proposedDescription: Absinthium is a perennial herb with silvery leaves and small yellow flower heads. Also called absinth wormwood, it comes from Eurasia and has been grown for its aromatic foliage. Outside gardens, it can become established in pastures, along roads and on disturbed ground. A plant can return from its roots for several years, while its seeds allow it to spread farther. Its strong scent and pale leaves are useful clues, but other wormwoods can look similar. Identifying the leaves carefully matters before removing a plant, especially where native species grow nearby.
identification:
Look for a branched plant roughly 2 to 5 feet tall with fine hairs covering the stems and both sides of the leaves. Lower leaves are deeply divided into narrow, rounded lobes; leaves higher on the stems become smaller. The yellow flower heads are tiny, about one-eighth of an inch across, rather than large, daisy-like blooms.

Common mugwort usually has greener upper leaf surfaces and broader, more pointed leaf divisions. Native Louisiana wormwood generally has narrower, lance-shaped leaves, sometimes with a few teeth near the tip, rather than absinthium's deeply divided leaves. Photograph the whole plant, a lower leaf and its underside, and any flower heads. Color alone is not enough to distinguish these plants.
actions:
If you think you have found absinthium, confirm the leaf features before deciding what to remove. Keep seed-bearing plants out of places where soil, hay or garden waste will be moved. For an established patch, preventing seed production is only part of the job: repeated mowing can reduce seed production but does not reliably kill the roots. Burning is not a dependable control method and can encourage its spread.

After control work, help desirable vegetation cover the disturbed soil and check the site again in following years. Washington's weed board reports that seeds can remain viable for three to four years. In a pasture, discuss control with an agricultural adviser; this plant can be toxic to livestock. Do not use its history in drinks or herbal products as evidence that it is safe to eat.

previousDescription: Absinthium has silvery leaves, small yellow flower heads and a strong scent. Its leaves are deeply divided and pale on both sides, unlike common mugwort's greener upper surfaces. This perennial herb comes from Eurasia and has long been grown for its aromatic qualities, including its use in absinthe. It also grows outside gardens along roads, railways and other disturbed ground, returning from the same plant each year.

proposedDescription: Despite the name achicoria azul, this member of the daisy family has pale yellow flowers. Its branching stems rise above a cluster of larger leaves close to the ground; the leaves become smaller farther up the plant. Small flower heads sit along the slender branches. Kew recognizes Launaea intybacea as an accepted species native across tropical and subtropical parts of the Old World. Regional floras describe it as an annual or biennial of seasonally dry places. Its presence in a catalog does not, by itself, show that a particular population is causing ecological harm.
identification:
Start with the leaves near the base. They can be spoon-shaped, toothed or deeply cut into backward-pointing lobes. Higher leaves are smaller and narrower, sometimes with small arrow-shaped lobes where they meet the stem. Look at several leaves rather than expecting every leaf to have the same shape. The branching flower stems carry small, pale yellow heads, with a narrow green covering around each head. Kew's Flora of Oman treatment describes that covering as about 9 to 13 millimeters long.

Photograph the whole plant, its lowest leaves, a leaf attached to the stem, and a flower head from both the side and front. These details are more useful than a distant picture of yellow flowers. A confident comparison with similar local daisies still needs a regional botanical reference or specialist review.
actions:
For a suspected sighting, record the location, date and habitat, along with close photographs of the leaves and flower heads. Include whether the plant is growing alone, in a patch or in cultivated ground. Those observations help a reviewer assess both identity and the setting in which it occurs. Avoid moving the plant or its seed heads to another site while identification is uncertain.

A photograph match alone is not a reason to clear surrounding vegetation or apply a herbicide. First confirm the plant with a regional botanist or Extension office, then discuss an approach suited to that population and its location.

proposedDescription: This tiny marine animal lives among seaweeds and other growth on the seafloor. Usually only a few millimeters long, it has an oval body whose sides curl downward. Algae living inside it contribute to its greenish or yellow-brown appearance and provide food through photosynthesis; the animal also eats small organisms. Convoluta convoluta is an acoel, a group distinct from the true flatworms despite the familiar flatworm label. Smithsonian records describe a northeastern Atlantic native range and introduced records in the Gulf of Maine. Those records describe observations at particular places and times, not its presence along every nearby coast.
identification:
Under magnification, look for an elongated oval animal usually around 2 to 4 millimeters long, although larger individuals have been reported. The sides curl toward the underside, producing a folded body rather than a broad, flat outline. Its color can be dark green or yellow-brown. Size, color and a curled outline together are useful clues, but they do not replace specialist identification of a tiny marine animal.

If you can document it without disturbing the habitat, include a close image with a size reference and a wider view of the seaweed or surface on which it was found. Note the location, date and water depth if known. A phone photograph may show the setting well while still leaving the species uncertain; keep that distinction in the report.
actions:
Avoid moving attached seaweed or small marine organisms between shorelines, harbors or aquariums. Clean visible organisms and debris from equipment before leaving a site, drain retained water where appropriate, and let equipment dry before using it elsewhere. These are general aquatic biosecurity steps, not a tested treatment for Convoluta convoluta.

Report a suspected new occurrence with photographs and location details for review instead of attempting to treat the surrounding habitat. Do not scrape away seaweed beds or use chemicals on the basis of an uncertain identification. Research in the southern Gulf of Maine found that these animals could eat very young mussels, but estimated a limited overall effect under the conditions studied. That finding does not establish the same impact everywhere the species occurs.

proposedDescription: The active gray pine needle aphid is a small, slender insect that feeds on pine needles. A thin wax coating can give its olive-green or gray body a pale appearance. Like other aphids, it releases sugary honeydew, which can leave surfaces sticky and support a dark fungal coating called sooty mold. Feeding may cause needles to yellow or fall, but these symptoms can also have other causes. Finding the aphids themselves is more useful than diagnosing a tree from discoloration alone. Lady beetles, lacewing larvae and other natural enemies can reduce their numbers as the weather warms.
identification:
Look closely along pine needles for narrow, spindle-shaped aphids about 2 to 2.5 millimeters long. They have thin legs, antennae and small dark spots on the body; some individuals develop wings. The pale coating is wax on the insect, rather than loose dust on the needle. A magnified photograph can help show the body shape and spots that are difficult to see with the naked eye.

Check both affected and apparently healthy needles, and photograph the whole branch as well as the insects. Record the type of pine if you know it. Yellowing, sticky honeydew or sooty mold can help you locate an infestation, but none identifies this aphid on its own. Identification from a general photograph of a damaged tree should remain tentative.
actions:
First check whether living aphids are still present and whether fresh damage is continuing. Notice natural enemies as well: lady beetles, lacewing larvae, hoverfly larvae and tiny parasitic wasps help keep these aphids in check. NC State notes that populations can be conspicuous in winter, when their natural enemies are less active. Continued observation may be more useful than treating old needle damage after aphid numbers have fallen.

If a valuable pine continues to decline, share close photographs and the pine's identity with an extension service or qualified plant-care professional. Horticultural oils are an option in NC State's guidance when natural control is insufficient, but they can remove the bluish surface wax from some pines and change their appearance. Any product must be appropriate for that tree and used according to its label.

proposedDescription: Acuminate scale is a small sap-feeding insect found on plant leaves. Adult females are flat, pale green to yellow-green, with a body that narrows toward the head and rounds toward the back. That shape can help you notice them, but closely related scales look very similar. USDA's identification guide records this species on a range of cultivated plants, including mango and gardenia. A scale found on one of those plants is not automatically acuminate scale: both its features and the host need to be checked. Published interception records also describe where infested material was encountered, not proof that the insect is established in every listed place.
identification:
Examine leaves for low, flattened, oval-to-triangular insects with a narrower front and a rounded rear. USDA describes adult females as pale green or yellow-green, without an obvious wax covering or a visible egg sac. Photograph the leaf surface, the insect close up and the plant as a whole. Include a size reference without moving the insect to another plant.

Kilifia americana and Kilifia deltoides are important lookalikes. Reliable separation uses tiny structures on a prepared specimen, including features of the legs and plates near the rear of the body. Those details are not usually visible in a phone photograph. Treat a visual match as a possible identification and arrange specialist confirmation when the exact species matters, especially for a nursery shipment or a new local report.
actions:
If a houseplant has suspected scales, separate it from other plants while you check the leaves and nearby plants. Photograph the insects before removing affected material so that useful identification details are not lost. UC IPM advises acting early on houseplant infestations; removing a limited number of affected leaves may help when the problem is small. Avoid passing infested plants or cuttings to someone else.

For a nursery, orchard or outdoor tree, request an identification before choosing a treatment. General houseplant advice is not a verified control program for acuminate scale on every host. Keep the plant name, purchase or arrival history, location and photographs together in the report. These details distinguish a contained infestation from wider establishment.

proposedDescription: A patch of white, wool-like material on a pine twig may be hiding Pineus boerneri. This adelgid, a close relative of aphids, feeds on pine trees beneath a protective covering of wax. Its youngest stages can crawl to a feeding site; after settling, they remain attached. Heavy infestations can damage shoots and cause needles to yellow or fall. Researchers have documented these effects in pine plantations, but the amount of damage depends on the tree and growing conditions. Other pine adelgids make similar white coverings, so the wax alone cannot tell you which species is present.
identification:
Look along pine twigs and stems for small patches of white wax. Under magnification, the covering may reveal eggs, young insects and rounded, reddish-brown adult females about a millimeter long. An infestation can resemble a fungal growth from a distance; seeing insects beneath the wax is an important first distinction. Photograph a complete affected branch and a close view of the colony, and record the pine species if known.

Separating Pineus boerneri from other pine adelgids requires more than these field clues. Published investigations have used carefully examined specimens to establish the identification. A photograph can support a suspected adelgid report without establishing the exact species. Do not assume a white patch on a spruce, hemlock or other conifer is this pine-associated insect.
actions:
Keep a record of the affected branches and check whether fresh damage is appearing, rather than judging the tree from old needle loss alone. Avoid carrying infested pine material or moving nursery plants to a new site while identification is unresolved. Published research describes spread through wind and the movement of infested material, making careful handling relevant even when an infestation looks small.

For a declining garden tree or a nursery or plantation outbreak, send close photographs and the host identity to an extension service or forest-health specialist. Ask how to submit a sample before mailing live insects or branches. Colombian researchers investigated a locally occurring lacewing predator; that is not a recommendation to purchase or release that insect elsewhere. A treatment choice should follow a confirmed identification and an assessment of current damage.

proposedDescription: Aegean wallflower is a familiar garden plant that can also grow in rocky crevices and cracks in old walls. Its fragrant flowers usually have four petals and are often yellow or orange, while cultivated varieties offer other colors. Narrow green leaves grow along stems that become woody near the base. It is a short-lived perennial, although gardeners often grow it over two seasons. Modern references may list it as Erysimum x cheiri, reflecting its treatment as a hybrid. That name and the older name Cheiranthus cheiri are useful when comparing garden labels or botanical records.
identification:
Look for an upright or bushy plant with narrow, pointed leaves and groups of fragrant flowers near the stem tips. Typical garden forms are about 10 to 50 centimeters tall, although cultivar and growing conditions affect size. The flowers are roughly three-quarters of an inch wide, usually with four petals arranged around the center. After flowering, long seed pods develop and eventually split open.

Take photographs of a flower face, a whole flowering stem, the lower woody portion and any mature pods. Other wallflowers can share the same colors and general shape, so a yellow four-petaled flower is not enough for a reliable species determination. If a plant came from a garden, keep any cultivar or purchase information with the observation. Hybrid garden plants can be especially difficult to name from a photograph alone.
actions:
For a plant growing beyond a garden, note whether it is an isolated escape or part of a patch producing seedlings. Photograph the flowers and pods before deciding whether management is needed. Where you want to prevent further self-seeding, remove developing seed pods before they open and collect the material rather than scattering it. Keep garden debris out of nearby natural areas.

A wallflower growing in masonry needs a different approach from one in a flower bed: do not pull apart old walls or disturb a protected structure to remove it. Ask the owner or site manager first. The references reviewed are botanical and horticultural accounts, not evidence that every escaped wallflower requires eradication or that this plant has the same impact in every region.

proposedDescription: African amaranth comes from South America, despite its common name. It is an inconspicuous herb with spreading or partly upright stems, narrow leaves and small flowers gathered near the stem tips. Its tiny fruits become strongly wrinkled as they mature, giving rise to another name, roughfruit amaranth. Regional floras describe it in disturbed places such as roadsides and cultivated ground. It may live for one season or persist as a short-lived perennial, so lifespan alone is not a reliable identifying feature. Neither a common name nor an overseas weed record establishes the status of a population near you.
identification:
Start with the low, spreading habit and narrow leaves, then examine the flowering tips. The flower clusters occur at the ends of stems and may also appear where leaves meet a stem. The mature fruit is particularly useful: it is only about 1.6 to 2 millimeters long, has a strongly wrinkled surface and does not open to release the seed in the way some other amaranths do. A hand lens or sharp macro photograph is often needed to see that texture.

Photograph a full branch, several leaves, the tip of a flowering stem and mature fruits beside a scale. General pictures of green foliage are less useful for distinguishing this plant from other amaranths. Published accounts differ in leaf dimensions and growth form; do not rule the species in or out using a single leaf measurement. A regional flora or herbarium can help resolve a doubtful specimen.
actions:
Photograph the patch before disturbing it, especially if mature fruits are available for identification. Keep fruiting material contained, and avoid moving soil or garden waste from the patch to a clean site. For a few confirmed, unwanted plants, remove the root crown as well as the visible shoots where this can be done without damaging surrounding vegetation. A plant with a surviving rootstock may grow again.

Revisit the location for new seedlings or returning shoots. In a crop, have the identification checked and choose a plan suited to that crop and setting. Preventing new seed and checking for regrowth are practical starting points; they do not guarantee that one removal will clear an established patch. Leave an uncertain plant in place long enough to obtain useful photographs rather than clearing nearby plants that may be different species.

proposedDescription: African asparagus fern climbs through other vegetation on thin, twisting stems. Despite its name, it is a flowering plant in the asparagus family, not a fern. Its glossy oval 'leaves' are flattened stems; small pale flowers are followed by berries that turn red as they ripen. Below ground, thickened roots store reserves while connected underground stems allow the plant to spread and return after its shoots die back. It is also widely known as bridal creeper. Outside its African native range, dense growth can shade nearby vegetation, while its underground network makes an established patch difficult to remove completely.
identification:
Look for shiny, pointed oval growths arranged alternately along wiry climbing stems. These leaf-like structures have several fine, roughly parallel veins and are broader than those of many other ornamental asparagus plants. Small greenish-white flowers have six parts that curve backward; later berries change from green through pink to red. Photograph the entire climbing plant, the leaf-like structures against a scale, and flowers or fruit when present.

If roots are already exposed during permitted work, photograph how the swollen storage roots attach to the underground stems. Do not dig up surrounding vegetation simply to obtain that picture. Different forms of this species can vary in the shape and arrangement of their underground growth. A familiar ornamental appearance should not substitute for checking the whole plant.
actions:
Start with small plants or the edge of a patch where removal will not damage surrounding vegetation. NSW guidance recommends digging out all connected underground stems for physical removal to work. Collect berries, including green ones, because fruit can continue to ripen after stems are cut. Keep that material and contaminated soil from being dumped elsewhere.

Cutting the climbing shoots can make a site easier to work in, but it will not reliably kill the plant beneath the ground. Return to look for new shoots and seedlings. For a large patch or plants intertwined with valued shrubs, seek a site-specific plan that protects those plants. Australian biological-control releases and seasonal treatment schedules are specific to that setting; they are not instructions to release insects or fungi in the United States.

proposedDescription: African bermudagrass spreads across the ground on runners that take root at their joints. Also called African stargrass, this warm-climate perennial is grown for forage and ground cover, but it can extend beyond the place where it was planted. Its flowering stems carry several narrow branches spreading from near the tip like a star. Common names have been applied inconsistently within this group, so the scientific name matters when comparing references. Unlike common bermudagrass, Cynodon nlemfuensis lacks underground spreading stems called rhizomes. Its above-ground runners are nevertheless capable of establishing new growth when moved.
identification:
Look for flat, narrow leaves on stems rising above a network of runners close to the soil surface. Botanical treatments describe leaves roughly 5 to 16 centimeters long and 2 to 6 millimeters wide, with considerable variation among forms. Several slender flowering branches spread from the top of each flowering stem. At a leaf's junction with its sheath, magnification can reveal a short fringe of hairs.

Photograph the flowering head, a leaf and its attachment, and a runner with rooted joints. Common bermudagrass can look very similar above ground but also produces underground rhizomes. Other stargrasses and cultivated hybrids complicate identification, so absence of an obvious underground stem in one photograph is not proof. Keep cultivar or planting records with a report if the grass was originally sown or planted for forage.
actions:
Check the edges of a planting for runners entering places where the grass is unwanted. Avoid moving live stem pieces or soil containing them to another site; stargrass is deliberately propagated from such pieces. Where removal is appropriate, collect connected runners rather than chopping and spreading them through the ground. Inspect disturbed edges again for regrowth.

Do not rely on repeated cultivation alone to eliminate a patch. Tropical Forages notes that resilient runners can survive ploughing and that cultivation can improve a stand. A larger escape needs a plan suited to the site, nearby plants and land use. In a working pasture, distinguish management of a useful forage from control of an unwanted escape. Appearance, forage use and presence in this catalog do not establish an identical ecological impact everywhere.

proposedDescription: African blackchin tilapia is a coastal African fish that can live in fresh, brackish and salt water. Adults often have dark patches beneath the mouth and across the lower head, although their coloring varies. It belongs to the cichlid family and is established in parts of Florida and Hawaii. The male shelters developing eggs and young in his mouth, a behavior called mouthbrooding. In Hawaii, introduced populations raise concerns about competition with native fish and changes to aquatic vegetation. Those concerns describe particular environments; they do not tell us how many fish are present or what effects they have in every recorded location.
identification:
Look for a small mouth, a body flattened from side to side, and irregular dark markings on the chin, throat or lower head. The back may appear olive or metallic green, while the sides are silvery with bronze tones. Large males can have a gold patch on the gill cover. Young fish may show a dark spot near the beginning of the soft-rayed part of the dorsal fin.

Take a clear side photograph that includes the complete dorsal fin, tail and gill cover, plus a view of the lower head if possible without unnecessary handling. Black coloring alone is not a secure identification: other tilapias change color with age and breeding condition. A specialist may need fin-ray and scale details that a distant photograph cannot show.
actions:
Do not move a suspected blackchin tilapia to another pond, canal or aquarium, or use it to stock a waterbody. Its ability to live across a wide range of salinities makes transfers between freshwater and coastal sites a concern. Record the exact location and date, and keep photographs with the observation rather than relying on a common name alone.

If you encounter an unfamiliar population or a fish die-off, contact the state fisheries or aquatic invasive-species program. Hawaii's aquatic-resources agency monitors both spread and disease events. Ask for instructions before retaining or transporting a live fish; rules differ among states. Removal projects described by agencies are supervised work, not a reason to net a whole pond or apply chemicals yourself.

previousDescription: African blackchin tilapia lives in warm waters, including coastal lagoons and estuaries where fresh and salt water mix. It feeds mainly on tiny algae and organic debris. The male has an unusual role in raising the young: he shelters the developing offspring in his mouth. Native to African coastal waters, the fish has been moved elsewhere through fish farming and other human activity, with populations recorded in Florida and Hawaii.

proposedDescription: African bowstring hemp grows a fan of stiff, rounded leaves that taper to sharp points. It is a succulent from Angola, often sold as a houseplant under the names African spear or cylindrical snake plant. Current botanical references usually call it Dracaena angolensis; Sansevieria cylindrica is the older name used in this catalog. Its leaves arise from connected underground stems, allowing new shoots to appear beside an established plant. Braided leaves in a shop are arranged by growers, not a natural growth form. A cultivated plant and a self-sustaining population outside a garden are different kinds of observations.
identification:
Check the leaf shape from more than one angle. The leaves are thick and nearly cylindrical, rather than simply narrow blades, with lengthwise ribs and faint darker bands across their gray-green surface. In larger forms they can exceed a meter in length, but dwarf cultivars are much smaller. Size by itself is therefore a poor test.

Photograph the base, the fan-like arrangement and a close view of the ribs and pointed tips. If flowers are present, look for a tall stalk bearing fragrant, pale tubular flowers with the narrow tips curling backward. Retail plants can consist of separate rooted leaf cuttings, so a tidy row or braid may conceal the plant's usual arrangement. Include that cultivation history when asking someone to identify it.
actions:
Keep unwanted leaves and underground stems out of outdoor dumping sites. This species can be propagated from leaf cuttings and divisions, so discarded living pieces are worth containing rather than scattering. When removing an unwanted clump with the owner's permission, check for connected underground stems and revisit the area for new shoots. Those precautions follow its documented growth habits; the references do not establish a tested eradication program for every setting.

Handle the stiff pointed leaves carefully, particularly where children or pets might brush against them. Do not use the plant as food. If you find it growing away from cultivation, record the size of the patch and any smaller plants nearby. That helps reviewers distinguish planted material from possible spread without assuming every household specimen is an ecological threat.
researchNotes: Preserves African bowstring hemp as the opening catalog name, as requested in saved feedback; other common and scientific names are separate. NParks and NC State disagree on flower-lobe count, so the draft does not assert a count. No unsupported naturalized distribution or harm claim. Containment and follow-up are explicitly precautionary deductions from propagation, not a validated management trial.

claims: Angolan origin, alternate fan, rhizomes, ribbed cylindrical foliage, flower shape, sharp-leaf hazard and cutting/division propagation.
Updated name, variable cultivar dimensions, rooted retail cuttings and artificial braiding, basal new growth, non-food plant hazards.

previousDescription: African spear is a succulent with stiff, round leaves that rise like a cluster of green rods. Faint bands cross the gray-green surface, and each leaf narrows to a pointed tip. New shoots grow from underground stems, gradually building a clump. Native to Angola, it is widely grown as a houseplant and can produce pale, fragrant flowers. You may find it labeled Sansevieria cylindrica in nurseries or older references; its accepted name is Dracaena angolensis.

proposedDescription: African boxthorn is a densely branched shrub from southern Africa, with rigid thorns and small clusters of fleshy leaves. Pale flowers give way to shiny orange-red berries. It was planted as a living hedge in some regions, but birds can carry its seeds beyond those boundaries. Established shrubs can form difficult-to-cross thickets and compete with nearby vegetation. In Australian landscapes, dense growth has also blocked livestock access to water. Those documented effects help explain why the plant is managed there; local records and conditions are still needed to understand a particular United States population.
identification:
Look for a woody shrub with stiff thorn-tipped branches and smaller spines along the sides. Mature plants can reach several meters tall. The leaves are smooth-edged, thick and usually gathered in small groups on short shoots; they are roughly spoon-shaped to oblong, often with rounded tips. Small cream, pale mauve or white flowers occur singly or in small groups, followed by round red berries commonly around a centimeter across.

Photograph the whole shrub, a leafy thorn-bearing branch and flowers or fruit. Include a scale without placing your hand among the thorns. Other Lycium species can also have spiny branches and red fruit, so neither feature alone establishes this name. A regional botanical key or herbarium review is especially useful where native relatives occur.
actions:
Avoid working barehanded in a mature thicket: the long, rigid thorns make handling and removal difficult. If removal is appropriate, plan how the cut material will be contained and moved before starting. Keep berries with the collected debris rather than spreading them along a track. Look for seedlings beneath nearby bird perches as well as immediately beside the original shrub.

Cutting the canopy does not necessarily kill the plant. The Victorian account records regrowth from cut stumps and broken roots, so follow-up checks are important after physical work. Large shrubs or plants beside waterways may need a coordinated site plan. Australian treatment calendars and legal classifications should not be applied automatically in the United States; use guidance appropriate to the location and confirm any product's permitted use before treatment.

Shrub stature, spurs and spine arrangement, leaf shape, flower colors and berry dimensions.

previousDescription: African boxthorn is a shrub with long thorns and small leaves clustered along its branches. Pale mauve or cream flowers develop into red berries. As it grows, its many branches can form a dense thicket several meters tall. Originally from southern Africa, it has become established elsewhere in open and coastal areas, pastures and roadsides. The long, rigid thorns are an important feature to notice before getting close.

proposedDescription: African bristlegrass forms lasting clumps topped by narrow, bristly flower heads. It has been grown for livestock forage, and some forms also establish along roadsides and in other disturbed ground. The species includes several varieties that differ considerably in height, leaf width and how they spread. Some produce abundant seed, while others spread mainly when stems fall over and root where they touch the ground. That variation matters when interpreting a record or planning removal. Its use as a pasture grass does not mean every stand is harmless, and its inclusion in a catalog does not mean all varieties behave alike.
identification:
Look for a tufted perennial grass with upright stems, sometimes connected by underground stems. Leaves are narrow and pointed, while the flower head is a tightly packed, upright cylinder surrounded by persistent bristles. The smaller flowering units fall away as they mature, but the bristles remain attached. Many forms have blue-green foliage and yellowish bristles.

Photograph the clump base, a complete flowering stem and the place where a leaf blade meets its sheath. A close view there can show the small fringed structure called the ligule. Flower heads may range from a few centimeters to several tens of centimeters long. Because closely related bristlegrasses share the bottlebrush appearance, an identification should use the whole plant and mature flowering material rather than head color alone.
actions:
First check whether the patch is a planted forage stand or unwanted growth beyond it. Where spread is unwanted, keep mature seed heads and rooted stem pieces out of soil, hay and garden waste moved to other sites. A variety that makes little seed can still spread through rooted stems, so simply removing flower heads may not be enough.

Return after cutting: established plants can persist under repeated cutting or grazing. Avoid treating livestock as a simple removal tool, because the grass's oxalate content can create animal-health problems under some feeding conditions. Ask an agricultural adviser about management appropriate to the variety and site. The sources describe forage biology and spread, not a single removal schedule that is proven to work everywhere.
researchNotes: Keeps the clear morphology the user liked and explains variety-dependent spread. AusGrass diagnostic treatment corroborates morphology independently of the forage-management synthesis. No cultivar-specific trait applied universally. Oxalate is included only as a reason not to improvise grazing treatment, without veterinary dosing or copied foreign chemical advice.

claims: Forage use, variety-dependent seeding and stem rooting, disturbed habitats, cutting persistence, blue-green foliage and oxalate concern.
Tufted perennial, rhizomes, leaf and ligule characters, long contracted heads and persistent bristles after spikelets fall.

previousDescription: African bristlegrass forms leafy clumps topped by narrow, bristly flower heads. Its leaves can have a blue-green cast, and the fine bristles around the flowers often look golden or yellowish. This perennial grass varies considerably in size and form, from shorter plants to tall, robust clumps. It has been cultivated for pasture and hay in warm regions. The combination of its clumping growth and bristly heads helps narrow the identification, but related grasses can look very similar.

proposedDescription: African clawed frogs spend most of their lives in water. Their flattened bodies, upward-facing eyes and broad webbed hind feet suit that way of life, while their small front feet help push food into the mouth. They come from sub-Saharan Africa and have been moved around the world for research and the pet trade. Released or escaped animals have established populations in some United States watersheds. They eat a wide range of small aquatic animals and can threaten native species through predation and disease transmission. An isolated sighting, however, is different from evidence that a population is reproducing locally.
identification:
Look closely at the feet. The front toes are unwebbed, while the large hind feet are fully webbed and carry black claws on the three inner toes. The head is small and wedge-shaped, with eyes on top, and the smooth back is often mottled olive or brown. Adults can exceed five inches in body length. Tadpoles look very different: they are partly transparent and have conspicuous whisker-like projections near the mouth.

African dwarf frogs sold as pets are an important lookalike. They remain much smaller, have webbing on the front feet, and have eyes positioned farther toward the sides of the head. Photograph the front feet and head position when possible. Do not rely on color alone, particularly for a captive animal with unusual pigmentation.
actions:
Never release a pet or laboratory frog into a pond, drain or stream, or relocate a wild frog to another waterbody. If one is found outdoors, record the location and photograph it without carrying it elsewhere. A clear image of the feet can be more useful for review than a distant picture of the whole pond.

Report a suspected new population to the relevant state wildlife or invasive-species program; California specifically requests reports through its invasive-species program. Ask that agency how to proceed before attempting collection. These frogs can carry pathogens affecting other amphibians, so keep aquarium water and equipment away from natural waters. Do not add chemicals to a pond or attempt a large removal on your own. A confirmed population needs a plan that also protects the other animals living there.

previousDescription: The African clawed frog spends almost all its life in water. Eyes on top of its flattened head help it look upward, while powerful, webbed hind feet propel it through the water. Three toes on each hind foot have the dark claws that give it its name; the smaller front feet have no webbing. Native to southern Africa, this smooth-skinned frog is also familiar from aquariums and scientific research.

proposedDescription: African cornflag is a South African perennial grown for its orange-red, sometimes yellow, flowers. It grows from a corm, a swollen underground stem, and produces long, strap-shaped leaves. Flowering stems rise above the leaves and carry tubular flowers in two opposite rows. Plants can spread through seed and small new corms, including when garden soil or discarded plants are moved. Its presence in a garden does not establish that it has escaped nearby; a record of plants growing beyond cultivation is a separate finding.
identification:
Look for a substantial clump of upright leaves and a flowering stem roughly 0.5–1.5 metres tall, often with a small number of branches. The flowers are uneven in shape: the upper lobe extends much farther than the others. Later, rounded capsules contain several orange seeds. Photograph the whole plant, a side view of an open flower, and the arrangement of flowers along the stem.

Crocosmia can look similar, but its flower lobes are more nearly equal. Names can also be misleading: Chasmanthe aethiopica has often been used incorrectly for this species. In the HortFlora treatment, true C. aethiopica has a one-sided flower arrangement and fewer flowers. Leaf fans alone are not enough to settle the identification.
actions:
If plants are appearing beyond a planting, mark the edge of the patch and photograph flowers before removing them. Keep seed capsules, corms and surrounding soil contained rather than dumping them in a vacant lot, ditch or natural area. A clump that disappears above ground may still have living corms below it.

For a small, confirmed patch on your property, ask your local extension service about removing the underground corms with as little soil disturbance as possible. Check the same spot during the next growing season. These steps address its known spread pathways; they are not a guarantee that one digging or cutting will clear an established patch.
researchNotes: Replaces the ornate flower description with visible features and separates corms from roots. Independent authored floristic and weed accounts support flower arrangement and propagation. Actions are conservative containment guidance based on those pathways; no US treatment trial or universal flowering calendar is claimed. Regional legal instructions are not transferred to US readers.

previousDescription: Tall sprays of curved orange-red flowers rise above the sword-shaped leaves of this South African plant. The flowers sit in two rows along branching stems, and each has a long upper lobe that arches over the shorter lower parts. Yellow-flowered forms also occur. Chasmanthe floribunda grows from a corm, an underground storage organ, and can spread through seeds and new corms. Its leaves die back during its dormant season before fresh growth returns.

proposedDescription: African feathergrass is a tall, clump-forming perennial with narrow, bristly flower heads. The underground stems, called rhizomes, let an established patch spread beyond the original clump and grow back after the leaves are cut. It has been planted as an ornamental and can move with soil, garden waste and machinery. You may find it listed as Pennisetum macrourum. Some current references, including Kew, place Cenchrus macrourus under Cenchrus caudatus; this profile retains the name used by our catalog so its records remain traceable.
identification:
Look for dense tussocks with rough leaf blades about 4–12 mm wide. The young leaves may be rolled, and older tips can curl. The cylindrical flower heads are commonly 8–30 cm long, with many slender bristles around the small flowering units. At the junction between blade and sheath, there is a dense fringe of hairs rather than a long, smooth membrane.

Photograph the entire clump, the flower head, and that leaf junction. Several ornamental fountain grasses have bristly heads, so a distant photograph is not enough. A grass specialist may need a flowering specimen to examine the spikelets and their bristles. Note whether shoots appear away from the main crown, but do not dig up or transport an uncertain plant just to check its rhizomes.
actions:
Avoid moving soil or machinery through a confirmed patch, especially when seed heads are present. Clean plant fragments and soil from equipment before leaving the site. Cutting off the visible stems alone leaves the underground rhizomes available to regrow.

Small plants may be removed by digging out their crowns and rhizomes where that can be done without damaging surrounding vegetation. Contain the material and ask about local disposal; do not put it in soil or garden waste that will be moved elsewhere. Larger patches need a follow-up plan with a weed specialist. Revisit treated ground for returning shoots and seedlings rather than assuming a single treatment has finished the work.
researchNotes: Kew currently treats macrourus as a synonym of caudatus, while the edited NSW flora retains macrourus. The alternative name is explained rather than changing the catalog or merging records. PlantNET provides authored diagnostic characters; NSW and Tasmanian weed agencies corroborate spread and regrowth precautions. No Australian herbicide label, seasonal calendar or legal classification is imposed on a US site.

previousDescription: African feathergrass grows in large clumps, with arching leaves and long, narrow flower heads surrounded by fine bristles. Underground stems spread outward and send up new shoots, allowing a clump to become a broad patch. It grows along waterways, roadsides and neglected pasture. Where it spreads densely, it can crowd out other vegetation. Pieces of underground stem can also travel in moved soil or discarded garden material.

proposedDescription: African fig fly is a small fruit fly with pale stripes bordered in black along its head and thorax. It can enter figs through their natural opening and is also found around damaged or overripe fruit. Its behavior varies with the crop: recent University of Kentucky guidance also reports infestation of ripening berries, so it should not be described as feeding only on fruit that is already damaged. It may occur alongside spotted-wing drosophila. Finding both flies near a crop does not, by itself, show which one caused the original injury.
identification:
Adults are roughly 2 mm long, with a yellowish-brown body, red eyes and clear wings. The contrasting lengthwise stripes on the head and the body section just behind it are the most useful first clue. Photograph the fly from above under good light, with a size reference if possible.

The markings help distinguish it from the more uniformly colored fruit flies commonly seen indoors, but a striped fly is not automatically this species. A specimen or a sharp close-up may be needed to distinguish related Zaprionus species. Larvae inside fruit are much less distinctive; keep a note of the fruit type, whether it was intact or damaged, and where it was growing.
actions:
Harvest ripe fruit promptly and remove fallen, damaged and overripe fruit from the growing area. Refrigerate harvested fruit when appropriate for the crop. This reduces opportunities for flies to breed and helps protect fruit quality; it does not establish which fly species is present.

If losses continue, send photographs and crop details to your extension office. Fine insect netting can help exclude flies when the mesh and edges are suitable, but it must fit the crop and its pollination needs. Monitoring traps can show that flies are active; they should not be treated as a stand-alone cure. Before using a pesticide, have the pest identified and check advice for that specific crop and product.
researchNotes: Preserves the user-approved simple explanation while correcting the older blanket claim that only damaged fruit is used. Kentucky 2026 guidance covers ripening berries and sanitation; the Virginia Tech account independently describes fig entry and damaged-grape associations. General fruit-fly symptoms are not represented as a species diagnosis, and no pesticide product or rate is recommended.

sources.title: University of Kentucky: African fig fly, ENTFACT-232

Adult striped appearance; figs; grape injury dependence and distinction from spotted-wing drosophila.

previousDescription: African fig fly has bright red eyes and pale stripes edged in black along its head and back. Those markings help distinguish this tiny insect from other fruit flies. Its young usually develop in damaged or rotting fruit, but they can also infest ripening figs and some berries. Originally from Africa, it has spread through warm regions and into parts of North America. Despite the name, figs are only one of its food sources.

proposedDescription: African jewelfish is a small predatory cichlid established in Florida, where it lives in habitats including canals, creeks and marshes. Its colors change: a tan fish with blue speckles can become much redder during breeding. Older Florida records often called it Hemichromis bimaculatus, which makes careful identification important when reading historical reports. More recent references use Rubricatochromis letourneuxi for the species covered here. Research has documented its expansion beyond the Miami area and effects on native fish communities in the Everglades; those findings do not imply equal effects at every location.
identification:
Look for a body flattened somewhat from side to side, bright blue spotting, and a conspicuous dark blotch on the gill cover. The tail is rounded. Breeding fish can be strongly red, but a subdued brown or tan individual should not be ruled out because it lacks that color.

Take a clear side photograph showing the head, full dorsal fin and tail, and record the waterbody and exact location. Closely related jewel cichlids can look very similar, particularly in aquarium strains. Color alone cannot resolve them. A museum or fisheries specialist may need fin counts, a specimen, or other diagnostic evidence to confirm a record outside its known range.
actions:
Never release an aquarium jewel cichlid into a pond, canal or other waterbody. If you can no longer keep one, arrange a return or rehoming through an aquarium retailer or an appropriate animal-care contact. Moving wild fish to a new site can also spread a population.

For an unfamiliar wild population, photograph it and report the location to the state fisheries or invasive-species program. Include the name you were given, but let the reviewer know if the identification is uncertain. Ask for instructions before collecting or transporting fish. Do not drain a pond or apply a fish toxicant yourself; those actions can harm the rest of the aquatic community and require professional planning.
researchNotes: Florida Museum supports visible diagnostic characters independently of the USGS literature synthesis and Belfiore/Schofield genetic study. The FWS 2026 report reconciles the newer genus and summarizes impacts. Historical misidentification is preserved without treating every aquarium jewel cichlid as this species. Actions are aquarium-release prevention and reporting guidance, not an unverified eradication method or a statewide possession ruling.

previousDescription: African jewelfish can show red tones and scattered blue flecks, but its colors change with its surroundings and breeding condition. A dark blotch on each side is a more consistent clue. This small African cichlid has an elongated body and rounded tail, and lives in lakes, floodplain waters and marshes, including some brackish habitats. It feeds on small aquatic animals such as insects and shrimp. Older references use Hemichromis letourneuxi; newer ones place it in Rubricatochromis.

proposedDescription: African jointgrass, often called limpograss in forage references, is a perennial grass that spreads through creeping stems and underground growth. It is grown as livestock forage in parts of Florida, especially on moist, poorly drained ground. Stems can root at their lower joints, allowing a planting to extend outward. In suitable climates it can keep growing later into the cool season than some other warm-season forage grasses. Its agricultural use and its behavior beyond a managed pasture are different questions; an occurrence record alone does not show that it is causing harm.
identification:
Look for long stems that trail or lean before their tips turn upward. Lower stem joints can produce roots where they contact the ground. The leaves are narrow, commonly about 2–6 mm wide, and the plant is generally smooth rather than densely hairy. Some stems or sheaths have reddish coloring.

The flowering structures are slender, inconspicuous spikes, sometimes occurring in small groups near the upper leaf axils, where leaves meet the stem. They do not form the broad, feathery head seen in many ornamental grasses. Photograph rooted joints, leaf bases and any flowering spikes. Several creeping pasture grasses look alike when mown, so a short lawn photograph is unlikely to establish the species.
actions:
Where limpograss is deliberately grown, check the boundary between the planting and adjacent ditches, wetlands or unmanaged ground. Photograph shoots that are extending beyond it and note whether they are connected by trailing stems. Do not move cut stems or soil from a suspected escaped patch to another moist site.

For a confirmed unwanted patch, discuss removal with an extension or land-management specialist, particularly beside water. Stem pieces capable of rooting need to be contained, and follow-up checks matter. Published advice on controlling other weeds inside a limpograss pasture is intended to protect the forage; it should not be mistaken for instructions to remove limpograss itself.
researchNotes: Uses the user-preferred natural seasonal phrasing. UF pasture guidance and the authored Tropical Forages account support rooted stems, wet-site use and identification. Recommendations to contain stems are explicitly precautionary; no unsupported US eradication method is claimed. Agronomic herbicide instructions for weeds within limpograss are not repurposed as control advice for this species.

claims: Forage use in wet Florida soils, vegetative establishment and cool-season growth.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Tropical Forages botanical and agronomic synthesis
claims: Growth form, rooting joints, leaf dimensions, hairiness and inconspicuous spike arrangement.

previousDescription: African jointgrass has long stems that bend across the ground and take root at their lower joints. Its narrow leaves sometimes develop reddish tips, and its flower spikes are small and easy to miss. This perennial tolerates wet, poorly drained soil. Farmers grow selected varieties for livestock because they keep growing into cooler weather when many other warm-season grasses slow down. Outside pastures, it can form thick patches in suitable wet ground.

proposedDescription: African mustard is a small annual with pink to violet flowers and slender seedpods. Its branches may spread low across the ground rather than stand upright. The lower leaves are broader and usually lightly toothed; those farther up are smaller. Fine, branching hairs cover much of the plant. It grows on open, disturbed ground and in dry habitats, including desert scrub. Older records may call it Malcolmia africana. An introduced roadside mustard is not automatically this species: flower color, leaf shape, pods, and hairs need to agree.
identification: African mustard has branching stems often 15–50 centimeters long, with broader, lightly toothed lower leaves and smaller leaves above. Its four pink or violet petals measure about 6–9 millimeters. Mature pods are narrow, usually 4–6 centimeters long, with scarcely any beak at the tip. A hand lens shows branched, star-shaped hairs without glandular tips. Blue mustard (Chorispora tenella) also has purple flowers, but bears stalked glands and often upward-curving pods with a conspicuous, elongated beak. Photograph the whole plant, lower leaves, an open flower, and mature pods beside a ruler. Close views of hairs and pod tips are particularly useful. Young plants without flowers or fruit need closer examination.
actions: Photograph a suspected African mustard patch while flowers and pods are present, and ask a regional herbarium or Extension office to confirm an unfamiliar occurrence. For a small, confirmed unwanted patch, remove plants before pods mature to reduce opportunities for seed release. If pods are already ripe, contain them during handling rather than shaking plants over the site. Clean adhering soil and plant material from tools before moving elsewhere, and revisit the patch after favorable growing weather. These are cautious prevention steps based on its annual, seed-producing life cycle. Extensive clearing is unnecessary for an uncertain identification and could remove similar native mustards.
researchNotes: Named lookalike gap resolved by comparing the full Morton/Jepson diagnosis with the independent Illustrated Flora of British Columbia account of Chorispora tenella. The 2024 Flora Mediterranea comparison also identifies these as lookalikes, but its old PDF redirects to an abstract; indexed key text was read and is labeled accordingly. That key says Strigosella pods lack constrictions, whereas Jepson allows some narrowing; pod constriction is therefore omitted as a diagnostic character. The comparison instead uses independently supported glandular versus branched hairs and long versus negligible pod beaks. UAE assessment supplies independent target-species morphology, not US impact or management status. Manual prevention is explicitly a cautious life-cycle inference, not an eradication claim; lack of a treatment trial alone does not prevent review.

sources.title: UAE National Red List — regional Strigosella africana assessment
University of British Columbia E-Flora BC — Chorispora tenella, Illustrated Flora of British Columbia
Homrani Bakali, Léger and Mombrial (2024) — Chorispora tenella: comparison with similar-looking species

claims: Annual with often prostrate branching stems; lower leaves 3–6 cm, shallow teeth; petals 6–9 mm; narrow pods 4–6 cm; branching hairs.
Jongbloed-based UAE assessment describes an annual with three-forked stem hairs and pale pink flowers; it does not assess US invasion impacts.
Annual not native to California; Malcolmia africana is an alternative scientific name.

Chorispora tenella has stalked glands, purple flowers, and frequently upcurved pods with a 7–20 mm beak; these contrast with the nonglandular hairs and scarcely beaked pods in the target-species flora.

The comparative key explicitly treats Strigosella africana as a Chorispora tenella lookalike and distinguishes their hair types and fruits; the pod-constriction character differs from Jepson and is not used here.

previousDescription: African mustard is a small annual with branching stems and pink to violet flowers, each with four petals. Its lower leaves are larger and lightly toothed, while those farther up the stems are smaller. Fine, branching hairs cover much of the plant, and slender seedpods develop as flowering progresses. It grows in open, disturbed ground and dry habitats. Flowers, pods and the shape of those tiny hairs are more useful for identification than the plant's overall size alone.

proposedDescription: African oil palm is a robust, single-trunked palm from tropical Africa, widely grown as a crop in warm regions. Palm oil comes from the flesh of its fruit; palm-kernel oil comes from the seed inside. Each heavy bunch holds many closely packed fruits. Long, feather-shaped leaves make a broad crown, and spines line their stalks. Younger trunks retain old leaf bases, while older trunks can become relatively bare. A planted crop tree and seedlings spreading beyond a planting are different situations; documenting where young palms appear helps distinguish them.
identification: African oil palm has one upright trunk, often marked by woody, roughly triangular old leaf bases, and can reach about 15 meters tall. Long feather-shaped leaves carry narrow leaflets in irregular groups pointing in several directions. Strong spines line the leaf stalks. Fruit bunches develop among the leaf bases; individual oval fruits may be red or black and reach about 5 centimeters long. American oil palm (Elaeis oleifera) is a close lookalike, but is shorter, has a more creeping trunk, and has regularly spaced leaflets arranged in one plane. Photograph the whole crown, trunk base, leaflet arrangement, and fruit from the ground. Seedlings without adult leaves or a visible trunk may need specialist examination.
actions: Check beyond a cultivated palm for young plants, noting whether they are in maintained ground or nearby natural vegetation. Before removing seedlings, confirm their identity and the land manager's wishes; a palm-shaped leaf alone is not enough. Keep collected fruit and planting material out of unmanaged areas. Do not climb a mature palm or stand beneath a fruit bunch while someone cuts it: the fruit clusters are heavy and leaf stalks are spiny. Arrange professional work on large trees. An unwanted planting needs a site-specific plan; being a major crop does not establish its ecological effect at your site.
researchNotes: The full USDA-supported Identifying Commonly Cultivated Palms account by Patti Anderson resolves the named lookalike with explicit Elaeis oleifera distinctions and supplies a clear mature size. It replaces reliance on the indexed UF landscape table for the identification paragraph. Independent Dransfield Flora of Tropical East Africa morphology and Dunford's OSU fruit account remain supporting sources. Precautionary advice follows the documented spines, heavy bunches and cultivation context; neither ecological harm at every US site nor a demonstrated escape-eradication protocol is asserted. The profile is ready for review with observation, containment and professional handling guidance; an unverified treatment trial is not a necessary gap.

previousDescription: African oil palm supplies two different oils: palm oil comes from the fruit's flesh, while palm-kernel oil comes from the seed inside. The tree has a sturdy trunk, long feather-shaped leaves and heavy clusters of red or orange fruit. Old leaf bases cover younger trunks, and spines line the leaf stalks. Native to tropical Africa, it is now widely cultivated in warm regions as a major crop. Its broad crown gives mature trees a distinctive silhouette.

proposedDescription: African olive is an evergreen shrub or small tree with a dense crown, opposite leaves and small dark fruits carried by birds. Escaped stands can shade out other vegetation, as documented in New South Wales. Its scientific name needs care: older accounts used Olea europaea subsp. cuspidata for both African and Asian brown olives. A recent revision separates the African plants as subsp. africana and retains subsp. cuspidata for Asian plants. A familiar common name therefore does not settle which subspecies a record represents. Leaf photographs, planting history and the identification source all help clarify that distinction.
identification: The African olive described in Australian weed guides commonly reaches 5-10 meters, with opposite leaves often ending in a small hook. Their undersides are green to yellow-brown. European olive (Olea europaea subsp. europaea), including escaped cultivated trees, usually has whitish or silvery leaf undersides and lacks the hooked tip. Small cream flowers are followed by purple-black fruit. These features help compare familiar olives, but they do not reliably distinguish the African and Asian brown-olive groups separated by recent genetic research. Photograph both leaf surfaces, leaf tips, their attachment to the stem, bark and ripe fruit. Keep the location and any nursery or planting records with the images so a botanist can assess the intended subspecies.
actions: For a confirmed unwanted African olive escape, remove small seedlings with their roots before they become fruiting trees, where digging will not damage nearby vegetation. Check again for seedlings and new shoots: cutting an established plant alone can leave a living base that resprouts. Keep fruit-bearing waste out of natural vegetation and arrange professional help for large trees or dense stands. If the subspecies is uncertain, keep photographs and the original name together when requesting botanical advice. Australian guidance supports these observations and prevention steps, but a local adviser should assess the plant and site before recommending a treatment program.

previousDescription: African olive is an evergreen tree or shrub with a dense canopy and narrow leaves growing in opposite pairs. The leaf tips often curve into a small hook, and their undersides are less silvery than those of familiar orchard olives. Small cream flowers develop into dark fruits. Planted for hedges and ornament, it has escaped cultivation in some regions, where its dense shade can change the vegetation growing beneath it.

proposedDescription: African pepperwort is a mustard-family herb with tiny flowers and small, flat seedpods. Its lower leaves are broader and toothed, while the upper leaves become narrow. It grows in gardens, roadsides, and other disturbed places and can persist beyond one growing season. Published floras describe considerable variation, including both hairless and hairy plants. The inconspicuous flowers are easy to overlook; a close view of mature pods and the hairs on their stalks usually provides more useful identification evidence. The name pepperwort is not a reason to taste an unidentified plant.
identification: Plants are often several tens of centimeters tall. The flattened pods are about 2–3 millimeters long, with a shallow notch at the end. Their short stalks curve outward and carry a row of fine hairs. White petals may be minute or absent. The related Lepidium pseudotasmanicum can have more deeply divided lower leaves; fruit shape overlaps and should not be used alone. Stems may be hairless or finely hairy; check the lower leaves and the row of hairs on each fruit stalk together. Photograph lower and upper leaves, stems, and several mature pods with a scale. A regional key is especially important if the plant does not match the usual hairless form.
actions: Keep a clear photographic record before removing an unfamiliar pepperwort. Similar species may be native, and their tiny differences are hard to judge without mature fruit. Once a small unwanted patch is confirmed, contain seed-bearing stems and lift plants where that can be done without disturbing neighboring vegetation. Check again for seedlings and surviving bases rather than assuming every plant dies after one season. Clean soil and seedpods from tools before leaving the site. For a larger patch, ask a local botanist or weed adviser to confirm the identification and plan removal around nearby plants.
researchNotes: VicFlora's substantive indexed treatment and the independently read 1988 Flora of New Zealand corroborate fruit dimensions and leaf pattern but differ over hairy forms and longevity. That variation is visible in the proposed identification rather than erased. VicFlora direct access timed out and Sydney exposed only navigation, so neither is labeled newly read full text. The pseudotasmanicum comparison is regional and not an exhaustive US lookalike list. Management guidance is clearly precautionary; no chemical efficacy claim.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria — Lepidium africanum
Manaaki Whenua — Flora of New Zealand, Lepidium africanum

claims: Annual or perennial to 70 cm, 2–3 mm fruits and minute petals; hairless-stem treatment; fruit shape alone unreliable against L. pseudotasmanicum.
Perennial treatment with hairy and glabrous forms; simple lower leaves, small elliptic notched fruits, one row of pedicel hairs; habitats and pseudotasmanicum comparison.

previousDescription: African pepperwort is a mustard-family herb whose tiny flowers are easy to miss. As it develops, small, flat seedpods line its branching stems, each with a shallow notch at the tip. Lower leaves are broader and toothed, while upper leaves are narrower. It grows in cultivated and disturbed ground and may last for one season or longer. Its pods and leaf hairs help distinguish it from similar pepperworts.

proposedDescription: African rock python, also called the northern African python, is a large, muscular constrictor from sub-Saharan Africa. Irregular dark markings cover a tan or gray-brown body, helping it blend into vegetation. It is nonvenomous, but a large snake can bite severely when disturbed. Its prey includes birds and mammals. Florida wildlife agencies monitor a localized introduced population in western Miami-Dade County. A single sighting elsewhere should be documented and investigated, not treated as proof that the species has established throughout that area.
identification: Adults found in Florida average about 10 feet long. Young snakes are much smaller, so size alone cannot identify one. Look from a safe distance for irregular, partly connected dark markings and a dark spear-shaped area on the head bordered by pale stripes. Burmese pythons generally have more clearly separated back blotches. African rock pythons also have dark mottling across the pale belly, but never lift or roll a snake to check this. Photograph the body pattern and head only if visible without approaching. A specialist can compare those images; a distant glimpse may not settle the identification.
actions: Give the snake space and keep children and pets away. Do not corner, grab, or try to move it. From a safe position, record the location, time, and a clear photograph. In Florida, report a suspected northern African python promptly through FWC's IveGot1 reporting service or its invasive-species hotline; include the location even if the snake moves out of sight. Elsewhere, contact the responsible wildlife agency. Let trained responders decide how to handle the animal. Never release an unwanted captive python outdoors; ask the wildlife agency about an appropriate surrender route.
researchNotes: Florida Museum and FWC species accounts were rechecked. Museum size ranges are internally inconsistent between its basic and detailed text, so the draft uses FWC's approximate Florida size rather than repeating a mismatched conversion. Museum northern-species diagnosis takes priority over older broad ADW usage that includes P. natalensis. FWC reporting guidance was read; no current legal-right-to-kill summary or handling procedure is added. Public prose preserves safe observation and separates records from establishment.

Approximate Florida size; localized western Miami-Dade population; prompt reporting with photograph and location through IveGot1; children/pet supervision.
Useful reports include clear photographs, precise location and date.

previousDescription: African rock python is a large, muscular snake with irregular dark patches on a tan, gray or brown body. A spear-shaped marking on its head and small heat-sensing pits along its lips are useful features. This nonvenomous snake constricts its prey, which includes birds and mammals, and often lives near water. Females lay eggs and coil around them while they develop, protecting the clutch until the young hatch.

proposedDescription: African senna, often sold as popcorn cassia, is a tropical African shrub with bright yellow flower spikes and dark unopened buds. It may stay small in a cold-climate summer garden but grow into a substantial woody plant where winters are mild. That difference matters when considering escapes. UF/IFAS classifies it as a high invasion risk in Florida using a predictive assessment. This is a warning about its potential to spread, rather than proof that every planted shrub has already harmed nearby habitat.

sources.title: University of Wisconsin Extension: Popcorn cassia

researchNotes: Wisconsin horticultural observations and the Flora of Zambia treatment support recognition independently. The Florida predictive assessment supports the prevention advice; its separate status assessment is incomplete, so predicted risk is not presented as measured ecological impact at each site.
previousDescription: Popcorn cassia gets its memorable name from the scent its foliage can release when rubbed, often compared with buttered popcorn. This tropical African shrub has long leaves divided into neat pairs of leaflets and upright spikes of bright yellow flowers. Dark buds at the tops of the flower spikes make the yellow blooms stand out even more. It can grow into a substantial shrub in a warm climate, while gardeners in colder places often know it as a seasonal ornamental. Flat pods follow the flowers, revealing its place in the bean family.
identification: Look for long leaves divided into many opposite pairs of oval leaflets, each ending in a small point. Flowers open progressively from the bottom of an upright cluster, with dark bracts still covering the buds above. Flat brown pods follow, their outlines indented between the seeds. The foliage has an unusual smell often compared with popcorn, although people describe it differently. Use the leaf arrangement, buds and pods together; scent alone is a poor way to separate this plant from other sennas.
actions: In Florida, choose an alternative rather than adding this shrub to the landscape. Around an existing plant, check for young seedlings beyond the bed, especially near disturbed ground. Collect pods before they scatter and keep seed-bearing trimmings out of natural areas. Photograph any apparently self-sown plants with the parent shrub and location noted. A plant growing in a pot is a different kind of record from seedlings establishing on their own. Where escapes are already spreading, ask the local invasive-plant program to help plan removal and follow-up.

claims: Growth form, paired leaflets, bud bracts, flowering sequence and pods
Exact-species leaf and leaflet morphology; tropical African shrub
Predictive high invasion risk in Florida; status assessment incomplete

proposedDescription: African tamarisk is a Mediterranean shrub or small tree with slender branches and sprays of tiny pale flowers. In its native range it grows around estuaries, coastal wetlands and waterways that may dry seasonally. Its fine foliage can make an entire tree look feathery from a distance. Several other tamarisks have spread extensively in the western United States, but their distribution and impacts cannot simply be assigned to this species. A report needs a checked identification before it can tell us where African tamarisk itself is growing.
