previousDescription: African tamarisk is a shrub or small tree with slender branches and tiny, overlapping leaves. Clusters of white to pale pink flowers grow along the branches, often on wood from the previous year. It belongs to a group of trees associated with riverbanks, shores and other open places near fresh or brackish water. Several tamarisks look very similar, making close-up leaf and flower details important for identification.

claims: Scale leaves, five-petalled flowers on older branches and riparian native habitat
Native Maltese coastal/estuarine setting and detailed flower characters

identification: The leaves are tiny, alternating scales pressed against the twigs, rather than the broad leaves of many streamside shrubs. White to pale pink flowers grow in cylindrical clusters, commonly on thicker wood from the previous year. Each flower has five petals. Record that position on the branch as well as close views of flowers and leaves. Specialists may need floral details that a whole-tree photograph cannot show. A general resemblance to saltcedar is enough to request help, but not enough to settle the species.
actions: If you find a possible escape, photograph the flowering branches and note whether it stands beside a planting or among naturally established vegetation. Avoid moving cut branches, seed-bearing material or wet soil to another waterway. Ask a herbarium or local invasive-plant specialist to check the name before arranging large-scale work. Streambanks may need protection and replacement vegetation during removal, so simply clearing a stand can create another problem. Keep the original identification and any later correction together when reporting the observation.

proposedDescription: African tuliptree is a tropical African tree widely planted for its large orange-red flowers. In Hawaii it has also spread into wet forests and pastures, where dense growth can crowd native vegetation. Its many winged seeds travel away from the parent tree, and a cut trunk can send up new shoots. A striking garden tree can therefore become an ongoing management problem in a suitable climate. The evidence from Hawaii is especially useful, but it should not be treated as a description of every place where this tree is cultivated.

sources.title: Universidad Francisco Marroquin Arboretum: Spathodea campanulata
Big Island Invasive Species Committee: African tulip

researchNotes: The university herbarium treatment supplies morphology; Hawaii's invasive-species committee supplies locally grounded spread and control guidance. No historical herbicide rate is copied. The draft avoids claiming all yellow-flowered plants are harmless, a conflict in ornamental summaries.
previousDescription: African tulip tree is hard to overlook in flower: clusters of large orange-red blooms sit above broad, feather-shaped leaves. The flowers have a flared, cup-like shape and often a yellow edge. This tropical African tree has been planted widely for shade and ornament, but its story continues after the flowers fall. Long woody capsules split open into boat-shaped halves, releasing many thin, winged seeds. Those flowers, compound leaves, and distinctive seed cases together make a more reliable impression than the common name alone.
identification: Look for large leaves divided into paired leaflets with one leaflet at the tip. The flower clusters sit above the foliage; swollen, curved buds open into broad cups with orange-red petals and often a yellow edge. Long woody seed capsules stand upright and split into boat-shaped halves, releasing thin seeds with papery wings. Photograph both the whole leaf and an open capsule if available. Yellow-flowered trees also occur, so flower color alone is not a reliable guide to whether a plant can spread.
actions: In affected tropical areas, avoid planting additional trees and check nearby forest edges for seedlings. Remove small, confirmed plants before they become difficult to handle, with the landowner's permission. Plan follow-up because cutting an established tree can produce vigorous regrowth. Large trees and brittle branches call for a qualified arborist, especially near buildings or paths. Keep cut material and seeds out of waterways and unmanaged land. For a spreading stand, use the local invasive-species program's current treatment guidance rather than assuming one cutting will finish the job.

claims: Compound leaves, orange flowers, canoe-shaped capsules and winged seeds
Hawaii invasion, resprouting, yellow-flowered plants, brittle branches and control

proposedDescription: The common warthog is an African wild pig adapted to open grassland and savanna. It grazes, digs for underground food and uses burrows for shelter. Escapes from exotic-animal ranches have established free-ranging populations in southern Texas, where researchers have studied it alongside wild pigs and native collared peccaries. These animals share parts of the landscape but are not the same species. A warthog sighting is useful information about an introduced animal; it does not by itself demonstrate a particular disease or the scale of local ecological damage.

sources.title: Journal of Mammalogy: occupancy and activity of peccary, wild pig and common warthog in southern Texas

researchNotes: Toronto Zoo's independent animal account supports recognition and defensive behavior. The 2025 Journal of Mammalogy study supports free-ranging southern Texas occurrence. Neither a sighting nor a modeled suitable area is treated as evidence of African swine fever.
previousDescription: The common warthog is an African wild pig with a broad head, curved tusks, and a mane running along its neck and back. The fleshy bumps on its face give it its name; males have more prominent sets than females. Despite its formidable appearance, much of its feeding is on grasses, roots, and other plant material. It favors open country and uses burrows as shelter. A sparse coat, long legs, give this savanna animal a silhouette quite unlike a domestic pig.
identification: Look for a broad, flattened head with fleshy facial bumps, long upward-curving upper tusks and shorter sharp lower tusks. The body is sparsely haired, with a coarse mane along the back, relatively slender legs and a tasseled tail. Warthogs often lower themselves onto their front wrist joints to graze. Native collared peccaries are smaller and lack the same conspicuous facial bumps and curved tusks. Photograph from a safe distance, ideally showing the head and body profile rather than approaching for a closer look.
actions: Give the animal room to leave and keep people and pets away from it. Do not feed, corner or attempt to catch it; a frightened warthog can injure someone with its tusks. Record the date, location, number of animals and any young, then contact the state wildlife agency or local land manager about an unexpected free-ranging sighting. Note whether fences or a nearby exotic-animal facility are present without assuming the source. Any capture or removal should be arranged through qualified people following local requirements.

claims: Morphology, grazing posture, burrows and injury risk
Established southern Texas populations from ranch escapes; comparison with other suids

proposedDescription: Air yam, also called air potato, climbs into shrubs and trees on fast-growing vines. Its most noticeable means of spread is the potato-like bulbil formed above ground where a leaf joins the stem. Fallen bulbils can start new vines, including very small ones, while underground parts can survive after the shoots are cut. In Florida and other warm parts of the United States, this growth can cover surrounding vegetation. The name is misleading: this is a yam relative, not a potato, and wild bulbils should not be treated as food.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS Plant Directory: Dioscorea bulbifera
Florida Museum: Five facts about air potatoes in Florida
US Forest Service: Dioscorea species review

researchNotes: UF/IFAS identification and management guidance is paired with the Forest Service yam synthesis. The museum account supplies the food-safety caution but overlaps UF expertise, so it is not counted as a separate confirmation of Florida impacts.
previousDescription: Air potato is a climbing yam whose most noticeable feature hangs above the ground. Rounded, potato-like bulbils form where the broad, heart-shaped leaves meet the stems; when they fall, they can start new vines. The plant climbs by twining around surrounding vegetation and can quickly cover shrubs and trees. It is a perennial, so underground parts can survive even when the visible vines die back. Despite the familiar name, those aerial growths are not potatoes, and the vine belongs to the yam family rather than the potato family.
identification: The broad, heart-shaped leaves grow alternately and have several strong veins radiating from their bases. Stems are rounded rather than prominently winged, and bulbils develop along the vine. Winged yam often has opposite leaves and angular, winged stems. Native yams can also have heart-shaped leaves, so leaf shape alone is not enough. Photograph a section showing several leaf attachments, the stem and a bulbil together. Do not taste a tuber or bulbil to try to identify the plant.
actions: Collect loose bulbils and prevent them from being carried in soil, yard waste or equipment. Bag reproductive material for disposal following local guidance; do not leave it in a brush pile where it can sprout. Cutting a vine helps stop its immediate climb but leaves underground reserves to regrow, so revisit the site and deal with new shoots. Avoid pulling heavy vines out of tree canopies. In Florida, ask Extension about the established air-potato beetle program and an integrated control plan for larger infestations.

claims: Alternate leaves, rounded stems, bulbils and Florida growth
Potential toxicity of wild bulbils; comparison with winged yam
Small bulbils and fragments regenerate; early control and follow-up
Bulbil collection and established biological-control program

proposedDescription: This rust fungus infects alder leaves, producing orange-yellow spore patches and sometimes causing early leaf loss. Repeated heavy attacks can weaken trees, although a rusty leaf does not mean an alder is about to die. Its full life cycle alternates between alder and larch, and researchers have confirmed that cycle in the eastern Alps. The fungus can also spread repeatedly between alder leaves without a nearby larch being obvious. Several similar rusts occur on alder, which makes careful diagnosis particularly important when checking older records.

sources.title: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Melampsoridium hiratsukanum
First Documentation of Life Cycle Completion of Melampsoridium hiratsukanum in the Eastern Alps

researchNotes: CDFA's species assessment and an independent 2021 Alpine field, microscopy and molecular study support biology and diagnostic limits. The Alpine impact findings are kept regional; practical guidance emphasizes diagnosis and nursery movement rather than an unsupported eradication treatment.
previousDescription: Alder rust causes orange-yellow patches on the undersides of alder leaves. Spots may also appear above, and badly affected leaves can curl, turn brown and fall early. The fungus releases spores that travel on the wind. Its life cycle can involve both alder and larch, although it can also repeatedly infect alder. Related rust fungi cause similar symptoms, so leaf spots alone cannot confirm which species is responsible.

claims: Similar rust taxa, disease cycle, California nursery spread
Host alternation confirmed; microscopy and DNA diagnosis; variable severity and repeated defoliation

identification: Turn an affected leaf over and look for powdery orange patches, then compare the upper surface for yellowing or browning. Note whether damage is scattered or affects much of the crown, and whether leaves are falling earlier than nearby healthy alders. These symptoms suggest a rust infection but do not identify this species. Specialists examine spore shape, surface ornamentation and the structures that release spores; DNA testing can help separate it from similar Melampsoridium fungi. Photographs of the host tree and both leaf surfaces support that work.
actions: If a nursery plant or unusual outbreak is involved, contact a plant diagnostic service before moving affected stock. Ask how to package a sample so that useful leaves reach the lab without spreading material around the site. Record when symptoms began and revisit the same trees to track recovery or repeated defoliation. Avoid removing nearby larches or applying fungicides solely from a photograph: the diagnosis and local growing conditions should guide any treatment. Keep confirmed laboratory results with the observation rather than replacing them with a visual guess.

proposedDescription: Aleppo pine is a Mediterranean evergreen widely planted in warm, dry landscapes. Young trees can be fairly upright, while older crowns often spread into irregular shapes with open spaces between branches. Its tolerance of heat and poor soil helps explain its popularity in California and the Southwest. A planted tree and a self-sown population are different things, however. When seedlings appear beyond a planting, check how far they have spread and what is growing around them. Their presence alone does not tell us how they are affecting that habitat.

sources.title: Oregon State University Landscape Plants: Pinus halepensis

researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Oregon State morphology and Stanford's separately observed campus trees corroborate paired needles, occasional threes and persistent cones. Cultivation is separated from escape and harm. Regional management uncertainty is retained as a decision boundary, not a reason to withhold basic recognition. Next: Record self-sown seedlings separately and seek local advice where they conflict with restoration.
previousDescription: Aleppo pine is a Mediterranean evergreen that often develops an open, irregular crown as it ages. Its thin, light green needles usually grow in pairs, giving the branches a finer texture than many familiar pines. Woody cones can remain on the tree for years, so several generations may be visible at once. The species is widely planted in warm, dry landscapes and tolerates heat and poor soils. Look at the needles, persistent cones, and spreading outline together; no single one of those features is unique to this pine.
identification: Look for fine, light-green needles carried mostly in bundles of two; occasional bundles of three also occur. The needles are generally about 6-10 centimeters long. Small woody cones have short stalks and may remain on branches for several years, so cones of different ages can be present together. Older trunks can become bowed or twisted. Related pines, including Eldar pine, may look similar from a distance. A useful identification photograph shows a needle bundle at its base and a cone still attached to its twig.
actions: Around a planted tree, check whether small pines are appearing beyond maintained ground, and distinguish seedlings from recently planted replacements. Record their distance from the parent and the habitat they are entering. Have an uncertain identification checked before removing young pines, especially where native species also occur. If a confirmed escape conflicts with restoration goals, discuss early removal and follow-up with the land manager. Mature trees near roads, buildings or power lines need professional assessment; their presence in this catalog is not a reason to cut them without a site-specific decision.

claims: Needle and cone characters, crown habit and Mediterranean origin
Two and three needle bundles, short thin needles, cones and local cultivated trees

proposedDescription: Solitaire palm is a single-stemmed rainforest palm from Queensland, Australia, also grown in warm American landscapes. Its slender trunk and compact crown can make it seem a modest garden plant, but reproduction beyond a planting still deserves attention. The 2026 UF/IFAS assessment recommends caution and management to prevent escape in central and southern Florida. Northern Florida has a different assessment, reflecting its different conditions. Those regional distinctions are more useful than treating every cultivated palm as either harmless everywhere or equally invasive everywhere.

sources.title: CSIRO Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants: Ptychosperma elegans

researchNotes: UF/IFAS description and current regional assessment are one institutional management lineage; the CSIRO-led Australian rainforest key independently supplies exact-species morphology and native ecology. A one-inch fruit measurement in the Florida summary conflicts with the botanical key and is omitted.
previousDescription: Alexander palm has a slender gray trunk marked with rings and a smooth green section just below its crown. Its long leaves divide into many leaflets with blunt or jagged tips. Small fruits ripen red beneath the leaves. Native to northeastern Australian rainforest, it is also grown in tropical gardens. The shape of the leaflet tips is particularly useful when comparing it with other palms of similar size and appearance.

claims: Solitary trunk, crownshaft, jagged leaflets and fruit clusters
Native Queensland rainforest, non-clumping habit and fruit morphology
2026 central/south caution and northern regional distinction

identification: Look for one pale, ringed trunk topped by a smooth green crownshaft, the sheath just below the fronds. The arching leaves are feather-shaped, and the individual leaflets have blunt, uneven tips that look as if they have been torn off. Branched flower clusters emerge below the crownshaft, followed by small red fruits. Several palms planted close together may look like a clump, so check whether each stem arises separately. Close views of leaflet tips, trunk rings and fruit are more informative than a distant silhouette.
actions: In areas where escapes are a concern, inspect beneath fruiting palms and along the nearest unmanaged edge for seedlings. Remove unwanted, correctly identified seedlings while they are small and keep fruits and plant waste out of natural areas. A nearby mature palm helps explain a possible seed source but does not replace identification. Record whether seedlings persist when maintenance stops. Leave work high in the crown to a qualified palm-care professional, and use local assessment guidance when deciding whether to retain an existing planting or replace it with a suitable native species.

proposedDescription: Alexandrian laurel is a broad-crowned coastal tree with glossy leaves and fragrant white flowers. It is native across parts of the Indian Ocean and tropical Asia into the Pacific, and has been planted elsewhere for shade and other uses. Its round fruits can float, helping seeds travel along shores. The Florida assessment does not currently label it a problem species, although the southern assessment remains incomplete. Its inclusion here should therefore not be read as a claim that every tree is damaging nearby habitat.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Calophyllum inophyllum regional flora accounts

researchNotes: The Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment, Singapore's national parks account and Florida's regional assessment provide distinct botanical and local-context evidence. The incomplete southern status is stated explicitly; no invasive impact or medicinal recommendation is inferred from traditional uses.
previousDescription: Alexandrian laurel is a broad-crowned tropical tree often associated with sandy or rocky shores. Its thick, glossy leaves grow in opposite pairs, with many fine, nearly parallel veins that are easy to see in good light. Fragrant white flowers with a bright center of yellow stamens are followed by round fruits. The short trunk and spreading branches can make a substantial canopy, which helps explain its long history as a shade and ornamental tree. The combination of polished leaves, close-set veins, and ball-shaped fruit is more distinctive than any one feature alone.
identification: The thick oval leaves grow in opposite pairs, with many closely spaced, nearly parallel side veins visible on both surfaces. Leaf tips are often rounded or slightly notched. Small clusters of white flowers have conspicuous yellow stamens, followed by smooth, round green fruits that turn brownish with maturity or drying. A mature tree often has a short trunk and spreading lower branches. Photograph the paired leaves, their veins and a fruit together; common names containing laurel are shared by unrelated trees and are not reliable identification on their own.
actions: If you notice seedlings beyond a coastal planting, record their location and whether they are rooted and growing rather than simply washed-up fruits. Keep unwanted fruits and nursery waste from being dumped into shore vegetation or waterways. Ask the land manager to confirm the species and local priorities before undertaking removal, particularly on an erosion-prone shoreline. Do not assume that reports about a different Calophyllum apply to this one. In a maintained garden, monitor reproduction and choose future plantings with local native habitat in mind.

claims: Native coastal habitat and botanical morphology
Opposite veined leaves, fruit and seawater dispersal
Not-problem assessments and incomplete southern status

proposedDescription: Alfalfa is a perennial forage legume that can persist along roadsides and field margins after escaping cultivation. Its deep root system and growing crown allow it to recover after cutting, which makes it valuable as a crop and explains why a roadside patch may return after mowing. Bacteria associated with its roots help supply nitrogen. An escaped plant is not automatically evidence of serious ecological harm: the Canadian biology review distinguishes survival outside cultivation from invasiveness. Local land use and the behavior of the actual patch still matter.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Biology of Medicago sativa
Kansas State University-hosted Missouri prairie plant identification guide: Alfalfa
Penn State Extension: Are My Forages Dead or Dormant?

researchNotes: CFIA supports perennial crop biology and the distinction between feral persistence and invasiveness. The USDA conservation-plant guide supplies recognition, and Penn State explains living crown/root regrowth. The separate subspecies record is not collapsed into this species-level profile.
previousDescription: Alfalfa is a perennial member of the pea family, best known as a hay and forage crop. Its branching stems carry leaves divided into three leaflets and clusters of small pea-shaped flowers, often purple. A deep root system and a persistent crown allow it to send up new shoots after cutting or winter dormancy. Bacteria in root nodules help it obtain nitrogen from the air. Plants can also grow beyond fields on roadsides and disturbed ground, where their flowers and coiled seedpods help distinguish them from superficially similar clovers.
identification: Look for leaves divided into three leaflets, with the terminal leaflet on a short stalk and small teeth concentrated toward the leaflet tips. Clusters of usually purple, pea-shaped flowers develop into curled or coiled pods. The stems arise from a persistent crown rather than from a creeping mat of runners. Similar clovers can share the three-leaflet appearance, so include flowers or mature pods in photographs. Flower color varies in the wider alfalfa group, and an image of one bloom alone may not resolve a subspecies or hybrid.
actions: When documenting alfalfa, say whether it is deliberately sown, left over from a former field or growing outside cultivation. For an unwanted small patch, preventing seed production is useful, but a single mowing should not be mistaken for removal of the perennial crown. Revisit the site for regrowth and plan any further work around the vegetation you want to retain. In a working pasture or hay field, consult the grower or Extension before treating it as a weed; removing a crop plant can undermine the purpose of the field.

claims: Crop biology, persistence outside cultivation and context-dependent weed interpretation
Three leaflets, terminal leaflet stalk, crown growth and purple flowers
Living crowns and roots support regrowth; identify desired forage before management

proposedDescription: This record concerns the cultivated alfalfa subspecies, rather than every plant in the wider Medicago sativa group. It is a perennial with a deep taproot and stems that regrow from the crown after cutting. Plants can survive beyond farm fields, including along roads and ditches. Distinguishing the subspecies matters because yellow-flowered relatives and fertile hybrids also occur. A county record identified only as Medicago sativa cannot automatically be made more precise by assigning it to this subspecies without supporting features or a checked specimen.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Biology of Medicago sativa
UBC E-Flora BC: Medicago sativa subsp. sativa

researchNotes: The Illustrated Flora of British Columbia gives the subspecies comparison and hybrid caveat; CFIA supplies the broader crop biology without establishing every occurrence at subspecies level. The draft keeps identification uncertainty visible and does not reinterpret species-level map records.
previousDescription: This is the commonly cultivated form of alfalfa, grown for hay and livestock forage. It has three-part leaves, purple to blue-violet flowers and seedpods that curl into tight coils. New stems grow from a lasting base above a deep root system, allowing the plant to regrow after cutting. It can also persist around field edges and disturbed ground. The coiled pods help distinguish it from yellow-flowered relatives.

claims: Persistent crop crowns, cultivated and feral populations; broader species context
Subspecies key, coiled versus curved pods, hybrids and roadside habitat

identification: Typical plants have three leaflets, the end leaflet on a short stalk, with teeth near the outer ends. Blue-purple flowers grow in compact clusters, followed by pods curled into tight spirals. The British Columbia flora contrasts these with the usually yellow flowers and curved, rather than spirally coiled, pods of subsp. falcata. Hybrids can blur that contrast. Photograph several flowering stems and mature pods from the same plant; if those features disagree, retain the broader species identification until a botanist can examine it.
actions: For a sighting, note whether the plant is a crop, a volunteer at a field edge or an established roadside escape. Include the fruit photographs rather than relying on a familiar purple flower. If removal is appropriate in a restoration bed, address the crown and monitor for regrowth; routine forage cutting demonstrates how readily a healthy plant can recover. Avoid spreading seed-bearing cuttings into nearby habitat. On agricultural land, coordinate with the owner before any intervention, because alfalfa may be an intended and useful part of the field.

proposedDescription: This red seaweed grows as branching tangles in sheltered bays and estuaries, including muddy places where many seaweeds cannot attach easily. It originated in the northwestern Pacific and has reached both coasts of the United States. Genetic research points to northeastern Japan as an important source of introduced populations and oyster movements as a likely pathway. Its effects depend on the setting: heavy growth can alter existing habitat, but a Chesapeake Bay study also found young blue crabs using its mats as shelter. Neither outcome describes every bay.

sources.title: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center NEMESIS: Gracilaria vermiculophylla
NOAA repository: Genetic identification of source and likely vector of a widespread marine invader
NOAA repository: Gracilaria habitat and juvenile blue crab study

researchNotes: NEMESIS and the 2017 genetic paper share pathway evidence and are not counted as independent confirmation of that claim. Wood and Lipcius provide an independent field study of juvenile crab habitat. Actions are precautionary containment and site assessment, not a universal removal prescription.
previousDescription: This red seaweed forms branching tangles of narrow, rounded strands in sheltered coastal waters. It may attach to shells or other firm surfaces, or gather in loose mats over mudflats and seagrass beds. Although classified as a red alga, its visible color can vary with growing conditions. Native to the northwestern Pacific, it has spread to estuaries elsewhere, where it can change the structure of shallow-water habitat. Those tangles can shelter small animals as well as crowd existing vegetation, so their ecological effects depend on the setting.
identification: Look for reddish-brown, cylindrical branches forming loose, tangled clumps rather than broad flat blades. Plants may attach to shells or other firm objects, become caught among animals' tubes, or accumulate as drifting mats. Color and branching change with conditions, and several native and introduced red algae look similar. A photograph can document the growth but may not establish this species. Include a close view of the branches and a wider view showing whether the material is attached, loose or mixed with seagrass.
actions: Record the date, shoreline location and approximate area covered, then share the observation with a local marine monitoring program. Do not move live seaweed, shells or fouled equipment to another waterbody. Remove hitchhiking material from gear where it can be contained and disposed of ashore. Avoid dragging a rake through a mixed seaweed and seagrass bed: that can disturb the habitat you are trying to protect. Where mats are changing access or vegetation, ask the responsible coastal manager to assess the site before removal.

claims: Branching morphology, habitats, introduction context and variable effects
Genetic source regions and likely oyster-associated transport
York River field evidence of juvenile blue-crab habitat in algal mats

proposedDescription: Grateloupia doryphora is a red seaweed associated with the southeastern Pacific coast. Its name also appears in older accounts of an introduced seaweed in the northeastern United States, but that history needs care. The Rhode Island population first called G. doryphora was later identified as Grateloupia turuturu. These are different species, so records and impacts reported under the older name cannot all be carried into this profile. Such an American introduction record needs a checked specimen or documented reassessment. Independent Peruvian collections document the true species attached to rock in intertidal and subtidal habitats.

sources.title: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Grateloupia turuturu, identification history
Gavio and Fredericq 2002: G. turuturu reassessment
Rodriguez et al. 2018: seaweeds of La Libertad, Peru

researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where the current assessment differs: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Smithsonian's current account confirms Rhode Island records called doryphora were reassigned to turuturu; the Peruvian catalog could not be recovered beyond a name-only index hit. A name-only index entry is excluded from evidence. The US historical misapplication remains material and no verified exact-taxon US population was established. Next: Obtain a modern voucher-backed US determination and original regional morphological treatment before release. Inherited reference not used as fresh substantive evidence (unavailable or superseded by the specified original): https://rnia.produce.gob.pe/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/MACROALGAS_DE_LA_COSTA_CENTRAL_DEL_PERU_CATALOGO.pdf .

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: Independent Peruvian field vouchers and the original molecular reassessment support a true Grateloupia doryphora profile without assigning the northeastern US invader records to it. The 2002 study sequenced a Peruvian Ancon collection separately from US G. turuturu. The 2018 La Libertad survey documents different HUT specimens and rocky intertidal/subtidal habitat. These are independent collections, not database copies. Next step: Review the narrowly scoped seaweed draft; keep historical US occurrence reassignment as a separate specimen audit. Fresh access: Gavio and Fredericq 2002: G. turuturu reassessment [full_text; Gavio-Fredericq-2002-original] https://suzannefredericqseaweedslab.com/grateloupia-turuturu.pdf — Peruvian G. doryphora sequence AF488817 from Ancon 2001 differs from the introduced Atlantic G. turuturu material. | Rodriguez et al. 2018: seaweeds of La Libertad, Peru [full_text; La-Libertad-2018-HUT-vouchers] https://www.scielo.org.pe/scielo.php?pid=S2077-99172018000100008&script=sci_arttext — G. doryphora recorded on rock in intertidal and subtidal habitats, with HUT25897 and HUT25893 specimen citations; independent of the 2002 Ancon collection. All inherited URLs remain retained in sources or the inherited notes. Previously accessed evidence is retained as provenance; only the accesses described here are claimed as fresh in this pass. No catalog IDs, occurrence mappings or public records changed. Local editorial review only; release remains deferred.
previousDescription: Grateloupia doryphora is a red seaweed described from Peru and recorded on rocky shores there. It belongs to a group of algae that can be difficult to tell apart by appearance. Its name was once used for some seaweeds later identified as Grateloupia turuturu. That naming history is important: reports under the older name may describe a different species, so they cannot all be treated as records of this one.

claims: Rhode Island historical doryphora records represent turuturu; genetic reassessment and related-species caution
Peruvian G. doryphora sequence AF488817 from Ancon 2001 differs from the introduced Atlantic G. turuturu material.
G. doryphora recorded on rock in intertidal and subtidal habitats, with HUT25897 and HUT25893 specimen citations; independent of the 2002 Ancon collection.

identification: A broad red blade is a starting clue, not a reliable identification. Several Grateloupia species produce flattened, branching seaweeds whose appearance changes with age and growing conditions. The confusion in the Rhode Island records shows why a confident-looking photograph can still receive the wrong name. Photograph the entire attached plant, its base and the branching pattern without pulling it off the shore. Include a scale and the tidal setting. A seaweed specialist may need reproductive structures or genetic evidence to separate the possibilities.
actions: If you encounter a suspected plant outside its documented range, send the photographs and exact location to a herbarium or marine monitoring program. Keep the original name attached to any older record and note who subsequently checked it. Avoid transporting living material on boats, gear or shells. Do not clear a patch on the assumption that it is the introduced species described in an old report. Wait for an identification and advice appropriate to that shoreline, especially where native seaweeds are growing together.

proposedDescription: Algerian sea lavender is a perennial plant that can spread through the upper edges of salt marshes. In the San Francisco Bay area, research has documented dense stands in the transition between tidal marsh and drier ground, where native plant cover can decline. That transition provides important room for marsh vegetation to move as conditions change. This plant produces many seeds, particularly in the less salty, less frequently flooded part of the marsh. A patch near a path or levee therefore deserves attention even when it is not growing in the wettest ground.

sources.title: Archbald and Boyer: invasion of Pacific estuarine transition zones

researchNotes: CDFA's 2024 assessment supplies exact-species morphology and notes subspecies uncertainty. Archbald and Boyer's original San Francisco Bay study independently supports upper-marsh spread and seed production. The draft does not assign a subspecies or transfer Bay-area findings to every coastline.
previousDescription: Algerian sea lavender is a perennial with a low rosette of spoon-shaped leaves and a much-branched spray of tiny pale pink flowers. The flowering stems rise above the foliage, giving the plant an airy outline. Native to the Mediterranean region, it can grow in salty coastal settings, including the higher edges of salt marshes. In parts of coastal California it has spread into marsh vegetation, where its position along the shore matters to how it interacts with other plants. Careful identification is useful because related sea lavenders have been confused in older records.
identification: Look for a low rosette of spoon-shaped leaves and a much-branched flowering stem rising above it, sometimes around half a meter tall. The small pale pink flowers occur in short, repeated clusters along the branches. Leaves are broader near the tip and narrow toward the base. Other sea lavenders, including native plants, can look similar. Photograph the rosette, branching stem and close flower clusters together. Some California plants have been assigned to a subspecies, but that name should not be assumed from a general photograph.
actions: Report a suspected patch to the refuge, park or local coastal restoration program, with its size and position relative to the marsh edge. Stay on established access routes rather than trampling sensitive vegetation for photographs. Prevent seed-bearing material from being moved in maintenance debris. Small confirmed populations are worth addressing before they expand, but removal in a marsh should follow the land manager's plan. Revisit treated areas for seedlings and recovery of native cover; one cleared patch does not establish that the surrounding seed supply is gone.

claims: Rosette, leaves, flower morphology and uncertain subspecies attribution
Field evidence on upper-marsh abundance, native cover and seed production

proposedDescription: Alligatorweed spreads across water and damp ground on stems that can root wherever their joints touch a suitable surface. Floating mats can fill the edges of ponds and channels, while plants on land form lower, tougher growth. A broken piece is enough to help it move to another site, making careless cutting or disposal part of the problem. Established infestations often need repeated, coordinated work. The same plant can look rather different in water and on a bank, so a small terrestrial patch should not be dismissed because it lacks a large floating mat.

sources.title: UF/IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Alligatorweed
Texas A&M AquaPlant: alligator weed management

researchNotes: UF/IFAS and USGS supply morphology and invasion biology; their underlying botanical references overlap. Texas A&M's management guidance is an additional practical source supporting fragment containment and the limits of one-time physical removal. No herbicide dosage or unapproved biocontrol release is prescribed.
previousDescription: Alligatorweed grows across wet ground and shallow water. Smooth leaves grow in pairs along its stems, and small white flower heads rise above them on short stalks. In water, hollow stems help support floating patches; on land, it can form a lower, denser cover. The stems take root at their joints, and broken pieces can start new plants. This helps it spread along shorelines, drainage channels and damp ground.

claims: Opposite leaves, stalked white heads and aquatic growth
Hollow aquatic stems, terrestrial variation and vegetative spread
Fragment regrowth, physical management limits and biological-control context

identification: Leaves grow in opposite pairs along the stem and have smooth edges. Small white flower heads resemble papery clover flowers and rise on stalks above the leaves. Floating stems are commonly hollow, but stems growing on land can be firmer and less obviously hollow. Note the leaf arrangement and stalked white heads together; other aquatic plants may share one feature without sharing the others. Photograph a flowering stem in place and include the shoreline or ditch setting rather than breaking off pieces to carry home.
actions: Keep fragments out of drains and waterways when cleaning equipment or maintaining a bank. Do not mow or rake an infestation into the water, and do not put live pieces in a garden pond or an ordinary loose brush pile. Contact the waterbody manager or local invasive-plant program before attempting removal from a substantial mat. Physical removal can leave rooted pieces behind, so plan containment and follow-up. Biological control is used in some regions, but effectiveness and availability vary; obtain local advice rather than moving insects or plants yourself.

proposedDescription: Allium leafminer is a small fly whose larvae feed inside onions, leeks, garlic and related plants. Adults make neat rows of punctures in the leaves, and the larvae tunnel downward toward leaf bases and bulbs. Damaged plants may become distorted, and injured tissue can spoil. The insect has spread through parts of the eastern United States, with separate spring and fall activity periods documented in affected areas. The timing changes with location and weather, so a calendar from another state is a guide to monitoring rather than a dependable treatment date.

sources.title: University of Maryland Extension: Allium leafminer

researchNotes: Maryland Extension provides diagnostic and damage guidance. North Carolina Extension adds independently documented local detection and practical crop-cover advice. Regional flight periods remain qualified; the draft does not convert northeastern dates into a nationwide schedule or prescribe pesticides.
previousDescription: Allium leafminer is a small fly whose young develop inside onions, leeks, garlic, and their relatives. Adult females make rows of tiny punctures in the leaves, and the larvae then tunnel downward through the plant. Infested leaves may become distorted, while the larvae and brown pupae can remain hidden among leaf layers or near the bulb. The adult is gray with yellow on the head, but the feeding pattern may be noticed first. Its concealed life inside a familiar vegetable makes it easy to miss until the plant is opened or growth changes.
identification: Start by looking for a line of small white punctures near a leaf tip, followed by winding mines or damaged inner leaves. Cream-colored, legless larvae can reach about 8 millimeters; brown pupae may be tucked into leaf bases. Adult flies are about 3 millimeters long, dark overall with yellow areas on the head and legs. These clues together are more useful than a photograph of a tiny fly alone. Other insects and diseases damage alliums too, so ask Extension to check a suspicious first finding.
actions: Inspect susceptible beds during local fly activity and photograph both the puncture rows and any larvae or pupae. Avoid sharing infested transplants or planting garlic from a suspect crop. Fine insect netting or row cover can keep adults out when installed before they arrive and sealed around the edges. Plant the next crop in a clean bed before fitting covers: covering soil where pupae remain can trap emerging flies inside with the plants. Ask local Extension about disposal of infested crop material and a monitoring schedule suited to your area.

claims: Adult and larval features, puncture rows, mines and damaged alliums
North Carolina field detection, local timing, sealed covers and rotation away from infested soil

proposedDescription: Allspice is an evergreen tropical tree grown for its aromatic berries, which are harvested unripe for the familiar spice. It comes from the Caribbean and Central America and is also planted in warm gardens elsewhere. A cultivated tree and a self-sown population are different records: the first shows where someone planted it, while the second can help document escape. Young plants establishing beyond a garden are worth recording. Whether they are displacing other vegetation needs a closer look at that site, rather than an assumption based on the tree's introduced origin.

sources.title: Indian Council of Agricultural Research, Indian Institute of Spices Research: Allspice

researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: NParks independently documents leaf and berry characters while ICAR-IISR verifies crop identity and Caribbean/Central American origin. The retained text makes no unsupported US invasion claim. Missing local harm or control evidence need not block an identification profile with observation and seed-containment advice. Next: Keep any regional escape or impact claim dependent on local evidence.
previousDescription: Allspice is a tropical evergreen tree whose dried, unripe berries supply the familiar kitchen spice. The name reflects a flavor often compared with a mixture of cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg, even though it comes from one plant. The tree has glossy, aromatic leaves in opposite pairs and clusters of small white flowers. Fruits darken as they ripen. Native to parts of Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean, it has long been grown beyond that range for spice and as an ornamental tree.
identification: Look for opposite pairs of glossy, leathery leaves with smooth margins and visible oil glands. Small white flowers develop in branching clusters, followed by rounded berries that change from green to dark purple or nearly black. Leaves commonly measure several inches long, and the plant develops a woody trunk rather than remaining a low herb. Related aromatic trees may look similar. Photograph the leaf arrangement, flowers or fruit and overall tree shape together. Do not taste an unfamiliar berry to decide whether you have found the culinary species.
actions: Around an existing planting, check for seedlings beyond the maintained bed and record whether young plants are establishing in nearby vegetation. Avoid dumping ripe fruit or seed-bearing pruning waste in natural areas. If you find an apparent escape, send photographs and the location to a local herbarium or Extension office for confirmation and regional advice. There is no need to infer harm from the scent or common name. Any decision to remove an established tree should consider its identity, local status and the surrounding habitat.

claims: Pimenta dioica crop identity, unripe berry use and native region
Opposite gland-dotted leaves, white flowers and green-to-purple-black berries

proposedDescription: The almond moth is a stored-food pest also known as the tropical warehouse moth. Its caterpillars feed in dried fruit, nuts, seeds, grain products and other dry foods, leaving silk and waste that can spoil more material than they eat. Adults do not feed. In cooler climates, heated storage buildings can provide conditions that outdoor winters do not. Finding a moth in a kitchen is a reason to inspect food supplies, not proof that every package is infested or that the insect is definitely this species.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: pantry pests

researchNotes: The Canadian Grain Commission supplies exact-species recognition, commodities, heated-building persistence and silk contamination. Minnesota Extension independently supports general stored-food sanitation; it is not represented as an almond-moth identification key. No Indianmeal-moth-specific timing or wing pattern is transferred.
previousDescription: The almond moth is a small gray moth associated with stored foods, including dried fruit, nuts, seeds, flour, and grain. Its caterpillars do the feeding, burrowing into food and producing silk that can bind pieces together. Webbing in stored material may therefore be more noticeable than the adult moth itself. The adults have faintly marked wings and resemble several other small pantry moths. Despite its name, this species is not limited to almonds; its broad diet and ability to develop in stored products explain its other name, tropical warehouse moth.
identification: Adults have gray forewings with relatively faint markings and a wingspan of roughly 16 to 30 millimeters. Look inside suspect packages for silk-bound food, feeding debris and larvae rather than relying only on a moth resting on a wall. Small holes in packaging and webbing around storage equipment are useful clues. Other pantry moths cause similar damage, and accurate separation may require an entomologist. Photograph the adult and the affected product, and keep the package details if the problem involves a recently purchased item.
actions: Inspect nearby dry foods, including pet food and birdseed, so that an overlooked package does not keep the infestation going. Seal and discard confirmed infested food, then vacuum shelf joints, cracks and spilled material; empty the vacuum afterward. Put unaffected foods into tightly closing containers. Do not spray insecticide into food or cupboards as a substitute for removing the source. If moths continue appearing, inspect again and ask Extension or a qualified pest professional for identification. In a commercial store, isolate the affected lot and follow the facility's food-safety procedures.

claims: Exact-species appearance, foods, silk damage and indoor persistence
General package inspection, disposal, vacuuming, sealed storage and avoiding cupboard insecticides

proposedDescription: The aloe aphid lives in sheltered parts of Aloe and Haworthia plants, where a colony can be easy to overlook. Its whitish wax makes it resemble a mealybug rather than a typical exposed, pear-shaped aphid. Reports from imported aloes in Korean greenhouses show how infested plants can carry it into new growing areas. Feeding can damage leaves, while sticky honeydew supports sooty mold. This is primarily a plant-health concern in the evidence checked here; a greenhouse finding does not establish an outdoor infestation across the surrounding county.

sources.title: Korean Journal of Applied Entomology: Aloephagus myersi on imported Aloe vera

researchNotes: The Korean diagnostic paper provides independently examined specimens, field appearance and feeding sites. Okinawa's plant-health account supports the host association and mealybug resemblance. Precautionary isolation and inspection are distinguished from a species-specific pesticide protocol, which these sources do not establish.
previousDescription: Aloe aphids often hide where a plant's leaves meet, so the first sign may be a pale, fluffy-looking patch tucked into the rosette. Beneath that waxy covering are small aphids feeding on aloes and some close relatives, including Haworthia. Their sheltered position and wax can make them resemble mealybugs at a glance. The species has traveled with cultivated succulent plants and has been recorded in greenhouses far from its probable African origin. Looking closely at the insects themselves matters more than judging the white coating alone.
identification: Check the bases of leaves and rolled or damaged leaf ends. Beneath a light, fuzzy wax coating, the small oval insects can appear orange-brown or dull green. The wax may leave two bare-looking strips along the back. These features help you locate a colony, but mealybugs and other small insects can still be confused with it. A specialist uses microscopic features, including its unusual lack of the paired tubes found on many aphids. Photograph the insects closely and include the whole host plant.
actions: Keep a suspect plant apart from other aloes and haworthias while you seek an identification. Inspect offsets and new purchases before sharing or moving them into a collection, paying attention to hidden leaf bases rather than only the outer foliage. Record where the plant came from and whether neighboring plants are affected. Ask Extension or a plant-health clinic for advice suited to that host and setting. Avoid treating every white patch as an aphid colony or using an unverified home mixture that may injure succulent leaves.

claims: Examined greenhouse specimens, wax pattern, feeding sites and diagnostic limits
Aloe and Haworthia hosts, leaf damage and mealybug resemblance

proposedDescription: Alsike clover is a perennial forage plant associated with cool, moist ground, including poorly drained pastures. Its pale flower heads often become pink as they age. Although it has been included in pasture mixtures, it needs particular care where horses graze. Veterinary guidance associates it with sunlight-related skin injury and, in some cases, liver disease. The substance and circumstances responsible are not fully understood. That uncertainty is a reason to identify the clover and assess the feed, not to assume that every clover has the same risk.

sources.title: Ontario: alsike clover poisoning in horses
Penn State Extension: plants toxic to horses

researchNotes: Purdue's livestock-plant account supplies morphology and explicitly notes unresolved causation. Ontario veterinary guidance and Penn State independently support recognizing risk and removing access to suspect pasture. No safe dietary percentage, definitive toxin or universal ecological-harm claim is inferred.
previousDescription: Alsike clover has rounded flower heads that begin pale and become pinker as individual florets age. Its leaves have three leaflets, usually without the pale chevron seen on many red or white clovers. The stems tend to grow upright rather than creeping along the ground and rooting at each joint. This short-lived perennial has been grown as forage and is often associated with cool, moist fields and meadows. Looking at both its leaves and its changing flower colors is more helpful than identifying it from a pink clover head alone.
identification: Look for three smooth leaflets with finely toothed edges, generally without the pale V-shaped marking often seen on red or white clover. Small rounded heads of pinkish-white flowers sit on stalks arising from upright or ascending stems. White clover usually has creeping stems, while red clover has larger flower heads and hairier growth. These comparisons are more useful together than flower color alone. Photograph the stem, leaflets and flower head, and ask someone experienced with pasture plants to confirm a suspect stand.
actions: Do not use an unidentified clover-rich patch or hay lot as horse feed while you are checking it. If a horse develops unusual sunburn-like lesions, appetite changes or other signs of illness after grazing, remove access to the suspect feed and contact a veterinarian promptly. Keep a sample or clear photographs of the pasture plants for that assessment. Review seed mixtures before renovating a horse pasture, and work with Extension on maintaining suitable forage. Treatment decisions for an animal belong with a veterinarian rather than a plant identification guide.

claims: Leaf and flower features, moist habitat and uncertain toxic mechanism
Horse photosensitization and liver concerns; identification and pasture prevention
Remove horses from suspect alsike pasture; distinguish other clover problems

proposedDescription: This small, hairy mustard has pale yellow flowers and rounded seed pods. It is associated with dry, open places in the Mediterranean region and southwestern Asia. Its North American history is much less straightforward: Flora of North America reports that most records assigned to Alyssum strigosum were actually the similar Alyssum simplex. The treatment does not confirm that A. strigosum is established in the region. A name on an old specimen label therefore needs checking before it becomes evidence of a current local population.

sources.title: Flora of North America, Al-Shehbaz: Alyssum simplex discussion of A. strigosum
Sirin et al. 2022: morphology, anatomy and pollen of Alyssum strigosum

researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where the current assessment differs: Fresh review 2026-10-31: FNA explicitly reports repeated misidentification as simplex and does not confirm strigosum establishment; the Cretan account supports native-region recognition. The unresolved historical California specimen affects the exact North American catalog concept, not simply confidence in a photograph. Next: Seek Davis 108 or a newer reidentified North American voucher and preserve its determination history.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: A new original Turkish specimen study independently supports the fruit-hair diagnosis of Alyssum strigosum while the North American record uncertainty remains explicit. Sirin and colleagues studied newly collected Konya material deposited at KNYA, including E. Sirin 693 from 2018. This is independent of Flora of North America and the uncertain Davis 108 historical record. A general species account does not require claiming present US establishment. Next step: Review the true-species draft; retain the separate request to reexamine historical North American vouchers before updating occurrences. All inherited URLs remain retained in sources or the inherited notes. Previously accessed evidence is retained as provenance; only the accesses described here are claimed as fresh in this pass.
