previousDescription: Alyssum strigosum is a small annual mustard from parts of southern Europe and western Asia. Its tiny fruits carry both star-shaped hairs and coarser, forked hairs, features that help separate it from related alyssums. These details may need magnification to see clearly. Some older North American records used this name for another species, A. simplex, which makes checking the original identification especially important.

claims: Small pale-yellow flowers, narrow leaves and hairy pods
Distinct forked fruit hairs and disputed North American records
Annual plants and fruits with coarse unequally forked hairs mixed with appressed stellate hairs; original KNYA specimens, anatomical and pollen observations.

identification: Look for narrow alternate leaves, branched stems and small flowers whose yellow petals have notched tips. The flowering stalk lengthens as the rounded pods develop. The most useful distinction is tiny: A. strigosum has star-shaped hairs mixed with much coarser, forked hairs on its fruit. In A. simplex, the fruit hairs are star-shaped, although some rays can be unusually coarse. A general picture of a yellow roadside flower will not resolve that difference. Detailed photographs of mature pods, preferably with magnification, are important.
actions: Ask a regional herbarium or botanist to review a suspected finding, particularly if it would represent a new locality. Include the whole plant, flowers, mature fruit and exact location, and follow the herbarium's instructions before collecting material. Do not relabel older records without keeping their original determination and the reason for any correction. Avoid moving seed-bearing soil or plants while identification is unresolved. Large-scale removal or a claim of ecological damage would require stronger evidence than the uncertain historical records currently available for this exact species.

proposedDescription: Pigweed aphid feeds on amaranths and can hide around their roots and stem bases rather than forming an obvious colony at the top of the plant. Florida researchers documented it on spiny amaranth and found that some older specimens had been given a different aphid's name. A later nursery record located a colony several inches below ground. These records make careful host and specimen identification worthwhile. They do not, by themselves, establish a major crop loss, a particular plant-virus risk or a need to treat every amaranth nearby.

sources.title: Florida Department of Agriculture TRI-OLOGY: Aphis amaranthi on Amaranthus spinosus
Aphids of Costa Rica: Aphis amaranthi diagnostic treatment

researchNotes: The 2000 Florida paper and later FDACS nursery observation supply separate occurrence details within a related agency lineage. The Costa Rican regional aphid treatment independently supports winged morphology and diagnostic features. Species-specific economic impact and virus transmission are not asserted; actions are diagnostic and containment-focused.
previousDescription: Amaranth aphids are small sap-feeding insects associated with amaranths, the plants often called pigweeds. They may gather low on the plant, around roots and stem bases, as well as on leaves or flower clusters. The aphids can be dull olive or reddish brown and are sometimes attended by ants. This less visible feeding position is a useful part of their story: an apparently clean upper leaf does not describe the whole plant. Closely related aphids can look similar, so color and host name alone do not settle the identification.
identification: Winged individuals can have a dark head and thorax with an olive-green to reddish-brown abdomen. Color is variable and is not enough to distinguish this species from the other aphids using amaranths. Specialists examine features such as the sensory structures on the antennae and the small tail-like tip of the abdomen. For an initial report, show the host plant, where the colony sits and a close view of several insects. Note whether they were on leaves, at the soil line or on exposed roots.
actions: If a colony appears on a crop or nursery plant, keep that plant and its root ball from being moved to another growing area until the insects are checked. Record any visible damage and whether neighboring plants are affected instead of judging the problem by aphid numbers alone. Send photographs to Extension and ask how to submit a specimen if needed. Avoid a broad spray based only on color or the presence of ants. Identification and the condition of the host should guide whether further management is warranted.

claims: Examined Florida specimens, host identity and historical misidentification
Independently dated underground colony on spiny amaranth
Winged coloration and microscopic diagnostic structures

proposedDescription: Amazon sailfin catfish is an armored, bottom-dwelling fish from South America that is traded for aquariums. Aquarium releases are a likely route into waters outside its native range. Introduced sailfin catfish populations have been recorded in the United States and elsewhere, but some contain hybrids or have uncertain species identifications. That matters when interpreting a map: a report of an armored catfish may be sound even when the exact species name needs revision. Evidence about a mixed population should not automatically be attributed to pure Pterygoplichthys pardalis.

sources.title: US Fish and Wildlife Service: Amazon sailfin catfish ecological summary
Guimaraes and colleagues: karyotypic and molecular analysis of Pterygoplichthys pardalis

researchNotes: USFWS's assessment documents introduction pathways and uncertainty in US populations. The 2023 lower-Amazon molecular study provides additional evidence on identification limits. This profile is ready as a qualified account; ambiguous occurrence records still need specimen-level review and are not silently reassigned.
previousDescription: Amazon sailfin catfish has rows of hard body plates, a tall back fin and a sucker-like mouth beneath its head. This freshwater fish is familiar in the aquarium trade as a pleco and spends much of its time against the bottom or other surfaces. Dark spots on its belly help distinguish it from some related catfish. Similar species and hybrids can complicate identification, so the underside pattern should not be used alone.

claims: Aquarium pathway, occurrence qualifications and hybrid identity limits
Armored South American fish, native and exotic genetic comparisons and limits of belly patterns and barcoding

identification: Look for a broad, flattened head, a downward-facing sucker mouth, rows of hard body plates and a large, sail-like dorsal fin. Belly markings have traditionally helped separate related sailfin catfishes, but researchers caution that color patterns and even a single DNA marker may be misleading in hybrid populations. An aquarium label saying pleco is not a species identification. Useful photographs show the side, spread dorsal fin and underside when those can be obtained safely without unnecessary handling. Leave a fish in the water rather than catching it just for a photograph.
actions: Never release an aquarium fish into a pond, stream or storm drain. If you can no longer keep one, seek a responsible aquarium rehoming option and keep it contained until that is arranged. For a wild sighting, note the waterbody, date, approximate size and number of fish, then report it to the state fish and wildlife agency. Do not move a captured fish to another waterbody. Follow local instructions about handling and disposition; a suspected nonnative identity does not remove fishing or wildlife requirements.

proposedDescription: Ambay pumpwood is a tropical South American tree with large, deeply lobed leaves. It readily occupies open or disturbed places, and researchers have documented self-sustaining populations along waterways and abandoned ground in parts of Indonesia and Singapore. Some of those trees were previously called Cecropia peltata, a related species. Checking the name changes how we understand both the introduction history and the appropriate response. The overseas evidence is informative, but it does not establish the same distribution or ecological effects in the United States.

sources.title: Conn and colleagues (2012): Status of Cecropia in Malesia
Fernandes and colleagues (2026): Sexual segregation and herbivory in Cecropia pachystachya

researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: The 2012 voucher-based revision and independent 2026 Brazilian field-study abstract corroborate the taxon, pioneer ecology and dioecy. The profile limits invasion observations to Indonesia and Singapore and does not assert US harm. Overlap between the 2010 and 2012 Malesian papers is not counted as another lineage. Next: Retain regional qualifiers and request vouchers for uncertain Cecropia observations. Inherited reference not used as fresh substantive evidence (unavailable or superseded by the specified original): https://lkcnhm.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/app/uploads/2017/06/2010nis199-209.pdf .
previousDescription: Ambay pumpwood has large, deeply divided leaves on long stalks. Their pale, hairy undersides become visible when the leaves turn in the wind. This fast-growing South American tree often establishes on open or disturbed ground, where it can soon rise above smaller plants. Male and female flowers grow on separate trees. The broad leaves make it noticeable even when young, although related Cecropia trees can look similar.

claims: Exact pachystachya naturalization in Java/Singapore, habitat, misidentification and intermediate plants
Dioecy, watercourse association and ecological observations in Brazilian campo rupestre

identification: Look for a relatively open, branching crown and very large leaves whose lobes spread outward like the fingers of a hand. The leaf stalk joins the blade inward from its edge, with prominent veins radiating from that point. Male and female flowers occur on separate trees, and flower or fruit clusters provide useful additional details. Related Cecropia species can look very similar, including plants with intermediate features. Photograph leaf surfaces, stalk attachments and reproductive structures rather than relying on the familiar umbrella-like silhouette alone.
actions: For a possible escape, record whether the tree was planted, whether seedlings are appearing nearby and what habitat they occupy. Send those details to a regional herbarium or invasive-plant program for a checked identification. Avoid distributing seed or dumping fruiting material along drainage channels. Do not treat every similar tree as this species or assume that a name used in an older source is still correct. Where a population is confirmed as spreading, plan removal and follow-up with the land manager, taking care to protect the riverbank or surrounding vegetation.

proposedDescription: Anisandrus maiche is a tiny Asian ambrosia beetle now recorded in parts of North America. Like other ambrosia beetles, it tunnels into wood and grows fungi inside its galleries as food for its young. Researchers in central New York found it overwintering as mature larvae inside those galleries and producing two generations in a year. That local study helps explain when beetles may emerge from infested wood. It does not mean that every tree with a pinhole is infested by this species or that the same flight dates apply throughout the country.

sources.title: USDA Agricultural Research Service: Rabaglia, Vandenberg and Acciavatti (2009), first North American records
USDA Agricultural Research Service: Milbrath and Biazzo (2024), Anisandrus maiche biology study

researchNotes: The 2009 first-record paper and independent New York rearing study support occurrence and life history; the latter is explicitly an abstract, not a full control trial. USDA's diagnostic key supplies body size and specialist traits. No disease transmission, guaranteed tree mortality or tested eradication method is inferred.
previousDescription: Anisandrus maiche is a tiny ambrosia beetle that spends much of its life out of sight inside wood. Females bore into woody plants and cultivate fungi in their tunnels; the fungi provide food for the developing young. Native to Asia, the species has also been documented in North America. Like other ambrosia beetles, it is easier to notice through its small entry holes than to identify by a casual look at the insect. Its partnership with fungi is central to its biology, and close examination is needed to separate it from similar wood-boring beetles.
identification: Females are only about 2.2 to 2.5 millimeters long. Separating them from other small ambrosia beetles requires close examination of body structures, including features on the wing covers and a small hair tuft associated with the fungus-carrying organs. A round entry hole or boring dust is therefore a clue to a wood-boring insect, not a species-level diagnosis. Photograph the affected wood and tree condition, and retain a beetle only if a diagnostic service gives instructions for submitting it.
actions: Avoid transporting suspect logs, firewood or nursery trees while an identification is being checked. Note the host tree, recent stress or injury and whether the material was cut or still alive. Ask Extension or a forestry diagnostic service to assess the insect and the tree together. Routine spraying based on holes alone may miss the cause and will not identify what is already inside the wood. If removal is recommended, arrange disposal locally and follow the advice on timing so that emerging beetles are not carried to another site.

claims: Examined first North American records and diagnostic key context
Central New York rearing observations, larval overwintering and two generations
Female body size and microscopic diagnostic traits

proposedDescription: Euwallacea similis is a small ambrosia beetle associated with wood, especially weakened trees and cut material. It is presumed native to parts of Asia and the Pacific and has established outside that region, including the southern United States. Reports of timber damage come mainly from tropical areas. Finding this beetle deserves an accurate identification, but it does not establish that a tree has the destructive disease associated with polyphagous or Kuroshio shot-hole borers.

sources.title: University of Florida and US Forest Service: North American Xyleborini identification tool
Netherlands NVWA: Quick scan for Euwallacea similis

researchNotes: Fresh UF/USFS diagnostic text and NVWA assessment support this restrained profile. NVWA finds insufficient evidence of major pathogen-vector impacts and no documented introduced-range timber damage. Practical actions emphasize diagnosis and containment, not an unverified species-specific treatment.
previousDescription: Euwallacea similis is a small, slender ambrosia beetle that lives in wood. Its light brown body is a useful first clue, although separating it from similar beetles takes a close look at the wing covers. Believed native to the Asia-Pacific region and introduced elsewhere, it usually colonizes weakened or stressed trees and can damage stored timber in its tropical native range. Its presence deserves attention, but the severe tree diseases associated with other Euwallacea species should not automatically be attributed to this one.
identification: Compared with other North American Euwallacea, the adult is unusually slender and light brown. Specialists examine the nearly square outline of the shield behind the head and the sloping rear surface of the wing covers. On that surface, rows of punctures diverge and a prominent pair of small bumps helps distinguish the species. Other Euwallacea and Xyleborus can look much alike in ordinary photographs. A hole in bark, sawdust, or a declining branch cannot identify the beetle or prove which organism caused the decline.
actions: If beetles appear in nursery plants or recently delivered wood, record the material, its origin, and the date before it is moved again. Photograph the insect beside a scale and ask an extension entomologist or plant-health service how to submit a specimen. Keep suspect wood and plants at the site while identification and any movement requirements are clarified. Have an arborist assess tree stress and structural problems separately. Avoid treating every nearby tree or transporting infested firewood on the assumption that all ambrosia beetles need the same response.

claims: Slender light-brown adult; subquadrate pronotum; divergent declivital striae and paired tubercles
Presumed Asia-Pacific origin and southern US introductions
Secondary colonization and tropical timber damage; uncertainty about pathogenic fungal impacts
Wood and woody-plant movement pathways

proposedDescription: American evergreen, often sold as arrowhead vine, changes dramatically as it grows. A small houseplant with arrow-shaped leaves can become a thick-stemmed climber in a warm, shaded landscape. In Florida, escaped vines spread across the ground and climb trees, where heavy growth can cover other vegetation. Stem pieces readily form new plants, making dumped cuttings an important escape route. Keeping a plant indoors is a different situation from allowing it to spread into a nearby wooded wetland.
researchNotes: UF documents Florida escape, vegetative spread, site impacts and removal precautions. NC State independently supports changing juvenile/adult foliage and cultivation biology. Florida invasion is not generalized to all indoor or cold-climate occurrences.
previousDescription: Arrowhead vine is the familiar tropical houseplant with pointed, arrow-shaped young leaves. Given warmth and something to climb, it becomes a much larger vine, and older leaves divide into several leaflets. Outside cultivation in southern Florida, it can blanket the ground, climb trees, and crowd native vegetation. Pieces discarded from gardens can take root, helping explain how an attractive indoor plant becomes a troublesome escape in warm natural areas.
identification: Young leaves are simple and arrow-shaped, sometimes marked with white, silver, or pink. Mature climbing growth develops much larger leaves divided into several spreading sections. Look along the same vine for this transition rather than expecting every leaf to match a houseplant photograph. Long leaf stalks and fleshy stems are helpful clues. Golden pothos can occupy similar places, but its leaves do not undergo the same division into separate spreading leaflets. Mature arrowhead vine can produce flowers enclosed by a pale, hoodlike bract.
actions: In places where it escapes outdoors, prevent cuttings and discarded pots from reaching drains, woodland, or wet soil. For a small accessible patch, wear gloves and long sleeves, lift vines carefully, and collect broken pieces; the sap irritates skin and eyes. Do not use a string trimmer, which scatters material and exposes the sap. Arrange contained disposal through the local waste service and revisit the site for rooted fragments. Large vines in trees need a coordinated removal plan that protects people, branches, and the plants beneath them.

claims: Florida invasion and wet woodland habitats
Stem fragments root; sap irritation; avoid string trimmers; contain removed material
Arrowhead juvenile foliage becomes divided adult foliage
Long stalks, climbing habit and spathe-bearing flowers

proposedDescription: Caprella scaura is a marine amphipod often called a skeleton shrimp. Its thin, jointed body clings to seaweed and branching growth on ropes, docks, and boat hulls. Those surfaces give it shelter and opportunities to travel between harbors. Its original native range remains uncertain, although several recent expansions are well documented introductions. An Italian lagoon survey found strikingly different abundances among sites, a useful reminder that one occupied dock does not tell us how the animal behaves throughout a coastline.

sources.title: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center NEMESIS: Caprella scaura
Cabiddu and colleagues: Occurence of the alien species Caprella scaura in three Tyrrhenian lagoons

researchNotes: Smithsonian supplies diagnostic and invasion-history synthesis; Cabiddu et al. independently report lagoon sampling and abundance differences. The older study calls the Indian Ocean native, whereas the broader synthesis treats origin as uncertain; the uncertainty is retained. Actions are pathway prevention, not a tested species-specific cure.
previousDescription: Caprella scaura is a tiny marine crustacean known as a skeleton shrimp. Its long, sticklike body grips seaweeds and branching growth on docks, boats, and other submerged surfaces. That habit makes harbors useful places to look for it and gives it opportunities to travel with vessel fouling. Introduced populations can become very abundant and compete with other small crustaceans. Its original range remains uncertain, so records need to distinguish well-supported introductions from places with an unclear history.
identification: A pointed spine projecting forward from the top of the head is an important clue. Mature males have prominent grasping limbs, while females develop a brood pouch beneath the body. Females and young animals can be much harder to separate from other Caprella. Body size and some features vary among populations, and older records include a complex of forms. A close side photograph showing the head and grasping limbs is more useful than a distant view of a fouled rope. Confirmation may require an amphipod specialist and a properly preserved specimen.
actions: For boat owners, the practical priority is limiting movement of attached marine growth. Inspect hulls, ropes, fenders, and other immersed equipment before moving to another harbor. Use a marina-approved cleaning service that captures removed material rather than scraping living fouling directly into the water. Do not transfer dock growth or live organisms to another site for identification. Photograph the fouling community and record the harbor, depth, and surface involved, then ask the local marine invasive-species program whether a sample is wanted. Let the local marine program guide any broader response so other marine life is protected.

claims: Uncertain native range; introduced coastal records and fouling pathways
Forward-pointing head spine and difficult female/juvenile identification
Original sampling found contrasting abundance and population composition among three Italian lagoons

proposedDescription: Amur corktree is a deciduous tree brought from eastern Asia for streets and gardens. Its deeply ridged, corky bark is memorable, but the seedlings beneath and beyond a planted tree often matter more to a woodland manager. Female trees bear dark fruit that birds carry away, and seedlings can establish in forest shade. In parts of the northern United States, escaped trees suppress native tree regeneration. A mature ornamental can therefore become a continuing seed source even when its own crown looks well contained.

sources.title: University of Illinois Extension: Invasive Amur corktree

researchNotes: Minnesota DNR independently supports opposite compound leaves, fruit dispersal and native-regeneration impacts. Illinois Extension supports seedling pulling and vigorous stump resprouting. The draft avoids a national regulation claim and does not repeat the DNR page fruit seed-count detail.
previousDescription: Amur corktree is an Asian tree once planted for its broad crown and unusual, deeply ridged bark. Its leaves grow opposite one another and divide into several leaflets; female trees carry dark berries that may remain through winter. Birds spread the seeds beyond gardens, and seedlings tolerate forest shade. In parts of the northern United States, escaped trees can fill the understory and make it harder for native trees and other plants to regenerate.
identification: Leaves grow opposite one another and divide into several smooth-edged leaflets. Mature bark is gray-brown and deeply furrowed; exposed inner bark is conspicuously yellow, although a healthy tree need not be cut for identification. Rounded fruits darken to black and hang in clusters, sometimes into winter. Ashes also have opposite compound leaves, but their fruits are winged rather than berry-like. Tree-of-heaven has alternate leaves. Record the arrangement of whole leaves on the twig, not just the apparent pairing of leaflets along one leaf.
actions: Start by surveying beneath fruiting trees, along bird perches, and into adjacent woods. Small seedlings can be pulled when soil is moist, taking care around native seedlings. Cutting a larger corktree once often leads to vigorous resprouting, so arrange a complete follow-up plan with a qualified land manager or arborist before felling it. Contain fruit-bearing branches during disposal and return in later seasons to find seedlings and sprouts. When replacing a landscape tree, choose a locally appropriate species and check current local restrictions on planting or sale.

claims: Forest invasion; moist-soil seedling removal; cut stems resprout
Corky bark, opposite compound foliage and dark fruit
Bird dispersal and suppression of native tree seedlings

proposedDescription: Amur goby is a small fish associated with the bottom of streams, but its name carries a complicated history. Rhinogobius brunneus once covered several related forms. Modern morphological and genetic work recognizes a more narrowly defined species in Japan and southeastern Korea. Older reports from Washington and Oregon used the broader name. Those reports are valuable historical records, yet they do not by themselves confirm that the introduced fish belong to the species as it is understood today.

sources.title: USFWS: Amur Goby Ecological Risk Screening Summary
Jeon et al. 2025: First Record of Rhinogobius brunneus from Korea

The older broad concept cannot be assigned to the revised species solely from those regional records. Next: Request voucher reassessment of introduced US Rhinogobius under the modern diagnosis.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: The current narrowly defined Rhinogobius brunneus can be described accurately while older Washington and Oregon identifications remain unassigned. The current Korean primary study supplies modern morphology and genetic context independently of the historical US risk account. The prior draft already separates those scopes; missing reidentification of US vouchers does not prevent a general species guide. Next step: Review the current-species draft and keep Washington/Oregon voucher reassessment outside its distribution claims. All inherited URLs remain retained in sources or the inherited notes. Previously accessed evidence is retained as provenance; only the accesses described here are claimed as fresh in this pass.
