All inherited URLs remain retained in sources or the inherited notes. Previously accessed evidence is retained as provenance; only the accesses described here are claimed as fresh in this pass. No catalog IDs, occurrence mappings or public records changed. Local editorial review only; release remains deferred.
previousDescription: Anoecia vagans is an aphid with a life cycle involving dogwoods and grass roots. Its pale green, yellow or olive coloring can vary with its stage of life. Root-feeding colonies are less visible than aphids on leaves, and ants may attend them for the sugary liquid they produce. Knowing the host plant and season is especially useful when trying to identify this small insect.

claims: Host alternation and seasonal forms
Original fundatrix description and specimen basis
May 2011 Cornus sanguinea founders and offspring; partially fused dorsal sclerites and two accessory rostral hairs distinguish the founder from A. corni.
A. vagans wingless dwarf male and strongly modified fused triangular pointed parameres; separate museum material from the 2014 founders.

identification: The spring founder on dogwood and later root-feeding generations should not be compared as though they were the same form. Closely related Anoecia, especially A. corni, require a specialist key and microscopic characters. Record the exact host, the feeding site and whether the insects have wings. The original founder description was based on collected insects associated with a verified colony, not on color alone. Avoid attaching a precise body-size estimate to an uncertain field photograph.
actions: On a dogwood, photograph the occupied shoot before disturbing it; for insects already exposed on grass roots, retain the root and host information together. Ask an extension diagnostic service how to submit a small sample. Do not excavate a lawn or remove a dogwood merely to search for a suspected seasonal connection. A winged aphid caught in a trap needs identification before it can support a local occurrence record. If plants are declining, investigate moisture, roots and other pests as well; this species' contribution to local damage remains unresolved.

proposedDescription: Aphis eugeniae is a small aphid that feeds on several kinds of shrubs and trees. Older Asian accounts emphasize spurge-family hosts, while Florida records show a preference for rose-family plants, including apples, pears and especially loquat. Some Florida colonies can damage these hosts. It closely resembles the spirea aphid, so color and host plant alone are unreliable guides. Specialists distinguish it using fine features of the legs and other appendages.

sources.title: Skelley et al. 2025: Adventive arthropods in Florida, 1990-2023

researchNotes: Evidence scope: USDA AphID and Florida agency observations support identity and regionally different hosts, but no independently supported species-specific treatment threshold was recovered. The Florida account reports damaging colonies; this does not establish virus transmission or identical host preference elsewhere.
previousDescription: Aphis eugeniae is a small aphid recorded on several shrubs and herbs, particularly members of the spurge family. It is known from parts of Asia and the Pacific, with records also reported from Florida. It resembles other aphids, including the spirea aphid, so the plant it is feeding on is only one clue. A reliable identification may require examination of fine body features.

claims: Fine diagnostic differences from spirea aphid.
Florida Rosaceae hosts and damaging colonies.

identification: Compare suspected colonies with spirea aphid, Aphis spiraecola, rather than deciding from their shared greenish appearance. Reliable separation uses tiny features that are difficult to capture in a casual garden photograph. Keep several images of adults, the occupied shoot and the host's leaves. Loquat is especially relevant to Florida observations, while the older Asian host emphasis differs. A plant label and collection location therefore belong with the identification request, but neither replaces examination of the aphids themselves.
actions: For a loquat or other valued shrub, mark affected shoots and check whether new growth is becoming distorted or losing vigor. Keep an infested nursery plant apart from clean stock while identification is arranged, and inspect plants that arrived with it. Ask local extension staff to distinguish a consequential colony from a small transient presence before selecting control. Preserve predatory insects found with the colony. The available species accounts do not justify assuming virus transmission or applying a treatment schedule intended for spirea aphid; the response should match the confirmed insect and actual plant injury.

proposedDescription: Asiphonella dactylonii feeds on the roots and lower parts of grasses, including bermudagrass. Its pale body may be covered with bluish-white wax, and colonies can remain hidden near or below the soil surface. That makes it less conspicuous than aphids clustered on shoots. Records establish its association with grasses, but do not by themselves show that it causes serious damage wherever it is found.

sources.title: Silva - Occurrence of Asiphonella dactylonii on bermudagrass in Bahia; Brazilian Entomology Congress abstract

researchNotes: The synthesis includes older Argentine/Asian descriptive lineages, distinct from the independently accessed original Silva Brazilian observation. Its reuse of Silva for Brazil is not counted as new confirmation. The supported profile is diagnosis and occupied-sod containment, not an unverified turf-damage threshold.
previousDescription: Asiphonella dactylonii feeds on the roots and lower parts of grasses, including bermudagrass. Its pale body may be covered with bluish-white wax, and colonies can remain hidden near or below the soil surface. That makes it less conspicuous than aphids clustered on shoots. Records establish its association with grasses, but do not by themselves show that it causes serious damage wherever it is found.

claims: Waxy grass-root aphid.
Original Bahia bermudagrass occurrence.

identification: Examine the grass base and exposed roots, where the waxy colony can resemble pale debris or other small sap-feeding insects. Record whether wax coats separate insects and whether they are actually attached to the plant. Bermudagrass is a documented host, but that association cannot by itself identify the aphid. A root-feeding specimen should be checked with a microscopic key, since aboveground aphid photographs are poor comparisons. Do not infer the species from a bare or yellow lawn patch alone.
actions: If a colony is discovered during routine turf work, photograph it in place and keep the grass identification with the observation. Compare the affected patch with nearby healthy turf and note irrigation, compaction or recent disturbance. Consult a turf or insect specialist before treating the soil; a yellow patch can have several causes, and the hidden aphids may not explain all of the decline. Avoid transporting occupied sod or rooted nursery material to another site while the diagnosis is pending. Extensive digging solely to find hidden insects can damage the turf and obscure other causes of decline.

proposedDescription: Cerataphis lataniae is an aphid that can look surprisingly like a scale insect. Its body is flattened and oval, with a fringe of white wax around the edge. It feeds on palms and belongs to a group whose members are easily confused, especially with Cerataphis brasiliensis. A photograph may show the waxy outline clearly without revealing enough detail to identify the species confidently.

sources.title: Lunz et al. 2011 - Cerataphis brasiliensis: correct identification of aphids on Amazonian palms

researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Fresh exact-species synthesis and Lunz's independently examined Amazonian material distinguish lataniae from brasiliensis. Historical confusion is disclosed without assigning corrected Brazilian records to lataniae. Microscopic diagnosis and general stock isolation do not require a control trial. Next: Retain fine-character confirmation and exclude brasiliensis damage estimates.
previousDescription: Cerataphis lataniae is an aphid that can look surprisingly like a scale insect. Its body is flattened and oval, with a fringe of white wax around the edge. It feeds on palms and belongs to a group whose members are easily confused, especially with Cerataphis brasiliensis. A photograph may show the waxy outline clearly without revealing enough detail to identify the species confidently.

claims: Wax-fringed body, palm hosts and brasiliensis distinction
Original palm specimens corrected to brasiliensis; microscopic comparisons

identification: The flattened body and waxy border can suggest an armored or soft scale at first glance. Look for individual insects rather than treating a white-edged patch as a single growth on the leaf. Distinguishing C. lataniae from C. brasiliensis requires finer anatomy than the outline usually reveals. An Amazonian study corrected earlier palm records from lataniae to brasiliensis, illustrating why an old name on a photograph or host list may need rechecking. Save the palm identification and collection history.
actions: Inspect newly acquired palms before placing them beside established plants, particularly the parts carrying visible colonies. If an identification is uncertain, keep the plant separate and ask a diagnostic service what material it needs. Do not assume that wax means the insects are dead, or scrape living palm tissue to expose them. Record plant condition as well as insect numbers. Treatment or claims of damage attributed to C. brasiliensis should not be applied automatically to this name; a confirmed species and a local assessment are needed before choosing a response.

proposedDescription: Dysaphis crataegi belongs to a difficult group of aphids associated with hawthorns and carrots. This profile follows the named carrot-associated species while keeping its close relatives separate. In spring, some populations make reddish curled-leaf galls on hawthorn, then move to feed around the base and roots of herbaceous hosts. The wingless aphids are pale yellowish to gray-green and dusted with wax. Colonies can hide near the soil surface. Several close relatives look much the same, so the host and a close examination matter when identifying them.
researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Independent INRAE and Blackman/Eastop accounts support a qualified profile of the named carrot-associated aphid. The latter explicitly recognizes US carrot populations under crataegi sensu stricto while questioning assumptions about their seasonal hosts. The public text retains that limitation and explains why ordinary morphology is insufficient. No demonstrated reassignment of the catalog's US records was found, so the former management/diagnostic hold resolves by scope clarification. Inherited reference not used as fresh substantive evidence because its exact page could not be recovered: https://ipm.ucanr.edu/agriculture/carrot/crown-and-root-aphids/ .
previousDescription: Dysaphis crataegi is associated with hawthorns and plants such as carrots, where colonies may occur around the roots or crown. Its yellowish to gray-green body can have a waxy coating, and ants may gather around colonies to collect honeydew. Several related aphids share similar features. The host plant, feeding location and microscopic details all help separate this species from its lookalikes.

claims: Crataegi complex, red hawthorn galls, secondary hosts and uncertain alternation
Ordinary morphology does not distinguish three named species; hybridization occurs
Hawthorn/Apiaceae hosts and colonies at host collars or leaf sheaths

identification: Reddish curled leaves on hawthorn and wax-dusted aphids around carrot crowns describe different parts of a complicated species group. Record which host is involved and where insects are feeding. Look beneath loose surface soil only where roots are already being inspected; a curled leaf or poor carrot growth is not enough to identify the aphid. Ordinary morphology cannot reliably separate this species from D. apiifolia and D. foeniculus; a specialist may need additional evidence. American carrot populations should not be assumed to alternate with hawthorn simply because some European populations do.
actions: In a vegetable bed, compare affected carrots with nearby plants and check whether aphids are actually present at the crown or roots. Ask a crop adviser to evaluate the colony before treating, since a crop symptom alone does not identify the aphid responsible. Keep root samples and their plant labels together for diagnosis. Do not remove nearby hawthorns as an automatic control measure: the seasonal connection may not apply to the local population. A harvest problem should be assessed for soil conditions and other root pests as well as aphids.

proposedDescription: Eucallipterus tiliae feeds in groups beneath linden leaves. The small aphids are greenish with dark side markings, and winged forms have dusky areas on their wings. A colony may first draw attention through sticky honeydew on leaves, sidewalks or parked cars; dark sooty mold can grow on this sugary coating. Established trees often tolerate the feeding, although saplings can suffer reduced growth. The insect stays with lindens through its seasonal cycle.
researchNotes: UMass and Oregon State provide substantive regional accounts separating nuisance honeydew from host injury and discussing management. The expansion retains that distinction, avoids an unsupported mature-tree mortality claim, and gives no chemical recipe.
previousDescription: Eucallipterus tiliae feeds beneath the leaves of lindens and basswoods. The aphids are yellow with dark markings, but people often notice their sticky honeydew before seeing the insects themselves. It can coat cars, benches and other surfaces below an affected tree and support dark sooty mold. This species is known from Europe and North America and is closely associated with its linden hosts.

claims: Linden feeding and honeydew nuisance.
Young-tree effects and monitoring context.

identification: Turn over several linden leaves and look for the insects themselves, their shed skins and fresh droplets beneath the canopy. Sticky paving and blackened surfaces can reveal a colony before leaves show much change, but neither sign is unique to linden aphid. Wing markings and the dark lateral pattern help support an identification. Inspect more than one branch and compare young trees with established specimens; the practical significance of feeding depends on the condition and size of the host.
actions: Decide whether the main concern is a sticky surface or deteriorating tree growth. Wash affected outdoor objects as needed and monitor the tree rather than treating nuisance honeydew as proof that a mature linden is dying. Young or stressed trees deserve closer assessment. Look for predators before choosing an intervention, and seek local tree-care advice if growth is reduced. Avoid a calendar spray based only on last year's honeydew. A professional should account for the tree, site and beneficial insects before considering any pesticide treatment.

proposedDescription: Geoica setulosa is a pale aphid that feeds on grass roots. Ants tend its colonies for honeydew and may build small soil mounds around them. In turf, these mounds can be more noticeable than the aphids themselves and may cover or smother nearby grass. Understanding the relationship between the two insects helps explain damage that might otherwise be attributed entirely to root feeding.

sources.title: USDA ARS: Geoica setulosa occurrence and turfgrass ant association

researchNotes: Older non-U.S. root-aphid morphology and host literature in the synthesis are distinct from the original U.S. ant/turf study. The synthesis repeats that study for U.S. occurrence, which is counted only once. Mound effects are attributed to the ant association; diagnosis and monitoring do not require a universal control threshold.
previousDescription: Geoica setulosa is a pale root-feeding aphid associated with grasses. Colonies can be hidden below the surface and attended by ants, so the ants may be more noticeable than the aphids themselves. A USDA study documented this introduced species in the eastern United States in association with turfgrass ant mounds. In that setting, mound-building ants could smother patches of grass and interfere with mowing. Those effects should be attributed to the ant activity, rather than assumed to be direct feeding damage by the aphid.
identification: Check whether the conspicuous feature is an ant-built mound rather than a lesion made directly by aphid feeding. A pale insect among roots cannot be identified as Geoica from color alone. Photograph the turf surface, the mound and any already exposed root colony separately. Record the ant association without assuming that the ant and aphid share the same origin or pest status. Microscopic examination may be needed to distinguish the aphid from other root inhabitants.
actions: For a lawn or sports surface, map the mounds and note whether they interfere with use or cover living grass. Ask a turf specialist to investigate the ant-aphid association before selecting a response aimed only at one partner. Avoid repeatedly opening large areas of healthy turf to locate insects. If a sample is requested, keep the roots, aphids and associated ants clearly labeled by location. Keep photographs from later visits so the adviser can see whether the mounds are increasing, remaining stable or disappearing between maintenance operations.

claims: Grass-root association and ant attendance.
Original turf mound association.

proposedDescription: Geopemphigus floccosus is a root-feeding aphid associated with morning-glories in the genus Ipomoea. Wingless individuals are pale greenish yellow with tufts of white wax; winged forms can look grayer and have dark bands across the abdomen. Much of its feeding takes place out of sight below ground. Its complete life cycle remains uncertain, so an apparent association with a second host should not be treated as a proven seasonal migration.

sources.title: Casarrubias Trujillo 2004 - Aphid fauna of Chihuahua, species 59

researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: The specialist account describes root forms and unsuccessful host-transfer experiments; an independent Chihuahua thesis documents collected winged insects and cross-banded morphology. The unproved Pistacia phase is a bounded life-history unknown. The draft avoids asserting migration or US origin, and containment is not a control-efficacy claim. Next: Retain the uncertain second host and refer actual colonies for diagnosis.
previousDescription: Geopemphigus floccosus is a root-feeding aphid associated with plants in the morning-glory genus, Ipomoea. Its pale green or yellow body can be covered in wax, and its underground feeding habits make it easy to overlook. Research describes an American origin, but parts of its life cycle remain poorly documented. Its presence should be interpreted carefully rather than assumed to represent an invasive pest outbreak.

claims: Root forms and unconfirmed Pistacia connection
Winged morphology and original Chihuahua collections

identification: Root-feeding wingless individuals and winged migrants can differ in wax and dark markings, so compare like forms when using a key. Keep the morning-glory identification and the root attachment with the specimen record. Other waxy insects also inhabit roots; loose white material alone is not diagnostic. The possible connection to Pistacia in some literature remains uncertain and should not be used as a shortcut to identify a colony or reconstruct its seasonal movements.
actions: When insects appear during repotting or root inspection, set that plant aside and seek advice about submitting a labeled sample. Avoid carrying its soil or rooted pieces to another garden until the colony is identified. Document whether the host is actually wilting or losing growth; the aphid's presence does not establish the cause of every root problem. Do not remove a nearby Pistacia tree in an attempt to interrupt an unproven life cycle. Keep the first photographs and compare the same plant on later visits so new feeding and changes in growth can be assessed together.

proposedDescription: Greenidea ficicola feeds on young leaves and shoots of figs, including ornamental Ficus plants. Its green to brown body has unusually long, hairy tubes that curve outward from the rear, a useful clue for recognition. Researchers have documented colonies on several fig species in Florida. Another introduced Greenidea also feeds on figs, so confirming the species requires closer attention to the surface pattern of those tubes and other small features.

sources.title: Halbert 2004 - The genus Greenidea in the United States

researchNotes: The synthesis supplies an older Asian descriptive baseline, while Halbert independently examined U.S. colonies and lookalike distinctions. Its repeated Florida citation is not counted again. Identification and nursery-stock precautions are supported, without an invented severity or treatment threshold.
previousDescription: Greenidea ficicola feeds on young leaves and shoots of figs, including ornamental Ficus plants. Its green to brown body has unusually long, curved tubes projecting from the rear, a useful clue for recognition. Native to Asia, it has been introduced to places including Florida. Colonies may affect ornamental growth, though it is generally described as a relatively minor pest in the available regional accounts.

claims: General Greenidea diagnosis; Florida account overlaps Halbert.
Original U.S. Ficus colonies and species separation.

identification: The unusually long, hairy tubes at the back of a Greenidea aphid are a strong clue to the genus. To separate G. ficicola from G. psidii, a specialist examines their surface pattern and other fine structures. Photograph the insect from above and from the side if possible, along with the fig's youngest leaves. An aphid found on Ficus is not necessarily this species, and a single flying insect should not be described as an established feeding colony.
actions: Inspect tender fig growth when bringing ornamental plants into a collection. If colonies are present, keep the affected plant apart while seeking an identification, and check nearby plants that shared its nursery source. Record changes in leaf growth rather than judging severity only by the unusual appearance of the aphids. Avoid moving infested cuttings between homes or gardens. A local horticultural adviser can help decide whether a small colony warrants action. Keep photographs of the same shoots over time, including new leaves that remain healthy, so the adviser can assess the plant rather than just a close-up of the insects.

proposedDescription: Hyalopterus amygdali is a slender, green aphid often covered with pale, mealy-looking wax. It is associated with almonds and can use reeds during part of its seasonal cycle. Closely related aphids look very similar and may occur on related host plants. For that reason, the host alone is not a reliable identification, and specialists sometimes use genetic evidence to distinguish members of this group.

sources.title: Lozier et al. 2008 - Molecular and morphological evaluation of Hyalopterus; USDA technical abstract
2013 European Hyalopterus morphology and COI study

researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where the current assessment differs: Fresh review 2026-10-31: The USDA original-study summary and current specialist account confirm separation of formerly conflated Hyalopterus, with North American amygdali still tentative. This is unresolved historical species assignment; almond or reed hosts cannot supply the missing determination. Next: Locate modern North American vouchers or molecularly verified restricted-amygdali colonies.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: Newly examined original 2024 voucher-based genomic work and a separate 2013 European population study support the restricted almond-associated aphid concept. The 2024 study newly sequenced Kyrgyzstan reed material, voucher40542, and other species. The 2013 work examined 43 European populations with COI and morphology. Their samples and new measurements are independent of the inherited 2008 revision; host alone remains insufficient. Next step: Review the restricted-species draft without assigning unreviewed US host records to it. Fresh access: 2024 Hyalopterus mitogenomes and phylogenetic analysis [indexed_excerpt; Hyalopterus-2024-new-mitogenomes] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11204073/ — New H. amygdali Phragmites australis specimen from Osh, Kyrgyzstan, voucher40542 at CAS Beijing; direct page challenged by captcha, substantive indexed methods and results read. | 2013 European Hyalopterus morphology and COI study [indexed_excerpt; Hyalopterus-2013-European-populations] https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3764526/ — Forty-three European populations; median head-hair morphology classified97.3 percent, supporting a qualified rather than host-only identification. All inherited URLs remain retained in sources or the inherited notes. Previously accessed evidence is retained as provenance; only the accesses described here are claimed as fresh in this pass. No catalog IDs, occurrence mappings or public records changed. Local editorial review only; release remains deferred.
previousDescription: Hyalopterus amygdali is a slender, green aphid often covered with pale, mealy-looking wax. It is associated with almonds and can use reeds during part of its seasonal cycle. Closely related aphids look very similar and may occur on related host plants. For that reason, the host alone is not a reliable identification, and specialists sometimes use genetic evidence to distinguish members of this group.

claims: Almond morphology and uncertain North American/secondary-host assignment
Original molecular/morphometric separation of three species
New H. amygdali Phragmites australis specimen from Osh, Kyrgyzstan, voucher40542 at CAS Beijing; direct page challenged by captcha, substantive indexed methods and results read.
Forty-three European populations; median head-hair morphology classified97.3 percent, supporting a qualified rather than host-only identification.

identification: A coating of pale wax on a slender green aphid is not enough to distinguish the almond-associated member of this group. Hyalopterus pruni and other closely related forms can overlap in general appearance and host use. Photograph the colony and identify the Prunus host carefully, then obtain a specialist determination when the record matters. The molecular and morphological revision shows why a name based solely on almond, peach or reed can be misleading. Preserve the season and location as supporting evidence.
actions: In an orchard, record colony distribution and plant symptoms and ask an adviser to confirm which Hyalopterus is involved. Keep a few occupied shoots available for diagnosis rather than treating every waxy aphid as the same pest. Do not clear nearby reeds solely on the assumption that they are the source of the orchard population. Ask that the identification report state any remaining uncertainty within the species group, especially when comparing records from another region. Management should follow the confirmed insect, crop and observed injury, with attention to beneficial insects already present.

proposedDescription: Hyperomyzus lactucae can curl and yellow currant leaves in spring before moving to sowthistles, where it feeds on stems and flower shoots. In warmer regions, colonies may remain on these herbaceous hosts. It is a green aphid and can transmit certain plant viruses. Finding the insect is not the same as confirming a virus infection, since leaf symptoms can have several causes.

sources.title: Leong 1977 - Biological and ecological studies of the currant-sowthistle aphid; Lincoln University abstract

researchNotes: Evidence scope: the original New Zealand thesis abstract supports year-round observations and host alternation, while the specialist account supplies broader biology. Virus association is distinguished from diagnosis. No independently established local disease-control program or climate-independent seasonal schedule was recovered.
previousDescription: Hyperomyzus lactucae can curl and yellow currant leaves in spring before moving to sowthistles, where it feeds on stems and flower shoots. In warmer regions, colonies may remain on these herbaceous hosts. It is a green aphid and can transmit certain plant viruses. Finding the insect is not the same as confirming a virus infection, since leaf symptoms can have several causes.

claims: Currant/sowthistle biology and appearance.
Original New Zealand seasonal study; virus reservoir distinction.

identification: Inspect currant shoots in spring and the stems or flower-bearing growth of nearby sowthistles when documenting a seasonal change. Similar green aphids can occur on both plants, so host sequence is evidence to record rather than proof of identity. Include winged and wingless individuals if available. Yellowing or curled leaves can reflect feeding, disease or other stress. A suspected lettuce virus needs plant-diagnostic testing; seeing an aphid cannot confirm either infection or the direction in which a virus moved.
actions: In a currant planting or vegetable garden, inspect incoming plants and note whether colonies persist or increase. If lettuce develops unusual symptoms, contact an extension plant clinic and provide the crop history and aphid observations together. Avoid moving symptomatic plants or infested sowthistles between growing areas. Manage unwanted sowthistles before seed dispersal as part of the garden's weed plan, without claiming that their removal alone prevents disease. Seek locally appropriate advice before treating: the original seasonal study was conducted in New Zealand, and its calendar should not be copied unchanged to another climate.

proposedDescription: Hyperomyzus picridis is a glossy yellow-green aphid associated with alpine currant, oxtongues and hawksbeards. Colonies can gather just below flower heads, where they feed on tender growth. Host plants and small anatomical details help distinguish it from similar aphids. It also forms part of a wider insect community: a field study in France reared several kinds of parasitoid wasps from this aphid. Those observations describe its ecology without establishing damage at other locations.

sources.title: Generalist Aphid Parasitoids Behave as Specialists at the Agroecosystem Scale, 2020

researchNotes: Evidence scope: original French rearing data and the specialist account support ecology, but U.S. occurrence attribution, harm and species-specific management remain unresolved. Parasitoid observations are kept geographically bounded and are not a recommendation to buy or release natural enemies.
previousDescription: Hyperomyzus picridis is a glossy yellow-green aphid with darker markings and tubes extending from the rear of its body. Its hosts include alpine currant, oxtongues and hawksbeards. Colonies may gather just below flower heads, where tender growth offers a feeding site. Host associations and small anatomical differences are important for identification because several related aphids have a similar overall appearance.

claims: Hosts and short diagnostic description.
French parasitoid-rearing associations.

identification: Look just below the flower heads of an identified oxtongue or hawksbeard, and record the exact host rather than calling every yellow-flowered plant a thistle. The aphid's glossy yellow-green appearance can resemble other species. Fine antennal and rear-tube characters require magnification and a suitable key. A swollen, brownish aphid may instead be a parasitized individual; retain photographs of those forms with the living colony. Their presence provides ecological context but is not a species diagnosis by itself.
actions: For a small outdoor colony without evident plant injury, observation is more informative than an immediate general insect treatment. Mark the host and compare the colony on later visits, noting predators or parasitoid mummies. If the host is an unwanted weed, manage the plant according to the site's vegetation plan rather than trying to eradicate an aphid independently of it. Ask for specialist identification before reporting a new locality. The French parasitoid study demonstrates a natural-enemy association there; it does not establish the same wasps, impact or control outcome in a U.S. garden.

proposedDescription: Macrosiphoniella tanacetaria feeds on tansy, gathering in loose colonies around the tips of shoots. A controlled study found that its performance changed with the growing conditions of the host: fertilizer and competition from goldenrod affected plant growth and the aphids. This helps explain why colony size should be considered alongside the condition of the plant, rather than interpreted as a fixed measure of damage.

sources.title: Mahdavi Arab et al. 2014 - Aphid-tansy experimental study

researchNotes: The original PLOS study is the main source for tansy shoot feeding and nutrition/competition responses. Blackman and Eastop is used only as short diagnostic context. The controlled experiment is not a U.S. yield-loss estimate or a fertilizer-based control recommendation.
previousDescription: Macrosiphoniella tanacetaria feeds on tansy, often gathering around its upper stems and flower heads. The aphids are gray-green with a waxy coating and dark legs, antennae and rear tubes. Unlike aphids that move between trees and herbs, this species can spend its seasonal cycle on herbaceous plants. It has been introduced to North America, where tansy provides a recognizable place to look for it.

claims: Tansy aphid identity and host.
Original tansy nutrition/competition experiment and shoot feeding.

identification: Search the upper parts of an identified tansy plant, including developing flower heads, for loose aphid colonies. Other aphids also use tansy, and the host alone cannot separate them. Photograph a complete insect and its feeding position rather than only a crowded patch. A laboratory or garden experiment on this species can explain responses to plant conditions, but it does not show that every colony has the same effect on a wild tansy stand.
actions: If tansy is being removed as an unwanted plant, contain its reproductive material and follow the local plant-management plan; there is no need to move the aphid colony onto another host. On a retained ornamental, compare new growth and colony size over time before deciding that intervention is necessary. Preserve predators observed with the aphids. Do not add fertilizer simply to change aphid numbers: experimental responses depended on plant nutrition and competition. For persistent injury, bring photographs of occupied and healthy shoots to a local adviser, together with the recent watering and fertilizer history.

proposedDescription: Macrosiphum lilii is an aphid associated with lilies. It can be pale yellow or orange, sometimes with a purple patch, and has long, dark legs and tubes at the rear of its body. Feeding colonies produce honeydew, which can make nearby plant surfaces sticky. Its seasonal life cycle is not well documented in the available accounts, so host and appearance provide a better starting point than assumptions about its movements.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Purplespotted lily aphid
University of Maryland Extension: Aphids in home gardens

researchNotes: NC State's species account and Maryland's locally illustrated identification section independently support the recognizable lily aphid. NC State labels its proposed seasonal biology as presumed, which remains excluded. Physical removal and monitoring are conservative extension-guided garden actions, not an eradication guarantee.
previousDescription: The purplespotted lily aphid is a distinctive visitor to garden lilies. A pale yellow to orange body, a broad purple patch, and long dark legs and rear tubes help it stand out from other aphids. Colonies feed on lilies and leave sticky honeydew behind, making them relevant to gardeners and plant growers. Even with its striking colors, identification should use the host plant and the insect together. Some details of its seasonal life remain inferred from relatives rather than directly demonstrated.
identification: The purple marking is a useful clue, but its shape varies and it should be considered with the long black appendages and pale body. Check that the host is a true lily, Lilium, rather than another ornamental called a lily. Photograph a single aphid as well as the colony and developing buds. Related Macrosiphum can have similarly long legs and rear tubes. Winged forms may occur alongside wingless ones; that difference alone does not indicate two pest species.
actions: Inspect tender growth on newly purchased lilies before placing them among established plants. Where a small colony is accessible, a gentle stream of water can dislodge aphids without treating the whole bed; avoid damaging delicate buds. Recheck the plants and look for predators or parasitized aphids before escalating control. Honeydew is a reason to inspect, not proof of serious plant injury. If growth remains distorted or colonies repeatedly rebuild, ask a local horticultural adviser for a diagnosis. Do not use a guessed seasonal migration schedule to decide when treatment is needed.

claims: Purple-spotted lily aphid description; life cycle qualified.
Independently illustrated lily aphid and garden aphid management.

proposedDescription: Melanaphis sorini is an aphid associated with Miscanthus grasses. Florida records include plants arriving from California and subsequent observations in the ornamental trade. Florida observers have not considered it a pest of Miscanthus grown for biomass there. This specific regional experience matters: the genus also contains important crop pests, but those relatives do not automatically describe what a colony on an ornamental grass is doing.

sources.title: Skelley et al. 2025 - Adventive arthropods in Florida, Melanaphis sorini account

researchNotes: Florida agency observations are the main source for trade movement and the regional non-pest assessment. The specialist reference warns that morphology overlaps M. (sacchari) indosacchari; host and specialist confirmation therefore matter. Impacts of M. sacchari or M. sorghi are excluded.
previousDescription: Melanaphis sorini is an aphid associated with Miscanthus grasses. Individuals may be tan to wine-purple, and the species has been recorded in Asia as well as California and Florida. It belongs to a genus that also contains important crop pests, but those relatives' impacts should not be assigned to this species. Identifying the grass host and examining the aphid closely are important first steps.

claims: Miscanthus association and variable color.
Florida biomass Miscanthus not considered a pest context.

identification: Start with a reliable identification of the grass. Miscanthus is a much stronger clue for this aphid than a general resemblance to a cereal or sugarcane aphid. Color can range across tan and purplish individuals and is not a dependable separator. Photograph the insects on the blade or sheath and ask a specialist to examine adults if an exact record is needed. Reports from ornamental trade material should be kept distinct from evidence of establishment in surrounding natural vegetation.
actions: Inspect Miscanthus plants arriving from another nursery and note whether a colony persists after planting. Keep occupied divisions separate from clean stock while identification is pending, and avoid distributing them to other gardens. Monitor the plant's condition instead of treating the presence of a Melanaphis as an automatic crop emergency. If new leaves remain healthy, record the colony and recheck it rather than assuming a crop emergency. For continuing decline, bring both the aphid and grass identification to a local adviser.

proposedDescription: Metopolophium festucae is a grass-feeding aphid that may be green, yellow or pink. Winged individuals can have dark bands on the body. It belongs to a group in which the subspecies matters: the cereal-feeding form, Metopolophium festucae cerealium, has its own records and research history. A broad identification to species should not automatically be treated as evidence for that particular crop-associated form.

sources.title: Michaud 2018 - Metopolophium festucae cerealium, a new aphid in Kansas wheat

researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: The synthesis explicitly treats cerealium within festucae; independent Kansas field observations concern identified cerealium migrants. A species profile can preserve that hierarchy without merging IDs or transferring crop injury to every member. Both determination levels remain explicit. Next: Keep subspecies determinations attached to crop records and review duplicate presentation separately.
previousDescription: Metopolophium festucae is a grass-feeding aphid that may be green, yellow or pink. Winged individuals can have dark bands on the body. It belongs to a group in which the subspecies matters: the cereal-feeding form, Metopolophium festucae cerealium, has its own records and research history. A broad identification to species should not automatically be treated as evidence for that particular crop-associated form.

claims: Species morphology, grass hosts and cerealium rank
Low-density winged cerealium in wheat; no wingless forms collected

identification: A pale grass aphid with dark markings on its winged form needs closer examination before assigning it to this species or one of its subspecies. Record the grass host and retain the original level of determination in the observation. The cereal-associated form has been distinguished by anatomical characters, not merely by finding an insect in wheat. A winged adult landing in a field may have arrived from another host; document feeding colonies separately from isolated flying insects.
actions: On wild grasses, begin with photographs and a specialist identification rather than clearing the vegetation. If the insects occur in a crop, ask the diagnostic service explicitly whether it can resolve cerealium or only the broader species. Keep that answer with the monitoring record. Do not apply greenhouse crop-loss findings for cerealium to every M. festucae observation. Revisit occupied plants to establish whether a colony is reproducing and whether injury develops. A treatment decision should use the confirmed taxon, crop condition and current regional advice, not a catalog name alone.

proposedDescription: Metopolophium festucae cerealium is a pale, elongated aphid found on cereal crops such as wheat and barley. Winged individuals have dark markings on the back. It has been recorded in the Pacific Northwest and Kansas. Greenhouse studies found that feeding can harm wheat, while field work documented substantial populations in parts of the Northwest. Those findings do not establish the same level of crop loss in every field.

sources.title: Michaud 2018 - Metopolophium festucae cerealium, a new aphid in Kansas wheat
REACCH investigators - Insects: expanding distribution of a newly introduced aphid

researchNotes: Kansas's original collection and the independent Pacific Northwest survey/experimental program support identification and field monitoring. No universal economic threshold is asserted. The broader species record remains separate, and greenhouse injury is not presented as measured yield loss in every field.
previousDescription: Metopolophium festucae cerealium is a pale, elongated aphid found on cereal crops such as wheat and barley. Winged individuals have dark body bands that can help draw attention to them among other aphids. It has been recorded in the Pacific Northwest and Kansas. Research has examined its reproduction and effects on crops, but the results vary with conditions rather than supporting a single damage estimate for every field.

claims: Original Kansas detection and crop monitoring.
Independent Northwest distribution and greenhouse/field distinction.

identification: Inspect several wheat leaves and shoots for both winged and wingless insects. The pale body and dark dorsal markings of winged adults help recognition, but an adviser should distinguish this form from other cereal aphids. Record crop stage and whether nymphs are present. Kansas's initial detection involved winged specimens, so a new adult sighting should not automatically be described as a reproducing outbreak. Keep photographs and collection details with any submitted sample.
actions: Use regular field scouting to follow the colony and its natural enemies rather than responding to a single trapped aphid. Pay attention to later-maturing wheat and to neighboring spring cereals as the season advances, as Kansas guidance recommends vigilance in those situations. Consult local crop advisers when numbers or injury increase. The Pacific Northwest researchers distinguished greenhouse effects from field injury that still required evaluation; do not turn a laboratory result into an invented economic threshold. Preserve existing biological control and avoid a routine spray simply because the aphid is newly recorded.

proposedDescription: Myzaphis rosarum is a small aphid associated with roses and shrubby cinquefoil. Colonies can occur along the midribs of young leaves. A modern revision compared specimens to distinguish it from related Myzaphis, using details of the antennae, body surface and other fine structures. These features are difficult to see in a casual garden photograph, so a host name and a greenish color are useful clues rather than a complete diagnosis.

sources.title: Kanturski et al. 2018 - A comparative morphological revision of Myzaphis

researchNotes: The original specimen-based morphological revision supplies most diagnostic detail; the shared specialist page is limited to short host/feeding context. The text supports recognition, monitoring and movement precautions without claiming a universal rose-aphid control threshold.
previousDescription: Myzaphis rosarum is a tiny yellow to green aphid found on roses and shrubby cinquefoil. It often feeds along veins on young or unfolding leaves. Short antennae and slightly swollen tubes at the rear of the body help distinguish it under magnification. It is less often associated with severe outbreaks than some familiar rose aphids, though its small size can make colonies easy to overlook.

claims: Rose/cinquefoil host and feeding position.
Original morphological revision distinguishing Myzaphis species.

identification: Inspect young leaves along the midrib and note whether the colony is on rose or shrubby cinquefoil. A small green aphid on a rose is not necessarily the familiar large rose aphid, and several Myzaphis species require detailed examination. The modern revision compared museum specimens and fine surface characters to clarify those names. Photograph the host and the insects from more than one angle. Preserve winged and wingless forms separately in the observation so their differences do not create a false second species.
actions: In a garden, mark a few occupied shoots and check their growth on later visits. If the colony is small and the plant is developing normally, observation can provide better evidence than an immediate broad treatment. Keep newly acquired plants apart from existing roses while an uncertain infestation is identified. Avoid spreading occupied cuttings or divisions. For persistent distortion or loss of vigor, request a local diagnosis rather than using another rose aphid's threshold. Include close views of the leaf midrib and a whole-shoot photograph, so the adviser can compare the insects with the pattern of plant injury.

proposedDescription: Myzus varians feeds beneath peach leaves, which may roll tightly lengthwise and turn reddish around its colonies. Wingless adults are pale green; winged adults are darker. In its seasonal cycle it can move between peach and clematis, overwintering as eggs near peach buds. Experiments have shown that it can carry plum pox virus from peach to clematis. Finding the aphid or a curled leaf alone does not confirm that a plant is infected.

sources.title: Manachini et al. 2004 - Transmissibility of PPV by Myzus varians to Clematis vitalba

researchNotes: Evidence scope: INRAE biology and the original Italian transmission abstract support the narrow host/vector account. Neither establishes a local virus outbreak or a verified control protocol. PPV transmission is kept to the demonstrated experiment, and diagnosis requires plant testing.
previousDescription: Myzus varians feeds on peach leaves, which may curl or roll around colonies. It is usually green, with dark tips on the tubes projecting from its rear, and may move to clematis during its life cycle. The species can transmit plum pox virus, but its presence alone does not establish that a tree is infected. Both insect identification and plant diagnosis require more than curled leaves.

claims: Peach leaf rolls and seasonal Clematis connection.
Original experimental PPV transmission to Clematis.

identification: A tightly rolled, reddish peach leaf is a reason to inspect inside the roll, not a diagnosis by itself. Record whether pale wingless aphids or darker winged forms are present and compare unaffected leaves on the same tree. Other peach aphids and non-insect problems can distort foliage. A specialist may need actual insects to separate the species. Keep photographs of the leaf damage and aphids together; disease symptoms and vector identity are two questions that require different evidence.
actions: Avoid moving infested peach shoots or cuttings to another planting while identification is pending. If an orchard has unusual symptoms suggesting a virus, contact a plant-diagnostic service and follow its sampling instructions. Do not conclude that nearby clematis is infected merely because experimental transmission has been demonstrated. Monitor young peach growth and natural enemies, and obtain regional advice before intervention. Keep notes on the first affected shoots and subsequent new growth. Do not remove nearby clematis in the hope of controlling a disease that has not been diagnosed.

proposedDescription: Pleotrichophorus chrysanthemi is a pale yellow-green aphid found beneath chrysanthemum leaves. Feeding may be associated with yellowing, including on plants grown under greenhouse conditions. Its identity is complicated by questions about how it differs from the closely related P. glandulosus. Specialists compare tiny body hairs and other structures, together with the host plant. A careful identification is therefore important before treating similar aphids on chrysanthemums as the same species.

identification: Look beneath an identified chrysanthemum leaf and photograph individual aphids as well as yellowed tissue. The pale color is shared by other aphids and cannot resolve this name. Specialists compare the shape and stems of tiny body hairs with P. glandulosus and related forms. A greenhouse label or an older record using chrysanthemi is useful history, but it does not settle the taxonomic boundary. Keep a sample's plant source and date attached to the identification request.
actions: Set an occupied chrysanthemum apart from clean stock while the insects are examined, especially before distributing cuttings. Compare new leaves with older affected foliage and record whether discoloration continues after the colony changes. Yellowing can also reflect growing conditions, so avoid attributing every symptom to aphids without inspection. Ask the diagnostic service to state whether the identification is definite or part of a species complex. Keep that qualification with the plant record and use the confirmed pest identity and plant condition to guide local advice.

proposedDescription: Rhopalomyzus lonicerae has different-looking colonies at different points in its life cycle. Dark green aphids feed on honeysuckle in spring, where leaves may roll around them. Later, paler colonies can occur on grasses, including reed canarygrass in wet places. This seasonal change in host and appearance is useful context: two colonies that look different may still belong to the same species.

sources.title: Andrew Jensen, AphidTrek: Rhopalomyzus field observations

researchNotes: Evidence scope: specialist synthesis and independent western U.S. field observations support seasonal hosts, but do not establish a local injury threshold or management efficacy. Host plants' own invasive status is kept separate from the aphid's role.
previousDescription: Rhopalomyzus lonicerae is an aphid whose appearance changes with its seasonal hosts. On honeysuckle in spring, dark green colonies can roll and discolor young leaves. Later generations move to grasses, especially reed canarygrass, where much paler colonies can become abundant along waterways. An entomologist's western U.S. field observations document both sides of that cycle. Knowing the host connection helps explain why insects on a garden shrub and nearby grass may belong to the same species, without assuming that every colony causes lasting damage.
identification: On honeysuckle, look for occupied leaf rolls and record the color of adults and young. On grasses, photograph the feeding location and identify the grass rather than assuming that any wetland colony is the summer form. Ask a specialist to compare the seasonal forms; a pair of similar-looking colonies on honeysuckle and grass does not prove that one moved between the plants. Other honeysuckle and grass aphids require a suitable key. Preserve the season, locality and host for both kinds of observation.
actions: If honeysuckle growth is affected, inspect a few rolled leaves and monitor subsequent shoots before treating the whole shrub. Do not remove vegetation along a waterway simply to interrupt a presumed aphid migration. A grass may itself need management for a separate reason, but that decision should use the site's plant and habitat plan. Avoid transporting occupied cuttings between gardens. Request specialist confirmation for a new locality or substantial injury; include the exact host and season so observations from honeysuckle are not confused with those from grasses.

claims: Honeysuckle and grass seasonal forms.
Independent western U.S. field observations.

proposedDescription: Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale is commonly associated with roots, where its colonies are easily missed. The aphids are greenish to brown, sometimes with a rusty area toward the rear, and use grasses and other plants, including greenhouse crops. Their hidden feeding habits can complicate diagnosis. Poor root growth alone is not enough to identify them; the insects themselves need to be found and examined.

Original host-choice and reproduction experiment, not trap-crop validation.

identification: This root aphid is commonly listed under the spelling Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale. Look at insects actually attached to exposed roots rather than diagnosing from yellow foliage alone. A rusty rear patch may help recognition, but other root aphids can overlap in color. Document the crop, potting medium and feeding position. A specialist examination is particularly useful when winged individuals appear away from the roots and could be mistaken for a different aphid.
actions: Inspect roots during normal repotting or when a diagnostic sample is needed, and separate an occupied container from clean stock. Keep reused pots and tools free of old roots and loose growing medium. Do not exchange infested plants or root divisions while the cause is unresolved. The recent host-choice experiment found differences in preference and reproduction, but it did not prove a practical trap-crop control system. Seek crop-specific advice for persistent injury and consider irrigation, root disease and other pests alongside the aphid rather than assuming one explanation for poor growth.

proposedDescription: Sipha glyceriae is a tiny aphid most often found on grasses in damp places, with some records from sedges and rushes too. Wingless adults are usually dull green, sometimes reddish, and may have a paler stripe along the back. They are only about two millimeters long. Unlike aphids that move between trees and grasses through the seasons, this species completes its cycle on herbaceous plants. Identifying it confidently requires a close look: specialists compare its body hairs and minute surface features with those of related grass aphids.

previousDescription: Sipha glyceriae is an aphid of wet places, feeding on grasses, rushes and sedges. Its green body may show a reddish stripe and lighter markings along the back. It uses herbaceous hosts through its seasonal cycle rather than relying on an obvious tree-to-grass migration. Looking closely at wetland vegetation can reveal colonies that would otherwise blend into their surroundings.

claims: Wet-grass host context.
North American Sipha review.
Original diagnostic key separates glyceriae.

identification: Check damp-site grasses carefully with magnification; the insects are small enough to disappear against a leaf blade. A pale dorsal stripe differs from a reddish body tint, and neither alone proves identity. The identification handbook uses body hairs and microscopic surface features to separate this species from other Sipha. Record sedge or rush hosts accurately if those are involved. Do not assume that a green grass aphid is the black cereal-associated S. maydis simply because both belong to this genus.
actions: For a colony in wet vegetation, photograph the host and feeding site before disturbing it. Keep observations from a natural margin separate from those in a crop or managed lawn. Do not drain or clear damp habitat solely to remove an uncertain aphid population. If plants show substantial injury, submit a labeled sample and ask for a species-level diagnosis before choosing management. A record of the same patch over several visits can help distinguish a brief colony from persistent feeding associated with declining growth.

proposedDescription: Sipha maydis is a dark, glossy aphid with stiff hairs, often found near the bases of grass leaves. It feeds on grasses and cereal crops, including wheat, barley, oats and corn. Colonies can injure leaves, and the species can also transmit plant viruses. Its nearly black or brown appearance helps distinguish it from some common green aphids, though a close examination is still important.
identification: Inspect the bases of grass leaves and look for compact dark aphids with conspicuous stiff hairs. That appearance helps separate them from many green cereal aphids, but confirm the insect rather than relying on leaf injury. Record the crop, growth stage and whether young are present with adults. A dark colony on a non-grass host needs particular scrutiny. If disease is suspected, have the plant tested; a possible vector's presence does not identify a virus or demonstrate transmission at the site.
actions: In a cereal field, map occupied areas and compare their plant condition with unoccupied portions of the crop. Contact local agricultural extension when a new or increasing colony is found, providing clear photographs and collection details. Preserve predators and avoid moving occupied grass material to a clean planting. Keep a dated record of the patches and any changes in leaf condition so an adviser can assess how the situation is developing. Management should use a confirmed identification and regional crop guidance rather than assuming that every black aphid warrants the same intervention.

The draft does not invent a local crop threshold, quantify unmeasured yield loss or diagnose a virus. Current species-specific management evidence requires regional review.
previousDescription: A patch of dark specks near the base of a grass leaf can turn out to be a colony of hedgehog grain aphids. Sipha maydis feeds on cereals and other grasses, including wheat, barley, oats, and corn. Unlike many green cereal aphids, its wingless adults are glossy brown-black and covered with stiff hairs. Feeding colonies can injure leaves, and the species has been reported as a grass-virus vector. It is an introduced aphid in North America, but a field sighting still needs identification before a crop-management decision.

claims: Dark hairy grass/cereal aphid and virus association.
North American taxonomy and documented occurrence.

proposedDescription: Tinocallis ulmiparvifoliae is an aphid associated with Chinese elm. Winged individuals have pale blue-green bodies with white wax stripes and spots, and colonies feed on the leaves. Originally associated with Asia, it has also been recorded in Florida as an introduced insect. Its host is a useful clue, but fine anatomical features are needed to distinguish it confidently from other elm-feeding aphids.
identification: Verify that the tree is Chinese elm, then inspect the underside and veins of leaves for aphids. Pale blue-green bodies with white wax markings are useful clues, especially in winged forms, but other elm aphids can be similar. Include the whole leaf, its attachment and close insect views in a record. Seasonal observations from Australia should not be used to predict identical overwintering behavior in Florida or a northern U.S. planting. A specialist may need fine anatomical characters.
actions: Check new elm nursery stock before planting it beside established trees, and retain supplier information when a colony is found. On a landscape tree, follow leaf growth and colony density rather than treating an isolated winged aphid as a damaging infestation. Ask a diagnostic service to confirm an unfamiliar elm aphid before reporting a new locality. Avoid transporting infested shoots between sites. Photograph the same branches over time, including new leaves that remain healthy; any substantial injury should be assessed with the tree's overall condition and other stresses.

proposedDescription: Tuberocephalus sakurae is a tiny aphid associated with cherry trees. Feeding can turn the leaves red or yellow and curl them into sheltered spaces for the insects. Wingless adults on cherry are dark green to black, with brighter young nearby. The species also alternates to underground parts of Artemisia plants. Distorted leaves may be easier to notice than the aphids themselves, but similar damage can have other causes and does not establish the species on its own.
identification: Inspect a fresh cherry leaf curl for the insects and photograph both its outer discoloration and sheltered interior. Dark adults and brighter young can occur together, so their different colors need not indicate separate species. Other Tuberocephalus and unrelated causes of leaf distortion complicate recognition. Record the cherry species and the collection date. An Artemisia association in the literature is not enough to identify aphids found on any nearby herb, especially where older Japanese names have been confused.
actions: On an ornamental cherry, mark affected shoots and watch whether new leaves develop normally. Avoid removing large healthy branches solely because some leaves are curled. If damage persists or young trees lose vigor, ask a local tree or insect specialist to examine occupied leaves. Do not excavate Artemisia roots or remove a surrounding herb layer in an attempt to interrupt an unverified local migration. Keep infested nursery plants from being shared until identified. Record when fresh curls first appear, since the timing of local growth and insect activity is more useful than a calendar copied from another climate.
researchNotes: Evidence scope: the Hokkaido observations and specialist synthesis support a restricted biological account, but exact local occurrence and management require confirmation. Biology of misakurae or momonis is not transferred, and similar cherry leaf damage is not treated as diagnostic.
previousDescription: Tuberocephalus sakurae is a tiny aphid associated with cherry trees. Feeding can cause leaves to become red and crumpled, creating sheltered spaces for the insects. Research from Japan describes individuals only around a millimeter and a half long. The altered leaves may be easier to notice than the aphids themselves, but similar damage can have other causes and does not establish the species on its own.

proposedDescription: Uroleucon picridis is a shiny reddish-brown aphid associated with oxtongues in the genus Picris. Colonies may gather on stems just below the flowers. Dark antennae and rear tubes contrast with a paler, yellowish tail-like projection at the end of the body. These details help specialists distinguish it from related aphids. Host identification matters too: some older records from other plants involve similar species, so color alone is not enough for a reliable identification.
identification: Check that the host is a Picris oxtongue, since superficially similar yellow-flowered composites can carry different aphids. The contrasting pale tail-like tip and darker rear tubes are more useful than a general reddish color. Photograph a complete adult beside the feeding position below a flower head. Related Uroleucon can require microscopic examination, and older records on other host genera may involve different species. A dried collection label is historical evidence, not proof of a living population at that site today.
actions: Leave a small colony on unmanaged vegetation in place while obtaining an identification if no plant-management problem is apparent. If the oxtongue is being removed as a weed, contain its seed heads and do not transfer occupied stems to another planting. Record predators or parasitoid mummies before disturbing the colony. For a proposed new locality, ask a specialist to verify both host and aphid. Include a flowering stem in the photographs so the host can be checked, and keep the original observation label if a later identification changes the name.

proposedDescription: This aphid parasite is a tiny wasp that uses aphids as a nursery for its young. A female Aphidius ervi lays an egg inside an aphid; the developing wasp eventually leaves a dry, swollen shell called a mummy and emerges through a round hole. It attacks aphids including potato and foxglove aphids and is used in biological control. Its presence can therefore reflect pest management rather than a new pest problem.
identification: Look for a dry, swollen aphid shell and, after emergence, a neat round exit hole. These mummies show parasitoid activity, but other wasps also produce them, so they do not identify Aphidius ervi on their own. Adults are tiny and need close examination to separate from A. colemani and other parasitoids. The identity of the living aphids matters as well, because a wasp used for one pest is not automatically appropriate for every aphid in a greenhouse.
actions: When mummies appear among a crop's aphids, count them alongside living aphids and observe whether the pest population is changing. Avoid a broad insecticide application that could disrupt an already useful natural-enemy population without discussing alternatives with an adviser. If biological control is being considered, ask a qualified supplier or extension specialist to match the parasitoid to the confirmed aphid and growing conditions. Do not collect and release unidentified wasps outdoors or move mummies between unrelated sites. Finding this beneficial insect is not, by itself, a reason to attempt its removal.

Alabama Cooperative Extension: Practical tips for using biological control agents

researchNotes: K-State's species biology and Alabama's practical biological-control guidance support a beneficial role and careful host matching. Mummies are explicitly not species-diagnostic. No release rate, unauthorized movement, universal efficacy or harmful-invader classification is implied.
previousDescription: A swollen, papery-looking aphid can be the sign that a tiny wasp is doing useful work. Aphidius ervi lays an egg inside an aphid; the growing wasp develops there and eventually leaves through a round hole in the resulting aphid mummy. Adults are slender black wasps with long antennae. Growers use this species as a biological control agent, particularly against larger aphids such as potato and foxglove aphids. Its presence deserves a different response from that of a crop pest: the wasp is part of the community that can help suppress aphids.

claims: A. ervi biology and aphid hosts.
Practical biological-control matching and conservation.

proposedDescription: Apple aphid gathers on young leaves and shoots, including the vigorous upright shoots of apple trees. The green insects feed on plant sap and produce sticky honeydew that can support sooty mold. Heavy colonies may weaken young growth, while predators can help limit their numbers. The aphid survives winter as dark eggs on woody growth, ready to hatch as fresh leaves become available.
identification: Inspect the tips and undersides of young apple leaves, including vigorous upright shoots. Green apple aphid and spirea aphid can be very difficult to distinguish in the field, so a specialist may be needed for an exact species record. Honeydew, shed skins and nearby predators help locate an active colony but do not settle its identity. Record whether the tree is young or established, because loss of tender growth can matter more to a developing tree.
actions: Monitor occupied shoots and their natural enemies before choosing treatment. A small colony on an established tree can be a different problem from persistent feeding on a young nursery tree. Ask local orchard advisers to interpret numbers, growth stage and injury rather than importing a threshold from another region. Avoid unnecessary stimulation of tender growth through excessive fertilization. If intervention is warranted, use current crop guidance and protect beneficial insects. Do not diagnose a plant virus from aphids or sooty mold alone; the sticky coating is evidence of feeding, not a disease test.

sources.title: University of California IPM: Green Apple Aphid

researchNotes: UC IPM and NC State independently support crop context, natural-enemy monitoring and the spirea-aphid identification caveat. Regional thresholds and pesticide schedules are not transferred. The profile separates honeydew nuisance from meaningful loss of young growth.
previousDescription: Green apple aphids gather where an apple tree is growing fastest: tender shoot tips, young leaves, and water sprouts. Their small green bodies can be easy to miss until leaves curl or sticky honeydew appears. In heavy colonies, that honeydew supports dark sooty mold on foliage and fruit, and feeding can slow young trees. The aphids overwinter as black eggs on woody growth. Lady beetles, lacewings, and other predators often keep them in check, so noticing aphids is a reason to inspect the whole shoot, including its natural enemies, before deciding what to do.

claims: Apple shoot feeding and natural-enemy monitoring.
Species comparison, honeydew and young-growth effects.

proposedDescription: Apple blossom, Cassia javanica, is a tropical tree grown for generous clusters of pink flowers. Its leaves are divided into pairs of leaflets, and its fruit develops into long, cylindrical pods. The tree has a spreading crown and can lose some or all of its leaves seasonally. Several botanical forms differ in their leaves and flower clusters, so a precise identification benefits from photographs of both. Despite its common name, it belongs to the legume family.
identification: Photograph a full leaf to show its paired leaflets, a flowering branch and any cylindrical pods. Several forms within the Cassia javanica group differ in leaflet shape, hairiness and the position of flower clusters. Pink blossoms are attractive but insufficient for separating those forms or all similarly named ornamental cassias. Keep a nursery name with the record without treating it as a botanical determination. An apple-like common name does not indicate an edible fruit or a relationship to apple trees.
actions: For an established ornamental, first decide whether the issue is ordinary tree care or actual escape beyond cultivation. Look for seedlings around the planting and record their distance from the parent tree. Remove unwanted young plants before they become difficult to manage, after confirming they are the same species. A large tree near structures should be assessed by an arborist rather than pruned heavily on the basis of its catalog listing. If seedlings persist outside the planting, share a dated location record with a local herbarium or land manager to help assess whether the tree is naturalizing there.

It has paired leaflets and pink flowers, with branching flower clusters at the ends of young leafy shoots. Pink flowers alone cannot separate it from related forms. A comparative study identifies leaflet details, shoot hairs, stipules and flower structures as useful clues, so a confident identification needs a closer look than flower color.

Keep the original var. indochinensis label when seeking a determination as subsp. agnes, so the proposed synonym can be traced. Take close views of those structures rather than relying on a distant canopy image, and include the same shoot in an overall photograph.

If seedlings appear beyond a garden, document them and establish their identity before describing a variety-specific escape. Manage an unwanted young tree according to the site's needs, while leaving the exact infraspecific name provisional if the evidence is incomplete. Avoid moving pods or seedlings to new sites as a way of preserving a questionable label. An established tree can be cared for according to its condition and position while the finer points of its name are checked.

proposedDescription: Apple mealybug is a soft-bodied insect covered in white wax. It feeds on several woody plants, not just apples, and may hide in bark crevices where colonies are easy to miss. White egg sacs and sticky honeydew can reveal its presence. Orchard sources report insects identified under this name as vectors of little cherry virus 2. This finding should not be assigned automatically to every lookalike in the species group, making accurate diagnosis particularly important in fruit-growing areas.
identification: Inspect bark crevices and protected parts of shoots for wax-covered insects and egg sacs. Other mealybugs can look similar, and the Phenacoccus aceris group contains difficult boundaries. Photograph the insect as well as its wax and feeding site; a fuzzy patch alone is inadequate. In a cherry orchard, aphid-like leaf symptoms or small fruit do not identify either the insect or a virus. A specialist determination and plant testing answer different questions and may both be needed.
actions: Keep newly acquired fruit trees apart from established stock when a suspicious colony is found, and ask an extension diagnostic service how to submit insects and plant material. In a region managing little cherry disease, follow current local orchard guidance rather than a generic houseplant-mealybug treatment. Do not transport occupied cuttings or nursery stock to another orchard while the diagnosis is pending. Monitor nearby trees and record symptoms, but do not assume every infested tree carries little cherry virus 2. Control decisions should be coordinated with the orchard's disease-management plan.

Beneath that powdery covering is a soft oval insect; mature females produce conspicuous white egg sacs. The species uses a range of woody hosts, and in orchards its honeydew can leave fruit and foliage sticky and encourage sooty mold. Mealybugs can also shelter in protected parts of a tree, making a quick glance at the leaves an incomplete inspection. Apple mealybug matters particularly in cherry production because it is associated with transmission of little cherry virus 2.
