proposedDescription: Applemint is a perennial herb with rounded, wrinkled, hairy leaves and a fruity scent. Small, pale flowers grow in spikes above the foliage. It spreads through underground stems, which can carry it beyond the edges of a garden bed. Native to parts of Europe and the Mediterranean region, it also grows outside cultivation in moist ground. Its soft leaves help distinguish it from smoother-leaved mints.
identification: Look for opposite, rounded leaves with a soft hairy surface and a strongly wrinkled texture. Flowering spikes and the arrangement of leaves help confirm that the plant is a mint, but hybridization and cultivated selections can blur species boundaries. Do not identify a volunteer solely by crushing or tasting a leaf. Photograph the whole shoot, both leaf surfaces and the flower head, and note whether stems extend underground beyond the original clump. Smooth-leaved mints may require a different determination.
actions: In a garden where applemint is wanted, keep its spreading underground stems within a monitored area and inspect the bed edge regularly. Remove escaped pieces with their connected roots where practical, rather than only clipping the visible tops. Avoid discarding rooted fragments into wet ditches or natural vegetation, where they may remain viable. Revisit cleared ground for new shoots. If a larger escape occurs beside a stream, ask the land manager for a plan that protects the bank and surrounding plants. A culinary garden use does not justify releasing it beyond cultivation.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Mentha suaveolens

researchNotes: Kew's botanical account and RHS cultivation guidance support the species' morphology and spreading habit. The actions address vegetative containment in gardens without assigning a nationwide invasive designation. Scent is not treated as an edible-plant identification test.
previousDescription: Apple mint brings a fruity mint scent and soft, rounded leaves to herb gardens. The leaves are hairy and wrinkled, and pale flower spikes rise above the patch in summer. This is a creeping perennial: underground stems let a small planting expand steadily into neighboring ground, especially where conditions stay moist. That vigor is useful in a contained planting but can become a nuisance in an open bed. Native to parts of Europe and the Mediterranean region, it has been grown and naturalized elsewhere; garden spread should be described separately from documented ecological harm.

claims: Accepted species, perennial habit and native range.
Leaf morphology, rhizomes and garden cultivation.

proposedDescription: Apple of Peru has pale blue, bell-shaped flowers followed by fruit enclosed in a papery covering. This annual member of the nightshade family comes from South America and can grow quickly in fertile, disturbed ground. It spreads by seed and may appear as a garden escape or field weed. Despite the familiar-looking fruit covering, it should not be confused with edible groundcherries.
identification: Examine the blue flower and the angular, inflated covering around the fruit together. Groundcherries also have papery fruit coverings, so the husk alone is a poor guide and should never be used to decide that an unknown fruit is edible. Include a whole leaf, stem and open flower in photographs. A young plant without flowers can be confused with other nightshades. Keep uncertain plants away from children or animals likely to investigate the fruit while identification is arranged.
actions: Remove a confirmed unwanted annual before its fruits mature, taking care not to spill seeds around the garden. Wear gloves for handling and keep fruiting plants out of a casual compost pile unless the disposal process reliably prevents seed spread. Check the area in later growing seasons for seedlings rather than assuming one removal finishes the problem. Do not promote it as a homemade insecticide or sample the fruit because of its common name. For a substantial field occurrence, use local weed advice that accounts for the crop and the actual species.

sources.title: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox: Nicandra physalodes

researchNotes: Missouri State and NC State provide independent botanical/extension descriptions of the annual, fruit and toxic-plant caution. The expanded actions emphasize seed prevention and safe identification, not pesticide experimentation or a claimed universal invasion impact.
previousDescription: Apple of Peru looks at home in a flower border, with pale blue bells and a papery case around each fruit. It is a summer annual in the nightshade family, native to South America and naturalized in parts of the United States. Plants grow quickly in disturbed, fertile ground and spread by abundant seed. That combination has carried this ornamental into crop fields and other disturbed sites. Its lanternlike fruits can suggest an edible ground cherry, but the resemblance is misleading: this plant should not be treated as a food plant.

claims: Annual weed recognition and fruit covering.
Independent botanical diagnosis and toxic-plant caution.

proposedDescription: Arabian jasmine is an evergreen shrub or scrambling climber with glossy, oval leaves and strongly scented white flowers. The flowers may turn pink as they age, and cultivated forms can have one or several layers of petals. Despite its name, its native range includes areas from Bhutan to India. It is widely grown in warm climates for its flowers and fragrance.
identification: Check the glossy simple leaves and the structure of several flowers, including whether a cultivated form has multiple petal layers. Scent is suggestive but is shared by many plants called jasmine. Other Jasminum and unrelated fragrant ornamentals need comparison with a botanical key. Photograph a leafy shoot and the flower from the side as well as above. A common name referring to Arabia is not evidence of native origin, and a pot label may identify a cultivar rather than the botanical species.
actions: For a retained garden plant, inspect the planting boundary and any stems that have spread into neighboring vegetation. Prune to suit the site and handle rooted pieces so they are not dumped into natural areas. If a volunteer appears away from cultivation, document it and ask local extension or herbarium staff to confirm the species before calling it an invasion. Keep a record of the parent planting and check whether the volunteer persists or produces additional growth beyond the cultivated area. Do not assume that fragrant white flowers identify material suitable for food, tea or homemade remedies.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Jasminum sambac
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Jasminum sambac

researchNotes: Evidence scope: independent horticultural description and Kew range information support identity, but no independently supported U.S. impact or targeted management evidence was established. The native-range correction is preserved and horticultural popularity is not equated with invasiveness.
previousDescription: Arabian jasmine is best known for the fragrance of its white flowers. This evergreen shrub can scramble over nearby support, carrying glossy oval leaves and blooms that may blush pink as they age. Cultivated forms range from simple flowers to richly doubled rosettes, so a garden specimen may look quite different from another plant of the same species. Despite its common name, Kew places its native range in Bhutan and India. Its long history in gardens and flower use is part of its story, but does not by itself demonstrate ecological harm where it has been introduced.

claims: Shrubby/scrambling habit, leaves and flowers.
Native range Bhutan to India.

proposedDescription: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass with fine leaves and a short, compact flower head. It grows in dry, open places and disturbed desert ground. Southwestern U.S. studies of mixed Schismus stands show that dry growth can connect fine fuels between shrubs; wet seasons can increase annual-grass cover. It closely resembles Schismus barbatus, another introduced desert grass. Small differences in the flower parts are more dependable for separating them than a photograph of their leaves.
identification: Collect clear photographs of mature flower parts as well as the low, fine-leaved clump. Schismus barbatus is a close lookalike, and separating the two often requires magnification of the lemma and its hairs. A carpet of short dry grass cannot be assigned to arabicus from color or height alone. Record whether other annual grasses are mixed through the patch. Their combined fuel contribution matters to a site assessment, but does not justify attaching every observed fire effect to one species.
actions: On a small managed site, address confirmed plants before seed maturation and avoid spreading dry seed-bearing material along trails or equipment routes. Coordinate larger desert work with the land manager so removal does not damage native annuals or disturb soil unnecessarily. Watch the site after wet seasons, when annual-grass growth can change quickly. Do not burn a patch as a casual weed-control measure: the relevant concern is its contribution to connected fine fuels. Use a regional restoration and fire-management plan rather than assuming a single removal produces lasting control.

sources.title: California Invasive Plant Council: Schismus arabicus
US Forest Service: Nonnative annual grass fuels and fire in California Mojave Desert

researchNotes:
Flora of Pakistan supplies independent morphology. Cal-IPC and the Forest Service share a fire-research lineage; the cited Mojave experiment pooled S. arabicus and S. barbatus because they could not be separated in the field. The overview now states that limitation explicitly.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.
previousDescription: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass that grows in dry, open places. After rain, its fine leaves and stems can fill spaces between desert shrubs; when dry, that growth can help fire move through areas that once had little continuous fuel. It closely resembles another introduced schismus grass, so small flower details are important for separating the two species.

claims: Original regional floral diagnosis.
Regional invasion account; shared fire literature.
Mojave study pooled arabicus and barbatus.

proposedDescription: Brachyrhynchus membranaceus is a flat bug associated with fungi and decaying wood. Its flattened body suits the sheltered spaces used by these insects. Originally known from the Old World, it has also been documented in the Caribbean and Central America. It feeds on fungal growth and has sometimes damaged cultivated bracket fungi. Finding this insect around wood does not by itself show that a healthy tree is being attacked; its documented food is fungal tissue.
identification: Look for a very flattened true bug in association with decaying wood or fungal growth, but do not identify it from that habitat alone. Other flat bugs occupy similar sheltered spaces, and a specialist may need fine body and antennal characters. Photograph the insect and the fungus or substrate separately. The microscopy study also documents unusual antennal development, so a single abnormal specimen should not define the normal species appearance. A bug on a trunk is not proof that it attacks living tree tissue.
actions: Leave a harmless-looking observation in natural deadwood undisturbed while seeking identification; removing every fungus-bearing log would erase useful habitat without an established benefit. If the insect is found in cultivated bracket fungi, separate the affected growing material and ask an agricultural or entomological adviser to assess the actual feeding. Avoid transporting occupied wood or fungal cultures to another site. Record damage directly rather than assuming it from presence. A useful report shows the affected fungus and the insect together, with photographs of any feeding injury and the condition of nearby growing material.

sources.title: USDA ARS: Henry et al. 2013 Brachyrhynchus membranaceus
Taszakowski and Kaszyca-Taszakowska 2020: Teratological cases of antennae in Aradidae

researchNotes: Evidence scope: the USDA original-paper abstract supports fungal feeding and limited cultivated-fungus injury; the separate microscopy paper concerns anatomy, not management. No healthy-tree attack or universal harmlessness is inferred. Local control evidence remains insufficient.
previousDescription: This aradid flat bug lives around decaying wood and feeds on fungi. Its flattened body suits the narrow spaces beneath bark and within woody material. Brachyrhynchus membranaceus has records in both the Old World and the Western Hemisphere, and has sometimes affected cultivated bracket fungi. Finding it in wood does not mean it is attacking a healthy tree; its feeding is associated with fungal growth.

claims: Original fungal-feeding and cultivated bracket-fungus injury account.
Independent microscopic specimen/antenna observations.

proposedDescription: Araucaria aphid feeds on young growth of Araucaria trees, including around the bases of needles on fresh shoots. Wingless individuals are broadly oval and bright yellow to orange, measuring only about one to one and a half millimeters long. Their tiny size makes a close look worthwhile. The species has been recorded in several tropical and subtropical regions, but that wide distribution does not clearly identify its original home. The host and color are useful clues rather than a complete diagnosis.
identification: Inspect fresh Araucaria shoots and the bases of young needles, where small insects can be concealed by the foliage. The broad oval outline and yellow-orange coloration help recognition, but other aphids on conifers need microscopic comparison. Keep the host tree's identity with the record rather than labeling every ornamental conifer an Araucaria. Photograph adults and younger individuals separately if possible. A broad tropical distribution does not, on its own, establish where the species originated or whether a particular locality represents an introduction.
actions: Check newly acquired Araucaria plants before moving them into a collection, especially where young shoots are crowded or discolored. If a colony is present, keep the plant separate and obtain an identification rather than treating it as a different conifer aphid. Record whether growth is actually affected and inspect for other causes of shoot decline. Avoid sharing occupied cuttings or nursery stock while the diagnosis is pending. Photograph the same growing tip over time so an adviser can see whether a brief colony coincides with continuing injury or the plant resumes healthy growth.

sources.title: Noordam 2004: Aphids of Java Part VI

researchNotes: Evidence scope: native origin remains uncertain and current local impact/management evidence was not established. Noordam's living-material account and the specialist synthesis support the restrained identification. Broad occurrence is not used as proof of either introduction or severe harm.
previousDescription: Araucaria aphid feeds on young growth of Araucaria trees. Wingless individuals are broadly oval and yellow to orange, measuring only around one to one and a half millimeters long. It has been recorded in tropical regions where its host trees grow. Its small size makes close examination useful, and its wider distribution should not be treated as a clear map of its original native range.

claims: Host/range context; origin uncertain.
Original living-material observations at young needle bases.

proposedDescription: Araucaria black scale can look like a dark speck attached to a leaf. The female shelters beneath a nearly circular, flattened brown-black cover with darker shed skins near its center. Despite the name, its hosts extend well beyond Araucaria: palms, olives and many other woody plants have been recorded. This broad host range makes examination of the insect especially useful. A dark spot on a familiar plant can suggest an armored scale, but it does not establish this species.
identification: Inspect the dark cover closely without assuming that a black spot on Araucaria is this particular scale. Other armored scales and non-insect marks can look similar. The female beneath the cover provides the microscopic characters used in identification, while the host and feeding position provide context. Photograph both sides of an affected leaf or twig. The Croatian survey documented several hosts, so a palm or olive occurrence is plausible but still needs the insect checked.
actions: Keep an occupied nursery plant separate from clean stock and avoid exchanging cuttings until the scale is identified. Mark a few affected branches and monitor fresh foliage for new settlement or declining growth. A local extension service can help determine whether the apparent covers contain active insects and whether intervention is warranted. Do not extrapolate a Croatian infestation level to every ornamental planting. Where treatment is considered, use the confirmed species, host and current local guidance; old cover appearance alone is a poor measure of whether a response has succeeded.

sources.title: Bjelis et al. 2024: status of Lindingaspis rossi in Croatia

researchNotes: ScaleNet's older morphological sources and the Croatian authors' original surveillance are complementary independent lineages. The source's erroneous author-year is omitted. No universal severity, local outbreak or chemical threshold is inferred; diagnosis and plant-movement precautions are the practical focus.
previousDescription: Araucaria black scale forms a small, round, dark covering on its host plant. The cover is usually brown to black, with darker remains of earlier skins near the center. Despite the name, it can feed on plants beyond Araucaria. Like other armored scales, the insect spends much of its life protected beneath this cover, making the covering more visible than the animal itself.

claims: Older morphological diagnosis and hosts.
Original Croatian surveillance and host infestation.

proposedDescription: Arborescent pricklypear is a Mexican cactus that can grow into a large shrub or small tree. Its gray-green pads carry white hairs and spines, while older growth develops a trunk. Yellow flowers are followed by fleshy fruit. Broken pads can take root, allowing plants to spread from discarded garden material. It has escaped cultivation in places including Australia, where dense growth can become a management problem.
identification: Look for upright, trunk-forming growth and broad gray-green pads carrying fine pale hairs as well as conspicuous white spines. Other prickly pears can become large, so photograph a mature pad, its spine clusters and any flowers or fruit. Small barbed glochids are easily overlooked and make bare-hand examination unwise. A detached pad may still be capable of establishing a plant; finding one beside a garden does not necessarily indicate a seedling or a new species.
actions: Where it has escaped cultivation, do not mow, slash or scatter the pads. Keep people and animals away from sharp material and arrange collection with tools and protective equipment suited to cactus work. Contain every loose segment and use local disposal advice so fragments are not dumped into suitable habitat. Large stands need a coordinated land-management plan and follow-up for surviving plants. The Australian weed guidance describes a regional problem; confirm the local status before applying that label to a Mexican native population or a planting elsewhere.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Opuntia leucotricha
NSW Department of Primary Industries: Aaron's beard prickly pear

researchNotes: NSW flora morphology and WeedWise management provide distinct botanical and agency lineages. The profile keeps Australian escape context separate from Mexican nativity and emphasizes fragment containment and spine safety. Australian legal rules and chemical recipes are not transferred.
previousDescription: Aaron's beard prickly pear can grow from a cluster of pads into a branching, trunked shrub. Its gray-green pads carry tiny pale hairs and flexible white spines, while yellow flowers are followed by fleshy fruit. Native to Mexico, it has escaped cultivation in parts of Australia, where managers document spread from detached plant pieces and dumped garden material. Those Australian impacts should not be assumed everywhere, but the way the plant travels is useful to understand. A broken pad can be more than waste: it may be the start of another plant.

claims: Hairy pads, white spines, flowers and fruit.
Australian spread/impact and safe fragment containment.

proposedDescription: Argentine ants are small brown ants often seen moving in long, busy trails. They form networks of shallow nests with multiple queens and can spread through gardens, buildings and natural areas. Native to South America, they have become established in many other regions. They collect sugary honeydew from sap-feeding insects and can displace other ants where their colonies become dominant.
identification: Workers in a trail are small and fairly uniform in size, with a brown body and a single waist node. Other small brown ants need comparison, so photograph a worker from the side as well as the whole trail. Follow the route to see whether ants are entering through a crack, using a plant bridge or tending sap-feeding insects outdoors. A large trail can connect several nests; removing the few visible workers is not the same as addressing the colony network.
actions:
Start indoors by sealing food, removing sugary spills and correcting accessible water sources. Seal entry gaps where practical and trim vegetation that bridges to the building. Once identification is confirmed, extension guidance favors a suitable bait strategy over repeatedly spraying visible trails; use only a product labeled for the site and keep it inaccessible to children and pets. Outdoors, assess the connected nests and honeydew-producing insects rather than treating every ant on the property. Do not move occupied pots or mulch to a new location.

Do not use insecticide sprays while using ant baits.

sources.title: University of California IPM: Argentine Ant

researchNotes:
UC identification/behavior and Texas A&M colony biology/management are separate extension lineages. Advice is conditional on confirmed Argentine ants and labeled household use. No homemade bait recipe or indiscriminate outdoor insecticide treatment is provided.

2026-11-01 safety continuity review: New bait advice loses the warning against combining it with sprays. Current source-specific support is recorded in the publication safety audit.
previousDescription: A busy ribbon of small brown ants along a wall or garden path may belong to Argentine ants. Workers are similar in size and move between shallow nests that can form part of a much larger network with many queens. Originally South American, this ant has become established in other regions and readily uses gardens and buildings. It feeds on sweet foods and tends honeydew-producing insects, which can complicate garden pest management. A trail in the kitchen is usually only the visible end of activity that extends outdoors.

claims: Uniform workers, trails and multiple shallow nests.
Household exclusion and bait-oriented management.

Baits section explicitly says not to use insecticide sprays while using baits. Argentine ant is a principal named target, with dedicated management subsection. Existing identification/Texas source supports bait selection but lacks combination warning.

proposedDescription: Argentine black and white tegu is a large, strong-bodied lizard with a banded tail. Young animals often have greenish heads. It eats a wide range of foods and can shelter in burrows during cold weather. Established populations in Florida are a concern because tegus eat native wildlife, including eggs and young animals; documented prey include alligator eggs and young gopher tortoises.
identification: Look for a large, robust lizard with black-and-white patterning and a heavy banded tail. Juvenile green heads can make young animals look different from adults. Other tegus and large lizards also occur in the pet trade, so a photograph showing the head, back and tail is more useful than a brief color description. Keep a safe distance and record the exact location and direction of travel. A single sighting outside an established range does not prove a breeding population.
actions: In Florida, report a suspected free-ranging tegu through the state's invasive-wildlife reporting system and include clear photographs when safely possible. Keep pets away and do not attempt to corner or handle a large unfamiliar lizard. Follow the wildlife agency's current instructions about removal; rules and authorized methods differ by place. Never release an unwanted pet. Owners needing an alternative should contact an appropriate reptile surrender or amnesty program. Where nests of native wildlife are vulnerable, qualified managers should assess the site rather than relying on improvised traps or poisons.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Florida Invader, Tegu Lizard
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Argentine black and white tegu

researchNotes: UF's Florida field/extension account and FWC's agency identification and reporting guidance support the regional profile. Prey observations are distinguished from speculative effects on every species. The text avoids capture instructions, pet release and jurisdiction-independent legal claims.
previousDescription: The Argentine black and white tegu is a large, ground-dwelling South American lizard with a banded or mottled body and a powerful tail. Young tegus often have green heads that fade as they grow. Adults eat a varied diet of fruit, insects, eggs, and small animals, and retreat into burrows during colder weather. In Florida, established populations raise conservation concerns because researchers have documented predation on native wildlife, including alligator eggs and young gopher tortoises. Its adaptable habits help explain why an escaped pet can become more than an isolated garden visitor.

claims: Florida populations, large lizard biology and prey observations.
Agency identification, reporting and pet surrender guidance.

proposedDescription: Argentine pepperweed is a hairy member of the mustard family with divided lower leaves and simpler leaves higher on the stem. Its small white flowers develop into flattened pods with a notch at the tip. The lower leaves may disappear as the plant matures, changing its overall appearance. Looking at both the remaining leaves and the seed pods helps distinguish it from other pepperweeds.
identification: A mature plant may have lost the deeply divided leaves that were obvious earlier, so examine the lower stem and any younger plants nearby. Close views of the flattened, rounded fruit and its shallow tip notch are particularly useful. Other pepperweeds can have similar tiny pale flowers, sometimes with petals too small to notice. Include stem hairs and fruit stalks in photographs. Do not identify a plant as edible pepperweed merely because its pods resemble a familiar mustard.
actions: In a cultivated bed, remove confirmed unwanted plants before mature pods scatter seed and watch the disturbed area for new seedlings. Keep fruiting material out of clean soil or seed mixes. For a plant in natural grassland, obtain a regional identification before disturbing neighboring mustards or assuming an invasive impact. The New Zealand and Australian floras describe the plant well but do not establish a U.S. ecological effect or a special control method. Record the location, population size and habitat if an escape appears unusual, so later observations can be compared.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Lepidium bonariense
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney: Lepidium bonariense

researchNotes: Two independently authored regional floras support the changing leaves and fruit diagnosis. The expanded actions are ordinary seed containment and verification, with no local harm claim or specific treatment efficacy inferred from botanical descriptions.
previousDescription: Argentine pepperweed is a small mustard relative whose seedpods are often easier to recognize than its tiny flowers. Lower leaves are deeply divided, while the leaves higher on a flowering stem become simpler. Hairy stems carry little pale flowers followed by flattened, rounded pods with a notch at the tip. Plants can look quite different as they mature and lose their lower leaves, so a complete photograph is more useful than a single flower. Records of naturalization describe where it grows outside its original range; they do not alone measure ecological damage.

claims: Changing divided leaves and mature pods.
Independent Australian diagnosis and habitat.

proposedDescription: Aonidiella taxus is an armored scale found on yews, plum-yews and Podocarpus. A pale, partly transparent cover hides the reddish female beneath it, often on the underside of a leaf. Feeding can leave yellow patches around the insects. Its life also involves much smaller visitors: researchers in Japan found several kinds of tiny wasps parasitizing this scale. The cover and host plant offer useful clues, but related scales can look alike and a confident species identification requires microscopic examination.
identification: Look beneath leaves of a correctly identified yew, plum-yew or Podocarpus for pale covers through which the reddish insect may show. Other armored scales can produce yellow feeding marks, so leaf color and host alone are not enough. Photograph the cover in place and ask a specialist whether a sample is needed for microscopic examination. Tiny emergence holes can indicate natural-enemy activity, but neither a hole nor a nearby wasp identifies the scale or proves that control is adequate.
actions: Inspect incoming conifer ornamentals before adding them to an established collection. Keep an affected plant apart while diagnosis is arranged, and record whether yellowing or twig decline is spreading. Avoid a general spray solely because scale covers remain visible; have active infestation assessed first. The Japanese study found several parasitoids, but that does not justify collecting and releasing wasps or assuming the same community exists locally. Use current local nursery or landscape advice if injury warrants intervention, and evaluate the plant's overall health alongside the insect observations.

sources.title: Uematsu1972: Studies on Marietta carnesi, I. Host Relation

researchNotes: Naturalis supplies detailed morphology and Uematsu's original Japanese study supplies an independent parasitoid association. Clear identification and movement precautions are supported; parasitoid presence is not promoted into an efficacy claim or release recommendation.
previousDescription: Aonidiella taxus is an armored scale found on plants such as yews, plum-yews and Podocarpus. A pale, partly translucent cover hides the reddish female beneath it. Feeding on leaf undersides can be associated with yellow patches. The young insects are mobile before settling down, and infested nursery plants can carry them to new locations even when the small scales are not immediately obvious.

claims: Pale cover, reddish insect and conifer hosts.
Original Japanese parasitoid associations.

proposedDescription: Arborvitae scale is a tiny armored insect associated with arborvitae, junipers and other conifers. Its cover can be oval or almost round, with a dull greenish-yellow color that becomes paler and browner with age. Infestations may accompany discolored foliage and dying twigs. A Pennsylvania study found a small parasitic wasp attacking this scale, and predatory mites sheltering in the empty scale covers afterward. Those observations reveal a small community around the insect, but do not establish a tested treatment for an infested tree.
identification: Compare several covers on affected conifer foliage, noting how their color changes with age. Other scales can inhabit arborvitae, so the tree's common name does not settle the insect's identity. Photograph discolored foliage and healthy-looking shoots as well as the insects. A diagnostic sample should retain the host and collection location. Empty covers may house other tiny animals; their presence should not be mistaken for proof that every visible object is a living scale insect.
actions: Mark affected twigs and monitor new growth before deciding how extensive an infestation is. For nursery plants, prevent movement into clean stock while the identification is unresolved. Have an extension service or qualified plant-health professional distinguish active scales from old covers and investigate other causes of dieback. The Pennsylvania parasitoid and mite observations are interesting evidence of natural enemies, but they do not establish a tested treatment. Do not transfer Connecticut crawler dates to another climate without local monitoring, and avoid releasing organisms collected from the covers.

sources.title: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, Bulletin 1059: armored scales
Schneider et al. 2019: arborvitae scale natural enemies (USDA ARS abstract)

researchNotes: The current Dynaspidiotus combination and older Nuculaspis usage are reconciled by ScaleNet; no unresolved taxonomy is asserted. Original Pennsylvania parasitoid/mite observations and Connecticut extension phenology are independent. Natural-enemy association does not demonstrate control efficacy, but supports a sound diagnosis/prevention profile.
previousDescription: Dynaspidiotus pseudomeyeri is an armored scale associated with conifers, including arborvitae. Its raised, oval cover is yellowish when young and becomes browner with age. The insect feeds beneath this protective layer, which can make it look like a small bump on the plant. Natural enemies include tiny wasps and mites, although their presence does not guarantee that a particular infestation will remain harmless.

claims: Current name and older Nuculaspis combination.
Connecticut regional phenology and conifer assessment.
Original Pennsylvania wasp/mite associations.

proposedDescription: Gymnaspis aechmeae is a tiny armored scale sometimes called flyspeck scale. Its dark covering can resemble a speck of dirt on bromeliads and other ornamental plants, including those grown in greenhouses. The female remains within the skin from an earlier growth stage and produces live young that can crawl to new feeding sites. Infested plants provide a route for it to move between locations.
identification: Inspect bromeliad leaves closely, especially where dark specks persist after loose dust has been removed gently. The covering can be small enough to escape notice during a quick nursery check. Other scale insects and leaf spots can look similar, so retain photographs of the whole plant and the occupied leaf surface. A specialist may need the female and its retained skin to identify the insect. Do not assume that every dark mark on a bromeliad is alive or is this species.
actions: Separate a suspect plant from other bromeliads and inspect plants that shared its source or growing space. Avoid distributing pups or divisions while an active colony remains unresolved. Ask a plant clinic to confirm the insect and assess whether fresh settlement is occurring before choosing treatment. Gentle observation is preferable to scraping or injuring the leaf to remove every speck. The California greenhouse detection is a historical event, not a current statement about all outdoor populations or legal status. Follow regional advice for an actual infestation rather than extrapolating from that record.

sources.title: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Fly speck scale assessment

researchNotes: ScaleNet biology and CDFA's original greenhouse detection/risk account are complementary. Source access recovered through indexed text is labeled accordingly. The expansion avoids presenting an old regulatory assessment as current law and gives conservative nursery containment rather than an untested eradication protocol.
previousDescription: Fly speck scale is aptly named: on a bromeliad, its small dark coverings can be mistaken for dirt. The insect has become a pest of bromeliad collections and greenhouse plants, where colonies can spoil the appearance of leaves. Mature females remain within a shed skin and produce mobile young rather than laying exposed eggs. Those crawlers can move between nearby plants, while the trade in living plants can carry the species much farther. Its native range is uncertain, so a precise origin story would overstate what the available evidence establishes.

claims: Retained-skin female cover and biology.
Original greenhouse detection and live-plant movement pathway.

proposedDescription: Mining scale can be easy to miss because plant tissue often partly hides its pale, rounded cover. The cover may be white, gray or yellow and is roughly three millimeters across at most. Howardia biclavis feeds on many kinds of woody plants. Researchers studying Mexican avocado orchards found it singly or in very small groups on branches, sometimes alongside other armored scales. Despite its common name, the exact way it becomes covered by plant tissue is not well understood, so it is better described as concealed than as a proven tunneling insect.
identification: Look for partly concealed pale covers on woody material, but do not cut into living bark simply to investigate a suspected scale. Other insects and normal bark features can create similar bumps. Photograph exposed covers and the surrounding tissue, and retain host identification with any sample collected on professional advice. Scale covers can become hidden beneath host tissue, but that observation does not show how the insect reached its concealed position. The name mining scale is not proof of an excavated tunnel.
actions: For an orchard or nursery, document which branches carry scales and whether growth or fruit is actually affected. Keep infested planting material from being moved into clean stock. A diagnostic service can distinguish Howardia from other armored scales found in the same orchard and advise on checking active stages. Avoid using a generic scale-generation calendar as though it had been measured for this species. Include unaffected branches in the comparison, so an adviser can judge whether the occupied areas are developing differently from the rest of the tree. Address any substantial decline through an integrated plant-health assessment.

sources.title: University of Hawaii CTAHR: Howardia biclavis
Lazaro-Castellanos et al. 2023: armored scales associated with Mexican avocados

researchNotes: Evidence scope: concealment biology and local management are poorly documented. CTAHR morphology and the Mexican authors' original branch observations are independent for those claims, while their shared background citations are not. Generic armored-scale generation times and a tunneling mechanism are excluded.
previousDescription: Howardia biclavis is an armored scale whose rounded, pale covering can become hidden by the host plant's outer tissue. This unusual feature has led to the name mining scale, although it is not a leaf-mining insect. It feeds on a range of woody plants. Because the covering blends into the plant surface, colonies may be less noticeable than exposed scales on leaves or stems.

claims: Partly concealed armored-scale recognition.
Original avocado branch observations; concealment mechanism uncertain.

proposedDescription: Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis leaves small brown, mussel-shaped covers on the leaves and sometimes stems of its hosts. Orchids are frequent hosts, and dense colonies can leave a patchwork of discolored feeding spots. The insect is not restricted to orchids: a Mexican orchard study also found it on avocado branches. Its covers can look much like those of other Lepidosaphes scales. A close view helps locate the insects, while microscopic features of the female are needed to distinguish similar species reliably.
identification: Examine the brown, elongated covers on an orchid leaf or stem and photograph the discolored tissue around them. Related Lepidosaphes can have nearly the same mussel-like outline, so microscopic features beneath the cover are needed for an exact determination. The avocado record broadens the known host context but does not make every scale on avocado this species. Keep the host name and feeding position with the sample. An orchid collection can contain several scale species at the same time.
actions: Set an affected orchid apart from clean plants and check newly acquired plants and divisions before sharing them. Monitor whether fresh feeding spots or small new covers appear, rather than judging success only by the disappearance of old covers. Ask a diagnostic service for identification and a plant-appropriate response if colonies persist. Do not scrub tender orchid tissue aggressively or apply a treatment intended for another host without checking suitability. The Mexican orchard observation does not establish the same impact or a treatment schedule in a household orchid collection.

sources.title: Lazaro-Castellanos et al. 2023: armored scales associated with Mexican avocados

researchNotes: Naturalis diagnosis and independent Mexican avocado collections support recognition and host context. The older geographic contradictions are excluded. No unverified management efficacy is claimed; the action text is diagnosis, isolation and observation appropriate to susceptible nursery material.
previousDescription: Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis is an armored scale associated with orchids. Its brown, elongated covering resembles a tiny mussel shell and may occur on leaves or stems. Feeding can discolor affected tissue. Newly hatched scales can crawl before settling, while established insects remain protected beneath their covers. Moving an infested orchid can transport the pest without the small colonies being noticed immediately.

claims: Mussel-shaped orchid scale diagnosis.
Original Mexican avocado collections.

proposedDescription: Fire bush scale often shelters between the corky ridges on winged euonymus twigs. Its female has a small brown, oyster-shaped cover with a pale body underneath. Lepidosaphes yanagicola also uses other deciduous trees and shrubs, including willow, maple and elm. Adult females can survive the winter and produce eggs the following summer. Heavy infestations sometimes accompany early leaf fall and twig dieback, although damage varies among locations. This is a different insect from Unaspis euonymi, another scale associated with euonymus.
identification: Inspect the spaces alongside corky wings on burning-bush twigs, where brown covers can be hidden. White male covers and dark female covers of Unaspis euonymi should not be treated as the same insect merely because the host is Euonymus. A close side view of the twig and an individual cover will help a specialist. The sources differ about occurrence on leaves, so absence or presence there should not be used as an absolute rule for excluding this species.
actions: On a planted shrub, mark infested twigs and check whether new shoots remain healthy or die back. Have active scales confirmed before responding to old covers. Consult local extension guidance about monitoring crawler emergence; Massachusetts or Illinois dates should not become a fixed calendar for every climate. Avoid moving infested shrubs or cuttings into another planting. Photograph the same sections of bark during follow-up visits, alongside current leaf and shoot growth. This helps distinguish persistent old covers from a colony associated with worsening plant condition.

sources.title: University of Illinois Extension: Winged Euonymous Scale

researchNotes: Independent Massachusetts and Illinois expert accounts support biology and crawler monitoring. Their leaf-location disagreement is not made into an absolute identification rule. Calendar dates are local observations, while the profile recommends diagnosis and monitoring rather than a universal schedule.
previousDescription: Lepidosaphes yanagicola is an armored scale with a brown, elongated cover. It occurs on woody plants, including the corky ridges of burning-bush stems, and has also been called firebush scale. Several scales use similar hosts, so the plant's name alone is not enough to identify it. In particular, it should not be confused with the different insect commonly called euonymus scale.

claims: Twig feeding, lookalike distinction and local monitoring.
Independent Illinois observations on winged Euonymus.

proposedDescription: Harper scale can blend into bark even when several insects are present. Its narrow, nearly flat tan covers are only about one to two millimeters long, with darker shed skins at one end and a pink or red female underneath. It feeds on a variety of woody plants and often settles in bark cracks. A specialist comparing specimens from California, Japan and Taiwan confirmed how widely the same species had been recorded. Its sheltered position and resemblance to other scales make microscopic examination important for a reliable identification.
identification: Search bark cracks for narrow tan covers with darker material at one end. Their flat shape can blend with bark and resemble other small armored scales. A pink or reddish insect beneath a cover is a useful clue, but examining the female's microscopic structures is still necessary. Photograph the bark surface before collecting anything, since position and host help interpret the sample. The historical comparison of specimens across regions confirms identity in those collections, not current abundance on a particular property.
actions: If found on purchased woody plants, keep the lot separate and ask a diagnostic service to identify a representative sample. Retain supplier, date and host information, and avoid distributing cuttings while an active infestation is unresolved. In a landscape, compare affected branches with unaffected growth and investigate whether visible decline has another explanation. Do not treat a historical low-damage report as a guarantee of safety, or a catalog listing as evidence of severe harm. Keep close photographs of the occupied bark alongside whole-branch images so a local adviser can compare the insects with the pattern of plant injury.

sources.title: Takagi 1970: Diaspididae of Taiwan, Part II

researchNotes: Evidence scope: original specimen comparison and Naturalis morphology provide substantive identity evidence, but local impact and management significance remain poorly established. Old California ratings or damage observations are not represented as current conclusions.
previousDescription: Neopinnaspis harperi is a small armored scale that can hide in bark crevices on woody plants. Its narrow, fairly flat cover is tan with a darker end, concealing a pinkish female underneath. The insect is only around one to two millimeters long. Available California accounts report limited known damage, and its small size and sheltered position make careful inspection more informative than a distant view of the plant.

claims: Flat narrow cover and concealed bark habitat.
Original Taiwanese specimens compared with other regions.

proposedDescription: Parlatoria camelliae is an armored scale found on camellias and other hosts. Its pale to gray covering has a darker patch made from earlier shed skins. Colonies can occur on either side of a leaf, often near veins, and feeding may discolor the foliage. Reports from places such as Galicia document its presence, but identification still requires attention to the insect rather than leaf discoloration alone.
identification: Check both leaf surfaces, especially near veins, for pale covers with a darker retained-skin patch. Camellias host several kinds of scale, and discoloration alone cannot separate them. Photograph a leaf showing the distribution of insects and a close view of individual covers. Ask for microscopic examination when species identification matters. The Galicia survey's affected plants are direct observations, but a small documented sample cannot establish the severity of every infestation or explain all yellowing in a collection.
actions: Separate newly acquired camellias carrying suspicious scales and inspect adjacent plants before exchanging cuttings. Mark a few occupied leaves and observe whether fresh colonies or new discoloration develop. Preserve useful diagnostic material until a specialist has identified the insect. Avoid stripping many leaves or treating an entire collection simply because one plant has old covers. If active feeding and decline continue, seek local advice that accounts for plant condition and other pests. Check the plants that shared the same nursery source, and keep each sample labeled so a diagnosis from one camellia is not accidentally applied to all of them.

sources.title: International Camellia Society: Research on scale insects in Galicia

researchNotes: ScaleNet morphology and the original Galicia laboratory/field survey are independent for complementary claims. Only limited discoloration was documented in that survey. Nursery containment is supported as a precaution, while severity and treatment are left to the confirmed local infestation.
previousDescription: Camellia parlatoria scale settles on leaves as small pale to grayish covers with a darker patch of shed skin. It has been recorded from more hosts than its common name suggests. Observations on camellia found insects on both leaf surfaces, often near veins; researchers in Galicia also documented discoloration on affected plants. Such marks can prompt a closer look, but leaf discoloration has many causes and several scale species share camellias. The insect under the cover, rather than the plant's symptoms alone, is what allows a specialist to identify it.

claims: Older morphology and host associations.
Original Galicia camellia observations with limited discoloration.

proposedDescription: Rutherfordia major is an armored scale associated with lychee and other tropical woody plants. Its initially pale covering may become covered by plant tissue and appear reddish or dark, helping it blend into bark. It has been introduced to places including the Galapagos. Movement of host plants is relevant to its spread, while the full history of its original distribution remains less certain.
identification: The scale can be partly obscured by host tissue, so a reddish or dark bump on lychee bark needs more examination than a color match. Photograph the surrounding branch and any exposed pale covering. Other armored scales occur on tropical fruit trees, and microscopic female characters may be needed. Keep a record of the host and where the plant originated. The name in an island checklist establishes a regional record; it does not prove the insect caused a nearby tree's decline.
actions: Inspect tropical nursery plants before sharing them and keep suspect stock apart while identification is arranged. Do not move occupied branches or propagation material to another growing site. In a lychee planting, document the affected parts and changes in vigor, then seek a specialist assessment rather than treating every concealed scale as the same pest. A record from another island or orchard does not explain the condition of your tree; compare occupied areas with nearby healthy growth. Any response should be based on an active infestation and local crop guidance, with the plant's other stresses considered.
researchNotes: Evidence scope: regional introduction is documented, but origin, measured local impact and management evidence are incomplete. The Galapagos no-impact-data entry is not converted into harmlessness or severity. Older Florida concern is not presented as a current loss estimate.
previousDescription: Lychee bark scale can be difficult to recognize because its normally white cover becomes obscured by plant tissue. The resulting patch may look reddish brown or almost black rather than snowy white. The insect uses a range of tropical woody hosts, not only lychee. Records from the Galapagos describe an established introduction associated with plant material, while older literature discusses possible importance on lychee in Florida. These are different kinds of evidence: an introduced population is not, by itself, proof of a measured ecological impact.

claims: Lychee/bark-scale morphology and literature.
Original Galapagos collection lineage: introduced, impact unknown.

proposedDescription: Selenaspidus albus is an armored scale with a small white disk for a cover. Slightly off-center, yellow-brown remains of earlier growth stages form a contrasting patch. The female's cover is usually less than two millimeters across, making a single insect easy to overlook. Euphorbia is a documented host, and crowded colonies have been reported on cultivated plants. A British botanical-garden report also found a heavy infestation on an imported Euphorbia kept in a heated glasshouse.
identification: On Euphorbia, look for separate white disks with an off-center yellow-brown patch rather than treating a pale crust as one continuous growth. Several scales can have this appearance, so a specialist may need insects beneath the coverings. Photograph the stem and plant label without breaking tissue unnecessarily; many Euphorbia plants have irritating sap. The British report concerns one imported glasshouse plant, and does not show that this scale was established outdoors in the surrounding region.
actions: Keep an occupied succulent apart from the rest of a collection and inspect plants received from the same source. Avoid exchanging cuttings while the infestation is unresolved. Ask a plant clinic how to obtain a sample without damaging the host or exposing skin to sap. Record whether new covers or injury appear after any advised intervention. Keep the plant label and purchase date with the diagnosis, particularly if several imported succulents arrived together. Different scale species may occur in the same collection, so check each affected plant.

sources.title: Malumphy et al.2010: First incursion of Contigaspis zillae, contextual S.albus record

researchNotes: Evidence scope: older morphology plus one independent glasshouse observation support a limited profile, but not outdoor establishment, full life history or management efficacy. The contextual report's focal Contigaspis biology is not borrowed. Host-sap handling is precautionary, not a toxicity claim about the scale.
previousDescription: Selenaspidus albus is an armored scale with a small, white, disk-shaped cover. A yellow-brown patch sits slightly off-center, marking the remains of earlier growth stages. It is associated with plants including Euphorbia. The covering is less than two millimeters across, so individual insects are easy to overlook; heavier colonies are more conspicuous and can warrant closer inspection of the host plant.

claims: Original morphology and Euphorbia host records.
Independent Wisley imported-plant infestation observation.

proposedDescription: West Indian red scale forms thin, partly transparent disks on leaves, often on the upper surface. Each female's cover has a pale edge and an off-center patch of darker shed skins. Citrus is a frequent host, but Selenaspidus articulatus feeds on many other plants, including rubber trees. Dense populations can cause yellowing and damaged leaf or fruit tissue. A field study in Brazil found that numbers on rubber trees changed with the season and differed among tree clones, so infestation levels should be assessed in their local setting.
identification: Inspect the upper leaf surface for thin disks with a pale margin and an off-center darker patch. The actual insect, rather than the yellowing around it, is needed for identification. Other round armored scales can occur on citrus or rubber trees. Include a healthy-looking leaf for comparison and record whether scales also occur on fruit or other tissue. The Brazilian study's seasonal peaks and clone differences are useful research findings, but they are not a universal identification or risk calendar.
actions: Monitor a consistent set of leaves or branches so changes in an orchard can be compared over time. Keep affected nursery plants from being moved into clean stock and obtain a diagnostic determination before selecting control. If leaf injury increases, ask a crop adviser to interpret it alongside plant vigor and natural enemies. Do not choose a rubber clone as resistant solely because it had fewer scales in one study, and do not import that site's seasonal schedule to another climate. Follow-up should assess active insects and new injury rather than old cover counts alone.

sources.title: Silva etal2020: Population Fluctuation of Selenaspidus articulatus in Rubber Tree

researchNotes: Naturalis morphology and the independent Brazilian field-sampling study support this scoped profile. The latter was recovered as indexed text, not claimed as a fresh full-paper read. Monitoring is useful, while clone resistance, thresholds and climate-independent control are not asserted.
previousDescription: Selenaspidus articulatus has a thin, partly transparent cover with a pale rim and an off-center darker patch. It feeds on citrus and many other plants, often on exposed upper leaf surfaces. Heavy infestations can cause yellowing and affect leaves or fruit. The name West Indian red scale appears in references, but a close look is needed to separate it from similar armored scales.

claims: Thin round cover and polyphagous leaf-feeding diagnosis.
Original Brazilian rubber-tree seasonal sampling.

proposedDescription: Unaspis citri is often noticed as a snowy white coating on citrus trunks and branches. That appearance comes largely from the white covers of immature males; females have darker, shell-shaped covers. Heavy feeding can weaken trees, contribute to branch dieback and cause bark to split. Its concentration on woody parts of the tree helps distinguish citrus snow scale from some scales found mainly on leaves.
identification: Inspect the trunk and woody branches as well as leaves. The conspicuous white material is largely the covering of immature males, while the females are darker and less obvious. This mixture helps distinguish snow scale from a fungal coating, but other citrus scales still require comparison. Photograph bark cracks, branch condition and both cover types. A white-coated trunk alone cannot show whether every cover contains a living insect or whether all nearby decline has the same cause.
actions: Keep citrus trees in good growing condition and correct water or nutrient problems with local advice, without overfertilizing. Have a suspected snow-scale colony identified and ask about monitoring active stages before choosing treatment. Inspect incoming citrus plants and avoid distributing occupied branches or cuttings. Trees with substantial bark splitting or dieback need a broader health assessment, not merely removal of the visible white material. Use current regional citrus guidance for any intervention and recheck active infestation afterward; do not transfer a fixed spray calendar or confuse old covers with treatment failure.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Citrus Snow Scale
Clemson Extension: Citrus insects and related pests

researchNotes: UF's detailed life-stage account and Clemson's independently maintained citrus diagnostic/management guidance support recognition and prevention. The snow is attributed correctly to immature male covers. No product rate, fixed calendar or universal damage threshold is supplied.
previousDescription: Citrus snow scale can make a trunk or branch look as though it has been dusted white. The snowy appearance comes from the covers of immature males; females remain beneath darker, shell-shaped armor. Colonies are usually concentrated on citrus bark and larger limbs, with leaves and fruit involved when infestations are severe. Persistent heavy feeding can weaken a tree and contribute to branch dieback and splitting bark. Inspecting both the white male covers and the less noticeable females gives a much clearer picture than looking only for a white coating.

claims: White immature-male covers and citrus bark injury.
Independent citrus inspection and plant-health guidance.

proposedDescription: This armored scale is listed as Andaspis punicae, though newer references also place it in Lepidosaphes. Its brown, elongated covering resembles a small shell on woody hosts, including lychee. Heavy populations may reduce plant vigor or damage branches. Changes in the scientific name can make records harder to connect, so both names are useful when checking the research behind an identification.
identification: Search under both Andaspis punicae and Lepidosaphes punicae when reviewing an identification, but keep the original label attached to its record. Long brown covers on lychee can resemble other armored scales. Photograph a branch with its occupied areas, and obtain a microscopic determination before attributing dieback to this species. The association with corky bark reported in Florida is not proof that the insect alone causes that condition. Plant symptoms and insect identity need to be evaluated separately.
actions: Inspect lychee propagation material before moving it between groves, and keep affected nursery stock apart while diagnosis is arranged. Record branch dieback and scale density over time rather than relying on a single view of old covers. Consult a local fruit-crop adviser if active colonies are associated with declining vigor. Historical experiments tested several interventions, but their products and results are not a current recommendation for every location. Do not attempt to import parasitoids independently or treat an unconfirmed corky-bark problem as a settled scale diagnosis.

sources.title: USDA ARS: Andaspis punicae in lychee

researchNotes: The current combination is reconciled while preserving the ID. ScaleNet morphology and the original Florida/Puerto Rico study abstract provide distinct evidence. Historical treatment results are not converted into current instructions; corky-bark causation remains unresolved and is explicitly not asserted. This does not block the narrower diagnosis and stock-movement guidance.
previousDescription: The scale historically called Andaspis punicae hides beneath a long, dark, mussel-shaped cover on woody plants. Current ScaleNet treatment places it in Lepidosaphes as Lepidosaphes punicae, so both names can appear in references to the same insect. Lychee is among its hosts, and research has linked infestations with loss of vigor and branch decline. The old name is worth retaining in a search, but a scale on lychee should still be identified carefully: several armored scales can share the crop and look like small pieces of bark.

claims: Current Lepidosaphes combination and diagnostic context.
Original Florida/Puerto Rico lychee observations; bark causation uncertain.

proposedDescription: Snout scale is a tiny armored insect found on citrus and other plants. The female remains enclosed within a shed skin from an earlier stage, producing a brown, elongated covering with a conspicuous ridge along its back. Dense colonies may also leave white secretions on the leaves. The 'snout' is a much smaller feature of the female's head, visible with close microscopic study. Several related Fiorinia species look similar in the field, so the shape of a brown cover alone is not a reliable identification.
identification: A brown ridged cover may suggest Fiorinia but does not identify the species. The female's projecting head feature is microscopic, not a large snout visible on the leaf. Similar adventive Fiorinia can be separated through detailed examination of females and other stages. Photograph the plant, leaf surface and distribution of colonies, and retain material only as the diagnostic service directs. Small differences between Taiwanese and Florida specimens make an overly rigid field description particularly unhelpful.
actions: Keep an occupied citrus or ornamental plant from being moved into clean stock while a specialist checks it. Inspect neighboring plants that arrived in the same shipment and retain their source information. Record fresh settlement and leaf condition rather than assuming all visible brown covers are active. Keep the insects and host labels linked, since several similar Fiorinia species may arrive through the same nursery pathway. For an unusual finding, contact the appropriate plant-health or extension service before discarding diagnostic material or sharing plants with others.

sources.title: Takagi1970: Diaspididae of Taiwan, Part II, Fiorinia proboscidaria
Ahmed etal2021: Taxonomic and identification review of adventive Fiorinia of the United States

researchNotes: Independent Taiwanese and Florida specimen studies support consistent species recognition, although field photographs cannot replace microscopic diagnosis. Minor head-lobe variation is not concealed. Identification and stock-movement precautions are supported without requiring a universal treatment threshold.
previousDescription: Fiorinia proboscidaria is a small armored scale sometimes called snout scale. Its elongated covering is glossy and golden-brown, and the female remains protected within an earlier shed skin. It occurs on citrus and other plants. Several related scales look much alike, so the cover's general shape is only a starting point; reliable identification depends on more detailed examination.

claims: Original Taiwanese adult diagnosis.
Independent Florida specimens, diagnoses and molecular tools.

proposedDescription: Aroma is a thorny shrub or small tree with finely divided leaves and hanging, two-tone flower heads. Pink or mauve sterile flowers contrast with the yellow fertile end, and clustered pods twist as they mature. Dichrostachys cinerea can establish from seed and spread through shoots arising from its roots, sometimes forming dense thickets. That growth occurs even within its native African range. A South African field study found root suckers among young plants under several fire and grazing regimes, showing why its spreading habit needs local context.
identification: The hanging flower head combines a pale pink or mauve sterile portion with a yellow fertile portion. Look also for spines, finely divided leaves and clusters of twisted pods. Many thorny legumes have divided leaves, so the complete combination is more useful than the local name aroma. Inspect the base and nearby shoots carefully: a young stem may be connected to an older plant through a root rather than being an independent seedling. Photograph without reaching through the thorns.
actions: Before removing a thicket, establish whether the shrub is native, introduced or being managed for woody encroachment at that location. Use a local land-management plan that accounts for grazing, habitat and follow-up. Cutting visible stems alone may leave connected roots, so monitor the boundary and new shoots after work. Wear protective equipment around thorny branches and keep cut material away from paths. Do not assume that burning or grazing will solve the problem; the South African study found root suckers under multiple disturbance regimes rather than identifying one universally effective treatment.

sources.title: Kew: Dichrostachys cinerea, Flora of Somalia and FTEA descriptions
Wakeling and Bond2007: Disturbance and root suckering in Dichrostachys cinerea

researchNotes: Regional floras, World Agroforestry and the original South African excavation study provide complementary evidence. Native woody encroachment is explicitly distinguished from alien invasion. Root-suckering observations support follow-up precautions but not a universal fire/grazing prescription.
previousDescription: Aroma is a thorny shrub or small tree with finely divided leaves and unusual hanging flowers: pink or mauve at one end and yellow at the other. Its pods become twisted as they mature. It can spread through both seed and shoots from its roots, producing dense thickets. Native across parts of the Old World, it has become invasive in some places outside that range.

claims: Thorny legume morphology and native context.
Original South African root-suckering study.
African tree morphology and twisted pods.

proposedDescription: Arrocillo is a coarse perennial grass that forms leafy clumps. Its broad blades may feel hairy or rough, while the flowering head opens into many slender, spreading branches. Tiny rounded spikelets sit in paired rows along those branches, a useful detail for identification. Paspalum paniculatum grows in disturbed clearings and other open ground. Its home range includes tropical America, while regional floras record it as introduced elsewhere, including the United States and Australia; a local record needs that regional context.
identification: Wait for a flowering head before trying to name an unfamiliar clump. Photograph the many branches from above and the paired spikelets close up, and include a blade, its hairy base and the lower stems. Other Paspalum species have far fewer flowering branches, but branch count alone is not a complete key. A young leafy clump without mature spikelets may need to be revisited. Record whether the plant is growing in a maintained lawn, pasture edge or less disturbed vegetation.
actions: If a confirmed clump is unwanted in a garden, contain the mature seed head before disturbing it and avoid carrying occupied soil to another bed. Check the spot for surviving growth and nearby seedlings during later visits. A pasture or natural-area population deserves a local botanical assessment before broad removal, since grasses in the same genus can have different regional roles. Share photographs and the location with an extension or herbarium service if the occurrence is unusual. Do not assume that an introduced record by itself means that the plant is damaging the site.

sources.title: New South Wales Flora Online: Paspalum paniculatum
Pohl and Davidse: Flora Mesoamericana, reproduced in WFO Paspalum paniculatum

researchNotes: NSW Flora and Pohl/Davidse's Flora Mesoamericana are independent regional treatments, with the latter accessed through its indexed WFO reproduction. No impact level is inferred from range data; seed containment and identification are precautionary reader actions.
previousDescription: Arrocillo is a coarse perennial grass that forms clumps with broad leaves and many spreading flowering branches. Small, rounded flower clusters line those branches. It grows in warm places such as clearings, plantations and other disturbed ground. Its natural distribution includes a broad area of the Americas, so a record in this region does not automatically mean the grass is an introduced species.

claims: Branched panicle and grass diagnosis.
Independent Mesoamerican treatment, habitat and range.

proposedDescription: Arrow bamboo has upright canes and long, broad leaves that make it popular as a screen. Beneath the soil, spreading stems can carry new shoots well beyond the original planting. It can form dense patches where it escapes cultivation. Records from places including Maryland and New Zealand illustrate why its underground growth matters when assessing a planting near neighboring gardens or natural vegetation.
identification: Follow a leafy shoot down to its cane and look for new shoots beyond the original clump. Broad leaves alone do not separate arrow bamboo from Sasa or Pleioblastus, which can also run through gardens. A photograph should include leaves, cane nodes and the planting's outer edge. Check for creeping underground stems only where digging is safe and permitted. The Maryland expert response identifies a running-bamboo problem, rather than providing a definitive species determination from every submitted image.
actions: Map the outermost shoots before starting work so you can see whether the patch expands. Coordinate with a neighbor if underground stems cross a boundary. A small patch may allow removal of canes and accessible rhizomes, followed by repeated checks for returning shoots; established stands require a longer plan. Avoid moving rhizome-bearing soil to another part of the property. Seek local advice on containment or removal near trees, utilities and buildings. Ordinary selective broadleaf lawn products will not solve a bamboo problem, and a single cutting should not be mistaken for eradication.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Pseudosasa japonica
Maryland Extension: Running bamboo identification and management response

researchNotes: Independent New Zealand flora and Maryland extension guidance support diagnosis, underground spread and the distinction from other running bamboos. The Maryland submitted plant is not overclaimed as a definitive P. japonica voucher. Removal expectations remain cautious.
previousDescription: Arrow bamboo forms a leafy screen of upright canes and long, broad green leaves. What happens below ground is just as important: running underground stems can send new shoots beyond the original planting. That habit has helped it escape gardens, with naturalized stands described beside rivers, roads, and woodland edges in New Zealand and reports of invasive growth in Maryland. An established patch is therefore more than the canes you can see. Identification and a plan for the underground growth are useful before attempting to remove or contain it.

claims: Broad-leaved running bamboo and regional occurrence.
Maryland running-bamboo diagnosis and management context.

proposedDescription: Arrowleaf elephant ear has large, arrow-shaped leaves held on long stalks that meet the leaf at its base. Thick underground growth and new shoots help it expand into patches. It favors warm, moist places and can grow along streams. In parts of Florida, escaped plants are considered invasive, where their large leaves and dense growth can crowd other vegetation.
identification: Look at the point where the leaf stalk meets the blade: it joins at the basal notch, a useful contrast with many Colocasia leaves whose stalk enters farther inside the blade. Photograph the whole leaf, that attachment and the base of the clump. Other large aroids and garden cultivars can still be confusing, especially without flowers. Underground growth may connect several leafy shoots, so a new stem beside the parent need not have come from seed.
actions: Before planting or sharing divisions in Florida, check the current UF/IFAS assessment for the relevant zone; its conclusions differ within the state. Keep garden material away from drainage channels and do not dump tubers or divided clumps beside streams. If an escape is confirmed, obtain a site-appropriate removal plan that accounts for underground parts and repeated visits. Along a bank, avoid tearing out a large patch in a way that leaves bare eroding soil. Wear gloves for routine handling and do not treat an ornamental elephant-ear label as an edible-plant identification.

sources.title: University of South Florida: Arrowleaf elephant's ear

researchNotes: NParks supplies botanical and propagation details; UF assessment gives zone-specific status; USF provides an independent Florida occurrence/recognition account. Central Florida invasive status is not generalized to all zones or the entire country. The underground-growth precaution is not an eradication guarantee.
previousDescription: Arrowleaf elephant's ear makes a bold patch of tropical greenery, with large arrow-shaped leaves held on long stalks. The stalk joins the blade at its base, a useful clue when comparing plants commonly called elephant ears. Thick underground growth produces offsets, allowing colonies to expand in moist places such as streambanks. It has a long history as a cultivated tropical plant, but it can also escape. Florida assessments describe invasive behavior in some regions, where dense growth can crowd or shade native vegetation; those regional findings should not be treated as a universal status.

claims: Leaf attachment and vegetative growth.
Florida zone-specific assessment.
Independent Florida identification and occurrence.

proposedDescription: Artist's pallet is grown for its heart- to arrow-shaped leaves, patterned in combinations of green, white, pink and red. It grows from underground tubers and produces small flowers grouped on a fleshy spike within a pale surrounding leaf-like structure. Native to tropical America, it is widely cultivated. Its colorful foliage is ornamental rather than edible, and the plant's tissues can cause irritation.
identification: Leaves usually attract attention long before the small flower structure appears. Photograph both the leaf pattern and its shape, but remember that cultivated caladiums include many selections and hybrids. A brightly colored leaf is not enough to settle the ancestry of a named cultivar. Check the label and growing history as well as visible features. Tubers can remain when seasonal foliage dies back, so loss of the leaves does not necessarily mean the planting has disappeared.
actions: Place caladiums where children and pets will not chew the leaves or tubers, and use gloves when dividing plants if sap contact is a concern. Keep divisions labeled and contained rather than discarding live tubers in a natural area. If a patch is unwanted, locate the remaining underground material and watch for renewed growth when conditions are favorable. For an unidentified escape, obtain a botanical determination before assigning an invasive status. This ornamental's tropical origin and irritating tissues do not by themselves show that it is a harmful invader at every planting site.

The broad blades range from heart-shaped to arrow-shaped and rise on long stalks from underground tubers. Its flowers are much less conspicuous, carried on a fleshy spike within a pale bract. This tropical American plant is widely cultivated, with garden forms that vary greatly in color and shape. An ornamental caladium should not automatically be described as an invasive threat, but its sap and tissues do deserve care around people and pets because they contain irritating compounds.
