proposedDescription: Diplosoma listerianum is a name used for closely related colonial sea squirts that form thin, soft sheets over submerged surfaces. Many tiny filtering animals share the same gelatinous covering. Colonies grow on docks, boat hulls and natural surfaces, giving them opportunities to travel with marine traffic. They can cover other organisms as they spread, but the long history of transport makes the species' original native range difficult to establish.
identification: Look for a very thin, soft colony in which the tiny individual animals are embedded in one shared sheet. Other colonial tunicates, sponges and films can resemble it, and colony color varies with background and condition. Photograph the colony underwater with a scale reference if that can be done safely. A marine specialist may need closer examination to separate similar species. A new colony on a hull is evidence of fouling, not a reliable clue to the species' original home. Genetic research has found deeply separated lineages within this name, so visual records should retain the broad species-complex qualification.
actions: Before taking a fouled boat or other marine equipment to another harbor, ask the marina or relevant authority about inspection and approved cleaning facilities. Arrange cleaning so removed growth and wash water are captured rather than scraped directly into the harbor. Do not transfer occupied ropes, floats or shellfish equipment between sites without appropriate advice. Record the location and substrate of an unusual colony and submit photographs to a marine monitoring program. Avoid experimental chemical or freshwater treatments in open water; a contained, professionally advised response is the appropriate way to address uncertain tunicate identification.

proposedDescription: Polyandrocarpa zorritensis is a colonial sea squirt made up of small, club-shaped individuals connected by root-like strands. Each has its own outer covering and two openings used in filter feeding. Colonies occur on docks, boats and natural surfaces such as mangrove roots, and can overgrow neighboring organisms. It was described from Peru, but that alone does not establish where it originally evolved.
identification: Unlike a thin sheet of tunic, this colony has individual upright bodies joined by connecting strands. Look for the two openings on each body and the network at its base. Other colonial sea squirts need comparison, so underwater photographs should show both individual shape and colony arrangement. Researchers also describe dormant rounded structures that can persist when conspicuous animals are scarce. A seasonal reduction in visible zooids therefore does not necessarily mean that an occupied rope or dock is free of the species.
actions: Inspect fouled ropes and equipment before moving them between marinas. Ask the harbor manager about identification and cleaning arrangements that capture removed material and wash water. Do not scrape an uncertain colony into surrounding water or try to alter harbor salinity. Laboratory differences in budding at different salt concentrations are not a do-it-yourself treatment recipe. Keep a dated photographic record if the colony appears to shrink and return, and share it with a marine monitoring program. The species' first description from Peru should not be used alone to decide whether a local population is native.

previousDescription: This sea squirt grows as a cluster of small, club-shaped animals, joined at their bases by rootlike strands. Each individual has its own tough covering and two openings through which it pumps and filters seawater. Colonies occur on docks, boat hulls, and natural surfaces such as mangroves. Introduced populations have been documented in several regions, and some colonies can overgrow other organisms. Its original home remains uncertain in the Smithsonian account, despite having first been described from Peru; the place where a species was named is not necessarily its native range. Experiments also show that salinity can limit its asexual reproduction, so success in one harbor does not predict equal growth in another.

Original salinity/budding experiments and dormant structures.

proposedDescription: Ash whitefly feeds beneath the leaves of trees and shrubs, including pears, pomegranates and citrus. Adults are small and white; immature insects have distinctive waxy structures and may carry tiny droplets. Feeding and honeydew can harm foliage and encourage sooty mold. In California, introduced natural enemies greatly reduced a once-serious outbreak, making this species a notable example of successful biological control.
identification: Turn over affected leaves to examine the immature stages, rather than relying only on clouds of flying adults. Pale wax and droplets on the immatures are helpful clues, while honeydew and dark sooty mold show why the leaves may look dirty. Other whiteflies also make honeydew, so a specialist may need a leaf sample. Compare young and old foliage and note whether the tree is losing leaves or merely carrying a light infestation.
actions: In places where natural enemies already suppress ash whitefly, avoid an automatic broad-spectrum spray that could disrupt that control. Monitor the undersides of several leaves and look for changes in infestation and tree condition before deciding whether action is needed. Obtain local advice if damage persists, particularly on a young or stressed plant. Check nursery plants before moving them to another site. The successful California biological-control program does not mean homeowners should purchase or release unidentified wasps or beetles; conservation of established natural enemies is the more useful first step.

previousDescription: Ash whitefly can cover the undersides of leaves with tiny sap-feeding insects. Adults are pale and wax-dusted, but the settled young are more distinctive, with a thick wax band and a fringe of fine tubes ending in droplets. Ash is only one host; pears, pomegranates, citrus, and other broadleaved trees can also support it. Heavy infestations can leave sticky honeydew and harm foliage or fruit. Its history in California also shows the value of natural enemies: introduced parasitoids greatly reduced a once conspicuous pest problem.

claims: Ash whitefly morphology and tree hosts.
California biological control and natural-enemy conservation.

proposedDescription: Ashy cinquefoil has small yellow flowers and leaves divided into five to seven toothed leaflets. Pale hairs on the undersides give the foliage a grayish cast, and hairy stems rise above the lower leaves. It favors dry, open places, including roadsides, grasslands and disturbed ground. This Eurasian plant has been introduced to parts of North America. Several yellow-flowered cinquefoils look similar, so the leaflet shape, gray undersides and hairs around the flowers are more useful together than flower color alone.
identification: Examine the pale undersides of several mature leaves and count their leaflets. Photograph the leaf tips, teeth, stem hairs and the small green structures beneath a flower. Potentilla intermedia can be similar; narrower leaflets and coarser hairs around the flowers help distinguish P. inclinata, but flower color alone is unreliable. A plant without flowers may be worth revisiting later in the season. Include habitat and location with the images so a regional botanist can compare the appropriate local species.
actions: For a confirmed unwanted garden plant, remove it before mature seed is scattered and check the same spot for renewed growth. Keep seed-bearing material out of clean planting soil. In grassland or along a road, confirm the identity and local status before removing a patch that may contain other cinquefoils. Ask the land manager how an unusual occurrence should be recorded. The gray foliage is a useful recognition clue, but it is not evidence that the plant is causing ecological damage or that a particular removal method will work at that site.

proposedDescription: Ashy geckos are tiny lizards that shelter in leaf litter, beneath bark and among rocks or woody debris, often near buildings. Young animals have bold bands and bright reddish tails; adults become tan to rusty brown with pale speckling. Sphaerodactylus elegans has been introduced to Florida, where other small geckos can complicate identification. Observations from Cuba also describe these geckos hunting flies and ants around a house during daylight. Their changing colors and secretive habits make a clear photograph more useful than a fleeting glimpse.
identification: A juvenile's bold bands and reddish tail can be much easier to notice than the adult's softer, speckled pattern. Photograph the whole animal without chasing it, ideally including the head and tail. Florida's native reef gecko and other small introduced geckos can complicate identification. Color changes with age mean that two differently patterned animals nearby may still belong to the same species. Daylight hunting observed in Cuba is a site-specific natural-history record, not a rule that every animal must be active at that hour.
actions: Leave an uncertain gecko undisturbed while seeking identification from clear photographs. Do not clear all leaf litter or spray sheltered areas merely because a tiny lizard is present. If found in a shipment of plants or landscape materials, notify the supplier or appropriate local wildlife contact before moving the material elsewhere. Never relocate an unfamiliar gecko to another outdoor site or release a captive one. An unusual sighting is useful when accompanied by date and location; it does not, by itself, demonstrate ecological harm or a breeding population.

The change in pattern as it grows means young and adult animals may look surprisingly different.

proposedDescription: Ashy pipewort forms a small tuft of very narrow leaves in wet ground. Slender stalks lift rounded, button-like flower heads above the foliage; these may look gray, yellowish or greenish rather than showy. Eriocaulon cinereum occurs in damp valleys and rice fields, including introduced populations recorded in California and Louisiana. Before flowering, its leaves can resemble a small grass. Mature heads are much more useful for recognition, although their tiny flowers still need close examination to distinguish this plant from other pipeworts.
identification: Look for the narrow basal leaves and upright stalks ending in compact rounded heads. Photograph several heads and the plant's base without trampling surrounding wetland vegetation. Other pipeworts are similar, and their minute flowers often need magnification for a reliable determination. A grass-like seedling cannot confidently be named from a distant photograph. Record whether the plant is in a rice field, a pond margin or another wet setting, since that context helps a botanist interpret the specimen.
actions: In an agricultural field, have the pipewort identified before deciding whether it is part of a crop-management problem. Clean visible plant material from equipment before moving between fields, and avoid moving seed-bearing mud into a new planting. In natural wetlands, do not drain or excavate a patch simply because the species has an introduced record elsewhere. Report an unusual occurrence to the relevant herbarium or land manager, with photographs and a precise location. Native pipeworts may occur nearby, and protecting them depends on getting the identification right first.

proposedDescription: Asia minor bluegrass, Polypogon fugax, is a loosely tufted annual with a compact flower head that may be pale green or tinged purple. Fine, short bristles edge the tiny flower clusters. Its stems can bend near the base and sometimes root at lower joints, while the leaves are often rough to the touch. It grows in moist places, including disturbed ground and farmland margins. Despite its common name, it belongs to Polypogon rather than Poa, and mature spikelets help separate it from similar grasses.
identification: Examine the flower head closely enough to see its small bristled spikelets. Include the leaf sheath, base of the stems and any rooting joints in photographs. Similar Polypogon and related grass hybrids can be difficult to distinguish without mature material, so a common name containing bluegrass is not a reliable guide. A loose clump in wet ground may look quite different from a pressed specimen. Ask a regional botanist to compare a complete flowering shoot when the identification matters.
actions: Where the grass is unwanted in a managed bed, collect mature seed heads before disturbing the clump and keep rooted stem pieces with the removed material. Check damp edges and recently moved soil for additional plants. At a field margin, record its extent and discuss any crop interference with local extension before selecting a response. Avoid broad treatment of a wet ditch while the identity is uncertain; other grasses and wetland vegetation may share the site. Its ability to root at lower joints makes careless movement of cut plants a poor containment practice.

proposedDescription: Asian bush mosquito has pale-banded legs and golden markings on its back. It uses small pools of water, including rock pools, tree holes, tires and other containers, and can thrive in relatively cool, wooded settings near homes. Its ability to use artificial containers helps it spread. The species can carry pathogens under some conditions, but finding it does not establish local disease transmission.
identification: The pale leg bands and golden lines on the thorax help narrow the possibilities, but several mosquitoes have banded legs. Local mosquito-control staff can identify an adult or larvae more reliably than a photograph of a bite. Check artificial containers in shaded places, including discarded tires and neglected water-holding items. A container with larvae should be addressed even before the species is known. Do not use the presence of this mosquito to diagnose an illness or to assume that a particular pathogen is circulating nearby.
actions: Empty and scrub water-holding containers regularly, store unused items so they stay dry and keep gutters draining. Cover rain-storage containers appropriately and maintain window and door screens. For personal protection, use an EPA-registered repellent according to its label and wear clothing that reduces exposed skin when mosquitoes are active. Contact the local mosquito-control program about persistent breeding sites or unusual collections. Do not drain natural rock pools or wetlands as a household response; concentrate on avoidable artificial breeding sites and follow current local public-health advice about disease risk.

previousDescription: Asian bush mosquito develops in small collections of water, from rock pools and tree holes to discarded tires and garden containers. Adults have golden markings on the upper body and pale bands on their dark legs. The species tolerates cooler conditions than many familiar container mosquitoes, helping it use wooded and residential settings. Females take blood meals, but a mosquito's capacity to carry a virus in a laboratory should not be confused with proof that it is causing local disease transmission. Around a home, reducing water-holding containers is a practical way to reduce breeding opportunities.

proposedDescription: Asian chestnut gall wasp causes rounded swellings on the buds, leaves and shoots of true chestnut trees. These galls start green or pink and later become woody and brown, sometimes remaining after the wasps have left. Heavy infestations can reduce shoot growth and nut production. The adult wasp is tiny, so the galls are usually the first sign people notice.
identification: Confirm that the host is a true chestnut, Castanea, and inspect buds, new shoots and leaves for rounded green or pink swellings. Old brown galls may remain long after the insects have emerged, so note their age and whether fresh galls appear on current growth. Other injuries can distort a shoot, and a tiny wasp nearby is not enough to name the cause. Photograph the gall's position on the tree and include the host's leaves for identification.
actions: Check nursery chestnuts and propagation material before purchase or movement, and ask about origin if gall wasp is a local concern. Apparently healthy dormant material can still be difficult to assess, so follow current plant-health advice rather than relying only on visible galls. Report a suspected new regional occurrence through the appropriate forestry or plant-health service. Avoid indiscriminate pruning of old galls, which may no longer contain the pest and can shelter natural enemies. For a small tree with fresh injury, obtain local advice about timing and management before cutting or treating it.

previousDescription: Asian chestnut gall wasp is usually noticed through the growth it causes rather than through the tiny adult wasp. Rounded green or pink galls develop on chestnut buds, leaves, and shoots, sheltering the larvae inside. Later, the galls turn brown and woody and may remain attached after the insects have left. Repeated gall formation can disrupt growth and flowering and reduce nut production. This pest attacks true chestnuts in Castanea, and its management has included carefully studied biological control; an old gall is not proof that a living wasp is still inside.

proposedDescription: Asian citrus psyllid is a small sap-feeding insect often seen with its body tilted upward as it feeds on tender citrus growth. Young insects are yellow-orange and produce curled, waxy tubes. Feeding can distort new leaves, but its greater importance is its ability to transmit the bacteria associated with citrus greening disease. Identifying the insect accurately helps distinguish that risk from ordinary leaf damage.
identification: Look on tender citrus flush for adults feeding with their rear ends raised and for flattened yellow-orange nymphs with white waxy tubes. Aphids, scales and leafminers can also affect young leaves, so include close photographs rather than relying on distortion alone. Citrus greening requires a separate official assessment: an unevenly yellow leaf does not prove infection, and finding a psyllid does not mean every tree nearby carries the bacterium. Record both the insect and the tree's location.
actions: Contact your state citrus or plant-health program promptly about a suspected new infestation and follow its sampling instructions. Keep citrus plants, cuttings and other potentially occupied material on site until you know the applicable movement guidance; do not mail a sample unsolicited. Inspect new flush during routine tree care and use clean, appropriately sourced planting stock. If disease is suspected, seek official testing instead of trying to treat leaf color alone. Coordinate any pest response with current regional advice, since neighboring trees and plant movement affect the usefulness of an individual household's efforts.

Yellow-orange young cluster on tender growth and produce curled white wax tubes. Feeding can distort shoots, but the greater concern is transmission of the bacteria associated with huanglongbing, or citrus greening. Infected trees can decline and produce poor fruit, and there is no cure for the disease. A psyllid sighting does not prove a tree is infected, but it is a good reason to follow local citrus plant-health guidance promptly.

proposedDescription: Asian cockroach usually lives outdoors in leaf litter, mulch and similar sheltered places. It closely resembles the German cockroach, but flies readily and is attracted to lights, especially around dusk. Adults may enter buildings from outside. That behavior matters when interpreting a sighting: one flying into a lit room does not necessarily indicate the kind of indoor infestation associated with its lookalike.
identification: A tan cockroach with dark stripes behind the head can strongly resemble the German cockroach. Ready flight toward lights and an outdoor mulch source favor Asian cockroach, but behavior alone is not a perfect identification. Save a clear photograph or a safely contained specimen for an extension service or pest professional. Note whether sightings occur around an open lit doorway at dusk or repeatedly within kitchens and other indoor hiding places; that pattern helps guide the inspection.
actions: Repair screens and door gaps, and reduce the attraction of bright lights immediately beside entrances where practical. Inspect nearby leaf litter or mulch as part of understanding the outdoor source, without treating every sheltered garden area. Persistent indoor sightings deserve species confirmation before selecting a control plan, because a German-cockroach infestation requires a different response. Do not assume that one flying adult calls for whole-house treatment. If an outdoor population becomes a nuisance, ask for a site-specific approach and use any control product only according to its label.

proposedDescription: Asian copperleaf is an annual plant with upright stems and toothed, oval leaves. Young growth may be reddish. Broad, heart-shaped structures surround the small flowers and developing fruit, providing a useful identification feature. Native to Asia, it has been recorded as a weed in parts of the American Midwest, where it can grow and produce seed beneath a crop canopy.

previousDescription: Asian copperleaf is a small annual plant that can blend into a garden bed or crop field until its flowers develop. Its upright stems carry toothed, oval leaves, often with reddish young growth. Look especially for the broad, heart-shaped leafy bracts around the flowers and fruits; several native copperleaf relatives look similar before flowering. Introduced from eastern Asia, it has become a concern in some Midwestern fields because it can grow beneath crop canopies and produce seed for future seasons.

proposedDescription: Asian drill snail has a thick, ridged shell, commonly about one to two inches long. It lives among shells, gravel and mud around oyster beds, where it bores through the shells of its prey. Small oysters are especially vulnerable, although it also eats other shellfish. Native to the northwestern Pacific, it has traveled with oyster shipments. Clusters of bright yellow, bottle-shaped egg capsules can offer another clue to its presence.

It lives around shell, gravel and muddy oyster habitats and feeds by boring through the shells of other animals. Native to the northwestern Pacific, it has traveled with oyster shipments. Its feeding makes it a concern where introduced populations overlap with shellfish beds.

identification: Examine the shell's raised ridges and projecting shoulders, but do not identify an oyster drill from a bored shell alone. Native predatory snails and other introduced drills also leave holes in shellfish. Photograph the intact snail from the side and from the opening, with a ruler nearby. Attached clusters of yellow egg capsules can strengthen a report. Young snails develop in capsules rather than through a freely drifting larval stage, making movement of infested oysters and equipment especially important.

For a new observation, record the location and photograph the snail and attached capsules for the local marine-pest or shellfish program. Growers can discuss targeted collection of adults and capsules with that program; University of Washington work found capsule removal particularly useful for reducing population growth. Avoid broad scraping of natural habitat simply because a shell has a drill hole.

proposedDescription: Asian flatsedge is an annual sedge of muddy river margins, ditches and fields. Its narrow leaves grow below branched flower clusters surrounded by longer, leaf-like bracts. The small yellow-brown scales in those clusters have green, pointed midribs. Originally associated with East Asia, it has also been recorded as a field weed in Europe. Close flower details help distinguish it from similar sedges.
