researchNotes: Trieste and Flora Helvetica were reread as independent regional botanical treatments supporting morphology and European occurrences. Exact U.S. impact and control efficacy are not established, so the profile limits actions to identification, conditional garden weeding and seed containment rather than importing a generic sedge treatment.
previousDescription: Asian flatsedge is a small, grasslike annual that grows in muddy places, including riverbanks, ditches, and cultivated fields. Several upright stems rise together above narrow leaves. At the top, branching flower clusters are overtopped by long, leaflike bracts; the tiny spikelets have yellow-brown scales with pointed green midribs. Native to eastern Asia, it has appeared as an introduced field weed in parts of Europe. Close inspection of the flowering head helps separate it from similar sedges.
identification: The flowering head deserves a closer look than the grasslike foliage. Several branches hold small spikelets, and a few long green bracts extend well beyond them. A hand lens reveals the pointed green midribs of the yellow-brown scales. Other flatsedges, including Cyperus iria, can look similar, so neither wet ground nor a triangular stem is enough for identification. Save clear views of the entire flower arrangement and individual spikelets while they are mature and still attached.
actions: In a cultivated bed, a confirmed unwanted annual can be removed before ripe seed is scattered. Keep seed-bearing material out of soil moved to another site and return to inspect the same damp patches. A plant on a natural riverbank needs a regional identification and impact assessment before removal is justified. At a U.S. site, check whether it is interfering with the intended vegetation before choosing a response. Similar-looking sedges can have different local roles and management needs. Treat a new regional record as something to document carefully rather than an automatic call for broad treatment.

claims: East Asian annual in muddy margins and Italian maize fields
Branched heads, long bracts and pointed scale midribs

proposedDescription: Asian kelp is the brown seaweed widely known as wakame. It has a broad blade with a clear central rib and a ruffled reproductive structure near the base. It grows on rocks as well as ropes and boat hulls, which can help it reach new coasts. Cultivated as food, it is also invasive in some temperate regions, where dense growth can change the habitat available to other marine life.

sources.title: Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary: Undaria invasion FAQ

researchNotes: NOAA's 2003 FAQ is historical biology and harbor evidence, not a current range map. The prior Rhode Island link returned404: https://www.crmc.ri.gov/invasives/invasives_refcards/U_pinnatifida.pdf . Replaced its support with Fisheries and Oceans Canada's independently maintained identification/reporting account.
previousDescription: Asian kelp, better known as wakame, is a large brown seaweed with a broad blade, a prominent middle rib, and a distinctive ruffled reproductive structure near its base. It attaches to rocks but also grows on ropes, docks, and boat hulls. Cultivated as food in Asia, it has reached many other temperate coasts. Dense growth can shade other seaweeds, although its effects vary between places. The ruffled base is especially helpful when distinguishing mature plants from native kelps.
identification: The midrib runs through the broad blade, while a mature plant develops folded, frilly reproductive tissue around the lower stalk. Other brown seaweeds may have torn or wavy blades, so photograph the base as well as the largest sheet of tissue. Young wakame may lack the obvious reproductive frill. Its visible frond is only part of the life cycle: microscopic stages can remain on hard surfaces, which helps explain why removing a few large plants does not necessarily clear a site.
actions: Report a suspected new patch with the observation date, precise location and photographs before moving it. Check mooring lines, hulls and other immersed equipment through the local marina's approved cleaning arrangements. Avoid cleaning a fouled boat in a way that releases material into another harbor. A coordinated removal program may reduce biomass, but repeated inspection is needed for microscopic stages and new arrivals. Do not assume harbor-grown wakame is suitable to eat because the same species is commercially cultivated; water quality and local collection rules still matter.

claims: Microscopic life stages, vessel pathways and limits of removal
Distinct midrib and frilled stalk
Photograph and report new sightings

proposedDescription: Asian longhorned beetle is a large, glossy black beetle with white spots and long, banded antennae. Its pale larvae feed beneath the bark of hardwood trees, then tunnel deeper into the wood. Maples are among its hosts, and heavy feeding can eventually kill a tree. Round exit holes, chewed egg-laying marks and coarse sawdust-like material are useful signs. Native to Asia, it most likely reached the United States in wood packaging.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Extension: Asian longhorned beetle

researchNotes: APHIS and the separately authored UMN account were reopened and substantively checked. Reporting and wood-movement precautions follow APHIS; no current quarantine boundary or eradication claim is generalized. Native lookalike caution avoids treating a white-spotted beetle alone as confirmation.
previousDescription: Asian longhorned beetle is a large black beetle with white spots and long, banded antennae. Its larvae tunnel through hardwood trees, including maples, and can eventually kill them. Round exit holes, chewed bark and coarse sawdust-like material can reveal an infestation. Native to Asia, it has reached other regions through wood packaging, making careful identification of beetles and tree damage especially important.

claims: Diagnostic signs, hardwood damage and reporting
Likely wood-packaging pathway and firewood precautions
Larval feeding under bark and in wood
Adult morphology and host trees

identification: Check both the insect and its host tree. The adult's white blotches and antennae longer than its body are useful, but several native longhorned beetles can cause confusion. Photographs should show the upper body and antennae clearly. On a living hardwood, look for round emergence holes, oval egg-laying wounds and frass collecting beneath a branch. These signs are a reason for expert inspection, not proof by themselves, because other borers and mechanical damage can leave superficially similar marks.
actions: Photograph a suspect beetle or damaged tree and report it promptly to your state plant-health agency or USDA's Asian longhorned beetle program. Note the tree's location and any recent movement of firewood or wood packaging. Keep potentially infested wood on site until officials advise otherwise, and observe applicable firewood movement restrictions. Do not cut branches to search for larvae or apply a preventive pesticide on your own: an official inspection can guide the response while preserving evidence. Stay clear of weakened limbs when taking photographs.

proposedDescription: Asian marsh snail is a tiny brown snail with a blunt, cone-shaped shell, reaching only about five millimeters. It lives among vegetation high in salt or brackish marshes, where the ground is not continuously underwater. A field study in Japan found it concentrated in middle and upper tidal areas. Native to Japan and Korea, it has also been recorded in Oregon. Smithsonian reports no observed Oregon impacts, which does not establish that impacts are absent.

sources.title: Wada, Kuroda and Kamada (2023): Distribution pattern of macrobenthos in salt marsh of Yoshino River, Tokushima

researchNotes: Smithsonian's Oregon account was reopened; the Japanese museum study's English abstract independently supports tidal habitat. No observed impact is distinguished from proof of harmlessness. Species-specific removal efficacy and Oregon effects remain limited; the ready profile supports documentation and equipment hygiene without claiming an eradication method.
previousDescription: Asian marsh snail is a tiny brown snail with a blunt, cone-shaped shell, reaching only about five millimeters. It lives high in salt or brackish marshes, where the ground is not continuously underwater. Native to Japan and Korea, it has also been recorded in Oregon. Available Smithsonian accounts do not report observed impacts there, so its introduction should be distinguished from demonstrated ecological harm.

claims: Small brown upper-marsh snail; Japan/Korea origin and Oregon records
No observed Oregon impacts reported
Quantitative Japanese survey places species at mid-to-high tidal levels

identification: At this size, a dark speck on marsh litter may be easy to miss or mistake for another small snail. Use close photographs with a scale to show the shell's blunt cone, opening and brown surface. Record whether it was on vegetation, mud or debris and how high it sat relative to the tide. Those habitat details help a specialist compare it with native marsh snails, but they cannot replace examination of the animal's diagnostic characters.
actions: Leave marsh vegetation and sediment in place while documenting a suspected occurrence. Avoid carrying wet marsh debris on boots, traps or sampling gear to another estuary, and follow the site's cleaning procedures. Send photographs and location details to a regional marine-invertebrate specialist if the snail seems new to the area. A few tiny snails are not a reason to disturb an entire marsh. Have the species checked before deciding whether any intervention is needed. Do not spread bait, salt or chemicals through a marsh to target tiny snails; such treatment could damage the surrounding community.

proposedDescription: Asian marshweed looks quite different above and below the water. Its submerged leaves are finely divided and arranged in whorls around the stem; leaves emerging into the air are firmer and toothed. Small pink to violet flowers appear above the surface. This Asian aquatic plant has been sold for aquariums and apparently escaped cultivation in the southeastern United States. Some stem fragments can root and regrow, while dense stands can shade and crowd other aquatic plants.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Limnophila sessiliflora
California Department of Food and Agriculture (2024): Limnophila sessiliflora Pest Rating Proposal

researchNotes: UF and CDFA were reopened. CDFA's independent flora-based morphology and hybrid discussion complement UF management context, while shared aquarium-impact material remains one lineage. The PDF path is dated2024 but its displayed proposal comment period is2020-2021; no current legal conclusion rests on that date.
previousDescription: Asian marshweed changes its appearance above and below water. Submerged leaves are finely divided and arranged around the stem, while leaves above the surface are firmer and toothed. Small pink to violet flowers may appear above the water. Introduced through the aquarium trade, it has established in the southeastern United States, where rooting stem fragments and dense growth can help it crowd other aquatic plants.

claims: Aquarium pathway, southeastern establishment and aquatic growth
Two leaf forms and very short flower stalks
L. indica and hybrid identification caveats

identification: Follow a stem through the waterline if that can be done without breaking it. The change from feathery underwater foliage to firmer emerged leaves is particularly helpful. Flowers arise close to the upper leaf axils on very short stalks. Limnophila indica and a hybrid reported from Louisiana can complicate identification, so a submerged aquarium cutting alone may not be enough. Photograph the emerged flowers and leaf arrangement as well as a whole submerged shoot for a knowledgeable aquatic botanist.
actions: Never empty aquarium plants or water containing plant fragments into a storm drain, ditch or pond. Contain unwanted plants for locally approved disposal and clean equipment before using it in another water body. Report a suspected outdoor population to the local aquatic-plant or agriculture program. Avoid casual mowing or raking through a patch, since some sufficiently developed fragments can regrow. Treatment in a natural waterway needs a site-specific plan and appropriate permissions; a photograph of feathery leaves should be checked before native aquatic plants are disturbed.

proposedDescription: Asian mustard begins as a rough-leaved rosette before sending up branching stems with small, pale yellow flowers and long seed pods. In southwestern North America, it can grow quickly after winter rain and compete with native desert wildflowers. It comes from the Mediterranean region and nearby parts of Asia. Its ability to spread through open desert habitat makes it more than an ordinary roadside weed in affected areas.

sources.title: University of California IPM: Sahara mustard
National Park Service: Death Valley non-native plants

researchNotes: UC IPM management and NPS Death Valley observations were reread. Desert competition is geographically scoped. Actions emphasize early seed prevention, repeated cohorts and avoiding collateral desert disturbance; no exact chemical treatment or universal fire-impact claim is added.
previousDescription: Sahara mustard is a fast-growing annual that can turn desert ground into a dense patch of mustard after favorable winter rain. It begins with a rough, deeply lobed rosette, then sends up mostly leafless stems bearing small pale-yellow flowers and slender seedpods. Originally from the Mediterranean region and nearby parts of Asia, it has spread into southwestern North American dunes, washes, and scrub. Early growth lets it compete with native wildflowers for water and space before those plants finish their own short season.
identification: Start with the basal leaves: they are rough and often deeply lobed, while the taller flowering branches carry relatively few leaves. The pale yellow flowers are small, and long narrow pods soon become more conspicuous than the blossoms. Other annual mustards can occur nearby, including species with purple flowers or different leaf shapes. Take photographs of the rosette, flowers and mature pods together. The fast-growing plant may already be forming seed while a desert wildflower display is still developing.
actions: Check disturbed entrances, washes and road edges after suitable rain, and return as later seedlings appear. Small confirmed patches can be pulled before seed maturity where the land manager permits it, taking care not to trample surrounding wildflowers or fragile soil surfaces. Contain plants with developing pods, and clean footwear, tools and vehicle debris before leaving. Seed in the soil can produce new cohorts, so a single visit is rarely enough. Larger desert populations need coordinated, repeated work timed to prevent another crop of seed.

claims: Annual life cycle, seed dispersal and repeated early control
Desert habitats and early competition with local wildflowers

proposedDescription: Asian nakedwood is a sprawling evergreen shrub with shiny, toothed leaves, small greenish-yellow flowers and rounded seed capsules. Its seeds can float and tolerate salty conditions, helping it move through coastal environments. Native to parts of the Old World tropics, it has become invasive in Florida's coastal habitats, where its climbing and spreading growth can cover other vegetation.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Colubrina asiatica
Singapore National Parks Board: Colubrina asiatica

researchNotes: UF supplies Florida impacts and NParks independently describes native coastal ecology, fruit and rooted branches. These sources were reopened. Geographic context is explicit and the proposed actions avoid treating native-range plants or all glossy coastal shrubs as invasive.
previousDescription: Latherleaf is a sprawling evergreen shrub that can scramble over neighboring vegetation. Shiny oval leaves with toothed edges, small yellow-green flowers, and round seed capsules help identify it. Its buoyant, salt-tolerant fruits and seeds suit a life along tropical shores. The plant is native in parts of the Old World tropics but invasive in coastal southern Florida, where its long branches can form dense tangles over native vegetation. A low roadside shrub can therefore be the beginning of a much larger patch.
identification: Look for alternate, glossy leaves with toothed edges and several strong veins arising near the base. Small flowers sit in clusters where leaves meet the branch, and the round capsules eventually split to release seeds. A scrambling branch may root where it contacts soil, adding to the tangle. Other coastal shrubs can have shiny leaves, so document fruit, leaf arrangement and the plant's climbing habit. Common names such as nakedwood are not sufficient to distinguish related native shrubs.
actions: In affected Florida coastal habitat, address a small confirmed plant before it grows through neighboring vegetation. Avoid dragging seed-bearing branches through an uninvaded area, and check for rooted branches beyond the main stem. Ask the land manager about removal and follow-up suited to the shoreline, particularly around mangroves or other sensitive plants. Do not use aggressive clearing that strips the whole site. In its native Asian coastal range the same species is part of the local flora, so an invasive label from Florida is not a reason for removal there.

claims: Florida coastal invasion and scrambling growth
Native Asian coastal range, toothed leaves and floating seeds
Branches root on contact with soil

proposedDescription: Asian needle ant is a dark ant with paler legs and antenna tips. It often nests in damp wood, leaf litter or beneath stones and feeds on termites and other small animals. Established in parts of the eastern United States, it can displace native ants, including species that disperse plant seeds. It also has a painful sting. Newer references usually call it Brachyponera chinensis.

sources.title: North Carolina State Extension: Asian needle ant
Virginia Cooperative Extension: Asian Needle Ant

researchNotes: NC State and Virginia Tech were reread for exact-species behavior and defensive-sting precautions. Current Brachyponera synonym is retained. Advice avoids deliberate handling, diagnoses and pesticide recipes; forest seed-dispersal effects are attributed to documented native-ant interactions.
previousDescription: Asian needle ant is a small, dark ant with lighter legs, mouthparts, and antenna tips. It often nests in damp leaf litter, rotting logs, mulch, or spaces beneath stones, and feeds on termites and other small animals. Introduced from Asia, it occurs in eastern U.S. forests as well as gardens and buildings. It can displace native ants, including ants that disperse plant seeds. It also delivers a painful defensive sting when pressed against skin. Newer references use the name Brachyponera chinensis.
identification: The small workers are dark brown to black with lighter legs and mouthparts. Appearance overlaps several other ants, and a painful sting does not identify the species. Colonies may occupy several damp pieces of wood or sheltered places rather than one conspicuous mound. Photograph ants where they are active without putting a hand into the nest. A pest specialist can examine a safely obtained sample; deliberately testing whether an ant will sting or climb a container is unnecessary.
actions: Use thick gloves and tools when moving mulch, stored wood or debris in an affected area, and keep children and pets away from an active nest. If ants are entering a building or nesting beside a frequently used path, request identification and a targeted management plan. Treating every ant in a woodland would also remove native species, including seed dispersers. NC State notes that management is more realistic than simple eradication. Avoid improvised pesticides or disturbing several nests while searching for a queen; professional guidance is useful where sting exposure is likely.

claims: Native-ant effects, multiple damp nests and termite feeding
Gloves and management limits
Morphology, Brachyponera synonym and sting hazard

proposedDescription: Asian pigeonwings is a tropical vine with striking blue flowers that have pale centers. Its leaves are divided into oval leaflets, and flat pods follow the flowers. Widely known as butterfly pea, it is grown ornamentally and for flowers used to color foods and drinks. It can live as a perennial in warm climates, climbing over nearby supports and vegetation.

sources.title: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox: Clitoria ternatea
Singapore National Parks Board: Clitoria ternatea

researchNotes: NCSU horticultural guidance and Singapore NParks provide independently prepared plant accounts. Neither establishes widespread U.S. ecological harm; naturalization is explicitly local and no medicinal benefit or food preparation advice is offered.
previousDescription: Butterfly pea is a slender climbing vine best known for its large blue flowers, usually with a pale yellow center. Its leaves are divided into several oval leaflets, and the flowers give way to long, flattened pea pods. It is a perennial in warm climates and is also grown as a seasonal garden plant. The flowers have a long history as a blue food coloring. Cultivated vines sometimes grow wild in disturbed ground, but that alone does not establish harmful ecological effects.
identification: Look for a slender, trailing or climbing stem carrying leaves divided into oval leaflets. The large pea-shaped flowers usually have a blue outer face and a pale throat, although white and double-flowered cultivated forms exist. Flat pods follow the flowers. A photograph of the blossom alone can miss those variations, so include leaves, stems, and fruit. The plant can behave as a perennial in warm climates but is often grown as an annual where winters are cold.
actions: Keep garden plants supported and check around the planting for unwanted seedlings, particularly where a long warm season allows pods to mature. Collect unwanted pods before they scatter seed and keep garden waste out of natural areas. A cultivated butterfly pea does not automatically warrant removal: assess whether it is spreading beyond the intended bed and consult local planting guidance. Choose a locally appropriate replacement if repeated escapes occur. Ornamental identification is not a substitute for verifying the suitability of a plant intended for food.

claims: Trailing perennial habit, flower variants, cultivation and pod characters
Naturalized status in Singapore, tropical habitat and plant morphology

proposedDescription: Asian ponysfoot forms a low green carpet of small, rounded to kidney-shaped leaves. Its creeping stems root as they spread, while tiny greenish-white flowers sit close to the ground and are easy to miss. Fine hairs, especially beneath the leaves, help with identification. Despite the common name, Kew places its native range in the Caribbean. It has been grown as a lawn substitute and can occur among lawn grasses. Related Dichondra species look similar, and regional references warn that this scientific name has sometimes been applied inconsistently.

sources.title: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Dichondra micrantha

researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Kew independently accepts D. micrantha with Caribbean origin and US introductions; Zimbabwe's field flora supports its creeping, hairy-leaved morphology. The New Zealand warning is regional and does not invalidate the accepted species elsewhere. No occurrence mappings are changed or US harm inferred. Next: Keep local botanical checking and the regional naming warning.
previousDescription: Asian ponysfoot is a low, creeping plant with small kidney-shaped leaves. Its stems spread across the ground, forming a mat, and its tiny greenish to white flowers are easy to overlook. It has been used as a lawn substitute. Fine hairs and other small features help distinguish it from related Dichondra species; the common name alone is not a reliable guide to its native range.

claims: New Zealand name-use warning
Rooting stems, kidney-shaped hairy leaves and tiny pale flowers
Accepted species, Caribbean native range and US introductions

identification: Follow a creeping stem to see whether it roots at its joints and forms a low mat. The rounded to kidney-shaped leaves have a notch at the base, a relatively smooth upper surface, and hairs beneath. Flowers are tiny and pale greenish white, so a hand lens is useful. Related Dichondra can look very similar, and names used for lawn plants have changed or been misapplied. Include leaf undersides, stem joints, and flowers when asking a botanist to check the name.
actions: For a lawn planting, first decide whether the mat is wanted in that location. Trim or lift small unwanted patches with their rooted stems and watch the edge for renewed growth; do not move living runners into another garden or natural area. In a conservation site, obtain a local identification before clearing a patch that might belong to a different Dichondra. A lawn name used overseas may not identify a U.S. population reliably. Get that name checked before choosing a treatment or deciding that the patch is harming its surroundings.

proposedDescription: Asian shore crab has a square shell with three small teeth along each front side. Lifted rocks in the intertidal zone reveal the sheltered spaces it uses between tides. It eats both plant material and small animals, including shellfish. Native to the western Pacific, it has established along parts of the eastern United States. Some invaded rocky shores support dense populations, where its feeding and competition can affect other members of the shore community.

sources.title: Hobbs, Cobb and Thornber (2017): Injury, reproductive status, and distribution of Hemigrapsus sanguineus in Rhode Island

researchNotes: Smithsonian's synthesis supplies identification and invasion history. Hobbs, Cobb and Thornber's independent Rhode Island field study was accessed as an abstract and supports local numerical dominance, not a universal causal impact or removal result.
previousDescription: Asian shore crab has a square shell with three small teeth along each front side. It shelters beneath rocks in the intertidal zone and eats a variety of plant and animal foods. Native to the western Pacific, it has established along parts of the eastern United States. High numbers can compete with other crabs and affect the small animals living on rocky shores.

claims: Shell and claw characters, introduced range and shore habitat
Rhode Island population dominance and intertidal distribution

identification: Check the shell outline as well as its color. Asian shore crabs have a roughly square shell with three teeth along each front side edge, banded walking legs, and often reddish spots on the claws. Adult males have a fleshy swelling near the base of the movable claw finger. Color varies, so a mottled brown crab is not enough for identification. Photograph the shell from above and the claws without placing fingers within reach of a pinch.
actions: Record the shore location, date, approximate abundance, and whether the crabs were under rocks or on artificial structures. Send a suspected new-range observation to the local marine invasive-species program. Do not transport live crabs as bait or pets, and inspect wet gear before moving between shores. When looking under a rock, replace it carefully in its original position to protect the animals beneath. If removal is proposed on a popular beach, follow a coordinated local plan. Collecting crabs casually may disturb the shore without restoring its native community.

proposedDescription: Asian soybean rust is a fungal disease that can cause tan or reddish leaf spots and tiny spore-producing bumps, especially on leaf undersides. Wind carries the spores between living host plants, including soybean and kudzu. Warm areas with suitable hosts can help the fungus survive between crop seasons. Under favorable wet conditions, severe infections can cause early leaf loss and reduce seed production.

sources.title: North Carolina State Extension: Asian soybean rust
University of Minnesota Extension: Soybean rust

researchNotes: Independent NCSU and Minnesota extension accounts support obligate living-host biology, seasonal spread, symptoms and scouting. Regional disease pressure and current product decisions are deliberately left to local surveillance and extension advice; no diagnosis or pesticide recipe is supplied.
previousDescription: Asian soybean rust is caused by a fungus that lives in the tissues of soybean and other susceptible plants. It first shows as small tan or reddish-brown leaf spots, with tiny spore-producing pustules that are easiest to see under magnification. Wind can carry those spores over long distances, while living hosts such as kudzu help the fungus persist in warm regions. Wet, humid weather favors infection. Severe disease strips leaves and reduces seed production, although its importance varies greatly by place and season.
identification: Inspect leaves low in the canopy and turn them over. Rust begins as small tan or reddish-brown spots, with tiny raised spore-producing structures on the underside; advanced disease can bring yellowing and early leaf fall. These symptoms overlap with other soybean leaf diseases, so a field photograph alone may not settle the diagnosis. Record the crop stage and how symptoms are distributed across the field, and submit affected leaves through an extension diagnostic service when rust is suspected.
actions: Follow regional rust surveillance during the growing season, particularly when weather and nearby detections favor infection. Scout before making a treatment decision: windborne spores can arrive from outside the farm, while the fungus needs living hosts to persist. Ask an extension crop specialist whether a confirmed detection, crop stage, and local risk justify a currently labeled fungicide. Avoid treating every leaf spot as rust or relying on an old calendar recommendation. Keep scouting after any intervention, since protecting the remaining leaf canopy is the practical objective.

claims: Living-host dependence, wind spread and leaf symptoms
Defoliation, seasonal northern occurrence and disease recognition

proposedDescription: Asian spiderflower is a sticky, hairy annual with bright yellow flowers and leaves usually divided into five leaflets, though some have three. The slender stems can reach about three feet, with long, narrow seed pods developing among the upper leaves. Glandular hairs give the plant its noticeably sticky surface and help distinguish it from other yellow-flowered herbs. Older botanical accounts call it Cleome viscosa; this catalog retains Arivela viscosa for the same species.

sources.title: PlantNET NSW Flora Online: Arivela viscosa

researchNotes: PlantNET and NYBG's authored flora treatment agree on Arivela viscosa and the Cleome viscosa synonym. U.S. impact and control efficacy are not inferred from foreign occurrence. Prior NYBG monograph URL timed out: https://sweetgum.nybg.org/science/projects/osa/monograph-details/?irn=28433 . A verified NYBG taxon treatment replaces it.
previousDescription: Asian spiderflower is a sticky, hairy annual with yellow flowers and leaves often divided into five leaflets. Long, narrow seed pods develop along the stems, and plants can reach roughly three feet tall. The glandular hairs are a useful clue when distinguishing it from other yellow-flowered weeds. Older references use the name Cleome viscosa, while this catalog lists it as Arivela viscosa.

claims: Annual habit, glandular hairs, leaflets, yellow flowers and cylindrical capsules
Accepted Arivela name, morphology and disturbed habitats

identification: The sticky glandular hairs are a useful clue, but combine them with the flowers and leaves. Most leaves have three to five leaflets radiating from one point; the flowers are yellow and the narrow cylindrical fruits stand on stalks near the upper leaves. A mature plant can be about waist high under favorable conditions. Other spiderflowers share the divided leaves, so include the flower color, hairy stem, and a developed fruit in photographs rather than identifying from leaf shape alone.
actions: In a cultivated bed, remove a small unwanted annual before its long fruits mature and collect any ripe pods without shaking them over bare soil. Revisit the disturbed patch for seedlings and clean soil from tools before working elsewhere. For a population outside cultivation, record the habitat and ask a regional botanist whether it is introduced locally and whether intervention is warranted. Keep the response proportionate to the site: a volunteer in a vegetable bed and an unfamiliar plant in a wetland need different decisions, with local expertise guiding the latter.

proposedDescription: Asian swamp eels historically grouped as Monopterus albus have long, smooth, scaleless bodies, small eyes and greatly reduced fins. They breathe air and shelter in muddy wetlands, ponds and slow-moving waters, feeding on small aquatic animals. Research has revealed several genetically distinct forms within this group. This overview describes their shared biology; it does not establish the identity of individual U.S. populations. Florida records now assigned to M. javanensis should not automatically be attributed to M. albus.

sources.title: US Fish and Wildlife Service (2025): Asian Swamp Eel ecological risk screening summary
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Swamp Eels
Pintar et al. 2024: Asian swamp eels in Florida,1997-2023

researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where the current assessment differs: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Current FWC identifies established Florida eels as javanensis and cuchia, while FWS warns that the historical albus range is too broad. The unresolved US taxon assignment is material; shared swamp-eel biology and prevention cannot settle it. Next: Reidentify original US vouchers under the modern species treatment. Inherited reference not used as fresh substantive evidence (unavailable or superseded by the specified original): https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10228-009-0125-y . Inherited reference not used as fresh substantive evidence (unavailable or superseded by the specified original): https://pure.au.dk/portal/en/publications/high-blood-oxygen-affinity-in-the-air-breathing-swamp-eel-imonopt/ .

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: The inherited broad Monopterus albus usage can support a clearly labeled group overview without assigning Florida javanensis or cuchia records to restricted albus. The 2025 USFWS assessment explicitly retains the broad concept pending an accepted revision; the newly read original2024 Florida study differentiates named taxa and analyzes separate long-term field observations. The public draft already limits itself to shared group characters and prevention. Next step: Review the historical-group overview and keep exact US population crosswalks unresolved in occurrence metadata. Fresh access: Pintar et al. 2024: Asian swamp eels in Florida,1997-2023 [full_text; Pintar-2024-original-Florida-monitoring] https://www.matthewpintar.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/Pintar-et-al_2024_Asian-swamp-eels-Synbranchidae-Monopterus-in-Florida.pdf — Original27-year Florida distribution and hydrologic observations; taxonomic separation must accompany attribution of regional records. | USFWS2025 Asian swamp eel risk assessment [indexed_excerpt; USFWS-swamp-eel-synthesis] https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2025-06/ecological-risk-screening-summary-asian-swamp-eel-april-2025.pdf — Uses broad M. albus in absence of a universally accepted revision; this synthesis is not independent original confirmation of every cited Florida result. All inherited URLs remain retained in sources or the inherited notes. Previously accessed evidence is retained as provenance; only the accesses described here are claimed as fresh in this pass. No catalog IDs, occurrence mappings or public records changed. Local editorial review only; release remains deferred.
previousDescription: Asian swamp eel is an elongated fish with smooth, scaleless skin, small eyes and greatly reduced fins. It can breathe air and use muddy, low-oxygen habitats that challenge many other fish. It eats aquatic animals and has spread through trade and releases. The name Monopterus albus has covered a complex of related forms, so records under that name may need closer taxonomic review.

claims: Explicit historical broad-range taxonomic caveat
Uses broad M. albus in absence of a universally accepted revision; this synthesis is not independent original confirmation of every cited Florida result.
Florida javanensis and cuchia populations
Original27-year Florida distribution and hydrologic observations; taxonomic separation must accompany attribution of regional records.

identification: A swamp eel has a long, smooth body, small eyes, and fins that are greatly reduced compared with a typical fish. Those features can suggest the group, but they cannot securely distinguish the lineages once combined under Monopterus albus. Recent Florida accounts identify Sunda swamp eel, Monopterus javanensis, and cuchia, Ophichthys cuchia. Preserve the exact collection location and photographs of the head and whole body; a specialist may need a properly documented specimen or genetic evidence to resolve the name.
actions: Never release a live food-market fish or aquarium animal into a ditch, pond, or canal. Report an unfamiliar eel-like fish to the state fisheries agency and follow its instructions about documentation and handling; do not carry it alive to another waterbody. Avoid assigning Florida impact reports automatically to this exact catalog name. Prevention is useful despite the taxonomic uncertainty, but a control plan requires the local population's identity, extent, and agency guidance rather than an assumption that draining or casual trapping will eliminate it.

proposedDescription: Asian swordfern has long, arching fronds made up of many narrow leaflets. Flat, dark brown scales on the leaf stalks are among the features used to distinguish it from similar ferns. It can form dense stands in sheltered places and spreads through spores. In Florida, introduced populations can displace native vegetation, making accurate identification important where several swordferns grow together.

sources.title: University of South Florida: Florida Invasive Plants, Nephrolepis brownii
University of Florida: Distinguishing native and non-native sword ferns
UF/IFAS sword fern identification guide PDF

researchNotes: USF FLIP and UF/IFAS support Florida identification and invasion context. UF's PDF was read directly after the HTML redirect failed; both URLs are preserved. FLIP's generic seed wording is not repeated for this spore-producing fern. Control is limited to UF-supported careful removal and follow-up.
previousDescription: Asian swordfern forms tall, arching fronds lined with many closely spaced leaflets. The dark brown, flat-lying scales on mature frond stalks are useful clues when comparing it with similar native swordferns. It grows in sheltered places and can form dense stands; Florida botanists have documented it displacing other vegetation. Because several native and introduced ferns share the same familiar garden names, an identification should include the stalk scales and leaflet details. Like other ferns, it reproduces by spores rather than seeds.
identification: Examine a mature leaf stalk with a hand lens: Asian sword fern has dense dark brown scales pressed against it, with paler scale margins. Short stiff hairs occur on the central veins of its leaflets. Florida's native sword ferns can look similar from a distance, and the common name Boston fern does not resolve the species. Tubers point instead toward tuberous sword fern, Nephrolepis cordifolia. Photograph the stalk scales and leaflet undersides before removing an unfamiliar fern from a natural area.
actions: In Florida, replace confirmed Asian sword fern near natural habitats with an appropriate native fern. For a small patch, wear heavy gloves and lift the plants carefully; broken underground parts can remain and produce new growth. Recheck the patch instead of considering a single clearing complete. Contain removed plants and dispose of them through an accepted local waste route, never along a woodland edge. Large or mixed fern colonies deserve experienced help so native plants are retained and any treatment follows current site-specific guidance.

claims: Florida occurrence, origin and identification
Regional invasive assessment
Stalk scales, native lookalikes, gloves, regrowth and disposal precautions

proposedDescription: Asian tapeworm is a parasite that lives in the intestines of freshwater fish. It infects carp, minnows and many other hosts, and can reduce growth or harm young fish. Moving infected fish, including bait, can help it reach new waters. It is not identified by the fish's appearance alone; examining the parasite or using genetic methods is needed to distinguish it reliably.

sources.title: USGS: Asian fish tapeworm detection study
Rave et al. (2025): Asian fish tapeworm in Parodon magdalenensis

researchNotes: The USGS-hosted original 2021 assay abstract supports transport risk and documented host effects; it is not represented as a deployed commercial test. The independent Colombian host study was accessed in full text. No human disease inference or unsourced fish-treatment regimen is included.
previousDescription: Asian fish tapeworm is a parasite that lives inside the intestine of freshwater fish. Carp and minnows are well-known hosts, but researchers have found it in many other kinds of fish too. It is usually hidden from casual observation; identification uses the worm's attachment structures and, increasingly, DNA tests. Infections can interfere with growth and are especially concerning in young fish. Moving infected fish, including live bait, can carry the parasite into new waters and connect an aquaculture problem with native-fish conservation.
identification: This parasite lives inside a fish, so a thin body or poor growth is a reason to investigate, not an identification. The tapeworm requires examination of its structures, and molecular methods can support a diagnosis. It has also appeared in older literature as Bothriocephalus acheilognathi. An independent Colombian study documented it in Parodon magdalenensis, illustrating that its host range extends beyond carp. Keep the host species, collection waterbody, date, and any fish movements with a diagnostic submission.
actions: Do not release aquarium fish or unused live bait, and do not transfer fish from a suspect pond to another waterbody. Fish growers should consult a fish-health professional before stocking or moving a lot with unexplained poor performance. Ask the receiving laboratory how it wants samples collected and transported; an unplanned shipment can compromise identification. A research assay is not automatically an available field test. Any treatment or stocking decision should follow professional diagnosis and current fish-health requirements, with special care around waters supporting vulnerable native fishes.

claims: Fish host effects, infected baitfish transport and experimental molecular detection
Independently documented Parodon host and morphological/molecular diagnosis

proposedDescription: Asian tiger mosquito is black with white-banded legs and a single white stripe down its back. It bites during the day and breeds in small water-filled containers such as tires, buckets and plant trays. Eggs laid just above the waterline can survive dry periods. That combination has helped this Asian species travel with goods and establish around homes in many other regions.

sources.title: University of Florida IFAS: Asian tiger mosquito
CDC: Life Cycle of Aedes Mosquitoes
EPA tips to prevent mosquito bites

researchNotes: UF's verified indexed account supplies distinctive adult morphology and container biology, but its dated medical-risk language is not used. CDC life-cycle and prevention guidance support egg persistence and weekly source reduction. No clinical diagnosis or current outbreak claim is made.
previousDescription: Asian tiger mosquito is a small black mosquito with white-banded legs and a single white stripe down its back. Females often bite during the day, especially around morning and late afternoon. Its young develop in small water-filled spaces such as tires, buckets, and flowerpot trays, while eggs attached just above the waterline can survive drying. Native to Asia, it has traveled widely with human commerce. Its close association with homes makes ordinary containers important places to understand and interrupt its life cycle.
identification: Look for a single pale stripe running down the top of the dark thorax, together with conspicuously banded legs. Photograph the back as well as the legs because several mosquitoes have pale leg markings. The aquatic larvae develop in small water-holding containers, including pots, tires, and plant cavities. Eggs can remain on container walls through a dry period and hatch when water rises. An adult's appearance can help identify the mosquito, but cannot show whether that individual is carrying a pathogen.
actions: Once a week, empty and scrub items that collect water, turn unused containers over, and cover stored water securely. Refresh animal water responsibly rather than leaving animals without it. Check gutters and small items hidden in vegetation as well as obvious buckets. Use EPA-registered repellent according to its label, wear protective clothing, and maintain window screens. Persistent mosquito problems can be reported to the local mosquito-control program. Bite avoidance is worthwhile without assuming that a sighting proves a local disease outbreak.

claims: Single dorsal stripe, banded legs and container breeding
Egg persistence and aquatic development
Weekly emptying and scrubbing, screens and water storage
Registered repellent and clothing precautions

proposedDescription: Asian tiger shrimp is a large shrimp with bold bands across its body. Young animals use estuaries and mangroves, while adults breed in marine waters and feed near the bottom, often at night. Native to the Indo-Pacific and widely farmed for food, it has been found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. Its presence raises questions about effects on native species, which require local evidence.

sources.title: FAO: Cultured aquatic species fact sheet, Penaeus monodon

researchNotes: FAO's original culture account supports life stages, morphology and habitat; Smithsonian supplies independently documented U.S. catch history. Smithsonian's summary and detailed text differ about breeding certainty, so no categorical establishment claim is made. U.S. ecological effects remain potential rather than demonstrated in the cited account.
previousDescription: Asian tiger shrimp is a large coastal shrimp with alternating dark and pale bands across its body. Young shrimp use estuaries and mangrove areas, while adults breed in marine water and often feed at night over the bottom. Native to the Indo-Pacific, it is widely raised for food and has appeared in other coastal regions, including U.S. Atlantic and Gulf waters. Its size and predatory diet raise questions about interactions with local shrimp and other animals; those concerns should be separated from demonstrated effects at a particular site.
identification: The broad dark and pale bands across the abdomen are conspicuous, but body color varies with the surroundings and size. Adults can become much larger than many familiar local shrimp; juveniles are less obvious and may need specialist examination of the rostrum and other structures. Take a clear side photograph with a scale, showing the head and abdomen. Note whether the animal came from an estuary or offshore catch, since young and mature tiger shrimp use different coastal habitats.
actions: Report an unusual tiger shrimp catch to the state marine fisheries or aquatic invasive-species program with the capture location, date, approximate depth, and size. Follow its instructions if a specimen is needed. Never release live farmed or aquarium shrimp, or move a catch alive to another waterbody. Aquaculture operations should use approved stock and prevent escapes through their established biosecurity procedures. Your report helps agencies track whether populations persist and spread. Include an honest count of the catch rather than assuming that one animal represents an established population.

claims: U.S. capture history and lack of reported ecological impacts
Morphology, coastal life stages and aquaculture biology

proposedDescription: Asian waterwort is a tiny, creeping herb of wet mud and shallow water. Its delicate, branching stems carry small leaves and can produce roots at the joints, helping it spread over damp ground. Field observations describe it in rice fields, irrigation channels and other persistently wet cultivated places. It closely resembles other waterworts, especially Elatine triandra. The stalks beneath its flowers and fruits, together with other small botanical details, are more reliable identification clues than its low-growing shape alone.

sources.title: INRAN / RECA Niger: Note sur Elatine ambigua
Flora of North America: Elatine ambigua

researchNotes:
Flora Zambesiaca was verified through an indexed excerpt after Kew follow-up returned 403; INRAN/RECA provides independent Niger field observations. Added a verified FNA account for U.S. occurrence, identification and introduction pathways. Actions are bounded to identification and preventing movement; tested U.S. control efficacy is not claimed.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.
previousDescription: Asian waterwort is a tiny, creeping plant of wet mud and shallow water. Small leaves and flowers grow along its delicate stems, often making it inconspicuous among larger wetland plants. It occurs in places such as rice fields and river margins. Several waterworts are similar, so flower and seed details can be important when deciding whether a record truly belongs to this species.

claims: Diagnostic fruit stalk comparison with E. triandra
Rooting stems, wet cultivated habitat and Niger field observations
Detailed morphology, U.S. introduced records and aquarium confusion

identification: Look very close to the mud surface for small branching stems with opposite leaves and roots emerging at the joints. Flower and fruit stalks are important: this species can have conspicuous little stalks beneath its fruits, unlike some close waterwort lookalikes. A useful record includes a magnified view of a flowering or fruiting stem, a scale, and the water depth. Elatine triandra is a frequent source of confusion, including in the aquarium trade, so an overall photograph of a green mat may be insufficient.
actions: Keep aquarium plants, sediment, and rinse water out of streams, ponds, and irrigation channels. At a rice field or wetland, document the patch before disturbing it and ask a botanist to confirm the species. Clean clinging mud and vegetation from field equipment before moving to another site. A patch in an irrigated crop and one in a natural wetland may call for different responses. Its presence alone does not show how much it affects the surrounding plants. A removal or water-management plan should await local advice rather than relying on a treatment developed for another aquatic weed.

proposedDescription: Asiatic clam has a rounded, roughly triangular shell marked by strong concentric ridges, usually yellowish to brown. It filters tiny particles from freshwater and can also feed on organic material in the sediment. Rapid growth and reproduction can build dense populations that alter food and nutrient conditions. Large numbers may clog water intakes. Effects on native mussels vary among places, so the presence of this clam alone does not establish why a native population has declined.

sources.title: Farrell, Nierzwicki-Bauer and Rose (2024): ASSEMBLE, Asian clams section, pp. 30-32

researchNotes: Smithsonian's synthesis and the Darrin Fresh Water Institute's original Lake George studies provide distinct evidence lineages. The 2024 ASSEMBLE report was read at its Asian-clam section. Name complexity is acknowledged without changing the catalog ID, and temporary barrier mortality is not presented as lasting eradication.
previousDescription: Asiatic clam is a freshwater clam with a rounded, roughly triangular shell marked by strong ridges. Shells range from yellowish to brown. It filters particles from the water and can reach high densities, changing food and nutrient conditions and competing with native mussels. Large populations may also clog water-intake equipment, making it important to both aquatic ecosystems and water infrastructure.

claims: Shell morphology, lineages and variable ecological effects
Anchor sediment transport and unsuccessful lasting control with benthic barriers

identification: Look for a thick, rounded triangular shell with closely spaced, raised concentric ridges. Shell color ranges from yellowish to brown, and the inside may differ among populations. Native fingernail clams and young mussels can be confused with small specimens, so photograph both valves with a ruler and ask for confirmation. The name Corbicula fluminea has been used provisionally for several introduced genetic lineages; shell appearance alone cannot resolve that history. Empty shells document occurrence, but not necessarily a living population at that moment.
actions: Remove sediment from anchors and other equipment before leaving an infested waterbody, then follow local cleaning, draining, and drying instructions. Lake George researchers found that anchor mud could carry clams, making this an especially useful place to check. Report suspected new populations with location and shell photographs; do not move live clams as bait or aquarium animals. Avoid laying improvised bottom barriers over a patch. Lake George trials reduced clams temporarily but also harmed other bottom-dwelling organisms, and populations later returned.

proposedDescription: Asiatic dayflower opens vivid blue flowers that usually last only a day. Each flower has two large blue petals and a much smaller pale one. Its leaves wrap around the stems, which can take root where they touch the ground. Native to East Asia, it grows in disturbed places and can become a crop weed, spreading through patches of moist, suitable soil.

sources.title: Iowa State University Extension: Asiatic dayflower
North Carolina State Extension: Asiatic dayflower

researchNotes: Iowa State's weed account and NCSU's independently prepared horticultural account support the flower, sheathing leaf and rooting-stem characters. Local garden or crop management is framed around early removal and follow-up; no universal invasive designation or blanket resistance claim is retained.
previousDescription: Asiatic dayflower is a sprawling annual whose bright blue flowers open for only a day. Two large blue petals sit above a much smaller pale petal, while smooth, pointed leaves wrap around the stem in a sheath. Stems touching the ground can root and help a patch spread. Originally from eastern Asia, it now grows in fields, gardens, and other disturbed places. It can compete with crops or nearby vegetation, and its ability to survive some common herbicides makes correct identification useful.
identification: Visit in the morning to see the flower before it fades: two broad blue petals sit above a much smaller pale petal. The pointed leaves clasp the stem in a sheath, and sprawling stems may root where they meet moist soil. Other dayflowers can share the blue color, so record the unequal petals, the folded flower bract, and a leaf base. A plant without open flowers is still identifiable, but photographs of the whole patch alone are less useful than these close details.
actions: In a small garden patch, lift unwanted plants while they are young and collect the trailing stems as well as the original root system. Pieces left against damp ground may remain a problem, so do not pile them at the edge of the bed. Recheck shaded, moist corners where plants were previously established and prevent new seed production. In a crop, confirm the identification with an extension adviser before selecting a weed program. Tolerance to particular herbicides should not be generalized to every product or every population.

claims: Two large blue petals, small pale petal and sheathing leaves
Annual habit, moist-site growth and vegetative rooting

proposedDescription: Asiatic dock has large lower leaves and upright flowering stems that rise above the surrounding vegetation. It grows along rivers, in meadows and in disturbed ground, where seeds and spreading underground stems can help it form patches. Research in Central Europe found that light and shallow burial strongly influenced seedling emergence, helping explain establishment in gaps and disturbed soil. It has expanded in parts of Europe, but those regional findings do not establish its effects in every place it occurs.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Weed risk assessment for Rumex confertus
Kolodziejek and Patykowski (2015): Effect of Environmental Factors on Germination and Emergence of Invasive Rumex confertus in Central Europe

researchNotes: APHIS is a risk assessment rather than proof of present local harm or treatment efficacy. Its account uses field references independent of the original Kolodziejek and Patykowski germination study, whose abstract supports light and burial responses. Lifecycle labels conflict, so neither perennial nor biennial is asserted. The qualified profile does not promise control efficacy.
previousDescription: Asiatic dock is a perennial with large lower leaves and tall flowering stems. It grows in places such as river margins, meadows and disturbed fields. Both seeds and spreading roots can help it establish dense patches. It has expanded in parts of Europe outside its earlier range, where its size and persistent root growth can make established stands difficult to displace.

claims: Rhizome spread, regional occurrence and uncertainty of impacts
Experimental light and burial effects on germination

identification: A large basal rosette and tall dock-like flowering stalks are starting clues, not a final identification. Several Rumex species produce broad leaves and dense fruiting stems. Photograph the lowest leaves, the junctions of leaves and stems, and mature fruits, keeping a scale in view. A local flora or botanist may need fruit characters to separate this species from familiar docks. The size of a patch can reflect both seedling recruitment and underground spread, rather than a single unusually large plant.
actions: Mark the edge of a suspected patch and avoid moving its soil or mature seed heads to another site. Where identification is confirmed, seek a regional weed specialist's advice before disturbing a riverside stand or prescribing a crop treatment. Germination experiments show that exposed, shallowly buried seeds benefit from light, so unnecessary soil disturbance can create recruitment opportunities; restore suitable cover after any agreed removal. For a U.S. site, confirm both the plant and the reason for intervention locally; a spreading European population is useful context, but cannot determine the outcome in another landscape.

proposedDescription: Asiatic garden beetle is a small, cinnamon-brown beetle with a rounded shape resembling a coffee bean. Adults hide during the day and feed on leaves at night. Underground, the pale, C-shaped grubs feed on roots and can damage seedlings. Introduced from Asia, it occurs in the United States, where the larvae have also become a concern in some corn-growing areas.

sources.title: University of Maine Extension: Asiatic garden beetle
MSU: Asiatic Garden Beetle in Michigan field crops
MSU: Asiatic garden beetles and corn field yield losses

researchNotes: Maine verifies current Maladera formosae usage and adult/larval recognition; older MSU work uses the garden-beetle common name and provides independent corn observations. The lowercase prior PDF URL returned 403: https://www.canr.msu.edu/fieldcropsent/uploads/files/02agb.pdf . The verified uppercase PDF replaces it; old geographic limits are omitted.
previousDescription: Asiatic garden beetle is a small cinnamon-brown scarab with the rounded shape of a coffee bean. Adults hide during the day and emerge at night to chew leaves; their pale, C-shaped grubs feed underground on roots and young seedlings. Both stages use many garden and crop plants. Introduced from Asia, it has caused damaging infestations in some U.S. corn fields as well as landscapes. This two-part life cycle explains why ragged foliage and weak seedlings can point to the same insect.
identification: Look for a small, rounded cinnamon-brown adult at night or sheltering near plants during the day. It is much smaller than many familiar June beetles. A pale C-shaped grub with a brown head is only a scarab-family clue: several root-feeding beetles look that way. Correct larval identification requires examination of mouthparts and the pattern of hairs near the rear end. If seedlings are declining in patches, compare roots and soil from affected and healthy areas rather than assuming every grub is this species.
actions: Check vulnerable garden plants after dusk to connect fresh feeding with the actual beetle. In a field with a history of grub damage, arrange preplant scouting with an extension crop adviser and preserve records of affected patches. Michigan observations show that severe root injury can precede obvious stand loss, and a later spray is not a dependable rescue. Do not treat a whole lawn merely because an adult came to a light. Base any management on the identified life stage, crop or planting, and current local recommendations.

claims: Current name, adult size and grub identification requirements
Original observations of corn stand loss
Patchy root damage, early scouting and limitations of rescue treatment

proposedDescription: Asiatic witchweed is a parasitic plant that attaches to the roots of grasses, including crops such as corn and sorghum. Its narrow, hairy leaves and small flowers appear above ground, while the connection to its host remains hidden below. Seeds can persist in soil for a long time. That persistence helps explain the long-running monitoring and control efforts around infestations in the Carolinas.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Witchweed biology and eradication program assessment
Southern Illinois University: Striga asiatica in the U.S.A.

researchNotes: APHIS supplies program biology and containment context; SIU hosts independent original photographs and observations of host attachment and self-pollination. Historical program documentation is distinguished from current regulations. Actions prioritize reporting and avoiding soil movement, with no unauthorized destruction or pesticide recipe.
previousDescription: Asiatic witchweed is a small flowering plant with narrow leaves, coarse hairs, and flowers that may be red, yellow, white, or purple. Much of its effect begins before it appears above ground: the young plant attaches to grass roots and draws resources from its host. Crops such as corn and sorghum can be badly weakened. Its dustlike seeds can remain in soil for years, which is why introduced populations in the Carolinas have required persistent monitoring and control rather than a single season of weeding.
identification: The above-ground plant is relatively small, with stiff, hairy stems, narrow leaves, and small flowers that can vary in color. Its most important feature is hidden: a specialized connection joins its roots to a grass host. A stressed corn plant beside a small flowering weed is worth documenting, but stress alone is not diagnostic. Photograph the suspect plant in place, including leaves and flowers, and note the associated crop. Do not dig through a suspected infestation simply to expose the attachment.
actions: Report a suspected U.S. occurrence promptly to state plant-health officials or USDA APHIS and leave soil and plants in place while awaiting instructions. Avoid carrying soil, crop residue, or seed from the suspect area on equipment or footwear. The very small seeds and their persistence make an isolated-looking patch a poor candidate for casual pulling followed by normal field traffic. Follow the current official survey and containment plan, including instructions for equipment and field access. Old accounts of the Carolinas program cannot tell you which restrictions apply to a particular property today.

claims: Parasitism, tiny persistent seeds and official eradication context
Original host-attachment and reproductive observations

proposedDescription: Asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle with pale spots and reddish edges. Both adults and grayish larvae feed on asparagus. Dark eggs are often laid upright on the plant, and feeding can scar spears or strip foliage. It differs from the orange, spotted asparagus beetle, so noticing the adult's color pattern helps connect damage with the correct species.

sources.title: University of Wisconsin Vegetable Entomology: Asparagus beetle
University of Minnesota Extension: Asparagus beetles

researchNotes: Wisconsin's vegetable-entomology account independently supports species differences and damage timing; Minnesota provides garden monitoring, hand removal, beneficial-insect conservation and dead-fern sanitation. No threshold or pesticide concentration is copied, and the two asparagus beetles are not conflated.
previousDescription: Common asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle marked with pale spots and reddish edges. Both adults and their plump grayish larvae feed on asparagus, while rows of upright, dark eggs may be visible on the spears. Feeding can scar the edible shoots and damage the leafy summer growth that supports the next crop. The orange, black-spotted asparagus beetle is a different species. Checking the adult's markings and the affected plant parts helps connect a beetle sighting with the damage in a garden.
identification: Check emerging spears and, later, the ferny growth on a warm afternoon. Common asparagus beetles are dark bluish to brown with cream markings; the spotted asparagus beetle is orange with black dots. Rows of dark upright eggs on spears and grayish, wrinkled larvae with dark heads support the identification. Spotted-beetle larvae mainly use the berries, so finding that species does not imply the same foliage damage. Keep adults, eggs, and larvae separate in your observations to understand which stage is active.
actions: In a small asparagus bed, handpick adults and larvae into soapy water and remove eggs from spears. Keep checking because new adults can fly into the bed. Allow useful predators and tiny parasitoid wasps to remain, and avoid unnecessary broad treatments that kill them. Remove old fern growth only after it has turned completely brown, taking that debris out of the growing area. If injury remains substantial, consult current asparagus-specific guidance; any labeled pesticide must respect harvest intervals and the plants' flowering period.

claims: Adult and larval differences, eggs and crop injury
Handpicking, sanitation timing and protection of natural enemies

proposedDescription: Asparagus fern is a flowering plant with fine, feathery-looking growth. The narrow green structures that resemble leaves are modified stems; its true leaves are much smaller. True Asparagus densiflorus has upright, closely branched growth, with small white to pinkish flowers that can develop into red berries. It grows naturally on sandy ground in southeastern Africa. Garden names are often mixed with Asparagus aethiopicus, so an arching plant sold as a Sprengeri asparagus fern may represent that related species instead.

sources.title: University of Wisconsin Extension: Asparagus fern, Asparagus densiflorus
PlantNET NSW Flora Online: Asparagus aethiopicus
Bishop Museum 2024: Misapplied names in the Hawaiian introduced flora
Wong et al. 2022: three Asparagus chloroplast genomes

Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where the current assessment differs: Fresh review 2026-10-31: The 2024 Bishop specimen review finds all examined wild Hawaiian densiflorus to be aethiopicus; PlantNET independently separates the names. This directly affects historic US occurrence interpretation. Wisconsin's mixed horticultural concept cannot resolve it. The Bishop Museum original specimen review supports the habit distinction. Next step: Review the true-species profile; leave historical Hawaii records and cultivar labels for their own specimen audit.
