previousDescription: Asparagus fern has fine, feathery-looking growth, but it is a flowering plant rather than a true fern. What look like tiny leaves are modified stems. Small pale flowers can be followed by red berries, and cultivated forms range from upright plumes to arching sprays. Names are sometimes confused with the related Asparagus aethiopicus, so garden labels alone may not establish the exact species.

claims: Horticultural name mixing and general cladode/berry appearance
Aethiopicus versus true densiflorus distinction
All examined wild Hawaiian densiflorus specimens reassigned; upright dense versus sprawling loose growth

New Hong Kong specimens K.H.Wong092,107,109 and genomes MZ337394,MZ337395,MZ424304; author discussion distinguishes growth habits but recommends cultivar-only Myers naming because species assignment is uncertain.

identification: First establish which asparagus fern the plant actually is. A recent Bishop Museum specimen review separates upright, densely arranged Asparagus densiflorus from the weakly sprawling Asparagus aethiopicus previously recorded under its name in Hawaii. Nursery labels and familiar cultivar names may not follow that distinction. Photograph the whole plant's posture, stem branching, clusters of green leaf-like structures, flowers, and berries. A botanist may need more than a photograph to resolve a garden plant, especially when published horticultural accounts combine the names.
actions: Keep an uncertain plant contained while its identity is checked, and collect unwanted berries before they are spread beyond the garden. Do not dump root masses or potting soil into natural areas. In a region where asparagus ferns escape, ask a local invasive-plant specialist which species is present and which removal approach fits the site. Do not transfer impact reports for sprawling A. aethiopicus to true A. densiflorus automatically. A correctly named plant makes local advice much more useful, especially when deciding whether a contained garden specimen or an escaping patch needs action.

proposedDescription: Aspen leafblotch miner spends its larval life inside the leaves of aspens and cottonwoods. Young larvae feed on sap, while later stages remove internal leaf tissue and leave a visible blotch. Silk can draw the mined area into a raised fold. The insect also pupates within its mine before emerging as a tiny moth. These altered patches on leaves are often easier to notice than the adults; a leaf mine still needs careful identification because other insects make similar marks.

sources.title: Pacific Northwest Insect Management Handbook: Poplar-Aspen leafblotch miner
Tozlu, Hayat and Ozbek (2002): Phyllonorycter apparella, a new record and a new pest of trembling aspen in Turkey

researchNotes: The PNW handbook provides practical cultural management and mining behavior; Tozlu and colleagues provide an independent original Turkish life-history study accessed as an abstract. Generation number and seasonal dates vary geographically. Feeding on poplar is not treated as proof that the moth is introduced or invasive locally.
previousDescription: Aspen leafblotch miner spends its larval stage inside the leaves of aspens and cottonwoods. Early feeding uses sap, while later feeding removes internal leaf tissue and produces a visible blotch. Silk can draw the mined area into a raised fold. The adult moth is tiny, so the pale, altered patches on leaves are often a more noticeable sign than the insect itself.

claims: Mine structure and small-plant cultural management
Original observations of larval feeding stages and pupation

identification: Inspect both sides of an affected aspen leaf. A blotch between the leaf surfaces, sometimes drawn into a raised fold by silk, points toward a leafminer, while open holes or chewing along the edge suggest another kind of injury. This moth is tiny and easily overlooked. Larvae and pupae inside a mine can help an entomologist distinguish it from other miners. Record the host tree, season, and whether the mines are scattered or widespread; a single mine does not establish the scale of injury.
actions: On a small tree, remove a few confirmed infested leaves when practical, as the Pacific Northwest handbook recommends, while leaving enough healthy foliage for the tree. For an established tree, monitor the extent and recurrence of mining rather than stripping the crown. Seek a local tree-health assessment if repeated heavy injury accompanies declining growth. The Turkish study describes a particular regional life cycle; its timing should not be copied as a spray calendar elsewhere. Planting a locally suitable, less susceptible tree may be preferable where serious infestations recur.

proposedDescription: This asthmaweed, Conyza bonariensis, is an annual or short-lived plant with narrow, hairy, gray-green leaves. Its many small flower heads release seeds carried by fine, fluffy hairs. Originally from South America, it grows in fields, orchards and along roads in other regions. Wind dispersal helps it reach newly disturbed ground, where a small plant can develop into a much-branched seed producer.

sources.title: University of California IPM: Hairy fleabane
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Conyza bonariensis

researchNotes: UC IPM supplies the practical horseweed comparison and California weed context; PlantNET independently verifies morphology and the Erigeron bonariensis synonym. The common name asthmaweed is not used to imply a health effect. Management emphasizes early seed prevention without claiming uniform herbicide resistance or ecological harm.
previousDescription: Hairy fleabane, also called asthmaweed, is a fast-growing annual or biennial with narrow leaves and a covering of grayish hairs. Branching stems carry many small flower heads that develop fluffy, wind-carried seeds. It grows in orchards, fields, roadsides, and other open, disturbed places. Native to South America, it has become a widespread agricultural weed elsewhere, where it competes for water and other resources. Its hairy foliage and branching pattern help separate it from similar fleabanes, though close comparisons are often needed.
identification: Young hairy fleabane and horseweed can be difficult to tell apart. Look for gray-green, often crinkled leaves and a mixture of short stiff hairs and longer soft hairs. Mature hairy fleabane tends to branch lower on the stem, while horseweed usually branches mainly above. The small flower heads have no showy daisy-like rays and later become pale fluffy seed heads. Photograph the stem base, leaves, hairs, and mature heads; height alone is unreliable because growing conditions change the size of the plant.
actions: Remove small unwanted plants before the fluffy seed heads form, preferably while the root system is still easy to lift. In orchards and other repeatedly disturbed sites, check the margins and gaps as well as the main planting rows, since windborne seeds can arrive from outside. Keep useful ground cover where it suits the crop and site. A mature seed-bearing patch requires care to avoid scattering seed during work. For persistent agricultural problems, seek a locally appropriate integrated weed program instead of assuming all populations respond alike to a herbicide.

claims: Hair types, branching and horseweed comparison
Flower heads, dispersal structures and synonymy

proposedDescription: Asthmaweed develops upright, leafy stems carrying many tiny flower heads in a broad, branching cluster. Narrow leaves and the nearly hairless bracts around the heads help distinguish this species from some similar fleabanes. Its small fruits carry fine, pale bristles. It grows in disturbed places, including roadsides and river margins. Modern treatments place Conyza floribunda in Erigeron as Erigeron floribundus; older records sometimes mix it with E. sumatrensis, so those records need a name check.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Erigeron floribundus
Liendo et al. (2021): Annual weedy species of Erigeron in the northern Iberian Peninsula: a review

researchNotes: Current floras and Liendo's original specimen revision resolve Conyza floribunda as Erigeron floribundus. Older E. sumatrensis concepts require screening of historical records, but do not block the qualified current identification profile. Liendo was verified as an indexed excerpt. No regional impact or treatment result is borrowed across the names. Blocked prior Kew reference retained for provenance: https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/60473415-2 .
previousDescription: Conyza floribunda is one of several plants called asthmaweed. It starts with leaves near the ground, then develops leafy stems carrying many small flower heads. Fine bristles help its seeds travel on the wind. Records include openings in coastal live-oak habitat in Texas. References may place these plants in Conyza or Erigeron, making scientific-name cross-checks useful when comparing information about them.

claims: Bract hairiness, branching and synonymy
Independent voucher review separating four species and documenting European spread

identification: Look for a tall, branching flower cluster that retains a strong central axis, with numerous small heads and narrow leaves along the stems. The bracts immediately surrounding the heads are mostly hairless, an important contrast with some other weedy fleabanes. A hand lens and mature flowering material are much more useful than a distant photograph. Erigeron sumatrensis has repeatedly been confused with this plant in older records, so record the name used by the identification source as well as the plant's location.
actions: If it is an unwanted plant in a cultivated bed, remove it before the heads release their fine-bristled seeds, collecting mature heads carefully. Check nearby disturbed ground for additional plants and avoid spreading seed with moved soil or garden waste. For a natural-area or agricultural infestation, have a specimen checked before importing management advice attached to another Conyza name. For a U.S. site, confirm the current name and the local reason for intervention. Similar appearance and overlapping older names can otherwise lead to a treatment aimed at the wrong fleabane.

proposedDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen tree with fine, jointed-looking branches and tiny, scale-like leaves. Its deep roots and tolerance of dry, salty conditions have made it useful for shelter plantings. Outside cultivation, it can spread along waterways. In parts of Australia, dense stands have altered river habitats and soil conditions, showing how a tree valued for protection from wind can become a problem in the wrong setting.

sources.title: Oregon State University Landscape Plants: Tamarix aphylla

researchNotes: Oregon State supplies morphology and drought/salt tolerance; Queensland independently documents regional waterway effects and spread. Added NSW's current guidance for seedling removal and follow-up. Older Oregon reproductive wording is not generalized globally, and no tamarisk biocontrol claim is transferred between species.
previousDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen shrub or tree with a spreading crown and fine, jointed branchlets. Its tiny leaves hug the twigs, and clusters of pale pink to white flowers appear among the foliage. Deep roots and tolerance of drought and salty soils made it useful for shade and shelter in dry landscapes. It can also escape cultivation. In parts of Australia, dense riverbank infestations have altered water flow and soil salinity, illustrating why a hardy planted tree can become a management concern in some settings.
identification: The foliage can resemble a she-oak or a conifer from a distance, but the tiny leaves closely sheath slender, jointed twigs. Small pinkish-white flowers occur in narrow clusters, and older trunks develop rough, furrowed bark. Casuarina produces woody cone-like fruits, while athel tamarisk has small seed capsules. Photograph a flowering twig and the trunk as well as the overall tree. Do not assume that the impact or reproductive behavior of another saltcedar species applies unchanged to this large tree.
actions: Check planted trees near drainage lines for young plants and report spread into waterways to the local land manager. Where removal is appropriate, small seedlings are easier to address than established trees with extensive roots. Mature riverbank trees need a planned approach that considers access, bank stability, regrowth, and replacement vegetation. Avoid dumping cut branches where floods can carry them away. Queensland's documented river impacts support careful prevention in susceptible places, but Australian restrictions and treatment instructions should not be treated as U.S. rules.

claims: Twig, bark and flower characters; drought tolerance
Australian river impacts, seed and plant-part spread
Small seedling removal and follow-up around waterways

proposedDescription: Atlantic ivy is an evergreen vine that can carpet the ground or climb trees. Young growth has lobed leaves, while mature flowering growth has less-divided leaves and produces fruit eaten by birds. Stems can also root as they spread. Introduced populations in the Pacific Northwest can dominate forest ground cover and add weight to trees. It is closely related to, but distinct from, English ivy.

sources.title: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: English and Irish ivy

researchNotes: Oregon State's independently produced management guide and Washington's cultivar-specific listing both explicitly include Irish/Atlantic ivy. Shared Hedera traits are used only within those accounts. The text avoids identifying H. hibernica from leaf shape alone or treating every ornamental cultivar as equally regulated.
previousDescription: Atlantic ivy, often called Irish ivy, is an evergreen climbing vine that can also make a thick carpet across the ground. Young shoots carry lobed leaves; flowering shoots have less-divided leaves and produce berries. Rooting stems expand a patch locally, while birds can carry seeds farther away. In invaded Pacific Northwest woodlands, dense ivy can cover native understory plants and add weight to trees. It closely resembles English ivy, and the species or cultivar should be confirmed when interpreting local weed guidance.
identification: Separate the juvenile and adult growth before comparing leaves. Ground-running shoots usually have lobed leaves and root along their stems; flowering shoots higher on a support carry less-lobed leaves and later dark fruits. English ivy and Atlantic ivy are difficult to separate confidently from one leaf, and cultivar names add another complication. Use a regional key or specialist when the exact name affects a report. In the Pacific Northwest, the management concern is especially clear where ivy is covering native ground vegetation or climbing trees.
actions: Wear gloves and protective clothing, then pull small ground patches carefully when soil is moist, collecting rooted stems. On a tree, cut accessible vines without cutting the bark and clear the lower stems; leave high attached vines to die rather than pulling down material from the canopy. Keep removed stems from touching moist soil and rooting again. Revisit for seedlings and resprouts over subsequent seasons, and restore appropriate ground cover. Large trees, steep slopes, or extensive mats may require an experienced crew.

claims: Pacific Northwest impacts, removal and follow-up
Explicit H. hibernica inclusion, growth stages and safe tree-vine removal

proposedDescription: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny sap-feeding insect that uses many host plants, including citrus and ivy. Its dark, oval immature stages sit on leaves and are easier to examine with magnification. Plants moved through trade can carry it between locations. A California assessment reported no significant known impacts at that time, so detection should be distinguished from evidence of serious damage.

sources.title: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Aleuroclava aucubae assessment
Seljak (2012): Six new alien phytophagous insects recorded in Slovenia
Seljak: Aucuba whitefly diagnostic figure and context

researchNotes: CDFA provides California detection and a dated impact assessment; Seljak's original record supplies an independent regional lineage. The paper abstract was accessible but its species section timed out; author-uploaded indexed figure context supplies diagnostic detail and is grouped with that study. Identification and prevention advice do not imply that regional treatment is necessary or proven.
previousDescription: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny plant-feeding insect found on a wide range of trees and shrubs, including citrus, ivy, and ornamental evergreens. Its immature stages stay on leaves; the late immature cases are small, dark, and oval, and reliable identification requires magnification. Trade in infested plants can move it between regions. California's 2022 assessment reported no known significant economic or environmental damage there, while European observations likewise found limited injury. Finding the insect and demonstrating damage to its host are separate questions.
identification: Turn over leaves and examine the tiny dark oval cases with magnification. Mature immature stages are well under a millimeter long and can look like small scales or specks rather than obvious whiteflies. Color and host plant are insufficient because other whiteflies also have dark cases. Reliable identification commonly relies on slide-mounted specimens examined by an insect diagnostic laboratory. Photograph the colony and record the host plant, but ask the laboratory how to collect material before clipping and shipping leaves.
actions: Inspect new nursery plants, especially leaf undersides, before placing them among established plants. Keep a suspect plant separate while identification is arranged and avoid giving away cuttings carrying the insects. Record actual yellowing or growth changes separately from the number of whiteflies, since a detection does not itself demonstrate damage. CDFA's 2022 assessment reported no significant known California impacts at that time. A pesticide decision should therefore follow identification and a current local assessment, not a treatment schedule borrowed from a more damaging whitefly.

claims: California records and no significant reported impact in 2022
Original Slovenian alien-species record
Small dark puparia and need for slide-mounted identification

proposedDescription: Australasian geranium is a low-growing herb with hairy, rounded leaves divided into lobes. Its small pink flowers have paler centers and usually appear singly or in pairs. Thickened roots support the plant in moist places such as gullies, creek margins and forested ground. The modest flowers and creeping or spreading growth can make it less conspicuous than familiar garden geraniums.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Geranium homeanum
Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Geranium homeanum

researchNotes: PlantNET and L.P. Smith's independent Victorian treatment were checked, the latter through substantive indexed text. PlantNET allows annual or perennial habit; the overview uses low-growing herb. Native Australian context is preserved, and unverified U.S. impact or treatment efficacy is not asserted.
previousDescription: Australasian geranium is a low, sprawling perennial with coarse hairs and rounded leaves cut into several broad lobes. Small flowers, pink toward the tips and paler at the base, appear singly or in pairs. A thickened, branching root supports growth from season to season. In Australia it is associated with moist places such as creek banks, wet gullies, and forest margins. Its modest flowers and leaf shape help distinguish it from the more conspicuous plants commonly sold as garden geraniums.
identification: Look for rounded to kidney-shaped leaves divided into broad lobes, with smaller divisions toward their tips. Coarse hairs cover the spreading stems, and the modest flowers are pink fading toward a pale center. Flowers occur singly or in pairs rather than in the showy rounded clusters of many cultivated Pelargonium. A complete record should include fruit as well as petals and leaves. Other small native geraniums can overlap in appearance, and the Victorian flora reports hybridization with related species.
actions: Where it belongs to the native vegetation, leave a healthy patch in place and avoid disturbing moist creek margins merely because the plant looks weedy. In a garden, identify unwanted volunteers before lifting them, and keep removed roots and seed-bearing material within an appropriate garden-waste system. A record outside its expected range is best documented with photographs and reviewed by a regional herbarium. A U.S. observation needs local assessment rather than an automatic invasive label. Keep a record of whether the plant persists or spreads beyond its original patch.

claims: Leaf divisions, hairs, flowers and moist-site habitat
Independent morphology, native status and hybridization warning

proposedDescription: Australian backyard mosquito has white-banded legs, a pale ring on its mouthparts and lyre-shaped markings on its back. It breeds in small water collections, including tree holes and containers around homes. Adults may bite during the day in shaded places. Originally associated with Australasia, it has also been detected in California, where container habitats can provide suitable places for it to reproduce.

sources.title: Northern Territory Department of Health: Common mosquitoes, Aedes notoscriptus
Santa Barbara Mosquito and Vector Management District: Australian backyard mosquito
EPA tips to prevent mosquito bites

researchNotes: Northern Territory health guidance supports distinctive morphology and dry-resistant eggs; Santa Barbara's district provides independent local detections and household prevention. EPA prevention guidance supports repellent use. Australian vector information is not converted into a California disease claim or veterinary treatment recommendation.
previousDescription: Australian backyard mosquito is a dark mosquito with white-banded legs, pale lyre-shaped markings on its back, and a white ring around the middle of its long feeding tube. Its young use tree holes and rain-filled containers, including plant trays, buckets, and drains. Females bite people and other animals, sometimes during the day in shade. Recent detections in California show how this adaptable mosquito can become a neighborhood concern. Its markings matter because it closely resembles other introduced Aedes mosquitoes.
identification: The pale band around the middle of the proboscis is especially helpful when separating this species from the similar-looking yellow fever mosquito, Aedes aegypti. Both can have lyre-like pale markings on the thorax and banded legs. A clear photograph of the head and back is more useful than a blurred image of the legs alone. Larvae occupy small water collections, and eggs laid just above the waterline can survive drying. Identification does not tell whether a mosquito is infected with a pathogen.
actions: Look for water in plant saucers, clogged yard drains, buckets, toys, and other small containers. Empty and scrub reusable containers weekly, and restore drainage where practical. Do not damage tree cavities while trying to remove a natural breeding place; obtain appropriate professional advice. Use label-directed mosquito repellent and protective clothing, and report suspected new detections to the local vector-control district. If concerned about a pet's mosquito exposure, consult its veterinarian. California detections do not establish local transmission of the diseases associated with this mosquito elsewhere.

claims: White proboscis band, lyre markings, container habitats and egg persistence
Local detections, lookalike comparison and weekly container sanitation
Label-directed repellent and protective clothing

proposedDescription: Australian brake is a fern with large fronds divided into many narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short base, and lines of spore-producing structures form along the undersides of the leaf edges. It grows naturally in Australasian forest and stream habitats and is also cultivated. Looking beneath a mature frond can reveal features that are less obvious from its overall shape.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Pteris tremula
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Pteris tremula

researchNotes: Two independently authored botanical treatments support morphology and native habitat, and New Zealand's flora notes California naturalization. Neither demonstrates U.S. ecological impact or species-specific control efficacy. The qualified identification and prevention profile retains regional native status and avoids extrapolated toxicological or grazing advice.
previousDescription: Australian brake is a large, lacy fern whose fronds divide repeatedly into narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short, scaly base, and the fronds can move delicately in a breeze. Lines of spore-producing structures run near the underside edges of fertile segments. It grows in sheltered forest, streamside, and garden settings and has been cultivated beyond its Australasian range. Looking beneath a frond provides useful identification details that are easy to miss when seeing only its feathery outline.
identification: Follow the branching of a frond: it is divided several times into narrow final segments, giving a delicate lacy appearance. The shiny brown stalk and marginal lines of spore-producing tissue are useful supporting features. In the New Zealand flora, Pteris epaleata is a close visual comparison, but its veins join into a network whereas P. tremula has free veins. Photograph the underside of a mature frond and the base of the plant; overall frond size changes too much to identify it alone.
actions: Retain it where it is part of the local native flora, and do not collect wild plants for garden use. With a cultivated fern, watch for volunteers around pots and damp sheltered beds and avoid dumping rooted plants or potting material into bushland. If a new population is found outside its expected range, document the location and obtain a fern specialist's identification. Naturalization is recorded in California, but that fact alone does not establish ecological damage or justify applying an invasive-fern control method developed for another species.

claims: Venation, marginal sori, P. epaleata comparison and range
Frond and stalk morphology and native habitat

proposedDescription: Australian cheesewood is an evergreen tree with glossy, wavy-edged leaves and fragrant white flowers. Orange capsules open to expose sticky seeds that birds can carry away. Native to eastern Australia, it has become weedy in some places outside its natural range. Its attractive foliage and scent explain its garden use, while bird-dispersed seeds help it move beyond planted sites.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Pittosporum undulatum

researchNotes: Stanford provides direct local tree observations and VicFlora independently supports species morphology and native Victorian occurrence. Follow-up access to VicFlora's regional expansion text failed, so no detailed range boundary or U.S. ecological impact is asserted. General garden containment is not presented as tested eradication.
previousDescription: Australian cheesewood, or sweet pittosporum, is a shrub or tree with glossy leaves edged in gentle waves. Fragrant creamy-white flowers are followed by orange to yellow-brown capsules that open around sticky seeds. Birds help move those seeds away from planted trees. Although native to parts of eastern Australia, it has spread beyond its earlier range and become an environmental weed in some Australian forests and coastal scrub. Its familiar garden appearance can therefore mean different things depending on the local setting.
identification: The glossy leaves are usually gathered toward branch tips and have noticeably wavy margins. In flower, the small creamy-white clusters are strongly fragrant; later, yellow-orange capsules open to expose sticky orange seeds. Those fruit and flower characters help distinguish it from other glossy evergreen trees used in gardens. The common names Victorian box and sweet pittosporum may refer to the same species. Include fruit, a leafy twig, and the whole tree in a record, since leaf waviness alone is not decisive.
actions: Check beneath nearby shrubs, trees, and fence lines for volunteers from a garden specimen, and remove unwanted young plants before they become established. Keep fruiting branches and garden waste out of natural vegetation. Before removing a mature tree, establish whether it is native to that locality and whether local guidance regards it as an escape problem. A substantial tree requires an arborist's assessment and an appropriate replacement plan. In a U.S. natural area, document seedlings and their spread before deciding on broader work. A planted tree and a growing stand of volunteers present different management questions.

claims: Fragrant flowers, orange capsules and sticky seeds
Native status, leaf and flower morphology

proposedDescription: Australian eelgrass is a freshwater plant with long, ribbon-like leaves rooted in the bottom. It spreads through runners and can form dense underwater beds. Female flowers reach the surface, and their stalks coil after pollination. Despite the common name, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations occur in places including California's Delta, where its underwater growth can change the structure of aquatic habitat.

sources.title: California Department of Parks and Recreation: Ribbon weed identification
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Vallisneria australis

researchNotes: California's agency sheet documents Delta occurrence and diagnostic features; PlantNET supplies an independent botanical treatment, runners and historical misapplied names. The text avoids marine-seagrass confusion and does not borrow impact or herbicide results from other Vallisneria. Reporting and transport prevention are the actionable scope.
previousDescription: Australian eelgrass, also called ribbon weed, is a freshwater plant with long, strap-shaped leaves rising from the sediment. Underground runners connect neighboring plants into tall underwater meadows. Small female flowers reach the surface on slender stalks, which coil back underwater after pollination. Despite the name eelgrass, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations have been documented in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, where distinguishing it from other ribbonlike aquatic plants helps track changes in submerged vegetation.
identification: Look for broad ribbon-like leaves rising in a tuft directly from the sediment, with rounded tips and visible lengthwise veins. Long, bare flower stalks can reach the water surface and later coil below it. Several Vallisneria share this general shape, and older names such as V. americana or V. gigantea have sometimes been misapplied to Australian plants. Record leaf width, tip shape, flowers, and location. A drifting leaf fragment alone may not be enough to distinguish this species from a native aquatic plant.
actions: At a suspected new site, photograph the bed from a safe position and report it to the local aquatic-plant program. Remove attached vegetation from boats, trailers, and gear before transport, and never release aquarium plants into freshwater. Avoid raking, cutting, or dredging a bed on your own: underwater work can disturb habitat and spread material without providing lasting control. California's Delta identification sheet supports early recognition there; any treatment should follow a coordinated site assessment that confirms the species and protects other submerged plants.

claims: Delta records, leaves and coiling female flower stalks
Stolon growth, floral details and misapplied names

proposedDescription: Australian fingergrass is easiest to recognize by its little windmill-shaped seed heads. Usually six to nine slender branches spread almost horizontally from the top of a stem, with the florets turning dark as they mature. Narrow leaves form a low, dense clump beneath flowering stems that can reach about knee height. Native to Australia, it grows on varied soils and flowers in response to rain. The detached seed heads can tumble in the wind, helping scatter seed.

sources.title: PlantNET NSW Flora Online: Chloris truncata
NSW Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development: Windmill grass

researchNotes: PlantNET and independently authored NSW agronomy guidance supply morphology, rain-responsive growth and tumbling seed-head dispersal. Both are Australian evidence, and no U.S. ecological impact or treatment outcome is inferred. The agronomy page was verified through substantive indexed text after direct follow-up timed out.
previousDescription: Australian fingergrass has a seed head shaped like a small windmill, with narrow branches spreading outward in a roughly horizontal plane. It forms low clumps with narrow leaves, and the flowering branches darken as they mature. Native to Australia, it responds to rainfall and grows on a range of soils. The spoke-like head is its clearest feature when seen among other grasses.

claims: Windmill head, mature dark florets and low crown
Rain-dependent growth, native habitat and detached-head dispersal

identification: Study a mature seed head from above and below. Its slender branches radiate from one point, while the small flowering units sit in rows along their undersides and darken when ripe. The low crown, narrow leaves, and roughly horizontal branches help distinguish it from taller windmill-like grasses, but several Chloris species look similar. Preserve photographs of the leaf-stem junction and an intact head with a scale. If a precise identification matters, a grass specialist should examine the spikelets.
actions: In its Australian native range, this grass can be a useful colonizer rather than a target for removal. At an unwanted garden or cultivated-site occurrence, prevent mature heads from blowing into adjacent ground and avoid transporting seed-bearing soil or clippings. Check the area after favorable rain, when new growth may become conspicuous. A record elsewhere should be reviewed against a regional flora before intervention. At a U.S. site, document where it is growing and whether it persists, then choose a response with local advice. A familiar Australian grass name does not settle those questions.

proposedDescription: Australian lovegrass is a loosely tufted perennial with narrow leaves and open, branching flower heads. Small, layered flower clusters sit along the fine branches, and hairs near the leaf joints can help with identification. It is native to eastern and southeastern Australia, where it grows in woodland and pasture settings. It should not be confused with other lovegrasses that have different ranges and impacts.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew GrassBase: Eragrostis leptostachya
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Eragrostis leptostachya

researchNotes: Kew GrassBase was verified in indexed text after direct follow-up was blocked, and PlantNET was read in full. These independent botanical treatments have different exact floret ranges, so only concordant characters are used. No ecological or treatment claims are transferred from other Eragrostis species.
previousDescription: Australian lovegrass, also known as paddock lovegrass, is a slender perennial that grows in loose tufts. Narrow leaves sit below an open, branching flower head made of many small, neatly stacked spikelets. A tiny fringe of hairs where the leaf meets the stem provides another identification clue. Native to eastern and southeastern Australia, it occurs in woodland and native pasture. Several unrelated concerns are attached to other plants called lovegrass, so the scientific name matters when deciding what a local observation means.
identification: Look for a loose clump with very narrow leaves and an open spray of small, many-flowered spikelets. A short fringe of hairs occurs where the leaf blade meets its sheath, and small rings of glands can be useful under magnification. These are specialist characters: a fine, airy seed head alone does not distinguish it from other lovegrasses. Photograph the whole flowering stem, leaf junction, and individual spikelets with a scale. Counts and measurements vary among treatments, so avoid relying on one floret count.
actions: Keep the native Australian context in mind before treating a paddock or woodland grass as an invader. If it is unwanted in a planted bed, prevent seed-bearing material from being moved with soil and seek an identification before broader removal. For an apparent occurrence outside its expected range, a local herbarium can check mature material and advise whether documentation or management is appropriate. For a U.S. occurrence, keep the response local and measured. Management advice for African lovegrass should not be applied simply because both grasses share a common-name ending.

claims: Tufted habit, hairy ligule, gland rings and open panicle
Independent morphology and woodland/native pasture habitat

proposedDescription: Australian redcedar can become a very large rainforest tree, with leaves divided into pointed leaflets and new growth often tinged red or pink. Older trees develop rough bark and may have broad buttresses at the base. Woody fruits release winged seeds. Its valuable timber led to extensive historical logging, and trees growing in open sites can look quite different from tall forest-grown specimens.

sources.title: Australian National Botanic Gardens: Toona ciliata
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Toona ciliata

researchNotes: ANBG's authored cultivation account and PlantNET's independent flora treatment support tree size, compound leaves, fruit and habitat. The unrelated palms reference already excluded from the prior draft remains excluded. This is a bounded cultivation/identification profile, without an unsupported U.S. invasion or disease-treatment claim.
previousDescription: Australian redcedar is a large deciduous rainforest tree with long leaves divided into many pointed leaflets. New foliage can flush reddish pink, while mature trunks develop scaly bark and substantial buttress roots. Small pale flowers are followed by woody capsules that release winged seeds. Its rich-colored, workable timber made it historically valuable and led to extensive logging in Australia. The shape also changes with its surroundings: forest trees can grow tall and straight, while open-grown trees develop broader spreading crowns.
identification: Unlike the conifers also called cedar, this tree has broad compound leaves made of many leaflets. Look for pointed leaflets with uneven bases, often reddish new growth, and dry woody capsules that split to release winged seeds. Mature forest trees may develop prominent buttresses, while open-grown trees can have a much broader shape. A seedling or bare winter twig can be less distinctive, so include a complete leaf, bark, and fruit in photographs. The Australian flora describes it as deciduous.
actions: Allow enough space for a very large tree before planting, with attention to buildings, paths, and the eventual root system. Use well-drained soil and local horticultural advice rather than assuming that a rainforest tree suits every warm garden. Retain established native trees where appropriate and have structural concerns assessed by an arborist. Watch cultivated specimens for unwanted seedlings near the planting and remove those early. Its timber value and ability to produce windborne seeds do not, by themselves, show that it is invasive at a particular U.S. site.

claims: Mature size, buttresses, woody fruits and well-drained soil
Deciduous habit, asymmetric leaflets and fruit morphology

proposedDescription: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, often blue-green, with a distinctive red patch on the claws of mature males. It comes from northern Australia and nearby regions, using streams, lakes and seasonally changing waters. Widely farmed for food, it can escape cultivation. It eats a variety of plant and animal material, making its establishment relevant to the waters and species it encounters.

sources.title: Joyce and Pirozzi: Stable-isotope study of farmed redclaw diet
Australian Government: Freshwater Pest Field Guide, redclaw

researchNotes: Queensland aquaculture guidance, an original Joyce/Pirozzi farm study, and the northern-Australia government field guide were independently checked. The study was verified through its indexed abstract and introduction after PDF follow-up timed out. Native-range and management rules remain geographically bounded; no food-safety claim is made.
previousDescription: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, usually mottled blue-green. Mature males have a soft, bright red patch along the outer edge of each large claw, a useful identification clue. It uses tropical streams, lakes, and billabongs in its native northern Australian range and is also farmed for food. It eats a varied diet that includes naturally occurring pond organisms and plant material. Movement for aquaculture has taken it beyond its home waters, where escaped populations can interact with local species.
identification: A mature male's soft red patch along the outer edge of each large claw is a useful clue, together with a mottled blue-green body. Females and young animals may lack that obvious male feature, so absence of the patch does not rule the species out. Take photographs of the whole animal and claws from a safe distance, with a size reference. Color alone is unreliable among aquarium crayfish. Females carry developing eggs and young beneath the abdomen, giving a single transported animal potential reproductive significance.
actions: Never release a pet, live food animal, or farmed redclaw into a stream or pond, and do not move a wild catch between waters. Report a suspected new population to the local fisheries or biosecurity agency and follow its handling instructions. Farms should maintain their approved escape-prevention and water-management systems, including after heavy weather. Native and introduced status differs even within Australia, so check local rules rather than assuming one rule applies everywhere. When reporting wild animals, include their abundance and habitat so fisheries staff can assess the population. Farm behavior alone cannot show what is happening in that waterbody.

claims: Native region, breeding, egg brooding and water-management needs
Farmed redclaw use both pond production and supplemental food
Male claw marking and region-specific introduced status

proposedDescription: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading plant that can form a mat over dry or salty ground. Its gray-green leaves have a fine coating, especially beneath, and its seed-bearing structures become fleshy and red. It has been planted for forage and erosion control. Animals can spread its seeds, and it has established outside cultivation in places including coastal California.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew: Atriplex semibaccata, Flora of Iraq and Flora of Tropical East Africa
California Invasive Plant Council: Australian saltbush

researchNotes: Kew-hosted Flora of Iraq/East Africa descriptions were verified by indexed text; Cal-IPC's authored California report was read directly. California occurrence and impacts are not generalized nationally. Its seed-bank duration is explicitly unknown, and chemical extrapolations from kochia/Russian thistle are excluded.
previousDescription: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading perennial that can form broad mats above a deep woody root. Small gray-green leaves often look dusted underneath, and the seed is enclosed in fleshy reddish structures. Native to Australia, it was introduced elsewhere for uses including forage and erosion control. It tolerates dry and salty ground and has colonized disturbed coastal habitats in California. Animals can carry its seeds, helping explain how a plant close to the ground can establish new patches some distance away.
identification: Look close to the ground for spreading stems with small alternate leaves, greener above and often noticeably scurfy beneath. The reddish structures around the seeds are enlarged fleshy bracts, not ordinary berries, and can dry to a more angular shape. Many native saltbushes share gray foliage, so a fruiting specimen is more useful than leaf color alone. Photograph the bracts and leaf undersides with a scale, especially in a coastal habitat where removing the wrong saltbush could disturb native vegetation.
actions: In an affected California site, hand-pull small confirmed plants before they produce seed, taking care around neighboring vegetation. Revisit the patch because seeds already in the ground can produce new plants. Collect fruiting material rather than scattering it while working, and avoid moving contaminated soil into an uninfested area. Large or sensitive coastal patches should be assessed with the land manager before clearing. If hand removal is impractical, obtain current local advice for this saltbush and habitat. A chemical program intended for another salt-tolerant weed may be inappropriate around coastal native plants.

claims: Prostrate form, leaves and distinctive fruiting bracts
California spread, animal dispersal and early manual removal

proposedDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers and persistent woody seed capsules. Older plants may have twisted trunks and textured bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it has been planted as a screen and windbreak and has become invasive in some other regions. Newer botanical references may list it as Gaudium laevigatum rather than Leptospermum laevigatum.

sources.title: Australian National Botanic Gardens: Leptospermum laevigatum

researchNotes: Stanford's observed tree account and ANBG's independent species account support morphology, garden use and regional escapes, without establishing U.S. control efficacy. ANBG says seeds are not retained on the shrub, so persistent woody capsules are not described as a long-lived canopy seed bank. Gaudium is a cross-reference only.
previousDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers, and flat-topped woody seed capsules. Older plants can develop wonderfully twisted trunks and shaggy bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it tolerates salt spray and has been planted as a screen or windbreak. It has also naturalized beyond its original range and become weedy in some regions. Recent botanical treatments may use Gaudium laevigatum, so both names are helpful when matching observations with planting records or identification guides.
identification: The broadest part of each small gray-green leaf lies toward its tip. White flowers are followed by squat woody capsules, and old specimens often develop strikingly twisted trunks with rough, fibrous bark. These features help separate it from other plants called tea tree, including the narrower-leaved New Zealand tea tree. Include a leafy twig, flower or capsule, and bark when requesting identification. The newer name Gaudium laevigatum may appear in a modern flora, while older garden records retain Leptospermum.
actions: Check whether the tree is native to the locality or is spreading from a planting before deciding on removal. In a garden outside its native range, watch nearby open ground for seedlings and do not dispose of capsule-bearing cuttings in natural vegetation. Replace an escaping screen with a locally appropriate species. A mature windbreak or dune planting needs professional planning before clearing, especially where its roots and canopy affect shelter or stability. For a U.S. planting, ask a local specialist whether the tree is producing an unwanted stand and what follow-up would be needed before undertaking major removal work.

claims: Twisted bark, leaf shape, capsules and newer generic name
Coastal origin, cultivation and regional naturalization

proposedDescription: Australian tortoise beetle is a rounded brown beetle, often mottled with darker marks, that feeds on eucalyptus. Adults and larvae chew the leaves, leaving curved or semicircular notches along the edges. Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath loose bark during the day, a habit also documented in Chilean field collections. Introduced populations occur in California. Established, well-cared-for trees often tolerate feeding, although heavy defoliation can add stress; finding beetles does not by itself show how seriously a tree is affected.

sources.title: UC Integrated Pest Management: Eucalyptus tortoise beetles
Villablanca and Villablanca Miranda (2022): Trachymela sloanei field record in Chile

researchNotes: UC IPM supplies California injury and management context; Villablanca and Villablanca-Miranda's original Chilean collection provides independent morphology and bark-shelter observations. Both were read substantively. The combined UC account is used carefully, without transferring another beetle's commercial-foliage damage claims to T. sloanei.
previousDescription: Australian tortoise beetle is a rounded brown beetle associated with eucalyptus. Adults and larvae feed on leaves, often leaving curved or semicircular notches along the edges. Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath bark during the day. Introduced populations occur in California. Mature trees can often tolerate some feeding, so the presence of beetles and the severity of damage should be assessed separately.

claims: Notched leaves, tree tolerance, cultural care and natural enemies
Original specimen diagnosis and eucalyptus bark shelter

identification: Examine fresh chewing along eucalyptus leaf margins and look for rounded, mottled brown adults. The Chilean study describes a strongly domed body with darker patches; specimens were collected beneath bark on eucalyptus. Other tortoise beetles can make similar notches, so the damage alone is not a species diagnosis. Photograph an adult and the affected leaves, and note whether the injury is restricted to a few shoots or widespread. Do not peel sound bark from a tree just to search for insects.
actions: Assess the tree's overall condition before treating damaged leaves. Established eucalyptus often tolerate this feeding, and appropriate watering and growing conditions can matter more than an insecticide. Preserve natural enemies and ask an arborist or extension service to investigate substantial or repeated defoliation, especially when other pests or drought are also present. Avoid moving infested nursery trees or bark material to new areas. An accurate identification is useful because a combined eucalyptus-beetle guide may discuss several species with different behavior and importance.

proposedDescription: Australian tubeworm lives inside a hard, pale tube attached to a submerged surface. A feathery crown reaches into the water to collect tiny food particles, then withdraws into the tube when disturbed. It favors sheltered brackish places such as estuaries, lagoons and docks. Many generations can build tangled, reef-like colonies, although reefs do not form everywhere it occurs. It also grows on boat hulls and structures. Despite its common name, an Australian native origin remains uncertain.

sources.title: Richards (2008), Marine Biological Association MarLIN: A fanworm

researchNotes: Smithsonian and Richards's MarLIN review are separate substantive syntheses with overlapping classic references and additional independent biological literature. The native range remains unknown; the common name is not origin evidence. Practical advice focuses on fouling transport and reporting, not an unsupported eradication method.
previousDescription: Australian tubeworm builds hard, pale tubes in brackish water. A feathery crown extends from each tube to collect food, while large colonies can form reef-like structures on submerged surfaces. It also grows on boats and marine infrastructure, which can help it travel. Despite its common name, its original native range is uncertain; the name should not be treated as proof of an Australian origin.

claims: Unknown origin, introduced occurrences and conditional reef formation
Tube and operculum morphology, brackish habitat and feeding

identification: Look for many thin, hard tubes with growth rings on a submerged surface. When the worm is extended, a small feathery crown projects from the opening; a specialist may examine the spiny plug used to close the tube. Other tube-building worms can look much the same when withdrawn, so an empty white tube is not enough for a secure identification. Photograph a living colony in place and record salinity context, substrate, and whether it is a thin coating or a substantial reef-like mass.
actions: Inspect hulls, buoys, and other immersed equipment before moving them between estuaries, and use an approved cleaning facility that contains removed fouling. Do not scrape a suspected colony into a new waterbody. Report a possible new occurrence to the local marine invasive-species program, especially on equipment about to be relocated. Large accumulations on infrastructure may need coordinated maintenance, while removing a naturalized reef can affect organisms using it. The species' uncertain origin and variable reef formation make a site assessment more useful than a blanket removal rule.

proposedDescription: Australian waterbuttons is a small, low-growing plant with finely divided leaves and tiny flower heads that look like buttons. The heads are cream to pale yellow and lack the showy outer petals of many daisies. Slender stems may lie along the ground or turn upward, and can root where they touch suitable soil. Look for it in lawns, roadsides, open grassland and other disturbed places. Its modest size can make the button heads easier to notice than the plant beneath them.

sources.title: PlantNET NSW Flora Online: Cotula australis
Kew-hosted Flora of Tropical East Africa (2005): Cotula australis

researchNotes: PlantNET and the independently authored Flora of Tropical East Africa agree on divided leaves and button heads; Kew's substantive treatment was accessed as an indexed excerpt. Lifecycle and native-range treatments vary, so neither is narrowly asserted. Lawn occurrence is not equated with ecological harm; routine garden advice is conditional on confirmed identity.
previousDescription: Australian waterbuttons is a small plant with finely divided leaves and tiny, cream to yellow flower heads that resemble buttons. The heads lack the showy outer petals of many familiar daisies. Stems can root where they touch suitable ground. Native to Australia and New Zealand, it also occurs in lawns, roadsides and other disturbed places elsewhere, often remaining close to the soil surface.

claims: Low habit, node rooting and rayless heads
Independent leaf and head morphology

identification: The tiny button heads stand on slender stalks above finely divided, somewhat fern-like leaves. They lack a ring of showy ray petals, and the plant commonly remains close to the ground. Examine the head and the leaf outline together: a small yellow button alone could belong to another daisy-family plant. A magnified photograph should show the bracts beneath the head, divided leaf segments, and the creeping or ascending stem. Rooting at stem joints can help a low patch persist.
actions: In a lawn or garden, decide whether the small patch is actually interfering with the intended planting before removing it. If unwanted, lift the connected stems and any rooted joints, collect flowering material, and check again for regrowth or seedlings. Avoid carrying soil from a confirmed patch into a conservation planting. In a natural area, obtain a local identification first because other small button daisies may be native. For a U.S. natural-area record, confirm the name and local significance before expanding the work. A small lawn weed is not automatically a threat to the surrounding habitat.

proposedDescription: Austrian pine has stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees are often roughly pyramid-shaped, while older trees develop broader crowns, deeply furrowed bark and brown cones. Native across parts of Europe, northwestern Africa and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles and mature bark are useful features when comparing it with other planted pines.

sources.title: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox: Pinus nigra

researchNotes: NCSU and Oregon State provide independently authored horticultural descriptions, although NCSU embeds an Oregon teaching video. Textual morphology and native range were compared separately. NCSU supports disease susceptibility but no treatment or diagnosis is inferred; the profile does not label all cultivated pines invasive.
previousDescription: Austrian pine is a substantial evergreen with stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees form a dense pyramid, while older trees develop a broad, rounded or flattened crown above stout branches. Brown cones point outward from the shoots, and mature bark becomes deeply furrowed. Native across parts of southern Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles are a practical first clue, while cone and bark details help distinguish it from other pines.
identification: Count needles at their base: they occur in bundles of two and are stiff, dark green, and sharply tipped. Mature cones are brown and relatively stout, and the trunk develops dark, deeply divided plates of bark. Other two-needle pines can be similar, so compare buds, cones, needle length, and bark rather than using needle count alone. Garden cultivars may be narrow, dwarf, or unusually colored, which makes the typical broad adult crown a useful clue but not a requirement.
actions: For an existing landscape tree, focus on its health and fit with the site. Provide space, sunlight, and drainage, and seek local advice before adding another specimen to a small yard. Brown needles or dying shoot tips deserve a diagnosis because this pine is susceptible to several diseases and insects; appearance alone does not identify the cause. Remove unwanted seedlings early where they spread beyond a planting. A planted Austrian pine is not automatically an invasive problem, and a mature tree should not be felled without a clear site reason.

claims: Needles, cones, site requirements and disease susceptibility
Independent tree morphology, cultivars and broader native range

proposedDescription: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial with small, four-petaled yellow flowers and toothed leaves that clasp the stem. Rounded seed pods follow the flowers. It can spread through both seeds and creeping roots, allowing patches to expand in damp fields, pastures and river margins. In parts of the western United States, dense growth can compete with other vegetation, including desirable pasture plants.

sources.title: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Austrian fieldcress

researchNotes: Burgenland Flora was verified through substantive indexed text and Washington's species account directly supports regional competition and vegetative spread. Hybrid complexity is acknowledged. Current treatment selection is referred to local expertise; no unsupported root-fragment control trial or nationwide regulatory claim is supplied.
previousDescription: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial in the mustard family, with small four-petaled yellow flowers and toothed leaves that partly clasp the stem. Its nearly round seedpods help separate it from mustards with long, narrow pods. It grows along moist riverbanks and in disturbed places such as pastures, roadsides, and fields. Creeping underground roots allow a patch to expand as well as spread by seed. In parts of the western United States, it competes with desirable forage and native vegetation.
identification: Follow the yellow flowers to the mature fruits: the nearly round pods are more useful than flower color for distinguishing this plant from many other mustards. Upper leaves partly clasp the stem, while lower leaves may have short stalks. Other yellowcresses and their hybrids can be difficult to separate, so include developed pods and several leaf positions in a record. A dense patch may be connected below ground by creeping roots, even when the visible stems look like separate plants.
actions: Avoid moving soil or root pieces from a confirmed patch into clean fields or stream margins. Mark its boundary and monitor for shoots beyond the visible edge. Because underground growth can persist after the tops are removed, a single mowing or pulling session should not be assumed to solve the problem. Ask a regional weed coordinator for a plan suited to the crop, pasture, or waterside habitat, and restore useful vegetation after control. Keep management claims local: Washington documents competition, while the European flora also describes native populations.

claims: Clasping leaves, globular pods, native regional context and hybrids
Pasture competition, creeping roots and local management referral

proposedDescription: Autumn olive is a spreading deciduous shrub with silvery foliage, fragrant pale flowers and small red fruits dotted with pale scales. Native to Asia, it was widely planted in the United States for landscaping and erosion control. Birds and small mammals carry its seeds into fields, roadsides and woodland edges. Its roots can add nitrogen to the soil, helping it grow on poor ground. In North Carolina and other affected regions, dense growth can crowd surrounding vegetation.
identification: Turn a leaf over to see the pale, silvery underside, then compare the speckled red fruits and small, fragrant flowers. Leaves occur alternately along the twig and have smooth edges that can look slightly wavy. Some branches bear sharp spines. Other silver-leaved shrubs, especially other Elaeagnus species, can be confused with it, so photographs should include both leaf surfaces and ripe fruit. Seedlings beneath bird perches or along a field edge may be the first sign that a nearby planting is spreading.
actions: Where autumn olive is invasive, stop planting or distributing it and prioritize young outlying plants before they fruit. Pull small seedlings when soil is moist, taking out the roots; wear gloves around thorny branches. Cutting a large shrub once is not a lasting solution because it can resprout. Arrange a follow-up plan with the land manager for established thickets, then watch for new shoots and seedlings. Restore appropriate vegetation to the cleared site rather than leaving bare ground, and follow local guidance on disposal of fruiting branches.

sources.title: Cornell Woody Plants: printable autumn olive account

researchNotes: Cornell's main URL timed out, but its official printable account was read in full and is retained as the same evidence lineage. NCSU supplies regional impacts; Maine's agency control guidance supports pulling and repeated follow-up. No edible-use recommendation or nationwide legal assertion is made.

claims: Silvery foliage, bird dispersal and North Carolina impact
Original Cornell account URL and species title; detailed text verified via official printable mirror
Fruit, leaves, growth and nitrogen fixation
Small-plant pulling and resprout monitoring

proposedDescription: Autumn zephyrlily is a small bulb-forming perennial with narrow green leaves and white, crocuslike flowers. Blooms rise above the grassy foliage in summer and autumn, often following rain. It comes from South America and is grown widely as an ornamental in borders and containers. The plants form compact clumps, and offsets develop around the original bulbs. In mild climates the leaves may remain green; in colder places the bulbs need protection from winter freezing.
identification: The narrow leaves emerge directly from the bulb, and each smooth, upright flowering stalk carries a single white, goblet-shaped bloom. Yellow stamens show in the center. Several other rain lilies have similar leaves, and flowering time changes with climate and rainfall, so leaf shape alone is not enough to name a clump. A photograph of an open flower, its stalk, and the basal foliage is most useful. Do not confuse this ornamental bulb with edible onions because the leaves look grassy.
actions: Choose a sunny position with moisture during growth and good drainage, especially through winter. In a cold climate, protect container plants or lift and store bulbs as local gardening guidance recommends. Separate offsets when a clump needs division, and remove spent flowers if you want to limit reseeding. Keep bulbs and removed plant material away from children and pets, and do not eat them. If an unwanted clump is removed, collect the small offsets too and monitor the spot. These garden practices do not imply that the species is invasive throughout its cultivated range.
researchNotes: NCSU was read for flowering, offsets and containment; GRIN independently confirms South American range. An additional RHS species account provides substantive morphology, drainage and bulb-safety guidance rather than counting taxonomy alone as a second biological source. Hardiness is expressed conditionally across climates.

claims: Bulb habit, rain-associated flowering, offsets and deadheading
South American native distribution
White goblet flowers, drainage, offsets and ornamental bulb caution

proposedDescription: Chenopodium hircinum is an annual herb from South America and a wild relative of quinoa. Its upright stems branch near the base, carrying alternate leaves that often have three uneven lobes. A pale, mealy coating and an unpleasant smell are useful supporting clues. The tiny whitish-green flowers grow in clusters along narrow spikes. Leaf shape varies considerably, so a familiar-looking leaf alone is not enough to separate it from other goosefoots; mature seeds can be important for identification.
identification: Compare leaves from several parts of the stem, since the lower, broader leaves and smaller upper ones need not match. The mealy coating, branching habit, and tiny clustered flowers help place it among goosefoots but do not separate it reliably from quinoa relatives or Chenopodium album. Mature seed characters may require magnification and an expert key. Record the plant's height, leaf variation, and fruiting clusters rather than submitting only one leaf. The unpleasant odor is a supporting observation, not a reason to crush or taste the plant.
actions: Have an unfamiliar field population identified before making crop or conservation decisions. If it is an unwanted annual in cultivated ground, preventing seed production and avoiding movement of seed-bearing soil are sensible containment steps while advice is obtained. Retain photographs and the location for a herbarium or agricultural service, which can request a specimen if needed. Its relationship to a food crop does not establish that a roadside plant is safe to eat. At a U.S. site, ask whether the plant is actually competing with the crop or changing the surrounding vegetation before planning work beyond routine garden weeding.

Mosyakin and Sokolova 2020: Lectotypification of Chenopodium hircinum

After direct article access timed out, the original Mosyakin and Sokolova 2020 abstract was retrieved in substantive search text: it independently establishes the quinoa relationship and importance of mature seeds for identification. A requested epitype does not invalidate the accepted species name. No U.S. ecological harm or tested control efficacy is claimed.

claims: Accepted name, annual habit and South American range
Annual growth, variable three-lobed leaves and clustered flowers
South American tetraploid quinoa relative; mature fruits and seeds important in diagnostic morphology

proposedDescription: Avocado is an evergreen tree from tropical America, grown for fleshy fruits with a single large seed. Its broad leaves form a dense crown, while small greenish-yellow flowers appear in branching clusters. Fruit size, skin texture and ripening season vary considerably among cultivated varieties. The trees grow best in warm, sunny places with good soil drainage. Avocados have been cultivated in the Americas since before European contact and remain an important orchard crop in tropical and subtropical regions.
identification: Look for simple, leathery leaves arranged alternately on the twigs, clusters of small greenish flowers, and a fleshy fruit surrounding one large seed. Fruit shape and skin can range from smooth green to dark and pebbled, so the supermarket appearance of one variety is not a universal identification guide. Young seed-grown plants may be hard to distinguish from other laurel-family trees without a label or flowers. A named nursery cultivar gives more useful information about expected fruit and local growing suitability than an unknown seedling.
actions: Plant where water drains freely and the mature crown has room, using a locally suitable cultivar from a reputable nursery. Avoid repeatedly saturating the root zone, and keep lawn equipment from injuring the trunk. Watch for leaf, shoot, or fruit problems and seek a diagnosis before treating them, since pests and growing conditions can produce overlapping symptoms. Remove unwanted volunteer seedlings where they interfere with another planting. This is a fruit-tree profile: cultivation and occasional self-sown plants do not establish ecological harm, and no broad removal recommendation is warranted.

sources.title: UF/IFAS: Avocado Growing in the Florida Home Landscape

researchNotes: NCSU and Crane's UF/IFAS home-landscape publication were checked independently. The prior UF HTML link loops, but its indexed text and official PDF were accessible; both belong to one lineage. Care is broad enough for different climates, without transferring Florida fertilizer or pesticide schedules elsewhere.

claims: Tree morphology, fruit and general growing needs
Florida drainage and cultivation context
Planting space, drainage, trunk protection and site care

proposedDescription: Avocado lace bug is a tiny leaf-feeding insect whose translucent wing covers resemble fine lace. Adults and spiny young gather beneath avocado leaves, where their feeding creates pale patches that can turn brown. Dark specks of waste and clusters of eggs are useful clues on the lower leaf surface. The insect also uses some other plants in the laurel family. Heavy infestations can cause early leaf drop, exposing fruit and branches to sun; small populations may cause little lasting damage.
identification: Turn over a damaged leaf and look for adults, dark spiny young, eggs, and sticky dark deposits in the same area. The lace-like upper surface of an adult is easier to see with magnification. Pale or brown leaf patches alone are not enough: mites, disease, and other stresses can also discolor avocado foliage. Photograph both sides of an affected leaf and the insects themselves. The association of a living colony with fresh injury is more informative than old damage on a leaf after the insects have gone.
actions: Check several parts of the canopy before deciding whether action is necessary. Small populations can be tolerated, while increasing injury or repeated early leaf loss deserves local extension advice. Maintain drainage and sensible irrigation, and preserve predators by avoiding unnecessary broad insecticide applications. Do not move infested avocado, camphor, or other host foliage into an unaffected area. Ask an agricultural office how to submit an unfamiliar insect. A dated California distribution statement in older guidance should not be used to decide where the bug can occur today.
researchNotes: UC IPM's direct guidance and the updated UF/IFAS/FDACS account were read, including Florida collection and injury observations. They share some literature but contain independent regional work. The UC 2006 county restriction is omitted as stale; no pesticide rate, diagnostic certainty from leaf damage, or current statewide range is inferred.

claims: Field recognition, tolerate low populations, plant care and movement prevention
Florida specimens, colony deposits and leaf injury

proposedDescription: Avocado scale is a small armored scale insect found on avocado, palms, tea and many other plants. Females sit beneath narrow, light-brown covers, often lined up along veins on the undersides of leaves. Their feeding can leave yellow spots, and heavy infestations may weaken foliage. Young mobile stages move to new feeding sites, while infested nursery plants can carry established colonies farther afield. Several related scales look very similar, so a microscope is usually needed to confirm the species.
identification: Use a hand lens on the lower leaf surface, especially beside veins. The female covers are narrow, pale brown, and slightly ridged, with a darker cast skin at one end. They can resemble other Fiorinia scales, and an old empty cover is not proof of a living infestation. A specialist may need a prepared adult female to confirm the name. Include the host plant, the pattern of yellowing, and close photographs of the covers when requesting help; the common name alone does not limit the host to avocado.
actions: Inspect nursery plants before purchase or transfer, and keep a suspect potted plant apart while identification is arranged. Avoid distributing infested cuttings or moving affected plants to a new garden. Check whether colonies and new leaf injury are actually increasing before seeking treatment, and consult extension staff for advice appropriate to the host, particularly for edible tea or fruit crops. Choose management with that diagnosis and the crop in mind, especially when leaves or fruit will be harvested. A treatment for a different scale should not be assumed effective here.

University of Hawaii: Insect and Mite Pests of Tea, p. 8

The latter cites Watson for background, so shared morphology is one lineage; its Maui tea record and photographs are independent observations. These support identification and regional occurrence. The ready profile gives inspection and referral advice, without presenting an unverified exact-species treatment as effective.

claims: Female covers, microscopic identification, hosts and dispersal
Maui tea occurrence, local leaf injury and observed colonies

proposedDescription: Froggattiella penicillata is a small armored scale insect associated with bamboo and other grasses. Females live beneath elongated protective covers, often tucked under leaf sheaths where they are easy to overlook. A Korean study found colonies on the stems of Sasa bamboo and described yellow covers with a darker yellow tip. Closely related scales can look similar without magnification. Its life history and economic effects remain poorly understood, so a sighting alone does not establish that it is causing serious plant damage.
identification: On bamboo, inspect accessible stems and the sheltered spaces around leaf sheaths for elongated yellowish or tan covers. Males have smaller, narrower covers than females. Other Froggattiella species can be nearly indistinguishable in the field; the differences involve pores and other microscopic structures on the insect, not merely the bamboo species. Have an entomologist examine a suitable sample before assigning the exact name. Photographs should show the colony's position on the stem as well as a close view of individual covers.
actions: Check bamboo nursery stock and divisions before moving them, because hidden colonies can travel with infested plant material. Set suspect container plants aside and obtain advice on sampling without carrying loose infested sheaths to other growing areas. Record plant condition and colony extent rather than assuming every scale cover represents serious injury. Ask for advice tailored to the confirmed insect and the condition of the bamboo instead of treating a few hidden covers automatically. In particular, an avocado pest label is misleading here: the documented hosts are bamboo and other grasses, so avocado-scale guidance should not be substituted.

proposedDescription: Avocado thrips is a small, straw-yellow insect that feeds on tender avocado leaves and young fruit. Fine dark lines cross the adult's abdomen, and the young are pale yellow. Feeding may bronze the leaves and leave rough brown scars on fruit as it grows, reducing its market quality even when the flesh remains usable. In California the insect became a major orchard pest after discovery in 1996. It often builds up during cooler periods when suitable young growth is available.
identification: Inspect tender leaves and beneath the calyx of small fruit. Active, pale adults have fine dark cross-lines. Western flower thrips, often abundant in avocado flowers, have more obvious stout hairs at the rear; their presence in flowers is not equivalent to an avocado-thrips infestation. A hand lens and specialist comparison help. Record live insects with fresh injury rather than naming the species from a scarred mature fruit alone.
actions: Scout young growth while fruit is small, when feeding scars can enlarge as the fruit grows. Record live thrips, fresh damage, and fruit stage for an orchard adviser. Protect beneficial insects and avoid treating every thrips in a flower. For a backyard tree, obtain an identification before using a product and consider whether cosmetic scarring warrants treatment. The original California discovery in 1996 began the formal description of this newly recognized pest; that history cannot serve as a current distribution map or universal treatment threshold.
