proposedDescription: Awl-leaf pearlwort, often sold as Irish moss, is a low flowering perennial that forms dense green mats. Its slender stems root where they touch the ground, and pairs of fine leaves give it a mosslike appearance. Tiny white flowers rise just above the foliage in summer. It grows best in cool, moist conditions and is often planted between paving stones or in rock gardens. It is a flowering plant rather than a true moss. The garden plant historically called Sagina subulata (Sw.) C.Presl was given the replacement name S. alexandrae because an earlier author had used subulata for a different plant.
identification: A close look reveals paired, slender leaves on creeping stems and tiny white flowers with five petals. True mosses do not make these flowers. Other pearlworts can look similar when not flowering, so inspect the flower, leaf tips, and stem arrangement rather than relying on the nursery name Irish moss. Golden garden forms can differ markedly in color from the usual green mats. Keep a nursery label or a flowering photograph if the scientific identity needs checking, because historical names in this group are easily confused.
actions: Use it where light foot traffic, cool conditions, and suitable drainage match its needs; repeatedly waterlogged or hot, dry sites are poor choices. Divide a garden clump when needed and collect removed fragments rather than depositing them in nearby natural vegetation. If a mat appears outside cultivation, confirm the species with a local botanist before deciding whether it needs removal. Use the nursery label as a starting point, because the name Sagina subulata has been applied to different plants. A garden escape needs local identification and assessment before it is treated as harmful.

proposedDescription: Axis deer is a spotted deer native to the Indian subcontinent, also known as chital. Adults retain white spots on a reddish-brown coat, and mature males usually carry three-pointed antlers. These social animals use woodland with grassy openings and access to water, feeding mainly on grasses but also browsing other vegetation. Introduced herds occur in places including Texas and Hawaii. In Texas, their ability to use limited forage can bring them into competition with native white-tailed deer.
identification: The spotted coat persists in adults, unlike the familiar juvenile spotting of white-tailed deer. Mature males generally have three tines on each antler, and a dark stripe runs along the back above pale underparts. Antlers may be absent in females or temporarily absent in males, so use the coat, body pattern, and local context together. Record photographs from a distance, with the number of animals and location. The Texas account documents births in different seasons, so the presence of a fawn is not a reliable seasonal identification shortcut.
actions: Do not feed, approach, capture, or relocate a free-ranging deer. If a herd appears outside a known managed area, share the location with the appropriate wildlife or land-management agency and let trained staff assess it. Landowners dealing with browsing or pasture competition should seek locally lawful exclusion or population-management advice; rules and practical options differ between Texas, Hawaii, and the native range. Keep observations specific: the Texas source documents forage concerns and calls for monitoring, rather than proving that every introduced herd has the same ecological effect.
researchNotes: University of Michigan's authored species account and Texas Tech's regional mammal account were read, including Texas reproduction and field observations. Broad precautionary actions avoid wildlife handling or hunting instructions. Historical population totals and present legal classifications are omitted; Texas forage effects are not generalized to every region.

claims: Native range, persistent spots and social habitat use
Antler/body diagnosis, Texas reproduction and regional forage observations

proposedDescription: Azalea lace bug is a tiny insect with patterned, lace-like wings that feeds beneath azalea and rhododendron leaves. The upper surface develops pale speckles, while dark waste spots and shed skins collect underneath. Young bugs lack full wings and become dark and spiny as they grow. Eggs can remain in leaves through winter, allowing new generations to appear the next growing season. Heavy feeding can turn foliage almost white or brown, although visible damage does not always mean the shrub is dying.
identification: Inspect the underside of a speckled leaf with a hand lens. Dark varnish-like spots, shed skins, and clusters of live lace bugs distinguish the pattern from simple leaf yellowing, though mites can also cause stippling. Adults have delicate wings with contrasting dark and pale markings; young bugs are wingless and increasingly spiny. Other lace bugs occur on related shrubs, so keep a close photograph of the insect as well as the host. Old pale marks remain after feeding stops and are not a reliable measure of today's population.
actions: Begin checking leaves as the first spring generation is expected locally, and repeat checks on both old and new growth. Keep azaleas adequately watered and avoid unnecessary insecticides that remove predators. A little cosmetic injury can be tolerated; increasing damage warrants advice matched to the plant and region. Choose less susceptible azalea varieties when replacing repeatedly affected shrubs. Do not assume that moving every plant into shade will solve the problem: shade relationships differ between eastern U.S. landscapes and Pacific Northwest conditions, and local experience should guide placement.

proposedDescription: Myosotis azorica is a forget-me-not native to the Azores, where it is a conservation concern. This upright, branching herb has simple, fleshy leaves covered with hairs and clusters of small dark-blue to violet flowers at the ends of its stems. Each flower has five petals. It grows in moist places, including rough slopes near waterfalls. Grazing can threaten its remaining habitat. This rare native plant warrants protection in its home range. A 2025 Hawaiian specimen review reassigned former local records to Myosotis latifolia, underscoring the need to check older names.
identification: Look for a hairy, leafy plant with branching upright stems and dense groups of small blue-violet flowers. The fleshy leaves and damp setting are useful clues, but they are not a reliable key to every Azorean forget-me-not. Closely related names, including Myosotis maritima, need careful botanical comparison. Photograph flowers, leaf surfaces, and the whole plant without pulling it up or entering a fragile slope. A record from Flores or Corvo should include enough location detail for a conservation team to relocate it discreetly.
actions: Leave wild plants in place and avoid trampling the moist ground around them. If you think you have found an overlooked population, send photographs and the location to the Azores conservation authority or a regional botanist rather than collecting seed or moving plants yourself. Local conservation work includes managed population reinforcement and protection of habitat. Grazing pressure should be addressed by the responsible land manager. Outside the Azores, verify an apparent identification before acting; a garden label or resemblance to a common forget-me-not is not a reason to remove a rare native species.

proposedDescription: Aztec marigold is an upright annual from Mexico and Guatemala, widely grown for its large flower heads. Cultivated forms often have rounded clusters of yellow, orange or cream flowers above divided, aromatic leaves. Plant height varies greatly with the variety, from compact bedding plants to taller cut-flower types. It favors sunny, well-drained places and flowers through much of the warm season. The familiar names African marigold and American marigold refer to the same species and do not describe its native range.
identification: The leaves are divided into narrow, toothed leaflets, and the large flower heads sit at the ends of upright stems. Many garden varieties have densely packed petals that hide the central disc, but flower fullness, color, and height vary. A single orange flower is not enough to distinguish every cultivated marigold or hybrid. Include a complete leaf and the green bracts beneath a head in photographs. The familiar garden names can be misleading about origin, and current botanical treatments do not always draw the same boundaries around related marigolds.
actions: Give garden plants sun and well-drained soil, and support tall varieties where wind or heavy rain may bend the stems. Remove spent heads to reduce their weight and encourage a tidier display; collect dry seed heads if unwanted seedlings are a concern. Pull volunteer seedlings while small when they crowd another planting. An ornamental growing well in a bed does not need invasive-plant control simply because it is outside its original range. Avoid assuming that planting a marigold will reliably cure a pest or soil problem without advice specific to that crop and site.

Kew's current broader synonym treatment includes Tagetes patula, so no hard French-versus-African marigold diagnostic is asserted. Added Kew garden interpretation is not an independent third lineage. No pest-repellent, medicinal or universal invasive claim.

proposedDescription: Aztec tobacco is an annual tobacco plant with broad, rounded leaves and relatively short, yellowish tubular flowers. Its foliage is noticeably wider than that of several other tobacco species. Native to Peru according to Kew's botanical account, it has been introduced across many regions, including parts of North America. It has a long history of ceremonial and medicinal use among some Indigenous peoples. Those cultural uses are part of its history, rather than advice to smoke, eat or prepare the plant.
identification: Broad leaves and short yellowish flower tubes are useful starting points when comparing this tobacco with other Nicotiana. The leaves are carried on upright herbaceous stems, and mature plants produce seed capsules after flowering. Confirm the combination of leaf shape, flower length, and fruit rather than naming a seedling from leaf width alone. Photograph the plant without tasting or experimenting with its sap. Cultivated tobaccos can occur near old gardens, and a local flora or herbarium can help determine which taxon has persisted.
actions: Treat it as a nicotine-containing plant, not an edible herb or a home remedy. Keep leaves, seeds, and discarded material out of children's and pets' reach, and do not make homemade insecticide from it. If an unwanted plant is setting capsules, prevent seed from scattering while arranging removal and use gloves for routine handling. Respect cultivated plants with cultural significance and the owner's wishes. An introduced occurrence should be documented accurately; it does not automatically establish ecological harm or justify clearing unrelated native plants nearby.

proposedDescription: Baby's breath is a branching perennial best known for the many tiny white flowers used in bouquets. Its open flower clusters rise above a leafy base and give the whole plant a rounded outline. Native across parts of Europe and temperate Asia, it favors sunny, well-drained sites and occurs along roadsides, fields and sandy ground. Garden escapes have become troublesome in some North American regions, including Great Lakes landscapes. The large, fleshy root helps established plants persist from year to year.
identification: Look for opposite, narrow leaves below a widely branching cloud of small white flowers. Each ordinary flower has five petals, although cultivated double forms can look fuller. The rounded flowering outline and persistent root distinguish this perennial from some smaller annual bouquet plants. It is not the blue-flowered plant commonly called bachelor's button. Take photographs of the lower leaves, branching pattern, and flowers before removing an uncertain plant, especially in dunes or grassland where native species may grow among the stems.
actions: In places where baby's breath escapes, prevent seed-bearing stems from being discarded in open ground. Detached plants can tumble and scatter seeds, so contain mature material during cleanup. Mowing or clipping established plants may leave a vigorous root alive; arrange a suitable follow-up plan with a weed coordinator instead of assuming one cut is enough. Report plants found in protected dunes to the land manager and stay on approved routes. Where removal is needed, protect nearby native vegetation and check the site again for seedlings and surviving crowns.

proposedDescription: Bacterial kidney disease is a slow-developing infection of salmon, trout and related fishes caused by Renibacterium salmoninarum. It can affect wild fish as well as those raised in hatcheries. Some infected fish show swollen organs, skin sores or bulging eyes, while others carry the bacterium without obvious illness. Infection can pass between fish and from parents through eggs. Because these signs resemble other diseases and healthy-looking carriers occur, laboratory testing is needed to identify the cause reliably.
identification: The bacterium itself cannot be recognized by looking at a fish in the water. Bulging eyes, skin lesions, unusual swelling, or unexplained deaths are reasons for a fish-health investigation, not a diagnosis of bacterial kidney disease. Some infected fish appear normal, which is especially important when broodstock or eggs are being transferred. A qualified laboratory may use molecular tests and other methods to establish the cause. Detection varies with the fish, tissue and test, so a negative result needs professional interpretation. Record the fish species, numbers affected, timing, and water conditions for the veterinarian or agency receiving the report.
actions: Report unusual illness or fish deaths to the responsible fisheries authority or an aquatic-animal veterinarian. Avoid moving live fish, eggs, water, or shared equipment from a suspect group until you receive instructions. Hatcheries should follow their established screening and biosecurity plans, including approved cleaning procedures; apparently healthy fish are not a substitute for testing. Do not add antibiotics or disinfectants to a stream, pond, or tank on the basis of appearance. Treatment and prevention need professional oversight because chronic carriers and infection within eggs make control difficult.

proposedDescription: Bagrada bug is a small shield-shaped insect, black with orange and white markings. Both adults and young feed by piercing plants, with cabbage, broccoli and other mustard-family crops especially vulnerable. Feeding on seedlings can leave pale patches, distort developing leaves or destroy the growing tip. The bugs also use wild plants around fields, moving into crops as conditions change. Originally from parts of Africa and Asia, this species has become an agricultural pest in California and other introduced regions.
identification: Adults are only about 5 to 7 millimeters long, smaller than the similarly patterned harlequin bug. Young stages are wingless and can be orange-red before darkening, so they do not always look like small adults. Examine seedlings for fresh pale, star-shaped feeding marks and damaged growing points, then look for the insects themselves. Bugs may be easier to see during warmer midday conditions than on a cool morning. Photograph the pattern and size; a bug resting on a plant does not necessarily show that it reproduces there.
actions: Inspect transplant trays before planting and monitor young brassicas closely, including field edges adjoining weedy ground. Deal with confirmed weed hosts as part of the farm's crop plan and seek local advice promptly when seedlings are being injured, since damage can develop quickly. Crop rotation choices differ between coastal and desert production areas, so avoid copying a regional program without checking its fit. Keep infested plant material from being moved to a new growing area. Treatment decisions should follow current crop-specific guidance, rather than a household recipe or the insect's striking colors alone.

proposedDescription: Paspalum notatum var. saurae is a name used for a perennial South American pasture grass, including the familiar Pensacola bahiagrass. Pensacola has narrow leaves, produces seed readily and can persist under heavy grazing. These traits helped make it a useful pasture grass in Florida. The name needs care: some botanical sources treat this variety as the separate species Paspalum saurae. Descriptions of broad-leaved bahiagrass cultivars should not automatically be applied to this narrower-leaved form.
identification: For a known Pensacola planting, narrow leaves and a persistent, low basal growth pattern are useful clues. A seed label or planting record is valuable because related bahiagrass cultivars differ in leaf width, growth, and genetic makeup, and a photograph alone may not establish the variety. Collect a record of the mature seed heads, leaf bases, and the patch as a whole for a grass specialist. The name Paspalum saurae may appear in botanical databases even when agricultural publications retain the older varietal name.
actions: Manage an intended pasture according to its actual cultivar, soil tests, and local forage advice. Heavy grazing tolerance does not mean that every site or stocking rate is suitable. If grass is moving from a pasture into a bed or conservation area, prevent seed-bearing material and soil from being transferred while the identification and site objective are checked. Ask for cultivar-specific advice before any selective herbicide use because bahiagrass types respond differently. The same plant can be a useful forage crop in one setting and unwanted in another, without being invasive everywhere.

proposedDescription: Bald brome is a short-lived grass that grows as a loose tuft or sometimes as a single upright stem. Its leaves and lower sheaths are hairy, while the flower clusters carry several pale-green, many-flowered spikelets with slender bristles. It is native across a broad temperate range from the Azores and Europe into Asia, and has been introduced elsewhere. Although its common name suggests a hairless plant, the floral details, rather than the absence of leaf hairs, are important for identification.
identification: Look at a complete mature flowering stem, including the hairy lower leaf sheaths and the shape of the spikelets. The New Zealand flora describes straight awns arising just below the tips of the floral scales, with smooth-looking rather than conspicuously hairy spikelets. Several annual bromes overlap in these features, so a field photograph should include a close view with a scale. The common name soft brome is used for more than one species; neither that name nor the word bald can settle an identification.
actions: In a garden or cropped area, prevent an unwanted confirmed annual grass from setting seed and collect mature heads rather than scattering them during cleanup. Check the surrounding patch for other bromes before treating it as a single species. If the grass occurs in a meadow or conservation site, ask a local botanist whether it is an introduced population and whether management is warranted. Keep seed-bearing soil and hay from being moved into clean sites. Local advice matters because similar-looking grasses may have different value, impact, and responses to treatment.

proposedDescription: Balfour's touch-me-not is an annual with upright, branching stems and two-toned pink and white flowers. Each flower has a narrow spur extending behind it, and the pointed leaves have regularly toothed edges. Native to the western Himalayas, it has been grown as a garden ornamental and sometimes escapes into disturbed ground. In Victoria, Australia, botanical accounts describe localized dense stands near old gardens. Its smooth stems and modest flower size help separate it from some larger, more familiar balsams.
identification: The flowers combine a pale upper portion with pink lower petals and a narrow, fairly straight spur behind the flower. Leaves are alternate, pointed, and regularly toothed, with glands near their bases. Smooth stems and this flower arrangement are more informative than the general balsam shape. Other garden Impatiens and escaped relatives can resemble it, so take a side view of the spur and a full leafy stem. Flowering dates given for southern Australia should not be expected to match a northern garden.
actions: Watch an ornamental planting for seedlings beyond its intended bed, especially along damp edges. In Oregon's Washington County, report suspected escapes to the local conservation district or state invasive-species hotline. Tualatin's guide advises pulling confirmed plants in spring before flowers and seedpods form, then containing the material and checking for regrowth over several years. Keep seed-bearing garden waste out of natural vegetation. On a stream bank or among native plants, coordinate with the land manager before clearing a stand. Local priority and impact vary, so record patch size and persistence rather than assuming every garden plant needs the same response.

proposedDescription: Ballmustard is an annual mustard-family plant of fields, meadows and disturbed ground. Small yellow flowers are followed by rounded fruits, giving the seed-bearing stems their distinctive beadlike appearance. Native to Eurasia, it has spread into parts of northern North America, including New England. The seeds can be difficult to separate from harvested canola or mustard because they are similar in size. That makes it relevant as an agricultural weed even where it is less conspicuous than larger flowering plants.
identification: Follow the small four-petaled yellow flowers down the stem to the rounded, beadlike fruits. Upper leaves clasp the stem, helping distinguish the plant from some other small yellow mustards, but several relatives have similar foliage. Mature fruits are particularly useful, so include them with a photograph of the lower and upper leaves. A crop seed sample may require a seed analyst rather than a field photograph. The rounded units mixed with a harvest are a practical clue, not a reason to assume every mustard weed is this species.
actions: Identify scattered plants before seed enters a crop harvest, and keep suspect seed lots separate while an agricultural adviser or seed laboratory assesses contamination. Clean equipment before moving from an affected field to a clean one. In a small non-crop patch, remove confirmed unwanted plants before fruit matures and check for new seedlings after disturbance. For canola or condiment mustard, use a locally appropriate crop program rather than an improvised treatment that could injure the crop. The decision should reflect seed contamination and field conditions, not an assumed nationwide ecological emergency.

proposedDescription: Balloon vine is a tendril-climbing plant named for its inflated, papery fruit capsules. The green capsules become brown as they mature, enclosing black seeds with a pale heart-shaped mark. Divided leaves and small white flowers grow along branching stems that scramble over nearby plants. It occurs across tropical and subtropical regions in thickets, river margins and disturbed ground. In parts of the southeastern United States, introduced growth can cover surrounding vegetation, but its native and introduced status varies around the world.
identification: An inflated, three-part capsule and a black seed with a pale heart-shaped scar are strong clues. Leaves are divided into smaller toothed leaflets, unlike the single broad leaves of many other climbing vines. Small white flowers and tendrils occur along the stems. Other Cardiospermum species, including larger balloon vines, need comparison when a precise identification matters; do not name a vine from an inflated fruit alone. Photograph leaves, flowers, and a mature capsule together, without scattering loose seeds while examining it.
actions: Where it is escaping, prevent capsules from ripening and remove small unwanted vines before they become tangled through neighboring plants. Work carefully around the supporting vegetation rather than pulling a large tangle down at once. Collect seed-bearing material and check the site for seedlings afterward; avoid dumping garden cuttings beside waterways. Before broad removal in a natural area, confirm both the species and its local native status. Its global history is complex, so a regional weed listing or a useful garden practice should not be treated as proof that every population is harmful.

proposedDescription: Balloon-flower is a perennial grown for buds that swell like small balloons before opening into broad, five-pointed bells. The flowers face outward or upward above leafy stems, appearing in late spring and summer. Native to eastern Asia, the plant returns from a fleshy root system that can be easily damaged by disturbance. It is commonly grown in sunny or partly shaded borders with well-drained soil. Its unusual unopened buds are usually the easiest feature to recognize.
identification: Watch a bud over several days: the inflated shape opens into a wide bell, commonly blue-violet but also white or pink in garden varieties. The leaves have toothed edges and may be arranged in pairs or whorls along the stem. Other bellflowers have similar open blooms, so an unopened bud, a leaf, and the whole plant together are more useful than flower color alone. Keep the planting marked through dormancy; the fleshy root below ground is easily injured when a seemingly empty border is cultivated.
actions: Choose a well-drained border with suitable sun or partial shade, and avoid repeated digging around an established crown. Deadhead spent flowers if you want a longer display and fewer seed heads. If a plant must be divided or moved, work carefully because the root system is fragile; replacing it from nursery stock or seed may be simpler. Remove unwanted seedlings while small, but there is no reason to treat a contained ornamental automatically as an invasive infestation. Check local planting guidance if it is spreading beyond cultivation into natural vegetation.

proposedDescription: Balsam woolly adelgid is a tiny sap-feeding insect hidden beneath white, woolly wax on true fir trees. Colonies settle on bark and branches, where their feeding can cause swollen twigs, distorted growth and declining crowns. Susceptibility varies among fir species: Fraser fir in the southern Appalachians and subalpine fir in the western United States can suffer severe damage. Introduced from Europe, the insect reproduces without mating in North America. Its small size means an infestation may go unnoticed until tree symptoms develop.
identification: First confirm that the host is a true fir, an Abies species; Douglas-fir is a different tree group. Look for small woolly patches on bark, especially around branch junctions, together with swollen shoot nodes and weakened growth. Resin, lichens, and other insects can also appear pale against bark, so use magnification and obtain a specialist diagnosis. A crooked leader or dying branch alone is not proof of adelgids. Photograph the insect covering and the whole crown rather than peeling extensive bark from a living tree.
actions: Report suspected new infestations to a forest-health specialist and avoid moving infested fir seedlings, branches, or firewood to unaffected sites. Tree-farm scouting and treatment timing should follow local crawler activity rather than a calendar copied from another region. High-value landscape trees may merit professional treatment, while a forest stand requires a broader assessment of host species, tree condition, and replacement vegetation. Do not assume that a product applied to the soil will reliably cure a damaged tree. Maintaining diverse, locally suitable plantings can reduce dependence on highly susceptible firs.
researchNotes: NCSU's Fraser-fir work and Utah State's western forest guidance are independent regional lineages. Both diagnosis and movement prevention were read directly. proposedDescription: Balsampear, also called bitter melon, is a fast-growing annual vine with curling tendrils and deeply lobed leaves. Yellow flowers develop into bumpy or ridged fruits that change from green to orange when ripe. The mature fruit splits open, exposing seeds wrapped in bright red flesh. Cultivated varieties are familiar vegetables in many warm regions, while smaller-fruited forms may grow outside gardens. The plant thrives in heat and humidity and can climb supports or spread across the ground.
identification: Look for an alternate, deeply lobed leaf, a curling tendril, and solitary yellow flowers on the same vine. Fruits vary markedly among cultivated forms: some are long and ridged, others short and strongly warty. The change from green to orange and the opening ripe fruit are helpful clues, but do not taste an unfamiliar vine to identify it. Other gourds can share yellow flowers and lobed leaves. A record showing the leaf, flower, unripe fruit, and mature fruit is much stronger than a single leaf photograph.
actions: Give an intended garden crop a sturdy support, sun, and well-drained soil, and keep the vine from covering neighboring plants. Collect unwanted ripe fruits before seeds are scattered and remove volunteer seedlings where they interfere with the planting. Do not discard fruiting vines beside waterways or natural areas. The immature fruit is a familiar cultivated vegetable, but mature fruits and seeds should not be eaten on the strength of a plant-identification profile. Avoid using the plant as a substitute for medical treatment, and check local guidance before treating an escaped vine as an ecological problem.

proposedDescription: This bamboo, also known as timber bamboo or Phyllostachys bambusoides, is a tall woody grass native to central and southern China. Its green canes carry long branches and pointed leaves that are bright green above and blue-green beneath. Young cane sheaths can be pinkish with purple mottling, a useful seasonal detail. It has a long history in cultivation, and its eventual size varies greatly with climate and growing conditions.
identification: Compare a new shoot with an older cane and photograph both leaf surfaces. Fresh cane sheaths can be pinkish and purple-mottled, while the pointed leaves are bright green above and blue-green beneath. Similar green bamboos, particularly P. viridiglaucescens, need comparison of sheath markings, branch length and leaves. Named garden forms can have yellow or striped canes, so cane color and the height of a clipped planting should not be used alone.
actions: Before choosing a planting site, allow room to inspect its margins throughout the growing season. Mark newly appearing shoots beyond the intended boundary and discuss containment with a knowledgeable nursery. Keep excavated underground stems contained during garden work; a small green shoot alone should not trigger removal of an unidentified bamboo collection. Photograph the same boundary after new shoots have expanded, keeping notes on which stems were present before the season began.

proposedDescription: Bamboo armored scale is a small scale insect that can remain well hidden on its host. Recorded colonies occupy the tight space between a bamboo leaf stalk and the stem, so an ordinary glance at the leaves may miss them. The species was originally described from Asian bamboo and has since been reported in other regions, including Saint Lucia. Closely related scales require microscopic comparison, making the host and concealed feeding site useful search clues rather than a complete identification.
identification: Use a hand lens where the bamboo leaf stalk presses against the cane; small attached scales can resemble debris in this sheltered junction. Photograph their position before disturbing them, and retain a short affected section if requested by the diagnostician. The host and feeding site help locate a colony but cannot settle the species. Specialist keys compare the pores and ducts of mounted females, details that an ordinary photograph of the bamboo cannot show.
actions: Tell the receiving diagnostic service which bamboo was involved and whether it recently arrived from another nursery. Ask how to package a short affected section before sending anything. Examine adjacent bamboo while keeping the original plant separate. A confirmed scale record does not establish the cause of every yellow leaf, so assess plant condition along with insect abundance.

proposedDescription: Bamboo pit scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect found on bamboo leaves and stems. Females are elongated and yellowish, sheltered beneath a translucent cover that can blend into the plant. A fringe of pale wax may help reveal a colony. Colonies occupy both leaf surfaces as well as stems, so an inspection should cover more than the most visible leaves. A Danish report records occasional problems in botanical-garden greenhouses. Its importance therefore depends on plant condition and setting, not simply the number of visible scales.
identification: Oval translucent covers with pale wax fringes on bamboo stems or leaves; color alone is unreliable. Examine both sides of several leaves as well as the canes, because colonies need not occupy just one surface. Look for a slightly raised, oval cover rather than a cottony mass. The wax fringe can be whitish or salmon colored. Other bamboo scales overlap in appearance, and confirmation depends on microscopic pores and other adult female structures.
actions: Record whether foliage remains vigorous or is declining, and show the diagnostician both occupied and apparently healthy leaves. Keep nursery labels with the photographs. Avoid spreading trimmings among bamboo collections while identification is pending. Once confirmed, ask an extension specialist whether monitoring or a targeted response fits the actual damage, plant size and growing setting.

proposedDescription: Bamboo powderpost beetle develops inside cut bamboo, where both adults and larvae make feeding tunnels. The insects can attack culms during processing, storage or use, turning internal tissue into fine powder and reducing the material's strength. Eggs are laid inside the bamboo, and the young remain concealed as they grow. Fresh powder and small exit holes may reveal an infestation before the beetles themselves are noticed. Research in Japan documents it as an important pest of dried bamboo products.
identification: Fresh fine powder and small exit holes suggest activity within the bamboo, but other borers can leave similar signs. Photograph the holes beside a ruler and note whether more powder appears after old debris is cleared. Retain an exposed adult for a specialist: these small brown beetles are more informative than dust alone. Surface holes reveal only part of an infestation because adults and larvae spend much of their time concealed within the culm wall.
actions: Keep purchase and storage details with any suspect bamboo furniture or poles. Ask a qualified pest professional to determine whether activity is current and whether the material remains sound. Do not rely on a homemade heating schedule; internal insects can survive uneven treatment. Bamboo used structurally deserves a separate assessment of strength before continued use.

proposedDescription: Stigmaeopsis celarius is a tiny bamboo-feeding spider mite that lives beneath silk shelters on leaves. The dense, oval roofs cover small colonies and help protect them from predators. Experiments observed nest defense by adults, but its effectiveness differed between sexes and behaviors. Several related bamboo mites look similar and older reports used this name more broadly. Webbing beneath a bamboo leaf is therefore a useful place to look, but microscopic examination is needed to identify the species reliably.
identification: Bamboo leaf mites require microscopic identification; webbing or leaf damage alone cannot confirm this species. Turn leaves over gently and photograph intact silk roofs, the surrounding leaf and any visible mites through a lens. Several members of the former celarius group make similar shelters. The pattern of tiny body hairs, interpreted with a current key or molecular work, matters more than simply finding silk on bamboo.
actions: Inspect replacement bamboo before adding it to a collection, and keep affected plants apart while samples are examined. Describe which bamboo species carries the mites and how much new foliage is affected. Inspect newly expanded leaves for fresh injury rather than judging the colony only from older marked foliage. A specialist can help decide whether the observed injury warrants intervention.

proposedDescription: Banana aphid is a small, shiny brown to nearly black insect that feeds on banana sap. Colonies produce sticky honeydew, which can attract ants and support black sooty mold. Its greatest importance is as a carrier of banana bunchy top virus, rather than the feeding injury alone. Winged forms can disperse to other plants. Older accounts assigned aphids from ginger and several other hosts to this species, but modern research separates many of those populations as Pentalonia caladii.
identification: Shiny reddish-brown to black aphids on banana; winged individuals have conspicuously dark wing veins. Look closely around sheltered banana tissues and developing growth, retaining a view of the colony as well as individual insects. Sticky leaves and sooty mold indicate honeydew but do not establish which sap feeder produced it. A banana host supports the identification; aphids from ginger need separate examination because the older broad host concept has changed.
actions: Record aphid colonies separately from suspected virus symptoms, since an aphid sighting does not diagnose a plant infection. Obtain clean planting stock from a reliable source and avoid sharing affected suckers. If bunchy top is suspected, contact the local plant-health service promptly for sampling and management instructions appropriate to the area, rather than treating aphids and assuming the plant is cured.

proposedDescription: Banana bud moth is a small brown moth whose caterpillars tunnel inside stems and other plant tissues. Despite its name, it attacks many plants, including palms, dracaenas, bananas and other tropical ornamentals. The pale caterpillars have a brown head and produce piles of fine plant waste held together with silk. Infested stems may weaken or collapse, and empty pupal cases can project from the tunnels. Damaged or stressed plants are especially attractive places for the nocturnal adults to lay eggs.
identification: Silk-bound powdery waste and projecting pupal cases; pale caterpillars with brown heads inside damaged stems. Inspect the base and damaged portions of the stem for small openings and fresh silk-bound waste. Photograph a caterpillar with its head visible if one is already exposed, but do not split sound stems merely to search. Other borers cause holes and collapse too; adult moth or larval examination may be needed to resolve the identity.
actions: Separate a suspect nursery plant from stock awaiting sale or planting and retain its purchase label. Review watering, drainage and accidental wounds that may be stressing it. Ask a diagnostic service how to contain or dispose of confirmed infested stems. Trimming visible damage alone may leave concealed larvae behind, so arrange follow-up inspection of the remaining plant.

proposedDescription: Pestalotiopsis disseminata is a fungus reported from many kinds of plants, sometimes causing blight, cankers or fruit decay and sometimes living within apparently healthy tissue. Symptoms depend on the host and growing conditions, so a spotted leaf alone does not identify it. Reports include banana fruit rot and a Thai field survey that attributed large banana leaf spots to this fungus. That survey adds a real leaf association, but its available methods do not establish modern genetic confirmation of the isolates. Microscopy and suitable DNA comparisons are important because closely related fungi can be confused.
identification: There is no reliable naked-eye diagnosis; laboratories compare fungal structures and DNA. Describe which organ is affected: a rotting banana fruit, a dying twig and a leaf spot are different diagnostic starting points. Include the healthy-to-damaged boundary in photographs. Similar fungi can produce overlapping symptoms and spore shapes; finding this fungus in tissue also does not automatically show that it caused the observed decline.
actions: Keep affected nursery stock or propagation material separate and avoid splashing water between plants while advice is obtained. Send a fresh sample using the laboratory's instructions, with the host name, symptom timeline and recent growing conditions. A diagnosis should guide any sanitation or treatment plan; removing unrelated healthy plants on the basis of a broad fungal name is unnecessary.

proposedDescription: Banana passionflower is a climbing vine with three-lobed leaves, hanging pink flowers and elongated fruits that ripen yellow. Often called banana poka in Hawaii, it can climb high into forest vegetation and spread across tree crowns. Birds and pigs disperse its seeds there. The vine is native to the Andes and was long confused with another banana passionfruit, Passiflora mollissima. Its vigorous growth is a serious problem in some Hawaiian forests, where it can smother the plants supporting it.
identification: Three-lobed leaves, pendent pink flowers and elongated yellow-ripe fruits; confirm against similar passionflowers. Photograph the flower from the side as well as the front, showing its long tube and how it hangs from the vine. Include the leaf lobes and any fruit attached to the same stem. Related banana passionfruits can look very similar, so a fruit nickname or a distant picture of pink blooms is insufficient.
actions: In an affected landscape, mark the main rooted stem and note seedlings beyond it before planning work. Keep ripe fruits and cut stems contained rather than dragging them through vegetation. Large vines suspended in tree crowns require advice from land managers or qualified tree workers. Revisit cleared ground for seedlings and rooted fragments, using the local management plan.

proposedDescription: Banded cichlid is a deep-bodied South American fish from the upper Orinoco and upper Negro river regions. Dark vertical markings cross the body, but the pattern must be interpreted carefully because several related fishes are sold as severums. In the modern identification of Heros severus, one middle body bar is shortened rather than extending fully between the upper and lower fins. Older aquarium and biological accounts can mix it with other Heros species, making confirmed identity especially important.
identification: Deep body and vertical bands; precise bar pattern and other characters require comparison with related Heros species. Take a clear side view showing every body bar, the tail base and the eye. In this species, the shortened fourth bar is an important comparison with H. liberifer, whose corresponding bar reaches between the fin bases. Color intensity changes with condition, so a seller's name or a single dark band should not decide identification.
actions: Keep aquarium provenance and photographs with the record, especially for stock sold simply as severum. If a fish is unwanted, arrange a responsible return or rehoming through an aquarium specialist. For a suspected wild occurrence, report the waterbody and date to the fisheries authority; avoid moving fish between waters while attempting to establish which Heros is involved.

proposedDescription: The banded elm bark beetle is a small Asian beetle that now occurs in North America. Adults are reddish brown with a darker band across the wing covers. Its pale, legless larvae tunnel beneath the bark of stressed elms, interrupting the tissues that move food through the tree. The beetle can also carry the fungus responsible for Dutch elm disease. Tree condition matters: in Utah, attacks on the common Siberian elm often cause little damage when disease is absent.
identification: Reddish-brown adults roughly 3-4 mm long with a dark wing band; white legless larvae and branching galleries beneath elm bark. Inspect freshly declining branches and photograph any exposed galleries without peeling bark from otherwise healthy trunks. The dark wing band is useful on adults, but small elm beetles overlap in size. Wilt can also arise from disease or other stress, and finding a beetle does not by itself establish that Dutch elm disease is present.
actions: Have an arborist or extension service assess the tree and decide whether disease testing is needed. Preserve a sample from recent activity rather than relying on old, empty holes. Follow local instructions for handling elm pruning waste and firewood. Maintain suitable watering and avoid trunk injury; the response should reflect tree health and confirmed risk, not beetle presence alone.

proposedDescription: Barbados aloe is an evergreen succulent with a rosette of thick, pointed leaves edged with small pale teeth. The leaves store water and contain the clear gel familiar from cosmetic products. Mature plants can send up tall stalks bearing tubular yellow to orange flowers, while young offsets form beside the parent plant. It is widely grown in pots and warm-climate gardens, where freely draining soil is important. The yellow latex near the leaf surface differs from the inner gel and should not be casually consumed.
identification: Thick toothed leaves in a basal rosette; offsets around the base; tubular flowers on tall stalks. Compare the thick leaves, marginal teeth and arrangement of offsets rather than relying on a pot label. Other aloes and agaves also form pointed rosettes. A photograph of a flowering stalk, if present, helps show the tubular blooms and their arrangement. Leaf spotting can vary with age and growing conditions.
actions: Use a pot that drains freely and check that water is not left standing beneath it. Let a local nursery help distinguish normal older-leaf loss from a growing problem before applying products. Keep discarded leaves and offsets out of natural vegetation. Household or medicinal uses of aloe products do not make an unidentified garden leaf suitable for eating.

proposedDescription: Barbados gooseberry is a climbing cactus with ordinary-looking, slightly fleshy leaves. Paired hooked spines help its branches catch surrounding plants, while older stems carry clusters of longer spines. Fragrant white or pale-yellow flowers are followed by round yellow to orange fruits. Native to tropical America, it has escaped from gardens in places such as eastern Australia, where heavy, tangled growth can smother other vegetation. Broken stems and even leaves can regrow, making dumped garden material a source of new plants.
identification: Leafy climbing cactus with hooked branch spines, longer clustered trunk spines and round yellowish fruit. Ordinary broad leaves can disguise its cactus identity until the paired hooks are visible. Photograph a young climbing shoot and an older woody stem, taking care around the longer spine clusters. Include flowers or fruit when available. A thorny vine without these combined features may belong to a different family.
actions: Map where stems touch soil before disturbing an escaped patch. Wear suitable protection and use tools that allow you to contain detached pieces without handling spines directly. Check disposal arrangements before cutting, because fragments left on moist ground may establish again. For growth tangled into trees or native vegetation, seek a site-specific plan that protects the supporting plants.

proposedDescription: Barbados nut is a spreading shrub or small tree native to tropical America. Its broad leaves have three or five pointed lobes, and small yellow-green flowers develop into rounded capsules that split as they mature. The dark seeds contain oil used in industrial products and investigated as a fuel source. The plant tolerates drought and relatively poor soil, which has encouraged cultivation far beyond its native range. Despite the common name, its seeds are not edible nuts and can cause poisoning.
identification: Alternate broad leaves with three or five pointed lobes, yellow-green flowers and yellowish capsules containing dark seeds. Show the leaf attachment, lobes and fruit in the same set of photographs. Leaves alone can resemble other Jatropha species and unrelated lobed shrubs. Mature capsules provide stronger evidence than a loose dark seed. Flower and leaf appearance may change across the season, so retain the original planting label when one is available.
actions: Do not leave fallen capsules where children, pets or livestock can reach them. Wear gloves for pruning and collect the resulting material rather than scattering it along a boundary. If exposure or ingestion is suspected, seek professional medical or veterinary advice. For an established ornamental, monitor nearby seedlings and choose any removal or replacement according to local guidance.

proposedDescription: Barbary fig is a large, branching cactus grown for its fleshy fruit. Its flattened, oval pads are stems, often forming a small tree with a distinct trunk. Many cultivated plants lack long spines, but small irritating bristles can still be present. Yellow flowers develop into rounded fruits that change color as they ripen. The species comes from Mexico and has been carried widely in cultivation. In New South Wales it sometimes escapes into surrounding vegetation, spreading through seeds and fallen stem pieces.
identification: Large flattened oval pads on a shrubby or tree-like cactus; yellow flowers and fleshy fruit; spines vary greatly. Look for the combination of broad flattened joints, a woody base and large fleshy fruits. Even apparently spineless pads may bear tiny bristles at their areoles. Other prickly pears overlap in form, and cultivated varieties differ considerably, so include pad dimensions, flowers and fruit rather than using spine number alone.
actions: Handle pads with tools and protective clothing, avoiding direct contact with their bristle-bearing spots. In places where escape is a concern, collect fallen pieces before they root and keep fruit waste contained. Ask local weed staff about disposal of a large planting. A cultivated food cactus should be assessed by its confirmed identity and actual spread at the site.

proposedDescription: Barbed goatgrass is a winter annual grass closely related to wheat. Its stiff, narrow leaves and short seed heads become especially noticeable when the very long bristles spread from the developing seeds. Native from the Mediterranean region into central Asia, it grows in California grasslands, rangelands and oak woodlands, including some dry, shallow soils. The bristles catch on clothing and animal fur, helping seeds travel. They can also lodge around livestock mouths or eyes, reducing the usefulness of affected pasture.
identification: Short cylindrical seed heads with exceptionally long, spreading bristles; narrow rigid leaves and hairy leaf sheaths. Examine a complete mature head rather than a detached bristle. Photograph the compact series of spikelets, the long awns and the lower leaf sheaths. Other goatgrasses and wild cereals can look alike before flowering. Seedling identification is especially uncertain, so retain a marked plant for later confirmation if doing so will not spread seed.
actions: Check boots, animal equipment and vehicle surfaces after work in an affected patch. Where livestock are involved, ask the agricultural adviser about grazing and seedhead hazards for that particular field. Small infestations need a plan before heads mature; large stands require coordinated follow-up. Avoid transporting contaminated hay or soil while the identity and local management requirements are being established.

proposedDescription: Barberton daisy is a perennial from southern Africa with bold daisy-like flower heads held above a low rosette of leaves. The leaves are elongated and often deeply lobed, while the flowers usually have red outer rays surrounding a darker center. This species helped give rise to the many hybrid gerberas sold as bedding plants and cut flowers. It favors bright conditions and moist but well-drained soil; saturated soil can damage its roots. In colder climates it is commonly grown seasonally or protected from frost.
identification: Lobed leaves in a basal rosette with solitary large daisy heads on upright stalks; garden hybrids vary widely in color. Photograph the leaf rosette and the underside of a flower head as well as its colorful face. A florist's gerbera may be a hybrid rather than the wild species, so color is not a dependable species test. The leaf lobes, flower stalk and plant label together provide better context for a botanical determination.
actions: Water the root zone without keeping the crown persistently saturated, and allow adequate drainage around container-grown plants. Retain labels when dividing or sharing a collection so horticultural hybrids are not recorded as confirmed wild G. jamesonii. If plants appear beyond a garden bed, document their position and persistence before deciding whether any local management is needed.

proposedDescription: Cryptocarenus heveae is a very small, dark-brown bark beetle recorded in South America. At roughly two millimeters long, it is difficult to recognize without a microscope. A specialist key uses details of the forehead, including a shallow depression and small central bump, to separate it from similar beetles. Researchers have caught it in ethanol-baited traps in a mixed Brazil-nut and rubber plantation in the southern Amazon. That finding documents its presence there, but does not by itself show which trees it was using.
identification: Tiny dark-brown beetle; forehead and other microscopic characters are needed for reliable species identification. A sharp dorsal and side image may help sort the specimen, but the shallow forehead impression and central bump need magnification. The beetle's trap label is part of its evidence: note the lure, collection date and location. Captures in a mixed plantation cannot reveal the breeding host without additional observations.
actions: Keep specimens from different traps or trees separately labeled. If damaged branches are present, photograph them and ask an entomologist whether a separate host-associated sample is useful. Do not cut healthy Brazil-nut or rubber trees merely because this species was caught nearby. Management decisions need a demonstrated connection between the beetle, the tissue and the injury.

proposedDescription: The black stem borer is a tiny ambrosia beetle from eastern Asia that has become a pest of orchard and nursery trees in North America. Females are shiny black and about two millimeters long. They bore into trunks or branches and grow a fungus inside their tunnels as food for themselves and their young. Stressed trees are especially attractive. Small entry holes, sometimes with thin toothpick-like strands of sawdust, may be easier to notice than the beetles themselves. Heavy attacks can accompany wilting and decline.
identification: Shiny black females about 2 mm long; small trunk holes and fragile sawdust strands are clues, not species-level proof. Inspect the lower trunk and branches for pin-sized openings and fragile projecting strands of boring dust. Rain or handling may remove the strands, so photograph them promptly. Other ambrosia beetles create similar signs; an adult specimen and current identification key are needed before assigning the holes to this species.
actions: Check drainage, transplant stress and recent injury alongside the insect evidence. Keep affected nursery blocks identified and avoid moving suspect trees into new plantings. Ask an extension specialist about monitoring during local flight periods and what to do with confirmed heavily attacked trees. Pruning or treating without diagnosing the underlying stress can leave the same vulnerability in replacement stock.

proposedDescription: Barnyardgrass is a variable annual grass common in damp, disturbed ground and cultivated fields. Its flattened stems may spread near the ground before turning upward, carrying broad, flat blades. The branched seed head is crowded with small spikelets and may have a purplish cast. One useful clue is the absence of a small membrane or fringe where the leaf blade meets its sheath. Introduced from Eurasia into North America, it is a familiar agricultural weed of irrigated fields, ditches and rice-growing areas.
identification: At the junction of the leaf blade and sheath, check for the absence of both a ligule and ear-like projections. Combine that clue with the flattened stem base, broad flat blades and crowded branches of a mature seed head. Awn length and branching can vary markedly. Related barnyard grasses share much of the vegetative appearance, so close views of mature spikelets and a regional grass key may be needed for a confident species record.
actions: In a garden, tackle a small confirmed patch while plants are young and before seedheads mature. In a crop, obtain advice matched to the crop and water regime rather than disturbing irrigation or applying a general lawn treatment. Clean soil and seed from tools before moving between beds, and inspect the same damp edges for later flushes of seedlings.

proposedDescription: Basil downy mildew is caused by Peronospora belbahrii, a microscopic water mold that infects basil. Leaves often turn yellow between the main veins, while gray to purple downy growth develops underneath. Symptoms may begin low on the plant and spread upward, making a healthy-looking crop decline quickly in humid conditions. The pathogen can arrive on seed or infected plants, and its spores travel through the air. Yellowing alone can resemble a nutrient problem, so the leaf underside provides an important clue.
identification: Yellow areas bounded by leaf veins with gray-purple downy growth underneath; a diagnostic laboratory can confirm uncertain cases. Turn yellowing leaves over in good light to look for the downy growth. Photograph the upper surface and matching underside, noting whether discoloration follows the veins. Nutrition problems and other leaf diseases can resemble the early stages. Record the basil variety, planting date and whether nearby pots are also affected.
actions: Space plants so air can circulate and water at the soil surface when practical. Start subsequent plantings with seed and varieties recommended for this disease by a local extension service. Bag confirmed infected plants for disposal according to local guidance, and inspect neighboring basil. Do not assume that removing visibly yellow leaves cures an infected plant.

proposedDescription: Basket plant is a fleshy perennial from Mexico that forms clusters of broad, glossy leaves. Long flowering stalks rise from the upper leaf bases and carry small, fragrant white flowers. Some cultivated forms have pale or purple markings, so leaf color alone is unreliable. Grown as an ornamental groundcover, it has escaped into hammocks and disturbed places in central and southern Florida, where it can displace existing vegetation. A plant growing outside cultivation should be assessed in its local setting before removal is planned.
identification: Glossy leaves clustered into rosettes; small fragrant white flowers on long stalks and tiny three-lobed capsules. Include the connection between rosettes and the long flowering stalks in photographs. Glossy leaves alone may suggest other members of the spiderwort family, including native plants. White flowers are small and short-lived, so a close view while open is more useful than a faded cluster. Variegated foliage is a cultivated form, not a separate identification rule.
actions: Check whether a patch remains within a maintained bed or has extended into neighboring vegetation. In areas with documented escape problems, contain removed rosettes and rooted pieces and inspect the boundary again after growth resumes. Where native spiderworts grow nearby, confirm each plant before removal. Seek local advice for extensive patches in hammocks or other sensitive habitat.

proposedDescription: Basswood thrips is a small, brown insect associated mainly with lindens and basswoods. Adults have narrow wings, and identifying them precisely requires microscopic details such as a tiny curved claw on the front foot. The insect feeds on young developing buds and leaves. Native to Europe, it has become a forest pest in the upper Midwest, where outbreaks can cause extensive loss of basswood foliage. Its early-season feeding can leave damage that is mistaken for frost injury rather than insect activity.
identification: Brown winged adults on developing basswood buds or foliage; a specialist should distinguish them from other thrips. Inspect basswood during bud expansion, when feeding activity and fresh injury are more informative than old summer damage. Collect close views of distorted new leaves and any tiny insects present. Brown coloration and narrow wings are only starting clues; the curved forefoot claw and other microscopic traits separate this thrips from relatives.
actions: Record when damage first appears and whether several trees show the same pattern. Ask a forest-health or extension specialist to compare insect injury with frost damage and other causes. Avoid making broad insecticide applications from leaf appearance alone. If sampling is requested, label the host and date carefully so the diagnosis can be related to the early-season life cycle.

proposedDescription: Bay Biscayne creeping oxeye, also called wedelia, is a fast-spreading groundcover with fleshy leaves and bright yellow daisy-like flowers. Its rounded stems creep along the ground and can form dense mats. Native to tropical America, it was planted widely for its flowers and rapid cover. Runners and broken pieces are particularly important in its spread, so cutting a patch can scatter material capable of growing again.
identification: Low mats of rounded trailing stems, fleshy irregularly toothed leaves and solitary yellow-orange flower heads. Follow a trailing stem to see how it grows through the patch, and photograph the leaves attached to it. Leaf lobing varies, so the name trilobata should not lead you to reject an otherwise matching plant with less obvious lobes. Yellow daisy heads alone overlap with numerous other groundcovers.
actions: Before working on an escaped mat, plan how to collect every cut runner without scattering it into neighboring soil or drains. Mowing can multiply the fragments that need attention. Monitor the edge and any disturbed soil afterward, and ask local extension staff about persistent regrowth. In regions where this is a garden escape problem, choose a locally appropriate replacement groundcover.

proposedDescription: Bean common mosaic necrosis virus is a plant virus that affects beans and related legumes. It can produce mottled, distorted leaves, but the result depends strongly on the bean variety. In some varieties, infection triggers darkening veins, wilt and widespread tissue death; in others it resembles ordinary bean common mosaic. Infected seed can introduce the virus, and aphids spread it between plants during brief feeding visits. Because related viruses can cause similar symptoms, laboratory testing is needed to distinguish them reliably.
identification: Leaf mottling or distortion, or dark veins and wilt in susceptible bean varieties; symptoms alone cannot separate BCMNV from related viruses. Photograph the whole plant and close views of mottled or darkened leaves, keeping the variety name with the record. Necrosis depends on host genetics, so it cannot be interpreted as a universal symptom. Aphids on a plant are not a species-level virus test; a diagnostic laboratory must distinguish this infection from BCMV and other problems.
actions: Keep seed-lot information and note which varieties are affected before consulting a crop adviser. Use a resistance recommendation that explicitly accounts for BCMNV, since resistance to another bean virus may not provide the same protection. Avoid saving or exchanging seed from suspect plants. Field decisions should consider confirmed infection, crop stage and local advice rather than relying on aphid control alone.

proposedDescription: Bd chytrid fungus is a microscopic fungus that infects amphibian skin. It releases swimming spores into water, allowing infection to pass through wet environments. Some amphibians carry it without obvious illness, while others develop chytridiomycosis, with abnormal skin shedding, weakness or loss of normal movement. Severe outbreaks have contributed to amphibian declines around the world. A skin swab can reveal infection, but visible illness is not specific enough to identify the fungus, and detecting it does not always mean the animal has developed disease.
identification: No reliable naked-eye identification; unusual shedding or weakness warrants expert assessment and laboratory testing. Watch from a distance for abnormal posture, sluggish movement or unusual shedding, but do not use these signs as a field diagnosis. Apparently healthy amphibians may also carry the fungus. A wildlife professional can arrange appropriate skin sampling and distinguish Bd from other causes of sickness, including the separate salamander pathogen Bsal.
actions: Leave wild amphibians at their original site and report unusual illness or multiple deaths to the wildlife agency. Remove mud and follow its cleaning and disinfection instructions before visiting another wetland. Keep captive amphibians and their water away from natural habitats. Treatment of an individual animal belongs with a veterinarian; adding disinfectant to a pond is not an appropriate response.

proposedDescription: Beach sheoak is a tall flowering tree whose fine, drooping branchlets can make it look like a pine. Its true leaves are tiny scales arranged in rings around those jointed branchlets, and the fruits form small woody, cone-like clusters. Native across parts of Asia and the western Pacific, it has been planted widely in tropical regions. In Florida, it is one of several introduced Casuarina species that have spread into native plant communities. Counting the leaf scales helps distinguish it from related sheoaks.
identification: Examine one joint of the slender branchlet with a lens: there are usually six to eight tiny leaf teeth in a ring. These scale leaves, together with the jointed branchlets and woody fruit clusters, distinguish its flowering-tree structure from a pine. Include the fruit cluster and bark in photographs rather than relying on a distant silhouette. Related Casuarina species and hybrids can be difficult to separate, particularly when the sample lacks mature reproductive material.
actions: Record seedlings and any spread beyond an intended windbreak before deciding on management. Large coastal trees require qualified assessment, especially where felling could affect buildings, dunes or neighboring vegetation. Use regional planting guidance when selecting a replacement. Do not infer that every fine-leaved tree near a beach is this species or that its presence alone justifies clearing the site.

proposedDescription: Beaked hawksbeard is a leafy herb with yellow, dandelion-like flower heads and toothed or lobed leaves. proposedDescription: Bean aphids are small, dark sap-feeding insects that gather on tender growth, leaves and stems. Adults are usually dull dark green to purplish black with lighter legs; both winged and wingless forms occur. Dense colonies can curl foliage and weaken young bean plants, while their sugary honeydew leaves surfaces sticky and encourages sooty mold. They can also carry plant viruses. Lady beetles, lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps often reduce colonies naturally, so the presence of aphids does not always mean treatment is needed.
identification: Adults are usually dull dark green to purplish black, with pale legs and two short tailpipe-like projections near the rear. The shinier cowpea aphid is a useful comparison on beans, although color alone cannot settle an ambiguous colony. Photograph several adults and the tender shoot they occupy. Shed skins, ants and sticky honeydew may draw attention to the insects first; a specialist can resolve mixed colonies in which more than one aphid species is feeding.
actions: Record whether new growth is actually distorted and whether lady beetle larvae, lacewings or aphid mummies are present. Recheck tolerable colonies before intervening. In a bean crop, ask for guidance tied to growth stage and any virus concerns; visible aphids do not establish which virus, if any, infects a plant. Preserve natural enemies wherever practical.

proposedDescription: Bean flower thrips is a small insect most often found inside legume flowers. Adults are dark brown, with pale areas on the narrow wings, while males can be smaller and lighter. proposedDescription: Bean root aphids are small, pale insects that feed on the roots of beans and many other plants. The wingless root-feeding forms are yellowish white with a dusting of wax and a light brown head and legs. This broad choice of hosts means the name describes only part of the aphid's way of life.

Inspect replacement plants for concealed root problems and avoid sharing suspect rooted material. Management of a crop root infestation needs local advice; removing unrelated Pistacia trees is not warranted by an uncertain aphid observation.

proposedDescription: Bean weevil is a small seed beetle that develops inside dry beans. Adults have mottled brown, black and gray wing covers and lack the long snout associated with true weevils. The larvae chew within seeds, often remaining hidden until an adult leaves a neat round exit hole. Infestations can begin in the field and continue through repeated generations in warm storage. identification: Small mottled beetles without a long snout; round holes in stored beans and pale larvae within seeds. actions: Label and isolate affected packages, check neighboring beans and clean spilled material from storage crevices. Use sound, clean containers for uninfested supplies. Do not mix suspect beans into a clean lot merely because adults are no longer visible.

proposedDescription: Beardless rabbitsfoot grass is a moisture-loving grass that forms loose tufts and can spread through creeping stems that root where they touch the ground. proposedDescription: Bed bugs are small, blood-feeding insects that hide in narrow spaces close to where people rest. Unfed adults are flat, oval and brown, roughly the size of an apple seed; after feeding they become fuller and redder. Young bugs are smaller and much paler. Skin reactions alone cannot establish the cause, so record exactly where the insect or signs were found rather than relying on the appearance of bites.

Coordinate with building management when appropriate and use a pest professional's integrated plan for inspection, containment and follow-up. Do not improvise room heating or apply outdoor products indoors. Keep monitoring after treatment according to the plan, because a single inspection without visible insects does not establish that all hiding places are clear.

proposedDescription: Beech leaf disease is caused by a microscopic leaf nematode, Litylenchus crenatae subsp. mccannii. A distinctive early sign is dark banding between the veins of beech leaves, especially when viewed against the light. More affected leaves may become thick, curled or misshapen, while damaged buds produce fewer leaves and the crown gradually thins. The nematodes spend winter in buds and affect developing foliage. American, European and Oriental beeches can develop the disease, so host species alone does not rule it out.
identification: Hold a leaf toward the light to check for dark interveinal bands, and compare nearby leaves for thickening and distortion. Confirmation needs specialist assessment. Record whether affected and apparently healthy leaves occur together on a branch; overall yellowing alone is less informative. Photograph the tree crown from a repeatable position so changes can be assessed over time. Banding is a useful warning sign, but other injuries can coexist, and a photograph cannot show the microscopic nematode itself.
actions: Record the first date of symptoms and the beech's planting history if known. Ask the local diagnostic service whether it needs leaves, buds or photographs at the current season. Avoid sharing cuttings or moving suspect nursery trees while the problem is assessed. Care decisions should follow current local tree-health advice rather than a homemade nematode treatment or indiscriminate pruning.

proposedDescription: The beech tree nematode is a microscopic roundworm that causes beech leaf disease. It lives in developing buds and leaves, where its presence is linked to dark bands between leaf veins and to thickened, distorted foliage. Heavy damage can prevent buds from opening normally and leave the crown sparse. Researchers distinguished this North American subspecies from the previously described Japanese Litylenchus crenatae using body features and DNA, and reproduced disease symptoms by introducing nematodes into beech buds.
identification: The nematode itself is too small for ordinary field identification. Dark bands between leaf veins are a useful warning sign, but laboratory examination confirms the organism. Photograph affected buds as well as leaves if poor bud opening is noticeable. Retain both a close view of the interveinal pattern and a whole-branch view showing healthy-looking foliage nearby. Laboratory staff use nematode body characters and genetic comparisons; the small organism cannot be confirmed from the visible bands alone.
actions: Keep reports tied to the original tree, with its host identity and symptom dates. Contact a tree-health service before taking material elsewhere, and request its sampling instructions. Continue observing crown condition while advice is obtained. If the tree is in a collection, avoid distributing young plants from the affected group until the movement risk has been professionally assessed.

proposedDescription: Beefsteakplant is an aromatic annual in the mint family, native to Asia and introduced in many parts of North America. It has opposite, toothed leaves on square stems, with small flowers grouped along upright spikes. Common ornamental forms have broad, crinkled, purple to reddish leaves. Plants produce abundant seed and may appear beyond gardens along roadsides or in other disturbed ground. Despite its history of cultivation, it can be troublesome in pastures because the plant is toxic to livestock.
identification: Check for opposite, broad toothed leaves, square stems and small flowers in narrow spikes. Leaf color varies among forms and is not enough for identification. Inspect the leaf arrangement and stem shape together, since purple foliage also occurs in many unrelated ornamentals. Small flower spikes and developing seed structures help distinguish a mature plant from other aromatic mint-family herbs. Do not taste a leaf to identify it, particularly when the plant is growing in a pasture or mixed forage.
actions: Mark suspect patches so they are not inadvertently cut into hay or offered as forage. Consult an agricultural adviser about confirmed plants and a veterinarian if animals may have eaten them. For unwanted garden volunteers, prevent seed production and check nearby disturbed soil later. Culinary cultivation of selected forms does not establish that an unidentified pasture plant is safe for livestock.

proposedDescription: Beet armyworm is a moth whose caterpillars feed on many vegetables, field crops and weeds. Young larvae gather together and scrape leaf surfaces, sometimes leaving thin, windowlike patches and loose webbing. Older caterpillars spread out, chew irregular holes and may enter developing fruit. They are usually green with lengthwise stripes and a small dark spot near the second pair of true legs. Adults are mottled gray-brown moths, while eggs occur in clusters beneath a covering of pale, hairlike scales.
identification: Look for smooth, striped caterpillars with a dark spot above the second true leg, scale-covered egg clusters and grouped young larvae. Similar armyworms require closer comparison. Look for groups of small larvae near a covered egg mass, then examine older caterpillars separately. Body color varies, so combine the smooth surface, striping and side spot with host and feeding observations. Include damaged fruit or foliage in the record; an adult moth at a light does not prove larvae are injuring the crop.
actions: Check new feeding damage during crop inspections and record the size of larvae, since timing affects management choices. Consult local extension guidance for the crop rather than transferring a recommendation from another vegetable. Conserve predators and parasitoids where possible, and avoid unnecessary treatments when injury is minor. Reassess fresh growth after any authorized response.

proposedDescription: Bell's honeysuckle is a dense, many-stemmed shrub produced by crosses between Morrow's and Tatarian honeysuckles. It bears opposite, oval leaves and paired tubular flowers, often pink when fresh and yellow as they age. Red or orange berries follow and can be carried by birds. The hybrid is variable, with leaves and twigs ranging from nearly hairless to lightly downy. In parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States it grows along woodland edges, roadsides and old fields, sometimes forming dense stands.
identification: Look for paired flowers and berries, opposite smooth-edged leaves and older stems with hollow centers. Hybrid identification needs comparison with both parent species. Compare hairiness on young twigs and leaf undersides as well as paired flowers. The hybrid can be intermediate between its parents, and a red berry or hollow old stem alone does not resolve that relationship. Photograph flowers at different ages if available. Native bush honeysuckles deserve careful separation before any clearing begins.
actions: Map confirmed shrubs and check for nearby seedlings in areas where local guidance calls for control. Plan work before berries are widely dispersed and contain fruiting branches. Cut established shrubs may require follow-up for regrowth, so obtain a method suited to their size and site. Retain surrounding native cover where possible to reduce unnecessary disturbance.
