proposedDescription: The brown-dotted clothes moth is a small, easily overlooked moth with mottled brown wings and a tufted head. Its larvae feed on dry plant and animal material, often in bird nests or poultry houses where feathers and other remains collect. Despite its name, it is only occasionally associated with damage to clothing. Stored animal specimens can also provide food. Adults resemble other small nest moths, so finding one indoors does not by itself show that fabrics are being damaged.
identification: Look for small, mottled brown forewings with dark spots and a hairy head. Similar Niditinea species may require specialist confirmation. A clear dorsal photograph should show the dark markings on the pale brown wings, as well as the hairy head. Traps sold for another clothes moth can also catch this species. A trap catch is therefore a reason to investigate, not proof that wool garments are being eaten.
actions: Inspect feathers, taxidermy and other stored animal material if catches continue, especially in attic storage. Isolate a suspect object while a specialist checks larvae and damage. Avoid disturbing occupied bird nests; outdoor nesting material can be a source without indicating an indoor collection infestation. Use monitoring records to locate the source before choosing any treatment.

proposedDescription: Browne's blechum is a low herb with paired leaves and upright flower spikes. The overlapping green bracts around those spikes are often more noticeable than the tiny pale flowers, giving the plant its other name, green shrimp plant. Its stems can spread along the ground and root where they touch the soil. Native to tropical parts of the Americas, it has become established beyond that range and is listed as invasive in Florida. The square-looking flower spikes are a useful starting point for recognizing it.
identification: Photograph the paired, oval leaves and dense spikes of overlapping leafy bracts, including any small pale flowers. Look at a flower spike from both the side and above to show the stacked leafy bracts that make it look squared. The small flower may be partly hidden. Trace low stems carefully: an upright flowering shoot may belong to a trailing section already rooted elsewhere.
actions: Check local invasive-plant guidance before moving it. For a confirmed unwanted plant, gather rooted nodes along the ground rather than removing only the visible flowering top. Keep moist fragments off bare soil during cleanup. Check beneath neighboring plants for overlooked stem sections, and avoid moving potting mix containing roots or seed to another garden bed. In mixed vegetation, identify each patch before disturbance.

proposedDescription: Brown knapweed is a perennial wildflower with purple-pink flower heads on upright, branching stems. Beneath each head are overlapping bracts with broad, brown, papery tips that look unevenly torn. Native to Europe, it has become established in North America in fields, meadows and disturbed ground, and can form large patches. It also crosses with black knapweed, producing plants that blur the usual identification clues. A close look at the bracts is more useful than flower color alone.
identification: Photograph the side and underside of a flower head to show its broad, irregularly torn brown bract tips; hybrids can be difficult to name. Check several heads because bract shape can vary within a patch, particularly where hybrids occur. The plant lacks the sharp spines of a true thistle, although its flower heads can give a similar first impression.
actions: Seek local identification help before management, and check your state's knapweed guidance before moving plants or seed. Record the size of the patch and whether it borders hay, pasture or natural grassland. Where local control is appropriate, limit seed movement on mowers and cut material. Ask an adviser how to handle a mixed or hybrid population, and keep surrounding desirable plants intact rather than clearing every purple-flowered stem in the same area.

proposedDescription: Browntail moths have white wings and a tuft of brown hair at the tip of the abdomen. Their caterpillars feed on trees and shrubs, including oaks, apples and cherries, and spend winter together in silk nests that hold dead leaves on branch tips. Established in parts of New England after introduction from Europe, they can strip foliage during outbreaks. The caterpillars' tiny hairs are also an important concern: they can irritate skin and breathing, even when carried on wind or left on surfaces.
identification: Look from a distance for dark, hairy caterpillars with white side markings and two red spots near the rear, or compact winter webs at branch tips. Winter nests are compact bundles of silk and retained dead leaves near branch tips. Web size or a white adult moth alone can be misleading when similar species are present.
actions:
Avoid touching caterpillars or nests. Consult local forestry guidance for safe management and reporting; avoid disturbing infested material in ways that send hairs into the air. Observe nests from the ground and record their position on the tree for a qualified adviser. Avoid mowing, blowing or shaking material beneath an active infestation if that would spread the hairs. Follow current local guidance for the season and setting, and use professional help for nests that cannot be reached safely without disturbing them.

Shed hairs can remain irritating for several years. Seek emergency medical care for difficulty breathing or swallowing, or swelling of the mouth, tongue or throat.

proposedDescription: Watersipora arcuata is a marine animal that grows in colonies, often as dark crusts with reddish growing edges. A colony is made up of many tiny connected individuals and can develop overlapping, curled layers. It attaches to hard surfaces such as rocks, docks and boat hulls, which can carry it between harbors. Records from Southern California and Hawaii reflect its history of introductions, although its original native range remains uncertain. Similar Watersipora species are hard to separate without examining their tiny skeletal features.
identification: A red edge and darker center can show where a colony is growing, but several encrusting marine animals share that pattern. Photograph the margin, surface and attachment site. The minute openings in the skeleton, rather than broad colony color, are what specialists compare among similar Watersipora species.
actions: Photograph suspected colonies and their location. Follow marina and local biofouling guidance; avoid moving fouled equipment or scraping organisms into another waterbody. Include vessel or equipment movement history when reporting an unfamiliar colony to a marina or biosecurity service. Plan maintenance before moving to a new harbor, using a facility that can contain the removed fouling. Leave growth on natural rock undisturbed while identification is pending, and do not assume that an apparently clean painted surface cannot carry this bryozoan.

proposedDescription: Buckhorn plantain grows as a clump of narrow, strongly ribbed leaves close to the ground. Slender, leafless stalks rise above them, ending in short flower heads ringed with pale, projecting stamens. Originally from Eurasia, it is now a familiar plant in lawns, paths, fields and other disturbed places across much of North America. Its low-growing leaves help it persist under mowing. Compared with broadleaf plantain, the leaves are much narrower and the flowering heads are usually shorter and more compact.
identification: Look for a basal rosette of narrow leaves with prominent lengthwise ribs and leafless stalks carrying compact flower heads. During flowering, pale stamens project around the short head, while the stalk itself carries no leaves. Broadleaf plantain has a wider blade, so include a whole leaf and the flowering head in identification photographs.
actions: Where removal is needed, remove the crown as well as the leaves before seed develops; mowing alone often leaves the plant alive. A few plants in a lawn may not need action unless they interfere with the intended use. Where a patch is unwanted, inspect the growing point after removal and revisit for remaining crowns or seedlings. Improve thin turf or other bare cover as appropriate for the site, since repeated mowing of the flower stalks does not remove the low rosette.

proposedDescription: Buckthorn aphids are tiny, soft-bodied insects that feed on plant sap. They are usually pale yellow or green, and colonies can gather on the undersides of potato leaves. In colder regions they spend winter as eggs on buckthorn, then move to other plants during the growing season. Their importance in crops is not just the sap they take: they can carry potato viruses between plants. Several aphids look alike, making a careful identification useful before deciding how to respond.
identification: Adults are roughly 1-2 mm long, pale yellow to green, with short antennae and short rear tubes. Winged forms have a darker head and thorax. Look beneath lower potato leaves and photograph a colony before disturbing it. Include winged and wingless individuals if both are present. Pale color and small size are shared by several aphids, and the short rear tubes need a close view rather than a distant photograph of curled foliage.
actions: Have crop colonies identified by an extension adviser before interpreting their virus risk. Record which plants carry colonies and how rapidly numbers change between visits. Virus concerns need a crop-specific assessment, since removing visible aphids does not reverse an infection already transmitted. Keep natural enemies in mind when considering treatment, and ask a crop adviser about the actual local risk before removing nearby shrubs or applying broad insect control.

proposedDescription: Buckwheat grows quickly into a soft, branching annual with arrowhead-shaped leaves and clusters of small white or pink-tinged flowers. Although its seeds are used like grain, it belongs to the knotweed family rather than the grasses. Farmers also grow it as a short-season cover crop, where its dense growth shades weeds and its flowers draw bees and other beneficial insects. Plants sometimes appear outside cultivation, especially on disturbed ground; that alone does not establish an invasive impact.
identification: Alternate arrowhead-shaped leaves, hollow stems that may redden, and clusters of five-parted white flowers. Follow the leaves up a stem to see their alternate arrangement and pointed, arrowlike bases. The small clustered flowers differ from the inconspicuous flowering spikes of true cereal grasses. A plant can begin flowering while still quite small, so height alone is not a reliable guide to maturity.
actions: For a deliberately planted buckwheat cover crop, decide when to end the planting before seed ripens if volunteers would interfere with the next crop. Monitor field edges and equipment for seed movement, particularly where buckwheat could contaminate another grain harvest. Retain the flowering crop for its intended use when suitable, while treating stray plants in neighboring beds according to that setting.

proposedDescription: The Budapest slug is a slender, ground-dwelling slug often found around gardens, cultivated fields and other disturbed places. Its brownish-gray body is densely speckled, with a pale yellow ridge running down the tail. A dark stripe along the otherwise pale underside is especially useful when separating it from similar keeled slugs. It can feed both above and below the soil surface, damaging root crops, bulbs and newly sown seed. A curled, horseshoe-like resting posture is another helpful clue.
identification: Usually 4-6 cm long; pale tail keel, spotted gray-brown body and a dark central stripe on the sole. The keel is the raised ridge along the tail behind the mantle, not a stripe painted on the skin. Photograph an extended animal to show that ridge and the dark spotting. The sole pattern is useful, but similar slugs and variable individuals can still need expert examination.
actions: Photograph the back and underside for identification, and inspect bulbs and root crops where feeding damage occurs. Keep a suspect slug contained briefly for a photograph rather than transferring it to another garden. If the crop damage is significant, ask local extension staff to distinguish this species from other slugs and choose monitoring or control appropriate to the affected planting.

proposedDescription: Buff coconut mealybugs look rather like tiny wax-covered cushions on their host plants. Adult females are orange to reddish brown, with yellowish wax and pointed tufts around the edge and across the back. Despite the common name, they feed on many plants, including palms, avocado and ornamental flowers. Their sap feeding produces sticky honeydew that can support black sooty mold, and ants may tend the colonies. Close inspection of a mature female is often needed to confirm the species.
identification: Oval females about 1.5-2.5 mm long, with yellow-orange wax and pyramid-shaped tufts; males form small white cocoons. Use a magnified photograph of a mature female to show the pointed wax tufts, especially those around the body margin. White cottony material alone is not enough: several mealybugs and other insects leave similar wax. Sticky leaves or black mold show a problem worth inspecting but do not identify the insect.
actions: Check protected leaf bases and the undersides of foliage before a nursery plant joins an established collection. Keep affected plants separate while the insect is identified and inspect neighboring pots for colonies. Note ant activity and the host plant in a report so an adviser can assess both the mealybug and conditions helping it persist.

proposedDescription: Buffelgrass forms coarse perennial clumps with rough leaves and fuzzy, bottlebrush-shaped seed heads. Originally planted as forage in dry regions, it is a serious problem in the Sonoran Desert, where it fills the spaces between native shrubs and cacti. Those connected patches carry fire through vegetation that is poorly adapted to burning. The seed heads change from reddish or purplish tones to tan as they mature, and seeds can travel on shoes, clothing, animals and moving water.
identification: Coarse bunchgrass with rough bluish-green leaves and dense cylindrical, bristly seed heads that turn tan. Look for a dense clump with older dry leaves beneath newer growth, and photograph a seed head before removing it. Fountain grass and native bunchgrasses can also have bristly heads, so the entire clump and leaves matter. Dry tan plants may still be important fuel even when they are no longer growing.
actions: Report new desert patches and join trained local removal efforts; follow up for regrowth. In the Sonoran Desert, give new small patches attention before they join into continuous cover between native plants. Work with a trained local group to protect cacti and other nearby vegetation. Clean tools and clothing after work, contain seed heads, and return after subsequent growth periods to check for plants missed beneath the original clump.

proposedDescription: Bukhara fleeceflower, also called silver lace vine, can cover a fence with a cloud of tiny pale flowers in late summer. This deciduous, twining climber has heart-shaped leaves and woody older stems. Its speed is part of its appeal in gardens, but also the reason it needs careful placement: shoots can scramble across nearby shrubs and quickly outgrow their support. Small winged fruits develop after flowering, often taking on a pink or reddish tint.
identification: Twining woody vine with alternate heart-shaped leaves and loose masses of small white to pinkish flowers. Follow a stem around its support to see the twining habit. The many tiny flowers can make a large vine look white from a distance, but a close view should also show the heart-shaped leaves and developing winged fruits. Other vines called fleeceflower may have different growth habits.
actions: Keep cultivated vines within their support with regular pruning, and remove unwanted growth before it spreads over neighboring plants. Choose a support and location that leave room for regular access to the whole plant. Check for shoots crossing into shrubs, gutters or adjoining property while they are still easy to reach. Where an established vine has become too large, plan staged work and support assessment rather than pulling down heavy tangled growth in one piece.

proposedDescription: The bulb and potato aphid lives in places that are easy to overlook: around roots, inside stored bulbs and on potato tubers. It feeds on a wide range of plants, including ornamental bulbs such as tulips and gladiolus, and can affect crops both in the field and in storage. It is also associated with transmission of plant viruses. Because colonies may remain hidden below ground, careful inspection of planting material is more useful than looking only at the leaves.

Look in the folds of bulbs and around sprouting tubers, where aphids can be hidden from an overhead inspection. Photograph a colony with the affected plant material and a scale reference. The host is a clue to where to look, but many aphids use roots or stored planting material.
actions: Separate suspicious bulbs or tubers from clean stock and check the surrounding storage area. Keep purchase labels and storage dates with a sample if an adviser requests one. Do not share apparently infested planting material while waiting for a diagnosis. In a crop, combine the insect identification with plant-virus advice instead of assuming every pale or distorted shoot has the same cause.

proposedDescription: Bulbil bugle-lily sends tall spikes of curved, trumpet-shaped flowers above fans of tough, swordlike leaves. This South African perennial grows from underground corms and is familiar in gardens for its salmon, pink, red or pale blooms. The bulbil-producing form develops small brown cormlets along the flower stems, each capable of starting another plant. In invaded open habitats, dense clumps can crowd out other vegetation; moving soil or dumping garden waste can carry the corms to new sites.
identification: Swordlike basal leaves and tall tubular-flowered spikes; inspect stems for brown bulbils in the bulbil-producing form. Include the base of the leaf fan and the whole flower spike in photographs. Look for small hard cormlets attached along the stalk after flowering; they are not ordinary seed capsules. Not every garden Watsonia plant produces those bulbils, so the presence of swordlike leaves alone does not establish the troublesome form.
actions: Keep corms and bulbils out of dumped garden waste. For small unwanted clumps, carefully collect underground corms and stem bulbils and monitor regrowth. Before dividing or moving a garden clump, check whether cormlets are scattered nearby. Keep excavated soil close to the work area and collect loose corms rather than shaking them into adjacent vegetation. proposedDescription: Bulbous bluegrass is a small, cool-season grass that gets an early start in spring and dries out early as conditions warm. It grows in tufts, with narrow leaves ending in the little boat-shaped tips typical of bluegrasses. Many plants carry an unusual flowering head full of tiny leafy bulblets, rather than an ordinary-looking spray of seeds. These bulblets and the swollen bases of the shoots help it persist and spread. It occurs on disturbed ground and has also been used to stabilize eroding soil.
identification: Small bunchgrass with boat-tipped leaves, swollen basal shoots and often sprouting bulblets in the flower head. A close view of the flowering head may show tiny green shoots emerging where ordinary grass flowers would be expected. Check the swollen bases separately, because they are easy to miss beneath old leaf sheaths. The combination is more useful than the plant's early spring growth alone.
actions: Photograph both the plant base and flowering head. Avoid carrying bulblets in soil or equipment when working through a patch. Record the clump while it is green and its head is developed; later dry growth is harder to recognize. Keep detached bulblets with any removed material, and brush them from tools before moving to another site. Assess the patch in the context of local pasture or habitat management instead of assuming that every occurrence of an introduced grass needs removal.

proposedDescription: Bulbous canarygrass, often called Harding grass, is a robust perennial that forms tall, leafy clumps topped by dense cylindrical flower heads. Slightly swollen shoot bases give it its other common name. Introduced from Mediterranean Europe as a forage grass, it has escaped into fields, ditches and streamside habitats. In affected western landscapes, established clumps compete with native vegetation for water and space. Most new plants arise from seed, although pieces of its short underground stems can also regrow.
identification: Coarse clumps with broad grass blades, swollen shoot bases, a membranous ligule and dense spike-like flower heads. Examine the leaf collar to see the thin membranous ligule, and include the base of a shoot if it can be viewed without disturbing nearby vegetation. A dense cylindrical head can resemble several other grasses. Mature spikelets, shoot bases and broad leaves together give a botanist a more dependable comparison.
actions: Remove small unwanted patches with follow-up checks; avoid cultivating established clumps into fragments, which can regrow. Map an unwanted clump before it blends into taller seasonal growth. Where digging is appropriate, keep removed underground pieces contained and check the same footprint later for shoots. On streambanks or wet ground, discuss the work with the land manager so soil disturbance does not create erosion or spread fragments into adjoining areas.

proposedDescription: Bull thistle starts as a low rosette of prickly leaves, then raises a branching stem with pinkish-purple flower heads. Unlike creeping thistles, it has a taproot and spreads by seed. The leaves are rough and hairy above, woolly beneath, and tipped with sharp spines; spiny wings also run down the stems. Originally from Eurasia, it readily colonizes disturbed soil and heavily grazed ground. Its prickles discourage grazing and can make neighboring forage harder for animals to reach.
identification: Spiny-winged stems, coarse prickly leaves with woolly undersides, and large purple heads surrounded by sharp bracts. Compare the upright stem with native thistles rather than identifying the plant from a purple flower alone. The continuous spiny wings down the stem and the coarse upper leaf surface are especially useful. A first-year rosette lacks the conspicuous tall flowering shape, so photograph both leaf surfaces carefully.
actions: Confirm the identification against native thistles. Remove small rosettes below the soil surface before flowering and revisit for seedlings. Use gloves and suitable tools when working around sharp rosettes. If a confirmed plant has already formed seed, contain the head before moving the stem. Coordinate pasture work with grazing and ground-cover management so bare ground does not invite another flush of seedlings. Preserve identified native thistles, which can occur near introduced ones and support local wildlife.

proposedDescription: Bur chervil has delicate, fernlike leaves, but its small hooked fruits are its most useful calling card. This Eurasian herb commonly grows as an annual, with hollow, branching stems and little clusters of white flowers beside the upper leaves. The burrlike fruits catch on animals and help the plant travel beyond the parent patch. In parts of the western United States it can form dense growth along waterways and beneath shrubs, although it also survives in drier grassland.
identification: Finely divided leaves, small white flower umbels beside upper leaves, and short oval fruits covered in hooked hairs. A close view of a mature fruit should show the hooked surface and the short, smooth beak at its tip. The small flower clusters sit beside upper leaves rather than forming one large showy umbrella. Fernlike foliage by itself is unreliable among the many members of the carrot family.
actions: Photograph ripe fruits for a reliable identification. Pull small confirmed patches before seed ripens and brush burrs from clothing and equipment. Do not taste an unfamiliar carrot-family plant as an identification test. Keep ripe burrs from catching on bags and cuffs while inspecting a patch. For locally unwanted growth, work before fruits become easily detached and check nearby shaded ground for additional plants. In riparian habitat, avoid pulling large mixed mats that would expose soil or damage the roots of neighboring shrubs.

proposedDescription: Burclover spreads low across the ground, with three-parted leaves that can easily be mistaken for an ordinary clover. Small yellow flowers give way to tightly coiled pods, often armed with hooks that cling to fur and clothing. Look for the tightly coiled pod after the yellow flowers fade; the fruit is much more distinctive than a three-leaflet leaf. The teeth along the leaflet margins also help when compared with true clovers. Some pods are less conspicuously hooked, so use several fruits and flowers for confirmation.

proposedDescription: Burmann's basketgrass is a low annual grass with spreading stems and relatively broad leaves. Several short side branches carry the spikelets, whose awns extend well beyond them. The rippled leaf surface is a useful clue, but broad leaves also occur in other basketgrasses with different regional status.

proposedDescription: Burmese fishtail palm gets its name from the jagged, fan-shaped leaflets that resemble little fish tails. Several slender trunks grow together in a clump, with new shoots arising at the base. Flowering follows an unusual sequence: a trunk flowers near its top first, then progressively lower down, and dies after its final flowering. The rest of the clump continues growing. Native to tropical Asia, this palm is widely cultivated in warm climates; its small fruits contain irritating material and should not be handled casually.
identification: Clustered smooth trunks and large, twice-divided leaves with broad, ragged-edged fishtail leaflets. The leaf is divided twice, with the distinctive ragged leaflets attached along smaller branches of the main leaf. Count the stems at ground level to distinguish a clustering palm from a single-trunked relative. Flowering on one trunk does not mean every stem in the clump will die together.

Leave healthy neighboring stems alone unless the whole planting needs removal, and check local planting guidance before establishing another clump.

proposedDescription: Burmese pythons are large, muscular snakes patterned with dark, irregular patches on a tan background. They are comfortable in water and can be remarkably difficult to notice among wetland plants. Native to Southeast Asia, they have an established invasive population in southern Florida, where they eat a wide variety of mammals, birds and reptiles. Their broad diet is well documented: one study of digestive contents from more than 1,700 Florida pythons identified 76 prey species.
identification: Large tan snake with dark puzzle-piece blotches and a dark arrow-shaped marking on the head; do not approach for a closer look. A distant photograph of the back pattern and head, taken without approaching, can help wildlife staff compare it with native large snakes. Water or dense vegetation may hide much of the body. Do not try to reveal the head or stretch out a snake to improve an identification photograph.
actions: Keep a safe distance, take a distant photograph and report suspected Florida sightings through the state wildlife reporting system. Keep people and pets back and note a precise location, direction of movement and time. Use the current wildlife reporting route for the area, particularly for a suspected new locality beyond known populations. Leave capture to trained, authorized responders. Owners of captive snakes should arrange an appropriate rehoming option rather than releasing an animal that has become difficult to keep.

proposedDescription: Bushkiller is a vigorous vine that uses tendrils to climb over shrubs, trees and garden structures. Its leaves have five toothed leaflets, and the small flowers are orange or salmon colored. The fleshy roots send up new shoots, particularly after they are disturbed, helping a patch recover even when the visible vines have been cut back. Native to Asia, Australia and nearby Pacific regions, it has escaped cultivation in the southern United States and is considered invasive in North Carolina.
identification: Climbing tendrils, alternate leaves divided into five shiny, serrated leaflets, and small orange-salmon flowers. Trace a complete leaf to its stem attachment to see how the five leaflets are arranged. Virginia creeper can also have five leaflets, so flower details and leaflet arrangement matter. A broad view of the vine shows its tendrils and the plants it is covering, while a close-up documents the small flowers.
actions: Seek a site-specific removal plan and revisit cut patches for new shoots. Identify where the vine enters the soil before cutting, and avoid disturbing roots unnecessarily during nearby digging. Root pieces can travel with moved soil even after the visible foliage is gone. For a canopy infestation, arrange safe access and a follow-up plan rather than pulling heavy vines from branches. Check the surrounding ground for shoots beyond the original crown.

proposedDescription: Bushy yate is an evergreen eucalypt from Western Australia that grows as a bushy small tree or a many-stemmed mallee. Its smooth bark varies from pale pink and gray-brown to reddish tones, sometimes with older bark collected around the base. Cream, greenish or yellow flowers add a softer contrast to the foliage. In its native landscape it grows on exposed slopes, rocky outcrops, coastal dunes and creek beds; it is also planted as an ornamental tree elsewhere.
identification: Bushy evergreen eucalypt with smooth, variably pink-gray bark and cream to green-yellow flowers; compare buds and fruit with a regional key. A general eucalypt silhouette is not enough for a confident name. Photograph unopened buds, open flowers and mature woody fruit on the same tree if possible, and include the bark at both the base and higher branches. Closely related yates can look much alike without those reproductive structures.
actions: Record flowers, buds and woody fruit for identification before managing a self-sown eucalypt; common names can cover similar species. Distinguish an intentionally planted tree from separate seedlings before deciding on management. Large-tree pruning or removal needs an assessment of branch weight, access and nearby structures; a common-name match alone is not a reason to remove a mature ornamental tree.

proposedDescription: Butter and eggs is the familiar yellow toadflax, with pale yellow, snapdragon-shaped flowers and a deeper orange-yellow center. Slender leaves line its upright stems, and each flower carries a long spur at the back. Once grown as an ornamental and dye plant, it now occurs along roadsides, in fields and in other open ground across much of temperate North America. A spreading root system lets it form persistent patches, making a few flowering stems part of a much larger plant.
identification: Narrow alternate leaves and two-toned yellow snapdragon flowers with long backward-pointing spurs. View an open flower from the side to show its long spur. The narrow leaves and orange-yellow raised center distinguish the familiar flowering form more clearly than a distant patch of yellow. A small cluster of stems may be connected underground, so visible stem count does not equal the number of separate plants.
actions: Remove small unwanted patches with their roots and monitor for regrowth; repeated management is usually needed. Avoid tilling an established patch casually because broken roots can produce more shoots. For a small confirmed infestation, plan repeat checks after removal and keep root pieces from being moved with soil. In mixed wildflower plantings, read the seed mixture before sowing and distinguish this species from desirable yellow-flowered plants before undertaking control.

proposedDescription: Butterfly tree is also known as purple orchid-tree, and both names fit: its rounded leaves are split into two lobes, while its showy flowers range from pink to deep purple. This small to medium tree comes from India and Myanmar and is widely planted in warm regions. Long, flat seedpods follow the flowers and may remain on the branches through winter. In Florida it has escaped cultivation and is considered invasive, so its ornamental appeal needs to be weighed against local spread.

proposedDescription: Butternut canker fungus attacks the bark of butternut trees, creating dead, sunken areas that can gradually encircle branches and trunks. Early damage may appear around leaf scars or wounds; older cankers become long cracks or open, dark-stained patches edged with ridges of living bark. As the disease advances, branches die back and the crown thins. Spores move between trees in rain splash and by other carriers. The disease has caused severe losses of butternut across its eastern North American range.
identification: On butternut, look for expanding branch dieback, dark sunken cankers, cracked bark and black-brown stained wood; laboratory confirmation may be needed. First confirm that the host is a butternut rather than a black walnut or a similar planted tree. Photograph the whole crown and individual bark lesions, noting whether dieback has increased between seasons. Several cankers may join into a larger damaged area, while smaller branch lesions can be easy to overlook.
actions: Ask a tree-health specialist to assess suspected cankers. Disinfect pruning tools between cuts and retain apparently healthy butternuts for conservation review. Avoid cutting into healthy bark merely to look for staining. Ask the specialist which samples, if any, are needed and how tools should be cleaned during work. Apparently healthy survivors can be important to conservation efforts, so discuss them before removal. Evaluate hazardous dead branches separately from the decision about retaining a living tree.

proposedDescription: Button burrweed stays close to the ground, forming small patches of finely divided, fernlike leaves. proposedDescription: Busy lizzy is a soft-stemmed tropical perennial best known as a colorful bedding plant for shady gardens. Compact mounds of glossy foliage carry flowers in white, pink, red, orange and many cultivated combinations, often from late spring until frost. In colder climates it is usually grown as an annual. For a previously affected bed, choose a resistant cultivar or suitable shade alternative. Keep good records of where diseased plants grew rather than assuming all impatiens types have identical susceptibility or that every yellow leaf indicates infection.

proposedDescription: Cabbage belongs to a remarkably varied species that also includes kale, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi. Centuries of cultivation have emphasized different parts of the same basic plant: leaves, flower buds or swollen stems. The leaves are usually thick and waxy, often blue-green, and flowering plants carry yellow, four-petaled blossoms followed by long pods. Wild cabbage and garden forms may look quite different, so a tight leafy head is only one possible expression of this species.
identification: Thick, waxy leaves, yellow cross-shaped flowers and elongated seedpods; cultivated forms vary widely in shape. Identify the cultivated form as well as the species when possible: a leafy kale and a swollen kohlrabi stem should not be expected to look alike. If a plant has bolted, photograph its waxy leaves, flower cluster and pods. A cabbage-like seedling alone may be difficult to separate from other brassicas.
actions: Identify volunteers before removal. Rotate vegetable beds and remove unwanted plants before pods split if reseeding is a concern. Manage planted vegetables for harvest and crop health, keeping volunteers only where they fit the bed plan. Inspect transplanted plants for caterpillars and disease before introducing them to clean beds. If saving seed, obtain advice on the crop's flowering and crossing behavior; seed from mixed flowering forms may not reproduce the parent plant's familiar appearance.

proposedDescription: Cabbage webworm is a small moth whose caterpillars feed on cabbage and other mustard-family plants. The larvae are pale gray-yellow with several darker stripes running lengthwise, and they shelter in silk among the young leaves. Feeding near the growing point is particularly damaging: young plants may be stunted or develop several small heads instead of one normal head. The adults are brownish moths with pale wing markings, but closely related webworms can look very similar.
identification: Striped larvae and silk webbing around brassica growing points; moth appearance alone does not reliably separate related Hellula species. Inspect the tender center of a young plant, where feeding can be concealed before obvious damage appears. Silk mixed with droppings is a useful warning sign, but diamondback moth and related webworms can also be involved. A clear larval photograph is more informative than a brown moth seen nearby.
actions: Check transplants before planting and revisit young crops frequently enough to find concealed feeding early. Keep affected plants and larvae available for a diagnostic photograph rather than discarding all evidence immediately. In a commercial crop, ask an adviser to match the response to the confirmed pest and crop stage, especially where multiple brassica caterpillars are present together.

proposedDescription: The small white butterflies visiting a vegetable patch may be the parents of imported cabbageworms. Keep beneficial predators in mind before choosing an insecticide; small, targeted garden actions can preserve the natural enemies that help limit repeated infestations.

Adults chew the leaves, while their larvae tunnel inside leaf stalks and stems, so the same pest can cause damage in two quite different places. The beetles are usually shiny metallic blue with orange-red legs, although pale and mixed-color forms occur. They are especially important in oilseed rape, where heavy feeding on newly emerged seedlings can destroy the growing point before plants have a chance to recover.
identification: Small beetle about 3-4.5 mm long, usually metallic blue with orange-red legs; pale larvae mine brassica stems and leaf stalks. Adults can jump when disturbed, so obtain a photograph before handling the leaf. Record the leg color and body shape as well as the metallic sheen. Leaf holes and internal tunneling represent different stages of attack; neither pattern alone separates this insect from all other brassica pests.
actions: Monitor emerging brassica crops for feeding and inspect stems if growth weakens; use local pest thresholds and advice rather than spraying on appearance alone. Note crop growth and recent weather, since slow-growing seedlings may be less able to replace eaten tissue. Ask a crop adviser how to assess larvae in leaf stalks and stems, and use guidance for the local crop rather than transferring a calendar from another country.

proposedDescription: Cactus moth caterpillars live together inside prickly pear pads, hollowing them out as they feed. Older larvae are bright orange-red with dark bands, a striking contrast to the unobtrusive gray-brown adult moth. Females stack eggs into slender sticks that can resemble cactus spines. Native cactus-feeding insects can produce similar damage, so report photographs of both the outside symptoms and any larvae already visible.

Keep nursery labels and purchase locations with a report if the cactus was recently acquired. Do not share pads for propagation or discard suspect pads where another cactus grows. Follow the plant-health service's instructions for sampling and disposal, and let trained responders decide whether nearby native prickly pears need a survey.

proposedDescription: Cadelle beetles live among stored grain and other dry foods, where both the insects and the places they hide deserve attention. The shiny dark adults have a noticeable narrow waist behind the front part of the body; the pale larvae have a black head and dark markings. Feeding damages grain kernels, especially the germ. Larvae can also bore into nearby wood or plaster, creating sheltered places that make an infestation harder to clear. Old grain residues and damaged storage surfaces are useful places to inspect.
identification: Adults are shiny brown to black with a distinct constriction behind the thorax. Larvae are whitish with a black head and dark rear projections. actions: Keep affected food or grain apart from clean stock while obtaining identification. Inspect cracks, old sacks and residues beneath equipment as well as the visible grain surface. Cleaning only the main container can leave insects hidden in storage materials. For a commercial store, seek an assessment of the grain and structure before filling the space again.

proposedDescription: Caesarweed has small pink flowers that look like miniature hibiscus blooms, but its hooked fruits are often the more memorable feature. They cling to clothing and animal fur, carrying seeds away from the parent shrub. Rough, sometimes lobed leaves and hairy stems help distinguish it before fruit forms. This widespread tropical plant grows in disturbed places, pastures, and forest openings; Florida treats it as invasive. Brush seeds from clothing and equipment before leaving a patch, and keep seed-bearing cuttings contained during removal.
identification: Look for alternate rough leaves, often shallowly lobed, pink flowers with darker centers, and burr-like fruits that split into five parts. Compare both surfaces of a leaf: the rough upper face and paler underside are useful when the plant is not flowering. actions: Check cuffs, bags and footwear before leaving an infested site so burrs are not dropped along the next path. If a confirmed patch is locally unwanted, work before the fruits become numerous and easy to detach. Keep seed-bearing waste contained during transport, and revisit the patch after removal rather than assuming that cutting the shrub removes seed already on the ground.

proposedDescription: Sweet flag grows at wetland edges in clumps of upright, sword-shaped leaves. A short, fleshy spike of tiny flowers appears to project from the side of a leaflike stalk, an unusual feature worth photographing. Names matter here: introduced Acorus calamus has often been confused in North American records with the native American sweet flag, Acorus americanus. The introduced North American form spreads through rhizomes and is sterile. Have a wetland plant specialist confirm the identification before removing a stand or moving divisions.

proposedDescription: Calico scale earns its name from the white patches on a dark, rounded adult female. Record which trees are affected and whether growth, leaf retention or branch health is changing. An adviser can check for live scales and natural enemies before recommending action. If monitoring is appropriate, revisit the same branches so changes are comparable. Do not transfer a crawler-treatment date from a distant region without checking local seasonal development.

proposedDescription: Callery pear is conspicuous in spring when clusters of white flowers cover the branches before or around leaf-out. Replacing a planted tree with a locally appropriate alternative helps reduce seed sources; removal also needs a plan for sprouts.

proposedDescription: Camellia scale hides beneath small brown, oystershell-shaped covers on the undersides of leaves. proposedDescription: Camphor scale is an armored scale that can hide in plain sight as small brown bumps on ornamental plants. proposedDescription: Camphor tree is a broad evergreen with glossy leaves that release a distinctive camphor scent when crushed. proposedDescription: Canada bluegrass is a low, spreading perennial whose flattened stems give it another helpful name: flat-stemmed bluegrass. proposedDescription: Canada thistle builds patches from a spreading root system, so the shoots above ground show only part of the plant. proposedDescription: Tall delphinium brings upright spires of blue to purplish flowers above a clump of deeply divided leaves. Its tall stems appreciate shelter and support, especially in wind or heavy rain. Remove spent spikes if you do not want seed, and keep all parts away from grazing animals or curious pets: this beautiful member of the buttercup family is toxic if eaten.
identification: Look for deeply lobed leaves and tall, stiff flower spikes; check a flower from more than one angle. Look at a flower from the side to show its projecting spur, and include a mature leaf with its deep divisions. Garden selections can have fuller flower spikes or unusual colors. A nursery hybrid label may describe cultivated ancestry more accurately than a confident identification as a wild species.
actions: Support tall stems, deadhead unwanted seed production, and prevent children, pets and livestock from eating plant material. Place supports early enough to guide the stems as they grow, and check ties after wind or rain. Keep pruned material away from grazing animals and dispose of unwanted seed heads securely. If a similar plant appears outside cultivation, confirm its identity before removal; native larkspurs and garden escapes can require quite different local decisions.

proposedDescription: Candlenut, or kukui, is a broad-crowned tropical tree whose pale green foliage can stand out across a wooded valley. Younger leaves are often lobed, while older leaves may be more oval. Small pale flowers give way to rounded fruits enclosing hard, dark seeds rich in oil, the source of the name candlenut. Long valued in Pacific cultures, it is naturalized in Hawaii and holds special cultural significance there. Fallen seeds readily produce seedlings, so watch planting boundaries and avoid distributing unwanted fruit or soil containing seeds.
identification: Look for broad alternate leaves, often lobed when young, pale terminal flower clusters and rounded fruits containing one or two hard dark seeds. Compare young and older leaves on the same tree before assuming that differently lobed foliage belongs to separate species. The pale canopy, broad leaves and rounded fruits together provide stronger clues than a single fallen seed. Photograph the fruit with its outer covering as well as the hard seed if already exposed.
actions: Keep seedlings only where a tree has room to develop its broad crown. When managing an unwanted patch, consult the landowner about cultural use and local ecological priorities before cutting established trees. Collect unwanted fruit from maintained paths without distributing it to new sites, and check the same planting edge for later seedlings after cleanup.

proposedDescription: Cane toads are large, warty amphibians that often appear around gardens, buildings, and water after dark. Their broad glands behind the eyes can release a milky toxin when threatened, making an encounter dangerous for a pet that bites one. Introduced populations are a management concern in Florida and other warm regions. Smaller native toads can look similar, so size alone is not enough for identification. Keep pet food indoors, supervise pets outside, and photograph an unfamiliar toad before seeking local wildlife guidance.
identification: Look for a large, heavily built brownish toad with conspicuous glands extending behind the eyes; compare carefully with local native species. In Florida, native southern toads have raised ridges on the head that cane toads lack. Photograph the head and shoulder glands from a safe distance, rather than handling the animal to compare them. Young cane toads can overlap native species in size, so a small animal is not automatically harmless or correctly identified.
actions:
Bring pets away from the area while identification is pending and remove attractants such as accessible food. Do not relocate a suspect toad to a pond or another property. Follow local wildlife advice for humane management only after confirmation, and obtain prompt veterinary help if contact with a pet has occurred.

For any authorized handling, use gloves and protect your eyes and skin. If a pet bites or mouths a cane toad, contact an emergency veterinarian immediately. FWC advises washing toxin forward out of the mouth for ten minutes without directing water down the throat, and wiping the gums and tongue.

proposedDescription: The New Guinea sugarcane weevil spends its most damaging stage hidden inside a plant. Pale, legless larvae tunnel through sugarcane and palms, often leaving a plug of fibers at a tunnel entrance. Feeding can weaken palm trunks or damage the growing tip, so the first visible sign may be a declining or unstable plant. The species has moved among tropical islands, with transported palms providing a pathway. Keep suspect plants on site and ask an agricultural or plant-health specialist to identify the insect before moving or treating them.
identification: Look for fibrous plugs over tunnels and pale legless grubs inside affected tissue; larvae alone need specialist confirmation. Record the affected host and photograph the tunnel opening, fiber plug and any exposed insect. A pale grub inside a palm is not a reliable species identification because several borers have similar larvae. Declining foliage or trunk weakness also needs assessment for other causes and for immediate structural risk.
actions: Keep people away from an unstable palm and arrange qualified inspection rather than cutting into the trunk yourself. Retain nursery or transport records for a recently acquired plant. Do not move infested stems, cane cuttings or palms while seeking plant-health guidance. Any cleanup should include the concealed material where larvae remain, using the disposal instructions provided for the confirmed pest.

proposedDescription: Canistel is a tropical fruit tree best known for its golden-yellow fruit and rich, sometimes egg-yolk-like flesh. The glossy leaves are simple and smooth-edged, and small cream flowers sit in their axils. Fruits vary from rounded to spindle-shaped, often ending in a point; several glossy brown seeds lie inside. Garden trees benefit from room to grow and good drainage. Pick fruit at the appropriate mature stage and let it soften before eating, and keep an eye on self-sown seedlings around a planting.
identification: Glossy alternate leaves, small cream flowers and yellow to orange fruits, often pointed, with large brown seeds are useful clues. Photograph the leaf arrangement and flowers as well as ripe fruit; several unrelated tropical fruits can be yellow and pointed. Canistel fruit shapes vary even among cultivated selections. The firm mature fruit usually needs time to soften, so yellow color alone does not describe the texture of a ready-to-eat fruit.
actions: Use well-drained planting sites, harvest mature fruit, and remove unwanted volunteer seedlings rather than moving them into natural areas. For an established garden tree, maintain access for harvesting without climbing weak outer branches. Keep fallen fruit from accumulating where unwanted seedlings are a concern. Obtain cultivar and harvest advice from local fruit-growing specialists, and confirm unfamiliar volunteer trees before keeping or sharing them. A cultivated fruit tree does not require removal simply because it originated elsewhere.

proposedDescription: Cantaloupes, honeydews, and several less familiar melons all belong to Cucumis melo, a warm-season vine with tendrils, rough leaves, and small yellow flowers. Fruit shape, rind and flesh vary greatly among cultivated groups, so a netted orange-fleshed melon is only one version of the species. Bees and other insects help flowers set fruit. In a garden, give the vines sun, space and well-drained soil, and avoid excess nitrogen that produces lush growth at the expense of fruit.
identification: Trailing or climbing vines bear tendrils, broad rough leaves, yellow flowers and highly variable fleshy fruits; cultivar identity is needed for finer distinctions. A flower with a small swelling behind it can be distinguished from a pollen-bearing flower without an obvious young fruit. Follow a vine back to its planting position when several cucurbits are tangled together. Leaf shape alone may not separate all cultivated melons or establish a named variety.
actions: Allow flower-visiting insects access when plants begin setting fruit, and use crop-specific advice if covers are being used for early protection. Keep leaves and fruit off persistently waterlogged ground where possible. Save the seed packet or plant label so harvest cues can be matched to the cultivar rather than assuming every melon develops netting or slips from its stem.

proposedDescription: Canterbury bells usually spends its first year as a leafy rosette, then sends up a tall stem lined with generous bell-shaped flowers. Blue, pink, purple and white garden forms make this European biennial a familiar cottage-garden plant. The lower leaves are long and toothed, with smaller leaves along the flowering stem. Seed escapes through small openings in the dry capsules, allowing new plants to appear nearby. Deadhead before capsules mature if you want to keep the display within its chosen bed.
identification: Look for a basal rosette of toothed leaves and an upright stem bearing large bell-shaped flowers; cultivated forms may be double. Compare the large open bells with the smaller flowers of other bellflowers, and photograph the leaf rosette as well as the stem. The upper leaves are smaller and sit close to the flowering stem. A double-flowered garden selection can obscure the normal flower shape, making its label useful.
actions: Keep track of first-year rosettes when weeding a planted bed so they are not discarded before their flowering season. If volunteers are welcome, leave room for a few replacement plants; otherwise collect fading flower stems before the capsules open. Check the neighboring bed after flowering and remove only the seedlings you have identified as unwanted Canterbury bells.

proposedDescription: Cape blue waterlily holds its fragrant flowers above a raft of broad floating leaves. Although blue is the familiar color, named forms and cultivated relatives can also flower pink or mauve. The leaves have a deep notch and a wavy edge, while a short upright, tuberous rhizome anchors the plant below. It comes from Africa and grows in still or slow water. Keep pond plants and discarded rhizomes out of natural waterways, and use more than flower color to distinguish this species from waterlily hybrids.
identification: Photograph the floating leaf margins as well as the raised flower. The colored extensions at the tips of the anthers are more useful than simply calling the flower blue. Photograph the flower center closely and note whether flowers stand above the surface. Pond hybrids may share these traits, so color and a floating leaf alone do not settle the name.
actions: Contain pond plantings and dispose of unwanted rhizomes away from waterways; obtain specialist identification before managing a wild stand. Keep the purchase label with photographs when asking a waterlily specialist for help. Do not dig into an unfamiliar wetland to examine the rhizome without permission and a clear sampling plan. During pond maintenance, collect underground pieces and keep the waste from drains, streams and ponds where it was not planted. Recheck contained plantings after divisions or major cleaning.

proposedDescription: Cape honeysuckle is a scrambling southern African shrub with clusters of bright trumpet flowers. It belongs to the trumpetvine family, and its compound leaves, usually with five to nine toothed leaflets, help distinguish it from true honeysuckles. Orange-red is typical, with yellow and other colors available in garden selections. Long capsules release winged seeds, and stems can be propagated by layering or cuttings. Give a planting room, prune it to the intended space, and keep rooted trimmings from being dumped beyond the garden.
identification: Look for opposite compound leaves with toothed leaflets, tubular orange-red flowers and long narrow seed capsules. Count leaflets on several mature leaves rather than a single young shoot. The flower tube has spreading, unequal lobes at its opening, while the long dry capsules provide another character after the display ends.
actions: Manage the plant's spread by pruning and checking for rooted stems or seedlings; contain discarded cuttings. Inspect stems where they rest on soil before trimming a spreading plant. Any rooted sections need to be managed with the original planting if its boundary is being reduced. Keep an access gap beside paths so pruning remains practical. In a garden where it is appropriate to grow, regular size management is more useful than assuming that every vigorous shrub is an ecological invader.

proposedDescription: Cape leadwort is a loose, scrambling shrub covered in clusters of pale blue flowers, with white-flowered selections also grown. Its small light-green leaves have little ear-shaped appendages near the base, a useful detail behind the name auriculata. Native to southern Africa, it is widely planted in warm gardens and can become a broad mass without pruning. Sunny conditions and good drainage suit it well. Keep a planting within its intended area and collect trimmings rather than dropping them at the edge of natural vegetation.
identification: Look closely at where each leaf joins the stem to see the small basal appendages. The flower has a slender tube ending in five spreading lobes, with several flowers grouped together. Its loose arching habit can look vine-like when tied to a support, although the plant is a shrub.
actions: Prune to maintain the intended boundary, use well-drained sites, and keep discarded plant material out of natural areas. Check low stems and the edge of the clump when reducing its size, including any suckering growth. Wear gloves if handling foliage because contact can irritate skin. In a container, make sure excess water can drain away rather than collecting beneath the roots. Retain healthy garden plants where suitable, while promptly checking any volunteers or spread beyond the intended bed.

proposedDescription: Fairy crassula spreads as a low succulent mat, with fleshy rounded leaves and airy clusters of small pale pink stars. Tiny plantlets may form among the flowers, drop to the ground, and become new plants; creeping stems also root where they touch soil. That easy propagation makes garden waste an effective way to start another patch. The South African species has become an environmental weed in parts of Australia and New Zealand. Collect every loose piece during removal and revisit the site for rooted fragments or fallen plantlets.
identification: A close photograph of the leaf surface can show the tiny pale or reddish dots without detaching the leaf. Look above the mat for loose flower clusters and the miniature plants that may replace flowers. These plantlets are different from the leaf-edge plantlets of some other commonly grown succulents.
actions: Contain cuttings and plantlets, remove rooted stems carefully, and monitor for regrowth rather than leaving fragments on bare soil. Work over a container or sheet when lifting plants from a small maintained bed so loose plantlets are easier to recover. Inspect the soil surface and nearby paving cracks after the main mat has been lifted. Do not leave rooted pieces in damp garden waste beside natural vegetation, and revisit after rain when missed fragments may become easier to see.

proposedDescription: Cape ricegrass is easiest to notice when its seed heads develop long, twisted awns. These bristles give the annual grass a tangled appearance and help its sharp seeds catch on clothing or animal fur. Narrow leaves and a compact seed head support identification, but flowering material is especially useful. In southern California desert areas, it can form dense patches and is a concern for native wildflowers and fire potential. Brush seeds from footwear before leaving a patch and report unfamiliar stands to the local land manager.
identification: Look for an annual tuft of narrow leaves with dense panicles and very long, twice-bent, twisted awns. The long bristles bend and twist beyond a compact head; photograph the whole head and a close view of an attached seed. Do not use a grass's dry brown color or its presence in a desert alone as identification.
actions: Clean seeds from clothing and equipment; document new patches and remove small plants before seed maturity where authorized. Avoid walking or driving through ripe seed heads when another route is available. Inspect footwear, animal bedding and field equipment before moving between sites. For a small confirmed patch, arrange work before the sharp seeds become easy to detach. Record both the patch location and its approximate extent so the land manager can plan follow-up with the surrounding native seasonal vegetation in mind.

proposedDescription: Cape ivy can drape a streambank or woodland edge in a thick green blanket. Its fleshy, lobed leaves resemble ivy, but clusters of tiny yellow flower heads reveal its place in the daisy family. In invaded coastal California habitats, the vine climbs over shrubs and trees and shades the plants beneath. Even small stem and underground pieces can start again after removal. Keep cut material out of waterways, collect fragments carefully, and expect repeated visits to clear regrowth rather than a single successful pull.
identification: Glossy fleshy leaves have five to seven pointed lobes; small clustered yellow flower heads lack the showy ray petals of some similar vines. Include the leaf base and the way the stem climbs in photographs. Ivy-like leaves by themselves can lead to confusion with unrelated ornamental climbers.
actions: Contain all fragments, protect nearby native plants during removal, and arrange repeated follow-up, especially near streams. Plan where cut vines will go before beginning work, especially on a bank where fragments can fall into moving water. Lift loose pieces without tearing out the native vegetation beneath them. Large tangles above head height need an assessment of the supporting branches. Return to the treated edge and cleared ground for small shoots rather than waiting for another blanket of growth.

proposedDescription: Fertile capeweed spreads a rosette of deeply lobed leaves close to the ground, then lifts yellow daisy heads with dark centers above it. Turn a leaf over to see the pale, woolly underside. This seed-producing species is an agricultural and environmental weed in parts of Australia and has established in coastal California. Its seeds travel with soil, equipment, footwear, and animals. Remove small plants before seed ripens and check the identification carefully: the creeping ornamental capeweed, Arctotheca prostrata, has different spreading habits and yellow flower centers.
identification: Photograph a fully open head from above so the dark center is clear, and turn over a leaf to show its woolly underside. Young rosettes can resemble other daisies before flowering. A creeping capeweed planting nearby does not prove that every similar seedling belongs to the same species.
actions: Prevent seed production, clean soil and seeds from equipment, and distinguish it from creeping A. prostrata before planning control. In a small confirmed unwanted patch, inspect for developing heads before soil disturbance or mowing scatters material. Remove soil and attached seeds from tools before using them elsewhere. Keep desirable ground cover where possible and check exposed patches for new rosettes after rain. If the plant is part of a mixed lawn or pasture, ask for advice suited to that use before undertaking broad control.

proposedDescription: Creeping capeweed was planted as a groundcover for its low rosettes and cheerful yellow daisies, but its runners can cross the intended boundary. Stems root as they creep, allowing a patch to expand even where the cultivated plants produce no fertile seed. California records describe escapes into coastal prairie and nearby urban ground. It is often confused with fertile capeweed, Arctotheca calendula; longer creeping stems and yellow flower centers help separate it. During removal, collect rooted runners and fragments so the cleared patch can stay clear.
identification: Check for long creeping stems and flower heads with yellow centers; fertile A. calendula usually has dark centers. Trace one runner gently along the soil to see whether it roots at several points. Those connected rosettes show how a patch expands. A yellow flower center supports the comparison with fertile capeweed, but a fading or closed flower may be misleading; use fresh, fully open heads.
actions: Avoid planting where it escapes locally; remove rooted runners, contain fragments and recheck the patch for regrowth. Start at the patch edge when lifting runners so attached rooted sections are less easily missed. Keep lifted material together rather than dragging it across clean ground. Revisit gaps between paving and the adjoining bed, where small retained pieces can be overlooked. Where a maintained planting is being replaced, choose locally suitable ground cover and continue watching its former boundary as the replacement establishes.

proposedDescription: Capybaras are the largest living rodents, with sturdy brown bodies, blunt muzzles, and short legs adapted to life beside water. Partly webbed feet and eyes, ears, and nostrils set high on the head help them swim while keeping watch. In their South American range, they live socially and graze on grasses and aquatic plants. An animal seen far outside that range may be an escape or release. Observe from a distance, keep pets away, and report the location to wildlife authorities rather than feeding or relocating it.
identification: A large brown rodent with a barrel-shaped body, blunt head, no visible tail and partly webbed feet; do not confuse young animals with nutria. A view of the rear body helps distinguish the tailless outline from a nutria with its long visible tail. Use an object already nearby for scale rather than approaching the animal. A swimming animal may show little more than its eyes and ears, so wait for a clearer view without cornering it.
actions: Do not feed, approach closely or release captive animals; document unexpected sightings and contact local wildlife authorities. Report the time, location and number of animals, noting any young or signs of an enclosure nearby. Keep dogs on a lead and give the animals an unobstructed route away from people. Feeding can encourage repeated visits and closer contact. If an animal appears injured or trapped, describe the situation to wildlife responders instead of attempting to catch it.

proposedDescription: Wigandia is a large-leaved shrub or small tree from tropical America, with showy lavender flowers above coarse, hairy foliage. The hairs are a reason to admire it without brushing past: they can irritate skin and sometimes provoke a stronger allergic reaction. Plants described from the Santa Monica Mountains have escaped cultivation into dense colonies near homes. Their big, toothed leaves and curling flower clusters give a useful starting point for identification, although local forms and older botanical names need careful comparison.
identification: Look for large alternate leaves with toothed, wavy edges, conspicuous veins beneath and dense hairs, plus lavender, five-lobed flowers. California plants can carry the name var. caracasana, so include any original plant label when seeking an identification. Photograph the undersides of leaves only where this can be done without contact; the coarse veins and dense hairs help show the foliage structure. Include a side view of an open flower and the curling cluster. A garden label or record of planting may help connect an escaped stand with the appropriate named form.
actions: Photograph leaves and flowers without touching the hairs. Wear protective clothing if handling is necessary, avoid relocating plants from escaped colonies, and seek local advice on established patches. Keep a safe working gap beside paths where the hairy leaves project into pedestrian space. If managing a confirmed escaped stand, plan how to carry cut material without brushing it against exposed skin or passersby. Ask a local botanist or land manager to check the identification and extent before treating an entire colony.

proposedDescription: Caraway is the familiar kitchen spice grown on a delicate-looking member of the carrot family. Finely divided leaves form below branched stems topped with small white or pink-tinged flower umbels; the aromatic, ridged fruits are commonly called seeds. It often grows as a biennial and can self-sow freely where conditions suit it. In a herb bed, harvest or remove ripening heads to limit volunteers. Wild carrot-family plants can be difficult to tell apart, so do not use a casual resemblance as a basis for foraging.
identification: Look for finely divided leaves, small compound umbels and narrow ridged aromatic fruits; a full botanical identification is needed for a wild plant. Include lower leaves, upper leaves and mature fruit in photographs because the leaf segments change along the stem. Several carrot-family plants have white umbrella-like clusters. The small ribbed fruits are a useful botanical feature, but smelling or tasting an unidentified plant is not a safe identification method.
actions: Harvest or remove seed heads to limit self-sowing, and keep uncertain wild Apiaceae out of food preparations. Keep cultivated caraway labeled, particularly where volunteers mix with other herbs or wild seedlings. Choose whether to retain a few identified plants for the next flowering season or remove ripening heads to limit spread. Avoid disturbing the roots of plants you intend to keep. Ask for a full botanical identification of an unfamiliar roadside or field-margin plant before considering any food use.

proposedDescription: Cardoon brings the artichoke family's bold outline to open ground: a broad rosette of deeply cut, gray-green leaves sends up tall stems topped with purple flower heads. This Mediterranean perennial is cultivated as a vegetable and ornamental, but wild plants also occupy California grasslands and other disturbed habitats. Its spiny leaves and substantial taproot make established plants awkward to remove. Seed and surviving root pieces can renew a patch, so a single cut rarely settles the problem.
identification: Very large, deeply lobed, spiny leaves with pale woolly undersides and purple thistle-like heads. Cultivated artichokes are close relatives and can complicate identification. Photograph the rosette, stem and outer bracts around a mature flower head. Some cultivated forms are less spiny, and flower shape alone does not establish whether a plant is an escaped wild form or a vegetable selection. Nearby garden plantings can help explain its appearance without proving its identity.

Revisit treated plants and check beyond the original rosettes for seedlings. Keep intentional vegetable plantings separate from decisions about escapes in surrounding habitat.

proposedDescription: Caribbean black scale can look like a row of small dark bumps along a fruit stem or twig. Mature females develop a tough, rounded covering with an H-shaped ridge; younger scales are paler and less distinctive. This sap-feeding insect uses many plants, including citrus, mango and guava. On citrus, its sugary honeydew supports sooty mold that can reduce fruit quality. Tiny natural enemies help limit populations, making a close inspection more useful than an automatic spray.
identification: Mature females are roughly 3-5 mm long, dark brown to black and hemispherical, with an H-shaped ridge. A close side view shows the female's raised dome, while a top view can reveal the H-shaped ridge. Other soft scales can share that outline, and young stages are harder to recognize. Record the host plant and include a twig with several stages when requesting expert identification.
actions: Inspect incoming plants and infested twigs. Preserve natural enemies; a neat round exit hole may indicate a beneficial wasp. Seek crop-specific advice before treating. Check whether the bumps contain live insects and whether honeydew is fresh before deciding that the problem is increasing. Look for ants tending the honeydew and for evidence of parasitic wasps. In a fruit planting, record affected branches and fruit rather than relying only on sooty mold elsewhere. Use local crop guidance to protect natural enemies while addressing a confirmed damaging population.

proposedDescription: Caribbean fruit fly is a yellow-brown fly whose patterned wings offer a useful first clue to its identity. Females place eggs beneath the skin of mature or overripe fruit, and the pale larvae feed inside before dropping to the soil to pupate. Guava, loquat and many other cultivated or wild fruits can serve as hosts. Because related fruit flies look similar and have different management implications, a suspected find deserves expert identification before fruit is moved.
identification: Brown S-shaped markings cross otherwise clear wings; a dark spot occurs near the rear of the thorax. White, legless larvae inside fruit are not enough for species identification. A clear top view of the adult's wings is particularly useful, but related Anastrepha flies may still require a specialist examination. Keep the host fruit name and collection location with the photograph.
actions: Photograph the fly and affected fruit, keep suspect fruit contained, and contact the local plant-health or agricultural office for identification and disposal guidance before transporting it. Keep the affected fruit away from fresh produce intended for transport or sharing. If the plant-health office requests a sample, follow its packing and delivery directions so larvae cannot escape along the way. Record whether the fruit came from a garden, market or shipment; that history helps responders decide where to investigate. Do not release a live captured fly after suspecting a reportable pest.

proposedDescription: Silver trumpet tree pairs golden, funnel-shaped flowers with foliage that catches the light in a silvery sheen. Native to South America, it is planted as a warm-climate ornamental. The leathery leaves spread from a single point like fingers, with five to seven leaflets and a silvery underside. Corky bark gives an established trunk a distinctive texture. Several yellow-flowered trumpet trees share this general silhouette, so a whole leaf and a close view of the bark are useful alongside the flowers.
identification: Photograph the five to seven leaflets joining at one central point, together with their grey-green upper and silvery lower surfaces. Include the corky trunk and a flowering branch. A distant yellow crown is not enough to distinguish related ornamental trumpet trees. Older labels may use Tabebuia argentea for silver trumpet tree, so keep the label with the photographs when seeking confirmation.
actions: Check local planting guidance and monitor seedlings around ornamental trees before assuming they need removal. Keep nursery labels and planting records where several yellow trumpet trees are grown together. Collect fallen leaves for comparison only where permission allows, instead of breaking branches from a mature tree. If seedlings appear outside the maintained planting, document their position and obtain local identification and planting advice before deciding whether the tree is spreading undesirably.

proposedDescription: Small white flower clusters make bur parsley easy to overlook until its hooked fruits catch your attention. This annual has finely divided leaves and only a few rays in each flower cluster. It belongs to the flora of Europe, northern Africa and parts of Asia, where it often grows in dry cultivated ground and field margins. Its conservation context matters: Switzerland regards it as vulnerable. A plant found among crops is therefore not automatically a candidate for removal.
identification: Twice- or three-times-divided leaves, small white umbels with few rays, and fruits about 6-12 mm long bearing rows of hooked spines. Mature fruit is important for separating similar carrot-family plants. Count the few main rays beneath a mature umbel and photograph the hooked rows on the fruit without carrying them to another site. A finely divided leaf and white flower alone can fit many carrot-family plants. Fruit size and spine arrangement are therefore better evidence than a distant flowering view.
actions: Leave a population in place while checking local conservation guidance, particularly in traditional arable habitat. Record whether it occurs among crops, beside a field or on recently disturbed soil. Clean attached fruits from clothing before leaving the site, containing them there rather than spreading them along a road. Share the record with a local botanist if the plant is unfamiliar or potentially significant.

proposedDescription: Carrotwood's glossy, leathery leaflets give this evergreen tree a tidy appearance, but its orange capsules reveal the feature that helps it travel: dark seeds wrapped in a bright aril that attracts birds. It is native to coastal eastern Australia, including rainforest near the sea and estuaries. In Florida, escaped trees invade a wide range of habitats and alter the understory. Young seedlings are much easier to tackle than the established trees they can become.
identification: Leaves are compound, usually with four to twelve leathery leaflets. Woody, yellow-orange capsules split into three sections to expose shiny black seeds with yellow-red coverings; inner bark can be orange. Look for the swollen base of the compound leaf stalk and several leathery, smooth-edged leaflets. Orange inner bark is a supporting clue, not a reason to damage an intact trunk for identification.
actions: In invaded areas, pull small seedlings with their roots and contain seed pods. Arrange suitable professional treatment for larger trees and continue checking for bird-dispersed seedlings. Check below bird perches and along the planting boundary, since seedlings may occur well away from the parent. Work on small plants before their roots become difficult to lift, where removal is appropriate and authorized. For a mature tree beside buildings or other vegetation, obtain a professional plan and keep the follow-up area under observation after the main work is finished.
