proposedDescription: The casemaking clothes moth's most revealing sign is often a tiny moving case rather than a moth. Its caterpillar builds a portable shelter from silk and fibers, feeding on vulnerable animal-based materials such as wool as it carries the case along. The adult is a small, buff moth with narrow, fringed wings and dark forewing spots. Stored textiles and the sheltered undersides of wool rugs deserve attention, especially when they have gone undisturbed for a long time.
identification: Look for a caterpillar inside a portable silk-and-fiber case and a buff adult with three dark forewing spots. Webbing clothes moth larvae feed in attached silk tubes instead of carrying a case. The fibers incorporated into a moving case can match the damaged textile and help locate the feeding site. Carpet beetle larvae can also damage wool, but they do not make these silken cases. A moth near a window is not by itself evidence that stored clothing is infested.
actions: Clean items using suitable laundering or dry-cleaning methods, vacuum rug edges and storage areas, and store clean woolens in sealed containers. Inspect folds, rug undersides and items that have been stored undisturbed, including nearby animal-fiber materials. Isolate affected pieces before moving them through the house. Choose cleaning methods that suit the textile care label; delicate or valuable objects may need a textile conservator. Recheck cleaned storage and newly stored items for fresh cases or damage so an overlooked source can be found.

proposedDescription: Spectacular cassia earns its common name with broad clusters of bright yellow flowers above a rounded crown. This tropical American tree has compound leaves and long pods that darken as they mature. Its appeal as an ornamental has carried it beyond its native range; in parts of East Africa and India, it has spread into forest edges, gaps and degraded land. Dense growth can hinder forest recovery, so seedlings near vulnerable habitat merit attention before they become seed-bearing trees.
identification: Compound leaves bear several pairs of leaflets; terminal clusters hold yellow flowers with unequal petals. Long, hanging, cylindrical or slightly flattened pods turn dark. Photograph a whole compound leaf, the flower cluster and a mature pod. Several commonly planted sennas have yellow flowers, so the number and shape of leaflets and the long pod are useful comparisons. A tree's ornamental setting does not exclude seedlings spreading into adjacent forest gaps.
actions: Where it is invasive, identify and remove small seedlings before seed set, contain pods, and monitor regrowth. Survey the area beyond the parent tree before beginning work in an invaded site, and record both small seedlings and established stems. Collect seed-bearing pods without scattering their contents. Where an established stand is being removed, plan repeated checks and recovery of suitable forest vegetation with the local land manager. Management needs to reflect the documented regional invasion and the condition of the particular habitat.

proposedDescription: Cassava is a tropical crop grown for its large, starch-rich storage roots, also familiar as the source of tapioca. Above ground, it forms a woody shrub with long-stalked, deeply divided leaves and milky sap. Farmers commonly propagate it from stem cuttings, a useful reminder that discarded stems can remain planting material. Although cassava is an important food plant, its raw parts contain toxins and require proper processing; the appearance of an edible crop does not make it safe to sample.
identification: A woody shrub with alternate, long-stalked leaves divided into narrow lobes, milky sap and thickened storage roots. Do not taste plant material to confirm identification. Look at the point where the long leaf stalk meets the deeply divided blade and include the alternating leaf arrangement. The storage roots belong below ground and do not need to be exposed simply to take an identification photograph. Other ornamental spurges can share milky sap, so sap alone proves little.
actions: Keep discarded stem cuttings out of natural areas and waterways. Use established food-safety guidance for processing cultivated cassava; do not eat raw roots or leaves. For an unexpected stand, record whether it is an active crop, an abandoned planting or growth beside discarded stems. Clear discarded stem sections from places where they could take root unintentionally. Keep children and animals away from raw harvested material awaiting processing. For unfamiliar volunteer plants, confirm the species before cultivation or harvest; the shape of a swollen root does not establish that it is a safe food crop.

proposedDescription: Castor bean is hard to miss: huge, star-shaped leaves rise on fast-growing stems, followed by clusters of prickly capsules. In warm climates it can become a substantial shrub, while frost-prone gardens often grow it as an annual. Escaped plants favor disturbed ground and waterways, and mature capsules scatter seeds that can establish new plants. Those attractive, mottled seeds are highly poisonous, so this is a plant to identify visually and keep away from children and animals.
identification: Large, glossy leaves have pointed lobes and toothed edges. Flower spikes bear petal-less flowers; rounded, spiny capsules contain smooth mottled seeds. Leaf and stem colors range from green to reddish purple. Photograph the attachment of the leaf stalk and the cluster of developing capsules from a safe distance. The mottled seeds should be recognized from reliable photographs rather than collected or handled to complete the identification.
actions: Avoid touching or collecting seeds. Wear gloves for necessary handling, prevent capsules from maturing, and obtain local disposal advice for unwanted plants. Keep children, pets and livestock away. Before working on a plant with mature capsules, arrange containment and disposal so seeds are not scattered onto accessible ground. Check the surrounding area for new seedlings after the main plant is removed. Where a tall specimen stands near a path, use an approach suited to its size and protect people from falling material. Do not leave cut capsules where children or animals can investigate them.

proposedDescription: Cat's-claw creeper climbs with tiny, three-pronged hooks that grip bark and other supports. Its yellow trumpet flowers may look inviting, but the woody vine can spread across forest floors and climb over trees, smothering vegetation in invaded areas. Underground tubers make it persistent after the visible stems are cut. Winged seeds travel by wind and water, while detached stems and tubers can also restart growth. Early identification is especially valuable around streambanks and woodland edges.
identification: Look for opposite leaves with two leaflets and a three-pronged, claw-like tendril, large yellow trumpet flowers and long flat capsules. Native crossvine has reddish-orange flowers; jessamines lack these claw tendrils. Examine a shoot tip to see the small hooked tendril between the paired leaflets. This is more informative than the yellow flower color alone. Young creeping stems can be inconspicuous beneath a larger climbing vine, and a visible canopy tangle may connect to several rooting points below.
actions: Remove small seedlings with their underground tubers where feasible, contain fragments and seed capsules, and revisit for regrowth. Trace ground-level growth before cutting so the extent of the infestation is clear. Keep tubers and stem fragments together during cleanup and prevent them from washing downstream. Avoid wrenching tangled vines from a tree where branches could fall. After planned treatment, check both the original rooting points and nearby bare ground for new growth, while retaining the native plants needed for recovery.

proposedDescription: Life plant has an unusual way of making a new generation: tiny plantlets can grow from the scalloped margins of its fleshy leaves, particularly after a leaf falls. This Madagascar succulent becomes an upright, shrubby perennial, with simple lower leaves and divided leaves farther up the stems. Drooping, bell-shaped flowers hang in branching clusters. Its easy propagation explains both its popularity and its tendency to become weedy; a discarded leaf can be more than garden litter.
identification: Smooth fleshy leaves have scalloped margins; upper leaves commonly divide into several oval leaflets. Look for small marginal plantlets and hanging bell-shaped flowers. Bryophyllum pinnatum is a widely used synonym. A fallen leaf with miniature plants at its notches is a useful clue, but other kalanchoes also make plantlets. Photograph the broad leaflet shape and the hanging flowers to strengthen the identification.
actions: Collect dropped leaves and plantlets when containing or removing it, and keep garden waste out of natural areas. Keep plants and trimmings away from grazing animals; do not use them as food or home remedies. Use a tray or other containment when moving a potted plant so fallen leaves are not left along the route. Inspect the ground beneath the pot and nearby cracks for small rooted plants. When an outdoor patch is locally unwanted, remove loose leaves as well as the standing stems and revisit the site. Keep collected material secure until appropriate disposal rather than passing it on as unidentified cuttings.

proposedDescription: Catnip's gray-green, aromatic leaves are familiar to many cat owners, but this mint-family perennial also attracts a lively mix of flower visitors. Small white flowers, often marked with pink or purple, crowd the tops of its square stems. Native to Europe and Asia, it has naturalized widely in temperate regions, especially along roadsides and field margins. It readily seeds around gardens and can become a nuisance, although that does not make every patch an ecological invasion.
identification: Opposite, softly hairy, triangular to oval leaves have coarse teeth and heart-shaped bases. Square stems carry crowded clusters of small two-lipped, whitish flowers with pink or purple markings. The softly hairy leaf surface and broad, toothed blades help compare it with ornamental catmints that have different flower colors or finer foliage. Scent is a supporting feature, not a substitute for those characters.
actions: To contain garden plants, remove spent flower stems before seeds mature or grow them in containers. Identify volunteer seedlings before removing them and avoid confusing catnip with other ornamental catmints. Check around the base of a garden plant for volunteers before they blend into neighboring herbs. If keeping the planting, allow room for its mature growth and use well-drained soil. Remove unwanted seedlings while their identity is clear, and leave other flowering plants undisturbed. A contained, managed planting can still provide flowers for visiting insects without allowing seed to spread throughout the bed.

proposedDescription: Caucasian bluestem forms dense clumps of pale green grass that turn straw-colored as they mature. Its branched seed head has a central axis extending beyond the shorter side branches, a helpful clue when comparing it with other bluestems. This warm-season perennial occurs under several regional common names, including forest blue grass in Australia. In Kansas, introduced stands have spread into native sites. Identification deserves care because the name "bluestem" also belongs to valuable native prairie grasses.
identification: Look for dense perennial clumps, mostly hairless leaf blades with a few long hairs at their bases, and a branched panicle whose central axis exceeds its branches. Mature spikelets may be needed for expert confirmation. Examine an intact flowering stem rather than a mown tuft. The plant is densely tufted rather than a lawn of creeping runners, and its numerous fine branches give the flowering head a more open outline than the compact spikes of some familiar pasture grasses.
actions: Photograph mature seed heads, leaf bases and the whole clump. Work from clean ground toward the affected patch so that clothing and machinery do not carry mature seed into uninfested prairie. Mark the clumps and revisit them while flowering heads are present; a specialist can then compare the spikelets with other Bothriochloa and native bluestems. Base any larger control project on that confirmed identification.

proposedDescription: Two-row stonecrop makes a low carpet of fleshy leaves, with creeping stems that root as they spread. Flowering shoots stand a little above the leafy carpet. Red or bronze winter foliage can belong to a named cultivar, so color alone is unreliable.

proposedDescription: Nettleleaf porterweed holds small blue-purple flowers along slender, curved spikes that rise above its wrinkled green leaves. Only part of a spike blooms at once, leaving a patterned stem behind as flowers fall. This tropical American shrub is grown ornamentally, but can spread through disturbed ground and degraded pasture in warm, moist regions. Seeds travel with contaminated soil, hay, equipment and garden waste. Other porterweeds are similar, making leaf texture and growth habit useful starting points rather than a final diagnosis.
identification: Opposite, toothed oval leaves have prominent veins and a wrinkled surface. Slender curved spikes bear small blue-purple, occasionally white flowers in succession; mature fruits sit in pits along the spike. Young stems can be four-sided and green or purple before becoming woody. Photograph both leaf surfaces, a whole spike, and the plant's height. Upright shrub growth and strongly textured leaves help with comparison, but flower color alone will not separate this plant from native porterweeds or cultivated selections.
actions: Confirm the species before removal, especially where native porterweeds occur. In unwanted patches, remove plants with their larger roots, contain seed-bearing spikes, clean equipment and check for seedlings. Check disturbed soil around a confirmed unwanted plant after removal, because small seedlings are easier to address than woody shrubs. Keep removed flower spikes contained and avoid moving soil from a seeding patch into clean ground. Where it is intentionally grown, watch the surrounding area for self-sown plants and choose locally appropriate replacements if it is escaping.

proposedDescription: Colombian datura virus can hide in an apparently healthy angel's trumpet, then show itself as pale mottling, wrinkled leaves or stunted growth. Brugmansia plants are important hosts, and moving infected cuttings helps carry the virus between collections. Aphids and transferred plant sap can spread it too. Related ornamental and crop plants can also be infected, including tomato. Because these symptoms overlap with other problems and some infected plants show none, reliable identification depends on laboratory testing.
identification: Look for irregular light-and-dark leaf mosaics, yellow flecks, vein banding, wrinkling or reduced growth on susceptible plants. These signs are not diagnostic, and symptomless Brugmansia can carry the virus. Check new and older leaves on the same plant, noting whether mottling is accompanied by puckering or smaller growth. Record which Brugmansia varieties are affected and whether cuttings came from a shared parent. Those observations help a laboratory choose samples; they cannot distinguish this virus from another virus or a mixed infection.
actions: Stop sharing or propagating suspect plants and contact a plant diagnostic laboratory. Use tested healthy stock for propagation, prevent sap transfer between plants, and follow diagnostic advice for removing confirmed infected stock. Keep the suspect plant's label and propagation history with your photographs. Separate it from plants being prepared for sale or exchange, and ask the laboratory how to package material before sending anything. Clean propagation tools between plants using its recommended procedure. A plant that looks better later should not automatically be treated as virus-free propagation stock.

proposedDescription: Cedar wattle is a tall Australian tree with unusually large leaflets for a feathery-leaved acacia. Sprays of pale yellow or cream flower balls appear above the foliage, followed by flat pods. In its native New South Wales range, it grows in rainforest and wetter eucalypt forest. Planting has carried it farther afield: it can escape into adjacent bushland and is documented as naturalized in South Africa. Its location matters when deciding whether a seedling belongs or needs attention.
identification: Twice-divided leaves have several pairs of branches carrying lance-shaped leaflets commonly 2-5 cm long. Look for pale spherical flower heads, flat pods, and dark, deeply fissured bark at the base of mature trees. The leaflets are much larger than those of many finely feathery wattles: each is a small lance-shaped blade, rather than a tiny dot along the leaf branch. Include a complete divided leaf and a ruler in photographs. Pale flower balls and mature flat pods provide useful additional checks.
actions: Record leaflets, pods and the planting context. Outside its native range, monitor nearby bushland for seedlings and seek local management advice; arrange professional assessment before removing large trees. Distinguish seedlings beyond a planting from the planted parent, and map their distance from the garden edge. If local advice calls for removal, deal with manageable seedlings before they become trees and continue checking beneath nearby vegetation. Do not cut a mature tree simply because it is an acacia; native status, ownership, safety and exact identity all matter.

proposedDescription: Greater celandine brings small yellow flowers to shady edges, gardens, and disturbed woodland. This leafy herb lives for more than one season or behaves as a biennial, spreading readily by seed where conditions suit it. Its deeply divided leaves and orange-yellow sap help separate it from other yellow-flowered plants. Originally from Eurasia, it has become established beyond its native range. The sap can irritate skin, so this is a plant to recognize without breaking its stems by hand.
identification: Look for clusters of four-petaled yellow flowers, lobed leaves, and long, slender seed capsules. Do not deliberately expose skin to the sap. The four broad petals and narrow upright capsules are especially useful together. Lesser celandine has glossy, less divided leaves and more numerous petals, so the similar common names are misleading. A flowering stem and an attached seed capsule make better photographs than a single yellow flower.
actions: Wear gloves when removing small unwanted plants, and work before they set seed. Recheck the area for seedlings. Keep sap off skin and eyes and collect removed flowering or fruiting stems rather than leaving them on disturbed ground. In a mixed woodland edge, identify neighboring plants before digging. Follow the original patch through the next growing period and remove only confirmed unwanted seedlings; one clearance does not show that the soil is free of seed.
researchNotes: Synthesized morphology and garden behavior with Kew's range and life-form account. Kept greater celandine distinct from lesser celandine; no unsupported nationwide impact claim. proposedDescription: This cellar spider belongs to the long-legged spiders that hang beneath loose webs in sheltered corners. Pholcus manueli has been recorded in cellars and other buildings, including a garage from which it was first described. Although its name was established from American specimens, the World Spider Catalog treats it as an Asian species introduced to the United States. Several cellar spiders look similar, so a web in a basement is a useful clue, not enough to identify this particular species.
identification: Long, thin legs and an inverted position in an irregular web suggest a cellar spider. The familiar Pholcus phalangioides and other pholcids can occupy the same sorts of sheltered spaces. Photograph the body from more than one angle without pulling the legs, and include a scale if possible. Adult anatomical details are needed for a reliable species determination.
actions: Photograph the spider and its web if documenting a sighting. Seek identification before treating a familiar house spider as this species. Leave an undisturbed spider in place when it is not causing a practical problem. If a web must be cleared, ordinary household cleaning is a more proportionate response than treating every room with insecticide. For a distribution record, retain the location, date and building context and ask a local arachnologist whether photographs or a specimen are needed.

proposedDescription: Centipedegrass is the pale-green, low-growing lawn grass often planted in warm parts of the country. It creeps across the soil on aboveground runners, gradually forming a coarse-textured turf rather than an upright clump. Its leaves alternate along the runners, giving them the appearance that inspired its common name. This grass is adapted to acidic, relatively low-fertility soils. Because it is widely cultivated, a patch beside a lawn should be described in that context rather than automatically labeled a harmful invasion.
identification: Look for light-green blades alternating along creeping runners and a slender, single seed spike. St. Augustinegrass has opposite leaves. Examine an unmown runner with several attached leaves. The blades have blunt or rounded tips, and fine hairs occur near the collar where blade and sheath meet. A single upright seed spike is useful when present, but frequent mowing can remove it before it is noticed.
actions: Keep planted turf within its intended area. For unwanted patches, confirm the grass before selecting a removal method with local extension advice. Trace runners at the lawn boundary rather than assuming every pale patch is the same grass. Where containment is needed, remove encroaching runners from the adjoining bed and check for rooted pieces. Ask for a turf identification before changing fertilizer or irrigation, since centipedegrass has different needs from other lawn grasses and extra fertilizer is not a remedy for every pale lawn.
researchNotes: Both university accounts support identification and turf ecology. Deliberately avoided equating cultivation or escape with demonstrated ecological damage. proposedDescription: Centipede tongavine is a tropical climbing plant whose leaves change dramatically as it grows. Young shoots creep or climb with relatively simple leaves; older shoots supported by a tree or another surface can produce much larger, deeply divided leaves. Aerial roots help the vine hold on as it climbs. Native across parts of Asia and the Pacific, it is grown ornamentally beyond that range. Its changing leaf shape makes identifying mature and juvenile plants together especially useful.
identification: Compare young and mature leaves and look for clasping aerial roots. Deeply divided mature leaves differ from the simpler juvenile foliage. Follow one stem from its smaller leaves to the higher, mature foliage if this can be done safely. The divided adult leaf can look unlike the juvenile plant below it. Golden pothos and other climbing aroids also change with age, so neither a houseplant label nor one detached leaf is sufficient.
actions: Keep cultivated vines contained and do not discard living cuttings in natural areas. Photograph several growth stages for identification. In warm outdoor settings, check where stems contact soil or climb into neighboring vegetation. Keep trimmings together and use a disposal route that prevents living nodes from rooting elsewhere. Do not climb trees to collect mature leaves: a photograph from the ground can document the growth stages while a local botanist advises on identity and appropriate containment.

proposedDescription: This microscopic diatom is known from freshwater plankton and is associated with the smaller freshwater forms of Actinocyclus normanii. Viewed through a microscope, its round silica shell has a patterned surface of pores that specialists use for identification. Its history in the Great Lakes is less straightforward than an introduction date might suggest: older sediment evidence has raised questions about whether it arrived recently at all. Even the boundary between named forms is uncertain, making careful identification more useful than a simple invasive label.
identification: Identification requires microscopy of the circular valve, pore arrangement, and specialized structures. Specialists compare coarse polygonal pores, the arrangement of pore rows, and details around the valve margin; small size alone does not securely identify the named form. Ordinary photographs of a pond cannot show these features. The freshwater form has been discussed under the spelling subsalsa, so retain the name originally attached to a sample as well as any later determination.
actions: Have a qualified diatom specialist examine samples. Record sampling details; do not attempt species-specific treatment based on water appearance. For a useful record, note the sampling date, water depth and whether the material came from living plankton or sediment. Preserve and label samples only as directed by the receiving laboratory. Do not add algicides or disturb sediment to address an unconfirmed identification; water-quality concerns need their own assessment, separate from the presence of this diatom.

proposedDescription: Skeletonema potamos is a tiny diatom that drifts in fresh and slightly brackish water, often as short chains of cells. Its delicate silica walls are so small that it can be overlooked even under a light microscope. Researchers studying the Danube found that it became a larger part of the river's plankton community as water temperatures rose. Its original range remains uncertain, and finding it in a water sample does not by itself establish a harmful bloom or a recent introduction.
identification: Specialists look for very small cylindrical cells joined in chains by marginal structures. Reliable identification may require detailed microscopy. The small cells may appear singly or in short chains, with delicate connecting structures near their edges. Those structures and the shape of the silica walls matter more than the general appearance of a chain. Other small centric diatoms can be mistaken for it, especially in routine low-resolution counts.
actions: Document the waterbody and sampling conditions and seek specialist confirmation. Avoid transporting untreated water or wet equipment between waterbodies. Keep any microscope images linked to the sample location and collection method. A specialist may request higher-resolution imaging or an additional sample rather than accepting an identification from one indistinct cell. Drain and clean field gear before moving between sites, following local aquatic biosecurity guidance; a record of this species alone is not a reason to treat a waterbody.
researchNotes: Combined USGS ecological context with the independent Danube study's original morphology and long-term observations. The warming relationship is regional and correlational, not a universal impact claim. proposedDescription: Cereal cyst nematode is a microscopic roundworm that feeds inside the roots of wheat, barley, oats, and other grasses. Damaged roots have more difficulty supplying the plant with water and nutrients, which can leave uneven patches of weak or stunted crop. After a female dies, her hardened body becomes a cyst that shelters eggs in the soil. Those persistent cysts make the problem longer-lived than one growing season, while the symptoms above ground can easily be mistaken for other crop stresses.
identification: Stunting and poor patches are warning signs, not a diagnosis. Root and soil samples need laboratory examination to distinguish related cyst nematodes. Compare weak patches with healthier plants of the same crop and growth stage. Small pale females or brown cysts on roots may support suspicion, but related cereal cyst nematodes can look similar. A laboratory needs the roots and surrounding soil, not just a photograph of yellow leaves.
actions: Use confirmed species identity to guide crop rotation and resistant-variety choices. Ask about sample timing before digging, and keep samples from affected and comparison areas clearly labeled. Avoid carrying adhering soil on machinery from a confirmed infested field into clean fields. Discuss rotations and suitable resistant cultivars with an agronomist after identification, because host response and effective resistance can differ between nematode species and local populations.
researchNotes: UC Davis biology and Oregon State's regional management synthesis independently support the draft. H. filipjevi is a distinct look-alike; resistance and diagnosis should not be generalized across species. proposedDescription: The cereal leaf beetle is a small insect with metallic blue wing covers and an orange-red area behind its head. Its larvae are easier to notice by what they leave behind: narrow strips of damaged tissue on cereal and grass leaves. A dark coating of their own waste often hides the larvae's pale bodies. Heavy feeding can reduce the leaf area a grain crop needs to fill its seeds, but natural enemies also help keep populations in check, making field monitoring important.
identification: Look for blue-winged, orange-thoraxed adults and waste-coated larvae feeding along leaves. Similar Oulema beetles may need expert separation. Larvae feed in narrow tracks that leave pale strips in the leaf, and their dark coating can make them resemble small slugs. Turn leaves gently to look for eggs and feeding stages. Adult color is suggestive, but closely related Oulema species can require examination of reproductive structures.
actions: Preserve beneficial insects rather than spraying automatically after a single sighting. Record how many stems or leaves were checked and the crop's growth stage rather than reporting only the worst damaged leaf. Revisit the field to see whether larvae are still feeding and whether natural enemies are present. Use current local crop thresholds to decide whether any intervention is justified; isolated adults do not establish an economically damaging infestation.
researchNotes: USU supports feeding, life cycle and crop management; the UK recording scheme independently supports adult morphology and look-alike limitations. Avoided assigning all striped leaf damage to this species. proposedDescription: Cereal rye is an upright annual grass grown for grain, forage, and soil cover. Its tall stems carry dense, bristly seed heads that may lean as they mature, while a network of roots helps hold the soil. It is a familiar agricultural plant that can also appear outside the places where it was sown. Despite the similar name, cereal rye is not the same as the ryegrasses used in many lawns and pastures. Identifying the seed head helps tell those grasses apart.
identification: Confirm the whole plant rather than relying on the name rye. Examine a mature head as well as the leaf blade. Rye carries its spikelets directly along a central axis, producing a dense grain head with long bristles, rather than a loose branching spray. Young plants without heads can be difficult to separate from other cereal crops and volunteer grasses.
actions: Where rye is unwanted, document whether it is planted or growing independently. Ask local extension about preventing further seed production. Check the sowing history before calling a patch an escape, particularly in cover-cropped fields and gardens. If volunteers are unwanted, address them before grain matures and inspect field margins afterward. For intentional cover crops, plan termination with the next crop and soil protection in mind; removing all green cover immediately may defeat the reason rye was planted.
researchNotes: Two university accounts support crop uses, growth form and identification. No unsupported ecosystem-damage claim was inferred from its presence in the editorial queue. Fresh review 2026-10-31: inherited source lineages checked against the exact taxon; public guidance emphasizes recognition and containment, not unverified control efficacy.

proposedDescription: Cerulean flaxlily forms clumps of long, sword-shaped leaves, with small pale flowers followed by glossy blue berries. Although its foliage may look grasslike at first glance, it spreads from underground rhizomes and carries its flowers on branching stalks above the leaves. Birds can disperse its fruit. Native across parts of the Old World tropics, it has also been grown as an ornamental. In Florida, UF/IFAS assesses it as invasive, so its attractive appearance should not be the only consideration when choosing a landscape plant.
identification: Look for leaves arranged in two ranks, pale flowers with prominent yellow-orange anthers, and shiny blue berries. The flowers and fruit sit on a branching stalk, unlike a grass seed head, and the blue fruits are berries rather than dry grains. Several other Dianella are cultivated and can look similar when sterile. Photograph the base, leaf arrangement and a flowering or fruiting stalk together.
actions: In Florida, follow UF/IFAS advice against its use. Elsewhere, check local guidance before planting and prevent unwanted fruit or rhizome spread. Do not use the blue berries as a taste test, and keep removed fruit out of areas where it can be spread. When local guidance calls for removal, account for the underground rhizomes and revisit for shoots rather than simply trimming the foliage. Confirm the species before replacing a planting sold under the broad nursery name flaxlily.
researchNotes: NParks supports morphology and dispersal; UF/IFAS supplies a separate Florida risk assessment. The Florida conclusion is explicitly regional, not a nationwide legal claim. Fresh review 2026-10-31: inherited source lineages checked against the exact taxon; public guidance emphasizes recognition and containment, not unverified control efficacy.

proposedDescription: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus affects crops in the cucumber family, including cucumbers, melons, pumpkins, and squash. Infected plants may develop mottled or distorted leaves, poor growth, or damaged fruit, although symptoms vary with the crop and conditions. The virus travels with contaminated seed and plant material and can also move on hands, tools, and other surfaces. That combination makes clean planting material and careful hygiene especially important in gardens, greenhouses, and farms where susceptible crops are grown.
identification: Mosaic-patterned leaves and abnormal fruit can suggest a virus, but laboratory testing is needed to distinguish CGMMV from other problems. Compare symptoms across the same crop and note when they first appeared, particularly after transplanting, pruning or harvest work. A normal-looking plant may still carry infection. Fruit symptoms can differ from leaf symptoms, and a mosaic pattern does not reveal which virus is present.
actions: Pause movement of suspect plants and contact a plant diagnostic laboratory or extension service. Follow their sampling and disinfection instructions. Keep seed lot labels and transplant records so a confirmed problem can be traced. Avoid sharing seedlings, tools or harvested plant material from a suspect area until you receive advice. Ask the laboratory what tissue it needs and how to package it. Use tested planting material and a crop-specific hygiene plan rather than relying on insect control alone.
researchNotes: APHIS and Agriculture Victoria support hosts, symptoms and transmission. Kept Australian legal/reporting requirements out of US guidance and distinguished suspicion from a confirmed diagnosis. proposedDescription: Chamberbitter is a small warm-season annual that can appear among garden plants, in lawns, and in other disturbed ground. Its neat rows of little leaves make a branch look like a miniature mimosa leaf, but those are individual leaves rather than leaflets. Turn a branch over and the round seed capsules underneath become a useful clue. Plants can make seed while still quite small, which is why repeatedly mowing the tops may leave the next generation ready to grow.
identification: Turn a leafy side branch over to find the small round capsules beneath it. The neatly paired-looking blades are simple leaves on a branch, not leaflets of one compound leaf. The close-fitting fruits help distinguish it from long-stalked chamberbitter, whose fruits hang on more obvious little stalks.
actions: Check nursery containers before bringing them into beds, and pull young unwanted plants while their roots are still manageable. Return often during warm weather, since small plants can already be producing seeds. Maintain suitable mulch in planted beds and correct unnecessary irrigation where practical. Mowing a lawn alone may leave this low-growing annual able to flower and reseed. When pulling, hold the stem near the soil so the young plant comes away with its root; avoid shaking ripe capsules into the bed.

proposedDescription: Chameleon plant is a spreading perennial with heart-shaped leaves and a strong scent when its foliage is crushed. Garden forms may have brightly patterned leaves, but the plant can also be plain green. What look like four white petals surround a short spike of tiny flowers. It thrives in moist ground and spreads through creeping underground stems, which can carry it well beyond a garden bed. Those hidden stems also make an established patch more persistent than its soft leaves might suggest.
identification: Look for heart-shaped leaves and a short flower spike surrounded by four white bracts. Leaf coloration varies among garden forms. Look beneath nearby vegetation for plain green shoots as well as the brightly variegated garden form. Heart-shaped leaves alone are shared by many plants; the short central flower spike and surrounding white bracts are better clues. Avoid assuming a patch has disappeared just because its leaves die back seasonally.
actions: Avoid planting it beside natural wetlands. Where removing a patch, collect creeping stems carefully and monitor for regrowth rather than only clipping leaves. Trace shoots beyond the obvious patch before starting work, and avoid scattering rhizome pieces through soil cultivation. A container can help keep an intentional planting manageable, but check any drainage openings and surrounding ground. If removing it from a mixed bed, work carefully around neighboring roots and plan repeated checks for fresh shoots rather than expecting one digging to finish the job.
researchNotes: NC State and RHS independently support moist-site growth, spreading habit and flower structure. White structures are bracts; no nationwide invasive designation asserted. proposedDescription: Chandelier plant is a succulent with narrow, mottled leaves and clusters of hanging orange-red flowers. Tiny plantlets develop at the leaf tips, detach, and become new plants, helping explain its other name, mother of millions. This Madagascar native has been grown ornamentally and can establish in warm, open habitats beyond gardens. Its ability to reproduce from small pieces makes garden waste an important concern. The plant is poisonous to livestock and pets, so identification matters around grazing land and homes.
identification: Look for slender, grooved leaves with a few teeth and plantlets near their tips. Related mother-of-millions hybrids have broader leaves. Inspect the end of a leaf for small developing plantlets and the narrow, almost cylindrical leaf shape. Broader, boat-shaped leaves suggest a related species or hybrid. Hanging flowers may be absent on young plants, while fallen plantlets can already be taking root around the parent.
actions: Keep animals away from the plant and collect fallen plantlets when removing it. Follow local disposal guidance; do not dump living material outdoors. Before lifting an unwanted plant, gather the small offspring scattered beneath it and keep them with the parent material. Do not mow through a patch and spread succulent fragments. In grazing areas, arrange removal and disposal so livestock cannot reach the cut plants. Revisit nearby cracks, bare ground and pot edges for new plants after the larger stems have gone.

proposedDescription: Changing forget-me-not earns its name as its tiny flowers age from pale yellow or cream to blue. Several colors can appear on the same curling flower cluster, a helpful detail when this small plant blends into grassy ground. It is a hairy annual with slender stems and narrow leaves, originally from Europe and now established elsewhere. Roadsides, ditches, open pasture, and other disturbed places can provide suitable habitat. A close view of the flowers is much more useful for identification than a distant patch of blue.
identification: Look for different flower colors on one cluster, small five-lobed corollas, and hooked hairs on the calyx. A hand lens helps. Compare newly opened and older flowers on the same stem, rather than flowers from separate plants. The tiny corollas are only a few millimeters across, and the curved cluster lengthens as fruits develop. Hooked calyx hairs are useful under magnification when distinguishing it from other small annual forget-me-nots.
actions: Include a close photograph of the calyx and a wider view of the leaves and branching stem. If it is an unwanted garden annual, remove confirmed plants before their nutlets are dispersed and check the same open soil for seedlings. In natural vegetation, seek local identification first; being an introduced forget-me-not does not by itself establish serious ecological damage.

proposedDescription: The channeled apple snail is a large freshwater snail that grazes on aquatic plants and can damage crops grown in wet fields. Its rounded shell has deep grooves between the coils, while conspicuous pink egg masses are laid above the waterline. Originally South American, it has been moved to other regions through human activity. In Hawaii, it became a serious pest of wetland taro. Several apple snails look alike, so shell color or a pink egg mass alone cannot settle the species identity.
identification: Photograph the shell, grooves, and egg mass without moving them. Expert examination may be needed to separate it from other introduced apple snails. Record whether eggs are attached above the water on stems or hard surfaces, and photograph the shell opening as well as its outer coils if already visible. Similar apple snails can vary in shell color, size and grooves. Do not rely on the label golden apple snail, which has been used for more than one species.
actions:
Do not release aquarium snails or move snails, eggs, or contaminated plants between sites. Ask local aquatic or agricultural authorities about suspected populations. Leave animals and eggs at the site while obtaining advice rather than transporting them for a casual identification. Check aquatic plants and equipment before moving them, and never empty aquarium water or unwanted pets into a ditch or pond. Where a crop is affected, use the local agricultural response plan and protect native snails from indiscriminate collection.

If an authorized response requires handling snails, wear gloves and wash your hands afterward.

proposedDescription: Charlock mustard, also called wild mustard, is an annual plant with clusters of bright yellow, four-petaled flowers. It often grows in cultivated fields and other disturbed ground, where its broad leaves and upright stems compete with crops for space and resources. Long seed pods follow the flowers, and seeds left in the soil can supply later generations. It belongs to the same plant family as many familiar vegetables, so recognizing its leaves, flowers, and pods together is more reliable than identifying it by color alone.
identification: Look for four yellow petals, rough or hairy foliage, and elongated pods. Other yellow-flowered mustards can be very similar. Examine lower and upper leaves together: their shape can change along the stem. Developing pods and their terminal beaks are more useful for distinguishing mustard species than the yellow flowers alone. Photograph a flower cluster with attached pods, and include the stem hairs and leaf attachment in close views.
actions: In crop fields, use local weed-management advice and monitor for later seedlings. Pull small confirmed plants when the ground allows roots to come free, before the pods become dry and shatter. Keep seed-bearing material contained if maturity has already been reached. In a field, combine timely control with crop competition and attention to seed return. Recheck disturbed patches after later germination rather than assuming all plants emerged at once.

proposedDescription: The charru mussel is a small, thin-shelled mussel found in estuaries, lagoons, and other sheltered coastal waters. Its shell can range from greenish to nearly black, with a purple inner surface. It filters suspended food from the water and can gather on shells, roots, docks, and aquaculture structures. Introduced populations have become locally abundant, but abundance alone does not measure their effects: field research has found that competition with other mussels needs more careful study than some broad claims suggest.
identification: Look for a relatively smooth, thin shell with a purple interior. Native and other introduced mussels require expert comparison. Include the whole attached group and the substrate in a sighting photograph. Color alone is unreliable because shells vary with age and condition, and crowded growth can obscure their outlines. A specialist may need an empty shell or an authorized specimen to examine interior features without confusing it with native mussels.
actions: Photograph suspect mussels in place and report unfamiliar fouling to local marine-resource staff. Avoid moving live mussels or fouled equipment between waters. Keep boats, ropes and aquaculture gear from transferring attached mussels to another estuary. Follow the harbor or farm's approved cleaning procedure, capturing removed fouling where required rather than washing living material into new water. Note approximate patch size and whether it is on natural habitat or equipment; repeated observations can show change without presuming an ecological effect.

proposedDescription: Chayote is a vigorous climbing vine best known for its pale-green, pear-shaped vegetable, also called mirliton or vegetable pear. The fruit contains a single large seed, and the vine uses supports to lift its cucumber-like leaves and developing crop above the ground. Separate male and female flowers grow on the same plant and attract pollinators. This tropical American crop is cultivated in warm regions around the world. Its presence in a garden is therefore different from a vine growing independently beyond cultivation.
identification: Look for tendrils holding the vine to its support, rough cucumber-like foliage and the characteristic single-seeded fruit. Fruits may be smooth or prickly, so prickles alone do not distinguish another species. Photograph the vine's flowers and attachment points when immature plants have no fruit to compare. The fruit is fleshy and broadly pear-shaped rather than a long cucumber, though size and surface ridges vary among cultivated forms.
actions: Keep cultivated vines on suitable supports and within the growing area. Document escaped growth separately from deliberately planted crops. Inspect beyond the trellis for shoots entering neighboring vegetation and guide or prune garden growth back into the allotted space. Collect unwanted fruits and living trimmings rather than dumping them beside waterways. When documenting a possible escape, record any nearby garden source and whether the plant persists independently; a planted food crop is not automatically an invasive population.

proposedDescription: Cheatgrass is an annual grass that often starts growing in fall, spends winter as a small plant, and produces seed early the following season. Its soft, hairy leaves give way to drooping, bristly seed heads, then dry vegetation as the season warms. In many western landscapes, this early-drying growth adds fine fuel between larger plants and can help fires spread. Repeated disturbance can favor more cheatgrass, making prevention of seed production and recovery of perennial vegetation important parts of long-term management.
identification: Look for soft hairs on the leaves and sheaths, a prominent membranous ligule, and nodding seed heads with long awns. Follow the seasonal change from soft green growth to reddish or straw-colored seed heads. The loose, drooping branches and long awns help separate it from grasses with compact upright heads. Other annual bromes can resemble it, so include the leaf sheath, ligule and mature spikelets in identification photographs.
actions: Clean seeds from boots and equipment. For established patches, plan control before seed maturity and pair it with recovery of suitable perennial cover. Remove clinging awns before leaving an infested site, especially from footwear, pet fur and field gear. Small unwanted plants are easier to handle before their seeds harden and detach. In larger areas, avoid leaving bare soil as the only outcome of treatment: coordinate follow-up and appropriate revegetation with local rangeland or restoration staff.

proposedDescription: Cheeseweed mallow gets its name from its round, segmented fruits, which look like tiny wheels of cheese. This annual herb grows in gardens, cultivated ground and other disturbed places, with rounded, shallowly lobed leaves and small pale flowers tucked beside the leaf stalks. Its deep taproot becomes woody as the plant matures. Seeds have tough coats and can remain in the soil, so removing young plants before they fruit is much easier than tackling an established patch.
identification: Rounded scalloped leaves; tiny white to pale mauve flowers; wrinkled, wheel-shaped fruits distinguish it from common mallow. Check flowers and mature fruit rather than identifying every round-leaved seedling as cheeseweed. The very short pale petals and rough, segmented fruit are useful distinctions from other mallows. Leaves have radiating veins and long stalks, while stems may spread along the ground or grow upright.
actions: Pull or hoe seedlings while small, removing the taproot before seeds develop. Mowing alone often leaves live buds. Work after soil has softened enough to release the root, and collect plants with developing fruits before the seeds scatter. Inspect newly disturbed soil and the edges of irrigated beds for fresh seedlings. If a plant has become woody, avoid repeatedly cutting only the top and leaving the crown to regrow; choose a method suited to the site and nearby desirable plants.

proposedDescription: Cherokee rose is a vigorous scrambling shrub whose long, hooked canes climb through nearby vegetation. Large white flowers with golden centers stand out against glossy leaves, usually divided into three leaflets; bristly orange-red hips follow. Despite its common name, the plant is native to parts of Asia and was brought to North America during colonial times. It can spread aggressively in the southeastern United States, where a locally native climbing plant is often a better garden choice.
identification: Glossy three-part leaves, hooked prickles, large single white flowers and bristly hips. Count the leaflets on several leaves and look for the glossy surface rather than relying on a single rose flower. The large solitary blooms and bristly, pear-shaped hips help separate it from many roses with clustered small flowers. Native climbing roses should be compared carefully before any removal.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves around the canes. Avoid new planting in regions where it spreads aggressively. Inspect the outer canes where they reach surrounding shrubs, and keep an intentional planting from growing into adjacent natural vegetation. Wear eye protection and protective clothing when handling thorny stems. For a large unwanted thicket, get local advice on staged removal and regrowth checks, especially where pulling canes could damage trees or disturb nesting wildlife.

proposedDescription: Cherry bark tortrix is a small, intricately patterned moth whose caterpillars live beneath tree bark. Cherries, plums, apples and other members of the rose family can serve as hosts. Eggs are laid on bark, often near wounds, and the larvae tunnel below the surface, causing cracking and sometimes conspicuous gum. The insect is established in parts of the Pacific Northwest. An adult moth may be easy to overlook; damaged bark near the base of a tree can be the first useful clue.
identification: Brownish forewings patterned with orange and metallic markings; pale larvae beneath loose or cracked bark. Look for damage at bark cracks and wounds, including the lower trunk, rather than assuming a leaf-chewing caterpillar is responsible. Fine orange and metallic markings on the adult's brown forewings can be hard to interpret in a blurred photograph. Other bark borers and diseases can produce gum or dieback.
actions: Photograph the trunk damage and contact an extension diagnostician. Avoid moving infested nursery trees or bark to new sites. Keep the host tree's identity, planting date and source with photographs of the whole trunk and close views of damaged bark. Avoid peeling away extensive bark to search for larvae, which adds injury. A diagnostic service can advise whether an adult, larva or bark sample is needed and whether neighboring host trees should also be inspected.

proposedDescription: Cherry laurel is a dense evergreen shrub or small tree with broad, glossy leaves and upright clusters of fragrant white flowers. Its dark fruits attract birds, which carry the seeds beyond planted hedges. In the Puget Sound region, escaped plants can thrive in forest shade and crowd native shrubs and tree seedlings. Branches touching the ground can also take root. Cutting a large plant once seldom finishes the job, because both roots and cut stems can produce new growth.
identification: Thick evergreen leaves with glands underneath near the midrib; upright white flower clusters and purple-black fruits. Turn an attached leaf over to photograph the small glands near its base. Its broad leathery leaves can resemble some hollies and other cherry laurels, so compare the leaf glands, edges and fruit as well as flowers. Hedge pruning may remove flowers and fruit, so document an untrimmed shoot if one is available.
actions: Dig small plants when soil is moist and watch for seedlings. Plan follow-up for cut stumps; keep foliage and fruit away from people or animals that might eat them. Inspect beneath bird perches and along woodland edges for young plants outside the hedge. If removal leaves exposed soil, stabilize and replant it with locally suitable vegetation rather than allowing another weed patch to form. Large rooted plants on slopes need a careful plan; repeated monitoring for stump shoots and seedlings is part of management, not evidence that initial identification was wrong.

proposedDescription: Cherry plum is a small deciduous tree that flowers early, often as its first leaves unfold. The species has green leaves and white blossoms, although familiar garden cultivars may have deep purple foliage and pink flowers. Small, smooth-skinned plums range from yellow to red and attract birds. Native to southeastern Europe and parts of Asia, it has escaped cultivation in several regions, including parts of the United States and southeastern Australia. A purple leaf alone identifies neither the species nor its local ecological impact.
identification: Finely toothed oval leaves, five-petaled spring flowers and small rounded plums; leaf color varies by cultivar. Flowers commonly occur singly or in small groups, and the finely serrated leaves may be green even near a purple-leaved garden parent. Include a short leafy twig and any fruit in photographs. Other ornamental plums and hybrids can be difficult to separate without these details.
actions: Photograph flowers, leaves and fruit together for identification. Check nearby uncultivated ground for volunteer seedlings before allowing a planting to spread. Check whether small shoots are seedlings or attached to a planted tree before digging near its roots. Where volunteers are unwanted, remove them while manageable and revisit after fruiting seasons. Have large trees assessed by a qualified arborist if removal is being considered; a garden specimen's color or ornamental origin alone does not establish a need to fell it.

proposedDescription: Chestnut blight is caused by a fungus that grows in the bark of chestnut trees. Infection can expand around a branch or trunk, interrupting its supply of water and nutrients and leaving wilted brown leaves above the damaged area. Sunken or cracked cankers may carry tiny orange fruiting bodies. The disease transformed eastern North American forests by devastating American chestnut. It also affects European sweet chestnut; ongoing breeding work seeks useful resistance, but an apparently healthy tree is not proof of lasting protection.
identification: Chestnut bark cankers, orange fungal structures, persistent wilted leaves above damage and new shoots below it; laboratory diagnosis separates look-alike diseases. Check the relationship between the canker and the dead leaves above it, and photograph any shoots below the damaged section. Orange structures can be minute and may not always be visible. Root diseases and other chestnut cankers can also cause crown decline, so the tree's full condition matters.
actions: Ask an extension or tree-health service to assess suspected cankers. Do not move suspect chestnut bark, wood or nursery plants. Keep a record of the tree's species and whether it is a planted hybrid or a naturally occurring chestnut. Do not strip bark to expose a suspected infection without diagnostic instructions. If branches or trees must be removed, ask how to handle the wood locally and arrange work safely; apparent recovery or sprouting does not establish that the fungus has gone.

proposedDescription: Chestnut brown rot can hide inside a nut that looks ordinary from the outside. This fungus damages chestnut kernels, which may become brown, chalky or sponge-like, reducing the quality of the harvest. It can also live in apparently healthy flowers and shoots, and has been associated with twig cankers. Research in Portugal confirmed that isolates caused disease in several sweet-chestnut varieties. Because other fungi produce similar symptoms, a cut nut or bark lesion is a starting point for diagnosis rather than a reliable identification on its own.
identification: Brown or pale chalky decay inside chestnut kernels; shoot cankers may occur, but testing is needed to identify the fungus. Photograph the outside and a cut surface of affected nuts, keeping track of which tree or stored lot they came from. Similar decay can have different causes, and a healthy-looking shell does not guarantee a healthy kernel. Twig cankers also overlap in appearance with chestnut blight and other diseases.
actions: Set aside representative affected nuts and ask a plant diagnostic laboratory for sampling instructions before moving nursery or grafting material. Keep suspect lots separate while asking for diagnosis, and record harvest and storage conditions for the laboratory. Do not select grafting wood from a tree solely because its foliage looks normal. A confirmed result can guide nursery hygiene and orchard decisions; applying a home remedy to the shell will not demonstrate that an internal infection has been eliminated.

proposedDescription: Chickenspike is an annual wetland herb with soft, upright stems and narrow flower spikes that rise above its leaves. The tiny white flowers are packed closely together, followed by small capsules containing numerous seeds. It grows in shallow water, ditches and flooded ground, and is familiar as a rice-field weed. Its native range spans tropical Africa, Asia and northern Australia. The fleshy lower stem and dense, tapering flower spike are useful clues when examining a plant at the water's edge.
identification: Soft or spongy stems, simple narrow leaves and dense cylindrical spikes of very small white flowers. Examine the smooth fleshy stem and the tightly packed terminal spike together. The light-green leaves are arranged singly around the stem, and the lowest stem may show spongy tissue associated with wet ground. A dense white flower spike alone can resemble unrelated wetland herbs, so include leaves and stem in photographs.
actions: Photograph the whole plant and flower spike without carrying wet soil or seed-bearing material between fields. In cultivated ground, identify young plants before they set capsules and coordinate weed work with the crop's water management. Keep muddy boots and tools from carrying material into a clean field. In natural wetlands, seek local guidance before pulling plants or altering water levels; its rice-weed reputation does not justify disturbing an entire wetland community.

proposedDescription: Chickpea milkvetch, also called cicer milkvetch, is a long-lived perennial legume grown for forage and soil stabilization. Its leafy stems carry many paired leaflets and clusters of pale yellow to white pea flowers. The inflated pods darken as they mature, and loose seeds may rattle inside. Native to Europe and the Caucasus region, it spreads through underground shoots as well as seed. Its agricultural usefulness is well documented; its presence in this catalog should not be read as proof that it is invasive everywhere.
identification: Many paired leaflets, pale pea flowers and inflated pods that turn black at maturity. Each divided leaf has many small leaflets, and the swollen mature pods provide a useful check beyond the pale flower color. Other milkvetches and locoweeds should not be judged interchangeable from a common name. Photograph flowers, leaves and pods on the same plant when possible.
actions: Confirm identification before treating a forage stand. Monitor the edges of plantings for seedling or underground-shoot spread. Keep the seed label and cultivar information for an intentional forage planting, and discuss any unexpected spread with the land manager. Inspect adjoining ground for new plants and avoid moving mature pods with equipment. Do not transfer the documented forage use of cicer milkvetch to an unidentified Astragalus; accurate species identification matters before making grazing or removal decisions.

proposedDescription: Chicory brings clear blue flowers to many roadsides and old fields, opening its flower heads along stiff, branching stems. Young plants begin as a rosette of leaves that can resemble a dandelion, above a substantial taproot with milky sap. This Eurasian plant has a long history of cultivation for leaves and roots, and is now naturalized widely in North America. Wild chicory favors disturbed ground and usually does not move far into undisturbed habitats. Its flowers often close around midday.
identification: Blue, strap-flowered heads along wiry stems; dandelion-like basal leaves and smaller leaves clasping the upper stems. Inspect a flower head closely: the blue strap-shaped florets have toothed ends and there is no yellow central disk. Visit in the morning if flowers were closed on an afternoon walk. A basal rosette by itself is easy to confuse with dandelions and other members of the daisy family.
actions: Confirm the plant before removing garden volunteers. Where unwanted, prevent seed production and remove the root rather than only clipping the flower stalk. If you want to keep a garden plant, manage its seed heads before they spread into unwanted places. When removing it, collect root fragments as well as the crown because pieces can regrow. Distinguish cultivated leaf or root crops from roadside volunteers, and do not use plants from a roadside or uncertain identification for food.

proposedDescription: Chilean evening primrose opens yellow flowers that take on orange or reddish tones as they age. It begins with a rosette of narrow leaves, then sends up a leafy flowering stem from a stout taproot. Usually annual or biennial, it comes from Chile and Argentina and has naturalized in disturbed places beyond that range. Flowers open toward evening and may remain open into the following day. The long floral tube and slender, upright seed capsules help distinguish it from other yellow-flowered plants.

The long tube below the flower and upright capsules help separate it from other evening primroses.

In a confirmed unwanted patch, work before dry capsules shed seeds and check disturbed soil for the next generation. Keep local flowering season in mind rather than applying Southern Hemisphere dates directly to a North American observation.

proposedDescription: Chilean gunnera makes a striking clump of enormous, rough-edged leaves on stout, prickly stalks. Despite the nickname giant rhubarb, it is not culinary rhubarb. Its leaves die back seasonally, leaving large buds on thick rhizomes ready for new growth. In invaded areas of Ireland it forms dense colonies in wet ground, along waterways and on coastal sites, shading smaller plants. Other large gunneras, including garden hybrids, can look similar, so the familiar umbrella-shaped leaf is only the beginning of an identification.
identification: Huge toothed leaves, prickly stalks, large rhizome buds and conical flower spikes; compare garden hybrids before naming a plant. Look at the entire clump and flower spikes as well as a leaf. Giant garden gunneras have often been sold under names that do not match current identifications, particularly the hybrid Gunnera x cryptica. Winter buds and old leaf stalks can reveal a dormant clump even when the large leaves are absent.

Large colonies beside water need a plan that protects the bank and neighboring plants, including follow-up for regrowth rather than only removal of the visible foliage.

proposedDescription: The Chilean recluse is a brown spider native to South America that has also been introduced elsewhere. actions: Avoid handling it bare-handed. Photograph it safely and seek identification from an entomologist or qualified pest professional. Keep hands out of unseen storage spaces and use gloves when sorting undisturbed boxes or debris. Reduce clutter where spiders have been confirmed and ask a qualified professional about targeted inspection. Do not infer this spider's presence from a skin mark or remove every brown spider in the building; identification of an actual specimen is the starting point.

proposedDescription: Chinaberry is a deciduous tree with a spreading crown, finely divided leaves and fragrant lilac-colored flowers. Where removal is appropriate, arrange safe tree work and planned regrowth checks; the need for management depends on local ecology and the tree's setting.

proposedDescription: Chinese banyan can begin life perched on another tree, then develop into a broad evergreen with hanging aerial roots. proposedDescription: Chinese fir is an evergreen conifer with a tall, tapering crown and spreading branches whose tips often droop. Keep pointed branches away from paths where people may brush against them. For a possible escape, document seedlings separately from the planted tree and include cones or a twig in the identification record. If browning is a concern, compare old interior foliage with new growth and ask an arborist to evaluate the tree rather than diagnosing disease from color alone.

proposedDescription: Chinese firethorn, in the traditional regional-flora sense of Pyracantha fortuneana used here, is a spiny shrub grown for its clusters of white flowers and bright red fruits. Its leaves are broadest toward the tip, with rounded or slightly notched ends and small teeth along the edges. Plants cultivated under this name have occasionally naturalized in Australia. The name itself needs care: some floras retain Pyracantha fortuneana, while Kew currently places it within P. crenulata. That disagreement matters when comparing photographs, records or management advice published under different firethorn names.
identification: Look for stout spines, spoon-shaped leaves, white flower clusters and scarlet fruits, and confirm which taxonomic treatment is being used. Firethorns and their cultivars can share bright fruit colors, so a red berry cluster does not settle the name. Include close views of leaf tips, margins and the young shoots, plus a whole branch showing the thorns. A regional flora may use a narrower concept than a global checklist. A population study found the sampled leaf traits did not reliably separate the traditional species.
actions: Wear gloves around spines and photograph leaves, flowers and fruits. Resolve the name before applying a species-specific management claim. Keep the original nursery label and the exact identification supplied by a botanist alongside photographs. Where an unwanted thorny shrub is already spreading, contain its fruit and protect hands and eyes during handling while seeking local management advice. Do not transfer a regulatory or ecological claim from another firethorn merely because the two names appear together in a synonym list.

proposedDescription: Chinese flame tree is grown for bright yellow flowers and colorful, papery seed capsules. The Taiwanese form, subspecies formosana, has large, twice-divided leaves and three-sided capsules that turn from red or pink to brown as they mature. Keep planting records or cultivar names when asking for identification of the Taiwanese form. Do not extrapolate Queensland weed behavior to every growing region; local climate, subspecies and actual escape records should guide decisions about an established tree.

proposedDescription: Chinese hackberry is a fast-growing deciduous tree with smooth gray bark and a broad, spreading crown. proposedDescription: Chinese hatplant is a scrambling woody shrub named for the small, colorful saucers around its flowers. Keep the stems on their intended support and inspect where they extend into neighboring vegetation. Record any separate plants beyond the garden, including whether there is evidence of a former planting. Collect unwanted rooted cuttings rather than discarding them beside a hedge or watercourse. Local observations of spread are more informative than assuming every vigorous ornamental is invasive.

proposedDescription: Chinese hound's tongue is often sold as Chinese forget-me-not for its sprays of small sky-blue flowers. proposedDescription: Chinese lovegrass is a small tuft-forming grass whose open seed heads carry flattened clusters of tiny flowers. These spikelets can turn purplish red as they mature, giving the airy heads a subtle wash of color. Its stems may rise from a leaning base, and plants grow as annuals or short-lived perennials. Native across tropical and subtropical Asia into parts of Queensland, it occurs in grasslands and along roadsides. Similar lovegrasses are difficult to separate, so close views of mature spikelets are more useful than a distant photograph.
identification: Open branched seed heads and flattened, many-flowered spikelets that may mature purplish red. A grass specialist should compare the spikelets and leaf joints. Hold a mature head against a plain background to show the loose branches and flattened spikelets. Include a scale and a clear view of several intact spikelets, because a purple tinge occurs in other grasses too. A hand lens can help, but a regional key may require finer floral details.
actions: Photograph mature seed heads and leaf joints for a grass specialist. Avoid moving seed-bearing soil or cuttings while identification is unresolved. Keep a flowering specimen only if collection is permitted and a receiving specialist requests it, with seeds contained during transport. Note whether the grass is in a lawn, roadside, damp hollow or natural grassland. If it is a confirmed unwanted annual in a bed, prevent seed return while protecting adjacent grasses whose identity has not been established.

proposedDescription: Chinese mantis is a large, slender hunter that waits among leaves and stems with its grasping forelegs folded. Adults range from green to tan or brown, often with a green line along the wings. The head swivels to follow nearby movement. Introduced to North America, it feeds on a broad range of animals it can overpower, including other beneficial insects. Its rounded, foam-like egg case remains on twigs after the adult season and can be mistaken for a small brown growth on the plant.
identification: Large mantis with a fairly square, vertically striped facial shield; rounded tan egg cases. Compare smaller native Carolina mantises carefully. Look at the face from a safe, close photographic angle and compare the body length with a visible reference. Young nymphs lack adult wings, so wing markings are unavailable at that stage. The round tan egg case is useful in winter, but an empty case does not show how many mantises remain nearby.
actions: Observe rather than release purchased egg cases outdoors. Confirm the species before removing an egg case, since native mantises occur alongside it. Preserve photographs and the twig location if an egg case needs identification. A mantis taking a pest insect is also capable of taking a pollinator, so purchased releases are not a selective pest-control method. In a mixed garden, avoid broad spraying prompted by one mantis sighting and seek local advice before disturbing egg cases that could belong to native species.

proposedDescription: Chinese mitten crab is named for the dense bristles that cover its claws like fuzzy gloves. It spends much of its life in rivers and other freshwater habitats, then moves toward saltier water to reproduce. Originally from coastal China and Korea, it has been carried to other regions through human activity. Where abundant, its burrows can undermine banks, and its feeding and migrations can interfere with native wildlife and fisheries. Small juveniles may lack the obvious hairy claws seen on adults.
identification: Hairy claws with pale tips, a notch between the eyes and four spines along each side of the shell; very small juveniles have less hair. Include the top of the shell, the claws and the front edge between the eyes in photographs. Adult hairy claws are striking, but small juveniles can be overlooked because the hair is sparse. Other crabs may have hairy limbs, so the shell spines and notch must be considered together.
actions: Photograph the crab and exact location, keep it from returning to the water if safely contained, and contact the local aquatic invasive-species authority. Never move it alive to another waterbody. If a crab is already caught, prevent escape without handling its claws, and request local instructions for identification and disposal. Do not carry it to another stream or keep it as a live curiosity. Record whether it was found in fresh, brackish or tidal water; that context helps investigators interpret a sighting along its migratory route.

proposedDescription: Chinese mysterysnails carry a rounded olive-brown shell with deep seams between its coils and a hard door that closes the opening. proposedDescription: Chinese obscure scale is a tiny armored insect found on woody plants, including crabapple. Ask which twigs or leaves to submit and avoid scraping all the scales away before a sample is taken. Wait for confirmation of living pests and species identity before choosing treatment; a historical report on crabapple does not establish that every crust on an apple branch is this scale.

Small white flowers precede the fruit, and its narrow leaves may have gently wavy edges. It comes from China and nearby parts of Asia, where it grows on slopes, in thickets and along riverbanks. Gardeners also know it as Photinia davidiana. The two names refer to the same plant in the accounts used here, rather than to two different red-berried shrubs.
identification: Evergreen narrow leaves, white flower clusters, red round fruits and initially hairy young shoots. Compare leaf margins and young shoots, because many evergreen shrubs have white flowers followed by red fruit. Its narrow leaves and initially hairy growth are useful alongside the flower clusters. Garden hybrids and other photinias can resemble it, so keep the nursery name when asking for an identification.
actions: Photograph flowers, fruit and leaf margins together to separate it from other photinias. Monitor unwanted seedlings near garden plantings. Watch the area beyond the planting for separate seedlings and record whether red-fruited shrubs were deliberately installed there. If unwanted volunteers are confirmed, remove them while small and check again after later fruiting seasons. Maintain an existing garden shrub according to its actual spread and local guidance; the alternative name Photinia davidiana is not evidence of a second invading species.

proposedDescription: Chinese privet is a densely branching shrub that often keeps its small leaves through winter in mild climates. Clusters of white flowers are followed by dark fruits that birds and mammals carry into new places. Introduced as an ornamental, it has become a major invader in parts of the eastern and southern United States. Seeds and root suckers both help it form thickets, which can replace a more varied layer of native plants. An old hedge can therefore be a continuing source of new plants beyond the garden.
identification: Opposite small oval leaves, often with hairs beneath the midrib; white flower clusters and dark purple-black fruits. Examine an untrimmed twig for opposite leaf pairs and hairs on the underside of the midrib. Several other privets have white flowers and dark fruits, while some native shrubs resemble it when sterile. Leaf size, twig hair and fruit clusters should be considered together rather than relying on an old hedge label.
actions: Choose a locally native hedge instead. Plan repeated follow-up for established thickets and check surrounding ground for seedlings and suckers. Start by locating small satellite plants beyond the main thicket, including those under bird perches. Protect native seedlings during work and avoid leaving all cleared ground bare. Large shrubs and root systems need a site-specific plan, particularly beside streams. Revisit for shoots from surviving roots and for new seedlings instead of assuming a cut hedge has stopped supplying new growth.
