proposedDescription: Chinese raspwort is a small perennial of wet tropical regions, native from southern China through parts of Southeast Asia and the Pacific to Australia. It is easy to overlook beside larger wetland plants. The New South Wales form has rough, four-ribbed stems, narrow toothed leaves and tiny flowers followed by ribbed fruits. Its Australian subspecies is treated separately in this collection, so a close look at the fruit matters when putting a precise name to a plant.
identification: In the NSW account, plants have four-ribbed stems, opposite lower leaves and tiny eight-ribbed fruits. Subspecies determination requires mature fruit. The leaf pairs near the base can give way to alternate leaves higher on a stem. Mature fruit details are much more informative than the tiny flowers alone. In the Australian treatment, the location of hairs and surface bumps on the fruit helps separate the two subspecies.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, stem, leaves and mature fruits. Ask a herbarium to check the subspecies before recommending removal. For a useful observation, include a scale beside the tiny fruits and note whether the plant is in standing water, damp open soil or a disturbed margin. Do not generalize the appearance of the New South Wales subspecies to every Asian or Pacific plant. Leave native wetland vegetation intact while a specialist checks the specimen and its regional context.

proposedDescription: This Australian subspecies of Chinese raspwort is a slender perennial of damp, open ground. proposedDescription: Chinese rose beetles often reveal themselves through the lace-like holes they leave between leaf veins. Adults emerge after dusk to feed on many kinds of plants, including garden ornamentals and crops. They are small brown scarabs covered with pale hairs, while their whitish grubs develop underground. A specialist may need detailed leg and reproductive characters to separate Adoretus sinicus from its very similar relative.
actions: Visit affected foliage with a light after sunset, photograph the beetles, and record which plants are actually being fed upon. Avoid digging out every grub nearby on the assumption that it caused the leaf injury. Keep any requested sample contained and labeled with host and time of collection, then use current local advice to decide whether the level of damage warrants action.

proposedDescription: Chinese silvergrass forms tall, arching clumps topped by airy flower plumes. A flowering stem with its leaf base is a better identification sample than a loose plume.

proposedDescription: Chinese tallow is often noticed for its autumn color and clusters of white seeds that resemble popcorn. The deciduous tree has broadly rounded leaves drawn out into slender tips and produces yellow flower spikes in spring. Brought from Asia as an ornamental and potential crop, it now invades wetlands, prairies and forests in the southeastern United States. Birds and water carry its seeds, while cut trees can sprout again. Removing seedlings early and planning follow-up for larger trees helps prevent a return.
identification: Alternate simple leaves with rounded bases and long tips; milky sap; three-part capsules opening to white seeds. Photograph the leaf attachment and slender pointed tip, and inspect the three-lobed fruit before or after it opens. The exposed white objects are seeds rather than fleshy berries. In autumn, leaf color can be conspicuous, but many unrelated trees also turn red and yellow.
actions:
Pull small seedlings before seed production. Use qualified help for mature trees and plan for stump sprouts and later seedlings. Inspect drainage routes and ground beneath bird perches around a seeding tree, where new plants can appear beyond the parent. Keep fruits and seeds contained during work, and avoid moving contaminated soil into restoration plantings. Larger projects should include suitable replacement vegetation and monitoring; cutting a trunk is a first operation, not evidence that roots or the seed supply have been exhausted.

proposedDescription: Chinese violet is a creeping perennial with opposite leaves, trumpet-shaped flowers and seed capsules that spring open when ripe. Garden forms can spread quickly in warm climates. The name covers more than one subspecies: the small white flowers with purple markings belong to subsp. micrantha, a serious smothering weed in parts of Australia, while other forms have larger, differently colored flowers. Stems can root where they touch moist soil, making dumped cuttings an effective way to start a new patch.

actions: Keep cut stems out of garden dumping areas and waterways. Where removal is appropriate, collect roots and stem fragments and check for regrowth. Trace sprawling stems to their rooted nodes before lifting a small unwanted patch. Collect loose fragments rather than scattering them with mowing or cultivation, and inspect the edge again for new rooted growth. In a mixed planting or natural area, identify the form first and obtain local guidance before clearing vegetation solely because its flowers resemble a picture of Chinese violet.

proposedDescription: Chinese wisteria's fragrant spring flower clusters can be beautiful, but the woody vine grows with enough force to overwhelm trees and shrubs. It climbs by twining and can also spread across the ground, where touching stems take root. The hanging seed pods are velvety, unlike those of native American wisteria. identification: Woody counterclockwise-twining vine; spring blue-violet flower clusters and velvety pods. Native American wisteria has smooth pods and generally blooms later. Japanese wisteria and hybrids make a single-character identification unreliable.
actions: Avoid planting near natural areas. Cut accessible stems carefully and arrange repeated follow-up; obtain local guidance for established infestations. Avoid pulling heavy entangled vines down from a tree, where they may bring branches with them. Arrange safe work on large stems and keep ground-level rooted sections in the follow-up plan. proposedDescription: Dioscorea oppositifolia is a tuber-forming climbing yam native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar. Its name has often been applied incorrectly to Chinese yam in North American writing. That distinction matters: descriptions of the invasive Chinese yam cannot simply be transferred to this species. The exact botanical identity therefore matters before interpreting a field sighting or choosing any removal method intended for the Chinese yam.
identification: The name Dioscorea oppositifolia and the common label Chinese yam do not reliably identify the same plant; compare botanical characters carefully. True Dioscorea oppositifolia is a leafy climbing plant with an underground tuber. Indian flora accounts describe broad leaves in opposite pairs, with conspicuous veins running from near the base toward the tip. A climbing habit and a yam-like tuber alone cannot separate it from other Dioscorea.
actions: Have the original taxon record checked before applying Chinese yam control advice or changing a species identification. Keep the source of a nursery label or earlier identification with photographs of the vine, paired leaves and any flowers or capsules. Ask a herbarium to distinguish the true species from Chinese yam before transferring occurrence records or deciding on removal. Avoid moving tubers or living cuttings while identity is uncertain, and do not dig up a large patch simply to test a name.

proposedDescription: Chinese yellowcress is a small annual mustard native to eastern Asia. proposedDescription: The chocolate moth, also called the cacao or tobacco moth, is a small moth associated with stored goods. Its larvae feed in products such as cocoa, tobacco, cereals and dried foods, so an indoor sighting is a reason to inspect supplies rather than assume the moth came from the garden. proposedDescription: Chocolateweed is a small upright herb or subshrub with toothed leaves and tight clusters of little flowers. proposedDescription: Christmas candlestick stands out for the rounded clusters of orange flowers spaced along its upright stems. proposedDescription: Christmas grass is a tufted tropical grass whose seed heads reward a closer look. proposedDescription: Chrysanthemum aphids gather around tender shoots, buds and leaf undersides, where they feed on plant sap. The small adults are dark reddish brown to nearly black; younger aphids are often dull brick red. Colonies can build quickly because females give birth to live young, and infested plants can carry them between greenhouses. Feeding may distort or stunt growth, while sticky honeydew supports black sooty mold. Regularly checking new shoots and incoming plants helps catch a colony before it becomes dense.
identification: Dark aphids with short black cornicles; wingless adults about 1.5 mm, nymphs brick red; colonies concentrate on chrysanthemum growth. Look at several stages together: wingless adults are compact and dark, while small nymphs have long legs and antennae against a brick-red body. Winged adults can appear as crowded colonies disperse. Cast skins and sticky deposits help locate feeding sites, but neither identifies the aphid without examining the insects themselves.
actions: Inspect chrysanthemums weekly and separate incoming plants for inspection. Remove heavily infested plants and seek crop-specific advice while conserving natural enemies. Pay particular attention to new terminal growth, stems and leaf undersides when stock arrives. Keep suspect pots apart from clean plants while obtaining advice. In a greenhouse, continue scouting while chrysanthemums remain present, since warmth and a continuing host can support feeding through winter rather than a single outdoor season.

proposedDescription: Cigarette beetles are tiny, rounded, reddish-brown insects that can turn up in far more than tobacco. Their larvae feed in dried products, including spices, grains, pet food and other stored plant material. The adult's head is tucked beneath its thorax, giving it a hooded appearance from above. Fine details help separate it from the similar drugstore beetle: cigarette beetles have saw-toothed antennae and lack rows of pits on their wing covers. Finding the infested material is more useful than treating a wandering adult.
identification: About 3 mm long, rounded and reddish brown; serrated antennae and smooth-looking wing covers distinguish it from drugstore beetle. Use a hand lens to examine the antennae and wing covers; reddish color and small size alone fit other pantry beetles. The pale larvae are curved grubs with legs, often concealed within the product. A beetle at a window may have flown away from its food, so record emergence sites if possible.
actions: Inspect dry goods and stored plant material, isolate suspect packages and ask an Extension or pest professional to identify the source. Check seldom-used spices, dried plant decorations and animal foods as well as everyday pantry staples. Keep confirmed infested material sealed for disposal or professional assessment, then clean remaining food debris from the storage area. Recheck unopened packages and replacement stock; removing adults alone leaves concealed larvae and their food source behind.

proposedDescription: True cinnamon is the Sri Lankan tree whose bark supplies the familiar spice. Fresh leaves often emerge red before turning glossy green, and several strong veins run from near the leaf base toward the tip. Small pale flowers are followed by dark, fleshy, single-seeded fruits. In tropical gardens the tree can become a substantial evergreen. Because other cinnamon relatives share aromatic leaves and bark, a scent alone is a poor identification test; leaf arrangement, veins and fruit provide a better starting point.
identification: Glossy, leathery leaves, reddish new growth and three to five strong basal veins; small pale flowers and dark oval fruits. Photograph a shoot showing paired or nearly paired leaves and the strong veins that run lengthwise from near the base. Include mature green leaves as well as reddish new growth, since color changes with age. Other aromatic laurels can look similar, so a nursery name or familiar smell should be checked against flowers and fruit.
actions: Use leaves and fruit for identification rather than tasting bark. Check local guidance before planting and watch for seedlings beyond cultivation. Keep any nursery label and planting history with the record. Where trees are cultivated for spice or ornament, distinguish deliberately planted young trees from volunteer seedlings. If growth appears outside the planted area, document it for local assessment rather than assuming either harmlessness or ecological damage from the tree name alone.

proposedDescription: Circular hemlock scale is a tiny armored insect that settles mainly beneath conifer needles. Females sit under rounded, dark brown covers with a raised center; heavy infestations can coat much of a needle. Feeding removes plant fluids and may lead to yellowing and premature needle loss, particularly on hemlocks. Also called shortneedle evergreen scale, it has a mobile crawler stage before the insects settle. Inspecting the lower crown with a hand lens can reveal a problem before thinning foliage becomes obvious.
identification: Female covers circular, dark brown and strongly convex, about 1-1.3 mm wide; usually on needle undersides. Confirm against other armored scales. Examine several needles from different branches, including the lower crown where infestation may first be noticed. Rounded scale covers differ from the loose white wool of hemlock woolly adelgid, but other armored scales still require comparison. Yellowing alone has many causes, so photographs should show the attached insects as well as the tree.
actions: Inspect lower needle surfaces with magnification. Have a diagnostic service confirm the scale and time any management to locally observed crawlers. Save a small affected twig only as directed by the diagnostic service, and keep nursery material from being transferred while an infestation is assessed. Record whether scales are alive and whether new needle loss is developing. Local crawler monitoring is more useful than applying a calendar date taken from another state.

proposedDescription: Citricola scale is a sap-feeding insect that can leave citrus foliage sticky with honeydew and darkened by sooty mold. Its appearance changes as it grows: young scales are flat and translucent beneath leaves, while mature females become oval, grayish bumps on twigs. Heavy populations can weaken trees and reduce fruit production. Ants, sticky leaves and black mold are useful clues, but checking the insects themselves matters because several other citrus pests leave the same signs.
identification: Look beneath leaves for flat young scales and along twigs for convex gray females, up to about 6 mm long. Brown soft scale is generally smaller and browner; identification should include life stage. Check the same tree at more than one growth stage: a leaf colony of nearly flat juveniles can later appear as larger females on woody growth. Brown soft scale often has mixed sizes together, whereas citricola populations are more synchronized in California. A close photograph with a size reference helps separate these overlapping appearances.
actions: Photograph both leaf and twig colonies and ask an extension specialist to confirm the scale. Preserve predators and parasitoids; management timing varies with local climate and the insect's stage. Note the scale stage, affected branches and presence of ants when seeking advice. Check whether fresh honeydew or new growth loss is increasing rather than judging only by old blackened leaves. Avoid choosing a treatment from color alone, since protecting natural enemies and timing work depend on the confirmed insect.

proposedDescription: Citron zephyrlily is a small bulb-forming perennial with bright yellow flowers held above a tuft of very narrow leaves. proposedDescription: Citrus black spot is a fungal disease that marks citrus fruit with several kinds of blemishes, from tiny dark speckles to sunken spots with pale centers and dark borders. Severe infections can cause fruit to drop before harvest. The fungus can reproduce in infected fallen leaves, helping the disease persist around a tree. Because symptoms vary with the fruit's age and can resemble other problems, a photograph is a starting point for diagnosis rather than a reliable confirmation.
identification: Hard-spot symptoms include small, circular, sunken lesions with gray or tan centers and dark margins. Other forms look quite different; have suspicious fruit and leaf symptoms assessed by a plant diagnostic service. Photograph several fruits and both leaf surfaces if affected. Raised corky canker lesions and other fungal spots can be confused with black spot in casual images.
actions: Photograph suspect fruit and contact local extension or the state plant health office. Avoid moving potentially infected citrus plants, fruit or fallen material until you receive local guidance. Keep the location, citrus variety if known, and date of first symptoms with the report. Ask the receiving service how material should be sampled before sending anything. Do not distribute fallen leaves, nursery stock or suspect fruit to another garden while the cause and any local movement requirements are being checked.

proposedDescription: Despite its name, citrus blackfly belongs to the whitefly family. Adults are dark and sooty-looking, and their young form conspicuous black, spiny patches beneath leaves. proposedDescription: Older citrus canker names need careful interpretation because bacterial species names and pathovar names carry different meanings. Dropping that final pathovar name changes the meaning. Resolving the original identification will help ensure that citrus symptoms and reporting advice are attached to the right organism.
identification: The species name alone cannot identify the historical citrus-infecting pathovar. Trace the original record, diagnostic result or cited name before assigning citrus canker symptoms to this entry. Bacteria cannot be identified by ordinary garden photographs. Host plant, lesion appearance and a complete laboratory name belong together, including any pathovar given after the species. A record using only a shortened historical name cannot establish that the organism is the citrus-infecting bacterium rather than another member of the genus.
actions: Ask a plant diagnostic service to interpret an incomplete or historical bacterial name before drawing conclusions about citrus canker. Keep the original identification with the plant history. proposedDescription: Citrus canker is caused by a citrus-infecting pathovar of Xanthomonas citri, a bacterium that attacks leaves, shoots and fruit. Its raised, corky lesions often have a yellow halo and can make fruit unsaleable; severe disease also causes leaf and fruit drop. Wind-driven rain helps bacteria reach young tissue and wounds. identification: Look for raised, rough or crater-like brown lesions, often with a water-soaked edge or yellow halo. Similar-looking damage needs laboratory or plant-health confirmation. Inspect leaves, young twigs and fruit together; a single brown mark is less informative than a repeated pattern across these tissues. Note whether lesions project above the surface, rather than simply being dark or depressed. Citrus black spot, scab and mechanical injury may resemble parts of the pattern and should remain in the comparison.
actions: Document symptoms without transporting the plant or affected material. Contact extension or the local plant health authority for sampling instructions and applicable movement requirements. Provide the tree location, planting history and recent movement of nursery material when reporting a suspicion. Do not share budwood or cuttings from the tree. Ask for local instructions before pruning, collecting samples or disposing of fallen material, since handling and movement decisions depend on diagnostic results and the regional disease situation.

proposedDescription: Huanglongbing, often called citrus greening, is a serious citrus disease associated with the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. Infected trees may develop unevenly mottled leaves, yellow shoots and small, misshapen fruit that remain partly green. The Asian citrus psyllid carries the bacterium between trees, and infected propagation material can also spread it. Symptoms may take time to appear, so a healthy-looking tree is not proof of freedom from infection. Confirmed disease has no cure.
identification: Asymmetric yellow blotching across a leaf's midrib is a useful warning sign. Small lopsided fruit and shoot dieback add concern, but nutrient disorders and other problems can look similar; laboratory testing is needed. Compare both sides of several leaves rather than relying on one yellow shoot. Uneven patches that cross the midrib differently are more concerning than a consistently symmetrical nutrient pattern, but neither pattern is conclusive alone. Record which part of the crown first changed and whether fruit size or shape also differs.
actions: Photograph suspicious foliage and fruit and contact the local plant health office. Avoid moving citrus plants, cuttings or suspect green waste until you have appropriate guidance. Keep nursery labels and propagation history available for the diagnostic service. Do not share budwood from a tree under investigation, even if another branch looks healthy. Follow the authority's sampling instructions; testing and any subsequent tree-management decisions need to account for the local disease program and the possibility of symptomless infection.

proposedDescription: Citrus leafminer leaves a delicate silver trail as its larvae tunnel just beneath the surface of new citrus leaves. The narrow, winding mine often contains a dark line of waste, and damaged leaves may curl around the developing insect. Young trees can lose valuable new growth, while established trees usually tolerate the injury. Feeding wounds can also make citrus canker infection easier where that disease occurs. The tiny adult moth is much less noticeable than its handiwork.
identification: Look for winding mines with a central dark line on tender leaves and a curled leaf edge where pupation occurs. Adults are tiny silvery moths with dark marks near the wing tips. Examine the newest expanding leaves, where the pale tunnel runs within the leaf rather than sitting on top like a loose thread. Older mines can remain after the insect has left. Rolled leaves without a visible mine may instead reflect aphids, psyllids or other injury, so check for the actual feeding trace.
actions: Keep damaged leaves that are still functioning, and avoid unnecessary pruning or excessive fertilization that prompts repeated flushes of tender growth. Where citrus canker is a concern, ask a local citrus adviser to assess the combined disease risk rather than treating every mine as an emergency.

proposedDescription: Citrus mealybug looks like a small moving fleck of white cotton, often tucked into a leaf joint, fruit cluster or other sheltered spot. Beneath its waxy coating is an oval sap-feeding insect with short filaments around the body. It attacks many ornamentals as well as citrus, including plants grown indoors. Colonies can weaken growth and leave sticky honeydew that encourages sooty mold. New plants deserve a close inspection because small colonies are easy to overlook.
identification: Females have white wax, a faint grayish stripe along the back and short marginal filaments, with the rear pair slightly longer. Look for cottony egg sacs and hidden colonies; related mealybugs can require expert examination. A magnified view should show a segmented insect beneath the white wax, rather than only a cottony patch. Compare the length of the tail filaments with the body; long-tailed mealybugs can be mistaken for this species. Check leaf axils, overlapping fruit and other sheltered joints that are hidden in a whole-plant photograph.
actions: Inspect and isolate newly acquired houseplants when insects are found. Remove small accessible colonies, then recheck crevices over several weeks; obtain pest-specific advice for persistent or extensive infestations. Keep infested pots from touching neighboring plants and inspect the supporting surfaces as well as the foliage. Where a few insects are removed by hand, return to the same hidden sites repeatedly to look for young stages. Avoid moving a plant back among clean stock merely because its obvious white colonies have disappeared.
researchNotes: UF provides host range and morphology; NC State's separately authored extension account provides inspection and repeated follow-up guidance. proposedDescription: Citrus rust mite is so small that the damage usually catches your eye before the animal does. Feeding on rind cells can leave oranges rusty brown and lemons silvery, changing the fruit's appearance. These pale, wedge-shaped mites also feed on leaves and green stems. In home gardens, light injury is often mainly cosmetic, but heavier infestations can matter in commercial production and may contribute to fruit drop. The similar pink citrus rust mite is a different species.
identification: A strong hand lens is needed: adults are less than about 0.25 mm long, pale yellow to brownish and wedge-shaped, with four legs near the front. Confirm the mite rather than relying on rind color alone. Look for living mites on affected fruit and foliage with magnification; old russeting can remain after the population changes. Pink citrus rust mite overlaps in size, and reliable separation uses fine body characters rather than rind color. Record the citrus type and whether new damage is appearing on developing fruit.
actions: Inspect affected fruit with magnification and assess the amount of injury before considering treatment. Garden fruit with superficial blemishes may not need intervention; growers should use local monitoring thresholds. Monitor more than one part of the canopy and keep dated photographs of the affected rind. A commercial fresh-fruit grower may have different quality thresholds from a home gardener keeping fruit for household use. Seek local advice before intervention, with attention to natural enemies and the number of active mites rather than discoloration alone.

proposedDescription: This clam worm lives out of sight in the mud of brackish estuaries, where its segmented body moves through a burrow. Native to the northwestern Pacific, Hediste diadroma has also been identified in estuaries on North America's Pacific coast. It gathers food from sediment and can filter suspended particles through a mucus net. Its resemblance to native worms makes casual sightings difficult to interpret, and the ecological effects of its introduction remain uncertain.
identification: A tapered, many-segmented worm with bristled side appendages and four eyes is consistent with this group, but not enough for species identification. Specialists use fine anatomical features and sometimes molecular evidence to separate similar Hediste. Include the head and side appendages in photographs, but do not try to name the worm from its segment count or color alone. Species separation depends on tiny jaw-area teeth and bristle structures. Native Hediste may share the same mudflat, so a worm found at an introduced-species locality is not automatically this species.
actions: Record the location and habitat without transferring worms or sediment between sites. Ask a marine invertebrate specialist to assess a suspected record; photographs alone may not resolve the species. Leave burrows and sediment in place during casual observation. Bait worms, attached mud and other collected material should never be released into a different estuary. For a suspected new locality, provide the original site, salinity setting and date to a marine specialist, who can decide whether a properly documented specimen is needed.

proposedDescription: Clammy goosefoot is a low, spreading herb whose small leaves and tiny flower clusters are easy to miss underfoot. Fine glandular hairs give it an aromatic, somewhat sticky character. The flowers sit close to the stems in the leaf axils, later producing minute dark seeds. Native to Australia, it has become established in other regions, often around disturbed or cultivated ground. Its modest appearance means close-up details are more useful than a distant photograph.
identification: Look for prostrate or partly ascending stems, small oval leaves with wavy or toothed margins, glandular hairs and dense, tiny whitish flower clusters where leaves meet stems. Confirm against other small goosefoots. A close side view can show the tiny flowers packed at the leaf bases rather than forming a conspicuous terminal spike. The leaves are small, with margins ranging from wavy to almost smooth. Examine the glandular hairs with magnification; the spreading habit and aromatic foliage together help narrow the choice among goosefoots.
actions: Photograph the leaf margins, flower clusters and growth habit. Ask a local herbarium or extension service to confirm uncertain plants before deciding whether removal is warranted. Record whether the patch is in a garden, track edge or natural vegetation and retain the date for a local comparison. If confirmed as an unwanted garden plant, contain flowering material instead of spreading it with soil. Native populations should be assessed in their own regional context before any control is proposed.

proposedDescription: Clasping heliotrope forms low, sprawling patches topped with curved clusters of blue-purple to pink flowers, each with a small yellow center. Its hairy, wavy-edged leaves sit close to the stems. This South American perennial can persist through a deep root system and regrow after its shoots die back. In introduced pasture settings it can compete with useful vegetation, and its toxicity to livestock makes a confirmed identification especially important around grazing land.
identification: Check for hairy, mostly stalkless leaves that partly clasp the stem and coiled flower clusters with blooms arranged along one side in two rows. It is often called blue heliotrope. The curved flower clusters gradually unfurl, with small blooms appearing along the upper side. Include the crowded flower head, hairy leaf surface and the way the leaf joins the stem in photographs. Related heliotropes can differ in flower color and growth form, while damaged plants may be difficult to distinguish without flowering shoots.
actions: Keep livestock away from suspected patches until a local agricultural adviser confirms the plant and assesses the situation. Record patch size and flowering details; obtain locally appropriate management advice. Avoid shifting soil or root fragments from a confirmed patch to clean ground. Mark its boundary and monitor regrowth after any locally approved control, since loss of the visible shoots does not necessarily remove the deep-rooted plant. Keep contaminated plant material out of animal feed and follow agricultural advice on grazing access.

proposedDescription: Clasping pepperweed has an unusual contrast between its leaves: the lower ones are finely divided, while the upper ones are broad and wrap closely around the stem. Small yellow flowers appear above them, followed by little rounded seed pods. This short-lived mustard comes from Eurasia and is introduced in North America, where it often grows on dry, disturbed ground. Seeing both the lower foliage and the flowering stem makes identification much easier.
identification: Look for deeply dissected lower leaves, strongly clasping rounded upper leaves, four small yellow petals and flattened, roughly oval fruits about 4 mm long. Other clasping mustards need comparison. The upper leaves can make the stem seem to pass through a rounded green shield. Check lower foliage before it withers, because its finely divided form provides a useful contrast. Mature pods are short and broad, unlike the long narrow pods of many mustards; a photograph showing flowers and fruit together is especially helpful.
actions: Include upper and lower leaves, flowers and mature pods in photographs. Consult a local flora or extension service if the plant cannot be distinguished from similar mustards. Note whether the plant occurs as scattered individuals or a dense patch within a crop or pasture. Where removal is warranted, act before mature pods shed and avoid moving seed-bearing material with soil. A regional assessment should separate ordinary disturbed-ground occurrence from an established agricultural problem or a locally regulated weed.

proposedDescription: Claspleaf pennycress is a small annual mustard with pale green foliage, tiny white flowers and flattened seed pods with a noticeable notch at the tip. Upper leaves clasp the stem, while lower leaves form a loose rosette. It occurs in dry, often lime-rich soils and can grow among crops and orchard vegetation. Botanical references may call it Microthlaspi perfoliatum, Thlaspi perfoliatum or Noccaea perfoliata, so matching the plant's features is more useful than relying on one name alone.
identification: Look for a low upright plant, oval to oblong clasping stem leaves, small white flowers and broadly winged, notched pods. Fruit shape helps distinguish it from other small spring mustards. The narrow wings around the flat pod widen toward its notched tip, giving a mature fruit more diagnostic value than the tiny flowers. Compare both sides of several pods and the stem-clasping leaf bases. Other pennycresses differ in pod proportions, so an immature round fruit may be misleading.
actions: Photograph mature pods beside a scale along with the upper leaf bases. Ask a local herbarium or extension specialist to resolve uncertain identification before treating it as a weed of concern. Keep a dated record while waiting for fruit to mature if identification is uncertain. In a planted bed, distinguish a few annual volunteers from a persistent crop-management problem. proposedDescription: Cotton leaf curl Gezira virus is a plant virus associated with leaf-curl disease in cotton and other members of the mallow family, including okra. Affected leaves may curl and develop thickened veins, but those changes are not unique to this virus. Reports from ornamental mallows have added another layer of uncertainty because findings in one host do not establish the same disease behavior in another. Reliable identification depends on a professional plant-health diagnosis.
identification: Curled leaves and thickened veins are warning signs, not a species-level diagnosis. Other viruses, pests and growing conditions can cause similar-looking damage. Include whole-plant views and close photographs of both leaf surfaces, showing whether veins as well as the blade are altered. Record whether the affected plant is cotton, okra or an ornamental mallow. A familiar leaf-curl appearance on one host does not show that an isolate behaves the same way on another.
actions: Document the host plant and visible symptoms and consult an extension plant pathologist or official plant-health service. Let qualified professionals determine whether further diagnostic assessment is appropriate. Keep the plant's source and the dates of new symptoms with the report. Avoid sharing cuttings or relocating suspect nursery plants until the diagnostic service advises on handling. For crop observations, describe whether the pattern is isolated or widespread; do not infer a particular virus solely from nearby whiteflies or a photograph.

proposedDescription: Climbing false buckwheat is an annual vine that threads its way through nearby vegetation with slender, twining stems. Its leaves are triangular to heart-shaped, and the small flowers are much less showy than those of a morning glory. As fruits develop, the surrounding flower parts form pale wings. Native across temperate Eurasia, it also occurs in disturbed North American habitats. It closely resembles native climbing false buckwheats, making mature fruit an important part of a useful record.
identification: Examine alternate, unlobed leaves and mature fruiting flower parts. In this species the latter are commonly about 4.2-6.5 mm long and narrow abruptly near the base; compare carefully with Fallopia scandens. Look for the thin sheath at a stem joint, a useful clue to the knotweed family rather than a morning glory. Measure several mature winged fruiting structures if this can be done without damaging surrounding vegetation. The transition from the broad winged portion to the narrow base matters when separating the native climbing relatives.
actions: Photograph ripe fruiting structures and leaf bases, not just the climbing habit. Seek a botanist's confirmation before removing a vine that could be a native lookalike. Trace the vine through its supporting vegetation gently so photographs do not damage the host plant. Record whether it is flowering or fruiting and revisit if only immature material is available. Where a non-native identification is confirmed and control is warranted, contain mature fruits rather than pulling them through neighboring stems and scattering them.

proposedDescription: Climbing nightshade scrambles through shrubs and fences, especially in moist places. Its purple flowers have petals that curve backward around a bright yellow center, and its berries ripen through several colors before turning glossy red. This perennial vine is native to Eurasia and has become established in North America, where it can spread through underground stems as well as seed. The attractive berries are not edible; all parts of the plant are toxic to people and domestic animals.
identification: Look for clusters of purple, backward-curving petals surrounding a yellow cone, red ripe berries and alternate leaves that may have two small basal lobes. It is also called bittersweet nightshade. Leaves on one plant can vary from unlobed to distinctly lobed at the base, so this difference alone does not indicate two species. Photograph the yellow anther cone and the reflexed purple petals when flowers are available. Berries change color while ripening, making a green-fruited shoot less immediately recognizable than a mature one.
actions: Keep children and pets from eating berries and wear gloves when handling the plant. Ask local extension for identification or management advice, particularly around waterways or mixed native vegetation. If a confirmed unwanted vine is removed, keep the berries and underground stem pieces contained rather than dumping them beside a stream or hedge. Check the original site for regrowth. In a mixed planting, trace stems to their base carefully so that native climbers and the shrubs supporting them are preserved.
researchNotes: Independent Utah State and NC State extension accounts agree on perennial habit, characteristic flowers, underground stems and toxicity. No ingestion or medicinal use is suggested. proposedDescription: Climbing fig can turn a wall into a dense covering of small, heart-shaped leaves. This woody evergreen vine, native to eastern Asia, attaches itself with short roots along its young stems. As it matures, it develops thicker branches with much larger, leathery leaves and may produce pear-shaped figs. That change can make the adult plant look surprisingly different from its familiar juvenile form. Its strong attachment to surfaces also deserves consideration wherever it is planted near buildings.
identification: Young climbing shoots have small heart-shaped leaves and attaching roots; mature projecting branches carry larger oval leaves and sometimes green-to-purple, pear-shaped figs. Compare the close-clinging juvenile mat with any stiff shoots projecting away from the support. Their larger leaves are a normal age-related change, not necessarily a different fig. The adhesive roots distinguish its climbing method from a vine that winds around a support or holds on with tendrils.
actions: Keep established garden vines within their intended space and assess the surface before allowing them to climb a building. Photograph both juvenile and mature shoots when requesting identification. Inspect a managed vine regularly around joints, fixtures and the edge of its support, where vigorous growth can make later maintenance difficult. Plan pruning while access is manageable and seek building or arboricultural advice before pulling old attached stems from a surface. Check discarded trimmings and nearby unmanaged ground for continued growth.

proposedDescription: Clinging jellyfish are small enough to overlook among seagrass and seaweed. Their transparent bells carry a conspicuous orange-brown cross, and sticky pads on the tentacles help them hold onto submerged vegetation. They occur in sheltered coastal waters such as bays, estuaries and ponds, rather than behaving like large jellies drifting conspicuously offshore. Contact can cause a painful sting, with reactions varying between people and populations. A clear photograph taken without touching the animal is the safest useful observation.
identification: Look for a transparent bell a few centimeters across, a colored cross and numerous fine tentacles associated with submerged plants. Small size and similar jellyfish make expert confirmation valuable. The cross and attachment pads identify a clinging-jellyfish type rather than resolving every member of the Gonionemus complex. Genetic studies separate northeastern Pacific G. vertens from some Atlantic and northwestern Pacific lineages historically given that name. A photograph cannot determine lineage or predict the severity of a sting.
actions: Avoid touching or collecting suspected animals. Follow local beach or marine-agency advice and report a sighting with its location and a photograph if one can be taken safely. Note whether the animal was attached to eelgrass, seaweed or another submerged surface and include the date and water body in the report. Observe from a safe position without pulling up vegetation to find more animals. Use current local advisories when planning water activities, since records and sting risk differ among populations.
researchNotes: Independent Rhode Island field confirmation and Swedish marine-agency account agree on appearance, vegetation association and variable sting severity. Historical sightings are not used as a current distribution map; medical treatment instructions are omitted. Fresh review 2026-10-31 retains separate source lineages, exact taxon scope and regional limits. Practical advice concerns observation and prevention rather than unverified eradication efficacy. The 2019 original study was read in full text and distinguishes northeast Pacific G. vertens from putative murbachii/Gonionemus sp. This profile explicitly treats historical use of the catalog name as a complex, not proof every population is introduced or equally toxic. Agency safety advice is retained; taxonomic labels need specialist interpretation.

proposedDescription: Clover dodder makes a fine tangle of yellowish, red or purple threads over other plants, with tiny rounded clusters of flowers along its stems. It draws nourishment directly from its hosts, which include clovers, heather and gorse, rather than supporting itself with ordinary green leaves. Include an undamaged host shoot in the photographs, because the host association helps interpret the plant without replacing floral identification.
actions: Photograph the flowers, threads and host plant. Seek local botanical or agricultural advice before removal, particularly in native heathland or conservation areas. Avoid carrying tangled host cuttings or contaminated seed between planting areas while identification is pending. In forage production, consult an adviser about affected crop material and seed sources. In native heathland, leave the association intact until a botanist assesses it, since a parasitic growth habit does not by itself make a plant non-native.

proposedDescription: The clover weevil, also called clover root curculio, is a small mottled brown beetle associated with clover and alfalfa. Adults nibble small semicircular notches along leaf edges, but the more serious injury happens underground. Pale larvae feed on roots and can leave scars or deep gouges that weaken plants. A thinning patch of forage may therefore reflect damage that is not visible above ground, although disease and poor nutrition can produce similar symptoms.
identification: Adults are about 4 mm long, mottled brown with pale markings and fine raised hairs. Larvae are white grubs with pale brown heads. Leaf notches and root scars are clues, not proof of the species. Several root-feeding weevils can notch forage leaves, so pair an adult specimen or detailed image with the root symptoms. The pale larvae are hidden in soil and are much less distinctive in a casual photograph. Record plant age and whether declining plants occur in patches, including areas with different drainage or crop history.
actions: Have an agricultural adviser assess declining forage and identify any insects found. Record whether damage involves leaf margins, roots or both rather than assuming every weakened patch has the same cause. Use the adviser's sampling instructions rather than digging up many plants at random. Keep field notes on previous forage stands and the timing of visible decline to help separate insect feeding from other root problems. Management should reflect the confirmed species and local crop situation, not the presence of a few adult leaf notches alone.
researchNotes: Independent UC and Utah State accounts describe adult versus larval injury. Geographic differences and limited California impact data are retained by avoiding universal severity or seasonal claims. proposedDescription: Cotton leafroll dwarf virus can be associated with curled or puckered leaves, distorted new growth and changes in the way cotton plants develop. Some affected plants become stunted, while others show elongated shoots with poor boll production. Symptoms vary with the cotton variety, growing conditions and the stage at which disease develops; some infected plants show little obvious change. Similar leaf distortion can result from insects or herbicide injury, so appearance alone cannot establish the diagnosis.
identification: Possible signs include cupped or crinkled young leaves, reddish veins and unusual shoot growth. These signs overlap with other cotton disorders and require professional diagnostic assessment. Compare affected and apparently normal plants of the same variety, including the youngest leaves and the upper canopy. Stunting early in development and elongated, poorly fruiting terminal growth later can look quite different. Record the growth stage and any recent field operations so that herbicide injury and other causes remain part of the assessment.
actions: Document symptoms and their pattern across the field and contact an extension cotton specialist or plant pathologist. Treat visual suspicion as a reason to investigate, not a confirmed virus record. Keep dated photographs and a simple map of affected rows for the diagnostic adviser. Do not assume that every curled leaf has the virus or that symptom severity predicts yield loss. Before changing crop management, obtain a diagnosis and region-specific advice based on the cotton variety, field history and current observations.
researchNotes: Separately authored Mississippi State and Alabama Extension accounts include their own regional observations. The draft avoids transferring severe losses from one region or strain to all infections, and contains no laboratory procedures. Fresh review 2026-10-31 retains separate source lineages, exact taxon scope and regional limits. Practical advice concerns observation and prevention rather than unverified eradication efficacy.

proposedDescription: Begonia cucullata forms a soft mound of fleshy stems and glossy green leaves, with small white or pink flowers held above the foliage. The leaves have a wavy, finely toothed edge, and the seed capsules are unevenly winged. Native to South America, this begonia is grown ornamentally and has escaped cultivation in some warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States. Its many garden relatives and hybrids make a flowering, fruiting specimen more informative than a familiar garden name.
identification: Look for succulent stems, broadly heart-shaped leaves with scalloped or toothed margins, white-to-pink flowers and three-winged capsules. Do not assume every bedding plant sold as wax begonia is this species. Look closely at the uneven leaf base and the fine teeth along the wavy margin, then include a mature winged capsule if present. Fleshy stems and familiar pink flowers alone also fit cultivated begonias. A nursery label may name a hybrid series rather than this botanical species, so retain it as context.
actions: Record whether plants are cultivated or growing independently beyond a garden. Photograph flowers and capsules, and ask a local botanist or extension service to distinguish species from cultivated hybrids. Where escaped seedlings are confirmed, contain them before the tiny seeds disperse and keep uprooted pieces from settling into damp ground again. Check the disturbed margins around a planting as well as the bed itself. Follow local planting advice, especially in warm regions where this species has established beyond cultivation.
researchNotes: UF's species account supports Florida escape context and capsule morphology; NParks independently provides species-level foliage and flower details. Characteristics of the entire wax-begonia hybrid group are not assigned to this taxon. Fresh review 2026-10-31 retains separate source lineages, exact taxon scope and regional limits. Practical advice concerns observation and prevention rather than unverified eradication efficacy.

proposedDescription: Cluster mallow carries small pale flowers close to the stem, tucked into tight groups where the leaf stalks join it. Its broad, rounded leaves usually have shallow lobes and scalloped edges, giving a leafy plant a much larger presence than its flowers suggest. It has a long history of cultivation and also grows in fields, roadsides and disturbed ground. Several mallows look similar, and published records themselves sometimes reflect misidentification, so mature fruit is especially valuable for checking a sighting.
identification: Look for rounded, shallowly five- to seven-lobed leaves and nearly stalkless flower clusters in the leaf axils. The small wheel-like fruit separates into segments whose surface details help distinguish similar mallows. Inspect where several flowers gather at a leaf base and compare their short stalks with those of nearby mallow species. Once petals fall, the ring of fruit segments remains useful. A hand lens can reveal the segment surfaces; photograph several mature fruits rather than relying on a single damaged or unripe one.
actions: Photograph open flowers and mature fruit as well as the whole plant. Request a botanical identification if the fruit characters are unclear; a broad leaf photograph alone is often insufficient. Keep garden provenance with observations near cultivation, since a cultivated mallow and a spontaneous population require different interpretation. If a confirmed unwanted patch is managed, collect fruiting material before moving it through the garden. Revisit uncertain plants for mature fruit instead of removing all similar mallows based on leaf size alone.
researchNotes: Independent Flora of Tropical East Africa and Flora Novae Angliae accounts both emphasize confusion among weedy mallows. Avoids uncertain fruit-edge measurements and does not repeat a potentially flawed regional range as definitive. proposedDescription: Clustered clover is a small annual that spreads low over the ground or lifts its stems slightly above surrounding vegetation. Its pink to purplish flowers gather in tight, rounded heads nestled directly against the stem at the leaf joints. Each leaf has the familiar three leaflets, but the almost stalkless flower heads help distinguish it from more familiar garden and pasture clovers. Native around Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, it has also become naturalized elsewhere.
identification: Look for hairless, prostrate or ascending stems, three small finely toothed leaflets and compact globular flower heads in the leaf axils. Heads are essentially stalkless, unlike those of many other clovers. Trace the flower head to its attachment point: the tight ball sits at a leaf joint rather than at the top of a long stalk. Examine several heads because young clusters can be partly hidden by the leaves. The plant is generally hairless, and the small leaflets broaden toward their tips.
actions: Photograph the attachment of a flower head to the stem and the leaflet edges. Consult a local flora or extension service when several small clovers occur together. Record whether flowering plants occur within a lawn, pasture or unmanaged vegetation and avoid identifying every pink clover by color. If a confirmed patch is unwanted in a bed, prevent mature heads from being scattered with soil. Where clovers form part of existing vegetation, check the local management objective before removing them.
researchNotes: Independent New Zealand and NSW floras agree on annual habit and head placement. Their reported flower lengths differ, so the draft uses shared qualitative characters rather than forcing a single measurement. proposedDescription: Clustered dock is a slender perennial with branching upright stems and small flowers arranged in separated whorls. Many of those clusters have a little leaf beneath them, giving the flowering stem a more leafy appearance than some other docks. It grows in damp places as well as cultivated and pasture ground, and has been introduced well beyond its native Old World range. The modest flowers are easy to overlook, but the mature fruit coverings provide useful identification details.
identification: Check for spaced flower or fruit clusters, leafy bracts beneath many whorls and three small, smooth-edged fruit valves, each with a prominent swollen grain. Mature fruit is needed to separate similar docks. Use a hand lens to inspect several ripe fruits, since the swollen grains on the three inner coverings can be hard to see in young flowers. The lower leaves are stalked and relatively broad compared with the narrow upper foliage. Hybrid docks and immature plants may not fit a simple photograph-based comparison.
actions: Include the lower leaves and close-up mature fruit in a record. Ask a botanist or extension service to check difficult plants, especially where several dock species or hybrids occur. Record the moisture conditions and whether the plant is growing in pasture, cultivation or a wetland margin. If control is locally justified, keep mature fruiting stems contained and avoid disturbing banks unnecessarily. Recheck the perennial base after management, and do not treat every leafy flowering dock as this species without examining fruit.
researchNotes: Independent Flora of NSW and Flora of Iraq accounts support flowering structure, fruit characters and habitat. proposedDescription: Coastal burnweed is an upright, short-lived herb with narrow, regularly toothed leaves and clusters of small cylindrical flower heads. Unlike a showy daisy, its heads lack a ring of spreading ray petals. Botanists now commonly treat this plant as Senecio minimus, while Erechtites minimus remains a name used in older records. It occurs naturally in Australia and New Zealand, including moist forest settings, so its presence there should not automatically be interpreted as an alien invasion.
identification: Look for narrow stem leaves with toothed bases that clasp the stem, small cylindrical heads and no showy ray flowers. Closely related Senecio species can require examination of head bracts and mature fruits. Photograph the toothed lobes where an upper leaf clasps the stem and the green bracts surrounding each flower head. These small structures are more useful than height alone. Plants intermediate with related Senecio occur, so unusual bract numbers or a poor fit to the leaf characters deserve a specialist check.
actions: Photograph leaf bases, flower heads and the whole plant. Confirm the identification and local native status with a herbarium before considering management. Include the surrounding habitat and any recent disturbance in the record. In its native range, an upright colonizing herb in wet forest is not automatically a weed needing removal. For an unexpected population elsewhere, obtain a confirmed identification and regional status assessment before moving flowering or seed-bearing material between sites.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand explicitly links Erechtites minimus to Senecio minimus; independent Flora of NSW supplies morphology and wet-forest context. Database ID retained. proposedDescription: Coastal wattle is a dense shrub or small tree with narrow, leathery leaf-like structures and round golden flower heads. Its most striking feature appears when the pods open: each dark seed is surrounded by a fleshy orange to scarlet loop. Native to coastal Western Australia and South Australia, it has been planted elsewhere for shelter and dune stabilization. Outside its native range it can become invasive; South African conservation assessments identify it as a threat to sensitive coastal plant habitat.
identification: Look for narrow phyllodes with three or four main veins, spherical yellow flower heads and thick pods that twist after opening. The conspicuous red-orange structure around each dark seed is especially useful. The leaf-like phyllodes are flattened stalks, with several strong lengthwise veins visible in good light. Open pods give the clearest view of the bright loop around the seed; yellow flower balls alone fit many wattles. Compare pods and foliage together, especially near plantings containing several Australian Acacia species.
actions: Record pods, seeds and foliage when seeking confirmation. Check local native status and land-management guidance before planting or removing coastal wattles, particularly in dune or conservation areas. Where coastal managers confirm an invasive population, ask for a plan that includes seedlings and follow-up after mature shrubs are removed. Keep pod-bearing branches from being scattered along access tracks. In native Australian coastal habitat, retain the same identification care and avoid treating a conservation threat reported overseas as a universal removal instruction.

proposedDescription: Coatbuttons carries little daisy-like heads on long, wiry stalks above a low tangle of hairy stems and coarsely toothed leaves. A yellow center is bordered by just a few short white, cream or pale yellow rays, giving each head its button-like appearance. The plant is native to tropical America and is now widespread in warm regions elsewhere. It readily occupies bare and disturbed soil, where sprawling stems can form small patches between taller plants.
identification: Look for rough-hairy, toothed leaves, long solitary flower stalks and a small yellow-centered head with only a few short, often three-toothed pale rays. Mature fruits carry feathery bristles. Check the rough hairs and opposite leaves on the lower stems, then look at the few short rays around the central disc. The pale ray tips are often divided into three teeth, unlike the long broad petals of many ornamental daisies. A mature head carries feathery bristles around the small dark fruits.
actions: Photograph the flower head from above and the leafy stems below it. Confirm uncertain plants with a local flora or extension service and note whether the patch is in disturbed ground or natural vegetation. Document whether low stems have rooted where they touch the soil. Where a confirmed patch is unwanted, remove young plants before mature heads disperse and keep rooted pieces out of fresh soil. Around native vegetation, first check local status and the management objective; widespread occurrence does not by itself establish ecological damage.

proposedDescription: Cochineal cactus grows into a branching shrub or small tree, with flattened green pads and slender scarlet flowers. Despite its often nearly spineless appearance, the pads can carry tiny irritating bristles. Native to Mexico, it has been planted widely in warm regions and sometimes grows beyond cultivation. It also has a long history as a host for insects used to produce cochineal dye. Its presence in a garden is different from an established wild population, so records need that context.
identification: Look for elongated, flattened green pads and red flowers with conspicuously projecting stamens. Other prickly pears can look similar; photograph flowers and the whole plant. The flattened pads are stems, with small areoles spaced over their surface. Tiny leaves may appear briefly on new growth, while mature plants can look almost spineless. The narrow red flowers and their projecting reproductive parts are more informative than a detached green pad when comparing other cultivated prickly pears.
actions: Avoid bare-handed handling. If a plant is spreading outside cultivation, photograph it and ask a local plant specialist to confirm its identity before removal. Keep broken pads and pruning waste contained, since a discarded pad can root where it lands. Do not move fragments into dunes, dry scrub or other unmanaged ground. For a large escaped plant, seek a handling and disposal plan that accounts for irritating bristles and follow-up checks for pieces left behind.

proposedDescription: Cockroach berry is a prickly, short-lived member of the nightshade family, with broad leaves, white star-shaped flowers, and round fruits that turn orange-red. It grows in disturbed ground in warm, moist regions, including places outside its native tropical American range. The bright fruit can make it conspicuous along a roadside or neglected patch, but appearance alone is not a safe guide to edibility. Similar prickly nightshades have often been confused with it, making careful identification especially useful.
identification: Check for yellowish prickles, broad sometimes lobed leaves, small clusters of white flowers, and orange-scarlet berries. Detailed fruit and seed features help specialists separate related species. Leaves on the same plant may differ in how deeply they are lobed, and prickles can occur on more than just the main stem. Include both leaf surfaces and the flower-to-fruit transition in a record. An orange fruit alone is insufficient because other nightshades share the color but differ in their reproductive details.
actions: Photograph the leaves, prickles, flowers, and fruit without tasting them. Wear gloves if handling a confirmed plant, and seek local advice before controlling a larger patch. Keep fruiting material contained during any locally approved removal so seeds are not spread along a path or into garden waste. Revisit disturbed soil for seedlings. In a mixed patch, confirm each plant before handling it; broad leaves and scattered prickles do not reliably distinguish every related species at a distance.

proposedDescription: Cockspur coral tree brings clusters of vivid red, pea-shaped flowers to a branching shrub or small tree. Its leaves are divided into three leaflets, and the branches carry prickles. Native to South America, it is grown as an ornamental in warmer regions and has been introduced well beyond its original range.
identification: Look for three-part leaves, prickly branches, and elongated red flowers held in clusters. Photograph leaves and flowers together; several cultivated coral trees share similar features. Each leaf is divided into three substantial leaflets rather than being a single deeply lobed blade. The scarlet flowers are elongated and arranged along a common flowering stalk. It is deciduous, so a bare specimen between growing seasons may be harder to recognize; leaf fall alone does not mean an ornamental tree has died. Close photographs should include branch prickles as well as flowers.
actions: Note whether the tree is planted or growing wild. Ask a local botanist or extension office to identify unexpected seedlings before deciding on management. Keep planting records or nursery labels with the observation, particularly where other coral trees grow nearby. If seedlings appear away from a planted specimen, map their positions and revisit them to see whether they persist. Wear protective gloves around prickly branches and use a qualified arborist for substantial tree work. Local guidance should determine whether a self-established population needs management; ornamental cultivation alone does not establish invasive harm.

proposedDescription: Taro is the plant behind a familiar tropical food crop and many garden elephant ears. Its large, heart- to arrow-shaped leaves rise from a thick underground corm. In warm wetlands, escaped plants can spread into dense patches along streams, ditches, and marshes, shading smaller vegetation. Pieces of the underground plant can help establish new patches when moved. Its value in cultivation and its ability to invade some waterways are both part of the story; the local setting matters.
identification: Photograph that attachment and the whole plant to distinguish similar elephant ears. A view from beneath the blade shows the stalk joining inward from the notch between the basal lobes. This helps distinguish taro from some Xanthosoma sold under the same elephant-ear name. Leaf size and color vary with cultivar and growing conditions, so they should support rather than replace the attachment character.
actions: Keep garden waste out of waterways. Wear gloves during removal and collect underground pieces; consult local wetland managers for established patches. Do not eat raw plant material. For a small confirmed escape, coordinate work with the landowner and avoid letting corm pieces wash downstream. Established wetland stands need a plan that protects neighboring native plants and stabilizes disturbed soil. Check for renewed shoots after work, since cutting away the large leaves alone can leave underground growing points intact.
researchNotes: NC State documents food and ornamental use and raw-plant irritation; UF documents Florida wetland escape and vegetative spread. Cultivation is not treated as proof of harm at every recorded location. Fresh review 2026-10-31 retains separate source lineages, exact taxon scope and regional limits. proposedDescription: Coconut palms are a familiar part of tropical coastlines, with a ringed trunk, long feather-like fronds, and large fibrous fruits. People have carried them widely for food, fiber, and useful materials. They also grow outside cultivation in suitable coastal habitats, where their ecological role depends on the place. Florida's assessment, for example, treats the palm differently across the state and identifies invasive behavior in the south with limited approved uses. A coconut record therefore needs more context than a garden label.
identification: Look for a single ringed trunk, a crown of long divided fronds, and large husked fruits. Young palms may still have the attached germinating nut. Look at the combination of a solitary trunk, arching feather-like leaves and the large fibrous fruit rather than identifying a palm from its silhouette alone. Dwarf and tall cultivated forms vary in stature. Seedlings may show simpler leaves before developing the divided fronds familiar on mature palms.
actions: Before planting near natural shorelines, check local guidance. Record whether a palm is planted or self-established; have a qualified professional handle removal of large palms. Observe fruit clusters and the crown from the ground, without climbing or standing beneath work in progress. For self-established seedlings near natural vegetation, document their number and distance from planted palms for the local land manager. Keep landscaping decisions tied to regional assessment and site conditions, especially where palms border sensitive shore or island habitats.

proposedDescription: Coconut scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that can gather in pale, closely packed patches on leaves. Coconut and banana are familiar hosts, but it also feeds on many other tropical crops and ornamental plants. Heavy infestations yellow and weaken foliage. Young insects, called crawlers, move before settling beneath a protective covering; infested nursery plants can carry them to new places. Predators and tiny parasitic wasps help suppress populations, so visible scales do not automatically mean broad insecticide treatment is needed.
identification: Look beneath leaves for small, flat, translucent covers with yellowish centers and nearby yellowing. Confirmation requires a specialist examining adult females under a microscope. Use magnification to distinguish the individual covers from leaf spotting or a continuous fungal coating. The insect beneath a cover is needed for microscopic confirmation; several tropical armored scales overlap in appearance. Photograph both the colony and the surrounding yellowing, and record the host plant rather than relying on the common name.
actions: Keep suspect plants from being moved or shared. Send clear photographs to extension or a plant clinic, and seek treatment advice that protects beneficial insects. Inspect adjacent leaves and recently acquired stock while awaiting identification. Keep a record of whether colonies are expanding and whether natural enemies are present. A plant clinic can advise how to submit a small affected sample safely; broad treatment based only on pale leaf patches can miss the cause and disrupt useful predators.

proposedDescription: Codling moth is best known for the caterpillar that tunnels into an apple or pear and feeds around the seeds. Adults are small, mottled moths that blend into bark; the damage inside fruit is usually more noticeable than the moth itself. It also attacks walnuts and some other fruit crops. Several generations can develop during a growing season, depending on climate. Successful management combines watching for moth activity with timely fruit protection and removing infested fruit before more insects emerge.
identification: Adults have a coppery patch near each forewing tip. Larvae become pale pink with a brown head; entry holes may have crumbly brown waste around them. Look for an entrance hole with reddish-brown frass and a tunnel toward the seed cavity, while remembering that other caterpillars can damage fruit. The coppery area at the moth's wing tip is more useful than its overall gray-brown color. Photograph a larva with the affected fruit and keep a size reference.
actions: Collect infested and fallen fruit promptly. Ask local extension about monitoring traps, fruit bagging, and seasonal management; timing varies with local weather and orchard conditions. Inspect developing fruit as well as the ground beneath the tree throughout the locally active season. Keep infested fruit contained so larvae cannot finish developing in discarded piles. Monitoring traps help establish timing, but a trap catch is not complete control; ask for a coordinated plan suited to backyard trees or commercial orchard conditions.

proposedDescription: Hairy willow-herb is a tall perennial with fuzzy stems and pink-purple flowers, often growing where the soil stays moist. Introduced from Eurasia, it can form dense patches along wetlands, ditches, and stream edges in North America. Underground stems help a patch expand, while silky-haired seeds travel on the wind. Its flowers can be attractive, but a crowded stand can leave less room for other wetland plants. Native willow-herbs and fireweeds make careful identification worthwhile before any removal.
identification: Look for hairy stems, opposite toothed leaves, four notched pink petals, and a pale four-part stigma. Photograph the flowers and leaf arrangement to separate lookalikes. The pale stigma divides into four lobes above the flower, and the long seed capsule later opens to release silky seeds. Include the stem leaf arrangement in photographs: native fireweed usually has alternate leaves and a terminal flower cluster. A hairy pink-flowered plant should still be compared with regional willow-herb species.
actions: For a confirmed small patch, seek permission and local advice before digging, remove underground growth, and prevent seed release. Avoid disturbing sensitive wetland vegetation. Work before capsules open where practical, and keep fruiting tops contained if mature seed is already present. Mark the treated area and inspect for shoots from remaining underground stems. Along a stream or wetland, coordinate with the responsible manager so follow-up does not damage native plants or leave an eroding bank.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR supplies identification and control; Native Plant Trust independently describes regional ecology and morphology. proposedDescription: Cogongrass is a spreading perennial grass that can turn varied vegetation into dense stands. Its extensive underground stems help it survive disturbance and move outward, while fluffy seeds and contaminated soil or equipment carry it farther. In the southeastern United States, it invades roadsides, pastures, and natural areas. The buildup of dry grass also increases fire danger and can change how habitats burn. Because a patch can regrow from underground pieces, controlling it usually takes a coordinated effort and repeated follow-up.
identification: Look for upright blades with a pale midrib noticeably off center and silvery, fluffy seed heads. Other grasses resemble it; have a specialist confirm suspected patches. Examine several blades, because the off-center midrib is variable and not enough by itself. The leaves arise from a spreading underground network rather than a single obvious bunch. Johnsongrass, pampas grass and silver beardgrass can cause confusion from a distance; photographs of leaf bases and flowering heads help an identifier assess the combination.
actions: Avoid mowing seed heads or moving soil from the patch. Clean equipment and contact local extension or land managers. Burning alone is not a solution. Mark the suspected boundary and arrange work so vehicles and mowing equipment do not carry material into clean areas. Have a land manager plan treatment and repeated monitoring beyond the first visible dieback. Avoid digging up rhizomes for casual comparison or attempting a burn; fragments and disturbance can complicate containment of the patch.
researchNotes: UF and Mississippi State support identification, rhizome spread, fire effects and persistent management. proposedDescription: Colocynth, sometimes called bitter apple, is a trailing relative of watermelon adapted to dry landscapes. Its rough, deeply divided leaves and small yellow flowers spread close to the ground, followed by round fruits that change from mottled green to yellow. Unlike a sweet watermelon, the fruit has intensely bitter flesh. The plant is native across parts of Africa and Asia and adjacent regions. Its desert ecology is well documented, but a record outside that range does not alone establish local invasive damage.
identification: Look for a sprawling vine with deeply lobed leaves, tendrils, yellow flowers, and small round yellowing melons. Do not use tasting as an identification test. Mature fruit is smooth and roughly spherical, with the mottled pattern fading as it becomes yellow. The rough leaf blade is divided deeply into further lobed sections. Other wild melons share these broad features, so record tendrils, flower shape and fruit size together rather than naming the plant from one detached melon.
actions: Photograph leaves, flowers, and fruit, and ask a botanist to confirm unexpected plants. Keep unidentified melons out of food and avoid spreading their seeds. Keep the record tied to its dry-ground habitat and any planting history. If a plant appears outside its expected range, provide photographs and location to a herbarium before disturbing it. Where removal is locally warranted, contain ripe fruit and avoid mixing seeds with compost, feed or planting material intended for another site.

proposedDescription: Colombian waxweed is a small, branching herb with rough, hairy leaves and tiny purple to pink flowers. It can be easy to overlook among grasses in a damp, disturbed patch. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has become established in other warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States and Hawaii. The flower's narrow tube and the plant's sticky hairs help distinguish it from superficially similar weeds. Its introduced presence alone does not tell us how strongly it affects a particular habitat.
identification: Look for a low, branching, hairy plant with small oval leaves and tiny purple flowers emerging from narrow tubes. A close photograph is more useful than a distant patch view. Use a close side view to show the tubular base of the flower and the small petals projecting from it. The leaves occur in opposite pairs, and fine sticky hairs can be difficult to see without magnification. Other small Cuphea may be cultivated nearby, making flowers and fruiting tubes useful alongside the whole-plant habit.
actions: Have unfamiliar plants identified before removal. Where management is warranted, address small patches before seed develops and avoid moving seed-bearing material into nearby natural areas. Record whether the plant is a single volunteer or a persistent patch in damp disturbed ground. Contain flowering stems during any approved removal and revisit the original area for seedlings. A local botanist can help distinguish an ornamental escape from this species before a larger management effort is planned around the common name.

proposedDescription: Colonial bentgrass, also called Rhode Island bentgrass, is a fine-leaved perennial introduced from Europe and nearby regions. Its airy flower clusters can give an unmown patch a soft haze. It has long been used in lawns, but also grows in fields, roadsides, and other open ground beyond cultivation. In some regions it becomes an invasive grass rather than staying a lawn plant. Separating it from related bentgrasses takes a closer look at the flowering branches and the small membranous flap where a leaf blade meets its sheath.
identification: Look for narrow leaves and a loose, branching flower cluster. The short membranous flap (ligule) at the blade-sheath junction helps distinguish it from creeping bentgrass and redtop. Spread a mature flowering branch gently for a photograph and include a close view of the ligule at the base of a leaf blade. A mown turf patch lacks many of these useful features. Related bentgrasses differ in ligule proportions and flowering structure, so a loose airy seed head alone is not conclusive.
actions: Keep lawn seed and soil from spreading into nearby natural grasslands. Ask a grass specialist to confirm suspect wild patches before choosing a restoration approach. Record whether the patch connects to a sown lawn or occupies an older grassland. Keep seed mixtures, mowing debris and moved soil from reaching nearby restoration areas. If a wild patch needs management, use a confirmed identification and a restoration plan that protects other fine-leaved grasses growing through it.
