proposedDescription: This colonial sea squirt forms thin living sheets over surfaces such as dock structures, ropes, rocks, and shellfish. Each sheet contains many tiny animals that filter food from the water. Colonies often look pale or marbled, but their appearance changes with conditions. It has spread through warm-water ports and can overgrow other organisms, creating concerns for aquaculture and some natural habitats. Its original home remains uncertain in parts of the scientific literature, even though introductions are documented in several regions.
identification: A thin, pale encrusting colony may be a clue, but color cannot confirm the species. Specialists examine microscopic structures and sometimes use genetic evidence. Colony thickness, color and outline change with season and condition; pale sheets can be discontinuous or form hanging growth on floating structures. Native and other introduced colonial tunicates may look similar. Record the surface occupied and photograph the edge and close texture, leaving species confirmation to microscopic or molecular examination.
actions: Photograph suspect growth and report it to local marine biosecurity staff. Follow approved hull and gear cleaning practices; avoid scraping live fouling into the water. Keep the precise site, date and recent vessel or equipment movement history with a report. Ask the marina or biosecurity service about an approved cleaning site before moving fouled gear. Contain removed material using their procedures rather than rinsing it back into the harbor, and arrange follow-up inspection where growth returns.
researchNotes: Smithsonian treats much of the range as cryptogenic; NIMPIS labels Caribbean origin. proposedDescription: Symplegma reptans is a colonial sea squirt that spreads as a low covering of many small animals joined within a shared outer layer. Native to the Indo-West Pacific, it has established in Southern California harbors, where it grows on docks, hulls, and other submerged surfaces. Colonies expand by producing new individuals through budding. At some sites they can cover large areas and potentially compete for space with other attached organisms. Its resemblance to related sea squirts has complicated identification and some early records.
identification: Look for flattened individuals visible within a thin, nearly transparent colony. Species-level identification requires a tunicate specialist; photographs alone may not separate related Symplegma. Coloration and overall patch size do not reliably separate related Symplegma, even when a colony is large and conspicuous on a dock. A specialist may need internal anatomical characters to check a colony. Record its appearance on the original substrate, including whether it grows among other fouling organisms or forms an almost continuous covering.
actions: Record the location and photograph the colony. Ask local marine specialists about identification and follow marina guidance for cleaning fouled equipment without releasing living material. Retain the date and berth or shoreline location for comparison with later observations. Avoid moving ropes, panels or other colonized items to another water body while a suspected record is assessed. Let marine staff specify specimen handling and cleaning arrangements; scraping a colony into the water does not provide a useful containment measure.

proposedDescription: Coltsfoot sends up yellow, dandelion-like flower heads before its broad leaves unfold. Later, the leaves form a low cover, with a pale, woolly underside that helps distinguish them from dandelions. Native across parts of Eurasia and North Africa, this perennial grows in moist disturbed ground and can spread into nearby habitats. Underground stems allow it to form persistent patches, while its fluffy seeds provide another route of dispersal. Removing only the visible leaves often leaves the living network below intact.
identification: Look for early yellow flowers on short, scaly or woolly stalks, followed by broad heart-shaped leaves with white-felted undersides. Dandelion leaves are differently shaped. The flowering stalk bears small scales rather than a rosette of deeply toothed dandelion leaves. Broad leaves expand later, so photographs from two visits may be needed to connect flowers and foliage at the same site. The white-felted underside helps, but butterburs and other broad-leaved plants still warrant comparison outside the flowering season.
actions: Where control is locally warranted, remove underground growth from confirmed small patches before seed spreads and monitor regrowth. Ask local land managers about established patches, particularly near wetlands. Mark the area while the early flowers are visible, then check for later leafy shoots beyond the original boundary. Where local advice supports removal, contain seed heads and underground fragments and plan repeat visits. In its native range or a sensitive habitat, establish the management need before disturbing the soil or neighboring plants.

proposedDescription: Comb bushmint is a branching, aromatic herb whose tiny pale flowers line curved clusters like the teeth of a comb. It can grow tall enough to look like a small shrub, with toothed, hairy leaves and angular stems. Native to tropical America, it now occurs in other warm regions, often around disturbed ground, thickets, and moist edges. Although it appears in weed records, Florida's assessment does not document it as a problem species there. Its local behavior deserves attention without assuming severe impacts everywhere.
identification: Look for toothed, hairy leaves and branching clusters of small whitish to pale mauve flowers arranged along one side. Confirm against other bushmints. Include the full branched flower cluster and a close side view of its one-sided rows. The opposite leaves and angular stems suggest the mint family but do not identify this species alone. Several bushmints have similar aromatic foliage, so flower arrangement provides a more useful comparison than a scent description.
actions: Photograph flowering branches and the whole plant. If it is spreading into a managed habitat, seek identification and local guidance before deciding whether control is needed. Note whether plants are scattered along disturbed ground or increasing within a particular planting or habitat. Where management is justified, contain mature flower clusters and check for subsequent seedlings. Keep the regional context with the record: a weed listing elsewhere and an assessment without documented Florida problems describe different evidence, not interchangeable outcomes.

proposedDescription: Rangoon creeper is a woody climber best known for fragrant flowers that change from white through pink to red as they age. Hooks formed from leaf stalks help it climb over supports, and its broad leaves grow in opposite pairs. Its native range includes Tanzania and tropical and subtropical Asia through northern Australia. Widely cultivated in tropical gardens, it has also been introduced elsewhere. The mix of flower colors on a single vine makes it especially distinctive when in bloom.
identification: Look for opposite oval leaves, hooked climbing structures, and clusters containing differently aged white, pink, and red flowers. Quisqualis indica is an older name. Compare young and older flowers in the same cluster, since their changing color is a normal feature of the vine. Photograph the long flower tube as well as the five spreading lobes and the opposite leaves. The hooked leaf stalks help distinguish its climbing habit from tendril-bearing garden vines.
actions: Record whether the vine is cultivated or spreading outside a garden. Contain prunings and ask local extension about management of confirmed escapes. Trace stems back to the planted base before removing growth from neighboring shrubs. Keep cut branches within appropriate garden-waste disposal and inspect the boundary of the planting over time. If shoots appear in unmanaged vegetation, document them for local assessment; vigorous growth on a maintained trellis alone does not demonstrate invasion.

proposedDescription: Common asparagus-fern looks soft and fern-like, but it is a flowering climber rather than a true fern. Its fine green sprays are familiar in houseplants and floral arrangements. Outside cultivation in warm regions, thorny shoots can climb through other vegetation, and birds carry seeds from its dark berries. Persistent underground growth makes established plants difficult to remove completely. Native to eastern and southern Africa, it has escaped cultivation elsewhere; Florida guidance recommends preventing escape and managing existing plants carefully.
identification: Look for fine, feathery sprays on wiry climbing stems, small flowers, and berries that ripen dark. Check for thorns and distinguish it from other ornamental asparagus species. The fine green branchlets form flattened, feathery sprays rather than the true fronds of a fern. Look for wiry climbing shoots and dark mature berries when distinguishing it from bushier ornamental asparagus. Juvenile potted plants may conceal the thorny, climbing growth that becomes obvious when an established plant reaches surrounding vegetation.
actions: Wear gloves, prevent berries from scattering, and remove the crown and underground growth where appropriate. Recheck for regrowth and keep discarded plants out of natural areas. Trace shoots to the crown before tackling a tangled patch so neighboring plants are not pulled out with it. Contain any berry-bearing stems and keep root pieces from being dumped where they can persist. After appropriate removal, inspect both the original crown position and nearby bird-perching sites for regrowth or new seedlings.

proposedDescription: Lemon balm is a perennial herb with wrinkled, toothed leaves that release a lemon scent when bruised. A member of the mint family, it produces small pale flowers visited by pollinators and has long been grown for kitchen and garden use. Native from the Mediterranean toward Central Asia, it has become established well beyond that range. Plants can spread and self-seed around gardens, so keeping an eye on seedlings is useful. Its familiar usefulness and occasional weedy behavior are both worth recognizing.
identification: Look for opposite, wrinkled oval leaves, square stems, and small pale two-lipped flowers. Scent can support identification but should not replace checking the plant's features. Check the paired leaves, puckered surface and scalloped teeth together with the small flowers clustered near the leaf joints. Other mints can have citrus scents, while cultivated leaf colors vary. Photograph an entire flowering shoot for comparison and avoid identifying an unfamiliar wild herb solely by rubbing or smelling a single leaf.
actions: Remove unwanted seedlings and trim flowers before seed forms if spread is a concern. Keep garden waste contained and confirm identification before using any wild herb. Inspect nearby bare soil for seedlings as well as the edge of the original clump. A container can help keep a garden planting manageable, but spent flowers still need attention where self-seeding is unwanted. Retain useful pollinator planting where appropriate while preventing spread into places where the gardener or land manager does not want it.

proposedDescription: Common bamboo forms large clumps of tall, jointed canes topped by leafy branches. Native to parts of Asia and widely planted in warm regions, it supplies material for buildings, tools, and crafts as well as garden screens. It is a clumping bamboo, so its growth differs from the long-running bamboos familiar in some gardens. That distinction matters when evaluating a sighting or planning management. Florida's completed assessment for its southern region does not document an invasive problem there; other regions need their own assessment.
identification: Look for a dense clump of substantial jointed canes and narrow, pointed leaves. Include the branch arrangement at a cane joint and any remaining sheath around a young cane in photographs. A yellow cane is not diagnostic: several unrelated cultivated bamboos share that color. The clustered growth form is useful, but a specialist may need sheath and branching characters to separate similar clumping species.
actions: Record whether the clump is planted and whether it is expanding beyond its intended area. Seek experienced help with large canes, and contain discarded rhizome pieces. Measure changes at the clump edge over time rather than judging expansion from one tall new shoot. Plan pruning or removal with safe access for the substantial canes and retain planting records for identification. If rhizome pieces are excavated, keep them contained and monitor the site for continued shoots before declaring management complete.

proposedDescription: Common Barberry is a deciduous shrub with branched spines, hanging yellow flower clusters, and red berries that can remain into winter. It grows in woodland, pasture, hedgerows, and disturbed ground, tolerating both sun and shade. Dense stands can crowd other vegetation, while birds carry its seeds to new sites. The shrub also serves as an alternate host for black stem rust, a disease of cereal crops. Its persistence comes from both long-lived seed and underground stems that send up shoots, so removing the visible branches alone rarely settles an established infestation.
identification: Look for a many-stemmed shrub roughly 8–10 feet tall, sometimes taller, with gray bark and two- or three-branched spines. Small oval leaves grow in clusters and have conspicuous sharp teeth. Spring flowers hang in elongated yellow clusters; the later fruits are oblong and red, with one to three seeds. Japanese barberry is a frequent confusion, but Common Barberry has toothed leaf margins and typically three-pronged spines. Hybrid plants can combine characters, so one spine or a distant photograph may be misleading. Photograph a complete branch, a leaf edge in focus, several spine junctions, and flowers or fruit. Include overall height and the date.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and eye protection when working among the spines. Prioritize isolated young shrubs and fruiting plants near fields or uninvaded habitat. Dig manageable plants carefully, keeping the root crown and attached underground stems together as far as possible; chopped fragments can produce new growth. Contain berry-bearing branches before carrying them away, and avoid shifting infested soil. Larger shrubs need a planned root-focused treatment and repeat inspections rather than a single cut. Ask local Extension or a weed specialist about suitable methods and reporting expectations in your area. Check the cleared ground for seedlings and returning shoots over subsequent growing seasons.

proposedDescription: Common barley is the cultivated cereal familiar from grain fields, brewing, and livestock feed. This cool-season annual sometimes appears along roadsides or in disturbed ground after seed escapes cultivation. Such plants should not automatically be described as a damaging invasion: the USDA guide describes volunteers as generally not persistent. The compact seed head often carries long bristles, although some cultivated forms lack them. Two-row and six-row barley differ in how many spikelets develop grain, a useful reminder that variation within this crop can change its appearance without indicating another species.
identification: Plants generally stand 2–4 feet tall, with hollow, jointed stems and flat leaves. At the point where a leaf blade meets its sheath, look for two overlapping, ear-like projections clasping the stem. The unbranched seed head has groups of three spikelets; long bristles may extend from them. In two-row forms only the middle spikelet produces grain, while all three are fertile in six-row forms. Wheat and cereal rye have single spikelets at each attachment point, rather than barley's groups. Photograph the leaf collar, an entire mature head, and a close side view of its attachments. Young plants without heads can be difficult to separate from other cereals.
actions: First establish whether the plants are a planted crop, a cover crop, or unwanted volunteers. Avoid removing a farmer's planting without checking its intended purpose. For a few escaped plants on your own ground, pull them before grain matures and collect any developed heads so seed is not scattered. Check nearby spilled feed, seed-storage areas, or recently disturbed soil for the source. In a production field, discuss volunteer management with the grower or Extension because timing depends on the crop rotation. Record repeated establishment outside cultivation if it appears to persist; isolated seedlings after a grain spill are a different situation from an expanding naturalized stand.

proposedDescription: Common bird's-foot is a small annual legume also called French serradella. Its softly hairy stems spread along the ground or rise above it, carrying leaves divided into many small leaflets. Small pink or whitish pea flowers develop into slender, jointed pods. Each pod segment holds a seed, giving mature fruits a beaded appearance. It is native to southwestern Europe and has been introduced elsewhere. The mature pods provide a useful way to recognize an unfamiliar patch after the flowers fade. A nearby planting or seed mixture may help explain an occurrence, but the plant itself still needs identification.
identification: Look for a branched, hairy annual up to about 50 centimeters high, often much lower because stems spread outward. Leaves have numerous paired, narrow oval leaflets and a terminal leaflet. Small groups of pink to white flowers sit above a conspicuously leafy bract divided into leaflets. Flowers are approximately 7 millimeters long. The flattened pods are about 12–30 millimeters long, slightly curved or straight, with constrictions separating three to seven seed-bearing segments. These fruits are more useful than a general photograph of the foliage. Photograph a whole leaf, the leafy bract below a flower group, and mature pods beside a scale. Identification among other Ornithopus species should use a regional botanical key.
actions: For an unexpected patch, record its location, approximate extent, and whether the ground was recently sown. Keep a photograph of mature pods for identification before deciding on removal. Where the plant is unwanted, lift small annual plants before pods harden and seeds separate. Collect fruiting material rather than dragging it through neighboring vegetation. Check seed mixtures or transferred soil if new plants repeatedly appear in the same place. Avoid distributing saved seed from an unidentified patch. For occurrences in conservation land, ask the land manager or a herbarium to confirm the species and determine whether management is warranted; management should reflect the habitat and observed spread rather than an assumption based on its presence alone.

proposedDescription: Common borage is an annual garden herb with bristly leaves and bright blue, star-shaped flowers. Native to the Mediterranean region, it is grown in herb and flower gardens and attracts bees. Plants often return through self-sown seed, rather than surviving as the same individual from year to year. Escapes beside a garden may therefore reflect ongoing seed production. The dark central cone of each nodding flower is especially distinctive against the blue petals. Flowers open in sequence as the curled clusters unfold, extending the display through summer. A persistent garden escape deserves attention without assuming that every volunteer damages surrounding habitat.
identification: Common borage grows roughly 1½–3 feet tall and has coarse gray-green leaves and stems covered with stiff hairs. Leaves alternate along the stem; lower leaves have stalks, while upper leaves become smaller and attach directly to the stem. Flowers are open stars about three-quarters of an inch across, with five pointed blue lobes and a prominent dark central cone formed by the anthers. Photograph a flower face and side view, the hairy stem, and a complete lower leaf. Other borage-family plants also have blue blooms, so color alone is insufficient. A hairy rosette without flowers should remain provisional until the leaf arrangement and eventual flower structure can be checked.
actions: Where seedlings are unwanted, remove them while small and before they produce another generation of seed. Wear gloves if the stiff hairs irritate your skin. Inspect the ground around the original planting and any place where garden debris was deposited, rather than treating a single seedling as the entire source. If retaining a garden plant, remove spent flowering stems before seed dispersal and check for volunteers beyond the bed. Do not move seed-bearing waste into natural areas. Ask local Extension about an expanding escape in sensitive habitat. Keep removal material separate from food crops and do not infer safe consumption from a visual identification; some botanical accounts flag potentially harmful plant compounds.

claims: Mediterranean annual with bristly gray-green leaves and blue star-shaped flowers.
Self-seeds and attracts bees; account includes toxicity cautions.
Annual commonly two to three feet tall with coarse hairy foliage and star-shaped blue flowers.
Readily self-seeds and attracts pollinators.
Alternate leaves become smaller and stalkless upward; flower has five pointed blue lobes.
Taprooted annual occurs in disturbed soil; flowers are about two centimetres across.
Five anthers form the dark central cone; flowers open progressively along curled clusters.
Plant contains small amounts of hepatotoxic pyrrolizidine alkaloids.

proposedDescription: Common brassbuttons is a low wetland plant named for its small yellow flower heads, which resemble buttons without surrounding petals. Fleshy stems can creep and root where they touch the ground. It occurs along streams and in both fresh and salty marshes, so a coastal location is helpful context but not a requirement. Introduced populations are widespread, though the Smithsonian account does not describe it as a highly aggressive invader. Local abundance and the plants growing alongside it matter when judging an occurrence. Its wetland setting also makes careless trampling or soil disturbance a concern during investigation.
identification: Plants commonly stand or spread about 5–25 centimeters, sometimes taller. Smooth, somewhat fleshy stems may lie flat and root at the joints. Leaves sit directly on the stem, with their bases forming a sheath; individual blades may be narrow and entire or irregularly toothed and lobed. Yellow flower heads are usually about 6–12 millimeters across and have no petal-like rays. Photograph the leaf bases around the stem, one entire leaf, a flower head from above and below, and the surrounding wetland. These details are more informative than yellow color alone. Other small wetland daisies require comparison, and a detached flower without leaves is unlikely to support a reliable determination.
actions: Photograph the patch from firm ground and note whether it is in freshwater, brackish water, or a tidal area. Ask the land manager to confirm identification and local priorities before disturbing a marsh or protected shoreline. For a small confirmed patch where removal is permitted, lift connected stems carefully and collect loose pieces, because rooted joints can maintain the plant. Keep seed-bearing or rooted material out of drains and waterways, and clean mud and plant fragments from footwear and tools. Revisit the marked location to check for surviving stems or seedlings. Larger wetland infestations need a site-specific approach that protects neighboring vegetation and avoids unnecessary sediment disturbance.

proposedDescription: Common brighteyes is a Mediterranean daisy-family herb with yellow flower heads and somewhat fleshy, often lobed leaves. The useful clue is beneath the flower: small bracts have a distinctive broad shape and pale, thin margins. It occurs in disturbed places such as field edges and roadsides in its native region. A familiar-looking yellow flower is not enough to identify an introduced occurrence, because many unrelated daisies look similar from above. Descriptions of related annual and perennial forms require care, especially when matching a plant found far from the area covered by a particular flora.
identification: Look closely at the green bracts wrapping each flower head and continuing down its stalk. They resemble small inverted hearts, with thin, translucent margins. Leaves can be somewhat fleshy and blue-green, with variable lobing or teeth. The typical Mediterranean form is described as perennial with a thick persistent stem base, but annual relatives or infraspecific treatments complicate comparison. Do not use the life cycle alone to assign an unfamiliar specimen. Photograph the whole plant, basal and upper leaves, the side of a flower head, and mature fruits. A regional herbarium should check an unexpected record rather than relying on a flower-only match.
actions: Document a suspected escape before removing it: record the location, patch size, and nearby plantings or disturbed soil. If identification is confirmed and the plant is unwanted, remove a small plant with its persistent base, while collecting developed flower heads and seed-bearing material. Watch the same site for renewed growth rather than assuming that cutting the stalk removes the plant. Avoid sharing seed or putting reproductive waste in natural vegetation. For a new regional occurrence, submit clear photographs to a herbarium or local botanical recording program. There is insufficient species-specific control evidence here to recommend a broad treatment or to claim that every introduced population is harmful.

Yellow flower heads, heart-shaped bracts and seed heads; conflicting life-cycle tag not adopted
Accepted Mediterranean perennial and introduced regions

proposedDescription: Common Buckthorn is a large shrub or small tree that can form a dense understory in woodland and along forest edges. It opens its leaves early and retains them late, extending the period when it shades plants beneath it. Female plants produce dark fruits eaten by birds, which carry the seeds elsewhere. Introduced as an ornamental and hedging plant, it has become a significant woodland invader in parts of North America. It also provides an overwintering host for soybean aphids. Removing a mature patch is a continuing project because cut stems can resprout and new seedlings can appear.
identification: Look for a shrub or small tree reaching roughly 20–30 feet, often with several stems. Oval leaves have fine teeth and several prominent veins curving toward the tip. Their placement is often opposite or nearly opposite, but vigorous shoots may show alternate leaves. Short, sharp points occur at the ends of many twigs. Small greenish flowers precede clustered black fruits on female plants. Native cherries and plums can resemble young buckthorn in bark appearance, so inspect leaves and twig tips rather than bark alone. Photograph leaf veins, attachment positions, terminal buds or spines, and fruit if present. Late-season green leaves are a useful search clue, not a diagnosis by themselves.
actions: Start with an inventory of fruiting shrubs and the least invaded areas. Removing berry-producing plants first limits further seed input. Small seedlings can be pulled from suitable soil; use a shrub-pulling tool for larger manageable stems, minimizing disturbance around desirable plants. A single cut of a mature stem commonly leads to resprouting, so arrange an appropriate stump treatment or a sustained follow-up plan with a local specialist. Work in sections if the infestation is extensive, then restore ground cover suited to the site. Walk the area each year for seedlings and sprouts, particularly in early spring or fall when buckthorn foliage is easier to notice.

proposedDescription: Common Burdock begins as a cluster of large, heart-shaped leaves, then sends up a branching flowering stalk. Its purple flower heads develop into the familiar hooked burs that cling to fur and clothing. This is an effective way for seeds to travel beyond the original patch. The plant commonly occurs in pasture, fence lines, and other disturbed ground, where its broad leaves can shade neighboring plants. A deep taproot supports its growth. Finding young rosettes before burs develop makes management easier and helps prevent painful tangles in animals' coats.
identification: First-year leaves can be 6–18 inches long, with wavy or coarsely toothed edges and pale, hairy undersides. The lower leaf stalks are hollow. In the flowering stage, the ridged, branching stems commonly reach about 5 feet. Purple to lavender flower heads are surrounded by narrow bracts ending in hooks; these remain as brown burs after flowering. Thistles may have similar purple flowers, but their surrounding bracts do not make the same hooked attachment mechanism. Greater burdock can be separated in part by its solid lower leaf stalks. Photograph a basal leaf on both sides, the leaf stalk, a flowering head, and a mature bur without pressing it into clothing.
actions: Remove small rosettes before the flowering stalk develops. Dig out the crown or sever the deep taproot below the crown using a suitable tool; pulling leaves alone leaves the growing point behind. Repeated cutting before flowering can prevent seed production, but inspect for replacement stems. Carefully collect any formed burs and keep them out of animal bedding, hay, and garden waste intended for spreading. Check clothing, pets, and tools after working in a patch. Re-establish suitable competing vegetation on disturbed ground and revisit during the following growing season. If burs are lodged in an animal's eye or sensitive tissue, arrange appropriate animal care rather than pulling them forcibly.

proposedDescription: Common Carp is a large, deep-bodied fish introduced to North America from Eurasia. It often feeds in shallow water, sucking material from the bottom and sorting out food. Where populations are abundant, this activity can uproot aquatic plants and stir sediment, reducing water clarity and changing habitat for other fish and waterfowl. It lives in lakes, rivers, ponds, and wetlands. Cultivated forms vary in color and scale coverage. Ornamental koi may belong to the related Amur carp rather than this species, so color alone cannot settle an identification. An unfamiliar capture should be identified carefully before any management decision.
identification: Look for a stout body, a long dorsal fin, and two pairs of short, whisker-like barbels around the upper jaw. Typical fish are bronze, olive, or brown with large scales, but color and scale coverage vary. Adults are often 12–25 inches long and may grow much larger. Native buffalo fishes and suckers lack carp's mouth barbels; grass carp also lack them and have a shorter dorsal fin. Photograph the fish's whole side and the mouth area, with the dorsal fin visible where possible, and record its measured length and waterbody. Juveniles or unusual cultivated forms may require expert review. Do not identify or remove a native lookalike solely from body color.
actions: Never release aquarium, pond, or bait fish into a new waterbody. Dispose of unwanted bait appropriately rather than emptying it into the lake or stream. If you find Common Carp in a waterbody where it is unexpected, record the exact location, date, photographs, and approximate number, and contact the fisheries agency. Follow local fishing and possession rules for any fish already caught; release and harvest requirements differ by jurisdiction. Do not attempt to drain, poison, or net an entire waterbody yourself. Effective population management depends on the connected waters, spawning habitat, and other fish present, and should be planned with the responsible landowner and fisheries professionals.

proposedDescription: Common catchfly is a small annual of fields, roadsides, and other disturbed ground. Its narrow flowering stems carry white, pink, or occasionally red-marked flowers above opposite leaves. The plant is introduced from Europe and has been recorded in scattered parts of North America. Short sticky hairs and longer ordinary hairs occur together around the flowers, a useful clue that is easy to miss in a distant photograph. Records of introduction do not by themselves demonstrate substantial ecological damage; the practical concern at a garden or restoration site is whether an unwanted patch is producing seed and expanding.
identification: Plants commonly stand about 15–45 centimeters tall and grow from a taproot. Lower leaves are broader toward the tip, while upper leaves become smaller and narrower. Leaves occur in pairs. The flower's green outer tube is about 7–10 millimeters long and has ten visible veins, short glandular hairs, and longer hairs without glands. Five petals may be white, pink, red, or spotted; their tips are entire or shallowly notched. Silene pendula has a longer fruiting flower tube, only short glandular hairs there, and more deeply divided petals. Photograph the flower tube and hairs closely, plus a whole stem and mature capsule. Petal color alone is unreliable.
actions: Check a suspected patch while flowers and capsules are present so identification can be documented. Where removal is appropriate, pull these annual plants before capsules open and contain any seed-bearing stems. Revisit disturbed ground for later seedlings, especially if soil has recently been moved or reseeded. Keep garden debris and contaminated soil from spreading into adjacent habitat. If the plants occur on conservation land, confirm identification with the manager before removing a small native pink-family plant by mistake. For persistent or extensive occurrences, ask Extension about a plan suited to the site; removal timing and follow-up should account for both newly germinating plants and mature seed already present in the soil.

Petals may be white, pink, red or spotted and entire or shallowly notched.

proposedDescription: Common Chickweed is a low annual that often makes bright green mats in gardens, lawns, and other moist ground. It grows particularly well during cool, wet weather and can complete a generation quickly. Its tiny white flowers appear to have ten petals, but each of the five petals is deeply divided. Seeds allow repeated flushes of growth during favorable weather, so a patch can return after a quick weeding. Young plants may flower while still quite small. In vegetable beds it competes for space, nutrients, and light.
identification: Look for smooth, pointed, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along soft stems. A single band of hairs along the stem is a useful close-up feature. Plants may remain only about 2 inches high in turf, becoming 4–6 inches high and more open in a garden or shade. The tiny white flowers have five deeply split petals. Mouse-ear chickweed and sticky chickweed have much hairier leaves and stems; the former is perennial, while sticky chickweed is annual. Photograph a stem section close enough to show its hair line, a pair of leaves, and an open flower. A mat seen from standing height can conceal several different weed species.
actions: Remove seedlings promptly, ideally before flowers appear, because plants can begin producing seed within weeks. In a small bed, shallow weeding works best while plants are young and the surface is relatively dry. Collect flowering or fruiting material instead of leaving it scattered across the bed. Where appropriate, replenish mulch and close gaps in desired ground cover. Review unnecessary irrigation if the same wet corner repeatedly fills with chickweed. Inspect during the cool growing season for another flush, rather than waiting for a dense mat. Mature patches with capsules need careful collection to avoid spreading seeds into freshly cleared soil.

UC describes rooting at nodes whereas Maryland's newer comparison says it does not; the public draft omits this disputed trait. claims: Single stem hair band, paired smooth leaves, deeply divided white petals.
Early weeding and removal of debris prevent seed and rerooting.
Winter annual can have multiple generations in cool wet conditions.

proposedDescription: Common comfrey is a perennial garden escape with broad leaves and hanging tubular flowers. It can persist around old homes, ditches, and damp disturbed ground long after a planting is abandoned. Pieces of its substantial root system can produce new plants, making soil movement and incomplete digging important routes of persistence. Garden plants sold as comfrey may also be hybrids or other species, so the familiar name does not settle identification. Historical medicinal use explains some cultivation, but it should not be presented as evidence of safety: extension sources warn that comfrey is unsafe to consume.
identification: Plants commonly reach 30–120 centimeters. Leaves are hairy and extend down the stem as narrow, flattened wings, especially useful when checking a flowering shoot. The hanging flowers may be whitish or purple and are about 12–18 millimeters long. Rough comfrey, Symphytum asperum, lacks the long leaf-base wings; Russian comfrey, S. × uplandicum, can have intermediate features and requires closer checking. Photograph the leaf attachment and the stem below it, a flower from the side, and mature fruits if present. Color is not sufficient to distinguish the species. An established garden clump with unusual characters should be checked against a botanical key rather than assumed to be this species.
actions: Before moving soil around an established clump, decide whether the plant is being retained or removed. If removing it, lift the crown and recover root pieces carefully; rotary cultivation can turn a localized clump into scattered regenerating fragments. Keep excavated roots out of soil or compost destined for other garden beds. Mark the spot and remove regrowth while small, repeating inspections through subsequent growing seasons. For a retained planting, watch its margins and avoid distributing unidentified root divisions. If an escape is spreading beyond a garden into damp habitat, document it and seek local advice. Do not use removed leaves or roots as a homemade medicinal preparation.

proposedDescription: Common corncockle is a slender annual with large pink to purple flowers, once a frequent weed of grain fields. Improved crop-seed cleaning and other farming practices have made it much less common in many agricultural areas. It also occurs in disturbed ground and may be grown as a flower. Long green points extending beyond the petals give the blooms a recognizable outline. The plant produces numerous seeds and is poisonous to people and livestock, making contamination of harvested grain or feed a more relevant concern than its attractive appearance suggests.
identification: Expect an upright, hairy plant roughly 2–3 feet tall with narrow leaves in opposite pairs. Leaves attach directly to the stem and may reach about 6 inches long. Solitary flowers are about 1–2 inches across, with five broad petals and five exceptionally long, pointed green sepals extending beyond them. Fine darker lines may mark the petals. The fruit is a capsule containing black, pitted seeds. Photograph a flower from both the face and side, the leaf pairs, and any capsule. Other pink-family plants can share hairy stems and pink flowers, so confirm the long sepals and narrow leaves together. Cultivars may vary in flower color.
actions: Keep suspected corncockle out of grain, hay, and animal feed. Document plants in a crop and alert the grower before harvest so contamination can be assessed. On your own noncrop ground, remove unwanted annual plants before capsules mature, collecting any developed capsules separately. Avoid sharing seed from an unidentified ornamental mixture and check future seed purchases for reliable labeling and cleanliness. Revisit the patch for seedlings after soil disturbance. Keep pulled material away from livestock and children. If a substantial area occurs in a field, obtain crop-specific advice rather than applying a garden treatment; control timing must account for the crop and the risk of seed entering the harvest.

proposedDescription: Common crupina is a winter annual of open grassland and rangeland. It starts as a low rosette, then produces upright branching stems with narrow purple flower heads. Dense infestations can replace desirable forage and reduce plant diversity. Its seed is relatively large and carries a dark ring of bristles. Two named varieties occur in North America; their differences are most useful on mature fruits, not in a distant photograph. Preventing seed production and movement is central to containment because the species reproduces by seed.
identification: Plants are usually 1–3 feet tall. Young seed leaves are thick and rounded, sometimes with a reddish midvein; later leaves are deeply divided and have small teeth and stiff hairs. Slender flower heads develop at branch tips and contain only a few purplish-pink florets. Their surrounding bracts lack the conspicuous spines or fringes seen in many knapweeds. Mature fruits are dark and barrel-shaped with a ring of stiff bristles. Photograph rosette leaves, stem leaves, several heads, and mature fruits with a scale. Ask a specialist to confirm a new occurrence, particularly if assigning a variety: rosette color and growth angle are not reliable field separators.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the relevant weed program and record its boundaries before disturbing it. Keep vehicles and livestock from carrying seed-bearing material away. Small confirmed plants can be hand-pulled before seed maturity where soil and access allow, but established infestations need repeated checks and a coordinated plan. Collect reproductive material securely; clean soil and plant debris from tools, boots, and equipment. Use clean hay and seed when managing surrounding land. Do not move plants to another site for identification without checking the receiving agency's instructions. Maintaining desired vegetation and watching the patch after removal are important parts of preventing renewed establishment.

claims: Winter annual reaches 1–3 feet.

proposedDescription: Common crupina variety brachypappa is one of the named forms of a purple-flowered annual that grows in rangeland and other open sites. It shares the divided leaves and small flower heads of Common crupina as a whole. The main reported distinction lies in the mature fruits: their attached bristles are shorter than those assigned to variety vulgaris. A 2023 genetic study of western US populations corroborated the two named varieties. Photographs of leafy plants alone cannot establish either one. A botanist may need mature fruit and a carefully chosen identification key.
identification: Common crupina generally reaches 1-3 feet tall, with divided leaves and small purple flower heads. Those features identify a candidate for closer examination, not variety brachypappa by themselves. Photograph mature fruits with an accurate millimeter scale, showing both the fruit body and its attached bristles. The current USDA-WSU account shows bristles only slightly longer than the fruit body, compared with noticeably longer bristles in variety vulgaris. Use that relative comparison with a specialist key, rather than an unsupported numerical cutoff. Leaf color and whether the rosette lies flat are unreliable in the field. Do not assign variety brachypappa from geography, green shade, or an immature flowering plant. Expert examination of mature fruits is needed.
actions: Contain suspected Common crupina while keeping the varietal identification provisional. Map the patch and contact a local weed program for identification and a site-specific handling plan. Keep loose mature heads off boots, tools, vehicles, and livestock equipment that will enter clean ground. Where removal is appropriate, deal with a small patch before seed matures and revisit for later seedlings. If a specimen is requested, follow the recipient's instructions rather than carrying uncovered fruiting plants. The reported difference in fruit bristles does not by itself justify a different homeowner treatment. Preventing seed movement remains useful even when a specialist cannot yet assign the plant to a variety.

proposedDescription: Common crupina variety vulgaris is a named form of the same purple-flowered annual found in rangeland and other open sites. It has divided leaves, small flower heads, and fruits bearing bristles. North American treatments distinguish this variety mainly by the relatively long bristles attached to mature fruits. Older literature uses the name variety typica for a longer-bristled form, while newer material uses variety vulgaris. A 2023 genetic study supports the two varieties in contemporary US usage. Historical labels should still be checked before reassignment. The shape and color of a young rosette do not reliably resolve its variety.
identification: Common crupina generally reaches 1-3 feet tall and has divided leaves and small purple flower heads. Document those features, then photograph mature fruits with a millimeter scale. The newer USDA-WSU account illustrates variety vulgaris with bristles noticeably longer than the fruit body; the older Washington treatment reports longer bristles under variety typica. Use the qualitative comparison, with the fruit body and bristles visible together, rather than a numerical cutoff from ambiguous older wording. Pale versus dark green leaves and upright versus flat rosettes are not reliable separators. Neither locality nor a photograph of flowers alone resolves the variety. Have a herbarium or weed specialist check mature material using the taxonomic treatment appropriate to the record.
actions: Record an uncertain plant as Common crupina until a specialist confirms its variety. Photograph and map the infestation, avoid moving seed-bearing plants, and contact the local weed program for a handling plan. Where removal is appropriate, taking out a small patch before seed maturity can reduce spread, but follow-up is necessary. Do not transport a loose specimen through uninfested ground; ask the receiving specialist how to submit it. Inspect footwear and equipment after entering a mature patch. A longer bristle does not establish a different management need. Continue watching for new plants around the original patch while the exact identification is being checked.

proposedDescription: Common dandelion is treated here in the broad officinale aggregate used by many references; its exact subspecies boundaries differ among floras. The familiar plant has a basal leaf rosette, yellow flower heads, a deep taproot, and wind-carried fruits. Its flowering stalk rises directly from the rosette, and the rounded seed head breaks apart as individual fruits drift away. That general appearance can identify a dandelion without proving this exact subspecies. Native North American dandelions are treated differently by different authorities, so applying an introduced label to every dandelion in a natural area would be misleading.
identification: Yellow heads, toothed basal leaves and rounded white seed heads suggest a dandelion. Check for a single head on each hollow, leafless, unbranched stalk; catsear commonly has branched flower stalks. These features still do not establish subspecies officinale. Photograph the complete rosette, the underside of a flower head, a flowering stalk, and mature fruits beside a scale. The outer bracts surrounding the head and small fruit characters are important in dandelion keys and may require specialist examination. Older broad species concepts have included both introduced Eurasian and native North American plants. A field identification must therefore follow a regional treatment that explicitly distinguishes the relevant taxa. A lawn photograph or the fact that a plant grows beside a path is insufficient.
actions: For familiar unwanted lawn dandelions, a weeding tool can lift the crown and deep taproot; simply mowing the leaves does not eliminate the plant, and remaining root pieces can regrow. Revisit the spot and maintain suitable turf or ground cover if preventing new seedlings is the aim. In native meadow or alpine habitat, confirm the taxon before removing a dandelion on the assumption that it is introduced. Keep photographs and location details for a local botanist. Avoid carrying ripe seed heads through a cleared planting. Treat the exact subspecies name as provisional until a regional key and the necessary plant features support it.

proposedDescription: Common dogmustard is a yellow-flowered mustard of fields, roadsides, railway margins, and other disturbed ground. Introduced from Europe, it can be a weed of cereal and oilseed crops. Its flower stalks often have small leafy bracts beneath them, a useful difference from several superficially similar mustards. Plants usually complete their life cycle in one season, although some floras include biennial behavior. Like many crop weeds, it spreads through seed. A new occurrence near a planting deserves identification and attention to seed movement, without assuming that every roadside plant causes the same level of harm.
identification: Plants range from small individuals to about 80 centimeters tall. Leaves are alternate, hairy, and often divided into lobes; their shape can change upward along the stem. Flowers have four pale yellow or whitish petals. Slender seed pods measure roughly 10–45 millimeters. Most or all of the flower and fruit stalks are subtended by small leafy bracts. In tall hedge-mustard, Sisymbrium loeselii, most such stalks lack bracts, and each pod valve has three veins rather than one. Photograph the flowering stem from the side, lower leaves, pod attachments, and a mature pod. A close view of those bracts is more useful than flower color alone.
actions: Remove isolated unwanted plants before pods mature, taking care to collect any stems already carrying ripe fruit. Inspect the surrounding disturbed soil for additional plants rather than relying on one visible flowering stalk. Avoid moving pod-bearing vegetation with mowing equipment or contaminated crop material. In a field, notify the grower and seek crop-specific management advice, since control options and timing depend on the crop being protected. Use clean planting seed and check suspicious seed contamination with a diagnostic service. Record persistent patches along access routes where seed can be redistributed, and revisit after the next period of germination.

proposedDescription: Common flax is the cultivated annual grown for linen fiber and linseed oil. Escaped plants can occur in fields, along roads and railways, and around disturbed places where seed has been moved. Its slender stems carry narrow leaves and blue flowers with five petals, followed by rounded capsules. An introduced crop volunteer is not automatically a major ecological invader; a few plants beside a grain-handling site may have a different significance from repeated establishment in natural vegetation. Other blue-flowered flaxes are perennial and can look similar, making life history and small flower details important when checking an unfamiliar plant.
identification: Plants generally reach 30–120 centimeters. Narrow leaves, usually 15–40 millimeters long, attach alternately and have smooth edges. Five blue petals surround the flower center, and rounded dry capsules are about 6–10 millimeters long. Compared with perennial flax, Linum perenne, Common flax is annual, typically has three leaf veins, and has longer sepals, about 7–9 millimeters at maturity, with tiny hairs along the edges of the inner sepals. Photograph a whole plant, the leaf veins, a flower from the side, and a ripe capsule. A blue flower viewed from above cannot establish the species, and a cultivated bed may contain another flax.
actions: Determine whether the plants are intentionally grown before treating them as volunteers. For unwanted escapes in a small garden or restoration plot, pull plants before capsules ripen and collect developed seed heads. Check recent seed mixtures, imported soil, and nearby cultivation if plants repeatedly appear. Keep seed-bearing waste out of adjoining natural ground and avoid spreading unidentified flax seed. Where an occurrence is well outside cultivation, record its extent and persistence so local botanists can assess whether it is naturalizing. In production fields, coordinate with the grower rather than removing or treating a crop; the appropriate response depends on why flax is present.

proposedDescription: Common frogbit is a floating aquatic plant that resembles a miniature water lily. Rounded to heart-shaped leaves collect in rosettes, and small white flowers may rise above them in summer. Plants can form crowded surface mats among other shallow-water vegetation. Besides growing shoots, the plant produces compact overwintering buds that detach and start new plants. These buds help it persist even when much of the visible foliage disappears. It is often called European frogbit, which helps distinguish it from American frogbit and other plants sold under similar common names.
identification: Leaves are typically about ½–2½ inches across, round or heart-shaped, and may have reddish-purple undersides. Plants usually float freely, though roots may reach the bottom in shallow water. Flowers have three white petals and a yellow center. Photograph a whole rosette, the leaf underside, connecting stems, roots, and any flowers or detached buds. American frogbit, Limnobium spongia, is a lookalike; comparison includes the amount of spongy tissue beneath the leaf, leaf shape, and root characters. These are easier to examine than to infer from an overhead photograph. Ask an aquatic-plant specialist to verify unfamiliar records, especially where native floating plants occur together.
actions: Report a suspected new occurrence with photographs and a precise waterbody location. Keep plants and detached buds from leaving on boats, anchors, boots, or sampling gear; inspect and clean equipment before visiting another waterbody. Do not empty aquarium or water-garden plants into drains or natural water. Hand removal may provide temporary control for a small patch, but should be coordinated with the landowner or aquatic-plant authority so fragments are collected and follow-up is arranged. The USGS account favors early-season removal after buds begin growing, before dense mats form. Large mats need an approved site-specific plan; do not introduce grazing fish or alter water levels on your own.

proposedDescription: Common globe amaranth is a warm-season garden plant with rounded pink, purple, or white flower heads. Most of the visible color comes from firm, papery bracts surrounding tiny flowers. Those bracts retain their color when dried, explaining the plant's popularity in arrangements. Hairy opposite leaves and stiff branching stems complete its appearance. It is usually grown as an annual and may produce self-sown seedlings. A garden volunteer is not necessarily a damaging invasion. Watch whether new plants remain within the bed or repeatedly establish in surrounding unmanaged ground.
identification: Plants commonly grow about ½–2 feet high, depending on cultivar. Leaves are simple, opposite, oblong to elliptical, and hairy, usually around 2–4 inches long. The compact heads look somewhat like clover but are made largely of dry-textured colored bracts; tiny whitish or yellowish true flowers may be visible between them. Photograph the full plant, a leaf pair, and a close-up of a head showing those small flowers. Red and orange globe amaranths may be selections of Gomphrena haageana or hybrids, so common names and color alone are inadequate. Retain nursery labels when available, but have naturalized specimens checked if their identity is uncertain.
actions: If plants are confined to an intentional flower bed, assess actual spread before deciding that control is necessary. Remove unwanted seedlings while small and collect spent heads before they scatter seed into nearby unmanaged ground. Keep discarded dried arrangements and seed-bearing garden waste out of natural areas. When a patch occurs beyond cultivation, record its location, size, and whether new plants return in later seasons. A herbarium can help distinguish this species from related ornamental globe amaranths. Inspect again after favorable germination weather and close gaps in the bed with suitable planting or mulch, keeping management proportionate to the observed escape and habitat.

proposedDescription: Common gorse is a dense evergreen shrub with stiff spines and golden-yellow pea flowers. Mature plants can form nearly impenetrable stands that displace grassland vegetation. Older bushes often accumulate dead material inside the living outer growth, and their oily foliage contributes to a serious fire hazard. Hairy pods split open and throw seeds away from the branches. Seeds can remain viable in soil for decades, so an apparently cleared patch may keep producing seedlings. Introduced for ornamental use, gorse is especially challenging where a long-established seed supply has built up beneath a thicket.
identification: Shrubs commonly reach several feet tall and can exceed 10 feet. Green angular shoots end in sharp spines, and mature foliage is strongly spine-like. Bright yellow flowers, about ½–¾ inch long, occur near branch tips. Their pea-flower shape may suggest Scotch broom or Spanish broom, but those shrubs lack gorse's dense array of obvious spines. Pods are short, flattened, and densely hairy, becoming brown at maturity. Photograph the branch structure, a flowering tip, and pods from a safe distance; include the bush's overall height. Young plants may have softer three-parted leaves, so the absence of a fully developed spiny thicket does not rule out gorse.
actions: Wear protective clothing and plan access before working near mature spines. Dig small plants with their crowns where feasible, then inspect for regrowth. Established shrubs can resprout after cutting, so a large patch needs a coordinated treatment and follow-up plan with local weed and fire-management advisers. Avoid leaving a pile of dry cut gorse against buildings or other vegetation. Prevent seed-bearing pods from being carried away on equipment or with soil. Re-establish appropriate cover on disturbed ground, and continue searching for seedlings over the long term. Do not use an improvised burn as a cleanup shortcut; fire and the persistent seed bank complicate safe management.

proposedDescription: Common Groundsel is a fast-growing annual of garden beds, nurseries, and disturbed soil, especially during cool conditions. Its small yellow flower heads soon open into white seed tufts carried by wind. Plants can flower when quite small, and several generations may develop in a favorable year. A particularly important detail is that flowers on pulled plants can still produce viable seed. Groundsel competes with young garden and crop plants, and it is also a livestock hazard because eating it can cause liver poisoning. Removing it promptly matters more than letting a patch reach a conspicuous size.
identification: Look for an upright, often branched plant up to about 2 feet tall, with alternate leaves that become deeply lobed. Upper leaves attach directly to the stem; young lower leaves have short stalks. The narrow yellow flower heads are wrapped in green bracts with conspicuous dark tips. Later, each head opens to show a white tuft of wind-dispersed fruits. Photograph leaves at two heights and the side of several unopened or flowering heads so the dark bract tips are visible. A tiny flowering individual may already be capable of setting seed. Other yellow-flowered members of the daisy family need comparison, particularly when flowers are absent or the image is distant.
actions: Pull or hoe young plants before flowering, then check the bed regularly during cool growing periods. If flowers are already present, remove the entire plant from the site rather than leaving it on the soil, because seeds may finish developing after pulling. Keep all removed material out of hay, feed, and livestock access. Inspect incoming nursery pots and nearby neglected corners that can supply windblown seed. Suitable coarse mulch can reduce establishment in garden beds, while keeping desirable plant cover reduces open space. Repeated small removals are usually more useful than waiting for a large flush. Seek local advice for extensive crop or pasture infestations.

proposedDescription: Common hawkweed is a yellow-flowered perennial whose scientific name is used differently among North American references. Some authorities recognize Hieracium vulgatum, while the Pacific Northwest flora uses Hieracium lachenalii and regards the former name as misapplied. These treatments may refer to different taxonomic boundaries rather than a simple spelling change. The plant described in the regional key has toothed basal leaves, several leaves along the flowering stem, and a group of small yellow heads. Native hawkweeds can look similar, so an unfamiliar plant needs both close examination and a clear choice of identification reference.
identification: The regional key describes plants about 20-80 centimeters tall, usually with four to seven stem leaves and four to twelve yellow heads. Basal leaves are gray-green, strongly toothed, and taper to stalks. Flower-head stalks and bracts carry combinations of simple hairs, star-shaped hairs, and dark gland-tipped hairs that need magnification. Smooth hawkweed generally has more stem leaves and more heads in the same key, but hair characters remain important. Photograph basal and stem leaves, the entire inflorescence, and close views of head coverings. Do not identify the species merely because a yellow hawkweed lacks runners; this group includes native lookalikes and difficult name usage.
actions: Document a suspected occurrence and avoid assigning an introduced-species label to all nearby hawkweeds. Request identification from a regional herbarium or weed specialist, providing close-ups of the leaf and flower-head hairs as well as the site location. Once a nonnative plant is confirmed and removal is appropriate, prevent mature seed from scattering and inspect the marked patch for returning growth. Work carefully among native vegetation rather than applying a broad treatment to every yellow flower. Record which scientific name and regional key were used for the determination. Keep uncertain plants marked for follow-up so that a later flowering or fruiting stage can supply missing evidence.

proposedDescription: Common Houndstongue is a biennial or short-lived perennial whose long hairy leaves form a low rosette before a flowering stem develops. Dull reddish-purple flowers produce four small hooked fruits that cling firmly to fur, clothing, and equipment. This makes trails, livestock movement, and contaminated material important opportunities for spread. It grows in pasture, roadsides, and other disturbed ground and can compete with forage. The plant is poisonous to livestock, including when dried in hay. A soft-looking rosette is therefore worth identifying before a mowing or haymaking operation carries it farther.
identification: Flowering plants reach roughly 1–4 feet. The first-year rosette has long, hairy, tongue-shaped leaves, often 4–12 inches long; leaves become smaller and attach directly to the stem higher up. Small burgundy to reddish-purple flowers have five lobes. Each flower develops four nutlets, each containing one seed and covered with tiny hooks. Photograph both the rosette and flowering stem, a leaf attachment, and the four-part fruit cluster. Other hairy rosettes can look similar before flowering, so record the leaf shape and hairs clearly rather than relying on texture alone. The mature hooked fruits are particularly helpful, but handle them carefully to avoid carrying them away.
actions: Prioritize plants in hay fields, livestock areas, and along travel routes before seed develops. Dig or pull small plants, removing the crown and as much root as practical, or sever rosettes below the crown. Recheck for sprouts and seedlings. Collect flowering or fruiting stems and keep even dried material away from livestock. Brush hooked fruits from clothing, animal coats, tools, and equipment before leaving the site, containing the removed seeds. Restore suitable competing vegetation where bare ground remains. For extensive pasture infestations, work with the local weed program and livestock adviser on a continuing plan; do not use grazing as a control method for this poisonous plant.

proposedDescription: Common house gecko is a small nocturnal lizard often seen on walls near lights, where insects gather. Broad toe pads let it climb smooth surfaces, and its pale gray to brown coloring can make it difficult to notice by day. Native to Asia, it has established introduced populations in parts of the United States and on many islands. Several other house geckos share buildings and look similar, so a gecko near a porch light is not automatically this species. Cargo and transported belongings are practical places to watch for accidental movement.
identification: Adults have a body length of about 42–60 millimeters from snout to vent, with a tail of roughly similar length when intact. The body is slightly flattened, the limbs are well developed, and a dark side stripe may run from the snout backward. The tail has rings of enlarged, pointed scales. Toe-pad scales are divided over much of each toe. Mediterranean and tropical house geckos can be confused with it, and diagnostic scale arrangements may need specialist examination. Obtain clear side and back photographs, including the tail and toes, without grabbing the animal or forcing it onto its back. A blurry silhouette or variable body color cannot establish species identity.
actions: Reduce entry into buildings by repairing screens and sealing gaps around doors, windows, and service openings after checking that animals are not trapped inside. Address indoor insect problems and unnecessary insect-attracting lights. Inspect boxes, nursery plants, and outdoor equipment before moving them to another region. Do not relocate a captured gecko to new outdoor habitat or release a pet. If one arrives unexpectedly in a shipment, keep the item contained where practical and ask local wildlife authorities for identification and handling advice. For persistent indoor problems, use exclusion-focused professional help. Photographs and shipping origin are useful evidence; broad insecticide spraying is not a reliable gecko-management plan.

Several introduced house geckos coexist in Florida.
