proposedDescription: Creeping cinquefoil is a low perennial that spreads through long, slender runners. Where each runner roots, another leafy plant can establish, allowing a small patch to stretch through grass or a garden bed. Its yellow flowers open in bright weather and close at night or in dull conditions. Native across parts of Europe and Asia, it has been introduced to North America. It can be unwelcome where it displaces desired planting, but it is also valued in wildlife gardens within its native range. An introduced record alone does not establish local ecological damage.
identification: Plants usually stay below 20 cm tall. Leaves commonly have five toothed leaflets spreading from one point like fingers; some have more. Yellow flowers are about 2 cm across and have five separate petals. Long, thin runners with rooted joints help distinguish the growth pattern from upright cinquefoils. Photograph the entire leaf, a flower with a size reference, and the connections between neighboring rosettes. Other Potentilla species can share yellow flowers and divided leaves, so flower color and a single leaf do not settle the identification. Use a regional flora or herbarium review for a definitive identification, especially if the plant is a new local record.
actions: For an unwanted small patch, gently raise the runners to find every rooted plant, then loosen and remove each taproot. A narrow weeding tool helps target roots without digging up the whole bed. Inspect nearby grass and under neighboring plants for runners that escaped the first pass. Avoid moving soil containing live roots or rooted stems to clean beds. Follow removal with suitable planting and repeat checks during the growing season. Decide management from the patch's behavior and location rather than its name alone. If it appears to be spreading into a natural area, document its extent and request local botanical advice.

A named lookalike is useful but is not a universal prerequisite for an honest recognition profile that already warns of other cinquefoils. No blanket US harm or eradication effectiveness is claimed. Next: Retain regional confirmation for new records and small-patch follow-up.

proposedDescription: Creeping cudweed, treated here in the broad Euchiton japonicus complex that includes the historical gymnocephalus names, is a small perennial with a basal rosette and clusters of tiny flowerheads above the leaves. Plants described under the closely associated name Euchiton japonicus spread by runners, with green upper leaf surfaces and pale, densely hairy undersides. The name Euchiton gymnocephalus has been used in different ways, so observations carrying that name need careful checking. Several cudweeds share a low, leafy habit and inconspicuous flowers. A useful record includes a complete plant, its connections to neighboring shoots, and mature flowerheads, rather than only a close photograph of the pale underside of one leaf.
identification: Creeping cudweeds in the Euchiton japonicus group may stand 10-35 cm tall, with basal leaves 4-18 cm long. Leaves are green above and covered with silvery hairs beneath; three main veins may be visible. Numerous tiny flowerheads gather in a rounded cluster at the stem tip, with leafy bracts beneath. These features help narrow the group, but do not securely identify every plant labeled Euchiton gymnocephalus. Photograph both leaf surfaces, a complete flowering stem, the basal rosette, and any runners connecting neighboring shoots. A botanist should compare mature flowerheads and growth form with Euchiton japonicus and E. collinus. A label or old observation using one of these names is not enough to establish that two plants are the same species.
actions: Keep a suspected occurrence documented while its identity is resolved. Record where it grows, the approximate patch size, whether stems root away from the parent plant, and whether the population returns in the same place. Send clear images to a regional herbarium or extension botanist, including any scientific name attached to the original observation. Avoid distributing rooted pieces or soil from the patch while checking it. If an unwanted garden specimen must be removed, lift the small rooted patch and retain photographs first. Broad removal of similar cudweeds in natural vegetation would be premature without identification and local management advice.

proposedDescription: Creeping inchplant forms low mats of small, fleshy leaves on branching stems that trail over pot rims or creep across soil. A stem joint can take root where it touches damp ground, making loose trimmings a ready source of new plants. Its tiny white flowers are easy to overlook among the leaves. This tropical American plant is widely grown in hanging baskets and warm gardens. Escape is a regional concern: Florida's assessment calls for preventing its spread from cultivation in central and southern parts of the state.
identification: A typical mat stands about 4–6 inches high, while trailing stems can extend more than 2 feet. The alternate, pointed leaves are usually 1–4 cm long and somewhat fleshy. Look for roots at stem joints and tiny white flowers tucked into the upper leaf axils, where leaves meet an ascending flowering stem. Flowers may appear in late spring and early summer in cultivation. Leaf color varies among cultivars and is a poor guide by itself. Fragrant inchplant (Callisia fragrans) has much larger leaves, commonly 15–30 cm long, rather than the small leaves packed along creeping shoots. Photograph an entire shoot beside a ruler, a rooted joint, and a flowering tip. Young cuttings may lack the mature proportions needed for a confident identification.
actions: Keep cultivated plants in containers where trailing stems cannot reach adjacent soil. Collect every cutting after trimming, and do not discard live pieces into woods, drains, or yard-waste piles beside natural vegetation. Lift small unwanted mats carefully and check beneath neighboring plants for rooted stems. Revisit the area to remove shoots that survived. Wear gloves if sap irritates your skin, and keep trimmings away from children and pets. Before planting it as groundcover, check its status with local extension staff. Photograph and map a patch spreading beyond cultivation, including the edge where new stems are rooting.

proposedDescription: Creeping indigo is a low perennial with small compound leaves, reddish flowers and narrow pods that point downward. Its stems can lie among pasture grasses, making a scattered plant easy to miss. It grows from a persistent woody base and occurs in open, disturbed ground. Authenticated plants have caused serious poisoning in grazing ponies, so suspected patches deserve prompt attention around horses. A closely related species, Indigofera hendecaphylla, shares the common name and was included in many older records. The distinction matters for identification, even though both deserve caution around grazing animals.
identification: Look for a prostrate plant that may rise to about 50 cm high, with leaves mostly divided into five to seven alternating leaflets. The leaflets are broadest toward their rounded outer ends and have a tiny point at the tip. Reddish flowers grow in narrow clusters. Mature pods point downward and measure about 10–18 mm long in the modern botanical treatment. Indigofera hendecaphylla usually has longer pods, about 22–27 mm, and longer flower clusters; small flower structures provide additional distinctions. A grazing patch cannot be identified from its common name or overall shape alone. Photograph a complete leaf, a flowering cluster and several mature pods beside a millimeter ruler. Keep the botanical identification separate from any veterinary assessment of an animal's symptoms.
actions: Exclude horses and donkeys from a paddock containing suspected creeping indigo while identification is checked. If an animal may have eaten it or develops unusual movement or behavior, contact a veterinarian promptly. For a few plants, physical removal must address the crown and deep root, followed by repeated inspections for seedlings. Keep removed plants out of feed and accessible grazing areas. Maintain vigorous pasture cover and adjust grazing pressure so bare, heavily used areas do not keep expanding. Larger infestations need extension guidance tailored to the forage and site. Do not assume mowing or drying makes the material suitable for animals.

proposedDescription: Creeping liriope resembles a small ornamental grass, but it belongs to the asparagus family. It was planted widely as a durable groundcover and spreads through underground stems that connect neighboring shoots. In suitable conditions those connections build dense patches and carry the plant into adjacent beds or woodland. Pale summer flowers are followed by dark, rounded fruits. The same spreading habit that fills a landscape bed can make an escaped patch difficult to remove. A border planting should therefore be assessed by its expansion beyond the intended area, especially near natural vegetation.
identification: Plants generally stand 6–18 inches tall. Narrow, arching leaves are usually dark green and may turn bronze-green in winter; some cultivated forms have white stripes. Their edges have fine teeth that are easier to see close up. Pale violet to whitish flowers sit on short summer spikes, often partly concealed among the leaves, and fruits mature dark purple-black. NC State lists Liriope muscari, Ophiopogon japonicus, and Carex morrowii as common confusions. Photograph the leaf width with a ruler, the flower spike, mature fruit, and the underground connections at a patch edge. A nursery label or a picture of grasslike leaves alone is insufficient.
actions: Check outside the original planting for connected shoots, particularly under shrubs and along woodland edges. Lift small outliers with their underground stems, then revisit the disturbed area for regrowth. Dispose of live divisions so they cannot become new groundcover elsewhere. Cutting off the leaves may tidy a bed but does not remove the spreading underground system. Where the plant is retained, keep it physically confined and inspect the boundary regularly. For an extensive escaped colony, seek a restoration plan before broad treatment: research on control warns that methods effective against liriope can also harm nearby trees and desirable vegetation.

proposedDescription: Creeping meadow foxtail is a long-lived pasture grass that forms thick sod on wet ground. Underground stems spread outward, and its light seeds travel with water or wind. It supplies forage on sites too wet for many other pasture grasses, but can escape into waterways and wetlands. In an Idaho wet meadow, researchers linked greater cover of the Garrison cultivar with lower survival of native common camas, particularly in wetter areas during some years. That finding concerns one cultivar and study site. A landowner's practical question is whether a forage stand is expanding into neighboring vegetation.
identification: Flowering stems are commonly about 50–120 centimeters tall, with flat leaves and a compact cylindrical head roughly 4–10 centimeters long. The head changes from green to dark purple or nearly black as it matures. Timothy, Phleum pratense, has a similar outline but its mature heads become buff-brown. Meadow foxtail, Alopecurus pratensis, is another close comparison; broader leaves and the dark mature head help distinguish Creeping meadow foxtail, but dimensions overlap. Look for spreading underground stems and a thin membrane at the leaf-and-stem junction. Photograph mature heads, leaves beside a ruler, that junction, and several connected shoots where they are already exposed. Seedlings and freshly clipped grass may require a specialist and mature flowering material.
actions: Before planting or expanding a forage stand, discuss alternatives with a local pasture adviser, especially beside canals, drains, and wetlands. Inspect downstream margins and neighboring damp ground for new patches. Prevent unwanted stands from shedding seed, and clean equipment before moving to another site. Where digging is appropriate, carefully lift small outlying clumps with connected underground stems and revisit for regrowth; this is containment, not a proven one-time cure. Avoid excavating wet banks to chase roots. Document larger escapes and coordinate work with the land manager. Pasture renovation should consider forage needs and neighboring vegetation; do not alter wetland drainage to control this grass.

proposedDescription: Creeping velvetgrass is a perennial grass with soft leaves and pale flowerheads. Beneath the surface, spreading stems connect shoots and help the plant occupy moist disturbed ground. Flora of North America records it as a European introduction and describes problems in some ungrazed pastures, prairie remnants, and oak savannas of the Pacific Northwest. That regional evidence should not be stretched into a claim of equal harm everywhere it occurs. Its close resemblance to common velvetgrass makes checking the lower stem and underground growth more useful than judging a patch by its softness.
identification: Plants usually reach 20–100 cm, sometimes taller. Leaves are 3–10 mm wide and hairy, while lower stem sections are hairless or only sparsely hairy; the joints themselves are hairy. Flowerheads are commonly 4–20 cm long, initially whitish-green and later straw-colored. Common velvetgrass, Holcus lanatus, forms tufts and has hairier lower stems. Under magnification, its flower bristles are strongly hooked, unlike the straight or bent bristles in creeping velvetgrass. Photograph the lower stem joints, an attached underground stem, and mature spikelets with a scale. A distant photograph cannot show these distinctions, and hybrids or unusual specimens may require a grass specialist.
actions: Identify a patch before removing it, especially where other grasses are mixed together. For a small unwanted colony, trace and lift the underground stems as completely as practical, collecting loose pieces before restoring the opening. Avoid transporting rooted turf or soil from the patch to a clean site. Watch the perimeter for new shoots, and document whether it expands into intact vegetation. A larger infestation in a prairie remnant or oak savanna warrants advice from the site manager or local restoration program. Plan follow-up and replacement vegetation before extensive disturbance, because a single cutting of the foliage cannot eliminate a living underground network.

proposedDescription: Creeping yellowcress is a yellow-flowered perennial that can arrive in a garden hidden among the roots of purchased plants. Its white, fleshy roots spread sideways and produce fresh shoots; even small broken pieces can start again. This makes an apparently simple weeding job surprisingly persistent. It occurs on damp disturbed ground as well as in nursery and garden settings. Hostas and daylilies are documented pathways for root fragments. Prevention starts with checking incoming plants, because moving an infested root ball may carry the problem to a new bed before any flowers appear.
identification: Look for low, branching shoots with deeply divided leaves and small four-petaled yellow flowers about 4–5 mm across. The most useful feature lies belowground: white horizontal roots linking or producing new shoots. Marsh yellowcress, Rorippa palustris, and southern yellowcress, Rorippa teres, instead have a taproot. Their young plants can be difficult or impossible to separate before creeping roots develop. Marsh yellowcress also has shorter, thicker seed capsules, generally under half an inch, compared with creeping yellowcress's slender pods, about 10–25 mm long. Photograph the whole plant, a lower leaf, ripe pods with a ruler, and carefully exposed roots. Leaf divisions vary, so a leaf-only picture should not be treated as definitive.
actions: Inspect the root balls of new perennials and avoid planting stock containing suspicious white creeping roots. Keep a suspect purchase separate while requesting identification from the nursery or extension office. For a small established patch, loosen soil carefully and collect the root pieces rather than chopping through them with a tiller. Recheck the bed repeatedly, since missed fragments can resprout. Do not distribute divisions, soil, or live material from an affected bed. Larger persistent patches need a site-specific control plan. If plants occur beside water, coordinate removal with the land manager so digging does not spread fragments or destabilize the bank.

proposedDescription: Crested latesummer mint is an annual herb introduced from Asia. It appears in yards, roadsides, railroad margins, and other disturbed places, where its short purple flower spikes provide a useful identification clue. Unlike a perennial mint patch that returns from surviving roots, an annual population depends on a new generation of plants. Native Plant Trust notes that this species can become invasive, but a scattered garden occurrence does not establish the size of its local impact. Watch whether it keeps producing seedlings and moves from disturbed ground into neighboring vegetation.
identification: An adult plant is usually 30–100 cm tall, with upright stems that are roughly square in cross-section. Leaves occur in opposite pairs, have toothed margins, and are not divided into leaflets. Small blue-purple flowers, about 4 mm long, crowd mainly onto one side of short terminal spikes. Purple giant hyssop, Agastache scrophulariifolia, is a documented lookalike: its flower clusters surround the axis and are generally longer. Photograph the flower spike from both sides, a paired set of leaves, and the stem. Flowerless seedlings are much less distinctive, and scent or a square stem alone only suggests the mint family. Include mature flowers.
actions: Remove an unwanted small population before its flower spikes mature into seed-bearing heads. Pull plants when the ground is soft, keeping soil disturbance limited around neighboring vegetation. If heads are already dry, contain them before carrying the plants away so seeds are not scattered along the route. Revisit the same ground during the following growing season and remove new seedlings before they reproduce. Avoid sharing plants or seed under a culinary or ornamental label until the species is confirmed. Where a patch is increasing outside a garden, record its extent and send photographs to a local invasive-plant or extension program.

Annual herb; nonnative naturalized status.

proposedDescription: Crested philippine violet is an upright shrub with dark green leaves and funnel-shaped flowers, usually lavender or purple but sometimes white. Leaves grow in opposite pairs, and their deeply marked veins can give them a puckered surface. Small, stiff points on the green parts surrounding each flower are useful identification clues. The plant is native to Asia and grown in warm gardens for its late-season flowers. It can produce many seedlings around an established planting. Watching those seedlings makes it easier to keep a garden clump within its intended space.
identification: Garden plants commonly reach 4–6 feet tall and 3–4 feet across. Leaves occur in opposite pairs and are elliptical to oblong, about 2–10 cm long, with hairs especially noticeable along the veins. Purple-blue flowers are roughly 4.5–6.5 cm long in the botanical treatment; cultivated plants also have white flowers. Look closely at the outer green flower coverings: their edges carry stiff, spine-like points. Coral creeper (Barleria repens) usually grows lower and spreads along the ground, and its floral coverings lack the conspicuous spines used to distinguish crested philippine violet. Flowers appear on new growth, often in late summer and fall in warm gardens. Photograph the paired leaves, the side of a flower, and those surrounding green structures; flower color alone cannot separate these ornamentals.
actions: Pull unwanted seedlings while they are small and before they flower. Check beneath the parent shrub and along the edges of adjoining beds, where new plants may be less obvious. Collect seed capsules before they release their contents, and contain seed-bearing branches during cleanup. Gather discarded cuttings too, since this shrub can be propagated from stem pieces. After removing a mature clump, inspect its base for returning shoots. Wear gloves when handling coarse or weather-damaged foliage. If seedlings are appearing beyond the garden, record their locations and remove small, confirmed plants where practical; seek local advice for established patches among desirable vegetation.

proposedDescription: Crested wheatgrass is a cool-season perennial introduced from Eurasia for forage and land rehabilitation. Its drought and cold tolerance helped make it a familiar grass in planted western rangelands. The name also covers a complicated group of related cultivated grasses in older literature, and commercial hybrids add to that difficulty. The exact species in this entry, Agropyron cristatum, is often called the fairway type. Its value in a pasture does not establish its suitability for restoring native plant communities. Management should distinguish a maintained forage stand from unwanted expansion beyond it.
identification: Plants in the crested wheatgrass complex commonly stand 30-90 cm tall. Fairway-type Agropyron cristatum generally has a short, broad, comb-like seedhead about 1-5 cm long, with spikelets projecting widely from the central axis. Agropyron desertorum tends to have a longer, narrower head, while A. fragile has more upright spikelets and narrower, usually awnless flower coverings. Cultivars and hybrids can blur these differences. Photograph several mature heads face-on and from the side with a ruler, plus the plant base and leaves. A broad seedhead is a useful clue, but exact identification may require a grass specialist and knowledge of the original seed mixture.
actions: Keep records of seed mixtures and cultivar names wherever this grass has been planted. Before using it beside native grassland, consult a local range or restoration adviser about alternatives and likely spread. Monitor the edge of existing stands and avoid moving mature seedheads or contaminated equipment into restoration areas. For a small unwanted outlier, remove the whole crown where practical and check for surviving growth and seedlings. Field restoration trials show that disturbance can increase grass density or open space for other weeds, so large stands need a replacement plan. If a restoration is the goal, decide how desired plants will establish after removal before disturbing a broad area of soil.

proposedDescription: Cretan brake is a fern with a few long leaf divisions spreading from each central stalk. Its open shape is quite different from the finely divided fronds of many familiar garden ferns. New fronds arise from a short, creeping underground stem, and fertile fronds carry spores along their leaf margins. It is widely cultivated and has escaped in warm regions, including parts of the United States. Several related ferns share its general shape, and nursery names can be misleading. Checking how the upper leaf divisions join the central stalk is especially useful.
identification: A complete frond can reach 1 m, although the leafy portion is often only 10–30 cm long in the North American treatment. Usually one to three pairs of side divisions flank the terminal division; the lowest pair may have backward-pointing branches. Fertile divisions are narrower than nonfertile ones and bear narrow spore-producing lines along their undersides near the margins. Young Pteris multifida can resemble it, but that species has thinner leaf tissue and more drawn-out tips on its lower divisions. White-striped Pteris nipponica is sometimes sold under a P. cretica name. Every division of P. nipponica has its own stalk; in Cretan brake, the terminal division usually joins at least one neighboring upper division through a strip of leaf tissue. Photograph that junction and both surfaces of a complete mature frond.
actions: Check shaded soil around cultivated plants for young ferns appearing beyond their containers or beds. Avoid dumping fern divisions or used potting material into natural vegetation. For an unwanted small garden clump, remove the crown and its attached short underground stem, then revisit the spot for new growth. Contain mature fertile fronds during handling to reduce scattering spores. If a plant is rooted in masonry or a steep bank, seek help before pulling it out and damaging the structure or soil. Have unfamiliar escapes identified before removing them, using photographs of mature fronds and their upper leaf junctions. Keep any nursery label as additional information.

proposedDescription: Cribellate spider, Metaltella simoni, is a small South American spider established in parts of the southern United States. Females and young spiders make tangled silk retreats beneath bark, boards, logs, and other sheltered surfaces; males may be found wandering. It also occurs around buildings and ornamental plants. A Florida account raised concern about possible competition with a native spider, but did not demonstrate a measured displacement trend. That distinction matters: encountering this introduced spider is useful distribution information, not by itself proof of ecological damage or a reason for broad spraying.
identification: Adults are roughly 7–9 mm long, excluding the legs. Males have yellow to orange-brown front bodies and legs, while females are browner; both have a mottled gray abdomen. The native Titanoeca brunnea is smaller, about 4–5.5 mm, and generally brighter orange, but appearance varies. Reliable separation can require microscopic inspection of mouthpart teeth and adult structures. Photograph the spider from above and side with a size reference without handling it. Web placement adds context but is not diagnostic. Young individuals and blurry indoor photographs should remain tentative identifications until reviewed by someone familiar with the group. Keep the original image resolution.
actions: For an indoor encounter, use a container and stiff card rather than bare hands if the spider needs to be contained for identification. Photograph it and ask a local extension or natural-history specialist how to submit the record. Check pots, stored boards, and other sheltered items before transporting them to a new property, and remove webs or hitchhikers without releasing an uncertain specimen elsewhere. Reduce unwanted indoor entry by sealing gaps and tidying stored materials near doors. Broad insecticide treatment is not supported by the reviewed ecological evidence. Preserve native spiders by confirming the identification before any targeted response outdoors.

proposedDescription: Crimson bottlebrush is an Australian evergreen shrub or small tree with bright red flower clusters shaped like bottle-cleaning brushes. Their showy parts are long stamens, and the narrow leaves have a lemon scent when bruised. Woody seed capsules can stay closed on branches for years, then release seed after branches are cut. Many garden forms have been selected, and some are hybrids. The name Melaleuca citrina refers to the same species in sources that place bottlebrushes in Melaleuca. Florida's university assessment rates it a high invasion risk; that prediction should not be mistaken for measured damage at every planting.
identification: An unpruned plant may reach about 10–15 feet high, though clipped shrubs are smaller. Alternate leaves are narrow, about 1–3 inches long, with visible side veins as well as a central vein. Red flower clusters are roughly 4–5 inches long, with flowering time varying by climate. Woody cup-shaped capsules persist after flowering. Weeping bottlebrush, Callistemon viminalis, has less obvious leaf side veins and stamens joined into a ring at their bases; Crimson bottlebrush has separate stamens. Check that flower detail with magnification rather than relying on red color or branch posture. Photograph leaves, the base of an individual flower, capsules, and the whole plant. Nursery hybrids can combine characters, so retain labels and seek botanical confirmation for an uncertain escaped plant.
actions: Inspect beneath and beyond cultivated plants for seedlings, especially after disturbance, and remove unwanted young plants before they become woody. Collect capsule-bearing prunings: closed woody fruits can release seed after branches are cut and dry. Keep them out of dumped garden waste and natural vegetation. Hard pruning can stimulate regrowth, so trimming alone is not reliable removal. An unwanted mature shrub needs a plan for its living base and follow-up shoots. Confirm an escaped plant with a regional botanist, retaining any nursery label. Before new planting, consult local guidance; UF/IFAS does not recommend this species for Florida because of its assessed invasion risk.

proposedDescription: Crimson clover is a cool-season annual often planted as a cover crop, forage, or flowering groundcover. Its upright red flowerheads are much more elongated than the rounded heads many people picture when they think of clover. Like other legumes, it can contribute to soil fertility through its association with nitrogen-fixing bacteria. It also protects bare ground while growing. Some cultivars readily reseed, allowing plants to persist beyond a planned sowing. Its agricultural usefulness and its potential to become weedy both deserve mention; an introduced clover is not necessarily causing ecological damage wherever it occurs.
identification: Crimson clover commonly reaches about 12–20 inches in cover-crop settings. Each soft-hairy leaf has three broad, rounded or wedge-shaped leaflets with small marginal teeth. Upright flowerheads are cone-shaped to cylindrical, usually 3–6 centimeters long, and become brown as seed matures. Spring flowering is typical of fall-sown plants where winters permit survival. Trifolium purpureum has much narrower leaflets and longer individual flowers. Trifolium dichotomum has shorter, more oval heads and flowers combining purple and white, rather than the usually red, elongated heads of Crimson clover. Photograph an entire leaf with a scale, a head from the side, and the plant's overall habit. Seedlings and mown plants lack these useful flowering characters and may need a regional key.
actions: Decide whether the stand is a planned cover crop or an unwanted escape before removing it. To prevent reseeding, end or remove unwanted plants before the flowerheads mature and scatter seed. Pull small garden volunteers while roots are easy to lift, then check for a new flush in the next cool growing period. Avoid moving ripe heads in mulch or uncleaned equipment. A field-scale cover crop needs a termination plan matched to the following crop and local conditions; one mowing is not automatically sufficient. If grazing is planned, seek forage advice because clovers can create bloat risk under some conditions.

proposedDescription: Crimson fountaingrass forms upright clumps topped by long, bristly flowerheads. It was introduced as an ornamental and has escaped into dry landscapes, including parts of the southwestern United States. Dry foliage can carry fire, and repeated burning can favor the grass rather than eliminate it. Seeds are its main natural means of spread and can move on wind, water, animals, clothing, or vehicles. The common name is also used loosely in horticulture, so a reddish nursery grass should not automatically be assigned to this species without checking its botanical identity.
identification: Clumps commonly reach about 2–4.5 feet tall at maturity. Long, slender leaves arch outward from a dense base, and purplish or rose-colored cylindrical heads carry conspicuous bristles. Flowerheads vary in size, so photograph one with a ruler rather than relying on color alone. Feather grass, Cenchrus longisetus, is a similar grass. A secure identification also requires close views of the spikelets and the bristles surrounding them; ornamental cultivars and related grasses can be difficult to separate from distant photographs. Include the plant base, leaf sheath, and several mature heads. Winter color and nursery labels can be misleading. Mature flowers are especially useful.
actions: Bag seedheads before disturbing an unwanted clump, then remove as much of the crown and roots as practical. Prioritize scattered plants beyond a large infestation so they do not start new seed sources. Clean shoes, tools, and vehicles before leaving an affected area, and do not move seed-bearing cut material to open ground. Revisit treated sites for several years because seed can remain viable in soil. Do not use burning as a household control method; this grass can recover rapidly afterward. For extensive roadside or desert infestations, coordinate with the land manager and use locally suitable replacement plants to reduce reinvasion.

proposedDescription: Crossflower is a small mustard with pale purple flowers and a strong, often unpleasant odor. It commonly begins as a low rosette in fall, then branches and flowers early the next spring. This timing lets it produce seed before a neglected bare patch receives much attention. Its narrow pods break into short seed-bearing sections, helping carry the next generation into new ground. It is a weed of disturbed dry sites and cultivated land in western North America. The same plant is frequently described by extension services as blue mustard or purple mustard.
identification: Plants are usually about half a foot to 1.5 feet tall, with a shallow taproot and branching stems. Tiny gland-tipped hairs make leaves and stems sticky. Leaves are alternate, with wavy or coarse-toothed margins; basal leaves may be more deeply lobed. Each pale purple flower has four petals arranged as a cross and is about half an inch across. Mature pods have a beaded lower portion and a long beak. African malcolmia, Malcolmia africana in the cited guide, is a documented lookalike. Photograph pod shape, a close view of hairs, and flowers: the pod's beak and crosswise breakup are more useful than purple color alone.
actions: Act while plants are still young rosettes, before early spring seed production. Dig, hoe, or pull small patches, removing the shallow taproot and collecting any developing pods. If flowers are already present, inspect promptly rather than postponing removal; seed can develop soon after flowering. Clean soil and plant material from equipment before working clean areas, and use crop or restoration seed with low weed contamination. Replant exposed soil with suitable vegetation or use an appropriate mulch in garden beds. In fields where it repeatedly returns, ask an adviser about crop rotation and follow-up, because one season of removal does not exhaust stored seed.

proposedDescription: Crow Garlic often first announces itself when a mower releases an onionlike smell from its leaves. It is a cool-season perennial that grows from bulbs, with foliage appearing in fall and dying back after flowering as summer temperatures rise. Aboveground, the flowering stalk may carry a cluster of tiny bulbs instead of many flowers. Underground bulb offsets add another means of persistence. This combination explains why a lawn patch can disappear for summer and then return. It is a common introduced weed of disturbed ground, but native onions must be distinguished before removal.
identification: Unmown plants can reach about 1–3 feet tall. The leaves are slender, hollow, and roughly round in cross-section, rather than flat grass blades. A tall stalk bears a rounded cluster of small aerial bulbs, sometimes mixed with white to purplish six-parted flowers. Native wild onion, Allium canadense, and cultivated garlic, Allium sativum, are listed as confusions. Photograph the intact bulb with offsets, a cut or naturally broken leaf showing its hollow center, and the head before and after its covering opens. Onion odor supports membership in the onion group but is not enough to identify this species or establish safe edibility.
actions: Loosen moist soil with a trowel and remove the bulb together with its smaller offsets. Pulling only the leaves leaves the plant able to return. Collect aerial bulb clusters before they fall, and keep bulbs out of soil or lawn material moved elsewhere. Recheck the site in fall and spring, when foliage is visible again. Mowing can reduce seed production and weaken plants but does not reliably kill the bulbs. Where a lawn patch is mainly a seasonal appearance issue, weigh repeated hand removal against simply tolerating it. Seek identification before removing native onions from meadows or woodland edges.

proposedDescription: Crown mayweed is the annual herb more often sold as German chamomile. Slender, divided leaves surround branching stems topped by white-and-yellow flowerheads. The raised yellow center becomes especially noticeable as a head matures. Plants grow readily from seed, and spent flowers can produce another generation in nearby bare ground. It is cultivated for flowers and fragrance and also occurs along roadsides and in fields and meadows. Its ability to reseed makes it a garden weed in some settings; the practical concern is whether seedlings are spreading into spaces where other plants are wanted, rather than the mere presence of a cultivated herb.
identification: Plants grow to about 2 feet tall, with alternate leaves divided into narrow, threadlike segments. Flowerheads have a domed yellow center surrounded by white rays and an applelike fragrance. The central receptacle is hollow, a useful distinction from solid-centered Anthemis lookalikes. Pineappleweed, Matricaria discoidea, lacks the white rays. Roman chamomile, Chamaemelum nobile, is a shorter perennial with creeping stems rather than the upright annual habit of this species. Examine a mature flowerhead from the side and, if needed, a carefully split center. Include the branching stem and a whole leaf in photographs. Scent alone cannot distinguish every plant sold as chamomile.
actions: Remove unwanted plants or cut off their flowerheads before seed ripens. As an annual, it returns through seed. Removing mature plants after their heads have shed seed will not prevent the next generation. Pull small plants from soft soil and inspect nearby open ground for later seedlings. Keep ripe heads out of seed-free mulch and areas where chamomile is not wanted. If retaining a garden planting, collect spent flowers regularly and monitor its edges. Do not eat or brew an unidentified daisy; resemblance to chamomile does not establish that it is suitable for consumption.

proposedDescription: Crown Vetch is a spreading perennial legume once planted extensively to cover road banks and other exposed ground. Its pink-and-white flower clusters rise above trailing stems and many small leaflets. Underground stems help a colony expand, while persistent seed creates a longer-term source of new plants. Dense growth can shade neighboring vegetation and spread into grasslands, forest edges, and other open habitats. Despite its name, it is not a true vetch and has no climbing tendrils. Its old use for erosion control means removal on a slope should include a plan to maintain soil cover.
identification: Trailing stems can reach 2–6 feet, creating a mound rather than a twining vine. Leaves have an odd number of oblong leaflets, commonly 11–25, with a final leaflet at the tip instead of a tendril. Pink, lavender, and white pea-shaped flowers form rounded or flat-topped clusters on long stalks. Narrow, segmented pods follow. American vetch, Vicia americana, has terminal tendrils, as do other true vetches. Flowering is generally from spring into summer, with timing varying by region. Check the end of a complete leaf and the flower-cluster arrangement; a small detached leaflet is not useful for separating the many legumes.
actions: For a small patch, repeatedly remove plants with their connected roots and underground stems, checking the perimeter for new shoots. Contain seed-bearing material before carrying it away. A garden patch can also be covered for a full growing season where doing so will not damage desired plants; inspect edges for escape. Large stands usually require repeated treatment over several years, so arrange follow-up before beginning. On a bank, replace lost cover promptly with suitable vegetation and erosion protection. Keep material away from horses and other animals for which it is unsuitable. Avoid moving infested soil into a restored area.

proposedDescription: Crucifer flea beetle is a tiny, dark beetle that chews small holes through cabbage-family crops. Newly planted seedlings are particularly vulnerable because a little feeding can remove much of their leaf area. Adults leap when disturbed and also fly between food plants. Their larvae develop belowground, while adults cause the familiar scattered holes in leaves. Broccoli, cabbage, kale, arugula, radish, and related crops can all be affected. The species is introduced in North America, but gardeners usually encounter it as a crop pest requiring early protection and close monitoring rather than an eradication campaign.
identification: Adults are about 2 mm long, oval, shiny, and uniformly dark. The hind legs are enlarged for jumping, which can make counting beetles difficult if plants are shaken first. Striped flea beetle, Phyllotreta striolata, is a close crop-associated lookalike with a broad yellow stripe on each wing cover. Several other flea beetles are also dark, so black color alone is insufficient. Look for beetles actually feeding on brassica leaves and record the host plant. Small round feeding holes support a flea-beetle diagnosis but do not identify the species. A sharp close-up showing the wing covers and a collected specimen may be needed for confirmation.
actions: Protect newly planted brassicas immediately with fine insect mesh or suitable row cover, sealing all edges so beetles cannot crawl underneath. Use a bed rotated away from last season's brassicas; otherwise insects may emerge beneath the cover. Check seedlings frequently and repair tears or lifted edges promptly. Remove harvested brassica residue and manage nearby mustard-family weeds that shelter beetles. Strong transplants can tolerate feeding better than very small direct-sown seedlings. In hot weather, choose breathable insect netting and monitor crop stress. If damage continues, ask extension staff to assess the crop's stage and damage before choosing a targeted treatment.

proposedDescription: Cryptomeria scale is an armored scale insect that lives beneath the needles of several conifers. Its small protective cover makes an infestation easy to overlook until the upper needle surfaces become yellow and mottled. Heavy feeding can lead to needle loss and weakened branches, with particular concern in nurseries and Christmas-tree plantings. The insect does not roam about once the female has settled; the tiny newly hatched stage, called a crawler, moves to new feeding sites. Old covers can remain after insects die, so visible scales do not automatically mean a tree needs another treatment.
identification: Use a hand lens to inspect the undersides of older, interior needles, beginning on lower branches. Mature females are about 1/20 inch across under rounded whitish covers with yellow centers, giving a small fried-egg appearance. Yellow stippling on the opposite needle surface can guide the search. Elongate hemlock scale, Fiorinia externa, occurs on some of the same hosts and has a more elongated cover; confirmation matters because management differs. Crawlers may appear in two seasonal waves in northeastern accounts, but local timing varies. Photograph both needle surfaces and the scales beside a millimeter ruler. A laboratory can resolve heavily layered or uncertain samples.
actions: Check incoming conifers before planting and keep infested stock from contacting healthy plants. If only one small branch is affected, prune and contain it when doing so will not compromise the tree. Look for live insects rather than reacting to old dry covers, and watch for round exit holes that indicate parasitoid activity. Track crawlers with extension guidance so any necessary treatment targets the exposed moving stage. Avoid unnecessary nitrogen fertilizer on an infested tree. For large trees or continuing needle loss, consult a qualified arborist or extension diagnostician; the undersides of needles must be assessed, and broad spraying can disrupt natural enemies.

proposedDescription: Cuban treefrog is a large Caribbean treefrog that has established populations in parts of the southeastern United States. It climbs plants and buildings using broad toe pads and often shelters in tight spaces during the day. Adults eat insects and other small animals, including native frogs. Warm rains stimulate breeding, and even water held in a bucket or other artificial container can serve as a nursery. Plants, vehicles, and boats can accidentally carry frogs to new places. Its changing color makes identification less simple than matching a photograph of one green or brown individual.
identification: Most individuals encountered are about 1.5–2.5 inches long in body length, although adult females may exceed 6 inches. Look for unusually large toe pads and eyes, warted skin on the back, and often dark bands on the hind legs. Color varies from pale cream to green, gray, or brown. Barking treefrogs and Cope's gray treefrogs are important native lookalikes. Small Cuban treefrogs may show a pale jagged line from the eye toward the rear leg and bluish leg bones visible through the skin. Photograph the back, side, and toes without stretching the animal. Tadpoles are difficult to identify, so uncertain ones need expert review.
actions: Inspect nursery pots, boat compartments, and camper awnings before moving them from an affected area. Empty unused containers that collect rainwater before they become breeding sites, and maintain pools. Reduce unnecessary outdoor lighting that attracts insect prey. Photograph suspected frogs and submit the location to a wildlife or extension program, especially beyond a known established population. If containing a frog for confirmation, avoid bare-skin contact with its secretions and wash hands afterward. Do not relocate it elsewhere. Once identification is certain, follow current wildlife-agency or veterinarian guidance for humane management; household chemicals and improvised killing methods are inappropriate.

proposedDescription: Cuchia swamp eel is an air-breathing freshwater fish native to southern Asia. Its long, brown body resembles an eel, but it belongs to a different fish family and lacks the paired fins of a true eel. It shelters in muddy water and burrows, feeding on small aquatic animals. Live-food imports have provided a pathway into the United States, where established populations have been documented. Recent sources use the name Ophichthys cuchia. Its ability to survive difficult water conditions makes preventing releases important, although the effects of introduced populations remain incompletely studied.
identification: Adults can approach 90 centimeters, or about three feet, long. Look for a tapering, brown body with distinct dark spots, no pectoral fins behind the head, and a single gill opening beneath the throat. The American eel, Anguilla rostrata, has visible pectoral fins. Asian swamp eels in the Monopterus albus group are harder to separate: cuchia has larger, more regular spots and paired air chambers that expand the sides of the head during breathing. Tiny scales near the tail and tooth arrangement require close examination. A photograph of the whole fish and the side and underside of its head can help a fisheries specialist; color alone cannot establish the species, particularly in young animals.
actions: Never release a live cuchia swamp eel bought for food, kept in a container, or caught elsewhere. Do not use it as live bait or transfer it to a backyard pond. Report an unfamiliar finless eel to your state fisheries agency or the USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species program, recording the waterbody, date, and location. Take photographs without entering unsafe water. If a fish is already contained, ask the agency how to handle it rather than moving it to another site. Avoid attempting to drain or chemically treat a pond yourself. Prevention and early reporting are practical landowner contributions while specialists assess an established population.

proposedDescription: Cucumber moth is a warm-climate moth whose caterpillars feed on cucumbers, melons, squash, pumpkins, and related crops. Young larvae scrape leaf tissue; larger ones shelter in folded leaves and may damage flowers or enter fruit. That hidden feeding can make a small caterpillar more consequential than the adult moth first suggests. The species originated in southern Asia and now occurs across many tropical and subtropical regions, including Florida. Infested plants and produce can transport immature stages. Its presence matters most in cucurbit plantings, where watching tender growth and folded leaves can reveal trouble before fruit damage becomes obvious.
identification: The adult has a wingspan of roughly 24–33 millimeters, with broad white wing areas enclosed by a dark brown border. The abdomen ends in a tuft, especially conspicuous in females. Mature caterpillars are about 25 millimeters long, green to yellow-green, with two pale lengthwise lines along the back. Look inside leaves held together with silk, and inspect damaged flowers and small fruit. A pupa may be enclosed in a loose cocoon between leaves. Melonworm, Diaphania hyalinata, is a close lookalike; wing pattern or caterpillar color alone may not settle the identification. Photograph the moth with its wings visible or the caterpillar from above, include its host plant, and seek extension confirmation when a new outbreak is suspected.
actions: Inspect cucumber, melon, and squash plants regularly, especially fresh growth and leaves folded with silk. In a small garden, open those shelters and remove the caterpillars you find; also remove badly damaged fruit that still contains larvae. Check purchased transplants before adding them to the garden, and keep infested plants or fruit from being carried to another growing area. Where practical, insect-excluding covers can reduce entry, but crop pollination needs must still be met. Preserve beneficial insects by avoiding unnecessary broad treatments. If damage continues or the moth is unfamiliar locally, send clear photographs and host details to extension for identification and crop-specific management advice.

proposedDescription: Cultivated garlic is the familiar bulb crop grown for its strongly flavored cloves. It is a perennial plant, although gardeners normally harvest it after one growing season. Each bulb contains several cloves, and an overlooked clove can produce another plant. Hardneck types also make a flowering stem that may carry small bulbs; softneck types usually do not. Garlic can persist around old gardens or appear in moved soil, but a volunteer plant is not by itself evidence of ecological damage. Where it is unwanted, understanding how cloves survive is more useful than simply cutting the leaves.
identification: Look for a clump of long, flat leaves and, when carefully lifted, a bulb divided into cloves under white or purple-tinged papery coverings. Plants commonly stand about one to two feet tall, with taller flowering stems in some types. In contrast, ordinary onion, Allium cepa, has rounded, hollow leaves and generally a single main bulb. Elephant garlic, Allium ampeloprasum, also forms segmented bulbs but is a different species with much larger bulbs. Hardneck garlic produces a firm central stalk, often curling before it straightens; softneck plants may lack that stalk entirely. Photograph a leaf cross-section and an intact bulb if identification is uncertain. Do not assume every onion-scented wild plant is cultivated garlic.
actions: Keep wanted garlic within a defined garden bed and lift bulbs carefully at harvest so that loose cloves are not left behind. Remove unwanted plants with their whole bulbs, checking the soil for separated cloves. Cutting foliage alone leaves the underground growing parts in place. Where a hardneck plant produces small aerial bulbs, remove the stalk before those bulbs scatter. Avoid dumping discarded cloves or bulb-bearing garden waste along fences, streambanks, or woodland edges. Recheck a cleared patch during the next growing season and lift any new shoots. There is no need to remove a contained food crop solely because it appears in an introduced-species catalog.

proposedDescription: Cultivated knotweed is a large perennial also widely called Himalayan or garden knotweed. Long pointed leaves and pinkish flower clusters give it a different appearance from the broad-leaved Japanese knotweed relatives. Beneath the surface, spreading underground stems allow a clump to expand and return after the tops die back. It has escaped ornamental plantings into roadsides, wet ground, and stream corridors, where dense stands can displace other vegetation. Small pieces moved in soil, floodwater, or garden debris can start new plants. That ability makes preventing fragment movement an essential part of any removal effort.
identification: Plants form dense clumps up to about six feet tall. Leaves alternate along the stems and are long, leathery, and lance-shaped, commonly five to twelve inches long, with pointed tips. Branch tips carry clusters of small pinkish flowers later in the growing season. The foliage is the clearest field contrast with Japanese knotweed, Fallopia japonica, and giant knotweed, Fallopia sachalinensis, whose leaves are much broader. Old reddish-brown stems may remain after winter dieback. Photograph a full leaf with scale, its attachment to the stem, and a flowering branch. Regional agency descriptions disagree about whether this species has hollow stems, so that feature should not be used alone to confirm or reject an identification.
actions: Do not mow through a patch or move soil containing its underground stems to a clean area. Mark the patch boundary and check beyond it for new shoots. A very small plant may be dug out if every root and underground stem can be recovered, but broken pieces can regrow. Collect fragments carefully and obtain local disposal advice before transporting them. Larger stands, especially beside water, need a coordinated, multi-season plan with a weed specialist or land manager. Repeated cutting requires sustained follow-up and careful debris handling; one cutting is not control. Restore cleared ground with suitable vegetation and continue checking for returning shoots.
researchNotes: Stem-cavity contradiction explicitly excluded from diagnosis. Alternate scientific combinations supported by NWCB; general knotweed management scoped to fragment control.

claims: Six-foot perennial with long lance leaves and pink flowers; rhizome fragments regrow; small-patch digging and repeated control required.

proposedDescription: Cultivated radish is an annual or biennial vegetable grown in many forms, from small red garden radishes to long white roots and crops harvested for leaves or pods. Plants that escape harvest can send up branching flower stems and set seed along garden edges, roadsides, and disturbed ground. The thick edible root varies greatly among cultivars, so an escaped plant may look unlike a supermarket radish. It is widely recorded outside cultivation in North America. Whether it needs attention depends on where it is growing and whether it is reproducing beyond the intended planting.
identification: Flowering plants can range from roughly four inches to more than four feet tall. Leaves are alternate, often rough-looking and divided into uneven lobes, with a larger end lobe. Flowers have four petals, usually white, pink, or purple, followed by firm pods that do not split open along their length. Wild radish, Raphanus raphanistrum, is a close comparison: its pods usually have strong narrowings between seeds and its root is slender. Cultivated radish generally has thicker pods tapering toward the tip, with little constriction, and a thickened root. These are combinations of features, not a flower-color test. Include mature pods, a lower leaf, and the root in identification photographs when available.
actions: Harvest planted radishes before they bolt if seed production is not wanted. Pull volunteers while young, removing the root, and check the edges of vegetable beds and places where crop waste was dumped. Once pods form, collect the seed-bearing stems before cutting or moving the plants; loose mature pods can carry seed into a new area. Keep cover-crop radish within its planned management schedule rather than allowing unwanted seed production. Recheck disturbed soil for later seedlings and establish cover where repeated bare ground favors weeds. If an unfamiliar radish is spreading into a neighboring field, confirm whether it is cultivated or wild radish before choosing a control program.
researchNotes: Taxonomic treatments differ; retain catalog Raphanus sativus and record cultivated-radish combination separately. Prevention advice derives from seed reproduction.

claims: Cultivated radish annual/biennial; roots variable by cultivar; food forage and cover crop; bolting with age/heat.
Escapes cultivation;10–130cm; four petals; unsplitting pods; wild radish distinguished by constricted pods slender root and usually yellow flowers.

proposedDescription: Cultivated tobacco is a large-leaved member of the nightshade family grown around the world for its leaves. In gardens it may also be kept for its clusters of tubular flowers. It usually behaves as an annual in colder climates, while plants can persist longer where winters are mild. Capsules produce numerous tiny seeds, allowing volunteers to appear near previous plantings. A cultivated or escaped tobacco plant is not automatically an invasive stand. Its more immediate household concern is its poisonous foliage, which should be kept away from children, pets, and grazing animals.
identification: An established plant usually has a sturdy upright stem, broad alternate leaves, and sticky hairs on its green parts. Plants commonly reach several feet tall; some cultivars approach ten feet. Leaves may be up to eighteen inches long and have smooth, unlobed edges. Branched clusters of long tubular flowers appear in summer and fall, often pink with a paler tube, followed by egg-shaped seed capsules. Nicotiana rustica is a named lookalike, usually with shorter, greenish-yellow flowers. Garden tobacco cultivars vary, so neither height nor flower color alone is decisive. Photograph a side view of an open flower, its green outer cup, and how a large leaf meets the stem; seedlings without flowers are harder to assign confidently.
actions: Remove unwanted volunteer plants before their capsules mature, and collect any seed-bearing flower stalks before handling the rest of the plant. Wear gloves and avoid unnecessary contact with sticky foliage; keep the removed material away from children, pets, and livestock. Do not make homemade pest sprays from tobacco leaves. For a plant you intend to keep, remove spent flower clusters if self-seeding is unwanted and inspect nearby bare soil for seedlings. Lift small volunteers with their roots rather than repeatedly trimming their tops. A spreading population outside a garden can be documented for extension, but the presence of a contained cultivated plant alone does not justify broad vegetation treatment.
researchNotes: Independent horticultural and botanical sources support identification. No general ecological impact claim is inferred from cultivation; actions are limited to seed containment and conservative handling of nicotine-bearing material.

claims: Large sticky alternate leaves;3–10ft; tubular summer/fall flowers; capsules many seeds; poisonous nicotine-containing plant.
Glandular hairy upright annual with egg-shaped capsules; N rustica green-yellow flowers; high toxicity.

proposedDescription: Cuming's lovegrass is a small, tuft-forming grass native across parts of Asia and Australia and recorded as a weed in Florida. It grows in open or lightly shaded disturbed places, including lawns, roadsides, and fields. Fine leaves and branched seedheads give it an inconspicuous appearance among other small grasses. It is usually annual, although botanical treatments also describe longer-lived plants. Its many small flower clusters eventually break apart to release seed. A few plants in a lawn and an expanding patch in a natural area present different management questions, so note the setting and extent when recording an occurrence.
identification: Plants range from only a few inches tall to about three feet, with wiry stems that may stand upright or bend near the base. Narrow leaves are generally just a few millimeters wide. The open, branched seedhead bears flattened, many-flowered clusters called spikelets, commonly about four to fifteen millimeters long. Each resembles a tiny stacked row of overlapping scales. Eragrostis brownii is particularly similar; botanical work separates Cuming's lovegrass partly by its very small, nearly rounded pollen-bearing anthers and usually annual habit. Those details need magnification and mature flowering material. A whole-plant photograph can suggest a lovegrass, but a reliable species determination usually needs an intact seedhead and specialist examination.
actions: Confirm the identification before removing an unfamiliar lovegrass from mixed native vegetation. In a garden or maintained verge where a small patch is unwanted, lift the entire tuft while the soil is moist and collect developed seedheads before carrying the plants away. Keep seed-bearing clippings out of clean soil and avoid sharing soil from the patch. Recheck the disturbed spot for new seedlings and maintain suitable ground cover so bare soil does not remain available. Photograph and record an expanding population outside cultivation for a local herbarium or extension office. These are limited containment measures based on its growth and seed production; a species-specific eradication program was not established by the sources reviewed.
researchNotes: Species-level treatment retained; no assignment to an infraspecific taxon. Limited containment inference explicitly distinguished from tested control.

claims: Tufted annual/perennial3–100cm; narrow leaves; flattened many-flowered spikelets; Florida weed; native Asian/Australian range.
Cumingii differs from brownii by minute nearly globose anthers and usually annual habit; occurs lawns fields roadsides; microscopic characters matter.

proposedDescription: Curly Dock is a perennial of pastures, roadsides, gardens, and other disturbed ground. Its long leaves form a low cluster before a tall flower stalk rises above them. Green flowers develop into conspicuous reddish-brown seed clusters that often remain standing after surrounding plants have faded. A substantial taproot lets an established plant return after mowing. Wet ground and excess irrigation can favor it, so repeated top removal may leave the underlying conditions unchanged. In agricultural settings it can compete with desirable plants; in cherry orchards it also hosts a leafhopper involved in spreading X-disease.
identification: Look first at the long, narrow leaves: their edges are strongly wavy, especially on the early rosette, the cluster growing close to the ground. Basal leaves can reach about twelve inches long, while flowering stems often reach three feet. Leaves are hairless, and a thin sheath surrounds the stem at each leaf attachment. Small green flowers become brown, three-sided, winged fruits in dense clusters. Broadleaf dock, Rumex obtusifolius, has much wider leaves; pale dock, Rumex altissimus, has similarly narrow but glossier leaves without the strongly curled margins. Photograph an entire basal leaf and mature fruit clusters. Damaged or very young leaves can obscure the distinction, and closely related docks may require examination of their fruits.
actions: Dig young plants while their roots are still manageable, removing the crown and as much of the thick taproot as possible. Established plants commonly regrow after mowing, so revisit the site rather than assuming a cut stalk means the plant is gone. Remove seed-bearing stalks before they shed and keep them out of clean soil or seed-free compost. Correct unnecessary overwatering where it favors dock, without draining natural wetland habitat. Fill cleared gaps with suitable vegetation and watch for seedlings. For extensive pasture patches or plants near a cherry orchard, consult extension about a site-specific plan that addresses both persistent roots and new seed production.
researchNotes: Flora and extension references support the curly leaves and fruit characters. Manual advice targets the crown and taproot rather than unsupported shallow pulling, with follow-up for regrowth and seedlings.

claims: Rosette leaves12in;3ft stems; wavy dull leaves; pale dock and broadleaf dock distinctions; winged brown fruits.
Perennial seed reproduction; hairless alternate leaves; thick branched taproot.
Wet overirrigated sites favor curly dock; taproot regrows after mowing/discing; deeper cultivation controls; host for X-disease vector.

proposedDescription: Curly plumeless thistle is a Eurasian thistle found in disturbed ground, pastures, roadsides, and fields. It grows as an annual or biennial, producing purple flower heads above spiny stems and leaves. The name is easy to confuse with the much more frequently reported spiny plumeless thistle, Carduus acanthoides. Botanical authorities caution that some North American records of curly plumeless thistle may belong to that other species. A careful identification therefore matters more than assuming that any small-headed, wing-stemmed thistle is this one. Preventing seed production is a reasonable first aim where a confirmed plant is unwanted.
identification: Plants are roughly one to five feet tall, with branching stems edged by narrow, spiny wings. Lower leaves are about four to eight inches long; their edges may be shallowly lobed or merely toothed, with small spines. Purple, occasionally pale, flower heads occur singly or in groups of two to five during summer and early fall. The rounded cup beneath each head is about twelve to seventeen millimeters across. Carduus acanthoides is an especially difficult lookalike, and differences described simply as softer spines or brittle stems are unreliable. Record the lower leaf underside, stem wings, and side view of a mature flower head. A herbarium specialist should examine doubtful material before a precise species record is accepted.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves when working around the spiny stems. For a few confirmed plants in a garden or disturbed area, remove the root crown before flowering and revisit the site for regrowth or seedlings. Collect developed flower heads before moving cut plants so that seed-bearing material is not scattered along the route. Avoid allowing a mature patch to pass through mowing equipment and then moving that equipment into clean ground. Maintain healthy surrounding vegetation and reduce avoidable bare soil. Where the identification is uncertain, obtain confirmation before clearing a larger area; native thistles and other introduced Carduus species require different assessments and may be mixed in the same site.

proposedDescription: Curly-Leaf Pondweed is a rooted underwater plant with leaves that resemble narrow, rippled ribbons. It often starts growing earlier than many native pondweeds and can form dense growth near the water surface in spring. As summer advances, it makes hard resting buds and often dies back. Those buds remain in the sediment and produce later growth, so a summer disappearance does not mean the population has been eliminated. Dense stands may hinder boating or swimming and alter nutrient cycling, although their effects vary among waterbodies. In some degraded waters, the plant also provides habitat that would otherwise be scarce.
identification: Leaves alternate along the stem, remain underwater, and usually measure about one-half to three and one-half inches long. Their edges have small, sharp teeth and often strong waves; young leaves can be flatter but still toothed. Color ranges from olive green to reddish-brown. Small flower spikes rise above the surface, and hard brown resting buds, called turions, resemble tiny prickly cones. Richardson's pondweed, Potamogeton richardsonii, is a native lookalike with broader, more pointed leaves that clasp the stem. White-stemmed pondweed, Potamogeton praelongus, can also cause confusion. A close photograph of the leaf edge and base is more useful than a distant mat. Check early-season plants carefully rather than requiring fully curled leaves.
actions: Inspect boats, trailers, anchors, and fishing equipment before leaving the water, remove attached plants, drain retained water, and dry equipment before visiting another waterbody. Report a newly discovered patch to the local aquatic invasive-species program with its location and close leaf photographs. For an established pond infestation, get advice before raking, cutting, or treating; aquatic work may require authorization and can affect native plants. Early-season removal before resting buds develop can reduce growth, but harvesting alone seldom eliminates the bud supply. Keep collected plants well away from the shoreline so runoff cannot return them. Plan follow-up over several seasons rather than judging success after the normal summer dieback.
researchNotes: Balanced ecosystem effects follow updated Wisconsin account; no blanket eradication promise or pesticide recipe.

proposedDescription: Currant stem girdler is a small metallic beetle whose larvae develop inside currant and gooseberry stems. Feeding tunnels interfere with water movement, causing affected shoots to wilt, weaken, and dry. Repeated attacks can seriously damage a shrub. The beetle is native to Eurasia and was recognized in North America only after specimens previously assigned to a similar species were reexamined. Its scientific name matters: gardening references also use currant stem girdler for the unrelated sawfly Janus integer. A wilted currant shoot therefore provides a reason to investigate, but does not by itself identify Agrilus ribesi.
identification: Adults are slender, metallic gold, green-gold, or copper-colored beetles about four to eight millimeters long. Mature larvae are pale, flattened, legless, and about fourteen millimeters long, with a broadened front end and two small points at the rear. Adults are most likely to be noticed in late spring or early summer; larvae spend much longer concealed in stems. Spiral galleries, localized swelling or darkening, and a D-shaped emergence hole support suspicion. Agrilus cuprescens looks nearly identical but is associated with roses and brambles; head and thorax details require expert examination. Janus integer is a sawfly rather than a beetle. Photograph the host, damaged cane, and any adult from above, and retain diagnostic material as directed by extension.
actions: Inspect currants and gooseberries for individual shoots that wilt while neighboring stems remain healthy. Prune dead or clearly affected canes, examine the cut stem for galleries, and keep suspect material contained rather than moving it with garden waste to another property. Ask extension or a plant diagnostic service how to submit a cane sample and dispose of the remaining material so concealed larvae cannot emerge. Check replacement plants before bringing them into the garden, and monitor nearby Ribes shrubs through the next growing season. Avoid treating every wilted shoot as this beetle: confirmation helps distinguish stem borers, sawflies, and disease before a larger management decision.

proposedDescription: Curtain fig psillid is a tiny sap-feeding insect of ornamental curtain fig, Ficus microcarpa. Colonies gather around tender new shoots, where feeding curls leaves and can stop normal shoot development. White, wool-like wax around the growing tips is often noticed before the insects themselves. Sticky honeydew can also support dark sooty mold on nearby foliage. Native to Asia, this psyllid has established outside its original range, including California and Hawaii. Infested nursery plants provide a practical reason to inspect new figs carefully. The host identity is important because other fig-feeding insects create somewhat similar symptoms.
identification: Adults are only about two to three millimeters long, with a brownish body, a strongly arched back, and clear wings marked with dark spots. Young stages are wingless and live among curled new leaves, producing conspicuous white wax; later stages develop visible brown wing pads. Look for colonies at shoot tips rather than assuming every white deposit is the insect. Homotoma ficus, the fig psyllid of edible fig, has a less strongly arched thorax and conspicuously hairy wing veins. Those details generally require magnification. A photograph of the whole affected shoot and a close side view of an adult help a diagnostician; include the fig species if known. White wax, curled leaves, or sooty mold alone are not a species-level diagnosis.
actions: Inspect new curtain fig plants before purchase or planting, concentrating on tightly curled shoot tips and white wax deposits. Keep a suspect potted plant separate from other figs and avoid moving cuttings or infested shoots to another property. Report an unfamiliar infestation to extension or your state plant-health office with photographs and the plant's source. A small, accessible affected tip can be contained during pruning, but heavy pruning or blanket spraying should wait for a diagnosis and tree-care advice. Check fresh growth after any intervention because hidden immature insects may remain. Preserve predatory insects where possible and ask an arborist for help if repeated shoot dieback is affecting a mature tree.

proposedDescription: Cutleaf blackberry is a vigorous bramble recognized by leaflets cut into narrow, jagged lobes. Its long, arching canes can build dense thickets, and tips that touch the ground may root into new plants. Birds and other animals also spread seeds after eating the fruit. The plant has escaped cultivation in North America and is particularly troublesome in parts of the Pacific Northwest, where it can overtop streamside vegetation. Its black fruit is familiar, but the deeply divided leaves distinguish it from many other blackberries. Removing visible canes alone leaves a substantial root crown capable of sending up replacements.
identification: Look for stout, ridged canes with curved prickles and leaves usually divided into five deeply cut leaflets. The plant can stand more than ten feet high where canes arch over one another, and individual canes may extend much farther. White to pale pink flowers have five petals with notched or lobed tips, followed by black clustered fruits. Himalayan blackberry, Rubus armeniacus, has broader, largely undivided leaflets with toothed edges. Native trailing blackberry, Rubus ursinus, is generally less massive. Photograph a complete compound leaf, its underside, and a section of cane with prickles. Hybridization can produce intermediate plants, so unusual leaf shapes should be checked rather than forced into a simple two-species comparison.
actions: Wear thick gloves, sturdy clothing, and eye protection when cutting through the canes. Start with small outlying plants and work toward the main patch. Cut enough top growth to reach and dig out the root crowns, taking care around desirable roots and unstable streambanks. Keep cut tips and roots off moist soil while they dry, since they can resume growth. Collect fruit-bearing material rather than spreading berries in ordinary garden waste. Repeated cutting can weaken plants, but requires sustained follow-up over several years. Replant cleared ground promptly with suitable vegetation, inspect for new shoots and seedlings, and obtain a restoration plan before opening a large thicket on an eroding bank.
researchNotes: Geographic ecological impacts are scoped to the documented invaded regions. Named lookalikes and hybrid limitations are supported, and repeated removal advice reflects persistent crowns rather than a one-pass eradication claim.

proposedDescription: Cutleaf geranium is a small annual or biennial with hairy stems, finely divided leaves, and modest pink flowers. It grows in disturbed grasslands, gardens, roadsides, orchards, and open woodland. After flowering, its pointed fruits split and scatter seeds nearby; some seeds can remain viable in soil for years. That persistence helps explain why seedlings may return after an apparently thorough cleanup. Introduced from Europe, it is widespread but generally described as a minor wildland weed rather than a uniformly severe invader. In dense local patches it can still compete with smaller plants and complicate restoration or garden maintenance.
identification: The leaves are roughly round in outline but divided into five to seven deep lobes, each cut again into narrow segments. Forked stems and leaves carry hairs, and flowering plants may sprawl or grow upright to about three feet. Small flowers have five pink to violet petals, usually in pairs, followed by a narrow, upright beak-like fruit. Flowering may begin in spring and continue much later in cool, moist conditions. Dovefoot geranium, Geranium molle, has less deeply divided leaves. Carolina geranium, Geranium carolinianum, is similar, but its flower-stalk hairs lack the tiny glands used to distinguish cutleaf geranium. A close view of the leaf and hairs on the flower stalk is more useful than flower color alone, especially before fruit develops.
actions: Pull or dig small patches before flowers develop into seed-bearing beaks, removing the slender root as well as the stems. Work carefully around nearby seedlings and desirable groundcover. Collect fruiting plants without shaking them across a clean area, and inspect shoes, tools, and moved soil for attached debris. Because buried seed can persist for years, revisit the site after later germination periods instead of expecting one cleanup to finish the job. Keep open garden soil mulched or planted where appropriate. Grazing is not a reliable control method for this geranium. For a larger patch in grassland or woodland, confirm the species and plan selective removal that protects surrounding native plants.
