proposedDescription: Cutleaf Teasel spends at least one season as a low cluster of leaves before sending up a tall, prickly flowering stalk. It flowers once and dies, leaving stiff seedheads that can remain conspicuous through winter. The heads contain many seeds, and moving them in dried arrangements or mowing mature stands can spread the plant. Introduced from Eurasia, it can form colonies in roadsides, fields, prairies, and other open habitats. Its large leaves shade the ground, giving later seedlings space around the dying parent. Preventing seed production and removing young plants are central to limiting a patch.
identification: Flowering stems commonly stand two to six feet tall and can be taller on favorable sites. They are ridged and prickly, with opposite leaves that join around the stem to form a cup. The upper leaves are deeply cut into irregular lobes. Dense oval flower heads carry many small white flowers in summer, with stiff pointed bracts beneath them that are shorter than the head. Common teasel, Dipsacus fullonum, usually has purple flowers, unlobed stem leaves, and longer basal bracts. Rare white-flowered common teasel means color alone is insufficient. Photograph the joined leaf bases, the divided upper leaves, and a side view of the flower head; a first-year rosette is less distinctive than a flowering plant.
actions: Dig young rosettes, removing the crown and as much of the deep taproot as practical. Wear gloves and protective clothing around mature stalks. Cut and bag flower heads before seed is dispersed, and contain them before carrying plants through an uninfested area. Do not use collected heads in outdoor decorations or leave mature stems in a brush pile. Check cut plants for renewed growth and inspect the area for seedlings for several years. Avoid mowing after seedheads mature, and clean equipment used in a patch before moving elsewhere. In a prairie or restoration site, prioritize scattered plants at the edge and coordinate larger removal work to protect existing native vegetation.
researchNotes: No burn recommendation or generalized legal claim; flowering-once life cycle explained without jargon.

claims: Rosette before2–6ft stalk; deeply lobed opposite cupped leaves; white flowers; short bracts; dig roots; collect stems.

proposedDescription: Cutleaf vipergrass is a taprooted herb with yellow flower heads and leaves that often divide into narrow, fingerlike lobes. Native to parts of Europe, Asia, and the Canary Islands, it has become established in disturbed ground in several western and central states. It usually lives for one or two growing seasons, although some plants persist longer before flowering. The flower heads open above a low rosette, then develop conspicuous tufts that carry the seeds. Its presence in a field or roadside does not by itself establish that it is causing ecological damage; the size and spread of the patch matter.
identification: Plants are commonly about 10–60 cm tall, with hollow, branching stems and a substantial taproot. Basal leaves can reach 20 cm long and are usually deeply divided, although some are narrow and unlobed. The yellow heads have a long, narrow cup of overlapping green bracts; the flowers project only a short distance beyond it. North American flowering records span May through July. Mature fruits are long and ribbed, with feathery bristles at their tips. Black salsify, Scorzonera hispanica, generally has undivided basal leaves, a distinction used in the Flora of North America key. Photograph both the lowest leaves and the side of a flowering or fruiting head. A yellow flower alone cannot distinguish vipergrass from the many other yellow members of the daisy family.
actions: Check a suspected patch while plants still have flowers and before the feathery seed heads open. For a few unwanted plants in an accessible garden or disturbed field edge, loosen the soil and lift the root crown and taproot with a narrow digging tool. Treat this as small-scale removal, and revisit the spot to check whether plants return. Bag mature heads before handling the stems so seeds are not scattered across the site. Keep seed-bearing material out of soil or yard waste that will be moved elsewhere. Where the plant is widespread in pasture or mixed with valuable vegetation, ask local extension or a weed specialist to help assess the patch and choose an appropriate approach.

proposedDescription: Cutworm moth, Hypena subidalis, is a moth placed in the family Erebidae. The original 1991 report documents specimens from Long Key and Bahia Honda in the Florida Keys; Mississippi State University's resource illustrates museum and specialist specimens. Older scientific names include Hypena pilosalis and Hypena triangularis. The broad name "cutworm" should not be taken as evidence that this particular species is damaging a lawn or crop. A moth seen near a damaged plant may simply be resting there; connecting an adult moth to feeding damage requires identification of the larvae and evidence from the affected plant.
identification: The illustrated reference specimens are labeled 25 mm and 27 mm, useful examples of scale rather than a complete size range for the species. A confident identification needs comparison with authenticated specimens and examination of the wing pattern, not a match based only on overall size or a brown moth silhouette. Take a clear photograph from directly above, showing both forewings, and a second view of the head and resting posture. Include the observation date and location and, if possible, a scale beside the moth without touching its wings. Worn individuals and photographs with hidden wing markings may be impossible to name confidently. A caterpillar cannot be assigned to Hypena subidalis simply because an adult moth was found nearby.
actions: Leave an isolated moth undisturbed while documenting it. If it is indoors, allow it to leave through an open window or gently guide it into a container for release immediately outside, rather than transporting it to another site. Where plants are being damaged, photograph the feeding injury and the insects actually present on the damaged tissue; keep those observations separate from the adult moth record. Ask an extension diagnostic service or a moth specialist whether a specimen is needed and how to submit it. Do not treat a garden on the strength of the catalog common name alone. Any pest-management decision should follow confirmation of the insect responsible for the damage.

proposedDescription: Cyanotis scale is a tiny armored scale insect associated with many kinds of plants, including ornamental Aglaonema, Hoya, and palms. It was described from Cyanotis in Sri Lanka, which explains its common name; it is not restricted to that host. The insect lives beneath a thin, pale cover that can be mistaken for a small blemish or bit of debris. Moving infested plants can carry scales into new collections. Because several armored scales look very similar on a leaf, a photograph may establish that a plant has scale insects without establishing that they are Cyanotis scale.
identification: The female cover is roughly 1 mm across, convex, and often irregularly lobed, with yellow shed skins near its center. It is thin and translucent, whitish to pale yellow-brown, and can incorporate hairs from the host plant. Male covers are smaller and more elongated. Look closely at leaf undersides and photograph several covers beside a millimeter scale, along with the host plant and both leaf surfaces. Coconut scale, Aspidiotus destructor, is especially similar in life. Specialists separate adult females using microscopic features of the rear body plate: in A. excisus, the central lobes sit in a conspicuous recess. That character cannot be judged through an intact scale cover. A diagnostic service may need preserved specimens prepared on microscope slides.
actions: Keep a suspect potted plant apart from other plants and avoid taking cuttings or sharing it until the scale has been identified. Inspect nearby Aglaonema, Hoya, and other plants that touched it, especially the undersides of their leaves. A small, accessible infestation can be documented and infested leaves selectively removed if the plant can tolerate that loss; contain the cut material before carrying it through the collection. Check remaining foliage repeatedly because tiny scales are easy to overlook. Send close photographs and the host name to an extension or plant diagnostic service before selecting a treatment. Do not infer that every pale scale on the plant is this species, or that a remaining cover proves the insect beneath it is alive.

proposedDescription: Cycad aulacaspis scale is an armored scale insect that can seriously injure cycads, including the plants often sold as sago palms. These plants are cycads rather than true palms. Dense infestations form a white crust on leaves, while feeding causes yellowing, browning, and eventual leaf death. The scale can also occupy stems and roots, where it is easily missed during an inspection. Native to Thailand, it was detected in Florida in 1996 and has spread through the movement of infested plants. White covers can remain after the insects die, so a white leaf is not by itself a measure of how many living scales remain.
identification: Female covers are white, roughly pear-shaped or irregular, and about 1.2–1.6 mm long. Male covers are narrow, white, and about 0.5–0.6 mm long. Examine the undersides of leaflets, the base of the leaves, and crevices around the trunk with a hand lens. False oleander scale, Pseudaulacaspis cockerelli, can look similar, but cycad aulacaspis scale females and eggs are generally orange beneath the cover; false oleander scale is yellow. Newly molted females can complicate that comparison, so color alone is insufficient. Photograph the distribution across the plant and a close view of intact covers. A specialist can confirm ambiguous samples. Healthy-looking upper leaf surfaces do not rule out an infestation beneath the leaves or below the soil surface.
actions: Inspect new cycads carefully before purchase and keep a suspect plant separate from the collection. Recheck leaf undersides regularly, including plants nearby, and clean tools before using them on another cycad. Bag severely infested fronds when they are removed and keep them out of home compost. Avoid stripping a plant of healthy foliage: cutting off fronds does not eliminate scales hidden on the stem or roots. Ask extension staff for a current treatment plan suited to the plant and setting, and assess living insects rather than counting old white covers. Continue inspections after apparent improvement because concealed scales can repopulate the leaves. Do not move an infested cycad or give away its offsets.

proposedDescription: Cyclaneusma needle cast is a fungal disease of pines that causes older needles to yellow and fall prematurely. The fungus Cyclaneusma minus affects several pine species, including Scots and Austrian pine. Repeated infection can leave a tree carrying mainly its youngest needles, giving the crown a thin appearance. Spores are released from infected needles still on the tree and from fallen needles, and spread with wind and rain. Symptoms may appear well after infection, making the timing confusing. Normal autumn shedding also removes older pine needles, so yellowing alone is not enough to diagnose this disease.
identification: Look for yellowing needles with brown bands, particularly needles approaching the end of their second growing season. Small, pale fruiting bodies can appear in the discolored tissue; their covers open under moist conditions to reveal a cream-colored spore-producing surface. These structures are only fractions of a millimeter across and usually need magnification. Photograph the whole crown, the distribution of affected needle age classes along a branch, and close views of bands and fruiting bodies. Normal seasonal needle drop and other needle-cast diseases can produce similar thinning. The related fungus Cyclaneusma niveum also occurs on pine needles and requires specialist examination to distinguish. Submit needles with developing symptoms as well as older affected material; a photograph of a bare branch cannot confirm the causal fungus.
actions: Improve air movement around affected pines by managing crowding and nearby weeds where practical, while avoiding damage to roots and bark. Give trees appropriate water during drought and address soil or nutrient problems rather than assuming every thin crown needs fungicide. In a plantation, remove unsalable, heavily diseased trees as part of a wider management plan. Ask a plant diagnostic laboratory to confirm the disease before scheduling any preventive treatment: infection and visible symptoms occur at different times, and treatment cannot restore needles already lost. Record which branches and needle age classes are affected, then compare new growth over subsequent seasons. For a large or declining landscape pine, have an arborist assess the whole tree.

proposedDescription: Cyclopoid copepod, Megacyclops viridis, is a very small freshwater crustacean often found among aquatic plants near shore. It feeds on a range of microscopic organisms and small animals, including mosquito larvae, and is itself food for fish. Records from the Great Lakes have prompted discussion about whether it arrived in ship ballast water or was overlooked as part of a wider northern distribution. Its environmental effects there remain insufficiently understood. This is an animal for careful microscopic study, not something a pond owner can reliably recognize as a moving speck in the water.
identification: Adults are only about 1.2–3 mm long in the USGS account, and size varies with population, season, and sex. Colors can include blue-green and olive, but color does not identify the species. A specialist examines adult females, especially the tiny fifth pair of legs and the paired tail branches and bristles. Megacyclops gigas is a close comparison: M. viridis has shorter tail branches and an inner tail bristle more than twice the length of the outer one. Historical Great Lakes records have also been confused with the Acanthocyclops vernalis complex. A useful submission needs a microscope image with a scale and the collection location, date, and habitat. Young stages usually lack the full set of adult characters needed for confident identification.
actions: Focus on preventing movement between water bodies rather than trying to remove individual copepods. Drain water from boats, bait containers, and other equipment at the place of use, and clean and dry equipment before taking it elsewhere. Do not transfer pond water, aquatic plants, or live plankton to establish a population in another pond. Although this species has been studied as a mosquito predator, introducing it yourself could move other organisms as well. If a specialist identifies it at an unexpected location, share the identification and collection details with the state aquatic invasive species program or USGS reporting system. Avoid treating an entire pond based on an unconfirmed observation of tiny swimming animals.

proposedDescription: Cypress Spurge forms low colonies of upright stems clothed in soft, narrow leaves that resemble miniature conifer branches. Yellow-green floral leaves brighten the stem tips in spring and may turn reddish as they age. This perennial was brought from Europe and nearby western Asia as an ornamental, including for cemetery plantings. It can spread through underground growth and, in fertile populations, seed, allowing a small planting to expand into nearby fields or open ground. Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes, and livestock should not eat it. Established colonies can be difficult to remove because shoots return from surviving underground parts.
identification: Typical plants stand roughly 6–15 inches tall, with branching stems and crowded leaves only about 1–2 mm wide and half an inch to a little over an inch long. The showy yellow-green structures at the tips are bracts surrounding very small flowers, rather than ordinary petals. Flowering is mainly in spring, with timing varying by climate; the bracts can become red later. Leafy spurge, Euphorbia esula, has similar flowers and milky sap but is usually taller and has broader leaves. Photograph a whole shoot, a close view showing leaf width, and the flowering tip. Do not break stems just to test for sap. A young or repeatedly cut plant may lack the usual height and branching pattern, so examine several shoots before deciding.
actions: Wear gloves and eye protection when working around this plant, and keep cut stems away from children, pets, and livestock. Avoid moving soil or root fragments from an infested bed into clean ground, and clean soil from tools and equipment before leaving the patch. Do not rely on mowing or pulling mature shoots to eliminate a colony; extensive underground growth makes those approaches unreliable. Ask local extension or the weed program for a plan suited to the size and setting of the infestation. Contain seed heads and root fragments during disposal. After control work, restore suitable vegetation to bare ground and inspect the area for several years, dealing promptly with new shoots or seedlings.

proposedDescription: Cypressvine is a fast-growing annual climber with finely divided green leaves and small scarlet flowers. Its slender stems twine around nearby supports, making it a familiar garden vine on fences and trellises. Hummingbirds and butterflies visit the tubular flowers, which can continue from early summer until frost. Native to tropical America, it has become naturalized beyond gardens in some parts of the United States. An annual vine can still be persistent in a planting: dry capsules release seeds that produce a new generation the following year. Whether it needs control depends on where it is growing and how readily it escapes the intended space.
identification: Stems can reach about 10–20 feet when supported, but remain thin and flexible. Leaves are cut into many narrow segments along a central axis, creating a much finer outline than the broad leaves of most morning glories. The red flowers are roughly three-quarters of an inch across, with a long tube and a five-pointed, star-shaped opening. Red morning glory, Ipomoea coccinea, has similar flowers but broad, heart-based leaves that may have several large lobes rather than numerous fine divisions. Photograph a complete leaf, the side and face of a flower, and the way the stem wraps around its support. Flower color alone is unreliable among cultivated vines, and hybrids with related morning glories can have intermediate leaf shapes.
actions: If Cypressvine is spreading beyond its intended support, remove unwanted seedlings while they are small and before stems become tangled through other plants. Clip mature vines into manageable sections rather than pulling hard on a shrub or fence covered with growth. Collect developing capsules before they split, and contain any mature seed-bearing material during disposal. Recheck the area the following spring for seedlings from previously shed seed. Avoid giving away seed or soil from a planting that is already difficult to contain. Keep seeds and discarded vines away from pets and livestock. Where it is escaping into a natural area, document the patch and ask the land manager which removal approach best protects surrounding vegetation.

proposedDescription: Daisy (Erigeron sumatrensis) is a tall fleabane with many small flower heads rather than a few large, showy daisies. A leafy stem grows upward before branching into a broad cluster of heads, which later release seeds with fine bristles. Native to Mexico and tropical parts of the Americas, the species has become established in many other regions. It occurs in California and parts of the southeastern United States, where older records sometimes used the names of other fleabanes. It is especially associated with disturbed ground, cultivated places, and roadsides. Confirming its identity matters because several close relatives share the same general appearance.
identification: Plants often approach a meter tall and may reach about 2 m. The stems and leaves are conspicuously hairy; lower leaves are broader and more toothed than the narrow upper leaves. Numerous small heads form a roughly pyramidal cluster, most evident in summer and autumn. The bracts enclosing each head are hairy. Erigeron floribundus differs in having nearly hairless head bracts and generally less hairy foliage. Erigeron bonariensis usually has narrower stem leaves and larger-looking heads; its inner bracts may have purple tips. These differences can be subtle. Photograph the whole branching pattern, lower and upper leaves, and sharply focused head bracts beside a scale. For difficult plants, a botanist should inspect mature heads and the tiny pits left on the head base after fruits detach.
actions: Identify the plant while it still has intact leaves and flower heads, then remove unwanted plants before their seed tufts open. Small plants in garden beds or disturbed soil can be pulled with the root crown when the ground is soft; check the site afterward for missed plants. Bag mature heads before carrying tall plants through the garden so seeds are not shaken loose along the route. Clean seed-bearing debris from tools and avoid shifting contaminated soil to new beds. Keep desirable vegetation established where bare ground repeatedly produces seedlings. If the patch is extensive or mixed with native fleabanes, have a local botanist or extension service confirm the identification before undertaking broad control.

Nesom resolves the US identity conflict and supersedes older conflation with E. floribundus. Conyza albida is deliberately excluded as a synonym; removal advice is conservative annual-weed containment.

claims: Annual to about 2 m; hairy foliage and bracts; pyramidal heads; summer-autumn flowering; E. bonariensis comparison.
US naturalization; hairy bracts distinguish E. sumatrensis from E. floribundus; detailed E. bonariensis comparison; historical misidentifications.
Accepted annual species native Mexico to South Tropical America; Conyza sumatrensis is a synonym.

proposedDescription: Daisy (Glebionis coronaria) is an upright annual with deeply divided leaves and yellow-centered flower heads. Often called crown daisy or garland chrysanthemum, it has been grown as both an ornamental and a leafy vegetable. Plants can escape cultivation into disturbed ground. In parts of coastal California, dense stands occupy dunes, scrub, and streamside habitats and can interfere with the return of native vegetation. That regional experience does not mean every cultivated plant has the same effect. The flowers may be entirely yellow or have white tips, depending on the form and the taxonomic treatment used.
identification: Plants commonly grow about half a meter to a meter tall, with larger individuals reported in favorable conditions. The leaves are divided repeatedly into toothed lobes, and the outer petal-like flowers are about 15–25 mm long. North American flowering records extend from April through July. The leaf surfaces are generally hairless. Yellow chamomile, Cota tinctoria, can look similar but has noticeably hairy leaves and small scales among the flowers on the head base. Photograph the whole plant, a leaf from each part of the stem, and both the face and underside of a head. Record whether the outer flowers are all yellow or white-tipped. Color alone does not settle identification, and white-tipped plants have been treated as a separate species by some botanists.
actions: Where this daisy is escaping cultivation, remove seedlings and small plants before flower heads mature into seed. Work after rain when roots lift more readily, while minimizing disturbance to neighboring plants. Collect mature heads into a bag before moving cut or pulled plants, and do not scatter garden waste along a natural-area boundary. Revisit the site after subsequent rains, when another flush of seedlings may appear. In dense stands, plan removal with the land manager so accumulated dead stems and bare ground are addressed alongside living plants. Reestablish suitable local vegetation where needed. Keep cultivated patches from setting seed if they are close to sensitive habitat, and ask extension staff about alternatives suited to the site.

sources.title: Flora of North America: Glebionis coronaria
California Invasive Plant Council: Glebionis coronaria
Kew POWO: Glebionis coronaria var. discolor

researchNotes: Uses the broad FNA and current Kew species concept, which includes var. discolor; the competing 2017 split is disclosed rather than silently merged. Cal-IPC impact evidence is regional. Manual seed prevention is conservative advice based on annual growth and rain-triggered recruitment, not a quantified eradication protocol.

claims: Deeply divided leaves; yellow sometimes white-tipped rays 15–25 mm; April–July bloom; introduced disturbed-site species.
Annual garden escape; rapid rain-triggered germination; dense coastal stands and persistent litter impede native plants.
Hairless leaves and absence of head scales separate Cota tinctoria; some authors recognize G. discolor.
White-tipped var. discolor retained as synonym of G. coronaria in current backbone.
Upright annual, divided leaves, typical garden height 0.5–1 m.

proposedDescription: Daisy is a small Mediterranean annual with yellow flower heads and a loose rosette of toothed or lobed leaves. The very broad common name can be misleading: this plant belongs to the dandelion-like part of the daisy family, and its heads contain only strap-shaped flowers. It grows in disturbed ground, field margins, and open grassland. As the heads mature, the surrounding bracts harden and curve around some of the fruits. This unusual fruit arrangement offers a much better identification clue than flower color alone.
identification: Plants are often below 8 inches tall, although some reach about 16 inches or more. Leaves vary from nearly whole to deeply divided, and a flowering stem may carry a few smaller leaves. Look for a stalk that thickens immediately beneath a yellow head. Mature heads have hardened, inward-curving bracts; fruits around the edge remain partly enclosed by them, while central fruits have a few coarse bristles. Dandelions and cat's-ears also have yellow strap-shaped flowers, so the flower head alone is insufficient. Photograph the base, the stalk beneath a head, and a mature head from the side. A botanical key may be needed where several similar annual composites occur.
actions: Check the identity before removing a yellow-flowered plant from mixed grassland. In a garden bed or other managed patch where Daisy is unwanted, lift small annual plants before their heads mature and collect any fruiting heads separately. Collect the heads gently so loose fruits do not fall back onto the cleared ground. Avoid shifting soil or mowing equipment carrying mature heads into clean beds. Keep a record of where plants recur and check those spots during the next growing season. On conservation land, ask the site manager to assess abundance and impacts before undertaking broad removal that could disturb other small annual plants.

sources.title: University of the Balearic Islands: Hedypnois rhagadioloides

researchNotes: Australian and Balearic floras corroborate annual habit and diagnostic thickened stalk/fruit structures. No species-specific U.S. impact or treatment trial was located; actions are explicitly cautious seed-prevention reasoning, without a claim of demonstrated control.

claims: Annual often below 20 cm, to about 40 cm; variable leaves.
Marginal fruits enclosed by hardened bracts; central fruits have bristles.
Stalk thickens beneath flower head; small annual with toothed leaves.
Occurs in fields, roadsides, and disturbed places.

proposedDescription: Dallisgrass is a coarse perennial grass that grows in expanding clumps, often standing above the surrounding lawn. Introduced from South America for forage, it also establishes along wet roadsides, ditch banks, and other managed ground. Short underground stems allow an established clump to survive from year to year, while abundant seed helps it reach new sites. In turf, the hard, uneven clumps can interfere with walking and mowing. Its seed heads can also carry an ergot fungus that makes affected material hazardous to livestock.
identification: Unmowed flowering stalks can reach 1–5 feet. The gray-green blades are broad, with a conspicuous central vein, and the base may be purple. A thin membrane sits where each blade meets its sheath. Look for several narrow seed-head branches arranged at different heights along the upper stalk, with rows of flattened, fringed spikelets. Crabgrasses are annuals and lack the short, thick, ringed underground stems of established Dallisgrass. Bahiagrass commonly has a simpler paired seed-head arrangement; young plants are less distinctive. Include the whole clump, a mature seed head, and a close view of the leaf collar when seeking confirmation, rather than relying on a lawn photograph.
actions: Dig young clumps before they develop extensive underground stems or shed seed, removing those stems with the crown. Mowing alone leaves the perennial base alive. Fill cleared lawn patches with appropriate turf so new seedlings have fewer openings, and adjust irrigation to support the desired grass. Clean mower decks after working in infested ground, inspect incoming sod, and avoid using contaminated soil for repairs. Check again through spring and summer for seedlings. Extensive infestations may justify a planned lawn renovation with local extension advice. If seed heads appear diseased in a pasture, seek livestock and forage advice before using that material as feed.
researchNotes: UC supplies detailed prevention and manual-management guidance; Tennessee independently corroborates the perennial clump, underground stems, leaf collar, and seed-head characters. Treatment recipes were deliberately omitted because turf species and product restrictions differ.

claims: Perennial clumps expand by short rhizomes; seed spreads on mowers.
Digging must remove rhizomes; mowing alone fails; fill bare turf.
Seed heads can carry livestock-toxic ergot.
Gray-green perennial with prominent leaf midrib and membranous ligule.
Hairy spikelets occur on alternating seed-head branches.

proposedDescription: Dalmatian Toadflax has yellow snapdragon-like flowers above broad, waxy leaves that clasp its upright stems. This perennial was grown as an ornamental before spreading into roadsides, rangeland, and other open habitats. A patch can expand through an extensive root system as well as by seed, so removing the flowers does not remove the plant. Disturbed or sparsely vegetated ground gives seedlings an opening. Established stands can displace other vegetation, making early detection and protection of healthy surrounding plant cover especially useful.
identification: Stems commonly reach 2–3 feet. The leaves are bluish or grayish green, broad and heart- to egg-shaped, with their bases wrapping around the stem. Yellow flowers have a conspicuous long spur projecting behind the blossom. Yellow toadflax, Linaria vulgaris, has similar flowers but much narrower, pointed leaves; leaf shape is more useful than flower color for separating them. Flowering can extend from late spring into fall where moisture permits, although timing varies with elevation and climate. Photograph a whole flowering stem, the leaf bases, and a flower from the side. Dense patches may contain shoots arising from shared roots, rather than many independent seedlings.
actions: Act on small new patches before they develop a large root system. Mark their boundaries and ask local extension or the weed-control office which measures fit the site; repeated follow-up is usually necessary. Avoid moving infested soil, and clean equipment before leaving a patch. Protect surrounding grasses and other desired plants, since exposed soil favors establishment. Removing flower heads can reduce seed production but will not stop established roots from making new shoots. Do not assume a single mowing or pull has finished the work. For a large infestation, use a coordinated plan that addresses root survival, seedling recruitment, and restoration of competitive vegetation.

sources.title: Colorado State Extension: Biology and Management of the Toadflaxes

researchNotes: Colorado State provides detailed biology and root-driven expansion; Minnesota independently identifies the broad waxy leaves and short-lived perennial habit. Public text avoids transferring Colorado calendar dates or jurisdiction-specific legal requirements nationwide.

claims: Broad clasping leaves distinguish Dalmatian from narrow-leaved yellow toadflax.
Roots produce new shoots; disturbance favors establishment; integrated management needed.
Short-lived perennial with waxy bluish-green leaves and stems.

proposedDescription: Daly river satinash is a tropical tree with glossy, aromatic leaves and clusters of small fruits that become purple to black. It is native across parts of tropical Asia and northern Australia, where it occurs in forests and near freshwater wetlands and streams. Its flower clusters form on older twigs below the leaves, giving the branches a distinctive appearance in bloom. The tree can become substantial, so an escaped seedling and a mature planted specimen present very different management questions. Its presence alone does not establish that it is causing ecological damage.
identification: Mature trees can reach about 15 meters in some floras and considerably taller in others. Leaves are opposite, usually elliptic to oblong, roughly 10–18 centimeters long, with visible side veins and often wavy edges. Bark is brown to gray-brown and may flake. Small flowers appear in branched clusters below the foliage; the bud covering falls away like a lid. Rounded fruits are about 1 centimeter across, with a depressed top and usually one seed. Other Syzygium trees can look similar, so dark fruit and aromatic foliage are not sufficient by themselves. Record leaf arrangement, veins, bud structure, fruit size, and whether the tree was planted.
actions: If Daly river satinash is producing seedlings outside a planting, map where they occur, especially along nearby wet ground or drainage lines. Remove unwanted seedlings while their roots are manageable, and contain fallen fruit during garden cleanup rather than dumping it beside waterways. These are conservative containment steps; they do not establish that every planted tree needs removal. For a large tree, seek a local arborist or land-management assessment before cutting, particularly where roots help stabilize a stream bank. Confirm the identification before choosing replacement planting, and monitor the seedling locations after fruiting to judge whether spread is continuing.

sources.title: CSIRO: Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants—Syzygium nervosum

researchNotes: CSIRO and PROSEA independently support morphology, native range, and habitat. No U.S.-specific invasion impact or tested control protocol was established. Seedling/fruit containment is framed as practical precaution, not evidence of harmfulness or a proven eradication method.

claims: Leaves about 9.6–17.5 cm, often wavy; bark flaky.
Clusters below leaves; globular fruit around 10 mm with one seed.
Tree can reach 40 m; occurs near freshwater swamps and streams.
Native distribution from Asia to northern Australia; fruit red to black.
Flower calyx falls as a lid.

proposedDescription: Damask rose is an old garden hybrid valued for strongly fragrant flowers, usually in shades of pink. Its prickly, open-growing branches and gray-green foliage give it a less compact appearance than many modern bedding roses. Most traditional forms flower in spring or early summer, while Autumn Damask forms can bloom again. Some cultivars have a long history in perfume production. A rose persisting beside an old homesite may be a remnant planting rather than a newly spreading population, and flower color alone cannot establish which old garden rose is present.
identification: Shrubs commonly stand around 5 feet tall and may reach about 7 feet. Stems carry numerous curved prickles and finer bristles. Leaves usually have five or seven toothed leaflets, with grayish hairs beneath. Fragrant flowers occur in loose clusters and are often semi-double, although cultivated forms vary. The long sepals fold backward when flowers open; flower stalks can bear gland-tipped bristles. Rosa gallica is a close relative, and distinctions among old hybrids and cultivars can be difficult. Photograph leaf undersides, stem prickles, flower stalks, and the green structures behind an open flower. A cultivar label or planting history can be as useful as a flower photograph.
actions: First establish whether the rose is an intentional planting, a surviving historic garden shrub, or an unwanted escape. Where removal is appropriate, wear sturdy gloves and eye protection, cut thorny branches into manageable pieces, and lift the accessible crown and roots. Watch the site for renewed shoots rather than assuming pruning has removed the plant. Keep discarded live root material out of natural areas. If preserving a historic rose, document its flowers and growth before major pruning and consult a knowledgeable rose grower. Avoid treating nearby roses solely because they share pink flowers; native species and other garden hybrids need separate identification.

sources.title: Mississippi State Extension: Notes from the Veterans Memorial Rose Garden
Trees and Shrubs Online: Rosa damascena

researchNotes: Mississippi State and the International Dendrology Society account support habit and identification. Sources differ on suckering/rhizomatous behavior, so no categorical spreading mechanism is asserted. Removal advice is conservative woody-shrub practice, not a species-specific eradication trial.

claims: Damask roses often 5 ft, open habit, downy gray-green foliage and thorny shoots.
Most bloom in spring; Autumn Damask repeats; Kazanlik used for perfume.
To 7 ft; five or seven leaflets, curved prickles and bristles.
Fragrant pink clustered flowers, long reflexed sepals; close to R. gallica.

proposedDescription: Dame's rocket moth is a small, slender moth whose caterpillars feed on dame's rocket and related host plants. The larvae can curl or join leaves with silk, and the moth's pale, streaked wings make it easy to overlook when resting on vegetation. It resembles the better-known Diamondback moth, but the two should not be assigned the same crop-pest behavior simply because they look alike. Research in Ontario found two generations in a year and young larvae surviving winter inside the host plant's growing tips.
identification: Adults have a wingspan of about 14–17 millimeters. Look for broad brown lengthwise streaks on a pale brown or whitish forewing and three dark bands near the tip of each antenna. Compared with Diamondback moth, the pattern generally looks more streaked and the adult slightly larger. Larvae on dame's rocket may hide in distorted leaves connected with a little silk; the white cocoon has an open, net-like structure. Host plant and feeding signs are helpful context, but do not prove the species. Photograph an adult closely enough to show the antenna tips, and record the plant on which any caterpillar was actually feeding.
actions: An adult near a porch light does not by itself call for treatment. If caterpillars are damaging a valued plant, inspect folded leaves and confirm both the insect and its host before acting. Removing a few occupied leaves is a reasonable small-scale response; widespread spraying is not justified by a single moth observation. Where dame's rocket itself is being removed as an unwanted escape, contain the cut material rather than transporting live caterpillars and host plants to a new site. Share unusual records with a local moth specialist, including the host, date, and close photographs. Do not assume this species is a substitute target for Diamondback moth control.

sources.title: Smith and Sears: Life history of Plutella porrectella

researchNotes: Guelph research abstract directly supports overwintering and two generations in Ontario; BugGuide supplies adult diagnostic characters from cited literature, and UKmoths adds cocoon observations. No economic-damage threshold or species-specific landowner treatment trial was established.

claims: Two generations annually in study; early larvae overwinter in Hesperis apical buds.
Wingspan 14–17 mm; broad longitudinal streaks and three dark antenna bands.
Larvae feed on Hesperis.
Larvae join or distort leaves with silk; open-mesh white cocoon under leaf.

proposedDescription: Dames rocket is a biennial or short-lived perennial with fragrant clusters of white, pink, or purple flowers. It was brought into gardens from Europe and can spread into woodland edges, roadsides, and open ground through plentiful seed. First-year plants form a leafy rosette; flowering stems rise in a later season. The blossoms attract insects, but the plant can still crowd other vegetation where it escapes. It is often mistaken for native phlox, a confusion that can lead to both accidental planting and removal of the wrong flower.
identification: Flowering plants commonly stand 3–4 feet tall. Each flower has four separate petals, and the lance-shaped leaves alternate along the stem rather than forming opposite pairs. Leaf margins are finely toothed. Phlox flowers have five petals, and common garden and woodland phloxes have opposite leaves with smooth edges. After flowering, Dames rocket develops long, slender seed pods typical of the mustard family. The overwintering rosette is less distinctive than the flowering plant. Check petal number and leaf arrangement together, and include a developing pod in photographs if available. Flower color and fragrance vary and are less dependable than those structural features.
actions: Pull small patches early, preferably while the soil is moist and before seed develops. Collect flowering and fruiting stems for contained disposal because detached material can still contribute seed; follow local disposal guidance. Return to inspect for missed rosettes and new seedlings rather than judging success after one spring visit. Check the ingredients of wildflower seed mixes and avoid adding Dames rocket to restoration plantings. Replace removed patches with appropriate native or other desired vegetation to reduce open soil. For extensive woodland infestations, coordinate with the land manager or extension office so control is timed around sensitive plants and does not damage similar-looking phlox.
researchNotes: Ohio State observations independently corroborate four petals and mustard-type pods; Wisconsin DNR and extension support spread, rosettes, lookalikes, and pulling. Wisconsin sources are treated as one regional evidence group, not inflated as independent confirmations.

claims: Four petals distinguish from five-petaled phlox; long narrow silique fruits.
Biennial or short-lived perennial 3–4 ft; first-year rosettes.
Alternate toothed leaves; prolific seed enables escapes.
Pull early and contain flowering material; distinguish phlox by petals and leaves.

proposedDescription: Dane's blood is a perennial bellflower with tight clusters of upward-facing purple, blue, or sometimes white blooms. The flowers sit together at the top of an upright stem, explaining its more familiar name, clustered bellflower. Native to Europe and parts of temperate Asia, it is widely cultivated in borders and can form expanding clumps through underground stems. Cultivars differ in height and flower color. A garden clump is not automatically a harmful invasion, but seedlings or expanding growth beyond a planting are worth tracking near sensitive habitat.
identification: Plants range roughly from 6 to 28 inches tall, depending on form and conditions. Leaves are simple and alternate, often oval to lance-shaped with rounded teeth and some hairiness. Lower leaves form a rosette. Bell-shaped flowers, about 1.5–4 centimeters long in the horticultural description, gather into rounded terminal groups and sometimes smaller groups at leaf joints. Harebell, Campanula rotundifolia, has much narrower upper leaves and more loosely arranged hanging bells. Flowerless rosettes can be difficult to separate from other bellflowers. Record the flower arrangement, upper and lower leaf shapes, and whether new shoots appear connected to an established clump rather than scattered as seedlings.
actions: To keep a planting contained, cut off spent flower clusters before seed matures and check its edges for expanding shoots. If an unwanted small clump is removed, lift the connected underground stems as carefully as the soil allows, then inspect for regrowth. Do not dump divided plants or garden soil at woodland edges. A maintained ornamental planting can be managed without treating every nearby bellflower as the same species. In a natural area, confirm the identification and extent first, especially where native harebells occur. Replant disturbed gaps with suitable vegetation and revisit them after the next growing season to see whether containment has worked.

sources.title: National Plant Monitoring Scheme: Identification guide

researchNotes: NC State and KPU corroborate size and diagnostic clustered bells; RHS directly recommends cutting after flowering to prevent self-seeding and describes rhizomatous growth. No blanket U.S. ecological-impact claim is made; root removal is conservative containment reasoning.

claims: Clumping perennial 6–24 inches, basal rosette, upward-facing clustered bells.
Alternate oval leaves with rounded teeth; flowers in terminal balls or leaf axils.
Rhizomatous vigorous perennial; cut after flowering to prevent self-seeding.
Harebell has narrow linear upper leaves and hanging bells.

proposedDescription: Dark rover ant is a tiny brown ant that can nest outdoors and enter buildings as workers or winged adults. It feeds on sweet resources such as nectar and honeydew, and may appear around kitchens, bathrooms, irrigated landscaping, and other moist places. Its small size makes it easy to confuse with several other household ants. Infestations can persist because nearby nests or separated parts of a colony may supply more ants after treatment. The main documented household concern is nuisance activity, rather than the conspicuous stings associated with fire ants.
identification: Workers are only about 1–2 millimeters long and reddish to nearly blackish brown. They have relatively large eyes, nine-segmented antennae, and a single waist node that is often hidden beneath the abdomen. Longer upright hairs occur on the abdomen among finer hairs. Brachymyrmex depilis is typically yellowish, but color alone will not distinguish every rover ant. Argentine ants, odorous house ants, and small fire-ant workers can also be confused with this species in casual photographs. A magnified specimen is usually needed to count antenna segments. Collect a few workers in a sealed container for identification and note where they enter or forage.
actions: Reduce accessible sweet food, wipe up spills, and correct leaks or persistently wet areas around the foundation. Check irrigation and heavy mulch close to the building, since excess moisture can favor nesting. Record indoor and outdoor activity so a pest professional can address connected sources rather than only ants on a countertop. Where treatment is needed, labeled ant baits placed at active foraging sites may be part of the plan; keep them inaccessible to children and pets. Do not assume a single spray will remove the colony. Persistent activity deserves a confirmed identification and coordinated follow-up, because nearby nests can reinvade treated rooms.

sources.title: UC IPM: Dark Rover Ant—Current Status in California
University of Florida: Dark Rover Ant
University of Georgia Extension: Insect and Arthropod Pests of Southeastern Neighborhoods: A Guide to Identification and Management

researchNotes:
UF direct fetch looped and its alternate page exceeded extraction limit; substantive indexed content was read. UC direct follow-up returned 403 but indexed article supplied morphology and treatment limitations. UGA gives independently authored practical baiting/vegetation guidance; old California occurrence statements were not reused as current status.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.

claims: Workers 1–2 mm, nine antenna segments, hidden waist node.
Satellite colonies can cause reinvasion and management difficulties.
Nests indoors and outdoors; nuisance workers and alates.
Reducing excess moisture in buildings and nearby mulch may reduce invasion.
Small dark workers can resemble several pest ants.
Bait where foraging and reduce dense vegetation around foundations.

proposedDescription: Darnel ryegrass is an annual grass historically associated with cereal crops and contaminated planting seed. Its upright seed spike can blend into a grain field, and its seeds were once difficult to separate from harvested wheat. Some seed lots carry fungi associated with toxicity, so suspected contamination belongs in a grain or forage assessment rather than a home food experiment. Modern seed cleaning has greatly reduced the plant in some regions. Occasional plants in disturbed ground should therefore be documented without assuming that an old account of severe crop infestation describes local conditions today.
identification: Plants are tufted and commonly around 1–3 feet tall, sometimes taller. Narrow spikelets attach edge-on to a stiff central seed-head stalk. A key feature is the long outer bract, or glume, which is about as long as the spikelet and can extend beyond it. Mature flowering scales become conspicuously plump. Italian ryegrass and perennial ryegrass have a similar overall spike, so a grass specialist should check mature spikelets rather than identify the plant from its leaves alone. Awns, the bristle-like extensions on the flowering scales, vary and may be absent. Photograph the complete spike beside a ruler and a close-up of several mature spikelets.
actions: If Darnel ryegrass is suspected in a cereal field, keep the affected seed or grain separate pending identification and advice from an agronomist or seed laboratory. Do not save visibly contaminated grain for sowing or assume it is suitable for feed. For a few plants outside a crop, collect mature heads into a bag before lifting the annual plants, taking care not to scatter seed. Use clean, appropriately tested planting seed and clean harvesting or mowing equipment before moving to an uninfested area. Recheck the site during the next crop or growing season; prevention of contaminated seed movement is especially relevant to this grass.

sources.title: Kew: Lolium temulentum—Flora of Oman and Flora Zambesiaca

researchNotes: Kew's floras and NSW flora agree on annual habit and long glumes; UW quotes FNA on variable awns and fungus-associated seed toxicity. Victoria documents reduction through modern seed supplies. INRA's conflicting glume wording was not used for diagnosis.

claims: Annual to 120 cm; long glume approaches or exceeds spikelet; mature lemmas plump.
Tufted annual, glume about equal to spikelet; formerly serious cereal weed.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of North America / University of Washington
claims: Awn presence and length vary; contaminated seeds historically caused poisonous flour.
Cereal/flax seed contaminant greatly reduced by modern seed supplies.

proposedDescription: Darwin's berberis is an evergreen shrub with small, glossy, spiny leaves and hanging clusters of orange-yellow flowers. Purple to nearly black berries follow the flowers and can carry its seeds beyond a hedge or garden when birds eat them. Native to Chile and Argentina, it has formed dense colonies in some regions where it was introduced. The combination of sharp spines, shade tolerance, and regrowth after damage can make established patches difficult to manage. Its attractive flowers therefore need to be considered alongside any observed spread into surrounding vegetation.
identification: Shrubs can grow to about 4 meters tall. Leaves are usually only 2–3 centimeters long, dark green and shiny, with sharp teeth that give them a miniature holly-like appearance. Branched spines occur beneath leaf clusters, and young stems may have rusty hairs. Flower clusters hang below the foliage; berries are about 6–9 millimeters long and may have a pale waxy coating. Holly is a common visual comparison, but its branching and fruit clusters differ. Other evergreen barberries and their garden hybrids can overlap in appearance. Include the stem spines, leaf margins, flower cluster, and ripe fruit in an identification record before removing an established ornamental.
actions: Pull or dig small seedlings before they become heavily armed shrubs, taking care around the sharp stem spines. For older plants, arrange a root- and stump-focused removal plan with a local weed specialist; cutting the branches alone may be followed by vigorous regrowth. Contain berry-bearing branches, and check beneath nearby bird perches for seedlings beyond the visible patch. Avoid moving rooted fragments or contaminated garden waste into woodland. Revisit treated ground regularly and restore suitable plant cover in bare areas. Where a population crosses a boundary, coordinating with neighboring landholders will reduce the chance of a cleaned area being reseeded from an untreated hedge.

sources.title: Bay of Plenty Regional Council: Darwin's barberry
NRM South: Weeds of Southern Tasmania

researchNotes: Tasmanian and New Zealand agency evidence supports spines, bird dispersal, thicket formation, and regrowth. Overseas control guidance is used only for biological/manual principles; no overseas regulation or chemical rate is presented as U.S. guidance.

claims: Evergreen shrub to 4 m, small holly-like leaves and branched spines.
Orange drooping flowers, purple berries; coordinate neighboring control.
Bird-dispersed seeds; dense colonies; resprouts after damage.
Replant bare sites following control.
Hand pull small plants.

proposedDescription: Date palm is the familiar cultivated palm that produces dates. Its crown of long, blue-gray feather-shaped leaves can rise high above a stout trunk, while shoots from the base sometimes form a clump. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, so only female palms produce fruit. Cultivated for thousands of years in hot, dry regions, it is also planted ornamentally. Seedlings or basal shoots may need attention where they spread beyond a maintained planting, but the presence of a crop or landscape palm alone does not establish ecological harm.
identification: Mature palms may reach roughly 50–80 feet. Leaves consist of many narrow, stiff leaflets along a central stalk, with sharp spines near the leaf base. The crown is often gray-green, and the trunk retains a pattern of old leaf bases. Large hanging clusters carry elongated yellowish to brown fruit on female plants. Canary Island date palm is a frequent source of confusion; both have feather leaves and spiny bases, so crown color alone is unreliable. Document the whole trunk, basal shoots, leaf arrangement, and mature fruit, with size measurements where safely accessible. Young seedlings and cultivated hybrids may require a palm specialist for confident identification.
actions: Remove unwanted seedlings while they are small, before their leaf-base spines and roots make handling difficult. Collect fallen fruit where seedlings repeatedly appear, and avoid dumping seed-rich fruit waste near waterways or natural habitat. Basal shoots should be assessed separately from seedlings because they are attached to the parent palm. For a tall palm or a dense clump, use a qualified arborist rather than climbing or cutting beneath heavy fronds. Protect eyes and hands from the stiff spines even on small plants. Keep a maintained planting under observation and seek local advice if seedlings are establishing beyond the property or into a sensitive site.

sources.title: University of Florida: Phoenix dactylifera, Date Palm
University of Florida: Ornamental Palms for South Florida
Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Phoenix dactylifera
Elsafy et al.: Phenotypic Diversity of Date Palm Cultivars

researchNotes: UF's species PDF timed out, but its publication abstract and palm tables were readable as indexed content. Independent HortFlora corroborates suckering habit, fruit, and long cultivation. No tested wildland-control protocol or U.S. impact claim is inferred from ornamental presence.

claims: Palm to 80 ft, adapted to dry climates; long-cultivated edible dates.
Blue-green feather leaves, spiny petioles; clumping or single stem.
Suckering palm to 20 m, old leaf bases, gray crown.
Fruit around 6 cm; ancient cultivation; female fruit production can promote spread.
Dioecious palm; feather leaves with basal leaflets modified into spines.

proposedDescription: Day jessamine is an evergreen shrub with glossy leaves and clusters of small, fragrant white flowers. Despite its name, flower scent is not a dependable identification test: accounts differ on when it is strongest. Its dark berries are more useful, and birds can spread their seeds away from planted shrubs. The plant has escaped cultivation and formed thickets in warm regions, including parts of Florida. The berries are poisonous to people and other mammals, so a fragrant garden shrub should not be treated as a source of edible fruit.
identification: Plants commonly reach about 6–8 feet, though floras give a broader range. Leaves are alternate, smooth-edged, elliptic to oblong, glossy above and paler beneath, often around 5–10 centimeters long. Small white to creamy flowers have narrow tubes about 1–1.5 centimeters long and short lobes at their tips. Ripe berries are purple to black. Night jessamine, Cestrum nocturnum, is similar but typically has white ripe berries and longer greenish flowers with more pointed lobes. Photograph fully ripe fruit as well as flowers and leaves; an immature green berry or a report of evening fragrance cannot reliably separate them. Avoid tasting any part for identification.
actions: Hand-pull or dig seedlings and small saplings where practical, especially before they begin producing berries. Collect fruiting branches and fallen berries during removal, and keep the material away from children, pets, and livestock. Look beneath nearby trees and fences where birds may deposit seed. Replace an escaping ornamental with a locally suitable plant instead of moving it to another outdoor site. Large shrubs or a dense thicket may need a professional control plan and follow-up for surviving growth. Do not put the cut foliage or berries into animal feed, and use gloves while collecting material so cleanup remains controlled and berries are not scattered.

proposedDescription: Daylily gall midge is a tiny fly whose larvae develop inside unopened daylily flower buds. Affected buds become unusually short and swollen, then fail to open or rot, while the leaves may remain normal. The damage is chiefly a loss of flowers rather than a decline in the whole plant. Early-flowering varieties are more exposed because their buds coincide with the fly's activity. Mature larvae leave the buds and enter the soil, where they survive until the next season, making prompt removal of affected buds especially useful.
identification: The adult fly is small and seldom noticed; the distorted bud is usually the first clear sign. Split an affected bud over a tray and look for numerous pale, almost transparent maggots up to about 3 millimeters long, sometimes in watery tissue. Compare it with a healthy slender bud on the same plant. A flower that simply failed to open is not enough to identify the midge, since weather and other damage can also affect buds. Photograph both bud forms and the larvae beside a scale. Keep the daylily cultivar and flowering date with the record, and seek extension confirmation for a suspected new occurrence.
actions: Inspect daylilies as soon as buds begin to develop and pick off swollen buds before larvae can drop to the ground. British Columbia guidance recommends freezing collected buds for 48 hours before disposal; do not place unfrozen infested buds in compost. Check nearby daylilies too, since removing buds from only one clump may leave a source close by. Avoid sharing plants with infested soil or intact affected flower stalks. Later-flowering cultivars may suffer less damage, although they are not a substitute for inspection. There is usually no need to discard an otherwise healthy plant solely because a few buds are affected.
researchNotes: British Columbia agency guidance and RHS independently support symptoms, one annual cycle, and early bud removal. American Daylily Society corroborates transport in soil/budded stalks. Older regional pesticide-registration statements are not represented as current nationwide law.

claims: Larvae around 3 mm in swollen buds; one generation, soil overwintering.

proposedDescription: Dead man's fingers is a green seaweed with soft, spongy branches that repeatedly fork like thick fingers. This subspecies has spread beyond its northwest Pacific origin on marine equipment, shellfish, and other transported material. It attaches to hard surfaces, including rock and shells, and fragments can establish elsewhere. Dense growth can overgrow other organisms, including shellfish, although effects vary among sites. The name has changed in much of the literature: records called Codium fragile subsp. tomentosoides commonly refer to the same introduced subspecies treated here.
identification: Fronds are often about 15–30 centimeters tall, with cylindrical green branches roughly 3–10 millimeters thick and a broad, spongy attachment at the base. The surface may look hairy. These features suggest Codium but do not prove the exact subspecies. Confirmation requires magnification of the small outer structures called utricles: in this subspecies they are cylindrical to club-shaped with a pointed tip. Related Codium species and other C. fragile forms can look very similar in shore photographs. Record the branching, attachment surface, depth or tidal position, and location. A marine botanist may request a carefully contained sample for microscopic or genetic examination.
actions: Do not tear apart an unfamiliar attached clump in the water, because fragments can spread and native lookalikes may be present. Photograph and report a suspected new site to the local marine invasive-species program, marina manager, or Sea Grant office. Inspect boats, ropes, fishing gear, and shellfish equipment before moving them between water bodies, and use established cleaning facilities that contain removed fouling material. Dispose of bait-packing seaweed on land according to local guidance, never into the water. Removal from an established bed should be planned with the responsible manager; repeated fragmentation and persistent attachment tissue can make casual hand clearing ineffective.

proposedDescription: Death cap is a mushroom that can cause fatal poisoning if eaten. It grows from a fungus living underground in association with tree roots, so removing visible mushrooms does not remove the whole organism. Caps can be greenish, yellowish, pale brown, or nearly white, and young mushrooms may remain enclosed in a rounded outer covering. The familiar green cap is therefore not a reliable safety test. Cooking, drying, and freezing do not make it safe to eat, and serious poisoning can begin only after a delay.
identification: Mature caps are commonly about 5–15 centimeters across. Look for white gills, a ring or skirt on the stem, and a loose, sac-like cup around the stem base. The cup may be hidden in soil or leaf litter, and the ring may be damaged or poorly developed. Young enclosed buttons have been mistaken for puffballs, while older mushrooms can be confused with paddy straw mushrooms and other pale species. Photograph the cap, underside, full stem, and intact base for an expert; a top-down photo is inadequate. These features are warning signs, not a test that makes an unidentified mushroom safe to consume.
actions: Keep children and pets away from suspected mushrooms. If anyone may have swallowed one, contact a poison center or emergency medical service immediately; do not wait for symptoms. For a pet, contact a veterinarian urgently. Retain a sample or clear photographs if this can be done without delaying care. In a yard, collect fruiting mushrooms into a bag for garbage disposal, wash hands afterward, and inspect again after rain or irrigation. Gloves can keep soil off your hands; touching an intact mushroom is not the same exposure as eating it. Do not use home compost, and report suspected new occurrences to local experts.

proposedDescription: Death's head cockroach is a large tropical cockroach named for the dark, face-like pattern on the shield behind its head. It normally shelters beneath decaying wood and vegetation, and is also kept in insect collections and captivity. Young insects lack the adults' full wings and spend much of their time concealed. Its imposing size and name do not establish that it is a typical kitchen pest. An isolated indoor sighting may involve a transported or escaped animal, so identifying its source matters before planning a household treatment.
identification: Adults are broadly flattened and roughly 5–7 centimeters long, with long antennae and wings extending over or beyond the abdomen. The dark shield behind the head carries paler marks that can resemble a face. Nymphs are wingless and patterned with pale spots rather than looking like miniature winged adults. Other large Blaberus cockroaches, including the Discoid cockroach and B. atropos, can be confused with it; a nickname based on the shield pattern is insufficient. Photograph the shield, the full upper surface, and the side of the insect beside a scale. An entomologist may need the specimen, especially for an immature insect or captive stock of uncertain origin.
actions: Contain an unexpected indoor specimen in a secure, ventilated container for identification rather than releasing it outdoors. Check whether it came from a pet enclosure, feeder-insect container, shipping box, or recently moved material. Repair enclosure gaps and inspect substrate and hiding places for nymphs if captive animals may have escaped. Remove accessible food debris and monitor the immediate area to establish whether this was one insect or a recurring problem. Repeated sightings warrant a pest professional's assessment. Avoid broad indoor spraying on the assumption that every large cockroach behaves like the German cockroach; treatment should follow a confirmed species and evidence of where it is living.
researchNotes: Lithuanian Zoo independently supports adult size, nymphs, diet and burrowing. UCR's historical text supplies morphology and rainforest habitat; its century-old 'only Key West' distribution claim is deliberately not treated as current. Prevention is containment/source tracing, not an unverified species-specific eradication claim.

claims: Adult 5–7 cm; skull-like pronotal pattern; burrows when threatened.

proposedDescription: Deer ked is a flattened, blood-feeding fly that mainly lives on deer and related mammals. Newly emerged adults have wings and search for a host; after settling on one they shed the wings and can look surprisingly tick-like. People often encounter flying adults in fall or find wingless insects while handling deer. Bites can cause persistent skin irritation. Finding microbes in a ked does not by itself prove that it transmits disease to people, and that distinction remains important when interpreting alarming reports about these insects.
identification: Adults are about 5 millimeters long, brown, flattened, and equipped with strong legs extending sideways. A newly emerged insect has one pair of wings; after finding a host, it sheds its wings and remains among the hairs. It has six legs, unlike an adult tick's eight, and can move quickly through fur or across clothing. Other deer keds occur in North America, including the native Lipoptena mazamae, so appearance and a deer association do not always establish L. cervi. Save a specimen and record whether it was flying, on clothing, or on a particular host. Close photographs should show the legs, head, and upper body.
actions: Check clothing and hair after walking through habitat where keds are active, and remove insects promptly. Light-colored clothing may attract fewer keds and makes crawling insects easier to see. Research found common tick repellents unreliable against this species; labeled permethrin-treated clothing may help kill keds that land, although it does not prevent all landings. Follow the clothing product's instructions and do not apply clothing treatments to skin. Hunters should inspect themselves after handling deer because wingless keds can transfer from the carcass. Seek medical advice for a troublesome or persistent bite reaction, and keep a specimen if identification would help.

proposedDescription: Deptford Pink is a slender annual or biennial with small, deep pink flowers dotted with white. Several blooms sit together at the tip of a wiry stem, surrounded by long, pointed green bracts. It grows in open grassland, roadsides, and disturbed ground, and has become established outside its European and Asian range. The plant's status differs greatly by region: it is an introduced wildflower in much of North America but a conservation concern in parts of its native range. A scattered occurrence should be assessed in its local habitat.
identification: Plants often stand about 20–50 centimeters tall, with a basal rosette and narrow opposite leaves along the stem. The small pink flowers have five toothed petals, usually marked with tiny pale dots. Hairy, pointed bracts surround the clustered flowers, and each flower sits above a long, narrow tubular calyx. Sweet William, Dianthus barbatus, can look similar but generally has larger, broader-leaved growth and larger flower clusters. Centaury may share the pink color but lacks the characteristic dotted, toothed petals and hairy surrounding bracts. Photograph the flower face, the side of the flower cluster, and leaf pairs; the thin leaves alone can be overlooked among grasses.
actions: Where Deptford Pink is unwanted in a managed bed, lift small plants before their capsules mature and collect any seed-bearing stems. This annual or biennial is best addressed by interrupting seed production, rather than treating the visible flowers as an isolated event. Avoid carrying mature capsules in mown material or garden waste to another site. In species-rich grassland, confirm the identification and discuss priorities with the land manager before broad removal, since disturbance can harm neighboring plants and create more open ground. Recheck the patch over subsequent seasons, recording whether numbers increase, remain scattered, or disappear as the surrounding vegetation closes.

proposedDescription: Dermestid beetle here refers specifically to Phradonoma nobile, a small patterned beetle in the same family as carpet beetles. The common name covers a much larger family and does not identify this species by itself. Published records include stored-grain environments and associations with insect material, but those observations do not establish that every household sighting represents a damaging infestation. A 2009 Arizona specimen formed the basis of the first published North American record. Correct identification is particularly useful when an unfamiliar dermestid appears in stored goods or a collection.
identification: An adult illustrated in the North American report measured 2.8 millimeters long; that single measurement is not a complete size range. The dark wing covers have two or three reddish cross-bands, with pale hairs over the lighter areas. Antennae and legs are reddish to brown. Closely related Phradonoma and Trogoderma beetles can be difficult to separate. A specialist checks structures such as spines along the front lower legs and details of the antennae and their grooves, not just the band pattern. Preserve an intact adult and photograph it under magnification from above and below. Larvae need a separate key and should not be assigned this species from hairiness alone.
actions: If found in stored food, dried biological material, or an insect collection, isolate the affected item in a sealed container and check nearby material for additional beetles, larvae, or shed skins. Keep a specimen and the exact source material available for an extension entomologist or diagnostic laboratory. Do not move potentially infested goods to another building before checking them. Routine cleaning of spilled dry material and protected storage can reduce opportunities for many dermestids, but confirmation should guide any more extensive treatment. One adult outdoors does not justify spraying a property, and a family-level carpet-beetle label is insufficient to select a species-specific response.

proposedDescription: Desert knapweed is a winter annual that starts as a low rosette and later sends up branching stems with small pink, purple or whitish flower heads. Plants can reach about five feet, but dry conditions may produce flowering plants only a few inches tall. That size difference makes small plants easy to miss. Desert knapweed can produce thousands of seeds, and California observations indicate that seeds remain viable in soil for at least five years. Its ability to grow in dry, sparsely vegetated ground makes early detection especially useful around desert roads, disturbed ground and nearby natural areas.
identification: Look for a rosette followed by branching upright stems, with narrow wings running along the lower flowering stems. Each flower head is roughly half an inch across and tall. The small florets may be inconspicuous, making some heads appear to have no petals. The head's base is hairy and surrounded by overlapping bracts tipped with short, pointed, light brown spines. Examine both large plants and very short flowering individuals after winter rain. Desert knapweed was initially misidentified in California as Volutaria canariensis; that name should not automatically be treated as a synonym. A regional flora or specialist may need flowers and mature fruits to confirm the species. Record the rosette, stem wings, bracts and location rather than relying on flower color alone.
actions: Mark the edge of a suspected patch and arrange identification before seed heads are moved. Where removal is appropriate, pull small plants before they flower and collect any developing heads so seeds are not scattered. Work from isolated plants toward the main patch, and clean soil and plant material from footwear, vehicles and tools before leaving. Revisit after further rain: germination can be staggered, so a single visit can miss later plants. Keep checking the site for several years because the seed bank lasts beyond one growing season. Report an unfamiliar desert infestation to the local weed program, especially where it is close to roads or undisturbed habitat.
researchNotes: California records were historically confused with V. canariensis; the draft preserves that distinction rather than listing it as a synonym. Seed persistence comes from field observations in the UC assessment, not a universal experimentally established limit. Removal guidance is supported by the California containment project; repeated follow-up is necessary.

proposedDescription: Desert wheatgrass is a long-lived grass introduced for forage and soil protection in dry rangelands. It grows in dense bunches, usually one to three feet tall, and begins growth during the cool part of the year. Its narrow, flattened seed heads distinguish it from many grasses with open, branching flower clusters. Desert wheatgrass tolerates drought and grazing, qualities that made it useful in planted pastures. Those same qualities can make it difficult to combine with less competitive native plants. Whether a stand needs management depends on the site's purpose: a seeded grazing field presents different choices from a native grassland restoration.
identification: Desert wheatgrass has flat leaves about 2–6 millimeters wide, generally smooth beneath and rougher above. Mature spikes are about 2.5–8 centimeters long and 5–9 millimeters wide, with closely arranged, flattened spikelets angled outward from the central stem. The small flowering parts can carry short bristle tips. Crested wheatgrass, Agropyron cristatum, generally has shorter, broader spikes with spikelets spreading at wider angles; Siberian wheatgrass, Agropyron fragile, has a narrower spike with more ascending, usually unawned spikelets. These distinctions require a mature seed head. Desert wheatgrass crosses with crested wheatgrass, and some planted varieties are hybrids, so a photograph of a leafy clump alone cannot reliably establish the exact species. Retain the seed mix or cultivar record when available.
actions: First establish whether the grass was deliberately planted for grazing or erosion protection. Avoid removing a large stand without a replacement cover plan, especially on dry or erodible ground. Near a native restoration, stop adding seed and check roadsides, soil stockpiles and adjacent ground for new clumps. Small, confirmed outliers can be dug with their crowns and roots, followed by checks for surviving growth and seedlings. Larger conversions need a local range or restoration adviser because competition, rainfall and replacement species affect success. Keep records of seeded cultivars so later surveys can distinguish planted hybrids from confidently identified Desert wheatgrass.
researchNotes:
USDA NRCS and USFS material supports morphology, planted uses, competition and hybridization. The unavailable Utah State compilation is not counted as independent corroboration. Manual outlier removal is a conservative inference, not a cited species-specific eradication trial. Taxonomic treatments sometimes combine A. desertorum with A. cristatum; mature material and planting records matter.
