proposedDescription: Destructive trailing ant is a very small ant also known as Singapore ant. Workers are pale brown to reddish yellow, with a distinctly darker rear section of the body. Their slow trails may lead to food, cracks or concealed indoor nests. The name reflects a particular household concern: colonies can occupy electrical equipment and damage wiring. Destructive trailing ant is now commonly placed in the genus Trichomyrmex, so searches under both scientific names are useful. Color and size provide an initial clue, but other small indoor ants look similar; a confirmed identification is helpful before choosing a control approach.
identification: Workers are approximately 1.5–3 millimeters long, with a yellowish or light brown head and middle body and a darker abdomen. Under magnification, the antennae have twelve segments, and two small nodes connect the middle body to the abdomen. Published identification keys describe the head and middle body as relatively smooth and shiny. Pharaoh ant, Monomorium pharaonis, is a useful comparison: it is also tiny and yellowish, but its head and middle body have more conspicuous fine surface texture in specialist keys. These are microscope characters, not dependable distinctions from a distant trail photograph. Collect several workers in a closed vial for an identification service, and record where trails enter walls or equipment. Avoid opening energized equipment to obtain a sample.
actions: Remove accessible food residues, keep animal food in closed containers and follow trails to learn where ants are entering. Check stored goods and movable equipment before taking them to another building. Have a pest professional identify the ant and choose a bait-based plan suited to the colony and food preferences; wiping away one trail does not locate every nest. If activity involves an outlet, appliance or damaged wiring, keep people away from the affected equipment and arrange an electrician's inspection. Do not spray liquid or insecticide into electrical fittings. Monitor the same routes after treatment and report continuing activity so the plan can be adjusted.

proposedDescription: Devil weed is a large brown seaweed native to waters around Japan and Korea that has become established along parts of the eastern Pacific coast. It attaches to hard surfaces, including rock, docks and boats. Young plants have a compact, fernlike appearance; older plants develop long branching stems and gas-filled floats that hold them in the water. Detached, buoyant plants can travel and remain capable of reproduction, making boat gear and drifting material important pathways. Research is still examining how Devil weed affects different marine communities. Its presence does not mean every nearby native seaweed is being displaced in the same way.
identification: Young Devil weed has flattened, regularly arranged blades with conspicuous notches, giving it a fernlike outline. Mature plants become loosely branched and may reach several meters long; guides commonly give about 3–5 meters. Look for the main stem, blade edges and small gas-filled floats, whose shape can range from rounded or oval to more elongated. Float shape alone is not a dependable identification test. The name Sargassum filicinum appears in older regional guides for material now included in Sargassum horneri. Other Sargassum species can look similar, particularly after blades are damaged or lost, so compare intact young and mature portions with a regional marine identification guide. Record whether the plant is attached or drifting, along with depth and the kind of surface beneath it.
actions: Leave an unfamiliar attached patch in place while you document and report it to a local marine monitoring program. Pulling plants without a coordinated plan can release reproductive material and damage the surrounding community. Before leaving a site, inspect anchors, lines, diving equipment and boat fittings for attached fragments; collect hitchhiking material for contained disposal rather than releasing it at the next harbor. Record the location, depth, approximate patch size and whether young or mature plants are present. Established populations can be difficult to remove completely, so prevention and early reporting are useful even where large-scale eradication is unrealistic. Follow local marine staff's instructions for any organized removal.

proposedDescription: Devil's backbone is a succulent whose leaf edges carry rows of tiny plantlets. Each plantlet can develop roots, drop to the ground and begin a new plant, which explains why it can spread beyond a pot without flowering. The upright stems bear broad, pointed leaves often marked with purple beneath, and mature plants may produce hanging pink or lavender flowers. Devil's backbone comes from Madagascar and is grown as an ornamental. It is easily confused with related plants sold under the same common names, especially a hybrid with narrower leaves. All parts should be kept away from animals and children who might eat them.
identification: Look for opposite pairs of thick, triangular to lance-shaped leaves with toothed margins and plantlets sitting in the marginal notches. Leaves can be large—often more than ten centimeters long and several centimeters wide—with purple blotches underneath. Plants may reach roughly a meter, although container-grown specimens can be smaller. Flower clusters rise above the foliage and carry drooping, bell-shaped pink to lavender flowers. Mother of millions, Kalanchoe delagoensis, has much narrower, nearly cylindrical leaves with plantlets concentrated toward the ends. Kalanchoe × houghtonii, a frequent source of mistaken records, has narrower, boat-shaped leaves than typical Devil's backbone. Measure a mature leaf and show its base, underside and full margin when seeking identification. Common-name labels alone do not establish which plant is present.
actions: Keep Devil's backbone in a place where fallen plantlets can be collected, such as a pot standing on a tray rather than directly over garden soil. Check nearby pots and cracks for new plants before moving or sharing containers. For a small unwanted plant, lift it carefully and gather loose leaves and plantlets at the same time; contain the material so pieces cannot fall into another growing area. Do not dump it in garden waste beside natural vegetation. Continue checking after removal because tiny plantlets are easy to overlook. Keep plants and discarded pieces away from livestock, pets and children. Confirm the species or hybrid before applying advice based on a regional weed listing.
researchNotes:
Flora of North America explicitly notes confusion with the hybrid; the profile gives supported leaf distinctions without transferring the hybrid's regional impact claims. NC State corroborates morphology and Madagascan origin. Containment recommendations follow the documented plantlet mechanism; no exact-species eradication trial or unsupported legal status is claimed.

proposedDescription: Devil's horsewhip is a variable herb with opposite leaves and long, narrow flower spikes. The small flowers are inconspicuous, but their stiff, pointed coverings become memorable when they catch on clothing or animal fur. Plants may live for one season or persist longer, sometimes developing a woody base. Devil's horsewhip occurs across warm regions of the world in disturbed ground and other habitats. The species includes several varieties with different histories and ranges, so a species-level record alone does not establish that a particular population is introduced or harmful. Mature flowers help resolve that finer identification.
identification: Plants commonly stand about 0.4–2 meters tall, with hairy stems and paired, oval to rounded leaves. The terminal spikes may reach about 30 centimeters; flowers become more widely separated along the lower part as the spike lengthens. Examine the stiff, pointed bracteoles surrounding each flower and fruit. Within Devil's horsewhip, the typical variety has relatively blunt leaves and flower coverings about 3–4 millimeters long, while variety pubescens has pointed leaves and longer coverings, about 6–7 millimeters. Japanese chaff flower, Achyranthes japonica, can resemble it, but a specialist key separates them using the edges of tiny structures between the stamens. Leaf shape or a burr-covered spike alone is insufficient for that distinction. A flowering piece with mature leaves is particularly useful for identification.
actions: Check the local identity and origin of a population before deciding that it needs removal, especially where variety pubescens may be native. Keep the hooked fruiting parts from traveling: inspect clothing, pets' coats and tools after passing through mature plants, and collect attached material for contained disposal. In a garden where a confirmed plant is unwanted, remove it before the spikes mature, taking the root crown rather than only breaking off the stem. Bag developed spikes before carrying the plant through other beds. Revisit the disturbed spot for seedlings and surviving growth. For a spreading patch in natural vegetation, seek a local botanical or land-management assessment before broad clearing.
researchNotes:
FNA supports the variable species concept and key characters; the Australian flora independently confirms habit and mature rigid flower coverings. CONABIO documents attachment to clothing and animals. The draft avoids treating every variety as alien and labels root-crown removal as practical garden containment, not a tested eradication protocol.

proposedDescription: Devil's horsewhip variety pubescens is the pointed-leaved form of a plant best recognized by its long, prickly flower spikes. Its flowers are small, but noticeably longer than those of the typical variety when examined closely. The name pubescens refers to hairiness, although hair alone is not a reliable way to recognize it. Kew treats this variety as native from southern Florida and the Caribbean into parts of tropical America, and introduced in Maryland and Texas. That regional distinction matters: finding Devil's horsewhip does not by itself justify removing a plant from natural vegetation.
identification: Use both mature leaves and flowers to identify this variety. Flora of North America describes elliptic to broadly egg-shaped leaves about 4–20 centimeters long and 2–5 centimeters wide, tapering to a distinct point. The flower coverings are about 6–7 millimeters long, compared with about 3–4 millimeters in the typical variety, which has rounder, blunt-tipped leaves. The Colombian treatment independently describes pointed, hairy leaves and similarly long flowers. The broader species can reach approximately two meters, but height does not separate its varieties. Older publications sometimes applied the name variety aspera to the long-flowered plant now called pubescens, so an old label needs checking against its description. A close view with a scale is more useful than relying on the amount of hair.
actions: Start with a botanical identification and local range check, particularly in southern Florida, where this variety is treated as native. Leave plants in natural habitat unless there is a site-specific reason to manage them. Around a path or garden where prickly spikes are unwanted, prevent seed movement by collecting mature spikes before cutting or lifting plants. Check trousers, footwear and animal coats for attached fruiting parts after working nearby. If removal is appropriate, lift the small plant's root crown and inspect the spot later for surviving growth or seedlings. Avoid transferring soil or seed-bearing cuttings to another property. These containment steps do not depend on assuming that the variety is invasive.

proposedDescription: Deviltree is a tropical evergreen tree with a straight trunk, leaves arranged in groups around the twigs, and clusters of small white flowers. Its long, slender fruits release small hairy seeds that can be carried by wind. Deviltree has been planted for timber and landscaping outside its Asian range, and seedlings can appear away from planted trees. Regional assessments differ: some Florida resources identify it as an invasive concern, while an older university assessment records limited documented problems and a reassessment in progress. Local observations of escape and regeneration are therefore more useful than assuming every planted tree has the same impact.
identification: Deviltree can grow into a large tree, roughly 30 meters tall or more, with smooth gray to brown bark and small buttresses at the trunk base. Leaves usually occur in whorls of four, sometimes three on flowering twigs, and feel papery or somewhat rough. Small fragrant white flowers form at branch tips. The narrow, smooth fruits are roughly 20–40 centimeters long and only a few millimeters across; opened fruits reveal the hairy seeds. Alstonia scholaris shares the common name devil tree and can be confused with it. NParks distinguishes Deviltree by its smaller buttresses and the absence of a small stipule at the leaf-stalk base; flower buds also differ in the direction their petals overlap. Show a complete leaf whorl and fruit, not only the trunk.
actions: Check beneath and downwind of planted Deviltree for seedlings, including in nearby unmanaged ground. Remove confidently identified seedlings while their roots are small, and revisit the area after the parent tree fruits. Avoid planting additional trees where local land managers have documented escape. If a mature tree is supplying seedlings to sensitive habitat, have an arborist or restoration professional assess removal and follow-up before cutting it. Large-tree work and any stump treatment require a site-specific plan; simply felling a tree should not be presented as guaranteed control. Record naturally established saplings separately from planted trees when reporting a population, because that distinction helps assess local spread.
researchNotes: USF and NParks independently support morphology and seed dispersal. UF/IFAS assessment language conflicts with the USF invasive listing and has an incomplete southern reassessment; the draft explicitly avoids resolving that policy discrepancy as a biological certainty. Seedling removal is supported by USF; pesticide rates there are deliberately omitted.

proposedDescription: Diamond burbark is a hairy herb or small shrub with yellow flowers and round fruits covered in hooked spines. Its lower leaves often have three shallow lobes, while the smaller upper leaves can be much narrower. That change in leaf shape on a single plant can make it look more variable than expected. Diamond burbark grows in disturbed tropical and subtropical places, including roadsides, and has become established outside its original range. The burrs are its most practical recognition feature: they can cling to clothing and carry seeds away from the parent plant.
identification: Look for erect, branching stems and alternate leaves with toothed edges. Lower leaves are commonly broad, diamond-shaped or egg-shaped and shallowly three-lobed; upper leaves are smaller and often unlobed. A hand lens shows star-shaped hairs, especially beneath the leaves. Plants often reach about one to two meters, though they can flower when smaller. Small yellow flowers are followed by nearly round burrs with hooked spines; measurements differ depending on whether the spines are included. Triumfetta pentandra is a close lookalike: specialist keys distinguish its five stamens from the roughly 10–15 in Diamond burbark, along with differences in fruit hairs. Urena lobata can have similar lobed leaves but larger pink to mauve flowers. Mature fruits and an open flower are more diagnostic than leaves alone.
actions: Prevent burrs from hitchhiking on clothing, animal coats and equipment when moving between sites. Collect them where they were picked up rather than dropping them along another path. In a garden or small disturbed patch where removal is appropriate, work before fruits mature; if burrs are already present, enclose the fruiting branches before lifting or cutting the plant. Check for surviving stems and new seedlings afterward. Avoid dragging fruiting branches through clean ground or putting them in an open pile beside natural habitat. Larger patches mixed with desirable plants need selective work and local advice, because broad clearing can expose more soil and damage the vegetation you want to retain.
researchNotes:
FNA, JCU and the Australian rainforest key corroborate the species, variable leaves and fruit characters. Habits and fruit dimensions vary among regional treatments, so the prose avoids a false single burr-size standard. Containment follows hooked-fruit dispersal; no species-specific manual eradication trial or nationwide U.S. impact claim is asserted.

proposedDescription: Diamondback moth is a small moth whose caterpillars feed on cabbage-family plants, including broccoli, kale and many mustards. The caterpillars often feed from beneath a leaf, leaving thin, translucent patches before larger holes develop. Despite their small size, numerous larvae can damage seedlings and spoil developing heads. Adult moths usually show a pale zigzag band that forms diamond-like marks when the wings are folded. Diamondback moth can arrive on infested transplants as well as by adult movement. It has developed resistance to many insecticides, making careful scouting, exclusion and protection of natural enemies especially valuable.
identification: Adults are slender, grayish brown moths with long forward-pointing antennae and a wingspan commonly around half an inch. The pale marks along the folded wings often form three diamonds, but their clarity varies. Mature caterpillars are pale green and roughly 8–11 millimeters long, tapering at both ends. The rear pair of fleshy legs projects into a conspicuous V when viewed from above. Disturbed larvae wriggle vigorously and may drop on a silk thread. Look under leaves for these larvae and loose, open silk cocoons. Imported cabbageworm and cabbage looper also attack these crops, but mature Diamondback moth larvae are smaller; the V-shaped rear legs help distinguish them. Feeding holes alone do not identify the pest. Check the larva and host together, especially on unfamiliar plants.
actions: Inspect cabbage-family transplants before planting, then check leaf undersides and growing points regularly for larvae, cocoons and fresh feeding damage. Handpick caterpillars in a small garden. Cover clean plantings with insect mesh or row cover, supported above leaves and secured at the edges so moths cannot lay eggs through gaps or against the mesh. Remove spent crop debris after harvest and watch nearby mustard weeds that may support larvae. Preserve parasitic wasps and other natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary sprays. If damage continues, consult local extension guidance for the crop and pest stage; resistance means repeated use of the same insecticide approach may fail. Adult trap counts alone do not measure the larvae damaging a crop.

proposedDescription: Diatom, in this entry, means Stephanodiscus binderanus, a microscopic freshwater alga with a silica shell. Its round cells can join into chains and drift in the water. It can become abundant in nutrient-rich conditions, and historical blooms have clogged water-treatment equipment and affected water's taste or smell. Its North American origin is less straightforward than older invasive-species lists suggest. Researchers found its remains in Lake Simcoe sediments dating to the late seventeenth century, challenging the idea that it arrived on the continent only during twentieth-century shipping. Abundance and water-quality effects should therefore be assessed separately from assumptions about introduction.
identification: Individual cells are only about 6–12 micrometers across, far too small for a shoreline photograph to identify. Under a microscope, the shell looks circular from above and barrel-shaped from the side. Neighboring cells can link face to face in chains through small marginal spines. The flat face has radiating rows of tiny pores and a faint central ring; specialist examination also checks the deep side wall and the arrangement of microscopic openings. Other round, chain-forming diatoms can look similar at low magnification. A water sample needs examination by a diatom specialist, with appropriate preparation and sometimes electron microscopy. Brownish water, odor or a clogged filter cannot by themselves distinguish this species from other algae or sediment.
actions: Report persistent taste, odor or filter problems to the water supplier or lake-management office and describe when and where they occur. Ask for a plankton assessment before assigning the problem to this Diatom; a species name requires microscopy. Around a shoreline property, keep fertilizer, soil and other nutrient-rich runoff out of the water and follow the watershed's nutrient-management plan. These steps address conditions associated with blooms without claiming to eliminate one microscopic species. Drain water from boats and equipment before moving between water bodies. Avoid adding an algaecide simply because the water looks brown: treatment decisions need a confirmed cause and a water-use assessment.

proposedDescription: Diffuse Knapweed begins as a low rosette and develops a branching flowering stem, often about one to two feet tall. Small heads usually carry white flowers, although purplish flowers also occur. The name refers to its spreading arrangement of branches, which can give a mature plant a rounded outline. Diffuse Knapweed reproduces by seed and can spread through disturbed grasslands and roadsides, particularly where competing vegetation is sparse. Preventing seed production is therefore central to management. Plants may flower in their first year, live for two years, or persist a little longer, so a fixed two-year schedule can miss some individuals.
identification: Rosette and lower stem leaves are deeply divided into narrow sections and covered with short hairs. Leaves become smaller and less divided higher on the stem. At each branch tip, examine the overlapping bracts beneath the flower head: their edges have comb-like teeth and the tip extends into a conspicuous slender spine. Spotted knapweed, Centaurea stoebe, generally has dark-tipped, fringed bracts without that long terminal spine. Color is less reliable because Diffuse Knapweed can have dark bract tips or purplish flowers too. The two species also hybridize, producing intermediate plants. Photograph the side of several mature heads and retain the rosette-to-stem leaf pattern. A distant view of white flowers is insufficient to separate Diffuse Knapweed from other knapweeds.
actions: Pull or dig scattered plants while the soil is moist, removing the root crown and avoiding unnecessary disturbance of surrounding grasses. Work before seed set; enclose and collect developed flower heads if plants are already reproductive. A broken stem or shallowly cut crown may regrow, so revisit treated plants and later-emerging rosettes. Repeated removal over several years can substantially reduce a patch. Keep desirable ground cover healthy, repair bare areas with appropriate vegetation and use clean seed or weed-free hay when bringing material onto the site. Check equipment after working in an infestation. Larger patches benefit from a coordinated local weed-management plan with follow-up, because removing standing plants does not remove the existing seed supply.
researchNotes: CSU supplies morphology and variable life span; the independent Forest Service review supports crown removal, seed prevention and multi-year follow-up. The draft does not repeat disputed allelopathy claims or promise one-pass control. Hybridization limits visual identification, especially where bract tips are dark.

proposedDescription: Diffuse-spotted knapweed hybrid results from crosses between Diffuse Knapweed and spotted knapweed. It is fertile, so finding a plant with mixed features does not mean it is a reproductive dead end. The hybrid can combine the branching habit of Diffuse Knapweed with darker flower-head bracts associated with spotted knapweed. Flowers may be white or purple, and individual plants vary considerably. Researchers have documented hybrid traits and genetic evidence in North American populations. That variation is useful to recognize in the field, but it also means an intermediate-looking plant needs closer examination before it is assigned this hybrid name.
identification: Examine several flower heads, mature fruits and the leaves on the same plant. Diffuse-spotted knapweed hybrid commonly has deeply divided gray-green leaves and much-branched stems. The head bracts can have a darkened tip with long marginal bristles, and their terminal projection may be shorter than in Diffuse Knapweed but longer than in spotted knapweed. Montana's field guide also emphasizes conspicuously enlarged outer florets and a tuft of bristles on the mature fruit. White versus purple flowers does not decide the identification. There is no dependable single height or bract color for all hybrids. A botanical specialist may need several heads and fruits, and research-level confirmation can involve genetic evidence. Do not assign every unusual Diffuse Knapweed plant to the hybrid from one photograph.
actions: Treat a suspected hybrid patch as potentially seed-producing while arranging identification. Avoid moving flowering stems, contaminated hay or soil from the patch to clean ground. Small plants can be removed with their root crowns before seeds develop, using the same practical containment approach applied to the parent knapweeds. Collect mature heads before carrying plants away, and check the site again for regrowth and seedlings. Keep a small, contained identification sample if requested by the local weed program. Protect existing grasses and restore gaps after removal. For a larger mixed population, map both obvious parent plants and suspected hybrids so management covers the whole seed-producing patch rather than only the most distinctive individuals.

proposedDescription: Digenean fluke, here Ichthyocotylurus pileatus, is a small parasitic flatworm with a life cycle involving snails, fish and fish-eating birds. In fish it occurs as an immature stage that becomes enclosed in a tiny capsule within internal tissues. Studies have found it in organs including the kidneys and swim bladder, and Great Lakes records extend back to the early twentieth century. A fish may carry more than one closely related fluke, so finding a cyst does not establish this species. The parasite's movement between hosts also means that identifying an infection is a fish-health task rather than a shoreline visual survey.
identification: The fish stage is microscopic: fully developed capsules in one European perch study measured about 0.29–0.54 millimeters long. Recently established larvae and developing capsules look different, so size must be interpreted with life stage. In that study, mature Ichthyocotylurus pileatus capsules were more oval and smaller than the generally rounder, larger capsules of Ichthyocotylurus variegatus. Specialists also examine the larva's suckers and internal structure. These comparative features apply to properly prepared material, not simply any pale spot in a fish. Record the fish species, capture location and affected organ, and ask a fish-health laboratory how to retain a sample. A photograph of the fish's exterior usually cannot reveal or confirm this internal parasite, and dissection alone does not establish species identity.
actions: Do not move suspect live fish, baitfish or water from their capture site into another lake or pond. Dispose of unwanted bait and fish parts through the locally accepted waste route instead of putting them into a different water body. Clean nets and equipment and drain retained water before travel. If several fish appear ill or an unfamiliar internal parasite is found during routine cleaning, contact the fisheries agency or an aquatic veterinarian with the location and host details. Ask before preserving a sample because the laboratory's method affects identification. Avoid treating a pond or removing snails or birds on the assumption that every host carries this fluke.

proposedDescription: Digenean fluke, here listed as Neascus brevicaudatus, is a microscopic fish parasite historically reported from the eye. Other literature links this name to Posthodiplostomum brevicaudatum, a fluke whose immature stages occur in fish and whose adults develop in fish-eating birds. The name needs care because records identified only as Neascus cannot be assigned to this species. The current Great Lakes account treats the reported introduction as probably unsuccessful, with no further reports after the 1990s. That is different from an established, expanding infestation. Eye abnormalities or dark spots on a fish are not enough to show that this particular parasite is present.
identification: The historical description summarized by USGS gives a body length of about 0.75 millimeters, with two main regions and a heart-shaped front portion tapering backward. Identification depends on microscopic anatomy, including the relative sizes of the oral and ventral suckers. The agency describes the fish stage as uncysted, while the broader literature uses the alternative combination Posthodiplostomum brevicaudatum for eye-associated immature stages. This history makes a modern specialist comparison essential. Several unrelated or closely related flukes inhabit fish eyes, and black-spot disease attributed only to Neascus is not a species diagnosis. Record the host fish, water body and precise tissue involved. Preserve material only after asking the receiving laboratory how it should be handled; an eye photograph cannot resolve the name.
actions: Keep fish and bait from a suspect population within their original water body rather than transferring them to another pond or lake. Drain live wells and bait containers before travel, and contain fish-cleaning waste for appropriate disposal. If a parasite is discovered or multiple fish show unusual eye damage, contact the fisheries agency or a fish-health laboratory and provide the host, date and location. Ask whether a specimen is needed before collecting additional fish. Do not treat a pond, kill birds or remove snails based on a presumed identification. A confirmed laboratory record would be more useful than a broad report of black spots, especially where establishment remains uncertain.

proposedDescription: Digitgrass is a perennial African grass widely used for grazing and hay. Its flower head has several slender branches spreading from near the stem tip like fingers. The species includes quite different forms: some make upright bunches, while others spread through above-ground runners that root as they grow. That distinction matters when managing an escape from a planted pasture. Some cultivars produce seed, while the familiar pangola type is sterile and spreads through runners. Digitgrass is not considered a serious weed everywhere it is grown; management should respond to its behavior at the site and the vegetation it is entering.
identification: Look for a perennial grass with narrow leaves and several fingerlike flowering branches. Plants commonly stand about 35–140 centimeters tall, with considerable variation among forms. Leaves may be smooth or hairy, and spreading forms can have long, hairy runners. The tiny spikelets are generally a few millimeters long; their hairs and arrangement are important in a grass key. A bunch-forming plant and a strongly creeping pangola plant may both belong within the broad modern concept of Digitgrass. Annual crabgrasses also have fingerlike seed heads, so that feature alone is insufficient. Examine the base for persistent crowns or runners, retain a mature flower head, and record the cultivar if the grass came from a known planting. A lawn-level photograph rarely resolves the species.
actions: Identify the form before planning containment. For a spreading cultivar, keep rooted runners and pieces of turf out of dumped soil or garden waste, and inspect the edge of the planted area for runners crossing into nearby habitat. For seed-producing forms, prevent unwanted seed production and avoid moving contaminated hay or seed. Small escapes can be lifted with their crowns and connected runners, followed by checks for pieces left behind. Maintain replacement cover where removal would expose soil. In a working pasture, discuss changes with a forage or restoration adviser rather than removing useful cover solely because the species is introduced. Document spread beyond the planting separately from the managed stand.
researchNotes: SANBI and Tropical Forages independently support variable growth forms, morphology and propagation. The broad species includes multiple former taxa and cultivars; the draft does not claim every Digitgrass plant spreads by both seed and runners. Tropical Forages explicitly distinguishes sterile pangola. No general invasive-impact or proven eradication claim is made.

claims: A perennial grass approximately 350–1400 millimeters tall.
Forms may be tufted or stoloniferous with hairy runners.
Leaves vary in hairiness and inflorescences have fingerlike branches.

The account does not generally consider it a serious weed.

proposedDescription: Dill is a familiar annual herb with finely divided leaves and broad clusters of tiny yellow flowers. Its leaves and mature fruits are used as seasoning, and its flowers attract bees and other beneficial insects. Dill also supports black swallowtail caterpillars where that butterfly occurs. Garden plants often reach two to three feet, with taller cultivars approaching five feet. Because Dill readily reseeds, seedlings may appear beyond the original bed the following year. That tendency calls for ordinary garden containment where volunteers are unwanted; it does not by itself show that Dill is damaging nearby natural habitat.
identification: Look for smooth, upright, hollow stems, finely divided threadlike leaf segments and yellow flowers arranged in umbrella-shaped clusters. Leaves are alternate and strongly aromatic, though smell should be used only as a supporting clue. Mature fruits, commonly called seeds, are flattened, oval and brown, with pale narrow wings along their edges. Fennel, Foeniculum vulgare, has similar fine foliage and yellow flower clusters, but its fruits are less flattened and lack Dill's narrow marginal wings. Cultivars differ in height and flowering time, so size alone is unreliable. If a volunteer is unfamiliar, show the whole plant, a leaf attachment and mature fruits to an experienced identifier. Do not use a resemblance to Dill as a reason to taste an unknown member of the carrot family.
actions: Keep Dill where you want it by collecting seed heads as the fruits turn brown or removing unwanted heads before they shed. Pull surplus seedlings while they are small; leaving a few chosen plants can provide herbs, flowers and caterpillar food without filling every bed. Before removing a plant, check for black swallowtail caterpillars and leave an occupied plant where practical. Sow new seed directly in its intended spot because established Dill transplants poorly. Avoid carrying mature seed heads into unmanaged areas or adding them to a cool compost pile where seed may survive. If volunteers recur, monitor the former bed through the growing season rather than assuming one weeding has removed the seed supply.
researchNotes: Maryland and NC State provide independent cultivation, self-seeding, morphology and wildlife information; PROSEA supplies the fruit distinction from fennel. The actions focus on seed containment in gardens and do not classify a useful annual as universally invasive. The cool-compost precaution is conservative seed containment, not a tested Dill seed-survival claim.

claims: Dill is an annual commonly two to three feet tall.

Cultivars can reach five feet.

proposedDescription: Discoid cockroach is a large tropical cockroach frequently kept as a feeder insect or laboratory animal. Adults have well-developed wings, although husbandry guides describe them as flightless, and females produce live young after retaining the developing egg case. Outdoor records include sheltered places beneath dead plant material and stones. Historical accounts also document occasional transport with tropical plants and temporary greenhouse populations. A single Discoid cockroach indoors therefore calls for checking its source, such as a feeder colony or incoming plant, rather than assuming it behaves like a common kitchen pest. Similar Blaberus species can be difficult to tell apart.
identification: Adults are commonly about 35–45 millimeters long. Both sexes have wings, while young nymphs lack the full adult wing covering. When documenting an adult, include the shield behind the head, the full wing outline and the underside; these views help a specialist compare structural characters. Death's head cockroach, Blaberus craniifer, and other Blaberus can look similar, and a shield marking alone is not a secure species test. University guidance explicitly warns that many members of this genus resemble one another. Keep the supplier or colony name with any sample, but do not treat it as proof if cultures have been mixed. Clear views from above and below, body length and the location found give an entomologist more useful evidence than a common-name label.
actions: Keep feeder or research colonies in secure, ventilated containers and check lids, vents and transfer areas before moving them. Although Discoid cockroach does not readily climb clean glass, do not rely on that alone to prevent escape; furnishings or accumulated material can provide a route out. Inspect incoming tropical plants and packing if an unexpected individual appears indoors. Capture it for identification and look nearby for additional adults or young. Do not release surplus colony animals outdoors. For repeated sightings in a building, remove food residues and ask an identification or pest-management service to confirm the species and source before choosing treatment. Finding one escaped feeder insect does not establish an outdoor breeding population.

proposedDescription: Ditch fimbry is a small, narrow-leaved sedge of wet or seasonally moist ground. Instead of a large branching flower cluster, it usually carries one oval spikelet at the stem tip, sometimes with one or two additional spikelets. This spare outline can make it resemble a spikerush. In the southeastern United States it occurs on moist sand or peaty soil in ditches, roadside clearings and other low, open places. Regional floras describe it as annual or perennial, so a single life-span rule is unreliable. Its presence identifies a wet-ground plant, but does not alone demonstrate substantial ecological harm.
identification: Plants form small tufts, often about 10–40 centimeters tall, with smooth, slender, grooved stems and very narrow leaves mostly around the base. The terminal spikelet is usually yellowish to pale brown, plump and oval, commonly about 5–8 millimeters long in the North American treatment. There may be two or three spikelets instead of one. Ditch fimbry resembles Eleocharis spikerushes, but its evident narrow leaf blades and detailed flower and fruit characters need checking in a sedge key. Mature fruits are pale, roughly 1.5–2 millimeters long, with fine surface patterns visible only under substantial magnification. Collect a whole tuft with basal leaves and mature spikelets when an authorized identification sample is needed. A clipped stem tip alone can hide important distinctions.
actions: Confirm the sedge before removing a wet-ground patch, especially where native spikerushes or other small sedges grow with it. In a maintained garden or drainage edge where Ditch fimbry is unwanted, lift small tufts before mature fruits are dispersed and collect the seed-bearing heads. Keep wet soil and plant material off tools before using them at another site. Recheck the patch for seedlings or surviving crowns. Avoid draining, filling or broadly disturbing a wetland merely to remove this plant; habitat damage could outweigh the benefit. If it is expanding through a restoration area, document its extent and ask the site's wetland botanist to assess selective management.
researchNotes:

No species-specific U.S. impact study or tested eradication schedule was found; useful low-disturbance containment is still possible after identification. The profile does not turn introduced status into a claim of major harm.

proposedDescription: Divine nightshade is a perennial herb with small star-shaped flowers and clusters of berries that darken as they mature. It may stand upright or sprawl, and larger plants can become shrub-sized. The species belongs to the black-nightshade group, whose members are often confused with one another. Divine nightshade is native across parts of the southeastern United States and tropical America, so it should not automatically be treated as an introduced invader. Although some regional traditions use related nightshades as food or medicine, an uncertain identification is no basis for eating the berries or leaves.
identification: Look for an unarmed plant with simple, egg-shaped leaves, their margins smooth or shallowly toothed. White, occasionally purplish flowers are about 1–1.5 centimeters across, often with a green or purple central star and yellow anthers. Berries are small, commonly about 5–8 millimeters across, and may appear dull green, purple or nearly black according to maturity and treatment. Solanum americanum generally has shorter anthers and a different combination of fruit sheen and calyx posture. Solanum douglasii has longer anthers; fruiting plants alone can be very difficult to separate. Specialists may also examine seed size and the small hard granules inside the berries. Show open flowers with a scale, mature fruit clusters and leaf attachments. Fruit color alone is not a safe identification rule.
actions: Check local native status and confirm the plant before managing a patch in natural vegetation. In a garden, remove an unwanted seedling while it is small and collect ripe berries before carrying a mature plant through other beds. Keep discarded fruit out of places where it could establish new plants, and inspect the site for later seedlings. Where children or animals might sample unfamiliar berries, limit access until the plant is identified. Do not taste fruit to distinguish it from another nightshade. If a population is spreading in a restoration area, ask a regional botanist to identify flowering material first; removing a similar-looking native species would not solve a misidentified weed problem.

proposedDescription: Dixie rosemallow is a large flowering shrub whose blooms can change color during a single day. Many open white or pale pink and deepen to rose as they age, so one plant can carry several shades at once. Broad, lobed leaves and hairy young growth give it a different texture from many familiar garden hibiscus plants. Native to China, it has been widely cultivated for its late-season flowers. Some plants persist or spread beyond gardens, but an old planted shrub alone does not show that a population is expanding.
identification: Look for a woody, often multistemmed shrub around 3–4 meters tall, with broad leaves usually 10–15 centimeters long. The leaves have several triangular lobes, toothed edges and long stalks; young stems and leaf undersides are hairy. Flowers may have five petals or many overlapping petals in double cultivars. Their change from pale to deep pink is useful when observed over time, though cultivar differences matter. Rose of Sharon (Hibiscus syriacus) generally has smaller, mostly three-lobed leaves, about 5–10 centimeters long. Photograph a whole branch, both leaf surfaces, a flower from the side and any hairy seed capsules. A single close photograph of a double flower can obscure the features needed for identification.
actions: Check around an established Dixie rosemallow for separate young plants, and note whether they occur beyond maintained garden beds. Where a confirmed volunteer is unwanted, remove it while small and revisit the spot for further growth. Keep seed-bearing capsules and fresh prunings out of streambanks and unmanaged ground: this plant produces seed, and cuttings root readily. Cutting a mature shrub to ground level can stimulate renewed growth, so treat pruning as maintenance rather than proof of removal. Ask a local horticultural or invasive-plant adviser about a larger escape near sensitive habitat. A planted specimen's presence alone does not justify clearing surrounding vegetation.
researchNotes: Independent NC State horticulture and Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria treatment support size, late flowering, color change and regrowth. Queensland weed key supplies seed/garden-waste pathway, but its legal status and broad impact language are not transferred to the United States. Its overly narrow Chinese-hibiscus color comparison is omitted because cultivated flower colors vary; the named H. syriacus comparison uses NC State leaf characters. Volunteer removal is bounded prevention, not a tested eradication guarantee.

Hairy young growth, paler hairy leaf undersides and hairy capsules; reproduction by seed and probable movement in water or garden waste.

proposedDescription: Dixie silverback fern forms upright tufts of finely divided fronds, dark green above and often strikingly white beneath. That pale underside is a natural waxy coating, not a disease. Its fronds arise from a short, scaly stem near the ground, and the spore-producing structures lie across the lower leaf surface. Originally from tropical America, it is cultivated and naturalized in many warm regions. It often occupies disturbed places such as rocky openings, road edges and cracks in paving. Finding it outside a pot warrants documenting the location, without assuming every occurrence causes ecological damage.
identification: The leafy part of a mature frond is commonly 15–45 centimeters long, divided into side branches that are divided again into smaller segments. The stalk may be another 10–50 centimeters long and is dark and glossy. Turn a frond gently to photograph its pale underside and the distribution of its tiny spore cases. Ordinary white-backed plants differ from golden-backed forms treated in the Australian flora as Pityrogramma calomelanos var. austroamericana: those have yellow wax and a different relative length of the lowest side branches. Color alone cannot settle every fern identification or varietal name. Include the entire frond, its stalk, the growing crown and close views of mature segments, without stripping the coating.
actions: Inspect nearby pots, paving cracks and disturbed soil for additional Dixie silverback fern plants before moving nursery material elsewhere. Photograph both sides of a frond first so a fern specialist can verify an unfamiliar escape. For a small, confirmed unwanted plant, carefully lift the growing crown and attached roots where this will not damage masonry or neighboring plants. Contain the removed material and avoid scattering fertile fronds during transport. Do not dump potting mix or garden waste into natural areas. Recheck the site for new growth; the advice reduces opportunities for spread but does not establish that one removal eliminates all spores.
researchNotes: Australian Tropical Herbarium and the independently authored Thailand/Laos/Cambodia fern flora were fully read, with Singapore NParks supplying native-region and growth corroboration. The Australian treatment includes golden var. austroamericana; no universal white-underside rule or unsupported reassignment to a separate species is made. Actions are precautionary handling and small-plant removal inferred from the crown/root and spore biology, not a published US treatment trial. No US harm level, exact introduction date or arsenic-remediation advice is asserted.

proposedDescription: Dog rose is a thorny shrub with arching branches, pale pink or white flowers and red rose hips. It is native to parts of Europe and western Asia and has become established outside cultivation in North America. Its compound leaves and curved prickles are familiar rose features, but distinguishing it from other wild and escaped roses takes a closer look. In some places it forms large shrubby patches in grassland. A rose growing along a fence may be a planted survivor, an escape or another species, so identification should come before control.
identification: Dog rose often reaches about 3 meters tall. Its leaves consist of toothed leaflets, and sturdy prickles curve backward from the stems. White-to-pink flowers appear in early summer, followed by red hips. Examine ordinary leafy shoots as well as flowering ones. Sweetbriar (Rosa rubiginosa) usually has small stalked glands on its leaflets and flower stalks, and more distinctly double-toothed leaflet edges; dog rose generally lacks those glands. Multiflora rose (Rosa multiflora) has conspicuously fringed leaf-base appendages, called stipules, which dog rose lacks. Photograph those appendages, both leaflet surfaces, prickles, flowers and hips. Close relatives and garden hybrids can overlap in appearance, so a whole-plant photograph alone may not establish the name.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and eye protection when working around dog rose's curved prickles. Confirm the species before removing a wild rose, especially where native roses grow nearby. For a few small unwanted plants, careful digging and follow-up inspection are reasonable first steps; keep hips contained rather than dropping them while carrying branches away. Record the extent of a larger patch and ask a local weed adviser for a plan that protects adjoining vegetation. Do not assume deer browsing will control it: Washington field assessment found browsing insufficient. Revisit treated ground for surviving growth and new plants rather than judging success from cut stems alone.
researchNotes: Go Botany provides target morphology and the gland-based sweetbriar comparison. King County independently identifies the multiflora stipule distinction; its multiflora-specific cutting schedule is deliberately not transferred to dog rose. Washington DNR's rapid expert assessment documents grassland thickets and inadequate browsing, with confidence limits explicitly acknowledged here. Small-plant digging and containment are conservative recommendations, not a claimed dog-rose eradication trial. No blanket legal control requirement is inferred.

proposedDescription: Dog's-tongue is a small perennial herb with broad lower leaves and narrow, upright clusters of tiny white flowers. Despite belonging to the daisy family, it has no showy ring of petals around a yellow center. Several small flower heads sit together along the flowering branches, each accompanied by narrow leaflike bracts. It comes from tropical America and has been recorded as introduced in Florida, including open sandy places. The common name is shared with unrelated plants, so a label saying dog's-tongue is not enough to identify it or infer its effects.
identification: Look for hairy lower leaves roughly 3–15 centimeters long, broad toward the tip and narrowing toward the base. Flowering plants in a published Thai treatment stood 10–40 centimeters tall; size alone is not diagnostic. The small white flower heads are grouped along spike-like branches and supported by narrow bracts. Elephant's-foot species such as Elephantopus mollis and E. scaber instead have broader bracts around their clustered heads. Under magnification, dog's-tongue has two longer bristles above each dry fruit with bent, N-shaped tips, another useful distinction. Photograph the basal leaves, entire flowering stem, side view of the heads and mature fruit with a scale. A leaf rosette without flowers is difficult to identify confidently.
actions: Before pulling a suspected dog's-tongue plant, take close photographs of the flower clusters and leaves and seek confirmation from a herbarium or Extension office if the plant is unfamiliar locally. Similar elephant's-foot plants should not be cleared solely because they have broad basal leaves. In a small, confirmed unwanted patch, lift the plant and its roots before dry fruits are shed, where soil disturbance will not harm neighboring plants. Contain flowering and fruiting stems, and clean plant fragments from tools. Check the patch again for surviving plants. These measures are cautious prevention; the sources do not establish a species-specific US eradication method.
researchNotes: Full Flora of North America treatment verifies introduced Florida records and leaf measurements. Independent Bunwong and Chantaranothai 2010 paper was read in full and provides the Elephantopus comparison and N-shaped fruit-bristle tips. The Thai height range is attributed rather than treated as a universal maximum. FNA and Thai accounts differ in fruit measurements, so no diagnostic fruit-length claim is made. Neither medicinal use nor ecological harm is inferred; management remains clearly bounded observation and manual prevention.

proposedDescription: Dogwood anthracnose is a disease caused by the fungus Discula destructiva, especially on flowering and Pacific dogwoods. It can begin as leaf spots and blight, then kill shoots and damage larger branches through cankers. Cool, moist, shaded conditions favor infection, which often starts low in the crown and progresses upward. Some trees decline severely, while other dogwood species and resistant cultivars tolerate infection better. Brown leaves alone are not proof of this disease: several leaf-spot fungi and growing conditions can produce similar symptoms, making examination of branches as well as leaves important.
identification: Look for tan or brown leaf blotches with reddish-purple margins, dead young shoots and progressive dieback, particularly on lower branches. Cankers are damaged areas of bark that can interrupt the movement of water through a twig or branch. Affected trees may produce many new shoots along the trunk or near diseased branches. Spot anthracnose, caused by Elsinoe corni, and Septoria leaf spots can resemble the early leaf symptoms but usually cause much less serious damage. Photograph the whole crown, the transition between healthy and dead foliage, spotted leaves and affected twigs. Record the dogwood species if known. Confirmation may require a plant diagnostic laboratory; photographs cannot show all the fungal features needed.
actions: Ask an Extension plant clinic or qualified arborist to assess a dogwood with recurring leaf blight and branch dieback. Follow the clinic's instructions for collecting a fresh sample rather than mailing only dried leaves. Remove and discard blighted shoots, and collect fallen infected leaves where practical. Reduce avoidable stress by protecting the trunk from mower damage, maintaining mulch over the root zone without piling it against the bark, and watering the root zone during prolonged dry weather. Seek professional advice before removing major branches or selecting a treatment for a valuable tree. For replacement planting, choose an appropriate disease-resistant dogwood rather than assuming every dogwood is equally susceptible.
researchNotes: UMass and University of Illinois Extension were fully read and independently support symptom progression, moist/shaded conditions, diagnostic lookalikes and sanitation/stress reduction. UMass identifies Discula destructiva explicitly and distinguishes highly resistant Kousa dogwood from susceptible flowering/Pacific dogwoods. Illinois notes fallen-leaf removal may have limited benefit, so no cure claim is made. No fungicide recipe, universal treatment success, exact introduction year or diagnosis from a photograph is asserted.

Prune blighted shoots, remove infected leaves, prevent trunk injury, water roots during drought and consider resistant planting material.

Plant clinics can examine or culture samples; branch sanitation and plant health are useful, while leaf removal alone may have limited benefit.

proposedDescription: The domestic cat is familiar as a house pet, but some cats live with little or no direct human care. Their coats vary enormously, but the quiet stalking approach and quick pounce are recognizable behaviors. Cats hunt birds, small mammals and other animals even when people provide food, so feeding alone does not prevent wildlife predation. An outdoor sighting cannot tell you whether a cat is lost, regularly allowed outside or living independently. That distinction matters: preventing roaming, finding an owner and arranging appropriate care can protect both the cat and nearby wildlife.
identification: An average domestic cat has a body roughly 46 centimeters long, with a tail around 30 centimeters, although breed and age cause substantial variation. Look for pointed ears, prominent whiskers and a compact, flexible body; coat color can be solid, patched, striped or spotted. Most have long tails, but some breeds have naturally short tails or none. Bobcats (Lynx rufus) usually have a short tail, cheek ruffs, ear tufts and a larger body, yet a young bobcat can be mistaken for a house cat. Tail length or a spotted coat alone is insufficient. Photograph the whole animal from a safe distance, especially the face, tail and any collar or distinctive markings. A cat's friendliness, wariness or lack of a collar does not establish ownership.
actions: Give an pet cat an enriched indoor home with places to climb, hide, scratch and play; an enclosed outdoor run can provide fresh air without access to wildlife. Discuss individual needs with a veterinarian, and keep identification and microchip registration current. For an unfamiliar cat, record its location and appearance and contact a local shelter or animal service about checking ownership and arranging humane help. Let experienced personnel handle a frightened or injured animal. Do not relocate a cat to another neighborhood or natural area. Where cats repeatedly visit a bird nesting area, share observations with the land manager and animal service so they can coordinate an appropriate response.
researchNotes: USDA APHIS supplies domestic-cat dimensions and the distinction between feeding and predation; Connecticut DEEP supplies the bobcat comparison. The independent feline veterinary statement supports enrichment, identification and controlled outdoor access, while recognizing individual welfare needs. No population-wide eradication claim or do-it-yourself capture method is inferred. Ownership cannot be determined from appearance; referral and observation are practical precautionary guidance rather than evidence that every outdoor cat is feral.

Cats prey on birds, mammals and other small animals, including when provisioned; identification and ownership need consideration.

proposedDescription: The domestic dog is a domesticated canid whose many breeds reflect a long association with people. Dogs serve as companions and working animals, and their size, coat and behavior vary widely. When allowed to roam, they may chase wildlife or provoke defensive responses from deer, elk and other animals, putting themselves and people nearby at risk. A dog alone outdoors may be a lost pet or escaped working animal rather than part of a feral population. Keeping dogs under reliable control is therefore both a wildlife precaution and an important part of responsible care.
identification: There is no single size or coat pattern that identifies every domestic dog. Breeds range from tiny dogs weighing only a few kilograms to animals weighing several tens of kilograms, with great variation in muzzle length, ear shape, leg length and tail carriage. Wolf-like breeds can resemble gray wolves (Canis lupus), while some lean, pointed-eared dogs resemble coyotes (Canis latrans). Tracks overlap in size and shape: splayed toes and a wandering trail may suggest a dog, but neither proves it. Record a side view of the whole animal, its face and tail, approximate size, location and any collar, harness or markings. Puppies differ from adults, and a distant photograph cannot reliably establish breed or hybrid ancestry. Ask a wildlife professional about an uncertain wild-looking canid.
actions: Keep an pet dog within secure fencing or on a leash appropriate to the setting, and supervise it around wildlife. Do not allow chasing, even when the dog seems playful; wildlife may defend themselves. Check gates and fence gaps after an escape, and keep pet food from attracting animals around the yard. If an unfamiliar dog is running loose, photograph it only from a safe position and contact local animal control with its location and direction of travel. Do not chase, corner or approach it, even if it looks friendly. Keep children and pets away, and leave capture to the owner or trained responders.
researchNotes: University of Michigan supports breed variation and the catalog's subspecific name; Colorado Parks and Wildlife independently supports controlling dogs near wildlife. CDC directly supports avoiding unfamiliar dogs and calling animal control for loose animals. The New Hampshire track comparison was read as an indexed excerpt because opening the PDF returned 403, and is used only for a qualified observation, never a definitive identification. No roaming observation is equated with established feral status.

proposedDescription: The domestic goat is a social browsing animal kept in many breeds for milk, meat, fiber and companionship. Goats readily eat leaves and shoots from shrubs and trees, and their climbing ability helps them reach vegetation above ground level. Those same habits make secure fencing especially important. Escaped or independently living goats can repeatedly browse young plants and strip bark; the effects depend on the habitat and the number of animals. A goat beyond a fence may still belong to a nearby farm, so observations should help locate its keeper before anyone assumes it is feral.
identification: Domestic goats vary greatly by breed, with adult shoulder heights ranging from roughly 30 centimeters in very small breeds to around a meter in large ones. Coats may be short or long, solid or patterned, and ears may stand upright or hang down. The short tail commonly curves upward. A beard can help distinguish a goat from a domestic sheep (Ovis aries), but coat texture, horns or beard alone should not be used as a universal test. Goat breeds also differ in coat texture, so an animal's overall shape and several features are more useful together. Split-hoof tracks and pellet droppings can resemble those of sheep or deer. Photograph the full animal, tail, head, ears and any ear tags without approaching. Include whether kids or other goats accompany it.
actions: Inspect goat fencing and gates regularly, including places where animals can climb, squeeze through or crawl underneath. Maintain shelter, water and adequate forage within the enclosure; tethering is not a substitute for suitable routine housing. If using goats for vegetation management, keep the work supervised and contained rather than releasing animals into unmanaged land. For loose goats, note the location, number, tags and nearby roads, and contact the likely owner, local livestock or animal service, or the responsible land manager. Keep dogs away and avoid chasing goats into traffic or steep ground. Established groups on conservation land need a coordinated assessment of browsing and humane management options.
researchNotes: Independent university zoology, government husbandry and New Zealand conservation sources support breed variation, browsing, fence escape and habitat effects. New Zealand damage observations establish a mechanism, not a claim that every U.S. goat population has equivalent impacts. The older ADW account contains inconsistent reproductive and geographic statements, which are excluded. Goat/sheep comparison is deliberately qualified; absence of horns or a beard is not treated as exclusionary. Fencing and reporting are prevention, not an eradication trial.

proposedDescription: The donkey is the domestic descendant of the African wild ass, familiar for its long ears, upright mane and strong association with people as a working animal. Donkeys have been carried far beyond their ancestors' range. In parts of the American Southwest, escaped or released animals contributed to the free-ranging burro populations present today. A donkey seen outside a pasture may instead be an owned animal that has escaped. These situations call for different responses, but both begin with keeping a safe distance and identifying the responsible owner or land manager.
identification: Look for long ears, a short upright mane, relatively narrow hooves and a tail with a tuft toward its end. Domestic donkey breeds span approximately 80–150 centimeters at the shoulder, so size alone is a poor identification guide. Some burros have a dark stripe down the back and another across the shoulders; leg stripes can also occur, but markings vary. Mules and hinnies are horse–donkey hybrids and can share the conspicuous ears and other features. A mule has a donkey father and horse mother; a hinny has the reverse parentage. Do not assign hybrid status from ear length alone. Photograph the animal's complete side profile, mane, tail and markings from a distance. Ownership information or an experienced equine assessor may be needed for an uncertain animal.
actions: Do not feed or approach a free-ranging donkey, including a foal that appears alone. Feeding can draw burros toward roads, and unfamiliar animals can bite or kick. Record the location and visible condition without blocking traffic or attempting to herd the animal. Report an apparent livestock escape to its owner or local animal service; for wild burros on Bureau of Land Management land, contact the responsible BLM office about injury, distress or conflict. Let trained personnel handle capture and movement. Owners should maintain secure enclosures and arrange knowledgeable equine care. Never release an unwanted donkey into open country or assume a young burro needs to be taken home.
researchNotes: BLM's Arizona guidance directly supports American introduction history, variable markings, roadside feeding risks and reporting injured wild burros. San Diego Zoo's combined African-wild-ass/domestic-donkey fact sheet explicitly distinguishes domestic breed heights; wild-ass averages were not transferred. The independent EU welfare guide supports ancestry, hybrid definitions and responsible care. Its husbandry scope excludes feral animals, so BLM rather than the EU guide supports wild-burro actions. No blanket U.S. legal status is asserted.

Bureau of Land Management — Wild Burros in Arizona
EU Platform on Animal Welfare initiative — Guide to Good Animal Welfare Practice for Donkeys and Donkey Hybrids

Escaped or released introduced burros contributed to southwestern free-ranging populations; back, shoulder and leg stripes vary.
Feeding attracts burros to roadways; keep a distance, do not assume isolated foals are orphaned, and report injured or distressed wild burros to BLM.
Domestic donkeys descend from African wild asses; mules and hinnies have reciprocal horse–donkey parentage.
Owners need informed care and appropriate handling; donkeys should not be abandoned.

proposedDescription: Dooryard dock is a tall perennial with broad, long leaves and upright clusters of small flowers that develop into brown fruits. It occurs in disturbed ground, fields, roadsides and some moist shore habitats. Introduced populations are documented in northeastern North America, but finding one plant does not establish that it is displacing nearby vegetation. Like other docks, it is easiest to recognize after flowering, when the thin structures surrounding each fruit have expanded. Those fruit details matter because several docks look very similar as leafy plants, and hybrids can further complicate an identification.
identification: Plants are often about 50–160 centimeters tall, with large lower leaves whose edges are gently wavy. Examine several mature fruits with a hand lens: the three inner flower parts enlarge into rounded or kidney-shaped wings, called valves, typically around 5–6 millimeters long. Their edges are smooth, and they generally lack the obvious central bumps found in some other docks. Patience dock (Rumex patientia) normally has a distinct bump on at least one valve; curly dock (R. crispus) usually has developed bumps on all three. Western dock (R. occidentalis) has a less distinct, unswollen joint on the small fruit stalk, unlike the conspicuous swollen joint of dooryard dock. Photograph the lower leaves, entire plant, fruit stalk joints and several fruits against a scale. Immature plants and suspected hybrids need expert examination.
actions: Confirm dooryard dock from mature fruit before removing plants among other docks. Where a small, confirmed plant is unwanted on your property, carefully loosen the soil and lift the root rather than only cutting off the leaves, then inspect the spot for renewed growth. Collect fruiting stems before moving material through the site, and keep them out of dumped garden waste or soil destined for another location. Clean adhering soil and plant material from tools. These are limited prevention steps, not a demonstrated eradication program. For an extensive patch, a shoreline location or an uncertain identification, send detailed photographs to a local botanical or land-management adviser before disturbing the ground.
researchNotes: Go Botany and Meise Botanic Garden independently support fruit characters and named comparisons. USGS GLANSIS supplied the leaf dimensions, perennial root and habitat account through a detailed indexed excerpt; subsequent full-page access returned 403, so that source is not labeled full text. This is Rumex longifolius DC., not the different R. longifolius Kunth homonym associated with R. crispus. Hybridization is an individual identification limit, not an unresolved catalog taxon. Manual removal and hygiene are explicitly bounded precautions rather than species-specific efficacy claims. GLANSIS control statements concerning curly and broadleaf docks are not transferred to this species.

USGS GLANSIS — Rumex longifolius Fact Sheet

claims: Introduced New England dock occurs in fields, roadsides and shores; mature fruit and stalk-joint features distinguish it from western dock.
Valves are rounded to kidney-shaped and commonly 5–6 mm; hybrids with other docks occur.
R. longifolius DC. has entire rounded valves lacking developed tubercles; R. patientia has a distinct tubercle on at least one valve and R. crispus usually has them on all valves.
Rumex domesticus Hartm. is a synonym; identification and original range have a complex history.
Perennial with a vertical tapering root, weakly wavy large leaves and stems reaching about 50–160 cm; occurs in disturbed and moist terrestrial habitats.

proposedDescription: Dothichiza canker is a fungal disease of poplars that often becomes most damaging when trees are stressed. Small twigs may die first; larger cankers can then interrupt the living tissue beneath the bark, killing branches or young stems. Newly planted trees and nursery stock deserve particular attention because transplanting and dry conditions can leave them vulnerable. The fungus has several older names, including Dothichiza populea, which still appears in forestry literature. Its presence on a damaged poplar does not mean that every nearby tree will suffer the same outcome.
identification: Look for dead twigs, yellowing leaves, early leaf fall, and sunken or discolored bark, especially near branch junctions. Older cankers may develop cracked bark and raised wound tissue around their edges. Small, dark, pimplelike fruiting bodies can form in affected bark, sometimes releasing pale spore tendrils in wet weather. Shoots growing below a girdled area are another sign of disrupted growth. Cytospora canker can also kill poplar branches and produce spore masses, so bark appearance alone does not establish Dothichiza canker. Record the host poplar, the position and extent of lesions, and recent drought or transplant injury. A plant diagnostic laboratory can examine the active canker margin and fungal structures.
actions: Reduce avoidable stress on valuable poplars: water newly planted trees appropriately during dry periods, protect trunks from equipment damage, and choose planting sites suited to the tree. Inspect nursery plants and cuttings before planting, and avoid taking propagation material from cankered trees. If a branch or stem is dying, seek a diagnosis before treating it as this particular disease. Ask an arborist or extension service whether affected branches can be removed safely or whether a severely cankered tree should be removed. Dead or weakened limbs near people require prompt assessment. Correcting site and watering problems also helps protect replacement trees.
