proposedDescription: European hare is a long-legged mammal of open fields, grasslands, and farmland. Unlike a rabbit, it rests above ground in a shallow hollow rather than living in a warren. Its young, called leverets, are born furred and with open eyes, ready to move soon after birth. Introduced populations can damage crops and young trees, particularly by clipping stems or gnawing bark. That agricultural role varies by place: in parts of its European range, declining populations are a conservation concern. A sighting alone is not a reason to begin control.
identification: Adults usually weigh about 3.5-5 kg, with a head-and-body length around 55-65 cm. The mottled brown coat has a pale underside; the long ears end in black tips. The upper side of the tail is dark. European rabbits are more compact, with shorter ears and legs, while European hare remains brown through winter rather than turning white like many mountain hares. North American native hares and jackrabbits can also have long black-tipped ears, so those features are not sufficient outside a known population. Record location and clear side views of the body, ears, and tail. Do not chase or handle an animal to obtain measurements.
actions: If young trees or crops are being damaged, confirm which animal is responsible before acting. Protect vulnerable planting areas with suitable exclusion fencing or individual guards, and check for gaps and renewed browsing. Hares range widely, so protection of a few valuable plants may be more practical than attempting to remove every visiting animal. Seek local wildlife or agricultural advice for substantial losses; permitted control methods and wildlife status differ by jurisdiction. Leave apparently healthy leverets where they are found and keep pets away. Mothers visit them briefly to nurse, so a youngster resting alone is not necessarily abandoned.
researchNotes: Bock's mammal review supplies current diagnostic comparisons, while Victoria contributes locally observed impacts and management. Victoria cites Bock and ADW among many references; the sources are not wholly independent for all biology. The advice avoids transferring Australian pest status or lethal-control rules to the United States.

claims: Head-body length 55-65 cm, typical mass 3.5-5 kg, black-tipped long ears; does not turn white in winter; young are born furred and mothers nurse briefly.
Bark and stem feeding damages young trees and crops; exclusion fencing is a recommended management measure; hares rest above ground.
Brown coat, pale underside and dark upper tail; uses open fields and shallow resting forms.

proposedDescription: European heliotrope is a gray-green annual that grows in open, disturbed ground and agricultural fields. Its small white flowers line a curled stalk that gradually straightens as they develop. In warm weather a plant can flower within weeks of germination, allowing seed production to continue through the growing season. It is a serious pasture concern in parts of Australia because eating it can cause cumulative liver damage in livestock. Seed can travel in contaminated fodder, on equipment, or with animals. Keeping new patches from setting seed is more useful than waiting for a dense stand.
identification: Plants commonly reach 30-50 cm, with branching, hairy stems and alternate oval leaves. The leaves are gray-green and may smell unpleasant when crushed, but there is no need to use smell for confirmation. White, five-lobed flowers with yellow throats are arranged along one side of a curved cluster, often in two rows. Fruits divide into four small nutlets. Spreading heliotrope (Heliotropium supinum) is a recognized lookalike, and the broader H. europaeum group has variable fruit and flower characters. Photograph the whole plant, leaf attachment, flowers, and mature fruits. Do not assume that every white-flowered heliotrope belongs to this species.
actions: Prevent livestock from being forced to graze an infested patch, and seek veterinary advice if exposure is suspected. Check hay and feed sources and clean soil and seed from machinery before moving between fields. Remove small plants before fruit matures, taking care to collect seed-bearing material. In suitable cropping ground, cultivation can kill this annual, but disturbed soil may produce another flush of seedlings that needs follow-up. Maintain competitive ground cover where compatible with land use. Established plants can be difficult to control chemically, so an agricultural adviser should help select locally appropriate methods for larger patches. Revisit treated ground through the warm season.
researchNotes: Tasmania provides morphology and dispersal; NSW specifically distinguishes annual common heliotrope management from perennial blue heliotrope, which can regrow from fragments. Kew notes variability within the species complex. Toxicity is supported, but no dosage or claim that a particular amount is safe is given.

proposedDescription: European larch is a large conifer that turns yellow and drops its needles in autumn. This seasonal change is normal, not a sign that the tree has died. Native to European mountain regions, it is a light-demanding pioneer that can establish after disturbance. It has also been planted widely for timber and ornament, including in northeastern North America, and sometimes seeds beyond cultivation. Its ecological behavior depends on location: naturalization alone does not establish that a particular planting is causing harm. The soft spring needles and persistent small cones make it recognizable through much of the year.
identification: Mature trees can reach 35-45 m or more in favorable conditions. Soft, light-green needles grow singly on new shoots and in dense clusters on older short shoots. They are roughly 1.5-4 cm long. Young twigs are pale straw or cream colored; older bark becomes furrowed. Upright, egg-shaped cones are commonly about 2.5-4 cm long. Japanese larch (Larix kaempferi) has cone scales that curl outward at their tips and conspicuous pale bands beneath the needles. Hybrids can blur these differences. Native tamarack and western larch are additional regional lookalikes, so retain cone and twig details when documenting a tree rather than identifying it from yellow autumn foliage alone.
actions: Check for self-sown seedlings beyond a planting, especially on open disturbed ground. If local land managers regard spread as a problem, remove young seedlings while their roots are manageable and revisit the site after further seed fall. Mature trees require a site-specific decision and professional help if removal is needed. For a retained tree, allow room for its eventual size and avoid poorly drained sites. Investigate isolated branch dieback, resinous cankers, or abnormal loss of needles during the growing season. Do not move suspect larch branches, nursery plants, or firewood until a forest-health adviser has assessed the possibility of European larch canker.
researchNotes: European forest atlas and Virginia Tech fact sheet support habit and morphology; the latter is hosted by URI but counted as Virginia Tech authorship. APHIS supports disease-related movement caution. The US Forest Service record labels the species noninvasive, while overseas sources describe invasion in some regions; no global invasive designation is inferred.

Straw-colored twigs, clustered older-shoot needles and upright cones; may seed into landscapes; several native and introduced larches are lookalikes.
Planted in southern Canada and northeastern United States; database labels species nonnative and noninvasive.

proposedDescription: European larch canker is a fungal disease that damages the living tissue beneath the bark of larch trees. Cankers can deform trunks, kill branches, and eventually kill a tree. The pathogen affects native larches as well as planted European larch, so the disease name does not restrict its hosts. In North America it has been documented in parts of eastern Canada and Maine. Tiny orange-centered fungal cups may appear around infected bark, but other fungi on larch look similar. A suspected case needs specialist confirmation before it is treated as a new outbreak.
identification: Look for depressed or swollen areas on branches and trunks, resin leaking from bark, and branches whose needles yellow or die prematurely. Young shoots can die before a conspicuous open canker develops. The fungus produces small, stalked cups, generally a few millimeters across, with an orange inner surface and a white hairy rim. Native Lachnellula fungi may also grow on larch and are often decomposers rather than this destructive pathogen. Photographs should show the whole affected branch, the canker edge, and any cups with a scale. A forest-health laboratory may need a sample for microscopic or other testing; orange cups alone do not establish the species.
actions: Leave suspect branches and wood at the site while contacting a state forest-health service or plant-health authority. Provide the tree's location, whether it was planted or naturally established, and when symptoms appeared. Ask how a diagnostic sample should be collected and delivered. Avoid moving larch nursery stock, cuttings, barked wood, or firewood from affected areas without checking current movement requirements. Quarantine boundaries and rules can change. Removal and disposal of infected trees may be part of an official response, but the correct approach depends on confirmation and the surrounding outbreak. Routine pruning or a garden fungicide should not be assumed to cure an infected trunk.
researchNotes: Maine reports distinguish native Lachnellula lookalikes and document 2025 detections beyond older coastal assumptions. Federal and Canadian overview pages retain older five-county descriptions; exact current boundaries are therefore omitted. Maine's page also mentions a proposed quarantine repeal, reinforcing the need to check operative requirements rather than present a proposal as law.

Maine Forest Service: 2025 forest health highlights

claims: Fungal cankers affect larch branches and trunks and can kill trees; movement restrictions are used.
Resinous depressed cankers and 2-6 mm cups with orange centers and white hairy exteriors; young twigs may die before open cankers form.
Native Lachnellula species also occur on larch and require expert differentiation; specimens were verified by a national fungal identifier.
2025 surveys confirmed European larch canker in Jefferson and Vanceboro, extending knowledge of occurrence.
Page describes a proposal to repeal the state's European larch canker quarantine; proposal is not treated as enacted.

proposedDescription: European mountain ash is a deciduous tree grown for white spring flowers, divided leaves, and conspicuous clusters of orange-red fruit. Birds eat the fruit and carry its seeds beyond gardens, allowing seedlings to establish in woodland and along disturbed forest edges. It has escaped cultivation in parts of northern North America and is a management concern in some regions. Despite its name and ash-like foliage, it belongs to the rose family rather than the true ashes. Native mountain ashes can look very similar, especially when young, making identification important before removing a volunteer tree.
identification: Trees are often about 20-40 feet tall, though larger individuals occur. The alternate leaves are divided into a central row of toothed leaflets, usually 9-15. White flowers form broad clusters, followed by small orange-red fruits about one-third of an inch across. Examine the winter buds: European mountain ash has conspicuous gray hairs and buds that are not sticky. American mountain ash (Sorbus americana) has few or no bud hairs and may have sticky buds. In western North America, Sitka and western mountain ash are further lookalikes and are generally more shrub-like. Growth form alone is unreliable for seedlings; include a close view of buds and a complete leaf.
actions: Confirm the species before removing young mountain ashes from a natural area. Where European mountain ash is spreading, pull or dig small plants from loose soil and remove the roots as thoroughly as practical. Check beneath bird perches and near mature fruiting trees for further seedlings. Cutting a larger tree alone can produce new shoots from the stump or root system, so plan follow-up before felling it. A local weed adviser can help select an appropriate stump treatment where needed, and an arborist should handle hazardous trees. In affected landscapes, choose a suitable native replacement and avoid distributing fruit-bearing garden waste.
researchNotes: Minnesota DNR provides bud comparison and resprouting guidance; King County independently supports escaped woodland populations and seedling removal. NC State supplies leaf and fruit measurements. An apparent copied reference to Amur cork tree in Minnesota's basal-treatment paragraph was not used. Regional concern is not presented as a nationwide removal requirement.

claims: Birds and mammals disperse seed; hairy nonsticky buds distinguish it from American mountain ash; cut stumps resprout.
Escapes into woodlands; native western mountain ashes are lookalikes; young plants can be dug or pulled.
Usually 20-40 feet; alternate leaves with 9-15 leaflets; fruits about one-third inch; rose family rather than true ash.

proposedDescription: European olive is the evergreen olive of Mediterranean orchards, valued for its fruit and oil. The subspecies includes cultivated and wild forms, so trees vary in fruit size and habit. Long-lived plantings can also supply seed to surrounding vegetation when birds and mammals carry the fruit away. In parts of southern Australia, escaped olives form dense stands that crowd out native plants. That regional invasion history should not be applied automatically to every orchard or garden. The silvery undersides of the leaves are a useful first clue, but other olive subspecies need to be considered.
identification: Look for opposite pairs of narrow, leathery leaves, gray-green above and distinctly silvery or whitish beneath. Leaves are commonly about 3-7 cm long. Small pale flowers develop in clusters, followed by fleshy fruits containing a hard stone. Cultivated trees usually have larger, fleshier fruit than African olive, traditionally treated as Olea europaea subsp. cuspidata. African olive often has greenish, yellow-brown, or rusty-scaled leaf undersides. These are supporting differences rather than an infallible single-character test: fruit size and leaf surfaces vary, especially in wild and horticultural material. Record both leaf surfaces and mature fruit, and seek herbarium confirmation if the subspecies affects a management decision.
actions: Where olives are escaping, inspect surrounding ground and bird perches for seedlings. Pull small seedlings from moist soil, including the root, and check for regrowth. Older trees have persistent root systems and need a planned approach; cutting alone should not be assumed to finish the job. Avoid unnecessarily disturbing large areas of soil during removal. Revisit cleared ground for new seedlings and shoots over subsequent years, and keep fruit-bearing waste out of bushland. For a substantial stand, arrange locally appropriate removal and follow-up with a weed-management professional. Decisions about retained orchard trees should consider both the crop and evidence of nearby spread.
researchNotes: Exact subspecies accepted by Kew; botanical comparisons corroborated by the dendrological treatment. Australian control evidence is applied conditionally to escaped populations. NSW Feral Olive page failed with HTTP 500 and was not counted as read evidence. The broader species name is not entered as a strict synonym of this subspecies.

sources.title: Trees and Shrubs Online: Olea europaea

claims: Accepts the exact subspecies and places its native distribution around the Mediterranean.
Opposite leathery leaves; subsp. europaea has larger and fleshier fruits than subsp. cuspidata, whose lower leaf scales can be rusty.
Escaped populations invade southern Australian vegetation; animals disperse seeds; remove seedlings with roots and follow up persistent regrowth.

proposedDescription: European Pine Sawfly larvae feed together on pine needles, sometimes raising their heads in unison when disturbed. Although they look like caterpillars, they belong to the same insect order as bees and wasps. They usually eat older needles, leaving the current season's growth at the branch tips. This can make a pine look stripped and untidy without killing it, though repeated attacks reduce growth and fullness. Mugo pine is a familiar garden host; Scots, red, and several other pines are also used. Small colonies are often manageable without treating an entire tree.
identification: Mature larvae are roughly 18-25 mm long, with shiny black heads and gray-green bodies marked by pale and dark lengthwise stripes. Young groups first scrape needles, which turn straw-colored; older larvae consume most of each needle. Egg-laying scars appear as small marks along needles, where eggs remain through winter. Adults are small, wasp-like insects; males are mostly black with feathery antennae and females are reddish brown. Other pine sawflies can cause similar damage. Record the larval head color, stripe pattern, host pine, and whether old or new needles are being eaten. The synchronized defensive movement is useful context, not proof of species.
actions: Inspect last year's needles in spring and act while colonies are small. Tolerate minor feeding on a healthy tree, or remove accessible groups by wiping or shaking them off while wearing gloves. A strong spray of water is another option for reachable larvae. Removing whole branches may disfigure a small pine more than the insects would. If feeding threatens a young or repeatedly defoliated tree, obtain local treatment guidance and target young larvae only when necessary. The caterpillar product Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki does not control sawflies. Check the same tree again the following spring, because infestations may recur and there is normally one generation each year.
researchNotes: Utah, Minnesota and Wisconsin extension independently corroborate life cycle and larval characters. Wisconsin supports manual removal and the important caterpillar-versus-sawfly treatment distinction. Published calendar dates are regional; profile uses seasonal monitoring rather than a nationwide application schedule or pesticide recipe.

claims: Black-headed striped larvae feed in groups on older needles; adult sexes differ; water spray and tolerance of low populations are options.
Larvae 18-25 mm; overwintering eggs in needles; one generation and multiple pine hosts.
Usually spares new foliage; repeated defoliation stunts; hand removal works for small colonies; caterpillar Bt is ineffective.

proposedDescription: European Pine Shoot Moth is a small moth whose caterpillars feed inside pine buds and shoots. A damaged terminal bud can force a side branch to take over, leaving a permanent bend in the tree's leader. Nursery stock, Christmas trees, and ornamental pines may lose shape and vigor even when the whole tree survives. Larvae begin near needles and then shelter within buds, often surrounded by silk and resin. That hidden feeding makes early detection more useful than waiting until many shoot tips have browned and died.
identification: Adults have orange-red forewings crossed by irregular pale or silvery lines and a wingspan around 18-23 mm. Older caterpillars are brownish, with a dark head and a dark plate immediately behind it. Examine browning or bent shoot tips for resin, webbing, and hollowed buds; do not identify the moth from a crooked leader alone. Other pine-tip insects and diseases can produce dieback. Rhyacionia pinicolana is a close moth lookalike, and difficult adults may require specialist examination of internal structures. A sample retaining the damaged bud, larva, and host identification is more useful than a photograph of an empty dead tip.
actions: Inspect young pines for newly damaged tips and avoid moving infested nursery plants or cut shoots to another planting. Prune out affected shoots promptly where this can be done without excessive loss of the crown, and contain the removed material so larvae cannot continue development nearby. For a valuable tree with a damaged leader, ask an arborist about restoring its form. Extensive nursery or Christmas-tree infestations need local monitoring and carefully timed management of exposed young larvae. Treatments applied after larvae are protected inside buds may miss them. Preserve natural enemies and reassess fresh damage rather than repeatedly treating old, already crooked growth.
researchNotes: Penn State provides pruning and treatment-timing principles; SENASA independently details stages and injury; Scion identifies R. pinicolana confusion. Penn State's page has a recent update banner but underlying authorship states revised 2004, so historical dates are not treated as newly trialed guidance. WSU direct access was blocked (403), and its snippet was not needed.

sources.title: Penn State: European pine shoot moth
Scion: Forest biosecurity import health standards review

claims: Pine bud injury produces permanent leader crooks; prune dead shoots when detected; exposed small larvae are the treatment target.
Adults span 18-23 mm with reddish silver-lined forewings; larvae have dark heads and feed inside buds and shoots with resin-associated injury.
R. pinicolana may be confused with this moth; adult genitalia distinguish them; infested shoots and branches are pathways.

proposedDescription: European pineneedle midge is a tiny fly whose larvae feed near the bases of pine needles. Affected needles bend down, discolor, and may fall, reducing the appearance of nursery or Christmas trees. Michigan research found one generation per year, with larvae spending winter in cocoons on the ground and adults appearing in spring. European studies also associate it with Scots pine and other pines. It is generally described as a minor pest in Europe, although conspicuous injury can occur. Bent needles warrant examination; they do not by themselves demonstrate a serious outbreak.
identification: The useful field signs are at the needle bases, where yellow to orange larvae live between paired needles or in small hollows. Needles may remain nearly full length but bend sharply downward, or show some shortening. These descriptions vary among studies and should not be turned into a rigid rule. Thecodiplosis brachyntera is another pine needle midge, and weather injury or other feeding can also distort needles. An expert may need larvae or reared adults to confirm the species. Collect fresh affected needles with their bases intact, note the pine species, and compare injured and healthy shoots rather than sending only fallen brown needles.
actions: Mark affected trees and record how much of the new foliage is injured, then compare later growth before deciding that control is needed. Have fresh material examined by an extension or forest-health diagnostic service, especially in a nursery or an area without confirmed records. Avoid distributing visibly infested plants until identified. Because larvae are sheltered at needle bases and later overwinter on the ground, a spray aimed at old brown needles is poorly matched to the life cycle. Commercial growers should ask about local emergence monitoring and current registered options if losses justify intervention. Old experimental product recommendations should not be used as present-day treatment instructions.
researchNotes: Two independent research groups support the biology: Wilson/Sapio/Simmons in Michigan and Skuhrava-associated European surveys. The Michigan abstract includes 1980s insecticide trials; these establish timing research, not current registrations. No validated home-garden removal protocol or adult measurement was found. Advice is limited to diagnosis, movement precaution and impact monitoring.

sources.title: Great Lakes Entomologist: Biology, injury and control of European needle-bending midge
Acta Societatis Zoologicae Bohemicae 80: Gall midges
Acta Societatis Zoologicae Bohemicae 75: Gall midges

claims: One annual generation in Michigan; eggs in new-needle sheaths; larval feeding causes drooping and shedding; larvae overwinter on ground.
Yellow larvae between Scots pine needles; needles bend at base; one annual generation and soil overwintering; minor European pest.
Orange larvae at needle bases, with shortened and slightly curled needles.
Lists European pineneedle midge and synonym Cecidomyia baeri; taxon record credibility marked unverified.

proposedDescription: European plum is the familiar cultivated fruit tree that supplies many plums, prunes, and related garden selections. White blossom appears in spring, followed by fruit that varies greatly in skin color, shape, and sweetness. Animals eating the fruit can carry seeds beyond cultivation, and trees sometimes persist around old homesteads or establish along woodland edges. A volunteer plum is not automatically an invasive plant. Cultivated varieties and different botanical treatments make this group unusually variable, so its identity is best judged from flowers, leaves, fruit, and planting history together.
identification: European plum is generally a small deciduous tree with simple, alternate, toothed leaves, commonly 5-10 cm long. Flowers are white and borne on distinct stalks. Fruit contains a single hard stone and may be yellow, red, blue, purple, or nearly black. In the narrow New England treatment, fruits are about 4-7.5 cm long and separate from a flattened, ridged stone; the smaller-fruited damson is treated separately as Prunus insititia. Cherry plum (P. cerasifera) usually has smaller fruit and less hairy leaf undersides. Broader horticultural treatments include forms that blur these distinctions. A nursery rootstock shoot may also differ from the named fruiting cultivar.
actions: If a plum is unwanted, first establish whether it is a seedling, an old cultivated tree, or a shoot arising from another tree's rootstock. Remove small unwanted plants and revisit for new growth without disturbing neighboring native plums unnecessarily. For retained fruit trees, remove rootstock suckers and plan pruning for a locally suitable growing-season window; RHS advises spring for young trees and summer for established trees to reduce silver leaf disease risk. Remove rotting or dried fruit that can carry brown rot into the next season. Keep discarded fruit and propagating material out of natural areas, and seek local orchard advice for persistent disease or vigorous suckering.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust uses a narrower concept separating P. insititia, while Kew and horticultural sources treat a broader cultivated complex. Measurements are explicitly tied to the New England treatment and do not promise cultivar identification. RHS pruning guidance is regional; UMass independently supports removing infected fruit as disease sanitation.

claims: Alternate leaves 5-10 cm; naturalizes near cultivation; narrow treatment distinguishes cherry plum and P. insititia using fruit and pubescence.
Accepted species treated as stabilized hybrid-derived lineage; introduced widely.
Small deciduous tree with white spring flowers and widely variable colored fruit; many cultivars.
Spring or summer pruning reduces silver leaf risk; remove rootstock suckers.
Unharvested infected fruit can persist and spread infection the next season and should be removed.

proposedDescription: European privet is a densely branched shrub long used for hedges. Clusters of small white flowers are followed by dark fruits that birds eat, carrying seeds into nearby woods and field edges. Plants can also recover strongly after cutting. In parts of eastern North America, escaped privets form persistent thickets and compete with surrounding vegetation. Several introduced privet species grow together, so a patch identified only as 'privet' may contain more than one species. The leaves and fruit are not food for people or pets, even though birds use the berries.
identification: Untrimmed shrubs can reach about 10 to 15 feet tall. The leaves occur in opposite pairs, have smooth edges, and are oval to lance-shaped, commonly up to about 2.5 inches long. They are dark green and relatively glossy; the amount of winter foliage retained varies with conditions. Flowers have small white lobes and develop in branching clusters, later producing black fleshy fruits. Chinese privet (Ligustrum sinense) is especially similar, with generally duller upper leaf surfaces, but the distinction can be subtle. Record leaves, young stems, flowers, and fruit rather than relying on a hedge silhouette. Regional botanical keys may be needed for confident species identification.
actions: Pull small plants when the soil allows the roots to come out intact. Roots and stump pieces left behind can resprout, so revisit the area instead of assuming that a cleared canopy means success. Cutting or mowing can open access through a thicket but needs follow-up. For established shrubs, ask a local weed adviser about a suitable targeted stump or other treatment that protects neighboring plants. Prevent fruit production on a retained hedge by removing flower clusters before berries form, and inspect nearby bird perches for seedlings. Replace escaped or repeatedly seeding plants with an appropriate local shrub where practical.
researchNotes: NC State provides species-level morphology and toxicity, while the North Carolina flora supplies a cautious Chinese-privet comparison. Penn State management explicitly covers a group that includes L. vulgare; its broad Asian-origin statement is not copied for this European taxon. Direct Penn State access was blocked, but substantive indexed management content was read.

sources.title: Vascular Plants of North Carolina: European privet

claims: Shrub to 10 to 15 feet with opposite glossy leaves, white flowers and black fruit; birds disperse seed; leaves and fruits toxic.
Similar to Chinese privet; upper leaf surface generally shinier; exact differences can be subtle.
Includes L. vulgare among managed privets; pull small plants with roots; cutting alone prompts root and stump sprouts.

proposedDescription: European rabbit is the species from which domestic rabbits were bred. Wild-type animals are compact, gray-brown grazers, but escaped domestic rabbits may be white, black, spotted, long-haired, or much larger. Groups often shelter in connected burrows called warrens. Where introduced populations become numerous, grazing can damage crops and prevent young plants from establishing, while burrowing changes the ground around them. A rabbit seen outdoors in North America may instead be a native cottontail or an escaped pet. That distinction should guide the response, rather than assuming every rabbit is an invasive wild animal.
identification: Wild-type adults commonly weigh about 1.5 to 2.5 kg and measure roughly 38 to 50 cm in total length. They have gray-brown upperparts, a pale belly, and a white underside to the short tail. Compared with European hare, the body is more compact, the legs and ears are shorter, and the ears lack the hare's clear black tips. Domestic forms vary too much for those measurements to apply universally. White tail flashes also occur in native rabbits and are not diagnostic. Photograph the animal from a distance, including the ears and whole body, and note any burrow use. Coat pattern alone cannot reliably establish species or ownership.
actions: Protect vulnerable beds and young trees with suitable rabbit-exclusion fencing or individual guards, checking regularly for gaps and digging beneath the barrier. A fence must account for burrowing as well as above-ground entry. If an animal appears to be an abandoned domestic rabbit, contact an animal shelter or rabbit rescue for identification and humane assistance rather than releasing it elsewhere. For an established wild population causing substantial damage, document feeding areas and burrows and consult local wildlife or agricultural staff. Coordinated management may be needed across neighboring properties. Do not close or destroy an occupied burrow without assessing the animals using it and the applicable humane-control requirements.
researchNotes: University of Michigan and Argentina's national parks account corroborate morphology and domestic variation. UK forestry and Victoria supply exclusion guidance; Australian eradication obligations and lethal methods are not generalized to US landowners. Current global conservation labels were omitted because retrieved secondary summaries conflicted.

sources.title: UK Forestry Commission: Rabbits and hares

claims: Wild animals typically 1.5 to 2.5 kg and 38 to 50 cm; domestic breeds vary greatly; pale underside and white lower tail.
Smaller ears and legs than European hare, no black ear-tip patch; forms colonies in excavated burrows; domestic color variants occur.
Fencing and individual tree protection are options for reducing rabbit damage.
Exclusion fencing needs a buried or outward secured lower edge and maintenance; assess non-target wildlife and coordinate management.

proposedDescription: European red raspberry is the Eurasian form of red raspberry, familiar from fruit gardens and sometimes found beyond cultivation. The perennial root system sends up canes and new shoots, allowing a patch to widen over time. Its red fruit is made of many small fleshy segments and comes away from the plant with a hollow center. Native American red raspberry is closely related and is treated as either a separate species or another variety or subspecies. Red berries alone cannot separate them, and a spreading raspberry patch should not be cleared before that distinction is checked.
identification: Look for upright or arching canes, divided leaves with pale undersides, small white flowers, and red raspberry fruits. Garden plants vary in height, prickles, and fruiting season, so no single cultivar appearance represents this variety. The most useful distinction from American red raspberry is on the flower-cluster stalks: European material generally lacks the tiny stalked glands found on the American taxon. These glands look like minute hairs with swollen tips and are best examined with magnification. Photograph young stems and flower or fruit stalks closely. Hybrid ancestry in cultivated raspberries can complicate an apparently simple native-versus-European determination, and uncertain plants deserve botanical review.
actions: Before controlling a wild patch, check the gland characters and whether native raspberries occur locally. In a retained garden row, regularly cut unwanted shoots arising outside the intended bed and keep access clear enough to notice new ones. Digging unwanted plants requires follow-up because roots can produce further shoots. Match pruning to the cultivar's fruiting habit; summer-bearing and fall-bearing raspberries are managed differently. Do not assume that removing every cane once will eliminate a patch. Keep rooted divisions and discarded plants out of woodland edges. For a natural-area infestation, agree on the identification and removal objective with the site manager before disturbing surrounding vegetation.
researchNotes: Exact variety is supported by NC State; Native Plant Trust independently describes the equivalent subspecies and diagnostic stalked glands. Minnesota cultivation advice applies to red raspberry garden cultivars, not a tested eradication method for genetically pure var. idaeus. Unknown garden ancestry remains an identification limitation, without inventing a new taxon-level gap.

sources.title: Native Plant Trust: Native and introduced red raspberries
University of Michigan CLIMBERS: Rubus strigosus

claims: Distinguishes Eurasian var. idaeus from native American var. strigosus, with glandular hairs absent from the former.
Inflorescence-axis stalked glands present in native subsp. strigosus and absent in introduced subsp. idaeus.
R. idaeus lacks glands compared with R. strigosus; raspberries detach from the receptacle leaving a hollow fruit.
Red raspberries send up suckers outside rows; cut unwanted shoots; management depends on fruiting type.

proposedDescription: European sea lavender is a small Mediterranean plant that has established in California coastal wetlands and nearby habitats. A low rosette of leaves supports branching stems carrying tiny pale pink to purple flowers. It spreads by seed and can form persistent stands among native marsh plants. Because it resembles both other introduced sea lavenders and the native California sea lavender, some populations were initially overlooked or misidentified. Its local importance comes from where it grows: even a short plant can occupy space needed by native salt-marsh vegetation.
identification: Plants are commonly up to about 30 cm tall, with smooth stems and spoon-shaped basal leaves approximately 1 to 4 cm long. The leaf tips are blunt, and each leaf narrows into a distinct stalk. Small groups of one to three flowers are spaced along the branching flowering stems. Algerian sea lavender (Limonium ramosissimum) tends to have larger leaves and more tightly grouped flowers, but intermediate-looking plants have been reported. Native California sea lavender (L. californicum) is another important comparison. Photograph the entire rosette, a leaf with a scale, and the arrangement of flowers along the branches. Expert examination is worthwhile before marsh vegetation is removed.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the wetland manager or local invasive-plant program before beginning work. Avoid carrying seed-bearing stems or muddy tools to another marsh. Small, scattered plants may be suitable for carefully supervised hand removal, followed by checks for recovery and seedlings. Research in southern California found that hand removal did not consistently suppress this species over time. For dense stands, professionally planned tarping performed better, with duration and site conditions affecting results. Scraping can damage native vegetation and should not be improvised across a marsh. Any treatment should include monitoring of both the target plant and the native plants expected to recover.
researchNotes: Catalog spelling 'European sea lavendar' is preserved in public copy; standard source spelling is supplied separately. CDFA morphology and Cal-IPC comparison support identification, with intermediate forms explicitly retained. The 2024 control paper's abstract was read; treatment effectiveness is site-bound and no universal tarp duration or chemical recipe is inferred.

sources.title: CDFA: Limonium duriusculum pest rating assessment
Lieberman and colleagues: Controlling non-native sea lavenders

evidence.independentSourceGroup: California Department of Food and Agriculture
claims: Plant to 30 cm with blunt spoon-shaped 1 to 4 cm leaves and sparse flower clusters; resembles L. ramosissimum and has been confused with L. californicum.
Seed-spreading Mediterranean species in California coastal and inland habitats; blunt leaves and looser flowers distinguish typical plants; intermediate forms occur.
Three-marsh trials favored tarping; hand removal did not consistently suppress L. duriusculum over time; scraping harmed native vegetation.

proposedDescription: European speedwell is a fleshy wetland perennial that creeps along muddy stream edges and other wet ground. Its stems can root where they touch the soil, producing connected patches with rounded leaves and small blue flowers. Introduced populations occur in northeastern North America. Dense local stands may affect neighboring vegetation, but USGS finds the evidence insufficient for a full assessment of its environmental impact in the Great Lakes. It closely resembles native American speedwell, so both identification and the actual extent of spread matter when deciding whether a patch needs attention.
identification: The smooth, thick stems may trail along the ground or turn upward. Leaves occur in opposite pairs on short stalks and have shallowly toothed edges. Typical leaves are oval or oblong, widest near or above the middle, with rounded tips. Native American speedwell (Veronica americana) generally has leaves widest below the middle and more pointed tips. In the New England key, European speedwell's slender style, the stalk above the seed capsule, is about 1.8 to 2.2 mm long, compared with 2.5 to 3.5 mm in American speedwell. A flowering or fruiting specimen showing several leaves is much more informative than a photograph of a dense green mat.
actions: Confirm the identification before removing plants from a stream or wetland, and record the patch boundary so changes can be checked. Avoid moving rooted stems or wet soil into another waterbody. If a small confirmed patch needs management, discuss selective removal with the land manager and collect loose material rather than letting it wash downstream. Rooting stems can make a quick cutback temporary. Broad clearing of wetland margins may remove native plants and leave open ground for recolonization, so treatment should have a clear local objective. Ask an aquatic-plant specialist about substantial stands or any proposed chemical treatment in water.
researchNotes: Native Plant Trust supports precise distinction from V. americana; USGS independently synthesizes ecology and uncertain Great Lakes impact. USGS direct access failed, but substantial indexed text was read; an apparent flower-length error was excluded. UK aquatic-weed guidance supports selective intervention in native habitat, not a North American eradication protocol; prevention advice is cautious inference from rooting growth.

sources.title: Environment Agency: Aquatic weed control technical report W111

claims: Opposite stalked rounded leaves; New England material is subsp. beccabunga; leaf shape and style length distinguish native V. americana.
Fleshy stems root at nodes; wetland margins are habitat; large local stands occur but Great Lakes impact evidence is inadequate.
Includes brooklime among emergent plants for which intervention should be selective and necessary; cutting does not reliably eradicate established plants.

proposedDescription: European spruce sawfly feeds on spruce needles, with larvae usually taking older foliage first. Its introduction once caused major forest damage in northeastern North America, but viruses and parasitic insects subsequently reduced those outbreaks. A few larvae on a tree therefore do not predict widespread decline. The adults are small, wasp-like insects; the caterpillar-like feeding stage is more likely to attract attention. Spruces with thinning foliage deserve a closer look because several unrelated insects can cause similar damage.
identification: Older feeding larvae reach about 15-20 mm and have a green body, brownish head and five pale lengthwise stripes. Young larvae and the final, nonfeeding stage lack that striped pattern. Females are roughly 6-9.5 mm, black with yellow markings and saw-toothed antennae. Gilpinia polytoma is a distinct, historically confused species; reliable separation can require microscopic adult characters. Photograph the larva from above and beside, its head, the host's needles and the feeding pattern. Missing needles alone cannot establish the species.
actions: Inspect accessible spruce branches before deciding that treatment is needed. Record whether feeding affects old needles, new growth or both, and whether damage is increasing. A gentle branch tap over a tray can reveal larvae for photographs and an extension identification. Keep suspect nursery spruces, branch cuttings and their potting soil from being moved elsewhere until identified: different life stages can travel with these materials. For repeated severe defoliation, ask an arborist or forest-health service to assess the tree. Routine broad treatment of a few larvae can interfere with the natural enemies that suppress this sawfly.
researchNotes: NRCan supplies an independent forest-health account; EPPO combines taxonomic keys, movement pathways and later biological-control literature. The old NRCan synonym list conflates historical uses of polytoma, so that name is not presented as a current synonym. Management is observation and pathway prevention, not an unverified treatment prescription.

sources.title: Natural Resources Canada: European spruce sawfly

claims: Larvae mainly consume older spruce foliage.
Historical outbreaks declined following viral disease.
Mature larvae are about 20 mm.
Late feeding larvae have five white stripes.
Gilpinia polytoma is a separate species requiring detailed identification.
Eggs and larvae can move on plants and cut branches; cocoons can occur in pot soil.

proposedDescription: European starling is the short-tailed, pointed-billed bird often walking briskly across a lawn or gathering in a noisy flock. Its dark feathers show green and purple reflections in good light, while fresh winter plumage carries many pale spots. Introduced to North America, it now uses farms, towns and other open landscapes extensively. It eats insects as well as fruit and grain, and nests inside cavities. Competition for nest sites and large concentrations around buildings or livestock feed are more useful concerns than the presence of a single bird.
identification: Adults measure about 20-23 cm long, with a compact body, short squared tail and pointed triangular wings. Breeding birds have a yellow bill; winter birds have a darker bill and conspicuous pale feather tips. Juveniles are plain gray-brown, sometimes with a patchwork of emerging spotted adult feathers. Common Grackles, blackbirds and cowbirds may join the same flock, so assess each bird rather than naming the whole group. Obtain a side view showing bill and tail, plus a flight image if possible. Color alone is unreliable in shade or at a distance.
actions: Reduce access to spilled grain, unsecured garbage and other concentrated food around buildings. Check damaged vents and eaves, then repair openings only after confirming that no birds or dependent young remain inside. Identify nest occupants before any intervention, because native birds use many of the same cavities. For a large recurring roost, consult a wildlife professional about exclusion suited to the building. Avoid sticky bird repellents: they can contaminate feathers of starlings and other birds. Scare devices often lose effect as birds become accustomed to them, so prioritize preventing access to the actual food or shelter.
researchNotes: Cornell provides the seasonal identification account; Illinois DNR provides separately authored exclusion and conflict guidance. Illinois-specific legal statements and unsupported disease generalizations are omitted. Named flock associates are not assigned unverified diagnostic measurements.

claims: Adults are 20-23 cm with short tails and pointed wings.
Bill and plumage change seasonally; juveniles are brown.
Mixed winter flocks occur.
Starlings use cavities and compete for nest sites.
Food restriction and exclusion can reduce conflicts.
Avoid trapping birds during repairs and avoid sticky repellents.

proposedDescription: European stickseed is a rough, hairy annual whose tiny blue flowers give way to fruits armed with hooked prickles. Those fruits readily catch on clothing and animal coats, carrying seeds away from roadsides, fields and other disturbed ground. Plants may grow as summer annuals or start as autumn rosettes. A patch can return from seeds even after the standing plants disappear. Its presence is especially worth noticing along routes where people, pets or equipment can carry the fruits into cleaner ground.
identification: Look for narrow, alternate leaves with unbroken edges, stiff pale hairs and small five-lobed blue flowers, sometimes white. Plants commonly stand several tens of centimeters tall. Mature fruit is essential: European stickseed has nutlets about 3-4 mm long with two, occasionally three, rows of hooked prickles. Native flatspine stickseed, Lappula occidentalis, normally has one row. Photograph several ripe fruits closely enough to count the rows, together with a whole plant and flower. A blue flower or a burr stuck to clothing is insufficient for a confident identification.
actions: Before plants shed their hooked fruits, remove small confirmed patches where digging is permitted and contain any fruiting material. Check clothing, boot seams, pet coats and equipment after passing through a patch, disposing of removed burrs where they cannot establish. Do not rely on one mowing: cut plants can regrow and increase seed production. Revisit the site for new seedlings over several seasons and restore suitable vegetation on bare disturbed soil. In pasture or crops, have the plant identified before choosing a management method; the native flatspine stickseed can occur in similar settings.
researchNotes: Go Botany supplies regional diagnostic characters and the Alaska Natural Heritage account supplies seed dispersal and mowing limitations from separate weed literature. The Alaska sheet's apparent 91 cm basal-leaf typo is excluded. Pulling and contained disposal are bounded seed-prevention advice, not a claimed eradication trial.

sources.title: University of Alaska: European stickseed biology

claims: Alternate entire leaves and blue flowers characterize the plant.
Nutlets are 3-4 mm with multiple rows of prickles.
Lappula occidentalis differs in fruit armature.
It reproduces by seed and burrs attach to clothing and fur.
Mowing or grazing can be followed by regrowth and increased seed production.
Seeds persist for several years.

proposedDescription: European turkey oak is a large deciduous tree from southern Europe and western Asia, often recognizable by the shaggy cups around its acorns. Planted trees can grow well beyond a garden's scale, reaching 20 m or more. Their leaves vary considerably, so a single unusually lobed leaf can be misleading. Look for the buds and acorns as well as the crown. A cultivated tree is not by itself evidence of harmful spread; seedlings establishing beyond planting sites provide more useful information about local behavior.
identification: Leaves are usually 7-12 cm long, dark green and rough above, with irregular pointed teeth or lobes. Young undersides are hairy. Slender, persistent bristles surround the buds, and the acorn cup has long curled-back scales that give it a mossy appearance. Acorns take two seasons to mature. Quercus castaneifolia and hybrids involving it or cork oak can complicate recognition; European turkey oak generally has fewer, deeper, less regular leaf teeth. Photograph several leaves, a twig with buds, bark and intact acorn cups, recording whether the tree was planted.
actions: Check beneath and beyond planted trees for self-sown seedlings, especially where a garden meets woodland or other unmanaged ground. Identify seedlings before removing them, since native oaks may be growing alongside them. Where unwanted spread is confirmed, remove manageable young plants with permission and monitor for further recruitment from acorns. Do not distribute acorns or transplant volunteers into natural areas. A mature tree needs a site-specific decision that considers its condition and nearby habitat; use a qualified arborist for large-tree work. The sources here do not justify automatic removal of every planted European turkey oak.
researchNotes: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria supplies detailed morphology and hybrid limits; Woodland Trust independently supports growth, seasonal leaves and diagnostic acorn cups. UK gall-wasp and conservation-impact claims are deliberately not transferred to US settings. Actions are bounded observation and prevention rather than a purported eradication protocol.

proposedDescription: European water plantain grows at shallow-water margins, lifting broad leaves and branching flower stems above a basal clump. Small three-petaled flowers develop into rings of dry fruits that can float away. The name needs care in North America: older accounts used Alisma plantago-aquatica for plants now treated as native species such as A. triviale and A. subcordatum. A water plantain beside a pond therefore should not be assumed to be the introduced European species from its general appearance or an old label.
identification: Flowering plants can reach roughly 0.5-1.8 m. Emergent leaves are broadly elliptic to oval, usually with a rounded or heart-shaped base and long stalks. The flower branches form successive whorls, and mature fruit clusters have a small central gap. Alisma lanceolatum generally has narrower leaves with wedge-shaped bases and tightly packed fruit clusters without that gap. Young plants can overlap. Native A. triviale and A. subcordatum require regional keys using flower and fruit measurements. Photograph leaf bases, open flowers with a scale, and ripe fruit heads from above and beside; retain location and planting history.
actions: Have a flowering or fruiting plant checked by a local herbarium or wetland botanist before removing it as an introduction. Protect the surrounding wetland while identification is pending. Keep garden-pond plants, mud and discarded rootstocks out of streams and natural ponds, because seeds float and the plant can reproduce from short underground stems. If an introduced population is confirmed, discuss containment with the land manager before disturbing sediment or working in water. Do not infer a control method from accounts of other Alisma species: native lookalikes and site access are central to a sound decision.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where the current assessment differs: Fresh review 2026-10-31: NZ Flora provides exact European-species morphology; UW directly documents historical Wisconsin use for two native species. The evidence preserves a genuine North American occurrence-attribution problem. The issue is not inability to recognize the genus or lack of a control trial. Next: Audit original catalog determination names against flowering or fruiting vouchers.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: A true European-water-plantain account can proceed without assuming older North American plantago-aquatica labels identify that species. Independent New Zealand flora morphology and North American herbarium nomenclature support the distinction. Fresh Burke records reveal differing regional/current treatments, so no new local range or native-status assertion is added. Occurrence uncertainty remains separate from the accurate general profile. Next step: Review the scientific-species draft; separately audit North American vouchers and regional native-status treatments before updating a map. No catalog IDs, occurrence mappings or public records changed. Local editorial review only; release remains deferred.

proposedDescription: European waterclover looks like a four-leaf clover growing in shallow water, but it is a fern. Four fan-shaped leaflets stand on slender stalks or float at the surface, while creeping underground stems connect the plants. It can also occupy exposed mud as water levels fall. Expansion within a pond is often vegetative. The clover-like leaves are a useful first clue, but several native waterclovers have a very similar appearance, so an unfamiliar patch should be documented before removal.
identification: Leaves divide into four wedge-shaped leaflets; the smooth stalks and leaflets may be floating, underwater or above the surface. Small brown spore cases, called sporocarps, develop near the leaf-stalk bases and are about 5 mm long. Their stalk arrangement matters. Hairy waterclover, Marsilea vestita, has hairy foliage and unbranched sporocarp stalks, whereas European waterclover has branched sporocarp stalks. Other Marsilea comparisons may need a specialist. Photograph leaf surfaces, the creeping stem and several mature spore cases with a scale. Do not identify the species from leaflet count alone.
actions: Photograph a suspected escaped patch and record its location, water depth and approximate extent. Submit the observation to the local aquatic invasive-species program, particularly where waterclover is being watched for new occurrences. Keep pond divisions, muddy equipment and aquarium waste out of natural waters. Inspect boots and tools for attached creeping stems before leaving the site. Avoid breaking up a patch with a rake while identification is uncertain, because native waterclovers can be involved and fragments are a potential transport concern. Plan any removal with the waterbody manager rather than assuming surface-leaf removal reaches the whole plant.
researchNotes: The USDA Forest Service account explicitly warns about native Marsilea lookalikes; Michigan provides independent current detection/reporting guidance. Both were read as substantive indexed excerpts, not claimed full text. The USGS native-range sentence conflicts with its introduced account and was not used. Expert identification needs alone do not invalidate this species profile.

proposedDescription: European white birch is a deciduous tree with pale bark, slender hanging twigs and small, sharply toothed leaves. Commonly planted forms include deeply cut leaves and strongly weeping branches. Its trunk changes with age: dark fissures can become prominent enough that an older tree looks much less white than a young one. A planted birch should be assessed for its actual local spread and health. In warm or dry settings, stress and bronze birch borer can be a more immediate concern than seedling establishment.
identification: Typical trees reach about 12-15 m, sometimes taller. The alternate leaves are usually 2.5-7.5 cm long, broadly triangular to diamond-shaped, with a long pointed tip and teeth within larger teeth. Young stems are hairless and resin-dotted. White bark peels less freely than paper birch, Betula papyrifera, and becomes darker with age. Cylindrical fruiting catkins are roughly 2-4 cm long. Photograph twig hairs or their absence, several complete leaves, bark and catkins. Cultivars can greatly alter leaf shape and branching, so bark color or a weeping outline alone is insufficient.
actions: If volunteers appear beyond a planted tree, identify them before removing seedlings among native birches. Map repeated recruitment rather than treating every pale-barked tree as an escape. Avoid distributing unwanted seedlings into natural areas. For retained landscape trees, address drought stress with site-appropriate care and have thinning crowns assessed for borers or other problems. Do not move suspect infested branches to another property. Large or failing trees need professional assessment; the sources support susceptibility to bronze birch borer but do not establish a universal invasive-management requirement for European white birch.
researchNotes: Oregon State and Colorado State independently document bark, leaves and twigs; Oregon State also supports borer susceptibility under stress. A typographic error in Oregon State's metric maximum height is excluded. Seedling monitoring and material containment are conservative recommendations, not claimed species-specific eradication research.

proposedDescription: European white waterlily is a rooted aquatic perennial with rounded floating leaves and large flowers, usually white around a yellow center. It grows from substantial horizontal underground stems in the mud of still or slow water. Garden waterlilies complicate its identification: many cultivars contain ancestry from several species and may resemble this one closely. A white waterlily in a pond can therefore be a native species, a planted cultivar or European white waterlily; flower color alone does not settle the question.
identification: Floating leaves are glossy and smooth-edged, commonly 12-25 cm long, with a deep notch and basal lobes that may overlap. Flowers are often 10-14 cm across and have numerous petals and yellow stamens. The creeping rhizome branches sparsely. Nymphaea mexicana usually has yellow flowers and a different, upright underground structure; fragrant waterlily, N. odorata, and white garden hybrids are much harder comparisons. Some hybrids cannot be reliably separated by ordinary photographs. Record leaf undersides, flower side and center, scent, planting history and seasonal changes. Avoid destructive collection of rhizomes merely to obtain an identification.
actions: Keep pond plants and their divided rhizomes within managed cultivation; never discard them in lakes, ditches or streams. For an unfamiliar wild patch, photograph it from a safe bank and ask a local aquatic botanist to distinguish native waterlilies and garden hybrids. Retain any nursery label, since it can help trace a planting even when the label itself is imprecise. If expansion obstructs a managed pond, discuss selective containment with the owner and aquatic-plant adviser. Broad removal based only on white flowers risks removing a native plant, and clipping leaves alone does not remove the rooted perennial.
researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Full NZ morphology and Frankfurt's own genetically checked conservation plants support a distinct N. alba while explaining cultivar confusion. Hybrid lookalikes require caution but do not invalidate a clearly scoped true-species profile. No claim is made that all white waterlilies or catalog observations are pure alba. Next: Retain the hybrid warning, professional identification and no wild planting advice.

proposedDescription: European yellow lupine is a hairy annual with yellow pea-shaped flowers above leaves divided into finger-like leaflets. It has been cultivated as well as occurring wild in its Mediterranean home range, so a roadside plant may originate from a nearby planting. Flowers give way to densely hairy pods containing several seeds. The annual habit matters when considering spread: preventing seed production addresses its next generation, while the presence of a cultivated crop does not establish an ecological problem in every surrounding landscape.
identification: Plants are erect or spreading, strongly branched near the base and can approach 1 m tall. Leaves usually have 5-11 leaflets, each about 2-4 cm long, with silky hairs. The yellow, strongly scented flowers are about 13-16 mm long and form upright clusters. Pods measure approximately 3-6 cm and are densely silky. Yellow flowers alone do not identify a lupine, especially around mixed ornamental plantings. Photograph the whole plant including its base, both leaf surfaces, the flower cluster and mature pods; note whether it completes its life cycle in one season.
actions: Check whether plants are part of an intentional crop before treating them as unwanted escapes. Where confirmed volunteers are spreading into adjacent ground, remove small plants before pods mature and contain seed-bearing material. Do not scatter surplus seed or discard mature pods along field margins. Recheck the area after the next germination period and avoid unnecessary soil disturbance that creates open establishment sites. Keep identification separate from feed decisions: an ornamental or wild lupine should not be added to livestock feed on the strength of a common name. Agricultural stands need crop-specific advice from local extension.
researchNotes: PlantNET supplies detailed morphology and cultivated/naturalized context; Kew independently establishes the accepted annual species and Mediterranean native range. No reliable named-lookalike key or US eradication trial was obtained, so no invented distinction or treatment efficacy is offered. Actions are annual seed-prevention and cautious crop identification.

proposedDescription: Evergreen bugloss is a coarse-leaved perennial with small bright blue flowers and a deep, persistent root. It can remain as a dense clump in shaded gardens and escape into nearby disturbed ground. The flowers have pale centers and are visited by pollinating insects, but the plant's size and spread can make it unwelcome among smaller plants. Its other familiar name, green alkanet, refers to the same species. Removing only the leaves leaves its root system capable of producing another season's growth.
identification: Upright bristly stems commonly reach 30-100 cm. The large basal leaves are oval with pointed tips and can reach 40 cm; leaves become smaller and less stalked up the stem. Bright blue, five-lobed flowers have a white center and sit in leafy clusters. Annual bugloss, common bugloss and viper's bugloss have narrower leaves and flower clusters that coil and unfurl more conspicuously. Photograph the basal leaf rosette, upper leaves and flower arrangement, not just one blue flower. Plants without flowers may need confirmation before digging.
actions: Remove unwanted seedlings while small, and dig established clumps when soil is moist enough to recover as much of the deep root as possible. Root fragments can regrow, so revisit treated ground. Cut and contain flowering or seed-bearing stems before moving the rest of the plant. Keep roots and seed capsules out of ordinary home compost and do not move contaminated soil or divisions to another garden. Where plants are retained, deadhead before seed develops. Gloves make the bristly foliage easier to handle. Disposal arrangements should follow local waste guidance rather than assuming every green-waste system destroys viable roots.
researchNotes: King County supplies direct identification, named comparisons and manual removal guidance; RHS independently supports deadheading and avoiding root/seed contamination of home compost. The King County image caption's incorrect two-year definition of perennial is excluded. Regional legal requirements are not generalized.

Digging should remove the taproot; fragments can resprout.

proposedDescription: Despite its catalog name, evergreen clematis is a deciduous woody climber; Clematis vitalba usually loses its leaves in winter. It is also widely called old man's beard because the pale, feathery seed heads remain conspicuous after flowering. Established vines can climb high into trees and cover shrubs, reducing light and adding weight. Ground-trailing stems and discarded fragments can also establish. The scientific name is especially important here, since other clematis sold as evergreen vines are different species.
identification: Look for a woody vine with ridged young stems, peeling older bark and compound leaves commonly divided into five leaflets. Small creamy flowers occur in clusters, followed by fruit heads with long feathery tails. A vigorous mature vine may climb tens of meters. Native western white clematis can resemble it and is generally smaller, but size and regional location are not sufficient to identify a young plant. Photograph a complete leaf, paired leaf attachment, open flowers, fruit heads and the stem base. Do not confuse the catalog's common name with proof of evergreen foliage.
actions: Confirm the vine before removing it where native clematis occurs. Dig small ground-level plants and their roots where feasible. For vines climbing a tree, sever accessible stems near the ground and remove a short section to separate upper growth from the roots; let high growth die in place rather than pulling down branches. Recheck for rooted stems and shoots emerging from missed roots. Keep cut stems off moist soil, and contain seed heads before transport. Extensive vines or unstable supporting trees need professional help. Repeated follow-up matters because both roots and stem fragments can survive incomplete removal.
researchNotes: King County provides management and regional comparisons; Go Botany supplies an independent flora account. The catalog common name is retained but its misleading evergreen implication is explicitly corrected. Native-Clematis comparison is not treated as a universal size-only key, and regional legal status is omitted.

claims: Woody vines bear commonly five leaflets and persistent feathery fruit heads.
Leaves die back in winter.
Roots and fragments can regrow; cut climbing vines and follow up.

proposedDescription: Exotic leafroller moth is an East Asian moth whose caterpillars tie leaves and other soft plant parts together into feeding shelters. Apples, crabapples, pears and plums are among its hosts, although its host range is much broader. The visible damage comes from the caterpillars rather than the adult moth. In the northeastern United States it has one generation annually, overwintering as eggs on woody branches. Rolled leaves deserve inspection, but many native leafrollers create similar shelters and need different identification.
identification: Adults have dull brown forewings with darker brown or reddish markings, including a band crossing the entire wing. Forewing length is about 7-9.5 mm in males and 8-12.5 mm in females. Mature larvae reach roughly 22 mm, with a gray-green body and orange-brown head. Archips xylosteana and several other Archips can look similar; the male wing fold and continuous band help, but genital examination may be needed. Photograph a resting adult from above, or a larva with its head and shelter visible. Record the host, date and black egg masses on bark.
actions: Inspect new growth and folded leaves on affected fruit trees in spring, recording the proportion of shoots with active larvae rather than treating old damage alone. Keep suspect nursery plants and pruned infested material from moving to another property until identified. Send clear photographs and host information to extension or the state plant-health service; they may request a specimen. On a small accessible tree, removal of a few occupied leaf shelters can be considered after identification, without stripping healthy foliage. An orchard outbreak needs a locally timed integrated-pest plan, not treatment selected from the moth's common name.
researchNotes: CAES provides Maier's direct regional host and life-cycle work. Tortricid ID contributes independently authored diagnostic morphology and comparisons, including Bradley et al. larval characters; its Maier-derived biology is not counted as independent confirmation. No unsupported insecticide regimen or trap-based diagnosis is supplied.

proposedDescription: Expanded lobsterclaw is a large tropical perennial with banana-like leaves and upright clusters of orange, yellow or red bracts. The conspicuous colored structures surround much smaller greenish flowers; they are not giant petals. Native to tropical America, it is cultivated for its appearance and has naturalized in parts of Hawai'i. A substantial clump can persist beyond the garden where it began. Knowing whether nearby plants were deliberately planted or have established independently is useful when documenting its local spread.
identification: Plants are commonly 2-3 m tall. The long leaf blades can reach 65-160 cm, with sheathing stalk bases and smooth margins. Upright flower clusters have roughly 8-17 spreading, pointed bracts arranged around the central axis, rather than a hanging chain. Small flowers inside are green to yellow-green, and mature fruits are blue. Other cultivated Heliconia and hybrids can be similar, so photograph the whole upright cluster from two sides, bract spacing, enclosed flowers and leaf stalks. Leaf shape alone is not enough for a species determination.
actions: Keep discarded clump divisions and soil containing underground stems away from streams, forest margins and unmanaged land. Check beyond the planted bed for new clumps and document their connection, if any, to the original planting. Where a small escape is confirmed and removal is appropriate, recover the underground growing portions as well as the leaves, then monitor for renewed shoots. Contain fruiting heads during disposal. Large clumps beside water or desirable vegetation need a site-specific plan. This profile does not imply that every cultivated expanded lobsterclaw requires removal or that cutting its leaves eradicates it.
researchNotes: Bishop Museum provides voucher-linked morphology and documented Hawaiian naturalization; Bogotá Botanic Garden independently supports tropical-American origin and ornamental use. Neither establishes a US treatment trial. Practical guidance is limited to preventing movement of planted material and checking confirmed escapes; cultivar identity may require expert review.

claims: Perennial herbs are 2-3 m with large leaves and erect spirally arranged bracts.
Fruits are blue.

proposedDescription: Fall dandelion is a perennial rosette plant that raises several yellow flower heads on branching stems. It often appears in grassland, lawns, road margins and other open ground, flowering later in the season than many familiar spring dandelions. The catalog uses Leontodon autumnalis; many modern references place the same species in Scorzoneroides as S. autumnalis. Its branching flower stems and small stem scales are more informative than the general dandelion-like flower. A scattered plant in managed turf is a different management situation from repeated establishment in a sensitive grassland.
identification: Leaves form a basal rosette and are deeply, irregularly lobed, usually smooth or only sparsely hairy. Flowering stems commonly reach 20-75 cm and branch above, carrying small scale-like bracts and more than one yellow head. Common dandelion, Taraxacum officinale, has hollow, unbranched flower stalks without these scales. Hairy catsear, Hypochaeris radicata, also branches but generally has conspicuously hairy leaves. Photograph the complete flower stem, basal leaves and mature seed head. A close-up of a yellow head alone cannot separate these plants.
actions: For a small unwanted patch, remove the basal crown and rootstock rather than simply clipping the flower stems. Work before seed dispersal and contain mature seed heads. Revisit after rain and in the next growing season to check for surviving crowns or seedlings. In turf, maintain a healthy grass cover and correct the site conditions leaving repeated bare patches. In species-rich grassland, confirm identification and protect neighboring plants before digging. Do not assume that a general lawn treatment is suitable for pasture or conservation land, where management goals and desirable vegetation differ.
researchNotes:
UMass supplies direct field identification and seed reproduction; the independent NZ flora provides dimensions and rootstock details. The Alaska/Southeast guide supplies the named dandelion/catsear comparisons and root-removal advice in a substantive indexed excerpt. The modern generic name is supported by BSBI's published nomenclature discussion.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.

proposedDescription: Fallow deer is a medium-sized deer with an unusually variable coat. The familiar form is brown with white spots, but dark and nearly white animals also occur, so spotting is not a dependable requirement. Mature males carry broad, flattened antlers. Introduced populations and captive herds occur far beyond the species' original range. They graze and browse in mixtures of woodland and open ground, and escaped animals can establish locally. A sighting should be interpreted with local herd history rather than assuming every deer of unusual color is wild or introduced.
identification: Males typically stand about 90-100 cm at the shoulder and are larger than females. Mature buck antlers widen into flattened, hand-like upper sections with points along the rear edge; young males may carry simple spikes, and females usually lack antlers. Common-colored animals have spotted flanks and a dark stripe continuing down the tail, but dark or white forms can lack that pattern. Photograph the whole animal from a distance, including tail, rump and antlers if present. Sika and axis deer also have spotted coats; spots alone cannot establish fallow deer, especially in antlerless animals.
actions: Observe from a distance and keep dogs away. Record the location, number of animals, apparent ear tags or fencing nearby, and any repeated browsing damage. Report a suspected escaped captive deer to the relevant animal-control or wildlife authority rather than attempting to capture, transport or release it. Do not feed it to keep it near the property. Owners of captive herds should inspect containment after an escape and coordinate recovery with qualified help. Management of an established free-ranging herd depends on local wildlife rules and land ownership; photographs and a clear record of damage are useful first steps.
researchNotes: Animal Diversity Web supplies independent morphology and life-history literature; New Zealand DOC corroborates coat variation and antler development. ADW's old treatment of Persian fallow deer as a subspecies is not adopted. Southern Hemisphere breeding dates and New Zealand hunting permissions are not transferred to US advice.

claims: Coat colors vary widely; mature males bear palmate antlers.
Males are commonly 0.9-1 m at the shoulder.

proposedDescription: False amaranth is an annual herb with slender flower clusters rising from the leaf joints. Its tiny flowers range from pale whitish pink to deeper red, so it can be easy to overlook among other field weeds. The plant occurs in cultivated and disturbed ground across parts of tropical Africa and Asia. A close examination of its small fruits is more useful than its resemblance to an amaranth. Local occurrence and establishment should be documented before assuming that one accidental arrival represents a persistent problem.
identification: Plants commonly reach 15-50 cm, sometimes about 70 cm, with simple or low-branched stems and alternate, stalked leaves. Leaf shape varies from narrow to broadly oval. Slender flower clusters can reach 30 cm. Each small group includes a fertile central flower and reduced side flowers that develop antler-like scales. The nearly rounded fruit is about 2-2.5 mm, rough or ridged, with a persistent style and a firm rim. These tiny structures distinguish it more securely than leaf color. Photograph a whole plant, leaf joints and magnified mature fruit; an amaranth-like seedling may need expert examination.
actions: If an unfamiliar plant appears in a nursery container, seed bed or imported growing material, keep it from producing seed while arranging identification. Photograph it before removal and retain a contained sample if extension requests one. Small confirmed plants can be removed before fruit matures; collect fruiting stems without scattering their contents. Check the same growing area for subsequent seedlings and avoid moving its soil to another property. These are precautions against accidental seed spread. The consulted sources do not support a species-specific chemical program or a claim of widespread ecological harm in the United States.
researchNotes: Kew reproduces the detailed Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment; IISc independently summarizes Indian flora records and disturbed-habitat occurrence. No reliable US impact or control study was located. Readiness is limited to accurate recognition and conservative prevention, with no invented named-lookalike distinction or US harm claim.
