proposedDescription: False baby's breath, treated here in the traditional broad Galium mollugo sense, is a perennial bedstraw with narrow leaves arranged around the stem and many small white flowers. It can sprawl through surrounding vegetation in fields, hedges and disturbed places. Its name should not be confused with garden baby's breath, which belongs to another genus. The scientific name also needs care: Galium mollugo has been used broadly to include plants other floras call G. album. That difference affects records and identification, so a familiar common name does not establish which botanical concept was recorded.
identification: Look for slender, roughly four-angled stems, rings of several narrow leaves and branching groups of small white flowers. The flowers are only a few millimeters across, and paired mature fruits lack the conspicuous hooked covering of some other bedstraws. Galium album is a particularly close comparison; different floras separate or combine it, and published differences include flower size, branch orientation and chromosome number. Photograph a complete flowering shoot, several leaf whorls and mature fruit with a scale. A distant view of white flowers cannot resolve the G. mollugo-G. album distinction.
actions: Confirm the local botanical name before acting on an occurrence report. For a small, unwanted and identified patch, remove the perennial crown and attached underground growth rather than only the flowering tips, then watch for regrowth. Contain seed-bearing stems and avoid moving contaminated soil or hay into clean sites. In pasture, ask extension to assess the stand and desirable forage before choosing a control method. Document the original label or report name alongside the current determination; that preserves useful history without treating every record called G. mollugo as proof of the same narrowly defined taxon.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where the current assessment differs: Fresh review 2026-10-31: The NZ flora and Canadian government inventory freshly confirm different album/mollugo circumscriptions; VicFlora's relevant body could not be recovered after initial metadata access. This is a real scope conflict, so a narrow occurrence assertion cannot be inferred from older broad records. Next: Compare original vouchers and author-cited names with a chosen current regional flora. Inherited reference not used as fresh substantive evidence (unavailable or superseded by the specified original): https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/9d6fb7e6-b1bd-40a8-939b-51e16d6197e4 .

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: Galium mollugo can be presented in the explicitly broad traditional sense while the album split remains visible. Independent New Zealand flora and Canadian agronomic account describe the traditional plant; the fresh Swiss checklist explicitly recognizes a mollugo aggregate including album. A named aggregate is a supportable concept, not a license to transfer narrow-species occurrences. proposedDescription: False beardgrass is the tall clumping grass commonly known as vetiver, grown for its aromatic roots and for erosion-control plantings. Its dense upright leaves and deep roots make an established clump substantial even when it produces little seed. Cultivar identity matters: the sterile cultivar 'Sunshine' is widely used, but that does not mean every plant assigned to the species is sterile. A planted barrier, an abandoned clump and a seed-producing escape should therefore be recorded separately when assessing local spread.
identification: Expect a dense perennial tuft with stiff, narrow leaves and stems that can reach roughly 1.5-3 m. Leaf blades are commonly 30-100 cm long and 4-10 mm wide, with rough margins. The small flap at the leaf-stem junction is a fringe of hairs. Flower clusters are open and branched, with paired spikelets. Roots are aromatic, but digging is unnecessary for an initial observation. Photograph the tuft base, leaf junction and mature flower cluster, and retain cultivar records. Appearance alone cannot establish that a plant is the sterile 'Sunshine' cultivar.
actions: Before adding false beardgrass to an erosion-control project, verify the planting material's identity and cultivar with the supplier and local conservation adviser. Do not distribute unnamed divisions as though their sterility were confirmed. Monitor beyond the planted row for new plants and note whether they arise from planted divisions or seedlings. If an unwanted clump must be removed, plan for its substantial rooted crown and stabilize the exposed soil afterward. Avoid destabilizing a bank through unplanned excavation. No blanket eradication recommendation follows from the species name alone, especially for an established, documented sterile planting.
researchNotes: AusGrass supplies field morphology; NC State independently discusses clumping growth and 'Sunshine'. Bowen and Estep's 2017 conference abstract reports no straightforward vegetative distinction between sterile and fertile material. The society's indexed abstract was read; its 33 MB proceedings exceeded the web reader limit and were not downloaded. This replaces the stale NC DOCKS link. Conflicting spikelet measurements in online floras are excluded.

proposedDescription: False oleander scale is a sap-feeding armored scale found on many ornamental plants, not just oleander. Its pale covers can look like flecks of white paint on leaves and green stems. Feeding may produce a yellow patch around each insect, and heavy infestations can weaken plants. The cover remains visible after the insect dies, so a plant with old scale marks is not necessarily undergoing active damage. Nursery movement is an important practical setting for inspection and early containment.
identification: Female covers are elongated or pear-shaped and white, with a reddish-brown remnant of shed skin near the narrow end. Male covers are smaller and often clustered; females are more scattered. Examine both leaf surfaces and green stems for these covers and surrounding yellow tissue. Pinnaspis strachani can look similar, but its shed-skin cap is generally yellow rather than reddish brown. Color is only a preliminary clue, and microscopic examination may be necessary. Photograph the host, colony and individual covers with a scale; ask a diagnostician to confirm whether living insects remain beneath them.
actions: Isolate an infested container plant from clean stock while obtaining identification. Inspect neighboring susceptible plants, especially leaf undersides and tender stems, and avoid giving away cuttings from the affected plant. Where only a few leaves or small shoots are heavily occupied, contained removal may reduce the source of crawlers without sacrificing the entire plant. Reinspect for newly settled scales rather than judging success by old white covers alone. For a persistent infestation, ask extension for host-specific integrated management and crawler timing. Do not improvise hot-water treatments or pesticide mixtures from nursery research.
researchNotes: Hawai'i CTAHR supplies an independent host/damage account; Argentina's official surveillance account supplies cover morphology and the Pinnaspis comparison. CTAHR content was read through indexed excerpts because later full retrieval timed out. Advice emphasizes containment and diagnosis; no unverified chemical or thermal schedule is used.

proposedDescription: The catalog's false scale insect is Pseudococcus nakaharai, more specifically known as Nakahara mealybug. It is associated especially with cacti and can occur around their roots, making an infestation easy to miss during a quick inspection of the upper plant. Plant-trade interceptions show why cactus collections deserve careful checking before plants are shared. ITIS treats it as native to the continental US; interceptions and greenhouse occurrences do not establish that every domestic population is introduced.
identification: Look for small oval mealybugs and waxy material on the cactus, root collar and accessible roots. The specialist account treats its visible wax-filament pattern as probable rather than firmly established, so filament counts should not be used as a field diagnosis. Pseudococcus viburni is a close microscopic lookalike. Separation uses the distribution of pores and ducts on a prepared adult female, including pores restricted to the hind tibia rather than both femur and tibia. Photograph the colony and host, but expect a laboratory specimen to be needed. A phone photograph of white wax cannot show these diagnostic structures.
actions: Keep a suspect cactus separate from the collection and stop sharing cuttings, offsets, pots or growing medium from it. Examine nearby plants and the root collar when routine repotting makes it accessible; avoid unnecessary damage to a valuable cactus just to search for insects. Ask extension or a plant-health diagnostic service how to submit a contained specimen. Record the plant's purchase history and any imported origin. Dispose of badly infested material only in a contained way that prevents insects moving to other plants. Species confirmation should precede treatment, and origin status should precede an invasive-species claim.

proposedDescription: False spiraea is a deciduous shrub that produces upright clusters of small white flowers above long leaves divided into many narrow leaflets. Its stems often arise in groups, and new shoots can appear beyond the original plant as root suckers. This habit can turn a single ornamental planting into a colony. The name resembles spiraea, but the compound leaves are an important clue that it belongs to Sorbaria. Local spread from a planted bed is more informative than the size of an individual shrub.
identification: Typical shrubs stand about 1.5-2.5 m, sometimes taller, with stout, largely hairless young stems. Leaves alternate along the branches and usually contain 13-25 pointed leaflets with finely doubled teeth. Dense white flower clusters can reach about 25 cm long and appear in early summer. The foliage resembles mountain ash, but the combination of a suckering shrub habit and upright flower clusters helps recognition. Photograph an entire compound leaf, its attachment to the twig, flowers and the pattern of shoots around the base. Cultivars vary in size and foliage color.
actions: Check the perimeter of a retained planting for root suckers and remove unwanted shoots promptly, following them back toward the source where this can be done without harming nearby plants. Do not give away rooted suckers where they could spread into natural ground. If removing a colony, account for the connected underground growth and revisit for new shoots; cutting stems once can simply rejuvenate the shrub. Contain root-bearing soil during transport. Choose any replacement planting for the actual site and available maintenance, rather than assuming a compact cultivar will never spread.
researchNotes: Colorado State independently describes leaflets, twigs and flowers; NC State supports root-sucker spread and pruning response. NC State's broad cultivar noninvasiveness assertion is omitted because cultivar identity and context are not established. Practical actions focus on the verified clonal pathway.

proposedDescription: False yellowhead is a sticky, strongly scented perennial shrub with numerous yellow daisy-like flower heads. Older stems become woody near the base, helping distinguish a persistent plant from an annual yellow-flowered weed. It grows in disturbed places in its Mediterranean region and has become problematic in some introduced settings. Contact with its sticky oils can irritate skin. Its close relative stinkwort is also sticky and yellow-flowered, so an identification should include the base, leaves and flower size rather than scent alone.
identification: Plants commonly reach about 1-1.5 m. The gray-green leaves are alternate, stalkless, pointed and often toothed, with bases partly clasping the stem. They are generally 2.5-10 cm long. Flower heads measure roughly 1-2 cm across, with conspicuous yellow rays around the center. Stinkwort, Dittrichia graveolens, is a slender annual with narrower leaves and smaller heads, usually under 1 cm. Photograph the woody base, leaf attachment and a measured flower head without rubbing the plant against bare skin. Young plants need particular care because the perennial base may be inconspicuous.
actions: Wear gloves and cover exposed skin when handling a confirmed plant. Keep livestock away from cut or discarded material rather than adding it to feed or bedding. Photograph and report a newly discovered population to the local weed program before spreading material through mowing or earthwork. For a small accessible plant on permitted ground, obtain guidance on removing the rooted base and containing flower heads before seeds disperse. Clean plant material from tools and revisit for regrowth. The safest plan for an extensive patch depends on its location and nearby desirable vegetation; no chemical recipe is implied here.
researchNotes: NSW WeedWise supports sticky foliage, irritation and livestock precautions; the independent Cyprus botanist's account supports the perennial-versus-annual comparison with D. graveolens. Cyprus measurements concern subsp. angustifolia and are used only where consistent with the broader NSW account. No Australian statutory requirement is applied to the US.

proposedDescription: Fan-bearing wood-borer is a small beetle whose males carry conspicuously branched antennae. Its larvae tunnel within hardwood, including felled timber and occasionally furniture, while adults consume little. Related evidence also records it in exposed dry wood of old broad-leaved trees. Small round exit holes can reveal a past infestation, but holes alone cannot show which beetle made them or whether insects remain active. The distinction matters before treating a building, a piece of furniture or dead wood outdoors.
identification: Adults are narrow, dark brown beetles about 3-5 mm long. Males have fan-like or comb-like antennae; females have shorter saw-edged antennae. Common furniture beetle, Anobium punctatum, is similar in size and setting but lacks the male's elaborate antennae and differs in thorax shape. Fan-bearing wood-borer exit holes are commonly about 1.5-2 mm, with fine or gritty boring material nearby. Photograph an adult with a scale, the antennae and the affected wood. Larvae and old holes usually require expert interpretation, and a hole diameter is not a species diagnosis.
actions: Set aside a suspect movable wooden object from unaffected items and retain any emerged adults for identification in a secure container. Record fresh boring dust and new holes over time, since old damage may be inactive. Avoid moving untreated suspect timber or firewood between properties. For valuable furniture or structural wood, consult a conservator or qualified timber-pest professional before treatment; heat, freezing or surface chemicals can damage objects or fail to reach larvae if applied casually. Do not remove habitat trees simply because similar holes occur in dead wood: assess tree safety and insect identity separately.
researchNotes: A museum integrated-pest resource supplies adult dimensions and object-associated damage; Ireland's NPWS survey independently documents outdoor dry-heartwood habitat. The older Forestry Commission account corroborates female antennae. Indoor prevention is conservative; no unverified treatment temperature, fumigation or structural-danger claim is included.

proposedDescription: Father-and-child plant is a small perennial cudweed with green upper leaf surfaces and densely pale-haired undersides. Short creeping stems can link neighboring rosettes, while upright shoots carry tight clusters of tiny flower heads. Older floras may list it under Gnaphalium japonicum or related historical names. It is native in parts of Australasia, so a foreign source calling it native does not determine its status at a US observation. The useful first task is to distinguish it from the many superficially similar cudweeds.
identification: Flowering stems commonly stand about 10-35 cm and carry a few small leaves above the basal rosette. Basal leaves are narrow-elliptic to spoon-shaped, often 4-18 cm long, green above and silvery-white with dense hairs below. Numerous tiny heads, each about 1.5-2 mm across, form a compact terminal cluster, sometimes with smaller clusters below. The leafy bracts beneath the cluster and creeping stems are useful details. Photograph both leaf surfaces, the stem base and a close flower cluster. Other Euchiton and Gnaphalium-like plants need a regional key; leaf whiteness alone is insufficient.
actions: Confirm a suspected occurrence with a regional flora or herbarium before removing small cudweeds among native vegetation. Where the plant is unwanted in a managed bed, lift the rosettes with their connecting creeping stems and monitor for remaining rooted pieces. Contain mature flower heads and avoid carrying contaminated potting soil or turf to a clean site. Record whether the patch enlarges vegetatively or new seedlings appear farther away. These are limited containment steps; the available flora accounts do not establish broad US ecological damage or a tested chemical control program.
researchNotes: The NZ flora and University of Tasmania key are independent descriptive treatments, with PlantNET corroborating size and stoloniferous habit. Historical synonym concepts are acknowledged without claiming all Gnaphalium records map automatically to this taxon. No named-lookalike distinction was found strong enough to invent a simple field rule.

proposedDescription: Faucet snail is a small freshwater snail with a smooth brown shell and a hard lid that closes its opening. Introduced from Europe, it occurs in parts of the Great Lakes and other US waters. It can act as an intermediate host for parasites that harm waterfowl, making prevention of further movement important even though individual snails are easily overlooked. Mud, aquatic vegetation and wet equipment can carry it between sites. Established populations are much harder to address than snails caught during equipment inspection.
identification: Adults usually remain below about 12-15 mm. The shell has roughly five to six whorls, a relatively high spire and an opening less than half the shell's height. The adult lid, called an operculum, is thick, whitish and marked with concentric growth rings; young lids may have spiral markings. Similar small snails in Amnicolidae and Hydrobiidae generally have thinner, brownish lids. Photograph the shell from the opening side, the lid and the opposite side with a millimeter scale. Do not force the animal from its shell, and do not identify an empty shell by color alone.
actions: Before leaving a waterbody, remove mud, plants and attached snails from boats, anchors, waders, decoys and other equipment, and drain retained water as required locally. Let equipment dry fully and follow the local aquatic-invasive program's approved decontamination method before another launch. Photograph a suspected new occurrence and report its exact location; ask before transporting a live sample. Never release aquarium snails or move them as bait. Do not add chemicals to a lake or pond to kill a suspected population. Open-water control remains difficult, so preventing transport is the practical priority.
researchNotes: USGS provides morphological and occurrence synthesis; Ohio DNR independently supplies the operculum comparison; North Dakota supplies equipment-prevention guidance and control limitations. No mirrored USGS/FWS account is counted as an independent group. Exact chemical or hot-water recipes are omitted from public instructions.

proposedDescription: Fawn melania is a slender freshwater snail recorded from Florida springs and streams. Its name carries an important uncertainty: some specialists treat it as a form of the variable red-rimmed melania, Melanoides tuberculata, while others provisionally keep it separate. A shell matching the traditional description therefore does not settle the species question. Published accounts describe introduced Florida populations, but their ecological effects are poorly documented. Possible competition with native snails should not be presented as a demonstrated impact of this particular taxon.
identification: Traditional descriptions give fawn melania a pointed, olive-green shell about 30-40 mm long, with reddish vertical markings, fine spiral lines, and 8-12 turns. The tip is often worn away. Fine upright ribs are most evident on the upper turns, and the shell base usually lacks a colored spiral band. The opening is teardrop-shaped. These are useful observations, not a definitive separation from Melanoides tuberculata. Photograph the entire shell, opening, base, and surface sculpture beside a ruler. Tarebia granifera is another possible confusion. A mollusk specialist should assess difficult material and explain which taxonomic treatment is being used.
actions: Keep aquarium snails, plants, gravel, and water out of streams, ponds, and drains that reach natural water. If a similar snail appears at a new outdoor site, photograph it in place and send the location and images to the state aquatic-species program or a museum mollusk specialist. Ask before collecting or transporting specimens. Clean attached mud and vegetation from equipment before moving between waters. Do not apply salt, bleach, or aquarium snail treatments to an outdoor population. Identification and site assessment should precede any removal plan, particularly where native snails may be mixed with the suspected population.

proposedDescription: Feather cockscomb is an annual grown for upright flower heads that retain their color and texture as they dry. The species includes several cultivated forms: feathery garden selections differ from plants with narrow, silvery or pink flower spikes. Escaped plants can occur in disturbed ground and cultivated fields. Each small flower has papery parts surrounding a seed capsule, so a fading head may still be producing seed. Its presence outside a flower bed is worth documenting, but an ornamental escape does not by itself demonstrate serious ecological harm.
identification: Feather cockscomb has upright, mostly hairless stems and alternate leaves with smooth edges and pointed tips. Plants may reach about 1-1.5 m, although garden selections vary considerably. The species' leaves can be narrow or broadly lance-shaped; flower clusters range from dense cylindrical spikes to the branching plumes of Plumosa Group cultivars. Small dark, shiny seeds develop inside capsules. Photograph the whole plant, a leaf attachment, and both fresh and mature flower heads. Crested cockscomb forms belong within the same broad cultivated species, so a different head shape alone does not establish a different species.
actions: Check the edges of beds and nearby disturbed soil for seedlings after flowering. Where feather cockscomb is unwanted, remove young plants before seed heads mature and collect old flower heads before moving the rest of the plant. Keep seed-bearing flower arrangements and garden waste out of natural areas. Use purchased seed or plants with clear names rather than distributing unidentified volunteers. A few seedlings can be handled individually, with follow-up for later emergence. If plants persist well beyond cultivation, record the extent and ask local extension staff whether escape is already documented in the area.
researchNotes: Smithsonian Hawaiian Flora provides species-level morphology; NParks independently describes the cultivated Plumosa Group and deadheading. The catalog common name emphasizes feathered cultivars while the scientific name covers a broader species. Geographic origin differs among accounts and is deliberately not asserted here; no universal invasive impact or control efficacy is claimed.

proposedDescription: Feathered mosquitofern is a tiny floating fern whose branching shoots form triangular pieces at the water surface. It can multiply into dense mats, shading water beneath them. A close association with nitrogen-fixing bacteria helps explain why this small fern can grow vigorously without obtaining all its nitrogen from the surrounding water. Plants may be green or reddish, so color alone is unreliable. Because other mosquitoferns look similar, a floating red or green mat should be identified before it is reported as this introduced species.
identification: Individual feathered mosquitofern shoots are commonly about 1-2.5 cm long. A fairly straight central axis carries side branches that become longer toward the base, producing a featherlike triangle. Tiny overlapping leaves have an upper surface lobe and a submerged lobe, with roots hanging below. Native mosquitoferns, including plants called Azolla caroliniana or A. microphylla in different accounts, require comparison rather than identification by mat color. Photograph separated shoots against a millimeter scale, the branching pattern, and the underside. Fine leaf structures and reproductive material may be needed for confident identification or subspecies assignment.
actions: Do not transfer floating plants or pond water to another waterbody. Inspect purchased aquatic plants and equipment for tiny fern fragments, and contain any removed material so it cannot wash back into water. For a suspected new outdoor population, contact the state aquatic-invasive-species program with clear close-ups and the location. In a small managed pond, repeated collection with a fine mesh may reduce the mat, but missed fragments can regrow; seek advice before disturbing larger infestations. Reduce avoidable fertilizer runoff into the pond. Broad chemical treatment or complete eradication cannot be recommended from a photograph.
researchNotes: USGS provides species identification and comparison with other Azolla; Florida agriculture's field guide independently supports the triangular floating habit and mat formation. Wisconsin DNR supplies bounded mechanical-removal and nutrient guidance. No subspecies is assigned, and no claim that skimming reliably eradicates an infestation is made.

proposedDescription: Feathertop is a perennial grass grown for soft-looking flower heads above arching leaves. The many long bristles give mature heads a broad, pale bottlebrush outline. Outside cultivation it can establish in disturbed places, and its bristled seed units can travel on animals, clothing, and equipment. Garden waste and deliberate planting are avoidable ways to move it further. A decorative grass beside a road still needs identification: several related fountain grasses have similar heads, and their appearance changes as the flowers mature.
identification: Feathertop forms a dense clump, generally no more than about 1 m tall. Narrow leaves arch outward and may roll inward along their edges. Flower heads are roughly 2-10 cm long, usually silvery or whitish and sometimes tinged purple. Their long, unequal, feathered bristles are a useful feature. Fountain grass, Cenchrus setaceus, generally has longer, narrower pinkish or reddish heads rather than feathertop's broad pale ones. Photograph the entire clump, leaf base, and a mature head with a ruler. Color alone is insufficient; close examination of the bristles and individual flower units improves identification.
actions: Where feathertop is escaping, stop moving divisions or seed heads to other gardens. Collect and contain mature heads before digging a small unwanted clump, and avoid scattering the bristled seed units along paths. Recheck the site for surviving growth and seedlings after removal. Clean footwear, clothing, mower decks, and tools used through seed-bearing plants before entering uninfested ground. Do not mow ripe heads simply to tidy a patch, because that can distribute seed. For a large roadside or natural-area population, document its extent and agree on a plan with the land manager before disturbing it.
researchNotes: Queensland's weed identification account and the French botanical conservatories independently describe morphology; New Zealand DOC supplies the ornamental pathway and attachment to clothing or animals. Public actions are bounded prevention and small-clump removal, not an unsupported claim of complete eradication. Flower color is expressed as variable across the sources.

proposedDescription: Fennel aphid feeds on members of the carrot family, including fennel and related cultivated herbs. Colonies of small sap-feeding insects may be noticed before the individual aphids can be identified. The name deserves care: close relatives share similar appearances, and fennel itself can host more than one aphid. Specialist accounts describe this aphid from temperate regions around the world. Knowing the host plant, the part being fed on, and the colony's appearance is more useful than naming it from a distant photograph alone.
identification: Wingless fennel aphids are described as gray-green, with a light wax coating, and about 1.6-2.3 mm long. This appearance overlaps with other Dysaphis. INRAE specifically warns that ordinary morphological characters do not separate Dysaphis foeniculus, D. apiifolia, and D. crataegi reliably. Photograph the colony and host plant, then take close views of several insects, including winged individuals if present. Record whether they occupy leaves, stems, or protected lower parts of the plant. Host association and specialist examination are important, but a colony on fennel should not automatically be assigned this species.
actions: Inspect fennel, dill, celery, and parsley before moving plants between gardens or giving away seedlings. Keep an infested potted plant separate while obtaining an identification, and avoid transferring infested cuttings or plant waste to another growing area. Record whether colonies are expanding and whether the plant is actually deteriorating before choosing treatment. Ask extension staff about crop-appropriate aphid management when a colony persists; identification matters especially for an unusual host or a new regional record. Avoid broad preventive spraying that would also affect aphid predators. These precautions reduce movement without assuming that every aphid on fennel is fennel aphid.
researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Fresh AphID and Blackman/Eastop support the named aphid, while independently authored INRAE explains its close, potentially hybridizing lookalikes. These references agree on the named taxa and the diagnostic limitation. No contradictory catalog concept was established; a profile can explicitly avoid visual species certainty and host exclusivity. Next: Keep identification qualified and request specialist review for exact records; do not imply ordinary microscopy always resolves the group.

sources.title: Blackman and Eastop: Dysaphis species accounts

claims: Apiaceous host associations and temperate distribution
Wingless size/color and basal colonies
Three species cannot be separated by ordinary morphology; host-neck/leaf-sheath colonies

proposedDescription: Feral horse refers to a domestic horse or its descendants living without routine human care. Free-ranging herds can occupy grasslands, marshes, and other open habitats, but their ownership and management differ among places. A horse outside a fence may also be a recently escaped animal. These distinctions matter when deciding whom to contact. Horses are social grazers, often moving and feeding in groups. Their familiarity to people should not be mistaken for an invitation to approach, feed, or handle them.
identification: Look for a large, long-legged animal with a long head and neck, a mane, a full-haired tail, and a single hoof on each foot. Coat colors and body size vary widely with ancestry; there is no color or marking that establishes feral status. University accounts describe domestic-horse heights broadly around 0.9-1.7 m, with exceptions. Other equids, including burros and mules, can complicate distant observations. Photograph from a safe distance and record any visible brand, halter, or other identification without approaching. Location, herd history, and the responsible land manager determine whether a horse is feral, managed, or lost.
actions: Give horses room to pass and retreat if they approach. Do not offer food, touch them, separate a foal from adults, or attempt capture. Secure food and pet food where horses can reach it, and drive cautiously where herds cross roads. Follow the viewing distance posted by the local land manager; one park's distance is not a universal rule. Report an injured horse, a road hazard, or a possible escaped domestic animal to the relevant land manager or local animal-control service, giving its location and visible markings. Population management belongs with authorized professionals who can address welfare, ownership, and habitat together.
researchNotes: University of Michigan Animal Diversity Web supports basic horse morphology and domestic variation; NPS provides independently developed field-safety guidance. No single federal management status or minimum viewing distance is generalized nationally. Feral status cannot be inferred from appearance, and the entry intentionally provides no capture, feeding, or veterinary instructions.

sources.title: National Park Service: Safety tips for viewing wild horses

claims: Horses have single hooves, long manes and tails, and widely varying body size and coat color.
Horses occupy diverse habitats and domestic ancestry produces substantial variation.
Feeding and approaching horses create risks; horses can bite, kick, or react suddenly.
Visitors should retreat from approaching horses and secure food.

proposedDescription: Feral swine are free-ranging pigs, including descendants of domestic pigs, introduced wild boar, and their crosses. Their rooting can turn over soil and vegetation while they search for food, damaging crops and natural habitats. Groups may be present well before a landowner sees an animal directly. Tracks, wallows, and repeatedly disturbed ground are useful early clues. Because pigs move across property boundaries, effective responses usually require neighboring landowners and wildlife staff to work together rather than treating each sighting as an isolated problem.
identification: Feral swine vary in color, size, hairiness, and body shape, so a dark coat or long snout is not required. Hoofprints usually have relatively blunt, rounded toes and a more squared or rounded outline than white-tailed deer tracks. Soft ground can also record the smaller rear toes. Look for rooting, muddy wallows, rubs on trees or posts, and beds alongside tracks. None of these signs alone is conclusive. Photographs from a trail camera, tracks with a scale, and an overview of disturbed ground help distinguish pigs from deer and other animals. Do not approach a group to obtain better identification.
actions: Report new sightings or fresh signs to the state wildlife agency or USDA Wildlife Services, especially where pigs are not already established. Provide the location, date, approximate number, and photographs. Never relocate pigs or release domestic pigs outdoors. Secure feed and other avoidable food sources, and coordinate with neighbors on access and monitoring. Seek a professionally planned removal approach; university guidance warns that shooting only a few animals may leave wary survivors that are harder to manage. Do not improvise poisons, traps, or pursuit near people, livestock, or wildlife. Keep people and pets away from injured or cornered animals.
researchNotes: USDA's technical series supplies track and rooting identification and its outreach brochure supports reporting and no relocation. Arkansas Extension independently explains Sus scrofa ancestry and coordinated management limitations. No disease diagnosis, hunting permission, trap construction, or lethal-method instructions are implied; local authorities must determine the appropriate response.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: Feral Swine technical series
University of Arkansas Extension: Feral hogs

claims: Tracks tend to be rounder and blunter than deer tracks; rooting and wallowing are important signs.
Report sightings or signs and do not relocate feral swine.
Feral hogs and wild boar are Sus scrofa; rooting is a common first sign.
Removing only a few pigs can educate survivors and hinder population control.

proposedDescription: Fern aphid is a small dark aphid associated with many kinds of ferns, including plants grown indoors and in greenhouses. Colonies often hide on the undersides of fronds. Connecticut's experiment station reports that it seldom causes severe injury on Boston fern, although other observations document distorted leaves on infested plants. This makes inspection more useful than assuming every colony requires treatment. The contrasting pale legs and patterned wings of adults can help draw attention to an insect that is otherwise easy to overlook.
identification: Wingless fern aphids are about 1.2-1.6 mm long, with a black body, pale legs, and pale antennae marked with dark rings. The paired tubes near the rear of the body are dark at their bases and pale toward their tips. Winged adults have conspicuous dark borders along the forewing veins and a pale spot within the darkened leading-edge region. Fern scale, Pinnaspis aspidistrae, instead forms fixed brown or white covers against the frond. Photograph the undersides of fronds and several aphids at close range. A fern host alone is insufficient because other aphid species also feed on ferns.
actions: Inspect frond undersides before buying, dividing, or sharing ferns. Separate an infested potted plant from neighboring plants while confirming the insect, and check whether new fronds are developing normally. Avoid moving infested divisions or discarded fronds into another collection. When a colony persists or distorts growth, ask extension staff for a treatment suitable for the particular fern and indoor or outdoor setting. Fern foliage can be sensitive to sprays, so do not apply a general garden mixture or assume a product safe on one plant is safe on another. Continued inspection is useful even when the initial colony appears small.
researchNotes: Blackman and Eastop provide detailed diagnostic characters; Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station independently reports host location, usually limited injury, and fern sensitivity to treatments. Actions emphasize inspection and isolation rather than repeating older chemical recommendations. Named scale comparison is supported by the same CAES page and does not purport to separate every fern-feeding aphid.

sources.title: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station: Fern pests

claims: Wingless adults are 1.2-1.6 mm, black with pale appendages; winged adults have dark-bordered veins.
Many fern genera are hosts.
Black fern aphids feed beneath Boston fern fronds and seldom cause severe injury.
Ferns are sensitive to some insecticide treatments; fern scale has fixed brown female and white male covers.

proposedDescription: Fern scale is an armored scale insect found on ferns and a range of other ornamental plants. The white covers of developing males may be conspicuous against a dark frond, while brown female covers are easier to miss. Feeding can leave pale spots and weaken heavily infested plants. The covers remain after an insect dies or an adult male leaves, so visible specks do not all represent living pests. Moving infested plants or cut foliage is an important way to carry this insect into a new collection.
identification: Female fern scale covers are generally about 1.5-2.5 mm long, brown, flat to slightly raised, and shaped like a small mussel shell. Male covers are narrower, white, and have three lengthwise ridges. The insect beneath a cover is much less obvious than the cover itself. Pinnaspis strachani can look very similar; scale-cover color is not a dependable separation, and authoritative identification requires slide-mounted females. Photograph both leaf surfaces, stems, and the differently shaped covers. A close view of live stages helps determine whether an infestation remains active, but it does not replace microscopic species identification.
actions: Inspect new ferns and foliage plants, especially the undersides of fronds, before placing them among an established collection. Keep affected plants separate and do not give away infested divisions or cut foliage. Track fresh pale spots and newly appearing covers rather than judging treatment success from old covers alone. For persistent infestations, obtain an identification and advice suited to the host plant. NC State notes that ferns are sensitive to pesticides; any labeled treatment needs careful host-specific use. Avoid transferring old chemical schedules between products or assuming that a remedy for aphids will also control armored scales.
researchNotes: NC State provides independent host observations, cover persistence, and treatment sensitivity; Naturalis synthesizes taxonomic work including Gill and Davidson/Miller and requires slide-mounted females to distinguish P. strachani. Hawaii independently documents transport on infested ornamental material. Microscopic identification is a normal diagnostic limit, not grounds to flag an otherwise supported species profile.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Fern scale insect

claims: Male covers are white and ridged; females have brown shell-shaped covers.
Covers persist after death; feeding causes pale spots and ferns can be pesticide-sensitive.
Female covers are 1.5-2.5 mm; P. strachani requires microscopic differentiation.
Infested plants and cut foliage spread the scale; many ornamental hosts are recorded.

proposedDescription: Ferngrass is a small annual grass with stiff flowering branches that can resemble a miniature branching spray. It grows in dry, open, disturbed places such as tracksides, gardens, gravel, and sandy ground. Despite its common name, it is a flowering grass rather than a fern. It has become naturalized outside its original Mediterranean and western Asian range. A few plants in a path do not establish a serious ecological impact, but seed-bearing plants can be worth removing where they are spreading into a managed garden or restoration site.
identification: Ferngrass usually forms a small rigid tuft about 5-40 cm tall. Its narrow leaves are mostly hairless, and the flower cluster has short, stiff branches arranged largely to one side. Individual flower units are roughly 3.5-10 mm long and contain several florets. Sea hard-grass, often called Desmazeria marina, generally has larger, broader flower units in a largely unbranched head. Photograph the whole plant and a mature head from the side and front, with a millimeter scale. The small membrane where the leaf blade meets its sheath and close views of the florets help a grass specialist confirm the identification.
actions: Remove small unwanted tufts before their flower heads shed seed, taking care not to pull neighboring desirable grasses. Collect mature heads rather than shaking them over nearby bare ground. Check paths, gravel edges, and moved soil for another flush of seedlings during the next growing season. Keep footwear and small garden tools free of seed-bearing debris before working in a clean restoration area. Where identification is uncertain, retain photographs and ask a herbarium or extension service to examine mature material before broad removal. These steps address seed movement; the sources do not establish a special eradication method for this species.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand provides a full morphological account and habitat; the University of the Balearic Islands independently supplies the Desmazeria marina comparison. Actions are explicitly conservative seed-prevention measures inferred from annual seed production, not a species-tested treatment claim. Regional flowering months have not been transferred to all US climates.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Catapodium rigidum
University of the Balearic Islands: Catapodium rigidum

claims: Annual rigid tufts 5-40 cm; short-branched one-sided heads and 3.5-10 mm spikelets.
Occurs on sandy or gravelly ground, tracksides and gardens.
Desmazeria marina has longer broader spikelets and usually an unbranched head.

proposedDescription: Fernleaf yarrow is a tall perennial grown for dense, flat clusters of yellow flowers above divided green leaves. Its stiff stems and long-lasting flower heads make it familiar in gardens and dried arrangements. It has naturalized beyond cultivation in parts of North America, but that does not make every planting a spreading problem. University horticultural accounts distinguish its relatively restrained clumping growth from more aggressive forms of common yarrow. Observing whether seedlings or expanding clumps actually appear beyond a bed is a useful starting point.
identification: Fernleaf yarrow commonly reaches about 3-4 feet tall, with deeply divided, fernlike leaves concentrated toward the base. Many tiny yellow flower heads form a broad, flattened cluster up to about 4 inches across. Flowering is chiefly in summer. Common yarrow, Achillea millefolium, also has divided leaves and flat clusters, but typical flowers are white or pink; cultivated forms and hybrids broaden that color range. Fernleaf yarrow generally has a taller, more rigid habit. Photograph basal and stem leaves, an entire flowering stem, and close details of individual heads. Garden labels are helpful, but hybrids can make a photograph-only identification uncertain.
actions: Keep an eye on the edge of a planting and remove unwanted seedlings before they establish. Cut spent heads before seed develops if volunteers are becoming a problem. Lift or divide expanding clumps where they exceed the intended bed, and keep unwanted rooted pieces out of natural-area waste piles. Do not remove unrelated native yarrows simply because they have similar divided leaves. If plants are persisting far from cultivation, record the site and obtain a botanical identification, particularly for yellow-flowered garden hybrids. A contained garden clump does not call for broad treatment solely because the species is introduced.
researchNotes: NC State supplies species-level dimensions, flower morphology, naturalization and division guidance. University of Georgia independently compares common and fernleaf yarrows; Colorado State independently describes comparatively restrained spread. Cultivar and hybrid uncertainty is stated as an identification limit, without asserting that every yellow yarrow belongs to this species.

sources.title: NC State Plant Toolbox: Achillea filipendulina
Colorado State: Flowers for mountain communities

claims: Perennial 3-4 feet tall with divided green foliage and flat yellow flower clusters.
Naturalized in parts of North America; division can limit overcrowding.
Fernleaf yarrow reaches about four feet and has yellow or gold flowers; common yarrow differs in typical color and stature.
A. filipendulina is described as not spreading aggressively in this horticultural setting.

proposedDescription: Feverfew is an aromatic perennial with clusters of small white-and-yellow flower heads. It is grown as an ornamental and has a long history as a cultivated herb, but garden plants can also seed into nearby open ground. Its divided leaves give a much fuller outline than the flowers alone suggest. Cultivars include double-flowered forms that look different from the familiar small daisies. Self-seeding can be vigorous under favorable conditions, so whether it stays within a planting depends partly on how spent heads and volunteers are managed.
identification: Feverfew usually grows about 1-3 feet tall as a branched mound. Green leaves are deeply divided into broad lobes rather than a single narrow blade, and their undersides bear hairs. Typical flower heads are about 12-20 mm across, with a yellow center and short white rays; double cultivars may form rounded heads. Chamomile is a common visual confusion, so photograph leaves as well as flowers rather than identifying from a daisy-shaped head alone. Include the whole plant, the underside of a leaf, and a side view of a head. The old name Chrysanthemum parthenium refers to the same species.
actions: Remove spent flower heads promptly if feverfew is producing unwanted seedlings. Pull small volunteers from moist soil and check disturbed spots near the original planting through the growing season. If removing an established plant, lift the rooted crown and revisit the spot for regrowth. Contain seed-bearing heads when clearing beds or handling dried arrangements, and avoid dumping them beyond the garden. Keep records of any persistent population away from cultivation and seek identification before removing similar wildflowers. A plant identified from an escape population should not be used as a medicinal preparation on the basis of its common name.
researchNotes: NC State provides self-seeding behavior, deadheading guidance, growth form and cultivar variation; Flora of Australia independently supplies measured flower and leaf characters plus the older scientific names. The chamomile comparison is framed as an identification caution rather than an unsupported complete key. No medical efficacy, dosage, or blanket ecological harm is claimed.

sources.title: NC State Plant Toolbox: Tanacetum parthenium
Flora of Australia, volume 37: Tanacetum parthenium

claims: Aromatic perennial 1-3 feet tall; self-seeding can be vigorous.
Prompt removal of spent flowers limits self-seeding; cultivars vary in head form.
Hairy plants have divided leaves and 12-20 mm heads with white rays and yellow disc flowers.

proposedDescription: Field bindweed is a perennial vine that trails over bare ground or twines through neighboring plants. White or pink trumpet-shaped flowers can conceal the persistence of the plant beneath them: established roots produce new shoots, and pieces moved in soil can start another patch. Seeds also remain a long-term source of seedlings. It is a troublesome weed in gardens and agricultural ground, where a single round of cutting or pulling seldom finishes the job. Early recognition is much easier to act on than a deeply established infestation.
identification: Field bindweed has alternate, arrow-shaped leaves, commonly about 0.5-2 inches long, and white to pink trumpet flowers roughly 1-1.5 inches across. Two small leaflike bracts sit below the flower rather than enclosing its base. Hedge bindweed, Calystegia sepium, has larger bracts covering the flower base and generally larger, more sharply pointed leaves. Wild buckwheat, Fallopia convolvulus, has tiny clustered flowers instead of an open trumpet and a thin sheath around the stem at leaf attachments. Photograph the flower from the side, its bracts, and several leaves. Flower size varies, so combine characters rather than relying on one measurement.
actions: Remove young seedlings promptly before a persistent underground system develops. For an established garden patch, repeatedly remove new shoots and track the area over multiple seasons; expect regrowth rather than assuming one pulling session has worked. Avoid moving infested soil or distributing cut root pieces through cultivation. Keep the vine from climbing through desirable plants, and collect seed-bearing material. Light-excluding coverings can help where practical, but inspect their seams and planting holes for emerging shoots. Large infestations need a site-specific plan with extension or the land manager. Protect nearby native morning-glories by confirming the identification first.
researchNotes: UC IPM supplies regeneration, persistence and repeated cultural-control guidance; Cornell independently provides a comparative key to field bindweed, hedge bindweed and wild buckwheat. Quantitative extremes for rooting depth and seed longevity are omitted to avoid overstating what any particular patch will do. No pesticide recipe or one-visit eradication claim is made.

claims: Perennial roots and fragments regenerate; seedlings are easier to manage than established plants.
Repeated cultivation and exclusion of light can suppress plants, with continued monitoring needed.
Small bracts below the flower distinguish field bindweed from hedge bindweed's enclosing bracts.
Wild buckwheat has small clustered flowers and a stem sheath.

proposedDescription: Field brome is an annual grass with an open, branching flower cluster and slender, awned flower units. It occurs in fields, roadsides, and other disturbed places and has also been grown as a cover crop. Its similarity to other bromes makes a mature flowering plant much easier to identify than a patch of green leaves. Introduced populations may behave differently among habitats, so the name alone does not establish the scale of a local problem. Preventing seed movement is a reasonable focus where it is unwanted.
identification: Field brome usually stands about 30-100 cm tall. Its leaf sheaths are hairy, and the flower cluster is loose and spreading, commonly 15-30 cm long. Mature flower units contain several overlapping florets, each with a straight bristle, or awn. The florets are roughly 7-9 mm long, with awns often 6-11 mm long. Rye brome, Bromus secalinus, usually has hairless sheaths and florets that spread apart more distinctly at maturity. Other bromes require examination of flower parts. Photograph the lower sheaths, complete head, and mature units against a millimeter scale; a grass specialist may need intact flowering material.
actions: Where field brome is unwanted in a small patch, remove or cut plants before seed matures and revisit for later-emerging seedlings. Contain mature heads rather than scattering them while moving cut vegetation. Check seed mixes and avoid transferring contaminated soil, hay, or equipment debris into clean planting areas. In a crop or pasture, confirm the brome species before choosing a management program, since several similar grasses have different life cycles and treatment responses. Maintain the intended vegetation after removal so bare ground is not left as an easy seedbed. These are prevention measures, not a guarantee that one season's work eliminates the seed supply.
researchNotes: Canadian Food Inspection Agency provides measured floret features and the documented cover-crop pathway; University of Tartu independently supplies whole-plant characters and the B. secalinus comparison. Annual seed prevention is a bounded inference from life history. No Canadian regulatory classification is presented as US law, and other Bromus treatment claims are not transferred.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Field brome seed identification

claims: Annual with 7-9 mm florets and straight 6-11 mm awns.
Occurs in disturbed places and was introduced as a cover crop.
Plants 30-100 cm with hairy sheaths and a loose head; B. secalinus has largely hairless sheaths and spreading mature florets.

proposedDescription: Field burrweed is a low annual of lawns and other closely managed ground. Its small green flowers are easy to miss, but the sharp points on mature fruits are difficult to ignore under bare feet. In warm-temperate lawns it commonly grows through the cooler part of the year and produces burs in spring. Plants may die as weather warms while the hardened burs remain. That makes finding the young plants more useful than waiting until a lawn has become uncomfortable to walk on.
identification: Field burrweed is freely branched and grows close to the ground, often only a few inches tall. Opposite leaves are finely divided into small segments, and inconspicuous flower heads sit low among them. The mature fruits bear sharp spines. Parsley-piert and knawel can resemble the small plants before fruit develops, so leaf shape and the central flower or fruit heads need close inspection. Photograph an entire plant, opposite leaf pairs, and a mature head with a scale; do not test burs with bare skin. A low, feathery lawn weed without visible fruit should be confirmed before treatment.
actions: Inspect thin lawn patches during cool-season growth and remove small plants before burs harden, collecting developing fruit heads with the plant. Wear gloves and footwear when working in a patch with mature burs, and keep children and pets away from heavily affected bare ground until debris is addressed. Maintain a dense lawn with the appropriate mowing height and soil-test-based care rather than excessive fertilizer. Killing mature plants does not remove their spines. If a larger lawn needs treatment, ask extension staff about timing and options suited to the turf species; local seasons and product suitability matter.
researchNotes: NC State independently describes morphology and winter-annual behavior; Clemson provides cultural turf management and the important persistence of burs after plant death. Clemson full-page access returned 403, so its substantive search text is honestly indexed_excerpt. Seasonal timing is qualified rather than transferring southern US calendar months nationwide.

claims: Low winter annual with opposite divided leaves, inconspicuous heads and spiny fruits; resembles parsley-piert and knawel.
Dense healthy turf reduces infestation; control before burs form matters because spines persist after death.

proposedDescription: Field clover is a small yellow-flowered annual whose leaves have three leaflets. Its compact flower heads make it easy to confuse with several other low legumes, especially before the flowers are fully open. It is widely naturalized, including in North America, and can occur among other plants in disturbed grassy places. A yellow clover in a lawn is not automatically evidence of a damaging infestation. Identification and the purpose of the site should guide whether to leave it, monitor it, or prevent further seed production.
identification: Field clover may stand or spread to about 30 cm. Mature heads are commonly around 10-15 mm across and hold many closely packed yellow flowers, often more than 25. Each flower is roughly 4-5 mm long. Lesser trefoil, Trifolium dubium, has smaller, less densely flowered heads. Black medick, Medicago lupulina, has a tiny point at the tip of each leaflet, unlike the more rounded leaflet tips expected here. Photograph a fully developed head, a three-leaflet leaf, and the leaflet tips close up. Count flowers on several heads rather than relying on one small or incomplete cluster.
actions: If field clover is unwanted in a small garden or restoration patch, remove plants before heads mature and retain the desired neighboring cover. Collect seed-bearing material rather than spreading it with clippings or soil. Check the site again during subsequent seedling emergence, especially where disturbance exposes bare soil. Confirm the species before treating a mixed patch of yellow-flowered legumes; black medick and other clovers are easily mistaken for it. In a lawn or pasture, decide whether the plant is interfering with the site's purpose before undertaking broad control. The sources support recognition and seed prevention, not a universal need to eradicate it.
researchNotes: The UK National Plant Monitoring Scheme gives explicit comparisons with T. dubium and Medicago lupulina; Uruguay INIA independently describes measured flowers and annual habit. The Australian weed account confirms North American naturalization without being used to transfer Australian harm claims. Practical actions are conservative annual-seed prevention rather than an unverified treatment protocol.

sources.title: National Plant Monitoring Scheme: Species identification guide

claims: T. campestre has dense 10-15 mm heads with many yellow flowers; T. dubium has smaller looser heads.
Black medick has a minute leaflet-tip point.
Annual plants reach about30 cm with yellow flowers4-5 mm long in compact heads.
Widely naturalized, including Canada and the United States.

proposedDescription: Field forget-me-not is a short-lived herb with tiny blue flowers carried above hairy leaves. As a flowering stem lengthens, older flowers give way to small fruits lower down. It commonly grows in cultivated or otherwise disturbed open ground. Plants in dry, exposed places can be much smaller than those in favorable conditions, which makes overall height a weak identification feature. Its flowers are smaller than those of the familiar woodland forget-me-not, but mature fruiting structures provide useful confirmation when several species are possible.
identification: Field forget-me-not is usually annual or biennial, often about 30 cm tall or less. Its leaves are hairy, oblong to spoon-shaped, and generally lack teeth. The blue flower is about 2-4 mm across. Woodland forget-me-not, Myosotis sylvatica, usually has a broader, flatter flower about 5-8 mm across. In field forget-me-not the green cup around a developing fruit bears spreading, often hooked hairs, and the fruit stalk is commonly longer than that cup. Photograph a flower against a fine scale, the lower leaves, and a mature fruit with its stalk. These details are more reliable than a distant view of blue flowers.
actions: Confirm the species before clearing a patch, especially where native forget-me-nots may occur. In a small unwanted garden population, remove plants before mature fruits detach, keeping seed-bearing stems contained during cleanup. Revisit open soil and path margins for seedlings rather than assuming all plants emerged together. Avoid moving soil or garden waste from a fruiting patch into another planting area. If plants occur in a natural area, send clear flower and fruit photographs to the land manager or a botanical specialist before broad removal. The available accounts support identification and cautious seed prevention, without establishing that every local population causes ecological harm.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand supplies the full life-history and fruit-stalk/calyx description; Native Plant Trust's Flora Novae Angliae comparison independently distinguishes M. arvensis from M. sylvatica by corolla size and shape. BSBI PDF fetch failed and is not relied on for additional claims. Management is limited to preventing seed movement in confirmed unwanted plants.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Myosotis arvensis
Native Plant Trust: Myosotis sylvatica comparison

claims: Usually biennial or annual, hairy, with small blue flowers and hooked calyx hairs.
Fruiting stalk is one to nearly three times the calyx length; plants vary with conditions.
M. arvensis flowers are2-4 mm with ascending lobes; M. sylvatica flowers are5-8 mm with spreading lobes.

proposedDescription: Field mustard belongs to a variable species that also includes familiar cultivated vegetables and oilseed forms. Escaped or volunteer plants can flower in fields, roadsides, and disturbed ground, producing clusters of yellow flowers followed by slender pods. A flowering mustard is therefore not necessarily a separate wild species from a nearby crop. Several related Brassica species look much alike and can complicate identification. The useful first step is to record the whole plant, leaves, flowers, and pods rather than assign the name from a yellow roadside display.
identification: Field mustard commonly has green to yellow-green leaves, with the upper leaves clasping the stem. Flower buds often sit below the uppermost open yellow flowers, giving the flowering tip a relatively flat outline. Oilseed rape, Brassica napus, tends to have a more waxy blue-green appearance, larger paler flowers, and buds projecting above the open flowers. Brown mustard, Brassica juncea, lacks the same clasping upper leaves. Cultivated forms vary, so compare several characters. Photograph lower and upper leaves, their attachment to the stem, the flowering tip, and mature pods with a ruler. Unusual intermediates may need specialist examination.
actions: Remove unwanted volunteers before pods ripen, especially around seed-production areas and newly established plantings. Keep mature pods contained when pulling plants, and inspect equipment or soil moved from a seed-bearing patch. Use clearly identified planting material and retain crop labels where cultivated forms are involved. In an agricultural field, ask extension staff to identify the mustard before selecting a control program or saving seed. Do not assume an escaped plant has the same crop qualities as a named cultivar. Where a small roadside population is the only concern, document persistence and spread before proposing broad intervention.
researchNotes: CFIA's crop-inspection comparison provides leaf clasping and flower-bud position; North Carolina's vascular flora independently contrasts B. rapa and B. napus. The species includes cultivated forms, so the description avoids a single crop shape, universal harm, or a claim that a flowering plant is safe to eat. Conservative seed prevention does not imply a tested eradication method.

sources.title: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Cruciferous crop identification
North Carolina vascular flora: Brassica napus comparison

claims: B. rapa generally has green clasping leaves and buds below open flowers; B. napus is waxier with buds above.
B. juncea upper leaves do not clasp the stem.
B. rapa resembles B. napus but is greener and has shorter petals.

proposedDescription: Field pennycress is an annual mustard best recognized when its broad, flat seedpods develop. Small white flowers continue near the top of the stem while the round pods mature below. Plants may begin in autumn or spring, and early seed production can let them replenish a patch before other garden or field work begins. It grows in agricultural and disturbed ground. The name reflects the coinlike fruits, which are much more distinctive than the young rosette of leaves.
identification: Field pennycress has mostly hairless stems and leaves. Upper leaves clasp the stem with small pointed lobes at their bases, while the lower leaves often wither as the plant matures. Tiny flowers have four white petals. Mature pods are about 10-17 mm long, flattened, broadly winged around the edge, and notched at the top. Shepherd's-purse, Capsella bursa-pastoris, has more triangular or heart-shaped pods. Thoroughwort pennycress, Microthlaspi perfoliatum, has smaller pods and rounded leaf-base lobes. Photograph the whole fruiting stem, a pod beside a ruler, and the upper leaf attachment. A young rosette alone is less dependable.
actions: Watch autumn seedlings and early spring growth so unwanted plants can be removed before their first pods mature. Pull or hoe small plants and collect any already developed pods. Do not rely on occasional mowing: Cornell notes that cut plants can branch and regrow quickly enough to produce seed. Recheck cleared ground and the edges of crop rows for another flush. In a production field, combine timely seedling control with a locally appropriate crop plan rather than importing a schedule from another climate. Keep seed-bearing waste and soil from the patch out of clean beds.
researchNotes: Cornell provides identification comparisons and evidence-based management limits, including early seed production and regrowth after mowing. The Illustrated Flora of British Columbia independently confirms hairlessness, leaf-base lobes and 10-17 mm winged fruits. No crop-use claim or broad legal status is inferred, and no herbicide recommendation is supplied.

proposedDescription: Field sowthistle is a perennial with yellow, dandelionlike flower heads on upright leafy stems. Its creeping roots can produce new shoots, allowing a patch to persist and expand even when flowering stems are removed. Wind-carried seeds provide another route to new ground. It can compete strongly with crops, especially in dense stands. The plant resembles annual sowthistles, but its persistent underground system changes what successful management requires: preventing seed alone will not eliminate an established patch.
identification: Field sowthistle commonly reaches about 0.6-1.5 m, with hollow stems, milky sap, and alternate leaves that clasp the stem. Leaf edges carry prickly teeth. Yellow flower heads are usually about 2.5-5 cm across, larger than the heads of annual sowthistle, Sonchus oleraceus, and spiny sowthistle, S. asper. Prickly lettuce, Lactuca serriola, has a distinctive row of sharp spines under the leaf midrib. Gland-tipped hairs often occur near the flowers, but some forms are hairless there. Photograph leaf bases, the underside of a leaf, flower heads with a scale, and the patch's growth pattern; do not require glandular hairs for every plant.
actions: Prevent mature seed from blowing away by removing developing heads, then continue checking for new shoots from the roots. In a small accessible patch, repeated removal of regrowth can gradually exhaust the underground reserves, but one cutting is insufficient. Avoid carrying root pieces in soil or equipment into clean ground. For larger crop or pasture infestations, plan repeated interventions and competitive vegetation with extension staff rather than relying on an isolated tillage pass. Keep a dated outline of the patch so improvement or expansion is visible. Confirm identification before broad removal of similar native yellow-flowered plants.
researchNotes: Cornell's detailed profile supports diagnostic comparisons and repeated regrowth suppression; Ontario independently confirms perennial reproduction by horizontal roots and seeds and agricultural competitiveness. The species-level catalog includes hairless-upper-stem forms, so glandular hairs are not treated as mandatory. Experimental eradication timelines are not generalized to a homeowner's patch.

claims: Perennial0.6-1.5 m with large yellow heads, clasping leaves and regenerating roots.

proposedDescription: Ficus thonningii, treated here in the broad African species sense, is an African fig tree that can develop a broad crown, multiple stems, and roots descending from branches. Some plants begin growing on another tree before their roots reach the ground. The name has also been applied to several close relatives, including trees called Ficus burkei and Ficus petersii in other treatments. That history matters when reading older records or identifying a cultivated tree. A familiar common name or nursery label alone does not establish which botanical concept a record represents.
identification: Broad descriptions of fig give heights of about 6-21 m, simple smooth-edged leaves, and small round to oval figs in or just below the leaf axils. The figs are often about 7-14 mm across and turn yellow or red. Leaves vary substantially in size, hairiness, and tip shape within published accounts. Ficus burkei, F. petersii, and F. natalensis are relevant comparisons, but different treatments draw their boundaries differently. Photograph a leafy fruiting twig, both leaf surfaces, the small bracts beneath a fig, bark, and any aerial roots. A specialist should check mature material and the name treatment; no single leaf outline reliably resolves this complex.
actions: Before planting or sharing material under this name, retain its nursery provenance and seek a reliable identification. Inspect around a cultivated tree for seedlings and record whether new plants appear beyond the intended planting. Small unwanted seedlings can be considered for removal after identification, but a large tree or a fig rooted into another tree or structure needs an arborist's assessment. Do not cut supporting roots or attempt major removal on the strength of an online name. Report suspected establishment beyond cultivation to a local herbarium or land manager, with photographs and the planting history if known.

proposedDescription: Fig scale is a small armored insect that feeds on leaves, twigs, and fruit. On figs, feeding on the fruit surface can leave raised, warty areas that reduce quality. The insect's protective cover changes in color and shape with its location and stage, so an infestation need not look uniform. In California fig production, a tiny parasitic wasp often keeps populations under control. That makes preserving natural enemies and checking for active damage more useful than automatically spraying every scale-covered twig.
identification: Adult female fig scale covers are shell-shaped and commonly around 2-3 mm long. Older overwintering covers on wood are dark brown; younger scales and leaf forms may be considerably paler. Crawlers are the tiny mobile stage that disperses before settling to feed. Other mussel-shaped scales, including oystershell scale, Lepidosaphes ulmi, can look similar. Cover color or a fig host is not enough for a firm species identification. Photograph occupied twigs, both leaf surfaces, fruit damage, and individual covers beside a fine scale. A diagnostic laboratory may need mounted specimens to separate closely related Lepidosaphes.
actions: Inspect new fig plants and cuttings before moving them into a collection, and avoid sharing visibly infested material. Check young wood as leaves unfold and compare several leaves and fruits for fresh activity. If there is little new damage, obtain advice before treating: UC IPM reports that Aphytis parasitoids often provide strong control in California orchards. Avoid routine broad-spectrum spraying that could disrupt those insects. For a persistent damaging infestation, ask local extension staff about timing and options for edible figs. Do not copy an old commercial-orchard spray rate into a home-garden treatment or assume that every remaining cover contains a live scale.
researchNotes: UC IPM provides California phenology, fruit injury and parasitoid-based management. ScaleNet's independent Ahmad/Ghani and Borchsenius records support measured covers, while Naturalis provides comparison with L. ulmi and regional variation. Generations per year are deliberately not generalized across climates. No unsourced hand-removal efficacy or chemical recipe is claimed.

proposedDescription: Fig whitefly is a tiny sap-feeding insect best known for yellowing and leaf loss on ornamental Ficus trees and hedges. A disturbed plant may release a cloud of adults, but an active infestation can also remain when few flying insects are visible. Immature whiteflies stay against leaf surfaces and are easily overlooked. Heavy populations can cause dieback and slow young-tree growth. Leaf loss alone is not a diagnosis, however, and a bare hedge should be checked for live stages and other possible causes before treatment or severe pruning.
identification: Adult Fig whiteflies are about 1.4-1.6 mm long, with white wings bearing faint gray-brown bands and dark red eyes. The small oval nymphs are pale green to tan and partly transparent, blending into a leaf. Older nymphs show conspicuous red eyes. Immatures can occur on both sides of leaves, while elongated yellowish eggs are often near the underside midrib. Greenhouse whitefly, Trialeurodes vaporariorum, and sweetpotato whitefly, Bemisia tabaci, are useful comparisons; wing bands help, but tiny adults still warrant close examination. Photograph both leaf surfaces, nymphs, and a resting adult rather than only the flying swarm.
actions: Inspect Ficus leaves before buying plants or moving cuttings. If a tree or hedge is infested, reduce unnecessary pruning while it recovers; heavy trimming adds stress. Bag infested clippings before taking them off the property, since immature whiteflies can survive on cut or fallen leaves. Look for live nymphs instead of judging the infestation solely by adults or empty cast skins. Preserve predators and tiny parasitic wasps by avoiding indiscriminate spraying. When damage continues, consult extension staff or a qualified landscape professional for a plan suited to the plant, infestation stage, and nearby environment.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS's identification guide and management sheet form one evidence group. Los Angeles County biologist Gevork Arakelian's UCR account independently supplies measured adults, leaf-surface occupancy and California observations. Named whitefly comparisons are supported by UF First Detector material, with no unsupported definitive species key. Older management guidance is restricted to pruning, containment and natural-enemy protection.

proposedDescription: Figleaf goosefoot is an annual of cultivated and disturbed ground, with inconspicuous green flower clusters rather than showy petals. Its name refers to the shape of its leaves, not to a relationship with fig trees. Middle leaves commonly have a long central section and two shorter lobes near the base. It resembles common lambsquarters closely enough that records based only on a casual glance may be unreliable. Mature leaves and seeds together give a much better basis for identification, especially where several goosefoot species grow together.
identification: Figleaf goosefoot has upright, often ribbed stems and variable leaves along the stem. Well-developed middle leaves are distinctly three-lobed, with an elongated, nearly parallel-sided central lobe; upper leaves may be narrower and less lobed. Tiny green flowers occur in clustered groups. Mature black seeds are about 0.9-1 mm across and have a honeycomb-like pitted surface visible under magnification. Common lambsquarters, Chenopodium album, overlaps in leaf appearance, while C. berlandieri generally has a less elongated central leaf lobe. Photograph several middle leaves, the full plant, and mature seed. Leaf shape alone may not resolve unusual plants or hybrids.
actions: Remove confirmed unwanted plants while young and before the green flower clusters mature into seed. Keep ripe material contained during cleanup, and check soil disturbed by the work for later seedlings. Avoid transporting seed-bearing plants, contaminated soil, or equipment debris into clean beds. In a crop field, obtain a species identification before assuming that control experience with common lambsquarters transfers directly. A mature seed sample may be useful to a diagnostic service; ask how to package it before sending it. Do not infer a local crop-loss estimate or a need for broad habitat removal from its resemblance to another weed.
researchNotes:

Full eFloras and INRAE requests timed out, so substantive indexed accounts are labeled honestly. Species-level variation and hybridization are acknowledged without creating a subspecies assignment or borrowing C. album yield-loss claims.
