proposedDescription: Fimbry is a small tufted sedge associated with wet or seasonally wet ground, including river margins and cultivated wet fields. Numerous tiny brown flower clusters form a branching head above narrow basal leaves. Older publications often call related plants Fimbristylis miliacea, but that name has been applied inconsistently to more than one taxonomic concept. Current US wetland references use Fimbristylis littoralis, while preserving the older name as a historical misapplication. Local identification should therefore be tied to a modern flora rather than to the common name alone.
identification: Accounts of fimbry describe leafy tufts commonly about 10-50 cm tall, with narrow leaves and many nearly round brown flower units about 2-3 mm long. Under the Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment, mature nutlets are three-sided, roughly 0.6-0.7 mm long, with a textured surface. Fimbristylis quinquangularis usually has more elongated, egg-shaped flower units; the Smithsonian treatment contrasts them with this species' rounder units. A North Carolina record proved to be F. caroliniana. Photograph the whole tuft, stem cross-section, leaf arrangement, branching head, and mature nutlets with magnification. Stem angles alone should not be treated as a universal rule because the published name concepts differ.
actions: Avoid moving unidentified sedges, wet soil, or seed-bearing plant debris between ponds, wet beds, and restoration sites. For a suspected new population, photograph mature plants and record the habitat and extent before asking a herbarium or local land manager for identification. Do not drain or broadly disturb a wetland to remove a plant identified only as fimbry. In a small cultivated bed, confirmed unwanted plants can be removed before seed matures, with follow-up for new seedlings. Broader management should wait for confirmation of the taxon and its local status; agricultural advice under an ambiguous older name may concern a different plant.
researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: A newly recovered Smithsonian flora explains the rejected ambiguous miliacea name using its two type sheets; the current USACE wetland list explicitly recognizes littoralis and marks old miliacea usage misapplied. This establishes a usable current species scope despite older database labels. One misidentified local specimen does not invalidate all modern littoralis records. Native/introduced status is not generalized nationwide. Next: Use current littoralis morphology, preserve old determination history, and verify doubtful local material.

proposedDescription: Fire star orchid grows on long, leafy stems that lean into surrounding plants. Its orange flowers have a yellow center and gather at the ends of the stems. Native from Mexico to Colombia, it is widely grown as an ornamental and has escaped cultivation in several tropical regions. It often occupies disturbed ground, roadsides, and grassland. Its conspicuous roots help the stems hold onto nearby vegetation; a planting can occupy more space than its small flowers suggest.
identification: Look for cane-like stems approaching 1 m, fleshy oval leaves spaced along them, and white roots emerging from the stem. Each orange flower has a three-part lip with fringed edges. The combination of roots, leafy canes, and the flower lip is more useful than flower color alone. The Florida flora separates it from Epidendrum amphistomum, whose flowers are greenish, yellowish, or white and lack the fringed lip margin. Garden hybrids can resemble the species, so keep nursery labels and show the entire stem as well as a close flower when seeking identification.
actions: Keep garden plants within a maintained bed or container and check where leaning stems meet neighboring vegetation. Remove unwanted rooted growth while it is still manageable, collecting living stems and roots rather than dumping them along woodland edges. Do not move unidentified orchids from an escaped patch into another outdoor planting. If plants are spreading beyond cultivation, document the extent and ask a local herbarium or extension office to confirm the identity before organizing removal.
researchNotes: Recognition combines Kew's species account with the independently authored Florida key. The flora was read as an indexed excerpt, not downloaded in full. Garden containment is a conservative inference from vigorous rooted stems, not a tested eradication prescription.

proposedDescription: Firespike is a tropical shrub with broad, glossy leaves and upright clusters of red tubular flowers. Descriptions of Odontonema tubaeforme place its origin in Mexico and Central America. It can grow roughly 2 m tall or more in favorable conditions and is cultivated for its conspicuous flowers. Escapes have been associated with discarded garden material. The name firespike is also applied to other Odontonema plants, so a familiar garden name does not by itself establish this species.
identification: Check for opposite, oval to elliptic leaves and red, two-lipped tubular flowers gathered at the shoot tips. The Australian rainforest account gives leaves about 11-18 cm long and flower tubes about 22-24 mm long. Record both leaves and open flowers, including a side view of the tube and protruding flower parts. In O. tubaeforme the small flower groups sit directly on the main flowering axis, with some arranged in whorls. O. cuspidatum, also sold as firespike, has stalked groups arranged oppositely or alternately. A specialist should resolve a nonflowering or nursery-labeled plant before attaching species-specific records.
actions: Keep prunings and uprooted plants out of natural areas and drainage channels. Collect stems during removal and use a contained garden-waste route, since propagation from plant pieces makes dumping a poor disposal method. Check beyond an established planting for new shoots and remove small unwanted plants before they enlarge. If the plant has escaped a garden, seek identification from an extension office or herbarium and include close views of flowers; advice based on another plant sold as firespike may not fit.

proposedDescription: Fireweed groundsel is an Australian perennial herb or small shrub with clusters of small yellow daisy-like heads. It often grows in relatively moist forests and can become conspicuous after fire or other disturbance. Plants reach around 1.5 m, with leaves that vary considerably among recognized varieties. That variability matters: a broad, toothed leaf and a narrow, nearly smooth-edged leaf can belong to the same species. Its presence in a species catalog should not turn an Australian native forest plant into a universal removal target.
identification: Look for an upright perennial with many small yellow flower heads at the branch tips. Each head has only a few outer yellow rays, commonly four to eight, around the central florets. Leaves may be narrow or broadly oval, and their undersides range from nearly hairless to covered in fine, tangled white hairs. Check several mature leaves, their attachment to the stem, and the narrow green casing beneath each flower head. Regional floras recognize several varieties; a single leaf photograph cannot reliably assign one. Flowering dates from Australian accounts should not be treated as a United States calendar.
actions: Confirm the species and local status before removing an unfamiliar yellow-flowered groundsel. In a garden where it is unwanted, remove small plants before mature seed heads disperse and collect the developing heads separately. Avoid moving seed-bearing cuttings or soil from the patch to another site. Record whether the plant is an isolated garden escape or part of established vegetation. A local botanist can distinguish it from other groundsels and determine whether intervention is appropriate; broad clearing based on the common name alone could remove unrelated plants.
researchNotes: Two independently authored regional flora accounts support the species-level description. They differ in seasonal emphasis and some fruit measurements, so neither is generalized to a US flowering calendar. Actions are cautious seed-containment advice, not evidence of US impact.

claims: Variable aromatic perennial to 1.5 m, yellow heads with 4-8 rays, forest disturbance colonizer.

proposedDescription: Fishhook waterflea is a tiny predatory crustacean that lives in open lake water. Its body is nearly transparent, but its black eye and long, hooked tail can stand out under magnification. It eats other small drifting animals, potentially competing with young fish for food. Introduced populations occur in the Great Lakes region. Anglers may first notice tangled clusters on fishing lines or other submerged equipment rather than individual animals. Movement of water and wet equipment can carry it between lakes.
identification: The body is about 1-3 mm long; the complete animal, including its tail, measures roughly 6-13 mm. Look for three pairs of barbs on the long tail and an S-shaped bend near its tip. Groups caught on a line can resemble wet cotton. Spiny waterflea is a named lookalike, so a tangled mass alone is not enough: the hook at the tail end is the useful detail to examine. Photograph a separated individual with magnification and a scale if possible, retaining the lake name and collection date for a report.
actions: Inspect fishing line, downrigger cables, nets, anchors, and boats before leaving the water. Remove attached organisms and mud, drain retained water at the access site, and let equipment dry completely before using it elsewhere. Follow the local aquatic-invasive-species program's decontamination directions when drying is impractical. Do not transfer bait water between lakes. Report a suspected new occurrence to the state aquatic invasive species program with location and photographs; established lake populations are difficult to control, so preventing another introduction is the most useful individual action.

proposedDescription: Fishpoison is a low shrub in the pea family, with many small leaflets, pale to purple flowers, and slender seed pods. It occurs widely in tropical regions and has a long history of cultivation and use. In Hawaii, accounts associate its arrival with early Polynesian settlement. The common name refers to historical use of the roots to stun fish; it is not an invitation to put the plant into a pond or stream. A planted specimen and an unwanted spreading population require different decisions.
identification: Plants may reach about 1.5 m. The compound leaves have pairs of small leaflets along a central stalk and a single leaflet at the end. Flowering branches carry pea-shaped blossoms; the narrow pods are roughly 2-4.5 cm long and split when dry. Check mature pods, leaflet shape, and the hairs on both leaf surfaces. Different regional treatments recognize variation within Tephrosia purpurea, and flowers alone do not settle subspecies identity. Photograph a whole leaf with its stalk and a ripe pod rather than relying only on the purple color.
actions: Keep seeds and cut branches out of waterways, and do not use this plant as a homemade fish-control treatment. Where an unwanted garden population is confirmed, collect pods before they open and remove small plants with their root crowns. Bag mature seed-bearing material for a contained disposal route instead of spreading it in mulch. Watch the disturbed soil for seedlings after removal. Ask a local botanist or extension office about the plant's status before removing an established population, especially where it has cultural or historical significance.

proposedDescription: Fishtail swordfern is an ornamental fern whose arching fronds carry leaflets with divided tips. The repeated forks give the frond its familiar fishtail appearance. It comes from tropical Asia and the western Pacific and is grown in gardens and containers. Florida extension records it escaping cultivation but explicitly distinguishes that history from the invasive status of other introduced swordferns. Its presence therefore calls for correct identification and attention to local spread, rather than assuming that every ornamental fern needs removal.
identification: Look for pale green, drooping fronds approximately 80-150 cm long. Many leaflets split near the end into two short points; some fork more than once. Round spore-bearing patches occur near the margins on the underside of mature fronds. UF's comparison separates this forked-leaflet plant from native Nephrolepis exaltata and N. biserrata as well as introduced N. cordifolia and N. brownii. Show several complete leaflets and the underside of a mature frond. A common nursery name such as Boston fern is not a reliable species identification.
actions: Keep unwanted divisions and root-bearing material out of woods, wetlands, and garden-waste dumps. If a container plant spreads into a bed, lift the unwanted clump with its connected underground growth and revisit the spot for new fronds. Avoid clearing other swordferns nearby until their identity is checked, especially where native species occur. For an escaped patch, document whether it is expanding and seek local advice on management priorities; Florida's account does not justify treating this species as equivalent to invasive tuberous swordfern.
