proposedDescription: Five-stamen tamarisk belongs to the saltcedar group of shrubs and small trees. Slender branches carry tiny scale-like leaves and clusters of small pinkish flowers. Tamarisks can occupy riverbanks, floodplains, and saline ground, where established stands may be difficult to remove. In North America, Tamarix chinensis and T. ramosissima have hybridized extensively. Many familiar saltcedar stands therefore cannot be confidently assigned to a single species from their outline or flower color.
identification: Plants are often multistemmed shrubs several meters tall, with minute leaves pressed close to the twigs. The five-parted flowers help distinguish the group from four-parted smallflower tamarisk, Tamarix parviflora. Separating T. chinensis from T. ramosissima or French tamarisk, T. gallica, requires close examination of the flower's nectar disc and the attachment of its stamens. These characters can be ambiguous even in flowering material. Record an uncertain plant as tamarisk and retain detailed flower photographs rather than forcing a species identification from a distant view.
actions: Remove newly established seedlings while they are small enough to lift with the root, provided the bank can be left stable. Recheck for seedlings and shoots: cutting an established plant alone commonly leads to regrowth. For larger riverside stands, plan work with land managers and consider bank stability, nesting habitat, and replacement vegetation before clearing. Keep cut material out of flowing water. A coordinated follow-up plan is more useful than repeated cutting without root control or restoration.

sources.title: US Forest Service FEIS: Tamarix species

researchNotes: Both substantive sources were read as indexed excerpts. Hybridization is an identification limitation of wild records, not a claim that the catalog species is invalid. The bounded profile avoids treating hybrid stand impacts as proven effects of genetically pure T. chinensis.

claims: Species separation relies on minute floral characters; established plants resprout and integrated restoration is needed.
T. chinensis and T. ramosissima hybridize extensively; seedlings can be hand-pulled; four-parted flowers distinguish smallflower tamarisk.

proposedDescription: Fivehorn smotherweed is an annual with narrow, softly hairy leaves and tiny flowers that become hooked fruits. It often grows on disturbed or salty ground, including fields, roadsides, and seasonal wetland margins. A mature plant can reach about 1.2 m. The hooks are small enough to miss without a close look, but they give this otherwise inconspicuous plant its name. Dense growth can interfere with desirable vegetation, and livestock should not be allowed to consume large quantities.
identification: Look for mostly alternate, narrow, flat leaves and small flower clusters along the upper stems and at leaf bases. At maturity, the enclosing flower parts bear five curved hooks, best checked with a hand lens. Kochia, Bassia scoparia, is especially difficult to separate at the seedling stage; fivehorn smotherweed is generally hairier, but mature fruit is stronger evidence. Russian thistles, including Salsola tragus, usually have more extensively branched, prickly growth. Photograph mature fruits and a leafy stem together; a young rosette alone may remain uncertain.
actions: Pull or dig small patches before their fruits mature, cutting the root below the soil surface if digging. Collect fruiting plants so the hooked fruits are not carried onward in debris. Check boots, tools, and equipment after working through a mature patch. Revisit disturbed soil for another flush of seedlings; cultivation can expose more seeds to favorable conditions. In grazed ground, prevent animals from concentrating on this plant and ask an agricultural adviser to help manage large infestations without leaving the site bare.
researchNotes: UC pages count as one source group; Montana's regional flora provides independent recognition. UC's web page incorrectly labels the family Brassicaceae, so the family label is not repeated. Management follows the Bassia weed report without chemical recipes.

claims: Summer annual to 1.2 m; seedlings resemble kochia; five hooks on mature fruits; livestock toxicity at high intake.
Hairy annual with hooked calyx segments; Russian thistles more branched and spiny.
Hand-pulling and digging control small infestations; tillage can stimulate new recruitment.

proposedDescription: Flag smut of wheat is a fungal disease that damages leaves and shoots rather than simply replacing the grain head with spores. Infected plants can be stunted and produce excessive shoots with few or no heads. A study of three DNA regions supports Urocystis tritici as the wheat pathogen, distinct from the narrower U. agropyri concept. Some extension guidance still uses the older, broader agropyri name. Keep that distinction when matching a laboratory result to a species record.
identification: Look for long gray to black streaks running along wheat leaves, especially as plants form additional shoots. The streaks later split, release dark spores, and leave the leaves frayed. Severe plants may be markedly shorter than their neighbors. These symptoms suggest flag smut but do not identify the fungus by themselves. Photograph whole plants beside healthy wheat and close views of unopened and ruptured streaks. A plant diagnostic laboratory should examine affected tissue; rust, other smuts, and physical injury require different interpretations.
actions: Contact an extension crop adviser or plant diagnostic laboratory before saving seed from an affected field. Keep potentially contaminated seed lots separate and clean soil and plant debris from equipment before moving to another field. Use seed from a reliable source and discuss resistant varieties, crop rotation, and professionally selected seed treatments for the next planting. The regional handbook describes infection before seedlings emerge, so spraying visibly damaged leaves is not a substitute for preventing early infection.

sources.title: Savchenko et al. 2017: What causes flag smut of wheat?

researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: The original 2017 multilocus revision directly resolves wheat isolates, including Kansas material, as tritici distinct from agropyri sensu stricto. APS actually lists both agents under flag smut. The new specimen-based research supports the exact wheat pathogen. Regional guidance using older broad agropyri remains disease-level context, not a claim that the narrow species are synonyms. Next: Use tritici for the revised wheat-pathogen concept; diagnostic labs should document the name treatment and host.

claims: Flag-smut list includes both agropyri and tritici
Disease symptoms, early infection and prevention under broad historical usage
Three loci separate wheat tritici from agropyri sensu stricto; sampled US wheat material

proposedDescription: Flame lily climbs with the curling tips of its leaves and bears striking red, orange, and yellow flowers. Its six narrow flower segments bend backward above spreading stamens. The stems die back seasonally, while thick underground parts remain alive and produce new growth. Native to Africa and Asia, it has escaped gardens in warm regions, including coastal habitats in Australia. Every part is poisonous if eaten, including the underground parts that can be mistaken for edible roots.
identification: Check for glossy, stalkless leaves with parallel veins and a slender tendril extending from each tip. Flowers have six wavy-edged segments, usually red or orange toward the ends and yellow toward the base. Climbing stems can reach several meters where they have support. Green capsules later darken and split to reveal seeds. The combination of leaf-tip tendrils and backward-curving flower segments is more useful than a lily-like bloom alone. Record the living leaves and flowers before seasonal dieback makes the plant harder to locate.
actions: Wear gloves and avoid contact with sap or underground parts. Keep children, pets, and livestock away from removed material. Dig small seedlings carefully and collect their underground growth; breaking and moving those pieces can spread the plant. Collect developing capsules before they open and do not dump plants or contaminated soil in natural areas. Mark the location and check for regrowth in the next growing season. Established patches may need a local weed specialist's follow-up plan rather than repeated removal of stems alone.
researchNotes: Two independent extension/government accounts support recognition and safe prevention. Australian impact is geographically bounded; no overseas legal status or pesticide recipe is generalized to US readers. Underground structures are described in plain language rather than unexplained jargon.

claims: Poisonous perennial climber with leaf-tip tendrils and six recurved flower segments; seasonal dieback.
Stems to 4 m; spreads through seed and underground fragments; protective clothing, seed prevention and digging small seedlings advised.

proposedDescription: Flamegold is a tree grown for yellow flower clusters followed by inflated pink to rose-colored capsules. The papery fruits later turn brown and release dark seeds. This profile concerns the Taiwanese subspecies formosana, rather than the closely related Fijian subspecies. In warm landscapes it can produce many seedlings and has escaped cultivation in the southeastern United States. The showy fruit is a useful recognition feature, but preventing seedlings from establishing beyond a planted tree is the practical management priority.
identification: Look for large leaves divided twice into smaller leaflets, with toothed margins and pointed tips. Trees can reach 18 m or more. The yellow flowers form branching clusters, followed by inflated capsules about 3-5 cm long. Compared with Koelreuteria elegans subsp. elegans, subsp. formosana generally has more strongly toothed, somewhat larger leaflets on longer small stalks. These differences overlap enough that a leaf alone is not ideal evidence. Record a whole compound leaf, flowers, and mature capsules when confirming the subspecies; do not confuse a single leaflet with an entire leaf.
actions: Pull seedlings promptly while their roots are small, checking garden beds, fence lines, and nearby disturbed ground after seed fall. Collect accessible fallen capsules before moving leaf litter or mulch elsewhere. Avoid sharing seed or seedlings from a tree that is spreading beyond its intended planting. Large trees near buildings or valued vegetation should be assessed by an arborist; removing the canopy is a different task from controlling the subsequent seedlings. Continue checking the area after any removal.

sources.title: Trees and Shrubs Online: Koelreuteria elegans, formosana treatment
USF FLIP: Koelreuteria elegans subsp. formosana

researchNotes: Exact subspecies retained. TSO's detailed subspecies treatment is preferred over FLIP's broad native-range wording and simplified leaf description. Seasonal dates are omitted because sources differ. Manual seedling prevention is supported; large-tree removal is referred to an arborist.

claims: Formosana is Taiwanese and differs from Fijian elegans in leaflet size, teeth and stalks; leaves twice divided.
Tree to 18 m; yellow flowers and inflated pink capsules; prolific seedlings should be removed promptly.

proposedDescription: Flamevine is a fast-growing woody climber with clusters of long orange flowers. It grips supports with branched tendrils and can extend over fences, shrubs, and trees. Native to South America, it is cultivated in warm regions and has escaped gardens in Florida and eastern Australia. Florida accounts often note its conspicuous cool-season bloom. Its vigor is the main practical concern in a garden: a small rooted cutting can eventually occupy much more space than the original planting.
identification: Look for opposite leaves, usually with two or three leaflets. The terminal leaflet may be replaced by a three-branched tendril. Orange tubular flowers have five short lobes at the opening, with stamens projecting beyond the tube; Florida extension describes flowers about 3 inches long. Inspect the junction between the leaf stalk and tendril, since orange flowers alone are shared by several unrelated garden vines. A flowering shoot with intact leaves is more useful than a close photograph of a single bloom. Growth height depends strongly on the supporting vegetation.
actions: Keep vines from reaching nearby tree crowns and trim growth that crosses beyond the intended support. Remove unwanted rooted stems before they become woody and extensive. Collect cuttings and rooted branches for contained disposal; this species is propagated by cuttings and layering, so dumping them can establish another patch. Monitor the base after cutting, since pruning is restraint rather than proof that the plant has died. Where it already covers a tree, seek help removing the vine without pulling down live branches.

sources.title: UF IFAS: Pyrostegia venusta Flame Vine

researchNotes: Regional impact statements are kept separate: UF's horticultural sheet describes escapes yet does not rate it a problem species, whereas the Australian guide calls it an environmental weed. Containment is justified by growth and propagation without claiming universal invasive status.

claims: Vigorous tendril climber; orange flowers about 3 inches; can cover trees; propagated by cuttings and layering.
Two to three leaflets, terminal tendril, projecting stamens; South American origin and naturalization in Australia and Florida.

proposedDescription: Flat grass scale is a sap-feeding insect associated especially with sugarcane. Colonies can be hidden between the stem and the wrapping leaf sheath, so a plant may carry insects that are not visible from the outside. Young females are pale, while older females become elongated and dark reddish brown. A Florida pest alert documented it on energy cane in 2016 and emphasized that its economic effects were poorly known. Finding scales calls for identification, not an assumption of severe crop loss.
identification: Gently inspect beneath a loose leaf sheath for elongated yellowish or beige insects, dark older females, and a narrow white wax fringe around their bodies. Mature females can resemble small dark seeds. Pink sugarcane mealybug, Saccharicoccus sacchari, may occur alongside them but is pink and more visibly coated with wax. Aclerda sacchari can be indistinguishable from A. takahashii in the field; reliable separation requires a specialist examining prepared specimens. Include the host grass and the insects' position on the stem in any identification request.
actions: Do not move infested cane pieces or ornamental grass divisions to another property while identification is pending. Inspect propagation material beneath its leaf sheaths and keep suspect plants separate from clean stock. Photograph a colony in place and ask a state plant-health office or extension entomologist how to submit a sample. Avoid stripping every sheath or treating an entire planting solely from a photograph: several grass scales and mealybugs resemble this species. A confirmed infestation should guide any crop-specific treatment decision.

sources.title: FDACS pest alert: Flat grass scale

researchNotes: Independent FDACS observations and USDA identification treatment support recognition. FDACS says little is known about economic impact, so no yield-loss estimate or control efficacy is invented. Actions emphasize clean propagation material and diagnostic submission.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
claims: Colonies hidden under cane sheaths; females darken with age; pink sugarcane mealybug differs; A. sacchari cannot be separated in the field.
Elongate yellow-brown body with darker apex; sheath/crown habitat; microscopic characters required for validation.

proposedDescription: Flaxleaf fanpetals is a slender, upright mallow with unusually narrow leaves and pale flowers marked by a dark center. It grows in open tropical habitats, including savannas and disturbed ground. Its native range includes parts of tropical America and Africa, so occurrence outside a garden is not automatically evidence of a harmful introduction. The narrow foliage makes it less obviously mallow-like than broad-leaved relatives, but the small segmented fruit and central column of stamens help reveal the relationship.
identification: Plants commonly stand well below or around 1 m. Leaves are narrow and pointed, often 3-10 cm long, with very short stalks and mostly unbroken edges. The pale flowers gather toward the shoot tips and often have a red-purple center. Mature fruits are small flattened discs that separate into several one-seeded sections. Regional flora accounts differ slightly in the number of sections, so count them as part of a complete identification rather than as a single decisive test. Include stem hairs, a whole leaf, flowers, and ripe fruit when asking a botanist to distinguish it from other Sida species.
actions: Confirm local status before treating a patch as invasive. Where it is an unwanted garden or field weed, remove small plants before the segmented fruits dry and break apart. Collect mature fruits instead of scattering them during mowing or cleanup, and avoid moving seed-bearing soil to another bed. Recheck open ground for new plants and maintain suitable ground cover where feasible. Because many fanpetals are similar, retain photographs of flowering and fruiting plants before removing a previously unrecorded population.
researchNotes: Independent Mexican and East African flora treatments agree on useful visible traits but differ in fruit-section counts, which are not over-specified. No species-specific eradication trial was located; actions are bounded prevention of seed movement and removal of unwanted plants.

claims: Narrow entire leaves 3-10 cm; pale dark-centered flowers; small flattened segmented fruits; native in Mexico.
Erect herb with narrow leaves and white or pink flowers; tropical American and African native range.

proposedDescription: Florida keys indian mallow is a hairy herb or soft-stemmed shrub with broad, heart-shaped leaves. Yellow to orange flowers usually have a reddish or purple center, followed by rounded fruits made of numerous joined segments. Despite its geographic common name, the plant has a much wider tropical distribution. Young shoots may feel sticky because they bear gland-tipped hairs. These details distinguish it more usefully than the general impression of a yellow-flowered mallow.
identification: Look for an upright plant around 1-2 m tall with toothed, heart-based leaves and conspicuously hairy young stems. The flowers arise at leaf bases or in short terminal clusters. Their yellow-orange petals and dark central patch accompany sticky, gland-bearing stems. The Florida key separates it from Abutilon grandifolium and A. hulseanum by those glandular stems; those relatives lack the same combination. Mature fruits contain many sections, rather than the few seen in some other mallows. Show a young shoot, flower center, and ripe fruit; foliage alone can leave the identification uncertain.
actions: For an unwanted small planting, remove plants before the fruits mature and collect any developed seed heads separately. Keep seed-bearing debris out of mulch intended for other properties. Wear gloves when handling sticky, hairy stems and wash tools after cleanup. Check the original site for seedlings, especially where removal leaves exposed soil. Have an unfamiliar wild mallow identified before clearing it, since related species may be native and the common name alone does not establish whether this plant is a local management priority.
researchNotes: Independent African flora descriptions and the Florida identification key support recognition; both were accessed as indexed text. The catalog common name is preserved without implying Florida origin. Conservative seed containment is an inference from fruiting biology, not a tested control program.

claims: Hairy glandular herb or shrub to about 1.5-2 m, heart-shaped toothed leaves, yellow-orange dark-centered flowers and many fruit segments.
Sticky gland-bearing stems and dark-based petals distinguish A. hirtum from A. grandifolium and A. hulseanum.

proposedDescription: Florida red scale is a small armored insect that feeds on leaves, green twigs, and fruit. Its circular coverings can look like dark spots stuck to the plant. Heavy infestations may cause yellowing and leaf loss, but natural enemies often keep populations in check. Citrus, palms, and many ornamentals can host it. The common name does not mean that every red or brown scale found in Florida belongs to this species; several armored scales are very similar.
identification: Adult female covers are about 2.0-2.2 mm across, dark reddish brown with a lighter brown center and visible concentric rings. Look on leaves and fruit as well as green twigs. Tiny winged males look quite different from the settled females. Chrysomphalus bifasciculatus cannot reliably be separated from this species in the field, and some Lindingaspis or Melanaspis scales can also resemble it on ornamentals. A close photograph can document the infestation, but authoritative identification requires microscopic examination of a prepared adult female.
actions: Inspect new citrus and ornamental plants before placing them beside established stock. Keep a heavily infested potted plant separate while an extension specialist confirms the scale and assesses whether it is still alive. Preserve beneficial insects: UF documents control by the tiny parasitic wasp Aphytis holoxanthus, so routine broad insecticide spraying can be counterproductive. Remove a few badly infested leaves or small twigs only when that will not seriously weaken the plant, contain the debris, and seek host-specific advice for persistent infestations.

sources.title: UF IFAS: A Guide to Scale Insect Identification
US Forest Service forest pest insect photo guide

researchNotes: UF's full identification section and independent taxonomic account support the field limits. Pruning and isolation are conservative household containment suggestions, not efficacy claims; chemical schedules and assumptions that every scale cover contains a live insect are avoided.

claims: Circular reddish-brown female armor 2.0-2.2 mm; occurs on foliage, green twigs and fruit; Aphytis holoxanthus provides biological control.
Microscopic slide-mounted females required; C. bifasciculatus indistinguishable in field.
Broad host range; foliage yellowing and possible leaf drop under heavy infestation.

proposedDescription: Florida tasselflower is a fast-growing annual with small pink to red flower heads above its leaves. The heads later produce many lightweight fruits with fine white hairs that carry them on the wind. It is common in warm disturbed places and can become a nuisance in nursery containers and landscape beds. Its name is easy to confuse with other tasselflowers, and color varies enough that a red bloom alone is not a dependable identification.
identification: Look for an upright plant with lower leaves gathered near the base and upper leaves that partly clasp the stem. The flower heads are bell-shaped, with the small tubular florets projecting from the enclosing green bracts; there is no ring of daisy-like outer petals. Emilia sonchifolia usually has a narrower, urn-shaped head. Emilia coccinea and E. praetermissa can also be confused with it. Record the head from the side and several leaves from different stem levels. Keep the original flower color in photographs, since dried material can lose a useful distinction.
actions: Pull plants from containers and beds before their heads turn into wind-dispersed seed. Collect developed heads before lifting the rest of the plant so cleanup does not shake seed into surrounding pots. Inspect incoming plants and reused pots, and keep potting materials free of weeds. Around managed nursery paths, regular mowing can reduce seed production, but plants growing among ornamentals are better removed individually. Revisit the area frequently during warm weather; this weed can complete its life cycle quickly.

sources.title: UF IFAS: Biology and management of tasselflower
Chung et al. 2009: Emilia praetermissa, a misidentified alien species
Manual de malezas comunes del Paraguay: Emilia fosbergii

researchNotes: Independent taxonomic and regional flora evidence supplements UF's practical nursery management. Color is treated as supporting evidence rather than a sole test. No regional claim of absence of a lookalike is extended nationally.

claims: Bell-shaped E. fosbergii heads; wind-dispersed seed; prompt hand-weeding, clean nursery materials and mowing reduce spread.
E. praetermissa has been misidentified as E. fosbergii; flower color changes in dried material complicate identification.
Annual upright herb with basal leaves, clasping stem leaves and red/pink/purple heads.

proposedDescription: Flower axistree is a small evergreen shrub or tree in the citrus family. It bears small white flowers and rounded fruits that change from pale colors to red as they ripen. Its leaves vary: some have only one leaflet, while others carry several. Native to parts of eastern and southeastern Asia, it is cultivated as an ornamental and has escaped in southern Florida. The berries can attract birds, making seedlings beyond a planted shrub worth checking.
identification: Plants are generally about 1-3 m tall. Leaves commonly carry two to four smooth-edged leaflets, sometimes one or five; individual leaflets may be oval, oblong, or lance-shaped. White petals are only about 4 mm long, and ripe fruits are about 1-1.5 cm across. Show the complete leaf attachment and the flower or fruit cluster, rather than assuming each leaflet is a whole leaf. Glycosmis species vary considerably, and a sterile plant with one leaflet may need botanical examination to distinguish it from related citrus-family shrubs.
actions: Check beneath the parent shrub and nearby bird perches for seedlings. Where the plant is unwanted or escaping, pull young seedlings with their roots and collect accessible fruit before moving garden debris. Keep fruiting branches out of natural-area waste piles. Confirm a suspected wild population before removing larger shrubs, then use a local extension or conservation adviser to plan the work. These measures limit seed movement without assuming that an ornamental specimen causes the same impacts in every region.
researchNotes: Fresh review 2026-10-31: Fresh Kew independently confirms accepted identity, native range and Florida introduction; a Florida agency account corroborates escape into disturbed hammocks, while acknowledging its morphology comes from Flora of China. Kew's scoped range/identity stream is independent of the repeated measurement lineage. Conservative seed containment does not need a separate eradication trial. Next: Retain the restrained Florida context and seek botanical confirmation for sterile plants. Inherited reference not used as fresh substantive evidence (unavailable or superseded by the specified original): https://efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200012451 .

claims: Variable leaflet counts, small white flowers, red fruit and NParks bird association
Cultivation escape and seed propagation; universal removal advice not adopted
Accepted species, Asian native range and Florida introduction
Escaped cultivation in disturbed southern Florida hammocks; morphology explicitly FoC-derived

proposedDescription: Flower of an hour is a branching annual mallow with pale flowers and a dark purple center. Each bloom lasts only briefly, but the plant remains recognizable by its deeply divided leaves and the inflated, veined covering around its fruit. It was introduced as an ornamental and now grows in fields, gardens, and other disturbed places across much of the United States. It reproduces by seed, so removing plants before their capsules mature is more useful than waiting for a long flowering display.
identification: Plants are often about 30-50 cm tall. Leaves alternate along hairy stems; later leaves divide into three to seven toothed lobes, while the first leaves are rounder. Five pale yellow or whitish petals surround a purple base. After flowering, a thin, bladder-like calyx with dark veins surrounds the hairy capsule. Seedlings resemble velvetleaf, Abutilon theophrasti, but flower of an hour has rounder, glossier seed leaves and develops deeply divided true leaves. Photograph both early and mature leaves if the plant has not yet flowered.
actions: Pull or hoe unwanted young plants before the capsules mature, taking care around nearby crop roots. Collect fruiting plants rather than leaving them to dry in the bed. Check soil brought in for landscaping and clean seed-bearing debris from cultivation tools before moving between sites. Because it is an annual, preventing seed return is the main long-term objective; revisit the patch for later seedlings during warm weather. In a crop, ask an extension adviser for options suited to that crop rather than using a general garden treatment.

sources.title: University of Missouri WeedID: Venice mallow

researchNotes: Three university identification accounts were read as indexed excerpts and agree on the US weed concept. Conservative annual-weed actions follow seed reproduction; no species-specific herbicide efficacy is asserted and Australasian taxonomic usage is not imported.

claims: Summer annual; lobed leaves, pale purple-based flowers and inflated veined calyx.
Plants 30-50 cm; flowers open briefly; rounded hairy capsules.
Velvetleaf seedlings resemble this plant; rounder glossy cotyledons and later deeply lobed leaves help distinguish it.

proposedDescription: Flowering Rush is a wetland perennial with narrow upright leaves and rounded clusters of pink flowers. In deeper water it may stay submerged and never flower, making established patches less conspicuous. It spreads through pieces and small buds from its underground stems, and some populations also produce viable seed. Dense growth can crowd shoreline vegetation and obstruct access to water. Small fragments carried on equipment or released during poorly planned removal can establish another patch.
identification: Look for long leaves with a triangular cross-section that often twist toward their tips. A separate round flower stalk bears an umbrella-like cluster of pink flowers, each with three petals and three similar-looking sepals. Plants commonly reach 1-4 feet above shallow water. Bur-reeds, Sparganium species, are useful lookalikes: they have ball-shaped flower or fruit clusters instead of the pink umbrella. Hardstem bulrush, sweet flag, and sedges can also resemble nonflowering plants. Have submerged or sterile material checked before disturbing the roots.
actions: Report a new patch to the local aquatic invasive species program and photograph its flowers, leaves, and shoreline setting. Clean mud and plant fragments from boats, waders, and tools, and drain and dry equipment before moving it to another waterbody. Do not plant or discard it in a natural waterway. Ask the relevant water manager about removal requirements before digging or cutting: broken underground pieces can regrow, and cutting has sometimes spread infestations. Small isolated plants need careful collection of every fragment and follow-up monitoring.
researchNotes: Seed fertility is described as population-dependent, avoiding the inaccurate blanket claim that all North American populations are sterile. Public-water permission is framed as a local check rather than a nationwide legal assertion; removal risks are explicit.

claims: Triangular twisting leaves; submerged nonflowering form; variable seed fertility; fragments and buds spread; cutting can worsen spread.
Pink flower umbels contrast with bur-reed balls; underground fragments regenerate.

proposedDescription: This forest pathogen causes willow scab, a disease of young leaves and shoots that is most noticeable during wet spring weather. Leaves brown, wither, and fall soon after they emerge, and small twigs may die back. The fungus can survive in infected twigs and fallen leaves, allowing rain to spread spores when new growth appears. Willow scab may occur alongside black canker, so a badly blighted willow can have more than one disease at once.
identification: Watch for brown patches along the midrib of newly expanded willow leaves, followed by rapid browning and leaf drop. Olive-brown spore growth may appear on infected tissue, and small dark cankers can develop on twigs. Black canker, associated with a different fungus, often becomes conspicuous later in summer and may affect larger wood. Venturia chlorospora also causes similar willow symptoms. Photograph the fresh leaf lesions and the boundary between living and dead twig tissue; a laboratory examination is needed to assign the fungus confidently.
actions: Collect fallen leaves and small infected twigs before the next spring flush, using a disposal route that keeps the material away from healthy willows. Prune accessible diseased twigs when practical, without removing excessive healthy canopy. Maintain the tree's vigor and discuss less susceptible planting choices if repeated blight makes replacement necessary. Ask an arborist or diagnostic laboratory to evaluate extensive dieback. Fungicide decisions should follow a confirmed diagnosis and a locally appropriate plan to protect new growth, rather than attempts to restore leaves already killed.

sources.title: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station disease guide

researchNotes: Catalog's broad common name is retained but the public text identifies willow scab clearly. Symptoms are not presented as species-proof. Sanitation follows independent extension guidance, with burning omitted because local disposal conditions differ.

claims: Wet-spring browning of new leaves and twigs, olive-brown spores, V. saliciperda scab; black canker differs.
Survival in old leaves and infected twigs; spring-rain spread; pruning and leaf cleanup advised; V. chlorospora also occurs.
Willow blight can combine scab and black canker; prune infected branches and maintain vigor.

proposedDescription: Forest redgum is a large Australian eucalyptus with smooth bark that sheds in patches or plates. Mature trees carry long narrow leaves and clusters of white flowers, followed by small woody capsules. It is widely planted outside its native range. The name refers to the horn-like caps on the flower buds in typical forms, a feature worth examining before the flowers open. Several subspecies and related redgums share much of its appearance, so bark alone is a weak identification.
identification: Trees can reach about 50 m, although planted individuals vary greatly. Adult leaves are usually narrow, roughly 10-20 cm long, while juvenile leaves are broader. Inspect unopened bud clusters: many forms have a long pointed cap above a short base. The woody fruits have valves that project above the rim. Eucalyptus camaldulensis is a named lookalike with generally shorter, beaked or bluntly conical bud caps, but variation and intermediate plants complicate the distinction. Record mature buds, fruits, adult leaves, and juvenile shoots if available; do not assign a subspecies from a single long-capped bud.
actions: Check beneath planted trees and along disturbed edges for unwanted seedlings, removing them while they can be lifted without major soil disturbance. Avoid distributing seed-bearing capsules or soil containing young plants to new sites. Have a large tree assessed by a qualified arborist before removal, especially near structures or utilities. If a population is spreading beyond cultivation, document the seedlings and ask a local botanist to verify the species. A planted redgum's identity and local behavior should guide management rather than its size alone.
researchNotes: Species-level text deliberately accommodates variation among subspecies; EUCLID's nominate-subspecies details are not applied to every plant. Independent flora accounts support recognition. No unsupported US ecological-impact or species-specific eradication claim is made.

claims: Tree to 50 m; smooth shedding bark; adult leaves 10-20 cm; pointed bud caps and exserted fruit valves.
Planted tree with smooth bark, horn-shaped bud caps and projecting fruit valves.
E. camaldulensis differs in bud-cap form; tree has small woody capsules.
Four subspecies recognized; bud and juvenile characters vary and intermediate plants occur.

proposedDescription: Formosa firethorn is a thorny evergreen or partly evergreen shrub with white spring flowers and dense clusters of orange-red fruit. It is native to Taiwan and widely grown as a hedge or barrier. Birds eat the fruit, and plants sometimes persist or escape beyond old garden sites. Its sharp branch tips make close inspection and pruning awkward, but the shape of the leaves is a useful way to distinguish it from other cultivated firethorns.
identification: Look for stiff, branching growth that may reach about 18 feet, with sharp thorns at the ends of some side branches. Leaves are commonly 1-3 inches long, broadest toward the tip, which is blunt, squared off, or slightly notched. Scarlet firethorn, Pyracantha coccinea, usually has leaves broadest around the middle and tapering toward the tip. White flower clusters appear in late spring or early summer; orange-red fruits can remain through winter. Photograph several mature leaves and a thorn-bearing branch, since pruning and cultivars can alter the shrub's outline.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and protect your eyes when reaching into the thorny branches. Remove unwanted seedlings while small, especially under bird perches or beyond a planted hedge. Collect fruit-bearing prunings and keep them out of woodland waste piles. If replacing a spreading shrub, plan safe access to its base and monitor the site for remaining seedlings or shoots. Confirm the species before clearing an unfamiliar firethorn; garden plants and escapes can belong to several similar species or horticultural selections.
researchNotes: Independent southeastern flora corroborates the leaf-tip distinction and escape history. NC State's phrase suggesting leaves themselves have sharp spines is not repeated; thorns are correctly placed on branches. Actions are conservative fruit and seedling containment.

claims: Thorny shrub to 18 feet; leaves broadest near blunt or notched tips distinguish P. coccinea; birds consume fruit.
Notched/truncate leaf tips key P. koidzumii; Taiwanese species sometimes escapes into southeastern woodlands.

proposedDescription: Formosa lily sends a leafy upright stem from an underground bulb and bears large white trumpet-shaped flowers. The outside of a flower may be flushed purple, followed by an upright capsule that dries and releases lightweight seeds. Native to Taiwan, it is cultivated widely and has escaped into disturbed ground in several warm regions. The stems die back seasonally, but the bulb remains alive. Removing only the visible flowering stem therefore does not remove the whole plant.
identification: Plants may reach 2 m, with many narrow alternate leaves up to about 15 cm long and 1 cm wide. The fragrant trumpet flowers can be about 15 cm long, with the segment tips bending backward. Long cylindrical capsules develop after flowering. Inspect the leaf width and arrangement along the stem as well as the complete flower in side view. Other cultivated white trumpet lilies can resemble it, and garden hybrids may blur the distinction. Keep flowering photographs and the planting history when seeking confirmation; a bare winter site can still contain bulbs.
actions: Remove developing capsules before they dry and split if a confirmed plant is spreading beyond its intended bed. Dig isolated unwanted plants carefully, lifting the bulb rather than merely pulling off the stem. Collect bulbs and seed-bearing material for contained disposal instead of dumping them with garden soil. Mark treated spots and inspect them during the next growing season for seedlings or surviving bulbs. On dunes or other sensitive ground, seek local advice before digging so removal does not destabilize surrounding vegetation.

sources.title: Bay of Plenty Regional Council: Formosa lily

researchNotes: Independent government accounts support morphology and bulb removal. Southern-hemisphere flowering months and local legal rules are not generalized to US readers. No named lily comparison was verified closely enough to supply a false definitive garden-hybrid key.

claims: Perennial bulb to 2 m; narrow alternate leaves; white trumpets to 15 cm; spread by bulbs and seed.
Wind-dispersed seed; seasonal dieback; dig scattered plants with bulbs; introduced ornamental affects local dunes.

proposedDescription: Formosan Termite is a wood-feeding social insect whose large colonies can damage buildings and trees. Colonies include pale workers, defensive soldiers, and winged reproductive adults. Although often associated with soil, it can also build nests above ground where moisture is available. Mud shelter tubes and discarded wings are useful warning signs, but old damage alone does not establish that termites are still active. Movement of infested timbers can carry colonies to new places.
identification: Workers are pale and about 3-4 mm long, but are poor specimens for species identification. Soldiers are roughly 4-5 mm long with orange-brown, teardrop-shaped heads and curved jaws; native Reticulitermes soldiers have more rectangular heads. Winged adults are yellowish brown, with equal-sized wings bearing fine hairs. Asian subterranean termite, Coptotermes gestroi, is a close lookalike requiring examination of tiny head hairs and other details. Save soldiers or winged adults for an identification service. Do not infer a species, or a hybrid, simply from the amount of damage.
actions: Arrange a professional termite inspection when live termites, indoor swarms, or fresh mud tubes appear. Keep a sample and photographs before disturbing the evidence. Do not move suspect railroad ties, firewood, or structural timbers to another property. Check moisture problems and have nearby trees assessed if termite activity may have weakened them. A colony can extend beyond one visible patch, so surface spraying or replacing one damaged board is not a complete treatment plan. Work with a licensed pest professional on control and follow-up inspections.

sources.title: UF IFAS: Asian subterranean termite comparison

researchNotes: Independent UF and Texas A&M accounts support recognition and timber-movement prevention. UF PDFs were opened and relevant identification text read; no claim is made that a swarmer near an outdoor light proves a building infestation. No pesticide or fumigation recipe is offered.

claims: Workers 3-4 mm; soldiers 4-5 mm; head shape, hairy wings, nests and live-termite confirmation; major structural pest.
Use soldiers or winged adults for identification; nests can occur above ground; recycled infested timber can spread termites.
C. gestroi and C. formosanus require fine head-hair examination for separation.

proposedDescription: This fouling bryozoan is a colony of tiny animals that share a branching, pale cream structure. Young colonies spread across a surface; older growth rises into thin, curling fronds. Each animal filters food from the water with a crown of tentacles. Large deposits have washed onto beaches in Brazil, where researchers studied blooms involving this bryozoan and other organisms. Its original native range remains uncertain. Historical records from Florida and the Gulf region do not establish that it is introduced or causing damage at every U.S. site.
identification: Colonies can reach about 6 cm tall and wide. Their lightly hardened, two-layered fronds curl and overlap, rather than forming the solid leaves of a seaweed. Individual chambers are only about 0.34-0.58 mm long, so a close photograph usually shows the colony's shape rather than enough detail for a firm identification. Other encrusting and upright bryozoans can look similar. Record whether the colony is attached to a shell, piling, rope or boat, and photograph both its growing edge and branching structure. A marine specialist may need a small, properly collected sample to inspect the chambers.
actions: Have an unfamiliar fouling colony identified before deciding whether removal is needed. Send photographs and the location to a marine extension service or local invasive-species program, especially if dense growth is affecting gear. Before moving boats, ropes or other equipment between waters, inspect attached growth and arrange cleaning where removed material can be captured on land. Do not scrape colonies into the water or move live samples to another shore. These are prevention measures for transferable marine fouling; the available evidence does not establish a household treatment or a reason to remove all local bryozoans.

sources.title: Rorig et al. 2017: Blooms of bryozoans and epibenthic diatoms

researchNotes: Smithsonian supplies the morphology and uncertainty in origin; the independent Brazilian study corroborates bloom occurrence without establishing U.S. harm. The university-hosted PDF failed to fetch, so the study is labeled indexed excerpt. Cleaning advice is conservative pathway prevention, not a species-specific control trial.

claims: Colonies form pale two-layered fronds; individual chambers require magnification.
Native range is uncertain and North American abundance information is limited.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Rorig et al. independent Brazilian field study
claims: Brazilian blooms involved this bryozoan and other species; causes were not conclusively established.

proposedDescription: This marine worm lives inside a hard white tube attached to a submerged surface. It extends a tentacled feeding crown into the water, then withdraws and closes the opening with a specialized plug. It belongs to the western Atlantic fauna, including parts of the U.S. coast, and has also been recorded outside that range. A Taiwanese study found it among fouling organisms on ropes and mussels. Boat and equipment movement matters because attached animals can travel with the surfaces they occupy.
identification: The tube may be smooth or have two lengthwise ridges and lacks a conspicuously raised rim at the opening. Those features alone cannot distinguish it from other tube worms. Identification depends on the plug, or operculum: its upper crown has curved spines with an outward-pointing secondary spine partway along each one. Hydroides dianthus lacks that external secondary spine, while H. elegans has a different arrangement of joined and branching spines. These are microscope characters, not a reliable shore-side color test. Photograph the tube and extended crown without pulling the worm out; specialist examination is needed for a new locality record.
actions: Keep hulls, mooring ropes and portable marine equipment free of excessive attached growth before moving them between harbors. Use a cleaning facility that captures removed material instead of brushing it into a marina. If unusual tube-worm growth appears on recently moved equipment, document its origin and destination and ask a marine identification service to examine it. Avoid transporting live fouling samples between water bodies. Because this species occurs naturally in the western Atlantic, its presence there is not by itself a reason for eradication; management should follow a confirmed identification and local context.

sources.title: Ferrario and Minchin 2017: Hydroides sanctaecrucis in Taiwan

researchNotes: The Taiwan paper was read in full and provides independent specimen observations alongside the Smithsonian's earlier taxonomic synthesis. A malformed size range in the database was deliberately omitted. Identification remains specialist-level; actions address transport of attached fouling and do not assume Atlantic populations are introduced.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Bastida-Zavala taxonomic studies synthesized by Smithsonian
claims: White tubes lack a raised opening rim; identification uses the opercular spines.
The western Atlantic is part of the native range.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Ferrario and Minchin Taiwan specimen study
claims: Specimens occurred in fouling on ropes and mussels.
Opercular secondary spines distinguish it from H. dianthus and H. elegans.

proposedDescription: Fountain palm grows slowly from a broad cluster of leaves into a palm with one trunk and a rounded crown. The name refers to the hanging tips of its fan-shaped leaves. Young plants may remain close to the ground for years, which can make an eventual tree look like a shrub in a garden bed. It is widely planted for its foliage, but seedlings outside cultivation deserve attention where local guidance identifies an escape risk. Its appearance and mature size depend strongly on growing conditions.
identification: The large fans have a central extension of the leaf stalk into the blade and deeply divided, drooping ends. Leaves can be roughly 4-6 feet long. The stout gray trunk develops closely spaced leaf scars as it grows. Brown spines along young leaf stalks are an important handling hazard; older palms may have fewer spines. A mature plant can approach 30 feet, although slow-growing landscape specimens may be much shorter. Other fan palms share the general outline, so photograph the leaf stalk, divided tips and trunk together. A small, trunkless plant should not be identified from height alone.
actions: Watch beneath fruiting palms and along nearby bed edges for seedlings. Remove unwanted seedlings while they are small enough to lift without damaging neighboring plants, wearing gloves and keeping clear of spiny leaf stalks. Collect fallen fruit where escape is a concern and avoid dumping palm waste in natural areas. Ask a qualified arborist to handle large plants or fruit clusters beyond safe reach. Before planting additional palms, check regional extension guidance: an ornamental that stays contained in one climate may establish beyond gardens in another.
researchNotes: Independent UF and LSU descriptions agree on the useful leaf, trunk and growth characters. Their landscape sizes differ, so the text distinguishes potential mature height from small slow-growing specimens. Seedling and fruit containment are precautionary garden advice; no nationwide invasive designation or chemical control claim is made.

claims: Palm can reach about 30 feet and has drooping fan-leaf tips.
Young petioles are spiny; potential escape warrants regional assessment.
Single gray ringed trunk bears a rounded crown and 4-6 foot leaves.
Plants grow slowly and can remain trunkless for years.

proposedDescription: Fountainbush makes a low, spreading shrub with green stems that rise and then arch toward the ground. Slender red flowers hang along those stems; yellow and salmon garden forms also occur. Hummingbirds visit the flowers, and flowering can continue through much of the year in warm conditions. Native to Mexico, it is often planted along walls or in large containers. It can root where arching stems touch soil, so a planted clump may gradually occupy more space. Garden vigor alone does not establish that it harms surrounding habitats.
identification: Look for slender, ribbed green branches and tubular flowers up to about 2.5 cm long. The shrub commonly stands 3-4 feet tall, with a spread of 6 feet or more. Leaves are sparse, tiny or absent on much of the flowering growth; occasional larger leaves can reach about 2 cm. Its stems can suggest horsetails, Equisetum species, but the conspicuous tubular flowers immediately separate this flowering shrub from those spore-producing plants. Photograph a flowering branch and its base, including any stems rooted into the soil. Flower color varies among cultivated forms, so red alone is not diagnostic.
actions: Keep arching stems within the intended planting area and lift or remove sections that have rooted beyond it. When reducing a clump, collect loose cut stems rather than leaving them on damp soil where propagation is possible. Check the edge again after new growth develops. Container culture can make spread easier to observe, provided trailing growth cannot reach nearby soil. Report persistent growth beyond cultivation if your regional invasive-plant program requests such records. Broad eradication is not automatically warranted: Florida extension treats it as a useful ornamental, while floras document naturalization in other regions.

sources.title: Kew: Russelia equisetiformis, regional flora descriptions

researchNotes: UF horticultural guidance and independently authored regional flora treatments support a bounded ornamental profile. The contrast between Florida's non-invasive assessment and naturalization elsewhere is retained without treating either as universal. Removal of rooted stems follows the documented layering habit; no tested eradication claim is implied.

claims: Arching shrub bears tubular flowers and can spread over six feet.
Propagation occurs through layers and stem cuttings.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of Tropical East Africa and Cayman flora
claims: Ribbed arching branches can root; leaves are often absent.
Flowers reach 2.5 cm; regional floras record roadside naturalization.

proposedDescription: Fourleaf manyseed is a small annual weed that can be easy to overlook until its branching stems carry many tiny fruits. It grows in disturbed ground, gardens and other open places rather than forming a tall, conspicuous stand. The leaves often sit in groups of four around a stem, giving the plant its name. The flowers are minute and pale, and the seed capsules are more useful than blossom color for recognizing a mature plant. Although usually annual, some regional accounts describe plants lasting longer.
identification: Stems commonly reach about 5-20 cm and are hairless, with small oval to spoon-shaped leaves. The leaves are often in whorls of four but can also appear in opposite pairs. Thin, pale triangular scales at the leaf bases are useful close-up details. Flowers have greenish sepals about 2-3 mm long and much smaller white petals; the capsules are about 2 mm long. Other small weeds can have paired leaves, so check several stem joints instead of relying on one. A magnified photograph of a joint and an open flower or mature capsule is much more useful than an overhead view of a seedling.
actions: Pull small patches before the capsules mature, taking the root with the stems and collecting fruiting material. Check the same disturbed soil for later seedlings, particularly where watering or cultivation keeps patches open. Avoid moving seed-bearing soil or nursery debris into clean beds. Covering bare garden soil with suitable plants or mulch can reduce available establishment sites. If the plant is tangled among valued seedlings, identify a mature piece first and remove it selectively. Routine mowing may miss this low-growing weed, so inspect close to the soil rather than assuming a short patch is seed-free.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Polycarpon tetraphyllum

researchNotes: Two independently authored floras supply consistent visible and reproductive characters. Identification stays at species level and does not assign an unverified subspecies. Manual advice follows the small annual and seed-capsule habit; no comparative herbicide effectiveness or universal persistence claim is asserted.

claims: Small hairless annual has 4-15 mm leaves and 2-3 mm sepals.
It occurs as a garden and pasture weed.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Webb Sykes and Garnock-Jones New Zealand flora
claims: Stems are commonly 5-20 cm with four-leaf whorls or opposite leaves.
Small pale stipules and capsules assist identification.

proposedDescription: Foxglove aphid feeds on many plants, not just foxgloves. In vegetables and greenhouse crops it can remain hidden among young leaves, where small scattered populations are easily missed. Its short life cycle allows numbers to rise quickly, and winged adults can move to new plants. Feeding and the viruses it can transmit are separate concerns: finding aphids does not establish that a plant has a virus. Careful inspection of fresh growth is more useful than waiting for a large, obvious colony.
identification: Many individuals are pale green or yellow and somewhat shiny, with darker green patches around the bases of the two small tubes near the rear of the body. These tubes are called cornicles. Black marks on the legs and antennae can help, but pink or orange forms also occur. Young aphids lack wings; adults may be winged or wingless. Green peach aphid has a characteristic inward-facing shape at the bases of its antennae that foxglove aphid lacks. Lettuce aphid, Nasonovia ribis-nigri, can be nearly indistinguishable in the field. Use magnified photographs or submit a specimen before selecting species-specific control.
actions: Inspect newly acquired plants and the youngest leaves of nearby crops, separating suspicious potted plants while identification is arranged. On celery, look inside the plant instead of checking only the exposed outer leaves. Record whether the population is increasing and whether leaves are distorted or discolored. Avoid moving infested cuttings to other growing areas. If numbers persist, ask extension staff for options suited to the particular crop and growing setting; the protected feeding sites make casual surface treatment unreliable. Do not apply commercial field-treatment rates to a home garden, and do not assume removing visible aphids reverses a virus infection.

sources.title: UC IPM: Foxglove aphid on celery

researchNotes: UC crop guidance and Cornell's independent greenhouse account agree on recognition. Cornell full-page retrieval failed, so only its displayed indexed text is credited. Advice emphasizes inspection and containment rather than translating commercial pesticide rates or claiming visible symptoms diagnose a particular virus.

claims: Aphids feed inside young celery growth and can transmit viruses.
Lettuce aphid is a close field lookalike; green peach aphid differs at antennal bases.
Foxglove aphids have green marks at cornicle bases and dark leg and antennal markings.

proposedDescription: Foxtail millet is a cultivated annual grass grown for grain and birdseed. Plants escaping from cultivation can appear around feeding stations, disturbed soil and discarded seed. The dense, bristly flower head gives it the familiar foxtail shape, but that outline is shared by several wild grasses. This profile treats cultivated foxtail millet separately from green foxtail, Setaria viridis. Their close relationship explains why older sources sometimes place them together. A volunteer millet plant does not by itself demonstrate a damaging local invasion.
identification: Plants can reach roughly 35-150 cm, with flat, narrow leaves and a dense flower head that may be lobed or nodding. Bristles beneath the small flower units can be yellowish or purple and reach about 15 mm. The mature head provides the important distinction from green foxtail: in foxtail millet, much of each spikelet stays attached while its upper fertile unit separates; green foxtail sheds the whole spikelet. This requires mature material and close examination. Setaria verticillata has backward-pointing bristle barbs, unlike the forward-roughened bristles in this group. Save a mature head for identification rather than relying on a seedling photograph.
actions: Where millet is unwanted, remove volunteer plants before their heads mature and collect any already formed seed heads. Clean spilled birdseed and dispose of sweepings without scattering them into bare soil. Check compost edges, feeding areas and recently disturbed ground for later seedlings. In a garden, maintain suitable cover on open soil after removal. In a crop or forage setting, identify the grass before acting because cultivated millet and weed foxtails may need different decisions. Do not move a questionable seed lot into a new field while its identity is unresolved.

sources.title: SANBI: Identification guide to southern African grasses, Setaria italica
Flora of New Zealand: Setaria key

researchNotes: Three independently authored floras support morphology, the narrow species concept and the crop context. A USDA dried-material page uses S. italica subsp. viridis inconsistently and was not used. Volunteer removal and spilled-seed hygiene are conservative prevention, not evidence of nationwide ecological harm.

claims: Annual plants are 350-1500 mm tall with bristles up to 15 mm.
Persistence of spikelets separates S. italica from S. viridis; bristle direction separates S. verticillata.
Foxtail millet is cultivated for grain and birdseed.

proposedDescription: Fragrant manjack is a tropical tree with broad leaves, small white flowers and soft fruit around a hard stone. Its sticky fruit pulp explains alternate names such as glue berry. Flowers form branching clusters near the ends of shoots, while young plants may have more strongly toothed leaves than mature trees. It is native across a broad part of Asia and the western Pacific region and is planted elsewhere. A tree's presence outside cultivation should be assessed locally; this description does not imply that all planted or naturalized trees are harmful.
identification: Leaves are usually arranged singly along the twigs, with pointed tips and blades that can reach about 16 cm in the Singapore account. The pale flowers are small, unlike the conspicuous orange flowers of Geiger tree, Cordia sebestena. Fruits are commonly about 1.5-2 cm long, with the persistent flower cup enclosing their bases and sticky flesh around a stone. Fruit color varies among regional descriptions and through ripening, so it is a poor stand-alone test. Photograph a flowering or fruiting twig, a leaf underside and the fruit's basal cup. Related Cordia species can require a regional flora or herbarium specialist.
actions: Check beneath established trees and nearby moist ground for seedlings if the species is escaping locally. Remove unwanted small plants before they develop substantial roots, and collect discarded fruit rather than dumping it beside waterways or woodland. For a large tree, obtain an arborist's assessment before removal. Cutting alone may lead to renewed shoots: forestry guidance records that the tree can recover well from cutting. Keep records of any regrowth and revisit the site. Confirm the species before managing a similar-looking native or valued tree, and base broader removal on regional evidence rather than the common name.

sources.title: Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants: Cordia dichotoma
Nepal government: Manual of Afforestation, Cordia dichotoma
Stone: Flora of Guam, Cordia key

researchNotes: Independent Singapore, Australian and forestry descriptions support recognition and conservative containment. Regional fruit-color and maximum-height differences are not forced into a single diagnostic value. The Guam excerpt includes adjacent species text; only the explicit Cordia key and labeled C. dichotoma paragraph were used.

claims: Broad leaves, white flowers and sticky stone fruits characterize the tree.
Fruit bases sit in a cup-like calyx and soft fruit becomes sticky when crushed.
Seeds are animal dispersed; trees coppice and recover from cutting.
C. dichotoma has small white flowers, unlike orange-flowered C. sebestena.

proposedDescription: French broom is a leafy shrub whose yellow pea-shaped flowers can make an established patch conspicuous in spring. It keeps many three-part leaves through the year, unlike the comparatively bare appearance of some other brooms. In affected western U.S. habitats, dense stands compete with other vegetation and complicate restoration. Mature plants produce abundant seed, while cut plants can resprout from the crown. That combination makes early removal and follow-up more useful than a single round of cutting.
identification: Shrubs commonly stand about 3-10 feet tall. Each leaf has three small leaflets, often with short silvery hairs, and the yellow flowers are about 9-12 mm long in small clusters. Mature pods are brown, flattened and conspicuously hairy, usually 1-3 cm long. Scotch broom, Cytisus scoparius, generally has fewer, smaller leaves and a more upright habit; Spanish broom, Spartium junceum, is another yellow-flowered lookalike. Photograph leaves, young stems and pods together rather than relying on blossom color. French broom's persistent leafy growth is especially useful when nearby brooms have lost much of their foliage.
actions: Pull seedlings before they produce seed, keeping soil disturbance as small as possible. A weed wrench can help remove established plants where roots can be extracted safely. Collect seed-bearing material and arrange disposal that will not scatter pods along a road or trail. Revisit cleared ground for seedlings and crown regrowth, since cutting above the crown may not kill the plant. Mulch appropriate sites and restore suitable vegetation to reduce open ground. For a large stand, contact the local weed program for a staged plan; do not improvise burning or release insects intended for another broom species.

sources.title: Oregon Department of Agriculture: French broom profile
Washington Noxious Weed Control Board: French broom

researchNotes: State agency accounts provide independent regional observation and management guidance, although Washington also cites Oregon. Recognition details and explicit pulling/resprouting advice were checked in the full Washington page. Conflicting older biocontrol statements are avoided, and no legal designation is generalized beyond its jurisdiction.

claims: Leafy 3-10 foot shrub differs from Scotch broom in persistent larger trifoliate leaves.
Flowers measure 9-12 mm and hairy pods 1-3 cm.
Pulling, reduced disturbance and follow-up are recommended; cut crowns can resprout.

proposedDescription: French flax is a slender annual with small yellow flowers held above narrow leaves. It often blends into sparse grass or disturbed ground until the flowers open. The plant grows from seed and finishes with small rounded capsules, rather than forming a woody shrub. Its native range includes the Mediterranean region, and it occurs as an introduced plant in some other regions. The name has also been confused with yellow-flowered ornamental shrubs, so the annual growth form matters when checking a record.
identification: Plants are usually about 10-50 cm tall, with smooth stems and narrow, hairless leaves roughly 5-20 mm long. Leaves alternate along the stem. Yellow petals are about 4-6 mm long, and the pointed sepals below them are about 3-4 mm long; the capsule is smaller, around 2-3 mm. Check the flower and capsule together with magnification. The ornamental yellow flax Reinwardtia indica is a shrub with much larger flowers and should not be folded into this annual species because an old name looks similar. A small yellow flower alone also cannot separate French flax from every other regional Linum.
actions: Have unfamiliar yellow flax checked before removing it from natural vegetation. Where French flax is confirmed and unwanted in a garden, pull small plants before the capsules shed seed, collecting any mature capsules. Revisit the patch during the next growing season and minimize the movement of seed-bearing soil. Replace unnecessary bare ground with suitable cover rather than repeatedly disturbing the whole area. For an occurrence beyond gardens, share photographs of leaves, flowers and fruits with a local herbarium or extension service. These steps address a small seed-producing annual without implying that every occurrence requires eradication.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Linum trigynum

researchNotes: The two regional floras consistently describe Linum trigynum L., the small annual. The NParks ornamental record is used only to prevent conflation with Reinwardtia, not as a synonym authority. Broad harm claims and precise local flowering months are omitted; manual prevention follows the verified annual seed habit.

claims: Annual reaches 10-50 cm with narrow leaves, 4-6 mm yellow petals and small capsules.
Alternate smooth leaves and sepals longer than the capsule support identification.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Singapore National Parks comparative ornamental account
claims: Reinwardtia is a shrub with flowers about 2.5 cm across, despite an overlapping historical name.

proposedDescription: French plantain is used for a group of cultivated bananas, while Musa x paradisiaca covers a broader hybrid background involving Musa acuminata and M. balbisiana. These plants form clumps of large leaves on stems made from tightly wrapped leaf bases. New shoots emerge beside older stems, allowing a planting to persist after a fruiting stem finishes. French plantains form a narrower cultivated group within that hybrid background. The group name does not establish a particular clone.
identification: Broad banana leaves, a thick stem of overlapping leaf bases and a hanging fruit bunch identify the general plant type, but they do not establish a cultivar. French plantains typically retain floral bracts and a substantial bud along the stalk below the fruit. Horn plantains have a cleaner stalk and a small or absent terminal bud; intermediate groups also exist. Photographs should include the entire bunch, the stalk below it and its terminal bud, not just a single banana. Leaf size and plant height vary greatly among cultivated forms. An origin label or nursery record is valuable when separating these hybrids.
actions: Keep unwanted clump expansion in check by removing young suckers and their connection to the underground base, where this can be done without harming retained plants. Do not dump living pieces of the base or rooted suckers into drainage channels or natural areas. If removing a whole planting, expect to revisit it for new shoots. Avoid sharing planting pieces from plants with unexplained decline, discoloration or distorted growth; obtain a plant-health diagnosis first. Before recommending broad removal or replacement, confirm the intended cultivar and local context. This hybrid crop label does not establish a harmful wild population.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Musa x paradisiaca
Musa species: bananas and plantains, Pacific agroforestry profile
University of Melbourne: Musa cultivated varieties
University of Melbourne: Musa cultivar-name sorting

researchNotes:

NCSU's broad hybrid page cannot establish a particular French-group identity. The mismatch remains an owner scope decision, not an absence of safe sucker containment. Next: Choose whether this record describes the broad hybrid or a French plantain group, without silently renaming it.

MGIS primary germplasm records identify named French plantain accessions as AAB plantains; Melbourne crop-name treatment and Hawaii descriptions independently explain the cultivar group. A general French-group profile need not pretend to identify a particular clone. French versus Horn retained bracts and bud; intermediate groups
French AAB group and multiple confusing cultivar labels
Primary germplasm accession identifies an AAB French plantain cultivar; direct page403, indexed accession metadata read.
French plantain group within acuminata x balbisiana AAB usage; cultivar-group scope rather than a single clone.

proposedDescription: French tamarisk is a deciduous shrub or small tree with slender reddish-brown branches, tiny scale-like leaves and clusters of pink to whitish flowers. It has been planted well beyond its western Mediterranean homeland, including coastal and dry landscapes. Its fine leaves can give a branch a soft outline, but close inspection reveals ordinary small leaves rather than needles. Several tamarisks are difficult to distinguish, and older records may use names broadly. Identifying the actual species matters before attaching local impact records or a management plan to it.
identification: Plants commonly reach about 2-5 m and can become taller. Leaves are roughly 1-3 mm long; narrow flower clusters are commonly 2-5 cm long. Most flowers have five petals. In the modern Iberian treatment, French tamarisk has petals that spread and fall, with stamens arising above or from the lobes of the floral disc. The Tamarix ramosissima group instead retains concave petals around developing fruit and has stamens between the disc lobes. Tamarix parviflora usually has four-part flowers. These small structures need magnification and fresh flowering material. A distant photograph of pink branches cannot reliably establish the species.
actions: Ask a botanist or local weed program to confirm flowering material before planning removal, especially where several tamarisks occur. Remove small unwanted seedlings while their roots can be lifted with limited disturbance, and revisit the site for new plants. Established tamarisks can resprout after cutting, so arrange a follow-up plan rather than treating a cut trunk as a completed removal. Keep cut material and disturbed soil out of waterways. Near a stream bank, coordinate work with the land manager to protect soil stability and replacement vegetation; impacts and appropriate priorities depend on the actual site.

sources.title: Natural History Museum Vienna: Tamarix gallica
Villar et al.: Synopsis of Iberian Tamarix

researchNotes: Modern taxonomic characters are used alongside an independent museum description, rather than transferring a generic saltcedar identification to T. gallica. The management source is an assessment and some older Tamarix records have naming uncertainty; advice is limited to confirmation, seedling removal and planned follow-up, not a species-specific herbicide protocol.

claims: Leaves measure 1-3 mm and narrow flower clusters 2-5 cm; flowers are five-parted.
Petal persistence and stamen insertion distinguish T. gallica from the T. ramosissima group.
Assessment records ready resprouting after cutting.

proposedDescription: This freshwater bryozoan forms small branching colonies on submerged surfaces. Each branch contains tiny feeding animals, which extend a circular crown of tentacles into the water. It can occur in water-system fouling, but a colony is not automatically a sign of damaged water quality. The species also participates in the life cycle of a parasite associated with kidney disease in salmonid fish. That association does not mean every colony is infected. Older North American records require particular care because some were later reassigned to Fredericella indica.
identification: Colonies are grayish, brown or sand-colored, with slender tubes branching somewhat like small antlers. Individual animals are commonly around 1.5 mm long and carry a circular feeding crown. Gross colony shape is insufficient to separate Fredericella species. The resting structures, called statoblasts, are especially important: F. sultana has smooth surfaces, while F. indica has conspicuously pitted surfaces under suitable magnification. F. australiensis is another similar species in comparative studies. Photograph colonies while submerged, noting their attachment surface, and seek specialist examination before reporting a new species occurrence. A fish disease diagnosis cannot be made from bryozoan appearance.
actions: Clean and drain portable aquatic gear before moving it between waters, paying attention to attached plants, branches and debris that can carry colonies or resting stages. Do not transfer live colonies for an aquarium or pond without appropriate identification and guidance. If fouling affects an intake, filter or hatchery, contact the operator or aquatic-health specialist so cleaning can be planned without spreading material. Report unexplained fish illness separately to a fish-health service. Removing visible bryozoans alone is not a demonstrated cure for fish disease, and unconfirmed colonies should not prompt chemical treatment of a water body.

sources.title: Identification of five bryozoan species in the Northern Mallee Pipeline

researchNotes: Independent Australian specimen evidence supplements the federal synthesis; the Wisconsin account documents the important historical misidentification. Federal full-page access returned 403, so only indexed text is credited. No current U.S. abundance or universal introduced status is inferred, and parasite association is distinguished from confirmed infection.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: USGS NOAA synthesis of Fredericella biology
claims: Colonies have branching tubes and circular tentacle crowns.
Older Great Lakes records were reassigned to F. indica; parasite hosting does not establish infection.
Electron microscopy of statoblasts established F. sultana among pipeline colonies.
Smooth F. sultana statoblasts contrast with pitted North American F. indica material.

proposedDescription: This freshwater bryozoan consists of many tiny animals living together in a soft, clear to yellowish colony. It attaches to submerged wood and other surfaces, where the animals extend tentacles to collect food from the water. Colonies are small enough to escape notice among other aquatic growth. The species also makes durable resting structures that can survive after the soft colony is gone. It has records outside its Asian native range, but occurrence and documented local harm are separate questions.
identification: Colonies are rounded or divided into soft lobes, generally no more than about 1.5 cm across. In an Okinawan specimen study, colonies attached to submerged wood measured up to about 5 mm. Definitive identification uses the oval resting structures, or statoblasts: groups of small hooked spines occur at their two ends. Their shape and surface details need microscopy. Cristatella mucedo instead forms elongated colonies and has a different arrangement of spines on its resting structures. Photograph the entire colony and attachment surface, but avoid assigning this name to every small gelatinous freshwater growth.
actions: Inspect boats, nets and portable equipment for attached growth and plant debris before moving them to another water body. Clean, drain and dry gear using the local aquatic-invasive-species guidance, and keep removed material on land. Do not move colonies on sticks, rocks or pond plants into a new pond or aquarium. If unfamiliar growth repeatedly obstructs equipment, preserve photographs and ask an aquatic specialist how to collect an identification sample. Avoid adding chemicals to open water on the basis of appearance alone. A confirmed record is useful for monitoring even when a practical local eradication method has not been established.

sources.title: Hirose and Mawatari 2011: Freshwater Bryozoa of Okinawa

researchNotes: The species account and key in the Okinawan paper were read directly, providing independent specimen evidence beyond the federal synthesis. USGS full retrieval failed and is labeled indexed excerpt. Gear hygiene is conservative pathway advice, not a validated eradication treatment; local ecological damage is not assumed.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: USGS synthesis of North American bryozoan research
claims: Colonies are lobed, yellowish and generally below 1.5 cm.
Statoblast spines are confined to the two poles.
Examined colonies occurred on submerged wood and reached about 5 mm.
