proposedDescription: Globose scale is a sap-feeding insect associated with stone-fruit trees, particularly plums. Mature females resemble small dark bumps on branches. Dense colonies can weaken a tree and leave sticky honeydew that supports sooty mold, but a few bumps on bark are not enough to identify the insect or decide whether treatment is needed.
identification: Mature females are strongly rounded, roughly 3 mm across, and dark brown to nearly black, with a shiny, finely pitted surface. Look for colonies on woody growth and record the host tree. Other soft scales can become similarly brown and convex, so photograph several individuals with a size reference and ask an extension specialist to examine a sample. The tiny moving young stages, called crawlers, can help determine treatment timing, but their appearance alone is not a reliable species diagnosis.
actions: Inspect the tree's vigor and the extent of infestation before acting. Pruning a limited amount of heavily colonized wood may help where the tree can tolerate it. As general soft-scale management, protect predators and parasitic wasps, and address ants that tend the insects for honeydew. If treatment is warranted, monitor for crawlers and obtain advice for the tree, scale and local conditions. Do not copy a calendar date from another country or assume a spray aimed at mature rounded females will reach the vulnerable stage.
researchNotes: ScaleNet supplies species-level adult morphology and taxonomic references; Turkish agricultural guidance independently describes stone-fruit hosts, honeydew and pruning. UC IPM supports the explicitly general soft-scale advice. Turkish crawler months are deliberately omitted because they cannot establish U.S. treatment timing.

sources.title: Turkish Ministry of Agriculture: Apricot pests, plum scale account

claims: Hemispherical mature females, dark shiny finely punctate surface and diagnostic dimensions.
Stone-fruit hosts, feeding and honeydew damage, and selective removal of heavily infested branches.
General scale monitoring, crawler timing, natural-enemy conservation and ant management.

proposedDescription: Globular spider beetles are small scavengers found in buildings and stored materials. They can matter in museums and collections as well as food-storage areas, where their presence may lead to an overlooked pocket of dry organic debris. Their rounded shape and long legs resemble a tiny spider, but they are beetles with six legs and antennae.
identification: Adults are roughly 3 to 5 mm long, with a rounded body covered in uneven brown and golden hairs rather than a smooth, polished surface. The antennae are long and slender. Other spider beetles can look similar: the golden spider beetle is more uniformly golden, while this species has darker patches in its hair covering. Photograph the beetle from above and from the side, with a size reference, and retain a contained specimen if identification is important. A distant image of a brown dot will not reliably separate these species.
actions: Look for the source as well as the insects: inspect stored dry materials and accumulated debris around the affected area. For household food, isolate infested packages, remove the source and clean nearby cracks before protecting unaffected supplies in sealed containers. For books, textiles, dried plant specimens or other collection objects, isolate the item and ask a conservator about treatment. Do not spray an object or apply heat or freezing without checking whether its materials can tolerate the method. Keep a record of where beetles recur so hidden sources can be investigated.
researchNotes: National Museums Scotland supplies the distinctive patchy appearance and collection-care context. Agriculture Canada's stored-product beetle guide independently describes the dense mixed hair covering and storage records. Minnesota Extension supplies explicitly general pantry sanitation. Older names include T. globulum; the draft avoids an uncertain native-range claim and does not treat a museum record as a county-wide outdoor occurrence.

sources.title: National Museums Scotland: Identifying collection pests
Agriculture Canada: Beetles associated with stored products

claims: Globular spider beetle size and patchy brown-gold appearance; spider beetle collection damage and debris associations.
T. globulus mixed dense golden and dark hair covering and stored-material associations.
General food-source removal, cleaning and sealed storage for pantry infestations.

proposedDescription: Glossy buckthorn is a woody shrub or small tree that can form a crowded understory. It tolerates both sun and shade and occurs in wet places as well as some drier, nutrient-poor habitats. Where it is invasive, a few fruiting shrubs can supply seedlings for years. The same species is also called alder buckthorn; that name does not make it an alder.
identification: Check several features together: alternate, oval to oblong leaves with smooth edges; curved side veins; and brown or gray twigs dotted with pale lenticels, the small pores in bark. Small greenish flowers develop into round fruits that become black. Smooth leaf margins help separate it from common buckthorn, but leaf shine alone is unreliable. Photograph a complete leafy twig, both leaf surfaces and any fruit. Native buckthorns and dogwoods deserve careful comparison before removal.
actions: Confirm the shrub before treating a woodland or wetland. Where removal is appropriate, start with small plants and prevent fruiting material from being scattered during the work. Revisit the site for new seedlings over several seasons, since seeds already in the soil can outlast the original shrubs. Ask a local invasive-plant program about established stems and wetland restrictions. A single cutting or a cleared-looking patch should not be treated as proof that the population is gone.
researchNotes: Cornell supports alternate leaves and entire margins; Michigan Tech KISMA independently describes bark, fruit, habitat tolerance and the need for repeated seedling checks. Management wording is deliberately bounded to sites where removal is appropriate.

claims: Leaves alternate with entire margins; woody perennial shrub or tree.
Pale lenticels, curved veins and black drupes aid identification.
Seeds remain viable for multiple years, requiring follow-up.

proposedDescription: Glossy privet is an evergreen shrub or tree with thick leaves and clusters of small pale flowers followed by dark fruit. Its size can make an old planting look quite different from a clipped hedge. Birds can carry the seeds away from the original tree, so seedlings beneath perches and along nearby woodland edges are worth checking where this species escapes cultivation.
identification: The leaves sit opposite or nearly opposite each other and are commonly about 3-6 inches long, with a glossy upper surface and a tapering tip. Look closely at the narrow, pale-looking band along the leaf edge and the prominent pale dots on young branches. Creamy flower clusters are borne at branch tips. Japanese privet is a close lookalike; a photograph of a whole tree is less useful than clear leaf, vein, twig and fruit details. Common names such as Chinese privet can refer to more than one species.
actions: Check whether local guidance recommends removal or managed retention before deciding what to do with a planted tree. Where replacement is appropriate, include seedlings around the tree in the plan. Removing accessible fruit clusters before birds disperse them can reduce one source of spread while larger work is arranged. Use an arborist for large trees rather than trying to fell them yourself. Continue looking for new seedlings after removal and keep fruit-bearing debris out of natural areas.
researchNotes: NC Cooperative Extension supplies diagnostic leaf and twig details and fruit-removal advice; UF/IFAS independently supports evergreen tree habit, flowers and bird-attracting fruit. Regional invasion assessments are not converted into a national presence or legal claim.

claims: Opposite thick leaves, narrow marginal band and conspicuous lenticels.
Removing fruit structures limits bird-mediated seed spread.
Evergreen ornamental tree with opposite leaves and bird-attracting fruit.
Management to prevent escape is advised in the Florida assessment cited by the profile.

proposedDescription: Glossy shower is a large tropical shrub or small tree grown for its yellow flower clusters. Flat hanging pods follow the flowers, making a mature plant easier to recognize than a young seedling. It has escaped cultivation in some warm regions; Hawaii extension describes it shading pasture forage. That regional record does not establish that a garden plant is invasive or present everywhere.
identification: Each alternate leaf is divided into opposite pairs of rounded or oblong leaflets, usually with no single leaflet at the end. Many descriptions report about six to ten pairs. The upper surfaces are smoother and darker than the finely hairy undersides. Yellow flowers gather near the upper leaves, and the pods are flat rather than cylindrical, turning dark brown when mature. Several sennas share yellow flowers and similar common names. Include the leaflet count, small glands along the leaf axis, flowers and mature pods in identification photographs.
actions: Before planting or sharing seed, check regional advice for this exact scientific name. Where an unwanted plant is producing pods, contain the pods during removal so the work does not scatter seed. Monitor disturbed ground nearby for seedlings. Do not rely on cattle to remove it: Hawaii extension reports that cattle avoid it. For established shrubs in pasture, request a locally appropriate management plan rather than copying an overseas chemical treatment. Preventing new seedlings is a prudent precaution, not a claim that pod removal alone eradicates a stand.
researchNotes: Singapore NParks and University of Hawaii provide independent descriptive treatments. Leaflet and pod measurements vary among treatments, so the draft uses a typical range and emphasizes combined characters. No medicinal or livestock-use advice is inferred.

claims: Large shrub or small tree with paired leaflets, yellow axillary flowers and flat pods.
Leaflets have smoother upper surfaces and finely hairy undersides.
In Hawaii the plant shades pasture forage and is not grazed by cattle.

proposedDescription: Glover's scale is a small armored scale insect associated especially with citrus. The conspicuous brown shape is a protective cover over the insect, not a beetle or a plant scar. Colonies can occupy leaves, fruit, twigs and bark. On woody branches the narrow covers often line up with the grain, which helps them blend into the surface and makes a quick inspection easy to miss.
identification: Look for elongated, narrow, brown covers about 3 mm long. Purple scale can occur alongside it and has a similar general shape, so finding a mussel-like scale on citrus is only a starting point. Examine both fruit and branches with a hand lens and photograph the insects beside a scale marker. The living female and eggs are beneath the cover; reliable separation from related armored scales may require a mounted specimen and specialist examination. Yellow leaves alone cannot identify this insect.
actions: Inspect citrus nursery stock before moving it into a collection, and keep a suspect plant apart while its identity is checked. Ask a citrus adviser whether the scales are alive and whether natural enemies are already active. UF/IFAS reports that parasitic wasps often keep Glover's scale under biological control, so an automatic broad-spectrum spray can undermine useful control. Base any treatment on a confirmed infestation and current advice for the plant and location. Do not move infested prunings to another orchard.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS provides cover shape, size, plant locations and biological-control context. SENASA independently describes citrus association and the covered female and eggs. The catalog spelling gloverii is retained; UF publications also use gloveri.

sources.title: UF/IFAS: A Guide to Scale Insect Identification

claims: Glover scale has narrow brown covers about 3 mm long and occurs on multiple citrus tissues.
Aphytis wasps commonly provide biological control.
Citrus is a host; females and eggs occur under the protective cover.

proposedDescription: Goat willow is a deciduous shrub or small tree whose catkins open before its leaves. Male trees carry silvery catkins that become yellow with pollen; female trees have greener, narrower catkins and later release tiny seeds with woolly tufts. Its broad leaves set it apart from the narrow-leaved willow image many people know. It can also hybridize with other willows, making some trees difficult to name confidently.
identification: Look for alternate, broadly oval leaves with a green upper surface and a softly hairy, grayish underside. The catkins are generally upright rather than long, dangling tassels. Photograph mature leaves on both sides as well as the current twigs and catkins. Gray willow is a particularly relevant comparison, and hybrids can blur the differences. A fuzzy spring catkin by itself does not distinguish goat willow from the other plants sold or described as pussy willow.
actions: Confirm the species and its local status before removing a willow near a stream or wetland. A planted tree may simply need enough room for its mature crown; an unwanted seedling is easier to assess before it becomes a large tree. Avoid dumping cut branches beside water or in damp ground, where living willow material may establish. For a suspected escape, record the location and whether plants are seedlings, rooted branches or part of an old planting. Get local advice before disturbing banks or removing mature trees.
researchNotes: RHS independently supports tree habit, leaf appearance and sex-specific catkins; University College Cork explains seed dispersal, rooting branches and hybrid confusion. Actions are precautionary site-management advice rather than an eradication protocol.

claims: Broad gray-backed leaves and catkins before leaf emergence; male and female catkins differ.
Seeds disperse with woolly tufts; branches can root.
Gray willow and hybrids can complicate identification.

proposedDescription: Goji gall mite feeds on goji plants and causes raised blisters in their leaves. The swollen plant tissue is much easier to see than the mites themselves. A plant can arrive with an infestation that becomes noticeable only after new growth develops, so recently purchased goji plants deserve a close look. Similar-looking leaf damage needs examination before it is assigned to this species.
identification: Check both leaf surfaces for bead-like galls, often only a few millimeters across, and for distorted new leaves. The mites are minute, pale and wormlike; they are not the larger eight-legged specks usually imagined when someone says mite. Published identification has used light and scanning electron microscopy, and several Aceria species can occur on Lycium. Photograph the host plant, whole affected leaves and close views of the swellings. A diagnostic service may need fresh leaf material rather than a photograph alone.
actions: Keep a suspect goji plant separate from other goji plants and avoid giving away cuttings until the problem is resolved. Contact a plant diagnostic service for sampling and disposal instructions, especially if symptoms appeared after a nursery purchase. Record where the plant came from and when the blisters first appeared. Do not assume that removing a few visibly galled leaves eliminates the mites. Treatment choices should come from current advice for edible goji plants; a product suitable for an ornamental shrub is not automatically suitable for a fruit crop.
researchNotes: Utah State Extension independently describes the tiny wormlike mite on goji. The Slovak primary report documents blistered leaves and microscopic confirmation. The draft avoids treating unconfirmed possible hosts as proven hosts or promising a treatment outcome.

sources.title: Utah State University: Goji in the Garden
Suvak: First record of Aceria kuko in Slovakia

claims: Goji gall mites are extremely small, pale salmon and wormlike.
Bead-like leaf galls and microscopic confirmation on purchased Lycium chinense.
Other Aceria species on Lycium make careful identification necessary.

proposedDescription: Gold-banded etiella moth is the adult stage of a caterpillar that feeds inside legume pods. Peas, beans and soybeans are among its hosts. The damaged seeds may remain hidden until a pod is opened, so a crop can look relatively normal from a distance. This sheltered feeding also makes the timing of inspection and any control decision more useful than spraying after damage is already well established.
identification: Adults have gray-brown forewings with a pale line along the leading edge and a conspicuous yellowish to reddish band crossing the wing. A research trap guide gives a wingspan of about 24-28 mm. Open suspect pods to look for chewed seeds, silk and droppings; these are clues to a pod borer, not proof of this particular moth. Photograph an adult and the contents of a damaged pod if possible. Other moth larvae can cause similar seed damage, and trap catches also require identification.
actions: Inspect developing pods in several parts of a crop rather than judging the problem from one damaged plant. Keep a record of crop stage and the proportion of pods affected, and ask an extension crop adviser to identify larvae or adults before selecting treatment. Regional guidance notes that earlier planting can sometimes allow lima beans to mature before pod borers become abundant. That is a local cropping decision, not a universal calendar rule. Avoid moving infested pods into clean seed stocks, and do not release biological-control insects without an approved program.
researchNotes:
ICAR provides independent host and pod-damage evidence; the Hungarian research trap guide describes adults and feeding signs; the PNW handbook supports the bounded early-planting point. Foreign trap schedules and pesticide directions are not transferred to US gardens.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.

sources.title: CSALOMON: Lima-bean pod borer — Etiella zinckenella
PNW Pest Management Handbooks: Lima bean pod borer

evidence.independentSourceGroup: ICAR National Bureau of Agricultural Insect Resources
claims: Larvae damage multiple legume crops and leave silk and frass within pods.
Forewing stripe and transverse yellow-red band; wingspan 24-28 mm.
Caterpillars chew seeds within pods.
Early planting can let lima beans mature before high pod-borer densities.

proposedDescription: Gold-of-pleasure, also called camelina, is a short-lived mustard-family plant cultivated for its oily seeds. It can appear as an intentional crop or as a volunteer outside cultivation, so the setting matters when deciding whether it is unwanted. Small pale flowers are followed by numerous swollen pods. Those pods are more useful for identification than a distant view of the yellow flowers.
identification: Look for simple leaves that clasp the stem, small flowers with four pale-yellow petals, and smooth, pear-shaped pods on slender stalks. Published descriptions commonly give mature pods as about 7-9 mm long. The plant is often nearly hairless or only sparsely hairy. Littlepod false flax, Camelina microcarpa, is a close relative with generally hairier stems and smaller pods and seeds. Photograph mature pods beside a ruler and include stem hairs and leaf bases; a seedling alone may be difficult to separate.
actions: First establish whether the plants belong to a crop or are unwanted volunteers. In an unwanted patch, preventing seed maturity is a sensible containment step, followed by checks for later seedlings. Keep loose seed out of neighboring beds and clean seed-handling equipment before moving between sites. For crop production or a persistent field problem, use local agronomic advice, since crop rotations and permitted treatments vary. Do not assume that an oilseed crop is suitable for sowing in a natural area merely because it has an agricultural use.
researchNotes: CFIA supports fruit dimensions and comparison with close relatives. USDA NRCS independently documents crop uses and advises checking local status. Their overlapping botanical citations are not used to imply independent experimental evidence for a control method.

claims: Four small petals, pear-shaped pods and distinguishing features of related Camelina species.
Camelina is grown for seed oil and meal.
Local status and suitability should be checked before use.

proposedDescription: Golden algae is a microscopic, single-celled organism that can form blooms harmful to fish and other animals that breathe through gills. A bloom may tint water yellow or golden brown, but not every bloom is toxic and cell numbers do not perfectly predict a fish kill. Its common name describes a visual effect; it does not mean that every golden-colored pond contains this species.
identification: Individual cells require microscopy. Water color, foam or dead fish can alert you to a problem but cannot distinguish golden algae from other algae, low oxygen or a chemical spill. Specialists examine the cells and may test the water for toxicity. Record the waterbody, date, color and where affected fish are concentrated. Useful photographs show the broader shoreline and affected fish without handling them. A home magnifier or phone photograph cannot establish the identity of this tiny alga.
actions: Report unusual fish deaths promptly to the relevant fisheries or water-quality authority and follow its sampling instructions. Do not eat fish found dead or dying during a suspected bloom. As a precaution, avoid moving untreated water, bait or wet equipment from the affected waterbody to another one. Pond owners should seek professional diagnosis before adding chemicals: treatments developed for managed hatchery ponds cannot simply be applied to a lake or stream. Follow any local access advisory while the cause is investigated.
researchNotes: Texas Parks and Wildlife supports bloom appearance, imperfect relationship between abundance and toxicity, reporting and the dead-fish precaution. EPA independently recognizes toxin-producing strains and fish kills. No claim of proven human poisoning is made.

sources.title: Texas Parks and Wildlife: Biology of Golden Alga

claims: Microscopic cells can give blooms a golden tint; abundance does not always predict toxicity.
Report fish kills and do not eat dead or dying fish.
Some Prymnesium parvum strains produce toxins associated with major fish kills.

proposedDescription: Golden chamomile is an herbaceous perennial with divided foliage and yellow daisy-like flower heads. It is grown in borders and for cut flowers, and cultivated forms can differ in height, hairiness and flower color. Older references often call it Anthemis tinctoria. A plant outside a garden should be identified on its leaves and flower-head structure rather than on the word chamomile alone.
identification: The branching stems can approach a meter tall. Leaves are divided two or three times into smaller lobes, giving them a finely cut appearance. Heads are usually borne singly at stem tips and can be roughly 3.5 cm across, with yellow centers and yellow rays that sometimes fade toward cream. Other yellow daisies can look similar from a distance. Photograph the leaf divisions, the underside and side of a flower head, and mature fruits if available; specialist keys use the small bracts and fruit details.
actions: For a planted specimen, check regional guidance before allowing it to seed into neighboring habitat or sharing divisions. Where plants are unwanted, removing flower heads before seeds develop is a reasonable precaution, followed by removal of small plants and checks for regrowth. Keep seeding debris contained rather than leaving it on an open compost edge. If the plant occurs in a meadow with similar native daisies, confirm its identity first. These are containment steps, not a species-tested eradication schedule.
researchNotes: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria HortFlora supplies habit, flowers and variability; the Burke Herbarium treatment independently provides leaf, flower and fruit characters from North American flora. No local invasive status or tested management efficacy is inferred.

claims: Perennial with divided leaves, solitary yellow heads and variable cultivated forms.
Finely divided leaves, yellow rays and ribbed fruits support identification.

proposedDescription: Golden clover is a short-lived, upright clover with dense heads of small yellow flowers. It usually grows as an annual, although some floras also describe biennial plants. Its leaves have the familiar three-leaflet arrangement, but the yellow heads can make it easy to confuse with other small clovers. A flowering stem with intact leaves is much more informative than flower color alone.
identification: Plants are commonly about 20-50 cm tall, with erect or ascending stems that do not root at their joints. The three oblong leaflets have fine teeth toward their outer ends and very short, nearly equal stalks. At the base of each leaf stalk are narrow, pointed stipules, the small leaf-like appendages that help in identification. The yellow flowers form dense rounded to short cylindrical heads. Compare other yellow-flowered clovers carefully, paying particular attention to leaflet stalk lengths and stipule shape rather than overall size.
actions: If golden clover is unwanted in a bed or restoration planting, identify it while flowers and leaves are present, then remove small plants before they set seed. Keep any mature heads contained during the work. Revisit open ground for new seedlings and limit repeated soil disturbance that leaves bare space for annual plants. In pasture or a species-rich meadow, first check the management objective and local flora so desirable clovers are not removed by mistake. These steps are general seed-containment precautions; the cited floras do not establish a tested eradication method.
researchNotes: British Columbia and New Zealand floras independently describe habit and leaflet characters. Their life-cycle treatments differ slightly, so annual or occasionally biennial wording is retained. No national invasive classification is inferred from introduced regional records.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Trifolium aureum

claims: Upright annual 20-50 cm with three finely toothed leaflets and pointed stipules.
Annual or biennial with non-rooting stems, almost equal leaflet stalks and dense yellow inflorescences.

proposedDescription: Golden oak scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that sits in shallow pits on oak twigs. The pits are changes in the bark caused by feeding, and their rims may become slightly swollen. Heavy infestations can accompany poor growth and twig dieback, but a few pits do not explain every unhealthy branch. Several closely related oak pit scales look much alike in the field.
identification: Use a hand lens to look for circular to oval scales about 1-2 mm across, colored golden, greenish or brown, nestled into small depressions. Young twigs are a useful place to inspect. Ordinary lecanium scales stand up as more obvious brown mounds rather than sitting within pits. The appearance of the pit cannot reliably separate Asterodiaspis variolosa from its close relatives. Photograph the oak leaves for host identification and a close view of affected twigs; exact naming may need microscopic examination.
actions: Check whether the affected twigs are still growing and whether dieback is spreading before choosing treatment. Have an arborist or extension diagnostic service assess a declining oak, since roots, drought and other pests may also be involved. Avoid moving infested nursery oaks between properties. If control is warranted, timing should be based on local crawler activity, not a calendar copied from another region. Preserve natural enemies where possible and do not strip healthy bark to look for insects. A confirmed pit-scale problem can guide care while the precise species is being resolved.
researchNotes: UMass explains size, damage and the difficult field separation of related species. Natural Resources Canada independently describes pit position, sap feeding and distinction from raised lecanium scales. Regional generation timings are omitted because sources differ.

sources.title: Natural Resources Canada: Insects of Eastern Forests

claims: Tiny golden to brown females occupy bark pits; related species look very similar.
Feeding can cause twig dieback and poor growth.
Oak pit scales are about 2 mm and sit in depressions, unlike raised lecanium scales.

proposedDescription: Golden trumpet is a tropical evergreen plant grown as a scrambling shrub or woody climber. Its large yellow flowers and glossy leaves make it a familiar garden ornamental in warm climates. It can escape cultivation in some tropical settings, and cut stems contain milky sap that can irritate skin and eyes. The attractive flowers should not be taken as a sign that the plant is edible.
identification: Look for simple, glossy leaves arranged opposite one another or in whorls around the stem, together with large yellow funnel-shaped flowers with five spreading lobes. Fruits, when present, are rounded prickly capsules. Several allamandas and garden forms have similar flowers; bush allamanda is generally more compact, so flower color alone is insufficient. Photograph leaf arrangement, flower size and the plant's growth habit. Do not snap a stem just to test for latex, since the sap is an irritant.
actions: Wear gloves when pruning and keep sap away from eyes. Keep cuttings and fruit away from children and pets, and do not use this ornamental as a home remedy. Where local guidance identifies it as an escape risk, contain prunings and remove unwanted new plants rather than dumping live stems at a garden edge. Check the base for continuing growth after cutting. For a planted specimen, make sure supports and pruning allow safe access without repeated contact with sap. Seek local advice before attempting to clear a large tangle among other vegetation.
researchNotes: NParks supports tropical evergreen habit and yellow trumpet flowers. NC State Extension independently supports leaf arrangement and irritant sap. Precautions follow these hazards without importing unsupported medicinal claims or species-specific eradication promises.

claims: Evergreen tropical climber with glossy leaves and large yellow trumpet flowers.
Leaves opposite or whorled; stems contain milky sap that can irritate skin and eyes.
Escapes cultivation in some tropical areas; propagated by cuttings; poisonous if eaten.

proposedDescription: Golden wattle is a shrub or small tree best known for rounded golden flower heads. It is native to southeastern Australia and is Australia's floral emblem, while also being a weed in places outside its native range. That contrast makes location important: an Australian name or ornamental use does not establish whether a particular planting is appropriate elsewhere.
identification: Mature foliage consists of broad, curved phyllodes, flattened leaf stalks that function as leaves. They are bright green, often sickle-shaped and can hang downward. Look for a fairly central main vein, a long narrowed base and a small gland set above that base. Flower heads are round and crowded into clusters on sturdy stalks. Acacia saligna and A. obliquinervia can resemble it, so photograph the entire phyllode, its base and gland, and a complete flower cluster. Golden balls alone do not identify a wattle.
actions: Before planting or distributing seed, check advice for this exact species in your region. Where it is unwanted, address small plants before they become seed-bearing trees and keep pods from being scattered during clearance. Follow up for seedlings rather than assuming that removing the visible stems completes the job. Established trees may need a local weed specialist or arborist. In its native range, confirm that a plant is an unwanted introduction at the specific site before removing it. The sources establish identification and regional behavior, not a universal removal prescription.
researchNotes: ANBG supplies growth form, phyllodes, floral emblem context and South African weed status. VicFlora independently supplies diagnostic gland, vein and inflorescence traits and named lookalikes. Containment actions are prudent general precautions.

sources.title: Australian National Botanic Gardens: Acacia pycnantha

claims: Shrub or small tree with sickle-shaped phyllodes and golden ball flowers.
Australian floral emblem; has become a weed in South Africa.
Central phyllode vein, gland separated from the base and stout flower stalks distinguish similar acacias.

proposedDescription: Golden-tuft alyssum is a low perennial often planted in rock gardens, where its small yellow flowers form dense spring clusters above gray-green foliage. It is also sold as basket-of-gold, and older references use Alyssum saxatile. The plant can remain after the brief mass of flowers has faded, so its foliage and persistent base are useful parts of the identification.
identification: Look for spoon-shaped gray-green leaves and branching flowering stems on a plant commonly only a few tens of centimeters tall. Each individual flower is small; the bright display comes from many flowers grouped together. Under magnification the stems bear branched, star-shaped hairs, while the fruits are hairless in the Austrian flora description. Other yellow-flowered mustard relatives can resemble it. Photograph a close flower, mature fruit, leaf shape and the whole mound rather than relying on a mass of yellow in a garden photograph.
actions: Check regional guidance before encouraging self-seeding beyond a garden. If seed spread is unwanted, trim off flowering stems before ripe seed is shed and watch nearby gravel or open soil for seedlings. A light post-flowering tidy also helps keep a cultivated plant compact, as botanical-garden guidance notes. Remove an unwanted plant carefully without scattering mature pods. In rocky natural habitat, confirm the species before disturbing similar low plants. These steps address garden containment; the cited sources do not demonstrate that a particular cutting routine eradicates an escaped population.
researchNotes: Dunedin Botanic Garden gives foliage, seasonal flowering and post-flowering care. Vienna Natural History Museum independently documents perennial habit, stature, stem hairs and hairless fruits. No regional occurrence or invasive status is extrapolated.

sources.title: Dunedin Botanic Garden: Tiny Flowers have Big Impact
Natural History Museum Vienna: Aurinia saxatilis

claims: Gray-green spoon-shaped leaves, yellow spring flowers and post-flowering cutting guidance.
Low perennial with star-hairy stems and hairless fruits.

proposedDescription: Goldenhaired bark beetle breeds mainly under the bark of recently cut pine logs, stumps and the roots or bases of dead and weakened trees. It is therefore often encountered in harvested wood rather than in a healthy tree canopy. Its presence matters when wood is moved, even where direct wood damage is limited. Finding the beetle in dead material does not by itself show that it killed the tree.
identification: Adults are small dark beetles, roughly 5-6 mm long, with conspicuous yellowish or reddish hairs visible under magnification. The hairs are especially noticeable near the rear slope of the wing covers. Reddish boring dust and galleries beneath bark are useful clues but are shared with other bark beetles. Hylastes species can look similar; this beetle is generally larger and hairier than Hylastes ater. Preserve location and host information and ask a forestry diagnostic service to examine an adult before assigning a species.
actions: Do not transport suspect bark-covered logs, firewood or logging debris to a new site while identification is pending. Photograph adults and galleries without damaging living trees unnecessarily, and note whether the material was freshly cut or already dead. Ask a forestry or plant-health authority about local wood-handling requirements and approved disposal. At a plantation or timber yard, include stumps, ground-contact logs and debris in inspections. Professional timber treatments are specialized operations; neither fumigation nor a household insecticide is an appropriate do-it-yourself response.
researchNotes: Scion supports pine breeding material, red frass and lookalike details; SENASA independently gives adult size, hairs and weakened-tree association. The broad host list in another historical source conflicts with Scion, so the draft emphasizes well-supported pine hosts.

sources.title: NZ Farm Forestry: Scion Golden-haired Bark Beetle account

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Scion New Zealand Forest Research Institute
claims: Breeds in inner bark of recently felled pine logs, stumps and dead roots; reddish frass.
Dark adults about 5-5.7 mm with yellowish hairs; attacks woody debris and weakened pine tissue.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Scion New Zealand Forest Research Institute
claims: Larger and hairier than Hylastes ater; transport in logs is significant.

proposedDescription: Goldenrain Tree is a deciduous ornamental with compound leaves, yellow flower clusters and papery, inflated seed capsules. The capsules may remain on bare branches, giving a useful winter clue. Seedlings can establish around planted trees and in disturbed ground in regions where the species escapes. A planted adult and a self-sustaining wild population are different observations and should be recorded separately.
identification: The leaves are usually divided once into a row of leaflets, although occasional leaves may be more divided. Leaflet edges are conspicuously toothed or lobed. Later, inflated capsules develop three papery sides and dry toward tan or brown. Related Koelreuteria species commonly have twice-divided leaves and different young capsule colors, so include a complete leaf rather than a single leaflet in photographs. Yellow flowers alone do not separate the species. Winter capsules, summer leaves and the tree's overall form make a useful combined record.
actions: Look for seedlings beyond the crown, especially in open soil and at the edges of nearby habitat. Where local guidance recommends control, remove young plants before they produce more seed and contain mature capsules during cleanup. Arrange professional work for large trees and monitor the site afterward. If retaining a garden tree, repeated seedling checks are a practical way to notice escape early. Do not distribute seedlings into natural areas merely because the parent is a common street tree; suitability depends on the region and planting site.
researchNotes: Maryland Extension independently describes reseeding and regional management concerns. The International Dendrology Society key supports the leaf-division and capsule distinctions among Koelreuteria species. No national legal status is asserted.

sources.title: University of Maryland Extension: Goldenrain Tree
Trees and Shrubs Online: Koelreuteria identification key

claims: Tree spreads through reseeding; compound serrated leaves and persistent capsules aid identification.
K. paniculata usually has once-pinnate leaves with toothed or lobed leaflets and green-to-tawny young capsules.

proposedDescription: Goldentop grass is a small tufted annual whose compact flower heads turn yellowish or golden as they mature. It is associated with open, disturbed ground and dry sites in regional floras. Its decorative-looking head contains both seed-producing and sterile spikelets, a useful distinction from grasses with a superficially similar soft or brush-like appearance.
identification: Look for flat, mostly hairless leaf blades and a conspicuous, thin membranous ligule where the blade meets the sheath. The ligule is relatively long and may shred with age. The compact head is only several centimeters long, with clustered spikelets of different forms; the fertile florets carry slender awns. Take a close photograph of the head from both sides and of the leaf collar. Foxtail-like appearance or golden color alone is not enough, especially once the head is dry. A mature specimen makes the unusual spikelet arrangement much easier to check.
actions: If it is unwanted, act while plants are small and before mature seed clusters can break away. Contain developed heads during removal and check the same bare patches after the next germination period. Clean soil and seed fragments from footwear and tools before leaving an infested site as a precaution against accidental movement. In a garden, avoid intentionally scattering ornamental seed into adjoining open land. For a mixed grass community, confirm the identity before broad removal; the botanical sources support recognition, not a species-specific treatment schedule.
researchNotes: VicFlora supplies mature head color, ligule and spikelet details; the UAE university flora independently describes annual tufted habit and mixed fertile/sterile spikelets. Their geographic records are not used as evidence of local presence.

claims: Long membranous ligule, yellowish mature panicle and distinct sterile and fertile spikelets.
Small tufted annual with flat blades and clustered dimorphic spikelets.

proposedDescription: Goldline snakehead is an elongated freshwater fish with a flattened head and long fins. It uses quiet or slow-water habitats such as canals, pools and vegetated lakes. Older records may call it bullseye snakehead or identify it as Channa marulius, but modern taxonomic work separates the two. A familiar common name can therefore hide an important identification difference.
identification: Look for a long body that is more cylindrical toward the head and tapers toward the tail, with an orange-ringed eyespot near the upper base of the tail fin. In larger juveniles and adults, black scales within the dark side blotches have conspicuous pale rear margins. The formal distinction from C. marulius also uses scale and fin-ray counts, which are not easy to judge from a casual photograph. Photograph the entire side, head and tail region and include a size reference. A general snakehead identification may be more defensible than an immediate species claim.
actions: Never release an aquarium fish or move a caught snakehead into another waterbody. If one is found outside a known managed fishery, record the exact location and contact the relevant fisheries authority for identification and handling instructions. Follow current local rules rather than assuming that retention, transport or release rules are the same everywhere. Do not handle a large fish unnecessarily to count scales; clear photographs may be the safest first record. Keep the original scientific name associated with any older report when discussing its possible reidentification.
researchNotes: Florida Museum independently supports body form, eyespot and habitat. Adamson and Britz primary taxonomic abstract supports separation from C. marulius and scale-margin characters. No unverified legal instruction or new local occurrence is asserted.

sources.title: Adamson and Britz: Channa aurolineata is a valid species

claims: Elongate body, flattened head, tail-base ocellus and quiet vegetated freshwater habitat.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Natural History Museum London taxonomic research
claims: White posterior margins on black scales and meristic differences separate C. aurolineata from C. marulius.

proposedDescription: Gooseberry gourd is a sprawling or climbing annual with small round fruits, sometimes called prickly paddy melon. It grows through disturbed ground and can trail for a couple of meters. The fruit may resemble a tiny melon, but this is not a reason to taste it. Several wild cucurbits share the name paddy melon, so fruit size and surface details are important.
identification: The alternate leaves are broadly shaped, with three to five lobes and additional teeth or smaller lobes. Their undersides and stalks are bristly. Male flowers occur in small groups, while female flowers are single or paired on the same plant. The round fruits are about 15-25 mm across, green with pale stripes before turning yellow, and carry scattered soft, often hooked bristles. Compare both fruits and leaves with other wild melons; a fruitless seedling is less straightforward. Photograph the whole vine and a fruit beside a ruler.
actions: Prevent unwanted plants from producing mature fruit, and collect existing fruits carefully rather than scattering them while pulling vines. Keep the material out of livestock feed and do not offer the fruits as food. Monitor disturbed soil for replacement seedlings. In a crop or pasture, ask a local adviser to confirm the wild cucurbit before selecting a control plan. These are prudent containment and exposure precautions; the identification sources do not establish that one pulling pass or a particular chemical treatment will eliminate a population.
researchNotes: NSW PlantNET supplies precise fruit and leaf traits. Charles Sturt University primary research independently confirms diagnostic morphological combinations and Australian subspecies identity. Catalog species is retained; older leptodermis usage is not silently adopted.

sources.title: Charles Sturt University: Identification of three cucurbitaceous weeds

claims: Annual vines with lobed bristly leaves and 15-25 mm striped, bristly fruits.
Combined vegetative, floral, fruit and seed traits distinguish wild melons; Australian plants assigned to subsp. myriocarpus.
Lists livestock-poisoning literature and potential seed contamination.

proposedDescription: Goosegrass is a tough, low-growing grass that often gains a foothold where traffic has thinned turf and compacted the soil. It is usually a summer annual, although it can persist longer in tropical conditions. Its flattened, pale-centered clumps can survive close mowing and still produce seed. Removing the visible grass without improving the worn patch leaves the same opportunity for the next generation.
identification: Look for radiating shoots with distinctly flattened, whitish or silvery bases. Leaves are folded in the bud, mostly smooth, and have a small membranous ligule at the collar. The seedhead has several finger-like branches, often with one or two set below the main cluster; the tiny flowers form orderly, zipper-like rows. Crabgrasses also have fingered heads, so check the pale compressed base and leaf collar as well. Photograph the whole clump and a close view of both features.
actions: Remove isolated plants with the central crown, the growing point at soil level, before seed develops. Simply clipping the leaves leaves that crown behind. Reduce repeated foot or vehicle traffic where practical, address compaction through appropriate lawn care, and repair thin turf with a suitable grass. Clean mowing equipment after working through flowering patches. For a persistent infestation, ask extension for options matched to the lawn species and growth stage; mature goosegrass can be difficult to control and resistant populations exist. Do not assume a crabgrass product will work equally well.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS supplies crown removal, compaction and prevention guidance. Penn State independently confirms folded leaves, bunch habit, ligule and lookalikes. Warm-climate persistence is qualified rather than calling all populations strictly annual.

claims: Flattened pale bases and fingered seedheads; compaction favors infestations.
Removing the crown controls isolated plants; healthy turf and equipment cleaning support prevention.
Bunch-type summer annual with folded vernation, membranous ligule and no auricles; crabgrass is a lookalike.

proposedDescription: Gophertail lovegrass is a tufted grass with a narrow, often woolly-looking flower head. Regional floras describe it chiefly as an annual, with stems that may rise straight or bend upward from the base. Its head can be tightly packed or broken into small lobes, so the outline varies. The name lovegrass covers many species, and a general resemblance is not enough for a confident identification.
identification: Look for narrow blades and a hair fringe at the leaf collar. The panicle contains many tiny, flattened spikelets, commonly with several flowers each, clustered into a compact or interrupted cylinder. Long hairs on the edges of the inner flower bracts contribute to the soft-looking head. The stems do not normally root at their lower joints in the North American treatment. Photograph mature spikelets under magnification, the collar and the base of the plant. Other small lovegrasses require comparison of these details, especially the arrangement and hairiness of the floral parts.
actions: If a patch is unwanted, remove small plants before the heads mature and keep ripe seedheads contained during cleanup. Check nursery containers and disturbed soil nearby for additional plants. Avoid moving soil or mowing debris from a seeding patch into clean areas. Before clearing a mixed grassland, have a mature sample checked so a similar native grass is not removed. Local habitat and land use should determine whether management is needed. The available floras support identification, while these actions are cautious seed-spread prevention rather than a proven eradication program.
researchNotes: Flora Zambesiaca as presented by Flora of Zimbabwe and Peterson's Flora of North America treatment on SEINet are independent botanical treatments. Kew reproduces the African description and is not counted as an additional group.

sources.title: SEINet: Eragrostis ciliaris, Flora of North America

claims: Annual tufted grass with woolly narrow panicles and long-ciliate palea keels.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of North America editorial treatment
claims: Tufted annual with non-rooting lower nodes, hairy sheath margins and lobed or interrupted panicles.

proposedDescription: Governor's plum is a shrub or small tree with small flowers and rounded red to purple fruit. Many plants have sharp spines, sometimes branching on the trunk. Its leaves, hairiness and overall size vary considerably, and botanical treatments differ in how broadly they define the species. It is cultivated in some places and escapes in others, so a fruiting plant should be assessed in its local setting.
identification: Look for alternate simple leaves with toothed or wavy edges, small yellowish flowers near the leaf bases and rounded fruit that darkens as it ripens. Spines may occur in leaf axils and on the trunk, but their presence and length vary. Male and female flowers are generally borne on different plants. Other Flacourtia species can resemble it; photograph the fruit tips, flowers, leaf arrangement and spines without handling them. A plum-like fruit does not make it a true plum or establish that an unidentified fruit is safe to eat.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and protect your eyes when working around the spiny branches. Check local recommendations before planting or distributing seedlings. Where the shrub is unwanted, contain ripe fruit during removal and inspect surrounding ground for young plants. Larger, densely spiny specimens are better handled with experienced help. Do not rely on leaf shape alone before clearing similar shrubs. A local invasive-plant adviser can recommend an approach for established stems; this profile does not transfer a chemical recipe from another country or habitat.
researchNotes: Kew-hosted African flora treatments document variation, spines and fruits. Florida Natural Areas Inventory independently provides alternate leaves and dioecious flowers through the Florida identification treatment. Taxonomic complexity is flagged without changing the catalog identity.

sources.title: Kew: Flacourtia indica, regional flora descriptions
Florida Natural Areas Inventory: Flacourtia indica

evidence.independentSourceGroup: African regional floras via Royal Botanic Gardens Kew
claims: Variable spiny shrub or tree with toothed leaves and rounded reddish fruit.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florida Natural Areas Inventory and Florida identification treatment
claims: Alternate simple leaves, axillary or trunk spines and male/female flowers on separate plants.

proposedDescription: Graceful twig ant is a slender, wasp-like ant associated with vegetation and hollow twigs. Its long body and large eyes make it look different from many compact ants seen around kitchens. It can deliver a painful sting if handled or disturbed, but its presence on a shrub does not automatically call for treatment. Nesting location and actual contact with people matter more than a single sighting.
identification: Adults are about 8-10 mm long, with a narrow body, very large eyes and two small waist segments between the middle body and abdomen. Color varies from dark brown or black to orange-brown or a mixture of orange and dark areas. That variability makes color alone a poor guide. Other twig ants can resemble it, so obtain clear side and head photographs without catching it in bare fingers. The large eyes and elongated waist are useful screening features; exact identification may require a specialist.
actions: Avoid breaking open occupied twigs or gripping vegetation where ants are active. Wear gloves when pruning and inspect hollow stems before carrying them indoors or sharing cuttings. If a nest is close to a frequently used doorway or work area, seek an identification and a targeted plan from extension or a pest professional. Keep unnecessary insecticide applications off otherwise healthy garden plants. For an isolated outdoor sighting, documenting the ant and leaving the nest undisturbed is often more proportionate than attempting to eliminate every ant in the area.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS supports adult size, variable color and sting risk. USDA Antkey independently emphasizes large eyes, two-segmented waist and low general pest significance. Antennal segment counts conflict between displayed accounts and are deliberately omitted.

claims: Slender arboreal ant with painful sting and variable dark or orange coloration.
Adults 8-10 mm, large-eyed and wasp-like with a two-segmented waist.
Very large eyes and two-segmented waist; painful sting but not generally a significant pest.

proposedDescription: Graham's manihot is a branching shrub or small tree grown for leaves divided into many narrow lobes. Its pale green, striped flowers are less conspicuous than the foliage. It is sometimes called hardy tapioca or ornamental cassava, names that can be misleading if interpreted as food advice. The catalog species is distinct from cultivated cassava, and its ornamental use does not establish that its parts are edible.
identification: Look for long-stalked leaves with roughly seven to thirteen lobes cut almost to the base, spreading like the fingers of an open hand. The lobes are mostly smooth-edged and hairless, with a paler lower surface. Small hanging flowers have greenish tissue marked with reddish or purplish stripes; rounded capsules contain three seeds. Compare the complete leaf, flowers and fruit with other Manihot species rather than identifying it from lobed foliage alone. The narrow lobes and their proportions are especially useful in photographs.
actions: Do not harvest leaves or roots as cassava on the strength of a common name. Before sharing seed or cuttings, check whether this ornamental is appropriate locally. Where unwanted seedlings appear, remove them early and contain mature capsules so seeds are not scattered through the garden. Recheck beneath and around the parent plant. Use gloves for pruning as a sensible precaution when handling an unfamiliar member of the spurge family. Management of a larger shrub should include follow-up for new growth; a single cut is not presented here as a proven eradication method.
researchNotes: NSW PlantNET gives precise leaf, flower and capsule characters. RHS independently describes ornamental habit and propagation, while NZPCN reports poisonous leaves and roots. Food use is explicitly not inferred from hardy tapioca.

sources.title: NZ Plant Conservation Network: Manihot grahamii

claims: Shrub or small tree with 7-13 deeply cut lobes, green purplish-striped flowers and three-seeded capsules.
Woody ornamental with palmate leaves and striped bell flowers; propagation by seeds and cuttings.
Leaves and roots are reported poisonous; seedlings documented outside a planting.

proposedDescription: Grand eucalyptus, also known as rose gum or flooded gum, is a very tall forest tree used in timber plantations. A mature specimen can greatly exceed the scale of an ordinary garden tree. Its trunk usually has a short rough-barked base with smooth pale bark above. Closely related eucalyptus species and planted hybrids mean that bark color alone is not a reliable name tag.
identification: Adult leaves are alternate, lance-shaped and darker green above than below. White flowers occur in groups, commonly seven, nine or eleven, and the small woody capsules provide an important clue: their valves curve inward when open. Eucalyptus saligna is a close lookalike whose open fruit valves are erect rather than incurved. Photograph a mature capsule from above and the side, buds, both leaf surfaces and the trunk base. Juvenile foliage can look different, so say whether a sample came from a seedling, regrowth or the mature crown.
actions: For a standing tree, begin with identification and a site assessment rather than assuming removal is needed. Its eventual size makes professional advice important near buildings, roads or utilities. Where unwanted seedlings occur beyond a plantation or garden, document them and consult local guidance before allowing a new stand to establish. Keep seed-bearing debris from being dumped in neighboring habitat as a precaution. Large-tree removal and follow-up belong in a locally appropriate plan; this account does not establish invasive status for every place where the tree is planted.
researchNotes: EUCLID provides diagnostic bark, leaf and valve details and comparison with E. saligna. PROSEA independently supports plantation use, very large stature and habitat. Shared Australian flora reproductions are not counted as extra evidence groups.

claims: Rough basal bark, discolorous leaves, grouped white flowers and incurved capsule valves; comparison with E. saligna.
Very large tree used in tropical and subtropical plantations; smooth upper bark and characteristic fruits.

proposedDescription: Granulate ambrosia beetle is a tiny beetle that tunnels into woody stems and grows fungi inside its galleries. The fungi provide food for the beetles and their young. Young or stressed ornamental and fruit trees can be seriously damaged, and infested nursery plants can carry the problem to another site. The insects are usually hidden by the time a tree begins to wilt.
identification: A useful early clue is a fine column of compressed boring dust projecting from a pinhole in the bark, often described as a toothpick. These fragile columns can disappear after wind or rain, leaving only tiny holes. Adult females are roughly 2-3 mm long and reddish brown. Other ambrosia beetles can make similar columns, so this sign does not prove the species. Photograph the dust columns before they break, the entire affected stem and the tree's condition, and arrange specialist examination of a beetle if needed.
actions: Inspect nursery trees and recent transplants regularly, especially lower stems. Keep suspect stock from being sold or moved until it has been assessed. Ask an arborist or extension specialist whether an attacked tree can recover and how infested material should be handled. Once beetles are inside, control options are limited, so do not assume a systemic insecticide will cure the problem. Address avoidable plant stress and follow locally timed monitoring advice for nearby vulnerable trees. Any removal should contain the breeding material rather than moving it to another landscape.
researchNotes: University of Georgia supports fungi, female size, toothpick signs and treatment limitations. Mississippi State independently explains that other ambrosia beetles can make similar frass columns and that columns disappear in weather. No pesticide recipe is included.

sources.title: University of Georgia: Granulate Ambrosia Beetle
University of Georgia IPM: Granulate ambrosia beetle

claims: Fragile dust columns indicate activity; control after boring is limited.
Females about 2.5 mm and young develop on cultivated fungi inside wood.
Other ambrosia beetles also make dust columns; rain and wind remove the signs; young trees can be badly damaged.

proposedDescription: Granulate mini-ponerine ant is a small, dark ant that is easily overlooked in soil and leaf litter. Museum records include nests in potted plants and piles of bark, which makes movement of planted material a practical concern. It is not usually seen in conspicuous outdoor trails. Workers and queens have a sting, although the species is not described as aggressive.
identification: Workers are only a few millimeters long, dark brown to nearly black, with very small eyes and a finely textured, dull-looking body. The waist has one upright node, and there is a visible constriction between the first large abdominal segments. Under magnification, the node is nearly rectangular in side view and the antennal stalks are relatively long. Similar Hypoponera and Ponera ants require comparison of the underside of the waist and other minute structures. A blurred photograph of a tiny brown ant cannot resolve this species.
actions: Avoid handling ants or breaking apart a nest with bare hands. If ants appear in newly purchased pots, keep those pots separate and have a specimen identified before distributing plants or soil. Ask the diagnostic service how to collect a sample safely. For occasional outdoor findings, record the substrate and location rather than treating an entire garden. If repeated indoor encounters or stings occur, seek a targeted assessment. The sources provide limited species-specific management evidence, so generic ant baits or broad soil treatments are not presented as proven solutions.
researchNotes: Mississippi Entomological Museum supplies original local observations, potted-plant association and diagnostic details; AntWeb independently supports the rectangular node and long scapes. Habitat biology remains limited, which is stated without inventing a control protocol.

claims: Small dark workers with tiny eyes and a rectangular petiole; nests recorded in litter, bark and potted plants.
May sting when disturbed; biology remains incompletely known.
Long antennal scapes, punctate body sculpture and rectangular node help distinguish close relatives.

proposedDescription: Grass Carp is a large freshwater fish that feeds heavily on aquatic plants. It has been stocked to manage vegetation, but too many fish can remove much more plant cover than intended. That can alter habitat for other animals and leave a pond looking very different. Stocked fish therefore need a planned management context; they are not a simple substitute for identifying the plants causing a problem.
identification: Look for a long, thick body with large dark-edged scales, an olive-brown back, silvery sides and a pale belly. The mouth faces forward and has no barbels, the whisker-like structures seen on common carp. Its dorsal fin is much shorter than that of common carp or goldfish. Bighead and silver carp have different scale and fin proportions. Photograph a whole side view and the head if this can be done without unnecessary handling. Appearance alone does not establish whether an individual is a sterile triploid.
actions: Do not stock, transfer or release Grass Carp without first checking the relevant fisheries authority's current requirements. Pond owners should identify the vegetation and assess how much cover should remain before considering fish-based control. If fish are already stocked, monitor plant coverage and outlet security with professional advice rather than adding more fish whenever growth returns. Report an unexpected catch where the species is being monitored. Follow location-specific handling rules, since a deliberately stocked fish and an unwanted escape may be managed differently.
researchNotes: USGS supplies diagnostic morphology and lookalike distinctions. Connecticut DEEP independently documents vegetation feeding and the risk of complete vegetation loss at high density. Triploid status is not claimed to be visually diagnosable, and no universal legal rule is asserted.

claims: Large dark-edged scales, terminal mouth without barbels and short dorsal fin distinguish Grass Carp.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection
claims: Grass Carp consume aquatic vegetation and can denude lakes when abundant; stocking is regulated locally.

proposedDescription: Grass-like starwort is a slender perennial whose weak stems weave through grasses and other low vegetation. The narrow leaves can be overlooked until small white flowers appear. Each flower has five petals split so deeply that it may look as though there are ten. It belongs to the chickweed family, but its narrow foliage and open branching flower clusters differ from the common garden chickweed mat.
identification: Look for opposite, stalkless, narrow leaves on smooth, distinctly angled stems. Leaf bases and the edges of the small flower bracts may have fine hairs even when the rest of the plant looks hairless. The deeply divided petals are about as long as, or a little longer than, the pointed sepals beneath them. Long-leaved starwort is a useful comparison: stem texture, sepal veins and mature seeds help separate similar plants. Photograph the stem angles, leaf bases and a flower from the side as well as above.
actions: Check a regional flora before deciding that a small white-flowered plant in grassland needs removal. Where this species is unwanted in a bed, lift small plants carefully and monitor for continuing growth rather than relying only on cutting flowers. Contain mature seed capsules during the work. In wet ground, avoid trampling or stripping surrounding vegetation simply to clear scattered stems. Ask for botanical confirmation when native starworts occur nearby. The cited treatments support recognition and perennial habit; they do not establish a single reliable eradication schedule.
researchNotes: NSW PlantNET and Germany's federal FloraWeb independently support smooth angled stems, narrow leaves and deeply split petals. The FNA checklist comparison with S. longifolia supports the lookalike caution. General containment advice is labeled accordingly.

claims: Slender angled glabrous stems, narrow sessile leaves and deeply bifid petals.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: German Federal Agency for Nature Conservation
claims: Perennial with smooth four-angled stems, narrow leaves and five deeply divided petals.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Flora of North America editorial treatment
claims: S. longifolia is a frequent lookalike; stem texture, sepals and seeds distinguish it.

proposedDescription: Grass-root antonina is also widely called rhodesgrass mealybug. It feeds in sheltered places on grasses, especially around stem joints beneath the leaf sheaths. Affected turf can yellow and thin in a way that resembles drought, so watering alone may not address the problem. The insect produces honeydew, which can leave grass sticky and support black sooty mold. Ants may visit this sugary material. Several predators and parasitoids attack the mealybug, making their presence useful information when assessing an infestation.
identification: Part the grass carefully and examine nodes, crowns and the spaces beneath leaf sheaths with a hand lens. Mature females look like small rounded cottony lumps; the underlying body is dark brown to reddish purple. A long, thin wax filament projecting from the body is a useful clue, and a honeydew droplet may hang from its end. Mobile young crawlers differ from the settled, saclike later stages. White material alone is not enough for identification because other grass mealybugs occupy similarly concealed places.
actions: Inspect several living stems at the edge of a damaged patch before treating the entire lawn. Photograph the concealed insects and ask an extension service to distinguish them from other turf pests. Record whether patches expand and whether ants or natural enemies are present. Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum spraying, which can remove beneficial insects. If treatment is warranted, seek advice for the grass species, site and locally permitted products; the protected feeding sites make timing and coverage important. Do not move suspect sod or divisions to clean areas.
researchNotes: UGA and UF/IFAS independently describe feeding sites, wax filaments, drought-like symptoms and natural enemies. The UGA page was read as full text; the UF species subsection was reviewed as an indexed PDF excerpt. Local generation counts are deliberately omitted.

sources.title: UGA Extension: Rhodesgrass Mealybug Biology and Management
UF/IFAS: Managing Scale Insects and Mealybugs on Turfgrass

claims: Mealybugs feed beneath sheaths at nodes, have woolly wax and long honeydew filaments, and produce drought-like turf damage.
Rounded cottony females, concealed feeding sites, honeydew, natural enemies and ant associations.

proposedDescription: Grassleaf spurge is a lightly built, branching herb that can appear in gardens and nursery areas. Its name is misleading if you expect every leaf to resemble a grass blade: the main leaves can be quite broad, while the smaller leaves around the flowering branches are narrower. Tiny flowers sit in cup-shaped structures typical of spurges, with small white appendages that are easier to see than the flowers themselves. Published floras describe different plant sizes and life spans in different settings, so neither height nor an assumed annual habit is a safe identification shortcut.
identification: Look for a loose, ascending or spreading plant with milky sap, broad oval to oblong main leaves and narrower leaflike bracts near the flowers. A Taiwan treatment describes alternate main leaves but opposite bracts, an arrangement worth photographing rather than judging from one stem tip. The flower cups bear small white petal-like appendages. Mature seeds have conspicuous pits arranged in rows, a specialist character useful when similar spurges are present. Do not deliberately break a stem to test the sap.
actions: If plants are unwanted in pots or beds, wear gloves and avoid getting sap on skin or in eyes. Remove small plants before their capsules mature and keep fruiting material contained during disposal. Examine neighboring pots and incoming nursery plants for similar seedlings. Photograph a whole plant, both leaf arrangements and the flower cups before asking for identification. These are practical containment precautions; the reviewed sources do not establish a particular removal schedule or herbicide treatment as reliably effective for this species.
researchNotes: The Taiwania original description and Kew-hosted Flora of the Cayman Islands provide independent morphology and habitat evidence. They differ in reported height and duration; the draft makes that variation explicit rather than forcing a single life history.

sources.title: Taiwania: Euphorbia graminea, a newly naturalized plant in Taiwan
Kew POWO: Euphorbia graminea, general information

claims: Milky sap, alternate main leaves, opposite narrow bracts, white cyathium appendages and pitted seeds.
Loose branching habit, annual or short-lived perennial description and occurrence in gardens and nurseries.

proposedDescription: Gray everlasting is treated here in the broad Gamochaeta americana complex that includes historical coarctata names. Older southeastern United States references used Gamochaeta coarctata for a small woolly cudweed with basal leaves and crowded flower clusters. A more recent regional treatment applies the name Gamochaeta impatiens to that plant. Kew, meanwhile, includes both names under a broader Gamochaeta americana. These treatments draw species boundaries differently, so the name on an older record needs to be interpreted alongside the flora that supplied it.
identification: Under the older United States concept, plants have a rosette of spoon-shaped to narrowly spoon-shaped leaves, woolly white undersides and much less hairy upper surfaces. Small flower heads crowd along the upper stems, with outer head bracts often rosy or purplish. These details describe the historical identification concept only. They do not resolve whether a particular specimen belongs to G. impatiens, G. americana or another cudweed. Close photographs of the leaf surfaces, basal rosette and individual flower-head bracts are more useful than a distant picture of gray stems.
actions: Keep the existing scientific name with the observation, but add its source and date rather than silently replacing it. Seek a herbarium or regional botanist familiar with recent Gamochaeta revisions before making a species-level report or removal decision. Preserve clear photographs and, where collection is permitted and requested, a properly documented voucher. Avoid moving seed-bearing plants or nursery soil while identification is pending. A local determination should guide management, especially where similar native cudweeds grow nearby.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Virginia's atlas explicitly states that Nesom's 2022 G. impatiens replaces earlier southeastern US use of G. coarctata. BioGator reproduces the older FNA morphological treatment. The older and revised treatments share Nesom's lineage and diagnose different concepts; a broad checklist cannot settle the intended catalog record.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: The historical coarctata account is supportable when explicitly scoped to the broad americana complex and contrasted with the narrower impatiens treatment. Nesom2022 reexamined types and MO/TEX-LL collections; the independent Freire morphometric analysis is reported as a separate study, not independently accessed here. Existing regional morphology and the original revision support the qualified concept; US records are not silently relabeled. Next step: Review the declared broad-concept draft; retain specimen-level coarctata/impatiens crosswalks as separate work. Fresh evidence/access: Nesom2022 Gamochaeta impatiens original revision [indexed_excerpt; Nesom-2022-original-Gamochaeta-revision] https://www.phytoneuron.net/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/35PhytoN-Gamochaetaamericana.pdf - Original type and herbarium comparison distinguishes US impatiens from South American coarctata/americana; broad lumping remains an alternative treatment. Inherited URLs and evidence remain provenance; only the specifically documented accesses are claimed fresh. Parent-read passages are explicitly attributed. No catalog, mapping or public-release changes; local review only.

Includes coarctata and impatiens within americana.
Original type and herbarium comparison distinguishes US impatiens from South American coarctata/americana; broad lumping remains an alternative treatment.

proposedDescription: Gray field slug is a small slug that often becomes noticeable when young plants develop ragged feeding damage. It is active in moist conditions and can shelter out of sight during the day, so an apparently empty bed may still contain feeding slugs. Color varies considerably: many are pale gray or buff with darker flecks, but some are much more uniformly pale or dark. The species can damage seedlings and crops, although finding one slug does not show that every nearby hole or missing seedling was caused by it.
identification: An extended adult is commonly around 3-5 cm long. The mantle, the smooth shield behind the head, is shorter than the tail section. A short ridge runs along the tail tip, and the breathing opening is in the rear half of the mantle on the right side. Dark mottling is common but not universal. Disturbed animals may produce milky mucus, but do not handle or irritate one merely to obtain that character. Unpatterned individuals can resemble other Deroceras species and may require expert examination.
actions: Check vulnerable seedlings after dusk or during damp weather, and photograph any slugs beside a size reference. Temporary refuge boards can help reveal activity if checked regularly; do not leave extra hiding places indefinitely beside tender plants. Reduce unnecessary damp debris around a small growing area while retaining habitat elsewhere for wildlife. Confirm the problem before using a bait, and follow a locally approved label with particular attention to pets and other animals. Crop-specific treatment thresholds and schedules should come from local advice, not a general identification page.
researchNotes: John Innes Centre and Oregon State Extension independently support size, mantle and tail characters, variable coloring and milky defensive mucus. Both were read as full text. Actions emphasize monitoring and modest habitat adjustments; no universal bait regimen is inferred.
