proposedDescription: Gray field speedwell is a low annual with small blue flowers and rounded, toothed leaves. It grows in cultivated and disturbed ground, including gardens and crop fields. Its stems spread close to the surface, so flowers may be easier to notice than the plant supporting them. The gray-green foliage helps suggest the name, but leaf color changes with light and growing conditions. Related speedwells can occupy the same kind of ground, making a flowering and fruiting plant much easier to identify than a seedling.
identification: Look for short-stalked, broadly oval leaves with several blunt teeth along each side. Lower leaves occur in pairs; the leaflike bracts farther up the flowering stem become alternate. The flowers are usually bright blue with a pale center and are only a few millimeters across. Mature capsules are small, paired-lobed structures with hairs. Common field speedwell, Veronica persica, generally has larger flowers and more widely diverging fruit lobes. Green field speedwell, V. agrestis, often has paler flowers; fruit hairs and shape deserve a close look.
actions: Photograph an open flower, the lower leaves and a mature capsule with a ruler before making a firm identification. A hand lens helps show the fruit hairs. In a cultivated bed where removal is wanted, lift young plants before seed develops and check the surrounding bare soil for later seedlings. This is a seed-containment precaution rather than a verified eradication program. Check regional status before removing plants from a wild site: abundance and conservation relevance differ between places, even for familiar garden weeds.
researchNotes: New Zealand Flora and the independent INRA weed account support annual habit, leaf arrangement, blue axillary flowers and hairy capsules. The BSBI account provides an additional regional comparison. The draft avoids conflicting fine capsule measurements across treatments.

proposedDescription: Gray poplar is a hybrid between white poplar and European aspen. A mature tree can be substantial, but a patch may instead appear as numerous young stems arising from spreading roots. That distinction matters: several stems close together are not necessarily independent seedlings. The foliage is variable, especially between ordinary branches and vigorous shoots. Its gray leaf undersides can be a helpful clue, although the amount of pale hair changes as leaves age. Published regional accounts document both large trees and dense sucker stands.
identification: Compare several mature leaves from ordinary branches rather than relying on one oversized sucker leaf. Leaves are broadly rounded to oval, with blunt or irregular teeth, and can be slightly heart-shaped at the base. Young undersides may be very pale, becoming grayer or less hairy later. White poplar generally retains a whiter underside, while gray poplar tends toward a less strongly white appearance on older leaves. Catkin details and the combination of leaf shape, hairs and shoot type may be needed to separate hybrids confidently.
actions: Before planting or removing a tree, consider the space occupied by both the crown and its suckering roots. Photograph mature branch leaves as well as any nearby shoots when requesting identification. If unwanted suckers are appearing, map their extent and ask an arborist to assess their connection to the main tree. Avoid casually cutting major roots near buildings or established trees. A single cut does not demonstrate that the underground plant has been controlled. Check local rules and habitat value before planning removal of a mature specimen.
researchNotes: Trees and Shrubs Online supplies the Bean morphology and comparison with white poplar; Flora of Zimbabwe independently documents hybrid parentage and root-sucker stands. Regional stature and weed status are not generalized to the user's location. The catalog hybrid identity is preserved.

claims: Variable leaves, age-dependent underside hairs and distinction from white poplar.
P. alba x P. tremula parentage, toothed gray-backed leaves and dense root-sucker stands.

proposedDescription: Gray sheoak can look like a pine from a distance, but its fine green hanging strands are jointed branchlets. The true leaves are tiny scales arranged around the joints. It can also send up shoots from its roots, creating groups of connected stems around an older planting. The species is native to part of eastern Australia and has been planted elsewhere. Whether a particular stand is appropriate to retain depends on its location and local guidance, not simply on the tree's presence in a catalog.
identification: Use a hand lens to examine the rings of tiny pointed leaf teeth at branchlet joints. A Victorian flora records commonly 12-17 teeth, sometimes more, and branchlet segments around 8-20 mm long. The branchlets droop, and mature woody cone-like fruits provide another useful feature. Counts from several normal branchlets are more informative than one unusual shoot. Other sheoaks can look very similar, and field guides use tooth counts, branchlet dimensions, fruits and suckering together; a pine-like silhouette alone cannot establish the species.
actions: Photograph a whole tree, its woody fruits and several branchlet joints before seeking confirmation. Note whether younger stems occur along roots beyond the crown. Where removal is appropriate, include those connected shoots in a professional management assessment and plan to check for further growth. Do not assume that felling the largest trunk finishes the work. Avoid moving rooted suckers or soil from a suspect stand. These are precautions based on the documented suckering habit; the sources reviewed do not establish a universal treatment method for every site.
researchNotes: VicFlora supplies diagnostic branchlet measurements and free root suckering; UF/IFAS independently treats field recognition of Florida Casuarina, including C. glauca. Florida concern is kept regional. No local occurrence, legal status or guaranteed removal result is claimed.

sources.title: UF/IFAS: Field Guide to Identify the Common Casuarina Species in Florida

claims: Drooping jointed branchlets, typical leaf-tooth counts and dimensions, and free root suckering.
C. glauca identification uses root suckers and numerous leaf teeth around branchlet nodes.

proposedDescription: Gray sugarcane mealybug feeds in protected spaces beneath the leaf sheaths of sugarcane and other grasses. Its wax coating can make the insects look like pale debris pressed against a stem. Finding the species requires opening those hiding places carefully; a quick look at the exposed leaves may miss it. Other mealybugs occur on sugarcane as well, so host choice alone does not establish identity. Published observations include gray and paler forms, making body color useful but insufficient on its own.
identification: The adult female is elongated to oval, with a gray body under white mealy wax and yellowish-brown legs. There are only a few short wax filaments along the sides, with the hind pair longest and thickest. A filamentous egg sac may cover the rear upper surface. Pink sugarcane mealybug and other Dysmicoccus species can be confused with it in the field. Definitive separation uses microscopic features of a prepared adult female, including the arrangement of wax-producing ducts and small bristle-bearing structures.
actions: Inspect leaf sheaths on several stalks, recording whether insects are scattered or concentrated in particular areas. Take close photographs before disturbing the colonies and ask a crop adviser or diagnostic laboratory how to submit material. Keep suspect propagation cane separate and avoid transferring it to uninfested plantings while identification is pending. Do not treat an entire crop solely because a few white insects are present. The reviewed sources establish recognition and host association, but do not supply a broadly applicable economic threshold or validated household treatment.
researchNotes: USDA identification material provides field characters. An independent Brazilian field report supports gray bodies, few lateral filaments and confirmed sugarcane occurrence; ScaleNet records color variation and historic confusion. No source-derived generic mealybug control is presented as species-tested efficacy.

sources.title: Brazilian Journal of Biology: First record of Dysmicoccus boninsis on sugarcane in Rio Grande do Sul

claims: Elongate gray body, white wax, short lateral filaments, egg sac and leaf-sheath feeding.
Collected sugarcane insects were morphologically identified; gray bodies bear a few short lateral filament pairs.
Gray and white forms are conspecific; historical confusion with other sugarcane mealybugs.

proposedDescription: Great globethistle is a tall perennial with rounded clusters of pale flowers above coarse, spiny leaves. The flower balls are made of many small individual flower heads, a structure that separates globe thistles from the more familiar open-topped thistles. Stems can reach roughly 2 m in favorable conditions. The plant has been grown ornamentally and is recorded outside cultivation in some regions. Its flowers attract visiting insects, but an attractive flowering plant can still need containment where local guidance identifies a problem.
identification: Look for deeply lobed leaves with slender spines at the tips and edges, green upper surfaces and densely pale, woolly undersides. Upper leaves clasp the stem. Gland-tipped hairs on the upper stems and leaf surfaces are useful close-up details. The terminal flower clusters are spherical and generally whitish to pale blue. Other cultivated Echinops species can have similar balls of flowers, so color alone is unreliable. Photograph stem hairs, both leaf surfaces and the entire flower cluster when seeking a species-level determination.
actions: Use gloves when working near the spiny foliage. If the plant is unwanted, contain maturing flower heads before they shed seed and arrange removal appropriate to an established perennial. Revisit the area for surviving growth and seedlings instead of assuming that cutting the visible stems is sufficient. Avoid dumping garden waste along roadsides or in grassland. Check local status before disturbing a natural-area population. These containment measures are prudent horticultural precautions; the cited botanical treatments do not prove a particular eradication method.
researchNotes: Cambridge Botanic Garden and the independent Flora of North America treatment via WFO support tall perennial habit, pale globular flower clusters and spiny bicolored leaves. NSW head-size wording differs from other treatments, so a disputed exact head diameter is deliberately omitted.

proposedDescription: Great yellowcress is a perennial of wet ground and shallow water edges, with yellow mustard-family flowers and underground rhizomes. A large patch can represent connected growth rather than many separate seedlings. The leaves change shape along the stem, and submerged or low leaves can look different from the leaves held above water. In some populations fruit develops poorly, so a stand without obvious mature pods is not necessarily young or dying. Wetland identification needs particular care because other yellow-flowered mustards may grow nearby.
identification: Look for upright stems with lower leaves that are often deeply lobed and upper leaves that are less divided, sometimes nearly entire. Flowers have four yellow petals. The fruits, when present, are short oval to oblong pods rather than the long slender pods of many other mustards. Roots and rhizomes should not be excavated just to confirm a casual observation. Other Rorippa species and their hybrids can be difficult to separate; photograph leaves from different stem levels and mature fruits together.
actions: Document the patch from firm ground, including its relationship to the waterline, without trampling soft banks. Seek botanical confirmation before removing wetland vegetation. Where management is required, prevent cut stems, rooted material and muddy equipment from being moved to another waterbody. Plan follow-up because the underground rhizomes can persist after visible stems are removed. Avoid an improvised herbicide application beside water; any treatment needs locally appropriate advice and permissions. The sources support rhizomatous persistence, not a one-step removal promise.
researchNotes: New Zealand Flora describes rhizomes, variable leaves, short fruits and poor seed set in clonal populations. The independent Conservatoire botanique national de Brest guide supports upper-leaf and short-pod distinctions. Regional measurements and hybrid variation warrant expert confirmation.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Rorippa amphibia
Conservatoire botanique national de Brest: Rorippa amphibia

evidence.independentSourceGroup: New Zealand Flora Volume IV authors
claims: Rhizomatous wet-ground perennial with variable leaves, yellow flowers and short, sometimes poorly developed fruits.
Simple or toothed upper leaves and short pods distinguish it from several related wetland mustards.

proposedDescription: Greater burdock begins with a rosette of large leaves and later sends up a tall, branching flowering stem. The purple flower heads eventually become hooked burs that cling to clothing and animal fur, carrying the enclosed seeds away. Its large leaves can resemble those of unrelated garden plants at first glance, but the woolly undersides and bur-forming flower heads are much more informative. It is usually a biennial, so a nonflowering rosette and a tall flowering plant may be different stages of the same species.
identification: Look for broad, heart-shaped basal leaves with pale woolly undersides and smaller leaves arranged alternately up the flowering stem. The stalks of the large lower leaves are normally solid and grooved on top. Purple flower heads sit on relatively long stalks in loose, roughly flat-topped clusters. The surrounding narrow bracts end in hooks. Lesser burdock usually has smaller heads and hollow lower leaf stalks; use several features together, especially if the plant is not in flower. Do not identify it as edible from leaf shape alone.
actions: Where removal is wanted, deal with rosettes before they develop mature burs and plan for the substantial taproot. Wear gloves and avoid crushing dry burs near your face, as their fine internal bristles can irritate eyes and skin. Contain burs during disposal, and remove attached burs from clothing and animal coats before leaving the patch. Recheck for seedlings rather than treating one cleared plant as the end of the problem. Seek local advice for large stands or plants close to sensitive habitat.
researchNotes: UMass provides species-specific life cycle, solid petioles and long-stalked heads. The independent Dutch taxonomic monograph confirms the lesser-burdock comparison; NC State supports bur dispersal and bristle irritation precautions. No medicinal or edible-use claim is made.

claims: Biennial habit, basal rosette, solid grooved petioles, long-stalked heads and hooked burs.
A. lappa differs from A. minus in solid basal petioles, larger heads and corymbose inflorescences.
Hooked burs disperse on fur and clothing; fine bristles can cause irritation.

proposedDescription: Greater European pea clam is a freshwater bivalve small enough to be overlooked among sand and fine gravel. Despite its name, a full-grown shell is only about a centimeter long. It is associated particularly with flowing water, although it also occurs in lakes. Its shell has clear concentric ridges, giving it a more strongly sculptured surface than many small freshwater clams. The species is native across parts of Eurasia and North Africa and has introduced populations elsewhere; a local record still requires proper identification.
identification: An adult shell is oval to somewhat angular, glossy yellowish or brown, with pronounced growth ridges. The raised beak near the hinge sits off center toward the rear rather than in the middle. Size and ribbing provide useful clues, but young specimens overlap other pea clams. Specialists also examine the hinge teeth inside an empty shell. Photograph both sides and the hinge of an already empty shell with a millimeter scale; do not force a living clam open for a photograph.
actions: Leave living clams and surrounding sediment in place while obtaining identification advice from a museum, aquatic biologist or local invasive-species program. Record the waterbody, substrate and exact location, since those details make a small shell observation more useful. Clean sediment from boots, nets and boats and drain equipment before visiting another waterbody. Never transfer live clams, aquarium contents or water between sites. These are general aquatic biosecurity precautions, not a proven species-specific eradication method; indiscriminate treatment could harm native freshwater mollusks.
researchNotes: USGS supplies shell shape, ridges, size and flowing-water ecology. The independent 2021 Morocco field treatment confirms strongly marked ridges, posterior beak and diagnostic hinge structure. A 2017 study cautions that shell proportions alone can vary within this species; the catalog name is retained.

proposedDescription: Greater knapweed is a perennial with deeply divided leaves and large purple flower heads on upright branching stems. The outer flowers are often enlarged, giving a head a loose, spreading fringe. It occurs in grassland and other open places, and its status varies substantially across regions. In parts of its native range it is a valued grassland plant; an introduced population elsewhere may receive different management advice. The word knapweed alone is therefore not a reason to remove it.
identification: Check for rough-textured leaves divided into distinct lobes, rather than merely toothed along the edges. The stems are ridged, and upper leaves become smaller. Beneath each flower head, overlapping greenish bracts carry dark brown or black fringed tips. Those dark appendages do not completely hide the underlying bracts. Common knapweed, Centaurea nigra, generally has less divided leaves and lacks the conspicuous enlarged outer flowers described in the BSBI comparison. Close photographs of the bracts are important because several other knapweeds also have fringed coverings.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, a lower leaf and the side of a flower head before deciding how to manage it. Check regional guidance, especially in species-rich grassland where removal could damage a native plant community. If this is an unwanted garden escape, prevent mature heads from shedding seed and arrange removal that accounts for its perennial root system. Watch for regrowth and seedlings after the initial work. Avoid transporting flowering or fruiting garden waste into open countryside. These are containment precautions, not a species-tested universal control schedule.
researchNotes:
New Zealand Flora and the Illustrated Flora of British Columbia independently describe perennial habit, divided leaves and fringed bracts. BSBI supplies a practical C. nigra comparison and evidence that regional conservation status differs. No invasive classification is generalized.

proposedDescription: Greater swinecress is a low plant that spreads across disturbed or trodden ground. Its small white flowers are easy to miss, but the rough little fruits are distinctive once you look closely. Older books often call it Coronopus squamatus; that name refers to the same species treated here as Lepidium coronopus. It may behave as an annual or a short-lived biennial in different treatments. Compacted paths, field edges and similar open ground are useful places to look, but habitat alone cannot confirm it.
identification: Look for mostly hairless, spreading stems and deeply divided leaves with narrow lobes. Flower clusters are short and crowded, and the tiny white petals extend beyond the sepals. Mature fruits are wider than long, with a coarse, warty or ridged surface and a short pointed tip rather than a clearly notched top. A hand lens is helpful. Lesser swinecress can resemble it vegetatively, so retain photographs of mature fruits and flowers rather than relying on the flattened growth habit or a common name.
actions: Before clearing a patch outside a cultivated bed, check a regional flora: a familiar disturbed-ground plant may still be uncommon locally. Where removal is appropriate, lift young plants before fruits mature and contain any fruiting material. Avoid carrying muddy footwear or soil from the patch to a clean planting area. In a garden, reduce repeated bare-soil disturbance where practical and check for new seedlings. These are reasonable seed-spread precautions; the botanical sources reviewed do not establish a particular herbicide or one-time removal method as reliable.
researchNotes: New Zealand Flora explicitly links Coronopus squamatus to Lepidium coronopus and describes corky warty fruits. Independent German FloraWeb confirms prostrate habit, divided leaves, six stamens and unnotched toothed fruits. Regional life-span variation is retained without changing taxonomy.

proposedDescription: Greater wax moth is chiefly a problem when its caterpillars reach stored comb or comb that a honey bee colony cannot adequately defend. The larvae tunnel through the material and leave silk, debris and damaged comb behind. Adult moths themselves are not the stage chewing through it. Greater and lesser wax moths can occur together, so the presence of moth damage does not automatically identify the species. A damaged hive also deserves a wider health check: weak colonies may be vulnerable for reasons beyond the moths.
identification: Adults are gray to brown moths that hold their wings in a roof-like position at rest. The body is commonly about 13-19 mm long. Young larvae are pale; older ones become grayer, retain a brown head and can approach 25 mm long. Silk-lined feeding tunnels and tough cocoons attached to hive wood are useful signs of wax-moth activity. Pupation sites can leave shallow gouges in the wood. Photograph both the insect and damage, because larval size varies and the smaller wax-moth species may share the same comb.
actions: Keep colonies appropriately sized and well supported, and inspect stored frames rather than leaving comb unattended for long periods. If damage appears, ask a local apiculture adviser to assess both the moth infestation and the reason the colony or stored comb was vulnerable. Freezing affected stored comb is an established option, but use a beekeeper-approved duration and procedure that reaches the whole load. Protect treated comb from reinfestation. Never substitute ordinary household mothballs for products specifically authorized for beekeeping equipment, and do not put storage treatments into an occupied hive.
researchNotes: Texas Apiary Inspection Service supplies adult and larval appearance, comb damage and practical prevention. NSW independently confirms stored or unattended comb risk and coexistence of greater and lesser wax moths. No freezing time, pesticide dose or diagnosis of colony failure is invented.

claims: Gray-brown roof-winged adults, pale to gray larvae, comb feeding, wood gouges, strong colonies and freezing stored comb.

proposedDescription: Greedy scale is an armored scale insect that can settle on leaves, stems and fruit of many woody plants. The part usually noticed is the small protective cover rather than the soft-bodied insect beneath it. Covers can remain in place after the insects die, so their presence alone does not prove that an infestation is still active. Several similar armored scales share the same hosts, making a host name or a few pale dots on a leaf an unreliable basis for choosing treatment.
identification: Adult female covers are roughly round and strongly convex, commonly about 1.5-2 mm across, although crowded individuals may be irregular. They range from pale or dirty white to brownish, with a yellow-brown to darker patch of retained immature skins near the center or slightly off center. The female underneath is yellowish. Latania scale, Hemiberlesia lataniae, can look very similar. A specialist may need to examine a prepared female under a microscope; cover color and shape alone are insufficient to distinguish these close relatives.
actions: Inspect several leaves and twigs and photograph the covers with a scale reference. Ask a diagnostic service how to submit a sample that includes living insects, especially on nursery stock or valuable fruit plants. Keep suspect potted plants apart and avoid moving infested cuttings to clean areas. Before deciding on treatment, establish whether scales are alive and whether fresh settling stages are appearing. Seek locally appropriate advice on any direct control. These are detection and containment steps; the reviewed sources do not justify a universal spray program.
researchNotes: University of Hawaii describes covers, size and host breadth. Chile's SAG independently describes the female and crawler stages; UK CSL documents difficulty separating H. rapax from H. lataniae. Conflicting male and honeydew claims in a different guide were excluded; no honeydew production is attributed here.

proposedDescription: Green citrus aphid also goes by spirea aphid, a reminder that citrus is only one part of its host range. Colonies can occur on fruit trees, spireas and various ornamentals, particularly around growing shoots. Both wingless and winged forms occur, and winged adults can move between plants. It resembles the green apple aphid closely enough that orchard advisers often discuss the two together. Useful management starts with the plant's condition and the insects present, rather than assuming every green aphid is this species.
identification: Wingless adults are small, about 1.2-2.2 mm long, and yellow-green to apple green. The pair of short tube-like structures near the rear, called cornicles, is black, as is the small tail-like projection beyond them. Antennae are relatively short, around half the body length. Winged adults also have a greenish abdomen and dark rear structures. These features help narrow the identification, but Aphis pomi and other aphids can overlap in appearance. Microscopic measurements may be needed for a reliable species distinction.
actions: Examine several growing shoots and record whether colonies are expanding, leaves are becoming distorted or plant growth is suffering. Look for lady beetles, hoverfly larvae and parasitized aphids before intervening, since natural enemies can suppress colonies. Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum treatments that may disrupt that help. On fruit crops, use a local crop adviser's monitoring and treatment guidance rather than a general aphid recipe. Keep newly purchased plants under observation before placing them among healthy plants. Photographs should include the host, colony and a close view of the rear body structures.
researchNotes: INRA provides detailed morphology and host breadth; Penn State independently documents similarity to apple aphid and natural enemy relevance in orchards. India's NBAIR confirms predator groups and additional hosts. Regional seasonal cycles and insecticide susceptibility are not generalized.

proposedDescription: Green Foxtail is a clump-forming annual grass with a narrow, bristly seed head. It can occur in cultivated ground, along roads and in turf, especially where there is room for seedlings to establish. Its green flower heads resemble small bottlebrushes, but several other grasses share that look. The plant grows from seed rather than from a persistent creeping root system, making seed production an important consideration when it is unwanted. A young nonflowering plant is easiest to identify by examining the leaf base as well as the blade.
identification: Look for a cylindrical seed head with fine bristles surrounding the small spikelets. Each spikelet commonly has only one to three bristles. The leaf blades are generally hairless, and the ligule at the junction of blade and sheath is a fringe of hairs. Giant foxtail usually develops a larger, drooping seed head; yellow foxtail differs in leaf hairs and seed-head proportions. Bristle direction helps distinguish green foxtail from bristly foxtail, Setaria verticillata, but that detail needs magnification and a regional key. Head color alone is unreliable.
actions: Remove small unwanted clumps before seed matures and contain any ripe heads during the work. Inspect bare patches and disturbed soil for later seedlings. In lawns, maintain a dense stand suited to the site with appropriate mowing and care; avoid creating bare ground through overly aggressive removal. In crop fields, obtain crop-specific advice because useful timing and permitted treatments differ. Photograph the seed head, leaf surface and blade-sheath junction when asking for identification. These steps target establishment and seed spread without promising that one pass will exhaust the seed bank.
researchNotes: NC State independently supports annual clumping habit, foxtail comparisons and dense-turf prevention. VicFlora supplies spikelet bristle counts, hairless leaves and bristle direction. The Ontario guide independently confirms a hairy ligule and seed reproduction; no regional emergence calendar is generalized.

proposedDescription: Green Iguana is a large, mainly plant-eating lizard that climbs well and readily enters water. Young animals are often bright green, but adults may be brownish, dark or seasonally orange, so the name does not describe every individual. A long tail makes up much of its total length. In places where it has been introduced, feeding and burrowing can create problems around gardens and built structures. Its native or introduced status depends on location; an observation should be assessed against the local wildlife authority's guidance.
identification: Look for a hanging flap of skin beneath the throat, a row of upright spines along the neck and back, and a long tail that often has dark bands. A conspicuously enlarged round scale below the ear opening is a useful close-view feature. Mature males commonly have heavier jowls and a larger throat flap than females. Do not rely on green coloration alone or approach to inspect the head. Photograph the animal from a safe distance, including its full tail and side of the head if naturally visible.
actions: Do not feed, chase, grab or relocate an iguana. Keep pets back and record its location and behavior for a local wildlife professional, particularly if it is burrowing near a structure. Never release an unwanted pet; contact an authorized surrender or rehoming program instead. Avoid handling droppings with bare hands and wash after contact with contaminated surfaces. A cold-stunned animal may recover and become active, so do not bring it indoors to warm it. Removal and transport requirements vary and should be checked with the responsible authority.
researchNotes: FWC supplies current Florida impacts, recognition and public precautions; Michigan's Animal Diversity Web independently supports climbing, swimming, variable color and the enlarged subtympanic scale. Native-range taxonomy is not narrowed from the older ADW account. Florida legal permissions are not generalized or restated.

proposedDescription: Green shield scale is a soft scale insect that feeds on leaves and young stems of many broadleaf plants, including tropical fruit trees and ornamentals. Mature females produce conspicuous white cottony egg sacs that can make a plant look dusted with fluff. Feeding insects also release honeydew, allowing black sooty mold to grow on the sticky surface. Old wax can remain after the scales have died, so white patches do not necessarily indicate a continuing active infestation. The name refers to one stage of an insect whose color changes as it matures.
identification: Young females are green and oval, becoming darker and eventually brown after laying eggs. Mature females are slightly domed and several millimeters long. The cottony egg sac develops beneath and behind the body and can extend around its margins. These features suggest a cottony soft scale, but other Pulvinaria species can be similar. Honeydew, ants, leaf curling and sooty mold are signs of sap-feeding insects rather than diagnostic proof of this species. Exact identification may require a specialist to examine a slide-mounted adult female.
actions: Check whether live scales and small mobile young are present beneath or near the wax. Photograph leaves, young stems and an intact female with its egg sac, and keep suspect potted plants from touching healthy plants. Conserve predators and parasitic wasps by avoiding unnecessary persistent broad-spectrum insecticides. Where ants are protecting colonies, seek plant-safe local ant-management advice. If the infestation remains damaging, ask an adviser about treatment timed to active young scales and appropriate for the host. Do not judge success solely by whether old white wax has disappeared.
researchNotes: UC IPM was read as full text for persistent old wax, natural enemies and management. USDA IDtools independently supplies field characters, and EFSA supports microscopic confirmation and nondiagnostic symptoms. Regional generation counts conflict and are deliberately omitted.

proposedDescription: Green swordtails are freshwater aquarium fish whose wild ancestors come from Mexico and Central America. They give birth to live young and can produce several broods in warm conditions. Released aquarium fish and escapes from outdoor ponds have established populations outside that range. They use vegetated streams as well as ponds, ditches and warm springs, so an apparently isolated ornamental pond can still become a source of fish for nearby water.
identification: An adult male has a long extension of the lower tail fin, the feature behind the name swordtail. Females lack that extension and are usually fuller-bodied. Wild-looking fish are often bronze or olive with a reddish stripe along the side; captive strains can be orange, red or other colors. A small female or juvenile is much less distinctive than a mature male. Platies and their hybrids can complicate identification, and USGS documents populations first called swordtails that were later identified as hybrids. Include a side view showing the whole tail and dorsal fin.
actions: Keep unwanted fish in captivity while arranging rehoming through an aquarium shop or experienced keeper. Never empty a tank or release fish into a pond, ditch or stream. Check that outdoor ponds cannot overflow into natural water. For a suspected wild population, record the waterbody, date and number seen and send clear photographs to the local fisheries or aquatic invasive-species program. Ask that program before collecting or transporting fish.
researchNotes: USGS supports native range, habitat, aquarium pathways and hybrid-identification limitations. NSW primary-industry guidance independently supplies field characters and prevention advice. Australian impact statements are not generalized into a claim of damage at an unspecified US site.

claims: Aquarium releases are a major pathway.

proposedDescription: Green wattle is an Australian tree with finely divided, dark green foliage and clusters of bright yellow flower balls. It has been planted beyond its native New South Wales range and can establish in open woodland and along disturbed edges. Mature trees can reach about 10-15 m. The fine-looking foliage belongs to a substantial woody plant, so identifying young trees early is more practical than waiting until a dense stand has developed.
identification: Look closely at a young twig: prominent ridges run along it like narrow wings. The leaves divide twice, with about 5-15 pairs of side branches, each bearing many narrow, well-spaced leaflets. Mature foliage and twigs are largely hairless. The flower heads are rounded, followed by flattened brown pods roughly 5-10 cm long. Other wattles have similar yellow heads, so flowers alone are not enough. Photograph the winged twig, a complete leaf and mature pods together. The combination of winged branches and widely spaced, hairless leaf divisions is especially useful.
actions: Check local guidance before planting this tree or giving away seed. Where removal is appropriate, identify small seedlings before disturbing surrounding plants and remove the entire young root system while soil is workable. Gather developing pods rather than leaving them with garden waste. Established trees require a site-specific woody-weed plan and safe tree work; cutting a large tree is not a complete follow-up strategy. Keep checking disturbed ground for seedlings after the initial work.
researchNotes:
VicFlora supplies diagnostic characters and Australian naturalization context. Indonesia's government invasive-plant guide independently describes stature, foliage and winged branchlets. The catalog name is retained; green wattle and early black-wattle refer to the same species here. Actions are prudent seed prevention and site assessment, not a verified eradication recipe.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.

proposedDescription: The greenhouse frog is a tiny ground-dwelling frog that can travel with potted plants and moist garden materials. Its eggs develop on land and hatch directly into miniature frogs, so it does not need a pond full of tadpoles to reproduce. Adults hide in leaf litter and other damp cover and become easier to notice after rain. A quiet series of high, birdlike chirps may reveal a frog that is otherwise almost invisible against brown leaves.
identification: Adults are generally about 1-3 cm long, brown, reddish brown or bronze. Some have mottled dark markings; others have two pale stripes running lengthwise along the back. The hind legs are banded, the skin is slightly warty, and the slender toes have little expansion and no webbing. A pale triangle can appear between the eyes and snout. Small native frogs and young treefrogs can be confusing, so include close views of the toes, side of the head and back, plus a sound recording if possible.
actions: Inspect pot rims, drainage holes, saucers and damp packing material before moving plants between properties. If a frog arrives unexpectedly in a nursery plant, keep the plant separate and photograph the animal before asking the nursery or local wildlife service for advice. Do not release it in a new place or move it to a nearby pond. For an outdoor sighting, record the location and call; those observations are more useful for checking a possible new introduction than an unverified name alone.
researchNotes: University of Florida and University of Georgia independently describe the frog, terrestrial development and plant-associated movement. Their regional range statements are not used to infer presence in a user's county. Handling and reporting advice is precautionary rather than a claim that removal is required everywhere.

sources.title: University of Florida: The Greenhouse Frog in the United States

proposedDescription: Greenhouse orthezia is a sap-feeding scale insect found on leaves and stems of many cultivated plants. Unlike a smooth, stationary-looking armored scale, the female carries conspicuous white wax plates and a long egg sac with her. It can be moved with living plants, making inspection of incoming greenhouse and nursery stock especially useful. Its unusual appearance helps find an infestation, but closely related ensign scales still need careful identification.
identification: Look for an oval, dark green to dark brown body with reddish-brown legs. White wax plates form rows along the middle and edges, leaving obvious dark bare patches between them. The ribbed white egg sac projects behind the female and may be about twice her body length. Praelongorthezia praelonga has much more wax covering its back and a differently shaped, longer egg sac. Another close relative, Insignorthezia pseudinsignis, requires microscopic characters for separation. Photograph an intact insect from above and from the side before disturbing its wax.
actions: Keep a suspect plant apart from clean stock and avoid taking cuttings or sharing it while identification is pending. Inspect leaf undersides, stems and nearby plants with a hand lens, including any white sacs rather than treating them as harmless debris. Send photographs and the host-plant name to a diagnostic service; ask how to package a specimen if one is needed. Use confirmed identification and the actual crop or houseplant setting to choose management with extension staff. Broad spraying based only on white wax can miss the correct pest.
researchNotes: USDA-associated IDtools provides detailed field and microscopic characters. An independent Florida Entomologist research article explains the confusion with Praelongorthezia praelonga. The older name Orthezia insignis is a synonym; the catalog's Insignorthezia name is retained. No species-specific pesticide directions are inferred.

claims: Females have wax plates separated by bare areas and carry a ribbed ovisac.
Insignorthezia pseudinsignis requires microscopic separation.

proposedDescription: The greenhouse slug is a small, dark slug associated with cultivated ground and plant movement. It is also called the jet slug or black-keeled slug. Like other garden slugs it is easiest to find when conditions are damp, while daytime hiding places can include pots, debris and soil crevices. Leaf damage alone cannot identify it: several unrelated slugs feed in the same settings, and some similar-looking species need anatomical examination.
identification: Its body can be gray or nearly black, with a raised ridge along the back behind the mantle. Take a top view and a clear side view while it is extended, showing the mantle, ridge, tail and breathing opening. A single dark silhouette is not enough for a confident name. Milax nigricans and species of Tandonia are important comparisons; specialist identification may involve internal reproductive structures. Published revisions have corrected earlier records of this group, so retain the original photographs even if an initial identification seems plausible.
actions: Inspect the bottoms of pots, trays and damp packing materials before moving plants. In a garden, check after rain or at dusk and record which plants are actually being damaged. Remove unnecessary moist shelter close to vulnerable seedlings and avoid transferring infested soil or pots into clean areas. If a new introduction is suspected, ask a local extension or plant-health service how to submit a specimen. These steps reduce accidental movement and improve diagnosis; they do not establish that this slug alone caused the damage or guarantee control.
researchNotes: University of California's slug guide supports color, identity and regional horticultural context; the PDF fetch was denied, so only indexed excerpts are claimed. An independent Swiss taxonomic revision documents misidentifications and the importance of anatomy. This draft deliberately avoids a photo-only species diagnosis. SANBI independently corroborates the dorsal keel, modified-ground habitat and confusion with M. nigricans.

proposedDescription: Greenleaf ticktrefoil is a trailing perennial legume grown as forage in warm, humid regions. Its stems scramble through nearby vegetation and can root where they remain against moist ground. The small jointed pods break into seed-bearing pieces that cling to clothing and animals. A planted forage patch and an unwanted escape therefore need different decisions, but both benefit from recognizing the plant before mature pods are carried elsewhere.
identification: Each leaf has three hairy leaflets, with the terminal leaflet usually larger than the side pair. Leaflets are broadly oval to pointed and may carry reddish-brown or purple markings. Stems often have hooked hairs and feel sticky. Slender flowering stalks carry pink to violet pea flowers; mature pods have several strongly separated segments covered in tiny hooked hairs. Other ticktrefoils share three-part leaves and clinging fruits. Document the whole leaf, stem hairs and a ripe pod rather than identifying this species from a single leaflet.
actions: Where plants are escaping cultivation, work before the jointed pods mature and remove attached pod pieces from clothing and equipment before leaving. Trace sprawling stems to their rooted nodes; lifting only the visible tips leaves established portions behind. Keep rooted cuttings and pod-bearing waste out of drains and nearby vegetation. On agricultural land, discuss changes with the grower because this may be an intentional forage crop. Monitor the edge of the managed area, especially shaded moist ground.
researchNotes: NSW Flora and the Tropical Forages research consortium independently describe leaves, hooked hairs, pods and growth. Agronomic tolerance information is not presented as a proven weed-control program. The catalog taxonomy is retained and no local occurrence or invasive status is inferred.

claims: Leaves have three hairy leaflets; jointed pods have hooked hairs.

proposedDescription: Greenwax golden bamboo is a vigorous woody grass that can form a tall, dense thicket. Its underground running stems can extend the planting beyond the visible canes. Young growth has a pale waxy coating, while older canes are green to yellow-green. This is a plant to assess by the space it occupies underground as well as the screen it creates above ground, especially near a property boundary or natural vegetation.
identification: The canes may reach roughly 8 m, with a groove along the internodes and usually two leafy branches at a node, features characteristic of Phyllostachys. Fresh internodes are white-powdery, and young nodes can be purple. Leaves are narrow, commonly around 10-15 cm long, with a paler, bluish underside. Several running bamboos look similar once their sheaths have fallen. For species confirmation, photograph fresh shoots and intact cane sheaths, including their small ear-like projections and bristles, as well as mature leaves and nodes.
actions: Map the outermost new shoots each spring and inspect beyond the apparent clump. If the planting is spreading into an unwanted area, remove or contain escaping rhizomes with a bamboo specialist or experienced landscape contractor. Cutting canes clears the view but leaves the underground system to produce more shoots. Keep excavated rhizomes out of soil moved to another site, and do not discard divisions in nearby woodland. Check local planting guidance before adding or sharing this bamboo.
researchNotes: Flora of China, accessed through World Flora Online, supplies diagnostic sheath and cane details. RHS independently documents vigorous thicket formation and running rhizomes. RHS horticultural size ranges are not treated as maximum possible size or evidence of US invasive status.

proposedDescription: The grey sea squirt is a solitary marine animal attached to hard surfaces, including mangrove roots, docks and vessel hulls. Despite its common name, it can be cream, yellow, orange, red or burgundy as well as pale gray. Water passes through the body as the animal filters food. Transport on marine structures and boats helps explain its broad distribution, while its ecological impacts remain poorly documented.
identification: Look for an individual soft-bodied sac covered by a translucent outer tunic, with two siphon openings. Color comes largely from the body wall beneath that covering and is not a reliable species test. Individuals can reach several centimeters long. Closely related Ascidia species may look alike in a dockside photograph; internal muscles, the digestive tract and other anatomical structures are used in specialist identification. Ascidia canaliculata has been confused with it historically. Photograph the attachment surface and both openings without removing the animal solely for a picture.
actions: Record the marina or shoreline, depth, substrate and approximate number present. Share clear photographs with the local marine biosecurity program if the animal appears unusual for the area. Before moving boats, moorings or aquaculture equipment, inspect sheltered fouling surfaces and follow local cleaning procedures. Arrange cleaning where removed organisms and wash water can be contained rather than scraped into another harbor. A specialist may request a specimen, but ask for collection and preservation instructions first.
researchNotes: Smithsonian NEMESIS supplies fouling habitat, variable coloration and explicit unknown impacts. An independent Zoological Studies taxonomic treatment supports anatomy-based distinction from Ascidia canaliculata. Native-range wording is cautious because the Smithsonian account itself discusses cryptogenic uncertainty.

claims: Solitary tunicate has variable body-wall coloration and a translucent tunic.

proposedDescription: Ground ivy, often called creeping Charlie, is a low perennial that spreads through lawns and garden beds on trailing stems. The stems root where their joints touch soil, making a connected mat rather than a collection of separate seedlings. Its small violet flowers and rounded leaves can be attractive, but repeated rooting lets it occupy gaps and return when only the leafy tips are removed.
identification: The leaves sit opposite one another on square stems. They are rounded to kidney-shaped, with broad scalloped teeth and long stalks. Blue-violet flowers arise beside the leaves, often in small groups. Crushed or mown foliage has a mint-like smell. Henbit and purple deadnettle also have square stems and purple flowers, but they do not form the same creeping, repeatedly rooted network. Speedwells and common mallow can resemble the leaves; check the square stem and rooted joints before deciding.
actions: For a small unwanted patch, loosen damp soil and lift the runners carefully, collecting rooted joints rather than snapping off the leaves. Revisit the area for pieces that were missed. In lawns, address thin turf and select grass or another groundcover suited to the light and soil so the same openings do not remain. Keep fragments out of newly planted beds. Larger infestations may need a seasonal plan with local extension guidance; one mowing or pulling session rarely removes the whole network.
researchNotes: University of Missouri provides the key field distinctions and rooted-stem habit. University of Minnesota independently describes mat formation and management context. No herbicide rate is carried into the draft, and the source's regional invasive characterization is not applied as a universal legal label.

claims: Opposite scalloped leaves, square stems and rooted nodes distinguish ground ivy.

proposedDescription: This ground mealybug feeds below the soil surface, where an infestation can remain hidden while a potted plant loses vigor. It has been recorded from roots of many kinds of plants. White wax around roots may be the first useful clue, but yellow leaves or slow growth alone have many possible causes. Looking at the root ball is therefore more informative than repeatedly treating the foliage.
identification: Look between the pot wall and outer roots for small, pale, segmented insects with a light powdery wax coating. Ground mealybugs lack the conspicuous fringe of long wax threads seen on many leaf-feeding mealybugs. Those features identify a group, not Rhizoecus falcifer specifically. Formal keys use microscopic structures, including antennal segments and pores. Keep a specimen intact for a diagnostic service and include the host name, root photographs and whether the plant recently arrived from a nursery.
actions: Isolate suspect pots and avoid sharing their trays, loose growing medium or drainage water with clean plants. Inspect neighboring root balls before moving a batch. Clean equipment that contacted affected soil and keep discarded roots in a closed container. A nursery adviser can help decide whether keeping a badly infested plant is practical, because insects hidden throughout roots are difficult to reach. These are containment steps while the exact species is confirmed, not evidence that a surface spray will clear the roots.
researchNotes: UC IPM supports root-ball inspection and containment for a group explicitly including this species. An independent published Italian identification key supports the need for microscopic species separation. ScaleNet documents the broad host record and original root-associated specimens. Group-level characters are clearly labeled.

proposedDescription: Kondo ground mealybug feeds below ground on plant roots. It has been studied in citrus orchards in Japan and alfalfa fields in California, as well as being included in nursery root-mealybug guidance. In affected alfalfa, declining plants can form roughly circular patches that expand slowly. Current taxonomic sources use Ripersiella kondonis, while many crop references retain Rhizoecus kondonis. Both names are useful when seeking an identification.
identification: Look for tiny, whitish insects crawling among the roots rather than on the leaves. Some individuals carry fine wax threads that resemble a loose net. When numerous, their wax can give nearby soil a bluish cast. In a field, the boundary between healthy and declining plants is a useful place to inspect roots. The insects and their immature stages live in the soil, so a clean-looking canopy does not rule them out. Other ground mealybugs are difficult to separate by eye; root symptoms and white wax alone cannot confirm Kondo mealybug.
actions: Keep suspect soil and rooted plants out of clean growing areas while obtaining a diagnosis. For field patches, record the boundary and inspect roots at its edge rather than sampling only dead plants at the center. In containers, inspect the root ball before sharing or repotting a declining plant. Ask a crop adviser for a plan suited to the affected host. UC guidance reports no established treatment threshold for alfalfa, and the insect can survive on several alternative plants, so crop rotation should not be assumed to eliminate it.
researchNotes: Species-specific UC alfalfa guidance supplies wax appearance, patch symptoms, root monitoring and management limits. Independent Japanese orchard experiments establish citrus association and soil-moisture sensitivity; their 1959 chemical recommendations are not reused. ScaleNet supplies the Ripersiella combination, and ITIS repeats that source rather than counting as an independent group.

proposedDescription: Groundnut bruchid is a seed beetle associated with peanuts and tamarind. The damaging stage is the larva, which feeds inside seeds while much of the infestation remains concealed. Adults emerging from stored material can reveal damage that started earlier. Keeping suspect pods or seed lots separate is useful both for protecting clean stores and for tracing where the insects came from.
identification: Adults are small brownish-gray seed beetles. Look for short wing covers that leave the end of the abdomen exposed, conspicuous antennae and enlarged hind legs, but seek confirmation rather than naming every beetle in peanuts as this species. Larvae are curved, cream-colored grubs with dark mouthparts. Eggs can be attached to pod surfaces, and round holes in pods or seeds show where beetles have emerged. Other stored-product insects also make holes. Photograph the beetle and the affected commodity together and retain an intact adult.
actions: Close the affected package or place the lot in a pest-proof container before inspecting nearby stored foods or seeds. Record the supplier and purchase date and keep the original label. Do not distribute suspect seed for planting or carry loose pods to another storage area. A plant-health or stored-product specialist can confirm the beetle and advise disposal or an approved treatment for the commodity. Avoid applying household insecticides to food or seed; sanitation and isolation can begin before a species-level diagnosis.
researchNotes: TNAU supplies seed-damage and immature-stage descriptions. The independent American Entomological Society revision supports the species and close-relative identification problem; the UNL-hosted primary report documents a Florida specimen without implying current local establishment. No storage treatment efficacy is invented. The USDA handbook additionally supports the enlarged hind-leg and antennal characters.

proposedDescription: Common guava is a tropical American fruit tree widely grown for its fragrant, seeded fruit. Outside managed orchards it can form thickets in suitable warm climates. Florida's invasive-plant program describes effects on forests and open woodland where dense guava crowds other vegetation. A productive garden tree and an expanding wild stand need different management, so first establish whether the plants are deliberately maintained or spreading beyond cultivation.
identification: The bark is smooth and flakes away in greenish to reddish-brown patches. Opposite oval leaves have prominent side veins and often a softly hairy underside. Young twigs are hairy and four-angled. White flowers have many long stamens; rounded or pear-shaped fruit turns yellow and retains a small crown of old sepals at its end. Strawberry guava has smaller, glossier leaves and generally smaller fruit, so use leaf texture, twig shape and fruit together. Photograph seedlings as well as the mature tree when documenting an escape.
actions: Where fruiting guava is permitted and retained, collect ripe and fallen fruit and check nearby beds, fences and woodland edges for seedlings. Do not dump fruit or pruned material in natural vegetation. Remove unwanted seedlings while their roots are manageable. For a mature unwanted thicket, consult a local woody-weed plan and arrange follow-up rather than assuming a single cut solves the problem. Verify the species before removing a valued fruit tree or a superficially similar native shrub.
researchNotes: University of Florida provides the natural-area impact context. Queensland-associated Lucid weed identification independently supports bark, twig, leaf and fruit characters. Claims are restricted to common guava, not generalized from strawberry guava; local presence and planting rules require local evidence.

claims: Guava is a cultivated fruit tree whose thickets can crowd vegetation in forests and woodland.

proposedDescription: Guava aphid gathers on tender shoots and the undersides of young leaves, especially on guava and other members of the myrtle family. It feeds by drawing sap from growing tissues. Its unusually long rear tubes make it easier to notice than many tiny aphids, but another Greenidea species has a very similar appearance. Finding a colony is an opportunity to confirm the insect before plants or cuttings are moved.
identification: Wingless adults are pear-shaped and pale to dark brown, with long yellow-brown tubes projecting backward from the abdomen and curving outward near their tips. These tubes, called cornicles or siphunculi, bear hairs. Winged forms are narrower and have even longer, darker tubes. Greenidea ficicola is a close lookalike. Specialists distinguish the surface pattern near the base and along the cornicles, plus antennal details, so a phone photograph may establish the genus without securely identifying the species. Include the host and young growth in photographs.
actions: Inspect fresh leaf flushes rather than only older leaves, and keep suspect nursery plants apart while identification is checked. Avoid exchanging infested cuttings. Record whether colonies occupy a few shoots or are increasing across the plant, and photograph predators or parasitized aphids present nearby. For a valuable crop or an apparent new introduction, ask extension staff or plant-health officials to identify specimens and recommend management for that host. The long cornicles alone do not justify a blanket treatment of every guava plant.
researchNotes: India's ICAR-NBAIR aphid database supplies diagnostic color, proportions and feeding sites. Independent Neotropical research explains the distinction from G. ficicola and broader host range. No specific virus transmission or treatment efficacy is claimed without species-level evidence.
