proposedDescription: Guineagrass is a tall, clump-forming tropical grass also known in older guides as Panicum maximum. It has been grown as forage and can become a large, persistent plant around disturbed ground and wet margins. Long leaves and an open, branching seed head give mature stands a much looser appearance than grasses with compact bottlebrush heads. A seedling is harder to recognize, making flowering material useful for confirmation.
identification: Mature clumps can reach about 3 m in favorable conditions. Leaves are long and may be around 2 cm wide; the surrounding sheath can be hairy. The seed head is an open panicle, sometimes up to 50 cm long, with branches arranged in whorls. Photograph a complete panicle, the point where a blade meets its sheath and the plant base. Other large panic grasses can resemble it, so height and leaf width alone are weak evidence. The old and new scientific names refer to the same grass in these sources.
actions: Prevent unwanted plants from setting seed before mowing or moving equipment through them. Small isolated plants are easier to address than a mature clump; include the crown when removing one and check the spot for regrowth. Keep seed heads and attached soil from being moved to a clean site. Near ponds or streams, seek locally approved management and protect the bank from erosion during removal. If it is an intentional pasture planting, coordinate with the land manager before changing the stand.
researchNotes: James Cook University supplies stature, leaf and panicle characters under the current name. Texas A&M independently provides habitat and prevention guidance under Panicum maximum. A source's broad North American distribution statement is not converted into county presence or a universal treatment requirement.

claims: Clumps can reach 3 m; leaves are long and panicles have many whorls.
Guinea grass occurs around aquatic margins and has a large branched flower cluster.
It should not be spread into new waterbodies.

proposedDescription: Gulf cockspur grass is a robust grass of wet ground, stream margins and shallow water. Its stems may bend near the base and root in mud, while a large, loosely branched seed head arches above broad leaves. Regional floras describe both annual and perennial plants. Its resemblance to other barnyard grasses makes a complete mature specimen more useful than a photograph of a single blade.
identification: Look for smooth, flat blades, often 15-60 cm long, and no ligule at the junction of blade and sheath. The panicle has spreading and somewhat drooping branches, with smaller branches on at least some of the lower ones. Tiny bristly spikelets may have short awns. A pale, soft-looking, arching panicle is a useful field clue, but related Echinochloa species vary greatly. Photograph the whole head, a close view of spikelets and the leaf collar; retain mature material for a grass specialist if the name affects management.
actions: Keep seed-bearing material and muddy equipment from moving between wet sites. Where an unwanted small patch is confirmed, work before seeds mature and limit soil disturbance along the bank. Check whether bent stems have rooted beyond the main clump before deciding the patch has been removed. For crop fields or extensive wetland growth, get identification and a site-specific management plan first. The presence of a large grass at a wet edge does not by itself establish that it is nonnative or harmful there.
researchNotes: VicFlora and Flora of Tropical East Africa independently support habit and diagnostic structure. Their annual/perennial descriptions differ, and broader sources disagree about native range; this draft does not resolve those conflicts by assertion. The catalog name is preserved and local origin remains unassigned.

sources.title: Kew: Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment

claims: Panicles have spreading, partly branched racemes and an arched pale appearance.
Robust stems can root in mud; blades lack a ligule.
Plants occupy shallow water, swamps and stream sides.

proposedDescription: Hairy beggarticks is a branching annual whose narrow fruits readily hitch a ride on clothing and animal coats. It grows in disturbed places, crops and garden settings in warm regions. The flower heads may be much less showy than those of related Spanish needles, but a mature plant can produce many barbed fruits. Recognizing it before that stage prevents an ordinary weeding job from spreading seeds along the route home.
identification: Leaves are opposite, often divided into three to seven toothed leaflets. Small heads have yellow centers and may lack the conspicuous white rays seen on Bidens alba, although some plants have short pale rays. Mature dark fruits project outward from the head and end in backward-catching barbs. Bidens bipinnata has more finely divided leaves. Because B. pilosa and B. alba are closely related and sometimes combined in references, document both flowers and mature fruits when an exact species name is needed.
actions: Pull unwanted young plants before the barbed fruits mature. If plants already carry seed, contain the heads before moving the rest of the plant and clean clothing, pet fur and tools on site. Inspect nursery pots and disturbed bed edges for the next flush of seedlings. Preserve nearby native Bidens where they occur rather than treating every Spanish-needles plant as the same weed. In agricultural plantings, choose management for the crop and growth stage with local extension advice.
researchNotes: University of Hawaii provides leaf, fruit and lookalike detail. University of Florida independently explains the B. alba/B. pilosa distinction and shared management context. Native or invasive status is not generalized from Hawaii; taxonomic overlap is explicitly noted.

sources.title: University of Florida: Spanish needles biology and management

claims: Opposite divided leaves and dark barbed fruits characterize the plant.
B. alba and B. bipinnata are lookalikes.
B. pilosa and B. alba are closely related; B. pilosa often lacks conspicuous ray flowers.

proposedDescription: Hairy bittercress is a small mustard that often appears in nursery pots, moist beds and thin turf. It can flower while still quite small, then scatter its seeds when the slender ripe pods spring open. That makes timing more important than plant size: a low plant tucked beneath a shrub may already be ready to seed the surrounding bed. Its growth season varies with climate and moisture.
identification: The first leaves make a low rosette. Later leaves have several small rounded leaflets and a larger terminal leaflet. Thin upright stems carry tiny white flowers with four petals, followed by long narrow pods that point upward. Hair is often easiest to see around leaf stalks and the rosette. Other bittercresses look similar, so include flowers, mature pods and the whole rosette in photographs. The combination of rounded leaflets, tiny four-petaled flowers and slender upright pods is more useful than the common name's promise of obvious hairiness.
actions: Remove seedlings before pods ripen, including those hiding in container edges and under benches. If mature pods are present, handle the plant gently and contain it before disturbing the stems. Keep nursery pots and purchased plants free of flowering weeds before planting them into a clean bed. Use mulch suited to the planting and check new gaps after watering or soil disturbance. Mowing may leave the low rosette intact, so inspect turf rather than assuming a short cut stopped seed production.
researchNotes:
Missouri and Cornell independently supply leaf, flower and explosive-pod characters. Tennessee's extension guide supports the low rosette's ability to survive mowing. Sources differ on seasonal behavior and roots, so the draft avoids a universal winter-only life cycle or a diagnostic root claim.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.

sources.title: University of Tennessee: W399—Hairy Bittercress(Cardamine hirsuta)

claims: Tiny four-petaled white flowers form narrow pods that eject seeds.
Rosette leaves have rounded leaflets and a larger terminal leaflet.
The weed occurs in nurseries and moist disturbed areas.
Low rosette growth can survive frequent mowing.

proposedDescription: Hairy buttercup is a low, conspicuously hairy plant with glossy yellow flowers. It occurs in fields and other open ground and can blend into a mixture of yellow-flowered buttercups. The flowering plant is easier to investigate than an isolated basal leaf, but ripe fruits are valuable when separating close relatives. Its appearance alone should not be used to decide that every buttercup in a field needs removal.
identification: Look for hairy stems and leaves divided into three main lobes or leaflets. Flowers usually have five shiny yellow petals; the hairy sepals bend sharply backward beneath them. The base lacks the obvious swollen bulb of bulbous buttercup. Mature fruits cluster into a head, and their surfaces may carry tiny raised bumps, although a regional flora notes that these can be sparse or absent. Photograph the underside of a flower, the plant base and mature fruit with a scale. A botanist may need those details to distinguish similar species.
actions: If plants are unwanted in a small managed area, confirm the identification and remove them before fruit matures. Keep fruiting material from scattering while it is carried away. In pasture, identify the buttercup species and assess the surrounding vegetation with an extension adviser before selecting a treatment or changing grazing. Record where patches persist and whether bare or disturbed soil is repeatedly recolonized. Wear gloves for routine plant handling and do not use an uncertain field identification to decide whether a wild plant is suitable as food.
researchNotes: University of Texas supplies detailed morphology, including reflexed sepals and a nonbulbous base. Southern Illinois University's field flora independently discusses fruit papillae and their variability. Sources differ in life-history descriptions, so the public draft avoids an unsupported universal annual/perennial statement.

claims: Hairy shoots have divided leaves, glossy yellow petals and strongly reflexed sepals.
The plant base is not bulbous.
Fruit papillae are useful but sometimes sparse or absent; the calyx is hairy.

proposedDescription: Hairy cat's ear is a perennial rosette plant with yellow dandelion-like flower heads. The leaves stay close to the ground while the flowering stems rise above them, allowing a plant to persist in turf even when its flowers are repeatedly cut. Seeds form fluffy heads and can move away from the original rosette. Its low, hairy leaves are often a better starting point for identification than a distant yellow flower.
identification: Look for a basal rosette of broad, elongated leaves with irregular lobes and dense hairs on both sides. Leafless flowering stalks often carry small scale-like bracts and branch to hold more than one yellow head. The heads consist of strap-shaped florets with toothed tips. Common dandelions usually have unbranched stalks carrying one head and much less hairy leaves. Other cat's ears can still be similar, so photograph a complete leaf, its hairs and the branching flower stalk together.
actions: For a few unwanted plants, loosen the soil around the crown and remove as much of the persistent root system as practical. Recheck the spot rather than counting removed flowers as removed plants. Prevent remaining heads from ripening while improving thin turf or replacing it with groundcover suited to the site. Keep a flowering specimen or clear photographs if the identification is uncertain. In pasture or a larger planting, seek local advice based on the confirmed species and the plants you want to retain.
researchNotes: UMass independently supports the hairy rosette, scaled scapes and perennial life cycle. Cornell corroborates perennial habit, rosette form and yellow heads. Advice is limited to small-patch removal, seed prevention and follow-up; no animal-disease or pesticide claim is inferred.

claims: Perennial has densely hairy basal leaves and leafless, often scaled flowering stems.
Perennial rosette plant has fuzzy leaves and yellow terminal heads.

proposedDescription: Hairy crabgrass, also called large crabgrass, is a warm-season annual that spreads outward through open or thinly covered soil. Lower stem joints can root and anchor a broad mat. It reproduces by seed, so a plant that is allowed to flower can leave a new problem even after the current year's growth dies. Gardens, crop fields and worn lawn edges provide the open conditions it readily occupies.
identification: Leaves and lower sheaths have conspicuous hairs, unlike the generally smoother foliage of smooth crabgrass. The stems are flattened and often bent near their lower joints. At the blade-sheath junction is a small membranous ligule. Several slender seed-bearing branches spread like fingers from near the top of a flowering stem. Photograph the hairs, ligule and whole seed head together; a finger-shaped head alone occurs in several grasses. Native or cultivated relatives can also resemble crabgrass.
actions: Remove young unwanted plants before the finger-like heads mature, lifting rooted lower joints as well as the central crown. In turf, repair worn areas and maintain a grass cover suited to the site so exposed soil is not repeatedly recolonized. Mulch bare bed soil where appropriate and check its edges. Clean seed-bearing clippings from tools before working a clean area. Crop management should match the crop and emergence stage; a treatment chosen for another annual grass may not work equally well here.
researchNotes:
South Dakota State supplies annual life history and practical field characters. University of California IPM independently describes rooted lower stems, hairy sheaths and fingerlike flowering branches. Control advice avoids copying dated herbicide-resistance or product claims into a general profile.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.

sources.title: South Dakota State: Grass weed identification
University of California Statewide IPM: Large Crabgrass (Digitaria sanguinalis)

claims: Annual hairy grass has flattened stems, a membranous ligule and finger-like seed heads.
Lower nodes root to form mats; lower sheaths are hairy.

proposedDescription: Hairy crabweed is better known to many gardeners as mulberryweed. It can arrive in nursery pots and quickly produce seeds among ornamental plants, especially in moist, shaded beds. Even a small plant can be reproductive, and some seeds are thrown away from the parent. Its resemblance to a young tree sometimes lets it remain in a pot long enough to spread through a plant collection.
identification: Look for alternate, roughly triangular to heart-shaped leaves with toothed edges and prominent veins. The thin, papery leaves and young round stems are hairy. Small feathery flower clusters sit where the leaf stalk meets the stem, becoming brown as fruits develop. A mulberry tree seedling has a superficially similar leaf but lacks the same hairy young stem and compact axillary flower clusters. Photograph the stem, leaf arrangement and clusters rather than relying on the outline of one leaf.
actions: Inspect purchased pots before placing them among clean plants. Pull seedlings while small, taking the crown and roots; a broken crown can regrow. Contain flowering or fruiting plants and dispose of them through an appropriate waste route rather than beside the bed. Mulch can reduce germination, but seeds landing on its surface can still grow. Recheck irrigated corners, container rims and propagation areas regularly, because a single clean-up can miss the next generation.
researchNotes: Delaware and NC State independently document identification, nursery movement and rapid seed production. Penn State independently supports regrowth after crown breakage. Flower-cluster color varies with age and treatment, so the draft emphasizes position and structure rather than one color.

claims: Hairy stems, alternate papery leaves and explosive seeds characterize the weed.
Plants flower when young and move with nursery stock; mulches and early removal aid management.
Broken crowns can regrow; remove roots and crown before seed set.

proposedDescription: Hairy cupgrass, also called woolly cupgrass, is an annual grass of crop fields, ditches and disturbed ground. Its soft-haired leaves can resemble a foxtail at first, but the mature seed head is built differently. Early plants may compete with a crop before their identity is obvious. Because the next generation comes from seed, finding isolated plants before they mature is particularly useful.
identification: Run a lens over a leaf rather than judging it from a distance: short soft hairs cover the blade, and one margin often has a noticeable crinkle. The sheath is also hairy, and the ligule is a short fringe of hairs. The seed head has branches with tightly arranged rows of oval spikelets, rather than a dense foxtail brush. Prairie cupgrass is a lookalike, but Missouri's key notes differences in inflorescence hair and the fertile floret's awn. Include close photographs of the collar and seed branches.
actions: Mark a suspected patch and obtain confirmation while flowering material is available. Remove a few unwanted plants before seeds mature and clean attached seed and soil from equipment. In fields, keep an eye on early-emerging plants and field entrances where machinery may introduce seed. Work with a crop adviser on a plan that fits this species and the crop; being an annual grass does not mean it responds like every foxtail. Revisit the area in following seasons to check for new seedlings.
researchNotes: Missouri and South Dakota State independently describe annual habit, fine hairs, crinkled leaf margins and distinctive seed heads. The public draft does not repeat dated herbicide-resistance statements or imply a treatment is currently labeled. Prairie cupgrass is identified as a comparison, not an interchangeable name.

sources.title: South Dakota State: Grass weed identification

claims: Hairy leaves often have a crinkled margin; spikelets form compressed rows.
Prairie cupgrass differs in inflorescence hairs and awn characters.
Woolly cupgrass is a seed-reproducing annual often confused with foxtails.

proposedDescription: Hairy fountain grass is a grass of open woodland margins, grassland and disturbed or cultivated ground. Older references call it Pennisetum pedicellatum. It can stand upright or bend at lower stem joints, and published treatments describe both annual and perennial forms. The name fountain grass covers several different species, so a fluffy-looking head or a nursery label is not sufficient to establish this identity.
identification: Plants can reach about 1.5 m. The flowering head contains small spikelet clusters surrounded by bristles. A grass key examines the short stalks of the spikelets, the size of their outer scales and a distinctive three-lobed scale enclosing the sterile floret. These are lens or microscope characters, not features reliably seen in a distant photograph. Collect photographs of a whole head and its base, the leaf collar and a detached mature cluster if collection is permitted. Cenchrus polystachios and related bristly grasses deserve comparison.
actions: Do not share unidentified fountain-grass seed or divisions. If a suspect plant appears outside cultivation, mark the location and ask a herbarium or extension service to examine mature flowering material. Contain loose seed heads before moving a confirmed unwanted plant, and clean equipment that has passed through a seeding patch. Local plant-health advice is especially useful where the species is regulated. Management should be selected after identification and site assessment; cutting off one flowering head does not demonstrate that a perennial plant is gone.
researchNotes: USDA-associated dissemination IDtools and an independent Botanical Survey of India flora provide substantive spikelet characters. Their habit descriptions differ, so both annual and perennial forms are acknowledged. The catalog name is retained alongside the older Pennisetum combination; no jurisdiction-specific legal conclusion is inferred from the tool title.

sources.title: Botanical Survey of India: Flora of Papikonda National Park

claims: Spikelet clusters and a three-lobed sterile lemma are diagnostic.
Annual or perennial plants reach about 150 cm.
The flora distinguishes stalked spikelets of C. pedicellatus from sessile spikelets of C. polystachios.

proposedDescription: This hairy nightshade is a small, usually annual herb whose ripe berries are orange to red, sometimes yellow. It belongs to the black-nightshade group, where closely similar plants have often been reported under the wrong name. The common name hairy nightshade is also used for other Solanum species. A record with that name alone therefore cannot reliably establish which plant was present.
identification: Plants are unarmed, without prickles, and may reach about 70 cm. Leaves are oval, with smooth to shallowly lobed edges and variable hairiness. Small white flowers occur in clusters and are followed by berries that can be slightly elongated. The orange-red ripe fruit is a strong clue among North American members of this group. Solanum retroflexum instead has dull purple berries with a pale bloom. Preserve the actual ripe-fruit color in photographs and include the flower, calyx and stem hairs; dried material can lose this useful distinction.
actions: Do not taste berries to identify the plant. Photograph flowers and fully ripe fruits before removing an unwanted garden specimen, then contain the berries so seeds are not scattered. Ask a botanical service to check an unusual report, especially where the name is not well documented. For crop or nursery infestations, seek management for the confirmed nightshade and the crop involved. A historical or catalog entry should not replace confirmation of a living plant at the site.
researchNotes: The primary Morelloid Solanum revision and independent VicFlora treatment support berry, habit and leaf characters. The revision questioned a Texas citation and described North American introductions as nonpersistent at publication; those dated findings are not asserted as current absence. Common-name ambiguity is flagged.

sources.title: Morelloid Solanum revision for North and Central America

claims: Orange-red, slightly elongated berries distinguish this species from many North American relatives.
Historical records can reflect misidentification.
Usually annual, unarmed herb with variable hairs, oval leaves and small white flowers.

proposedDescription: Hairy spider beetle is a stored-product insect associated with cereal foods, grain and animal feeds. It can live in mills, granaries, warehouses and homes, with damp grain particularly favorable. Larvae feed among food particles and produce silk, leaving webbed granular material. Finding a beetle away from food is a reason to inspect nearby dry stores, not proof that the building itself is being eaten.
identification: Adults have the rounded, long-legged appearance shared by spider beetles, but the useful species characters are much smaller. On the wing covers, some rows carry erect hairs markedly longer than those between them, and flattened pale scales may also be present. White-marked spider beetle, Ptinus fur, is an important lookalike. Larvae are pale grubs and are not readily named from a casual photograph. Save an intact adult, photograph it from above with a scale, and note the exact material in which it was found.
actions: Inspect flour, cereals, bran, pet food and stored grain, including spills in cracks and under shelving. Seal suspect packages while checking the rest of the store. Remove accumulated food debris and correct moisture problems rather than relying on treatment of exposed adults alone. Keep clean products in well-sealed containers. For a commercial grain lot, seek stored-product advice before movement or treatment; do not apply household insecticides directly to food, feed or packaging surfaces that contact it.
researchNotes: The Canadian Grain Commission provides food associations, larval signs and wing-cover hair characters. A USDA Forest Service taxonomic monograph independently distinguishes P. villiger from P. fur and P. clavipes using setae and scales. The profile does not infer structural timber damage from the family name.

sources.title: Canadian Grain Commission: Hairy spider beetle
USDA Forest Service: Ptinus diagnostic treatment

claims: Cereal products, damp grain and feeds may be affected; larvae leave silk and granular material.
Unequal wing-cover hair lengths help identify adults.
Long erect setae and appressed white scales separate P. villiger from similar Ptinus.

proposedDescription: Hairy vetch is a scrambling legume often grown as a cover crop. Tendrils let its stems climb neighboring plants, and an established planting can form a dense tangle of foliage and purple flowers. Outside its intended area, seed production can create volunteer plants in later crops or nearby vegetation. Recognizing a deliberately managed cover crop is as important as noticing an unwanted escape.
identification: Compound leaves carry many narrow leaflets and end in branching tendrils. In the typical hairy form, stems and leaves have abundant soft hairs. Numerous purple to violet pea flowers line one side of a long flower cluster. Other vetches share tendrils and divided leaves, and some forms within Vicia villosa are less hairy. Photograph the full flower cluster, the base of an individual flower and the leaflets. A botanist or crop adviser can separate it from tufted vetch and other similar species.
actions: If it is an intentional cover crop, follow the grower's termination plan and prevent unwanted seed production. Pull small escapes before pods mature, taking care not to drag seed-bearing vines through clean vegetation. Watch fence lines and the margins of planted fields for new plants. Do not assume an unfamiliar vetch is suitable livestock feed simply because related plants are forage crops; ask a forage adviser about the identified plant and intended use. Choose control that preserves neighboring crops and native legumes.
researchNotes: USDA NRCS independently documents leaflets, tendrils and many-flowered racemes. UC IPM explains variation among weedy vetches and the difference between typical hairy vetch and less hairy forms. The species-level catalog scope is preserved rather than restricted silently to one subspecies.

sources.title: USDA NRCS: Forb seedling identification guide

claims: Hairy vetch has divided leaves ending in tendrils and one-sided racemes of purple pea flowers.
Weedy vetches include hairy and less hairy forms within Vicia villosa.

proposedDescription: This wallaby grass is a slender perennial that grows in loose to crowded tufts. It is also called slender wallaby grass, a useful name because the catalog's hairy wallaby grass is shared with another species. Narrow leaves and an elongated flowering head can make it look inconspicuous among other pasture grasses. Species identification depends heavily on the tiny flowering parts rather than the overall amount of hair.
identification: Leaves are very narrow, flat or rolled inward, and may carry scattered long hairs. Slender stems can reach roughly 75 cm to 1 m in the regional floras. The flower head is narrow and elongated, with relatively few spikelets and conspicuous outer scales. In a mature floret, the inner scale called the palea extends beyond the notch between the lemma's lobes. That detail helps distinguish this species from similar wallaby grasses. Photograph the entire head and retain mature spikelets for a grass specialist rather than identifying from a tuft alone.
actions: Before removing a wallaby grass in a meadow or restoration planting, have a mature specimen checked so desirable grasses are not lost. If an unwanted population is confirmed, map its extent and prevent seed-bearing material from being carried in hay, soil or mowing equipment. Small plants can be addressed individually with minimal disturbance to neighboring vegetation. Follow up at the same growth stage the next season. The shared common name is not evidence that advice for Rytidosperma pilosum applies without checking.
researchNotes: NSW Flora and the independent Flora of New Zealand treatment support narrow leaves, slender habit and elongated heads. NZPCN corroborates the palea distinction but is not counted as an independent flora source. The shared catalog common name is flagged; species-specific eradication evidence was not located.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Rytidosperma penicillatum

claims: Slender tufted perennial has narrow often inrolled leaves and an elongated narrow inflorescence.
Mature spikelets have long glumes, extended awns and a relatively long palea.
The palea exceeding the lemma sinus and narrow inflorescence aid separation.

proposedDescription: Hairy wallaby grass is a perennial grass whose small flowering parts are more distinctive than its general tufted appearance. The same English name is used for Rytidosperma penicillatum, so using the scientific name prevents two different plants from being combined. Older references may also use other genus names. A mature flowering head is especially useful when confirming a suspected plant outside its known local flora.
identification: Look for hairy leaf sheaths, including hairs arising from small raised bases. The relatively compact head is often about 4-6 cm long and holds a few large spikelets. Each spikelet contains several florets, whose scales have organized hair tufts and a bent central awn with a twisted lower portion. GrassBase describes the palea as shorter than the full lemma, unlike the conspicuously projecting palea used to recognize R. penicillatum. These details need magnification. Keep the head intact and include close views of a sheath and a mature floret.
actions: Ask a herbarium or local grass specialist to verify the species before disturbing a natural grassland or sowing a collected seed lot. Do not transfer seed or divisions under the shared common name alone. For a confirmed unwanted patch, contain ripe heads and minimize movement of seed-bearing soil and clippings. Removal should preserve neighboring native grasses and be followed by checks for seedlings. Species-specific control evidence is limited here, so an ordinary mowing schedule should not be described as proven eradication.
researchNotes: Kew GrassBase and the independently authored Flora of New Zealand treatment provide substantive inflorescence and floret evidence. The catalog species is retained and distinguished from R. penicillatum. No local presence, ecological harm or treatment success is inferred from inclusion in an invasive-species catalog.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Rytidosperma pilosum

claims: Sheaths are pilose with tubercle-based hairs; florets have tufted hairs and bent twisted awns.
The panicle is contracted and spikelets have several florets.
The compact to somewhat loose panicle has few large spikelets on short stalks.

proposedDescription: Hairy woodrose is a twining vine with large, five-part leaves and white morning-glory-like flowers. In warm conditions it can climb through shrubs and along fences, covering supporting vegetation. Long coarse hairs on the stems and flower coverings make it distinctive at close range. Some newer references call it Distimake aegyptius, so both names may appear when looking up a plant or an old observation.
identification: Each leaf is divided like a hand into five leaflets. Stems and leaf stalks have long yellowish to brownish hairs. The white flower is funnel-shaped, with its petals joined together; the outer sepals are especially hairy and remain around the developing fruit. The ripe capsule is rounded to egg-shaped and pale brown. Other vines can have five-part leaves, so check the flower shape and hairy sepals rather than assuming a leaflet count identifies it. Photograph one complete leaf and a flower from both front and side.
actions: Trace an unwanted vine to its rooted base before cutting or pulling it away from a shrub. Work before the capsules mature, and contain any fruiting material before carrying it off site. Remove seedlings from disturbed ground near the original plant and check supports for overlooked stems. Do not discard vines or seeds along a watercourse. If it occupies natural vegetation, get a local assessment of identity and status before planning extensive clearance; the species has a broad, complicated tropical range.
researchNotes: India's weed-research handbook and an independent Australian weed account support hairy stems, five-part leaves and climbing growth. The Leon Levy preserve lists the newer Distimake name. Conflicting annual/perennial and origin statements are not silently resolved; the catalog taxonomy remains unchanged.

sources.title: Leon Levy Native Plant Preserve: Distimake aegyptius

claims: Twining hairy stems bear five leaflets and pale brown capsules enclosed partly by the calyx.
Fast-growing vine can cover supporting vegetation; exact tropical origin is obscure.
Merremia aegyptia is listed as a synonym of Distimake aegyptius.

proposedDescription: The hairy-clawed shore crab is an East Asian coastal crab whose identity needs particular care. For many years, two very similar crabs were recorded together under Hemigrapsus penicillatus. Researchers separated Hemigrapsus takanoi in 2005, and later genetic work supported that distinction. Older records, especially reports of an invasion in Europe, cannot automatically be assigned to the species in this profile.
identification: Adult males have a patch of fine hairs on each claw. The original species description distinguishes H. penicillatus by smaller hair patches and a different distribution of dark spots, including spots on the underside. These are comparison features, not a dependable identification from one casual photograph. Independent Korean research found individuals with mixed external characters that genetically belonged to H. penicillatus. Females, juveniles and worn or preserved specimens can be especially difficult to separate. Include sharp photographs of both claws, the upper shell and the underside if this can be done safely and legally.
actions: For an unexpected shore-crab sighting, record the precise shore location, date and habitat and send images to a marine identification service or local aquatic biosecurity program. Retain the uncertainty in the record until a specialist checks it; a photograph labelled with the older name is not enough to establish a new population. Do not move live crabs, bait or shoreline material to another waterbody. Ask the receiving program whether it needs a specimen before collecting one.
researchNotes: The 2005 taxonomic paper supplies the species split and original visible characters. Independent Korean molecular work confirms separate species but documents overlap in those characters. This important limitation is kept in the public draft; European H. takanoi invasion evidence is not reassigned to H. penicillatus.

sources.title: Asakura and Watanabe: Hemigrapsus takanoi, a sibling species of H. penicillatus
KIOST: Taxonomic study of H. penicillatus and H. takanoi

claims: The two species differ in male claw hair patches and pigmentation; older records combined them.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Lee and colleagues Korean molecular study
claims: COI sequences support the species distinction; mixed morphological characters occur in H. penicillatus.

proposedDescription: Hairypink is a slender annual with small pink flowers and narrow leaves. It grows in open, dry, disturbed ground and can occur in pasture or along tracks. Its flowers are easy to overlook because a tight head may show only one open flower at a time. The brown bracts around that head remain useful for recognizing the plant after the bright petals have disappeared.
identification: Plants are commonly about 20-60 cm tall. Leaves sit in opposite pairs, with their bases joined into a sheath around the stem. The leaves are narrow and grasslike, but the swollen stem joints and five pink or purple petals show that this is not a grass. Each petal has a notched tip. Look for gland-tipped hairs on the middle part of the stem and compact flower heads enclosed by overlapping brown bracts. Related Petrorhagia species are similar, and hybrids with P. nanteuilii are reported. Photograph the stem hairs, leaf sheath and flowering head together rather than relying on flower color.
actions: Where removal is appropriate, pull small annual plants before their capsules ripen, keeping the flower heads together if seed may already be present. Check disturbed soil around the original patch later in the season. Avoid carrying mature heads on mowing equipment or in garden waste. In a species-rich grassland, obtain a positive identification before clearing fine-leaved plants that may include native pinks or grasses. Restoring appropriate ground cover can reduce the open patches where new seedlings establish.
researchNotes: Australian botanical descriptions and the Bishop Museum Hawaiian flora independently support habit, stem hairs, leaf sheaths and flower structure. Hybridization makes a species-level photograph identification less certain; no unsupported claim of nationwide invasiveness or quantified impact is added.

sources.title: Plants of South Eastern New South Wales: Petrorhagia dubia
Bishop Museum Plants of Hawaii: Petrorhagia dubia

claims: Annual with glandular middle stems, opposite narrow sheathing leaves and notched pink petals; hybrids occur.
Slender annual with swollen nodes, tight flower heads, sheathing leaves and glandular hairs.

proposedDescription: Hammer sedge, often called hairy sedge, is a perennial that can extend through the soil on long rhizomes. A patch may therefore consist of connected shoots rather than separate seedlings. It occurs in grassy and disturbed places, including damp ground. Its place in the local vegetation matters: it is native in parts of its range, so finding it is not by itself a reason to remove it.
identification: Look for narrow, hairy leaves and conspicuously hairy leaf sheaths around upright, three-sided stems. Lower sheaths may be reddish brown. The flower arrangement is especially useful: the upper spikes bear male flowers, while lower, often stalked spikes bear female flowers. As fruits develop, each is enclosed in a hairy, strongly veined sac with a long beak divided into two teeth. These sacs are about 5-9 mm long. Other hairy sedges can look similar before fruiting, so include a close photograph of a mature female spike and the leaf sheaths for confirmation.
actions: Mark the edge of a suspected spreading patch and obtain an identification while fruiting material is available. If the plant is unwanted and local guidance supports removal, lift a small patch carefully and trace its underground rhizomes; cutting leaves alone leaves those connections in place. Keep contaminated soil and root pieces out of clean beds. Revisit the area for new shoots. Seek site-specific advice before disturbing wet ground or removing sedges from a natural meadow, where neighboring plants may be valuable habitat.
researchNotes:
Flora of New Zealand and a separate New England Carex field guide support the rhizomatous habit and diagnostic hairy reproductive sacs. The catalog common name is retained, while the widely used hairy sedge name aids recognition. Actions are conditional on local status rather than assuming every sedge patch is invasive.

proposedDescription: Hardheads is also widely known as Russian knapweed. This perennial can build dense colonies through an extensive root system, with new shoots arising from buds below ground. A patch that appears to have been cleared can return from surviving roots. It is a particular concern in pasture and hay because it is poisonous to horses, making correct identification useful even where only a few stems are visible.
identification: Plants commonly stand about 30-90 cm tall and branch above their leafy bases. Lower leaves are lobed, while upper leaves are smaller and less divided; fine hairs can give foliage a gray-green appearance. Pink to lavender, occasionally white, flower heads sit at branch tips. The overlapping bracts below each head have smooth, papery margins rather than the conspicuous spines seen on some other knapweeds. Dark brown to black, scaly root crowns are another useful clue. Older references often use the name Acroptilon repens for this same plant.
actions: Keep suspected plants out of horse hay and obtain confirmation from a weed or forage adviser. Mark the full patch, including scattered shoots beyond its obvious edge. Avoid casually tilling it into pieces, because root fragments can produce new plants. Plan repeated treatment and follow-up with the local weed program; a single mowing is unlikely to remove the underground system. Re-establish suitable competitive vegetation after control and check equipment before moving from an affected field to a clean one.
researchNotes: Colorado State and Washington State's weed board independently describe creeping roots, papery flower bracts and horse toxicity. The catalog's Rhaponticum name is preserved, with Acroptilon explained as an older name. General integrated management is supported; dated product and biological-control availability statements are omitted.

proposedDescription: Hardy fuchsia is a woody shrub from southern South America, familiar in gardens for its hanging red-and-purple flowers. It can grow into a substantial shrub or scramble through surrounding vegetation. Cultivated plants are variable, and the name fuchsia also covers many hybrids and other species. An escape from a garden needs a closer look before it is recorded as Fuchsia magellanica.
identification: Leaves grow opposite one another or in groups of three around the stem. They are oval to lance-shaped with finely toothed edges. The flowers hang on slender stalks, usually singly or in pairs in the upper leaf axils. Their red or pink tube opens into four long red sepals surrounding shorter purple petals, with the stamens and style extending beyond them. Older stems develop brownish, peeling bark. Fruits become dark, elongated berries. Photograph the leaf arrangement, an entire flower from the side and any fruit; double-flowered or unusually colored garden forms can be harder to place.
actions: Before planting, check whether hardy fuchsia is an escape concern in your region. Watch beneath established shrubs and along nearby boundaries for seedlings or unwanted shoots. Remove small escapes with their roots when the soil can be disturbed without harming surrounding plants. Keep cut stems and fruiting material out of woodland edges, waterways and informal garden-waste piles. For a large established thicket, identify the plant first and agree on a removal and follow-up plan with the land manager.
researchNotes: Flora del Cono Sur provides detailed flower, leaf and fruit characters and the South American context. The Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria horticultural treatment independently documents cultivated variability and naturalization. The profile avoids assigning the behavior of every garden fuchsia hybrid to this species.

sources.title: Flora del Cono Sur: Fuchsia magellanica

claims: Opposite or three-whorled toothed leaves, red sepals, purple petals and dark elongated berries identify the shrub.
The species is an erect or scrambling shrub with variable cultivated forms and solitary or paired flowers.

proposedDescription: Hare's ear mustard is an annual mustard with unusually smooth, broad leaves clasping the stem. It grows in open disturbed ground and can be mistaken for a young crop mustard before flowering. Mature plants develop long, narrow seed pods above the leaves. Those pods, together with the way the leaves meet the stem, are much more useful for identification than a general impression of yellow flowers.
identification: Plants are often 10-50 cm tall, sparsely branched and bluish green, with little or no obvious hair. The leaves are fleshy, oval to spoon-shaped and generally lack teeth or deep lobes. Stem leaves wrap around the stem with rounded bases. Flowers have four pale yellow, yellow-green or whitish petals. Slender upright pods may reach 4-14 cm long and are approximately cylindrical to four-sided. Turnip and related crop mustards can also have clasping leaves, but often have brighter yellow flowers and a different leaf outline. Include both lower and upper leaves and a developed pod in photographs.
actions: Pull small unwanted plants while pods are still immature and remove the root crown with them. If pods are already dry, contain the seed-bearing stems before moving the plants. Recheck open soil for later seedlings and keep seed-bearing debris off cultivation equipment. In a crop field, confirm the identification before choosing a treatment, especially where planted brassicas or their volunteers are present. A local extension office can help distinguish a new weed record from an ordinary crop escape.
researchNotes: VicFlora supplies measured leaf, flower and pod characters. North Carolina's botanical account independently explains the clasping, unlobed leaves and confusion with Brassica rapa, including past misidentifications. Actions use the documented annual habit and seed production without implying proven regional abundance.

claims: Glaucous annual with fleshy clasping leaves, pale flowers and long slender pods.
Blunt unlobed leaves deeply clasp the stem; Brassica rapa can be confused with this species.

proposedDescription: Harestail grass is an annual grass with soft, oval flower heads that resemble small pale tails. It is native to the Mediterranean region and is also grown ornamentally. Dry sandy ground, tracks and disturbed coastal places suit it well. The same heads that make it attractive in a dried arrangement contain the structures that produce its next generation, so collecting or moving mature heads can move seed.
identification: The whole plant has a soft, gray-green appearance. Leaves and their enclosing sheaths are densely hairy, and the upper sheath may look inflated. Flower heads are compact, oval to somewhat elongated, commonly a few centimeters long, and densely covered with silky pale hairs. They may begin greenish or slightly purplish before becoming cream-colored. Other fluffy-headed grasses, including Polypogon species, can be confused with it; those often have more elongated heads and favor wetter places. Photograph the leaf sheath, the complete head and the base of the plant, because a detached decorative head loses useful clues.
actions: Check local planting guidance before using it in a garden near dunes or other open natural vegetation. Remove small unwanted plants before the heads mature, lifting the whole annual plant. If seed heads are already dry, bag them before carrying the plants away. Do not scatter dried arrangements outdoors or dump them at a beach access point. Recheck the patch for seedlings and retain appropriate surrounding vegetation rather than opening a large area of bare sand during removal.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand provides life history, hairiness and head dimensions. The University of the Balearic Islands independently describes dry sandy habitat and comparison with Polypogon. Practical prevention follows seed-bearing annual growth; it is not presented as a tested eradication program.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Lagurus ovatus
University of the Balearic Islands Virtual Herbarium: Lagurus ovatus

claims: Softly hairy annual with dense oval silky heads and an inflated upper sheath.
Dry sandy habitats and soft white oval heads distinguish it from many Polypogon grasses.

proposedDescription: Harmal peganum, more often called African rue or harmal, is a bushy perennial of dry ground. It can persist beside roads, in disturbed pasture and around heavily used farm areas. A deep root system makes an established plant much harder to remove than its small aboveground size suggests. Seeds and pieces of roots can move with soil or equipment, and the plant is toxic to livestock.
identification: Look for a rounded plant roughly 30-80 cm tall with bright green, hairless leaves divided into very narrow, fleshy segments. White flowers have five petals around a yellow center, backed by narrow green sepals. The fruit is a small rounded capsule divided into several chambers. Its fine leaves can suggest a young grasslike or feathery plant from a distance, but the five-petaled flowers and rounded capsules provide a better check. Photograph a whole branch with leaves, flower and fruit when available; do not identify it from dried fragments in hay alone.
actions: Keep suspect material out of feed and prevent animals from grazing the affected patch while identification and management are arranged. Avoid using cultivation or repeated chopping as an improvised fix, because surviving roots and fragments can regrow. For a small plant, careful removal may be possible, but follow-up is essential. An established patch warrants a multiyear plan with a local weed adviser. Clean soil from machinery before leaving it, use clean seed and maintain suitable vegetation around disturbed ground to reduce new establishment.
researchNotes: Nevada agriculture guidance supports the visible characters, toxicity and root persistence. Canadian plant-health guidance independently documents seed and root-fragment movement and prevention. New Mexico State's control guide supports the need to address the deep root system; no herbicide recipe or grazing treatment is supplied.

claims: White five-petaled flowers, finely divided fleshy leaves and rounded capsules; roots persist and all parts are toxic.
Seeds and root fragments move with equipment; clean seed and ground cover are preventive measures.

proposedDescription: Hawthorn mealybug is a small sap-feeding insect associated with woody plants such as hawthorn, mountain ash and serviceberry. Colonies can be concealed in bark crevices before becoming obvious on new twigs or leaves. Their sticky honeydew may be noticed before the insects themselves. Heavy populations can weaken twigs, but finding a few mealybugs does not establish the cause of every leaf or branch problem on a tree.
identification: Adult females are rounded, reddish insects about 3 mm long, partly covered by white wax. Younger stages are smaller and more elongated, with reddish-brown coloring. Examine protected bark cracks and twig undersides as well as foliage. In the seasonal pattern described by extension sources, immature insects overwinter under bark and females move onto twigs in spring. Apple mealybug can look similar, but has a raised ridge or crest along its back. A close photograph should show the insect's body beneath the wax and the plant it occupies; loose white wax alone is not a species identification.
actions: Check affected twigs for live insects, honeydew and actual dieback, and record whether the population is increasing. Inspect nearby susceptible plants before moving nursery stock. Preserve predators where possible and ask an extension service or arborist to identify a persistent infestation before treating the entire tree. Bark cracks and wax can shelter insects, so a treatment aimed only at exposed adults may miss much of the population. Choose any intervention for the confirmed pest and plant rather than treating every white deposit as a mealybug.
researchNotes: Colorado State provides body form, host associations and sheltering behavior. University of Illinois independently describes seasonal movement and the crest that helps distinguish apple mealybug. The draft does not generalize a local introduction history into a claim that the species is foreign throughout North America.

sources.title: Colorado State Agricultural Biology: Hawthorn mealybug
University of Illinois: Hawthorn and apple mealybug

claims: Globular red females carry white wax; colonies feed on woody Rosaceae and produce honeydew.
Insects overwinter in bark crevices and move onto twigs; apple mealybug has a raised dorsal crest.

proposedDescription: Hazel aphid is often called filbert aphid in orchard guidance. It feeds on hazel foliage and can leave sticky honeydew beneath a tree. Colonies may be inconspicuous when small, while heavy, sustained infestations can affect nut development. Hazel also supports other aphids, so a sticky leaf or a pale insect is a starting point for inspection rather than a firm identification.
identification: Look mainly on leaf undersides for small, pale yellow to light green aphids. Myzocallis coryli has much less prominent rear tubes, called cornicles, than the darker green hazelnut aphid Corylobium avellanae. The latter also has longer legs and often gathers along shoots and leaf midribs. Under magnification, the pale winged adults of M. coryli have dark rings on their antennae and a small dark mark near the leading edge of the forewing. Photograph several individuals and the part of the hazel they occupy. Tiny nymphs are harder to identify from color alone.
actions: Inspect a consistent set of leaves over time and note both aphids and their natural enemies. Ladybirds, hoverfly larvae, lacewings, predatory bugs and spiders have all been recorded in these colonies. Avoid disrupting them for a small, stable infestation. In a nut orchard, ask the local crop adviser how to assess sustained pressure and possible effects on the crop. Before moving nursery hazels, inspect the leaves and shoots and isolate plants with a substantial infestation until the problem has been assessed.
researchNotes: Pacific Northwest university guidance distinguishes filbert and hazelnut aphids and supports the crop-damage context. Independent field research in Poland documents predators in Myzocallis coryli colonies. A Scottish field survey supplies finer visible characters. No unverified virus-transmission claim is included.

Pale adults have ringed antennae and a dark mark by the forewing pterostigma.

proposedDescription: Heartleaf madeiravine is usually called Madeira vine. This long-lived climber has fleshy leaves and stems that wind through shrubs and trees. Established vines can cover and weigh down other vegetation. Its most important spread structures are the irregular tubers formed along the stems and below ground. A vine can therefore remain a problem after its visible canopy has been cut away.
identification: Leaves are glossy, smooth-edged and somewhat succulent, commonly with a heart-shaped base. Small fragrant white or cream flowers crowd into long hanging clusters. Look along older stems for rough, knobbly aerial tubers attached near the leaf joints; these are a much stronger clue than a heart-shaped leaf alone. The tubers may be greenish or brown and vary greatly in shape. Fleshy climbers such as Malabar spinach can resemble the foliage, so photograph the stem joints and flower clusters as well as a leaf.
actions: Do not start by pulling a large vine out of a tree: easily detached tubers can rain onto the ground and establish new plants. First map the affected area and arrange a method that contains falling tubers and plant fragments. Small plants may be lifted carefully with their underground tubers, but recheck the soil for missed pieces and new shoots. Keep all viable material away from waterways and ordinary garden-waste dumping areas. A canopy infestation needs a local weed professional's plan and repeated follow-up, not a single cutting visit.
researchNotes: NSW field guidance documents tubers, climbing habit and persistence. South Africa's Agricultural Research Council independently describes aerial-tuber reproduction, smothering and management difficulty. Fruitlessness is geographically qualified in the sources and is not made a universal species claim here.

sources.title: NSW Local Land Services: Weed identification guide, Madeira vine

claims: Fleshy heart-shaped leaves, hanging flowers and aerial tubers; tubers persist and spread with soil and garden waste.
Aerial tubers fall and root; vines smother vegetation and fragments complicate removal.

proposedDescription: Heath false brome is a perennial grass that forms tufts connected by wiry underground rhizomes. A spreading patch can become much denser than its individual flowering stems suggest. It belongs to a group of similar grasses, some native in the same regions where it occurs. Checking the species and the purpose of managing the site is essential before treating a patch in a meadow or woodland edge.
identification: Flowering stems are upright and fairly stiff. The seed head is narrow, with elongated, many-flowered spikelets attached on very short stalks along its central axis. Each small flower has a short bristle-like awn. Leaves are relatively stiff, and their underside is dull and rough rather than shining. The small membrane where a leaf blade meets its sheath, called the ligule, is useful under magnification. The closely related Brachypodium rupestre is particularly difficult to separate; regional keys compare ligule length and the fine prickles on the leaf underside. A whole flowering stem and close views of these details are more useful than a distant grassy patch.
actions: Mark the patch boundary and check whether it expands between visits. Seek a grass identification before mowing or removing vegetation in a natural site. If management is justified, plan for the connected rhizomes and follow-up regrowth rather than assuming one cut will remove the plant. Do not transfer soil containing rhizomes into clean areas. Keep mature seed-bearing material contained during work, and choose restoration plants suited to the local habitat so the cleared patch does not remain open ground.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand and the independent Flora of North America treatment describe the rhizomes and many-flowered spikelets. Swiss InfoFlora explicitly separates B. pinnatum from B. rupestre within an aggregate, supporting the diagnostic caution. The catalog remains at species level, not silently broadened to the aggregate.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Brachypodium pinnatum
Flora of North America treatment: Brachypodium pinnatum

claims: Rhizomatous perennial with stiff stems, narrow leaves and short-awned many-flowered spikelets.
Spikelets have very short stalks; leaves are rough and dull beneath.
Species-level distinction from B. rupestre uses ligule length and leaf-surface prickles.

proposedDescription: Heather is a small evergreen shrub that can turn open ground pink or purple when it flowers. It is a characteristic native plant of many European heathlands and moors, and also a widely planted ornamental. Outside its native setting it can escape cultivation. Its preference for open, acidic, nutrient-poor soils helps explain why the surroundings are as useful to record as the plant itself.
identification: The tiny leaves are usually only 1-3 mm long and look like overlapping scales pressed against the twig. They occur in opposite pairs, with successive pairs turned at right angles, forming four rows. Small pink, mauve or sometimes whitish flowers line the upper shoots. Garden cultivars vary in foliage and flower color. Many Erica species are also sold as heath or heather, but their leaves are typically longer and more needle-like, often arranged in whorls. Take a close side view of a leafy twig and a flowering shoot; a distant pink mound is not enough to separate these shrubs.
actions: Check local advice before planting heather near heathland, bogs or open upland habitat. If it is an unwanted escape, record seedlings beyond the planted area and remove small plants before they set seed, taking care not to damage the surrounding ground. Monitor the patch afterward for new growth. Do not use burning as a casual garden control method: heather's response to fire is complex and seedlings or shoots can reappear. In native heathland, management should follow the site's conservation plan rather than treating the species itself as a weed.
researchNotes: University of Connecticut and KPU botanical teaching accounts independently describe scale leaves and differences from Erica. USDA Forest Service ecology supports acidic open habitats and postfire regeneration. Native habitat value and introduced-population management are distinguished without asserting current presence at an unspecified site.

sources.title: University of Connecticut: Heath and heather
USDA Forest Service FEIS: Calluna vulgaris

claims: Calluna has tiny opposite scale-like leaves and small pink-purple flowers; Erica leaves are more needle-like.
Opposite leaf pairs rotate at right angles, producing four rows on the twig.
Heather occupies open acidic nutrient-poor habitats and can regenerate after fire.

proposedDescription: Hedgehog gourd is an annual climbing or trailing plant in the cucumber family. Its pale green fruit is densely covered in soft bristles and becomes yellow as it ripens. The species comes from tropical Africa and has been carried to other warm regions. It can grow in disturbed ground and cultivated places, where its trailing stems may become mixed with other vines before the distinctive fruits appear.
identification: Stems are angular and rough with stiff, spreading hairs, especially along the ridges. Leaves are broad, roughly heart-shaped at the base, and toothed around the edge; they may be unlobed or shallowly divided into three rounded lobes. Leaf stalks are conspicuously long and hairy. Bright yellow flowers develop near the leaf joints. Mature fruits are oval, usually about 4-6 cm long, with dense soft bristles covering most of the surface. Other Cucumis species can also have prickly fruit, so photograph the fruit, leaf shape and stem hairs together. A young vine without fruit may need a botanical key.
actions: Do not assume an unfamiliar wild cucumber is edible because it resembles a cultivated vegetable. For a small unwanted patch, identify the vine and remove it before fruits ripen, collecting any developed fruit rather than leaving it on the soil. Check among nearby plants for additional stems and later seedlings. Keep fruit and seed-bearing material contained during disposal. At a nursery, field or restoration site, record where the vine appeared and inspect incoming soil or plant material before moving it onward.
researchNotes: Kew's African flora treatments describe annual growth, yellow flowers and bristly fruit. NSW Flora independently supplies leaf, stem and fruit characters from Australian material. Edibility and medicinal-use listings are not turned into consumption advice, and local invasive status is not inferred from the catalog.

sources.title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Cucumis dipsaceus, African flora descriptions

evidence.independentSourceGroup: African floras via Royal Botanic Gardens Kew
claims: Annual climbing or trailing herb with yellow flowers, bristly stems and oval fruits that turn yellow.
Broad toothed leaves have long hairy stalks; 4-6 cm fruits are densely covered in soft bristles.

proposedDescription: Hedgemustard is an annual of open, disturbed ground, including field margins, roadsides and neglected garden edges. It starts with divided leaves near the ground and later sends up a branching stem with small yellow flowers. Its most distinctive feature appears as the flowers fade: short, slender pods lie tightly against the stem, making a fruiting branch look noticeably different from many other mustards.
identification: Plants are often about 30-100 cm tall and have stiff hairs on stems and leaves. The lower leaves are deeply divided, with a broad terminal lobe and smaller side lobes. Upper leaves become smaller and more narrowly lobed. Flowers have four small yellow petals, only about 3-4 mm long. The seed pods are commonly around 1 cm long, narrow gradually toward their tips and sit on short, stout stalks pressed close to the flowering axis. Mustards with long spreading pods are likely to be something else. Photograph both the lower leaf shape and a fruiting branch to make identification easier.
actions: Pull or hoe young unwanted plants before pods mature. Once the pods have dried, handle the stem gently and contain it before moving it through a clean bed or field margin. Check the same disturbed soil for later seedlings. Keep crop borders and nursery containers under observation, since small plants can be overlooked until their stems elongate. If the plant is among cultivated brassicas or uncommon native mustards, seek identification before broad treatment. Preventing seed production is more useful than merely removing the yellow flowers after pods have already formed.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand and the University of Washington Burke Herbarium independently describe the annual habit, divided leaves and tightly appressed pods. Identification is centered on reproductive structure, avoiding a generic yellow-mustard description or unsupported food and medicinal claims.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Sisymbrium officinale

claims: Hairy annual with divided leaves, small yellow flowers and tapering pods appressed to the stem.
Short stout fruit stalks and tightly erect pods distinguish this disturbed-ground annual.

proposedDescription: Hemerocallis aphid is a small, pale aphid associated especially with daylilies, and it also occurs on Agapanthus and some other ornamental hosts. Colonies can feed near the base of leaves, where they are easy to miss during a quick inspection of flowers. Heavy feeding can distort or discolor foliage, buds and flowers, while honeydew leaves affected surfaces sticky. The amount of damage varies, so inspect the insects and new growth together.
identification: Wingless adults are pale yellow-green to greenish white and approximately 1.6-2.4 mm long. Color alone will not distinguish them from other pale aphids on daylilies. Specialists compare the two rear tubes, or cornicles, with the small tail-like projection between them: in this species the tubes are long, slender and cylindrical or tapering toward their tips. Green peach aphid has relatively shorter, more swollen tubes. These proportions and surface details require magnification. Include the host plant name, a close view of several insects and the part of the plant where the colony is feeding.
actions: Inspect the bases of new leaves and developing flower shoots before dividing or sharing daylilies. Keep substantially infested plants apart from clean nursery stock while seeking identification and appropriate management advice. Record distorted growth and honeydew, and check whether live colonies remain before repeating any intervention. Avoid moving affected divisions to another garden. If this is an unfamiliar pest in a commercial collection, send photographs or a requested sample to the plant diagnostic service. These steps reduce movement of infested plants without assuming that every pale aphid is this species.
researchNotes:
Blackman and Eastop's specialist descriptions and host key provide size, color and diagnostic cornicle comparisons. Julius Kuehn-Institut independently assesses movement on host plants, feeding damage and establishment risk using reported outbreaks. Its dated legal assessment is not presented as current regulation, and virus transmission is not assumed.

Long cylindrical or tapering cornicles distinguish it from the shorter swollen cornicles of M. persicae.
Aphids move with host plants and can cause damaged foliage, buds and flowers and honeydew.

proposedDescription: Hemp aphid, also called cannabis aphid, feeds on leaves and stems of Cannabis plants. Colonies can build quickly, leaving honeydew and pale shed skins on the crop. Heavy feeding may cause yellowing, wilting and reduced plant vigor. Both indoor and outdoor plantings can be affected, and moving infested planting material can carry a colony into a new growing area.
identification: Adults are small, soft-bodied insects roughly 2 mm long, with long antennae and two rear-facing tubes. Color changes with season and life stage: pale cream or yellow forms may be followed by greenish, pinkish or light brown ones. Some have faint lengthwise green stripes. The close relative hop aphid looks very similar. Both can have small horn-like projections near the antenna bases, but hemp aphid has distinctive swollen-tipped hairs that need a microscope to see clearly. Other aphids also occur on hemp, so host plant and color alone do not confirm the species.
actions: Examine leaf undersides and stems regularly, keeping track of live colonies, shed skins and beneficial insects. Hold infested cuttings or plants back from sale or transfer until the infestation has been assessed. In a crop, ask an extension specialist to confirm the aphid and select management suited to the growing system and crop use. Protect natural enemies where possible. Before choosing any pesticide, verify that the product is permitted for that crop and location; recommendations for another aphid or a different crop cannot simply be transferred to hemp.
researchNotes: North Carolina State documents seasonal appearance, reproduction and microscopic separation from hop aphid. Oregon agriculture guidance independently supports movement precautions and the diagnostic swollen-tipped hairs. The draft avoids unsupported disease-vector claims and does not repeat old distribution limits as current facts.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Cannabis aphid in industrial hemp
Oregon Department of Agriculture: Cannabis aphid pest alert

claims: Seasonal color varies; colonies feed on leaves and stems; hop aphid requires microscopic comparison.
Swollen-tipped hairs distinguish hemp aphid from hop aphid; infested plants should not be distributed.

proposedDescription: Hemp-leaf ragwort is a tall, leafy perennial from South America. Its deeply divided leaves and clusters of yellow flower heads can make it stand out above surrounding pasture plants. The species is important in livestock management because poisoning has been documented in cattle, and material mixed into hay is a concern. Wind-carried seeds also make a flowering patch worth noticing before it begins to disperse.
identification: Plants commonly reach about 1-2 m tall and branch toward their upper parts. Leaves alternate along the stem and are divided nearly to the midrib into a few pairs of long, very narrow segments. The terminal flower clusters contain many small yellow heads, each with short yellow ray florets around a central disk. Mature fruits carry white hairs that help them travel in the wind. Other ragworts and groundsels also have yellow heads; the tall leafy habit and finely cut leaves help narrow the choice, but a botanist should check the whole flowering plant.
actions: Keep suspected plants and contaminated cuttings out of livestock feed, and ask a forage adviser or plant diagnostic service to confirm the identification. If an animal may have eaten the plant, contact a veterinarian rather than waiting for visible illness. For a newly found patch, record its size and flowering stage and consult the local weed authority about removal before seed dispersal. Contain mature seed heads during handling, remove the plant thoroughly where practical and monitor for regrowth and seedlings. Do not use livestock grazing as an improvised control method.
researchNotes: EPPO's species assessment provides the deeply divided leaf and flower characters, seed dispersal and hay concern. An independent Brazilian field-outbreak study documents S. brasiliensis involvement in cattle poisoning and delayed or acute disease courses. European establishment risk is not converted into a claim of widespread invasion elsewhere.

sources.title: Mendez and colleagues: Senecio poisoning in cattle in southern Brazil

claims: Tall perennial with deeply divided narrow leaf segments and yellow heads; wind-dispersed seeds and hay contamination are concerns.
S. brasiliensis was implicated in field outbreaks; illness included chronic and acute courses with liver lesions.

proposedDescription: Hen's eyes is more commonly known as coral ardisia. This evergreen shrub was planted for its glossy foliage and hanging clusters of red fruit, but it can escape into moist, shaded woodland. In Florida, dense stands are a recognized invasive-plant problem. Its fruit often remains conspicuous long after flowering, making winter a useful time to look beneath the leaves for an overlooked plant.
identification: The shrub usually has several stems and can grow to about 2 m tall. Leaves alternate along the stems and are shiny, dark green, oval to narrowly elliptical, with a distinctly scalloped edge. Small swellings occur in the notches along that edge. Pale pink or white flowers hang in clusters beneath the foliage and develop into rounded, usually bright red fruits; white-fruited plants also occur. Shoebutton ardisia can look similar, but its leaf margins lack the same scalloping and its ripe fruit becomes dark rather than red. Photograph the leaf edge and the fruit cluster together.
actions: Where coral ardisia is an unwanted escape, remove young plants with their roots before they build a fruiting population. Contain ripe fruit during the work and check beneath nearby parent shrubs for seedlings. Do not move fruiting branches into woodland waste piles or share plants from an affected site. Established clumps need a removal plan and follow-up for surviving plants and new seedlings. Ask the local extension or invasive-plant program for a method suited to the woodland or pasture involved, and verify local planting restrictions before buying or distributing it.
researchNotes: Florida agriculture and University of Florida provide detailed identification and the documented Florida invasion context. An independent South African botanical treatment confirms evergreen habit, leaf margins and persistent red fruits. Management avoids making a definitive poisoning claim from a source that labels the plant only potentially toxic.
