proposedDescription: Henbit is a small annual in the mint family that often appears during cool weather in gardens, thin lawns and cultivated ground. It can flower while still quite low, producing pink-purple tubes among rounded leaves. Many plants establish in autumn and flower the following spring, although spring-germinating plants also occur. Its ability to set seed while growing close to the ground makes early recognition helpful.
identification: Stems are square in cross-section and may be green or purplish. Leaves grow in opposite pairs and have rounded, scalloped edges with a visibly crinkled surface. Lower leaves have stalks, while upper leaves attach directly and clasp the stem. The pink to purple flowers emerge in groups from those upper leaf axils. Purple deadnettle has more triangular upper leaves on stalks, often with a purple tint. Ground ivy also has rounded leaves, but its leaves remain stalked and its creeping growth is more conspicuous. Compare the upper leaves, rather than relying only on flower color.
actions: Pull or shallowly hoe small unwanted plants before they make mature seed, including the low spreading portions at the base. Check again during the next cool growing period. In lawn areas, repair thin patches and choose turf or another ground cover suited to the available light; repeatedly treating henbit without addressing bare ground leaves room for another generation. In a crop, use the grower's weed-management plan and confirm the plant before treatment. Keep removal proportionate to the site, since a few plants outside a crop or formal bed may not require broad control.
researchNotes: University of Wisconsin explains cool-season growth, lookalikes and lawn competition. University of Missouri independently details square stems, petioled lower leaves, clasping upper leaves and flowers. Sources differ on how much low stems root, so the draft emphasizes visible leaf distinctions without asserting that rooting never occurs.

claims: Cool-season annual habit; upper clasping leaves distinguish henbit from other deadnettles and ground ivy.
Square stems bear stalked lower and stalkless upper leaves; pink-purple tubular flowers arise in upper leaf whorls.

proposedDescription: Herb sophia, also called flixweed, is a mustard that starts as a low rosette before sending up a slender, branching flowering stem. Its finely cut foliage gives disturbed ground a gray-green, almost fernlike cover. It reproduces by seed and can compete with crops, especially where soil is regularly disturbed. Recognizing the rosette makes removal easier than waiting until the plant has a full crop of narrow pods.
identification: Look for alternate leaves divided repeatedly into narrow segments, with fine branched hairs on the leaves and stems. Tiny pale yellow flowers have four petals. The long, thin seed pods stand on slender stalks along the flowering branches. Pinnate tansymustard can look similar, but generally has less finely divided leaves and shorter pods. Ragweed has greenish flower clusters rather than these yellow mustard flowers. Photograph a whole plant, a lower leaf, and mature pods together; foliage alone is less useful for separating related mustards.
actions: Remove unwanted plants while they are still rosettes or before pods mature, and check the same patch for later seedlings. Collect plants with developing seed rather than scattering them through mowing or soil movement. Keep disturbed ground covered where practical. In crops, match control to the crop and the weed growth stage with local extension advice. Keep flowering plants out of livestock forage; UC IPM reports that large quantities can be toxic to cattle. A suspected feeding exposure belongs with a veterinarian.
researchNotes: Ontario and Cornell independently describe the foliage, life cycle and lookalikes. UC IPM supports the livestock warning. Seed prevention is a practical priority for this seed-reproducing weed; no county presence or universal control prescription is inferred.

claims: Gray-green finely divided leaves, star-like stem hairs and seed reproduction.
Winter annual or biennial habit; pinnate tansymustard has less divided leaves and shorter fruit.
Rosette stage and potential cattle toxicity when flowering plants are consumed in quantity.

proposedDescription: Hessian fly is a small fly whose larvae feed on wheat stems beneath the leaf sheaths. Infested young wheat may stay short and unusually dark green, while damage higher on older stems can leave plants weak enough to lodge. The adult is easy to overlook. Finding the immature stages at the base of the plant or near a stem joint is more useful than trying to identify a passing fly.
identification: Adults are delicate, mosquito-like flies about one-eighth inch long. Newly hatched larvae are reddish or orange, becoming pale as they feed. Their brown resting cases resemble small flax seeds and sit against the stem under a leaf sheath. Carefully peel back sheaths on affected tillers and photograph these cases in place. Drought, nutrient problems and other insects can also stunt wheat, so leaf color and lodging alone do not establish Hessian fly damage. A crop specialist can check a sample containing both the stem and the suspected larvae.
actions: Scout affected patches and record the variety, planting date and stage of the crop. Once established stem damage is apparent, a rescue spray is not a dependable answer. For the next crop, use locally tested resistant varieties, control volunteer wheat, and discuss planting dates with extension. Traditional fly-free dates are regional guides whose performance can change with warm autumn weather. Resistance also varies among fly populations, so use current local ratings rather than assuming a variety resistant elsewhere will protect your field.
researchNotes: Oklahoma State supplies diagnostic stages and symptoms; Kansas State and Penn State independently support preventive management and limitations of historical planting dates. No fixed calendar date or pesticide program is transferred across regions.

proposedDescription: Hibiscus snow scale is an armored scale insect that feeds on many kinds of woody and herbaceous plants. A heavy colony can look like white flecks spread over stems and foliage. The white material is the insects' protective covering, not a fungus. Hibiscus is only one possible host, so a plant name alone cannot identify this scale. Several similar Pinnaspis species require close examination to separate.
identification: Female covers are small, elongated and often slightly curved, roughly resembling a narrow mussel shell. The conspicuous male covers are white and felted. Crawlers are the mobile young stage; after settling on a feeding site, they build a cover and become much harder to notice as insects. Examine both leaf surfaces and young stems with a hand lens. Other snow scales can produce nearly identical white colonies. Keep clear photographs of the host and scale arrangement, but expect a diagnostic laboratory to need adult females for a firm species identification.
actions: Set a suspect nursery plant apart from other stock and avoid sharing cuttings until its identity is checked. Inspect neighboring plants, including different species, because this insect has a broad host range. Remove heavily affected disposable plant material only where that is practical, and contain it for local disposal. Ask extension or a plant diagnostic service about live-scale assessment and crawler monitoring before treatment. White covers can remain after an insect dies, so judge continuing infestation by living insects and fresh growth, not the number of old covers alone.
researchNotes: The UK overseas-territories field guide supports host breadth, cover form, crawler behavior and laboratory identification. The UNAM treatment independently describes female and male covers. Isolation and diagnostic submission are prudent containment steps, not a claim of proven eradication.

proposedDescription: High mallow is a tall, spreading herb with conspicuous pink to purple flowers. It grows as a biennial or perennial and is associated with gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Its flowers and rounded leaves resemble several other mallows, including low garden weeds. A flowering stem usually gives a clearer identification than a young rosette. A cultivated plant is not, by itself, evidence that the species is spreading locally.
identification: Leaves are alternate, rounded to kidney-shaped, and shallowly divided into about five to seven toothed lobes. Flowers sit in groups where leaves meet the stems. Each has five broad petals with a notch at the tip and darker purple veins running toward the center. The fruit forms a flat ring of small segments, often described as a cheese wheel. In high mallow, mature segments have a conspicuous netlike surface. Smaller-flowered mallows can share the leaf shape and ring-shaped fruit, so include a flower-size reference and ripe fruit in photographs.
actions: If the plant is unwanted, remove young plants before the fruits harden and release seed. In a garden, remove spent flowering stems if you want to limit self-seeding. Check disturbed edges and moved soil for new seedlings rather than assuming one removal finishes the job. Where the plant is established outside cultivation, document its extent before choosing a larger removal project. Keep the identification separate from decisions about local weed status, and avoid collecting it as food on the strength of a common name.
researchNotes: Flora of Victoria and the University of the Basque Country independently support flower, leaf and fruit characters and disturbed habitats. Actions are modest seed-containment measures; neither source establishes a need for broad control in every location.

proposedDescription: Highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza is a disease caused by particular influenza A viruses. The scientific name Influenza A virus is broader than this disease: it includes many viruses that are not highly pathogenic H5 bird flu. This overview concerns that narrower H5 disease. It can affect wild and domestic birds and some mammals. An animal can carry an avian influenza virus without showing obvious illness, so appearance cannot confirm freedom from infection.
identification: There is no field mark that identifies the virus. In poultry, warning signs can include sudden deaths, reduced feeding or egg production, breathing difficulty, swelling or discoloration around the head, and poor coordination. Those signs overlap with other illnesses. Wild birds may appear weak, uncoordinated or be found dead, but a single dead bird does not establish H5 infection. Laboratory testing through animal-health authorities is needed to identify the virus and its subtype. Observe from a distance and record the location, animal species and number affected.
actions: Avoid direct contact with sick or dead birds and other potentially infected animals, and keep pets away. Report unusual poultry illness to a veterinarian or state animal-health office; report sick or dead wildlife through the local wildlife agency. Do not move animals or collect carcasses for testing without instructions. If you have had an unprotected exposure, contact your health department for current guidance. If illness follows an exposure, seek medical advice promptly and tell the clinician about the animal contact. Follow current CDC and USDA advice because outbreak guidance can change.

proposedDescription: Hiller's spider beetle is associated with stored products and accumulated food residues. An Australian government assessment describes it as a likely scavenger and a potential minor pest of feed mills and warehouses. That is a narrower claim than saying it routinely damages sound grain. Finding a spider beetle indoors is a reason to look for an infested material or hidden residue, but the exact species still needs confirmation.
identification: Adults are about two to three millimeters long, dark reddish brown, with a narrowing front portion that gives the body a gourd-like outline. Fine golden hairs occur in sparse rows on the wing covers. The Agriculture Canada key distinguishes this beetle by the hind trochanter, a small leg segment, reaching the wing-cover margin. Those details require magnification and comparison with other spider beetles. Photograph the insect beside a scale and keep it contained for an entomologist. Record whether it emerged directly from stored food or was merely walking nearby.
actions: Inspect the product where the beetle was found and nearby dry foods, animal feed and spilled material. Isolate suspect packages, clean accessible cracks and shelf edges, and store unaffected goods in tightly closed containers. In a warehouse, retain the product name, lot and location so inspection can follow the source. Do not treat a whole room based only on one unidentified beetle. These are general stored-product hygiene measures; a specialist should confirm this species and determine whether an active infestation is present.
researchNotes:
The Agriculture Canada Bousquet key adds an exact adult diagnosis and documented warehouse/feed-mill context. Nagoya's municipal account independently describes 2-3 mm dark reddish-brown adults and scavenging-associated storage occurrences. The Australian assessment overlaps Bousquet for occurrence and is not counted as another independent study. Nagoya supplies a separate practical account; hygiene remains general prevention. proposedDescription: Himalayan balsam is a tall annual of moist ground, particularly stream margins and other places where water can carry its seeds. Large pink to purplish flowers hang from soft, upright stems. Mature seed capsules burst open, throwing seeds away from the parent. Dense stands can leave little space for other low vegetation, then die back at the end of the season. Preventing another seed crop is central to managing an established patch.
identification: Look for hollow, easily broken stems that are often reddish, with swollen joints. Long, pointed leaves have sharply toothed edges and grow in opposite pairs or groups of three. Small glands occur near the bases of the leaf stalks. The flowers have a deep, helmetlike shape and a short curved spur; white-flowered plants also occur. Native jewelweeds share soft stems and explosive fruits, so check the leaf arrangement and flower form rather than identifying every touch-me-not as Himalayan balsam. Photograph leaves attached to the stem as well as a side view of a flower.
actions: Work before seed capsules mature. Small plants can be pulled with their roots where access and soil conditions allow, but arrange disposal so pulled plants do not reroot or finish ripening seeds. Return to the patch for missed plants and new growth through the season. Along streams, coordinate with the land manager and neighboring sites because seeds can arrive from upstream. Avoid trampling banks or leaving large areas of bare soil. Restore suitable ground cover after removal and keep watching in later seasons.
researchNotes: USGS provides diagnostic structure and life history. Swedish Environmental Protection Agency guidance independently supports mechanical removal before seed spread. The sources concern different regions; their legal classifications are not transferred to the reader's location.

proposedDescription: Himalayan berry is a vigorous blackberry that forms tangled thickets of long, prickly canes. It spreads both through seed in its fruit and where cane tips root into the ground. Established patches can block paths and overgrow other vegetation. The name Rubus bifrons is used for Himalayan blackberry by the regional management sources consulted here; blackberry naming has changed across sources, so an older label should be checked against its actual species treatment.
identification: The stout canes arch outward and carry strong prickles. Leaves are divided into broad, toothed leaflets, commonly five on first-year canes and three on flowering growth. Clusters of white to pale pink flowers develop into glossy black aggregate fruits. Cutleaf blackberry has deeply divided, lacy leaflets. Native trailing blackberry is generally more slender and trails close to the ground, but leaf shape and cane habit should be considered together. Photograph both sides of a complete leaf, a cane with prickles, and flowers or fruit rather than relying on the berries alone.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and protective clothing, and plan how to reach the root crowns safely. For a small patch, cut access through the canes and remove crowns where feasible; substantial root pieces can resprout. Cutting alone needs repeated follow-up. Check for rooted cane tips beyond the main patch and dispose of material without leaving viable pieces against moist soil. On banks or wildlife habitat, stage removal and replace cover rather than stripping the entire site at once. Check for active nests before clearing dense growth.
researchNotes: King County and Metro Vancouver independently provide practical identification and management. King County treats R. armeniacus and R. discolor as former names for its R. bifrons concept; that regional usage is recorded without silently changing catalog taxonomy. No local legal duty or presence is inferred.

proposedDescription: Himalayan grain moth is a small moth that can use stored grain, but its larvae also feed in decaying organic material. A moth attracted to a porch light does not show that a nearby pantry is infested. The North Carolina species account describes it as a minor stored-grain pest and notes that its outdoor habitats are poorly documented. This is a species for which careful identification matters more than the common name suggests. The accepted name currently includes a provisional synonym, M. ravicapitis; unresolved variation means a specialist should qualify difficult records.
identification: Adults are ocher-brown with a heavy dark overlay on the head, body and forewings. The forewing has small dark spots, including a pair near its basal third, and the antennae have narrow rings. These subtle marks can be hard to see on worn moths. Related Martyringa species may require examination of structural characters, including genitalia, by a specialist. Take sharp dorsal and side photographs before disturbing the moth, and retain the date and whether it was found in grain, compost, decaying wood or at light. A Japanese comparative study also separates xeraula larvae from M. ussuriella by microscopic arrangements of eyes and body hairs. Those features require a specialist and do not turn a pantry photograph into a confirmed identification.
actions: If larvae or adults are emerging from a stored product, isolate that container and inspect nearby materials for activity. Remove spilled grain and residues, and use tightly closing containers for unaffected food or feed. Keep a specimen and its product association for identification before considering treatment. If a single adult was outdoors, a photograph and location record are more useful than treating the surrounding vegetation. These steps address a possible stored-product infestation; they are not evidence that this moth requires control wherever it is found.

proposedDescription: Himalayan honeysuckle is an upright shrub with drooping clusters of pale flowers framed by dark purple bracts. Its berries ripen through red to purple-black and can be carried away by birds. It is grown ornamentally, but escaped plants can form persistent patches in suitable climates. Despite the common name, it has a distinctive cane-forming habit and is not a twining honeysuckle vine.
identification: Stems arise together from the base and are green, relatively soft and hollow when young. Large leaves grow in opposite pairs and end in long points; their bases may be heart-shaped. The hanging flower clusters are particularly useful: short white to purplish tubes sit among conspicuous purple leaflike bracts. A cluster can hold berries at several stages of ripening at once. Hollow stems alone can suggest knotweed, but the paired leaves and drooping purple-bracted flowers distinguish this shrub from typical knotweeds.
actions: Check beneath nearby shrubs and bird perches for seedlings if a fruiting plant is escaping its planting bed. Remove young unwanted plants with their roots while they are manageable, and contain fruiting material so berries do not scatter. Established plants can regrow after cutting, so revisit cut sites rather than treating a bare stump as completion. For a large patch, ask a local weed service about root removal or an approved treatment plan. Replace cleared cover with suitable plants and keep garden waste out of gullies, stream margins and natural areas.
researchNotes: Oregon State supports habit, paired leaves, flower clusters and berry development; the independent Australian weed treatment supports hollow stems and detailed morphology. Auckland Council supports follow-up and revegetation. Management is framed for unwanted or escaping plants, not as a blanket claim of invasive status.

claims: Opposite pointed leaves; pendulous purple-bracted flowers; berries change from green through maroon to black-purple.
Hollow green stems; deciduous multistemmed shrub; tubular flowers and dark berries.
Follow-up treatments and replanting dense ground cover can reduce reinvasion.

proposedDescription: Hiptage is a woody perennial that can grow as a shrub in open ground or climb high into surrounding trees. Its clusters of fragrant flowers are followed by distinctive winged fruits. In warm, moist settings, climbing growth can cover other vegetation, and wind or water can carry the fruits beyond the original planting. The fruit is often the easiest feature to recognize when a large vine has flowers out of reach.
identification: Leaves are opposite, oval to elongated, and shiny on the upper surface. The pale flowers have pink and yellow markings and fringed petal edges. Each mature fruit has three broad, papery wings of unequal size around its seed-bearing center, rather than the two-winged pair familiar from many maples. Photograph a complete fruit, a flower and a leaf pair still attached to the stem. Several tropical vines have opposite leaves, so the foliage alone is less distinctive than the combination of flowers and three-winged fruit.
actions: Prevent an unwanted plant from producing and dispersing fruit. Pull isolated seedlings when the soil allows the roots to come out, collecting stem and root fragments. Do not haul fruiting vines through uninfested areas. Large vines intertwined with trees need a planned removal; pulling the entire canopy down can damage supporting trees or people below. Contact a local weed specialist for a treatment suited to the site, especially near water. Recheck for seedlings and regrowth, and use locally suitable vegetation to fill cleared gaps.
researchNotes: Queensland government and the Indian Institute of Science independently support habit, paired leaves, flowers and winged fruit. Queensland supports hand removal of young plants and wind/water dispersal. Its pesticide permits and legal restrictions are not presented as applicable outside that jurisdiction.

proposedDescription: Hispid starbur is a rough-haired, branching annual whose small yellow flower heads turn into hard, prickly fruits. It grows in disturbed ground and cultivated places, and its burrs can cling to wool, clothing and harvested material. The flowers are easy to miss, while mature fruits can make an unnoticed patch troublesome to walk or work through. Removing plants before those burrs harden helps limit further movement.
identification: The plant stands upright and branches repeatedly. Opposite leaves are broadly oval, hairy and coarsely toothed, sometimes narrowing toward the stem without a clear stalk. Tiny yellow flower heads occur near the leaf junctions. The wedge-shaped fruits carry hooked prickles and two longer, spreading spines at the upper end. This combination is more useful than the common name, since several unrelated burr plants are called starbur. The related Acanthospermum australe generally has a lower, spreading habit and lacks the same pair of prominent long fruit spines.
actions: Wear gloves around fruiting plants and collect burrs before moving through a clean area. Small patches can be removed before fruit maturity, taking care not to shake ripe burrs onto the ground. Check shoes, clothing, animal coats and equipment after working in an affected patch. In a crop, record whether burrs are already entering harvested material and seek crop-specific advice before treatment. Revisit recently disturbed soil for seedlings. Keep identification samples contained so the very feature needed for diagnosis does not spread the plant.
researchNotes: The NSW flora supplies fruit anatomy and wool-contamination evidence; the Indian Institute of Science independently describes leaves and heads. A Paraguayan weed manual supplies the explicit A. australe comparison. Actions target seed-bearing burr movement without claiming a tested eradication method.

proposedDescription: Hoary alyssum is a grayish, hairy mustard that grows in dry, disturbed ground, pastures and hay fields. Plants may live for one season or persist longer, but spread is through seed. It is especially important to recognize where horses graze or hay is made because it can be toxic to horses, including in dried forage. A small white-flowered plant in a hay field deserves a closer look before cutting.
identification: Stems are upright and often branch near the top, usually reaching about one to three feet. The oblong leaves and stems have fine, star-shaped hairs that give the plant a pale cast. Each white flower has four petals, but deep notches split their tips so the flower can seem to have eight. Hairy, oval seed pods swell below the flowers and end in a short point. Other white-flowered mustards can look similar at a distance. Check the divided petal tips, gray foliage and inflated pods together.
actions: Keep suspect forage away from horses until the plant is identified. If horses may have eaten contaminated hay or pasture, contact a veterinarian immediately and retain a forage sample. Remove small patches before seed production, including the root crown, and inspect again for seedlings. Maintain useful pasture cover and avoid moving seed in hay or machinery. For a hay field or extensive pasture infestation, develop a local weed-management plan before harvest. Drying or baling should not be treated as making contaminated material safe.
researchNotes:
University of Minnesota supports identification and equine forage risk; British Columbia independently describes morphology and habitat. Montana weed guidance explicitly notes toxicity in cured hay and root-crown removal. No safe dietary percentage or veterinary treatment is inferred.

2026-11-01 safety continuity review: New wording makes visible illness a prerequisite for veterinary advice despite possible delayed symptoms. Current source-specific support is recorded in the publication safety audit.

proposedDescription: The name hoe nightshade has been applied to small, hairy nightshades of cultivated and disturbed ground, and historical scientific-name usage needs careful interpretation. Older regional floras used Solanum physalifolium broadly, including plants now treated as Solanum nitidibaccatum. Recent North American floristic work excludes true S. physalifolium from that region. A useful report should therefore preserve photographs and specimens rather than turn an old name into a confident local identification.
identification: Plants covered by the older treatments are low, branching herbs without prickles, with hairy oval leaves, small white star-shaped flowers and rounded berries. Gland-tipped hairs and the green calyx surrounding the developing fruit are important details. The amount of calyx expansion, berry surface and mature fruit characters help separate related black nightshades, but their interpretation depends on the taxonomic treatment. Photograph stem hairs under magnification, open flowers and ripe fruits together. A green berry or a fuzzy leaf alone cannot distinguish this historical species concept from its close relatives.
actions: Keep uncertain nightshade fruits out of food and animal feed. If the plant is unwanted in a garden, remove it before ripe berries scatter and keep fruiting material contained. For a distribution record or a crop diagnosis, ask a herbarium or extension botanist to check the material against a current key. Include the name of any older reference used. Do not spread the plant by moving soil containing berries, but postpone species-specific claims about invasiveness or range until the name is resolved.

proposedDescription: Holly oak is a Mediterranean evergreen tree with a dense crown and leathery leaves. Young leaves can be sharply toothed like holly, while older growth may carry nearly smooth-edged leaves on the same tree. Its acorns reveal that it is an oak. It is planted as a shade or street tree in suitable climates, and its presence in cultivation should be distinguished from seedlings establishing beyond the planting.
identification: Leaves are alternate, typically a few inches long, dark and glossy above, and pale with fine felted hairs underneath. Their shape ranges from oval to narrow and pointed. Acorns are elongated to oval and sit in cups covered with small, closely pressed scales, often enclosing roughly half the nut. Coast live oak can have a similar evergreen habit and toothed foliage. Examine the leaf undersides and acorn cups together rather than relying on spiny margins. Photograph both juvenile and mature foliage if they differ strongly on the tree.
actions: For a suspected escape, record whether the tree was planted and look for independently rooted seedlings beyond its canopy. Pull only unwanted seedlings that you can remove safely and identify confidently; native oaks may be mixed among them. A mature tree needs an arborist and a site-specific decision if removal is proposed. Avoid moving acorns or nursery plants into natural areas without checking local planting guidance. If the tree is part of a managed landscape, monitor its offspring before assuming that its ornamental use creates an invasion problem.
researchNotes: Oregon State and Stanford independently describe evergreen foliage, pale undersides, variable teeth and acorn cups. The action text is observation and cautious seedling containment, not an unsupported claim that this planted tree is invasive everywhere.

claims: Evergreen tree with variable leathery leaves, downy undersides and scaled acorn cups.
Variable toothiness and furry leaf undersides; comparison to coast live oak; acorn form.

proposedDescription: Holly scale is an armored scale that can feed on several ornamental plants, not just holly. Its small covers sit against leaves, twigs or fruit and can be mistaken for harmless surface marks. Feeding may damage tissue around the attachment point and weaken heavily infested growth. The name also appears as laurel scale or bay tree scale, which makes the scientific name useful when requesting a diagnosis. Turkish research also records it on cedar, fir and spruce, so inspect conifers as well as broad-leaved hosts.
identification: Female covers are flat and roughly circular, about one to two millimeters across, gray to light brown with a yellowish old skin slightly off center. Male covers are more elongated, with the old skin closer to one end. The living female beneath the cover is yellow. Many armored scales have similarly plain covers, so a hand lens can establish that scales are present but cannot reliably name this species. Authoritative identification requires a slide-mounted adult female examined under a microscope.
actions: Inspect leaf undersides, twigs and fruit on suspect plants, and note whether damage is increasing on new growth. Keep an affected nursery plant separate while a diagnostic service checks it. Do not move infested cuttings to another garden. Ask for advice on checking whether insects beneath the covers are alive and on monitoring their mobile young stage before choosing a treatment. Keep the host name and purchase history with the sample, especially when several ornamental species are affected.
researchNotes: A newly read Turkish forestry review reports D. britannicus feeding on cedar, fir and spruce and cites Ayhan and Ulgenturk's Ankara phenology: two generations, overwintering as second-stage nymphs. That independently authored Turkish research lineage supplements the Gill/Ferris diagnosis in Naturalis. Local timing and efficacy are not extrapolated to US gardens; ITIS remains nomenclature only.

sources.title: Ulgenturk and Dokuyucu 2019: Pest scale insects in Turkish forests

claims: Flat circular female covers; elongated male covers; feeding injury; slide-mounted females required for species diagnosis.
Taxonomic name and holly, laurel and bay tree scale common names only.
D. britannicus feeds on cedar, fir and spruce; cited Ankara research documents two generations and second-instar overwintering.

proposedDescription: Hollyhock is a familiar garden plant with tall flowering stalks and large open blooms. It usually grows as a biennial or short-lived perennial, often making a leafy base before flowering. Plants may appear along roadsides or around old gardens after escaping cultivation. Flowers vary widely in color, so the tall habit, leaves and fruit are more useful than expecting one particular shade.
identification: Look for upright stems that can exceed six feet, with large rounded leaves on long stalks. Leaves are shallowly lobed and feel hairy, especially when young. Flowers open along the upper stem and may be white, pink, red or purple; garden forms can be double. Beneath a single flower, an outer cup of several green lobes sits outside the main calyx. Mature fruits break into numerous flattened segments arranged in a ring. Other mallows have similar ring-shaped fruits, but commonly lack the combination of very large flowers and a tall, nearly unbranched flower stalk.
actions: If self-sown plants are unwanted, remove seedlings while small and cut spent flowering stems before the fruit segments mature. Keep seed-bearing garden waste out of unmanaged ground. Where a plant grows away from a garden, record whether it is one isolated escape or part of a reproducing patch. Confirm small nonflowering plants before removing them because other mallows can have similar leaves. For a cultivated hollyhock, ordinary garden maintenance may be enough; its inclusion here does not establish that every planting requires removal.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand and the North Carolina vascular flora independently describe habit, flowers and escaped habitat. The RHS account supports the range of cultivated colors and short-lived growth. Actions are limited to unwanted seed spread, without an unsupported invasive-impact claim.

proposedDescription: Varroa destructor is a parasitic mite of honey bees and a major concern in managed colonies. It feeds on bees and reproduces in capped brood cells, and it can transmit viruses such as deformed wing virus. A colony can carry a damaging mite load before many mites are obvious on adult bees. Routine measurement is therefore more useful than waiting to see mites or visibly deformed bees.
identification: Adult females are reddish to dark brown, flattened and oval, with the body wider than it is long, roughly one to two millimeters across. They may hide between the abdominal segments of an adult bee or occur on pale developing brood. Under magnification, a mite has eight legs. The bee louse, Braula, is a six-legged fly and has a different body outline. Deformed wings are a warning of associated disease rather than a species-level identification of the mite. A photograph of a removed mite with a scale can help a beekeeper or inspector confirm it.
actions: Use a standardized mite-monitoring method recommended for your region and record the result for each sampled colony. Keep the queen out of any adult-bee sample. Compare results with current local thresholds and choose only treatments approved for the hive conditions, temperature and honey-super status. Check again after treatment to see whether it worked, and continue monitoring because colonies can be reinfested. An apiary inspector or extension beekeeper can help interpret counts and avoid repeating an ineffective treatment. Visual inspection alone should not replace regular sampling.
researchNotes: University of Florida supports morphology, the Braula distinction and virus association. Ontario independently supports standardized sampling, repeated monitoring and reinfestation. The draft deliberately does not transfer Ontario numerical thresholds or older treatment-method lists into a universal recommendation.

claims: Flattened reddish-brown females wider than long; eight legs versus six in Braula; associated deformed wing virus.
Standardized monitoring before and after treatment; visual checks inadequate; reinfestation can occur.

proposedDescription: Honey bee tracheal mite lives inside the breathing tubes of adult honey bees. This makes it very different from the larger varroa mites visible on the outside of bees. Heavy infestations can contribute to poor colony performance and losses, but early infestations may go unnoticed. A weak colony or crawling bees can have many causes, so this diagnosis needs laboratory evidence rather than a visual judgment at the hive entrance.
identification: The mites are microscopic and occur in the large breathing tubes in the bee's thorax. A laboratory can dissect bees and look for mites, eggs and darkened areas in those tubes, or use an appropriate molecular test. Closely related Acarapis mites live externally and must be distinguished from A. woodi. Finding a tiny mite on a bee does not prove tracheal-mite infestation. Keep colony records, including when weakness began and what other pests were measured, so a diagnostic result can be interpreted in context.
actions: Contact an apiary inspector or bee diagnostic laboratory before collecting a sample, and follow its instructions for the number of bees and preservation method. Keep samples labeled by colony rather than pooling unexplained losses from several hives. Avoid moving or selling suspect live bees until you have advice on the diagnosis and applicable movement rules. Continue checking other common causes of colony decline, including varroa and food shortage. Any treatment should follow current local beekeeping guidance and the product label; household recipes are not a substitute for a confirmed diagnosis.
researchNotes: WOAH supplies diagnostic standards and distinguishes microscopy from molecular methods. NSW independently describes the internal parasite and its external relatives. Regional absence statements and old treatment options were not generalized. Actions emphasize diagnostic submission, not self-dissection or an unverified therapy.

claims: Mites inside adult bee tracheae; laboratory diagnosis by microscopy or molecular methods; related mites can complicate testing.
A. woodi is internal; A. dorsalis and A. externus live externally; colonies may perform poorly.

proposedDescription: Honey-flower is a large, spreading shrub grown for its blue-green foliage and tall dark red flower clusters. It can send up new shoots from a persistent root system, so a plant that dies back above ground may return. Birds visit its nectar-rich flowers, but the leaves and roots are poisonous. The attractive foliage and the word honey should never be taken as signs that the plant is safe to eat or feed to animals.
identification: Each large leaf is divided into a row of sharply toothed leaflets along a visibly winged central stalk. The foliage is pale blue-green, with a strong unpleasant smell when disturbed. Thick, hollow stems carry upright clusters of maroon to rusty-red flowers. Pale, inflated, papery capsules follow, enclosing shiny black seeds. This combination separates it from plants with simple lobed leaves, such as castor bean, despite an occasional shared common name. A photograph showing the entire divided leaf and the flower or fruit cluster is particularly useful.
actions: Keep cut foliage and roots out of livestock feed and away from animals that may browse discarded garden material. If an unwanted plant is removed, plan for the rootstock and suckers rather than only cutting the stems. Collect mature capsules before they can be carried away, and inspect the margins of the planting for new shoots. In natural areas, use a local weed plan and restore cover after removal. Wash hands after handling and seek professional advice after a suspected ingestion rather than relying on traditional-use descriptions.
researchNotes: SANBI provides independent native-range morphology, suckering, capsules and toxicity evidence; Flora of New Zealand confirms hollow stems, winged leaf stalks, fruit and naturalized growth. No medicinal uses or pesticide methods are endorsed.

proposedDescription: Honeyweed is an upright herb in the mint family, with deeply divided leaves and rings of small flowers spaced along the upper stems. It can grow in disturbed ground and has also been cultivated. The name Leonurus sibiricus was historically misapplied to this plant in some regions, so older records require care. The two honeyweed entries in this catalog should not be combined simply because their common names match.
identification: Stems are four-sided and hairy. Lower leaves are broad in outline but divided into several lobes; leaves higher on the stem become narrower and more finely cut. Pink, reddish-purple or sometimes white flowers crowd into rings at the leaf junctions. Each flower sits in a persistent green cup with pointed teeth. Compared with true L. sibiricus, the calyx is generally smaller, with more nearly equal, upright teeth rather than a distinctly downward-bent lower portion. Photograph the lower and upper leaves plus a side view of flowers and calyx teeth.
actions: Before recording an escape under either honeyweed name, check flowering material with a current regional flora or botanist. Remove unwanted young plants before the persistent flower cups contain mature seed, and collect seeding stems rather than dragging them through the site. Revisit disturbed soil for seedlings. If it is being grown deliberately, keep seed-bearing waste contained and watch beyond the planting. Do not use the plant medicinally on the basis of a catalog identification or a common name shared with another species.
researchNotes: Flora of China and NSW independently provide morphology; NSW explicitly corrects historical misuse of L. sibiricus. Kew now places L. japonicus in Paraleonurus, a nomenclatural update flagged without changing the catalog. The draft uses the catalog name consistently and excludes medicinal claims.

sources.title: Flora of China via WFO: Leonurus japonicus

claims: Divided leaves, flower whorls and pointed calyx teeth.

Name treated as synonym of Paraleonurus japonicus.

proposedDescription: This honeyweed is the true Leonurus sibiricus, an annual or biennial herb with finely cut leaves and pink to purple-red flowers. It is distinct from Leonurus japonicus, although the latter has often been sold or reported under the same name. Because the catalog contains both species, an identification needs to follow the scientific characters of the plant rather than the label on a seed packet.
identification: The stems stand upright and bear leaves divided into three main parts, each cut further into narrow segments. Flower clusters form dense rings around the stem. The flower tube is surrounded by a hairy calyx with sharp tips, and the lower calyx teeth spread or bend downward more distinctly than in L. japonicus. Flora of China describes flowers about 1.8 cm long, but size should be used with the calyx and leaf characters, not alone. Photograph an open flower from the side and the entire green calyx after flowering; a distant picture of the plant is unlikely to settle the distinction.
actions: Have a botanist check uncertain flowering material before submitting a species-level record. If you are preventing spread from an unwanted garden plant, remove it before seed matures and contain the dried flowering stems. Keep its original label and any source information with the observation, since these can reveal a misapplied name. Check the site again for seedlings. Do not assume accounts of medicinal use or management written for L. japonicus apply to this species just because both have been called honeyweed.
researchNotes:
Flora of China describes true L. sibiricus; the independent NSW treatment explicitly contrasts its calyx with L. japonicus. This is sufficient for a cautious identification draft, while historical reports and commercial names remain taxonomic traps. No regional presence or medicinal use is inferred.

claims: Annual/biennial; finely divided leaves; hairy calyx and spreading anterior teeth; approximately 1.8 cm corolla.
True L. sibiricus differs by a more distinctly two-lipped calyx with deflexed lower lip.

proposedDescription: Hood canarygrass is a tufted annual grass with dense, short flower heads. The uppermost leaf sheath often swells around the base of the head, giving it a partly enclosed appearance. It is documented as a crop weed in Australia, but a dense grass head alone does not identify it. Several canarygrasses share that general shape, and the small units within the head provide the strongest distinction.
identification: Leaves are narrow and flat, with a thin membranous ligule where the blade meets the sheath. The compact head is usually cylindrical or oblong, sometimes broader toward the top. Under magnification, the spikelets occur in groups: a central fertile spikelet is surrounded by several shorter, unequal sterile ones, commonly six. These groups detach together as they mature. The fertile spikelet has firm outer scales with a projecting tooth or flange on the keel. Keep an intact mature head for identification; a photograph of an immature, still-enclosed head may miss the decisive characters.
actions: In a small unwanted patch, remove plants before the spikelet groups break away. Keep mature heads contained and clean seed-bearing debris from equipment before moving between fields. Check crop seed and disturbed field margins as possible sources rather than assuming the plant arrived from a nearby natural area. For a crop infestation, ask extension to confirm the grass and advise on timing within that crop. A generic treatment for another canarygrass may not fit the same growth stage or farming system.
researchNotes: Flora of New Zealand and NSW Flora independently agree on inflated upper sheaths and grouped fertile/sterile spikelets. Actions concern seed containment; no herbicide susceptibility, county occurrence or livestock toxicity is inferred from the genus.

proposedDescription: Hooked bristlegrass is an annual grass whose bristly seed heads catch on fur, clothing and one another. The tiny hooks point backward, which distinguishes it from many other foxtail grasses. Plants may stand upright or sprawl, forming loose tufts in disturbed ground. The sticky feel is mechanical: it comes from the bristle barbs rather than a coating of sap.
identification: The leaf blades are flat and fairly broad for a small weedy grass. Flower heads are compact and spike-like, often with small gaps or short branches near the base. Several stiff bristles project around the small spikelets, and close inspection shows their barbs facing toward the base of the head. Heads may be green or purple-tinged and often become tangled together. Other Setaria species can have almost identical bottlebrush-shaped heads, so the direction of the bristle barbs is more useful than color. Photograph the whole head and a magnified bristle.
actions: Remove unwanted plants before the heads mature and begin catching on passing animals or equipment. If ripe heads are present, bag them before handling the rest of the plant. Check trouser cuffs, socks and animal coats after crossing a patch, and dispose of collected seed debris where it cannot return to soil. Recheck disturbed areas for new seedlings. For crop or pasture infestations, obtain a confirmed identification and local advice; the presence of hooked bristles alone is not a reason to apply a broad grass herbicide.
researchNotes: SANBI and the independent AusGrass treatment support annual habit and inflorescence structure. SANBI explicitly identifies backward-barbed bristles as diagnostic. The southern African book reproduces SANBI content and is not counted as another source group.

claims: Loosely tufted annual; spike-like heads; retrorse bristle barbs entangle heads.
Small compressed spikelets with a sterile lower and fertile upper floret; mature spikelets fall entire.

proposedDescription: Hop aphid is a small sap-feeding insect that uses hops during the growing season and Prunus trees, including plums, for part of its life cycle. Colonies gather on leaves and can enter developing hop cones. Their honeydew and feeding can make an infestation important even when the individual insects are hard to see. Checking early growth and following the crop into cone development is more useful than inspecting only at harvest.
identification: Wingless adults are pale green, often with a darker stripe along the back, and have an elongated soft body. Winged forms have darker markings. Like other aphids, they carry two small tubes near the rear of the abdomen. Hop aphids also have prominent fingerlike projections on the head near the antennae; these require magnification and help distinguish them from other aphids. Inspect the undersides of leaves and the interior of suspect cones. Photograph a whole colony and a close side or top view of an individual, including the head.
actions: Monitor the same marked plants regularly and record whether colonies are increasing or entering cones. Look for predators and parasitized aphids as well as live pests. Avoid excessive nitrogen that produces lush susceptible growth. If a commercial crop is at risk, use current local scouting guidance and discuss selective options that preserve useful insects. Timing matters because aphids established inside cones are harder to manage. Do not use a calendar spray or a threshold borrowed from another climate without checking whether it fits the crop and conditions.
researchNotes: INRAE supplies independent diagnostic head and body characters and host alternation. The multiauthor hop field guide hosted by Michigan State supports scouting, nitrogen restraint and natural-enemy considerations. Regional dates and treatment thresholds were omitted.

sources.title: Field Guide for Integrated Pest Management in Hops

claims: Pale elongated wingless aphids; dark dorsal markings in winged forms; prominent frontal tubercles.
Primary Prunus hosts and secondary hop host.
Monitor before cone establishment; avoid excess nitrogen; preserve predators and parasitoids.

proposedDescription: Hophead philippine violet is a small, spiny shrub with yellow tubular flowers packed into upright clusters. The overlapping bracts beneath the flowers give the heads a hoplike appearance. It has been grown as an ornamental and can form thorny growth where it escapes in warm climates. Despite the common name, it is neither a true violet nor necessarily a purple-flowered plant.
identification: Look for narrow, smooth leaves in opposite pairs, often with a conspicuous reddish central vein. The stems are roughly four-sided, with sharp spines at the leaf junctions. Yellow to pale orange flowers emerge from dense terminal spikes surrounded by broad, overlapping, sometimes purplish bracts. Dry capsules follow the flowers. Other Barleria shrubs can also be spiny and yellow-flowered, so include the leaf midrib, spine arrangement and entire flower head in photographs. A close image of a single flower without its bracts is less informative.
actions: Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling the spiny branches. If an unwanted garden plant is beginning to escape, remove seedlings and collect mature capsules before they open. Keep thorny, seed-bearing waste contained rather than dumping it at a woodland edge. For a large thicket, ask a local weed specialist about an appropriate removal plan and revisit the site for regrowth or seedlings. Record whether plants are cultivated or independently established; that distinction is useful when assessing spread beyond the original planting.
researchNotes: James Cook University and Singapore NParks independently describe the red midrib, spiny stems and tubular flowers. Brisbane provides the bracted spike and escaped-thicket context. NParks lists a conflicting leaf-arrangement field; the draft follows JCU and Brisbane opposite-leaf descriptions and flags the discrepancy here.

claims: Spiny shrub; opposite leaves with red midvein; compact spike of yellow-orange tubular flowers.
Four-sided spiny stems; narrow leaves; yellow tubular flowers and capsules.
Paired leaves, overlapping purplish bracts and thorny escaped thickets.

proposedDescription: Horehound is a gray-green perennial herb of open, disturbed ground and pasture. Its broad, wrinkled leaves and small white flowers can make it look like a soft garden mint, but mature flower cups become hooked burrs. Grazing animals often leave it behind, allowing it to compete with more useful pasture plants. Burrs can then carry its seeds beyond the patch.
identification: Leaves grow in opposite pairs on branching stems and are covered with pale hairs. Their surfaces are strongly crinkled, with rounded teeth along the edges. Small white flowers cluster in rings at the upper leaf junctions. After flowering, the persistent cups harden into tight brown burr clusters. Compare it with other woolly mints using the white flower rings and mature hooked cups, not smell alone. Photograph an entire stem with several leaf pairs and both a flowering and a fruiting cluster.
actions: Pull or dig small unwanted plants before burrs mature, removing the upper part of the taproot to reduce resprouting. Check again for seedlings and surviving crowns. Clean burrs from clothing, animals and equipment before leaving the patch. In pasture, maintain competitive cover and avoid relying on heavier grazing to solve the problem: animals may preferentially remove other plants. Extensive infestations need a site-specific plan. The Navajo-region guide does not recommend burning alone because it can stimulate germination, so do not treat fire as an easy cleanup method.
researchNotes: South Australia independently supports identification and pasture competition. The Bureau of Indian Affairs guide supports taproot removal, follow-up and the limitations of grazing and fire. Regional legal obligations and herbicide lists are not transferred into general directions.

claims: Hairy perennial with opposite crinkled leaves, white axillary flower clusters and brown burrs; unpalatable pasture competitor.
Remove top of taproot; repeat for seedlings; grazing and burning alone are poor choices.

proposedDescription: Horn flies are small blood-feeding flies that spend much of their adult life on cattle. Large numbers repeatedly bite and irritate an animal, disrupting feeding and contributing to production losses. The larvae develop in cattle dung, so the flies have both an on-animal stage and an off-animal stage. Effective management depends on knowing which fly is present and measuring the pressure on the herd.
identification: Adults are gray-brown to black and about half the size of a house fly, roughly 3.5 to 5 mm long. Their wings lie nearly flat over the body, and two dark stripes run along the thorax. They often gather over the back and shoulders with their heads directed downward. Stable flies are larger and commonly concentrate on the legs; face flies gather around the eyes and muzzle. Photograph the body region occupied as well as the insects. Head tossing, skin twitching and tail swishing show irritation but do not identify the fly species.
actions: Count flies on a representative set of animals and keep records through the season. Use local livestock guidance to interpret those counts because dairy cattle, calves and beef cattle may need different decisions. Discuss a combination of suitable on-animal products, application methods and manure-stage approaches with extension or your veterinarian. Check whether the chosen method is working and consider reinvasion from nearby herds. Follow labels for use on the class of cattle involved, and do not keep repeating the same ineffective product or improvise diluents.
researchNotes:
UF/IFAS supplies species biology; the University of Georgia description is explicitly adapted from UF and is counted with that source group. Nebraska provides independent monitoring and management evidence. No universal economic threshold, product rotation interval or treatment schedule is specified.

proposedDescription: Horn nut is an aquatic plant associated with the hard, two-horned fruits sometimes called bat nuts. Floating leaves form a rosette above stems rooted in bottom mud. Trapa taxonomy varies among floras: some recognize Trapa bicornis, while Flora of China includes it within a broad T. natans. This account concerns that horn-nut form, without borrowing distribution claims for the distinct North American two-horned trapa described as T. bispinosa.
identification: Floating leaves are broad and diamond-shaped, with toothed upper margins and swollen, spongy portions of the leaf stalks. Small flowers have four white petals. The mature dark fruit has two broad, sideways-projecting horns that may curve downward like a buffalo's horns. Underwater structures look very different from the floating rosette. A photograph of the leaf mat is not enough to separate Trapa forms. Record both leaf surfaces, flower color and a mature fruit. Do not confuse these fruits with the edible corms of Chinese water chestnut, Eleocharis dulcis.
actions: Do not plant loose fruits in ponds or release aquarium or water-garden material into natural water. If an unfamiliar Trapa appears, photograph it and report it to the local aquatic-plant program before disturbing a large patch. Keep fruits and plant material from moving on boats, nets or equipment. Any removal should prevent dropped fruits and be coordinated with the waterbody manager. Accurate naming is especially important here because a report of a two-horned fruit can otherwise be assigned to the wrong Trapa species.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: FRPS recognizes a two-horned T. bicornis form, whereas Flora of China explicitly declines narrow taxa because fruit variation overlaps. The two Chinese floras substantiate a taxon-boundary conflict. Their overlap is not treated as two independent confirmations of a narrow invasive taxon. Inherited links not used: https://www.nparks.gov.sg/sbg/research/publications/gardens-bulletin-singapore/-/media/sbg/gardens-bulletin/4-4-31-2-02-y1978-v31p2-gbs-pg-84.pdf. The PDF exceeded the bounded retrieval size and was not downloaded; the accessible Chinese flora treatments supply the competing concepts.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: An original2023 genome study independently supports the cultivated bicornis entity alongside the traditional two-horned flora account. Wuhan researchers newly assembled bicornis and incisa genomes. This is independent of the older FRPS/Flora of China treatment and permits a named horn-nut profile while broad natans lumping remains explicit. Next step: Review the bicornis horn-nut account; do not equate it with North American bispinosa from horn count alone. Fresh evidence/access: 2023 chromosome-level Trapa genome assemblies [indexed_excerpt; Trapa-2023-original-genomes] https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-023-02270-4 - New cultivated large-seeded bicornis and wild incisa genome assemblies; direct Nature access failed, substantive indexed abstract/methods read. Inherited URLs and evidence remain provenance; only the specifically documented accesses are claimed fresh. Parent-read passages are explicitly attributed. No catalog, mapping or public-release changes; local review only.

proposedDescription: Hornfaced bee is a solitary mason bee introduced from Asia for pollination of spring-flowering fruit crops. Females use nest cavities rather than forming a honey-bee colony. It closely resembles another introduced mason bee, Osmia taurus, and distinguishing them matters when documenting their spread or evaluating purchased nesting material. A bee using a garden nest block cannot be identified simply from the nest structure.
identification: The body is dark with pale tawny to bronze hairs. Females have two conspicuous hornlike projections on the front of the face and orange-brown pollen-carrying hairs beneath the abdomen. The facial horns separate this pair of introduced species from familiar native blue orchard bees, but not from O. taurus. In O. cornifrons females, the center of the lower facial margin has a small pointed projection; in O. taurus it is indented. Males require different, finer characters. A sharp face-on photograph is much more useful than a distant side view.
actions: Photograph visiting bees and nesting activity without blocking occupied holes. Do not move occupied nest blocks or purchase and release cocoons simply to establish an unidentified population. If you manage orchard pollinators, use a reputable source, keep provenance records and seek advice on identification and nest hygiene. Support locally appropriate pollinators with flowering plants and suitable nesting habitat. A suspected non-native bee should be documented and checked, rather than destroyed on the basis of color or a rough resemblance to this species.
researchNotes: Independent Canadian establishment research and an Environmental Entomology review provide diagnostic comparisons with O. taurus and native Osmia. Ecological association is not rewritten as proof that O. cornifrons alone caused native-bee decline. Movement restraint is preventive guidance, not an eradication claim.

sources.title: Canadian establishment study: Osmia cornifrons and O. taurus

claims: Spring fruit pollination; female facial horns and scopal color; difficult distinction from O. taurus.
Female O. cornifrons has a median clypeal projection versus indentation in O. taurus; males need separate characters.

proposedDescription: Horntail snail is a small land snail with a delicate amber shell and a pointed fleshy projection at the end of its tail. It can shelter in moist plant material and nursery settings, making movement with plants a practical concern. Feeding studies show that it can use seedlings and various cultivated plants, although the amount of damage depends on the setting. A chewed leaf alone cannot show which snail caused it.
identification: The body is brown, and the thin shell is glossy amber, commonly around a dime in diameter in adults. Look for the small tail horn and a flap of flesh extending back over or around the shell. The similar jump snail, Ovachlamys fulgens, also has a tail horn and comparable colors, but has a more slender body and a more prominent horn. Photograph the snail while extended, including its tail, shell profile and a size reference. A closed shell by itself may conceal the most useful characters.
actions: Keep a suspect nursery plant and its potting material separate, and contact your state plant-health agency or extension office before moving it. Inspect pot rims, undersides and damp debris without handling snails barehanded. Use gloves if handling is required and wash afterward. Do not ship live snails as an identification sample unless the receiving agency gives instructions. Record where the plant came from and whether more snails are present. Follow official disposal or treatment guidance rather than scattering bait around an unidentified snail population.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS provides biology, nursery-monitoring guidance and the jump-snail comparison, drawing on independent feeding research. FDACS independently supplies an official diagnostic sheet and reporting contact. Parasite potential is not presented as proof that any individual snail carries a pathogen.

claims: Amber shell, tail horn, mantle flap, jump-snail comparison and plant-feeding studies.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
claims: Delicate dime-sized amber shell and caudal horn are diagnostic screening clues.

proposedDescription: Horsefly's eye is a small, soft-stemmed herb of wet ground, including rice fields, pond margins and seasonally wet riverbeds. Its thin branches and reduced upper leaves can make it resemble a tiny rush until the flowers open. It is an annual, so a patch may change greatly as water levels rise and fall. Its occurrence in a wet place is not enough to establish either its identity or an ecological impact.
identification: Stems are smooth, fleshy and much branched near the base, with faint lengthwise lines. The lower leaves are larger and broader than the upper ones, which may shrink to small scales. Leaves have smooth edges and little or no stalk. Tiny white, pink or pale purple flowers stand on slender stalks; the lower lip spreads outward while the upper lip is shorter and upright. The fruit is a very small rounded capsule. Photograph a complete plant with the base, leaf arrangement and an open flower, since a bare upper stem can be misleading.
actions: For a suspected new occurrence, record the water depth or wet-soil condition and ask a local botanist to check flowering material. Avoid moving mud or wet plants from the site to another pond or field. In a garden or production area where the plant is unwanted, remove small plants before capsules mature and inspect again as water recedes. Do not drain or treat a wetland solely because this species has been named. Any larger control decision should consider the site, confirmed identity and the plants growing with it.
researchNotes:
Flora of China and the Indian Institute of Science independently support succulent branching stems, reduced leaves, small flowers and wet habitats. No documented species-specific control trial or broad ecological-impact conclusion was found; actions are limited to identification and prudent containment.

proposedDescription: Horseradish is a perennial mustard grown for its thick, pungent roots. The large leaves die back in cold weather and new shoots rise from the surviving underground parts. Those roots also make it persistent outside its intended bed: even a small piece left behind can produce another plant. Harvesting a patch and removing a patch are therefore different jobs.
identification: The basal leaves are large, shiny and elongated, with wavy or toothed edges, and may resemble dock leaves at first glance. Flowering stems carry clusters of small white flowers with four petals. The stout roots are pale to white. Docks have very different small greenish flowers and seed clusters, so wait for reproductive details if the leaves are ambiguous. Photograph the rosette and a flowering branch together. Do not taste an unknown root to identify it, and avoid digging up a plant merely to test its smell.
actions: Keep a cultivated patch in a clearly bounded area and watch for shoots outside it. When removing unwanted plants, dig carefully and collect root pieces rather than chopping and redistributing them through tillage. Revisit the site and remove new shoots from missed fragments. Keep roots out of dumped garden waste and soil moved to new beds. In a field or natural area, map the patch before selecting a wider control approach. Expect follow-up rather than assuming that removal of the main root has eliminated the plant.
researchNotes: NC State supports root-fragment regeneration and colony formation. Wisconsin independently describes harvest and root propagation; RHS corroborates docklike leaves, white flowers and winter dieback. Food use is context only, with no identification-by-tasting advice.

claims: Large rosette leaves, four-petaled white flowers and regeneration from small root pieces.
Roots persist and are used for propagation; careful digging avoids breaking roots.
Vigorous perennial with docklike leaves and pale fleshy roots; winter dieback and spring regrowth.

proposedDescription: Horseradish flea beetle is a small leaf beetle associated especially with horseradish and related mustard crops. Adults chew small holes in leaves, while its larvae can burrow in leaf stalks and veins. The adult feeding can resemble damage from several other flea beetles. Checking the beetle itself helps avoid treating every small hole as evidence of this particular species.
identification: Adults are about one-eighth inch long. Much of each wing cover is yellowish, bordered by black along the outside and by a broader black band down the middle of the back. This can look like a black beetle with two broad yellow stripes. The central dark band is widest around the middle. Other striped Phyllotreta species can look similar, so record the host plant, beetle size and a sharp dorsal view. Leaf-stalk mining or damaged veins may support the diagnosis, but leaf injury alone cannot name the insect.
actions: Inspect fresh leaves and leaf stalks, especially when plants are young, and determine whether beetles are still actively feeding. Keep a specimen for extension if the stripes are unclear. A mature horseradish plant with limited cosmetic damage may not need treatment; the Connecticut handbook notes that control is seldom necessary in its setting. If seedlings or a commercial crop are being damaged, use local crop guidance to choose a response. Avoid applying a broad treatment solely because an older leaf has holes.
researchNotes:
Wisconsin supplies the species comparison and feeding damage; Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station independently describes the yellow wing covers, central black stripe and larval petiole mining. The Connecticut control assessment is labeled regional rather than universal.

proposedDescription: Horseradish tree, also called moringa or drumstick tree, is a cultivated tropical tree with finely divided foliage and long hanging fruits. It is unrelated to the familiar horseradish crop despite the shared common name. The leaves and immature pods are used as vegetables in some food traditions, but that does not make every part suitable for use or establish a medicinal benefit. For identification, the long fruits and small leaflets are especially helpful.
identification: The pale gray trunk has lengthwise wrinkles. Each large leaf branches two or three times into many small, oval to rounded leaflets, creating a light, open appearance. Creamy white flowers occur in clusters. The long, narrow pods hang downward and become brown and three-sided as they dry, splitting lengthwise to release rounded seeds with three papery wings. Other trees can have finely divided leaves, so include a complete leaf, a flower and a mature pod in photographs. The seed wings are useful when pods are no longer attached.
actions: Where a planted tree is producing unwanted seedlings, collect mature pods before they split and check beneath and beyond the canopy for new plants. Keep seed and pruning waste out of natural areas. Remove small unwanted seedlings while their roots are manageable; larger trees need a safe, site-specific removal plan. Record whether an observation is a planted tree or an independently established plant. Use regional planting guidance to decide whether cultivation is appropriate rather than assuming that a useful crop cannot escape.
researchNotes: Indian Institute of Science and Singapore NParks independently support trunk, compound leaves, pale flowers and pendulous pods. Indian forestry material provides three-sided dry pods and winged seeds. Health claims, growth-rate extrapolations and universal invasive status are excluded.

proposedDescription: This plant is also widely called sour fig or highway iceplant. It is a trailing succulent that roots at its joints and forms heavy, dense mats. Native to South Africa, it has escaped coastal plantings in several other regions. Its thick stems and leaves store water, so detached pieces can remain viable long enough to spread in dumped garden waste. Flower color varies with age and hybrid ancestry, which can complicate identification.
identification: Leaves are long, fleshy and sharply triangular in cross-section, usually green but sometimes reddening with age. Large flowers contain many narrow petal-like parts around yellow stamens. In typical C. edulis, flowers open yellow and can fade toward pale pink. Fleshy, figlike fruits follow. Related Carpobrotus species and hybrids can have pink or purple flowers from the start, so color alone is not a secure identification. Photograph a freshly opened flower, older flowers and the shape of a leaf without breaking off material unnecessarily.
actions: For a small confirmed patch, lift the shallow-rooted stems carefully and collect all fragments. Keep removed pieces off moist soil where they could root again. Large mats on dunes or slopes should be removed in stages under a restoration plan so bare ground does not erode. Check for regrowth and seedlings after removal, and replace the mat with suitable local vegetation. Do not dump succulent cuttings over a bank. In places with native Carpobrotus, have uncertain plants checked before clearing them.
researchNotes: SANBI supplies independent native-range morphology and rooting habit. The Western Australian Weeds Society supplies practical fragment-regrowth and hybridization evidence; Argentina national parks independently corroborates succulent triangular leaves and trailing habit. Unsupported medicinal advice in SANBI was not used.

sources.title: Weeds Society of Western Australia: Carpobrotus

claims: Node-rooting mat-forming perennial; triangular succulent leaves; yellow flowers fading pale pink and fleshy fruit.
Hybridization complicates identification; hand-pulled plants regrow from fragments.

proposedDescription: Hound's tongue root weevil is an insect used in Canada to suppress houndstongue, Cynoglossum officinale. Adults feed on the leaves, but larvae inside the roots cause the more consequential damage. It can also use some related native plants, so biological-control benefits and non-target risks need to be considered together. An insect that damages a weed is not automatically appropriate to collect and release elsewhere.
identification: Adults are small brown weevils, about two to three millimeters long, with pale markings forming a cross on the back. The larvae are pale, curved grubs with brown heads inside the roots. Adult feeding leaves rounded or oval holes in leaves, but those holes are not unique to this weevil. Photograph an adult on its host with a size reference and record the plant species. A root containing a white grub should be checked by a specialist because several insects can use damaged roots.
actions: Do not collect, redistribute or release these weevils on your own. Report a suspected occurrence to your local weed or plant-health program and retain photographs and host details. If houndstongue needs control, use methods approved for your location rather than moving insects from another patch. Ask officials before transporting plant roots that may contain larvae. Monitor nearby related plants if a professional program requests it, but do not interpret occasional feeding as proof of population decline without a proper assessment.
researchNotes: Montana Extension provides diagnosis and documented movement concerns. Catton and colleagues provide independent experimental target/non-target population evidence. Their finding for Hackelia micrantha is not generalized to all native Boraginaceae. The draft avoids a new legal assertion based solely on older release-status documents.

sources.title: Catton et al.: Target and nontarget population effects

claims: Brown adults with white cross; root-feeding C-shaped larvae; concerns about unauthorized movement and native relatives.

proposedDescription: House mice live around buildings, stored food and farms as well as in fields. They contaminate food, gnaw materials and build nests in sheltered spaces near a dependable food supply. A single mouse indoors can be a sign to inspect the building, but droppings or a fleeting glimpse may not identify the rodent species. Control works best when entry points, food access and the animals already inside are addressed together.
identification: An adult house mouse is a small gray-brown rodent with relatively large ears and a sparsely haired tail about as long as the head and body together. The belly is usually lighter without the sharply contrasting white underside typical of many deer mice. Look for small droppings, fresh gnawing and nests made of shredded material, but use a clear photograph or professional identification if the species matters. Young rats can be confused with mice; their proportions, feet and head differ, so body length alone is unreliable.
actions: Store food and animal feed in rodent-resistant containers, remove spills and reduce clutter that hides nesting sites. Seal gaps around pipes and doors, including openings only slightly larger than a quarter inch. Use appropriately placed snap traps where children, pets and wildlife cannot reach them, or work with a pest professional. Check traps regularly. For droppings or contaminated nesting material, follow current public-health cleanup instructions rather than sweeping or vacuuming dry material. Persistent activity after trapping usually means an entry route or food source still needs attention.
researchNotes: Missouri and Utah State provide independent extension guidance on appearance, entry gaps and integrated control. Health-related cleanup wording is conservative and directs readers to current instructions rather than reproducing older disposal advice. No disease is diagnosed from rodent presence.

claims: Food contamination, nesting signs, large ears and small entry openings; sanitation, exclusion and population reduction.
Gray-brown fur and long naked tail; door sweeps, sealed gaps, food storage and snap traps.

proposedDescription: House sparrows are stocky, social birds closely associated with buildings, farms and urban food sources. They often feed in groups and use holes in structures or nest boxes. Their status differs greatly across their range: a species introduced in one country may be a declining native bird in another. A useful identification should come before any decision about nest boxes or nuisance birds.
identification: The bill is short and thick, the head rounded and the back streaked brown and black. Breeding males have a gray crown, chestnut around the head, pale cheeks and a black throat bib. Females and young birds are plainer buff-brown with a broad pale eyebrow and unstreaked grayish underparts. Nonbreeding males can have less obvious black and chestnut. Many native sparrows have stronger breast streaking or different head patterns, so photograph the face, breast and back together. The familiar repeated chirping is helpful context but not a substitute for seeing the bird.
actions: If birds are entering a building, identify them and locate the opening before planning exclusion. Remove accessible food spills and secure stored grain.
