Do not seal a cavity while birds or dependent young are inside; ask local wildlife authorities or a qualified professional about appropriate timing and rules. At nest boxes, monitor which species is using the box and seek locally suitable advice if there is a conflict with native cavity nesters. Avoid poisons or improvised traps that can harm other birds.
researchNotes: Cornell independently supplies detailed sex- and season-specific field marks. RSPB supports social behavior, feeding and building-cavity nesting and demonstrates that conservation status is region-dependent. No blanket legal exemption or universal removal recommendation is inferred.

claims: Stocky bill and body; male gray crown/black bib; female pale eyebrow and streaked back; seasonal variation.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Royal Society for the Protection of Birds
claims: Social birds using seeds, grain and scraps; nest in building cavities; UK conservation concern.

proposedDescription: Human flea is one of several flea species that can bite people. Its common name does not mean that a flea found on a person is necessarily this species; cat, dog and other fleas can also feed on humans. Adults take blood meals, while immature stages develop in the surrounding environment. Solving a flea problem therefore usually requires finding its animal or environmental source, not just treating the bites.
identification: Adults are small, wingless insects compressed from side to side, with strong hind legs for jumping. Species identification requires magnification. Human flea lacks the rows of thick spines called combs that occur below the head and behind it in cat and dog fleas. Its head is broadly rounded, and a distinctive bristle lies below the eye. Other fleas also lack combs, so this feature alone is insufficient. Preserve a specimen as directed by a diagnostic service; a photograph of a bite cannot identify the flea that caused it.
actions: Ask a pest professional or extension entomologist to identify a captured flea and investigate animal resting areas, bedding and nearby wildlife access. Vacuum accessible areas and launder washable bedding as part of a coordinated plan. Have a veterinarian advise on any affected pet, using products intended for that animal. Never apply a household or veterinary insecticide to human skin. Seek medical advice for a severe reaction or illness after bites and mention the exposure. Continue follow-up because immature stages may remain after adults become less visible.
researchNotes: CDC DPDx and UF/IFAS independently support microscopic diagnosis and the distinction from other biting fleas. The draft does not amplify historical disease associations into a claim that this flea is an efficient plague vector. Control steps are general integrated flea management, not a species-specific eradication trial.

claims: Several species bite humans; P. irritans lacks genal/pronotal combs and has rounded head with ocular bristle below eye.
Diagnostic comb, head, bristle and internal characters distinguish human flea from related species.

proposedDescription: Hyacinthbean is a twining bean grown for its flowers, pods and other uses. It can behave as an annual or a short-lived perennial, climbing through supports and nearby vegetation on long stems. Cultivated plants vary considerably: flowers can be white, pink, red or purple, and the pods and seeds also differ in color. A plant beside a garden may be cultivated, self-sown or discarded; its location alone does not establish that it is spreading in the surrounding habitat.
identification: Look for leaves divided into three broad leaflets, often roughly triangular or diamond-shaped, and upright flower clusters rising above the foliage. The pea-shaped flowers are followed by broad, flattened pods, sometimes curved or slightly inflated, with a persistent pointed tip. Mature seeds have a conspicuous elongated white scar along one edge. These features together are more useful than purple coloration, which is absent in many varieties. Other climbing beans can have similar leaves, so include photographs of the flowers, whole pods and mature seeds when seeking an identification.
actions: Where a cultivated vine is producing unwanted seedlings, collect pods before they split and remove volunteer plants while they are small. Keep pods and seed-bearing garden waste out of nearby natural areas. Check the original planting and the ground beneath supports during the next growing season. If a vine is established away from cultivation, document its extent and whether young plants are present before deciding on removal. Treat these as practical steps to limit seed escape, rather than proof that the species needs control everywhere. Do not use an identification profile as food-preparation advice.
researchNotes: NSW Flora and the Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment supplied through Kew independently support the distinguishing leaf, flower, pod and seed characters. Cultivated variability is retained. The draft makes no claim of a local invasive designation and does not infer food safety from the existence of agricultural uses.

sources.title: Flora of Tropical East Africa through Kew: Lablab purpureus

claims: Twining annual or short-lived perennial with trifoliolate leaves, variable flower colors and broad flattened pods.
Flowers and pods vary; compressed seeds bear a conspicuous elongated white aril.

proposedDescription: Hydrilla is a rooted underwater plant whose branching stems can grow upward and form dense growth near the surface. It can spread when stem fragments are moved between waters, and it also produces resting structures that help populations persist. A patch may therefore return after its visible shoots have disappeared. Its close resemblance to other submerged plants makes careful identification especially important before anyone begins cutting, raking or treating a waterbody.
identification: Inspect several points along a stem. Small, pointed leaves usually occur in whorls of four or more, although the number varies. A hand lens can reveal teeth along the leaf edges and sometimes small teeth beneath the central vein. Elodea commonly has three leaves per whorl, but leaf count alone is not decisive; Egeria can also have larger whorls. Hydrilla produces small pale, potato-like tubers below the sediment, which these lookalikes lack. Do not uproot a suspected patch simply to search for them. Clear close photographs of intact stems and leaf edges can support an initial expert assessment.
actions: Report a suspected new occurrence to the relevant water manager or aquatic invasive species program, with the location, depth and approximate patch size. Avoid driving boats through dense growth or pulling plants in ways that release fragments. Inspect boats, trailers and equipment and follow local clean, drain and dry requirements before moving to another waterbody. Keep aquarium and pond plants out of natural waters. Established infestations need a site-specific management plan that accounts for fragments and resting structures; casual cutting is not a reliable way to eliminate the plant.
researchNotes: USGS NAS and Penn State Extension provide independent substantive accounts of morphology, lookalikes and vegetative spread. Washington invasive species guidance corroborates the tuber distinction. Leaf-whorl counts are explicitly variable. No local biotype, distribution, herbicide choice or treatment outcome is inferred from the catalog entry.

sources.title: USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species: Hydrilla verticillata
Penn State Extension: Aquatic Invasive Species in Pennsylvania

claims: Submerged rooted plant; toothed whorled leaves, variable morphology, fragments and resting structures important for spread.
Hydrilla resembles other submerged plants and spreads through fragments, tubers and turions.
Underground pale tubers help distinguish hydrilla from similar waterweeds.

proposedDescription: This hydroid is most likely to be noticed as a small jellyfish in brackish water. Its conspicuous swimming stage is only one part of the life cycle: the attached polyp is minute and has been much harder to observe. Maeotias marginata is associated with the Black Sea and Sea of Azov region and has been recorded in other estuaries. California monitoring has found it during warmer, lower-salinity conditions, but those observations do not establish a universal seasonal schedule.
identification: The jellyfish has a rounded, hemispherical bell that can reach about five centimeters across. Four main canals radiate from the center, with additional shorter canals between them. A mature animal has numerous fine tentacles around the edge and four frilly lips beneath the bell. Young individuals are relatively clear; older ones may look milky white, with pinkish or brownish coloration at the margin. Smaller individuals are harder to distinguish from other hydromedusae. The extremely small polyp lacks tentacles in the cultured stage described by researchers, so a visible branching hydroid colony should not automatically receive this name.
actions: Photograph a suspected jellyfish in the water, including a view from above and from the side if possible. Record the date, precise location, approximate size and any available salinity information. Send observations from a potentially new area to the regional aquatic monitoring or invasive species program. Avoid moving live animals, collected water or fouled equipment between waterways. Finding one jellyfish does not reveal the size or origin of the population, and removing visible individuals is not an established means of controlling its full life cycle.
researchNotes: Smithsonian NEMESIS provides a full-text species synthesis with diagnostic anatomy and documented uncertainty about the polyp. California Department of Fish and Wildlife supplies independent field monitoring evidence. Seasonal statements are limited to that monitoring context. The draft does not convert potential food-web effects into a demonstrated decline in fish populations.

sources.title: California Department of Fish and Wildlife: 2023 Fall Midwater Trawl Summary

claims: Bell anatomy, mature size and coloration; minute poorly known polyp; brackish-water ecology.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: California Department of Fish and Wildlife
claims: Independent estuary monitoring recorded Maeotias during warmer, lower-salinity conditions.

proposedDescription: Moerisia lyonsi is a very small hydroid with an attached polyp stage and a free-swimming jellyfish stage. The polyps can grow on shells, stones, debris and other submerged surfaces. Both stages are easy to overlook, and a population may be present without an obvious jellyfish bloom. Its native range is uncertain. Reports using only the name Moerisia cannot automatically be assigned to this particular species.
identification: A polyp is roughly one to two millimeters tall, with a spindle-shaped body and several beaded tentacles. It grows from a creeping connection along the surface, and buds may form on the body. The jellyfish is only a few millimeters across. Four canals run outward across its bell, and reddish eye spots occur near the tentacle bases. As it develops, it gains more tentacles around the rim. These are microscope-level characters, rather than features that can usually be resolved in a casual photograph. Identification also requires comparison with related small hydroids and attention to which life stage was examined.
actions: If you find a suspected colony during routine inspection of submerged equipment, photograph its location and seek advice from an aquatic invertebrate specialist before collecting it. Record whether the material was attached or swimming and whether the water was fresh or brackish. Do not move live colonies or water to another site. Follow the relevant cleaning procedures for equipment, without assuming that an ordinary rinse eliminates every life stage. Any local response should begin with a confirmed identification; removing a few visible jellyfish is not evidence that the organism has been eliminated.
researchNotes: NEMESIS separates original Boulenger/Calder morphological descriptions from Purcell and colleagues' 1999 Chesapeake feeding experiment; the latter's abstract was read directly. These underlying author lineages support a narrow morphology-and-Chesapeake-biology account, even though the synthesis also cites the feeding paper. California and Barnegat identity questions remain qualified rather than generalized.

sources.title: Purcell and colleagues: Prey, feeding rates and asexual reproduction rates of Moerisia lyonsi

claims: Polyp and medusa morphology from Boulenger and Calder; regional Moerisia identities and native range require caution.
Original study abstract describes low-salinity Chesapeake populations, feeding and asexual reproduction.

proposedDescription: Hyssop loosestrife is a small annual of damp ground, including places that are wet for part of the year. It is much less conspicuous than the tall, purple-flowered loosestrifes people may recognize from wetlands. Its narrow leaves and tiny flowers can blend into low vegetation or recently exposed mud. The shared common name does not mean that it has the same life cycle or should receive the same management as purple loosestrife.
identification: Look for a slender, mostly hairless plant with weakly four-angled stems and narrow, unstalked leaves. Plants are often only a few tens of centimeters tall. Some lower leaves may be opposite, while others are alternate. The flowers sit singly or in pairs where leaves meet the stem, rather than forming a large terminal spike. Their small pinkish or pale petals project from a narrow, ribbed flower tube; petals can be inconspicuous or absent. Elongated seed capsules develop inside that persistent tube. Purple loosestrife is a much larger perennial with showier flowers, so overall size, flower arrangement and growth form are useful distinctions.
actions: Document an unfamiliar patch with close photographs of the stem, leaf arrangement and flowers or capsules. Include a wider view showing the wet-ground habitat. Before removing it, confirm both the identification and whether local guidance calls for management. Where removal of an unwanted annual patch is appropriate, act before mature seed is shed and limit disturbance to the surrounding wet soil and vegetation. Revisit the site after the next period of suitable moisture, since one visit may miss later seedlings. Do not transfer mud or seed-bearing material into another wetland.
researchNotes: E-Flora BC and the New Zealand Flora independently describe the annual habit, narrow leaves, axillary flowers and persistent calyx around the capsule. Their size ranges overlap but vary, so the draft avoids a rigid height cutoff. No local status or equivalence to invasive purple loosestrife is assumed.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: University of British Columbia E-Flora BC
claims: Small glabrous annual, narrow leaves and tiny solitary or paired axillary flowers; distinction from larger perennial loosestrifes.
Four-angled stems, small pink petals, tubular ribbed calyx and capsules.

proposedDescription: Iguanatail is a tough, evergreen plant that forms upright clumps of stiff leaves. Thick underground rhizomes allow a clump to expand and connect neighboring shoots. It has been grown as an ornamental and can persist where garden material is discarded. The familiar snake-plant appearance is useful for recognizing the group, but several related species are cultivated and their names are easily confused.
identification: Look for broad, flat, dark green leaves marked with paler patches or bands. The leaf edges have a reddish to orange-red margin, a useful distinction from the green, yellow or white margins typical of common forms of the related snake plant traditionally called Sansevieria trifasciata. The substantial rhizomes are orange. Flowering plants produce a tall cluster of narrow, pale flowers that may be cream, white or lightly mauve and are scented at night. Orange berries can follow in parts of its range. A photograph should show the whole clump, leaf markings and a close view of the margin; leaf color alone is insufficient.
actions: Keep divisions, leaf pieces and rhizomes out of garden waste dumped on undeveloped land. Where an unwanted small clump is being removed, trace the connected shoots and collect the underground rhizomes rather than cutting off only the leaves. Check for regrowth and avoid scattering pieces while digging or transporting material. In a natural area, confirm the identification and follow local management guidance before disturbing the site. These steps address the plant's capacity for vegetative persistence; they do not establish that every cultivated clump is invasive or that one removal visit will eliminate it.
researchNotes: SANBI supplies an independent native-range botanical account, and Franck's Florida taxonomic revision provides diagnostic comparisons and evidence of vegetative spread there. Kew treats the catalog name as a synonym of Dracaena hyacinthoides; the catalog name is preserved. The Florida observation of no fruiting vouchers is not generalized into global sterility.

sources.title: Franck: Taxonomic treatment of Sansevieria in Florida
Kew Plants of the World Online: Sansevieria hyacinthoides

claims: Flat marked leaves with red margins, orange rhizomes, pale scented flowers and orange berries.
Leaf-margin color distinguishes hyacinthoides from trifasciata; Florida plants form colonies through thick orange rhizomes.
Catalog name is treated as a synonym of Dracaena hyacinthoides.

proposedDescription: Illyrian cottonthistle is a large, spiny thistle that begins as a low rosette and later produces an upright, branched flowering stem. Its pale, woolly surface gives a plant a gray-white appearance. In affected pasture, broad rosettes can occupy space needed by other plants, and dense stands of mature stems can obstruct movement. Those effects are documented in regional weed guidance and do not establish its status at an unverified location.
identification: Look for a strongly spined rosette with densely woolly leaves. As the plant bolts, leafy tissue continues down the stem as prominent, spiny wings. Mature plants can reach around two meters, with branching concentrated toward the upper part. The combination of white wool, large spiny leaves and broad stem wings points toward the cottonthistle group. Other Onopordum species, especially Scotch thistle, can be very similar. Do not assign the species from a distant photograph or the pale color alone. Useful identification photographs show the lower leaves, the winged stem and several views of the flower heads and their surrounding bracts.
actions: Where local guidance calls for control, inspect for rosettes before the plants become tall and difficult to handle. Wear sturdy gloves and protective clothing around the spines. A small number of young plants may be removed with the root crown, while avoiding unnecessary soil disturbance. Seek local advice for larger infestations or uncertain identifications. If heads have begun developing seed, keep them contained during removal and follow the local disposal procedure. Recheck the ground for seedlings in later seasons. Cutting tall stems once is not a reliable substitute for preventing seed production and following up.
researchNotes: Agriculture Victoria and NSW WeedWise provide independent regional agency accounts of habit, woolly foliage, spiny stem wings and pasture impacts. Species separation from other Onopordum remains an expert identification step rather than an oversimplified visual claim. Manual actions are prudent early intervention, not a tested guarantee of species eradication.

claims: Erect annual or biennial thistle to about two meters, densely woolly leaves and conspicuously winged spiny stems.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: New South Wales Department of Primary Industries
claims: Gray-white thistle with rosettes and spiny mature growth; documented pasture impacts and seed-production concern.

proposedDescription: Inchplant is a trailing perennial often grown in hanging baskets or as a groundcover. Its jointed stems can root where they touch a suitable surface, allowing a loose piece or an escaped garden planting to become established. The striped foliage is conspicuous, but cultivated varieties differ in how much green, silver and purple they show. A pot on a windowsill and a spreading patch outdoors are different situations and need different responses.
identification: The leaves are pointed, somewhat fleshy and usually display two broad, silvery bands along the upper surface, with green or purple between them. Their undersides are typically purple. Leaves clasp the stem through a sheath and occur along the trailing shoots. Small flowers have three pinkish to purple petals; they may be absent on indoor plants. Other cultivated Tradescantia can have purple or striped foliage, so include the leaf underside, attachment to the stem and flowers when available. Check whether the stems are rooting at their joints, rather than judging only the color of the upper leaves.
actions: Keep pruning pieces and unwanted plants out of natural areas, drains and streams. Where a small unwanted outdoor patch is being removed, collect the creeping stems and rooted joints, then revisit for overlooked pieces and regrowth. Work carefully around other plants so fragments are not spread through the site. Gloves are sensible if the sap irritates your skin; wash exposed skin after handling. Follow local advice for an established infestation. Regular clipping may keep an ornamental compact, but scattered clippings can also create new plants, so disposal is an important part of the work.
researchNotes: NC State Extension and Singapore NParks independently support the trailing habit, striped foliage, purple undersides, small three-petaled flowers and propagation from stems. Their leaf-arrangement wording is inconsistent; the draft avoids the conflicting label rather than combining it into a false description. Skin precautions reflect the documented possibility of sap irritation.

sources.title: NParks Flora and Fauna Web: Tradescantia zebrina

claims: Trailing stems root at nodes; silver-striped leaves with purple undersides, sheathing bases and three-petaled flowers; sap can irritate skin.
Low trailing ornamental with silver-purple foliage, purple leaf undersides, pink flowers and propagation by stem cuttings.

proposedDescription: Incised halberd fern is a large fern of moist, shaded places. It produces pale green fronds from a short, stout rhizome and can form substantial groundcover where conditions suit it. It has been cultivated as an ornamental, and Florida accounts identify discarded garden material as a possible route into natural areas. A fern appearing in a wet woodland should still be identified carefully, because related native ferns can look very similar.
identification: A frond is divided into broad leaflets, with a large terminal section at its tip. The lowest leaflets have conspicuous extended lobes, contributing to the halberd-like outline. The fronds can be roughly a meter long or more. Turn over a mature frond without breaking it to look for the spore-bearing spots, called sori. These occur in rows and have small rounded to kidney-shaped covers attached along an edge. The arrangement of the leaflets, their basal lobes and the sori are more useful than size alone. Some related species have different sorus arrangements or lack these covers, and rare native lookalikes require specialist attention.
actions: Photograph the whole frond, its lower leaflets and the underside of a mature leaflet before considering removal. In Florida or another area with similar native ferns, ask a local botanist or land manager to confirm the identification. Keep unwanted ornamental ferns and their rhizomes out of woodland and wetland waste piles. Where a confirmed escaped patch is managed, use the locally agreed approach and check for regrowth. Do not assume that a general garden herbicide recommendation is suitable for a wet natural area or that cutting the fronds removes the underground plant.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS provides the Florida introduction account, habitat information and warning about native lookalikes. NParks independently supplies frond and sorus morphology, drawing on botanical treatments. These support a review-ready descriptive draft. The sources do not establish a universal control method, so management is limited to identification, waste containment and local planning.

sources.title: NParks Flora and Fauna Web: Tectaria incisa

claims: Large pale green fronds, lobed basal leaflets and covered sori; escaped ornamental in wet Florida habitats with native lookalikes.
Large divided fronds with enlarged basal lobes; sori in rows with kidney-shaped covers distinguish related ferns.

proposedDescription: India mockstrawberry is a low, creeping perennial that spreads through long runners. New plants root along those runners, gradually forming a patch in lawns, beds and other suitable ground. Its three-part leaves and bright red fruits resemble a strawberry, but the flowers provide a particularly helpful distinction. Whether a patch needs removal depends on the planting and local guidance; its presence alone does not show that it is harming the surrounding habitat.
identification: Look for three hairy leaflets with rounded teeth around their edges. The flowers are solitary and have five yellow petals. Wild strawberries such as Fragaria virginiana have white flowers, making a flowering specimen much easier to identify than leaves alone. Below a mockstrawberry flower or fruit, the conspicuous green outer bracts have three teeth at their tips. The red, rounded fruit has noticeable bumps on its surface. Some cinquefoils also have yellow flowers, so combine flower color with the three leaflets, runner-forming habit and strawberry-like fruit rather than relying on one feature.
actions: If an unwanted patch is small, follow the runners and lift the rooted plants along their length. Removing only the original clump can leave connected young plants behind. Revisit the area for regrowth and avoid moving rooted runner pieces with garden waste or transplanted soil. Mowing alone may leave this low-growing plant in place. Confirm the identification before removing a native strawberry or another similar groundcover. Photographs of the yellow flowers, the green bracts beneath a fruit and the connected runners will help an extension service distinguish the plants.
researchNotes: University of Missouri Weed ID and NC State Extension independently support the diagnostic yellow flowers, trifoliolate leaves, runners and red fruit. Kew and NC State use Potentilla indica for this taxon, with Duchesnea indica as a synonym; the supplied catalog name is preserved. No edible-use or medicinal recommendation is inferred from resemblance to strawberries.

sources.title: University of Missouri Weed ID: Indian mock-strawberry
Kew Plants of the World Online: Duchesnea indica

claims: Creeping perennial with runners, hairy trifoliolate leaves, yellow five-petaled flowers and red fruit; comparison with white-flowered wild strawberry.
Former Duchesnea indica; long stolons, yellow flowers, three-toothed outer bracts and ability to persist under mowing.
Duchesnea indica is treated as a synonym of Potentilla indica.

proposedDescription: A single Indian banyan can become a spreading stand of trunks. Roots hanging from its branches thicken into supports when they reach the ground. Seeds carried into another tree can also start life above ground, with roots eventually surrounding the host. This tropical fig is widely planted for shade, but its large root system and ability to establish outside cultivation deserve attention near buildings and natural areas.
identification: Look for broad, leathery leaves arranged alternately, prominent leaf veins, and paired round figs that ripen reddish. Mature trees have a heavy, fluted trunk and descending aerial roots. The Indian Institute of Science describes figs about 2 cm across. Young trees may lack the conspicuous supporting roots, so include the leaves and figs in photographs rather than relying on the overall shape. Other large figs also produce aerial roots; that feature alone does not identify a banyan.
actions: Check walls, fenceposts and the forks of nearby trees for young plants, especially around a fruiting banyan. Photograph any seedlings growing away from the planted tree and distinguish those from deliberately maintained landscape trees in a report. Avoid planting this species beside structures or sensitive habitat. An established banyan or a seedling rooted high in a host tree needs a planned removal assessment, not simply cutting visible roots. Ask an arborist and local extension service about safe removal and follow-up where control is warranted.
researchNotes: IISc supplies independently documented foliage, figs and prop-root characters; UF describes epiphytic establishment, infrastructure risk and removal difficulty. Florida guidance does not establish harmful status everywhere. Actions avoid unsupported homeowner chemical directions.

claims: Alternate leathery leaves, paired red figs and aerial prop roots.
Animal-dispersed seeds establish in tree canopies; roots can damage infrastructure; physical removal can be difficult.

proposedDescription: Indian hedgemustard is an upright, short-lived mustard of disturbed ground and cultivated places. Its pale yellow flowers give way to long, narrow pods that spread away from the stem. The plant changes shape as it grows: broad, divided lower leaves are replaced by narrower leaves higher up. A flowering plant without mature pods can easily be mistaken for another roadside mustard.
identification: Look for grayish hairs, a basal rosette of divided leaves, and stem leaves with a long, arrow-shaped end lobe. The uppermost leaves can be narrow and undivided. South Australian flora describes rigid, sometimes curved pods about 6-10 cm long on short, thick stalks. Those long spreading pods distinguish it from common hedgemustard, whose much shorter pods lie close to the stem. Photograph a lower leaf, upper leaf and attached mature pods together; yellow four-petaled flowers alone are not enough.
actions: If an identified plant is unwanted in a bed or disturbed patch, remove it while young, before pods dry and scatter seed. Gather fruiting material carefully rather than dragging it through clean ground. Watch the disturbed spot for new seedlings and keep soil from the patch out of new planting beds. These are seed-prevention precautions for a short-lived weed, rather than a tested species-specific eradication prescription. For a crop-field infestation, confirm the mustard with an extension service before choosing crop-specific control.
researchNotes: Independent Flora of South Australia and Flora Zambesiaca descriptions agree on leaf changes, hairs and long pods. Management is explicitly limited to conservative seed-prevention advice; no local occurrence, legal status or chemical efficacy is inferred.

sources.title: Flora of South Australia: Sisymbrium treatment

claims: S. orientale has gray hairs and 6-10 cm spreading pods; S. officinale has short appressed pods.
Annual or biennial with divided basal leaves, arrow-shaped stem leaves and pale yellow flowers.

proposedDescription: Indian heliotrope carries a narrow flower spike with a curled tip, rather like a slowly unrolling tail. Only a few tiny flowers open at a time, while the older part develops fruits. This hairy annual grows in open, often damp or disturbed places, including field edges and drains. Its presence in a garden does not tell us how common it is elsewhere in the surrounding county.
identification: The egg-shaped or oblong leaves have wavy margins and a rough covering of short hairs. Their blades extend down toward the leaf stalk. Small white or light purple flowers, about 3-4 mm wide, have a yellow center and sit along the curling flower spike. Leaves may be alternate or nearly paired. Photograph the complete spike, the leaf surface and the way the blade joins its stalk. A close view of mature fruits helps a botanist distinguish this plant from other heliotropes.
actions: Pull or hoe young plants where they are unwanted, preferably before the flower spikes develop mature fruit. Revisit damp disturbed patches after removal rather than assuming one pass has cleared the seed supply. Keep seeding material out of soil or nursery pots being moved elsewhere. WIKTROP documents manual removal in agricultural settings, but its overseas chemical recommendations are not instructions for a US garden or crop. Do not turn a plant identification into advice to eat it or use it as a home remedy.
researchNotes: NParks provides detailed morphology and seed reproduction; CIRAD-associated WIKTROP independently documents wet disturbed habitat and manual control. Native-range wording differs between resources, so the draft does not assert a precise origin. Medicinal-use claims are deliberately not promoted.

claims: Hairy wavy leaves, curled spikes, tiny pale flowers and seed propagation.
Occurs in disturbed damp habitats; pulling and hoeing are described management methods.

proposedDescription: Indian jujube is a thorny shrub or small tree grown for fruit and shade. In suitable warm environments it can spread into dense thickets that restrict access and displace other vegetation. Animals eat the fleshy fruits and carry the seeds away. Cutting back an established plant is not necessarily the end of it: damaged roots and the swollen woody base can produce vigorous new shoots.
identification: Young branches often zigzag, with a curved thorn near a leaf joint. Leaves are rounded to oval, glossy above and whitish or rusty-haired underneath, with small teeth along the edge. Small pale flowers grow in leaf forks. The rounded fruits are roughly 1.5-3 cm across and change from green through yellow to reddish brown, surrounding a hard stone. Photograph the underside of a leaf, a thorn-bearing twig and fruit. Do not assume a plant labeled simply jujube is this species.
actions: Inspect beneath fruiting trees and along nearby animal routes for seedlings. Wear protection against the thorns and keep collected fruit and seed-bearing waste from being dumped into natural areas. Before tackling an established thicket, arrange a plan that includes regrowth checks; repeated top cutting can leave the living base behind. Australian agencies describe cut-stump and other treatments, but local US requirements and site conditions must guide any pesticide use. Report an escaping population with its location, size and whether plants are producing fruit.
researchNotes: Queensland and Northern Territory government guidance independently support thicket formation, distinguishing foliage and animal seed dispersal. Queensland specifically notes regrowth after damage. Australian restricted-plant rules are not presented as US law.

sources.title: Northern Territory: Chinee apple management guide

claims: Zigzag thorny branches, pale leaf undersides, ripening fruit and dense thickets.
Animals disperse fruit seed; damaged lignotubers and cut roots regrow.

proposedDescription: Indian lovegrass is a small tufted annual that can be easy to overlook until its delicate seed heads spread open. It grows in disturbed ground and cultivated places, where fine branches hold many narrow spikelets. Each spikelet contains several tiny flowers. The plant is much less conspicuous than large perennial lovegrasses, and the small hairs around its leaf bases and flowering branches are useful clues.
identification: Look for narrow blades, usually only a few millimeters wide, and a fringe of hairs where each blade meets its sheath. Longer hairs occur at the sheath opening and at some lower seed-head branch junctions. The open seed head has fine branches arranged in whorls at its lower nodes. NSW flora describes spikelets about 3-9 mm long, with multiple florets. Use a close photograph or hand lens for these parts; an airy seed head alone cannot reliably separate similar lovegrasses.
actions: For an unwanted small patch, remove plants before the spikelets break apart and release seed. Keep seed-bearing cuttings and soil from the patch out of clean beds and equipment. Leave an identifiable flowering sample or clear photographs for a local grass specialist if the name is uncertain. Recheck disturbed soil for seedlings rather than treating every fine-leaved grass as the same weed. These measures aim to limit seed movement; the reviewed floras do not establish a particular herbicide or a species-specific eradication program.
researchNotes: NSW flora and the University of British Columbia flora independently support the annual habit, sheath hairs, fine whorled panicle branches and spikelet dimensions. The action paragraph explicitly distinguishes prudent seed hygiene from tested control efficacy.

claims: Tufted annual; hair-fringed sheath and ligule; open panicle and small many-flowered spikelets.
Fibrous-rooted annual; hairs at sheath summit and lower panicle nodes; narrow flattened spikelets.

proposedDescription: Indian marshweed can look quite different above and below water. Submerged stems carry whorls of finely divided leaves, while shoots above the surface have shorter leaves and small pale flowers. It is a rooted freshwater perennial that can form dense underwater growth. Aquarium labels and a feathery appearance are not reliable identification: several related marshweeds are difficult to separate and have different regulatory histories.
identification: Photograph both submerged and exposed shoots if possible without disturbing the patch. Underwater leaves are finely split, often in whorls of six to twelve. Above water, look for solitary flowers on visible stalks, pale flower tubes with pinkish or purplish lobes, and small paired bracts below the flower. Stalk length and the calyx surrounding a developing fruit are useful specialist characters. The leaves alone are not enough to distinguish it confidently from L. sessiliflora or other Limnophila.
actions: Never empty aquarium plants, water or trimmings into a stream, pond or storm drain. If a marshweed appears in outdoor water, photograph it in place and ask an aquatic-plant specialist to confirm the name before attempting control. Record whether it is rooted, flowering and spreading beyond a planted area. Avoid breaking up a stand while investigating it or moving live samples between water bodies. Treatment advice for a different Limnophila species should not be assumed to work or be lawful for this one.
researchNotes: Kew floral descriptions and the California pest assessment support amphibious growth and identification using stalked flowers. CDFA partly cites floristic sources; its independent risk assessment is distinguished from morphology derived from shared floras. No congener herbicide recommendation is adopted.

sources.title: Kew: Limnophila indica, Flora of Iraq and tropical Africa descriptions
California Department of Food and Agriculture: Indian marshweed assessment

claims: Aquatic perennial with divided submerged leaves and stalked aerial flowers; calyx not striate at maturity.
Rooted amphibious freshwater plant with dense underwater growth; species-specific California assessment.

proposedDescription: Indian meal moth is usually a pantry problem rather than an insect feeding on living plants outdoors. Its caterpillars eat stored dry foods and leave silk, shed skins and droppings among them. Flour is only one possible source: nuts, dried fruit, pet food and birdseed can also support an infestation. A caterpillar on a wall may have wandered away from the food to find a place to pupate.
identification: Adult moths have a conspicuous contrast between the paler inner part of the forewings and coppery outer portions. They often make weak, wandering flights around food storage areas. Look inside packages for pale caterpillars and silken threads that bind food together. Larvae or cocoons may be tucked into shelf corners or container edges. Photograph a resting adult with both wings visible, and note the food it came from; larvae alone are harder to identify than the two-toned moth.
actions: Inspect all dry goods nearby, including rarely used ingredients, pet food and decorative dried plant material. Seal and discard infested food, clean spilled material and shelf crevices, and put remaining susceptible goods in insect-resistant containers. Check new packages before storing them and use older food first. Traps can help reveal continued moth activity, but they do not replace finding the infested food. Avoid spraying food or food-contact surfaces to solve an infestation that is developing inside a package.
researchNotes: Utah State and Minnesota extension independently support stored-food hosts, webbing, wandering larvae and sanitation. Advice focuses on removing the breeding material. No promise is made that trapping adults alone clears an infestation.

sources.title: Utah State Extension: Indian meal moth
University of Minnesota Extension: Pantry pests

claims: Copper-tipped adult wings; off-food pupation; stored-food hosts; sanitation and pest-proof containers.
Pantry pests infest many dried goods; contaminated food disposal and cleaning are central management.

proposedDescription: Indian mulberry, often called noni, is a tropical shrub or small tree with glossy leaves and unusual pale, knobbly fruit. Many small flowers join to form each fruit, which becomes soft and strongly scented when ripe. The plant has a long history of cultivation and transport through the Pacific. That history matters when interpreting a record: a planted noni tree and a self-established population are different observations.
identification: Look for large, smooth-edged leaves in opposite pairs, with obvious curved side veins. White tubular flowers open in rounded or oval heads. The developing fruit resembles a lumpy, miniature pineapple and becomes yellowish white. Stems can be four-angled. University of Hawaii guidance separates noni from the Hawaiian Morinda trimera partly by its larger, pale, soft fruit; M. trimera has smaller, firm, dark green fruit. Photograph leaves, flowers and fruit together rather than relying on the smell.
actions: When reporting this plant, note whether it was deliberately planted and whether seedlings are appearing beyond the cultivated area. Keep fruit and garden waste from being dumped into nearby natural vegetation. Before removing a tree in a Pacific landscape, establish its identity and local context; this catalog entry is not a blanket recommendation to remove culturally important plantings. The sources document traditional uses, but this profile does not recommend noni products as a treatment for any illness.
researchNotes: NParks and University of Hawaii botanical material independently describe foliage, flower heads and fruit. Older Hawaii references use inconsistent native/introduced wording; the draft therefore explains cultivation history without resolving indigenous status by assertion. No therapeutic claims are adopted.

claims: Opposite glossy leaves; many-flowered heads and soft pale ripe fruit.
Noni has larger pale soft fruit than M. trimera; leaves and fruit vary between cultivated forms.

proposedDescription: Indian murainagrass forms a low perennial mat by sending creeping stems across the ground. Those stems root at their joints, so a patch can persist even when its short flowering shoots are cut. Its seed heads are small and narrow, with golden hairs that become easier to see close up. It is one of several fine tropical grasses whose identity is easily lost when lawns are regularly mown.
identification: Look for creeping, branching stems with rooted joints and upright shoots roughly 10-40 cm high. Short leaf blades may have stiff hairs. Each flowering shoot carries one narrow seed head, commonly 2-7 cm long, rather than a broad open spray. Under magnification, the hairy spikelets occur in groups of three, a useful feature behind the genus name. Photograph an intact seed head and a creeping stem with its leaf joints; a photograph of a mown green mat rarely resolves the species.
actions: If it is spreading from turf or a planting into an unwanted area, map the edge of the mat and check whether runners have already rooted beyond it. Avoid carrying rooted pieces in discarded sod or soil. Remove small unwanted patches with their rooted stems where this can be done without damaging surrounding vegetation, and watch the edges for regrowth. A grass specialist can confirm the flower structure before larger management work. The reviewed botanical sources do not establish a particular herbicide program for this species.
researchNotes: AusGrass and Flora of China material independently corroborate rooting stems, solitary racemes and hairy spikelets; Kew confirms the accepted taxon and broad introduced range. Removal wording is cautious containment guidance, not a sourced claim of eradication efficacy.

sources.title: World Flora Online, Flora of China: Polytrias indica

claims: Perennial mat; lower nodes root; solitary racemes bear spikelets in threes.
Rooting decumbent stems, short hairy leaves and golden-haired spikelets.
Accepted perennial species with introductions including Florida, Hawaii and Puerto Rico.

proposedDescription: The familiar rubberplant houseplant can grow into a substantial tree outdoors in a frost-free climate. Its thick shiny leaves and pointed pinkish new-growth coverings are often recognizable long before it develops a trunk and aerial roots. This species is widely cultivated, so a record may represent a planted specimen rather than an escaping population. A large tree and an indoor potted plant also present very different management questions.
identification: Leaves are alternate, thick and glossy, usually oblong or oval with a pointed tip and a strong central vein. NParks describes blades about 10-30 cm long. Pink to purplish leaf coverings surround new growth and fall away as leaves expand. Small figs grow at leaf joints and ripen yellow; they are not the large edible figs sold as fruit. Mature trees may send down aerial roots. Include a shoot tip and the leaf arrangement in photos, since many other tropical plants have glossy leaves.
actions: Keep unwanted cuttings and potted plants out of dumped garden waste. When documenting a tree, record whether it is planted and look separately for young plants away from it. Choose outdoor planting space with its eventual tree size in mind, and use an arborist for large-tree work. Wear gloves when pruning and avoid getting the irritating milky sap on skin or in eyes. There is no reason to remove a contained houseplant simply because the species appears in this catalog.
researchNotes: NParks supplies detailed leaf, stipule, fig and sap-hazard characters; UF independently documents landscape size and cultivation context and does not classify it as a universal problem. Actions distinguish prevention and structural care from invasive-species treatment.

claims: Thick alternate leaves, pink-purple stipules, yellow figs, aerial roots and irritating sap.
Tropical landscape and indoor tree; regional assessment does not treat it as universally problematic.

proposedDescription: Indian sandalwood is an evergreen tree grown for its fragrant heartwood. Its roots connect to other plants and obtain part of their water and nutrients through those connections. It still has green leaves and makes its own food through photosynthesis. That combination makes it a root hemiparasite, rather than a vine growing over another tree. Cultivated trees and plants establishing outside cultivation should be distinguished in a report.
identification: Look for opposite pairs of smooth, oval to narrowly oval leaves, often paler underneath. The small flowers grow in clusters and change from greenish to reddish or purplish tones. Round, single-seeded fruits become dark purple or black at maturity. World Agroforestry describes fruits about 1 cm across. Leaf shape alone is not enough to separate sandalwoods; photograph flowers or fruit and the arrangement of several leaves. Cutting into the trunk to check for fragrance is unnecessary and damages the tree.
actions: Record whether the tree was planted and whether there are younger plants beyond the cultivated area. Include nearby vegetation in a photograph, but do not dig up roots to search for host connections. If removal is being considered, have the identity checked first and discuss the root connections with a qualified local specialist. Avoid distributing unidentified seedlings as ornamental trees. The sources describe cultivation and biology, not a single removal method suitable for every place where sandalwood occurs.
researchNotes: Kew Flora of Tropical East Africa and World Agroforestry independently support morphology; the American Phytopathological Society explains root hemiparasitism. Native-range boundaries are not asserted because treatments differ. Host connections do not by themselves establish harmful impact at a recorded site.

claims: Opposite leaves, changing flower color and dark mature fruit.
Small clustered flowers, opposite leaves and approximately 1 cm single-seeded fruit.
Sandalwoods are root hemiparasites; Santalum album is cultivated for fragrant wood.

proposedDescription: Indian sandbur is a tufted annual grass with a seed head made of small, prickly burs. Those burs can catch on fur, clothing and equipment, moving seeds beyond the original patch. They also make a mature infestation unpleasant to walk through. Open, disturbed ground is a useful place to look, but a prickly grass should not be identified from its common name alone: several sandburs have a similar appearance.
identification: Look for upright or spreading grassy clumps with narrow leaves and a cylindrical cluster of burs at the end of each flowering stem. The burs enclose the small grass flowers and become easier to detach as they mature. Feedipedia describes flower clusters roughly 3-15 cm long and burs enclosing one to three spikelets. For identification, photograph the entire seed head and the individual attached burs beside a scale. The arrangement of the bristles matters more than whether a plant simply feels spiny; a local grass specialist may need a specimen.
actions: Check shoes, animal coats and equipment before leaving an infested area, removing burs where their seeds can be contained. If a small patch is confirmed and removal is appropriate, work before the seed heads mature and wear gloves. Collect seeding material without shaking it across clean ground. Revisit the patch for later seedlings rather than assuming one removal finishes the job. For a pasture or larger infestation, arrange locally appropriate control with extension staff; do not move contaminated hay or soil into unaffected sites.
researchNotes: Broome local-government weed guidance supports annual habit, bur transport and early removal. The INRA/CIRAD Feedipedia account independently describes burs and grass morphology. These sources do not establish current U.S. county distribution; detailed Cenchrus identification still requires examination of the burs.

sources.title: Shire of Broome: Weed management strategy

claims: Annual clumps, cylindrical bur heads, attachment to animals and removal before seed.
Flower clusters 3-15 cm long, prickly burs enclosing one to three spikelets.

proposedDescription: Indian shot, or canna lily, is a tall perennial with broad leaves and red or yellow flowers. Beneath the stems are thick, branching rhizomes that let a clump survive and spread. In warm, wet settings, escaped plants can form dense stands along waterways. Garden cannas include hybrids as well as this species, so a conspicuous canna beside a stream still needs a closer identification.
identification: The leaves are large, smooth and pointed, with their bases wrapping around the upright stem. Flowers grow in terminal clusters. In Canna indica, the brightly colored, petal-like parts are relatively narrow compared with many garden hybrids. The fruit is a bumpy capsule that dries brown and contains hard, rounded, dark seeds. Photograph the flowers from the front and side, a fruit if present, and the whole clump. Broad leaves and flower color alone do not reliably separate cultivated canna hybrids.
actions: Keep rhizomes, seeds and garden waste out of drains and waterways. Small unwanted plants can be dug out where access and site conditions allow, but all rhizome pieces need to be collected: fragments left behind can regrow. Check the site again for new shoots. Large wetland patches need a coordinated plan that avoids spreading fragments or damaging the bank. Florida IFAS assigns this species a high invasion risk in its assessment; that regional finding should guide local decisions rather than be assumed to apply equally everywhere.
researchNotes: NSW WeedWise provides distinguishing flower parts, fruit and rhizome management. The independent UF assessment supplies Florida risk context. Hybrid confusion is stated explicitly, and Australian pesticide directions are not transferred into U.S. advice.

claims: Narrow flower parts compared with hybrids, bumpy capsules, rhizome fragments regrow.
High invasion risk in Florida assessment.

proposedDescription: Indian swampweed is an aquatic plant that can grow submerged or extend onto damp banks. Its stems break readily, and loose pieces can root and start new patches. That makes aquarium disposal and the movement of plant-covered equipment especially important. Dense growth can crowd other aquatic plants and obstruct use of a waterway, but a photograph of a few underwater leaves is not enough to establish the species.
identification: Leaves grow in opposite pairs along the stem and usually have smooth edges. The NSW flora describes them as oblong, about 2-6 cm long and 0.5-2 cm wide. When growing above water, the plant can produce small, pale bluish-white, two-lipped flowers in the leaf axils, where leaves meet the stem. Photograph several stem joints and any flowers without pulling the plant apart. Underwater growth can look different from the flowering bank form, and other aquarium plants also have paired leaves.
actions: Never empty aquarium plants or water into a creek, pond or storm drain. If you find a suspected patch outdoors, record its location and photograph it before attempting removal. Avoid raking or chopping it: Texas A&M notes that roots and stem fragments can survive mechanical removal and regrow. Clean visible vegetation from equipment before moving elsewhere and contain removed material away from water. A waterbody manager or extension specialist can plan control and follow-up; a large removal or treatment can create additional problems as plant material decomposes.
researchNotes: The NSW flora independently supports leaf and flower identification. Texas A&M supplies fragment-regrowth and management limitations; UC Davis documents dense growth and transport pathways. Guidance emphasizes containment, not unsupervised aquatic herbicide use.

claims: Opposite oblong leaves, axillary two-lipped flowers and aquatic or bank growth.
Mechanical removal leaves viable fragments; large decay events can reduce oxygen.
Brittle stems root at nodes and dense growth obstructs waterways.

proposedDescription: Indiantree spurge, often sold as pencil tree, is a succulent shrub or tree with a network of slender green branches. It may look like a cactus, but it belongs to the spurge family. Its milky sap is irritating, which matters when someone handles a broken branch or clears discarded cuttings. A cultivated plant in a pot is different from a population growing outside a garden; include that distinction when reporting it.
identification: Look for smooth, rounded, pencil-like green branchlets rising from older woody branches. The plant is largely leafless in appearance rather than covered with the obvious pads or ribs of many cacti. NC State describes a spineless, much-branched plant that can become a substantial tree outdoors in a warm climate. Do not snap a branch to test for milky sap. Photographs showing the branching pattern and any small leaves are a safer starting point, especially for cultivars whose new growth changes color.
actions: Keep children and pets away from broken stems and fresh pruning debris. UC guidance recommends gloves, eye protection and covered skin for handling this plant; dried sap can also be irritating. Avoid a removal attempt that puts sap near your face, and arrange professional help for a large specimen. Keep discarded cuttings contained rather than leaving them along a natural area or drainage channel. If plants appear to be establishing beyond cultivation, record their extent and ask a local botanist or extension service to confirm the identity and appropriate response.
researchNotes: NC State independently describes the spineless succulent growth form. UC Agriculture and Natural Resources supplies handling precautions for fresh and dried sap. The draft does not claim invasive impact in every region or offer medical treatment instructions.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Indian tree spurge

claims: Spineless succulent shrub or tree with green pencil-like branchlets and woody older branches.
Fresh and dried sap can irritate; protective clothing and eye protection for handling.

proposedDescription: The Indo-Pacific gecko is a small, mostly nocturnal lizard that catches insects. It can live around buildings and other sheltered places, but its appearance overlaps with several other house geckos. Its original tail has a particularly useful clue: a saw-like edge. A replaced tail may lose that feature, so an apparently smooth-tailed animal should not be ruled in or out from that character alone.
identification: Look for a flattened head, pale tan to gray-brown body, and patterned legs and tail. The University of Hong Kong describes rows of darker markings with pale spots, a yellowish underside, and prominent small spines along the sides of an original tail. Toe pads have divided adhesive plates. Close relatives require comparisons of chin scales, back scales and tail structure that may not be visible in an ordinary phone image. Take clear photographs from above and the side without grabbing the tail or forcing the animal into a position.
actions: Record where the gecko was found and whether it arrived with nursery plants, freight or household belongings. Do not release a transported animal into a new place or move it elsewhere outdoors. If it is still associated with a shipment, contact the relevant local wildlife or agriculture office for instructions. Avoid injuring a gecko simply to obtain diagnostic photographs. A report with several views and the original location is more useful than an uncertain name attached to a single blurred image.
researchNotes: Hong Kong university morphology and independent primary herpetological work support diagnostic characters. Recent work uses H. garnotii sensu lato and reports sexual males in a related population; the profile deliberately avoids a universal all-female claim. Specialist review is needed for difficult house-gecko records, not assumed from color.

sources.title: University of Hong Kong: Garnot's gecko
O'Shea and colleagues: Timor-Leste herpetofauna update

claims: Original tail has saw-like lateral spines; regenerated tail lacks them; nocturnal insect-feeding gecko.
Comparison with house geckos requires tail, dorsal and chin-scale characters.

proposedDescription: The Indo-Pacific swimming crab is a coastal crab that has reached parts of the western Atlantic beyond its original range. Its flattened rear feet work like paddles, while stout claws and a spiny shell give it a compact, armored appearance. Researchers consider it a possible competitor and predator of native animals, although the strength of those effects is not equally documented in every invaded location.
identification: Look for a roughly hexagonal shell, six prominent teeth along each front side, and flattened ends on the last pair of legs. The upper surfaces of the claws carry dark-tipped spines; spines on the rear leg segments are also important for identification. Smithsonian descriptions note dark green coloration with purplish inner surfaces on the legs and claws, but color varies and is not a sufficient test. Include the shell edge, claws and rear legs in photographs. Native swimming crabs can look similar, so have unusual records checked.
actions: Note the exact shore or waterbody, date and circumstances of the observation, including whether the crab was in fishing gear or attached to transported material. Photograph it without placing fingers near the claws. Do not move a live crab to another waterbody or use an uncertain nonnative crab as live bait. Ask the local marine resource agency how it wants a suspected new occurrence documented. These are reporting and spread-prevention steps; the available sources do not establish a practical homeowner eradication method for an open coastal population.
researchNotes: Smithsonian NEMESIS supplies shell, claw and swimming-leg features and appropriately qualified impact evidence. South Carolina DNR independently documents regional introduction context. Historical dates are not turned into present county occurrence claims; no unsupported eradication promise is made.

sources.title: South Carolina DNR: Spiny hands crab

claims: Hexagonal carapace, six anterolateral teeth, spiny claws and paddle-like rear legs; impacts incompletely documented.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
claims: Indo-Pacific origin and western Atlantic introduction history.

proposedDescription: Intermediate wheatgrass is a long-lived, cool-season grass planted for pasture, hay and soil stabilization. It spreads through underground stems and can form a dense sod. Selected forms are also grown for the perennial grain sold as Kernza. Those uses are important context: a planted field should not automatically be treated as an invasive infestation, even though the grass is introduced and can spread beyond a planting.
identification: Plants commonly stand around 2.5-4 feet tall, with narrow, flat leaves and a straight seed spike roughly 4-8 inches long. Utah State describes closely set, slightly overlapping spikelets, each containing several florets, without long awns. Small clasping projections occur where a leaf blade meets the sheath. Some plants are noticeably hairier than others, so hairiness alone is not a dependable separation from the pubescent form. Photograph a mature spike, leaf collar and the pattern of growth across the ground for a grass specialist.
actions: When documenting a patch, distinguish seeded pasture or restoration plantings from plants spreading into surrounding vegetation. Photograph the boundary and any separate young patches. If it is unwanted in a natural area, plan control around its persistent underground stems rather than assuming a single mowing removes it. Consult the site manager before disturbing a forage or erosion-control planting. For new restoration work, choose seed mixes suited to local conservation goals and check the full species list rather than relying only on a product's common name.
researchNotes: Utah State supports detailed field characters and vegetative spread; USDA NRCS supports forage and stabilization uses; University of Minnesota establishes the Kernza relationship. No uniform legal or harmful status is inferred from its introduced origin.

sources.title: USDA NRCS: Intermediate wheatgrass plant guide

claims: Sod-forming rhizomatous perennial; spikelets, awnless lemmas and leaf-collar characters.
Introduced forage grass used for hay and soil stabilization.
Kernza is grain harvested from selected intermediate wheatgrass.

proposedDescription: Introduced pine sawfly larvae feed on pine needles and can make an otherwise healthy-looking branch suddenly appear thin. They resemble caterpillars, but they are the young of a sawfly, a relative of bees and wasps. White pine is an important host, although other pines can also be used. Feeding may involve older needles first and, in later generations, both older and newer needles.
identification: Mature feeding larvae are about 3/4-1 inch long, with a black head, two dark stripes along the back, and a mottled pattern of yellow, white and black. Photograph several larvae, their host pine and the affected needles. The USDA identification tool notes that late-stage larvae can be easier to separate from similar Diprion species than the adults, whose identification may require microscopic structures. Needle loss by itself is not diagnostic: other sawflies, caterpillars and tree-health problems can produce similar damage.
actions: Inspect a suspected tree while larvae are actively feeding and note whether damage is limited to a few branches or spread through the crown. Have the insect identified before selecting a treatment intended for caterpillars. On a small, accessible tree, ask extension staff whether physical removal is sufficient; larger trees and substantial defoliation need an arborist or forest-health assessment. Keep a record of the date and check again later in the season, since Minnesota observations include more than one generation. Local timing will differ with climate.
researchNotes: University of Minnesota provides larval appearance, host preferences and seasonal feeding patterns. USDA Diprion ID independently addresses difficult adult separation and diagnostic larval coloration. Seasonal examples are attributed to Minnesota and no unverified pesticide recommendation is supplied.

sources.title: University of Minnesota: Introduced pine sawfly

claims: Black-headed spotted larvae, white pine preference and feeding on different needle ages.
Larval mottling and specialist characters separating adults from similar Diprion.

proposedDescription: Irish potato is the familiar food crop grown for its underground tubers. Plants can also reappear from tubers left in a garden, discarded in a pile or missed during harvest. These volunteer plants matter especially around potato production because infected tubers can carry disease into another season. A volunteer potato is not, by itself, evidence of a damaging invasion of nearby natural habitat.
identification: The above-ground plant has soft green, compound leaves with a slightly rough texture and small flowers that range from white to purple. Underground tubers have the small buds commonly called eyes. Florida's plant-identification guide distinguishes these from sweet potatoes, whose edible roots lack those eyes and whose above-ground growth is a trailing vine. Do not use an unknown plant or an unexpected fruit as food to confirm its identity. Photograph the foliage and flowers, plus any tuber already exposed during ordinary garden work.
actions: Remove unwanted volunteer plants and remaining tubers as part of garden or crop sanitation, particularly where potatoes were diseased. Keep discarded potatoes from forming a sprouting cull pile beside a new crop. Use certified disease-free seed potatoes for planting rather than assuming saved or grocery-store tubers are clean. If foliage develops rapidly expanding dark lesions or widespread collapse, seek a plant-disease diagnosis instead of assuming the plant itself is the problem. Rotation and volunteer control help reduce disease carryover; the appropriate response depends on the disease and growing situation.
researchNotes: UF supports leaf, flower and tuber identification. UMN independently supports certified planting stock, volunteer and cull-pile sanitation, and disease carryover. Crop status is clearly separated from ecological invasion, and this draft does not diagnose late blight from a photograph.

sources.title: University of Minnesota: Late blight of tomato and potato

claims: Compound slightly rough leaves, white-purple flowers and tubers with eyes.
Infected tubers and volunteer plants can carry late blight; cull-pile and seed hygiene.
Certified disease-free seed tubers and rotation guidance.

proposedDescription: This tiny marine isopod is a wood-boring gribble, not an insect. It lives in submerged timber and excavates narrow galleries near the surface. Repeated attack and erosion can gradually weaken wooden marine structures. The catalog's broad common name, isopod, covers many unrelated-looking crustaceans, so reports need the scientific name and an expert identification rather than a photograph of damaged wood alone.
identification: Limnoria are only a few millimeters long and resemble miniature, segmented woodlice. Under magnification, L. quadripunctata has a Y-shaped raised ridge on the fifth abdominal segment and two pairs of small bumps on the broad tail plate. The British Myriapod and Isopod Group warns that these features can be difficult to see. Similar gribbles occur in the same kind of wood, and some occur together. Photograph the animal and gallery if safely accessible, but leave microscopic confirmation to someone familiar with marine isopods.
actions: Report suspected damage to the owner or manager of a dock, piling or other marine structure. Do not cut into a load-bearing timber or enter unsafe water to collect an animal. Record whether the material is a fixed structure, driftwood or transported timber, along with the waterbody and date. Avoid moving infested wood to another coastal site. Marine engineers and resource managers can assess structural condition and suitable protection; treatments used historically are not a reason to apply preservatives directly in the water.
researchNotes: BMIG supplies species-specific ridges and tubercles. A CSIRO primary report independently documents this species attacking marine timber and emphasizes species-specific protection. No broad native-range claim is made; historical confusion among Limnoria can complicate old records.

sources.title: British Myriapod and Isopod Group: Limnoria quadripunctata
CSIRO: The occurrence of Limnoria in Australia

claims: Small marine wood borers distinguished by a Y ridge and four tail-plate tubercles.
Identified L. quadripunctata in attacked marine timber; historical identification and protection limitations.

proposedDescription: Italian bugloss is a bristly perennial grown for its bright blue flowers. It produces upright, branching flowering stems above a leafy base and may be found outside cultivation. It is recorded as nonnative in California, but that does not mean every garden plant is causing ecological harm. Describing whether it was planted or growing independently is especially useful for this ornamental species.
identification: Look for coarse hairs, oblong to lance-shaped leaves, and blue flowers around 2 cm across on branching stems. The green calyx beneath each flower is divided almost to its base. Older flowers may shift toward blue-purple, and cultivated forms vary. Other blue-flowered members of the borage family can look similar. Photograph a whole flowering stem, a lower leaf and the calyx from the side; a close crop of a blue flower alone leaves out useful identifying details.
actions: If plants appear beyond a garden, record the distance from any planted clump and whether there are several sizes of plants. Where removal is appropriate, prevent seed maturation and follow up for regrowth rather than assuming the top growth is the entire perennial plant. Wear gloves around the coarse hairs and keep removed seed-bearing material out of garden-waste dumping sites. Ask a local botanist to confirm unfamiliar plants before clearing a patch, especially where other borage-family wildflowers occur. These are cautious garden-containment steps, not a tested eradication protocol.
researchNotes: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria and RHS independently describe the bristly perennial, leaves and flowers. Calflora supplies California nonnative context. The draft avoids importing medicinal uses or claiming a documented control trial that these sources do not provide.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria HortFlora: Anchusa azurea

claims: Bristly perennial, blue flowers to 2 cm, deeply divided calyx.
Mostly basal lance-shaped coarse-haired leaves; branching stems; aging blue-purple flowers.
Nonnative perennial in California.

proposedDescription: Italian pear scale is a tiny armored scale insect that feeds on the woody parts of fruit trees. It often hides beneath moss or lichens on older bark, where a small infestation can be easy to miss. Heavy aggregations can weaken a tree or contribute to bark damage, but small populations may cause little noticeable harm. Finding the scale is a reason to inspect the tree carefully, not an automatic reason to spray.
identification: Adult females sit beneath a small, roughly circular, pale gray cover about 1.5 mm across, with a brown peak slightly off center. The insect underneath is pinkish, reddish or purple, a useful clue separating it from some other orchard scales. Photograph a section of affected bark and a close view with a scale reference. Several armored scales look alike from above; a laboratory may need a specimen to confirm the species. Bark cracking or poor growth by itself does not identify this insect.
actions: Inspect sheltered bark on branches and the trunk, especially during routine dormant-season checks. Record the host tree and whether there is actual dieback or only a few scale covers. UC IPM notes that damaging infestations are unusual in California and that sprays can perform poorly when insects are sheltered. Have an extension specialist assess live scales and tree condition before treatment. Avoid stripping healthy bark or removing all lichens simply because they are present; confirm the pest and the need for action first.
researchNotes: UC IPM supplies scale-cover details, modest-impact context and management limitations. Norway's NIBIO independently describes reddish females on bark and damage from serious infestations. Orchard and regional differences are retained rather than presented as a universal treatment threshold.

sources.title: UC IPM: Italian pear scale on prune

claims: Gray covers, reddish females, bark feeding, low-impact small populations and spray limitations.
Females overwinter on bark; reddish body and branch deformation under heavy attack.

proposedDescription: Italian plumeless thistle is a spiny thistle that starts as a low rosette before producing branching flowering stems. In suitable disturbed ground or grassland it can form dense, prickly patches. Its narrow flower heads and spiny stem wings are useful clues, but it is easily confused with slenderflower thistle and other thistles. Native thistles also support wildlife, so getting the identification right matters before removal.
identification: Look for deeply lobed, spine-edged leaves whose bases continue down the stem as narrow, spiny wings. The leaf undersides and parts of the stems can have a pale, cobwebby coating. The University of Texas treatment describes small groups of one to five narrow heads, surrounded by pointed bracts. Photograph the lower leaves, stem wings and the entire flower-head cluster. The shape and grouping of heads help distinguish it from thistles with large solitary heads, but close relatives still need careful comparison.
actions: Deal with a confirmed small patch before seed matures, using gloves and tools that keep spines away from skin. Contain flowering or seed-bearing material rather than leaving it on disturbed ground. Follow up for new rosettes and check places where soil or equipment could have carried seeds. For a new occurrence, contact the local weed program before undertaking a large clearing effort. Portland includes Italian and slenderflower thistles in an early-detection program, illustrating why the correct local response may be reporting and coordinated removal rather than routine mowing.
researchNotes: The University of Texas flora provides independent morphological detail. Portland's municipal program supplies local response context, with the two similar Carduus species explicitly grouped. No Portland requirement is generalized to other jurisdictions; physical advice is conservative seed prevention.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: University of Texas Plant Resources Center
claims: Decurrent spiny stem wings, woolly leaf undersides and clusters of one to five heads.
Local early-detection response for Italian and slenderflower thistles.

proposedDescription: Italian stone pine is the broad-crowned pine associated with Mediterranean landscapes and commercial pine nuts. A young tree is much more compact than the umbrella-shaped adult, so age can change the first impression considerably. It is planted as an ornamental in suitable climates. Records of planted trees and records of seedlings establishing away from them should be kept separate when describing its spread.
identification: Mature trees develop a wide, rounded crown on a substantial trunk. The long needles occur in pairs; Oregon State gives a typical length of 10-15 cm. Mature cones are broad and heavy-looking, often 8-15 cm long, with large seeds. Photograph a needle bundle at its base, a mature cone and the whole tree. Crown shape alone is unreliable for a young specimen, and other pines also carry two needles per bundle. A cone-and-needle comparison is more useful than an umbrella silhouette by itself.
actions: Check the ground beyond planted trees for self-established seedlings and photograph them before deciding whether they need removal. Include information about nearby landscaping and any recent planting. Do not cut a mature ornamental tree merely because it appears in an introduced-species catalog. If an unwanted seedling is correctly identified, removal while small is easier to plan than work on an established tree. Larger trees require an arborist's assessment of safety and site constraints. Choose locally appropriate planting stock rather than releasing ornamental seedlings into natural habitat.
researchNotes: Oregon State supplies needle and cone measurements. NC State independently describes the transition from shrubby young growth to an umbrella crown and its ornamental use. Long cultivation complicates native-range reconstruction, so the draft avoids an overly precise origin statement or blanket invasive label.

claims: Paired 10-15 cm needles, broad cones and umbrella crown.
Young shrubby form changes to a tall trunk with umbrella crown; ornamental cultivation.

proposedDescription: Italian toadflax is a narrow-leaved perennial with yellow, snapdragon-like flowers and a long spur behind each flower. It belongs to a group that includes the more familiar yellow toadflax. Similar-looking plants should not be assumed to be the same species, especially when an observation would be a new regional record. European accounts place it in dry grasslands, where its slim flowering stems rise above narrow foliage.
identification: The Swiss flora describes flat, bluish leaves and an otherwise hairless plant, including the flowering cluster. Flowers are golden yellow with an orange-yellow raised throat. The flower body is about 1 cm long excluding the spur, which is approximately as long again; the capsule is only about 4-5 mm. These proportions help separate it from common yellow toadflax.
