Examined females from Celtis and Osmanthus in Yunnan; key uses short stout dorsal setae and conical cerarian setae for P. japonicus.

proposedDescription: Japanese millet is a cultivated annual grass used for grain, forage and other agricultural purposes. Escaped plants can occur near places where it has been sown or where birdseed has spilled. It belongs to the same difficult grass group as barnyardgrass, so a sturdy grass beside a feeder is not automatically a different species from one growing in a field.
identification: Look for stout upright stems and fairly broad, flat blades. At the junction of the blade and sheath, the ligule is absent, an important Echinochloa clue. The dense seed head has upright or spreading branches carrying clusters of plump spikelets, which can become purplish or dark brown. The lower glume is much shorter than the spikelet. These small floral parts help separate related species; photographs should show a mature head, individual spikelets and the collar area rather than just broad leaves.
actions: Keep the original seed label when Japanese millet has been deliberately planted, and record whether a suspected escape is adjacent to that planting. Clean up spilled birdseed and remove unwanted volunteers before seed ripens if you are trying to prevent another generation. Avoid assuming that an unidentified Echinochloa is a suitable forage crop. A local agronomist can help confirm mature specimens and choose management that fits the crop or habitat. Regional reports of escape justify checking nearby ground, but they do not establish that every planted stand is invasive or requires removal.
researchNotes: New South Wales Flora supplies diagnostic characters and birdseed or cultivation escapes. Missouri Extension independently distinguishes Japanese millet from other millet crops. A conflicting extension table labeling this taxon browntop millet was excluded rather than propagated.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Echinochloa esculenta
University of Missouri Extension: Growing millets

claims: Annual stout grass, ligule absent, dense panicle, dark spikelets; birdseed use and cultivation escapes.
Japanese millet is Echinochloa esculenta; distinct from browntop millet; grain forage and cover crop context.

proposedDescription: Japanese netvein hollyfern forms a tuft of sturdy, glossy fronds whose broad leaflets look rather like holly leaves. It stays green in mild conditions but can lose foliage in colder weather. This is a fern, so the brown structures beneath fertile fronds are spore-producing clusters rather than flowers, seeds or automatically a sign of insect damage.
identification: Each frond is divided once into broad, pointed leaflets that curve slightly like a sickle. The leaflets are leathery, with irregular teeth and a network of veins. Turn a mature frond over to look for many rounded spore clusters arranged on both sides of the leaflet midrib. Other hollyferns can look similar, so include the stalk scales, leaflet margins and underside in photographs. A close image of one leaflet usually gives more useful evidence than a picture of the entire glossy clump.
actions: For a retained garden plant, provide shelter, shade and soil that holds moisture while draining well. Check frost exposure before interpreting damaged fronds as disease; damaged foliage can be removed when new growth begins. Before sharing divisions or planting near natural habitat, consult local guidance, because the species has naturalized in some regions. Keep a record of spontaneous plants outside the original bed. If removing an unwanted clump, distinguish its actual crown from neighboring ferns first and monitor for additional small plants rather than broadly clearing the surrounding vegetation.
researchNotes: RHS independently supports tufted habit, cultivation and frost-damaged frond care. Flora of New Zealand supplies venation, sori and naturalized habitat evidence. Florida's separate assessment is not generalized to other regions.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Cyrtomium falcatum

claims: Tufted leathery sickle-shaped fronds; shade and moist well-drained soil; cold deciduous behavior and frost care.
Net veins, toothed falcate pinnae, round sori and naturalized lowland or urban habitats.

proposedDescription: Japanese pagoda tree is a large deciduous tree with a rounded crown, divided leaves and creamy summer flowers. It is also called Chinese scholar tree and was long known as Sophora japonica. The familiar Japanese name reflects its cultivation history rather than a simple statement about origin. Mature trees can become much broader and taller than a young nursery specimen suggests.
identification: Leaves alternate on the branches and divide into several pairs of leaflets plus an end leaflet, usually seven to seventeen leaflets altogether. Creamy, pea-shaped flowers gather in large terminal clusters. The smooth pods narrow sharply between seeds, producing a distinctive string-of-beads outline. Young stems can remain green for several years before becoming brown. Compare the pods and a whole leaf with other compound-leaved trees, and do not use the presence or absence of flowers alone: young trees may take years to flower well.
actions: Allow generous space when assessing whether an existing tree fits its surroundings. Have substantial branches and storm damage assessed by an arborist rather than attempting large cuts from the ground. Where regional guidance identifies escape concerns, check beyond the crown for seedlings and avoid distributing seed. The pods and seeds should not be treated as food. If the tree flowers poorly, consider maturity and local summer conditions before applying fertilizer or diagnosing illness. Any replacement decision should take account of the mature canopy, nearby structures and the site's local planting guidance.
researchNotes: NC State provides the leaf count, beaded pods, green stems and structural cautions. RHS independently supports mature size, pea-shaped flowers and delayed flowering. Sources differ on exact years to flowering, so the draft uses no fixed age threshold.

sources.title: Royal Horticultural Society: Japanese pagoda tree

claims: Alternate compound leaves, seven to seventeen leaflets, beaded pods, young green stems, toxic seeds and storm vulnerability.
Large rounded deciduous tree, creamy pea-like flowers and flowering dependence on maturity and warm summers.

proposedDescription: Japanese pear rust is a fungal disease whose life cycle connects susceptible pears and related plants with junipers. Japanese pear is an important host, while infection can persist on juniper for more than one season. The fungus is only one of several Gymnosporangium rusts, so a rusty pear leaf or an orange growth on a juniper does not by itself establish this species.
identification: On pear, look closely at both leaf surfaces: small upper-surface structures are followed by tube-like spore structures beneath. On Chinese juniper, brownish-orange spore masses can develop on leaves and green stems. These signs help locate material for testing but overlap with other rust fungi. Record the host species, date, recent wet weather and whether nearby junipers also show symptoms. A plant diagnostic laboratory may need microscopic examination or molecular testing to distinguish the fungus reliably.
actions: Photograph symptoms before removing affected material and ask a diagnostic service how to package samples. Keep suspect nursery junipers or bonsai separate and avoid moving them to another property while the problem is unresolved, because infection can be hidden. Do not remove every nearby juniper based on leaf spots alone. Once the disease is confirmed, discuss susceptible hosts and locally appropriate prevention with an orchard adviser or plant-health authority. Treating visible pear leaves alone does not address a perennial infection on the alternate host, and a symptom-free winter inspection does not establish that a juniper is clear.
researchNotes: EPPO supplies the alternate-host cycle, detailed signs, latent juniper infection and diagnostic requirements. A 2023 original comparative infection study independently confirms G. asiaticum on Chinese juniper; it postdates the 2022 EPPO synthesis and is not counted as its underlying duplicate.

sources.title: BMC Genomics: Comparative transcriptome analysis of infected juniper branches

claims: Pear and juniper alternate hosts; tube-like pear aecia; orange telia on juniper; persistent and latent juniper infection; molecular diagnosis.
Gymnosporangium asiaticum and G. yamadae infect Chinese juniper with different symptoms.

proposedDescription: Japanese pearlwort is a tiny, tufted flowering plant that can be mistaken for a little grass or a patch of moss until its white flowers appear. It is an annual or short-lived biennial in botanical treatments. The delicate stems and narrow leaves make it easy to miss in a casual survey, and several other pearlworts share almost the same general appearance.
identification: Examine a flowering plant with a hand lens. The leaves are narrow and linear, while small white flowers sit on slender stalks. The species commonly has five sepals and five petals, with petals slightly shorter than the sepals. The ripe capsule opens into valves, and seed-surface details can matter in a formal identification. A moss will not produce these flowers or capsules. Count parts on several intact flowers and photograph the upper stems, leaves and ripe fruit rather than relying on one damaged bloom.
actions: Keep a small flowering sample or clear close photographs before removing an unfamiliar pearlwort from a cultivated bed. Where it is unwanted, act before ripe capsules scatter seed and check the same gaps again later. Avoid transferring loose soil from a seed-bearing patch into new pots. In a natural setting, seek a regional botanical identification first, since small native and introduced pearlworts can be difficult to distinguish. The flora evidence supports recognition of the species, but does not supply a tested control schedule or justify a blanket invasive label.
researchNotes: Indian Institute of Science independently describes a tufted annual with linear leaves and white flowers. Digital Flora of Shanghai supplies floral details, while Kew supports annual or biennial lifespan. No regional flowering calendar is presented as universal.

Kew Plants of the World Online: Sagina japonica

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Indian Institute of Science regional flora
claims: Small tufted annual, linear leaves, white flowers on long stalks and valved capsules.
Five sepals and petals; petals shorter than sepals; narrow leaves and small capsules.
Accepted species, annual or biennial life form and regional native and introduced ranges.

proposedDescription: Japanese primrose is a moisture-loving perennial with upright flower stems rising from a broad rosette of leaves. Flowers appear in separated tiers around the stem, giving it the candelabra appearance that gardeners recognize. Red-purple is a familiar color, but white and other garden forms occur. A flowering group beside water can be striking without being enough to establish its local ecological status.
identification: Look for broad, pale green, crinkled leaves gathered at the ground and relatively bare upright stems carrying several rings of flowers. The flowers in a tier open around the stem rather than forming a single ball at its tip. Other candelabra primroses share that arrangement, so flower color alone is not decisive. Photograph a complete stem, individual flowers and the leaf rosette. Retain any cultivar label, especially where several primroses or garden hybrids have been planted together.
actions: For a retained garden planting, maintain dependable moisture and protect it from intense drying heat or wind. Check the soil before repeatedly watering a wilting plant; moisture-loving does not mean that every poorly drained site is suitable. Cut back spent flower stems if you want to limit seed production, and watch for seedlings beyond the intended bed. Before moving divisions into a streamside or other natural area, check local recommendations and the site's conservation needs. If plants decline, inspect the crown and foliage and obtain a diagnosis rather than automatically treating all primrose problems as the same disease.
researchNotes: RHS supplies rosette and tiered-flower characters, moisture needs and post-flowering pruning. New York Botanical Garden independently describes this species growing beside its stream and distinguishes other candelabra primroses. Garden observations are not converted into wild occurrence claims.

claims: Deciduous perennial, broad crinkly rosette, whorled flowers, moist humus-rich soil and cutback after flowering.
Japanese primrose with one to six flower whorls; red-purple to white flowers; moist shade and stream-edge garden culture.

proposedDescription: Japanese privet is an evergreen shrub or small tree often clipped into a hedge. Left to grow freely, it produces clusters of fragrant white flowers followed by dark fruit. Its thick leaves can make it look tidy even when seedlings are beginning to appear elsewhere. The degree of escape and the recommendations for planting vary by region and should be checked locally.
identification: Look for opposite, leathery leaves, commonly around two to four inches long, and branched clusters of small white flowers. Garden selections may have wavy margins or variegation. Glossy privet is a close lookalike, and heavily clipped plants may lack useful flowers or fruit. Photograph several mature leaves with a size reference, the twig arrangement and any fruit clusters. A broad evergreen leaf or the nursery name waxleaf privet is not enough to separate all the species and cultivars sold under similar names.
actions: Before adding a hedge, check the current regional assessment for Japanese privet and consider a locally suitable alternative where escape is a concern. For an existing planting, look beneath bird perches and along neighboring edges for seedlings. Remove unwanted seedlings while small and contain fruit-bearing debris. Shearing can reduce flowering, but it should not be treated as proof that a hedge cannot spread. Larger established plants require a plan for roots and follow-up growth; use local extension advice rather than transferring an unrelated privet treatment without checking the species and site.
researchNotes: Clemson independently describes Japanese privet habit and leathery foliage, with genus-level seed dispersal cautions. UF/IFAS provides species-level landscape and current regional assessment material. Direct fetches of Clemson and UF publication failed, so those sources remain indexed excerpts.

claims: Japanese privet is evergreen with leathery two to four inch leaves; shearing removes flowering branches; birds disperse privet seed.
Japanese privet species-level landscape description.
Florida planting guidance includes assessment-specific management restrictions.

proposedDescription: Japanese raisintree is a deciduous tree with a spreading crown and an unusual fruiting display. The swollen, branching stalks beneath the small fruits give rise to its raisin name. It has been planted as an ornamental in many places and has escaped in some regions. A tree's familiar garden use therefore does not settle whether it is appropriate beside nearby natural habitat.
identification: Look for alternate, broad oval to heart-shaped leaves and loose clusters of small, fragrant, greenish-yellow flowers near branch tips. The small rounded fruits sit above stalks that become conspicuously thickened as the season progresses. Gray or gray-brown bark and the overall branching form provide supporting clues. Photograph the entire fruit cluster with its stalks, rather than just a detached brown piece. Other broad-leaved trees can look similar when sterile, and a name based on food should not substitute for a botanical identification.
actions: Before planting or sharing seed, check local guidance for Hovenia dulcis, especially where it is already escaping. Around an existing tree, look for young plants beyond the maintained lawn and record whether they occur beneath likely bird perches. Contain fruiting debris if removal is planned, and use an arborist for work on a mature crown. Keep follow-up checks focused on seedlings as well as the original trunk. If retaining a tree in a cooler climate, consider cold wind and poorly matured shoots when evaluating damage instead of immediately assuming a pest problem.
researchNotes: NC State supports swollen fruit stalks, bark, bird attraction and regional escape concerns. RHS independently describes foliage, flower clusters and climate-related shoot injury. Food and medicinal claims, including inconsistent fruit-versus-stalk wording, are deliberately excluded.

claims: Deciduous tree with swollen fruit stalks, gray bark, bird-attracting fruit and regional naturalization.
Alternate broad leaves, branched greenish-yellow flower clusters and cold damage to unripened shoots.

proposedDescription: Japanese rose, or kerria, is a deciduous shrub with slender arching stems and bright yellow spring flowers. It is a member of the rose family, but its simple leaves and green shoots give it a different appearance from a typical garden rose. New shoots arising around the clump can gradually create a broad thicket, even when the original plant was small.
identification: Look for bright green young stems and pointed oval leaves with conspicuous teeth along the edges. Flowers are carried singly on short leafy shoots. Wild-type plants usually have five yellow petals, while familiar double garden forms resemble small yellow pompons. Both can belong to the same species. Photograph a leafy shoot and the whole flower rather than relying on the name Japanese rose, which can be confused with actual roses in conversation or on an old planting label.
actions: For an established garden clump, decide how much space it can occupy and check its edges for new suckers. Remove unwanted suckers as part of routine maintenance rather than waiting for a dense patch to develop. Provide well-drained soil and avoid excessive feeding, which can encourage unwelcome growth. Some shade helps protect the flower display from fading in strong sun. If a plant has moved beyond the garden, confirm local recommendations before transferring divisions elsewhere. Cutting only the tall stems will change the appearance quickly, but it does not by itself account for the shoots spreading around the base.
researchNotes: NC State and RHS independently support the arching habit, spring flowers and garden care. RHS explicitly describes suckering and sucker removal. The draft does not infer that every vigorous garden clump is an ecologically invasive population.

claims: Arching deciduous shrub, yellow spring flowers, five-petaled and double forms, drainage and restrained fertilization.
Green stems, toothed leaves, suckering thickets and removal of unwanted suckers.

proposedDescription: Japanese sedge, also called Asiatic sand sedge or calligraphy sedge, is a low perennial adapted to coastal sand. Its underground stems can produce dense mats of stiff leaves on dunes and upper beaches. In parts of the introduced range it competes with dune vegetation, so management needs to consider both the sedge and the fragile ground supporting it.
identification: Look for short, stout plants with triangular stems and stiff, arching yellow-green leaves. The leaf margins have small sharp teeth, and brown scales surround the stem base. Compact flowering heads often sit below the taller leaves. These features distinguish the plant from many beach grasses, but other sedges need comparison. Photograph the stem base, an intact flower head and the leaf arrangement without trampling a larger area of dune. Avoid running bare fingers along the sharp leaf edges just to test their texture.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the beach or dune manager, with a location and photographs. Keep vehicles, collected sand and plant debris from carrying material away from the patch. Small outlying plants may be removable under an approved site plan, but all underground material must be considered and follow-up is necessary. Do not excavate a broad dune face on your own: removal and revegetation need to protect the site from erosion. Established mats are a restoration problem that calls for repeated monitoring, not simply a one-day clearing exercise.
researchNotes: Michigan's state profile supports coastal habitat and diagnostic characters. Lower Hudson PRISM independently provides rhizome and follow-up management guidance. Its statement about mixed-sex inflorescences was not used because it conflicts with other treatments.

sources.title: Michigan invasive species program: Calligraphy sedge
Lower Hudson PRISM: Asiatic sand sedge

claims: Low perennial coastal sedge; triangular stems, basal scales, serrated leaves and dune impacts.
Rhizomatous mats, stiff yellow-green leaves, underground material removal and repeated monitoring.

proposedDescription: Japanese stiltgrass is a summer annual that can form a soft-looking carpet across woodland edges, damp paths and shaded lawns. Its sprawling stems may root at the nodes, allowing a few plants to occupy more ground during the season. The plants die, but seed left in the soil can keep a patch returning for years, especially when disturbed ground remains open.
identification: Look for relatively broad grass blades with a pale, silvery line along the midrib and a spreading, branched habit. Examine several leaves under good light; the stripe can be less obvious in some views. Native grasses such as nimblewill, cutgrasses and rosette panicgrasses can be mistaken for it. A complete plant, its stem nodes and mature seed head are better evidence than a single striped blade. Compare texture and growth form carefully before removing an entire woodland ground layer.
actions: For a small confirmed patch, hand-pull plants before seed heads mature and keep disturbance to the surrounding soil modest. Clean shoes, tools and mowing equipment before leaving, since seed travels readily on them. In a lawn, maintaining suitable dense turf and preventing seed production can help, but woodland work needs different priorities from lawn care. Revisit the site for several seasons, including after fresh disturbance. If seed heads are already present, contain the material instead of carrying loose plants along a path. A cleared patch this year does not mean its seed bank has been exhausted.
researchNotes: Rutgers supports lookalikes, silver midrib, rooting nodes and multi-year seed persistence. Penn State independently supports hand removal before seed heads, contaminated equipment pathways and limits of turf management. Lawn recommendations are explicitly separated from woodland restoration.

sources.title: Penn State: Japanese stiltgrass in lawns

claims: Silvery midrib, rooting nodes, lookalike grasses and seed survival up to five years.
Annual grass; hand pulling before seed; equipment and footwear spread; turf density alone may not suppress established infestations.

proposedDescription: Japanese sweet coltsfoot, also called giant butterbur, is a perennial that makes a bold patch of broad leaves in moist ground. The flower shoots appear early, before the full summer foliage develops. Underground rhizomes let a planting spread well beyond its original clump. Leaf size varies considerably among forms and growing conditions, so spectacular size is a clue rather than a requirement.
identification: Look for rounded to heart-shaped leaves carried on long stalks from the ground. Early flower shoots are thick and upright, bearing clusters of small pale flower heads rather than a single daisy. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Other butterburs can look similar, and a large summer leaf without flowers may not be enough for a confident identification. Photograph the leaf base and underside, the way its stalk meets the blade, and any early-season flower clusters.
actions: Think about the available space before planting or dividing it. Where containment is needed, monitor the perimeter for shoots arising from the rhizome system and avoid moving soil or divisions into nearby wet habitat. Cutting off the large leaves can hide the patch temporarily without removing the underground plant. Obtain local advice before attempting broad excavation beside water, where disturbance can affect the bank. For a retained ornamental, provide consistently moist, sheltered ground and remove old foliage as new growth approaches. Published food traditions are not a reason to taste an unidentified butterbur or assume every plant part is safe.
researchNotes: RHS describes vigorous rhizomatous spread and garden care. University of Tokyo's botanical catalogue independently supports dioecy, long-stalked heart-shaped leaves and early inflorescences. Leaf dimensions differ greatly, so no single size cutoff is imposed.

sources.title: University of Tokyo Museum: Faces and Flora catalogue

claims: Large rounded leaves, early cream-white flowers, vigorous rhizomatous spread, moist sheltered culture.
Dioecious perennial, long-stalked heart-shaped leaves and early rhizome-borne flower clusters.

proposedDescription: Japanese wisteria is a woody climbing vine with long hanging flower clusters. Its showy spring display can disguise the scale of its later growth: established stems can climb through trees, while surface runners root wherever they meet suitable ground. In regions where Asian wisterias escape, a flowering canopy may be connected to a much wider network below.
identification: Leaves are divided into many leaflets, commonly fifteen to nineteen in this species. Long drooping clusters carry fragrant, pea-shaped flowers that open progressively from the cluster base toward its tip. Fuzzy hanging pods follow the flowers. Chinese wisteria and hybrids can overlap in appearance, so leaflet number or twining direction alone should not settle the identification. Photograph a complete leaf, several flower clusters at different stages and mature pods. A garden label can help but does not rule out hybrid ancestry.
actions: Before removal, trace the vines to their bases and look for runners rooted away from the main trunk. Keep rooted pieces and seed pods contained rather than dumping them at a woodland edge. Do not pull a heavy vine from a tree canopy if branches could fall or bark could be stripped. Plan repeated checks for regrowth after cutting and obtain local advice for large established plants. When replacing an ornamental, choose a species suitable for your region and support structure. A single pruning can make the site look clear while living stems and roots remain.
researchNotes: NC State provides species morphology and rooting-runner evidence. Maryland independently treats Chinese, Japanese and hybrid wisterias together, supporting the diagnostic caution and management context. No edible-use advice or pesticide concentration is transferred from source text.

sources.title: University of Maryland: Chinese and Japanese wisteria

claims: Commonly fifteen to nineteen leaflets; sequentially opening long clusters; velvety pods; rooting runners.
Asian woody perennial vines include Japanese, Chinese and hybrid plants requiring careful identification.

proposedDescription: Japanese yellow loosestrife is a low, branching herb with small yellow flowers and rounded to oval leaves. Regional floras describe it in moist places, including stream margins and damp forest edges. Despite the loosestrife name, it is not purple loosestrife, and advice for that much taller wetland plant should not be assumed to apply here.
identification: Examine the stems and both leaf surfaces for fine hairs. Leaves are paired opposite each other and carry small gland dots that may be easier to see with magnification. Yellow flowers arise singly from the leaf axils on short stalks; the green sepals remain around the developing capsule. Creeping or low-growing relatives can share the same general look. Photograph the leaf arrangement, stem hairs, a flower from the side and any fruit. These details are more useful than a distant image of a yellow-flowered patch.
actions: Record whether the plant is part of a deliberate groundcover planting or is growing independently in a moist natural area. Seek a regional flora-based identification before removing it from a stream margin, where similar plants and sensitive ground may be present. If an unwanted garden plant is confirmed, contain seed-bearing material and check for further plants before moving nearby soil. The sources reviewed support its identity and habitat but do not demonstrate a reliable species-specific eradication method. Local status and the purpose of management should guide any larger intervention.
researchNotes: Indian Institute of Science and New South Wales Flora provide independent morphology and habitat treatments. Shanghai flora corroborates opposite leaves and solitary axillary flowers. No blanket invasive status, aggressive rooting rate or control efficacy is inferred.

proposedDescription: Japanese yew is an evergreen conifer more accurately known as a podocarp or Buddhist pine. It is not a true yew in the genus Taxus. In gardens it may be clipped into a narrow hedge, but unconfined plants can become trees. The long, flat leaves give it a broad-leaved appearance even though it produces cones rather than ordinary flowers.
identification: Look for stiff, narrow leaves several inches long with a conspicuous central midrib and smooth edges. Female plants can carry a seed above a swollen, colored fleshy receptacle, an arrangement quite different from a typical berry. The cultivar Maki is more compact and has smaller leaves, so size alone is not decisive. Photograph a complete shoot and any seed-bearing structures. If the only name available is Japanese yew, compare both Podocarpus and true yews before making decisions based on a common name.
actions: For a retained hedge or tree, pay close attention to drainage: this species does poorly in persistently wet soil. Consider its eventual size when deciding how close to structures it should remain. If yellow spots or leaf loss appear, inspect leaves and twigs for scale insects and obtain an identification before treating. Beaded structures on the roots are not automatically a pest; podocarps can have normal root nodules. Avoid removing healthy roots merely because they look unfamiliar. Check regional planting advice before distributing seedlings or adding plants beside natural habitat.
researchNotes: NParks and LSU independently support leaf, seed-bearing and cultivation characters. UF/IFAS adds scale symptoms and the important root-nodule lookalike caution. The draft avoids source wording that calls gymnosperm structures true fruit.

claims: Evergreen conifer, narrow five to ten centimeter leaves, well-drained soil and intolerance of wet conditions.
Stiff flat leaves with prominent midrib; female seed-bearing structures; smaller Maki selection.
Scale-associated leaf spots and drop; beaded roots can be normal nodules rather than pests.

proposedDescription: Jaraguagrass, also called thatch grass, is a tall, tufted grass associated with warm open habitats and pasture introductions. Mature stands can leave substantial dry material. In Hawaii, fire specialists identify it as a fire concern, but the importance of a particular patch depends on local climate, surrounding vegetation and how the land is managed.
identification: Look closely at the flowering head rather than trying to identify a tall grass by height. The head is assembled from pairs of short flowering branches, each associated with a narrow bract. Rusty or reddish hairs on the spikelets are an important clue in the Hawaiian key. Other Hyparrhenia species can be very similar, and small hairs at the branch bases may be pale. Photograph the whole head and a close view of one paired unit, with a size reference and an intact mature specimen if requested.
actions: Report a new patch to the relevant land or weed manager where this grass is a concern. Keep mature seed heads from being carried on equipment or mixed into material moved to another property. In a dry stand, discuss fuel reduction and plant control together rather than treating burning as a simple removal method; the species can regenerate after fire. Arrange follow-up checks for regrowth and seedlings after any work. If it is part of a pasture system, seek locally appropriate forage and vegetation advice before making changes that could leave bare ground or redistribute seed.
researchNotes: New South Wales Flora supplies paired-raceme morphology. Bishop Museum independently distinguishes red spikelet hairs in Hawaii. Pacific Fire Exchange provides a regional fire-risk assessment; its Hawaii conclusion is kept regional and no burning prescription is inferred.

sources.title: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Hyparrhenia rufa
Bishop Museum: Hawaiian biological survey records
Pacific Fire Exchange: Hyparrhenia rufa fire risk

claims: Tall annual or perennial grass with paired racemes and awned spikelets.
Hawaiian Hyparrhenia key separates H. rufa by red hairs on spikelets.
High regional fire risk and regeneration after fire.

proposedDescription: Java plum is a large evergreen tree with a dense crown and clusters of dark, oblong fruit. It is also called jambolan and is widely cultivated in warm regions. Animals eat the fruit and carry its seeds, helping explain why seedlings may appear away from an old planting. Invasion assessments vary even within Florida, so local guidance matters.
identification: Leaves are opposite, smooth-edged, glossy and somewhat leathery, often with a conspicuous yellowish midrib. New foliage can be pinkish. Small fragrant flowers have many stamens, giving their clusters a soft, brushlike appearance. The fruit changes from green through reddish purple to shiny dark purple or black. Other Syzygium trees can have similar leaves; photograph the leaf veins, entire flower cluster and ripe fruit together. A dark fruit alone is not enough to establish Java plum.
actions: Check the regional assessment before planting or distributing seedlings, particularly in places where the tree is known to escape. Around an existing tree, inspect nearby edges and animal perches for young plants and record how far they occur from the parent. If removal is recommended, include fruit and seedlings in the plan instead of focusing only on the trunk. Have large trees assessed by an arborist, and contain seed-bearing debris so it is not dumped into natural areas. Continue monitoring after work because animals may bring seed from other nearby trees.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS establishes the South Florida impact and explicitly different zone assessments. NParks independently supplies morphology and animal dispersal evidence. Florida Natural Areas Inventory repeats UF material, so it is not counted as another independent source.

claims: Large evergreen tree escaped cultivation and became invasive in South Florida.
Assessment differs between North, Central and South Florida.
Opposite glossy leaves, yellow midrib, pink flush, many-stamen flowers, dark oblong fruit and animal dispersal.

proposedDescription: Javanese bishopwood is a substantial tropical tree with a dense, rounded crown. It has been widely planted for shade and street landscaping, but has also escaped cultivation in places such as southern Florida. Young foliage can have a bronze cast. Its most useful everyday identification feature is the three-part leaf, which should be examined as a whole rather than as separate leaves.
identification: Each long leaf stalk carries three shiny leaflets, with the middle leaflet often larger and more distinctly stalked than the side pair. Leaflets are broadly oval to elliptic and have small teeth along their edges. Tiny greenish flowers lack showy petals and occur in clusters near leaf axils. Small rounded fruits may become brown, reddish or dark. Several unrelated plants have three leaflets, so include the woody branching, leaf stalk and fruit in photographs instead of treating leaflet number as a complete identification.
actions: Check regional recommendations before planting another tree or moving seedlings from an old planting. Where removal is appropriate, map the seedlings as well as mature trees, and contain fruit-bearing debris during work. A large bishopwood needs professional assessment for safe pruning or removal, especially near buildings and roads. Keep records of any new growth after work so follow-up can be directed to actual surviving plants. In a place where the species belongs naturally, the same vigorous tree may have a different role; do not transfer a Florida impact label without checking the local context.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS supplies the introduced Florida context and diagnostic trifoliate foliage. Chiang Mai University's Forest Restoration Research Unit independently describes leaf arrangement and dimensions in the native-range restoration context. Inconsistent leaflet sizes were not converted into a hard cutoff.

claims: Large dense-crowned tree, alternate trifoliate toothed leaves, tiny flowers and small fruits; Florida escape history.
Spirally arranged trifoliate leaves, oval or elliptic hairless leaflets and shallowly toothed margins.

proposedDescription: Javanese glorybower is a traditional name for a red-flowered tropical shrub usually described with large, hairy, heart-shaped leaves. However, the scientific name has been applied inconsistently. Some institutional sources place Clerodendrum speciosissimum with C. buchananii, while other botanical treatments distinguish them. The traditional speciosissimum concept is used here, with the related buchananii treatment kept explicit.
identification: A shrub matching this general description has opposite broad leaves and a terminal cluster of red to orange flowers with projecting stamens. Those characters also fit related glorybowers. The lengths of the calyx, corolla tube and lobes are important in treatments that separate C. speciosissimum from C. buchananii. Photograph a full flowering branch, both leaf surfaces and individual flowers beside a ruler. The similarly named hybrid C. x speciosum is another plant and should not be substituted merely because a search returns it.
actions: Keep the original plant label, collection location and any photographs together when seeking a botanical determination. Avoid sharing a plant as this exact species until the name is resolved. If a broad-leaved glorybower is spreading beyond a garden, document runners and new plants so local advisers can assess the actual growth pattern. Contain any material removed during that work. Have flowering material checked before choosing a species-specific treatment or interpreting regional invasive-status advice. Retain the identification source with the plant record so later comparisons use the same botanical concept.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: NParks still merges C. speciosissimum into C. buchananii; the freshly recovered Flora Zambesiaca text explicitly distinguishes their floral dimensions and calls for revision. The Florida account's calyx dimensions overlap buchananii. This is a substantive identification conflict that a broad red-flowered description cannot solve.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: A traditional speciosissimum account can acknowledge the buchananii boundary without requiring that every cultivated specimen be reassigned first. Meerts2023 newly examines Central African herbarium material, largely buchananii, and explicitly compares floral dimensions; NParks independently describes the broader cultivated plant. Dimensions are comparisons within declared treatments, not a universal resolved key. Next step: Review the qualified traditional-concept account and separately verify flowering vouchers before regional occurrence changes. Fresh evidence/access: Meerts2023 Central African Clerodendrum treatment [indexed_excerpt; Meerts-2023-original-Clerodendrum-specimens] https://phytotaxa.mapress.com/pt/article/view/phytotaxa.594.1.1/50550 - BR/WAG collections and floral comparisons; most African material called speciosissimum fits buchananii; further Asian-taxonomy work needed. Inherited URLs and evidence remain provenance; only the specifically documented accesses are claimed fresh. Parent-read passages are explicitly attributed. No catalog, mapping or public-release changes; local review only.

proposedDescription: Jerusalem cherry is a small ornamental shrub often grown in a pot for its bright orange-red berries. It belongs to the nightshade family and is not an edible cherry or a pepper. Outside cultivation it can persist in suitable moist, disturbed places. The colorful fruit makes the plant conspicuous, but it also makes careful labeling especially useful.
identification: Look for narrow oval to lance-shaped leaves with smooth, slightly wavy edges. White, star-shaped flowers occur singly or in small groups, followed by rounded orange-red berries about the size of a small marble. The plant lacks prickles. Other nightshades and ornamental peppers can be confusing when only fruit is shown. Photograph the flowers, leaf attachment and a complete branch with fruit at different stages. Do not taste a berry as an identification test; the plant is poisonous.
actions: Keep a labeled plant and any fallen berries out of reach of children and pets. If removing an unwanted plant, collect loose fruit as well as the shrub so seeds are not left scattered through the bed or dumped with garden waste. Look for subsequent seedlings in the same moist gaps. Before moving a potted specimen outdoors permanently, check local advice about escape from cultivation. For an unfamiliar fruiting shrub in a natural area, seek confirmation before clearing it. The plant's decorative use is not evidence that its fruit or leaves can be eaten safely.
researchNotes: New South Wales Flora independently supplies the unarmed shrub, leaf, flower and fruit characters and naturalized habitat. Queensland Poisons Information Centre supports toxicity. Sources disagree on flower diameter, so that dimension is omitted; no medical treatment advice is given.

proposedDescription: Jetbead is a deciduous shrub with a loose, arching outline, white flowers and shiny black fruits. The fruits often remain on the branches after the leaves fall, giving the shrub its common name. It has escaped ornamental plantings in parts of eastern North America. Despite the species name scandens, the plant normally presents as a shrub rather than a climbing vine.
identification: Look for opposite, pointed oval leaves with strongly toothed edges and a wrinkled or corrugated upper surface. The showy white flowers usually have four petals, an unusual and helpful feature among familiar rose-family shrubs. Black fruits commonly occur in groups of four, though fewer can develop. Compare the leaf arrangement and petal count with kerria and other flowering shrubs. Photograph a leafy twig, a flower face-on and a fruit cluster; an isolated black fruit could belong to many unrelated plants.
actions: Check local invasive-plant recommendations before planting or distributing seedlings. If removal is recommended, include small plants beneath and around an old shrub, and keep the persistent fruits contained while cutting or transporting branches. Do not treat the attractive black fruits as food. For an uncertain plant, wait for flowers or obtain an expert identification before clearing nearby shrubs with similar leaves. Revisit the area after removal for new growth and seedlings. Where a planting is retained while a replacement is arranged, reducing fruit production can be one precaution, but it is not proof that spread has stopped.
researchNotes: NC State and Oregon State independently support opposite toothed foliage, four-petaled white flowers and persistent black fruits. Fruit number varies in the Oregon treatment, so four is described as common rather than universal. Management remains a bounded precaution.

claims: Deciduous ornamental shrub; four-petaled white flowers; groups of black fruit persisting through winter; poison warning.
Opposite doubly toothed corrugated leaves; solitary four-part flowers; variable fruit count; escape caution.

proposedDescription: Jimsonweed is a robust summer annual with broad leaves, large trumpet-shaped flowers and prickly seed capsules. It can grow rapidly in disturbed ground and crop fields. The flowers may be white or purple, and the stems can also take on a purple color. All parts are poisonous, so this is a plant to identify by observation rather than by tasting or experimenting.
identification: Mature leaves are broadly oval with a few large, irregular triangular teeth, while the earliest seedling leaves may have smooth edges. The thick branching stems are largely smooth. Upright funnel-shaped flowers emerge near leaf or branch junctions, followed by egg-shaped capsules covered in stiff prickles. Ripe capsules split into four sections. Other Datura species require comparison, especially when flowers or fruit are missing. Photograph the whole plant, leaf outline and an intact capsule; a common name such as moonflower can refer to entirely different plants.
actions: Remove confirmed unwanted plants before the prickly capsules mature, keeping hands protected and avoiding unnecessary contact with the foliage. Contain any capsules already present so seed does not spill during transport. Keep removed material out of animal feed and away from children or pets. Recheck disturbed soil for later seedlings instead of assuming the first removal ends the problem. In a crop or pasture, ask an extension adviser to assess the infestation and contamination risk before harvest. Do not rely on ornamental flowers, a historical use or a familiar common name as evidence of safety.
researchNotes: University of Missouri provides detailed morphology and seedling changes. Cornell independently confirms annual weed biology, and Queensland Health supplies toxicity evidence. No medical use, symptom-management instructions or unsupported pesticide advice is included.

proposedDescription: Jio is the catalog common name for Commelina benghalensis, more widely called Benghal dayflower or tropical spiderwort. It is a spreading herb with broad leaves and small blue to purplish flowers. One especially important feature is hidden: it can produce self-pollinating flowers and seed-bearing capsules underground. A patch with no visible flowers can therefore still deserve attention.
identification: Look for broad oval leaves, short hairs on the upper surface and a sheathing leaf base that often carries longer reddish hairs at its opening. Above-ground flowers sit in folded green bracts. These characters overlap with other dayflowers, including Virginia dayflower, so red hairs or blue petals alone are not decisive. Underground flowering structures are a useful additional clue when a specimen is examined. Photograph the leaf sheath, flower bract and whole growth habit, and ask a diagnostic service whether roots and lower stems are needed.
actions: Where this species is unwanted, prevent soil and plant fragments from being moved out of the patch while identification and management are arranged. Inspect the base and rooting stems rather than removing only visible flower shoots. Do not assume mowing or taking off blue flowers prevents all seed production, because the plant can also reproduce below ground. Keep removed material contained and revisit the site for new plants. In a crop field, obtain local extension guidance early: management must fit both the crop and this plant's unusual reproductive biology, rather than following a generic dayflower recommendation.
researchNotes: SANBI independently describes hidden self-pollinating flowers and seed capsules. Mississippi State provides a practical comparison with other dayflowers. Lifespan varies among regional treatments, so the draft uses herb rather than imposing a universal annual or perennial label.

claims: Spreading herb with broad leaves, sheath bristles and underground self-pollinating flowers and capsules.
Comparison with Virginia and other dayflowers; broad leaves, upper-surface hairs and subterranean flowers.

proposedDescription: Job's tears is a robust grass best known for the smooth, beadlike structures carried among its flower clusters. Those hard coverings surround the grain and have long been used as beads. The plant grows in warm, moist settings, including stream banks and disturbed wet ground. Its cultivated forms and local life span vary, so a garden label may be useful context.
identification: Look for stout stems with broad, flat, tapering leaf blades. The conspicuous rounded or teardrop-shaped coverings can mature to pale, bluish or grayish tones and have a polished surface. A slender male flowering branch emerges above the structure that encloses the female portion. This combination is much more distinctive than the leaves alone. Photograph an intact flowering or fruiting cluster from the side, showing both the beadlike part and the projecting branch. Other broad-leaved grasses are difficult to exclude before these structures develop.
actions: Before planting or sharing seed-bearing beads, check local guidance about the species and its ability to establish outside cultivation. Around an existing planting, look along drainage routes and nearby moist ground for volunteers. If it is unwanted, collect the seed-bearing clusters before they are shed and keep them out of discarded soil or streamside garden waste. Continue checking the site after removal. A craft use does not establish that collected material is nonviable, and a grain-crop tradition should not be treated as confirmation that an unidentified wild grass is suitable for food.
researchNotes: Kew's Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment independently supplies the hard cupule, leaf morphology and wet habitat. NParks supports tropical perennial behavior and seed-bearing structures. Food and medicinal source claims are not turned into consumption advice.

claims: Coarse grass with broad blades, polished bony cupule, projecting male raceme and stream or swamp habitat.
Seed enclosed within involucre, perennial in warm climates, moist habitats and bead use.

proposedDescription: Johnny jumpup, also called heartsease or wild pansy, is a small, short-lived violet that often returns from seed. Its cheerful flowers commonly combine purple, white and yellow, although the balance of colors varies. It is related to cultivated pansies, and a volunteer beside a flower bed may need closer examination before it can be assigned to this species.
identification: Look for small pansy-like flowers with five petals, a spur behind the lower petal and green sepals that are no longer than the petals. Leaves are oval to lance-shaped, and the leaflike structures at their bases are deeply divided. Flower color alone is not enough. Field pansy can be especially difficult to separate when plants are not flowering; Flora of North America notes that the usual variety cannot be distinguished from it vegetatively. Photograph the flower front and side, sepals and leaf bases together.
actions: If you welcome it in a garden, allow for seedlings to appear beyond the original clump. If you want to limit that spread, remove developing seed capsules before they dry and eject seed, then check nearby gaps for volunteers. Keep the soil moist but well drained rather than repeatedly soaking a struggling plant. In a natural area, confirm the species before treating every small violet as a garden escape. This plant's readiness to reseed does not alone establish an invasive impact, and advice for large hybrid pansies should not automatically determine its identification or management.
researchNotes:
NC State supports floral characters, self-seeding and capsule dispersal. Flora of North America independently provides the important inability to separate V. tricolor var. tricolor from V. arvensis using vegetation alone. No foraging advice is carried over.

proposedDescription: Johnsongrass is a tall perennial grass that spreads through both seed and a network of underground rhizomes. It was introduced as a forage plant in some regions but is now a troublesome weed of crops, roadsides and other disturbed land. A patch can expand even when seed production is reduced, because established underground stems continue sending up shoots.
identification: Look for long, mostly hairless blades with a conspicuous pale or white midrib. At the blade base there is a membranous ligule, but no clasping auricles. Established plants have substantial rhizomes, which help separate them from similar annual sorghums. A white midrib by itself is not diagnostic. Photograph the collar where blade and sheath meet, a complete flowering head and any underground stem exposed during an authorized inspection. Young plants without flowers or rhizomes may need a weed specialist's comparison.
actions: Prevent seed production and keep contaminated soil or rhizome pieces from moving to clean ground. A casual tilling pass can redistribute living pieces, so any cultivation should be part of a deliberate local plan. Small patches require attention to underground material and repeated new shoots; mowing once only removes the visible growth. Clean machinery before it leaves an infested area. If the grass is in pasture or hay, seek livestock and forage advice before using it, especially after drought or frost. Its history as a forage crop does not guarantee safety under every condition.
researchNotes: Missouri supplies morphology and rhizomatous growth. FAO independently supports targeting both seed and rhizome production; Kentucky extension adds the caution about fragmenting rhizomes and stressed forage. No general grazing safety threshold or pesticide recipe is provided.

claims: Perennial rhizomes, mostly hairless blades, white midvein, membranous ligule and absent auricles.

Cultivation can spread rhizomes; drought or frost can create livestock toxicity concerns.

proposedDescription: Jointed goatgrass is a winter annual grass that closely resembles wheat while young. It is particularly troublesome in winter-wheat systems because its growth timing overlaps the crop and its seed-bearing pieces can contaminate grain. Mature heads make the name easier to understand: they look like narrow cylinders built from a stack of joints.
identification: Look for upright hollow stems, narrow flat leaves and fine hairs along leaf edges or sheaths. The flowering spike is slender and cylindrical rather than open and branching. At maturity it breaks into firm sections that enclose the seeds; loose sections can be mistaken for bits of straw. The upper part of the spike may carry long awns. Photograph an intact head and a detached joint beside a ruler, along with the leaf collar. Seedlings need particular care because visual similarity to wheat is substantial.
actions: Use clean seed and clean harvesting equipment before entering an uninfested field. Map small patches early enough to stop seed production, and include adjoining roadsides or field margins in the plan. If jointed heads are present, contain them rather than carrying loose stems through the crop. Ask a local agronomist about rotation and treatment options that fit the actual wheat system; similar crop and weed biology makes a generic grass-control approach unreliable. Continue surveillance for several years, since seed can persist in soil and apparent success in one season may not remove the source of future plants.
researchNotes: Washington's weed board supports identification, clean seed and machinery, and prevention of seed production. Colorado State independently describes the jointed spike and wheat-like annual habit. Conflicting rotation durations in the Washington page are not reproduced as a fixed prescription.

proposedDescription: Joseph's-coat puts its color into leaves rather than a conspicuous flower display. Ornamental forms of Amaranthus tricolor combine green, yellow, red, pink, or copper, sometimes making the upper growth look quite different from the leaves below. Other forms are mostly green. This upright annual can become a substantial, branching plant during a warm growing season, so a small nursery seedling does not tell you its eventual size. Cultivar choice makes a considerable difference to both height and color.
identification: Look for broad, pointed or rounded leaves that narrow toward their stalks, with blades ranging from roughly diamond-shaped to oval. Color alone is unreliable because green forms belong to the same species, and several unrelated ornamentals share the name Joseph's-coat. The flowers are much less noticeable than the foliage. When identifying a volunteer amaranth, photograph its flowering clusters and mature fruit as well as its leaves; a colorful leaf is not enough to separate all the cultivated and weedy relatives.
actions: Give an identified ornamental planting a sunny position and enough room for the stated cultivar dimensions. Moderate watering supports garden growth, although established plants can tolerate some dryness. Keep the cultivar label if you want to repeat a particular color scheme, and check nearby seedlings before assuming they are the same selection. Remove unwanted volunteers while small. The common names and the existence of vegetable forms do not establish the identity or suitability of an unknown plant for eating.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS supports ornamental cultivar variation; Singapore NParks supplies growth and cultivation information, and the Thai flora supports leaf form. Identification cautions and keeping cultivar labels are practical deductions rather than diagnostic guarantees. No nutritional or medicinal recommendations are made.

proposedDescription: Jujube is a deciduous fruit tree with shiny leaves, often zigzagging branches, and fruits that change from green to brown as they mature. The brown fruit eventually softens and wrinkles, explaining the familiar name Chinese date, although this tree is unrelated to date palms. Cultivars differ in fruit quality, tree size, and thorniness. A less obvious feature is its ability to send up shoots from roots some distance from the trunk, which matters when choosing a place for it in a garden.
identification: Check the combination of glossy, finely toothed leaves, small clustered greenish-yellow flowers, and fruit containing a hard stone. Branches may carry paired spines, with one straighter and the other hooked, but some cultivars are nearly or completely thornless. The leaves fall seasonally, unlike those of many evergreen fruit trees. Record the fruit and branching pattern together; a thorny shoot alone is not enough for identification, particularly when it comes from beneath the graft of a cultivated tree.
actions: Allow access around the tree so you can notice and remove unwanted root suckers early. On grafted plants, those shoots can belong to the rootstock and should not be assumed to produce the named cultivar's fruit. Choose well-drained soil and provide regular irrigation when a good fruit crop is the aim, even though the tree tolerates drought. Protect the trunk from physical injury. If fruit performance is disappointing, check the cultivar and local growing conditions before applying extra fertilizer or assuming every jujube needs the same pollination arrangement.
researchNotes: Arizona Extension independently supports root suckering, cultivar thorn variation, irrigation, and injury precautions. UF/IFAS provides a Florida crop perspective and graft/rootstock context. The arboretum entry supports visible leaf, flower, and branch characters; it is grouped with Arizona rather than counted as a third independent institution.

proposedDescription: The jumping snail is a tiny land snail whose name describes an unusually energetic escape. When disturbed, it can flick itself away using the rear of its foot and a hornlike structure near the tail tip. It has been recorded on ornamental plants, including orchids, and can be overlooked among pots and moist plant material. Laboratory research found that isolated individuals could produce viable eggs without mating, so finding only one snail does not establish that a plant shipment is free of a reproductive population.
identification: An adult shell is only about 5 to 7 millimeters wide, with roughly four or five whorls. Look closely at the extended animal for the distinctive tail horn, and photograph both the shell and the body beside a scale. Small brown shells occur in many unrelated snails, and the shell alone can be misleading. A specialist may use detailed morphology or DNA to confirm an unfamiliar record; a published Argentine discovery used both approaches rather than relying only on its jumping behavior.
actions: If you notice a suspect snail on newly acquired plants, keep those pots separate while arranging identification through a plant-health service. Inspect pot bases, sheltered crevices, and associated plant material without transferring the material to another garden. Photograph the animal where found and retain the purchase location and date. Do not release it elsewhere. These are containment precautions, not a demonstrated eradication treatment; the laboratory reproduction findings also should not be read as a fixed outdoor development schedule.
researchNotes: USDA identification material supplies shell and tail characters. Barrientos is the original laboratory reproduction study; its life-history claims repeated by identification sites are counted in the same evidence lineage. Beltramino and colleagues provide a separate original morphology/DNA-confirmed Argentine record. Containment advice is conservative inference, not tested control.

proposedDescription: Amynthas agrestis is one of several earthworms commonly called jumping worms. They live close to the soil surface and can leave a loose, granular layer that resembles coffee grounds. In affected North American woodlands and gardens, their rapid processing of surface organic matter can change the conditions that plants and other soil organisms depend on. They also travel with everyday gardening materials, including soil, mulch, and potted plants. Their presence calls for careful containment, even when the individual worms seem easy to collect.
identification: Mature jumping worms usually have a smooth, pale collar that wraps completely around the body and lies almost flush with the surrounding skin. They may thrash strongly or move with a snakelike motion when disturbed. Those features help distinguish the group from familiar earthworms with a raised, saddle-shaped collar, but they do not establish Amynthas agrestis specifically. Amynthas tokioensis and Metaphire hilgendorfi look similar. Juveniles are harder to assess, and granular soil by itself is only a clue.
actions: Keep soil and yard waste from an affected area on site rather than sharing plants with intact root balls or moving mulch elsewhere. Check incoming plants and clean adhering soil from tools and footwear before working in another location. Photograph mature worms and ask your extension service how to confirm and report a local finding. Removing visible adults may reduce their numbers, but it will not reliably eliminate the small cocoons already in soil. Avoid improvised chemical treatments; prevention and limiting further movement remain the most practical priorities.
researchNotes: Michigan and Minnesota agency guidance independently support group recognition and spread prevention. The text explicitly separates group characters from species-level identification and avoids claiming that an ordinary photograph proves A. agrestis. Management limitations apply to the jumping-worm group; no unvalidated household treatment is recommended.

proposedDescription: Junglerice is a warm-season annual grass that takes advantage of moist, disturbed ground, especially where irrigation continues through summer. It forms clumps that may stand upright or spread low across the soil. In rice fields it can resemble the crop before flowering and compete with it; in orchards and garden beds, repeated summer emergence can make a patch seem to return just after it has been cleared. The plant reproduces by seed, so preventing another seed crop is central to keeping a small problem from growing.
identification: Look first at the junction where the leaf blade meets its sheath: junglerice has neither a ligule nor auricles. The leaves often show purple bands running across the blade, but those markings can be faint or absent and are not a required character. Mature flower heads have short, compact branches. Barnyardgrass is a close lookalike, while crabgrasses and dallisgrass can also confuse a quick inspection. Photograph the collar region and a complete flower head rather than relying on banding alone.
actions: Pull or hoe young plants before they set seed, then revisit irrigated edges and other damp patches through the growing season. In crop fields, confirm the species before changing a weed program. Sri Lankan rice guidance uses early weeding and appropriate water management, but flooding is not suitable for every crop or site. Some populations resist commonly used herbicides, so repeated treatment failure deserves diagnosis rather than a stronger dose. Keep records of where surviving plants occur and seek crop-specific extension advice.
researchNotes: UC IPM supports identification and California habitat; its related orchard publication explains variable leaf banding and documented or suspected resistance. These two are one UC evidence group. Sri Lanka's rice agency independently supports annual seed reproduction, rice competition, and early mechanical control. Regional crop advice is not generalized to all gardens.

proposedDescription: Juniper fiorinia scale is a minute armored scale insect with a particularly confusing naming history. Fiorinia pinicola is retained as a valid species in ScaleNet and a modern review of United States Fiorinia, but older accounts sometimes placed it under names also used for other scales. Records include conifers and additional woody hosts, so neither the word juniper nor a plant's identity is enough to settle the diagnosis. An infestation may appear as scattered dark flecks on foliage before the insects themselves are recognized.
identification: The 2021 review describes an oval, medium- to dark-brown covering with a conspicuous lengthwise ridge. Two overlapping shed skins create an indentation near the front, and heavily occupied leaves can carry white secretions. Older descriptions mention a frosted wax layer and a whitish rear extension. These are preliminary clues rather than a reliable field test. Closely related Fiorinia can look alike, and prepared specimens are needed to compare the microscopic lobes and ducts. A normal garden photograph cannot resolve those structures.
actions: Photograph the affected plant and close views of the scales, and record which plant parts carry them. Before treating a valuable specimen, ask an insect diagnostic service to establish the scale's identity and whether living insects remain under the coverings. Keep newly purchased affected stock separate while that assessment is arranged. Do not borrow spray timing or life-cycle claims from elongate hemlock scale, ordinary juniper scale, or phantasma scale simply because the names sound similar. A local diagnosis should determine what monitoring or management the actual plant needs.
researchNotes: The 2021 original Fiorinia review was recovered at its ScaleNet-hosted PDF mirror. Its direct field description adds overlapping first- and second-instar skins, a brown ridged cover and white secretions on heavily occupied leaves. Ferris 1950 morphology, quoted explicitly in ScaleNet, and the modern authors' examined material are separate lineages. The ScaleNet citation to that same 2021 review is not counted again. Common-name caution remains without a catalog contradiction. Inherited links not used: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9616077/ ; https://mrec.ifas.ufl.edu/lso/phantasma/pdf/CIRCULAR-Phantasma-Scale.pdf. The PMC route presented an access challenge and the Florida circular route redirected away from the cited content; neither is relied on. The retained original Fiorinia review and ScaleNet treatment support the revised text.

proposedDescription: Corchorus aestuans is a leafy herb with small yellow flowers and slender, angular seed capsules. It is often called jute, a name that also covers other Corchorus species and can obscure important differences. Floras record it in warm regions, including moist or marshy sites in parts of India. Its ordinary green foliage is easy to overlook, but the details at the base of a leaf and the shape of a ripe capsule are much more informative than its general resemblance to a small mallow.
identification: The leaves are usually oval to broadly oval, with toothed edges and a pointed tip. One or both of the lowest teeth may extend into a narrow, threadlike point. Inspect mature capsules for lengthwise angles or wings and the projecting, divided tips at their ends. The Florida flora distinguishes this species by capsules with three or four compartments and forked terminal awns. Other jutes can have rounded capsules or differently shaped, unwinged fruits, so leaves alone are a poor basis for a final name.
actions: If a volunteer appears in a cultivated bed, take close photographs of the leaf base, yellow flower, and mature capsule before deciding what it is. Remove unwanted plants before their capsules release seed, provided the planting is yours to manage. In a natural area, establish local status before treating a plant as a weed. A record labeled jute does not prove that it is a commercial fiber crop or suitable for food. Preserve the scientific identification with any observation you submit.
researchNotes:
Independent Botanical Survey of India and North American flora treatments support flowers, leaves, habitat, and diagnostic fruit differences. Removal before seed release is a conservative gardening inference rather than a species-specific control trial. The generic common name does not support food, fiber performance, or a blanket invasive designation.

proposedDescription: Themeda quadrivalvis is most usefully called grader grass, although kangaroo grass appears among its common names. It forms upright clumps with cane-like stems and branched seed heads that turn warm reddish-brown or golden as they mature. In parts of Australia it has spread through roadsides, pastures, and other disturbed ground, where dense stands compete with desirable vegetation and add dry fuel. The common-name overlap matters: the better-known Australian kangaroo grass, Themeda triandra, is a different species and should not be removed on the strength of a shared label.
identification: Grader grass is usually an annual, sometimes lasting into a second year, and can reach roughly 2 meters or more. Its narrow leaves are spaced along relatively hairless stems. The drooping flower heads contain fanlike groups of small spikelets and bent, twisted awns. Themeda triandra is perennial and generally has larger individual spikelets; other Themeda grasses also require comparison. Photograph an intact seed head and the plant base, and have uncertain specimens checked before controlling a mixed grassland patch.
actions: Where control is appropriate, dig out a few plants before seed matures and monitor the disturbed spots for seedlings. Cutting below the flower heads at early flowering can limit seed production, but it does not kill the plants. Clean seed-bearing debris and mud from machinery, footwear, and clothing before leaving a patch. Maintain healthy pasture cover rather than creating bare ground through overgrazing. Ask the local weed authority about disposal and site requirements, because management status differs between Australian jurisdictions and cannot be inferred for other countries.
researchNotes: Queensland and NSW government treatments support morphology, impact, and management. NSW full text establishes the comparison with T. triandra and limits of slashing. Catalog commonName 'Kangaroo grass' is potentially misleading but does not invalidate the supplied scientific ID; no catalog field was edited. Legal status is deliberately left location-specific.

Cane-like stems and golden seed heads
Pasture and grassland invasion

proposedDescription: Tilletia indica is the fungus responsible for Karnal bunt, a disease of wheat, durum wheat, and triticale. It is often called partial bunt because infection can replace only part of a grain with a dark mass of spores. A crop may look fairly ordinary in the field, with the problem becoming apparent after threshing exposes the affected kernels. Its importance extends beyond the amount of grain visibly damaged: grain movement and export requirements can make even a small confirmed finding significant for a grower or grain handler.
identification: Look for kernels with blackened, sooty areas, often near the base or along the groove, while part of the outer coat remains intact. Heavily affected kernels can look hollowed like a small boat. A fishy smell may accompany severe infection, but smell is not a safe or sufficient identification test. Other bunt fungi and discolored grain can be confused with it. Confirmation depends on a diagnostic laboratory examining spores and, when appropriate, using molecular tests to distinguish related fungi.
actions: If you suspect Karnal bunt, keep the grain lot identified and separate, and contact your plant-health authority or crop diagnostic service before moving or disposing of it. Preserve field, seed-source, and storage records so the finding can be traced. Use clean planting seed and follow locally applicable sanitation and movement requirements. Avoid judging an entire lot from a few visible kernels or deciding that a clean-looking field excludes infection. Treatment choices and any official restrictions should follow a confirmed diagnosis and current regional guidance.
researchNotes: USDA APHIS and UC IPM independently support grain symptoms and disease significance. Plant Health Australia's diagnostic protocol supplies confirmation limits and related-species confusion. No claim about current quarantine boundaries, a specific treatment, human health, or universal host susceptibility is made. Sample containment is a precaution pending official direction.

proposedDescription: Keeled wormseed, also called keeled goosefoot or green crumbweed, is a small aromatic herb that may spread along the ground or stand upright. Its green leaves and tiny clustered flowers make it easy to dismiss as an ordinary garden weed. That would be a poor assumption everywhere: the Victorian flora describes it as rare there, occurring on sandy or gravelly ground near the Snowy River and its tributaries. The scientific name Dysphania carinata is more useful than its varied common names when checking a local record.
identification: Look for oval to elliptic leaves, generally no more than about 3 centimeters long, with edges that may be wavy or nearly smooth. Glandular and other hairs cover the plant, and minute flowers cluster in the leaf axils. It closely resembles Dysphania pumilio in general appearance. The more useful distinction lies in the five flower-covering segments, which have a pronounced ridge or keel with coarse hairs. Mature seeds are very small and stand vertically within the fruit; magnification is needed for a dependable comparison.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, leaf edges, and close views of mature flower clusters before assigning a species name. A local herbarium or flora specialist can help with the tiny fruit characters. In a river corridor or conservation area, leave the plant undisturbed while checking local significance rather than assuming that a goosefoot-like herb needs removal. If it is a confirmed unwanted volunteer in your own cultivated bed, remove it before seed dispersal. Do not infer culinary or medicinal use from the name wormseed or from other Dysphania species.
researchNotes: NSW Flora Online and VicFlora are independent regional flora treatments by different authors. Their seed-size and color descriptions vary slightly, so the public text avoids an overly precise merged measurement. Victorian rarity is geographically bounded; no global invasive or threatened status is asserted. Garden removal is conditional practical inference.
