proposedDescription: Lacy sea lettuce is a sheetlike green seaweed recorded under the name Ulva pertusa and now widely treated as Ulva australis. It grows in shallow coastal settings, including lagoons, and can resemble several other sea lettuces. The change in name reflects taxonomic work, not a visible change in the alga. This profile keeps the catalog identifier while making the newer name available for comparison with current identification resources.
identification: Look for a translucent green blade with irregular holes, wavy edges and a relatively thick, wrinkled base near its attachment point. Older blades can split into strips. Holes alone are not conclusive, because wear and grazing can also perforate seaweed. Closely related Ulva species overlap in appearance, and microscopic cell features or DNA examination may be needed. Photograph the attached whole blade, its base and its margins, with a scale. A washed-up fragment without its base often leaves the identification uncertain.
actions: Record the shore, date, tidal position and whether the seaweed was attached or drifting. Send photographs of an unusual population to a local marine recording program or herbarium rather than assuming a green accumulation belongs to this species. Clean seaweed from boats and equipment before moving between sites, following local disposal guidance. Do not transplant attached material or discard aquarium seaweed into coastal water. Large accumulations need local assessment of species and conditions before a management response is chosen.
researchNotes: CIESM supplies blade morphology and habitat. Hanyuda and Kawai's independent type-specimen DNA study supports the pertusa/australis synonymy and molecular identification context. Generic marine hygiene advice is precautionary, not an assertion of a local invasion.

sources.title: Hanyuda and Kawai: Genetic examination of Ulva australis type

claims: Perforated blade with thick concentrically wrinkled base; shallow coastal lagoons; related species overlap.
Type-specimen genetic study supports synonymy of Ulva pertusa with Ulva australis.

proposedDescription: Ladder brake is a fern with long, narrow fronds divided once into many slender leaflets. It often appears on lime-rich surfaces, including old mortar and masonry, as well as in disturbed ground in suitable climates. A plant growing from a wall crack may be small, while a shaded specimen can carry much longer fronds. Its spreading units are microscopic spores, so it never produces flowers or seed pods.
identification: Look at the underside of a mature frond. In ladder brake, the spore-bearing structures form lines along the leaflet edges. Swamp fern, Blechnum serrulatum, can look similar, but its spore lines lie nearer the leaflet midrib. Ladder brake's leaflets are simple rather than deeply divided into smaller segments, another useful feature when comparing other Pteris species. Photograph an entire frond, a leaflet underside and the base of the plant. An unfertile young frond may not show enough detail to settle the name.
actions: If the fern is unwanted, identify it while the fronds are intact and remove small plants carefully before more spores are released. Avoid forcing roots from fragile mortar or damaging a historic wall. For established plants, plan follow-up rather than assuming removal of the fronds has removed the growing base. Ask a local botanist about uncertain ferns and local management priorities, especially where several similar species occur together.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS supplies spore placement and the Blechnum comparison. North Carolina's flora independently supplies simple pinnae, lanceolate blade and masonry habitat. Remediation claims about arsenic are omitted because they do not support casual household use.

claims: Once-divided fronds; spore lines at leaflet margins distinguish it from swamp fern.
Simple unlobed pinnae and narrow lanceolate frond; old lime-mortar walls.

proposedDescription: Lady's thumb is an annual smartweed often found in cultivated or disturbed ground. It develops branching stems and compact pink flower spikes, sometimes reaching about a meter tall. The familiar dark mark on many leaves gives the plant its common name, but some leaves lack that mark. A spot is a useful clue, not a reliable shortcut around examining the rest of the plant.
identification: Leaves alternate along the stem and are narrow oval to lance-shaped. The stem joints are swollen and often reddish. At each leaf attachment, look for the thin sheath that wraps around the stem; its upper edge has conspicuous bristly hairs. Flower clusters are generally upright and pink to purplish. Pale smartweed, Persicaria lapathifolia, can look similar, but its sheaths lack the same bristly fringe and its clusters are often paler or nodding. Photograph the sheath closely, as well as flowers and leaves, rather than relying only on the thumb-shaped blotch.
actions: In a garden bed, remove unwanted seedlings before they flower and set seed, taking care to distinguish them from wanted plants nearby. Record whether a larger patch occupies damp disturbed soil, crop rows or a water margin. Keep seed-bearing plants out of soil or waste moved to a clean area. For extensive crop infestations, ask extension staff for a plan matched to the crop and growth stage instead of applying a treatment based only on the common name.
researchNotes: USGS supports annual habit, variable leaf spot, swollen nodes and crop habitat. Alaska's university comparison independently supports the bristly ochrea and distinction from P. lapathifolia. Advice is seed prevention and identification, with no chemical prescription.

claims: Annual with alternate leaves, variable dark blotch and swollen reddish nodes.
P. maculosa has bristly sheath margins and pink erect clusters, unlike P. lapathifolia.

proposedDescription: Lamarck's bedstraw is a slender annual that can be easy to overlook among dry grasses and other low vegetation. Fine branching stems spread into a loose, wiry framework, with tiny leaves grouped around the joints. Its flowers and fruits are much smaller than those of many familiar garden weeds. The plant has been recorded in disturbed lowland habitats in western North America, while Australian floras also describe it from dry, open places.
identification: Look for rings of six to eight narrow leaves on the lower stems, with fewer leaves around the upper flowering branches. The leaves are only a few millimeters long and may end in a small bristle. Minute yellowish flowers can have a reddish tint. Mature fruits are tiny paired structures with a finely bumpy surface, rather than the conspicuous hooked burrs of some other bedstraws. A hand lens is useful. Photograph lower leaf whorls, branching flower stalks and mature fruit; a distant view is unlikely to separate this species from related annual bedstraws.
actions: Confirm a suspected plant before clearing a patch, since other bedstraws may be part of the local vegetation. If removal is appropriate, work before the small fruits disperse and keep collected material together. Note the size of the patch and nearby disturbance, then revisit during the next growing season. For a record outside a familiar range, submit clear close-ups or ask a herbarium how to prepare a specimen.
researchNotes: VicFlora provides detailed whorl, flower and fruit characters. Burke Herbarium independently supports annual life history and disturbed low-elevation habitat in Washington. Broad management claims are avoided for this small, less-documented species.

claims: Slender annual with lower whorls of six to eight leaves, tiny yellow-red flowers and papillose fruit.
Annual recorded in disturbed low-elevation sites; regional Washington distribution.

proposedDescription: Lambsquarters is an upright annual that often appears quickly in cultivated soil, vegetable beds and other disturbed places. Its young foliage commonly has a pale, floury coating, especially underneath. As the plant grows it branches and produces dense clusters of tiny green flowers. Because it reproduces through seed, a small overlooked seedling can become a much larger source of future weeds if left through the growing season.
identification: Leaves alternate along the stem and vary from broad, roughly triangular shapes to narrower leaves higher up. Their edges may be irregularly toothed or nearly smooth. The mealy coating and generally hairless, grooved stems help distinguish it from many pigweeds, although related goosefoots still require close comparison. Stems may carry reddish or green stripes. Flowers are small and lack showy petals, appearing in clusters at leaf joints and branch tips. Photograph young leaves from both sides and an older flowering branch to show the change in shape.
actions: Pull or hoe unwanted seedlings while they are small, before roots and seed clusters develop. Check regularly around crop rows and recently moved soil, where new seedlings may continue to appear. Contain mature seed-bearing plants instead of shaking them across a bed. Mulch or replant bare ground where appropriate to reduce repeated disturbance. Ask extension staff about persistent crop problems, and do not use an uncertain identification as a reason to taste or gather the plant.
researchNotes: Penn State supplies annual, seed reproduction, leaf and root traits. UMass independently documents the mealy coating, striped stems and flower arrangement. The text avoids edible-use advice and does not claim a single native range for the broad complex.

claims: Summer annual reproducing by seed, alternate toothed leaves and branched taproot.
Mealy leaf surfaces, hairless grooved striped stems and small green flower clusters.

proposedDescription: Lanceleaf rattlebox is an erect annual legume with narrow leaflets and clusters of small yellow flowers. It occurs in disturbed ground, including sandy fields and roadsides, and has also been cultivated outside its African range. As the flowers finish, inflated pods darken and hold the seeds associated with the rattlebox name. Several related plants have similar flowers and pods, making the leaves and flower size important parts of the identification.
identification: Each leaf is divided into three relatively narrow leaflets. The upper surfaces are nearly hairless, while the undersides may have sparse hairs. Flowers are about 8-10 mm long, yellow with darker purplish-brown veins or markings. The pods are roughly 2-3.5 cm long and become black when mature. North Carolina's flora distinguishes this species from Crotalaria ochroleuca partly by its much smaller flowers. Photograph a complete leaf, an individual flower beside a scale and mature pods rather than relying on yellow color alone.
actions: Have an unfamiliar rattlebox confirmed before using land containing it for collected forage or moving seed-bearing material elsewhere. In a small unwanted patch, remove plants before the pods mature and gather any dark pods already present. Keep contaminated soil and cut plants out of clean garden or restoration areas. Record the site and revisit after soil disturbance. For a larger agricultural patch, ask extension staff for a species-specific plan rather than treating all rattleboxes as interchangeable.
researchNotes: NSW Flora provides annual habit, leaflets, flowers and mature pod characters. North Carolina flora independently provides disturbed sandy habitat and the C. ochroleuca comparison. Forage advice is identification precaution, not an unsupported species-specific poisoning assertion.

claims: Three narrow leaflets; small yellow marked flowers; hairy pods become black.
Sandy disturbed habitats; flowers 8-10 mm versus 18-20 mm in C. ochroleuca.

proposedDescription: Lantana is familiar as a flowering garden shrub, but the name Lantana camara has also been applied broadly to a complicated group of cultivated and escaped plants. Some current Florida resources distinguish the widespread ornamental weed as Lantana strigocamara. That difference matters when interpreting a photograph or a local invasive-plant record. This account uses the broad cultivated-and-escaped camara complex, rather than assigning every plant to a narrow species.
identification: Plants commonly called lantana have opposite toothed leaves, dense rounded clusters of small tubular flowers and fleshy fruits that darken as they ripen. Flower clusters may include several colors, and color changes alone do not identify a species or cultivar. Queensland guidance describes square stems with small backward-curving prickles and a heavily branched, sometimes scrambling habit. Other lantanas and garden hybrids can share much of this appearance. Photograph leaves, stems, flower clusters and fruit together, and keep any nursery label or planting history with the record.
actions: Before planting or moving a lantana, check local recommendations for the exact species or cultivar. Do not assume that a colorful nursery selection is harmless outside cultivation or that every lantana should be removed. For a shrub spreading into nearby vegetation, seek local identification and management advice. Contain fruit-bearing cuttings and avoid dumping garden waste on open ground. Large tangled shrubs may need staged work and follow-up rather than a single trim.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: The UF page at the camara URL now explicitly heads its account Lantana strigocamara. Queensland still uses broad L. camara. Shared shrub features cannot reconcile narrow L. camara with the horticultural weed complex. The draft preserves that distinction and does not transfer invasive status.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: The broad cultivated-and-escaped camara complex is a defensible declared subject despite narrower strigocamara naming. The2024 Bishop original specimen discussion explicitly considers broad camara sensu lato versus strigocamara alternatives. Queensland and Florida supply independent regional descriptions; neither establishes a universal narrow taxon assignment. Next step: Review the declared broad-complex account; retain narrow identification and regional occurrence audits separately. Fresh evidence/access: Bishop2024 Hawaiian Lantana taxonomy [indexed_excerpt; Bishop-2024-Lantana-original-review] https://hbs.bishopmuseum.org/pubs-online/pdf/op156p171-177.pdf - Hawaiian strigose plants are not camara sensu stricto; broad camara or strigocamara treatment is debated and some named hybrid determinations are doubtful. Inherited URLs and evidence remain provenance; only the specifically documented accesses are claimed fresh. Parent-read passages are explicitly attributed. No catalog, mapping or public-release changes; local review only.

claims: Broad L. camara concept: opposite toothed leaves, square prickly stems, colored clusters and dark fruit.
Account discusses ornamental L. strigocamara, exposing a taxonomic scope mismatch.
Hawaiian strigose plants are not camara sensu stricto; broad camara or strigocamara treatment is debated and some named hybrid determinations are doubtful.

proposedDescription: Large gray willow is a deciduous shrub or small tree that often forms a broad, many-stemmed crown. It favors wet ground, including stream edges, swamps and lake margins. In regions where it has escaped cultivation, it can form dense stands and regenerate from seed or surviving woody growth. Its soft early catkins make it attractive, but a wetland planting needs more thought than its appearance alone might suggest.
identification: Leaves are oval to somewhat broader toward the tip, with wavy or finely toothed margins. Their undersides are gray and hairy, and young twigs are often densely hairy as well. Catkins appear before or around leaf emergence, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Goat willow, Salix caprea, has often been confused with this species, and willows can be difficult to identify from one leaf. Photograph mature leaves on both sides, young twigs, buds and catkins, and include the plant's overall shape and habitat.
actions: Ask a willow specialist or local herbarium to confirm an unfamiliar wetland shrub before removal. Avoid planting cuttings beside natural waterways or moving pruned branches where they could establish. A confirmed unwanted stand needs a plan that accounts for regrowth, seedlings and the stability of the bank. Do not clear a large waterside area at once without suitable advice. Mark the original extent and revisit after management to look for new shoots and seedlings.
researchNotes: NSW Flora supplies morphology and frequent confusion with S. caprea. Bay of Plenty independently supports wetland setting, seed dispersal and resprouting. Regional ecological impacts are framed as introduced-region behavior, not a universal status.

claims: Many-stemmed tree or shrub with hairy gray leaf undersides; often confused with S. caprea.
Wetland and stream-edge tree; disperses seed and resprouts to form thickets.

proposedDescription: Large watergrass is a robust perennial grass that can float or rise above shallow water. It spreads into mats, supported in part by its swollen, spongy leaf sheaths. Florida observations document large colonies that crowd other aquatic vegetation. Its size sets it apart from the more delicate watergrasses, but a floating grass mat still needs careful examination before a species name is assigned.
identification: Look for thick creeping stems, broad leaf blades and conspicuously inflated sheaths. At the junction of blade and sheath, the membranous ligule can be unusually long. Male and female flowers occur in separate clusters on the same plant: the male cluster is open and terminal, while female clusters are denser and arise from leaf axils. This arrangement is more useful than leaf width alone. Photograph both kinds of flower cluster if present, along with the swollen sheath and a stem joint. Other watergrasses and floating grasses can overlap in general appearance.
actions: Report an unfamiliar expanding mat to the local aquatic-plant program with the location, approximate area and photographs. Clean boats, trailers and other equipment before leaving the waterbody, collecting attached plant pieces for appropriate disposal. Avoid chopping or dragging a mat through open water because fragments can contribute to spread. Large infestations require a coordinated aquatic-management plan that protects nearby vegetation and access. Follow the site's instructions before collecting a specimen or attempting removal.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS supports Florida mat behavior, diagnostic sheaths and equipment hygiene. FWS quotes Martínez-y-Pérez's independent taxonomic revision for floral morphology and aquatic biology; that underlying revision is distinguished from UF's Kunzer/Bodle Florida account.

sources.title: FWS: Tropical American Watergrass risk summary

claims: Robust floating grass, spongy sheaths, long ligules, separate male/female panicles; clean gear.
Independent revision describes axillary female panicles and wetland or slow-water habitat.

proposedDescription: Large yellow loosestrife is an upright garden perennial that expands through underground rhizomes. Its yellow flowers and leafy stems can make a handsome colony, but the same growth can carry it beyond the space originally intended. It has escaped from gardens in several regions, often around discarded plant material. This is a Lysimachia in the primrose family, rather than the unrelated purple loosestrife often discussed in wetland management.
identification: Leaves grow in groups around the stem, and yellow flowers cluster in the upper leaf axils. The flowers may have small reddish marks near their centers. To distinguish it from yellow loosestrife, Lysimachia vulgaris, examine the flower arrangement and the green sepals behind the petals: L. vulgaris has a more terminal branched cluster and darker sepal margins. Other garden Lysimachia can also resemble it. Photograph a whole flowering stem, a leaf whorl and the back of a flower rather than relying only on its yellow color.
actions: Choose a contained garden position only where local guidance supports growing it, and inspect the edges of an existing clump regularly. When reducing an unwanted colony, collect underground rhizomes as well as the upright shoots. Do not dump divisions or soil containing roots along a hedge, ditch or woodland edge. Revisit the area for shoots emerging from missed pieces. If a plant outside cultivation is uncertain, ask a botanist to check its flower and sepal characters before management.
researchNotes: NC State supplies rhizomatous garden growth; Flora Helvetica independently supplies leaf whorls and green sepals. BSBI supports escape via discarded material and the vulgaris comparison. Conflicting seed-set generalizations are avoided.

claims: Rhizomatous upright perennial forms colonies and can escape cultivation.
Leaves whorled three to six; yellow flowers with reddish basal dots; sepals without red margin.
Discarded garden material and rhizomes support persistence; flower position distinguishes L. vulgaris.

proposedDescription: Large-flower primrose-willow is an aquatic perennial associated with shallow water and wet margins. Creeping stems can first form floating mats, then produce upright flowering shoots. Bright yellow flowers make the patch conspicuous, but they do not settle its identity. The name Ludwigia grandiflora has sometimes been used loosely for a group of similar creeping water primroses, so an exact species record deserves more care than a general report of the weed.
identification: Leaves can change shape as the plant develops: early floating growth may have rounded leaves, while later shoots carry narrower, pointed blades. Roots can develop at stem joints. Similar Ludwigia species share yellow flowers and overlapping leaf forms, and water conditions can alter their appearance. Specialists may need mature flowers, fruits and sometimes DNA evidence to separate them. Photograph floating and upright growth, a flower face, its underside and any fruits. Record the water depth and whether the patch is attached to the bank.
actions: Never introduce creeping water primrose to open water or discard pond plants into a drainage channel. Clean fragments from boats and equipment before moving to another site. Report a newly noticed mat to the local aquatic-weed program, especially if it is expanding. Avoid mowing or fragmenting the stand in the water. Ask the program to confirm the species and plan any removal, since a large mat can be difficult to handle without spreading pieces.
researchNotes: NC DEQ supports growth stages, leaf change and fragment spread. SFWMD's independent field report flags L. grandiflora as a catch-all name and emphasizes identification limitations. Draft stays species-aware and does not transfer hexapetala-specific impact claims.

sources.title: SFWMD: 2024 South Florida Environmental Report chapter 7

claims: Aquatic perennial with floating then upright growth; leaves change form; roots from fragments.
L. grandiflora sometimes used for creeping water primrose complex; identification can require DNA.

proposedDescription: Largefruit amaranth often spreads close to the ground, its branching stems weaving through paving edges, garden soil, and other disturbed places. Unlike many familiar upright pigweeds, this species is a perennial with a persistent base. Young growth can be hairy, while the small green flowers gather into narrow, rather inconspicuous clusters. The enlarged fruits are more useful for recognizing it than the flowers, which easily disappear against the foliage.
identification: Look for long-stalked leaves that are broadly oval to diamond shaped, sometimes with gently wavy margins. Flower clusters occupy the stem ends and upper leaf joints. As they mature, the fruits project beyond the surrounding flower parts and enclose a much smaller, shiny seed. A spreading habit alone is not enough: several amaranths can become flattened by trampling. Photograph the stem base, a whole leafy branch, and mature clusters with a ruler. A local flora or botanist can check the fruit characters.
actions: In a garden where removal is wanted, work on a small patch before mature fruits are scattered and lift the persistent base along with the shoots. Simply clipping the visible stems may leave the plant in place. Keep fruiting material contained, then revisit the same cracks or bed edges for surviving growth and seedlings. Outside managed ground, confirm the identification and local significance before disturbing vegetation. Record whether the plant is rooted in a pavement joint, cultivated bed, or other disturbed setting; that context helps make a useful observation.
researchNotes: NSW Flora and VicFlora independently support the spreading perennial habit and diagnostic fruit characters. Their flower-part counts vary, so this draft avoids a rigid count. Removal guidance is a cautious practical inference from the persistent base and fruit-bearing growth, not a tested eradication protocol.

claims: Spreading perennial; rhombic leaves; inflated fruit exceeding perianth and small glossy seed.
Prostrate perennial with hairy young stems; terminal spikes; indehiscent fruit; disturbed habitats.

proposedDescription: Largeleaf maidenhair has a simpler, bolder outline than the finely divided maidenhair ferns often grown indoors. Each arching frond carries a small number of broad leaflets, and fresh growth can emerge reddish pink before turning green. Botanical treatments describe it from tropical American forests, including streamside settings. Those habitat records describe where the fern grows; they do not establish that every cultivated or newly observed plant is an environmental problem.
identification: Follow one frond from its shiny, dark stalk to the tip. The blade is divided once, with broad, mostly opposite leaflets and a terminal leaflet. The leaflets are roughly triangular to oval, with relatively symmetrical bases, and their surfaces and main axes are hairless. On fertile fronds, long spore-bearing lines run along the leaflet margins, interrupted near the sterile tip. Other maidenhairs can share dark stalks or pink new growth, so include both mature and young fronds and a clear underside photograph when seeking confirmation.
actions: Leave an unidentified wild fern rooted while you document it, especially in forest or streamside vegetation where similar species may belong. For a cultivated plant, retain the nursery name and photograph the whole pot as well as the leaflet details. Keep unwanted plants and potting material out of streams and natural vegetation. If an apparently escaped population is found, record its extent and setting and ask a local herbarium or land manager to confirm its identity before deciding whether any removal is appropriate.
researchNotes: UNAM's Mexican flora treatment and the Jardim Botanico do Rio de Janeiro Flora do Brasil account provide independent substantive morphology. No species-specific invasion impact or removal trial was established; actions focus on documentation, avoiding disposal into natural habitats, and local identification.

claims: Once-pinnate fronds; broad opposite glabrous pinnae; dark stipes; marginal sori; streamside forest habitats.
Short creeping rhizome; opposite broad pinnae; reddish young fronds; linear marginal sori.

proposedDescription: Largeleaf marshpennywort is a small, creeping lawn and disturbed-ground herb whose name can suggest something much larger than the plant itself. Its stalked, lobed leaves sit above slender stems, with conspicuous pale hairs giving parts of the plant a fuzzy appearance. A Louisiana botanical report documented how easily it can be filed under the wrong name: the original specimen had been identified as Bowlesia incana. Careful close-up examination matters more here than the common name.
identification: Look for shallow, usually five-lobed leaves with rounded teeth between the lobes and hairs on the leaves and stalks. The leaf stalk joins at the leaf base rather than at the center of a little umbrella. A useful distinction from Bowlesia is hair structure: this Hydrocotyle has simple hairs, whereas Bowlesia has star-shaped hairs. A hand lens or sharply focused macro photograph is helpful. Capture the creeping stem, the upper end of a leaf stalk, both leaf surfaces, and any tiny flowers or fruits.
actions: Start by mapping the patch and recording whether it is in turf, a nursery pot, or damp disturbed soil. Avoid transferring soil or plant fragments from an uncertain patch to other beds while identification is pending. In a small managed area, any desired removal should include the connected creeping stems rather than just the leaves, followed by checks for surviving growth. If the observation could be a new local record, send detailed photographs to a herbarium before clearing the whole patch, since a useful specimen may be requested.
researchNotes: Thornhill and Krings' original Louisiana report supports the Bowlesia comparison and simple hairs. The New Zealand Plant Conservation Network's independent illustrated key supports the hairy appearance and leaf-outline distinction. No regional abundance or blanket invasive designation is inferred from these records.

sources.title: Thornhill and Krings: Hydrocotyle bowlesioides in Louisiana
New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Trilepidea July 2022

claims: Lobed hairy leaves; simple hairs distinguish Bowlesia incana; documented Louisiana misidentification.
Illustrated pennywort key describes conspicuous whitish hairs and angular or rounded leaves.

proposedDescription: The larger pine shoot beetle uses different parts of a pine during its life cycle. Breeding takes place beneath the bark of recently cut material, stumps, or badly weakened trees, while newly emerged adults can feed inside the shoots of living pines. That shoot feeding may leave damaged tips in the crown or on the ground. A fallen pine shoot is a clue worth examining, but several insects and weather events can produce similar damage.
identification: Adults are small, roughly 3.5 to 5 millimeters long, and dark brown to black. Their compact shape is shared with many bark beetles, making a phone photograph alone an uncertain route to identification. Look inside a naturally broken shoot for tunneling and photograph the entrance, damaged tip, and whole tree. Specialists use fine antennal and body characters to separate this species from related Tomicus beetles and other bark beetles. Keep the pine's identity, location, and date with any photographs or submitted specimen.
actions: If unusual shoot damage is appearing across several pines, contact a forestry or extension service before moving cut branches, logs, or nursery trees elsewhere. Infested pine material can carry the beetle over much greater distances than an individual normally travels. Inspect nearby stored pine wood and note when trees were cut or became stressed. Leave decisions about removing standing trees to an arborist or forester; shoot damage by itself does not establish a severe trunk infestation or justify felling an otherwise healthy tree.
researchNotes: UF/IFAS provides adult morphology and identification context; Maine Forest Service independently describes breeding material, shoot feeding, and movement in pine products. Historic quarantine language on agency pages is not reproduced. Actions emphasize diagnosis and avoiding movement pending local advice.

sources.title: Maine Forest Service: Pine Shoot Beetle

claims: Adult size and coloration; diagnostic antennal features and bark beetle lookalikes.
Breeding under bark of cut or weakened pines; adults feed in shoots; infested pine products move beetles.

proposedDescription: The larger shothole borer is a small bark beetle associated with weakened trunks and branches, including those of fruit trees. Its presence can therefore be part of a larger tree-health problem rather than the first cause of decline. Beneath occupied bark, a lengthwise mother gallery gives rise to smaller larval tunnels spreading across the grain. These galleries can help an expert understand the infestation, although they should be examined on already detached or dead material.
identification: Adults are about 3 to 4.5 millimeters long, with a dark reddish-brown body and brown to reddish wing covers. The surface is relatively smooth and shiny. Identification relies on details of the face and underside that distinguish Scolytus species, so round holes in bark are not enough to assign a name. Photograph the whole affected tree, its leaves or fruit for host identification, and the damaged branch. A close, well-lit beetle photograph is useful, but a specialist may still need a specimen.
actions: Have an arborist or local plant-health service assess declining fruit trees and the stresses affecting them. Note recent drought, physical injury, or dying branches without assuming any one factor caused the attack. Avoid carrying suspect branches or firewood to another orchard or garden while the beetle is being identified. If dead material is removed, ask about appropriate local disposal and keep a record of where it came from. Do not strip healthy bark to look for galleries; that creates another wound on an already vulnerable tree.
researchNotes: The University of Ljubljana species account supplies host and gallery information. Smith and Cognato's original Nearctic Scolytus revision supplies independent adult diagnostic morphology. The Slovenian generation count is not generalized to other climates, and no specific treatment efficacy is claimed.

sources.title: Smith and Cognato: A taxonomic monograph of Nearctic Scolytus

claims: Weakened fruit-tree hosts; adult size; longitudinal mother gallery and transverse larval tunnels.
Scolytus mali adult color, size, face and abdominal diagnostic characters.

proposedDescription: Larkdaisy is a branching herb with small, rounded purple flower heads that stand out against rough-textured leaves. Plants may sprawl or grow upright, and the base can become woody as the season progresses. It is cultivated ornamentally, while botanical records also document it outside gardens in disturbed places and pasture. A flowering plant beside a garden is therefore worth recording in context, without assuming that one escaped individual represents a widespread local problem.
identification: Look for toothed leaves arranged alternately along ridged, hairy stems. The leaves often broaden toward their tips and can show small gland dots. Each mauve or purple head sits among a conspicuous set of leafy outer bracts, with smaller inner bracts surrounding the florets. Those green, leaflike bracts are useful when comparing it with other purple-flowered members of the daisy family. Photograph a whole stem, the upper and lower leaf surfaces, and a flower head from both above and below.
actions: If it is being grown deliberately, keep track of seedlings beyond the planted area and avoid dumping spent flowering material into adjoining land. Where an unwanted garden patch is small, remove it before mature seed is scattered and check later for new plants. The woody base may need more attention than the soft upper shoots. For a patch in pasture or natural vegetation, document its size and location and seek local identification and management advice before broad clearing. Nearby desirable plants may be easy to overlook beneath the branching growth.
researchNotes: NSW Flora and Singapore NParks independently describe morphology and cultivated or disturbed-site occurrence. Suggested seed containment and follow-up are conservative gardening actions inferred from a seed-propagated herb; no claim of universal invasive status or validated eradication method is made.

sources.title: NParks Flora and Fauna Web: Centratherum punctatum

claims: Branching annual herb with woody base, hairy stems, toothed gland-dotted leaves and purple heads with leafy bracts.
Rough alternate toothed leaves, terminal or axillary purple heads and propagation by seed.

proposedDescription: Latania scale is an armored scale insect that spends much of its life beneath a tiny protective cover attached to a plant. Colonies can look like pale specks or small crusts on leaves, stems, or fruit. The covers remain much easier to see than the insects themselves. Finding a few scales does not automatically mean a plant needs treatment: their importance depends on the host, whether the insects are alive, and whether damage is developing.
identification: Female covers are usually round, convex, and roughly 1 to 2 millimeters across, often grayish white with an off-center yellowish or brown patch from earlier growth stages. On stems they may appear browner. Several armored scales look very similar, especially greedy scale, and reliable separation can require microscope examination of the insect beneath the cover. Photograph the colony in place, the host plant, and any affected fruit or foliage. Include a size reference; a magnified white bump without context is difficult to interpret.
actions: Inspect adjacent leaves and branches before deciding how extensive the infestation is. A local extension service can help distinguish live scales from empty covers and identify the species if management depends on that distinction. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary broad insecticide use, and address ants or dusty conditions where these interfere with biological control. For valuable plants or fruit crops, ask for advice tailored to that host and location. Do not move heavily infested cuttings to other gardens while you are working out what is present.
researchNotes: UC IPM explicitly compares latania and greedy scales and emphasizes natural enemies. Argentina's official SINAVIMO account independently supplies species-specific cover morphology and stages. No cover-only identification or crop-wide treatment threshold is asserted.

sources.title: UC IPM: Greedy Scale and Latania Scale

claims: Similar convex armored scales need close identification; natural enemies and ant or dust management matter.
Female cover approximately 1 to 2 mm, gray-white and convex with subcentral colored exuviae; colonies on plant surfaces.

proposedDescription: Latin American fleabane makes loose cushions of wiry stems carrying small daisy heads, often with white and pink flowers visible together. It is familiar in rock gardens and wall crevices, and botanical records describe escapes into other moist or disturbed settings. Its cheerful flowering habit can make it easy to overlook seedlings outside the original planting. Whether those escapes need action depends on the surrounding habitat and local guidance.
identification: Look for yellow flower centers surrounded by slender pale rays that can become pink as the heads age. Lower leaves are commonly divided into three lobes or bear a few distinct teeth, while upper leaves are narrower and often unlobed. The heads sit on slender stalks above a branching, spreading plant. Other small daisies can share the flower colors, so include the lower leaves and stem arrangement in photographs. Mature heads produce tiny fruits with a tuft of fine hairs, another useful detail for a botanical identification.
actions: Keep an eye on nearby cracks, drains, and bed edges if you grow it ornamentally. Where seedlings are unwanted, remove small plants before they mature, taking care around masonry and any neighboring vegetation. Established plants may have persistent underground growth, so a single trim should not be treated as complete removal. Contain flowering and fruiting waste rather than tipping it onto nearby land. If a colony appears away from gardens, record its extent and habitat and ask a local botanist or land manager whether it is a concern in that setting.
researchNotes: VicFlora supplies the rhizomatous habit, leaf variation, flower dimensions and escape records. IISc's India Flora account independently supports the white-to-pink rays, yellow discs, and wall-crevice habitat. Suggested containment is proportionate horticultural guidance rather than a regional invasive designation.

sources.title: Indian Institute of Science: Erigeron karvinskianus

claims: Sprawling rhizomatous herb; lobed lower and narrow upper leaves; white to crimson rays and hairy fruit pappus.
White rays becoming pink, yellow discs, and occurrence in moist places and wall crevices.

proposedDescription: Laurel willow is a broad-leaved willow whose glossy foliage can look surprisingly unlike the narrow leaves many people associate with the genus. It grows as a shrub or tree in wet settings, and planted trees occur beyond its Eurasian range. The name needs particular care in North American records: a New Zealand taxonomic treatment notes research assigning North American material previously called Salix pentandra to a hybrid. A garden label or older observation should therefore be checked rather than accepted automatically.
identification: Look for hairless, shiny dark-green leaves with paler undersides and fine, closely spaced glandular teeth. Small glands also occur near the top of the leaf stalk. Catkins appear with the leaves, and male flowers usually have around five stamens, sometimes more. These details help separate it from other willows, but hybrids can combine their parents' features. Photograph both leaf surfaces, the stalk glands, a leafy twig, and catkins if available. Include the planting history when known, since cultivated willows can be especially difficult to name.
actions: Treat an uncertain tree as a willow awaiting confirmation rather than removing it on the basis of a broadleaf appearance. A herbarium or willow specialist can advise whether a specimen is needed and which seasonal features matter. On streambanks, consult the land manager before cutting or digging because the work can disturb the bank and adjacent vegetation. Keep cut branches out of waterways and avoid distributing cuttings from an uncertain planting. For a confirmed tree, management should follow its local ecological role and condition.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Glenny's New Zealand treatment freshly confirms the North American hybrid issue and cites Zinovjev 2011; Flora Helvetica independently treats true S. pentandra. The potential reassignment of North American specimens to S. x meyeriana is a real identity issue. General willow containment cannot settle it.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: True Salix pentandra can be described without assigning uncertain North American hybrid records to it. Fresh original Zinovjev2011 text documents hybrid misidentification, while independent Swiss morphology and the New Zealand discussion support the general species comparison. An uncompleted US voucher audit is not a barrier to a bounded species guide. Next step: Review the true-species draft; preserve the separate pentandra versus meyeriana voucher question. Fresh evidence/access: Zinovjev2011 Salix pentandra and hybrids [indexed_excerpt; Zinovjev-2011-willow-vouchers] https://www.mapress.com/phytotaxa/content/2011/f/p00022p060f.pdf - Boreal Eurasian true species and US cultivated hybrid specimens; does not authenticate every historical North American pentandra record. Inherited URLs and evidence remain provenance; only the specifically documented accesses are claimed fresh. Parent-read passages are explicitly attributed. No catalog, mapping or public-release changes; local review only.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Salix pentandra
InfoFlora and Flora Helvetica: Salix pentandra

claims: Glossy broad leaves, petiole glands, male stamens and hybrid comparisons; warning about North American misidentifications.
Hairless glossy leaves with glandular teeth, catkins accompanying leaves, usually five stamens and wet habitats.
Boreal Eurasian true species and US cultivated hybrid specimens; does not authenticate every historical North American pentandra record.

proposedDescription: Laurel wilt is a tree disease caused by the fungus now called Harringtonia lauricola, formerly Raffaelea lauricola. The catalog retains the older fungal name. The redbay ambrosia beetle can introduce the fungus as it bores into a host, after which the tree's water-conducting tissue becomes blocked. Redbay, sassafras, avocado, and other members of the laurel family can be affected. Susceptible trees may decline rapidly, making an early, well-documented report useful.
identification: Watch for wilting foliage that changes from green to olive or reddish brown, sometimes beginning in part of the crown. Dead leaves may remain on evergreen hosts. Small beetle entrance holes or delicate tubes of boring dust can accompany the decline, but neither proves laurel wilt. Dark staining in the sapwood is another clue that a trained diagnostician may examine. Photograph the whole crown, leaves, trunk symptoms, and host features. A plant disease clinic may need appropriately collected wood to confirm the cause.
actions: If a laurel-family tree develops unexplained rapid wilt, contact an extension office, forestry service, or plant disease clinic, particularly where the disease has not been confirmed before. Ask how to collect and package a sample before cutting into the tree. Avoid moving suspect firewood, logs, or plants to other locations, since beetles can travel in infested material. Obtain local advice on removal and disposal of confirmed trees, and check nearby susceptible hosts. Similar-looking decline has other causes, so a photograph alone should not trigger a definitive diagnosis.
researchNotes: NC State's extension account explicitly updates the fungal name and describes diagnosis and movement precautions. Virginia Department of Forestry independently describes host symptoms and the beetle association. The record preserves its ID and older name while distinguishing the fungus from its insect vector.

sources.title: NC State Extension: Laurel Wilt Disease
Virginia Department of Forestry: Laurel Wilt

claims: Harringtonia lauricola synonymy; xylem blockage; wilt, sapwood staining, diagnostic samples and wood movement.
Redbay ambrosia beetle vector, laurel-family hosts and rapid wilting and browning.

proposedDescription: Lavender scallops is a succulent with rounded, fleshy leaves whose blue-gray coloring and scalloped edges give it a soft, patterned appearance. It can stand upright or lean outward as stems lengthen. Hanging, bell-like flowers appear in branched clusters above the foliage. The species comes from Madagascar and is widely cultivated; a flora record of an escaped roadside plant in Zimbabwe shows why garden waste deserves attention, without establishing the same behavior in every climate.
identification: Look for opposite leaves that broaden toward the tip, with a smooth surface and a series of rounded teeth along the edge. Flower clusters carry downward-facing tubes in muted reddish, pink, or purple tones. Variegated garden forms have cream margins that may be tinged pink, but that coloring is not a requirement for the species. Other kalanchoes have fleshy leaves and hanging flowers, so photograph the entire plant, a leaf pair, the leaf margin, and a flower cluster rather than relying on color alone.
actions: For a plant you want to keep, use a container with freely draining soil and avoid keeping the root zone constantly wet. Because stems are used for propagation, collect unwanted cuttings rather than leaving them on surrounding soil or tipping them into natural vegetation. Check the ground around outdoor pots for established fragments or seedlings. If plants appear well beyond cultivation, record the setting and extent and ask a local botanist to verify them before deciding on removal. Retain the cultivar label when available, since ornamental forms can complicate identification.
researchNotes: Flora of Zimbabwe supplies species-level morphology and a documented escape, while NParks independently describes a variegated cultivated form and stem-cutting propagation. Cultivar colors are explicitly separated from the species description. No broad invasive status or leaf-plantlet mechanism is asserted.

claims: Succulent perennial with blue-gray scalloped leaves, pendent flowers and documented roadside escape.
Opposite fleshy leaves, cultivar-specific cream margins, hanging tubular flowers, well-drained soil and stem-cutting propagation.

proposedDescription: Lawn marshpennywort is a low perennial whose slender creeping stems can thread through grass, garden soil, or damp litter. Its small, rounded leaves are often only about a centimeter across, so the plant may first appear as a fine green mat rather than a collection of separate stems. Botanical treatments differ somewhat in the amount of hair they describe, and the New South Wales flora notes that its local species concept is under revision. Those details make careful regional identification worthwhile.
identification: Look for rounded to kidney-shaped leaves with shallow lobes and scalloped edges. The stalk attaches at the notch or base, not in the center of the blade as in some larger pennyworts. Tiny flowers gather in small, headlike groups, followed by minute ribbed fruits. Do not identify it from a round leaf alone: several Hydrocotyle species have similar outlines. Photograph the attachment point, leaf hairs, creeping stem, and any fruit, using a ruler to show how small the plant is.
actions: In a lawn or bed, first decide whether the patch is actually interfering with the intended planting. If removal is wanted, follow the connected stems through the vegetation and check for remaining rooted portions afterward. Avoid shifting infested soil or pot contents into another bed. A patch in a wet natural area deserves a local botanical check before disturbance, since pennywort names and native status vary by region. Note moisture conditions, shade, and the patch's extent when requesting help; these observations are useful alongside the close-up photographs.
researchNotes: The Smithsonian Hawaiian flora and NSW Flora provide independent morphological treatments. Differences in hairiness and the NSW revision warning are retained rather than flattened into a rigid universal key. Actions are low-disturbance observation and garden containment, not an invasive-species designation.

sources.title: Smithsonian Flora of the Hawaiian Islands: Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides

claims: Slender creeping stems; non-peltate small shallowly lobed leaves; small umbels and ribbed fruit.
Small crenate leaves, creeping stems, variable hairs and regional taxonomic revision warning.

proposedDescription: Lawn daisy, also called English daisy, is the familiar low plant with a yellow-centered flower head surrounded by white or pink rays. Its leaves stay close to the ground, allowing it to persist among regularly mown grasses. It is a perennial, although garden forms may be grown for a shorter season. Whether it counts as a weed is often a matter of the lawn's purpose: Oregon State includes it among plants that can be retained in an ecolawn and provide food for visiting pollinators.
identification: Look beneath the flowers for a compact rosette of spoon-shaped leaves. The flower stalks are leafless, which helps distinguish lawn daisy from taller daisies with leaves distributed along an upright stem. Garden cultivars can have pink or red flowers and extra rows of rays, so flower fullness is variable. For an uncertain plant, photograph the rosette and a complete flowering stalk together. A close-up of the flower alone can hide the growth pattern that makes this species recognizable.
actions: If the daisies suit the way you use the lawn, leaving them in place is a reasonable choice. Where a small patch is unwanted, lift the whole rosette with its rooted base and revisit the spot for surviving plants or seedlings. Mowing off flower heads alone does not remove the low-growing perennial. Keep soil disturbance modest and repair bare patches according to the needs of the surrounding turf. In a garden bed, check for seedlings outside the planted group rather than assuming ornamental varieties will stay exactly where they were placed.
researchNotes: Oregon State supplies lawn context, mowing tolerance and the option of retention; NC State independently describes basal leaves, leafless stalks, perennial growth and seed or division propagation. No medicinal or food-use material is carried into the draft.

sources.title: Oregon State University: Broadleaf Weeds in Lawns
NC State Extension Gardener: Bellis perennis

claims: Low perennial with spoon-shaped leaves and white or pink flowers; can remain in ecolawns and support pollinators.
Basal rosette, leafless flower stems, variable garden flower forms and propagation by seed or division.

proposedDescription: Laxman's bulrush is a cattail, with narrow upright leaves and the familiar brown, cylindrical flowering head. It grows at shallow water margins and in other wet ground, and it is also cultivated as a pond plant. Compared with some larger cattails, the female portion of its flower spike is relatively short. That compact head can be a useful starting point, but cattail identification needs more than a distant view of a brown cylinder.
identification: Look for leaves only a few millimeters wide and a clear gap between the lower female spike and the longer male section above it. Flora Helvetica describes plants commonly around 60 to 120 centimeters tall, with a female spike usually about 3 to 5 centimeters long, although size varies. The leaves are well developed and may extend beyond the flowers, helping distinguish it from the smaller Typha minima. Photograph a whole flowering shoot, leaf width against a ruler, and both spike sections while the male part is still visible.
actions: In a garden pond, monitor how far the underground growth is spreading and keep removed divisions and old plant material out of nearby ditches or wetlands. Horticultural guidance warns that the roots can spread rapidly in shallow water and may damage pond liners, so placement deserves thought. An unexpected wild patch should be identified before any digging or cutting begins. Wetland work can disturb other vegetation and the water's edge; ask the land manager or local conservation staff what action is appropriate for a confirmed population.
researchNotes: Flora Helvetica and the University of Greifswald's Mongolian flora independently support narrow leaves and separated male and female spikes. RHS adds species-page horticultural spread and liner cautions. The draft does not turn a garden warning into a universal wetland impact claim.

sources.title: InfoFlora and Flora Helvetica: Typha laxmannii

claims: Narrow leaves, short female spike, longer male spike and separation gap; comparison with T. minima.
Leaves up to 5 mm broad, separated spike sections, short female heads and shallow-water habitats.
Rhizomatous pond-margin plant; rapid spread in shallow water and potential pond liner damage.

proposedDescription: Xanthomonas oryzae is a bacterial species that includes distinct disease-causing forms in rice. The form called pathovar oryzae causes bacterial leaf blight, while pathovar oryzicola causes bacterial leaf streak. The catalog's broad species name should not be read as a diagnosis of one particular disease. Both can damage leaves, but their early symptoms and biology differ, and late-stage injury can look much alike.
identification: Leaf blight often begins as water-soaked injury near a leaf tip or margin, spreading toward the base and becoming yellow to light brown as tissue dries. Leaf streak begins as narrower, water-soaked lines between veins that can lengthen and merge. Severe blight in young plants can produce rapid wilting known as kresek. Other rice problems can resemble these symptoms. Photograph whole plants and close views of newly developing lesions, and record the rice variety, crop stage, field location, and where symptoms first appeared. A laboratory needs to establish the bacterial identity.
actions: Contact a rice extension specialist or plant-health service when an unfamiliar outbreak appears, and follow their instructions for collecting samples. Avoid transferring suspect plants or contaminated water to unaffected production areas while the cause is being investigated. Keep field and seed-lot records so a confirmed finding can be traced. For future crops, locally suitable resistant varieties are an important option, but resistance should be matched to the disease and regional bacterial populations. Do not choose a treatment simply because a leaf is yellow or streaked.
researchNotes: IRRI's diagnostic guide independently describes early blight and streak symptoms. EFSA's pest assessment supports pathovar distinctions, contaminated-water spread and resistant-cultivar options, drawing on several studies. The public draft explicitly retains the broad species scope and does not assign all leaf blight to an unspecified isolate.

sources.title: IRRI: Diagnosis of Common Diseases of Rice
EFSA: Pest categorisation of Xanthomonas oryzae pathovars oryzae and oryzicola

claims: Different early symptoms of bacterial leaf blight and leaf streak; late-stage similarity and kresek.
Distinct pathovars, rice hosts, spread through contaminated water and resistant cultivars as a mitigation option.

proposedDescription: Leaf smut of rice is caused by Eballistra oryzae, a fungus still called Entyloma oryzae in many crop guides. It produces small dark spots in leaf tissue and is generally treated as a minor disease in the United States extension accounts reviewed here. A heavily spotted leaf may look alarming, but its appearance does not by itself indicate a major yield threat. The first useful step is to distinguish leaf smut from the other leaf and grain diseases that share parts of its common name.
identification: Look for small, black, slightly raised or rectangular marks on the leaves, often becoming noticeable later in the crop's development. Numerous lesions can darken a leaf, and affected tips may die. The location matters: leaf smut marks occur in the foliage, unlike diseases centered on the developing grain. Photograph individual lesions close enough to show their shape, then include the whole leaf and plant. Record crop stage and whether grain symptoms are present, since a second disease may be occurring at the same time.
actions: Ask a rice extension adviser to confirm an unfamiliar pattern before considering treatment. Texas A&M and Arkansas guidance do not recommend routine fungicide control for leaf smut, so spotting alone is a poor reason to spray. Review nitrogen management with the adviser if the field has received excessive fertilizer, because Arkansas observations associate leaf smut with overfertilized rice. Keep notes on the variety, affected area, and timing, and compare subsequent crops rather than assuming every dark leaf spot has the same cause.
researchNotes: Index Fungorum verifies the Eballistra/Entyloma name relationship. Independent Texas A&M and Arkansas crop accounts support symptoms, generally minor importance, and no routine fungicide recommendation; Arkansas supplies the excess-nitrogen association. Regional observations are not inflated into a guarantee of negligible loss everywhere.

sources.title: Arkansas Rice Production Handbook: Management of Rice Diseases

claims: Eballistra oryzae is the current combination based on Entyloma oryzae.
Small raised black leaf spots; late-season minor disease; no routine control recommended.
Rectangular black leaf spots, excess-nitrogen association and no routine fungicide recommendation.

proposedDescription: Dysaphis crithmi is described in specialist aphid literature as an aphid associated with rock samphire, Crithmum maritimum, particularly around sheltered leaf bases. The common name leaf-curling plum aphid points toward a different insect: university plum guidance uses that name for Brachycaudus helichrysi. Combining the two would give readers the wrong host plant and could lead to an incorrect diagnosis.
identification: For Dysaphis crithmi, the reviewed specialist account describes wingless adults as gray to greenish gray, dusted with wax, and about 1.7 to 2.2 millimeters long. The host and feeding position are useful clues, but neither confirms the species by itself. Several aphids can occur on rock samphire, and a specialist may need microscopic characters. Photograph the entire host, the colony in its original position, and individual aphids as clearly as possible. A curled plum leaf should not be assigned to this scientific name from a common-name match.
actions: If you are trying to identify aphids on a plum tree, use a local fruit-crop identification service and keep that observation separate from rock-samphire observations. For aphids on rock samphire, record the location and whether they occupy the sheathing leaf bases, then seek specialist confirmation. Avoid choosing a control method from advice for the similarly named plum aphid. Keep the original name and source attached to the observation so a specialist can trace the identification and explain any correction.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Fresh specialist and university accounts confirm that the scientific and common labels point to different insects. The common-name/host mismatch remains. Plum-control information is retained only as evidence of the mismatch and is not assigned to D. crithmi. Trace the original catalog label and obtain an aphid specialist's taxon correction recommendation.

proposedDescription: Centrocoris volxemi is a small true bug in the leaf-footed bug family, documented in Utah and Idaho after its arrival in North America. University of Idaho observations describe it as a possible household nuisance as well as an insect found outdoors. Russian thistle is an important recorded feeding plant. Its appearance on another plant does not necessarily mean that plant is a host, a distinction emphasized in California's pest assessment.
identification: Adults are about a third of an inch long, roughly 8 millimeters, with a mottled brown-and-white appearance. Those broad features overlap with other true bugs, so the family-level common name is not enough for a confident species identification. Take a sharp photograph from above and another from the side, with a size reference if possible. Include the antennae, legs, and body outline rather than only the wings. Record whether the insect was on living Russian thistle, on another plant, or entering a building.
actions: For insects gathering at a house, begin with identification and practical exclusion, such as checking gaps around doors and window screens. Avoid crushing individuals indoors because they can release an unpleasant smell. Send clear photographs to an extension service if the species is unfamiliar in your area. Do not move bugs or occupied plant material elsewhere, even if they are feeding on an unwanted weed. The reviewed California assessment did not establish crop or environmental damage, so their presence alone should not be treated as proof that nearby garden plants are being harmed.
researchNotes: University of Idaho supplies its own Idaho collection history, appearance and household-nuisance guidance. CDFA provides an independent host-evidence assessment and explicit uncertainty about impacts. Historic California absence and pest-rating statements are not presented as current range or law. Door and screen checks are conservative exclusion advice.

proposedDescription: The variegated leafhopper is a tiny grape-feeding insect listed in older vineyard guides as Erythroneura variabilis and placed in Erasmoneura in taxonomic treatments. Both adults and immature stages remove the contents of leaf cells, leaving pale stippling behind. Large populations can reduce leaf function, but a few insects or scattered feeding marks do not automatically call for treatment. Vine condition, population trends, and the activity of natural enemies all matter.
identification: Adults are around 3 millimeters long and mottled in brown, green, and white, often with a reddish cast. Newly hatched nymphs are almost transparent and later become yellowish or orange brown. Similar grape leafhoppers differ in markings and immature coloration, and specialist keys use much finer anatomical features. Examine leaf undersides for nymphs and photograph both the insects and the feeding pattern. Keep the vine's location and variety with the record, rather than identifying the species from leaf stippling alone.
actions: Check several vines and leaves at regular intervals to see whether nymph numbers and damage are increasing. Record the counts in a consistent way so an adviser can interpret the trend. Preserve predators and tiny egg-parasitic wasps by avoiding unnecessary broad insecticide applications. UC guidance notes that treatment decisions differ with grape use, region, canopy size, and leafhopper species, so a threshold from another vineyard may not fit yours. If the vines are declining or identification is uncertain, bring clear photographs and monitoring notes to a local viticulture or extension specialist.
researchNotes: UC IPM provides species-specific coloration, feeding injury and monitoring context under Erythroneura variabilis. Dmitriev's original 2008 Erasmoneura treatment independently supplies placement and diagnostic key characters. The account distinguishes practical field clues from definitive anatomical identification and omits regional numerical treatment thresholds.

claims: Variegated adult and nymph colors; stippling damage; monitoring and management depend on crop and natural enemies.
Erasmoneura variabilis appears in original taxonomic key using male anatomical characters.

proposedDescription: Leafy spurge names can conceal an important difference between closely related plants. The name Euphorbia esula has often been applied to the troublesome North American plant now treated as Euphorbia virgata. Montana's botanical guidance explicitly marks that older usage as a misapplication, while European floras distinguish true E. esula by its leaf shape and other characters. This account concerns true variety esula; importing a general North American leafy-spurge account would risk describing the wrong taxon.
identification: Begin with several mature leaves from the middle of a stem. In true E. esula, leaves tend to be widest above the middle and narrow gradually toward the base. E. virgata has much narrower leaves whose sides are more nearly parallel through the middle, with a more abrupt narrowing at the base. These are comparison clues, not a complete identification key. Photograph the entire shoot, representative leaves with a ruler, and flowering structures. A botanist may need finer leaf and floral details to settle the name.
actions: Record the plant's location and setting, but keep any management recommendation provisional until its identity is confirmed. Ask a herbarium or local weed specialist whether the observation belongs to true E. esula, E. virgata, or another similar spurge. Do not move plants or soil from an uncertain patch to a new site while that check is underway. If a regulated weed is confirmed, seek local guidance for that taxon. Keep the original identification and the botanist's determination together so later reports can distinguish the two species.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Montana explicitly marks Euphorbia esula as misapplied to E. virgata; Flora Helvetica distinguishes true esula by leaves widest above the middle and narrowed at the base. The catalog variety cannot inherit the North American virgata invasion account merely through the common name leafy spurge.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: A true esula-variety profile is supportable when virgata invasion records are explicitly excluded. Fresh Meise treatment recognizes narrow esula and distinguishes the introduced narrow-leaved complex. Independent Swiss flora and Montana misapplication notes support the existing comparison without claiming a US identity. Next step: Review the true-esula account; leave historical leafy-spurge occurrence crosswalks unresolved.
