proposedDescription: Maltese cross is a perennial garden flower with dense clusters of bright scarlet blooms. It may also be listed under its older name, Lychnis chalcedonica. A plant beside a house or in a maintained bed may be an intentional ornamental; records outside cultivation should distinguish that setting from a self-established population. Flower color alone is not enough to decide its identity or local impact.
identification: Upright, hairy stems carry opposite leaves that attach without obvious stalks. The leaves are broadly lance-shaped to oval, and the crowded flower cluster sits at the stem tip. Each flower has a tubular, veined calyx and deeply divided petals that give the familiar cross-like appearance. Cultivated forms can have pink or white flowers rather than scarlet. Photograph the entire stem, a leaf pair and a close view of the flower tube. After flowering, capsules open at the tip; a flowering or fruiting specimen is more informative than foliage alone.
actions: Note whether plants are spreading away from an old garden, and record the number and extent of separate clumps. Where the plant is unwanted, remove faded flower heads before seed develops and keep any removed root divisions out of nearby natural areas. Its perennial underground growth means cutting flowers alone does not remove an established clump. Revisit the site for regrowth and seedlings. The references establish identification and garden propagation, but do not justify treating every planting as an ecological threat.
researchNotes: Flora of North America description is supplied through World Flora Online; NC State independently describes garden habit and propagation. The two hostnames of NC State are one source group. No unsupported national impact or legal status is asserted.

sources.title: Flora of North America via World Flora Online: Silene chalcedonica

claims: Hairy perennial stems, sessile leaves, crowded scarlet flowers and toothed capsules.
Upright ornamental habit, flower colors and perennial cultivation.
Deadheading and propagation through seed and root divisions.

proposedDescription: Mammoth wildrye is a coarse perennial grass that spreads through underground stems called rhizomes. It has been planted to hold inland sand and reduce wind erosion. That useful role does not rule out unwanted spread into neighboring vegetation, but neither does its catalog listing mean every established planting should be removed. Site history and local assessment are important parts of a record.
identification: Look for stout upright stems, long tough leaves and a thick, elongated flowering spike. The foliage can have a blue-green cast; the upper leaf surface and edges feel rough. Several spikelets cluster at each level along the main spike, unlike grasses with single spikelets or a loose branching flower head. Photograph the whole stand, the leaf collar and both sides of a mature spike. Measurements vary among regional descriptions, so a single height or spike length should not be treated as decisive. A grass specialist can separate it from other wildryes.
actions: Check the edges of a planting for new shoots and record whether it is advancing into nearby habitat. Avoid moving soil or sod containing live rhizomes, which are also used deliberately to establish the grass. Where removal is warranted, plan for underground regrowth rather than assuming one mowing will finish the job. On dunes or erosion-prone ground, coordinate replacement vegetation before disturbing an extensive stand. USDA recommends locally appropriate control advice; its favorable assessment of the Volga cultivar is not a universal assessment of all sites or material.
researchNotes: USDA NRCS supplies original cultivar assessment, rhizome spread and erosion-control context. Kew GrassBase supplies independent structural characters. Conflicting spike dimensions are avoided, and the cultivar assessment is not generalized to the species everywhere.

sources.title: USDA NRCS: Mammoth wildrye plant guide

claims: Rhizome spread, inland sand stabilization, cultivar-specific environmental evaluation and follow-up context.
Robust rhizomatous perennial, tough rough leaves and clustered spikelets.

proposedDescription: Man to man, or shiny bush, is a small fleshy herb that grows in moist, sheltered places. It can appear in garden beds, beside walls and in other damp crevices. Its delicate stems and tiny flowers make it easy to overlook until several plants are present. Common names vary widely, so the scientific name and clear photographs are especially useful when reporting it.
identification: Look for smooth, branching stems and shiny leaves that are broadly heart-shaped to triangular. The leaves are small and thin compared with many familiar ornamental peperomias. Slender upright spikes carry the very small flowers and later dark fruits, rather than large showy blossoms. Photograph a complete plant, the point where a leaf joins its stalk and a close view of a fruiting spike. The leaves are not shield-shaped with the stalk attached in the middle of the blade. Other cultivated peperomias can have thicker, wrinkled or densely crowded foliage.
actions: Where it is unwanted in a maintained garden, remove the small plant with its roots before mature fruits are scattered. Work carefully around nearby seedlings and avoid shaking fruiting plants over fresh soil. Contain removed material rather than leaving fleshy stems in another damp bed, and check moist edges and cracks for subsequent seedlings. Record the setting before clearing a suspected new wild population. The sources support garden identification and removal, not a blanket claim of serious ecological damage. Do not use online medicinal descriptions as instructions to eat or treat illness with this plant.
researchNotes: Singapore NParks supports foliage, propagation and careful garden removal; Smithsonian Flora of Micronesia independently distinguishes its leaf and fruit characters from other Peperomia. Medicinal uses are not converted into recommendations.

sources.title: NParks: Wildflowers in Singapore management guide

claims: Small shiny triangular leaves, slender spikes, moist habitat and propagation.
Removal with roots while avoiding seed dispersal.
Non-peltate flat leaves and ribbed fruit distinguish the species.

proposedDescription: Manchu tubergourd, also called red hailstone or goldencreeper, is a perennial climbing vine that can persist through a network of underground tubers. Shoots can cover fences, shrubs and other vegetation. Those tubers are important to both spread and control: cutting the visible vine does not remove the stored growth below ground, and discarded tubers can start another patch.
identification: Look for hairy climbing stems, curling tendrils and heart-shaped leaves with a deep notch at the base. Yellow flowers are tubular near the base, opening into five lobes. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Where pollination occurs, cucumber-like fruits can mature red, but the absence of fruit does not rule the species out. Some documented populations have only male plants. Photograph the leaf base, tendril attachment and flowers. If digging is authorized, document the tubers without scattering them or moving contaminated soil to another location.
actions: Record the full boundary of the patch, including shoots away from the main climbing mass. Prevent tubers and soil from being dumped beside waterways or shared with garden plants. Small patches may be excavated carefully, but missed or broken-off tubers require repeated checks. Do not assume that one cutting or a single treatment has eliminated it. For vines tangled in shrubs, work from the ground rather than pulling heavy growth overhead. Local managers can help plan repeated treatment and disposal while protecting the vegetation underneath.
researchNotes: Minnesota DNR and Ontario crop weed guidance independently support tuber persistence, hairy heart-leaved vines and garden escapes. Male-only Minnesota observations are not represented as universal or necessarily current for every population.

claims: Tuber spread, hairy vine, separate sexes and male-only regional observations.
Perennial tuberous vine, deeply notched heart leaves and persistence in disturbed agricultural places.

proposedDescription: Manchurian walnut is a deciduous tree grown for its large divided leaves and, in some forms, its nuts. The name has been used broadly in some botanical treatments and more narrowly in others. Japanese walnut and heartnut may be included within it or listed separately. That naming history matters when matching a cultivated tree or an older record to this profile.
identification: Look for very large leaves divided into numerous toothed leaflets along a central stalk. Young shoots and leaf stalks can be hairy, and the leaflet undersides are often noticeably downy. Long hanging male catkins appear in season. Nuts develop within husks; mainland forms commonly have thick, rough shells with prominent ridges and pits. Photograph a complete leaf, the underside, young shoots and any mature nuts. A label or documented planting origin can be as useful as a single visible trait. Nut shape varies, so it should not be used alone to resolve the broader species complex.
actions: Record whether the tree was deliberately planted and whether seedlings are establishing beyond the planting. Do not remove an unfamiliar walnut solely because a catalog name appears to match. Ask an arboretum or botanical specialist to review uncertain material, particularly where native walnuts or hybrids occur. Retain the original label wording alongside any updated identification. Compare any seedlings with the planted parent and note their distance from it. A planted walnut and a self-sustaining population are different observations; neither should be inferred from a name on a map.
researchNotes: Fresh full-text dendrology and Arnold Arboretum field accounts support the identification scope and a documented Korean forest collection. The broad versus narrow walnut treatment is explained rather than silently reassigned. Independent original collection context can corroborate a descriptive profile without a second complete key or United States control trial. Review as a recognition and provenance profile; obtain specialist identification before management.

sources.title: Arnold Arboretum: Plant collecting in Korea

claims: Large pinnate leaves, hairy shoots, ridged nuts and competing taxonomic treatments.
Documented collection in Korean forest; not management or impact evidence.

proposedDescription: Mango is a widely cultivated evergreen fruit tree. In warm climates it may also grow outside maintained gardens, but a fruit tree in cultivation and a spreading wild population are different observations. Florida assessments distinguish regional levels of concern, so the species should not be described as equally problematic throughout the United States. Record the setting and evidence of recruitment rather than assuming impact from the name alone.
identification: Look for long, leathery, unlobed leaves that hang slightly downward from the branches. New growth often has a coppery or reddish color before becoming deep green. Many tiny pale flowers form large branching clusters near the tips of shoots. The fleshy fruit contains a large central stone, but size, shape and skin color vary considerably among cultivated varieties. Photograph mature leaves, new shoots and any flower or fruit clusters. A dense crown or red young leaves alone will not distinguish mango from every other tropical tree.
actions: Note whether seedlings occur beyond the orchard or garden and whether fallen fruit is reaching nearby natural areas. Where containment is needed, collect unwanted fruit and keep fruit-bearing waste out of unmanaged vegetation. Have young trees identified before removal. Avoid unnecessary contact with damaged stems or sap, which can cause reactions in some people. Mature trees require appropriate tree-work planning, especially near buildings. The reviewed references support identification and regional assessment; they do not call for removing every productive mango tree or provide a single treatment suitable for all sites.
researchNotes: UF tree description and Florida assessment are one institutional group; Singapore NParks independently supports foliage and fruit structure. Regional concern is preserved, and horticultural cultivation does not become a universal invasive-status assertion.

sources.title: UF IFAS: Mangifera indica tree fact sheet

claims: Evergreen crown, reddish new growth, fruit variability and sap sensitivity.
Different regional recommendations within Florida.
Long entire drooping leaves, flower panicles and large fleshy drupes.

proposedDescription: Mango shield scale is a small sap-feeding insect found on mango and many other host plants. It belongs to the soft scales, which can produce sticky honeydew that supports dark sooty mold. A dirty-looking leaf is therefore a clue to investigate, not a diagnosis: several scale insects and other sap feeders can produce the same effect.
identification: Inspect leaf surfaces, especially the undersides, for flattened to slightly raised, roughly triangular insects. Young females can be yellow-green and older ones brown, sometimes with reddish flecks. They lack a conspicuous cottony egg sac; eggs are held beneath the female. Photograph several insects in place with the host leaf and a scale reference. Distinguishing this species from similar soft scales requires microscopic features, including the plates near the rear of the body and the tiny hairs around its edge. A phone photograph may establish a likely scale infestation without establishing this species.
actions: Keep an infested potted plant separate from other plants while arranging identification, and avoid giving away affected cuttings or foliage. Record the host, recent plant purchases and whether sticky deposits or sooty mold are spreading. Ask a plant diagnostic service how to submit a sample without transporting loose insects. Treatment should follow confirmation and the insect life stage; a dark leaf coating alone is not a reason to spray. For an unusual infestation, contact the relevant plant-health authority before moving nursery material elsewhere.
researchNotes: USDA identification tool supplies detailed field and microscopic characters; EFSA independently synthesizes pest biology and detection limitations. Interceptions are not treated as proof of establishment in every origin or destination. No unsupported product or treatment efficacy is claimed.

sources.title: EFSA: Pest categorisation of Milviscutulus mangiferae

claims: Triangular females, color changes, absent ovisac and microscope-based separation.
Honeydew, sooty mold, broad hosts and difficult early detection.

proposedDescription: The mangrove-boring isopod is a small crustacean that shelters in burrows in mangrove roots and other suitable material. Its relationship with mangroves is more complicated than a simple damage label. Studies document root injury and altered root growth, but the outcome depends on the site and conditions. Its origin and introduction history are also uncertain in parts of its range.
identification: Look for small openings or damaged sections in submerged or tidally wetted mangrove prop roots. These signs alone cannot identify the animal: other borers, decay and physical injury can also damage roots. Photograph the whole root, the location of the holes relative to the water and any visible animal without breaking living roots. Experimental work found that water depth and the part of the root available for colonization influenced where this isopod settled. A crustacean specialist may need a specimen to separate it from related species, so ask about collection before disturbing the habitat.
actions: Record the tide, root condition and extent of damage, and share a suspected new occurrence with the coastal land manager. Do not cut healthy mangrove roots or apply a chemical treatment simply to remove a suspected borer. Avoid transporting affected wood or attached marine growth to another waterbody. An observation of holes does not establish a new invasion or prove this animal caused all visible decline. The available studies support careful documentation and specialist assessment, not a broadly tested removal method for living mangrove systems.
researchNotes: Independent field study from Kerala and experimental root-colonization study support site-specific effects. Smithsonian synthesis is used for uncertain introduction history, not counted again as independent evidence of those experiments. No universal destruction claim or treatment prescription.

claims: Water depth, root position and root diameter affect colonization.

claims: Observed burrowing and damaged prop roots at two sampled localities.
Uncertain origin and mixed documented effects; review pending.

proposedDescription: Manila grass is a warm-season perennial turf grass that forms a close mat through aboveground runners and underground stems. It is intentionally planted in lawns, but those same spreading structures can cross a maintained edge. A lawn planting is not itself evidence of ecological harm. Records outside cultivation should explain where the grass is growing and whether its patch is expanding.
identification: Look for narrow, stiff, pointed leaf blades and spreading stems that root at their joints. A small fringe of hairs occurs where the blade meets its sheath. Flowering stems carry a short spike-like head with small spikelets arranged along it. Closely related zoysias and cultivated hybrids can look similar, particularly when frequently mown. A botanical key uses fine measurements of the spikelets and their stalks to separate Manila grass from Japanese zoysia. Photograph an unmown flowering shoot, the leaf junction and a runner rather than relying only on the overall lawn texture.
actions: Check the boundary between turf and neighboring beds or natural vegetation for rooted runners. Where the grass is unwanted, keep removed sod and soil containing live stems from being spread elsewhere. Follow up after edging or removal because underground growth can produce new shoots. Before treating a larger escaped patch, confirm the grass and plan to protect nearby desirable turf or native grasses. Seasonal browning can be normal winter dormancy, so it does not by itself show that removal has succeeded or that the plant has died.
researchNotes: University of Georgia supplies independently authored turf biology and dormancy context, explicitly covering multiple zoysias. New Mexico State grass key supplies species-level distinctions and warns of hybrid difficulty. Group-level characters are not presented as decisive species diagnosis.

sources.title: New Mexico State University: Grasses of New Mexico

claims: Stolons and rhizomes, hairy ligule, narrow pointed blades and frost dormancy.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: New Mexico State University grass flora
claims: Spikelet and pedicel measurements distinguish Z. matrella; hybrids complicate identification.

proposedDescription: Manna gum is a tall Australian eucalyptus with pale upper bark that sheds in long ribbons. It has been planted beyond its native range. Florida assesses it as a high invasion risk using a predictive tool; that is a warning about potential behavior, not proof that every Florida county has an established population. A useful observation distinguishes a planted tree from seedlings growing beyond cultivation.
identification: Look for smooth white, gray or yellowish bark above any rough lower trunk. Juvenile leaves occur in opposite pairs, while adult leaves are narrow and arranged separately along the shoot. Flower buds and woody capsules usually occur in groups of three in the New South Wales treatment. The small capsules have valves projecting above their rim. Photograph bark, both young and mature foliage if available, and intact bud or fruit clusters. Related gums can share ribbon bark and narrow leaves, and regional treatments differ in which closely related forms they include.
actions: Record nearby seedlings, their distance from the apparent parent and the surrounding habitat. Avoid distributing seed-bearing branches or planting additional trees where local guidance discourages this species. Small uncertain seedlings should be identified before removal. Large trees and hanging bark require appropriate professional tree-work precautions; do not climb or fell an established tree simply to obtain an identification sample. Where management is necessary, arrange follow-up for regrowth or new seedlings and choose replacement vegetation suited to the site.
researchNotes: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney supplies species morphology and taxonomic scope; UF independently supplies a predictive risk assessment. The assessment is not described as a county occurrence survey or a demonstrated national impact.

claims: Ribbon bark, juvenile opposite leaves, three-flowered groups and exserted fruit valves.
Predictive high invasion risk, distinct from documented county occurrence.

proposedDescription: The many-striped skink is now commonly placed in the genus Eutropis, although older records use Mabuya multifasciata. It is a sturdy, day-active lizard from southern and southeastern Asia. Published observations document introduced populations in southern Florida. Those records establish particular occurrences, not a reason to assume that any brown skink seen elsewhere is this species.
identification: Look for a glossy bronze-brown body with overlapping scales that have raised lengthwise ridges. Dark fine stripes may be present on the back, but their prominence varies. The sides can be dark with pale spots or show orange coloring, and some animals have yellow beneath the head. It is not reliably identified by a fixed number of stripes. Take clear photographs from above and the side while leaving the animal undisturbed. Include the whole body if possible. A specialist may need to examine head-scale arrangement to distinguish it from other skinks.
actions: Record the exact location, date, number seen and whether small individuals are present as well as adults. Share an unusual sighting with a local wildlife or invasive-species reporting program. Do not release a captive skink or relocate a wild one to another park or garden. Avoid grabbing it by the tail or using traps that could catch native lizards. The species feeds mainly on insects and bears live young, but the reviewed Florida occurrence report does not by itself establish the scale of its ecological impact.
researchNotes: NParks supplies morphology and life history from the native range; the independently authored 2018 Florida population report establishes a specific introduced locality. ITIS supports the Mabuya-to-Eutropis name link, not a third biology source.

proposedDescription: Maqui is a many-branched shrub or small tree with dark berries. It is native to parts of southern South America, but its movement to islands illustrates why location matters: research from the Juan Fernández archipelago documents invasion of native vegetation there. That island history should not be presented as proof of the same impact at every United States occurrence.
identification: Look for opposite, evergreen leaves with toothed margins and a pointed oval shape. Young twigs and leaf stalks are often reddish, and the leaves can hang downward. Small cream-yellow flowers develop in clusters. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, with dark berries developing on fruiting plants. Photograph a leaf pair, the red-tinged stalks and flowers or fruit when present. A nonfruiting plant cannot be excluded solely because berries are absent. Other shrubs with dark berries need comparison, so avoid identifying it from fruit color alone.
actions: Document whether plants are cultivated or establishing beyond a garden, especially along moist edges and disturbed woodland. Birds eat the fruit and can move seeds, so record seedlings away from the parent as well as the main shrub. Where local managers recommend containment, keep fruit-bearing waste out of natural areas and avoid distributing the plant. Do not target birds as a household control measure. A site-specific plan is needed before removing a larger stand; the reviewed island literature does not supply a universally tested United States treatment.
researchNotes: University of Talca hosts botanical information attributed to Fundación R. A. Philippi. Independent Chilean ecological research supports bird-mediated invasion on Juan Fernández. Geographic limits are explicit, and speculative bird-control proposals are not recommended.

claims: Opposite toothed leaves, reddish shoots, separate sexes and black berries.

proposedDescription: Margined buttercup is a small yellow-flowered buttercup recorded in disturbed places, including roadsides and seasonally moist ground. It can resemble several other annual buttercups. The mature fruits are more informative than flower color, and regional descriptions differ in the fruit forms they report. A yellow blossom alone is not enough to identify this species.
identification: Look for upright, sparsely hairy stems and broad lower leaves with rounded teeth or shallow lobes. Flowers have five yellow petals and hairy sepals that bend backward. The fruits gather into a small rounded head. In the North American flora, the individual fruits have sharp bumps or short spines on their faces but a smooth margin and a short, straight beak. European accounts include smoother-fruited forms, creating additional overlap with related species. Photograph the lower leaves, the back of a flower and a mature fruit head with a size reference.
actions: Before clearing a patch, obtain identification from someone familiar with local buttercups, including native species. Record the habitat and whether the plants occupy disturbed soil or a wetter natural area. If removal is appropriate on managed ground, contain mature fruiting material and avoid moving seed-bearing soil to a new place. Return during a later flowering season to check for additional plants. Keep close-up fruit photographs with the location record: a smooth-looking fruit from an overseas garden should not be used as the sole comparison for a North American plant.
researchNotes:
Fresh FNA indexed text and Christos Petrou's independently authored Cyprus field account support recognition; fruit differences are geographically scoped. FNA explicitly excludes the smoother European form from its North American treatment. This is regional variation, not a reason to require an unsupported management claim. Retain the North American fruit qualification and request mature fruit for uncertain identifications.

proposedDescription: Neotoxoptera oliveri is a small aphid recorded from several herbaceous hosts, including violets, chickweeds and some onion relatives. The catalog label marigold aphid is not enough to establish the host range or identify an infestation. A Florida inventory published in 2025 reports this species from herb nurseries and herb gardens, illustrating why the plant's identity and growing setting are worth recording.
identification: Wingless adults are described as dark red to almost black and roughly one to two millimeters long. Like other aphids, they have paired tube-like structures near the rear of the abdomen. In this genus those tubes are club-shaped, and winged forms have dark-bordered wing veins. These are specialist comparison features, not details that every phone image will capture. Photograph the host plant and a close group of insects, including winged individuals if present. Winged individuals can provide characters that are missing from an entirely wingless colony, helping an aphid specialist test a tentative identification.
actions: Keep affected nursery plants separate while seeking confirmation, and avoid sharing infested stems or flowers. Record exactly which plant parts hold the insects, whether the plant is declining and whether the population is increasing. A diagnostic service can explain how to retain a small sample for examination. Do not assume that this aphid transmits a particular plant virus or choose a treatment solely from its common name. Keep the host label with any submitted sample, and ask the diagnostic service to distinguish this species from other dark aphids before deciding whether intervention is needed.
researchNotes: Fresh Skelley and colleagues' 2025 Florida inventory supplies independent state specimen evidence: FDACS sample E2006-0111 and records confined there to herb nurseries and herb gardens. Blackman-Eastop and its AphID derivative remain one diagnostic lineage. Noordam's uncertain Java specimens are retained only as an identification caution, not confirmation. The Florida collection record closes the second-lineage gap without importing a control claim. Review a scoped aphid-recognition profile; retain expert confirmation and do not infer virus transmission.

proposedDescription: Cannabis is an annual plant with a long history of cultivation for several purposes. It can also persist as escaped plants in disturbed ground. The names hemp and marijuana do not provide a reliable visual identification of a plant's chemical composition. This profile concerns recognizing and documenting the plant, not determining its legal classification or how it may be used.
identification: Look for leaves with several narrow, sharply toothed leaflets radiating from one point. Lower leaves are often opposite and upper leaves may be alternate. Plants vary greatly in height and branching. The small flowers lack showy petals; pollen-producing flowers can form loose branching clusters, while seed-bearing flowers are grouped more closely along the shoots. Photograph a whole leaf, its attachment and any flower clusters. Similar-looking plants, including kenaf, can have a single deeply lobed blade rather than separate leaflets. Leaf shape and smell cannot establish cannabinoid content or distinguish regulated categories with certainty.
actions: Record whether the plant appears cultivated or self-established and document it without entering private property. If its identity or handling requirements are uncertain, seek guidance from the responsible land manager or local authority before collecting, transporting or removing material. Do not taste an unknown plant or assume that appearance establishes a permitted use. For an unmanaged population, useful records include the number of plants, the disturbed habitat and whether mature seed is present. The sources support identification, not a universal ecological-impact claim.
researchNotes: UF peer-reviewed identification guide and Native Plant Trust flora independently support leaf, flower and habitat traits. No numerical legal threshold, cultivation instructions, potency estimate or medical claim is included. Older popular taxonomy separating industrial and drug forms was not adopted.

sources.title: UF IFAS: Cannabis identification and look-alikes

claims: Botanical identification and limits of visually distinguishing chemical categories.
Compound toothed leaves, small flowers, dry fruit and disturbed-ground occurrences.

proposedDescription: The lacy crust bryozoan is a colony of many tiny animals, often forming a pale, net-like layer across kelp. A colony begins when a swimming larva settles, then grows by budding additional individuals. In parts of the northeastern United States it is an introduced fouling organism that can weaken kelp tissue. Its effects should be described for the affected region rather than assumed everywhere.
identification: Look for a thin, flat, whitish crust spreading over a seaweed blade or another firm surface. Under magnification the colony has a regular pattern of small adjoining compartments, each belonging to an individual animal. That appearance differs from bushy branching bryozoans, but other encrusting species still need comparison. Photograph the colony edge, a close view of its pattern and the entire host surface. Include the location and depth if known. Do not tear attached kelp from a natural bed simply to obtain a specimen; photographs can help a marine specialist decide what further evidence is needed.
actions: Inspect marine equipment and cultured seaweed before moving them between sites. Follow the relevant facility's cleaning procedures, keeping removed fouling material on land and out of another waterbody where possible. Aquaculture guidance recommends removing fouling from gear and considering harvest timing, but treatments suitable for equipment are not automatically safe for living kelp or shellfish. Report an unusual occurrence with clear images. A white crust alone does not establish this species or explain every damaged kelp blade.
researchNotes: Smithsonian Ocean explains colony growth and regional kelp effects; the northeastern aquaculture management guide independently supplies equipment and crop-management context. Host-safe treatment limits are retained and no blanket freshwater or brine recipe is applied.

claims: Larval settlement, budding colonies and regional kelp damage.
Flat kelp crust, weakened tissue and containment during gear cleaning.

proposedDescription: Eualetes tulipa is a marine worm snail: despite its irregular tube-shaped shell, it is a snail rather than a worm. Adults remain attached to hard surfaces and feed from the surrounding water. Records include harbors and other altered coastal habitats. Its native range and identification history are complicated, with older records published under names such as Vermetus alii.
identification: Look for a hard, winding tube fixed to rock, a seawall or another solid surface. A live animal may be visible at the opening, but an empty tube cannot reliably establish its species. Several worm snails and tube-building worms can look similar in an underwater photograph. Capture the complete tube, opening and attachment surface without breaking coral or other living habitat. Specialist examination may be needed. A Brazilian study corrected earlier identifications only after closer observation, illustrating why a familiar tube shape is not sufficient evidence on its own.
actions: Record the location, depth, surface type and whether there are isolated tubes or a dense group. Share a suspected new record with a marine monitoring program rather than moving attached shells to another shore. Inspect and maintain boat hulls and equipment through appropriate facilities, containing removed fouling material instead of releasing it at a new site. Do not scrape living natural habitat as an improvised control measure. The research documents occurrence and density patterns, but does not establish a safe, generally effective eradication method for every coastal setting.
researchNotes: Bishop Museum Pearl Harbor inventory supplies independent Hawaiian specimen history. Skinner and colleagues provide an original Brazilian density study and identification corrections. Smithsonian synthesis is used only for wider uncertain origin and hull-fouling context, not counted again as independent Brazilian evidence.

proposedDescription: The maritime gardensnail, also called vineyard snail, is a land snail that can gather on vegetation, posts and other objects above the soil. Agricultural concern includes contamination of harvested grain and interference with machinery, not only feeding on plants. It can travel with equipment and goods, so a small cluster on stored material is worth documenting before that material is moved.
identification: Adults generally have a pale, rounded shell, often with brown spiral bands, although some are entirely white. An open, circular hole is visible at the center of the underside. Fine growth scratches and the shape of the shell opening help specialists compare it with other pale snails. Photograph the top, side, underside and opening with a ruler, without releasing it elsewhere afterward. Several related or similar species share white shells and bands; neither color nor climbing behavior is enough to confirm this species. Young shells can be especially difficult to distinguish.
actions: If snails are attached to incoming equipment, nursery stock or cargo, pause movement and contact the relevant agricultural inspection service. Keep photographs and shipment details together. Do not transport live specimens unless the receiving diagnostic service explains how to contain them. For an established agricultural infestation, management needs to account for seasonal activity and snails resting above ground. Australian seasonal recommendations should not be transferred directly to a United States calendar. Historical eradication reports demonstrate coordinated response, not a guarantee that one household treatment will eliminate a population.
researchNotes: USDA IDtools provides comparative shell diagnosis; South Australia SARDI/PIRSA independently supplies crop contamination, resting behavior and regional management. Historical Tacoma assessment is not used to claim present-day distribution or regulatory status.

claims: Pale banded shells, whorls and comparison with C. neglecta.

proposedDescription: Maritime pine is a large Mediterranean pine planted for timber, shelter and ornament. It can establish beyond plantings in suitable environments. Florida identifies invasion risk through a predictive assessment, with recommendations differing by region. That assessment should guide caution about planting and escape, but it does not establish that a particular county already contains a wild population.
identification: Look for a deeply fissured, dark reddish-brown trunk and long, stout needles held in pairs. The sheath around each needle pair persists at the base. Large woody cones often occur in groups and may remain on the tree for years. Their scales have raised, angular exposed surfaces with a prominent point. Photograph a complete needle pair with its base, a mature cone and the bark. Other two-needle pines can look similar, so combine these features rather than identifying a tree from its coastal location or rough trunk alone.
actions: Check open ground around a planting for seedlings and younger trees of different sizes. Record whether those recruits are outside maintained areas and whether nearby vegetation is changing. Where removal is appropriate, seek confirmation before pulling small pines, particularly in places with native pine species. Mature trees require a safe professional plan, and cone-bearing waste should not be distributed into unoccupied habitat. Revisit managed sites for seedlings. The reviewed sources support identification and regional risk awareness, not a single treatment prescription for every stand.
researchNotes: NSW flora supplies cone and bark morphology; International Dendrology Society supplies paired needle characters; UF independently provides predictive risk. Risk is not confused with observed occurrence, and no control guidance for a different pine species is transferred.

claims: Deeply fissured bark, persistent clustered cones and angular cone scales.
Long stout paired needles and persistent basal sheaths.
Region-specific predictive invasion risk.

proposedDescription: Japanese ardisia, also listed as marlberry, is a low evergreen shrub that can spread into a dense groundcover. Its underground growth makes a patch larger than the stems visible above it. Florida guidance identifies particular concern in the north of the state, with different assessments farther south. That regional context matters when deciding whether a planted groundcover has become a management problem.
identification: Look for short upright stems with glossy, finely toothed leaves concentrated toward their upper portions. Small white or pale pink star-shaped flowers occur in groups. Round fruits are initially red and can become dark as they mature, so fruit color changes with stage. Photograph the plant at ground level, the leaf margins and any flowers or fruit. Taller ardisias can share similar leaves and berries, but Japanese ardisia typically forms a much lower mat. Published summaries differ on leaf arrangement, so that feature is not used alone as a decisive shortcut here.
actions: Trace the edge of the colony before work begins and look for connected shoots beyond the obvious patch. Where removal is appropriate, collect berries and seedlings and address the underground runners as well as the upright stems. Simply clipping the foliage can leave a substantial network capable of regrowth. Avoid moving contaminated soil or divisions to another property. Revisit cleared ground repeatedly, especially beside shaded woodland. For established colonies, arrange a sustained removal plan that protects surrounding roots and native groundcover.
researchNotes:
UF CAIP supplies regional impacts and underground removal considerations. Flora of China independently resolves red-to-blackish fruit maturation; NC State provides additional horticultural context. Conflicting leaf-arrangement summaries are excluded as a decisive character.

claims: Low colonies, shaded forest effects and persistent underground runners.
Low stoloniferous habit, toothed leaves and red fruit becoming blackish.
Evergreen groundcover, runner spread, flower and cultivar context.

proposedDescription: Marsh cudweed is a small woolly annual found on damp ground, including pond margins, wet meadows and disturbed places. Its flower heads are much less showy than those of familiar daisies. Regional references differ about whether all North American populations should be considered introduced, so its local origin and ecological role need to be assessed separately from its identity.
identification: Look for a low plant that commonly branches near the base, with narrow, unlobed leaves covered in pale woolly hairs. Tiny brownish flower heads sit in tight clusters at branch tips and sometimes in leaf axils. The leaves immediately below the clusters usually extend beyond them. There are no large strap-shaped petals surrounding a yellow center. Photograph the whole branching pattern, leaf surfaces and a close view of a head cluster. Several plants formerly grouped with cudweeds now belong to other genera, making the arrangement of heads and surrounding leaves useful for comparison.
actions: Record whether it occupies recently exposed mud, a disturbed margin or a maintained planting. Small damp-ground annuals can be mistaken for one another, so have uncertain plants checked before removing vegetation from a wetland edge. Where removal is justified on managed ground, address plants before seed dispersal and avoid transferring seed-bearing mud to another site. Do not drain or disturb a wetland simply to eliminate a suspected patch. Include the surrounding vegetation in your photographs so a local botanist can assess the patch in its habitat, rather than treating a single woolly plant as evidence of a harmful invasion.
researchNotes:
Fresh FNA and independently authored Flora of China support the woolly annual, axillary and terminal head clusters, and moist habitats; Native Plant Trust confirms the differing regional origin summary. The unresolved continent-wide introduction history can remain explicit without preventing an accurate recognition profile. No universal invasive status or tested control efficacy is claimed. Keep the North American origin uncertainty visible and use local habitat context for any management decision.

proposedDescription: Marsh parsley, also called slender celery, is a finely divided annual herb found in gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Its airy foliage and tiny white flowers can resemble several members of the carrot family. The common names do not make it an edible herb, and a safe identification should rely on leaves, flowers and mature fruit together.
identification: Look for a slender, upright, hairless plant with leaves repeatedly divided into thread-like segments. Lower leaves have stalks; upper leaves attach more directly to the stem. Small white flowers form modest umbrella-like clusters rather than the large, dense flower platforms of wild carrot. The mature fruits are small, oval and ribbed, without the conspicuous hooked or bristly covering found in some carrot relatives. Photograph the lower and upper foliage, an entire flower cluster and ripe fruit with a size reference. A close fruit view is especially helpful when leaves alone look familiar.
actions: Do not taste the plant or use a crushed-leaf smell as the deciding identification test. Record the habitat and whether it is confined to disturbed ground or extending into sensitive vegetation. Where it is unwanted in a maintained bed, remove identified young plants before fruit matures and keep seed-bearing waste from being scattered. Recheck the same moist or recently disturbed areas for later seedlings. Management should match the setting: sources describe it as a weed in some places, but that is not evidence of equally severe ecological harm throughout its range.
researchNotes: NSW flora and the Paraguay weed manual independently support fine divided foliage, small umbels and ribbed fruit; Queensland Lucid account supports comparison with Daucus. Australian legal wording is not transferred to the United States, and no food-use inference is made.

claims: Hairless annual, thread-like leaf segments, small white umbels and oval fruits.
Finely divided leaves, ribbed fruit and disturbed-ground habitat with examined specimen.
Small umbels and unadorned ribbed fruit contrast with carrot relatives.

proposedDescription: European marsh thistle is a tall, spiny plant of damp open places, wetland edges and disturbed woodland. It starts as a low rosette and later produces a flowering stem, sometimes after more than two growing seasons. A population can therefore contain inconspicuous rosettes as well as tall plants. Mapping both stages helps reveal the extent of a developing infestation.
identification: Look for long, deeply lobed rosette leaves and upright stems with conspicuous spiny wings running down their length. Flowering stems branch mainly toward the top and carry clusters of relatively small purple heads. Leaves become smaller farther up the stem. Native swamp thistle can occupy similar habitat but lacks those spiny stem wings, so examine the stem as well as the flowers. Photograph the lower leaves, stem wings and clustered heads. Do not assume every purple thistle is introduced or that every spiny thistle has the same life history.
actions: Report new patches with location and life-stage details, particularly at the edge of a known infestation. Where authorized, small rosettes can be pulled or dug while minimizing disturbance to wet soil. Flowering plants need carefully timed work and follow-up; mowing at the wrong stage can allow renewed growth and seed production. Contain mature heads and clean equipment before leaving. Larger wetland patches need a coordinated plan that protects native thistles and surrounding habitat. A single pass through the tallest stems is unlikely to address all the plants present.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR supplies local identification and mechanical guidance; the independent SUNY New York field study supports life-stage mapping and adaptive response. Forest Service synthesis qualifies mowing and uncertain seed persistence; no unqualified mowing cure or biological-control release is recommended.

proposedDescription: Marshpepper knotweed, or water-pepper, is an annual of wet ground, ditches and stream or pond margins. It can form groups of plants through repeated seed production, especially where wet soil is disturbed. Its common name reflects a reported peppery taste, but tasting an unknown smartweed is unnecessary and should not be used as an identification method.
identification: Look for narrow, pointed leaves arranged one at a time along a smooth stem. A thin tubular sheath surrounds the stem at each leaf junction and has a fringe along its upper edge. Slender, often nodding flower clusters carry small greenish-white or pinkish flowers that may appear only partly open. Fine glands on the flower coverings and mature dark fruits help specialists distinguish it from similar smartweeds. Photograph a leaf junction, the whole flower cluster and ripe fruit. Several native relatives grow in the same kinds of wetlands, so the general wetland habit is not enough.
actions: Record the patch boundary and whether the ground has recently been disturbed. Before removing plants from a natural wetland, confirm the identity and agree on a site-specific plan with the land manager. For a small unwanted patch in managed ground, prevent mature seed from moving with soil or plant waste and check for new seedlings later. Avoid broad clearing that removes neighboring native smartweeds or leaves more bare wet soil. The sources describe its annual biology and wetland behavior, not a single treatment that is appropriate beside every waterbody.
researchNotes: NC State and Native Plant Trust independently support annual habit, wetland setting and structural characters. Taste is not recommended, and glandular flower coverings plus fruits are presented as specialist comparisons rather than a simple guaranteed diagnosis.

claims: Annual wetland herb, nodding flowers and dark fruits.
Alternate entire leaves, fringed tubular stipules and glandular flower parts.

proposedDescription: Martinique trimezia is a yellow-flowered perennial in the iris family, also known as yellow walking iris. That common name can cover more than one garden plant. A recent Florida flora warns that the similar Trimezia steyermarkii has often been called T. martinicensis. This distinction needs resolving before older Florida observations or horticultural descriptions are assigned confidently to this species.
identification: Look for a clump of long, narrow leaves and a yellow flower on an unwinged flowering stem. The pattern at the base of the outer flower segments is important: the Florida key distinguishes a contrasting band in T. martinicensis from purplish or brownish spots in T. steyermarkii. The Bahia flora describes brown stripes on true T. martinicensis, so brown coloration alone is not a reliable separator. Compare the arrangement of markings together with leaves, stems and underground structures. Photograph an open flower from the front and side, the complete stem and the leafy clump. A label or leaf-only photograph cannot settle this comparison.
actions: Record the original plant label, whether it was deliberately planted and whether new clumps occur beyond the garden. Ask a botanical specialist to check the flower pattern before assigning the species name or deciding on management. Keep divisions and discarded underground material out of natural areas while the identity is uncertain. Florida lists low predictive invasion risk under T. martinicensis, but that assessment should not be transferred automatically to a misidentified relative. Keep the original determination alongside any later correction, and let the land manager assess a confirmed escape in its actual setting.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Fresh UFM text still describes brown-spotted flowers under martinicensis; Franck's October 2026 flora separates that pattern as T. steyermarkii and calls true T. martinicensis rare to absent in Florida. This affects the identity attached to historical Florida records, not merely uncertainty about control. UF's 2025 low-risk assessment cannot resolve which concept its observations represent. Obtain a curator decision supported by flowering vouchers and the revised Trimezia key.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: The independent Bahia flora supports true martinicensis and clarifies that basal brown striping is compatible with that species. Parent accessed the substantive2016 original Bahia treatment, including reexamined Ribeiro45 CEPEC type of connata. Florida provides an independently authored comparison with steyermarkii. Brown coloration alone is not an absolute separator; architecture and pattern need comparison. Next step: Review the qualified true-species draft and leave Florida voucher assignments unchanged. proposedDescription: The legume pod borer is a moth whose caterpillars feed inside or around the flowers and pods of beans and other legumes. They can tie plant parts together with silk, making feeding less obvious from a distance. Damage matters most when flowers or developing seeds are affected. Reports from different regions should not be confused with proof of a newly established population at every sighting.
identification: Look for webbed flower clusters, damaged pods and droppings near feeding sites. Those signs can also be caused by other caterpillars. Adult moths have brown forewings with pale patches and largely white hindwings bordered with brown. Photograph both wings when possible, rather than only the most conspicuous forewing patch. For larvae, a specialist may need microscopic features of the hairs, their bases and mouthparts. Keep the host name and damaged plant part with the photographs. An insect found on a shipment is not necessarily feeding on every plant included in that shipment.
actions: Inspect flowers and young pods regularly where the pest is known, and seek identification early rather than waiting until many pods are damaged. Keep infested harvested material from being carried to other plantings. Crop specialists can advise on monitoring, including suitable pheromone traps, and locally appropriate management timing. International crop guides discuss several approaches, but they are not universal instructions for United States crops or climates. Do not select a pesticide or release a control organism solely from a photograph or a foreign production guide.
researchNotes: USDA LepIntercept supports specialist larval diagnosis and warns that non-legume host claims can be doubtful. World Vegetable Center independently supplies webbing, pod damage and monitoring context. Mississippi State adult images and description supplement diagnosis; its reused USDA larval text is not counted twice.

claims: Larval microscopic diagnosis, legume flowers and pods, uncertain incidental hosts.
Webbed plant parts, pod damage and pheromone monitoring.

proposedDescription: Marvel of Peru, or four-o'clock, is a familiar garden plant with flowers that often open late in the day. It can live as a perennial where winters are mild and is grown as an annual in colder places. Both seed production and persistent swollen roots can matter when it becomes unwanted, so removing the visible stems may not finish the job.
identification: Look for a branched plant with opposite, pointed oval leaves and smooth leaf margins. The stems can be brittle. Trumpet-shaped flowers occur near the ends of stems or in leaf axils and may be white, yellow, pink, red or mixed colors on the same plant. Their colorful outer portion is formed from fused sepals rather than true petals. Photograph the whole plant, a leaf pair and an open flower. A plant seen earlier in the day may have closed flowers, so return later rather than excluding it because no open blooms are visible.
actions: Where it is spreading beyond an intended bed, remove developing seed and watch for seedlings nearby. If a mature plant is unwanted, account for its swollen underground root and revisit the spot for regrowth. Do not share discarded roots or seed-bearing garden waste with areas where the plant is not wanted. Wear gloves if your skin is sensitive and keep roots and seeds away from children and pets. Its ornamental value and capacity to spread should both be described without assuming the same ecological impact in every region.
researchNotes: NC State and Wisconsin Extension independently describe late-opening flowers, self-seeding and perennial roots. Their native-range and hardiness details differ, so precise universal limits are avoided. Toxic parts are identified without providing medical or consumption advice.

claims: Late-opening flowers, tuberous roots, self-seeding and regional perennial habit.

proposedDescription: Mascarene Island leaf-flower, also called long-stalked phyllanthus, is a small upright plant often found in nursery pots, irrigated beds and disturbed ground. Its tiny leaves can make the side branches resemble compound leaves, but they are separate leaves on a stem. Plants can flower when still small, so waiting for a tall weed can allow seed production to begin unnoticed.
identification: Look for a slender, often reddish or brown stem with small oval leaves arranged along delicate side branches. Tiny flowers and round green capsules hang beneath the foliage. The capsules have visible stalks, an important distinction from chamberbitter, Phyllanthus urinaria, whose fruits sit much closer to the stem. Photograph the underside of a branch so those attachments are clear. Do not identify it only by the fern-like outline. Regional floras and nursery guides differ in typical height, and a well-watered plant may look very different from a small seedling.
actions: Check pot surfaces, drainage holes, tears in nursery fabric and damp ground near irrigation equipment. Remove young identified plants before mature capsules scatter seeds, keeping roots and fruiting material contained. Repair unnecessary leaks and match watering to the cultivated plants rather than leaving surrounding ground continually wet. Recheck incoming nursery stock and recently weeded containers. Older plants can recover after their tops are damaged, and chemical performance varies, so a single contact treatment should not be assumed to provide lasting control. Preventing repeated seed production is central to keeping a nursery patch from returning.
researchNotes: UF nursery research and NC State guidance support early hand removal, irrigation attention and explosive seed spread. NSW flora independently supports small stalked flowers, capsule and leaf structure. No herbicide dose or universal efficacy claim is supplied.

claims: Stalked capsules versus chamberbitter, seed expulsion and recovery after contact injury.
Nursery refuges, early hand weeding and irrigation management.

proposedDescription: Maskell scale is a tiny armored scale insect that feeds on several conifers, including junipers, arborvitae and Japanese cedar. Infestations can cause yellowing, browning or twig decline, but those symptoms have other causes too. Old scale covers may remain after the insects have died, so the amount of visible debris is not necessarily the size of the living infestation.
identification: Look closely around the bases and undersides of foliage for small, pale brown to whitish covers shaped like elongated oyster shells. Adult female covers are only about one and a half millimeters long. Young mobile stages, called crawlers, are pale and much harder to see. Photograph the affected branch, the host's normal foliage and magnified scales with a size reference. Related armored scales require comparison, and a diagnostic service may need to examine insects beneath the covers. A photograph of browned needles alone cannot confirm this pest.
actions: Have the identification and presence of live insects checked before treating. Record which host is affected, where decline begins and whether fresh growth is acquiring scales. Monitoring crawler activity is more useful than applying the same calendar date everywhere; published timing comes from particular regions and varies with conditions. Avoid moving infested nursery plants to new sites. Appropriate watering and other plant care can reduce additional stress, while any treatment needs to match the susceptible life stage and host. Recheck living populations after treatment rather than judging success by old covers alone.
researchNotes: UMass provides morphology and regional biology limitations; Bartlett research laboratory independently documents sheltered feeding, retained dead covers and diagnostic timing. Rutgers timing is cited within UMass and is not counted as a separate independent line. No universal calendar, product or release recommendation.

proposedDescription: Mat amaranth, also called prostrate pigweed, is a summer annual that spreads close to the ground in dry fields, roadsides, gardens, and other open places. It is native to part of North America, so its presence does not automatically represent an introduced invasion. In a vegetable bed or newly planted field, however, a spreading plant can compete with the plants someone is trying to establish.
identification: Look for a low mat of branching stems with alternate, small leaves that are broadest toward the tip. Flowers are inconspicuous green clusters tucked into the leaf axils, rather than the conspicuous terminal spikes of several other pigweeds. Mature seeds are dark and shiny. Young plants can resemble other amaranths before their growth form develops. Prostrate spurges are another common source of confusion, but have different leaf arrangements and milky sap. A photograph showing both a whole branch and its leaf joints is more useful than a single leaf.
actions: If the plant is unwanted in a cultivated bed, remove small plants before the axillary flowers develop mature seed, taking care not to scatter seed-bearing material. Keep disturbed ground covered with appropriate vegetation or mulch rather than repeatedly leaving open soil. Photograph uncertain seedlings and ask an extension weed specialist to confirm them before treating a larger area. In natural vegetation, first establish whether this native annual is actually causing a management problem; an isolated roadside plant does not by itself justify eradication.
researchNotes: Native status is explicit in Missouri and Kew. Removal before seed is a prevention inference from annual seed reproduction, not a species-specific efficacy trial.

proposedDescription: Matgrass is a small, tough perennial bunchgrass from Eurasia. Its name describes the dense, wiry clumps it can build rather than a soft lawn. In parts of the western United States it is a concern in grazed grasslands because livestock tend to leave it while eating more palatable grasses. Its quiet appearance makes a small infestation easy to overlook among other pasture plants.
identification: The leaves are narrow, stiff, rough, and tightly folded, with older outer leaves often spreading sideways around the clump. Closely packed shoots grow from short underground stems. Flowering stems bear an unusual narrow head with the spikelets arranged along one side, giving it a comb-like or bristly appearance. That arrangement is more helpful than leaf color alone. Other fine-leaved bunchgrasses may look similar before flowering. Photographs should include the entire tuft, the base of the leaves, and a close view of a mature flower head.
actions: Mark a suspected patch and seek identification from a local weed program before moving soil, turf, or hay from it. Oregon's early-detection guidance specifically encourages reporting this species. Do not assume heavier grazing will solve the problem, since low palatability can favor matgrass over surrounding forage. Small clumps are tightly rooted, so any authorized removal needs to account for the underground base and subsequent regrowth. Keep records of the patch boundary and revisit it during flowering, when previously missed plants are easier to recognize.
researchNotes: Oregon and New Zealand sources are independent regional treatments. Management wording avoids promising hand-removal success; regional reporting advice does not imply nationwide regulation.

proposedDescription: Matrimony vine is the sprawling, sometimes climbing shrub also sold as goji or wolfberry. Long arching shoots, small purple flowers, and orange-red berries can make it conspicuous along old gardens and disturbed ground. Cultivated plants can spread through both seed and root suckers. Whether that spread is an environmental concern depends on the region and setting; a fruit planting is not evidence that the species is invasive throughout the country.
identification: Look for slender woody stems with scattered thorns and simple, smooth-edged leaves. Leaves may be alternate on young shoots and clustered on older growth. The flowers have a funnel-shaped base and five spreading lobes; berries develop afterward. Related Lycium species can be difficult to separate, especially when flowers are missing. Bittersweet nightshade also has purple flowers and red berries, but often has lobed leaves and a different flower structure. Retain close photographs of flowers, their green bases, leaf clusters, and thorns for identification.
actions: Watch the ground around an existing planting for suckers and seedlings, particularly beyond the maintained bed. Remove unwanted young growth before it becomes another fruiting shrub, and continue checking the area rather than relying on one pruning. Wear gloves around thorny stems. Do not identify a wild berry as edible from its color or the common name goji. Before removing an extensive thicket, obtain local advice that distinguishes this species from other boxthorns and accounts for its ability to send up new shoots.
researchNotes: USU supports suckering and seed spread; Michigan provides diagnostic comparisons. USU's broad origin wording is not repeated because it appears to conflate the genus with this species.

proposedDescription: Mauritanian grass is a large perennial bunchgrass native to the western and central Mediterranean region. It has been cultivated outside that range and is recorded as established in parts of California. A mature clump can be substantial, with flowering stems rising well above the leaves. Flora of North America notes that plants dry rapidly in summer, an important consideration where ornamental plantings meet fire-prone vegetation.
identification: The plant forms dense clumps with underground stems, long narrow blades, and tall flowering stalks. Leaf surfaces are strongly ribbed, their edges are finely toothed, and their tips taper to a long point. The large, loose flower clusters have drooping branches that tend to face one side. A close view of the papery ligule where blade and sheath meet helps a grass specialist separate it from superficially similar ornamental grasses. A distant photograph of a large grassy mound cannot reliably distinguish it from pampas grasses or other tall bunchgrasses.
actions: Document plants growing beyond a maintained planting, including the clump size, flowering heads, and nearby seedlings. Ask a local herbarium or invasive-plant program to confirm the identification before undertaking removal. Avoid transporting ripe flower heads or pieces of the underground base into another landscape. In a fire-sensitive setting, have a qualified local professional assess the vegetation around buildings. For a large clump, ask that specialist to plan access and disposal before disturbing the base; photograph the same spot afterward to document any new shoots or seedlings.
researchNotes: Fresh FNA text via SEINet confirms the distinctive large clumps, ribbed serrate leaves and drooping panicles; Kew independently lists California introduction. Identification and introduction evidence support a limited descriptive profile. Absence of a tested local removal program does not block observation, identification and avoiding movement of seed-bearing material. Review scoped actions without promising removal efficacy.

proposedDescription: Mauritius hemp is a massive rosette-forming succulent grown for ornament and historically for fiber. Despite its common name, a planting can spread through little plantlets produced on the towering flower stalk. Those plantlets, called bulbils, can fall and establish around the parent. Florida assessments identify it as invasive in natural areas, while its behavior and management priority elsewhere need to be checked locally.
identification: Look for a broad rosette of long, stiff, sword-shaped leaves and, on a flowering plant, a very tall branched stalk. After flowering, small leafy bulbils can hang where someone might expect ordinary fruit. Leaf margins and tips vary among forms, so the absence of conspicuous teeth is not enough to exclude the species. Agaves and other Furcraea species can have similar silhouettes. Photograph the leaf base, margins, tip, flower stalk, and any bulbils rather than relying on the overall rosette alone.
actions: Where removal is appropriate, prioritize preventing mature bulbils from reaching fresh ground. Do not give away plantlets from an invasive planting or dump stalks and rosettes at a natural-area edge. Small plants can be dug out, but a large rosette or tall stalk warrants professional help to avoid injury and accidental dispersal. Use protective clothing when handling sharp leaves. After removal, inspect the surrounding soil repeatedly for overlooked bulbils and new plants. Consult local land managers before disturbing coastal or protected vegetation around a suspected escape.
researchNotes: FNAI and municipal South African material support morphology and bulbils independently. PROTA supports digging; this is not a pesticide recommendation. Regional invasive status retained.

proposedDescription: Mauve pittosporum scale is a tiny armored scale insect found on leaves and small stems of a wide range of woody and ornamental plants. Pittosporum is only one host; records also include pines, apples, and several other plant groups. The insect has been reported in California, but a scale-covered shrub elsewhere should not be assigned this name without examination. Its protective cover can remain visible after the insect underneath has died.
identification: Colonies can look like small gray or tan flecks stuck to the plant. The mature female and her eggs are purple beneath the covering, while younger females can be beige. These colors are clues, not a definitive field test. Chaff scale, Parlatoria pergandii, is an important lookalike; Henderson also warns that P. fulleri cannot be reliably separated in the field. Specialists distinguish the species using microscopic pores and ducts on a prepared adult female. Photographs of an entire colony, the affected plant, and the exact leaf or twig surface help document the problem but rarely settle the species.
actions: Keep an infested potted plant separate from other stock while obtaining an identification. Record the host name and whether damage involves leaves, twigs, or fruit. Ask an extension or plant-health diagnostic service how to submit a small infested cutting in a secure container. Avoid moving cuttings or nursery material from the plant until the identification is resolved. Treatment should follow confirmation that scales are alive and causing meaningful injury; old covers alone do not demonstrate that another treatment is needed.
researchNotes: Fresh Henderson 2011 morphology and original host records, alongside Gill/McKenzie material summarized in Naturalis, support a scoped scale-recognition profile. ScaleNet is not counted as a new author lineage merely because it is another website. Henderson's own New Zealand observations and Gill's California account are distinct; no current pesticide or statewide legal claim is imported. Retain microscopic confirmation and add P. fulleri to the lookalike warning.

proposedDescription: Max chrysanthemum is a white-flowered perennial daisy associated with gardens and occasional escapes. The scientific name Leucanthemum maximum is useful here because the familiar label Shasta daisy is also applied to cultivated hybrids. The species is native to southwestern Europe and introduced elsewhere. Its presence in a catalog of introduced species should not be read as a claim that every garden daisy is an invasive plant requiring removal.
identification: Flowering stems carry large heads with white outer rays and a yellow central disc. Leaves are comparatively narrow, elliptic, and regularly toothed. The Flora of New Zealand treatment distinguishes it from oxeye daisy by the larger flower heads and narrower, regularly serrated leaves. Size alone is unreliable in garden plants, especially where hybrid cultivars are involved. Photograph lower leaves as well as the smaller leaves higher on the stem, the underside of the flower head, and the whole clump. A nursery label may document a cultivar but does not independently establish a wild escape's identity.
actions: Record whether a plant is deliberately cultivated, persisting at an abandoned garden, or producing new plants beyond the bed. If preventing escape is the goal, remove spent heads before mature seed is dispersed and keep discarded plant material out of nearby grassland. Have ambiguous plants checked before applying oxeye-daisy control recommendations. Keep records of any new seedlings and their distance from the original clump. A hybrid garden daisy and a confirmed wild L. maximum should remain separate observations until their identities are checked.
researchNotes: Fresh New Zealand flora, indexed GRIN treatment and California occurrence account support the named species, with the garden-hybrid caveat intact. The common label Shasta daisy is ambiguous, but the scientific species concept can be described without assigning every cultivar to it or borrowing oxeye-daisy impacts. Retain the cultivar distinction and limit actions to confirming and preventing unwanted garden escape.

proposedDescription: This May beetle belongs to a large group whose adults and soil-dwelling larvae are often called June beetles and white grubs. Phyllophaga hondura was verified in a Homestead, Florida nursery after larvae found beside pygmy date palm roots in December 2002 were reared to adults and identified by a specialist. A separate Mexican forest-site specimen also documents the species. These observations establish particular records, not a claim that every white grub is this beetle or that it causes widespread crop damage.
identification: The Florida diagnostic account describes brown adults about 11-14 millimeters long. A notched front margin of the head, a hairless plate behind the head and a dusted-looking body surface help specialists recognize them. Females have pronounced swellings on the exposed rear abdominal plate; male genital structures also help confirm identity. These details require close examination. The larvae could not be separated reliably from native Florida Phyllophaga in that account. Photograph the adult from several angles beside a scale, and preserve the host and collection circumstances with the record.
actions: If grubs occur around declining plants, document actual root feeding rather than assuming the insects caused every symptom. Keep any specimen securely contained and contact an extension diagnostic service before treatment or movement of affected planting stock. Do not transport soil or rooted plants from a suspected imported infestation while seeking advice. Provide the diagnostician with the plant species and a photograph of damaged roots; a treatment intended for a different lawn grub or an overseas coffee pest may not address the insect actually present.

Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: The freshly read Evans-Smith checklist names P. hondura Saylor and lists Belize, Costa Rica and United States; recovered IHCAFE indexed text instead credits Mankins and gives broad coffee-grub traits. The checklist does not establish which United States population or identification supports the record, while the biological account's taxon attribution remains questionable. Group-level white-grub characters cannot settle this. Trace Saylor's description and a United States voucher; reconcile the IHCAFE identification before assigning its biology to the catalog species. Inherited links not used: https://repositorio.catie.ac.cr/bitstream/handle/11554/3346/Plagas_invertebradas_de_cultivos_anuales.pdf?isAllowed=y&sequence=1. proposedDescription: Mayan cichlid is a Central American fish that has established populations in southern Florida. It can occupy fresh and brackish water, which helps explain its occurrence in canals, marshes, and estuarine environments. It feeds on a variety of aquatic animals. Scientific publications have used several combinations for its name, including Cichlasoma urophthalmus and Mayaheros urophthalmus; those naming differences should be checked when comparing records rather than treated as separate fish.
identification: Look for a deep-bodied fish with several dark vertical bars and a conspicuous dark eyespot near the base of the tail. Red coloration can occur on the throat and fins, but changes with condition and age. It resembles native sunfishes at first glance. Cichlids have one nostril opening on each side of the head and a lateral line divided into two sections, unlike the continuous line and two openings of sunfishes. Photograph the side of the fish with the tail base visible; the eyespot and bar pattern are especially useful.
actions: Never release aquarium fish or transport a catch alive to another water body. Photograph an unexpected catch and report its precise location to the state wildlife agency or the USGS nonindigenous-aquatic-species reporting program. Check current local fishing rules before deciding whether a caught fish can be retained. A population report helps managers track spread, but does not authorize private stocking, poisoning, or alteration of a wetland. Keep equipment free of attached organisms and follow local guidance when moving between waters.
researchNotes: USGS and NOAA profile share literature and are one source lineage. Independent FWC field-based profile corroborates Florida establishment and diagnosis. Current generic placement needs taxonomy review; catalog ID retained. Action wording is conservative aquatic containment, not an eradication claim.
