proposedDescription: Mazapan is a woody ornamental mallow with long, hanging flowers that never open into the broad flat shape familiar from many hibiscus plants. It is also called Turk's-cap mallow, a name shared with related plants. Its regional status deserves care: the University of Florida's current assessment describes it as not a problem species in Florida, while other regional sources report invasive behavior elsewhere. Neither statement establishes its behavior in every landscape.
identification: The shrub has simple, pointed leaves and solitary or clustered drooping flowers. The overlapping petals form a narrow, elongated flower, often red, with the reproductive column near or beyond its end. Related Malvaviscus species and cultivated forms can be confused, especially in photographs without a whole flower and its green base. Some references place this plant under Malvaviscus arboreus as a variety or subspecies. Record the actual scientific name on a nursery label and photograph both leaves and hanging flowers before trying to connect a plant to an occurrence record.
actions: First establish whether a plant is a maintained ornamental or an escape spreading into surrounding vegetation. Check current local recommendations before deciding removal is necessary; Florida's assessment does not support treating every planting as a weed. Keep discarded branches and unwanted nursery material out of natural areas, and document any self-established plants beyond the garden. If identification or spread is uncertain, consult a local extension office with photographs and the planting history. Avoid applying an invasive rating from another country directly to a United States site.

proposedDescription: Meadow brome is an introduced grass of fields, meadows, and disturbed ground. In this profile the name means Bromus commutatus, a species native to Europe and western Asia, rather than every forage grass sold under a similar common name. Correct identification matters because closely related bromes can occur together and differ in agricultural importance. Its presence in a field is a starting point for assessment, not proof that the surrounding habitat needs treatment.
identification: Flowering plants have a loose branched head with relatively large, many-flowered spikelets. In the Rothamsted identification guide, the branches supporting meadow-brome spikelets are mostly longer than the spikelets themselves, and the spikelets are usually hairless. Soft brome generally has a more compact head and hairy spikelets. Rye brome becomes easier to distinguish when mature florets separate and gaps appear within the spikelet. Lower leaf sheaths can also help, but their hairiness should not be used alone. Collect photographs of mature heads and leaf sheaths together.
actions: Mark patches before seed is shed and seek an extension or herbarium identification if the brome species is uncertain. Avoid moving mature seed heads on mowers or harvested material into an uninfested area. For a cultivated field, use a management plan designed for the confirmed brome and crop rather than borrowing one for smooth brome. Keep a mature flowering sample or clear close-up with the field record, since a recently mown patch may no longer show the characters needed to distinguish the bromes.
researchNotes: Fresh Native Plant Trust flora and Stephen Moss's Rothamsted guide independently support the species and brome comparisons. The guide includes an original ADAS comparison of 28 meadow-brome populations, so field characters are more than repeated website text. Missing natural-area control trials do not block scoped actions. Retain mature-spikelet confirmation and crop-specific local advice.

proposedDescription: Meadow fescue is a perennial forage grass that has become naturalized in the United States. It grows in meadows, grasslands, roadsides, and streamside settings, sometimes within deliberately planted pasture. You may encounter the names Festuca pratensis or Lolium pratense in floras and seed information. Those alternative names make checking a scientific identification more useful than assuming that every plant called fescue has the same behavior or management needs.
identification: Plants form tufts, sometimes with short underground stems, and bear a branched flower head rather than the simple spike of a ryegrass. The little ear-like projections at the junction of leaf blade and sheath, called auricles, are prominent, curved, and hairless. Tall fescue has hairs along its auricles, a helpful distinction when examined closely. Meadow-fescue spikelets contain several florets and have no obvious long awns. Hybridization with perennial ryegrass can complicate identification. Photograph the collar region with a close-focus camera and include an intact mature flowering stem.
actions: Determine whether the plant is part of an intended forage stand or an unwanted population in a restoration area. For the latter, avoid adding seed mixtures containing meadow fescue and document its extent before planning removal. Ask a botanist to check plants with intermediate characters, especially near ryegrass plantings. A pasture-maintenance recommendation may be unsuitable for a streamside restoration site. Include nearby ryegrass and other fescues in the site photographs, and retain the seed-mixture label when available. That context helps the adviser distinguish intentional planting from spread into adjacent vegetation.
researchNotes: Recovered exact Colorado flora excerpt confirms hairless sickle-shaped auricles and United States naturalization; FEIS narrative independently supports European origin, forage history and ryegrass hybridization. FEIS's native metadata conflicts with its own sourced narrative and is not used. The public profile avoids a universal removal method and does not require resolving that metadata error. Review the scoped recognition profile and preserve local forage-versus-restoration context.

proposedDescription: Meadow foxtail is a perennial grass with a soft cylindrical flower head and a long history of use in hayfields and pasture. It favors moist, fertile ground and can form dense stands. It is native in parts of Europe and introduced in North America. A foxtail-shaped head is not itself a sign of an invasive grass: several unrelated grasses share that silhouette, and their seasonal growth and management differ.
identification: Look for hairless stems and leaves, loose tufts, and a short membranous ligule where the blade joins its sheath. The flowering head is soft because the small flower units carry fine awns. Timothy has a superficially similar cylinder, but its individual units have two stiff horn-like tips and feel much rougher. Meadow foxtail also tends to flower earlier than timothy, though local weather changes the calendar. A close image of separated flower units is more useful than the head outline alone. The basal leaf collar lacks auricles.
actions: Record flowering plants early in the growing season; a late-summer survey may miss a population after the distinctive heads have passed. In a restoration planting, check seed-mixture labels and avoid introducing it where native meadow vegetation is the goal. Where it is already abundant, seek advice that considers the site's moisture, desired vegetation, and existing use as pasture. Do not drain or disturb wet ground simply to remove a grass. Photograph the same patch at flowering and later in the season; note whether the grass is persisting within the planted area or appearing in neighboring vegetation.
researchNotes:
Exact indexed Gateley and vegetative-grass monograph text independently confirms early flowering, soft awned heads, short ligule and absent auricles. The inherited Forest Service compilation was readable but its exact meadow-foxtail context was not recovered reliably; it is excluded. A local control trial is unnecessary for cautious recognition and site assessment. Keep flowering calendars relative to timothy and avoid transferring British habitat impact to every American population. Inherited links not used: https://www.fs.usda.gov/pnw/pubs/pnw_gtr694.pdf. proposedDescription: Meadow hawkweed is a yellow-flowered perennial that can spread into dense patches in grasslands and other open ground. Modern references often call it Pilosella caespitosa. It belongs to a difficult group of introduced hawkweeds, several of which spread through runners as well as seed. In the Pacific Northwest, distinguishing these plants from native hawkweeds is an essential first step before removal.
identification: Look for a basal rosette of hairy leaves and an upright stem carrying a cluster of yellow, dandelion-like flower heads. Leaves are concentrated near the ground rather than distributed along a leafy stem. Creeping runners can connect neighboring rosettes. Those traits help recognize the introduced meadow-hawkweed group, but they do not always identify this particular species. Native Washington hawkweeds lack the spreading runners, according to King County guidance. Photograph rosettes, runners, stem leaves, and the hairs beneath the flower heads, and ask a specialist to use a regional key.
actions: For a confirmed small infestation, carefully dig or pull the entire root system and connected runners rather than just removing the flower stalk. Bag flowering or seeding heads before disturbing them so seed is not shaken across the site. King County advises against composting those heads. Restore suitable competing vegetation in cleared ground and revisit the patch over several years. For a larger population, obtain a coordinated plan from the local weed program. A single mowing does not address the network of surviving rosettes and roots.
researchNotes: King County is group-level management explicitly including H. caespitosum. Alberta and BC keys support Pilosella caespitosa synonym and native comparison; regulation not generalized nationwide.

proposedDescription: Meadow knapweed is a common name used for plants in a hybrid complex involving black and brown knapweed. The scientific name Centaurea debeauxii needs careful comparison with that complex: current botanical sources distinguish it from the hybrid also called Centaurea x moncktonii. Confirmed meadow-knapweed hybrids are a management concern in parts of the United States, where they can replace desirable meadow and pasture vegetation. Their control advice should not be applied to an uncertain identification.
identification: For plants identified as the meadow-knapweed hybrid complex, look for several upright, ridged stems with pink to purple flower heads. Leaves are generally less deeply divided than those of spotted knapweed. Fringed margins on the overlapping bracts below each flower are more useful than flower color alone. Young leaves and buds can look cobwebby. Seedlings have a taproot, while older plants develop a clustered root system below the crown. Photograph the flower base and basal leaves for a specialist; these features do not settle the exact botanical concept on their own.
actions: Have a local weed specialist confirm the plant before starting removal. For a confirmed unwanted meadow-knapweed patch, isolated seedlings are easier to remove than older plants, whose entire root crown needs attention. Bag plants carrying flowers or seed heads and clean tools, footwear and machinery before leaving the patch. Minnesota guidance warns that mowing does not control meadow knapweed and can spread seed. Revisit treated ground for surviving crowns and seedlings, and plan work around desirable vegetation. Keep the identification and its supporting source with the record.

proposedDescription: Meadow pea, also called meadow vetchling, is a scrambling perennial with bright yellow pea-shaped flowers. It uses tendrils to lean through surrounding vegetation rather than standing as a rigid shrub. In New England it is a non-native plant of fields, meadows, and disturbed places. The word pea in its name describes its relationship and flower form; it should not be used as an assurance that an unidentified wild pod is suitable for food.
identification: Each leaf normally has a single pair of narrow leaflets with a tendril extending beyond them. The stems are angled, and the yellow flowers occur in small elongated clusters. Mature pods become dark and split to release seed. This combination helps distinguish it from many vetches with numerous paired leaflets and from related ornamental peas with pink or purple flowers. Nevertheless, both flowering material and leaves are needed for a confident identification. Photograph a complete leaf, the stem at a node, a flower cluster, and any ripe pods.
actions: Record whether a patch is spreading from a former planting or persisting among established meadow plants. If seed escape is a concern, keep ripe pods and discarded plants out of natural areas and avoid moving contaminated soil. Seek local advice before disturbing a large stand, particularly where it is intertwined with native plants. Cutting the visible stems does not establish that its underground perennial growth has been removed. After any agreed work, revisit the marked patch for new stems and record whether they arise inside the original clump or beyond it. Keep photographs of nearby desirable plants to guide careful follow-up.
researchNotes: Fresh Native Plant Trust and RHS text independently supports paired leaflets, angled stems, yellow flowers, tendrils and dark pods. No taxon mismatch was found. Absence of a United States control program or nationwide invasive status is accommodated by restrained observation and containment actions. Review as a local recognition profile, with no food-use or blanket invasive claim.

proposedDescription: Meal moth is a stored-food moth whose caterpillars feed in grain products, animal feed, and other dry provisions. It is especially associated with damp or moldy grain and neglected storage residue. Finding an adult indoors is a reason to inspect stored materials, but the flying moth itself is not the feeding stage. A moth in a distant room may have developed from a caterpillar that wandered away from the food to pupate.
identification: The adult has a broad pale tan band through the middle of each forewing, bordered by wavy pale lines and darker reddish-brown areas at the base and tip. This differs from the more simply divided forewing of the common Indianmeal moth. Caterpillars are whitish with a dark head and dark plate just behind it. Silken webbing, shed skins, droppings, and irregular feeding damage are useful signs within a package or bin. Save a photograph of the moth with wings visible and inspect nearby pet food, birdseed, and old cereal products.
actions: Find and remove the infested food source, sealing it before disposal. Empty and clean the storage area, including seams and spilled material beneath shelving, then place replacement dry goods in sound, tightly closed containers. Address moisture problems rather than treating the moth as an isolated flying nuisance. Continue checking older packages after cleanup because wandering larvae may already have left the original source. For commercial grain or a persistent household infestation, use an extension or stored-product specialist to confirm identification and develop a sanitation-based plan.
researchNotes: Canadian Grain Commission morphology and moisture association combined with NC State pantry management. Sanitation advice is family-level guidance applicable to documented stored-food pest.

proposedDescription: Mealy plum aphid is a wax-covered sap feeder associated with plums, prunes, and related fruit trees. Large colonies can weaken growth and produce sticky honeydew that supports black sooty mold. In its seasonal cycle, eggs overwinter near buds, spring colonies build on trees, and winged forms can move to reeds or cattails before returning in autumn. Those movements help explain why populations on a tree change during the year.
identification: Wingless adults are pale green to whitish green, with three darker lengthwise stripes partly obscured by powdery white wax. Winged adults have a darker thorax and crosswise bands on the abdomen. Colonies often occupy leaf undersides or slightly curled leaves. White wax alone does not distinguish this aphid from mealybugs or other wax-producing insects. Photograph the colony and individual insects if possible, and record the tree species. Look for live aphids rather than interpreting old leaf distortion as proof that a colony remains active.
actions: Inspect new growth early, before curled leaves conceal large colonies. In a home orchard, a firm stream of water can dislodge accessible aphids, while avoiding excessive nitrogen and watering can reduce lush growth that favors them. Preserve lady beetles, lacewings, hoverfly larvae, and other natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary broad-spectrum sprays. If injury is substantial or recurring, ask a fruit-crop extension specialist about timing appropriate to your tree and region. Leaves already distorted will not straighten simply because the aphids have been suppressed.
researchNotes: UC prune and apricot accounts are one lineage; PNW handbook independent management corroboration. No pesticide rates or transfer of California treatment calendar.

proposedDescription: Dysmicoccus grassii is a mealybug with a well-documented association with banana production in the Canary Islands. Its naming history also follows plant trade: the original material was found on imported bananas, and an older name, Dysmicoccus alazon, is now treated as a synonym. These records establish a real species and an important crop association, but they do not by themselves demonstrate an outdoor infestation at any United States location.
identification: Females hold eggs in a white cottony sac beneath the body. ICIA describes short rear wax filaments, about one-eighth of the body length, and no clear lengthwise dorsal stripes. Young stages are small and easily overlooked among plant surfaces or wax. This appearance identifies a mealybug problem more readily than it identifies D. grassii itself; several species on bananas and ornamental plants can look similar without magnification. A reliable determination requires the microscopic characters described in the specialist literature. Record the host, the exact part occupied, and whether insects were on fruit, foliage, or planting stock, and photograph intact colonies before disturbing them.
actions: Keep suspect imported plants or propagation material separate while asking a plant-health diagnostic service for identification. Retain labels and origin information, which are particularly useful for a species historically moved with bananas. Do not move infested pieces into another collection or discard them where living plant material could persist. The Canary Islands have published integrated-management guidance, but its production conditions and available controls should not be assumed to apply locally. A confirmed identification and local crop advice are needed before selecting a treatment.
researchNotes: Fresh ICIA original crop-research text and ScaleNet's Leonardi/Marotta type and synonym records support a scoped D. grassii account. ICIA biological observations are distinct from the taxonomic type revision; ScaleNet is credited to those underlying authors. Canary Islands management conditions are expressly not transferred to United States crops. Retain diagnostic confirmation and origin labels; no treatment efficacy is claimed.

proposedDescription: The insect listed here as Eriococcus araucariae is treated in current scale-insect references as Uhleria araucariae, a felt scale associated especially with Araucaria trees. Although Araucaria mealybug is a documented common name, it belongs to the felt-scale family rather than the true mealybug family. It has moved widely with ornamental hosts, and heavy honeydew production can leave foliage coated with dark sooty mold.
identification: Females are concealed by a white, felted, oval wax covering. Newly mature females can be brownish yellow with two purple lengthwise markings; older females become purple. These colors and the host are suggestive but do not provide a complete diagnosis. Other scales and true mealybugs also live on Norfolk Island pines and related ornamentals. Specialists examine adult females for features such as the shape of enlarged hairs and microscopic ducts. Photograph the affected twigs, the wax coverings, and the whole host, while preserving the plant's label if one exists.
actions: Separate an affected container-grown Araucaria from other plants until its pest has been identified. Ask an extension diagnostic service how to collect a small infested twig without distributing live crawlers. Keep discarded infested foliage contained, and do not share cuttings from the plant while the infestation is unresolved. Record actual live insects and new injury rather than relying only on lingering sooty mold. The available literature confirms the insect and host relationship, but a current species-specific treatment recommendation for your location still requires professional review.

proposedDescription: Ferrisia malvastra is a mealybug recorded from many plant families and from material intercepted in international plant trade. It has a complicated history of confusion with other Ferrisia, particularly the striped mealybug. The original type material came from Malvastrum in Texas, and its origin across the United States is not fully settled. A record needs local context before it can tell us whether the insect is introduced there.
identification: Adult females have a gray body beneath white mealy wax, with two lengthwise areas where the wax is thinner or absent. Long, fine crystalline wax rods project from the back, and the most conspicuous rear filaments are about half the body length. They often occupy sheltered parts of a plant. These field features overlap with related Ferrisia. USDA's identification account emphasizes how difficult it is to separate F. malvastra from F. terani by morphology alone; prepared specimens and sometimes molecular evidence are needed.
actions: Photograph undisturbed insects, record the host and its source, and keep an affected nursery or houseplant apart from other plants while obtaining an identification. Avoid distributing cuttings or moving infested material between collections. Do not assume that two dark stripes prove striped mealybug or that a treatment reported for that species has been tested on this one. A plant-health diagnostician can determine whether a live colony is present and whether the specimen warrants further specialist examination. Retain the laboratory's determination with the plant record, especially if the first report used the broader striped-mealybug name.
researchNotes: Fresh USDA text supports the F. malvastra/F. terani boundary; the Jansen-Alferink inventory supplies independently examined material. Difficult morphology is not a taxonomic contradiction: Kaydan-Gullan molecular evidence supports distinctness. The independent Dutch record strengthens pathway context without proving an outdoor United States infestation. Retain specialist identification and local context; do not import F. virgata treatment claims.

proposedDescription: Golden mealybug is a distinctive sap-feeding insect associated with Araucaria and Agathis trees, including ornamental relatives of Norfolk Island pine. It comes from Australia and has also been recorded in New Zealand and California. Unlike many familiar mealybugs that use a wide variety of houseplants, its documented hosts are concentrated in the Araucariaceae. A host record is useful context, but should accompany rather than replace an insect identification.
identification: Adult females are broadly oval to almost round, deep purple, and decorated with tufts of golden wax along the middle of the back and around the edge. They are only a few millimeters long. First-stage nymphs carry white wax before later stages develop the golden tufts, and males develop in white wax cocoons before emerging as tiny winged adults. Egg sacs extend behind females and can look different from the insects themselves. Photograph several life stages if present, especially the colored wax, host twigs, and egg sacs.
actions: Inspect young stems and small branches when checking a suspected host. Keep an infested potted tree separate from other Araucaria or Agathis while a diagnostic service reviews photographs or a contained sample. Do not distribute cuttings or move a visibly infested tree into another collection. Note whether there are living insects, sticky honeydew, and new plant injury; those observations help determine whether intervention is warranted. Keep a record of which branches carry new young insects, and share that with the adviser. Old wax, empty cocoons and living females can occur together and need to be interpreted separately.
researchNotes: Fresh Martin 2018 original observations describe the changing wax color through nymphal stages; ScaleNet independently attributes southern California pest records to Brown and Eads 1967. The modern life-stage account and older California observations are distinct author lineages. Their age and regional limits remain visible; no current treatment schedule is claimed. Review a recognition and containment profile, preserving white wax on first instars.

proposedDescription: Imported mealybug, Pseudococcus importatus, is strongly associated with orchids in taxonomic and plant-quarantine records. Its original description involved insects on Vanda material; a later Dutch greenhouse record documents it on Maxillaria splendens. That history makes orchid collections and imported planting stock relevant places to investigate a suspected finding. The word imported is a common name, however, and does not prove where a particular insect came from or whether an outdoor population is established.
identification: At first glance an infestation may appear as small waxy insects or cottony material on an orchid. Those are mealybug clues, not diagnostic characters for this species. Pseudococcus importatus requires examination of a prepared adult female, including the distribution of microscopic pores and tubular ducts. Historical taxonomic work even describes orchid specimens assigned only tentatively because their duct patterns differed from the types. Photograph the insects in place and record the orchid genus, affected plant part, nursery source, and whether additional plants share the symptoms.
actions: Isolate a suspect orchid from the rest of a collection and stop exchanging divisions or cuttings until the pest is identified. Ask an extension or plant-health laboratory how to send an intact specimen; photographs alone may not be enough. Keep packaging and plant labels if the orchid was recently acquired, as those details help trace a possible pathway. Do not infer that every mealybug on an orchid is this species or apply an imported-pest label to an unconfirmed specimen. Tell the diagnostician whether the orchid was kept indoors, in a greenhouse or outdoors, and whether the insects have appeared on neighboring plants.
researchNotes: Newly read Jansen-Alferink 2023 supplies independent specimen evidence, supplementing the original taxonomic literature. This supplies independent evidence beyond McKenzie and the Gimpel-Miller revision. McKenzie's tentative Compton specimens remain a historical caution, not the sole basis for species recognition; quarantine and greenhouse records are not outdoor establishment. proposedDescription: Odermatt mealybug is a small plant-feeding insect documented on foliage and fruit, including citrus and ornamental plants. It has been recorded in Florida and intercepted on plants moving through international trade. Recent research has also questioned how sharply it is separated from the related Comstock mealybug. That uncertainty does not erase the existing name, but it makes expert identification especially important when interpreting a new record.
identification: Adult females are oval, covered in pale wax, and may show two lengthwise dark lines formed by exposed areas between body segments. They have numerous marginal wax filaments, with the hind pair reaching roughly half the body length. These features overlap with several other Pseudococcus species. Identification uses microscopic structures, including pores on the hind legs and ducts on the body. A recent study retained P. odermatti while calling for additional morphological and molecular work. Photograph intact females and their host, but do not treat a photograph as a definitive species determination.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants or cuttings separate and avoid moving infested fruiting branches between sites while seeking diagnosis. Preserve the host name, date, source, and any shipping information alongside the specimen record. Ask a plant-health laboratory whether adult females suitable for microscopic examination are available before discarding all the material. Do not substitute a Comstock-mealybug treatment solely because the insects are closely related. Local decisions should follow confirmed identification, observed damage, and applicable crop advice; an interception elsewhere does not demonstrate a local outbreak.

proposedDescription: Obscure mealybug is a wax-covered insect that feeds on grapes, ornamentals, and several fruit crops. It can hide beneath bark and in sheltered plant parts, making an infestation less obvious than the sticky honeydew or contaminated fruit it produces. In California vineyards it is one of several mealybugs that need to be distinguished before management decisions are made. The older names Pseudococcus affinis and Pseudococcus obscurus may appear in records.
identification: Females are soft, oval, and coated with white powdery wax, with wax filaments around the body margin and a longer hind pair. Eggs are placed in a cottony sac; young crawlers are yellowish to orange-brown. This separates their reproductive pattern from longtailed mealybugs, which produce live crawlers, but does not by itself distinguish obscure from grape mealybug. Tiny stages may be impossible to identify reliably in the field. Photograph adults as well as wax masses, and record whether they occur under bark, on shoots, or within grape clusters.
actions: Inspect protected plant surfaces and nearby stock, not just exposed leaves. Separate infested nursery plants and avoid moving contaminated propagation material. In vineyards, work with a local extension specialist to identify the species, monitor colonies and ants, and choose measures that preserve useful natural enemies. Removing a few visible insects is not proof that sheltered colonies are gone. Keep monitoring after intervention, and use fresh adult specimens when confirmation is needed; an official German outbreak investigation could only complete morphological identification once adults were available.

proposedDescription: Mediterranean amaranth is a small annual whose North American history is unusually tangled. Flora of North America warns that the name Amaranthus graecizans was repeatedly misapplied to the common native species A. albus and A. blitoides. Some old reports may therefore refer to a different plant entirely. A record carrying this name needs a specimen-based review before it is used to describe a present-day invasion.
identification: Like several other small amaranths, it has simple alternate leaves and inconspicuous green flowers in clusters at the leaf joints. Those broad characters do not separate it reliably from its lookalikes. Identification depends on mature female flowers, the relative lengths of their bracts and floral parts, and the form of the tiny fruit and seed. The North American treatment describes fruits about 2-2.5 millimeters long that open around their circumference, with black seeds about 1-1.3 millimeters across. Seedlings or distant photographs are especially poor evidence. Photograph a complete branch and close views of mature axillary clusters, and keep the original identification label attached to any specimen record.
actions: If you think you have found this species, ask a herbarium or extension botanist to examine flowering or fruiting material before deciding on control. Record the exact location and whether the plant arrived with seed, nursery soil, or disturbed fill if that history is known. Avoid spreading ripe material while it is being evaluated. Historical records do not establish a current United States population. Resolving the identity, including whether an old record actually represents a native amaranth, is the useful first step.

proposedDescription: Mediterranean flour moth is a stored-product pest best known from flour mills, food-processing facilities, warehouses, and sometimes homes. Caterpillars do the feeding; adult moths do not eat the stored food. Their silk can bind flour and grain residues into masses and, in industrial settings, obstruct handling machinery. An infestation therefore calls for attention to hidden food deposits and storage conditions, not just the moths flying around a room.
identification: Adults have gray forewings with darker and paler markings and a wingspan of roughly an inch. Caterpillars are whitish to pinkish, with a distinct head and small dark spots at the bases of their body hairs. Heavy silk on the food surface is a useful clue. Several other flour and pantry moths resemble them, so a gray moth alone is not a firm identification. Mature larvae leave their food to pupate, which means cocoons may be found away from the original infested package or machine.
actions: Identify and remove infested food, seal discarded material, and clean accumulated flour from cracks, shelves, and nearby storage surfaces. Keep replacement provisions in tightly closed containers and check older packages rather than simply replacing the most obvious one. Continue monitoring after cleanup for larvae that had already wandered away. In a mill or commercial store, have a stored-product specialist inspect equipment and inaccessible residues; do not improvise pesticide use in food machinery. A specimen-based identification helps distinguish this moth from other pests with similar webbing.
researchNotes: Canadian species account and NC State general pantry IPM support copy. Industrial machinery claim from Canadian source; no unverified fumigation or heat procedure.

proposedDescription: Mediterranean fruit fly, often shortened to Medfly, is a serious agricultural pest whose larvae develop inside many kinds of fruit and vegetables. Infested produce is an important route by which it reaches new areas. It is established in Hawaii, while mainland detections have prompted official response programs. A suspected finding deserves prompt reporting, but neither a small fly near fruit nor a maggot in a damaged fruit identifies this species by itself.
identification: Adults are smaller than a house fly, with a dark patterned thorax, a tan banded abdomen, and clear wings marked with brown bands and gray flecks. Larvae are pale, legless maggots feeding in the fruit's flesh; affected fruit may decay or fall early. Other fruit flies can produce similar damage. Diagnostic protocols favor examination of an adult under magnification, using the wing pattern, body markings, and sex-specific features. Photograph the fly and damaged produce, but keep the material contained rather than carrying it to another property.
actions: Report a suspected Medfly to the state plant-health authority or local extension office and follow their instructions for a sample. Do not move potentially infested produce, plants, or waste while identification is pending. Check the official quarantine guidance for your area, since boundaries and restrictions can change. Declare agricultural products when returning from international travel. If officials are surveying nearby, cooperate with access for monitoring traps. An individual property treatment is not a substitute for the coordinated detection and response needed for this pest.
researchNotes: APHIS page fully read; EPPO diagnostic protocol independent technical source. Current quarantine boundaries deliberately not asserted. Adult diagnostic superiority retained.

proposedDescription: Mediterranean gecko is a small, introduced lizard often seen on building walls after dark. Porch lights attract the insects it hunts, and cracks around masonry and fixtures provide daytime shelter. In much of its introduced range it is closely associated with people and buildings. Its presence should not automatically trigger pest treatment: household guidance emphasizes preventing unwanted indoor entry rather than poisoning these insect-eating lizards.
identification: Adults are usually about four to five inches long including the tail. Their pale body carries darker mottling and conspicuous raised bumps, while the tail often has dark bands that are especially clear in youngsters. Large eyes have vertical pupils, and expanded toe pads help the gecko climb smooth surfaces. The common house gecko can look similar but is generally smoother and has a more elongated snout. Color changes with lighting and condition, so photograph the back, toes, and tail as well as the whole animal.
actions: If geckos are entering a building, repair weather stripping and seal gaps around doors, pipes, windows, and soffits after checking that animals are not trapped inside. Photograph an unusual outdoor population and share the location with a local wildlife agency if it lies beyond known occurrences. Do not transport captured geckos to another neighborhood or natural area. For an animal indoors, seek local advice about humane handling and applicable rules. Sticky traps cause prolonged injury and are not needed for the basic exclusion approach described here.
researchNotes: Texas A&M fully read for diagnosis and exclusion; Indiana provides independent regional account. Avoided repeating Texas recommendation to release outside without regard to local introduced-wildlife rules.

proposedDescription: Mediterranean mussel is a marine bivalve that attaches to hard surfaces and has been introduced beyond its original range. Genetic surveys established its presence in California, where it can coexist with native bay mussels and their hybrids. It belongs to a difficult complex of blue mussels in which shell appearance, local conditions, and hybridization can make a simple photograph misleading.
identification: The shell is generally dark blue to purplish black and roughly triangular or pear-shaped, with fine growth lines. The pointed end may curve downward, and the lower edge can be slightly concave. These are tendencies rather than a dependable checklist. Mediterranean mussels can overlap in appearance with Mytilus edulis and M. trossulus, and older shells are especially difficult to assign. A specialist may need anatomical or genetic evidence. Photograph both valves, the shell outline, attachment surface, and surrounding mussel bed without damaging a natural colony.
actions: Do not move living mussels, fouled ropes, shellfish equipment, or attached debris between coastal sites. If you find an unfamiliar mussel on a boat or structure, document the location and contact the local marine invasive-species program for sampling instructions. Arrange hull or equipment cleaning where removed organisms and wastewater can be contained rather than released into another harbor. Avoid treating every dark mussel as this species or attempting to clear a shoreline yourself. Confirmation is important because native and introduced mussels may occur together and look very similar.
researchNotes: Fresh Naturalis shell account and NEMESIS's independently authored California genetic studies confirm both recognition limits and coexistence with M. trossulus and hybrids. Expert identification and hybrid zones are valid species-profile cautions, not evidence that the name itself is unusable. NEMESIS is not counted as independent of the studies it summarizes. No shoreline eradication claim is made. Review the scoped profile; request genetics or expert examination for doubtful local specimens. Inherited links not used: https://nas.er.usgs.gov/Queries/FactSheet.aspx?SpeciesID=107. The USGS route did not yield substantive exact-species content in this pass; the retained NEMESIS and Naturalis accounts support the scoped California and identification claims.

proposedDescription: Mediterranean pine beetle, also called Mediterranean pine engraver, is a small bark beetle associated mainly with pines. It often breeds in recently cut, fallen, or stressed trees, though attacks can contribute to the death of living pines. It was discovered in California in 2004. Wood packaging and bark-bearing wood are important pathways, so finding beetles in delivered wood is a different situation from identifying the cause of decline in a standing tree.
identification: Adults are only a few millimeters long and reddish brown to dark brown. From above, the head is largely hidden beneath the front body shield. The rear of the wing covers is scooped inward and edged with four spines on each side, with the second particularly conspicuous. These structures require magnification and can resemble those of other engraver beetles. Larvae are pale, legless grubs beneath bark. Yellowing or browning needles alone are not diagnostic; drought, disease, and other insects can produce similar symptoms.
actions: Leave suspect pine logs and firewood at their current site while obtaining advice from an extension forester or state plant-health office. Photograph the tree, bark symptoms, galleries if already exposed, and any securely contained beetles. Do not strip healthy trees merely to search for larvae. Have stressed landscape pines assessed for their broader water and site needs, and ask a qualified professional how infested wood should be handled locally. A correctly identified specimen is more useful than assuming every small bark beetle requires the same response.
researchNotes: FAO morphology and Wyoming survey guidance independently support biology; no current Wyoming absence claim repeated. Firewood advice is pathway containment, not unsupported salvage prescription.

proposedDescription: Mediterranean recluse spider is a small, inconspicuous spider that has traveled beyond the Mediterranean region, often in human environments. Introduced populations may remain closely associated with buildings. Because several harmless brown spiders are mistaken for recluses, an identification should rest on the animal rather than on fear, a vague violin-shaped marking, or an unexplained skin lesion. The common name does not mean every brown spider indoors is dangerous.
identification: Adults have a relatively plain brown body and long, slender legs without the conspicuous spines seen on many other spiders. Recluses have six eyes arranged in three pairs, but that feature requires a good close view and is not unique to this species. The darker mark on the front body is also insufficient on its own. Distinguishing Mediterranean recluse from other Loxosceles can require adult reproductive structures examined by a specialist. Photograph a stationary spider from a safe distance with a size reference rather than handling it.
actions: Keep hands out of hidden spaces where a suspected spider is resting, and use a secure container only if collection can be done without contact. Ask an extension entomologist or qualified pest professional to confirm the species before planning a building response. Record the room, date, and whether repeated sightings occur. Reduce opportunities for accidental contact when sorting stored items by using gloves and checking material carefully. If someone develops concerning symptoms after a suspected bite, seek medical advice; a photograph or safely contained specimen can assist identification without delaying care.

No treatment recipe is included. Lack of a species-specific building-control trial does not prevent advice to avoid contact, obtain an identification and seek clinical assessment for concerning symptoms. proposedDescription: Mediterranean sage is a woolly biennial that begins as a ground-level rosette and later produces a tall, branching flower stalk. It is a weed of open, disturbed and grazing landscapes in parts of the western United States. Mature plants can break loose and tumble, distributing seed as they travel. Recognizing the first-year rosette gives landowners a chance to act before that mobile seed-bearing stage develops.
identification: The rosette has broad gray-green leaves covered with dense, felt-like hairs. On flowering stems, leaves occur in opposite pairs and the stem has the square outline typical of the mint family. Pale cream to white, two-lipped flowers are grouped along the branches. Common mullein is a frequent rosette lookalike, but its leaf attachment and later yellow-flowered stalk differ. Native and ornamental sages also deserve consideration. Photograph the basal leaves, their stalks, the arrangement of stem leaves, and a close view of an open flower.
actions: For a small confirmed patch, sever or dig out the root below the soil surface and remove the plant before seeds mature. Wear gloves and keep flowering or seed-bearing material contained rather than leaving it where it can tumble away. Revisit the area for missed rosettes and new seedlings. Avoid assuming that cutting the upper stalk alone has removed the plant. Larger infestations need a local weed-management plan that considers grazing, desirable vegetation, and follow-up. Report unusual new populations to the relevant county or state weed program.
researchNotes: Oregon and Colorado regional management/identification sources used. Seed structure errors in a separate Forest Service excerpt were not repeated. No biological-control release instructions.

proposedDescription: Mediterranean scale is more often called black parlatoria scale or ziziphus scale in plant-health references. It is an armored scale insect associated especially with citrus, where dense colonies can mark fruit and cause yellowing or loss of leaves. Florida has documented introductions, and the insect also occurs in other warm regions. A historic pest alert describes a particular event; it does not establish the current status of every citrus-growing area.
identification: The mature female's covering is small, elongated, and shiny black to very dark brown, with fairly parallel sides. A smaller dark shed skin sits at the front, and a pale papery flap can project at the rear. Male covers are smaller and lighter. Dense colonies may be especially noticeable beside leaf veins or on fruit. This dark, elongated armor differs from the rounded, raised bodies of many soft scales. Photograph individual covers and their arrangement on the host; a plant-health specialist should confirm an unfamiliar population.
actions: Do not move infested citrus plants, cuttings, or fruit to another property while identification is pending. Contact the local extension or state plant-health office with clear photographs and the plant's origin, especially if it was recently purchased or brought from another region. Keep detached leaves and twigs contained for any requested examination. Record live scales and fresh yellowing rather than relying only on persistent covers. Management should follow the local citrus program, since natural enemies, crop stage, and regulatory status all affect the appropriate response.
researchNotes: Recovered Stocks's exact December 2016 Florida alert and fresh SENASA account corroborate dark parallel-sided female covers, pale posterior flap and citrus damage. Stocks reports original Miami inspection observations; SENASA independently supplies biological description. The event remains explicitly historical, and current local control or regulatory status is not asserted. Review recognition and plant-health referral actions; retain the date limitation.

proposedDescription: Medusahead is a winter annual grass that can degrade western rangelands. Its long barbed awns and silica-rich tissues make mature plants poor forage, while slowly decomposing litter builds a dense thatch. It often stays green later than neighboring annual grasses, drawing attention as other vegetation dries. Its impacts are tied to particular landscapes and climates; a careful identification is needed before managing a suspected new patch.
identification: Plants form small, loose bunches with narrow leaves and compact seed heads carrying very long, rough awns. The head's central axis remains intact as seeds fall, often leaving a persistent bristly skeleton. Barley grasses and native squirreltail can look similar from a distance. Photograph a mature head, its attachment to the stem, and the leaf collar; also note whether nearby annual grasses have already dried. Do not run bare hands through ripe heads, since the barbs can catch on skin and clothing.
actions: Mark and report a suspected new infestation before mowing, digging, or driving machinery through it. Clean footwear, tools, and equipment after leaving an affected area, and keep seed-bearing material from being moved with hay or soil. Maintain healthy desirable vegetation around the patch and work with a local rangeland or weed specialist on timing. Control depends strongly on growth stage and follow-up restoration, so a one-time mowing or an improvised burn is not a complete plan. Revisit treated ground for new seedlings over subsequent growing seasons.
researchNotes: UC IPM morphology and ecology cross-checked with BC prevention alert; erroneous BC rainfall figure not repeated. No claim of available biological control agents or unsafe burn prescription.

proposedDescription: Mexican black scale is a soft scale insect that can settle on the leaves and stems of many kinds of woody plants. Its dark, rounded adult females can look like small bumps attached to the plant. Feeding colonies may attract attention when several life stages occur together, but a common name or a black shell is not enough to identify the species. Florida entomologists have long recognized it among several closely similar black scales. That regional history does not establish which species is present on a particular shrub today.
identification: Young females are initially pale pink and translucent, becoming gray to black as they mature and grow more convex. A raised pattern resembling the letter H crosses the upper surface. This useful clue also occurs in related black scales, including Saissetia oleae and Saissetia neglecta. Mexican black scale keeps its eggs beneath the female's body rather than producing a conspicuous external cottony egg sac. Reliable separation of the similar species uses microscopic characters on prepared specimens, including the legs and the arrangement of bristles around the body margin.
actions: Photograph the entire affected plant, its label if available, and close views of both young and mature scales. Keep newly purchased infested plants separate from other stock while an extension diagnostician identifies the insect. Ask how to package a sample before moving clipped material between properties. Avoid choosing a treatment solely from the H-shaped ridge. Tell the adviser which plants have fresh colonies and whether the scales appear alive; the prepared specimen can distinguish species that look alike on a shrub.
researchNotes: Fresh USDA and Dekle diagnoses are supplemented by independent specimens in Jansen-Alferink 2023. The H-shaped ridge is shared and microscopic confirmation remains required. An independent specimen record closes any concern that the two diagnostic pages merely repeat one lineage; no modern control claim is needed. Review as a soft-scale recognition profile and retain S. neglecta comparison.

proposedDescription: The Mexican bromeliad weevil threatens some of Florida's native bromeliads, the plants often seen growing on tree branches. First detected in the state in 1989, it spread through infested plant movements as well as the flight of adult beetles. The damaging stage is the larva, which tunnels inside the plant near its base and can destroy the central growing tissues. A bromeliad may therefore be seriously injured before an observer sees an adult weevil. Susceptibility varies among bromeliads; a small air plant should not automatically be treated as an infested host.
identification: Typical adults are black, about 11 to 16 millimeters long, with a yellow or orange band crossing the wing covers and an obvious curved snout. Recent research also documents a dark form lacking the usual band, so color alone cannot rule the insect out. Larvae are pale grubs with darker heads, concealed in plant tissue, and pupation occurs in a fibrous cocoon. Florida also has other Metamasius weevils. The native M. mosieri is generally smaller and has a different red and black pattern, but uncertain specimens need specialist comparison.
actions: Inspect purchased bromeliads and watch established plants for damaged bases, tunneling, or unusual decline. Photograph the beetle and the affected plant without moving potentially infested specimens into another garden. Contact Florida extension staff for identification and current handling advice. Leave wild bromeliads in place and avoid collecting them as a response to an infestation. Treatment decisions for plants high in trees require professional guidance and consideration of the surrounding habitat.
researchNotes: UF account provides Florida history and life stages. Independent 2024 original research documents melanic adults, preventing an overly absolute band-color diagnosis. No blanket susceptibility claim or pesticide recipe.

proposedDescription: Mexican fan palm is familiar as a tall, narrow silhouette above streets and gardens. Native to northwestern Mexico, it also establishes beyond cultivation in parts of California, including riparian areas and orchards. A deliberately planted avenue and a group of seedlings spreading along a watercourse are different management situations. California guidance identifies escaped populations as a concern, particularly where palms alter vegetation or accumulate dry fronds. Its presence in a landscape elsewhere does not by itself establish the same ecological impact or legal status.
identification: Look for a single slender trunk topped by a relatively compact crown of bright green, fan-shaped leaves. The leaf stalks have sharp teeth, and older dead leaves can remain hanging below the living crown. California fan palm, Washingtonia filifera, generally has a thicker trunk and a broader, grayer crown. The two can hybridize, making intermediate plants difficult to name confidently. Height is not a sufficient character: both species can become large, and young seedlings have not developed the mature trunk and crown proportions.
actions: Remove unwanted seedlings while they are small and manageable, using gloves and avoiding the toothed leaf stalks. Confirm uncertain plants near native palm habitat before undertaking removal. For established escaped palms, California guidance describes cutting below the growing point; tall trees and heavy hanging fronds should be assessed by a qualified tree professional. Do not climb into a dry leaf skirt or attempt to fell a palm near power lines. Revisit the site for new seedlings after the mature seed source is addressed.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC supports regional impacts, identification and physical removal. UF independent horticultural table supports single trunk, large eventual size and comparison with W. filifera. Hybridization limits photo-only identification. No nationwide invasive claim.

proposedDescription: Mexican flamevine is a tropical climber grown for its vivid orange flower heads. It can climb a support or spread across nearby vegetation when left to its own devices. Its presence in this catalog should not be read as a recommendation to eradicate every garden specimen. The University of Florida assessment reviewed here classifies it as not a problem species in Florida and assigns low invasion risk. That conclusion is specific to the assessment and region, while a vigorous vine may still need ordinary garden containment.
identification: The leaves are dark green, alternate along the stem, and shaped somewhat like an arrowhead, with toothed edges. Bright orange, daisy-like flower heads contrast with the foliage and are followed by fluffy seed heads. A plant may climb roughly 12 to 20 feet where conditions permit. Stems touching soil can form roots, so a trailing branch may become attached at more than one point. Older references and nursery labels may use Senecio confusus or Senecio chenopodioides. Those names should be reconciled before treating different records as separate plants.
actions: Keep a cultivated vine on a suitable support and check the ground beneath trailing stems for rooted sections. If it has grown beyond the intended planting, trace those rooted points before removing the unwanted growth. Collect the cut material rather than leaving living stems against damp soil or dumping them at a woodland edge. Photograph any apparent escape well away from cultivation and ask a local botanist or extension office about its status. Regional evidence should guide any larger control decision.
researchNotes: Two independent extension lineages: UF risk assessment and NCSU plant description. UF low-risk/not-problem conclusion is intentionally retained rather than assuming all catalog taxa are invasive. Actions are garden containment consistent with documented rooting, not an eradication claim.

proposedDescription: Mexican fruit fly is a regulated pest whose larvae feed inside fruit, especially citrus and mango. An infested fruit can look reasonably sound while feeding damage develops beneath the skin. The insect matters to home growers as well as commercial orchards because moving fruit can carry hidden life stages into a new area. United States restrictions and response areas change with detections. Use the current USDA or state agriculture notice for the location in question rather than assuming that an older outbreak map still applies.
identification: Adults are yellowish to pale orange flies with patterned wings and pale stripes on the thorax. Females have a conspicuous, elongated egg-laying structure at the rear of the body. The wing pattern includes curved and angled yellow-brown bands, but several related Anastrepha species have similar markings. Species confirmation can require examination of the female's egg-laying structure or other specialist characters. Larvae are pale, legless maggots inside fruit; their appearance alone is not a dependable household identification. Small punctures, internal tunnels, and decay can accompany infestation.
actions: Report a suspected fly or infested fruit to the state plant health authority and retain photographs showing the fruit, its source, and the insect. Do not carry suspect fruit to another property or mail specimens without instructions. Where an active quarantine requires sanitation, USDA advises removing ripe fruit from trees and the ground and double-bagging it for disposal rather than composting it. Follow the current local directions for fruit movement, disposal, and access by survey staff.
researchNotes: APHIS current response guidance opened; independent EPPO diagnostic synthesis indexed. Does not state current quarantine boundaries. EPPO stresses species-level difficulty and female aculeus examination; larvae are not presented as visually definitive.

proposedDescription: Mexican gray squirrel, also called Mexican red-bellied squirrel, is native to Mexico and Guatemala. An introduced population was established on Elliott Key in Florida in the twentieth century, and Biscayne National Park lists the animal among its nonnative wildlife. That localized history should not be expanded into a claim that every unusual gray squirrel in the southeastern United States is this species. A report needs a precise location and a careful comparison with the squirrels already present in the area. The sources reviewed here do not provide a current population estimate.
identification: Despite the common name, coat color is variable. Some individuals have a grayish back and reddish, orange, or chestnut underparts; others are much darker, including black forms. The animal has the long, bushy tail and climbing build of a tree squirrel. A red belly is a useful observation to photograph, but it is not a complete identification on its own. Capture views of the back, belly, face, and tail if the squirrel naturally presents them. Young animals, shade, and poor photographs can make color comparisons unreliable.
actions: Observe from a distance and record the date, exact location, number of animals, and behavior. In Biscayne National Park, send a suspected nonnative wildlife observation to park staff with photographs rather than attempting capture. Do not feed squirrels or move one between islands, parks, or neighborhoods. An animal that seems injured should be referred to the appropriate wildlife authority. Decisions about population management belong with land managers and require confirmed identification and current local information.
researchNotes: Original Mammalian Species account and independent National Park Service page support range, introduced Elliott Key history, color variation and reporting. NPS page is historical context, not confirmation of present population size or distribution.

claims: Native range, introduced Elliott Key population and variable red-bellied and dark pelage.
Mexican red-bellied squirrel listed among introduced wildlife; useful reporting details and avoiding releases.

proposedDescription: Mexican groundcherry is the name used here for Physalis philadelphica, a husked-fruit plant also associated with cultivated tomatillos. Kew places its native range in Mexico, Central America, and parts of the Caribbean, while floras elsewhere document introduced plants. A vegetable grown in a garden, a volunteer near a compost pile, and a persistent population outside cultivation are different observations. The reviewed sources do not establish that this species causes ecological harm throughout the United States. Records also need care because related names have been used inconsistently. The broad species concept used here includes immaculata in the 2023 Mexican revision, although other authorities place that name with P. ixocarpa.
identification: The New Zealand flora describes a sprawling annual with stalked, variably toothed leaves and solitary yellow flowers with a darker purplish-brown center. The calyx enlarges into a ribbed, papery covering around the berry. These features help place a plant among the groundcherries, but the lantern-like husk is shared with other Physalis species. Flower size, the dark markings, anther details, the fruiting calyx, and mature fruit are more informative together than a photograph of a husk alone. Cultivated selections can further complicate comparison with wild plants.
actions: For a plant outside cultivation, photograph open flowers, leaf attachment, and mature husks, and record whether a vegetable plot or discarded garden material is nearby. Ask a regional botanist to distinguish it from native groundcherries and reconcile the name before removing a natural-area population. In a garden, keep unwanted volunteer plants and discarded fruits from spreading beyond the managed bed. Do not taste an unidentified groundcherry to determine its identity; preserve its flowers and fruit for visual comparison instead.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Fresh New Zealand and Kew flora accounts support the general plant description, while Kew's current var. immaculata treatment places that name in P. ixocarpa, unlike the North American varietal treatment. The neighboring species and variety records may represent overlapping or different concepts. This requires a coordinated catalog-scope decision, not simply a missing control trial. proposedDescription: Mexican mint is a succulent, aromatic herb also sold as Cuban oregano or Indian borage. The catalog retains Plectranthus amboinicus, while current botanical and Florida assessment sources use Coleus amboinicus. Its many geographic common names are not a dependable guide to its origin. Although it is familiar in home gardens, the 2026 University of Florida predictive assessment assigns it high invasion risk and does not recommend it for Florida planting. That is a regional risk assessment, not proof that every cultivated plant has already escaped or caused damage.
identification: Look for thick, fleshy leaves in opposite pairs on succulent, often square stems. The leaves are softly hairy with rounded teeth along the margins, and they have a strong oregano-like scent. Older stems can become somewhat woody. Flowering plants carry small purplish flowers in clusters along an upright stalk, but foliage is often the most conspicuous feature. These characters distinguish the plant from ordinary culinary oregano, which has much smaller, thinner leaves. Fragrance can support an identification, but should not replace a botanical comparison or encourage tasting an uncertain specimen.
actions: Because the plant readily propagates from cuttings and division, keep trimmings and unwanted plants out of natural areas and shared garden-waste piles where living pieces might remain. In Florida, consider a locally recommended alternative when replacing a planting. Inspect the edges of existing beds and containers for plants establishing beyond their intended space. Photograph suspected escapes and ask extension staff about locally appropriate removal and disposal. Avoid treating the familiar culinary name as evidence that unrestricted planting is harmless.
researchNotes: Current UF 2026 high-risk predictive rating verified in full text. NCSU morphology and propagation read in full text. Current Coleus combination retained in prose while catalog ID unchanged. Risk prediction is explicitly distinguished from demonstrated local impact.

proposedDescription: Mexican tulip poppy is an ornamental perennial valued for bright yellow flowers above finely divided, blue-green foliage. Gardeners in colder climates may grow it as an annual. Its native range includes western Texas and extends south into Mexico, while California floristic records classify it as nonnative there. Location matters when assessing a plant found outside a garden: a yellow-flowered poppy in its native region calls for a different response from an ornamental spreading beyond a planting.
identification: The flowers are carried above the foliage and have broad, overlapping yellow petals surrounding conspicuous orange stamens. Cambridge University Botanic Garden describes the leaves as deeply divided, with smaller lobed segments and a glaucous, or bluish-gray, surface. From a distance, the color and divided leaves can suggest other poppies. A close view of the flower center, leaves, and whole plant is more useful than a distant yellow patch. Compare suspected wild plants with a regional flora instead of identifying them from the common name or assuming that a garden label settles a wild record.
actions: Record whether the plant is deliberately cultivated, persisting at an old homesite, or growing independently away from gardens. In or near its native range, confirm status with a local botanical specialist before removing plants. If a garden specimen produces unwanted volunteers, keep those plants within the managed planting and avoid disposing of seed-bearing material in nearby open land. Include nearby planted specimens in your photographs so a botanist can assess a possible garden origin.
researchNotes: Fresh Cambridge, Kew and Calflora treatments support recognition and geographically qualified status. Western Texas native range and California nonnative status are compatible. No claim of universal U.S. introduction, harm or treatment efficacy is needed. Editorial review can proceed with the regional qualification intact. proposedDescription: Mexilhao mussel, more often called brown mussel, is a marine bivalve that attaches to hard surfaces with strong byssal threads. Populations can form dense beds, providing structure for other organisms while changing the surfaces they occupy. Smithsonian accounts document introductions beyond its native range, including the Gulf of Mexico, and United States records include historical Texas observations. Those records do not establish that the mussel is currently present at every previously reported site. Its value as food in some regions also does not settle its ecological status or the safety of collecting it elsewhere.
identification: The shell is elongated, with an angular upper portion near the hinge and a more rounded lower outline. Adults are commonly brown or reddish brown, sometimes with lighter or greenish areas and pale patches where the outer covering has worn away. The lower shell margin is relatively straight. Similar Perna and Mytilus mussels overlap in general appearance, so shell color is not sufficient. Specialists can compare internal muscle scars, hinge characters, shell proportions, and features of the living mantle to establish identity.
actions: Photograph a suspected occurrence in place and record the location, substrate, approximate abundance, and whether it is attached to a vessel or fixed structure. Ask the local marine resource authority how to submit a specimen. Do not move live mussels as bait, food stock, or aquarium material between waterways. If they are found in vessel fouling, seek an appropriate haul-out and waste-containment procedure rather than scraping living organisms into another harbor. A new observation should be checked against the dated local records before deciding on a response.
researchNotes: Fresh FAO diagnosis and Smithsonian synthesis distinguish brown mussel recognition from dated Texas occurrence. FAO morphology and Hicks-Tunnell field records are independent lineages; USGS repeats those field records. Historical Gulf records are not presented as current presence. Observation and movement precautions do not require a species-specific eradication trial. Review the scoped profile; verify any new local occurrence before a response decision. proposedDescription: Mickey mouse plant is a southern African shrub whose unusual fruit display helped make it an ornamental. Yellow flowers are followed by glossy dark fruits set against a bright red floral base. Birds can carry the seeds beyond gardens, and discarded garden material is another pathway. New South Wales guidance describes it as an environmental weed where it forms persistent infestations. That documented regional problem is a reason to examine local escapes carefully, while United States status and any removal requirements should be checked with the relevant local authority.
identification: Leaves are narrow to elliptic, with fine teeth along their edges; young growth may have a bronze or brown tint. The flowers have five yellow petals and numerous stamens. After the petals fall, the remaining calyx enlarges and turns red, supporting several small fruits that change from green to black. This sequence is more useful than the common name, which is also used loosely for other ornamental plants. Small plants may conceal a substantial taproot with a distinctive bend, making them harder to remove intact than their height suggests.
actions: Confirm identification before removing a shrub, especially when it has neither flowers nor fruit. Where local management calls for removal, small seedlings can be dug out carefully with the entire root; pulling until the stem snaps can leave a plant able to recover. Collect fruiting material so birds cannot continue dispersing seed from discarded branches. Keep garden waste out of bushland and waterways. Revisit treated ground for seedlings and regrowth, and ask a qualified weed adviser about established plants with larger root systems.
researchNotes: NSW official weed account provides regional impacts and root-aware hand removal. Independent Singapore National Parks account verifies floral/fruit sequence. No US legal status inferred from Australian guidance. Avoid fixed fruit counts because descriptions differ slightly.

claims: Bird and garden-waste spread, persistent taproot, small-plant digging and follow-up.

proposedDescription: Ichthyosporidium hertwigi is a microscopic fish parasite name that needs specialist review before it can support a confident distribution or impact statement. Modern marine taxonomy links the name with Glugea hertwigi, while fisheries sources often retain Glugea for the parasite reported from smelt. A research paper discussing Ichthyosporidium also describes an old I. hertwigi record from connective tissue of fish gills. These records should be reconciled using the underlying taxonomy and host evidence rather than joined solely because the species epithet matches.
identification: This is not an organism that can be recognized reliably in a shoreline photograph. Microsporidian diagnosis depends on examining infected tissue and microscopic spores, sometimes with molecular evidence. A pale lump, damaged gill, or sick fish can have many causes and cannot establish this species. The host's identity, the tissue involved, the collection location, and the diagnostic method are all important parts of a usable record. Photographs can document an affected fish, but they are supporting observations rather than a substitute for laboratory identification.
actions: If several fish appear affected, record the location and circumstances and contact the fisheries or aquatic animal health authority. Do not transfer suspect live fish, bait, or water to another waterbody while seeking advice. Ask the laboratory how it wants samples collected and preserved before handling or shipping them. Do not attempt a home treatment based on this provisional name. A response should follow the identified parasite and affected tissue, not a match to an ambiguous historical name. Confirming the parasite and affected fish is the next step.

proposedDescription: Mile a minute vine, or Cairo morningglory, is a perennial climber that can spread over shrubs and other vegetation. The common name is shared with unrelated vines, so the scientific name matters when interpreting a report or choosing a response. The University of Florida assessment assigns Ipomoea cairica high invasion risk and does not recommend it for planting in Florida. Australian weed guidance also documents vigorous spread and practical control concerns. Those regional findings should be kept distinct from a claim that every occurrence across the United States has the same status.
identification: Leaves are alternate and deeply divided into five to seven finger-like lobes, often nearly to the base. The conspicuous flowers are funnel-shaped, usually pink to purple with a darker throat, though white forms occur. Twining stems can root where they touch the ground, and broken pieces can establish new plants. This combination separates it from the Mikania vine also called mile-a-minute, which has opposite, undivided leaves and small clustered flowers. A nonflowering fragment should be photographed with several leaf attachment points visible.
actions: Do not dump cut stems or garden waste near waterways or natural vegetation. For a small confirmed infestation, guidance supports removing the root crown and collecting living fragments so they cannot root again. Where vines climb through shrubs or trees, cut the climbing stems and allow the upper growth to die rather than forcefully tearing it through the canopy. Check the ground repeatedly for rooted pieces and regrowth. Larger infestations need a site-specific plan that protects the vegetation being uncovered.
researchNotes: UF high-risk assessment verified in full text. Independent NSW account supports diagnostic lobes, fragment regeneration and physical control. Common-name collision with Mikania and other mile-a-minute plants explicitly addressed. No Australian legal rules generalized to USA.

claims: High invasion risk and not recommended for Florida planting.

proposedDescription: Mile-a-minute is a fast-growing perennial vine that can cover shrubs, young trees, and nursery plants, reducing the light reaching the vegetation beneath it. Native to tropical America, it has become a serious weed in several other tropical regions. Florida's documented introduction near Homestead was confirmed after investigations that included DNA analysis. Older publications describe the early response area, but those historical counts should not be treated as a current distribution map. A suspected new occurrence deserves prompt attention because both wind-carried seeds and living stem fragments can spread the plant.
identification: The leaves occur in opposite pairs and are triangular to heart-shaped with pointed tips. Slender stems twine through surrounding vegetation. Small white or greenish-white flower heads occur in clusters, followed by tiny seeds with fine bristles. Florida has similar native Mikania species. Climbing hempweed, M. scandens, tends to have darker leaves, reddish leaf stalks, and pinkish flowers; Florida Keys hempvine, M. cordifolia, has hairier leaves and stems and larger flower heads. These tendencies help guide comparison, but uncertain plants should be checked by a specialist before clearing.
actions: Photograph the leaves, stem joints, and flower heads and report a suspected Florida occurrence to the state plant industry authority. Avoid mowing or scattering cut vines: fragments can regenerate, so cutting alone is not an effective solution. Follow local instructions for uprooting, collecting material, and approved disposal rather than placing living stems in ordinary garden waste. After removal, inspect the original patch and nearby vegetation for regrowth or seedlings. Protect similar native vines by securing identification first.
researchNotes: UF full-text extension account and independent Australian biosecurity page support morphology, threats and fragment dispersal. UF historical discovery/counts not presented as current extent. Native Mikania lookalikes included. Historic incineration recommendation not copied; disposal deferred to current local approved method.
