proposedDescription: Mile-a-minute vine is an annual climber that can turn a sunny stream edge or disturbed woodland into a blanket of triangular leaves. Its thin stems hook onto surrounding plants, allowing one season's growth to cover young trees and shrubs. In the Mid-Atlantic, seedlings emerge from an established seed supply even though the old vines die each autumn. That annual life cycle makes preventing new seed an especially useful part of management.
identification: Look for light green, triangular leaves arranged alternately on slender stems. Backward-pointing barbs occur on the stems and beneath the leaves. Small, round collars of leaflike tissue surround the stems at the nodes, a particularly useful feature when flowers are absent. The small flowers eventually give way to conspicuous blue fruits. Other climbing knotweeds may have triangular leaves, so photograph the collars, barbs and fruit rather than relying on the overall tangle. Seedlings are easier to overlook than the sprawling summer growth.
actions: Pull small seedlings and young vines before they set seed, using gloves to protect against the barbs. Work carefully where vines cover desirable plants so removal does not pull those plants apart. Revisit the patch through the growing season and in following years; a cleared surface does not mean the seed supply is exhausted. If fruit is already present, contain it during removal and obtain local disposal guidance. Report a new patch outside a known infestation area to the local invasive plant program.
researchNotes: Independent Penn State and Maryland extension accounts support annual growth, diagnosis and early removal. Regional context is Mid-Atlantic rather than a nationwide invasive designation.

claims: Annual barbed vine with triangular leaves; identification and seasonal control.

proposedDescription: Miles' firefish, also called devil firefish, is one of the lionfishes recorded outside their native Indo-Pacific range. In the western Atlantic, agencies often report it together with the very similar red lionfish, Pterois volitans. These predators shelter around reefs, wrecks and other structure and eat small fishes and crustaceans. A record of a lionfish therefore does not automatically establish which of the two species was present.
identification: Lionfish have alternating reddish-brown and pale bands, a broad head, fanlike pectoral fins and long, conspicuous dorsal spines. The spines are venomous and should never be touched to improve a photograph. Pterois miles and P. volitans are difficult to separate in ordinary underwater images; specialist examination of fin characters or genetic evidence may be needed. Small juveniles already have the striking banding and oversized-looking fins. Photograph the fish from a safe distance, including a side view, and record depth and the kind of structure where it was sheltering.
actions: Never release an aquarium lionfish into coastal water. Report an unfamiliar sighting to the relevant marine wildlife agency or the USGS nonindigenous aquatic species reporting program, retaining the original photographs and location. Leave capture to trained divers or an authorized removal program with appropriate equipment. Do not handle a live or dead fish casually, because the spines remain a hazard. If a spine puncture occurs, seek prompt medical guidance and identify the animal as a lionfish.
researchNotes: NOAA and USGS are separate agency evidence lineages. USGS treats Atlantic records as a volitans/miles complex; draft deliberately does not assign every lionfish observation to miles.

claims: Banded appearance, venomous spines and introduced lionfish context.
Combined volitans/miles treatment; reef and artificial habitats; fish and crustacean prey.

proposedDescription: Miliaris pit scale is a small bamboo-associated insect now treated in authoritative identification resources as Bambusaspis miliaris. Asterolecanium miliaris is an older name retained in this catalog entry. Colonies can occur on bamboo stems and on either leaf surface. The insect's protective covering makes it look more like a tiny attached fleck than a moving garden pest, and a photograph of discolored foliage alone cannot establish its identity.
identification: Look closely for pear-shaped coverings that are flat or only slightly raised. Their color can be green, brown or translucent pale yellow, with fine white or salmon-colored wax around the margin. The covering may show a faint ridge down the middle and fine crosswise lines. An older covering can contain the shrunken female toward its front end. These are useful field clues, but related bamboo scales overlap in appearance. The authoritative key separates this species using microscopic pores and other features of a prepared adult female, including comparison with Bambusaspis mimicum.
actions: Inspect the stems and both sides of leaves before moving or dividing bamboo. Keep suspect nursery material separate and contact an extension diagnostic service for sampling instructions; intact coverings and a piece of the host plant are more useful than crushed insects. Record the bamboo's name if known and whether the material was recently purchased. Avoid distributing infested cuttings while identification is pending. A confirmed diagnosis should precede any treatment decision, especially where other scales or natural enemies are present.
researchNotes: An independent 2017 Canary Islands collection confirms this bamboo scale on both leaf surfaces, supplementing USDA diagnosis. ITIS confirms the accepted Bambusaspis combination. The genus change is an unambiguous synonym, not a competing biological concept. Identification, inspection and containment advice can proceed without claiming U.S. damage or tested treatment. Review with the older catalog name explained and no change to the catalog ID.

proposedDescription: This milkweed is a slender, branching shrub often called narrow-leaf cotton bush or swan plant. It is native to southern Africa and has become a weed in some other warm regions. The familiar word milkweed can be misleading in an American garden: this is not one of the native Asclepias species. Its inflated fruits release silky-haired seeds, allowing a planted shrub to become a source of plants well beyond the original bed.
identification: The narrow, pointed leaves usually stand in opposite pairs along the stems. Creamy, drooping flower clusters are followed by inflated, pale green fruits covered in soft, bristlelike projections. Each fruit narrows into a curved beak, giving it the swanlike outline behind one common name. Balloon cotton bush, Gomphocarpus physocarpus, is a close lookalike with rounder fruits lacking that pronounced beaked end. Young, nonfruiting plants are harder to separate. Broken stems release milky sap, but deliberately breaking a plant is unnecessary for identification.
actions: Where local guidance calls for removal, tackle young plants before the pods open and remove the crown with as much root as practicable. Wear gloves and keep sap away from skin and eyes. Contain seed-bearing material rather than carrying open pods through the site. Keep removed plants out of livestock feed, and obtain local disposal advice for a large infestation. Recheck for seedlings and regrowth after the initial work. Before using it in a wildlife garden, check regional weed guidance and consider locally appropriate native milkweeds.
researchNotes: SANBI and New Zealand flora provide independent morphology; Western Australian biosecurity guidance supports crown removal and containment. Management is explicitly conditional on local context.

proposedDescription: Mimosa psyllid is a tiny sap-feeding insect associated with Albizia trees, including the ornamental mimosa or silk tree. Native to Asia, it has been recorded in North America and Europe. Heavy colonies can dry out new growth, cause leaves to drop early and leave sticky honeydew beneath the tree. Because mimosa itself is invasive in parts of the United States, damage to this tree has a different ecological meaning from damage to a native woodland species.
identification: Adults are only about two millimeters long. Their color changes with season, from yellowish green toward pinkish or brown tones, and the eyes are reddish. Clear wings and the habit of jumping help distinguish psyllids from many other small insects. Eggs and immature stages occur around young foliage; nymphs can produce waxy material. Look for insects on the undersides and margins of the small leaflets, not just for sticky deposits below the tree. Honeydew, sooty mold and yellowing are clues shared with other sap feeders, so a close specimen examination is needed.
actions: Before treating a declining mimosa, confirm both the host tree and insect with an extension diagnostic service. Photograph young shoots, affected leaflets and the insects together. Avoid moving infested nursery trees or cuttings to another property. Do not deliberately transport or release this psyllid to control mimosa: an observation that it damages the tree is not authorization for biological control. If the tree is unwanted in your region, discuss tree removal and follow-up seedling management rather than automatically protecting it with repeated insecticide applications.
researchNotes: EPPO supplies biology and plant-trade pathway; USDA's original North American report independently confirms arrival and host association. No release recommendation is inferred from the early paper's speculative biological-control discussion.

proposedDescription: Mimosa tree, or silk tree, is a small Asian tree planted for its fine foliage and pink summer flowers. It readily escapes into sunny disturbed places in parts of the southeastern United States, including roadsides and open ground. A spreading crown can be attractive in a yard while the tree's seeds establish beyond it. Its status varies with region, so an ornamental planting and an established wild population should be recorded separately.
identification: The leaves are divided twice: each main leaf carries several pairs of side branches, and each side branch holds many small paired leaflets. The flowers form soft pink clusters whose long stamens make a powder-puff effect. Flat, elongated seed pods follow the flowers and can persist after the leaves fall. Multiple trunks and a broad crown are common. Woman's tongue tree, Albizia lebbeck, has fewer, larger leaflets on each side branch and is a particular comparison in warm parts of Florida. Photograph a complete leaf as well as flowers or pods to show the branching pattern.
actions: Where mimosa is considered invasive, choose another tree for new planting and remove volunteer seedlings before they become difficult to handle. Check nearby open ground and disturbed edges, not only directly beneath the parent tree. Established trees need a removal plan that addresses regrowth and subsequent seedlings; simply cutting the trunk does not demonstrate lasting control. For a large tree, use a qualified tree professional and seek regional extension advice. Do not distribute pods or rooted seedlings from an escaping planting.
researchNotes: UF synthesis and Missouri weed identification provide independent institutional accounts. Draft avoids applying Florida assessment statewide elsewhere.

proposedDescription: Mimosa webworm is a small moth whose caterpillars tie leaves together with silk and feed inside the resulting shelter. It attacks mimosa and honeylocust, including common landscape honeylocust cultivars. Homadaula albizziae, the name in this catalog, is a synonym of Homadaula anisocentra in the cited insect literature. In Missouri and Kansas, two generations can produce much more conspicuous browning late in summer than early in the season.
identification: Inspect browned clusters of leaflets for silk, feeding damage and slender caterpillars. Full-grown larvae are roughly half an inch long and may be greenish or brown, with pale lengthwise stripes. They can move backward rapidly when disturbed and descend on a silk thread. Adults are small gray moths with dark spotting. Pupae shelter in cocoons in bark crevices, debris or nearby structures. Webbed foliage is more informative than a distant view of a brown canopy, which can also result from drought, disease or other insects.
actions: Check susceptible trees early in summer for the first small webs and active caterpillars. Ask extension staff or an arborist to identify the problem while the infestation is still localized. Dense late-season webbing can shield the larvae, making a late spray poorly timed; do not assume that brown foliage requires immediate treatment. Record when the first webs appear so next year's inspection starts earlier. If replacing a repeatedly affected tree, diversify the planting and avoid introducing invasive mimosa where local guidance advises against it.
researchNotes: USDA explicitly establishes synonymy. Missouri and Kansas extension independently describe seasonal biology and diagnosis; Kansas supports avoiding ineffective late treatment after dense webbing forms.

proposedDescription: Miniature flatsedge is an African wetland sedge often grown as a compact ornamental beside water. Its upright stems end in rounded sprays of fine rays, creating a small papyrus-like silhouette. The name miniature papyrus in a nursery is not a dependable scientific identification: Cyperus prolifer has been sold under several names, including names misapplied from other sedges. Its presence in a planted pond also does not by itself establish that it is invasive locally.
identification: The true leaves are reduced to sheaths around the stem bases. The stems have a somewhat flattened triangular cross-section and arise from creeping underground rhizomes. At the top, numerous slender rays form a rounded or hemispherical head. Fertile wild plants can carry reddish-brown spikelets at the ray tips. Older heads may produce plantlets that root when a leaning stem reaches wet soil. Some cultivated material lacks fertile spikelets, which makes identification from a garden photograph more difficult. A full view of the plant, the stem base and a mature head is more useful than the tuft alone.
actions: Keep pond plants and divisions contained and do not discard them into streams, wetlands or drainage channels. Check for stems that have bent over and rooted beyond the intended planting. If you find an apparently escaped patch, record whether it is connected to a garden, photograph mature heads and consult a herbarium or local aquatic plant specialist. Avoid removing an unidentified sedge from a natural wetland, where native species may look similar. Management recommendations should follow confirmation of the species and its local status.
researchNotes: Fresh Kew Flora Zambesiaca morphology and range independently corroborate the NParks ornamental account. Their authorship and observations are distinct. Recognition and vegetative-spread precautions are supported; the profile does not infer local invasiveness or prescribe an untested control. Review the scoped profile and confirm the identity of any reported escape.

claims: Leaf sheaths, rounded heads, plantlet rooting, often sterile cultivated material and misapplied nursery names.
Accepted identity; African and western Indian Ocean range; rhizome, leafless culms and rounded inflorescence.

proposedDescription: Minor ambrosia beetle, also called the punky wood ambrosia beetle, lives in wood together with a fungus that serves as food. In Florida, its association with the white-rot fungus Flavodon subulatus is especially noticeable in dead wood and broken branches. The fungus breaks down both lignin and cellulose, leaving pale, softened wood. This is not evidence that every living tree near an occupied log is being killed by the beetle. FDACS documented a separate Florida collection in Marion County in 2018.
identification: Adults are dark brown, compact beetles. Compared with many related species, adults are bulky, with similarly sized bumps on the sloping rear of the wing covers. Several native and introduced ambrosia beetles look similar, so a casual photograph rarely establishes the species. In colonized wood, closely grouped, circular entrance holes can be surrounded by patches of white rot. A pale fungal crust may also be present. Photograph the whole branch or log, the gallery openings with a scale, and any safely collected beetle without assuming that the fungus alone identifies its carrier.
actions: Ask an extension entomologist to examine suspect material, particularly for a report outside the known regional range. Record the tree species and whether the wood was living, recently dead or already decayed when found. Do not move infested firewood or untreated woody material to another area. If a decaying limb threatens people or property, consult a qualified arborist about the structural hazard. Avoid treating surrounding healthy trees solely because an ambrosia beetle was found in a dead branch.
researchNotes: Fresh UF/IFAS guidance supports the beetle-fungus association and explicitly recommends no specific management; an independent FDACS field collection confirms Florida occurrence. UF-associated papers count as one biological lineage, while the FDACS collection is an independent occurrence lineage. Advice is restricted to diagnosis, wood movement and structural safety, without a claim that this beetle kills surrounding healthy trees. Review the scoped profile; new locations and tree-health concerns need local assessment.

claims: Dark bulky beetle, clustered circular holes, white rot, specialist diagnosis and limited management evidence.
October 2018 Marion County collection, E-2018-6342.

proposedDescription: Hairy mint is the hybrid between spearmint, Mentha spicata, and apple mint, Mentha suaveolens. Often called hairy mint or mojito mint, it is a perennial herb grown for aromatic leaves. The multiplication sign sometimes written as an x in its name indicates hybrid origin. Nursery names and mint scents overlap considerably, so a plant labeled simply mint should not automatically be recorded as this hybrid.
identification: Hairy mint bears opposite pairs of oblong leaves with toothed margins and a softly hairy surface. Purple flowers are crowded into rings that together form a terminal, spikelike cluster. The combination is useful, but leaf shape, hairiness and flower arrangement overlap with its parents and other mint hybrids. Scent can help describe a specimen but is not a reliable identification test by itself. Photograph both leaf surfaces, the stem attachment and a mature flower spike before asking a botanist to confirm the name.
actions: Keep cultivated mint within a maintained bed or container and check the surrounding soil for unwanted growth. When thinning a patch, collect rooted divisions and cut stems instead of dumping them beside a ditch or woodland edge. This hybrid is propagated by division and stem cuttings, so discarded living pieces deserve attention. Record escaped plants separately from an intentional herb planting. If accurate identification matters for a natural-area record, seek a herbarium determination rather than choosing the closest nursery photograph. Do not infer a regional invasive designation from this catalog entry.
researchNotes: IPNI rechecked the spicata x suaveolens parentage; NParks independently supports paired hairy leaves, purple spikes and vegetative propagation. Bavarian flora documents cultivated escapes. A nationwide impact claim or treatment trial is unnecessary for this identification and garden-containment profile. Regional invasiveness remains unasserted. Review the hybrid identification cautions and keep any future local status claim tied to regional evidence.

proposedDescription: Mint flea beetle feeds on mint in two quite different places during its life. Adults make small holes in leaves, while the pale larvae feed below ground on roots and rhizomes. In Oregon mint fields, root injury can become apparent as weak, patchy spring growth. The older name Longitarsus waterhousei appears in some crop literature, so checking the scientific name is useful when comparing past records or management advice.
identification: Adults are tiny, elongated oval beetles, yellowish to orange-brown with a darker head. Their enlarged hind legs allow them to jump abruptly. Numerous small holes between the leaf veins can suggest adult feeding, but the holes alone are not diagnostic. Larvae are slender and whitish, with a pale brown head and three pairs of legs. Underground injury may resemble water stress or damage from other soil pests. Related Longitarsus beetles, including L. membranaceus in European identification resources, require close comparison rather than identification by color alone.
actions: Do not establish a new mint patch with rootstock from an infested planting; moving rooted material is an important spread pathway. Examine leaves for fresh holes and ask an extension crop specialist about sampling if spring growth is uneven. Keep notes on the date, adult beetles and affected area, because the underground and aboveground stages occur at different times. Commercial growers should use current local mint guidance for treatment decisions rather than carrying over old product recommendations. In a small herb bed, confirm the insect before treating all leaf damage as flea beetle injury.
researchNotes: Oregon IPM account was read in full and supplies life stages, symptoms and rootstock pathway. UK recording scheme independently supplies adult morphology and confusion species. Old chemical guidance was deliberately not reproduced.

proposedDescription: Miscanthus mealybug can remain hidden inside an ornamental grass while the plant gradually loses vigor. Colonies occupy protected leaf sheaths near the crown and can also infest roots. Yellowed or twisted leaves, shortened flower stems and reduced flowering may be the first visible signs. Some extension publications use the spelling Miscanthiococcus, but CDFA and the ScaleNet-based ITIS record use Miscanthicoccus for this mealybug. Preserve the scientific name with a submitted sample.
identification: Carefully separate a few lower leaf sheaths and look for tightly packed insects with white, powdery wax. Purple spotting on infested stems is a useful reason to inspect more closely. Sticky honeydew and black sooty mold may accompany a colony, but neither proves that this particular mealybug is present. The adult females and small immature stages are much easier to miss than insects exposed on leaves. Other mealybugs occur on ornamental grasses, so the host name and a close look at the insects are both important for a reliable determination.
actions: Inspect crowns and roots before dividing Miscanthus or bringing nursery plants into a collection. Set suspect pots apart and avoid sharing divisions until the insects have been identified. Contact an extension diagnostic service with photographs of the colony, purple stem markings and the plant label. Nursery managers should discuss current, crop-appropriate options with an adviser; hidden colonies complicate treatment, and a method suitable for one cultivar can injure another. Reinspect after any response rather than judging success solely by cleaner upper leaves or new growth.
researchNotes: The 2020 CDFA assessment uses Miscanthicoccus miscanthi and documents its own nursery interceptions; ITIS/ScaleNet also accepts that spelling. The extension variant does not establish a different taxon. Nomenclature is resolved without changing the catalog ID. CDFA's original interception records and NC State's diagnostic account are independent evidence; shared background citations are not counted twice. Conflicting origin labels are not used for a blanket native or introduced claim. Review the corrected spelling explanation; retain diagnostic confirmation before moving infested divisions.

proposedDescription: Regional sources use Cenchrus polystachios for perennial mission grass, a tall African grass. The scientific name needs care: USDA GRIN distinguishes that use from the formally named grass now placed under Setaria parviflora, and refers the mission-grass usage to Cenchrus setosus. We retain the catalog entry while its identity is checked. The guidance below follows the mission-grass resources linked here and should not be applied to an observation from its name alone.
identification:
The following features describe perennial mission grass in Northern Territory guidance. Confirm that this is the plant intended by a record before using these details to identify it.

Mature plants may reach about three meters. The elongated leaves are hairy, and their color can turn reddish purple under stress. Slender stems may root at lower joints. The flower head is a dense, narrow, bristly cylinder, often golden when mature. Its small seed units bear hairs that can catch on animals, clothing and equipment. Annual mission grass, Cenchrus pedicellatus, and young spear grasses can look similar before flowering. A specimen with the leaf collar, stem base and intact seed head is much more useful than a photograph of a distant clump.
actions:
These steps follow Northern Territory guidance for perennial mission grass. A record using this catalog name needs its identity checked before that guidance is applied.

Identify suspect plants before mowing or moving soil through them. Where mission grass is a local target, prevent seed production and clean seed-bearing material from equipment before leaving the area. Small populations deserve early advice from the local weed program because mature seed can develop quickly. Plan follow-up inspections after treatment and after rain, and include the surrounding disturbed ground. Large dry stands need a coordinated management plan that considers fire and nearby vegetation; do not use an improvised burn as a control method.
researchNotes: Northern Territory government provides morphology, comparison and seed movement; UF/IFAS independently supports Florida applicability. Australian flowering seasons are not transferred to U.S. calendar dates. Name-research cross-check on 2026-11-01 identified conflicting uses of Cenchrus polystachios. USDA GRIN 511148 distinguishes the misapplied mission-grass usage from the formal name. No synonym or occurrence reassignment is justified by the bare catalog name. Status changed to research_gap; regional morphology and actions remain explicitly attributed.

proposedDescription: Orange jasmine is a warm-climate shrub or small tree with fragrant white flowers and glossy foliage. It is also called mock orange, a name shared with unrelated shrubs such as Philadelphus. Murraya belongs to the citrus family, and its connection with Asian citrus psyllid matters near citrus production. A hedge can provide suitable new growth for the insect even when it is being grown purely for ornament.
identification: Look for alternate compound leaves with several glossy, oval to somewhat wedge-shaped leaflets. Small clusters of white flowers have a strong citruslike fragrance, and the fruits ripen orange to red. The University of California's living collection describes an evergreen shrub with orange-red mature fruit and documents variation among cultivated material. True mock oranges in the genus Philadelphus have simple leaves, so photographing an entire leaf with its leaflet attachments is especially helpful. Distorted new shoots, tiny insects or waxy deposits call for a separate pest examination; they do not establish citrus disease by themselves.
actions: Inspect tender new growth before purchasing or moving plants, especially in a citrus-growing region. Follow local plant-movement guidance and contact the agricultural department about suspected Asian citrus psyllid rather than carrying an infested branch elsewhere. UC IPM advises removing Murraya in or near citrus orchards where it can support psyllid reproduction. For an ordinary residential hedge, discuss local pest and planting guidance with extension staff before deciding on removal. Record whether a sighting is a maintained hedge, a seedling or an established plant beyond cultivation.
researchNotes: UCR living collection and Indian Institute of Science provide botanical evidence; UC IPM supplies citrus-specific actions. Murraya paniculata complex taxonomy is acknowledged through a separate original molecular study; no unsupported infection diagnosis is made.

proposedDescription: Mohintli, also called Mexican honeysuckle or muicle, is a small shrub with bright orange tubular flowers. It belongs to the acanthus family rather than the true honeysuckles. Native-range botanical records place it in Mexico and Central America, extending into northwestern South America in some treatments. It is widely cultivated in warm gardens, including the southwestern United States. Garden use in a dry region does not determine its behavior in a moist tropical landscape.
identification: The leaves are simple, oval and arranged opposite one another. Their soft, finely hairy surface gives them a velvety feel without needing to crush or pick them. Flower clusters sit toward the ends of the stems, with narrow orange tubes that stand out against the yellow-green to green foliage. Older stems become woody. The small green fruit capsules are less conspicuous than the flowers. Other orange-flowered garden shrubs can resemble it at a distance, so include the opposite leaf arrangement and the flower's side profile in photographs rather than relying on color alone.
actions: For an observation outside cultivation, record the distance from the nearest garden and whether several plants occur along a stream, trail or dumped vegetation. Ask a local botanist to confirm the species before removing vegetation in a natural area. Keep unwanted cut stems out of drainage channels and natural vegetation because the plant is readily propagated from cuttings. In a maintained garden, use regional planting guidance and remove unwanted growth deliberately. Traditional dye or medicinal uses are not evidence that home preparations are safe or effective.
researchNotes: Arizona's account and CICY herbarium records corroborate morphology and native-range context; KISC's dated survey lists Justicia spicigera as naturalized on Kauai. Regional survey status is not a nationwide impact assessment. Identification, documenting escapes and retaining cut stems can be reviewed without a tested US eradication method. Review the scoped garden-escape advice; obtain local management guidance only if a confirmed population requires intervention.

proposedDescription: Moist sowthistle is a form of perennial sowthistle with underground roots that allow an established patch to survive after the flowering stems are gone. It occurs in disturbed ground as well as damp settings, so its common name should not be used as a habitat test. In Alaska, the subspecies uliginosus is distinguished from the more glandular form of perennial sowthistle. Older references may call it Sonchus uliginosus or use the name glabrescens.
identification: Early plants form a rosette that can resemble a dandelion. Later, upright leafy stems carry branching clusters of yellow flower heads made entirely of strap-shaped florets. Stem leaves are alternate, clasp the stem and have softly prickly or toothed edges. Broken tissue contains milky sap. The important subspecies feature is the lack of conspicuous gland-tipped hairs on the flower stalks and the green bracts around each head. Photograph those parts close up. A tall sowthistle without mature flowers is difficult to assign confidently to subspecies, and annual sowthistles can resemble young plants.
actions: Do not treat a cut stem as proof that a perennial patch is gone. Prevent seed maturation while planning repeated follow-up that addresses the underground root system. Avoid moving soil or root fragments from an infested area into clean ground. For pasture, cropland or a wetland margin, ask local extension or weed staff for a site-specific plan that protects surrounding vegetation. If the record requires subspecies identification, arrange examination of a flowering specimen before submitting a definite name.
researchNotes:
Alaska-focused USDA-hosted guide and Swiss Flora Helvetica independently support the glandless diagnosis. Forest Service review supports root-based persistence and integrated control. No species-level record is silently promoted to subspecies.

2026-11-01 publication reference review: Live references, preserved archived originals, and any narrowed public wording are documented in the names-800-public-profiles-20261101 audit. Source access limits are not treated as resolved biological evidence gaps.

proposedDescription: Molassesgrass is a sprawling African perennial introduced into tropical regions as forage. In Hawaii it can form dense growth in dry to moderately moist open ground, including disturbed natural areas. Its sweet smell explains the common name, but its ecological importance comes from the way a thick grass layer changes vegetation and adds fuel. Established mats can recover after fire, making repeated burning a poor assumption for lasting control.
identification: The dull green leaf blades are hairy and sticky, with a noticeable sweet odor. Stems spread outward and can root to extend a patch. At the junction of blade and sheath, the ligule is a line of hairs rather than a broad membrane. The flower cluster begins as a fairly dense, purplish panicle and opens as it matures. Many tropical grasses produce reddish or purple flowering heads, so combine that feature with the sticky leaves and spreading habit. Record whether a patch is green, flowering or dry, since its appearance and fire implications change with season.
actions: Keep seed and stem material from moving on equipment or with dumped vegetation. In an area where molassesgrass threatens native vegetation, seek a coordinated weed and fuel-management plan before cutting a large stand. Do not burn a patch casually: recovery can be rapid and surrounding plants may be harmed. Check treated ground for surviving runners and new plants, particularly along its edges. Hawaii land managers should use local recommendations appropriate to the site and nearby native plants rather than general pasture advice imported from another tropical region.
researchNotes: Hawaii invasive species page repeats CTAHR and is one lineage. A follow-up search located the current FEIS review and independent D'Antonio original field research. Fire response is site-dependent, so draft says can recover rather than always increases after fire.

proposedDescription: The European mole cricket is an underground insect with powerful front legs built for digging. Its North American records have been concentrated in northeastern states and associated with plant nurseries, according to the Mississippi Entomological Museum. It should not be confused with every mole cricket found in a southern lawn. The United States also has native mole crickets and other introduced species whose distributions and management differ.
identification: The body is elongated and brown, with a broad shield behind the head and shovel-like forelegs. A close view of the digging fingers on those legs is important for identification. European mole cricket resembles the native prairie mole cricket, Gryllotalpa major, in size and number of these fingers; specialists distinguish them using additional leg structures. A recording of a calling insect can help document an observation, but location and a clear specimen image remain valuable. Soil tunnels, bare turf or damaged roots cannot identify the species without the insect itself.
actions: If a mole cricket appears in nursery stock or outside an expected range, photograph its upper surface and front legs and ask an extension entomologist for a determination. Keep the plant label and purchase information with the record. Avoid moving suspect soil or rooted plants to another property until advice is available. Do not apply a southern turf-pest treatment solely because the animal has digging legs. First determine whether it is this introduced species, a different introduced mole cricket or a native species, and whether measurable plant injury is actually occurring.
researchNotes: Hill's museum diagnosis and SINA's separate song and locality observations support recognition, nursery association and cautious species determination. The draft explicitly separates European from native and other introduced mole crickets. Historical locality accounts and expert referral do not require a current nationwide distribution or control trial. Review the dated distribution wording and require an insect determination before recommending any turf treatment.

proposedDescription: Moleplant is an upright spurge also sold as caper spurge or gopher spurge. Its blue-green foliage and unusually orderly leaves make it recognizable in gardens and on disturbed ground. The common names can suggest a pest-repelling use, but they do not establish that planting it controls moles or gophers. In Washington it is on a monitoring list rather than the state's noxious weed list, an important distinction from a required-control designation.
identification: The narrow leaves stand in opposite pairs. Each pair is rotated a quarter turn from the one below, creating four vertical ranks along the stem. A pale midrib is often conspicuous. Near the branching flower display, the leaves become broader and more rounded. The yellow-green flowering structures are small and lack the showy petals of many garden plants. The stems have a waxy appearance, and damaged tissue releases milky sap. Other spurges also contain latex, so the leaf arrangement is a safer and more useful feature than breaking a stem to test it.
actions: Wear gloves when handling this plant and keep its sap away from eyes and skin. Do not eat the seeds or other parts, and keep removed material away from children, pets and livestock. Where plants are unwanted, arrange removal before seed is scattered and inspect the site for seedlings afterward. Avoid using it as a substitute for a sound wildlife-management plan. For a plant found outside cultivation, document the four-ranked leaves and flowering top and check local weed guidance before choosing a response.
researchNotes: Washington weed board read in full and NC State independently support morphology and latex hazard. Washington page's unusual fruit-lobe count was not reproduced. No mole-repellent claim endorsed.

proposedDescription: Monarch fern is a creeping tropical fern with leathery, lobed fronds and rounded clusters of spores underneath. It is also known as wart fern and appears in sources under Microsorum scolopendria. Its names have often been confused with those of the related Microsorum grossum, especially in Hawaiian horticulture and historical records. For that reason, a familiar local name or a nursery label is not enough to establish the narrow scientific species.
identification: Monarch fern has a scaly, creeping rhizome and glossy fronds divided into several broad lobes. Young fronds may be less divided than mature ones. Round spore-bearing patches, called sori, occur beneath the frond and can produce visible raised areas on its upper surface. They are part of the fern's normal reproduction, not insect eggs. Narrower taxonomic treatments describe P. scolopendria as usually epiphytic with relatively few pairs of lobes, while larger, mostly ground-growing plants with more lobes may belong to P. grossus. Recent specimen and DNA work supports these distinctions, but occasional terrestrial plants and hybrid signals mean growth position alone is insufficient.
actions: For an escaped or unusual fern, photograph the complete mature frond, its underside and the exposed rhizome without tearing it from a tree. Record whether it grows on soil, rock or bark and whether a cultivated planting is nearby. Ask a fern specialist or herbarium to review it before assigning a definite species or organizing removal. Keep garden divisions and discarded rhizomes out of natural areas. Where an unwanted planting is being removed, account for the creeping rhizome rather than cutting only the fronds.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Fresh comparison still finds the Hawaiian key's narrow epiphytic concept, NC State's broader horticultural description, and Anderson-Fung's statement that Polynesian records called scolopendria belong to grossum. This is a species-concept conflict affecting Hawaiian record identity, not merely a change of genus. Impact claims from grossum cannot be assigned to the unchanged scolopendria ID. Have a fern taxonomist reconcile catalog source specimens and Hawaiian occurrence records against the scolopendria/grossum distinction.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: New original2026 voucher-based work distinguishes scolopendria, grossum and membranifolium and supports a carefully narrowed fern profile. Parent full text covers25 Niue2024/2025 plus one Cook specimen with CHR vouchers, chloroplast clades and nuclear hybrid signals. This independent lineage complements the inherited Hawaiian key; epiphytic habit is frequent but not absolute. Next step: Review the narrow scientific-species account; leave old Hawaiian and horticultural records for specimen reassessment. proposedDescription: Moneywort, often sold as creeping Jenny, makes a low carpet of rounded leaves. It is a perennial groundcover from Europe and temperate Asia that has escaped cultivation in North America. Damp lawns, streambanks and pond margins provide places for its trailing stems to spread. The familiar golden-leaved garden forms belong to the same species, and an attractive planting can require attention when it reaches adjoining natural vegetation.
identification: Leaves occur in opposite pairs along stems that lie close to the ground. Each leaf is nearly round, suggesting the coins behind the name moneywort. Yellow, cup-shaped flowers open along the leafy stems. Roots can develop at the nodes, and slender underground stems also help a patch persist. Ground ivy is sometimes called creeping Charlie too, but its leaf edges, scent and purple flowers differ. Use the combination of paired round leaves, yellow flowers and rooting stems. A flowerless green mat should be photographed close enough to show the leaf attachment and margins.
actions: Keep trailing growth from reaching a stream or escaping from a container into nearby soil. Lift small unwanted patches carefully, collecting rooted nodes and underground growth rather than just clipping the tops. Mowing alone does not control a plant that grows so close to the ground. Revisit cleared edges for surviving pieces and newly rooted stems. For an established patch in a wetland or along water, get local management advice before disturbing the bank or considering treatment. Use locally suitable groundcovers where garden drainage leads directly toward natural habitat.
researchNotes: NC State botanical account and USGS/NOAA management synthesis provide separate sources. Regional overseas description is supplementary, not evidence of U.S. control obligations.

proposedDescription: Monk orchid is a small terrestrial orchid with mottled leaves, often growing quietly in leaf litter. Native to tropical Africa, it is established in parts of tropical America and Florida. Its inconspicuous flowers are easy to miss, while the patterned leaves remain noticeable near the ground. Florida assessments vary by region, with caution advised in central and southern Florida; that is more precise than calling every occurrence an equally severe invasion.
identification: Each small, clustered pseudobulb generally carries one leathery leaf. The leaf is dark green with pale gray-green mottling and a slight lengthwise fold. A slender flowering stalk rises above the foliage and carries several small flowers that open in sequence. The flowers have subdued cream, greenish or brownish tones and a more conspicuous pale lower lip marked with purple. Hanging capsules develop after flowering and contain tiny seeds. Native ground orchids can also have patterned leaves, so photograph the leaf, the visible pseudobulb and a flower without uprooting the plant.
actions: Confirm identification before removing an orchid in a natural area. Share clear photographs and the habitat description with a local herbarium or land manager, especially when the plant is not flowering. Do not collect wild orchids for the garden or distribute seed-bearing plants. In a maintained planting where escape is a concern, manage developing capsules and unwanted seedlings with local guidance. A single photograph cannot show whether a population is expanding or displacing native plants; repeated observations of the same patch are more useful for that assessment.
researchNotes: UF profile and UFM arboretum independently describe morphology. Current UF assessment supersedes older all-zone caution wording: North not a documented problem, Central/South caution as of 2026.

claims: Pseudobulb with one mottled leaf, sequential flowers and capsules.
Leathery mottled foliage and small partly buried pseudobulbs.

proposedDescription: Monk parakeets are social South American parrots that have established populations in several United States cities after escapes and releases from captivity. They can be surprisingly successful in cold urban climates. Their large communal stick nests provide a home throughout the year, rather than serving only as a temporary breeding site. When a colony builds on electrical equipment, the nest becomes an infrastructure issue that needs the utility's involvement.
identification: Look for a green, long-tailed parakeet with a gray face and breast and a pale pink, strongly curved bill. Blue flight feathers show especially well when the bird is flying. The birds often travel in noisy groups and can disappear against leafy trees while feeding. A bulky stick structure with separate chambers is a strong clue, particularly on a pole or other urban structure. Other escaped parrots may also be green, so the gray front of the body is more useful than color alone. Photograph the bird and nest from the ground without approaching wires.
actions: Never release a pet parakeet outdoors. If you can no longer keep one, contact an appropriate rescue or animal-care organization. Report a nest on a transformer or power structure directly to the utility, and leave removal to trained personnel. For nests on private trees or buildings, ask the local wildlife agency about humane options and applicable requirements before acting. Avoid dismantling an occupied nest yourself. Record the colony's location and observed activity from a safe distance if you are contributing to a bird survey.
researchNotes: Cornell supplies field diagnosis and nesting biology; USDA Wildlife Services provides independent conflict and management evidence. No unsupported instruction to trap, kill or relocate birds.

claims: Gray face/breast, green body, pink bill, blue flight feathers and communal stick nests.
Utility nest conflicts, introduced populations and professional management context.

proposedDescription: Pithecellobium dulce is a thorny tropical American tree often called Manila tamarind, madras thorn or opiuma. The catalog name monkeypod can cause confusion because that name is also widely used for a different tree, Samanea saman. In Hawaii, P. dulce has established in dry pastures and disturbed natural areas, where dense growth can displace other plants. Its coiled pods and unusually small number of leaflets are better guides than its common name.
identification: A complete leaf is divided twice but ends in just four leaflets, arranged as two pairs. Short spines occur on the branches and can also be present on the trunk. The small pale flowers are crowded into clusters. Thick pods curl or twist as they mature and may become pinkish or reddish, opening to reveal dark seeds surrounded by pale pulp. This differs from the much more finely divided foliage of the tree commonly sold as monkeypod. Include a full leaf, a thorn-bearing twig and a pod in identification photographs when available.
actions: Before planting or sharing seedlings, check regional guidance under the scientific name. Where the tree is unwanted, remove young volunteers before a thorny thicket develops and keep seed-bearing pods from being moved with garden waste. Wear sturdy gloves and arrange professional help for large branches or established trees. A removal plan should include follow-up inspections for surviving growth and new seedlings. For a population in dry natural habitat, consult the local land manager rather than copying old pasture herbicide recommendations. Keep the record distinct from observations of Samanea saman.
researchNotes: Hawaii CTAHR read in full supplies diagnosis and local impact; NParks is independent botanical corroboration. Common-name collision explicitly documented without changing catalog identity.

proposedDescription: Monkeypox virus causes the infectious disease mpox. Recognition and care depend on clinical assessment and laboratory testing. The scientific virus name and the disease name are different: current virus taxonomy places it in the species Orthopoxvirus monkeypox. Infection can spread through close contact with an infected person, contaminated materials or infected animals. A person's identity or appearance does not establish infection.
identification: Mpox can cause painful or itchy lesions, sometimes with fever, swollen lymph nodes, muscle aches or fatigue. Some people have only a few lesions, and symptoms do not always arrive in the same order. Lesions can resemble other infections or skin conditions, including chickenpox or herpes, so photographs and symptom lists cannot provide a diagnosis. A healthcare professional can assess the illness and arrange laboratory testing, commonly using material collected from a lesion. Do not try to identify a viral clade from the rash or collect a diagnostic sample yourself.
actions: If you develop an unexplained rash or have a possible exposure, contact a healthcare provider or public-health clinic promptly. Until assessed, avoid close skin contact and sharing towels, bedding or clothing. Do not pick or open lesions. Ask a clinician about vaccination after exposure and whether vaccination is recommended for your circumstances. If mpox is confirmed, follow the care team's instructions about preventing spread, including around pets. Seek urgent medical help for severe symptoms, eye involvement or difficulty breathing.

proposedDescription: Montbretia is a garden hybrid grown for arching sprays of orange flowers above narrow leaves. It returns from underground corms and can build dense colonies that survive after the foliage dies back. Escaped populations occur in coastal California and other mild regions. Movement of garden waste and soil is especially important because small corms can start a new patch even when no flowers or seeds are visible.
identification: The leaves are smooth, narrow and sword-shaped, grouped near the base. Slender flowering stems branch in a zigzag pattern and carry orange to reddish, funnel-shaped flowers, often with yellow centers. Beneath the soil, corms and their smaller offsets are a more persistent part of the plant than the seasonal leaves. Other Crocosmia species and cultivars can look similar, and flower color alone cannot reliably identify this hybrid. Photograph the whole clump, flowering stem and any corms exposed during authorized garden work. Do not dig a wild site simply to obtain a photograph.
actions: Dig small unwanted patches carefully, collecting the corms, offsets and connecting underground parts. Avoid scattering soil containing corms elsewhere in the garden or along a watercourse. Do not dump divisions on a roadside or offer them to neighbors where local guidance discourages planting. Check the site over subsequent growing seasons, since missed corms can produce fresh leaves. Large colonies beside streams need a management plan that protects bank stability and native vegetation. Removing flowers alone does not address the underground growth that sustains the patch.
researchNotes: NSW government read in full supplies morphology and physical control; Cal-IPC independently supplies California escape context and hybrid parentage. Avoids transferring Southern Hemisphere calendar dates.

proposedDescription: Sinomegoura citricola has been reported on many woody and cultivated plants in Asia and from limited detections in the United States. A Florida alert documented it on mango fruit, while a California report described a colony on lemon. Those observations are useful detection records, not proof of a widespread, damaging population throughout either state. The catalog name moon aphid is less consistently used than the scientific name Sinomegoura citricola.
identification: Wingless adults are shiny chestnut to reddish brown and somewhat spindle-shaped. A conspicuous black tail-like structure, the cauda, projects from the rear and is longer than the paired tubes beside it. Those tubes have pale bases and darker tips, and the antennae show banding. These characters are easier to evaluate under magnification than in a phone photograph. Other brown aphids occur on citrus and ornamental plants, so the host alone cannot confirm the species. Record whether insects are on fruit, leaves or young stems, and photograph the colony before disturbing it.
actions: Ask your state plant diagnostic service to examine a suspected colony, especially on mango fruit or recently acquired plants. The Florida alert recommends gently collecting adults with a small paintbrush for submission to the plant industry laboratory; obtain the laboratory's packaging instructions first. Keep infested material from being moved or shared while identification is pending. Avoid assuming that the colony is transmitting a particular disease. A useful report includes the host plant, date, location and whether the same insects remain present on a later visit.
researchNotes: The CDFA report's indexed text independently documents the lemon detection and diagnostic cauda; Florida's original mango alert supports detection and submission. AphID's negative vector statement conflicts with the older Taiwan citation. Neither disputed virus assertion is needed for this detection profile. The draft makes no vector claim and tells readers not to diagnose disease from aphid presence; that scoped omission resolves the publication hold for the proposed text. Review the detection-only profile; consult Wang 1981 and modern transmission work before adding any plant-virus claim.

proposedDescription: Aurelia coerulea is one of several closely related animals commonly called moon jellyfish. For many years, moon jellies from widely separated coasts were often grouped under Aurelia aurita. Molecular work has revealed distinct species hidden within that familiar appearance. Smithsonian's invasion account documents A. coerulea in California, while its status in some other regions remains debated. Seeing a moon jelly therefore does not establish either the exact species or its introduction history.
identification: The swimming stage has a rounded, translucent to whitish bell, often with four pinkish or orange horseshoe-shaped reproductive structures visible through it. Short tentacles fringe the bell, and oral arms hang beneath. These features help recognize a moon jelly, but they are shared across the complex. Size, color and the number of jellies in a bloom are insufficient for identifying A. coerulea. Its life cycle also includes a small attached polyp stage that is much less obvious than the swimming jelly. A species-level determination may require expert morphology and genetic evidence.
actions: Photograph jellies in place without handling them, and record the date, waterbody and approximate number. Describe the observation as a moon jelly unless a specialist has confirmed the species. Send an unusual bloom or new-location record to the relevant marine monitoring program, which can decide whether sampling is needed. Do not release aquarium jellies, attached polyps or aquarium water into coastal waters. A large aggregation by itself is not a reason for improvised removal; local managers need to distinguish ordinary bloom dynamics from a verified new introduction.
researchNotes: Smithsonian's California account and the Dutch study's DNA-confirmed mixed Aurelia populations independently support cryptic identity. The Azores paper documents the limits of classic morphology. Expert or genetic diagnosis is an appropriate identification limit, not a reason to invent a visible species key. Mediterranean origin disputes remain disclosed without generalizing them to California. Review the moon-jelly observation language and avoid converting unsequenced sightings into exact-species records.

proposedDescription: Ipomoea carnea is a large, woody morning-glory that may grow as a shrub or scramble over surrounding vegetation. This differs from the delicate annual vines many people associate with the name morning-glory. Botanical treatments distinguish an erect form, subspecies fistulosa, from a climbing form, subspecies carnea. Florida references often concern the erect subspecies, so those records should not be silently generalized to every form of the species.
identification: Woody morning-glory has stout, hollow stems and alternate leaves on long stalks. Leaves are broad and often heart-shaped at the base, with an undivided margin and pointed tip. Young growth can be finely hairy. Clusters of large pink to pinkish-white, funnel-shaped flowers appear toward the ends of shoots. Several woody Ipomoea species have similar flowers, so include the leaf shape, stem habit and the small sepals behind the flower in photographs. A leafless branch or a single flower without the rest of the plant is a weak basis for a subspecies determination.
actions: Do not plant or distribute a suspect woody morning-glory where regional guidance identifies it as a weed. If it is spreading beyond a garden, record the extent and whether the stems stand upright or climb, then ask a local botanist to confirm the taxon. Keep cuttings and rooted material out of drains and natural vegetation. For a substantial patch beside water, seek a site-specific management plan rather than assuming that cutting the visible stems will finish the job. Retain the exact name used by the determining botanist in any report.
researchNotes: Kew's botanical treatment distinguishes climbing carnea from erect fistulosa; FDACS explicitly links its Florida account to fistulosa and explains rooting stems and suckers. The parent-species profile can retain both forms while explicitly limiting Florida advice to its named subspecies. This is a nested taxonomic scope, not evidence that the catalog species must be renamed. Review the subspecies distinction; preserve the determiner's exact name for any local report. proposedDescription: Morning-glory leafminer moth is best noticed through the translucent patches its caterpillars make inside leaves. It uses plants in the morning-glory family, including bindweeds and sweet potato. The small moth is recorded widely, and crop significance depends on the host and degree of damage. Mines on an unwanted bindweed have a different practical meaning from substantial mining in a sweet-potato planting.
identification: A young larva begins a narrow, winding mine that later expands into a broader, pale blotch. Frass can be pushed outside the mine and hang in chains or collect on silk beneath the leaf. The caterpillar and later exposed pupa are more informative than a dried brown patch alone. Adults are very small and easily confused with other narrow-winged moths. Other leafminers can also start a winding tunnel, so photograph both leaf surfaces, the transition from narrow mine to blotch and any visible larva. Include a photograph of the host plant's leaves and flowers to support identification.
actions: In a food crop, inspect several plants to learn whether fresh mines are increasing before choosing a response. Ask extension staff to distinguish this moth from other miners and leaf diseases, using leaves with active mines rather than only old damage. Avoid moving infested slips or leafy plant material between plantings. Keep any collected sample contained and follow the diagnostic service's instructions. A few mines do not automatically justify broad insecticide use, which may also affect natural enemies. Do not deliberately move the moth onto bindweed as an informal biological-control experiment.
researchNotes: North Carolina state moth account and Queensland crop guide provide independent regional treatments; UK mine observations supplement diagnostic details. Exact current U.S. treatment thresholds unavailable, so actions remain monitoring and referral.

proposedDescription: Moroccan toadflax is a delicate annual flower native to Morocco and widely grown in gardens. Escaped plants have been documented in several regions, including occasional records along trails in southern California. Its presence outside a flower bed deserves an accurate record, but the evidence does not support treating every garden planting as an invasive population. The variety of flower colors sold in seed mixes can make recognition less straightforward than a single photograph suggests.
identification: Slender leafy stems carry small, two-lipped flowers with a conspicuous backward-pointing spur. Flowers may be purple, pink, reddish, yellow or combinations with a contrasting pale throat. Narrow leaves and a fine branching habit can be inconspicuous before flowering. Rounded seed capsules follow the blossoms. Other annual toadflaxes share the spurred flower, and related ornamental material can complicate identification. Photograph both the front and side of a flower, the narrow leaves and a mature capsule. Yellow color alone does not separate it from perennial invasive toadflaxes, whose growth and management are quite different.
actions: If unwanted plants appear beyond a garden, document them while flowering and remove them before mature seed is scattered, where removal is permitted. Keep seed mixes and garden sweepings out of trails and natural vegetation. Record whether plants recur in following seasons or appear only after recent sowing. For a conservation-area report, ask a local botanist to examine a complete flowering specimen or detailed photographs. Avoid labeling an unfamiliar toadflax from its color alone, and do not substitute management advice for perennial yellow toadflax without first confirming the species.
researchNotes: Prigge/Gibson original regional botanical description and independent Iberian field records support annual ornamental escape context. Actions are bounded seed-containment inference; no severe U.S. impact claim.

proposedDescription: Morrow's honeysuckle is an upright deciduous shrub from eastern Asia that has spread through parts of eastern North America. It can occupy woodland edges, abandoned fields and other places where birds deposit its seeds. A dense patch shades smaller plants and is more work to remove than scattered young shrubs. It belongs to the bush honeysuckles, so it should not be confused with the twining growth of Japanese honeysuckle.
identification: Leaves occur opposite one another and are oval, with a noticeably hairy underside. Paired white flowers turn yellow with age and sit on relatively long, hairy stalks. Red berries follow the flowers. Tatarian honeysuckle generally has hairless leaf undersides and often pink flowers; Amur honeysuckle has more strongly pointed leaves and shorter flower stalks. Hybrids can blur these distinctions. Native honeysuckles also deserve protection, so do not identify a shrub from red fruit alone. Close photographs of the leaf underside, flower attachment and twig are more useful than a wide photograph of the thicket.
actions:
Confirm the identification before clearing shrubs, especially where native honeysuckles grow nearby. Pull very small plants when soil conditions allow the roots to be removed without excessive disturbance. Larger shrubs often resprout after cutting, so plan repeated follow-up or a professionally advised cut-stump approach appropriate to the site. Prevent new fruit production where practicable and inspect nearby bird perches for seedlings. Replace removed cover with suitable native vegetation and keep checking the area; an open patch can receive more seeds from surrounding shrubs.

Contain berry-bearing branches during removal and follow local disposal guidance rather than dumping them in natural areas.

proposedDescription: Mosquitograss is an annual grass native from the Mediterranean region toward Central Asia. The common name is not an indication that it repels mosquitoes. It is a member of the wheat tribe and is also found in older references as Haynaldia villosa or Secale villosum. In its native range it grows in dry pasture, uncultivated ground and disturbed roadside habitats. Those observations establish ecology, not a current impact assessment for every United States locality.
identification: Plants form tufts with slender stems and narrow, somewhat hairy leaf blades. At the leaf collar, curved clasping projections and a short membranous ligule are useful features for a grass specialist. The flowering structure is a single oblong spike with hairy parts and spikelets set broadside against the central axis. Mature sections of that axis can break apart. Several wild barley and wheat relatives have similarly bristly heads, making a distant photograph unreliable. A full stem with its base, leaf collar and mature head provides much better material for comparison with a botanical key.
actions: If you find this grass outside a known planting or research plot, photograph the stand before disturbing it and note whether mature seed is present. Ask a herbarium or extension botanist to verify the identification, retaining the scientific name on any original label. Keep seed-bearing material and contaminated soil from moving to a new site while the record is assessed. Do not assume that a common-name match proves identity or that a seed-bank accession represents a wild population. Local control advice should follow confirmation of both species and setting.
researchNotes: GrassBase morphology, Trieste's independently authored native ecology and ITIS nomenclature were freshly recovered. ITIS labels continental-US occurrence incidental. The draft does not assert established US populations or ecological harm. Identification and careful seed handling can be reviewed while incidental records remain distinct from establishment. Review the recognition profile; require a local voucher before any US establishment assertion.

proposedDescription: Moss-rose is a low, succulent annual grown for bright flowers in sunny gardens and containers. It is native to South America and can reseed around a planting. That garden behavior should not be confused with a demonstrated ecological invasion: NC State's horticultural account explicitly describes self-seeding without treating it as invasive in its garden context. Many named cultivars and related ornamental purslanes are sold together, so the label matters when identifying an escape.
identification: The stems spread close to the ground and carry fleshy, narrow leaves. Flowers are large relative to the plant, with colors including yellow, orange, pink, red and white. Cultivars may have single or doubled flowers, and many close at night or during dull weather. Common purslane has broader, flatter leaves and much smaller yellow flowers, but cultivated hybrids can blur simple comparisons. Photograph a whole shoot with leaves and an open flower, and preserve the nursery label if there is one. A closed bloom at dusk does not mean that the plant has stopped flowering.
actions: In a garden where seedlings are unwanted, remove spent flowers before seed develops and pull volunteer plants while small. Avoid dumping seed-bearing potting mix or plant debris into natural areas. If plants appear far from cultivation, record the habitat and whether they recur, then seek confirmation rather than assigning a broad invasive label. Keep observations of ornamental hybrids distinct when their identity is uncertain. For a natural-area restoration, choose species appropriate to the local plant community instead of treating a drought-tolerant bedding plant as a substitute for native groundcover.
researchNotes: NC State and NParks provide independent horticultural evidence. UF older document appears to reverse the usual grandiflora/oleracea leaf comparison and was not used for that claim. Regional invasion evidence is not inferred.

proposedDescription: Moth mullein spends its early life as a leafy rosette before sending up a tall flowering stem. It is a biennial of open disturbed places and can appear along roadsides, in fields and around neglected ground. Its slender stalks and relatively smooth foliage make it look less bulky than common mullein. The name refers to a plant, not the caterpillars of the unrelated moth sometimes called the mullein moth.
identification: The rosette leaves are oblong, with irregularly toothed or sometimes lobed edges. Later stem leaves become smaller toward the top. Individual yellow or white flowers stand on distinct little stalks along an elongated flowering axis, often showing purple tones around the stamens. Rounded capsules follow them. Common mullein usually has thick, woolly leaves and tightly crowded flowers, while moth mullein is much less hairy and its flower stalks are visible. Photograph the first-year rosette and, when available, a flowering stem close enough to show those stalks and the purple-haired stamens.
actions: For a small unwanted population, identify the rosettes before flowering and discuss removal with the landowner or local weed adviser. Preventing mature capsules from being scattered is more useful than waiting until dry stems are shaken during mowing. Record both rosettes and flowering plants when mapping a patch, since counting only tall stems misses the next cohort. Avoid disturbing broad areas of soil just to remove a few individuals. On a sensitive site, verify the identification first and arrange follow-up inspections after removal to check for new seedlings.
researchNotes: Missouri's weed account and the independent New Zealand flora agree on biennial rosettes, sparse hair, stalked flowers and rounded capsules. The draft offers conditional small-patch planning and seed containment, not a tested control efficacy claim. Missing US treatment trials do not block that limited scope. Review identification and conditional removal wording; use local site advice for any actual treatment.

proposedDescription: This plant is usually called baby's tears or mind-your-own-business. The catalog name mother of thousands is also used for unrelated succulent plants, so it is particularly important to use Soleirolia soleirolii when seeking advice. It forms a fine, green carpet in damp, sheltered places and can spread beyond ornamental plantings. Coastal California botanical records document escapes in moist shade, while garden behavior elsewhere depends strongly on climate and site.
identification: Tiny, almost round to kidney-shaped leaves crowd slender, branching stems. Leaves are only a few millimeters across, and the stems root where they contact a suitable surface. Fine hairs are present, but this member of the nettle family does not have the conspicuous stinging hairs of familiar nettles. The minute pale flowers are easy to overlook. Mosses can look similar from a distance, but a close view shows the plant's distinct leaves and branching stems. It also differs entirely from the thick-leaved Kalanchoe plants that produce plantlets along their leaf edges.
actions: Lift unwanted mats carefully and collect the small stem pieces, which can regrow if left behind. Avoid mowing through a patch and spreading chopped stems into clean parts of the lawn. Check pot bases, paving joints and the edges of damp beds for rooted extensions. Dispose of unwanted divisions through an appropriate garden-waste route rather than dumping them beside water or woodland. In a natural site, confirm the plant and consult local guidance before clearing a green mat that might include native mosses or small herbs.
researchNotes: Victoria/New Zealand flora, UC Irvine local specimen account and RHS management are distinct lineages. Common-name collision explicitly separated. RHS removal details derived from rooting-fragment biology and read guidance.

proposedDescription: Mottled rustic moth is a Eurasian species established in parts of North America, including the Pacific Northwest. Adults visit lights, so a porch observation may be the first indication that it is nearby. The larvae feed on a range of low-growing plants. A moth at a light does not show which plant its caterpillars used, and the available regional accounts do not justify treating every encounter as a damaging garden infestation.
identification: Mottled rustic adults are small to medium-sized brown moths with a slightly brassy cast to the forewings. Two darker marks, one rounded and one kidney-shaped, sit on each forewing, and the outer portion has a grayish band. The hindwings are pale with a yellowish tone, a useful comparison with related Caradrina whose hindwings are whiter. Pattern strength varies, and worn individuals are difficult to identify. Photograph the moth from above while it rests naturally, including a size reference nearby. Do not force the wings open; a specialist can advise if further evidence is needed.
actions: For an unusual locality, submit a dated photograph to a regional moth recording program and describe the habitat around the light. If caterpillars are damaging plants, photograph the larvae and affected plant separately rather than assuming they belong to the visiting adult. Avoid spraying a whole planting in response to one moth. Keep any diagnostic sample contained and ask an entomologist how to handle it. Distinguish a confirmed species record from a tentative identification based only on a blurry image of a brown moth.
researchNotes: The PNW account was recovered through its original indexed host, and the Ulster Museum account independently supports glossy marked forewings, nocturnal herb-feeding larvae and attraction to light. BugGuide overlaps PNW literature and is grouped with it; BAMONA provides separate verified sightings rather than a second biological account. The new Ulster account supplies independent biology. No garden-damage or eradication claim is needed. Review the moth recognition and observation advice, retaining caution for worn specimens and unassociated larvae. The inherited PNW-new address redirected to an inaccessible migration page; substantive text was recovered at the original PNW host listed below. proposedDescription: Mottled spurge is a branching succulent often mistaken for a cactus. It is grown as a houseplant and, in frost-free climates, can become a large shrub or small tree. Pale markings along the green stems give it a patterned appearance. Crested forms sold as coral cactus can look very different from the upright plant, and a grafted specimen may combine two species. A pot label therefore needs to be interpreted with the plant's actual growth form.
identification: The stems are angular and ridged, with paired spines along the edges. Small leaves may appear briefly near growing tips, but plants are usually almost leafless. Green branches often show pale central streaks or mottling. Injured tissue releases irritating milky latex, but cutting the plant to test that feature is unsafe and unnecessary. Several succulent Euphorbia species overlap in appearance. Photograph the branching pattern, ridge edges and spine pairs; for a grafted plant, include the junction between the upper plant and its supporting stem.
actions: Wear gloves and protect your eyes when pruning or handling broken pieces, because the latex can injure skin and eyes. Keep the plant and its cuttings away from children and pets, and do not eat any part. Contain discarded stems rather than leaving them where people or animals may encounter the spines and sap. If you find a thicket beyond cultivation, ask a local botanist to confirm the species and advise on removal. Do not assume that advice for removing a true cactus applies unchanged to this spurge.
researchNotes: NC State's species account and NParks' separate Cristata account support stem recognition, crested variation and irritating sap. Uncertain native limits and absence of US control trials do not invalidate a horticultural recognition and handling profile. NParks is explicitly cultivar evidence, not proof of wild establishment. Review the cactus-versus-spurge distinction and handling precautions without adding a broad invasion claim.
