proposedDescription: Firespike, the more familiar name for mottled toothedthread, is a tropical shrub cultivated for upright clusters of red tubular flowers. Its native range extends from Mexico into Central America. Hawaiian herbarium records document plants outside cultivation, including along a stream, alongside a long history of ornamental cultivation. Those different settings are a reminder to describe local behavior rather than assigning one impact level to every planting.
identification: Large, opposite leaves have an oval outline and taper to a pronounced point. The flowering clusters rise at the ends of stems, carrying many narrow red tubes with short lips at their openings. The plant can grow into a substantial shrub in a warm, sheltered site. Related Odontonema species have similar foliage; the color and shape of the flowers and the hairiness of the flowering axis help a botanist separate them. Older literature sometimes applies the name O. strictum to material treated as O. cuspidatum. Photograph the leaves, complete flower cluster and a close side view of individual flowers.
actions: Keep an ornamental planting within its intended bed and watch adjacent damp ground for plants beyond the maintained area. Collect pruned material instead of dumping it along streams or in woodland. For an apparent wild patch, document whether it is connected to a garden and send photographs to a local herbarium or invasive plant program. Use the scientific name from a confirmed determination when reporting it, noting any older label separately. A garden-care recommendation is not a tested eradication method for a naturalized streamside population.
researchNotes: Kew's Flora Zambesiaca diagnosis and Bishop Museum's independent voucher records support red tubular flowers, opposite leaves and naturalization in Hawaii; Bishop also flags O. strictum as misapplied. The old name can be retained as a caution without changing identity. Streamside observations and containment advice are supportable without a nationwide impact level or tested eradication trial. Review local-behavior wording and retain the exact name on future voucher determinations. Smithsonian PDF failed parsing and exact-source search did not recover its relevant passage; Bishop's freshly read misapplied-name record supplies that caution instead. Unused inherited source: https://repository.si.edu/bitstream/handle/10088/17551/SCtB-0098.pdf (not substantively recovered here or superseded by the explicitly identified recovered source).

claims: Red tubular corolla and native Mexican/Central American shrub.
Naturalized streamside and other Hawaiian specimens with red flowers.

proposedDescription: Mountain ebony, commonly called orchid tree, is an Asian tree with large flowers and distinctive two-lobed leaves. It belongs to the pea family, despite the orchid name. In Florida it has escaped cultivation, and regional assessments distinguish greater concern in the south from other parts of the state. A seed-producing ornamental near disturbed ground can become a source of volunteers beyond the original landscape.
identification: Each leaf is simple but split at the tip into two rounded lobes, giving it a hooflike outline. Large flowers have five broad, overlapping petals, usually in pink to purple tones, sometimes white. The upper petal may have contrasting markings. Long, flat pods follow the flowers. Bauhinia purpurea is a close comparison: botanical keys emphasize its narrower, less-overlapping petals and generally three fertile stamens, compared with five in B. variegata. Cultivated hybrids add further uncertainty. Photograph the complete flower and its central stamens, as well as leaves and mature pods, instead of relying only on the leaf silhouette.
actions: Where local guidance discourages orchid tree, choose a suitable alternative and remove volunteer seedlings while their roots are manageable. Inspect the ground beyond the planting, including disturbed edges where seeds may establish. Mature-tree removal should include professional assessment of size, access and regrowth, followed by checks for seedlings. Do not distribute pods or rooted volunteers from an escaping tree. Confirm the species before removing a different Bauhinia or a cultivated hybrid, because similar-looking ornamentals can have different reproductive behavior and regional recommendations.
researchNotes: UF provides Florida biology and prevention; South African botanical weed guide independently supplies B. purpurea diagnostic comparison. Florida categories not exported to other states.

proposedDescription: Mouse barley is a cool-season annual grass familiar along western roadsides, pavement cracks, disturbed ground and neglected turf. The name covers a variable species complex, with several subspecies recognized in botanical treatments. Its bristly heads may look harmless while green, but the dry, barbed seed units can catch in fur and clothing and injure animals. Managing it before the heads harden is more practical than dealing with scattered dry fragments later.
identification: Young plants form grass tufts with flat, narrow blades and small clasping projections at the leaf bases. Flowering stems carry dense, upright heads with numerous long, straight bristles. As the heads mature, they break into small units. Many grasses called foxtail or wild barley look similar; subspecies within H. murinum require details of the spikelets and floral parts that are difficult to see in a casual photograph. Show the whole plant, leaf collar and intact head when requesting identification. Do not rely on the common name foxtail, which is applied to several unrelated grasses.
actions: Pull, hoe or dig young plants before seed heads mature, removing the crown rather than clipping the tips. Ordinary mowing can miss low-growing plants, so inspect the treated patch afterward. Collect dry heads carefully and avoid dragging them through clean areas. Keep desirable groundcover healthy and close gaps that invite new seedlings. Check pets after walks through dry grass, and seek veterinary help for a suspected embedded awn rather than trying to probe it out. A local weed adviser can help with larger pasture or roadside patches.
researchNotes: UNR management factsheet read in full and Prigge/Gibson botanical account are independent. Species-complex uncertainty retained; awn injury advice avoids diagnosis or treatment instructions.

proposedDescription: Mouseear cress is a small annual mustard often found on disturbed ground, garden edges and other open sites. It is also the laboratory plant widely used in genetics research. A plant with that familiar scientific name is not necessarily an escaped experiment; wild populations occur independently of research cultivation. In North America it is introduced, but that fact alone does not establish serious ecological harm at a particular location.
identification: A low rosette of spoon-shaped to narrow leaves forms first, followed by slender flowering stems. Basal leaves usually have simple or branched hairs, while the upper stem leaves are smaller. Tiny white flowers have four petals in a cross. Narrow, upright to spreading seed pods develop below the continuing flowers. Native Arabidopsis relatives can be mistaken for it: A. lyrata generally has larger flowers and longer, flatter pods, while A. thaliana has shorter, very narrow pods that are more rounded in cross-section. Photograph the rosette, flowers and mature pods together for a reliable comparison.
actions: In an ordinary garden, unwanted plants can be removed while small and before the pods release seed. Hold the plant near its base and minimize disturbance around neighboring seedlings. Recheck the spot because additional annual seedlings may emerge. If the plant occurs among rare vegetation or in an unfamiliar natural setting, verify it before removal rather than treating all small white-flowered mustards alike. Keep labeled research material within the facility's own containment procedures; a field-guide identification should not replace those requirements. Record whether an observation is cultivated or growing independently.
researchNotes: Burke Herbarium and Native Plant Trust support diagnosis and native lookalikes. UC IPM supports explicitly general annual-weed hand removal; no claim of species-specific eradication trial or ecological severity.

proposedDescription: Mouseear hawkweed is a low, spreading perennial now commonly treated as Pilosella officinarum. The older name Hieracium pilosella remains widespread in weed literature. It can form mats in open, relatively low-fertility ground, including grasslands and roadsides, where runners allow a small patch to expand. Its status and reporting requirements vary by region, and yellow flowers alone are not enough to distinguish it from the many other plants in the daisy family.
identification: Leaves form low rosettes and have long hairs on the upper surface. The underside is pale and felted with dense, fine hairs. Each mostly leafless flower stalk usually carries a single pale yellow head; the outside of the outer rays may have a reddish stripe. Slender aboveground runners connect new rosettes. Dandelions lack this combination of hairy leaves and connecting runners, while other hawkweeds may carry several flower heads or leaves along the flowering stem. Look closely at the leaf underside and the connections between rosettes before deciding that an entire patch is one species.
actions: Photograph the rosettes, runners and flowers and check local weed guidance before disturbing a suspected new infestation. For a confirmed small patch where self-removal is advised, lift the entire interconnected mat, including rooted runner sections, and revisit for regrowth. Avoid carrying fragments or seed-bearing heads into clean grassland. Some jurisdictions ask residents to report hawkweeds and leave treatment to their biosecurity team, so follow the local process. Protect native hawkweeds and other yellow-flowered herbs by confirming identity rather than clearing all similar plants.
researchNotes: Thurston County supplies U.S. occurrence/diagnosis; Bay of Plenty Council independently provides biology and small-patch digging; NSW supports jurisdiction-specific report-first handling. Accepted synonym preserved without changing catalog ID.

proposedDescription: Mozambique tilapia is a cichlid native to southeastern Africa that has been moved widely for aquaculture and other purposes. It can live in fresh and brackish water, and introduced populations occur in warm regions outside its native range. Records need careful interpretation because related tilapias and hybrids have sometimes been reported under this name. A photograph of a dark fish beside a pond is rarely enough to establish a new species record.
identification: The body is deep and compressed, with a long dorsal fin and a relatively large mouth. Nonbreeding fish are generally grayish or greenish, sometimes with dark flank blotches. Breeding males can become very dark with a paler lower head and colored fin edges, so color changes with sex and condition. Juveniles may show vertical bars. Cichlids have one nostril opening on each side and an interrupted lateral line, unlike the paired nostrils and continuous lateral line typical of sunfishes. Separating Mozambique tilapia from other tilapias requires closer examination, especially where hybrids occur.
actions: Never release aquarium or aquaculture fish into a pond, canal or stream, and do not move a captured tilapia to another waterbody. If an unusual fish is caught, photograph both sides, the tail and head, record the exact waterbody and contact the relevant fisheries agency. Follow local rules for retaining or disposing of the catch rather than assuming a universal rule applies. Report suspected escape pathways, such as a pond overflow connection, to the responsible owner or agency. Identification may require a specimen or genetic work, so label uncertain records as provisional.
researchNotes: USGS explicitly warns of hybridization and misidentification; Smithsonian STRI provides independent diagnostic detail. Prevention guidance follows aquatic introduction pathway and does not invent local harvest regulations.

proposedDescription: Mount Etna broom is a large shrub or small tree associated with Mediterranean landscapes. It is grown for a cloud of yellow flowers on slender green branches. Recent botanical work uses Genista etnensis as the correct spelling, while Genista aetnensis remains common in horticulture and in this catalog. Native populations and introduced populations need to be distinguished: research on expansion around Vesuvius does not make every occurrence elsewhere an equivalent invasion.
identification: The branches are long, green and often drooping, giving mature plants a light, open outline. Leaves are few and simple rather than divided into three leaflets, and can be inconspicuous. Yellow pea-shaped flowers occur in open groups, followed by short, somewhat egg-shaped pods with a curved tip. Several other brooms have green stems and yellow flowers. A close view of the leaf structure, pods and branching pattern is therefore more useful than flower color alone. Young plants may not yet have the tree-like form suggested by photographs of old garden specimens.
actions: Keep the original nursery name when documenting a cultivated plant, but include the alternative spelling when searching botanical records. If seedlings appear away from a planting, photograph them and map their relationship to the parent tree before deciding on management. Avoid distributing seed from plants that are reproducing beyond cultivation. In a natural area, ask a local botanist to distinguish this species from other brooms and assess the significance of the record. A Mediterranean study of invasive behavior should not be used as a ready-made treatment plan for an unidentified American population.
researchNotes: The 2022 original phylogeographic study and Bean/Spencer botanical treatments independently confirm etnensis spelling, sparse linear leaves and yellow flowers on green branches. An orthographic spelling difference is not a conflicting species concept. The profile separates Mediterranean invasion observations from an unverified American setting and does not promise control. Review the spelling explanation while preserving the catalog ID and locally confirmed population context.

proposedDescription: Mueller's saltbush is an Australian herb of low-lying and disturbed habitats, with introduced records in parts of Africa. Bishop Museum records document naturalized plants in Hawaii, including a patch on a Maui beach; these local records do not establish nationwide harm. Descriptions differ in how tall it grows and how long it lives. A local identification and documented location are needed before drawing conclusions about its spread in the United States.
identification: Plants are often upright and branched, with broad, stalked leaves that narrow toward the base. Leaf edges may be wavy or coarsely toothed, and a pale mealy coating can be most apparent on the underside. The small flowers occur in clusters around the leaf axils. Mature fruiting structures are important: paired bracteoles surround each fruit and become thickened, with a rounded outline and toothed upper portion. Many saltbushes have similar grayish foliage, so photographs of leaves alone are insufficient. Include close views of mature fruiting bracts, the stem and the overall plant habit.
actions: For a suspected occurrence outside cultivation, record the exact habitat, date and whether mature fruit is present. Ask a herbarium to compare the material with regional Atriplex keys before assigning the name. Keep collected fruiting material contained and avoid spreading soil from a questionable patch until identification is settled. Do not infer salt tolerance, forage suitability or a control method solely from the common name saltbush. Local management decisions should wait for a verified determination and evidence that the population is established in that setting.
researchNotes: PlantNET and Brenan's East African treatment agree on axillary flowers and thick fruiting bracts. Fresh Bishop Museum evidence adds naturalized Hawaiian records, including a Maui beach specimen. Annual versus potentially longer-lived habit can remain qualified. The independent Hawaiian voucher resolves the prior lack of US context without implying nationwide harm or changing the taxon. Review the Hawaiian occurrence wording and require fruiting material for new identifications.

proposedDescription: Mugo pine is a European mountain pine widely planted as an evergreen landscape shrub. Garden forms range from compact cushions to much larger, spreading plants. The name also sits within a taxonomically variable group, so a small nursery cultivar should not be used as the model for every wild population. A planted specimen or compact nursery cultivar does not by itself demonstrate invasive behavior in the surrounding landscape.
identification: The stiff green needles occur in bundles of two and commonly curve slightly. Short, egg-shaped woody cones develop among the branches, and many cultivated plants have several stems rather than one tall trunk. Size alone is a poor clue because cultivars vary greatly. Several other pines also have two needles per bundle; examine the needle length, cone scales, buds and growth form together. European treatments distinguish shrubby mountain-pine forms from taller relatives using cone shape and other details. Photograph the needle bases and intact cones, and retain a nursery label if the plant was purchased.
actions: If a planted mugo pine produces seedlings outside its intended bed, document them and remove unwanted volunteers while small, where permitted. Check whether the plants are actually seedlings or low branches still connected to the original shrub. Avoid treating a large established landscape plant as an emergency solely because it appears in this catalog. For apparent naturalization near a sensitive habitat, ask a regional forester or botanist to verify the identity and evaluate the local concern. Any removal of a substantial tree should account for its size, nearby structures and the intended replacement vegetation.
researchNotes: NC State's needles, cones and buds and EUFORGEN's independent European forestry account support the broad range of mountain-pine growth forms. The draft is about identification and conditional volunteers around plantings. A universal US impact claim is neither made nor required, and cultivar size is explicitly not treated as a species diagnostic. Review the landscape context and obtain a regional determination for any apparent naturalization. Oklahoma page opened but its diagnostic text could not be retrieved after timeout; the substantive NC State and EUFORGEN accounts were read instead. proposedDescription: Mugwort is a strongly scented perennial that can form persistent colonies in gardens, fields, roadsides and disturbed edges. Its underground rhizomes make it difficult to remove once established. Cutting the stems may tidy a patch for a while without eliminating the plant beneath it. In eastern North American landscapes, identifying a small patch early is usually much easier than disentangling a mature colony from valued plants.
identification: Leaves are alternate and often deeply lobed, with green upper surfaces and pale, felted undersides. The foliage can resemble garden chrysanthemums or ragweed, so turn a leaf over rather than relying on its outline. Stems may become reddish or purplish. Small, inconspicuous flower heads occur near the upper portions of the stems; they lack the showy petals expected on many garden flowers. An aromatic smell from disturbed foliage can support identification, but scent alone is not a dependable test. Photograph both sides of a leaf and the arrangement of leaves along the stem.
actions: Avoid rototilling a patch: chopping and redistributing the rhizomes can create more plants. For a small infestation, carefully remove as much of the underground system as possible and keep returning for new shoots. Repeated cutting or light exclusion can weaken growth, but expect sustained work rather than a single successful pass. Do not move rhizome-contaminated soil or divisions of nearby ornamentals into clean beds. For a large colony, ask extension for a site-specific plan that protects neighboring plants, and restore cover once suppression has created space.
researchNotes: Maryland and UConn extension independently support rhizome biology, leaf diagnosis and repeated control. Advice distinguishes temporary cutting from eradication and avoids pesticide specifications.

claims: Rhizomatous perennial, mowing tolerance, avoid tilling and sustained suppression.
Pale leaf undersides, lobed alternate leaves, inconspicuous flowers and repeated management.

proposedDescription: The multicolored Asian lady beetle is both a predator of plant-feeding insects and a familiar autumn house visitor. Native to eastern Asia, it is now widespread in North America. Adults seek sheltered places for winter and can gather in large numbers around buildings. Indoors they are a nuisance rather than a sign that the house is being eaten: they do not reproduce there or damage structural wood. Their defensive liquid can stain surfaces.
identification: Adults are rounded and domed, with colors ranging from pale orange to red or black. Spots vary greatly and can be absent, so counting them is unreliable. The pale area just behind the head often contains a dark M- or W-shaped mark, although it may merge into a larger patch. Larvae look very different: they are elongated, dark, spiny-looking insects with orange markings. Other lady beetles can look similar, including native species. Photograph the back and the area behind the head before assigning a name based only on color.
actions: Before autumn gatherings begin, repair screens and seal gaps around windows, doors, siding and utility openings. Remove indoor clusters carefully with a vacuum and empty or contain the collected material promptly. Avoid crushing beetles against walls or fabrics, which can release staining secretions. People sensitive to the insects should arrange removal that avoids stirring up their material. Outdoor adults and larvae often consume aphids, so a few on a plant do not call for a broad insecticide treatment. Do not buy and release more of this already widespread introduced predator.
researchNotes: Maine account read in full; Penn State independently supports life stages, exclusion, vacuum handling and avoiding purchased releases. Color-pattern variability and native lookalikes retained.

proposedDescription: Multiflora rose is a thorny Asian shrub that can turn open ground and woodland edges into dense, arching thickets. It was formerly planted for purposes including hedges and erosion control, but its ability to spread by seed and by rooting cane tips makes it difficult to contain. Birds carry the small rose hips away from parent plants, so seedlings can appear well beyond an old hedge. Local weed status varies, and identification should precede removal.
identification: The leaves are divided into several toothed leaflets, usually five to eleven. At the base of the leaf stalk, the narrow stipules have a conspicuous fringed or comb-like edge. That fringe is a particularly useful clue. Numerous small white, occasionally pinkish, flowers occur in clusters, followed by small red hips. Arching canes bear curved prickles and may root where their tips touch the soil. Native and cultivated roses can share individual features, so photograph the stipules, whole leaf and flower or fruit cluster instead of identifying a plant simply because it is thorny.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and clothing that protects against the canes. Pull or dig small plants with their root crown when conditions allow, and check for rooted cane tips around the main shrub. Larger thickets usually need repeated treatment; a single cut commonly leaves living roots capable of regrowth. Avoid spreading hips during removal, and inspect the area over following seasons for seedlings. Repeated mowing can suppress accessible patches over time, but protect nearby native plants and follow local guidance for any other treatment. Replant cleared ground with vegetation suited to the site.
researchNotes: UConn and Penn State independently support stipule diagnosis and vegetative spread; Maryland supplies sustained management. Not all native roses share one flower color, so no universal pink-versus-white rule.

claims: Fringed stipules, compound leaves, tip rooting and repeated cutting.
Diagnostic stipules, arching canes, hips and identification cautions.
Repeated mowing and sustained follow-up for established thickets.

proposedDescription: Munk's rhubarb is a large perennial dock, not the rhubarb grown for pie stalks. Its broad leaves and stout underground rhizomes help it persist around old gardens, roadsides and disturbed meadows. Native to parts of Europe and western Asia, it has been introduced to northeastern North America. Flora of North America describes it as uncommon there and specifically notes that it has not been reported as a serious invasive weed.
identification: Look for a substantial clump with very broad, rounded to oval basal leaves, often with a deep heart-shaped notch where the stalk joins the blade. Mature stems carry dense branched clusters of small flowers and later brown fruits. The three inner fruit coverings have smooth edges and lack the swollen grainlike bumps seen in many other docks. Burdock also has broad leaves, but its hooked flower heads and burs are quite different. Leaf size alone is not enough to distinguish a young dock.
actions: Photograph a whole clump, a basal leaf and mature fruit clusters before deciding whether removal is warranted. In an old garden, record whether the plant is spreading or simply surviving where it was planted. If local land managers want a small patch removed, address the underground rhizomes and inspect the site for regrowth. Keep excavated roots and mature seed heads out of dumped garden waste. Do not harvest a plant as culinary rhubarb on the strength of this common name.
researchNotes:
FNA supports persistence, morphology and restrained North American impact language; Kew independently supports native and introduced ranges. Removal advice is precautionary, not a species-specific efficacy claim.

proposedDescription: Lophosceles frenatus is a muscid fly recorded in specialist insect catalogues. The common label 'muscid fly' describes its family rather than a distinctive appearance or a particular kind of damage. A museum collection list records this species from Greenland, and the Palaearctic Diptera Catalogue indexes the name. A separate Russian field account records adults in coastal meadow and tundra. These records do not show that the fly is an introduced pest in the United States.
identification: This is a specialist identification, not a house-fly image match. A comparative museum study found tiny hairs on the upper surface of the leading wing vein across its first three defined sections in Lophosceles frenatus. Four examined relatives, L. cinereiventris, L. impar, L. minimus and L. mutatus, had those hairs only on the second and third sections. This useful distinction requires magnification and a correctly oriented wing; it is not a complete key to every muscid fly. Photograph the wings, head and body from several angles and retain the location and date. An entomologist can assess the specimen alongside the rest of its anatomy.
actions: If you encounter a possible specimen, record the date, location and immediate habitat without disturbing the surrounding area. Ask a local museum or university entomology service whether it accepts fly identification requests and what information it needs. Do not infer that this insect bites, transmits disease or damages crops from its family name. Avoid a control campaign based on an unconfirmed image match. A useful observation here is a carefully documented specimen record that allows a specialist to resolve the identity and regional context.
researchNotes:

proposedDescription: Musky stork's bill is an aromatic annual or short-lived herb that often begins as a low leafy rosette. Its small pink flowers give way to long, pointed fruits that explain the birdlike common name. Originally Mediterranean, it appears in disturbed ground, cultivated places and other open sites outside its home range. An established patch can contain plants of very different sizes, so the biggest specimen is not necessarily a different species.
identification: Each leaf is divided into several broad, toothed or lobed leaflets. These are generally less finely cut than the feathery leaflets of redstem filaree, Erodium cicutarium, but leaf shape varies and can mislead. Musky stork's bill has small pink flowers in stalked clusters and elongated beaked fruits. For a difficult identification, mature fruit segments are especially useful: their pits bear numerous tiny sessile glands. Ordinary photographs may not resolve those details. Scent can be a supporting observation, but should not replace examination of leaves and fruits.
actions: In a garden bed, remove unwanted young plants before the long fruits mature, taking care to distinguish nearby desired seedlings. Collect fruiting material rather than dragging it through an uninfested area. Photograph a full leaf, flowers and ripe fruits if the identification matters to a local survey. Where it appears in pasture or natural vegetation, ask local extension whether management is justified for that site. A species record alone does not establish substantial ecological harm.
researchNotes: Info Flora supports annual habit, aromatic foliage and fruit dimensions; Meise's alien-plant manual independently documents leaf variation, misidentification and diagnostic fruit glands. Actions are low-impact garden prevention.

claims: Aromatic annual, broad toothed leaflets, pink flower clusters and long beaked fruits; Mediterranean origin.
Frequent confusion with E. cicutarium; variable leaves and sessile glands in fruit pits.

proposedDescription: Muster John Henry, also called stinking Roger, is a tall annual marigold from South America. It carries small, tightly grouped flower heads rather than the large showy blooms familiar from bedding marigolds. The aromatic foliage and upright stems can become conspicuous in disturbed ground, along roads or near cultivation. Its behavior varies by region, so a garden escape should be documented locally rather than assumed to be a serious weed everywhere.
identification: The leaves are divided into narrow, toothed leaflets with visible gland dots. Lower leaves tend to stand opposite one another, while upper leaves may alternate. Near the stem tips, many slim cylindrical flower heads form crowded clusters. Each head has a few tiny cream to yellow rays above a long greenish tube of fused bracts. Mature fruits are narrow and dark with a small crown of unequal scales or bristles. Ordinary garden marigolds usually have much broader, more conspicuous heads; a close photograph of a single head is useful.
actions: Check nearby disturbed soil for seedlings if a cultivated plant has been allowed to set seed. Where removal is appropriate, pull young plants before flowering and contain mature heads during cleanup. Keep seed-bearing garden waste away from creek banks and vacant land. Wear gloves if the aromatic foliage irritates your skin. Do not make home pesticide preparations or assume that planting it will solve another weed problem. Local extension can help assess whether a patch needs routine garden care or a wider response.
researchNotes: Kew's Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment and NSW botanical flora independently support diagnostic heads, leaves and annual habit. No borrowed hemispheric flowering calendar or pest-control efficacy claim.

claims: South American annual with aromatic divided leaves and narrowly cylindrical flower heads.
Opposite divided gland-dotted leaves, fused involucral bracts, tiny rays and dark fruits.

proposedDescription: A mute swan can look like a familiar ornamental pond bird while still changing the wetland around it. This large Eurasian waterbird was brought to North America for parks and estates, and escaped or released birds established wild populations. Feeding can remove submerged vegetation used by other wildlife, while territorial pairs may drive other waterbirds away from nesting areas. The scale of those effects depends on the waterbody and number of birds.
identification: An adult has white plumage, an orange bill and a conspicuous black knob at the bill's base. Its neck often forms a graceful S curve, although posture alone is unreliable. Native trumpeter and tundra swans have mainly black adult bills; many tundra swans also show a small yellow mark near the eye. Young mute swans may be gray or dusky with darker bills and a much less obvious knob. A distant white bird or an immature swan needs closer review before its species is recorded.
actions: Watch from a respectful distance, especially around nests and young. Keep dogs away and give a defensive bird room to retreat rather than approaching for a photograph. Do not feed swans or release captive birds onto public water. Record the location, number of birds and clear bill photographs for the local wildlife agency when reporting an unfamiliar population. Leave nest, egg and bird management to authorized professionals, who can account for native swans, local rules and the needs of the wetland.
researchNotes: Minnesota DNR and California DFW independently support identification, juvenile confusion, introduction and habitat concerns. No nationwide legal status or permission to control birds asserted.

claims: Eurasian introduction; vegetation and territorial impacts; orange adult bill and gray young.

proposedDescription: Myoporum thrips is a tiny insect with an outsized effect on the new growth of Myoporum trees and shrubs. Feeding twists tender leaves into swollen, folded shelters where the insects can continue developing. Coastal California landscape plantings have suffered serious damage, and in Hawaii the insect attacks native naio, Myoporum sandwicense. A damaged ornamental and a damaged native forest tree therefore raise different management priorities even when the pest is the same.
identification: Adults are slender, dark brown to black and only a few millimeters long, with fringed wings. Younger stages are paler and can be hidden deep in distorted leaves. Look closely at the freshest growth for tight curling, gall-like swellings and insects protected inside the folds. Other thrips can look very similar, including Cuban laurel thrips, which produces comparable damage on figs. Confirm the host plant as well as the insect; leaf distortion by itself does not identify Klambothrips myopori.
actions: Inspect new Myoporum plants before moving them into a garden or restoration area. Avoid transporting visibly infested shoots, and contain pruned material so insects are not carried to another site. In Hawaii, report suspected damage on naio through the state invasive-species reporting system and follow local advice about plant movement. For repeatedly damaged landscape plants, discuss less susceptible replacements with extension or a qualified nursery. Established insects are sheltered inside curled tissue, so broad spraying without identification and a site-specific plan may miss the problem.
researchNotes: UC IPM supports morphology, sheltered life stages and replacement strategy; Hawaii DLNR independently supports native naio concern and reporting. Older California host observations not treated as current universal resistance claims.

proposedDescription: Myrtle-leaf milkwort is an evergreen South African shrub grown for its mauve, pink or sometimes white flowers. In its native range it occupies several habitats, including dunes, rocky slopes and woodland edges. It can also escape cultivation in mild coastal climates overseas. A flowering garden shrub is not automatically an invasive population, but seedlings spreading into nearby open vegetation deserve attention, particularly where local weed programs already recognize this species.
identification: The shrub has many simple leaves along slender branches, usually oval with rounded tips, although leaf shape varies considerably. Flowers cluster near branch ends and resemble little pea flowers. Look closely at the lower, boat-shaped part of the flower: it ends in a distinctive brushlike crest. Unlike a typical pea flower, there is no large upright banner petal. Small flattened, winged capsules follow flowering. Nursery hybrids and other milkworts complicate identification, so photograph the leaves, whole flower and fruit rather than relying only on flower color.
actions: Inspect the ground around cultivated plants and the nearest disturbed edges for seedlings. Small unwanted seedlings can be removed while roots are manageable, with care around desirable native vegetation. Collect mature capsules and keep seed-bearing cuttings out of dumped garden waste. If an established shrub is spreading into a reserve or dune system, coordinate removal and follow-up with the land manager. Ask a local native-plant nursery about replacement shrubs suited to the same coastal conditions, and revisit cleared ground for new seedlings.
researchNotes: SANBI and NSW Flora independently describe floral structure, variable leaves and naturalization. Cal-IPC confirms California assessment exists; no blanket national invasive rating applied.

claims: Evergreen variable shrub, crested pea-like flowers without banner, winged capsules and nearby seedlings.
Leaf and flower dimensions, capsule, ornamental naturalization in NSW.

proposedDescription: The estuarine mysid in this entry is now usually called Orientomysis aspera; Acanthomysis aspera is its earlier scientific name. Native to coastal East Asia, it was recorded in California's San Francisco Estuary in 1992. It is one of several introduced mysids there. Changes in the estuary's mysid community are well documented, but the effect of this particular species is difficult to separate from that of more abundant introduced relatives.
identification: Like other mysids, it has a slender shrimp-like body, stalked eyes and a small shield over the head and thorax. Adult females carry developing young in a pouch beneath the body. Species identification depends on fine structures, especially the tail plate, its pattern of spines and features of the antennae and tail appendages. These details require magnification and a specialist key. Hyperacanthomysis longirostris and Orientomysis hwanhaiensis occur in the same regional literature, so a generic photograph of a mysid is not a reliable species match.
actions: Do not move live estuary water, bait or small crustaceans between waterbodies. Drain and clean sampling or boating equipment according to local aquatic-species guidance before visiting another site. If a monitoring sample contains an unfamiliar mysid, retain its collection location, date, salinity if measured and sampling method, then ask the monitoring program how specimens should be handled. Avoid attempting to remove a mysid population with chemicals or indiscriminate netting. A verified identification is more useful than an unsupported report based on overall shape.
researchNotes: Koshiishi and colleagues' Ariake Sound survey independently collected Orientomysis aspera chiefly near shore or in estuaries. Smithsonian supplies California history and detailed diagnosis; WoRMS confirms the combination. The Japanese field survey is independent of the Fukuoka-Murano revision shared by WoRMS and Smithsonian. Species-specific California impact uncertainty can remain explicit; it does not block accurate recognition limits and water-movement precautions. Review the expert-identification scope and keep any future impact attribution separate from more abundant introduced mysids.

proposedDescription: Mystery fluke is a minute parasitic flatworm whose developing stages can injure fish gills. Its life cycle links snails, fish and fish-eating birds or mammals, making movement of live aquatic animals an important concern. In the United States, published fish-health accounts describe infections in warm waters and springs. The parasite is particularly significant when vulnerable native fish share habitat with suitable snail hosts; it cannot be recognized simply by seeing snails in a stream.
identification: The stage found in fish forms small cysts in the gills. Heavy infections can distort or enlarge gill tissue, but visible swelling and breathing difficulty also have many other causes. Diagnosis requires examination of gill material by a fish-health laboratory, often with microscopy or additional tests. Adult flukes live in the final host rather than appearing as conspicuous worms on fish skin. Red-rimmed melania, Melanoides tuberculata, is an important snail host, but not every individual snail carries this parasite.
actions: Never release aquarium fish, snails, plants or aquarium water into natural waterways. Keep newly acquired aquatic animals separate while seeking advice on an appropriate health check, and do not transfer sick fish between ponds. Contact a fish-health professional or the responsible wildlife agency if fish show persistent gill problems or unusual mortality. Preserve photographs and details of animal purchases or transfers; ask before collecting sensitive wild fish. Do not treat an entire pond on the assumption that this fluke is responsible, because an accurate diagnosis and host-specific plan are essential.
researchNotes: AFS fish-health chapter gives U.S. regional context, cyst diagnosis and host cycle; independent Kannur University research supports three-host cycle and additional snail-host complexity. No current occurrence list or medical treatment advice.

proposedDescription: Naked grass-mealybug is a small scale insect with a complicated naming history. Older records may use Phenacoccus nudus, Heterococcus graminicola or Heterococcus occidentalis, which current taxonomic accounts place under Heterococcus nudus. ITIS lists it as native in the continental United States and Canada. That matters: the presence of a mealybug name in an invasive-species catalogue does not, by itself, establish that this particular insect is an introduced threat.
identification: Grass-associated mealybugs can be difficult to separate even when examined closely. The name 'naked' should not be used as a simple field test, and an insect's amount of visible wax is not enough to identify it. Specialist work on Heterococcus uses microscopic pores, ducts, antennae and other body structures. Miller and McKenzie's revision separates adult females from H. pulverarius by their eight or nine antennal segments, slender legs and absence of three-loculed pores. These are microscope characters, not a dependable phone-photo test. A small pale insect on grass should remain provisionally identified until a qualified entomologist examines it.
actions: If insects are associated with declining grass, photograph the plant and affected area as well as the insects, and record whether they occur on leaves, stems or roots. Send those observations to local extension before choosing a treatment. Ask how to collect a specimen without losing the plant association needed for identification. Avoid moving infested nursery material while the problem is assessed, but do not remove native grassland or apply broad insect controls merely because this species is suspected.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: The full Miller-McKenzie revision now supplies a species diagnosis: elongated adult females, 8-9 antennal segments, slender legs and no trilocular pores, with leaf-sheath association. ITIS still labels the species native in the US and Canada. This improves the draft but the current taxonomy catalogue and revision are not demonstrated independent biological lineages. A separate modern account and the reason for catalog inclusion remain unresolved; no introduced-pest claim is made. Seek a separately authored modern species account or original field study and have the owner review the native-status catalog rationale.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: An independent original cytogenetic study and separately collected grass specimens resolve the former single-lineage evidence gap. Gavrilov and Trapeznikova newly examined nudus chromosomes and reproduction, independently of Miller-McKenzie1970 morphology. The2011 Crete survey documents a separate2009 Sorghum collection. Native-status concern is retained without inventing invasive harm. Next step: Review the general mealybug draft; leave catalog native-status rationale to separate owner review. proposedDescription: Nakedstem dewflower, often called doveweed, can disappear visually into a lawn until a dense patch has formed. This creeping summer annual belongs to the dayflower family, despite its grasslike leaves. It grows especially well in warm, wet conditions and can occupy poorly drained ground where turf is already struggling. Fleshy stems trail across the surface and root at their joints, while seed allows the weed to return in later seasons.
identification: Look for shiny, narrow leaves with parallel veins on succulent creeping stems. The small lavender flowers have three petals and appear on relatively bare stalks. Those flowers are a useful clue that the plant is not a grass. Marsh dayflower, Murdannia keisak, is a related lookalike that usually grows larger; its green sepals are about as long as the petals, whereas doveweed's sepals are shorter. Photograph a flowering shoot and a rooted stem joint to make an identification request more useful.
actions: Begin by checking irrigation and drainage in affected lawn areas. Watering less frequently, where appropriate for the turf and weather, can reduce persistently wet surface conditions. Remove small patches carefully before seed develops, gathering rooted stem pieces rather than scattering them with equipment. Clean clippings and soil from tools before moving elsewhere. A large infestation may require several seasons of management, so ask extension for a plan matched to the lawn species and site. Avoid draining or altering an actual wetland to address a garden weed.
researchNotes: Clemson supplies lawn prevention and seed persistence; NCSU corroborates morphology and M. keisak distinction, though its management referral overlaps Clemson. Separate institutional descriptions support the ready draft.

claims: Wet-soil lawn weed, grasslike leaves, three lavender petals, rooting stolons and irrigation management.

proposedDescription: Nanking cherry is a cold-hardy Asian shrub planted for early spring flowers and small tart cherries. It usually forms a dense, spreading outline rather than the tall trunk of an orchard cherry tree. Birds use its fruit, and some plantings are maintained as hedges or shelter. The sources reviewed describe a cultivated fruiting shrub; they do not establish that every planting or occasional seedling represents a damaging invasion.
identification: New growth is noticeably hairy. The alternate, toothed leaves are often wrinkled above and densely downy beneath, a useful clue behind the alternative name downy cherry. White or pale pink flowers appear before or around leaf emergence. The round red fruits sit on very short stalks close to the branches. Other shrub cherries can look similar, so include leaf undersides and fruit attachment in photographs. Flower color or a handful of red fruits alone does not distinguish this species from all other Prunus.
actions: Check the edges of a planting for volunteer seedlings, especially where birds perch or fallen fruit collects. Remove unwanted seedlings while small if they are moving into a managed natural area, but first distinguish them from locally native shrubs. A healthy garden plant does not need removal solely because its species is nonnative. If a shrub declines or develops dead branches, seek a diagnosis rather than attributing the problem to invasiveness; cankers and other pests can affect cherries. Keep any proposed replacement or pruning work consistent with local habitat goals.
researchNotes: Colorado State provides morphology; NDSU independently supports cultivated use, native range, birds and canker susceptibility. No unsupported invasive impact or control requirement. Management framed as observation and optional seedling removal.

claims: Hairy toothed leaves, short fruit stalks, white flowers and dense spreading shrub habit.
Cold-hardy Asian shrub; bird-used fruit and branch canker susceptibility.

proposedDescription: Napoleon's plume is an ornamental shrub or small tree better recognized by its butterfly-shaped leaves and large pink flowers. It has been planted widely in tropical regions and can naturalize beyond gardens. Native to Madagascar, it is one of several orchid trees whose similar leaves can make garden escapes difficult to identify before they flower.
identification: Each rounded leaf is split into two broad lobes, as if a butterfly had opened its wings. The five-petaled flowers usually have red or purple markings, with one petal more strongly colored. A particularly useful feature is the single fertile stamen, which helps separate it from several other orchid trees. Long, flattened brown pods develop after flowering and split to release seeds. Leaves alone identify a bauhinia much more readily than they identify this species, so obtain a flower photograph whenever possible.
actions: Watch for seedlings beneath and beyond cultivated trees, especially near disturbed edges and waterways in warm climates. Remove unwanted seedlings before they become woody, and contain mature pods during pruning or cleanup. Do not dump branches bearing pods beside roads or natural areas. If an established tree is spreading into conservation land, discuss removal and follow-up with the land manager rather than cutting it without a plan. A regional botanical or extension service can confirm the species and help choose a locally appropriate replacement.
researchNotes: USFS supports single fertile stamen and explosive pods, but its older Asian-origin claim conflicts with modern Kew. Kew Madagascar range adopted explicitly; stable morphology independently supported by NParks. No broad national impact claim.

claims: Bilobed leaves, marked flowers with one fertile stamen, dehiscent pods.

proposedDescription: Narrow swordfern is often sold or recorded under names such as tuberous sword fern and fishbone fern. It spreads with runners and can produce underground tubers, helping established clumps persist after the visible fronds are removed. In Florida it is a nonnative fern capable of forming dense stands in natural areas. The name 'Boston fern' is used loosely in horticulture, so a nursery label does not reliably distinguish this plant from native sword ferns.
identification: Inspect the whole plant rather than one frond. Small potato-like tubers attached to the runners are an especially useful positive clue among the sword ferns compared in Florida guides, but a plant without visible tubers is not automatically a different species. Closely spaced leaflets often overlap the frond's central axis. Their tips tend to be blunter than those of native Nephrolepis exaltata. Tiny scales with distinctly dark attachment points and the shape of the covers over spore clusters provide further specialist characters.
actions: Confirm the identification before removing ferns in a natural area, where native relatives may grow beside them. For a small confirmed patch, gather runners and tubers as well as fronds, and keep the material out of dumped garden waste. Check the cleared area repeatedly for regrowth. Avoid sharing divisions from an uncertain garden fern. For a large stand or sensitive habitat, ask a local land manager or extension specialist for a removal plan that protects neighboring vegetation and accounts for repeated follow-up.
researchNotes: UF IFAS supports Florida distinction and management context; independent New Zealand flora supports tubers, runners and spore-cover characters. No claim that all tuber-bearing ferns globally are this species.

proposedDescription: Narrowleaf bittercress is a small mustard whose leafy flowering stems can rise from a low rosette in a second growing season. It has become an unwanted plant in parts of North America, including sites addressed by Minnesota weed programs. The species is easy to overlook among other spring herbs before its stems and slender pods develop. Its modest flowers are less useful at a distance than the way the leaves attach to the stem.
identification: Look for leaves divided into numerous leaflets, with rounded leaflets on the basal rosette and narrower, more pointed ones higher on the plant. At each stem-leaf attachment, a pair of narrow pointed lobes clasps the stem like tiny ears. This is an important distinction from many other bittercresses. The small white flowers may have reduced petals or no obvious petals at all. Long, narrow pods project from the upper stem. Photograph the clasping leaf bases as well as the overall plant; a leafy rosette alone may remain uncertain.
actions: Have a suspected new patch checked before disturbing a mixed woodland herb layer. If removal is recommended, work while plants are young and before ripe pods release seed. Place flowering or fruiting plants directly into a container rather than carrying them loosely along a trail. Clean footwear and tools after working in a patch, and revisit the site for overlooked rosettes and new seedlings. Consult the local weed program about priorities and disposal, because a regional listing does not automatically describe requirements in another state.
researchNotes: Minnesota identification guide and Sorbonne/Jussieu botanical account independently support auricles, compound leaves and reduced petals. U.S. management is localized; no legal category exported between states.

claims: Annual/biennial rosette and flowering stages; pointed clasping auricles and differing leaflet shapes.
Clasping pointed auricles; compound leaves; white often reduced petals; elongated siliques.

proposedDescription: Narrowleaf cattail forms tall stands along wetland margins, with underground rhizomes connecting many shoots. Dense expansion can crowd other marsh plants, and the species can hybridize with broadleaf cattail to produce Typha x glauca. Its North American history is not described consistently: some authorities treat it as native in eastern coastal settings, while others treat it as introduced or emphasize its recent inland expansion. Local ecological context matters more than a blanket label.
identification: Leaves are long, narrow and straplike, rising from the base. The flowering stalk carries a brown female spike below a male spike, usually with an obvious bare gap between them. Broadleaf cattail typically has wider leaves and little or no gap. Those characters are useful clues, but hybrids can be intermediate and mixed stands are common. Measure several plants and photograph flowering spikes, leaf width and the surrounding wetland. An old brown seed head alone may not preserve all the characters needed for a confident determination.
actions: Ask the wetland manager to confirm both the identification and the management objective before cutting or digging. A stand may provide wildlife cover even where its expansion is a concern, and disturbing saturated soil can spread rhizome fragments. Keep excavated material and muddy equipment from being moved to another wetland. Where restoration is warranted, use a planned approach that accounts for water levels, other vegetation and repeated monitoring. Avoid introducing garden cattails into ponds connected to natural waters.
researchNotes: The North Carolina guide explicitly separates coastal native from inland nonnative context; Minnesota's account addresses its own regional problem. Bansal et al. independently explain hybridization, rhizome expansion and variable management results. These regional native-status treatments need not be forced into one nationwide label. The draft preserves hybrid uncertainty and asks for a local wetland objective; no universal origin or treatment claim is required. Review regional qualification and retain expert confirmation of hybrid stands before a restoration response. The inherited PMC page returned a browser challenge and targeted search did not recover its substantive text; it is not counted as newly read evidence. Unused inherited source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3399161/ (not substantively recovered here or superseded by the explicitly identified recovered source).

proposedDescription: Narrowleaf cottonrose is a small woolly annual, also known as French cudweed and formerly placed under Filago gallica. It often grows in open, sparsely vegetated ground rather than forming the conspicuous patches associated with larger weeds. Botanical floras describe it in grassland, roadsides and disturbed places. Its pale covering of fine hairs makes the entire plant look grayish, but many unrelated little cudweeds share that appearance.
identification: Look for narrow, almost threadlike leaves along short branching stems. The leaf edges roll inward or under, giving the blades a stiff appearance. Tiny flower heads sit in compact groups, with the surrounding leaves extending noticeably beyond each cluster. There are no broad, showy daisy petals. Close inspection of the scales around the heads and the small fruits is often needed to separate Logfia from Filago and other woolly members of the daisy family. A photograph should show the branching pattern and a cluster with its surrounding leaves.
actions: If a few plants appear in a garden or restoration plot, confirm their identity before removing other small woolly annuals nearby. Pull unwanted plants before the heads mature and collect the fine seed-bearing material. Avoid scraping a broad area of soil just to eliminate a few scattered plants, since bare ground may favor another flush of annual weeds. For a conservation-site observation, record substrate, associated vegetation and whether plants are isolated or numerous. The available descriptions support recognition and monitoring, not an assumption of major ecological damage.
researchNotes: VicFlora and Flora of New Zealand independently support morphology; INRA confirms confusion with Gnaphalium and Filago. No uncertain Hawaii native/introduced status copied from Kew.

proposedDescription: Narrowleaf firethorn is a spiny evergreen shrub with clusters of white flowers followed by conspicuous orange or yellow-orange fruits. It is widely cultivated, and botanical floras document escape into scrub, roadsides and other open habitats. A hedge can therefore be a seed source beyond its planted boundary. Firethorns include many similar species and garden cultivars, so the common name or fruit color should not be treated as a definitive identification.
identification: Examine several mature leaves and young shoots. This species usually has narrow leaves with mostly smooth, slightly rolled edges and blunt tips. The undersides remain densely pale and woolly, as do the short leaf stalks. Young shoots are also hairy. Other firethorns often have less hairy leaf undersides and more conspicuous teeth. The stems bear true spines, helping distinguish firethorn from similar fruiting cotoneasters. Photograph both leaf surfaces, a thorny shoot and ripe fruit; hybrids or cultivated selections may still require botanical review.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and eye protection when working around the spines. Check beneath bird perches and along nearby fence lines for young plants, and remove unwanted seedlings before they become strongly rooted. Gather fruiting cuttings so seeds are not scattered in garden waste. For a large escaped shrub, plan removal with follow-up rather than assuming a single pruning will finish the job. Where spread threatens native vegetation, discuss a suitable replacement hedge with a local nursery or land manager.
researchNotes: New Zealand and Victoria floras independently agree on persistent underside hairs and narrow entire leaves. Review literature warns of cultivar confusion. Actions are precautionary and do not assert a particular control efficacy.

proposedDescription: Narrowleaf hawksbeard is an annual with small yellow flower heads held on branching stems. Introduced from Europe to North America, it occurs in roadsides, fields, ditches and other disturbed open ground. It begins with basal leaves near the soil, then produces a taller flowering stem whose leaves are much narrower. This change in appearance can make seedlings and mature plants seem unrelated during a casual survey.
identification: The lower leaves are lance-shaped to spoon-shaped and may be toothed or deeply lobed. Upper leaves are narrow, stalkless and clasp the stem with small basal lobes; their edges often roll inward. Several yellow heads develop on one branched plant. That differs from a typical dandelion's single head on each unbranched, leafless stalk. Other hawksbeards remain close lookalikes, and mature fruits can help: those of this species are small, dark reddish brown and marked by ten ribs. Include stem leaves and the outer flower-head bracts in photographs.
actions: Remove small unwanted plants while the taproot is manageable and before seed heads disperse. Collect flowering material instead of leaving it where seeds can finish developing. In a field or restoration area, note the patch boundaries and whether bare ground or repeated disturbance is helping establishment. Avoid moving contaminated soil or seed-bearing clippings to another site. A local botanist or extension office can check an uncertain hawksbeard identification, especially where native yellow-flowered relatives occur. Follow-up observation is more useful than treating every dandelion-like flower as the same weed.
researchNotes: Burke Herbarium supports North American distribution and diagnostic characters; UBC Illustrated Flora independently corroborates narrow clasping rolled leaves and annual taproot. No quantitative impact claim.

proposedDescription: Narrowleaf lupine is an annual Mediterranean legume also known as blue lupin. It has been cultivated and has naturalized in some regions, but an escaped crop plant and a persistent invasive population are different situations. Botanical accounts describe it in open ground, including sandy soils. Its upright flowering stems and hand-shaped leaves make the genus recognizable, while the particularly slender leaflets help narrow the identification.
identification: Each leaf has several narrow leaflets radiating from the end of one stalk. The upper surfaces are relatively smooth, while the undersides carry silky hairs. Blue to purplish pea-shaped flowers rise in a terminal cluster, followed by hairy pods containing several rounded or oval seeds. Flower shade and plant height vary, and white-flowered forms occur. North America has many native lupines, so neither blue flowers nor a palm-shaped leaf proves this species. A useful identification set includes a full leaf, hairs beneath it, flowers and mature pods.
actions: Before removing a wild lupine, ask a local botanist or extension service to distinguish it from native species. Where confirmed plants are unwanted, remove them before pods dry and split, keeping mature pods contained. Check the following growing season for seedlings, particularly near a former planting or disturbed soil. Do not scatter leftover crop seed into natural areas. Avoid assuming that a wild plant is suitable for food or livestock merely because cultivated lupins have agricultural uses; variety and local agricultural guidance matter.
researchNotes: NSW flora and independent Israeli botanical description support narrow leaflets, hairy pods and annual habit. VASCAN confirms regional ephemeral rather than blanket established status; public copy avoids unsupported U.S. invasive designation.

claims: Cultivated naturalized annual, narrow leaflets, blue corolla and hairy pods.
Annual habit, palmately arranged narrow leaflets, occasional white flowers and splitting pods.

proposedDescription: Garden nasturtium is familiar for its round leaves and brightly colored flowers spilling from beds and containers. Some forms remain compact while others scramble over neighboring vegetation. It is commonly grown as a warm-season annual and can spread by self-seeding. Whether it stays within a flower bed or persists beyond cultivation depends on local conditions, so observations of escaped plants should distinguish a planted display from seedlings establishing on their own.
identification: The leaf stalk attaches beneath the blade, away from the edge, giving the leaf a small parasol shape. Veins radiate outward across the rounded surface. Flowers have five petals and a conspicuous backward-pointing spur; cultivated colors include yellow, orange, red and cream. A leafy seedling may resemble other round-leaved plants, but the shieldlike leaf attachment and spurred flowers together are more useful. Despite the common name, garden nasturtium belongs to Tropaeolum and should not be confused with true watercress.
actions: If the plant is spreading beyond its intended bed, gather developing fruits before they drop and pull unwanted seedlings while small. Check the base of fences, nearby banks and places where garden waste has been deposited. Keep seed-bearing cuttings within a contained disposal stream rather than dumping them beside open land. Where a trailing patch covers desired vegetation, work gently from the edges so those plants are not uprooted with it. Ask a local weed program about persistent escapes in sensitive coastal or riparian habitats.
researchNotes: NC State full text supports growth forms and self-seeding; independent Botanical Survey of India flora supports peltate leaves and spurred flowers. NC State page incorrectly lists Nasturtium officinale as previous name; that error is explicitly not adopted.

claims: Climbing and bush forms, parasol leaves, spurred flowers and self-seeding.
T. majus peltate leaves, five petals, elongated spur and cultivated ornamental habit.

proposedDescription: Natal glorybower is an African shrub or small tree also known as tinderwood. Modern Kew taxonomy places Clerodendrum glabrum under Volkameria glabra, while older botanical and horticultural accounts retain the familiar Clerodendrum name. It bears scented flowers and conspicuously odorous leaves, making it memorable when encountered in a garden. The evidence reviewed describes its native-range biology well, but does not establish a clear United States invasion history or species-specific management need.
identification: The simple leaves are arranged opposite one another or in groups of three, and their edges are usually smooth. They may fold slightly upward along the midrib. Young branches have small pale raised dots. Rounded flower clusters contain pinkish or mauve flowers with projecting stamens, followed by pale yellow ripe fruits in the southern African account. Related glorybowers and the broader Volkameria complex can differ in hairiness and flower details. Photograph a branch showing leaf arrangement, the flowers and ripe fruit; an unpleasant leaf smell is only a supporting clue.
actions: If an unfamiliar shrub is producing seedlings outside a planting, record how far they occur from the parent and seek a botanical identification. Keep fruiting prunings out of dumped garden waste while the identification is reviewed. Do not assume that it shares the aggressive root behavior of every other plant called glorybower. Where plants occur on conservation land, let the land manager decide whether monitoring or removal is appropriate. No broad control recommendation is justified without better regional evidence.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: SANBI describes var. glabrum, and the 2021 southern African tree checklist retains Volkameria glabra and V. eriophylla separately. Kew instead includes eriophyllum under V. glabra; its copied regional flora explicitly compares the two former species. The genus transfer is clear, but the concurrently different circumscriptions affect which hairy or nearly hairless plants the species profile covers. This is more than the ordinary need for a local occurrence record. Have the catalog owner identify its taxonomic authority and obtain a US voucher determination against the same circumscription. The old Kew synonym URL was blocked and not substantively recovered: https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn%3Alsid%3Aipni.org%3Anames%3A862099-1 . The accepted-name page and its regional-flora text were recovered instead.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: The traditional southern African glabrum concept can be described while broader Volkameria synonymy remains explicit. SANBI independently describes the local plant; regional flora records distinguish hairy eriophylla while Kew combines it. This is a stated circumscription difference, not a need to assign unexamined US specimens before writing a general profile. Next step: Review the traditional glabrum account and retain local occurrence and broader synonym crosswalks separately. proposedDescription: Natal plum is a dense evergreen shrub often planted as a hedge in warm coastal gardens. Glossy foliage, fragrant white flowers and red plumlike fruits make it attractive, but the strong thorns deserve equal attention. It belongs to the dogbane family, not the true plum genus Prunus. Plantings vary greatly in height because dwarf forms are common, so size alone is a poor way to decide whether two shrubs are the same species.
identification: Leaves are thick, smooth-edged and arranged opposite one another. The conspicuous thorns often fork into two points. White flowers have overlapping lobes that create a star or pinwheel appearance, and oval fruits turn red to purplish as they ripen. Damaged stems release milky latex, although there is no need to break a branch for identification. Other Carissa species and compact cultivars can be confusing; photographs should include the forked thorns, paired leaves and a flower rather than fruit alone.
actions: Keep thorny branches away from paths and play areas, and use sturdy gloves and eye protection when pruning. Inspect nearby ground for volunteer seedlings if fruit regularly falls outside the bed. Remove unwanted young plants before their thorny structure makes access difficult, and collect fruiting cuttings rather than dumping them. Check local guidance before choosing it for a natural-area boundary. Do not treat every plant part as food because the ripe fruit has culinary uses; identification and ripeness matter, and the latex should be avoided.
researchNotes: NC State supports leaves, latex caution and ripe fruit; independent Stanford field account corroborates bifurcate thorns and fragrant flowers. No regional invasive severity or whole-plant toxicity exaggeration.

claims: Evergreen opposite leathery leaves, white flowers, red fruits, latex and naturalization.
Forked thorns, fragrant white flowers and older C. grandiflora name.

proposedDescription: The naval shipworm is a clam transformed for life inside submerged wood. Its long soft body looks wormlike, but two small shell valves at the front act as cutting tools. It can tunnel through driftwood, pilings, boats and other timber, leaving damage far more extensive than the small entrance holes suggest. Centuries of transport in wooden vessels have obscured its original range, and its native or introduced status needs regional interpretation.
identification: A piece of affected wood may contain winding tunnels lined with a thin chalky layer. The animal remains inside, with siphons reaching the water through a small opening. Species identification relies heavily on the paired hard structures called pallets, which close the tunnel when the siphons withdraw. In Teredo navalis these are broadly paddlelike, with particular blade and stalk proportions. Other shipworms make similar tunnels, so photographs of bored wood establish wood-borer activity much more readily than they establish this species.
actions: If pilings, a dock or a wooden vessel show suspected damage, arrange a professional structural or marine inspection before relying on the timber. Photograph exposed tunnels and keep the date and location of the finding. Do not transport waterlogged infested wood to another waterbody or attempt to treat submerged structures with household chemicals. A marine laboratory can advise whether a small sample is needed for identification. On natural shorelines, leave ordinary driftwood in place unless the responsible land manager requests a documented sample.
researchNotes: Smithsonian supports cryptogenic global history and damage; Fisheries and Oceans Canada independently supports pallet-based identification and similar shipworms. No unsupported claim that every coast population is introduced.

proposedDescription: Navigating big-headed ant is a tiny reddish-brown ant with two noticeably different worker sizes. A minority have oversized heads, while the more numerous small workers look much less distinctive. It is recorded as an introduced ant in the southeastern United States and Hawaii. Older records may call it Pheidole moerens, reflecting a later taxonomic correction. Local abundance does not justify assigning it the severe impacts documented for every other big-headed ant.
identification: Look for the large-headed workers among a trail of small reddish ants. Under magnification, workers have a two-part waist, clubbed antennae and small spines near the rear of the thorax. Separating this species from related Pheidole requires fine head sculpture and other specialist characters, especially on major workers. In Hawaii the small workers can resemble little fire ants, which do not have a separate oversized-headed soldier caste. Mixed colonies or a limited photograph can still mislead, so apparent worker size differences are a clue rather than a complete diagnosis.
actions: Inspect pots, soil, hollow twigs and other materials before moving them between properties or islands. If identification is uncertain, use the local ant-survey program's collection instructions and submit a sample that includes both worker sizes when possible. Record whether ants are outdoors in wood or litter, or entering a building. Do not apply a species-specific treatment solely from a phone-image match. In Hawaii, reporting an uncertain little-fire-ant lookalike can prevent both missed detections and unnecessary treatment.
researchNotes: Mississippi museum specimen work supports U.S. history and morphology; Maui program supplies independent local survey observations and LFA comparison. Maui full text states impacts uncertain, not a major pest; preserved that restraint.

proposedDescription: Dothistroma needle blight is a fungal disease that can thin the foliage of susceptible pines after repeated infections. Dothistroma septosporum is one cause of this disease. Moist conditions favor spore production and infection, so dense plantings and frequently wet foliage can be important parts of the setting. A tree may lose older needles while retaining green growth at branch tips, giving the crown a sparse, tufted appearance rather than killing it all at once.
identification: Reddish-brown spots can expand into bands around individual needles. The needle tip beyond a band dies while the base initially remains green. Tiny black fruiting structures may emerge through affected tissue. These clues are useful, but brown spot and other needle diseases can look similar, and weather injury can also brown needles. Note which pine species is affected and whether damage is concentrated on older needles or lower branches. A plant-disease laboratory may need symptomatic needles to distinguish the cause.
actions: Reduce unnecessary wetting of the canopy by adjusting irrigation, and allow room for air movement when planning or thinning plantings. Gather information on when symptoms began, recent weather and any nearby affected trees before requesting a diagnosis. Avoid removing large numbers of healthy branches just to expose the trunk. If disease is confirmed, ask extension or a qualified arborist about a plan for that pine and location. Treatments cannot turn already dead needles green, so judge progress by subsequent foliage and repeated observations.
researchNotes: Montana and Minnesota extension independently support symptoms and canopy moisture management; BC supports splash dispersal and host-region differences. Avoids exporting regional host rankings or calendar and gives no pesticide recipe.

proposedDescription: Stigmina deflectens is a fungus associated with needlecast of junipers. Symptoms can resemble those caused by other juniper diseases, and a local laboratory assessment is needed to understand an affected plant. It should not be confused with better-publicized Stigmina diseases of spruce simply because the genus name is shared. Browning juniper foliage is a reason to investigate, not evidence that this fungus is responsible.
identification: An older USDA diagnostic account describes minute brown fungal structures along the sides of the central vein on the upper surface of needles, appearing after foliage begins to brown. Both the leaves and the structures are very small. The same account warns that similar fungi can occur on juniper foliage and that the disease is unlikely to be recognized from visible symptoms alone. A close photograph may document damage, but confirming the species requires microscopic examination by a plant-pathology service.
actions: Record the juniper's identity, the pattern of browning and the date symptoms were first noticed. Photograph the entire plant and several affected shoots, including the boundary between green and brown foliage. Ask a diagnostic laboratory how to collect and package a sample before cutting or mailing branches. Avoid moving suspect nursery plants until the problem is assessed. Do not choose a fungicide or remove a healthy neighboring juniper on the basis of a generic needlecast label. Management should follow a confirmed diagnosis and current local plant-health advice.
