proposedDescription: Nepalese firethorn is an evergreen shrub with spiny branches, white flower clusters and bright red fruits. Native to the Himalayan region, it has been cultivated in many mild climates and has escaped into some roadsides, scrub and stream margins. Birds can carry firethorn fruits beyond a hedge, so seedlings may appear well away from the original planting. Regional accounts describe differing levels of spread; the plant is not equally troublesome in every setting.
identification: Look for relatively narrow leaves with fine teeth along most of the edge. Both surfaces of mature leaves are essentially hairless, unlike narrowleaf firethorn, Pyracantha angustifolia, whose undersides are densely pale and woolly. Young twigs can have rusty hairs that disappear as they age. The small round fruits become red or crimson. Broadleaf firethorn and ornamental selections remain possible lookalikes, so compare several mature leaves and include close photographs of their undersides, margins and fruit. Thorns distinguish firethorns from otherwise similar cotoneasters.
actions: Wear gloves and protect your eyes when reaching into a shrub. Remove unwanted seedlings while they are small, particularly along reserve boundaries and beneath bird perches. Contain ripe fruits and fruiting branches during cleanup. Do not assume that clipping the top of an established escaped shrub will prevent its return; plan follow-up with the land manager. Where a hedge is producing persistent escapes, consider a locally appropriate replacement, and check regional guidance before planting additional firethorns.
researchNotes: NSW flora supplies independent morphology; NZPCN independently supports close-species comparison; Cal-IPC provides California escape and bird-dispersal context without universalizing its rating.

proposedDescription: Nepalese smartweed is a low, spreading annual with small rounded clusters of pinkish or white flowers. Its natural range extends through parts of Africa and Asia, so its name captures only a small part of its geography. Stems can root at their lower joints and rise from a sprawling base. Unlike the long flower spikes of many familiar smartweeds, this species presents its flowers in little heads close to the upper leaves.
identification: The leaves are oval to somewhat triangular and may carry a dark central blotch, although the blotch is not a dependable identification mark. The blade tapers down along the stalk, which often has small earlike lobes near its base. A thin sheath surrounds the stem at each leaf joint, as in other members of the knotweed family. Flower heads commonly have a leaf immediately beneath them. Mature dark fruits are distinctly pitted. Related head-flowered smartweeds can look very similar, so include the leaf bases, sheaths and ripe fruits in a botanical review.
actions: For a suspected escape, record whether plants are rooted outside a maintained bed and whether they recur in later seasons. Remove small unwanted plants before fruit develops only after distinguishing them from local native smartweeds. Collect rooted stem portions rather than leaving them on damp soil. Keep soil and plant fragments out of dumped garden waste. In a wetland or streamside setting, ask the land manager to verify the species and decide whether action is warranted before disturbing the vegetation.
researchNotes: Flora of Bhutan and Flora Zambesiaca via Kew independently support head flowers, auriculate decurrent leaves and rooting annual habit. No U.S. impact or distribution assertion beyond observed-sighting guidance.

claims: Annual habit, globose heads, leaf subtending head, auriculate leaf stalks and pitted fruits.
African and Asian native range, lower-node rooting and decurrent leaf bases.

proposedDescription: Nettleleaf goosefoot is a branching annual of disturbed, often nutrient-rich ground. The name Chenopodiastrum murale is used in current botanical treatments, while Chenopodium murale remains common in older references. It can develop a bushy outline and reddish tones as it matures, but lacks the conspicuous flowers of many garden weeds. Its small green flowers and variable toothed leaves make careful comparison more useful than a quick match based on color.
identification: Leaves alternate along the stems and are usually diamond-shaped to broadly triangular, with coarse, uneven teeth. Young parts may have a light meal-like coating, but the plant is not necessarily densely white or gray. Tiny flowers form branching leafy clusters toward the tips and in upper leaf axils. Mature seeds are black, flattened and sharply edged, with minute pits visible under magnification. Other goosefoots have overlapping leaf shapes, so photograph mature leaves, the arrangement of flower clusters and fruiting material. The common name does not make it a stinging nettle.
actions: In cultivated ground, remove unwanted seedlings before the inconspicuous flowers develop mature seeds. Gather seed-bearing plants carefully rather than shaking them over a clean bed. Maintain desired ground cover where practical and avoid repeatedly leaving bare, enriched soil beside a patch. If the plant appears in hay, pasture or a food garden, seek local identification and management advice rather than assuming it is interchangeable with another edible goosefoot. Keep a dated record of recurring patches so follow-up can focus on places where seedlings repeatedly emerge.
researchNotes: Kew FTEA and New Zealand flora independently support morphology, including seed details. Name update is explained without modifying the catalog ID. No edibility recommendation or national invasive severity claim.

proposedDescription: Nettleleaf velvetberry belongs to the porterweeds, flowering plants with slender spikes that can look deceptively alike. Kew accepts Stachytarpheta urticifolia as a species native from the Caribbean into northern South America. Other major treatments include it within S. cayennensis. That disagreement matters when interpreting reports of escaped plants: a record under one name may represent a broader group than the plant intended here. A local specimen needs careful identification before information about Cayenne porterweed can be applied to it.
identification: Sharply toothed, broadly oval leaves accompany dark blue to purple flowers with a lighter throat. These are clues, not a complete identification. A published comparison of regional floras found disagreement even over the number of calyx teeth, the little points surrounding the flower base. Pale flowering S. cayennensis, S. jamaicensis and hybrids complicate identification further. A photograph of one blue flower cannot reliably resolve this group. Young plants without developed flower spikes are especially difficult to assign.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, leaf edges, stem, flower spike and flower bases, including a ruler for scale. Record whether it was planted or appeared independently, and keep nursery labels with the observation. Ask a regional herbarium which taxonomic treatment it uses before recording a confirmed species. Avoid sharing seed or moving flowering cuttings from an uncertain escaped population. If removal is appropriate locally, collect reproductive material securely and revisit the site for seedlings. Preserve nearby native porterweeds until identification is settled.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Fresh full-text reading of Chandler, Westaway and Conn's original comparison confirms conflicting calyx and leaf characters and difficulty locating the urticifolia type. Kew accepts it but records alternative cayennensis treatments. Two sources substantiate the conflict rather than eliminate it. Assigning an unverified local plant to one narrow concept could transfer the wrong diagnostic or invasive claims. Resolve the taxon concept against a modern revision and inspect catalog-linked US vouchers before narrowing this profile.

A named aggregate might be possible, but the current exact-species scope is not demonstrated by these conflicting characters. Next step: Have a taxonomic reviewer define the intended type-linked or broad cayennensis concept before promoting the exact profile. proposedDescription: Neverdie is a fleshy perennial plant in the stonecrop family. Its thick leaves help it occupy seasonally dry settings, and older plants can become small, upright shrubs. Kew places its native range in tropical and southern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, with introductions including Florida and several Caribbean islands. An introduced occurrence is not, by itself, evidence of damaging invasion. For an observation near a garden, the useful first distinction is between a maintained planting and plants establishing beyond cultivation.
identification: Look for opposite, fleshy leaves with rounded or blunt teeth along the edges. South African descriptions report oval to oblong leaves, often folded along the midline, on rounded upright stems. The yellow to orange flowers have elongated tubes and small spreading lobes. The leaf stalk and clasping leaf base deserve close photographs. Many other kalanchoes have similar succulent foliage, so a leaf alone is insufficient. Do not assume that this species produces the conspicuous rows of tiny leaf-edge plantlets associated with some other kalanchoes.
actions: Keep an unfamiliar succulent out of food or home-remedy preparations. Photograph a flowering stem, a pair of leaves and their attachment to the stem before making a species record. For unwanted plants on your property, collect loose stems and leaves along with the rooted plant, and keep that material out of natural areas and garden-waste dumping sites. Check the surrounding ground for additional plants. Where an apparent escape is extensive, ask local extension staff to confirm the identity and regional significance before planning broader removal.
researchNotes: Two independent botanical lineages support identity and range. No species-specific US ecological impact or eradication efficacy asserted; vegetative debris containment is precautionary, not a claim of demonstrated regeneration from every leaf.

claims: Succulent shrub, leaf morphology, tubular yellow to orange flowers.
Accepted species, African and Arabian native range, introduced Florida and Caribbean records.

proposedDescription: The New Guinea flatworm is a land-dwelling predator of snails and other small invertebrates. It shelters in damp places beneath pots, stones and leaf litter, so movement of planted containers and their associated soil deserves attention. Researchers documented Florida and Puerto Rico records in a study published in 2015. Its ecological significance comes especially from predation on land snails, including vulnerable native species; it should never be released as a garden snail-control animal.
identification: This animal is broad and flattened rather than cylindrical like an earthworm. Its dark brown to nearly black upper surface usually carries a narrow pale stripe down the middle, while the underside is much lighter. The head narrows into a snout with two eyes set behind its tip. The Florida wildlife agency notes that strong light can make the stripe difficult to see. Unlike hammerhead flatworms, it lacks a broad, sideways-expanded head. Color and body length alone are insufficient, particularly when an animal is contracted or photographed only from above.
actions: Inspect pot bases and damp packing materials before moving plants between properties. Photograph a suspected flatworm with a size reference, taking views of the head and back without handling it barehanded. Report an unfamiliar occurrence to your state wildlife, agriculture or extension office with its location and the circumstances of discovery. Keep suspect plants and soil from being distributed while you seek advice. Do not transport live specimens across state lines without instructions from the receiving authority. Avoid disturbing adjacent native snails while documenting the animal.
researchNotes: FWC field account and original 2015 PeerJ records are separate lineages. Historical records are dated; no claim of complete current national distribution. Barehand avoidance is a precaution, not a claim of direct disease transmission.

claims: Body and head characters, damp habitats, prey and movement considerations.

proposedDescription: New World screwworm is a fly whose larvae feed on living animal tissue. Livestock, pets, wildlife and people can be affected. The problem begins when females lay eggs around wounds or body openings; developing larvae burrow into the tissue and can rapidly worsen the injury. This is an urgent animal-health and public-health concern, not an ordinary household fly nuisance. Where it occurs and how officials are responding can change quickly. Follow the linked USDA guidance for current information; earlier eradication does not mean there is no present risk.
identification: Warning signs include maggots or pale egg masses in a wound, an enlarging or foul-smelling injury, and unusual pain or irritation. An affected animal may stop eating, become depressed or separate from the group. Larvae may be deep within a wound rather than plainly visible on the surface. These signs require assessment even when the wound began as a small injury. Other flies also cause wound infestations, so appearance alone cannot confirm New World screwworm; laboratory identification belongs with trained professionals.
actions: Immediately contact a veterinarian, your state animal-health office or USDA if an animal has suspicious wound larvae. Follow their instructions about examination, samples and animal movement. Do not wait for a photograph-based identification before seeking help. A person with suspected wound infestation should obtain prompt medical care and tell the clinician about travel and animal exposure. Avoid trying to remove or treat larvae using improvised chemicals. Check current official animal-travel requirements before moving pets or livestock from affected places.
researchNotes: Current APHIS status and reporting pages checked 2026-10-29. Avoids outdated US absence claims and does not reproduce volatile case counts. CDC independently supports human risk, living-tissue feeding and prompt clinical assessment; no treatment recipe or diagnostic certainty offered.

proposedDescription: The name New Zealand burr can be misleading for Acaena magellanica. This creeping perennial occurs in southern South America and on several southern islands; the common name does not describe its full range. Its burrs are useful clues: they can attach to clothing or animals and carry the plant's fruits away. Any proposed US observation should be checked against a regional botanical key and a documented specimen; the reviewed evidence does not establish a US population.
identification: Candidate plants form low mats with leaves divided into several paired, toothed leaflets and a terminal leaflet. The foliage often appears grayish or bluish green. Small flowers are packed into rounded heads, followed by fruits bearing stiff spines with hooked tips. The Argentine national-parks account describes creeping plants and three or four fruit spines; the New Zealand treatment describes four conspicuous barbed spines. Other Acaena species also make mats and burrs, and the count, length and surface of the fruit structures matter more than the common name.
actions: Photograph leaves from above and below, a complete flowering or fruiting head, and individual mature burrs beside a scale. Record any nursery label and whether the patch was deliberately planted. Brush attached burrs from footwear, pets and equipment before leaving the site, collecting them rather than scattering them along a trail. Avoid moving rooted mats or contaminated soil into natural areas. Ask a herbarium to resolve the name before removing a population believed to be rare, native or a different ornamental burr species.
researchNotes: Fresh Argentina and New Zealand accounts agree on the creeping habit, divided leaves and hooked fruit. Kew confirms southern South American and subantarctic range; the NZPCN endemic tag conflicts with its own wider distribution text. The geographic metadata error does not demonstrate a different taxon concept. The draft can describe the supported species and require documentation for any proposed US record without claiming established US populations or harm. Ready for editorial review. Keep US occurrence verification as a record-level task, and do not infer an invasive designation from the common name. The inherited Kew base URL could not be recovered substantively after blocking; the same taxon's general-information page was read through indexed text. proposedDescription: New Zealand flax mealybug is associated with Phormium, the ornamental plant with long, strap-shaped leaves. Colonies can remain tucked into the crowded bases of those leaves, making a casual inspection of the foliage misleading. The Royal Horticultural Society reports that this insect can survive outdoors through British winters, unlike many greenhouse mealybugs. Outdoor survival in the United States depends on local conditions. Modern ScaleNet records place the species in Trionymus, while many practical references retain Balanococcus diminutus.
identification: Look for small insects surrounded by fluffy white wax in sheltered parts of a Phormium clump. Sticky honeydew and dark sooty growth can accompany feeding, although neither symptom identifies the species by itself. The host plant is a useful starting point, not a substitute for examining an insect. The USDA identification resource distinguishes this mealybug from similar Trionymus species using microscopic ducts with a strongly hardened collar. That character cannot be checked reliably in a phone photograph, and immature individuals may need specialist examination.
actions: Before bringing a new Phormium into a collection, inspect the leaf bases as well as the exposed blades. Keep a suspect pot separate from other plants and avoid passing along divisions until the insects have been identified. Photograph the colony, the entire host and any sticky or sooty areas. A plant clinic can advise how to submit a sample without spreading live insects. If infested leaves or plants are removed, contain the debris and clean tools before using them on other clumps. Use locally appropriate professional guidance for persistent infestations.
researchNotes: ScaleNet confirms revived Trionymus combination; USDA diagnostic source and RHS horticultural account independently support identification and host context. Oregon State also documents a Phormium infestation. No extrapolation of British winter survival to all US climates.

claims: Phormium association, wax, honeydew, sooty mold and British outdoor survival.
Microscopic distinction from similar Trionymus and quarantine observations.
Current Trionymus diminutus combination and nomenclatural history.

proposedDescription: New Zealand geranium, here the type-matching New Zealand form, is a small perennial cranesbill, not the showy bedding plant commonly sold as a geranium. Its identity needs unusually careful regional checking. New Zealand botanists describe several forms under this name and distinguish the typical native plant from unresolved related forms. Australian treatments also warn that some plants assigned to the name differ from the New Zealand type. A record in a disturbed place therefore does not establish either a foreign origin or the correct species.
identification: The most useful visible clue is the short hair covering on stems and leaf stalks: in the typical form, hairs point backward and lie close against the surface. Leaves are palmately divided into five to seven main sections, which divide again into narrower lobes. Small pinkish to pale flowers develop into elongated, beaked fruits. Mature seeds and the shape of the rootstock can help specialists separate this plant from Geranium solanderi and related cranesbills. Juvenile leaves and a single flower are not enough to settle the identification.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, both leaf surfaces and close views of stem hairs with good side lighting. Include flowers and mature fruit whenever possible, and record the surrounding habitat. Do not dig up a plant merely to inspect its root, especially in a protected site or native-range population. Ask a regional herbarium which form or species concept applies to the observation. Until that is resolved, avoid distributing seed and avoid treating an uncertain cranesbill patch as an invasive-species removal target.

Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: The current VicFlora update explicitly calls this an unresolved species complex and distinguishes most Victorian plants from the New Zealand type. NZPCN independently distinguishes three races and gives a type-matching diagnosis. This is a real circumscription problem with conservation consequences, not a missing control trial. A unified US description requires determining which entity its material represents. Secure catalog-linked US vouchers and compare them with the New Zealand type concept and the revised Australian treatment.

Fresh NZPCN text expressly defines its described form as type-matching; the independent Victorian treatment explains the excluded divergent material. proposedDescription: New Zealand hebe is a coastal shrub better known botanically today as Veronica speciosa. It is native to parts of New Zealand, where naturally occurring populations belong in a conservation context. The plant is also grown ornamentally for its glossy foliage and rich magenta flower clusters. A garden specimen outside that range is not automatically an invasive population. Nursery plants need extra care in identification because hybrids are frequently sold under the species name.
identification: Look for a stout, spreading shrub with opposite pairs of broad, dark green, leathery leaves. Flower clusters arise as compact spikes beside the leaves and contain many magenta to reddish-purple flowers. The New Zealand Plant Conservation Network highlights a fine pink or red margin on the fleshy leaves, with tiny hairs along that edge. Photographing that detail can be more useful than a distant picture of the flowers. Similar hebe cultivars may combine broad leaves and colorful spikes, so the overall appearance does not prove that a plant is the wild species.
actions: Keep the nursery label and any information about the plant's origin. Photograph a mature leaf edge, the arrangement of leaves on a branch and a complete flowering spike before requesting identification. If plants are appearing outside a maintained garden, record seedlings separately from the original shrub and ask local botanical staff whether escape has been documented nearby. Avoid putting prunings or seed-bearing material into coastal habitat. Within its native range, leave wild plants undisturbed and consult conservation authorities before collecting or managing them.
researchNotes: NZPCN and University of Auckland botanical accounts support species characters and native setting. Modern Veronica name noted without changing ID. Nursery-hybrid warning retained; no unsupported US impact or broad invasiveness claim.

claims: Magenta flowers, distinctive leaf margin, coastal native habitat and hybrid confusion.
Shrub habit, opposite leathery leaves and reddish magenta lateral spikes.

proposedDescription: The New Zealand mud snail is a tiny freshwater snail that can travel unnoticed on wet fishing gear, boats and equipment. Introduced populations in North America include females that reproduce without mating and give birth to live young, allowing a small introduction to grow. Some invaded streams support extremely dense populations. Effects vary with the waterbody, but prevention is particularly important because established populations in natural waters are difficult to control.
identification: Adults are usually only a few millimeters long, with an elongated, coiled shell that is gray to brown. Hold the shell tip upward and the opening generally appears on the right. A living snail has a small lid, or operculum, that closes the opening. USGS describes deep grooves between the shell's whorls, but shell sculpture varies between populations. Numerous native freshwater snails are also small and right-coiled. Specialists may need a close examination, and empty shells lose some useful features, so a confident identification should not rest on size alone.
actions: Inspect and scrub waders, boot seams, nets, anchors and other equipment before leaving the water, removing mud and attached organisms. Drain retained water and follow the receiving state's current mud-snail decontamination guidance before using gear elsewhere; a quick rinse or a short air-dry is not dependable. Avoid felt-soled waders where they can retain contaminated material. Do not move live snails to another waterbody for identification. Photograph a suspected occurrence and report it to the state aquatic-invasive-species program, including the site and equipment or habitat where it was found.
researchNotes: USGS technical morphology and Minnesota field-management account used as distinct agency treatments; Minnesota law and fixed drying periods are not generalized nationally. No chemical or heat treatment recipe provided.

claims: Shell characters, variation and introduced population context.
Clonal reproduction, gear pathways, specialist identification and prevention.

proposedDescription: New Zealand nightshade, also called poroporo or kangaroo apple, is a softly woody shrub native to New Zealand and parts of the southwest Pacific region, including eastern Australia. It often occupies open or disturbed ground, forest edges and coastal settings. Some populations are conservation concerns in their native range. Its presence in a garden or an introduced-range record should therefore be described in its local context, rather than treated as evidence that the plant is harmful everywhere.
identification: Look for a shrub without prickles, bearing alternate leaves that may be long and narrow or deeply divided into a few large lobes. This mixture of leaf shapes can occur on the same plant. Flowers are blue-violet to paler shades with a prominent yellow center, followed by rounded to oval orange or reddish fruit. New Zealand botanists emphasize that nonflowering material cannot reliably separate this species from its close relatives. Solanum laciniatum is a particular source of confusion, so mature flower form and other reproductive details should accompany a record.
actions: Do not taste berries or use leaf shape as a guide to edibility. Keep unknown fruit away from children and pets. Photograph the whole shrub, both divided and undivided leaves, a fully open flower and mature fruit if present. Record whether the plant was cultivated and whether independent seedlings occur nearby. Where an escape needs management, ask local extension or botanical staff to confirm the species before removing it. Contain fruit-bearing material and check the site for subsequent seedlings; leave native-range wild populations undisturbed without appropriate guidance.
researchNotes: NSW flora and NZPCN support morphology and native context. NZPCN var. aviculare evidence is labeled in sources; no variety-wide statements about every form or unsupported US invasion impact. Poisonous-plant warning avoids food-use advice.

claims: Unarmed shrub, variable leaves, flowers, fruit and disturbed habitat.
Native range, poisonous status and limits of sterile identification.

proposedDescription: New Zealand spinach is a low, fleshy plant also known as warrigal greens. It has been cultivated as a vegetable, but escaped plants can occupy beaches, dunes and coastal wetland margins. California assessments describe local displacement of native vegetation, including problems on the Farallon Islands. That regional concern should not erase its native coastal role elsewhere. Botanical references also use the spelling Tetragonia tetragonoides for the same familiar name, so both spellings can be useful when checking records.
identification: The plant spreads outward on succulent stems and bears thick, roughly triangular to diamond-shaped leaves. Small yellow flowers sit where the leaves meet the stem, rather than forming a conspicuous flower head. Mature fruits become hard and angular, with hornlike projections that are particularly useful for identification. Young, nonflowering shoots can be confused with other fleshy coastal plants. Photograph leaf surfaces and fruit together; a broad green leaf alone is a poor basis for distinguishing the species or confirming a new occurrence.
actions: Where this plant is an unwanted escape, map the patch and check its edges for smaller plants before beginning removal. Work carefully around fragile dune vegetation and avoid trampling neighboring native plants. Collect mature fruits with the removed material so they are not scattered along paths or moved in soil. Revisit after suitable growing conditions to look for seedlings. Do not dump garden-grown plants on beaches or marsh margins. Use a regional identification guide before acting on a coastal population, especially where related or native plants occur.
researchNotes: Independent California impact assessment and New Zealand botanical account support regional framing and morphology. Life span differs across sources, so no universal annual/perennial claim. Spelling variant noted without ID changes. NSW notes possible entities within broad concept; diagnostic confirmation advised.

claims: Fleshy habit, yellow axillary flowers, California coastal habitats and local impacts.
Native coastal context, triangular fleshy leaves and horned woody fruits.
Spelling correction and broad-concept caution.

proposedDescription: Ngaio tree is a New Zealand evergreen that has also been widely planted as a screen or ornamental shrub. In coastal California it has escaped into woodland and streamside settings, where dense stands can crowd native vegetation. Its status is different within its native range, and local plantings should be assessed accordingly. The foliage is toxic to livestock, so grazing is not an appropriate way to manage an unwanted stand.
identification: Look for a shrub or small tree with glossy, somewhat fleshy leaves dotted with translucent glands. Holding a leaf against the light can make those dots easier to see without damaging the tree. Young growth may be sticky and bronze-green. Small white flowers carry purple markings, and fruits become reddish purple. Serrated, gland-spotted leaves help separate ngaio from Myoporum insulare, but hybrids can blur that distinction. Distorted shoots may also reflect feeding by myoporum thrips; damage alone does not establish the tree's identity.
actions: Photograph the foliage against light, a leaf edge, flowers or fruit, and the whole plant. Check nearby natural areas for seedlings beyond the original hedge. When removal is warranted, start with small plants where they can be lifted without disturbing sensitive habitat, and seek a site-specific plan for mature trees. Cutting alone should not be assumed to finish the job; monitor surviving bases and new seedlings. Keep cut foliage away from livestock and contain fruit-bearing branches. Choose replacement plants suited to the local habitat, and avoid moving prunings into creek corridors or coastal scrub.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC and NZPCN provide independent regional ecological and botanical accounts. Avoids livestock grazing because toxicity is documented. Does not claim thrips-resistant cultivars are safe or advise introducing thrips.

claims: California escape, dense stands, flower/fruit appearance and livestock toxicity.
Native context, gland-spotted serrate leaves, M. insulare and hybrid confusion.
Translucent leaf dots and sticky bronze-green young growth.

proposedDescription: Night and afternoon, also called pastel flower, is a small perennial herb or low subshrub in the acanthus family. Kew recognizes its native range in eastern Australia and New Caledonia and records introductions in Florida, Puerto Rico and South Carolina. Those records establish occurrence outside the native range, not the degree of ecological harm. In its native region it grows in several coastal habitats, particularly moist forests, which helps explain why a shaded garden observation can be plausible.
identification: Plants commonly stand only a few tens of centimeters tall, with hairy branches and simple, mostly untoothed leaves that range from narrow to broadly oval. Leaf undersides may be purple. The showier flowers occur toward the top of an elongated flowering shoot and are white to mauve, sometimes with darker spots on a lower lobe. Less conspicuous flowers lower down may remain closed and self-pollinate. This difference between flower types is useful to notice. Other small members of the acanthus family can look similar, especially before flowering.
actions: Photograph an entire flowering shoot, the upper and lower flower positions, both leaf surfaces and any capsules. Record whether the plant is an intentional groundcover or has appeared away from a planting. Avoid assuming that a lack of showy blooms means there is no seed production. If an unwanted patch is removed, contain stems bearing capsules and check nearby shaded ground for additional plants. Ask local extension or herbarium staff to confirm unfamiliar escapes and their significance. Finding it outside its native range does not by itself mean that removing it will benefit this site; confirm local priorities first.
researchNotes: Independent NSW flora and Kew distribution support identity and US occurrence. No direct species-specific US impact evidence found; draft deliberately makes no damaging-invasion claim. Closed lower flowers are species-level flora evidence, not inferred from genus.

claims: Small perennial, leaf variation, showy terminal and often closed lower flowers.
Accepted name, native eastern Australia/New Caledonia and specified introduced regions.

proposedDescription: Night jessamine is a woody shrub whose small flowers become strongly fragrant in the evening. Despite the familiar name, it belongs to the nightshade family rather than the true jasmines. It was introduced to Hawai'i as an ornamental and has naturalized in some wetter forest settings. Its ability to grow in shade makes an escape beneath trees worth checking. A fragrant garden shrub and an expanding forest population require different local responses.
identification: Look for arching or wavy branches carrying alternate, shiny, oblong to oval leaves. The flowers occur in clusters and have long, narrow, pale greenish or creamy tubes with small pointed lobes at their tips. Mature berries are white. This combination helps separate it from day jessamine, Cestrum diurnum, whose mature berries are dark and whose flowers open during the day. Flowering time and scent are supporting clues, not substitutes for leaves and fruit. Nonflowering young shrubs are much easier to confuse with other ornamental species.
actions: Do not eat the berries or use the leaves as a tea; keep unknown Cestrum material away from children, pets and livestock. Photograph leaves, an entire flower cluster and mature fruit before requesting identification. Where a confirmed escape is unwanted, check beyond the planted shrub for seedlings and collect fruit-bearing material during removal. Large woody plants or infestations within forest should be handled through a local management plan that protects neighboring vegetation. Revisit treated ground for surviving plants and seedlings, and avoid dumping branches into moist woodland or streamside areas.
researchNotes: University of Hawaii species account supports regional invasion and distinction from C. diurnum. NC State genus account supports toxicity caution and specifically describes C. nocturnum form; toxicity symptoms and chemical control recipes not transferred. USFS Hawaii report independently documents management target.

claims: Night flowers, white fruit, alternate leaves, day-jessamine distinction and wet-forest invasion.

proposedDescription: Nightblooming cactus is one of the climbing cacti grown for dragon fruit. Modern botanical references generally call it Selenicereus undatus, while Hylocereus undatus remains common in horticultural information. Kew places its native range from Mexico to Honduras and records introductions in several warm regions, including Florida and Hawai'i. It can become a substantial mass of fleshy stems on a support. Cultivation or an introduced-range record alone does not demonstrate that every planting threatens nearby habitat.
identification: Look for jointed, green, climbing stems with broad, wavy ribs, usually presenting a three-sided form. Small spines occur along the edges, and aerial roots help stems attach to supports. Large pale flowers open at night. The familiar cultivated form develops red-skinned fruit with white flesh and many small dark seeds. However, dragon-fruit cultivars include other species and hybrids, so fruit color or the common name is not sufficient for a botanical identification. A nonflowering stem should be recorded cautiously when its provenance is unknown.
actions: Keep labels or cultivar records with garden plants and photograph stem edges, flowers and fruit when seeking confirmation. Wear protective gloves when handling stems, and support heavy growth before pruning so it cannot fall onto people or neighboring plants. Collect cut segments rather than leaving them against trees or on open ground, because pitayas are readily propagated from cuttings. Where a plant has escaped cultivation, ask local botanical or extension staff to confirm its identity and assess the site. Avoid distributing unidentified cuttings or dumping them in warm coastal or woodland habitat.
researchNotes: Kew confirms Selenicereus synonymy and range; UF horticultural account supports cultivated biology and cutting propagation. Cultivar/hybrid identification caveat retained. Native status of all pitaya cultivars not assumed, and no unverified broad invasive impact asserted.

proposedDescription: The familiar nightcrawler is a European earthworm introduced to North America, where it is often encountered in lawns, gardens and fishing bait. It makes deep burrows and comes to the surface to collect food. In northern hardwood forests that developed without these worms, removal of the protective leaf-litter layer can alter the ground environment for native plants. This regional effect should not be simplified into a claim that all American earthworms are foreign: North America also has native earthworm species, including western groups documented by the Forest Service.
identification: Adult nightcrawlers are comparatively large, often several inches long, with a swollen reproductive band called the clitellum. In this species that band is saddle-shaped rather than an even ring around the body. It lies farther back from the head than the pale, smooth-looking band of an adult jumping worm. Movement can help draw attention to a worm, but behavior alone does not identify it. Young earthworms lack a fully developed clitellum and are especially difficult to identify from photographs.
actions: Never release unused fishing worms or their bedding into woods, shoreline soil or a compost pile near natural habitat. Contain unwanted bait for disposal according to local guidance. Remove adhering soil from equipment before moving between sites, and be cautious when transferring soil, plants or mulch into relatively undisturbed forests. Photograph adults with the head and reproductive band clearly visible if identification matters. Do not apply pesticides or attempt broad soil treatments to remove earthworms. Consult local extension staff about protecting forest litter and distinguishing introduced worms from native species.
researchNotes: UMN supports species-level northern hardwood effects and clitellum; USDA Sam James regional synthesis independently confirms European origin and native western earthworms. Minnesota DNR jumping-worm comparison is supporting regional guidance, not counted as wholly independent research from UMN.

proposedDescription: Nightflowering silene, or night-flowering catchfly, is an introduced annual of fields, roadsides and other disturbed ground in parts of North America. It starts as a low rosette and later produces an upright flowering stem. Its common name reflects flowers that often open in the evening, but an absence of open flowers during a daytime visit does not mean the plant is finished growing. Seed production is the important stage to watch when managing unwanted plants.
identification: The leaves occur in opposite pairs and carry conspicuous hairs. Upper stems and flower stalks can feel sticky because some hairs have glands. Pale pinkish or whitish petals are deeply divided, and the fused green calyx surrounding each flower has ten visible longitudinal veins. As fruit develops, that enclosing structure enlarges around a capsule. Silene conica has many more calyx veins, while several other campions differ in flower size or reproductive structures. Photograph the calyx from the side as well as the flower face; a closed flower can still provide valuable features.
actions: Check an uncertain plant again near evening, and include a basal leaf, stem leaves and a developing capsule in photographs. Confirm the identity before removing unfamiliar campions from a natural area. In a garden or disturbed patch where control is appropriate, remove plants before capsules mature and collect any seed-bearing material securely. Since reproduction is by seed, revisit the patch for new rosettes instead of assuming one visit has exhausted the seed supply. Clean soil and plant debris from tools before using them elsewhere, and avoid spreading contaminated soil into new beds.
researchNotes: Penn State life-cycle account and Native Plant Trust regional flora are independent. Ontario crop account corroborates seed reproduction. Avoids conflicting capsule-tooth/style counts found in some secondary summaries and does not claim all flowers open or all pollination is by moths.

proposedDescription: Giant devil's fig is a large, prickly nightshade. The intended species is Solanum chrysotrichum described by Schlechtendal, native from Mexico into Central America. A different historical name with the same spelling belongs to another plant, and some older records used Solanum hispidum incorrectly. These naming problems matter when interpreting an observation or a report of weed impacts. Botanical accounts document introduced populations overseas, but the exact US occurrence evidence needs further checking.
identification: A mature giant devil's fig is a tall, woody shrub with very large, broadly oval leaves divided into prominent lobes. The undersides are especially hairy, and young stems and leaf stalks often look rusty because of their dense, star-shaped hairs. Stems may carry sparse, broad-based prickles. Branched clusters bear white, deeply star-shaped flowers, followed by yellow to orange-yellow berries. Several prickly nightshades share portions of this appearance. Photographs should include the hair covering, prickles, leaf bases and flower clusters, rather than relying on a single berry.
actions: Do not taste the fruit or infer edibility from resemblance to familiar crops. Wear gloves when approaching a prickly specimen and avoid brushing its stems against exposed skin. Record a suspected escape with a location, whole-plant photograph and close details, then consult a herbarium or extension office. Keep fruit-bearing cuttings and soil from being moved to another property while identification is pending. If local removal is recommended, plan for the size of the shrub and check afterward for surviving growth and seedlings.
researchNotes: PlantNET independently supplies a clear diagnosis for S. chrysotrichum Schltdl.; Kew confirms that correct-author taxon, while ITIS lists a continental US introduction that is not specified in Kew's range. The homonym and misapplied hispidum warning are useful identification cautions, but no recovered evidence demonstrates that this catalog ID intends a different species. Unknown US establishment and impact can remain explicit scope limits. Ready for editorial review with the correct authorship and provisional US occurrence context retained. A future US record should be tied to a specimen before local impacts are attributed.

claims: Rusty stellate hairs, large lobed leaves, prickles, white flowers and misapplied S. hispidum.
Accepted correct-author taxon and native/introduced distribution.
Continental US introduced designation needing voucher reconciliation.

proposedDescription: The Nile monitor is a large African lizard that has established populations in parts of southern Florida following escapes or releases from captivity. It is an agile swimmer and climber, often seen near canals, ponds and other water edges. Its broad diet includes many small animals and eggs, creating concern for native wildlife where introduced populations occur. A single sighting outside a known population is worth reporting, but it does not by itself demonstrate that a breeding population has become established there.
identification: Look for a long-bodied lizard with powerful clawed feet, a narrow head and a very long tail that is flattened sideways for swimming. The body is olive to dark brown or nearly black, with yellowish markings forming bands or spots; pale markings also occur around the jaw and head. A dark, forked tongue may be visible. Young animals are much smaller than the large adults shown in many photographs. Tegus, iguanas and even young alligators can cause confusion at a distance, so photograph the head, body and tail together if it is safe.
actions: Keep people and pets back and do not attempt to corner, catch or handle the animal. Florida wildlife officials specifically recommend reporting a photograph and location rather than trying to capture a monitor. Note its direction of travel and nearby water or shelter without following it into unsafe terrain. Secure small pets and poultry, and do not leave food that could attract wildlife. Never release an unwanted captive monitor; contact the appropriate wildlife agency or an authorized surrender program for current options.
researchNotes: FWC current field guidance and UF/IFAS identification guide support separate agency/university treatments. No nationwide establishment claim, unsupported prey-population decline or capture/killing instructions. Regulatory details intentionally deferred to current authorities.

proposedDescription: Nile tilapia is an African and Middle Eastern cichlid widely moved for aquaculture. Escape or release can place it in warm natural waters, where its effects depend on the habitat and the other species present. Females protect eggs and young in their mouths, an important part of the fish's reproductive biology. US records require particular care: Nile tilapia has often been confused with blue tilapia, and farmed stocks can contain hybrids that later escape.
identification: A typical Nile tilapia has a deep, compressed body, a long dorsal fin and a fairly squared-off tail crossed by regular dark bands. Those tail bands help separate typical individuals from blue tilapia, whose tail lacks the same distinct regular striping. Breeding colors and fin-spine counts may provide additional clues, but coloration changes and hybrids complicate the picture. USGS warns that conventional visible characters often cannot assign a reliable species name to introduced US tilapia populations. Young fish and photographs showing only one fin should be treated especially cautiously.
actions: Do not release aquarium, food-market or aquaculture fish into ponds, canals or streams, and never move a caught fish alive into another waterbody. Report an unfamiliar wild tilapia to the state fisheries agency with clear side and tail photographs, the exact waterbody and an approximate size. Follow local fishing and possession rules rather than assuming that nonnative status permits any action. Keep stocked systems secure against escape and obtain agency guidance before stocking. Where species identity is uncertain, record the fish as an unidentified tilapia pending expert examination.
researchNotes: USGS taxonomic and introduction synthesis plus FAO cultured-species biology are independent lineages. Hybrid uncertainty is explicit; occurrence table is not treated as proof of current establishment. No unverified national fishery rules or universal ecological-effect claims.

proposedDescription: Nit grass is a small annual grass from the Mediterranean region that has become established in disturbed habitats elsewhere. Its narrow flower head can be easy to overlook among other grasses. The important identification details are much smaller than the whole plant, and photographs of a distant patch rarely show enough to separate it from related grasses.
identification: Look for a tuft of slender stems with narrow leaves and a dense, pale green, somewhat shiny flower head. Each tiny spikelet contains one flower. Its two outer coverings, called glumes, are swollen around the base and taper above it. The smaller inner covering bears silky hairs and usually a bent bristle. These details need a hand lens or a sharp close-up. Similar Gastridium species differ in the proportions of their glumes and bristles; a spike-shaped head alone does not establish the name. Include a ruler in photographs without crushing the head.
actions: Record whether the grass is in a garden, roadside, pasture or less disturbed vegetation, and photograph the leaf collar as well as a mature head. If the identity is uncertain, ask a herbarium or extension service to examine the reproductive parts before treating a larger patch. Where removal is appropriate, avoid scattering mature heads or carrying seed-bearing soil elsewhere. Keep the location marked and check for new annual plants in the next growing season. The available sources describe recognition and habitat more clearly than tested control methods for this exact species.
researchNotes: PlantNET and Go Botany provide independent botanical treatments. Exact-species management trials were not located; actions are cautious documentation and seed-containment steps rather than a claimed validated treatment program.

proposedDescription: Noble yarrow is a perennial introduced through cultivation, with clusters of small pale flower heads above divided leaves. North American records need context: Flora of North America distinguishes established Montana plants from records elsewhere that represented cultivated specimens. A garden record should not be read as proof that the species has spread into surrounding habitat or become invasive there.
identification: Look closely at the leaves rather than relying on the familiar yarrow-shaped flower cluster. Noble yarrow has relatively short, broadly outlined leaves divided into lobes, with small intermediate divisions. The stem leaves can clasp slightly at their bases. Numerous tiny heads form a broad cluster, and the plant has a persistent root rather than the short life of an annual. Hairiness and flower details vary among published treatments. Photograph a lower leaf, a stem leaf at its attachment, and the side of several flower heads. Other yarrows and cultivated selections can resemble it.
actions: For a possible escaped plant, note its distance from a planting and whether seedlings or additional clumps occur beyond the garden boundary. Seek a botanical identification before removing wild yarrow, because the familiar common-yarrow group also contains native North American plants. Avoid distributing divisions or seed from an unconfirmed escape. If a land manager decides removal is warranted, retain clear photographs and revisit the site to distinguish regrowth from new seedlings. Evidence for this species does not support treating every yarrow patch as the same management problem.
researchNotes:
FNA supplies cultivation versus establishment distinctions; Flora Helvetica independently describes foliage and small crowded heads. Their hairiness and ray-count descriptions differ, so no single numeric shortcut is used. No nationwide harm claim or species-specific treatment efficacy is asserted.

proposedDescription: Musk thistle, also called nodding thistle, is a prickly plant of pastures, roadsides and other open ground. It usually grows first as a low rosette and later sends up flowering stems. Large plants can produce substantial seed, so preventing another generation matters more than simply cutting down a conspicuous stem after its seeds have dispersed.
identification: The large pink-purple heads often lean sideways or downward. Beneath each head, broad pointed bracts overlap like the scales of a small pine cone. Leaves are deeply lobed with sharp margins, and spiny wings run along portions of the stem, with interruptions near the heads. Rosettes are comparatively smooth and may become quite broad. Native thistles can also have spines and purple flowers, so photograph the underside of the head, the stem wings and both leaf surfaces. Do not use a purple flower by itself as a reason to remove a thistle.
actions: Confirm the identification, then prioritize young rosettes and plants that have not set seed. For a small patch, an approved mechanical approach must address the root crown; cutting only the upper stem can leave an opportunity for further flowering. Contain flower heads that may already hold seed rather than dragging them across the site. Keep desirable vegetation covering disturbed ground and inspect the area over multiple seasons, since the seed bank can outlast the visible plants. For pasture-scale infestations, use a coordinated local weed-management plan instead of repeated late mowing alone.
researchNotes: North Dakota agency diagnostic characters and the Forest Service evidence synthesis support recognition and seed-bank management. Native thistle protection is explicit. No biological-control release or pesticide recipe is recommended.

proposedDescription: Nodeweed is a small, branching plant with yellow flower heads tucked close to its leaves. It occurs widely in warm disturbed ground, including cultivated areas and roadsides. Its broad tropical American origin and introductions elsewhere mean that local context matters: being weedy in a garden is not the same as being a nonnative ecological threat in every part of its range.
identification: Look for rough, toothed, broadly oval leaves with several strong veins rising from near the base. The tiny yellow heads sit in crowded groups at leaf junctions and toward the branch tips, rather than on long showy flower stalks. Examine a mature head if one is available: it produces two noticeably different fruit types. The outer fruits are flattened and winged, while central fruits are narrower and carry longer pointed appendages. Those small structures help separate nodeweed from other yellow-flowered weeds. Photograph the branching habit, leaf junctions and a close-up of the heads.
actions: When recording a patch, include its size and whether it is confined to cultivated soil or spreading into adjacent vegetation. Where routine garden removal is appropriate, work before fruits mature and keep fruiting material contained. Check shoes, gloves and equipment after handling plants with mature heads, since pointed fruits can travel with animals or people. Avoid moving soil from the patch to a new planting area. For a natural-area report, first establish the regional status and identification rather than assuming that a tropical weed necessarily requires broad removal.
researchNotes: Kew establishes tropical American origin and botanical detail; NParks and the specialist daisy-fruit key provide independent descriptive context. An alternate manual erroneously listing African/Asian origin and alternate leaves was rejected. Actions are low-risk containment, not an efficacy claim.

claims: Tropical American origin, leaf veins, axillary heads and dimorphic fruits.
Yellow stalkless heads in leaf axils, roadside habitat and seed reproduction.
Central spiny and marginal winged fruits and proposed dispersal roles.

proposedDescription: Ventenata is a slender annual grass that can become abundant in western grasslands and pasture. Its fine appearance can disguise the amount of ground it occupies until the seed heads emerge. It commonly establishes in autumn, then flowers and dries during the following growing season. A useful report catches the plant while its identifying structures are still intact.
identification: Look for narrow leaves, dark reddish or nearly black stem joints, and a long translucent flap where the leaf meets the stem. Mature flower heads open into delicate branching sprays with bent, twisted bristles on the upper flowers. Young heads are more tightly gathered, so the silhouette changes with age. There is another trap after maturity: the bent-bristled upper flowers can fall away, leaving a straight-bristled lower flower behind. Photograph both fresh and older heads when possible, plus a close-up of the leaf collar and stem joints. Other annual grasses require comparison at this scale.
actions: Mark the patch while it is identifiable and note whether it occurs in hay ground, pasture, a trail margin or native grassland. Keep mature seed heads from travelling on mowing equipment, footwear or collected hay. Clean equipment before moving from an affected field to an uninfested one. Ask the local weed program to plan treatment around the annual growth cycle and the plants you want to retain. Return during the next germination and heading periods to check the boundaries; a single visit after dry stems disappear will not show whether new plants are establishing.
researchNotes: OSU and MSU independent extension material supports identification; the Montana field guide adds a specifically sourced post-maturity diagnostic trap. Prevention advice is tied to seed containment; no unsupported mowing efficacy or universal legal status is claimed.

proposedDescription: North African knapweed is an annual with pink-purple flower heads and a branching habit. California records place it in grassland settings, while agricultural research in southern Spain documents vigorous growth in cereal fields. Those are different settings, not evidence of the same impact everywhere. Its ability to emerge over an extended season makes a single early inspection easy to miss later plants.
identification: Look for lobed leaves and thistle-like purple heads on a tall, branching plant. The overlapping bracts around the head and the mature fruits are important for separating knapweeds. A specialist seed guide describes the fruits as smooth, flattened and roughly 3 to 4 millimeters long, with pale longitudinal markings and a persistent tuft of bristles. Photograph the head from the side and below, not only the colored flowers. Several other knapweeds have similar blooms, and a reliable identification may require a specimen examined with magnification.
actions: Report a suspected new patch with its location, approximate extent and clear photographs before it is disturbed. Where the plant is confirmed and removal is appropriate, prevent mature heads from shedding during handling and keep affected soil or seed-bearing material on site until disposal is arranged. Recheck after later rains, because research from its Mediterranean growing region records staggered emergence. In cropland, seek a plan specific to the crop and local registrations; treatments tested in Spanish wheat cannot simply be transferred to an American grassland or garden. Record follow-up plants instead of assuming the first clearance was complete.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC provides California habitat and watch context; IFAPA original field work supports staggered emergence and crop-specific limits. The specialist seed guide supplies fruit detail. No unsupported U.S. herbicide recommendation or statewide occurrence extrapolation.

proposedDescription: The northern curly-tailed lizard is a ground-dwelling Caribbean lizard established in parts of Florida. Sidewalk edges, parking areas and other sunny developed places can provide shelter and feeding opportunities. It eats a range of small animals, including insects, and has also been observed taking other lizards. A record of one individual helps document its location but does not measure its effect on a whole local wildlife community.
identification: The raised, curled tail is a helpful first clue, especially when the lizard pauses on open ground. Look also for a sturdy body and rough-looking scales with raised ridges along the back. Photograph the animal from the side and above if you can do so without approaching closely. A tail may be held differently while running, so a single silhouette can be misleading. Include the full body, feet and surrounding surface rather than only a close view of the tail. Other introduced lizards occur in the same Florida neighborhoods.
actions: Record the location and the number of animals you actually saw, noting any young individuals separately. Do not feed the lizards or relocate one to another yard or natural area. If one arrives in nursery stock, landscaping materials or a vehicle, contain the material where practical and ask the relevant wildlife authority how to proceed. Leave burrows and animals alone while obtaining identification; improvised traps can catch native reptiles too. Repeated photographs from the same place can help distinguish a one-time sighting from a persistent group without disturbing the animals.
researchNotes: CNAH/SSAR supports taxonomy and introduced Florida context. Meshaka synthesis supplies urban habitat and separately attributed feeding observations. The draft does not inflate individual predation observations into quantified population effects; practical actions focus on reporting and non-relocation.

claims: Caribbean origin, Florida introductions and keeled scales.
Shelter under hard surfaces, urban habitats and independently cited diet observations.

proposedDescription: Northern root-knot nematode is a microscopic plant parasite that feeds within roots. Affected plants may grow unevenly, yellow or wilt, while their roots develop small swellings. Despite its name, it is not confined to northern states: it has also been investigated in Florida strawberry and vegetable production. The host plant and a laboratory diagnosis matter when deciding how to respond.
identification: Inspect roots from declining plants for small, rounded galls, sometimes with extra branching around them. Aboveground stress alone is not diagnostic; nutrient problems, other diseases and damaged irrigation can produce similar symptoms. Even the presence of galls does not identify this particular root-knot species. Specialists examine the nematodes and may use molecular or biochemical tests to separate it from relatives. Photograph the whole plant, the affected patch and washed roots, but follow a diagnostic laboratory's sampling instructions before washing or discarding the actual sample.
actions: Contact a plant diagnostic laboratory before choosing a treatment or rotation crop. Ask whether it needs fresh galled roots, soil, or both, and keep the samples from drying or overheating as directed. Avoid moving suspect transplants and root-zone soil to an unaffected bed, and clean soil from tools before working elsewhere. Once the species is confirmed, plan around the crop: some grasses and cereals can interrupt its host cycle, but that does not make every rotation suitable. Use clean planting material and revisit the affected area rather than assuming healthier-looking foliage proves the roots are free of nematodes.
researchNotes: UF species-specific detection research and UC Davis Nemaplex support biology and diagnosis; UGA sampling instructions support the referral. Obsolete DBCP mention and hot-water recipe on Nemaplex deliberately excluded. Rotation advice remains crop- and diagnosis-dependent.

proposedDescription: Northern snakehead is an introduced predatory fish found in several U.S. waterways. It has a long, mottled body and can breathe air, an adaptation that helps it survive conditions that challenge many other fish. Its presence deserves careful documentation, but accurate identification comes first because native bowfins are often mistaken for snakeheads and should not be harmed because of that confusion.
identification: Look for a broad, somewhat flattened head, dark irregular blotches and a long dorsal fin extending along much of the back. The fin underneath the rear body is also long. That lower fin is an especially useful contrast with bowfin, whose anal fin is short. Snakehead pelvic fins sit close behind the pectoral fins; bowfin pelvic fins lie farther back. Photograph the entire side of the fish with the fins visible, plus the head. A long dorsal fin or dark body color alone is not enough for a dependable identification.
actions: If you catch a suspected snakehead, record the exact waterbody and location and promptly contact the state fisheries agency for identification and handling instructions. Do not move a live fish to another waterbody or keep it for release elsewhere. Requirements for possession and handling vary, and established fisheries may have different reporting priorities from a new detection. Maryland, for example, asks anglers to remove captured snakeheads and report catches through its invasive-fish program. Follow the rules for the place you are fishing, and never use a suspected invasive fish as live bait.
researchNotes: USGS supplies diagnostic comparison with native bowfin. Maryland DNR provides locally scoped catch handling and reporting, not a falsely nationwide mandate. No unsupported walking-on-land distance or universal ecological damage rate.

claims: Long dorsal and anal fins, pelvic-fin position and native bowfin distinction.
Current state handling request and reporting route.

proposedDescription: Norway maple is a Eurasian shade tree widely planted along streets and in gardens. In parts of the United States, its wind-carried seeds establish in nearby woods, where dense shade and abundant seedlings can make it harder for other plants to grow. A planted adult and a spreading woodland population are different observations, so record the seedlings and surrounding habitat as well as the tree.
identification: Leaves occur in opposite pairs and have broad, pointed lobes. Green and purple-leaved cultivated forms both occur. A freshly detached leaf stalk often releases milky sap, especially early in the growing season; the feature can be less obvious later. Paired winged fruits spread widely apart, and the mature bark develops ridges. Native sugar maple can look similar, so compare several features rather than autumn color alone. Photograph opposite leaves, a fruit pair if present, and the buds or bark. Do not cut branches from a tree you do not own.
actions: Check beneath and beyond mature trees for seedlings, particularly at woodland edges. Confirm their identity before pulling small plants, since native maple seedlings may be mixed in. Where removal is appropriate, remove young seedlings with their roots while the soil is workable and revisit the area for new arrivals. Established trees require a planned approach with the property owner and a qualified tree-care professional, especially near buildings or utilities. Choose suitable native replacements rather than another seed-producing Norway maple, and maintain groundcover after removal so the opened space does not simply become another weed patch.
researchNotes:
University of Maryland supplies impacts and management context, with Nebraska extension botanical characters independently supporting identification. Sap test qualified by season. No statement that every planted tree must be immediately removed.

proposedDescription: Norway rats live around buildings, farms and other places that offer food and shelter. They often use ground burrows, including spaces beneath slabs or beside foundations. Besides damaging stored food and structures, their waste can create health concerns. An effective response removes the conditions supporting the rats while dealing safely with the animals already present.
identification: Compared with a roof rat, an adult Norway rat usually has a heavier body, blunter muzzle and smaller-looking ears. Its tail is shorter than the combined head and body; roof rats typically have a longer tail and a more slender build. Young rats can be confused with mice, so size alone is unreliable. Burrows, gnawing and droppings help locate activity, but photograph signs without touching them. Note where you see fresh damage and when activity occurs. A single dropping does not reliably establish the species or the size of an infestation.
actions: Secure food, animal feed and rubbish in resistant containers, reduce clutter and close accessible gaps around doors and utility entries. Use a pest professional when activity is extensive or difficult to reach. If traps are used, position and protect them so children, pets and wildlife cannot reach them. Do not dry-sweep or vacuum droppings or nesting material; follow CDC guidance for wet disinfection and protective gloves. Keep monitoring after the first captures, because remaining food or entry points can support another infestation. Seek health advice if illness follows a possible rodent exposure.
researchNotes: CDC diagnostic key supports rat-versus-mouse/roof-rat distinctions; Utah State IPM supports exclusion and food management. Current CDC cleanup instructions are linked. No unqualified poison recommendation or species-specific disease diagnosis.

claims: Body, ears, muzzle and tail proportions compared with roof rat and mouse.
Burrows, food sources, exclusion and protected control planning.
Wet disinfection, gloves and no dry sweeping or vacuuming waste.

proposedDescription: Norway spruce is a European evergreen widely planted as a landscape and forestry tree. Mature trees can be recognized from their hanging branchlets and long cones, but young trees are less distinctive. A planted spruce is not by itself evidence of an invasive population. When documenting an apparent escape, the useful question is whether young trees are establishing beyond the original planting.
identification: The needles attach individually to short woody pegs, rather than growing in the bundles typical of pines. Those pegs leave the twig rough after old needles fall. Needles have an angular cross-section, while the long, papery seed cones hang downward. Mature side branchlets often droop beneath the larger branches. Fir cones stand upright, and fir needles usually attach without the same persistent woody pegs. Photograph a cone with a scale reference, a twig and the overall branching pattern. Needle length and tree shape can vary with age and growing conditions.
actions: Distinguish deliberately planted trees from seedlings growing on their own, and note the distance between them. For suspected spread into sensitive habitat, send photographs and a location to the land manager or a regional herbarium before arranging removal. Do not cut a large tree simply because it is nonnative; consider site goals, safety and habitat effects. Where confirmed seedlings are unwanted, remove them while small with the owner's permission and check for further recruitment. Leave seed-bearing cones and excavated soil at the site until appropriate disposal is arranged rather than distributing them to new areas.
researchNotes:
The Nebraska identification manual was recovered as substantive indexed text and Stanford's independent observed-tree account was read in full. Both support the needle pegs, hanging cones and cultivated European tree context. Widespread ecological harm and a control trial are not needed for a profile that distinguishes plantings from volunteer recruitment and offers only conditional seedling observation and owner-approved removal. Ready for editorial review with regional establishment and treatment efficacy left unclaimed.

proposedDescription: The noxious bamboo mealybug is a small sap-feeding insect that can remain hidden beneath the sheaths wrapped around bamboo stems. Its waxy covering and sheltered position make an infestation easy to overlook when plants are moved or divided. A 2026 Florida diagnostic circular describes it as common on bamboo in that state. Published records place it on several bamboo genera, but finding wax on bamboo is not enough to name this particular species. Other mealybugs occupy similar protected spaces, and their treatment may differ.
identification: Inspect an already loose sheath for concentrated white wax and the insects beneath it, without stripping healthy stems simply to search. Photograph the whole bamboo, the affected stem joint and a close view of the colony. Living Antonina pretiosa cannot reliably be separated from A. nakaharai by appearance. Specialists examine slide-mounted specimens: A. pretiosa has abdominal plates and lacks, or has only a few, dorsal multilocular pores near the anal opening. Record the bamboo name if known and whether the insects occur on new shoots, older stems or both.
actions: Keep an affected potted bamboo apart from other plants while obtaining identification, and pause moving divisions, cut stems or nursery stock from it. Ask an extension diagnostic service how to submit a sample containing insects, wax and the relevant sheath. Include when the bamboo arrived and where it came from if that information is available. Do not apply a treatment intended for another bamboo insect based only on the common name. A confirmed identification and assessment of the plant condition should come before a control plan.
researchNotes: The Hendricks revision's exact passage was recovered through indexed text. A newly accessed May 2026 FDACS original circular directly compares pretiosa with nakaharai, confirms pretiosa as a common Florida bamboo insect, and requires slide-mounted specimens. This adds independent current diagnostic evidence, beyond ScaleNet's inherited bibliography. A specific treatment trial is unnecessary for isolation, documentation and diagnostic referral; no crawi or nakaharai control claim is imported. Ready for editorial review; identification remains a specialist task and treatment efficacy is not asserted. proposedDescription: Nun's orchid is a large ground-growing orchid cultivated for tall stems of nodding flowers. It has become naturalized in places including Florida, Hawaii and Puerto Rico, where records include wet wooded habitats. A planted orchid and an independently growing woodland population tell different stories, so that distinction matters when reporting it. Some current botanical references place the plant in Calanthe as Calanthe tankervilleae; the older Phaius name remains widely used.
identification: Broad, strongly pleated leaves rise from the base beside a separate, upright flowering stem. The flowers have a striking contrast between pale outer surfaces and reddish-brown inner surfaces, with a pinkish to purple, partly tubular lip. Photograph both the front and back of a flower, its lip, the whole flower stem and the leaf bases. Cultivated hybrids and closely related swamp orchids can complicate identification. Leaf size or flower color alone is not a reliable way to settle the name, especially on plants with a nursery history.
actions: If you find one outside cultivation, record whether it is near a garden, discarded potting material or an apparently undisturbed wetland. Photograph it in place and ask a botanist or land manager to confirm the identification before removing an unfamiliar orchid. Do not collect wild plants or transfer them to another natural area. Keep garden divisions and spent plant material out of wetland edges. For a confirmed escaped population, let the managing agency decide whether monitoring or removal is appropriate for that location.
researchNotes: Go Orchids supplies independently described US naturalization and morphology; the Thailand flora's indexed treatment supports habitat and floral distinctions. Kew explicitly maps Phaius tankervilleae to Calanthe tankervilleae. The unambiguous combination can be explained without renaming the catalog ID. Missing local removal trials do not block conservative observation and containment; P. wallichii and Australian relatives remain excluded. Ready for editorial review; retain the catalog identifier and explain the accepted combination in prose.

proposedDescription: Nut scale is a sap-feeding soft scale found on a range of woody plants, including oak, elm, hazel and linden. The name does not mean it is limited to nut trees. Established females can resemble small rounded growths on branches, while the younger stages are much less conspicuous. Heavy colonies can weaken a host, but a few scales do not automatically mean a tree needs treatment or removal.
identification: Mature females are strongly domed and roughly 5-6 millimeters across, ranging from brown to gray-brown. Young stages are much smaller and can be pinkish or orange-yellow. Inspect several twigs and leaf undersides rather than judging the tree from one bump. Photograph colonies with a size reference, the host leaves and a wider view of the branch. Several soft scales look similar to an unaided eye; a specialist may need a specimen to distinguish nut scale from other rounded brown scales. Note whether you see living insects, mobile young or only dead females.
actions: Keep a record of the affected branches and whether the tree shows reduced growth or substantial leaf damage. Ask an extension service or qualified arborist to identify the scale and assess the severity before treating a large tree. Do not move infested nursery plants to a new site while that assessment is pending. If management is warranted, its timing should follow the locally observed vulnerable stage rather than a calendar copied from another country. Avoid stripping bark or pruning healthy major limbs simply to remove scattered scales.
researchNotes:

The Italian park account separately describes woody hosts and juvenile movement; NIBIO independently corroborates strongly domed females and leaf-to-twig seasonal movement. Different European emergence dates need not be reconciled into a US calendar. The draft correctly asks for local stage assessment and does not assert a treatment threshold or universal harm. Ready for editorial review with local timing and management efficacy explicitly left open.
