proposedDescription: Malus pumila is a botanical name historically used for the cultivated apple. Many current references place it under Malus domestica, while older floras retain the earlier name. Apple trees have been planted so widely that a tree along a road or in an abandoned field may be a surviving planting, a seedling or part of a former orchard. That history matters when interpreting an occurrence. A familiar edible crop can grow outside cultivation without every such tree representing a damaging invasion, and native crabapples should not be swept into the same category.
identification: Orchard apples are deciduous trees with simple, oval, toothed leaves and clusters of showy flowers, followed by fleshy fruits with a central core. Young twigs and leaf undersides may be hairy. Fruit size, color and flavor vary widely among cultivated apples and their seedlings, so a small sour fruit does not establish that a tree is a native crabapple. Flower, leaf and fruit photographs together are more helpful than fruit alone. A visible graft union and regular orchard spacing can suggest cultivation, although neither is necessary for an apple tree to have a planting history.
actions: Before removing an apple from an old property or natural area, identify it and check the site's planting history and management goals. Keep unwanted fruit and seedlings from being moved into nearby undeveloped land. If you want to retain a tree, an extension fruit specialist or arborist can help assess its health and maintenance needs. For a suspected native crabapple, seek a botanical identification before acting; the broad label apple is not precise enough to support a removal decision.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: Kew and Flora of China clearly connect M. pumila with cultivated apple; EPPO likewise replaces its paradise-apple code with M. domestica. An older government germplasm treatment explicitly distinguishes M. pumila from the domesticated-apple usage. The current synonym is clear, but the inherited catalog concept still needs to be tied to orchard apple versus historically narrower germplasm usage. This decision should not be silently made by changing an ID. Ask the catalog owner to confirm the intended apple concept and review potential duplicate M. domestica records; retain the draft's protection of native crabapples.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: The cultivated-apple interpretation of pumila is well supported by current nomenclature and does not require resolving possible catalog duplicates first. Fresh Kew treatment lists pumila as a rejected synonym of domestica; EPPO independently defines the cultivated crop and FOC supplies morphology. The old germplasm alternative is retained as historical provenance, not allowed to silently redefine all garden apples. proposedDescription: February daphne is a small shrub valued for fragrant flowers that appear in late winter or early spring, often before the leaves. Daphne mezereum comes from Europe and western Asia and can escape gardens into shaded woodland. In Washington it is on a monitoring list rather than the state's listed noxious-weed roster, so reporting an occurrence is distinct from an automatic legal requirement to remove it. Its bright fruits also deserve care around people and animals: this is a poisonous ornamental, not a berry plant to taste.
identification: The shrub usually stays only a few feet tall. Pink, lilac-purple or sometimes white flowers cluster directly along the woody stems. Narrow, smooth-edged leaves develop later and may appear crowded toward the branch tips. Rounded fruits ripen close to the stems, commonly becoming red, with yellow-fruited forms also known. The seasonal sequence of flowers on relatively bare stems followed by foliage is a useful clue. Other daphnes and shrubs can share the common name spurge laurel, so include flowers, leaves and fruit when confirming the scientific name.
actions: Keep the fruit and other plant parts away from children, pets and livestock, and avoid using them in food or homemade remedies. Wear gloves when handling cut material because contact can irritate skin. If you find plants spreading beyond a garden in Washington, report the location to the county weed program and ask for current guidance. Bird-dispersed seeds can produce plants away from the original shrub, so inspect nearby shaded ground. For removal, follow local advice and secure fruit-bearing material rather than dumping it in woodland.
researchNotes: Washington monitoring status checked directly, not described as a listed noxious weed. Independent NCSU morphology/toxicity supports cautious handling. Regional agency referral is the supported management action.

proposedDescription: Kangaroo thorn is an Australian shrub with stiff spines and bright yellow flower heads. Acacia paradoxa has been planted as a hedge, but it has also established outside cultivation in California's coastal ranges. The California Invasive Plant Council places it on its Watch list, reflecting concern about its potential to spread rather than a claim that it dominates every suitable habitat. Its dense, prickly growth can make a small planting difficult to approach once it expands. A confirmed wild occurrence is worth distinguishing from other yellow-flowered acacias nearby.
identification: The apparent leaves are small, flattened leaf stalks called phyllodes, usually elliptical and sometimes wavy along the edges. They are much smaller than the long, strap-like foliage of several other common acacias. Stiff spines occur along the branches, and the flowers form rounded yellow balls. Mature plants are spreading shrubs, often wider than they are tall. Photograph the phyllodes, their attachment to the stem, the spines and the flower heads. Older labels may use Acacia armata. Neither yellow flowers nor thorns alone provides a reliable identification.
actions: Avoid planting or moving this shrub into places where it could escape into coastal woodland. For a suspected California escape, record the extent of the patch and contact the local weed program or land manager for advice. Wear sturdy gloves and eye protection when working near its rigid spines. Keep seed-bearing material contained during any removal work, and avoid disturbing a large thicket without a follow-up plan. Nearby seedlings and plants beyond the original hedge are especially useful to document.
researchNotes: The current Cal-IPC profile and Wrigley-Fagg description hosted by ANBG were reread: California coastal escapes, Watch assessment, spines, short wavy phyllodes and yellow flower balls are supported. The draft gives cautious reporting and seed containment, not an unsupported species-specific removal protocol. Lack of a California control trial is a scoped limitation. Ready for editorial review; no current legal status inferred from old lists and no propagation recipe included.

proposedDescription: Paraguay burr is a low, spreading plant of the daisy family whose fruits readily draw attention to an otherwise modest weed. Acanthospermum australe is native to tropical South America and part of the southern Caribbean and has been introduced into the southeastern United States and other regions. It occurs in sandy ground and disturbed places. Its hooked fruits can accompany material moved from a patch, so the fruiting stage matters when deciding how to handle plants. Its distribution alone does not establish the level of damage at a particular site.
identification: Stems lie close to the ground and can root as they spread. The opposite leaves are broadly oval, triangular or diamond-shaped, with toothed edges and small gland dots, especially beneath. Tiny pale yellowish or white ray flowers surround the small flower heads. The mature burrs are elongated, with ribs bearing hooked prickles. Unlike the related bristly starbur, Acanthospermum hispidum, they lack the pair of large, projecting terminal spines. A close photograph of a mature burr is therefore particularly useful, alongside a view of the whole plant and opposite leaves.
actions: Before moving through a fruiting patch, note where it begins and ends so you can avoid carrying burrs onward. Check footwear, clothing and equipment afterward and collect attached burrs for contained disposal. If the plant appears in a garden or crop, confirm its identity and ask local extension staff for advice suited to that setting. Do not assume that a control recommendation for another burr-producing species will work equally well. Record newly observed patches in natural areas for the responsible land manager.
researchNotes: Kew and the full NSW flora were checked, and the exact Flora of Australia burr description was recovered through indexed text despite the oversized PDF. It confirms hooked rib prickles and absent terminal spines. The fruit characters, range and containment rationale are supported; a missing local removal trial is not a barrier to identification and careful handling advice. Ready for editorial review. No species-specific herbicide, grazing impact or universal invasive designation is asserted.

proposedDescription: Neoergasilus japonicus is a tiny freshwater copepod, a crustacean whose adult females can attach to fish. Native to eastern Asia, it has been recorded in several United States waters, including the Great Lakes region. Fish movements and aquaculture have helped it spread internationally. Its presence on a fish does not establish how much harm it causes to the surrounding fish community: the United States Geological Survey notes that evidence is insufficient to assess its Great Lakes environmental impact. Many different fish species can serve as hosts.
identification: Adults are generally less than a millimeter long, so reliable identification requires magnification. Attached females may occur near the bases of fins, particularly the dorsal fin. Their segmented bodies and specialized appendages distinguish them from worms or larger external parasites, but those details are difficult to judge in a field photograph. Larvae, males and immature females are free-living rather than attached parasites. That life cycle means an apparently clean fish is not proof that its transport water contains no copepods.
actions: Do not move live fish or their holding water from one waterbody to another. If you notice tiny organisms attached to fins, record the fish species, capture location and date and contact a fisheries biologist or aquatic-animal diagnostic service. Ask how to preserve a sample before collecting one. For aquarium or aquaculture fish, seek professional identification and treatment advice instead of applying a treatment based on appearance alone. Keep suspect fish and their water contained while receiving that advice.
researchNotes: The original Italian diagnostic study, the 2024 host/distribution paper and the USGS account were recovered. USGS still explicitly says Great Lakes impact evidence is insufficient; that limit is retained. Several independent studies support identity, fin attachment and fish-transfer pathways. A quantified Great Lakes impact or species-specific treatment is unnecessary for conservative transport and diagnostic advice. Ready for editorial review. proposedDescription: Parrotfeather is an aquatic perennial whose feathery shoots can rise above the surface like miniature green trees. Myriophyllum aquaticum comes from South America and was spread widely through the pond and aquarium trade. In shallow, slow-moving water it can form dense growth that crowds other plants, interferes with recreation and obstructs channels. Even a small patch deserves attention because broken stem pieces can establish elsewhere. Local rules matter: King County, Washington, requires control of this regulated weed, but that requirement should not be assumed to apply identically in every jurisdiction.
identification: Above-water leaves are blue-green and finely divided, arranged in whorls around the stems. Submerged growth can look like other watermilfoils, including native species, so photograph the emergent shoots as well as anything beneath the surface. The plant roots into sediment and produces long spreading stems with many fibrous roots. Its tiny flowers are far less noticeable than the foliage. A pond planting may remain green and attractive while its stems extend beyond the original container, making the edges of the patch important places to inspect.
actions: Do not release pond plants or aquarium contents into natural water. If you find parrotfeather in a ditch, lake margin or stream, report it to the local aquatic-weed program before cutting or raking it. Removal must capture fragments and address rooted material; careless cutting can create pieces that drift away. Small manual projects may require repeated work over several years. Keep removed plants away from water and follow local disposal guidance. Established infestations need a site-specific plan that protects nearby native vegetation and meets aquatic-management requirements.
researchNotes: King County current species page supports jurisdiction-specific status; 2017 guide supports fragment containment and persistent manual work. Independent Bay of Plenty ecology/morphology. No obsolete occurrence count or hemisphere-specific flowering season generalized.

proposedDescription: Parsley is a Mediterranean herb grown in gardens for its leaves, usually as an annual even though its natural life cycle is biennial. Petroselinum crispum commonly spends its first season building a leafy rosette, then flowers and produces seed in its second season if it survives the winter. Volunteers around an herb bed are therefore quite possible. A self-sown culinary herb is not automatically an invasive natural-area problem. Parsley also serves as food for black swallowtail caterpillars, an interaction worth recognizing before treating leaf loss as a reason to spray.
identification: Curly-leaved cultivars form dense, crinkled foliage, while flat-leaved types have more open, divided leaves with toothed segments. Flowering stems rise well above the first-year foliage and carry clusters of small greenish-yellow flowers in the umbrella-like arrangement typical of the carrot family. Seedlings initially look much simpler than mature plants. Other members of that family can resemble flat-leaved parsley, including dangerous lookalikes, so a parsley-like leaf or smell is not enough to identify a wild plant for eating. Use a known, labeled crop for the kitchen.
actions: Harvest outer leaf stalks from an established garden plant, leaving the center to continue growing. If you do not want volunteers, remove flower heads before mature seed is shed. Check for swallowtail caterpillars before cutting back a plant and decide whether some foliage can be left for them. Pull unwanted, confidently identified seedlings while small rather than moving them into unmanaged ground. For an unfamiliar parsley-like plant outside the garden, photograph the leaves, stem and flowers and obtain an identification before harvesting or removing it.
researchNotes: Two independent extension horticultural sources; public response concerns routine garden management rather than an unsupported invasive designation. No medicinal claims from NCSU repeated. Lookalike caution limited to avoiding wild-food misidentification.

proposedDescription: Atrichonotus sordidus is a South American broad-nosed weevil recorded outside its home region, notably in Australia and New Zealand. Older work calls it Floresianus sordidus. The concealed, root-feeding stage has been studied in New Zealand pasture, where larvae were found beneath ryegrass and white clover. Those observations explain why a plant may show trouble before the insect is noticed, but they do not establish that this species is responsible for damaged turf in the United States. The US introduction history of the related A. taeniatulus must not be assigned to A. sordidus.
identification: Adults belong to the broad-nosed weevils, a group in which the snout is relatively short rather than the long, narrow projection seen in some other weevils. A firm species identification needs an entomologist familiar with the group. The described larvae are small, strongly curved grubs, reaching about five millimeters, with fine yellowish hairs and a distinct head capsule. Their distinguishing structures include minute hairs, mouthpart details and breathing openings that require magnification. A curved grub from the soil cannot be identified as this species simply because grass or clover is nearby.
actions: If you suspect a weevil problem in a lawn, pasture or potted plant, retain information about the affected plant and the exact place where insects were found. Ask an extension diagnostic service how to submit both adults and larvae if available. Keep soil and root material from a suspect shipment together until it has been checked. Do not apply a pasture treatment based solely on the name of an overseas pest; diagnosis should establish the insect, its life stage and whether it is causing the damage.
researchNotes: May's original larval account and the Lanteri-Morrone revision independently support A. sordidus, its New Zealand root-feeding observations and Australian/New Zealand introductions. The revision distinguishes the US introduction history of A. taeniatulus. No recovered evidence demonstrates a different entity behind this catalog ID. The draft can accurately describe the overseas observations while declining to infer US establishment or attribute local turf damage to this species. Ready for editorial review. Keep relatives' US records separate and request a local specimen determination for any proposed US observation.

proposedDescription: Pantomorus tessellatus is a name that requires caution when reading older accounts of introduced weevils. It has been used in a complicated taxonomic history involving Aramigus and Aracanthus. Recent specialist work explains that the introduced South American weevil long called Aramigus tessellatus is now treated as Aramigus pallidus, while the original species named tessellatus belongs in Aracanthus. As a result, a record carrying the older name cannot safely be assigned the introduced species' host plants, distribution or pest behavior without checking what the author meant.
identification: The broad-nosed weevils involved can appear as small, oval beetles covered with gray or brown scales. That general appearance does not distinguish the taxonomic alternatives. Specialists examine the head and snout, position of the antenna grooves, shoulders of the wing covers, legs and other fine structures. Some populations in the historical Aramigus complex are highly variable, adding another reason not to identify a beetle from a mottled color pattern alone. An adult specimen, its original label and the name of the person who identified it can be more informative than a photograph without context.
actions: For a suspected record, keep the original scientific name attached to the observation and ask an entomological collection or diagnostic laboratory to check it against current taxonomy. Include the location, date, host plant and any evidence of feeding. Do not assume that an insect resting on a plant caused its damage. Until its identity is resolved, avoid moving suspect nursery material and use a crop-specific diagnosis rather than copying management advice for the historically misnamed weevil.

proposedDescription: Patience dock is a substantial perennial herb with large leaves and tall, branched flower stalks. Rumex patientia comes from Eurasia and has been grown as a vegetable, later appearing outside gardens in disturbed places. North American records include roadsides and open ground across a broad area, including the Pacific Northwest. Its size can make it conspicuous, but an introduced roadside plant is not necessarily a priority invasive species at every site. Identification matters because several docks overlap in appearance, and their names are sometimes applied incorrectly.
identification: The broad, elongated leaves are generally smooth, with edges that are flat or only gently wavy. Flowering stems can reach roughly three to six feet and branch mainly above the middle. Small flowers crowd the upper branches, later producing brown fruits enclosed by enlarged, papery inner flower parts called valves. In patience dock these valves are broad and usually have smooth or nearly smooth edges, with one conspicuous grain-like swelling. Greek dock, Rumex cristatus, can be confused with it and has more distinctly toothed valve margins. Mature fruit provides a stronger identification clue than a large green leaf.
actions: Photograph the basal leaves and a close view of ripe fruiting branches before deciding which dock is present. Ask a botanist or extension service to check plants that do not match clearly, since related docks can also hybridize. If an unwanted plant is growing in a garden, prevent mature seed heads from being moved with soil or yard waste while you obtain suitable local management advice. Avoid harvesting an unfamiliar wild dock merely because this species has a history as a cultivated vegetable.
researchNotes:
Burke's FNA description and the exact R. cristatus comparison were recovered, alongside independent Pakistan and Flora Helvetica accounts. Broad, nearly entire fruit valves with one usually prominent tubercle remain useful characters. The text qualifies normal variation and referral for hybrids. A field identification requiring ripe fruit does not make the species concept unresolved. Ready for editorial review with no edible-use instructions and no blanket claim of ecological harm.

proposedDescription: Immigrant pavement ants are among the small ants most often encountered around sidewalks and buildings in the northern United States. Tetramorium immigrans arrived from Europe and commonly nests in soil beneath paving, stones or structures. Workers search for a wide range of foods and may enter through cracks. They can be a household nuisance, but they do not excavate structural wood like carpenter ants. Their ecological role is mixed, and their widespread presence does not mean every outdoor colony needs treatment. Older North American references often call them Tetramorium caespitum.
identification: Workers are dark brown to nearly black and about three millimeters long. Under magnification, the head and middle body show fine ridges, the waist has two nodes, and a pair of short spines projects from the rear of the middle body. The antennae have a distinct enlarged club at the tip. Winged queens and males are larger than workers, so size differences do not necessarily mean several species are present. Related Tetramorium ants can be difficult to separate; a close diagnostic examination is more reliable than identifying every small dark ant near concrete as this species.
actions: If workers enter a home, follow their route to locate the entry point and the food attracting them. Clean up spills, keep food and pet food contained, and seal accessible cracks once the route is understood. A few outdoor ants do not justify treating an entire yard. If activity persists or you are unsure of the species, ask an extension service or pest professional to identify specimens and assess the nest location. Distinguishing pavement ants from carpenter ants or termites prevents unnecessary structural work.
researchNotes: UF taxonomy/morphology and Maine local observations independent; PNW handbook supplies exclusion guidance applicable to listed pavement ants. No generalized severe ecological impact or unsupported structural-damage claim.

proposedDescription: Acyrthosiphon primulae is associated with primroses, not the pea crops suggested by the familiar name pea aphid. Pea aphid refers to Acyrthosiphon pisum, a different species. This primrose-associated aphid has also been called Microlophium primulae, so both names appear in older horticultural and taxonomic accounts. Blackman and Eastop cite a California museum collection. Published observations describe colonies on cultivated Primula, sometimes with many insects but little visible distortion of the foliage. That host association is a useful starting point, although it does not mean every aphid found on a primrose belongs to this species.
identification: The wingless aphids are pale yellow to yellow-green, with relatively long legs and long, tapering cornicles, the paired tubes near the rear of the body. They gather on the undersides of leaves, where pale shed skins can remain caught among the leaf hairs. Winged forms have darker abdominal markings. These features help describe a suspected colony, but similar aphids require microscopic examination for confirmation. Photograph the underside of the leaf and the whole host plant, and record the Primula name if it is known. A label saying only green aphid leaves important uncertainty.
actions: Inspect a suspected colony before deciding whether it needs intervention: note new growth, leaf condition and whether the plant is otherwise thriving. Keep an infested new potted plant separate while seeking identification, and avoid sharing affected plants until the insects have been checked. For a United States occurrence, ask an extension diagnostic service to confirm both the aphid and its host. Advice written for pea aphids in legumes should not be applied automatically to this primrose-associated insect.

proposedDescription: Pea leafminer is a tiny fly whose larvae feed inside leaves of many crops and ornamentals. Its name hides an important identification problem: older North American records included the closely related Liriomyza langei. Molecular work separated those populations from South American L. huidobrensis. A winding mine in a California leaf therefore cannot establish this species, and historical distribution statements need to be checked against the revised taxonomy.
identification: Adults are mostly dark flies only a few millimeters long, with yellow areas on the head and behind the thorax. Pale larvae live between the leaf surfaces, leaving mines that become conspicuous as damaged tissue loses color. Feeding punctures and mines indicate leafminer activity, but several species produce similar signs. Even specialist examination of adult structure does not reliably separate L. huidobrensis from L. langei; molecular identification may be needed. Photograph both leaf surfaces and the whole host plant, and retain the plant label and purchase history if available.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants apart from other stock and contact an extension diagnostic service before moving or discarding heavily mined material. Ask how to submit intact leaves and any emerging adults in a contained sample. In established crop infestations, a locally designed integrated pest-management program should protect parasitoids and account for the insect's protected feeding site inside leaves. Avoid repeated broad insecticide applications based only on the appearance of mines. Record new damage over time, because old mines remain visible after the larva has left.
researchNotes:
Inherited review history, retained for provenance and superseded where this assessment differs: The full EPPO diagnosis, exact global-review taxonomy passage and original 2014 molecular survey were recovered. All 664 sampled California flies in that survey were L. langei, and the 2024 diagnostic standard recommends molecular separation. Historical US records cannot establish L. huidobrensis merely from mines or adult appearance. The gap is reassessment of the catalog's US identity, not routine expert diagnosis alone. Trace the entry's US vouchers and request molecular or otherwise validated species-level determinations under current diagnostic guidance. Keep the observation and containment advice without asserting established US populations.

Fresh follow-up 2026-10-31: New original2024 global molecular work supports a true huidobrensis account while California langei reassignment remains explicit. The global study adds original geographic samples independently of the earlier California survey and supports the narrow species concept. It does not justify assigning old US records to huidobrensis. Next step: Review the scientifically scoped leafminer draft; retain separate molecular checks for uncertain US records. proposedDescription: Peach is a familiar deciduous fruit tree from Asia, grown in many cultivated forms. Nectarines belong to the same species and differ in having smooth fruit skin. Trees can persist around former gardens and occasionally occur in disturbed places, but a surviving planted tree does not prove that an invasive population is spreading. North Carolina botanists specifically caution that some records may represent persistent trees rather than independent reproduction.
identification: Leaves are alternate, narrow and pointed, with finely toothed edges. Small glands may be visible near the base of the blade or leaf stalk. Pink flowers, usually with five petals, appear before or around leaf emergence; ornamental forms can have additional petals. The fleshy fruit contains one large, rough stone and is usually fuzzy unless it is a nectarine. Other cherries and plums share parts of this pattern, so photograph the leaf attachment, flowers and fruit rather than relying on pink blossom alone. Mature bark becomes rougher than that of young shoots.
actions: When reporting a possible escape, look for seedlings beyond the original tree and record whether the site was formerly cultivated. Remove unwanted young volunteers only after confirming the identity and obtaining permission. For a maintained fruit tree, use local orchard guidance for pruning and pest problems instead of treating the tree itself as an invasive emergency. Keep pruned or wilted foliage away from livestock, and do not eat the seed inside the stone. Preserve cultivar labels when available, since fruit and growth form vary considerably.
researchNotes: NC State horticulture and NC Parks regional botanical account independently support recognition and persistence caveat. No ecological-harm claim is inferred from cultivation escape.

proposedDescription: Peach scale is also called grapevine scale or European peach scale. It feeds on a range of woody plants, so its common name does not limit it to peach trees. Colonies are important in some grape-growing regions, where sap feeding and honeydew can reduce plant quality. The same level of damage should not be assumed for every American garden tree. Other soft scales can occur alongside it and complicate identification.
identification: Mature females are dark brown, broadly oval to elongated, and attached to stems or other feeding sites. Their shape and size change as they develop. Unlike armored scales, the domed surface is part of the female's body rather than a separate detachable shield. Young stages are smaller and paler and may be difficult to see beneath leaves or near bark crevices. Compare several insects, not just one brown bump. Related lecanium scales can look similar; a diagnostic service may need prepared specimens to settle the species.
actions: Mark affected branches and record the host, honeydew, sooty mold and any loss of growth. Inspect incoming nursery plants before placing them among established stock, and avoid sharing infested cuttings. Ask extension to identify the scale and determine whether living populations warrant action. Management timing should follow local crawler activity rather than a calendar from an Australian vineyard. Preserve natural enemies where possible and assess new growth after any treatment; old dead females can remain attached and are not proof that control failed.

proposedDescription: Peach twig borer is a small moth whose caterpillars damage tender shoots and fruit of peaches and other stone fruits. Early feeding can kill a shoot tip; later generations may enter fruit. It is different from the peachtree borer that attacks the lower trunk and crown. That distinction matters because a treatment aimed at one insect may miss the other entirely. Damage and seasonal importance also vary among growing regions.
identification: Young larvae are pale with a dark head. Older larvae become chocolate brown, with pale bands between the body segments that give them a striped appearance. The adult is a small gray moth with narrow, mottled wings and forward-projecting mouthparts. Wilting shoot tips also resemble oriental fruit moth damage, so look for a larva rather than identifying the pest from wilt alone. Photograph the damaged shoot or fruit and any caterpillar with a size reference. Adult moths may require specialist examination because related Anarsia species can be very similar.
actions: Inspect new shoots and developing fruit during the growing season, and use a local orchard monitoring program to decide when action is justified. Ask extension about suitable traps and how to interpret catches alongside actual damage. Larvae protected inside shoots or fruit are harder to reach, making timing more useful than repeated unscheduled spraying. Keep suspect fruit contained when sending a sample, and avoid transporting infested nursery material. For a home tree, confirm whether injury is in shoots, fruit or the trunk before buying a treatment or removing the tree.
researchNotes: UC IPM and Oklahoma State independent extension accounts support stages, injury and oriental fruit moth comparison. British taxonomic split cautions against unaided adult identification. No pesticide rates or universal generation counts.

proposedDescription: Pear blight beetle, also called European shot-hole borer, is an ambrosia beetle that excavates wood and cultivates fungi inside its tunnels. The common name does not mean it causes bacterial fire blight. It has been investigated in Oregon nurseries, including sites in the Willamette Valley. Tiny entrance holes can be the first visible clue, but holes alone cannot distinguish this beetle from other wood-boring insects.
identification: Adults are compact, dark beetles with the head partly hidden beneath the hoodlike front of the body. Females and males differ markedly in size and form, making an isolated photograph difficult to interpret. Look for small, round entrance holes, boring dust and changes in the affected branch or tree. Several ambrosia beetles make similar holes and fungal galleries. Photograph the insect if present, the hole beside a ruler and the whole affected plant. Record the host species and whether the tree was recently transplanted, damaged or growing under stressful conditions.
actions: Ask an extension or plant-health diagnostic service to identify beetles from an affected tree before arranging treatment. Avoid moving infested nursery trees, branches or firewood to another property. Review irrigation and other stresses with the nursery manager or arborist, because prevention should include the condition of the host. Protective treatments, where recommended, need to match adult flight rather than be applied after larvae are already sheltered inside wood. For a damaged landscape tree, assess structural condition separately from pest identity and do not assume that filling the holes will solve the infestation.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. The original assay and Oregon observations support diagnosis referral and stress prevention without a universal trapping or spray schedule. Experimental assay performance does not establish routine field diagnosis from any sawdust sample. Source lineage and access details are recorded in batch-63-notes.md.

proposedDescription: Pear leaf blister moth is a leaf-mining moth associated especially with apple and also with pear and several other woody hosts. The larva feeds within the leaf, producing a rounded blotch rather than chewing an open hole. Heavy populations can reduce useful leaf area, but scattered old mines are not a measure of current larval numbers. Its common name should not be confused with damage caused by pear leaf blister mites.
identification: The characteristic mine is nearly circular and lacks a long introductory corridor. Dark waste accumulates in concentric rings inside the pale area, which later turns brown. A mature larva leaves the mine and makes a small white, boat-shaped cocoon outside it, sometimes in sheltered bark or fruit crevices. Other leafminers produce long winding tracks or tent-like mines, but damaged or overlapping mines can be ambiguous. Photograph the upper and lower leaf surfaces and hold the leaf against light for a clear view of the internal pattern without opening it.
actions: Keep the host name, location and date with photographs and ask a diagnostic service to confirm an unexpected occurrence. Do not transport mined nursery foliage or suspect fruit to another growing area while identification is pending. In an orchard with a confirmed population, monitoring should distinguish fresh occupied mines from empty damage and take parasitoids into account. Avoid blanket spraying simply because brown spots are visible. Management thresholds and seasonal timing from European apple production need local interpretation before they are applied to an American garden or orchard.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. European morphology can support recognition while US establishment and treatment decisions remain explicitly local. proposedDescription: Pear thrips is a minute insect that feeds in developing buds of fruit trees and many deciduous forest trees. Sugar maple is an important host in the Northeast, despite the pear name. When emergence coincides with slow bud opening, feeding can leave distorted or tattered foliage. Outbreaks vary considerably between years, and an otherwise healthy maple may recover without a lasting decline.
identification: Adults are slender, dark brown to nearly black and only about one to one and a half millimeters long. Their narrow wings have long fringes that need magnification to see. Pale larvae feed on expanding tissues. Brown scars along leaf veins or stalks, misshapen new leaves and damaged blossoms can suggest thrips feeding, but frost and other injuries can look similar. Photograph fresh damage and any insects collected from buds or flowers. A close-up of a dark speck is usually not enough to distinguish pear thrips from other thrips.
actions: Start observations around bud opening and bloom rather than after the leaves have fully expanded. Tapping flowers over a pale surface can reveal adults, but a specialist should interpret the insects and crop-specific counts. Do not apply orchard thresholds to a large shade tree without advice. Ask extension about the tree's ability to recover and whether treatment can still reach the insect's vulnerable stage. Protect healthy roots and avoid adding unnecessary stress to a defoliated maple. Record recovery as well as damage so the next season's decision is based on the tree's actual condition.
researchNotes: Penn State fruit guidance and UMass shade-tree account provide independent practical contexts. Fixed dates and numerical orchard thresholds omitted from general public copy.

proposedDescription: Pear trellis rust is a fungal disease that alternates between susceptible pears and junipers. Bright leaf spots on pear are one phase of a life cycle that also involves persistent infections on juniper branches. It is not the only rust affecting pears: in the Pacific Northwest, another pear rust uses incense-cedar instead. Identifying the rust correctly matters before deciding which nearby plants are involved.
identification: On pear, look for orange to yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface. Later, projections develop beneath the spots and form the lattice-like structures behind the trellis name. On a compatible juniper, infected branches can swell and produce orange gelatinous spore structures during wet spring weather. Photograph both sides of an affected pear leaf and any suspicious juniper growth without assuming they are connected. Other rusts can also make orange spots or horns. A diagnostic service may need plant material and details of the nearby hosts to distinguish them.
actions: Seek a diagnosis before removing a valued juniper or starting a spray program. Record when pear spots first appeared and whether compatible junipers are nearby. Where recommended, pruning infected juniper branches can reduce a local source, but spores can arrive from beyond one property. Avoid moving infected nursery plants to new sites. Ask local extension about options for edible versus ornamental pears, since product permissions and useful timing differ. Do not expect removing fallen pear leaves alone to eliminate a fungus that persists in a living juniper host.
researchNotes: OSU distinguishes Pacific Coast rust; RHS independently explains living alternate hosts and management limits; CDFA supports trellis structures. No foreign pesticide availability generalized.

proposedDescription: Pearl millet is a warm-season annual grass grown for grain, forage and ornamental use. Many agricultural references call it Pennisetum glaucum, while Cenchrus americanus is used in newer classifications. A planted field or trial plot is different from a self-sustaining escape. For a plant beyond cultivation, the useful question is whether it produces new generations without being sown again.
identification: The plant has upright, leafy stems, broad blades with fine teeth along the margins and a hairy ligule at the leaf collar. A dense, cylindrical, spike-like flower head develops at the top. Cultivars vary greatly in height, head shape and color, and ornamental selections may have purple foliage. Other plants called millet belong to different genera and can have very different heads. Photograph the entire plant, the leaf collar and a mature head, and keep any seed-package or crop-variety information with the record. Do not identify a grass solely from a field's common-name label.
actions: For an apparent escape, record whether plants recur away from sowing or spilled birdseed and whether they produce another generation. Keep unwanted seed-bearing material out of restoration sites and verify the identity before removing a useful forage planting. Livestock management needs crop-specific advice: drought or other stress can create nitrate concerns even in a familiar forage. Ask a forage adviser about testing suspect feed rather than assuming that a green stand is safe.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Crop identification is well supported; cultivation and a self-sustaining escape are different observations. No inference that a useful forage crop is invasive throughout the United States. Source lineage and access details are recorded in batch-63-notes.md. proposedDescription: Pearl wattle is an Australian shrub or small tree grown for silvery foliage and yellow flowers. It is native to part of eastern Australia and has escaped cultivation elsewhere, including other Australian regions. A documented planted specimen in California confirms horticultural use, not a widespread invasion. When evaluating a tree, the useful distinction is whether it is staying within a managed planting or producing independent seedlings in surrounding vegetation.
identification: Mature foliage consists of oval, leaflike flattened stalks called phyllodes. They are usually silvery gray to blue-green, with soft hairs, a prominent main vein and a tiny point at the tip. Young branchlets have a pale, powdery appearance. Bright yellow spherical flower heads are carried in clusters above or among the foliage, followed by broad, flattened pods. Seedlings can briefly have divided true leaves, so young and mature plants may look surprisingly different. Photograph a young shoot, a mature phyllode and any pods to separate it from other gray-leaved wattles.
actions: Check beneath a fruiting tree and along nearby disturbed ground for seedlings before they become large shrubs. Avoid distributing seed from a planting that is escaping. Where removal is warranted, obtain local advice on young plants and arrange qualified help for a substantial tree. Keep seed-bearing debris out of bushland and other natural vegetation, and revisit after soil disturbance for new seedlings. Do not copy Australian weed classifications or seasonal treatment calendars directly to a United States site; establish the local status and management objective first.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Independent botanical and field accounts support a planting-versus-escape profile; overseas weed behavior is geographically bounded. proposedDescription: Pennyroyal is a perennial mint that occupies seasonally wet ground, including ditches, seeps and wetland margins. In California it can persist in places that once supported native wetland vegetation, although the extent of its ecological effects is not equally well documented everywhere. It spreads by seed and by creeping growth, so a patch may survive after its visible stems have been cut.
identification: The stems are square in cross-section and bear opposite, rounded to oval leaves. Dense rings of small pink, violet or bluish flowers surround the upper stem at the leaf nodes. Leaves are often gray-green and softly hairy, and the plant has a strong mint scent. Its habit varies from low and spreading to upright, so height alone is unreliable. Other mints also have opposite leaves and square stems; the separate flower whorls and the whole flowering shoot provide more useful evidence than a crushed leaf alone.
actions: Confirm the plant before disturbing wetland vegetation, particularly where native mints grow nearby. Small patches can be dug with their creeping stems, followed by repeated checks for regrowth and seedlings. Keep fragments and seed-bearing material out of drainage channels, and clean mud from tools before moving to another wet site. Plan follow-up work rather than expecting one removal to exhaust an established seed bank. For larger wetland infestations, involve the land manager or local weed program so control protects surrounding plants and water.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC original profile/field card plus independent Chico botanist scorecard support morphology, fragments and repeated removal. Wetland context retained without quantified displacement claims.

proposedDescription: Pepper flowerbud moth is a small moth whose larvae feed in developing pepper buds and fruit. Ground cherries can also serve as hosts. It has been recorded in the Gulf Coast region and farther north, but the published North Carolina record is sparse. A damaged pepper does not by itself establish this insect, since several caterpillars and other pests can enter similar plant parts.
identification: Larvae are whitish, with an amber-colored head and a similarly colored plate immediately behind it. They tunnel through flower buds and young fruit, sometimes causing premature fruit drop. Pupation may occur within the fruit or after it reaches the ground. These features help direct a diagnosis but are not a substitute for examining a specimen. Photograph the larva from the side and above, with the damaged bud or fruit and a size reference. Retain information about whether the plant was a cultivated Capsicum pepper or a Physalis ground cherry.
actions: Inspect fresh buds and recently dropped young fruit rather than relying only on old damaged peppers. Keep suspect produce contained while seeking identification from extension or a plant-health service, and ask how to submit a larva without allowing it to escape. Record the proportion of affected buds and whether damage continues on new growth. Avoid transporting infested plants or fruit to another garden. Do not substitute a potato tuber moth or general fruit-borer treatment schedule without confirming that it fits this species and the crop.

proposedDescription: This small pepperweed is an annual or biennial mustard from Eurasia. Its name appears in older North American records, but Flora of North America cautions that most such reports represent misidentified Lepidium densiflorum. That distinction is central to any report of an apparent escape. A roadside pepperweed with tiny flowers is not enough evidence to place this species on a local invasive-plant list.
identification: Plants branch near the base and farther up the stem. Lower leaves can be lobed or toothed, while upper leaves become narrow and may have nearly smooth edges. Flowers are minute, with petals absent or reduced. The most useful distinction is in mature fruit: L. apetalum has small elliptic pods widest around the middle, whereas L. densiflorum has pods widest above the middle. Fine hairs and the shape of the fruit tip also matter in a botanical key. Photograph several ripe pods beside a scale and include both lower and upper leaves.
actions: Ask a herbarium or extension botanist to check a fruiting specimen before initiating species-specific control. Include the exact location, habitat and any connection to imported soil or seed. Avoid scattering mature pods while collecting an authorized sample, and follow the recipient's packaging instructions. Where a pepperweed is unwanted in a garden, identify it and address seed production early, but do not assume that every similar plant is an introduced invader. Preserve the distinction between a verified occurrence and an older name on a record.

proposedDescription: Peregrine saltbush, also called sprawling saltbush, is an Australian plant recorded as introduced in California and Utah. It often occupies disturbed ground. Depending on conditions it can behave as an annual or persist longer, and its stems may sprawl or rise into a low bush. Those traits describe its occurrence; they do not establish a severe ecological effect at every site where it appears.
identification: Leaves are mostly alternate, short-stalked and often diamond-shaped, with coarse irregular teeth. A fine scaly coating can make them look gray or mealy, especially underneath. The flowers are small and clustered in leaf axils. Around each developing female fruit, paired bracteoles enlarge into a flattened, roughly diamond-shaped enclosure with teeth mainly on the upper half. These structures are much more useful than leaf color for separating saltbushes. Photograph mature fruiting bracteoles from several angles, as well as the whole plant. Native Atriplex species can look similar when young or drought-stressed.
actions: Have a fruiting plant checked before removing saltbush from a restoration area or other natural habitat. Record whether the population is confined to recently disturbed soil or is expanding into intact vegetation. Keep soil and seed-bearing debris from the patch out of clean planting areas. If removal is appropriate, work before mature fruits scatter and return to check subsequent growth. For larger populations, ask the local land manager to choose a method suited to the habitat; an Australian management designation is not automatically a United States requirement.

proposedDescription: Perennial cornflower, or mountain bluet, is a European garden perennial that can spread beyond flower beds by both seed and creeping underground stems. It forms persistent patches rather than behaving like an annual bedding flower. Washington places it on a monitor list rather than classifying it as a listed noxious weed. Its local importance therefore needs to be assessed in context, especially near meadows and other open vegetation.
identification: The plant is hairy, with broad, usually unlobed leaves whose bases extend down the stem to form narrow wings. Large flower heads usually stand alone at shoot tips. The inner florets are violet and the enlarged outer florets are commonly blue, though garden selections vary. Overlapping bracts beneath the head have dark, deeply toothed margins. Annual bachelor's button has narrower, smaller leaves and lacks the creeping rhizomes. Include the lower leaves and the base of a flower head in photographs, rather than recording only the blue petals.
actions: For a small unwanted patch, dig carefully enough to remove the underground stems and revisit the site several times during the growing season. Fragments left behind can produce new shoots. Prevent flowers from developing seed, and contain seed-bearing material during disposal. Established patches may need repeated work over several years, so record their boundaries and check the edges as well as the center. Avoid sharing divisions from plants that are escaping. In natural vegetation, seek local advice before broad soil disturbance that could damage desirable neighboring plants.
researchNotes: Washington identification and UAA Alaska management evidence independent; Alaska report references original control observations. Regional monitor status distinguished from statutory noxious listing.

proposedDescription: Perennial pea is a climbing ornamental that persists through underground growth and can escape along roadsides, abandoned gardens and other disturbed places. Unlike an annual sweet pea, an established plant can return after its stems die back. California reports locally dense stands, while King County, Washington, treats it as a weed of concern. Those regional assessments do not mean every cultivated plant has the same impact.
identification: Broad, flattened wings run along the green stems and leaf stalks. Each leaf has a pair of leaflets and a branched terminal tendril that grips neighboring vegetation or a fence. Pea-shaped flowers are held in clusters above the leaves and are commonly pink, with white and other garden forms also occurring. Long flattened pods follow. Narrow-leaved everlasting pea is a close lookalike, so leaflet width alone should be considered alongside the stem, stipules and flowers. Do not identify a climbing pea from flower color alone.
actions: Watch the edges of a planting for shoots spreading into adjoining vegetation and prevent pods from scattering seed. Before clearing a natural area, confirm the species so native peas are not removed with it. A removal plan needs to account for persistent underground growth; cutting the climbing stems once does not demonstrate eradication. Ask the local weed program about follow-up methods suitable for the site and revisit marked patches for returning shoots. Keep the plant and its pods away from livestock feed, and do not treat its pea-like seeds as edible garden peas.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC supports rhizomes and livestock concern; Michigan original botanical project supplies paired-leaflet morphology; King County supplies regional management status. Control prescription intentionally limited to persistence/prevention.

Two leaflets, winged stems, branched tendrils and L. sylvestris comparison.
Weed-of-concern status and discouragement of new plantings.

proposedDescription: Perennial ryegrass is a widely planted pasture and turf grass that also grows outside cultivation. Its value in a managed lawn does not prevent it from competing with desired plants in a meadow or restoration site. The relevant question is the purpose of the site and which plants should be there. Some botanical treatments combine closely related ryegrasses under broader names, making a precise identification especially useful before control.
identification: The grass forms tufts with fibrous roots. Leaf undersides are conspicuously shiny, while the upper surface has lengthwise ridges. New leaves are normally folded in the shoot, and short ear-like projections may occur where the blade meets the sheath. The flowering stem carries a narrow spike with flattened spikelets set edge-on to the central axis. Typical perennial ryegrass lacks the long awns of Italian ryegrass, whose young leaves are usually rolled. Hybrids and variable plants can complicate this comparison. Photograph the leaf collar and an intact mature flowering spike.
actions: Check the seed mixture used at the site before treating a grass that may have been deliberately planted. In a sensitive grassland, identify native grasses first and prioritize small patches near valuable vegetation. Careful hand removal before seed set can be practical for limited patches, with as little soil disturbance as possible. Large areas need a restoration plan that addresses both the unwanted grass and replacement cover. Revisit treated ground to check recruitment and avoid bringing ryegrass seed back in erosion-control mixes or contaminated materials.
researchNotes: Penn State identification plus independent GOERT conservation management support ready status. Broad taxonomic lumping acknowledged, exact treatment follows input ID.

claims: Bunch growth, folded young leaves, membranous ligule and auricles.
Awnless versus Italian ryegrass, hybrids and careful small-patch removal before seed set.
Shiny leaf undersides, ridged upper blades and edge-on spikelets.

proposedDescription: Perennial veldtgrass is a southern African grass introduced for uses including forage and stabilization. In California it can invade sandy habitats and develop dense cover among shrubs. Individual tussocks may eventually merge into an almost continuous grassy layer. Its persistence means that removal is a continuing restoration task, particularly where nearby plants remain a seed source.
identification: Look for an upright tuft of numerous stems with flat leaves that may be green, bluish or tinged reddish purple. The blade margins are often noticeably wavy near the base. Loose branching flower heads rise above the foliage, and the small spikelets can have a mauve cast. A hand lens reveals structures within each spikelet that distinguish this grass from other Ehrharta species. Panic veldtgrass and annual veldtgrass also occur in California, so reddish color or a grassy clump alone is insufficient. Photograph the leaf base, the whole head and individual spikelets if possible.
actions: Confirm the species before removing grasses from dunes or shrubland. Small patches can be pulled or dug, but the whole plant must be removed to prevent resprouting. Work carefully because disturbed soil may stimulate new seedlings, and return to check the cleared area. Contain mature seed heads and clean footwear and tools before leaving the patch. Mowing alone has inconsistent results and should not be treated as a reliable cure. Larger infestations need a site-specific plan that protects native vegetation and includes repeated follow-up against reinvasion.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC Pickart account and Victoria flora supply independent botany; EPPO control derives from Pickart/Frey and is grouped as shared management lineage, not independent replication.

proposedDescription: Perennial wallrocket is a yellow-flowered mustard also grown as wild rocket. Outside cultivation it occupies roadsides, rubble and other disturbed ground, and it is a crop or pasture weed in some regions. It has a persistent root system rather than the purely annual habit suggested by a short-lived salad crop. Australian weed regulations and European agricultural observations should not be read as a blanket statement about its impact across the United States.
identification: Leaves are usually hairless, somewhat blue-green and deeply divided into narrow lobes, with smaller leaves higher on the stem. Four bright yellow petals form each flower. Long slender pods develop on stalks, with a short additional stalk between the main flower stalk and the pod itself. The stem can become woody at the base. Annual wallrocket, Diplotaxis muralis, generally has smaller, less leafy stems, but mature flowers and fruits are needed for a reliable comparison. Photograph the pod attachment closely, along with lower and upper leaves.
actions: Check whether a patch originated from a garden planting before reporting an escape. Prevent unwanted plants from setting seed and keep soil or mature pods from being moved into clean beds. Because established plants have a substantial root system, clipping the flowering stalks is containment rather than proof of removal. Seek locally appropriate advice for persistent populations, especially in crops or native vegetation. Do not transfer a foreign herbicide recommendation to an edible garden. Revisit the site after management and record whether growth returns from old crowns or new seedlings.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Perennial-root and fruit characters support recognition; Australian agricultural impacts and controls are not generalized to US sites. Local establishment, measured harm and treatment efficacy are not inferred beyond the cited regional evidence. Prevention and sampling advice is editorial guidance, not a tested eradication protocol. proposedDescription: Perfumed passionflower is a vigorous tropical vine grown for its large red flowers. Its grape-like leaves explain the alternative name grape-leaved passionflower. Hawaiian herbarium records include both cultivated plants and vines recorded along forest trails, so the setting of an observation matters. In a cold-climate conservatory it is a managed ornamental; in a warm landscape, growth beyond the planting deserves closer attention.
identification: The leaves are deeply divided into three lobes, usually with toothed margins and a darker upper surface. Young stems and leaf stalks have conspicuous reddish or rusty hairs. Tendrils attach the vine to supports. Flowers have scarlet petals and sepals surrounding a shorter central corona, and the oval fruit can be green with pale speckles. Some other red passionflowers have unlobed leaves, which makes foliage useful alongside the flower. Photograph leaf undersides, the leaf stalk and its small glands, and a complete flower rather than using flower color alone.
actions: Keep cultivated vines on a support where their growth can be checked, and watch neighboring vegetation for stems or seedlings beyond the intended planting. Avoid dumping cuttings or fruit in forest margins. If a vine is climbing through a tree, obtain advice before pulling it down, since forceful removal can damage the support plant. Report an apparent new wild population with its location and whether a garden or abandoned nursery is nearby. Ask the local invasive-species program about regional priorities before adopting control advice for a different passionflower species.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Vouchered Hawaiian context and independent horticultural description support a careful escape-recognition profile. Local establishment, measured harm and treatment efficacy are not inferred beyond the cited regional evidence. Prevention and sampling advice is editorial guidance, not a tested eradication protocol. proposedDescription: Persea mite is a spider mite best known as a pest of avocado. Colonies feed beneath small silken shelters on the leaves, and heavy infestations can cause premature leaf drop. Loss of foliage can expose fruit and branches to sunburn. The mite also occurs on other plants, but finding it near an avocado does not mean every neighboring tree is a feeding host.
identification: Turn over an affected leaf and look for small, roundish silvery patches of silk. Feeding beneath them produces discrete yellowish or brown spots, initially most evident underneath and later visible from above. The mites themselves are tiny, greenish or yellowish, with dark food spots in the body. Several avocado mites and beneficial predatory mites may occur together. Silk shelters and the spot pattern are useful clues, but reliable species confirmation requires magnified examination; specialists may examine slide-mounted adult males. Keep intact leaves available for a diagnostic sample.
actions: Monitor living mites on several leaves rather than judging the problem from accumulated brown spots alone. Ask extension to distinguish pest mites from predators before selecting treatment. Maintain appropriate irrigation and address other avocado stresses, since a weakened tree tolerates leaf loss poorly. Preserve beneficial mites and avoid unnecessary broad insecticide applications. Commercial predator releases require appropriate species and timing, so seek advice before purchasing them. Keep infested nursery plants separate and record whether new leaves remain healthy after management; old feeding spots will not disappear.
researchNotes: UC management and independent EFSA diagnostic synthesis support practical guidance. EFSA incorporates UC biology but also original morphological/taxonomic work; grouped accordingly.

proposedDescription: Persian ryegrass, often called Persian darnel, is an introduced annual grass that can be troublesome in spring grain crops of the northern Great Plains. It emerges around the same time as the crop and may go unnoticed until seed heads become visible. Preventing seed return is especially valuable because this weed's seed bank is relatively short-lived compared with that of many persistent perennial weeds.
identification: Young plants have narrow, smooth leaves with shiny undersides and often a reddish stem base. The short, membranous ligule contrasts with the longer papery ligule of wild oat, while downy brome has much hairier foliage. Mature plants tiller from the base and carry a flattened-looking spike with spikelets in two rows. Seed and awn characters vary among descriptions, so do not decide from the presence of an awn alone. A seed laboratory can compare the floret surface and its attachment structures with annual ryegrass, which can be difficult to separate.
actions: Inspect fields while grasses are young enough for a useful management decision, and keep suspect seedlings with their leaf collars intact for identification. Map patches before harvest and avoid carrying contaminated seed or material into clean fields. Work with an agronomist on a combined plan that limits new seed production and suits the crop rotation and tillage system. Some populations resist particular herbicide groups, so repeating the same approach without checking results can fail. Revisit mapped patches in following seasons to distinguish successful suppression from a temporary reduction in visible plants.
researchNotes: Montana guide supplies original regional ecology and resistance context; CFIA seed diagnosis independent. Awn conflict between Montana and CFIA explicitly avoided rather than resolved by assumption.

claims: Seedling comparisons, early crop competition, seedbank and resistance.
Annual life cycle and distinction from annual ryegrass using florets.

proposedDescription: Persimmon wilt is associated with the fungus Nalanthamala diospyri, which older references call Cephalosporium diospyri or Acremonium diospyri. American persimmon is an important susceptible host. In a grafted orchard, the identity of the rootstock matters as much as the named fruiting variety: Florida guidance warns that infected propagation material can threaten susceptible American persimmon rootstocks. Wilting alone cannot identify the fungus.
identification: Look for persistent wilting, dying branches and decline of the tree top, and record whether symptoms began in one part of the canopy or throughout it. Other fungi, root damage and water stress can cause similar changes. Pink spore masses have been described beneath the bark of trees killed by this wilt, but stripping healthy bark to search for them creates wounds and is not a sensible field test. A plant diagnostic laboratory should examine appropriate tissue and interpret the result alongside the host, graft and site history.
actions: Use clean, traceable scion material when propagating persimmons and avoid taking cuttings from a declining tree. Contact extension promptly for sampling instructions and keep pruning tools clean between trees. Avoid unnecessary bark wounds. Once infection is confirmed, arrange removal and disposal according to local guidance rather than moving suspect wood or propagation material elsewhere. Check nearby trees and record their rootstocks if known. Do not assume a general fungicide spray will reverse an established vascular wilt, and have a hazardous dead tree assessed independently of the disease diagnosis.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Host-specific pathology and propagation advice are usable without asserting that the pathogen is introduced. Historic pathology supports biology, not a current geographic survey or a general insecticide prescription. Source lineage and access details are recorded in batch-63-notes.md.

claims: Type strain from wilted American persimmon in Tennessee.
Host/rootstock susceptibility and clean propagation guidance.

proposedDescription: Peruvian groundcherry, also known as cape gooseberry or poha, is cultivated for its husked fruit and has naturalized in Hawaii. It is a short-lived, softly woody perennial in suitable climates, though cold can limit its persistence elsewhere. The familiar papery lantern is shared by many Physalis species, including native groundcherries, so a garden escape should be identified before it is treated as this particular plant.
identification: The stems and leaves are densely hairy. Leaves are generally oval with a pointed tip and a heart-shaped base, sometimes appearing as unequal pairs near a node. Solitary pale yellow flowers hang from the leaf axils and have distinct purplish-brown marks near the base of the corolla. The calyx enlarges into a papery enclosure around a rounded yellowish berry containing many seeds. Other groundcherries have similar flowers and husks; include hairiness, leaf shape, mature fruit and the whole plant in a photographic record.
actions: Keep a cultivated planting within its intended area and collect unwanted fallen fruit before it becomes a source of volunteers. Record seedlings beyond the bed and check whether they survive and reproduce independently. Before clearing a wild patch, have it compared with local Physalis species. Avoid moving fruit-filled soil or garden waste into natural vegetation. Hawaiian management literature expresses uncertainty about chemical susceptibility, so ask for current local advice rather than treating an old tentative recommendation as established control. Keep unidentified groundcherries out of harvested produce until a knowledgeable person has confirmed the plant.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. An independent flora corroborates recognition; speculative chemical control in the Hawaii guide is excluded rather than required for clearance. The Hawaii guide labels proposed chemical efficacy as probable. Public actions remain seed/cutting containment and local advice. Source lineage and access details are recorded in batch-63-notes.md. proposedDescription: Peruvian peppertree is an evergreen ornamental with a loose, drooping canopy. Although it is often called California pepper tree, it is native to South America. In California it can establish beyond plantings in washes, slopes and other suitable places, with impacts assessed as limited rather than uniform across the state. An old shade tree and an expanding population of seedlings call for different management decisions.
identification: Leaves are alternate and feather-like, divided into many narrow, pointed leaflets. The long leaves and hanging branches create a fine, weeping appearance. Small pale flowers are carried in branching clusters, followed by rounded pink to red fruits on fruiting trees. Brazilian peppertree has fewer, much broader leaflets and a less finely divided look. Photograph a complete compound leaf, its attachment to the branch and any fruit. Common names can be confusing, so use the scientific name when seeking advice or comparing nursery records.
actions: Inspect beneath the tree and along nearby drainage lines for seedlings, and record whether they are spreading into natural vegetation. Remove small unwanted seedlings where permitted before they become substantial trees. Established plants can produce root sprouts after removal, so arrange follow-up checks over several years. A mature tree requires an arborist's assessment and an appropriate removal plan rather than casual cutting. Keep fruit-bearing debris out of undeveloped land. Where the tree is retained, monitor recruitment and ask the local weed program which nearby habitats deserve priority protection.
researchNotes: Virginia Tech dendrology and Florida botanical key independent of UC DiTomaso management lineage. Limited California impacts kept contextual; no food safety claim.

claims: Drooping compound leaves with numerous narrow leaflets.

proposedDescription: Peruvian primrose-willow is a shrubby wetland plant that can form dense stands along shorelines and in drainage areas. Florida programs identify it as an invasive management concern. A 2026 federal review treats southeastern US populations as introduced. Older sources differ over its origin, so local records still need careful interpretation. It is important to separate this upright shrub from the creeping water-primrose complex rather than attaching every floating yellow-flowered mat to the same name.
identification: Young stems and alternate leaves are hairy. The leaves are pointed, often broad enough to appear oval rather than narrowly willow-like. Large yellow flowers are usually solitary and have four broad petals. Mature fruits are relatively short, stout, hairy capsules with four angles. The Florida-native relative Ludwigia octovalvis can also have hairy foliage and four-petaled flowers, but its capsules are longer and round in cross-section. Photograph flowers and mature capsules as well as the overall growth habit; these details are more useful than a distant shoreline photograph.
actions: Do not plant or move a suspect primrose-willow into a pond or drainage channel. Report expanding stands to the waterbody manager and include photographs of the fruiting stems. Avoid breaking up vegetation or moving seed-bearing debris through the water while identification is pending. Aquatic control should be planned by people familiar with the site, neighboring native plants and any permit requirements. Check treated shorelines for seedlings and renewed growth, and keep equipment free of mud and plant material before using it elsewhere. Control advice for creeping water-primroses may not suit this upright shrub.

proposedDescription: Pestilence wort is better known as common butterbur, a large-leaved perennial introduced from Europe. It favors moist ground and can spread into dense patches through fleshy underground stems. The broad foliage shades surrounding plants, while fragments can start new growth after disturbance. A patch beside a stream therefore needs attention to both the visible leaves and the material hidden in the soil.
identification: Thick flowering stalks emerge in early spring before the large leaves have fully expanded. Their clustered flower heads are usually pink to purplish. Later, broad heart- or kidney-shaped leaves rise on long, hollow, ridged stalks; the undersides are woolly. Giant butterbur has similar huge leaves but usually paler white to yellowish flowers. Burdock produces prickly burrs and has a different flowering habit. Native Petasites also occur, so compare spring flowers and leaf form rather than deciding from size alone. Photographs from more than one season can be especially helpful.
actions: For a small confirmed patch, careful digging can remove plants, but expect to revisit repeatedly for shoots arising from missed fragments. Keep excavated roots and rhizomes contained, and inspect the disposal or temporary storage area for regrowth. Avoid moving contaminated soil to another bed or streambank. Large colonies near water need a plan that limits erosion and protects desirable vegetation during removal. Ask the local invasive-plant program about disposal and follow-up. Do not spread divisions from an ornamental planting into natural areas, even if the plant was originally purchased as useful ground cover.
researchNotes: UMass morphology and Minnesota DNR management provide independent guidance; regional differences and native lookalikes explicit.

proposedDescription: Petty spurge is a small annual weed of gardens, disturbed soil and nursery containers. It is easy to overlook because its flowers are green and blend into the foliage. Unlike perennial spurges that spread through underground runners, this species depends on repeated seed production. Removing a few plants before they mature can therefore prevent a much larger crop of volunteers in the same bed.
identification: The plant grows upright and branches into pale green, leafy stems. Small oval leaves and broader leaflike bracts surround inconspicuous flower structures near the shoot tips. Damaged tissue releases milky sap, but deliberately breaking a plant is unnecessary for identification. Petty spurge can resemble a small leafy spurge; the latter's persistent underground spread is an important difference. Prostrate garden spurges have a much flatter habit. Photograph the branching top, ordinary stem leaves and developing fruit, since several green-flowered spurges can look alike in a quick overhead view.
actions: Wear gloves when pulling plants and keep the irritating sap away from skin and eyes. Remove young plants before seed develops, preferably when the soil allows roots to lift without excessive disturbance. Check nursery pots and the ground beneath benches, where inconspicuous plants can replenish the seed supply. After clearing a garden bed, suitable mulch can reduce new emergence, but continue checking gaps and edges. Keep mature seed-bearing weeds out of clean potting material. For persistent nursery problems, confirm the species and ask extension for current crop-safe options rather than assuming that guidance for perennial leafy spurge applies.
researchNotes: NC State nursery guide and UC Marin hand-removal guidance independent. No unverified seed-dormancy duration or herbicide efficacy claim.
