proposedDescription: Phantasma scale is an armored scale insect affecting palms and other ornamental plants. It has been found in Hawaii and Florida, where nursery movement and landscape plantings make careful inspection important. Dense populations can produce yellowing and leaf loss. The adult female remains enclosed within the shed skin of an earlier stage, which helps explain why an apparently simple surface infestation can be difficult to identify and manage.
identification: Look on both sides of leaves, including folds where early colonies may be hidden. Numerous tiny white male coverings can give foliage a whitewashed appearance. Female coverings are less conspicuous and may look translucent, brownish or reddish; red bands are sometimes present but are not universal. Fiorinia fioriniae is extremely similar in the field. Reliable identification requires a specialist to examine prepared specimens under a microscope, so photographs are useful for screening but should not be treated as final confirmation of a new occurrence.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants separate and avoid moving infested palms or cut foliage between sites. Send a sealed sample to extension following their instructions, with the host name and purchase history if known. Inspect nearby plants rather than assuming that only palms can carry the scale. Preserve lady beetles, lacewings and parasitoid wasps that may be attacking the population. Ask for current guidance matched to the host and scale stage before treatment, and assess living insects afterward because empty coverings can remain attached long after an insect dies.
researchNotes: Original 2015 taxonomy and 2021 Florida field survey are separate research lineages; UF Collier supplies current sample/conservation guidance. Mirrors of survey counted once.

proposedDescription: Pharaoh ants are tiny household ants that can establish persistent colonies in warm indoor spaces. They exploit food and water in buildings and can spread through concealed cavities. Colonies have an unusual management complication: disturbance or repellent treatment may split them into additional nesting groups. Seeing fewer workers immediately after spraying therefore does not necessarily mean the infestation has been resolved.
identification: Workers are very small, generally yellowish to reddish with darker areas, and have a two-segmented waist. Under magnification the antenna has twelve segments with a three-segmented club at the tip, and the body lacks the conspicuous thoracic spines seen in some other ants. Thief ants are a close household lookalike, and a microscope may be needed to distinguish them. Photograph trails and collect a few workers for identification as directed by a pest professional. Record where the ants find water and food, rather than concentrating only on the point where they emerge.
actions: Have the species confirmed before using an ant spray. A coordinated bait program is usually more appropriate, allowing workers to carry a suitable product back to the colony. Place commercial baits only as directed and keep them inaccessible to children and pets. Reduce competing food sources, fix leaks and monitor trails so bait placement can be adjusted. In an apartment building, coordinate through management because colonies may occupy connected spaces beyond one room. Avoid repellent products around an active bait program, and continue monitoring after visible activity falls.
researchNotes: UF and Minnesota independent extension lineages support identification and budding/bait response. Avoids universal tropical origin claim and does not prescribe homemade toxicant recipes.

claims: Colony budding, trail/resource location and nonrepellent bait approach.

proposedDescription: Phialophora wilt is a fungal disease of carnations that can move with infected planting material. It affects the plant's water-conducting tissues and may develop gradually, making a slowly fading greenhouse crop easy to mistake for a watering problem. The pathogen can persist in soil and infected plants, and spores can spread with water. Clean propagation stock is therefore more valuable than waiting for a conspicuous outbreak.
identification: Affected plants wilt and their leaves become yellow to straw-colored. The vascular tissue inside stems can turn dark brown, while advanced plants may show surprisingly little soft tissue rot. Compared with Fusarium wilt, symptoms are less characteristically confined to one side, but this is a clue rather than a reliable diagnosis. Root problems and other carnation diseases overlap in appearance. Record which plants and benches are affected, whether the pattern follows a cutting batch or irrigation route, and how symptoms changed over time. Submit appropriate tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory.
actions: Start with disease-free cuttings and keep incoming batches identifiable. Separate suspect plants while arranging diagnosis, and avoid taking propagation material from them. Remove confirmed infected plants promptly according to nursery guidance and review sanitation of benches, containers and growing media before replanting. Keep drainage or irrigation water from carrying contamination into healthy stock. Ask a greenhouse specialist about suitable media treatment and current crop-protection options; treatment intended for a water mold or a different wilt may not address this fungus. Monitor neighboring plants after removal because symptomless material may still require attention.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Two extension pathology teams support recognition and clean-stock advice; uncertain invasion history is not converted to a crop-management hold. Local establishment, measured harm and treatment efficacy are not inferred beyond the cited regional evidence. Prevention and sampling advice is editorial guidance, not a tested eradication protocol. proposedDescription: Philippine evergreen is a tropical foliage plant widely grown indoors and in shaded warm-climate landscapes. Its silver-marked leaves have also been selected into many ornamental forms, so a nursery label may refer to a cultivar or hybrid rather than a readily recognizable wild species. Introduction records include Puerto Rico, but presence in cultivation does not establish ecological harm. A plant kept alive in a maintained bed is different from seedlings establishing independently in nearby vegetation.
identification: The plant has short, upright stems bearing simple, pointed, lance-shaped leaves in a spiral arrangement. Typical foliage is glossy dark green with silver-gray markings, although cultivated forms vary. The flower structure is a pale upright spadix surrounded by a greenish-white spathe, followed by fleshy berries that turn orange to red. Other Aglaonema and related aroids can have similar leaves and flower structures. Photograph the whole plant, stem, leaf attachment and any flowers, and preserve a cultivar label rather than forcing an identification from the variegation pattern alone.
actions: Keep discarded divisions, stem pieces and potting material out of tropical woodland or drainage areas. If plants appear beyond a managed bed, record whether they are rooted independently and whether seedlings or fruit are present. Seek a botanical identification before removing unfamiliar aroids from natural vegetation. For a houseplant, ordinary containment and responsible disposal are more appropriate than treating the pot as an invasive-species emergency. Ask local extension about regional status before planting outdoors, especially near humid forest habitat, and distinguish persistent planted clumps from evidence of wider spread.

proposedDescription: Philippine ground orchid is a terrestrial orchid that has escaped cultivation in tropical regions, including parts of the Caribbean, Florida and Hawaii. Its attractive flowers do not make it ecologically interchangeable with native orchids. UF/IFAS assigns it a high predicted invasion risk and does not recommend general planting in Florida. Risk assessments describe potential as well as observed behavior, so local records still matter.
identification: Clumps arise from crowded pseudobulbs near the soil surface. Long, broad leaves have deep lengthwise folds, giving them a pleated appearance. A tall stalk carries several pink to purple flowers, usually opening a few at a time, and seed capsules may develop while other flowers remain open. The flower's lip is distinctly lobed, with contrasting yellow and pink markings. Native terrestrial orchids and cultivated hybrids can be confusing. Photograph the folded leaves, base of the clump, full flower stalk and a close flower view before deciding which orchid is present.
actions: Avoid planting or sharing this orchid where regional advice discourages it, especially beside native orchid habitat. Keep discarded pseudobulbs and seed capsules out of natural vegetation. Report a new wild clump with its location and distance from gardens, and ask a botanist to confirm the identification before any removal. Where a land manager approves control, arrange containment before mature capsules open and follow up for new plants. Do not transfer a treatment for another invasive orchid automatically: the protected basal growth and the surrounding native vegetation require a site-specific approach.

proposedDescription: Epicoccum sorghinum is a fungus formerly known as Phoma sorghina. It has been associated with leaf spots, blights and other symptoms on several crops, rather than one uniform disease called Phoma blight. A United States study confirmed it causing leaf spot on rice in Texas. Independent Ethiopian work also identified it among rice sheath-rot fungi. These findings concern particular hosts and tested isolates; they do not identify every spotted rice leaf or every fungus called Phoma.
identification: Visible symptoms depend on the host and can overlap with many other diseases. The Texas report described dark lesions that developed paler centers and dark margins, but those features are not unique to this fungus. Tiny fungal structures within a spot cannot normally be identified to species with an ordinary photograph. Laboratories use culture characteristics and DNA sequence evidence, interpreted with the affected host and symptoms. Photograph whole plants and close views of both leaf surfaces, and record whether lesions also occur on sheaths or stems. Note cultivar, irrigation conditions and the first date symptoms were observed.
actions: Contact a crop diagnostic service before choosing a disease-specific treatment. Keep a representative sample from the advancing margin of damage according to the laboratory's instructions, rather than sending only completely dead tissue. Retain seed-lot and planting records so linked plants can be assessed if the identification is confirmed. Avoid moving suspect propagation material into clean production areas. Management findings from a different host or country need local interpretation, especially when several pathogens occur together. Monitor new lesions after any recommended action, because the old necrotic tissue will not return to healthy green.

proposedDescription: Phytophthora cinnamomi is a soilborne water mold that damages roots of many woody and herbaceous plants. On avocado it is a major cause of root rot. It moves with contaminated plants, soil and water, so prevention depends on what enters a site as well as how a sick plant is treated. Wet, poorly drained ground favors disease, and adding more water to a wilting tree can make the underlying problem worse.
identification: An affected avocado may have a sparse canopy, small pale leaves, brown leaf tips and dying twigs even while the soil remains wet. Fine feeder roots become dark, brittle and scarce. These signs suggest root dysfunction but are not unique to this pathogen. Other Phytophthora species and noninfectious drainage problems can look similar. The whole pattern, including roots and site history, should guide sampling. A laboratory must confirm the organism; a photograph of a declining canopy cannot identify the species.
actions: Use healthy nursery stock from a reliable supplier and inspect roots before planting. Improve drainage and match irrigation to actual soil moisture rather than routinely watering a wilted plant. Avoid working in soggy soil and carrying mud on footwear or equipment between sites. Keep runoff from suspect areas away from clean plantings. For an infected avocado, seek an integrated plan that addresses roots, irrigation and any professional treatment. Tolerant rootstocks are not immune, and replacing a dead tree with another susceptible plant in untreated infested soil may repeat the problem.
researchNotes: UC avocado guidance and independent Tasmanian plant-health diagnosis support species-level laboratory caution and integrated prevention. EPPO diagnostic standard corroborates laboratory identification.

proposedDescription: Pigeonpea is a cultivated food and agroforestry shrub, often grown as an annual even though it can persist for several years in a suitable climate. It has been moved widely through agriculture. Growing outside its original range does not necessarily make pigeonpea invasive. UF/IFAS currently describes it as not a documented problem species across Florida's assessment zones. Volunteer plants should still be evaluated in their local setting.
identification: The shrub has many slender branches and leaves divided into three leaflets. Leaf undersides are paler or silvery and carry fine hairs. Pea-shaped flowers are yellow, sometimes with reddish coloring on the outside. Flattened pods are visibly depressed between the seeds. Cultivars vary in stature, flowering time and seed color. Other three-leaflet legumes can resemble seedlings, so photograph a complete leaf, flowers and mature pods rather than trying to identify a young volunteer from one leaflet. A crop label or seed source can provide useful context.
actions: Record whether plants beyond a field are isolated volunteers or are reproducing over successive seasons. Keep unwanted mature pods out of restoration soil and avoid dumping crop residues where seedlings would be difficult to monitor. Remove confirmed unwanted volunteers early where permitted, while preserving deliberately managed food plantings. Before sowing near a natural area, ask local extension whether pigeonpea is suitable for that location and objective.

proposedDescription: Pike killifish is a predatory livebearing fish introduced to southern Florida. Despite the name and long jaws, it belongs to the livebearer family rather than the true pikes. It eats small fishes and can affect native fish populations. Historical Texas records should not be read as proof of a current population there; USGS describes that introduction as apparently lost, while Florida populations are established.
identification: The body is elongated, with a pointed snout, long toothed jaws and a lower jaw that projects beyond the upper. Irregular rows of dark spots run along the sides, and a larger dark mark may occur near the tail base. The dorsal fin begins well behind the anal fin. Females grow larger than males. The pike-like head is striking, but combine it with body pattern and fin placement to distinguish this fish from native elongated species. Photograph the entire side of a specimen beside a scale without moving it to another waterbody.
actions: Never release an aquarium fish into a canal, pond or stream, and do not use an unfamiliar live fish as bait elsewhere. If a captive fish is no longer wanted, seek a responsible aquarium or animal-care placement. Report a suspected new wild occurrence to the state fish and wildlife agency or USGS nonindigenous-species reporting program with the exact location and photographs. Follow local instructions for any captured fish rather than relocating it. Waterway-scale removal or treatment belongs with fisheries managers, who can assess native species and whether control is practical.
researchNotes: USGS occurrence synthesis and Florida Museum original collection/morphology support independent evidence. Prevention follows documented aquarium/farm release pathways; no unsupported home eradication.

proposedDescription: Pine bark anobiid beetle is associated with dead conifer material that retains bark. Its larvae feed mainly in the bark and the outermost sapwood, so their presence does not automatically mean the deep structural attack associated with some other wood borers. Emerging adults can nevertheless make holes through coverings placed over infested timber. Correct identification can prevent both unnecessary treatment and overlooked secondary damage.
identification: Adults are small, pale yellow-brown to darker brown beetles with fine hairs and a relatively soft body covering. Larvae produce galleries and granular boring dust; emerging adults leave small round exit holes. A particularly helpful clue is dust containing both dark bark particles and pale wood particles near remaining bark strips. Other beetles also make round holes, and old holes can persist long after activity ends. Photograph the beetle if present, the hole beside a scale, the dust and the wood's remaining bark. Retain a specimen for a timber-pest specialist rather than diagnosing from a hole alone.
actions: Inspect incoming bark-covered conifer objects or timber before placing them with stored material. Isolate a suspect movable item and clean beneath it so fresh dust can be distinguished from old debris. Bark removal and exclusion from finished timber can prevent this particular problem, but structural work should be assessed by a qualified person. For an important wooden object, consult a conservator before heat or cold treatment. Do not apply broad woodworm chemicals simply because exit holes are visible, and check any damaged covering for water-entry problems.

proposedDescription: Pine oystershell scale, also called Oriental pine scale, is an armored scale associated with pine needles. It is native to Asia and has been introduced to the United States. The common name overlaps with other scales, including Lepidosaphes newsteadi, so a report should retain the scientific identification. Several related pine scales are treated together in risk assessments, but evidence for one should not automatically be assigned to all of them.
identification: Look for small brown, shell-like coverings attached near the bases of pine needles. Feeding can produce yellowing around the attachment area, and heavy infestations may be associated with broader needle decline. The covering protects the insect but is not enough to identify it confidently. Several Lepidosaphes species have similar elongated armor, and reliable separation requires microscopic examination of prepared adult females. Photograph the needle base, the whole shoot and the host pine, and keep an intact sample available for an extension or plant-health laboratory.
actions: Inspect nursery pines carefully before moving them into a collection, especially compact plants where needle bases are difficult to see. Keep a suspect plant apart while identification is pending and avoid sharing infested cuttings or branches. Ask a local adviser whether living scales are numerous enough to warrant management and how to monitor the mobile crawler stage. Do not use another pine scale's seasonal schedule without checking it. Evaluate fresh growth and living insects after any action, because attached empty armor and old yellow needles can remain visible.

proposedDescription: Pine woolly aphid, treated here as the historically named Pineus pini group, is an adelgid associated with pine shoots and bark. White wax around colonies can make an infestation conspicuous, but the name has been used inconsistently for closely related Pineus species. International forestry accounts warn that some records combine P. pini, P. boerneri and older names without preserved specimens. A cottony patch on a pine therefore deserves identification before it is assigned a particular distribution or damage history.
identification: The insects are tiny, usually concealed beneath gray-white, threadlike wax. Eggs and young stages can occur together on twigs, and mobile crawlers provide a means of spread. Affected shoots may lose needles or decline when populations are damaging, particularly on young nursery plants. Other adelgids, aphids and harmless material can produce superficially similar patches. Photograph the colony in place, the pine's needles and the overall branch condition. A specialist may need insects from beneath the wax and the exact host species to narrow the identification.
actions: Keep suspect nursery stock separate and avoid moving colonized shoots between properties. Ask a forest-health or extension service to identify the adelgid and assess actual shoot injury. Record whether the tree is growing normally, whether fresh colonies are increasing and whether predators are present. Native natural enemies can help limit populations in some regions, so unnecessary broad spraying may be counterproductive. Treatment timing and expectations should follow local advice for the confirmed species. Do not import a foreign outbreak calendar or assume that every white-waxed colony requires removal of the tree.

proposedDescription: Pineapple mealybug is a small sap-feeding insect that often stays hidden at the base of a pineapple plant. It also uses other bromeliads and many unrelated plants. In Hawaii, where it occurs on the major islands, its importance includes its association with pineapple mealybug wilt. Feeding can also leave pale patches and damage the base of developing fruit. Ants often attend colonies, collecting honeydew while protecting the mealybugs from their natural enemies.
identification: Look beneath lower leaves, around the plant butt, and on exposed roots for oval insects covered with white powdery wax. The body beneath is pink or pink-orange, with 17 pairs of wax filaments around its margin. Small moving crawlers may be easier to overlook than established females. Gray pineapple mealybug, Dysmicoccus neobrevipes, is a close lookalike that more often occupies aboveground foliage and fruit. Body color and feeding position are useful clues, but a specialist should confirm the species because the two can occur together.
actions: Inspect planting material and the roots of potted bromeliads before moving them beside healthy plants. If colonies are found, keep affected material separate and ask extension staff about both mealybugs and the ants tending them. In pineapple production, remove infested crop residues and manage host weeds around the planting as part of a coordinated plan. Preserve predators and parasitoids; controlling the insects while protective ants remain can give poor results. A wilting pineapple needs diagnosis because appearance alone cannot establish virus infection.
researchNotes: UH management and US occurrence paired with independent USDA identification tool. UF profile derives substantial biology from UH and is not counted separately. No universal claim of parthenogenesis or current pesticide recommendation.

proposedDescription: Pineapple weed is a small aromatic annual commonly noticed along worn paths, pavement edges, and disturbed garden soil. It can also grow in turf and nursery beds. Its name comes from the pineapple-like scent of the foliage and flower heads. Flora of North America treats it as native to northwestern North America and spread elsewhere, including eastern parts of the continent. A weed catalog entry therefore does not make it a foreign invader everywhere. Local abundance and the purpose of the site help determine whether removal is useful.
identification: Young plants begin as a low rosette. The first pair of leaves is opposite, while later leaves alternate and divide into very fine, soft-looking segments. Smooth stems branch and can stay low or rise above a foot. Rounded yellow-green flower heads sit at branch tips without the conspicuous white rays of familiar chamomiles. Use the combination of finely divided leaves, rayless heads, and characteristic scent; a yellow button alone is not enough. Flowers may appear through much of the growing season, followed by small seeds.
actions: Where plants interfere with a bed or path, pull small individuals before the heads set seed. Their shallow root system usually makes removal manageable, although larger plants can have a wider fibrous network. Recheck the same bare patches for new seedlings rather than expecting one visit to finish the job. In turf, discuss the underlying poor growing conditions with a local extension office. Avoid removing every small aromatic daisy from natural vegetation without checking its identity and local status first.

proposedDescription: Pineneedle toadflax is a North African plant also known as Linaria reticulata; the New England treatment describes it as annual, while a later herbarium account gives a conflicting perennial description. Its spurred flowers resemble miniature snapdragons. Reports from North America need particular care: a New England flora lists Connecticut, but a published voucher audit found no certain specimen and reported that reviewed North American material belonged to Moroccan toadflax instead. That disagreement leaves the identity of historical escapes unresolved. A garden label or old county record should therefore be checked against the actual plant.
identification: Look for slender upright stems and narrow, linear leaves. Lower leaves may occur in whorls, with upper leaves arranged alternately. Typical flowers are purple to red-purple with darker netlike veins and a conspicuous yellow palate, the raised area closing the mouth of the flower. The New England key gives flowers about 15 to 18 mm long and a shorter spur of 5 to 7 mm. Moroccan toadflax has larger flowers, a largely white palate, and a longer spur. Cultivated color mixtures complicate identification, so photograph the spur, calyx, and leaf arrangement together.
actions: If an unfamiliar plant appears outside a flower bed, record its location and whether seedlings recur the following season. Send flowering photographs to a local herbarium or extension office under both Linaria pinifolia and Linaria reticulata. Avoid distributing seed from escaped plants while their identity is being checked. In a managed garden, removing unwanted plants before mature seed develops is a sensible containment step, but a regional specialist should advise on any larger roadside population. There is no basis here for treating it like perennial yellow toadflax.

proposedDescription: Pinguin is a large terrestrial bromeliad native to tropical America, including parts of the Caribbean. Its tough rosettes have been used as living barriers, a role made effective by the sharply hooked teeth along the leaves. In Florida it is a nonnative ornamental escape that can form dense colonies. A plant's status therefore depends strongly on location: a Florida escape and a population within its Caribbean native range require different decisions.
identification: The plant forms a broad rosette of long, narrow, arching leaves that can reach roughly two meters. Large hooked teeth line the margins. Inner leaves and bracts turn red around flowering, while the stout flower cluster has conspicuous whitish, powdery or woolly surfaces. Flowers have rose to purple petals, and the mature fruits are fleshy, yellowish berries. New rosettes develop on spreading underground or near-ground connections. The combination of terrestrial growth, fierce marginal teeth, red inner foliage, and a pale-coated flower cluster is more useful than the common name, which is also applied loosely to other bromeliads.
actions: Before removing a colony, confirm both the species and whether it is native at the site. In Florida landscapes where an escape is unwanted, stop moving offsets and inspect the colony edge for younger rosettes. UF/IFAS recommends uprooting; stout gloves, protective clothing, and tools that keep hands away from the hooked leaves are important. Large thickets merit professional help. Remove connected growth carefully and revisit the site for surviving rosettes. Keep discarded plants out of adjacent natural vegetation, where vegetative pieces may establish another patch.
researchNotes: Independent NYBG morphology/native context and UF escape/control guidance. UF page route says bromelia-balansae but its page heading and content identify B. pinguin. Its capsule wording conflicts with botanical berry descriptions; use berry.

proposedDescription: Pink disease is a fungal disease of woody plants in humid tropical environments. The fungus, Erythricium salmonicolor, also appears in older literature as Corticium salmonicolor. It can infect citrus and many other trees and shrubs, producing cankers that kill bark and may girdle a branch. Warm, wet conditions and dense canopies favor disease development. The name describes fungal growth on affected wood, not a pink discoloration of leaves or fruit. Its significance in a particular US planting needs local diagnosis and disease-history context.
identification: Inspect branch forks and the undersides of declining limbs. Early growth can look like a thin white or pink cobweb on the bark. Later stages include small pink pustules, orange-red spore structures, or a salmon-colored crust extending over a canker. Bark may crack and shoots beyond the infection die. Different stages need not be present at once. Similar dieback can have other causes, and another fungus may occupy the same damaged branch, so the visible color is a lead for a diagnostic laboratory rather than proof by itself.
actions: Photograph the whole branch and close views of the fungal growth before pruning. Ask extension staff or a plant clinic how to submit a representative sample. For confirmed disease in ornamentals or citrus, remove affected branches and dispose of diseased material as locally advised. Selective thinning can improve air movement through an overcrowded canopy. Large cankers or weakened overhead limbs call for an arborist. Treatment decisions should be specific to the host and site; published plantation guidance does not provide a universal cure.

proposedDescription: Pink hibiscus mealybug feeds on tender growth of many tropical and subtropical plants, including hibiscus. Its feeding saliva can distort leaves and shorten the spaces between them, producing crowded, bushy shoot tips. This damage can be much more conspicuous than the insects themselves. The species was detected in southern Florida in 2002 and has also established in parts of other warm US regions. Local biological control programs are important, so an infestation does not automatically call for repeated broad insecticide treatment.
identification: Adult females are roughly 3 mm long, with pink bodies largely hidden beneath white mealy wax. Their marginal wax filaments are short or inconspicuous, unlike the prominent fringe of several common mealybugs. Egg sacs shelter eggs that change from orange to pink; tiny crawlers disperse to new feeding sites. Inspect folded leaves, soft shoot tips, buds, and stem crevices. Honeydew and black sooty mold can accompany colonies. Curled shoots may resemble virus injury, but finding wax-covered insects still does not establish the species without expert examination.
actions: Inspect new plants carefully and keep suspect nursery stock away from established plantings while identification is arranged. Send close photographs and host details to extension staff or the state plant-health service. Small localized colonies may be removed with affected plant parts, with clippings contained for appropriate disposal. Avoid disrupting tiny parasitoid wasps and other natural enemies; introduced Anagyrus kamali has provided effective suppression in established programs. Ask for local advice before applying a product, particularly where beneficial insects are already keeping the population low.
researchNotes: UF diagnostics paired with independent UC IPM cultural management and species-specific parasitoid success. UF's old conditional Florida establishment wording not repeated. No present-day county limit inferred from dated UC text.

proposedDescription: Pink queen, often sold as spider flower or cleome, is a tall South American ornamental grown for airy clusters of flowers. The plant has circulated under several names, including Cleome hassleriana, Cleome houtteana, and Tarenaya houtteana. Current authorities differ in the genus used: Kew places the hassleriana name within Cleome houtteana, while some regional floras use Tarenaya houtteana. In Florida, UF/IFAS displays a high predicted invasion risk while marking the assessment incomplete. That combination calls for care when choosing new plantings, rather than a blanket claim that every garden plant is already causing ecological damage.
identification: Typical plants stand three to six feet tall. The lower and middle leaves divide like fingers into five to seven leaflets, while upper leaves are smaller and simpler. Hairy stems may carry paired spines at the bases of leaf stalks. Pink, purple, or occasionally white flowers have long projecting stamens that create the familiar spiderlike appearance. Elongated cylindrical seed capsules follow the flowers. A musky odor may be noticeable. Flower color alone is unreliable because cultivated selections vary; include the leaves, stem spines, and developing fruits when asking for identification.
actions: Before buying seed or plants in Florida, check the current UF/IFAS assessment and choose a locally appropriate alternative where escape is a concern. In an existing bed, watch beyond the planting edge for volunteer seedlings. Remove unwanted volunteers and prevent mature capsules from being carried into natural vegetation with garden waste. Wear gloves around the spiny stems. If plants are spreading along a roadside or into a natural area, document the population and seek local botanical advice before assigning the name from a nursery label alone.

proposedDescription: Pink woodsorrel is a bulb-forming perennial that can turn a small garden introduction into a persistent colony. Native to South America, it has been introduced in several US regions and grows in yards, flower beds, roadsides, and other disturbed habitats. Its ability to leave many small bulblets behind makes removal more demanding than its delicate flowers suggest. Florida's completed 2025 UF/IFAS assessment does not classify it as a documented problem species statewide, although individual gardeners may find dense patches difficult to manage.
identification: Leaves arise on long stalks from the base, each with three rounded, heart-shaped leaflets. Pink, lavender, or rose-purple flowers occur in loose clusters above them. With magnification, tiny orange oxalate deposits may be visible along the leaflet margins or across their surfaces; the sepals also have orange marks near their tips. A cluster of small bulbs is an important underground clue. Clover has a different flower structure, and native yellow-flowered woodsorrels should not be identified as this species merely because they have three leaflets. Names containing corymbosa often refer to forms included within Oxalis debilis.
actions: Check incoming pots and soil for unwanted woodsorrel. For a small established patch, loosen the soil and lift the entire bulb cluster rather than simply snapping off the leaves. Collect the small bulblets carefully, then revisit for missed growth. Mowing does not remove the underground source, and cultivating an infested bed can distribute surviving pieces. Keep removed bulbs and contaminated soil away from clean beds. Seek site-specific advice for a large infestation instead of borrowing chemical instructions written for yellow woodsorrel.

proposedDescription: Pinkhead smartweed is a low, trailing perennial grown as a ground cover for its patterned leaves and small pink flower balls. Native to Asia, it has escaped cultivation in several warm regions. Hawaiian field surveys document it along roads, on lava, and in forest settings, where managers have worked to limit its spread into selected native habitats. It is sometimes called Japanese knotweed, but that common name can cause confusion with the much taller invasive knotweeds. Use the scientific name when seeking advice.
identification: Look for long, slender branches that scramble over the ground and can root where they touch it. The alternate oval leaves are generally under 6 cm long and often carry a reddish or darker V-shaped marking. Fine hairs occur on leaves and stems. The small pink flowers crowd into dense round or oval heads, usually less than a centimeter across. A papery sheath surrounds the stem at each leaf junction, as in other members of the knotweed family. The combination of low mat-forming growth, oval marked leaves, and compact flower balls distinguishes it from upright smartweeds with elongated flower spikes.
actions: Avoid planting it next to vulnerable Hawaiian native vegetation. Dig out small unwanted patches, collecting trailing stems as well as rooted portions, and use local disposal arrangements that prevent garden waste from establishing elsewhere. Recheck treated ground several times through the year. After surviving plants are controlled, restore suitable ground cover to reduce reinvasion. Large patches in natural areas need a coordinated management plan; do not transfer an overseas herbicide recipe to a US site. Photographs and a mapped patch boundary help land managers prioritize follow-up.
researchNotes: Hawaiian primary field survey establishes regional concern, NSW botanical flora supplies morphology, Auckland council full text supplies digging, disposal and repeat checks. No quantitative chemical recommendation transferred; regional impact scoped to Hawaii.

proposedDescription: Pit scale, Pollinia pollini, is a tiny sap-feeding insect associated especially with olive trees. It shelters around buds, branch junctions, and cracks in bark, where colonies can be difficult to notice until shoots decline. Reports from Mediterranean olive-growing regions describe leaf distortion, loss of leaves, and drying branches. California has historical introduction records, but published accounts disagree about the extent of eradication and do not establish its present pest importance. A suspected US finding deserves identification rather than an assumption based on the common name.
identification: Adult females are orange-red beneath a grayish wax covering that can conceal groups of females and young insects. Yellow immature stages are mobile; established females are small and rounded. Search closely where buds meet twigs and in sheltered bark crevices. Despite the name pit scale, this species does not produce pits in the host. It may even shelter beneath dead black scales, so a familiar dark scale covering can hide a different insect underneath. Distinguishing it from other olive scales requires microscopic characters, including the adult female's pores and reduced appendages.
actions: If olive twigs carry unexplained waxy colonies, photograph the insects and affected growth and contact extension staff or the state plant-health service. Ask how to package a twig sample while keeping the insects contained. Record which trees are affected and whether live yellow crawlers are present. Hold suspect nursery plants apart from clean stock while identification is pending. Avoid choosing a spray from the name pit scale alone: treatment timing and necessity depend on the actual insect, local population, and orchard conditions.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. The profile can describe olive-scale recognition while explicitly leaving current US occurrence unconfirmed. Argentine seasonal timing and treatment references are not US instructions; conflicting California history is not resolved by assertion. proposedDescription: Pitch canker is a fungal disease of pines caused by Fusarium circinatum. It can affect seedlings as well as established trees, and its appearance changes with the stage of infection. Monterey pine has been especially affected in coastal California. Douglas-fir can also carry infections, usually with more limited visible damage. Infected planting stock and wood are important reasons to keep suspected material from moving to another site.
identification: Look for dying shoot tips, yellowing or reddish needles, and conspicuous resin around affected branches or stems. Beneath diseased bark, tissue may be honey colored and soaked with resin. Seedlings can collapse without those distinctive signs, or develop resin near the soil line. Bark beetles, other canker fungi, drought and poor growing conditions can produce overlapping symptoms. A photograph of brown needles alone cannot establish pitch canker; a diagnostic laboratory needs suitable tissue to confirm the fungus.
actions: Photograph the whole tree and affected branches, then contact extension or a qualified arborist before pruning or removing it. Keep suspect firewood, nursery plants and branch debris at the site until local handling advice is available. Avoid unnecessary injuries to healthy trees. Some affected trees recover, so immediate removal is not always the appropriate response. If pruning is recommended, follow professional sanitation and disposal instructions and monitor the remaining crown for new symptoms.
researchNotes: Two independent institutional sources support diagnosis and movement precautions; dated California county counts omitted.

proposedDescription: Pitscale grass is a small annual grass whose beadlike flowering structures are much more distinctive than its leaves. Botanical works also call it Hackelochloa granularis. It occurs across warm regions, and Flora Neomexicana records introduced plants on dry plains and foothills in the southwestern bootheel of New Mexico. That regional record does not mean that every rough-haired grass in an American pasture belongs to this species.
identification: Plants grow in tufts, with branching stems and conspicuous hairs arising from swollen bases on the leaves and sheaths. The leaf bases can be heart shaped. Short flowering branches carry paired spikelets: one is rounded, hard and deeply patterned with pits, while its companion is flatter and projects beyond it. A hand lens helps reveal the tiny, almost grenade-shaped fertile spikelet. Seedlings lack this strongest character and can resemble unrelated annual grasses. Photograph a complete mature flowering branch, its attachment and the hairy leaf sheath.
actions: For a suspected new occurrence, record the location, habitat and size of the patch, and ask a regional herbarium to check the flowering material. Keep collected heads contained so loose seed is not scattered. Avoid moving soil or mowing equipment directly from a seeding patch into uninfested ground. In a garden, removing a confirmed unwanted annual before seed release is a reasonable precaution, but extensive treatment in natural vegetation should wait for identification and local advice.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Independent floras support recognition and seed containment; no nationwide ecological harm or tested removal efficacy is inferred. proposedDescription: Pitted beardgrass, also called Indian bluegrass, is a warm-season perennial that spreads through creeping stems. It has been used as pasture and groundcover in tropical regions. Its ability to form a close mat and tolerate grazing can also change the balance of vegetation where it spreads beyond a planting. A pasture recommendation from Australia does not establish that it is suitable for an American restoration site.
identification: Look for narrow gray-green leaves and runners that root at their joints, often with a pink or reddish color. Flower heads carry several slender branches arranged near the top of a short central axis. The small spikelets occur in pairs, and a conspicuous depression in the outer covering gives the species its name. Fertile spikelets also have a sharply bent, twisted awn. Related beardgrasses share the branching head and can be hard to separate without magnification. Include the runners, leaf collar and close views of mature spikelets in identification photographs.
actions: Before introducing this grass for forage or erosion control, ask local extension whether it is appropriate for the site. For an unexpected patch, map its edge and check whether runners are entering neighboring vegetation. Keep soil and rooted fragments from being moved into clean areas. Seek a grass specialist's determination before planning removal, especially where native beardgrasses grow nearby. Existing pasture should be managed with attention to desirable cover rather than abruptly exposing soil to erosion.

proposedDescription: Pittosporum pit scale is a sap-feeding insect that settles on stems and leaves and can distort new growth. In California it particularly favors pittosporum and ceanothus, although its host list is much wider. Heavy infestations may leave swollen, misshapen twigs and smaller leaves. The insect has also appeared under the older combination Asterolecanium arabidis, a useful name when comparing extension references.
identification: Settled scales are small, oval and largely motionless. A fringe of pale wax surrounds the body, and pittosporum pit scale also has a lengthwise wax fringe on its upper surface. Feeding can leave ring-shaped depressions in bark; at crowded growing tips, distortion may obscure individual pits. Newly hatched crawlers are the mobile stage. Other pit scales occur on ornamentals, including smaller species lacking the upper wax fringe. Host identity and close photographs help, but an expert may need a mounted specimen to distinguish similar scales confidently.
actions: Inspect new nursery plants and the growing tips of established shrubs before exchanging cuttings. Photograph living scales and the associated twig distortion, rather than assuming old pits mean an active infestation. Ask extension to confirm a damaging population and assess whether treatment is needed. Avoid carrying infested prunings to another garden. Where intervention is justified, timing against susceptible stages matters; obtain plant-specific advice and follow the product label rather than applying repeated broad treatments merely because a few scales are present.
researchNotes: UC IPM supports field traits and management timing; USDA historical taxonomic treatment supplies independent identity lineage.

proposedDescription: Plantago asiatica mosaic virus, usually shortened to PlAMV, is a plant virus of particular concern in commercial lilies. It also infects other plants, including the plantain from which its name comes and heavenly bamboo. Infected bulbs can carry it into new plantings. Unlike several other familiar lily viruses, no biological vector is known for PlAMV; contaminated sap, handling and growing media are important concerns.
identification: Lilies may show reddish or brown dead streaks and spots on leaves, sometimes with poor growth. Some infected plants show little or no obvious damage. Symptoms vary with the lily cultivar, growing conditions and other viruses present. Lily mottle virus, lily symptomless virus, cucumber mosaic virus and nonviral disorders can complicate the picture. Neither a healthy-looking bulb nor a photograph of mottled foliage proves whether PlAMV is present. Diagnostic testing is needed to identify the virus and distinguish mixed infections.
actions: Buy tested planting material from a reputable supplier, and retain labels so affected lots can be traced. Separate suspect plants from propagation stock and stop sharing bulbs until a diagnostic service has advised you. Avoid transferring sap between plants on hands and tools, and do not reuse suspect potting media for fresh lilies. Commercial growers should review bulb washing, packing and sanitation with their plant-health adviser. Insect treatment alone will not address the documented mechanical and planting-material pathways of this virus.

Independent Xu/Ming December2022 original assay study, later than the review, supports diagnostic separation of the named lily viruses. Current EPPO species name Potexvirus marmorplantagonis; catalog ID retained.

proposedDescription: Rhinacloa cardini is a small member of the plant-bug family, Miridae, with a broad Neotropical distribution. Published Florida records date to 1999, and reported host associations include two species of Enterolobium, trees in the pea family. Those records establish the insect's occurrence and associations; they do not by themselves demonstrate damaging feeding or a need to treat every tree on which it is found.
identification: The Cuban revision describes males about 2.4 to 2.7 millimeters long, weakly oval and pale green. Dark spots on the hind thighs and stout dark hairs along the sides of the thorax and forewings are useful close-up clues. These are tiny characters, and related plant bugs can look similar. A specialist may need the male genital structures to confirm the species. Photograph the dorsal surface and hind legs with a size reference, and record the plant on which the bug was found. A leaf blemish alone cannot identify it.
actions: If you find unfamiliar bugs on an Enterolobium tree, document whether the foliage is actually damaged and preserve the host information with the observation. Ask extension or an insect collection for identification before treating the tree. A single insect landing on a plant does not prove that the plant is its host. Avoid moving infested nursery material while a suspected new record is being checked. There is no basis here for introducing the insect elsewhere or applying a routine control program.

proposedDescription: Plantain signalgrass is an annual grass also called creeping signalgrass or Brachiaria plantaginea. It is associated with disturbed ground and crops, and Florida botanical guidance records it from scattered disturbed sites in the state. Its ability to root at low stem joints can make a plant appear more persistent than its annual life cycle suggests. Regional occurrence should be checked independently of the different common names used for signalgrasses.
identification: The stems may bend along the ground before rising, with smooth lower joints that can produce roots. Leaves are relatively broad for a small weedy grass, taper to a point and may have hairs along the sheath margin. Several flowering branches are spaced along the main axis rather than forming one compact head. Oval spikelets sit in rows on one side of each branch. Other Urochloa species have similar arrangements, so leaf width alone is unreliable. Photograph the leaf collar, lower joints and an intact flowering head, ideally with close views of the spikelets.
actions: Remove confirmed unwanted garden plants before mature seed is shed, including rooted lower stem sections. Inspect the area again for seedlings after soil disturbance. Clean seed-bearing debris from tools and avoid carrying contaminated soil to another bed. In crops, obtain a local identification and management recommendation because useful timing depends on the crop and growth stage. Preserve nearby native grasses by checking the flowering structures before clearing a mixed patch. A photograph of a young, unflowering plant may need follow-up later in the season.
researchNotes: UF regional account and Argentine plant-health botanical description support identity; conflicting origin/life-cycle wording in an Indian compilation was not used.

proposedDescription: The pleated tunicate is a solitary sea squirt that often grows in crowded groups on docks, hulls and aquaculture equipment. Each individual filters water through its own two openings. Long-distance transport by vessels has blurred its original distribution, and its native region remains uncertain. Southern California harbors support introduced populations, but a confident worldwide origin should not be inferred from an old regional field guide.
identification: Look for an upright oval body with a thick, leathery, pale tan or whitish covering. Large rounded lumps and grooves give many individuals a cobblestone appearance. Two short siphons open near the upper end, often with darker stripes inside. Unlike stalked club tunicates, mature pleated tunicates attach without a long narrow stalk. Color and surface texture vary, and other solitary sea squirts can resemble them. Photographs should show the entire attachment, both siphons and neighboring organisms; an expert may need internal anatomy for a firm determination.
actions: Check boat hulls, ropes and other submerged equipment before moving between harbors. Follow the marina's cleaning and waste-capture rules, keeping scraped organisms and wash water out of another waterbody. Do not transplant clusters to an aquarium or a different dock. Photograph an unfamiliar fouling population in place and report its location to the local marine invasive-species program. Aquaculture operators should seek site-specific advice before cleaning stock, because handling methods can affect both the cultured animals and the spread of fouling organisms.
researchNotes: Native-origin conflict between older USGS wording and Smithsonian synthesis resolved by stating uncertainty. Australian government morphology provides independent lineage.

proposedDescription: Plume albizia is a shrub or small tree with finely divided foliage and pale bottlebrushlike flower clusters. Also known as plume acacia or brush wattle, it has escaped cultivation in parts of coastal California, where Cal-IPC lists it on its Watch list. Its behavior elsewhere varies with climate and habitat. An ornamental specimen and a reproducing population beyond cultivation deserve different management decisions.
identification: The large leaves divide twice into many small leaflets, producing a fernlike outline. Cream to greenish yellow flowers form elongated, dense clusters rather than the round pink puffs of familiar silk trees. Flattened brown pods contain several conspicuous seeds, with thickened edges and bulges over the seeds. Young foliage may have golden hairs that become less apparent with age. Black wattle and other finely leaved trees can look similar before flowering. Photograph the full leaf, its stalk, the elongated flower heads and mature pods to support identification.
actions: Watch the ground beyond planted trees for seedlings, especially along drainage lines and disturbed edges. Pull or dig small confirmed volunteers while their roots are manageable, and keep pods out of garden waste dumped in natural areas. Larger plants need a site-specific removal plan and follow-up for seedlings. Before replacing a tree, check local recommendations for suitable alternatives. Avoid moving soil from beneath a seeding specimen into restoration ground. A local weed program can help distinguish a contained planting from a population that is spreading.

proposedDescription: The plump spider beetle is a small beetle associated in published accounts with stored organic material, including dried plant collections. Some references use the name Sphaericus gibboides, which the Natural History Museum treats as a synonym. Reports from a museum or pantry should be checked carefully: several unrelated beetles can emerge from dried goods, and the common name does not establish which species is present.
identification: Adults are tiny, about 1.5 to 2.5 millimeters long, with a rounded dark body and short yellowish scaly hairs. A specialist key separates this species by its heart-shaped wing covers, scarcely visible surface punctures and a basal antennal segment similar in color to the others. These details need magnification; a rounded beetle silhouette alone is not enough. Photograph the upper surface and antennae with a size reference. Keep the packaging or collection label with the find, since larvae and damaged material alone rarely settle the identity.
actions: Place suspect dried material in a closed container while arranging identification, and inspect nearby packages or specimen cabinets for additional insects. Remove loose food debris and keep replacement goods in sound, tightly closing containers. Do not spray food, herbarium sheets or other collection objects. Valuable specimens need advice from a conservator or collection manager before any treatment, because heat, cold or chemicals can damage the material. A confirmed identification and a search for the actual breeding source are more useful than repeatedly killing wandering adults.

proposedDescription: Potato mop-top virus affects the quality of potato tubers, sometimes leaving internal blemishes even when the crop above ground looks healthy. It is carried through soil by Spongospora subterranea, the organism that also causes powdery scab. These are related problems but not interchangeable diagnoses: powdery scab can occur without the virus. Preventing contaminated soil and planting material from entering clean production areas is especially important.
identification: Cut tubers may reveal rusty brown arcs, rings or flecks inside the flesh. Similar marks can result from tobacco rattle virus, potato virus Y and other disorders, so appearance alone is insufficient. Some infected tubers have no visible symptoms. When foliage is affected, yellow blotches, chevron-shaped patterns or shortened stem sections may occur, with expression influenced by weather and variety. Powdery scab instead produces external pustules and lesions, sometimes with root galls. Photograph both the whole tuber and a clean cut surface, and ask a diagnostic laboratory how to submit samples.
actions: Use planting stock with appropriate testing and traceability, and discuss field history with a potato adviser. Keep soil on equipment, footwear and harvested material from moving between suspect and clean fields. Do not save suspect tubers for planting or assume that removing visibly affected plants clears a field. Once virus-carrying Spongospora is established, management is difficult. A confirmed diagnosis should guide variety choice, sanitation and future planting decisions rather than a treatment chosen only from the appearance of brown rings.
researchNotes: Cornell collaborative symptom account and Idaho disease-management bulletin; no current certification guarantees or curative treatment promised.

proposedDescription: Podocarpus aphid forms small colonies on tender growth of podocarpus, a common ornamental shrub in warm parts of the United States. Its bluish purple color makes a colony noticeable against the narrow green leaves. Feeding can affect new growth, but finding aphids is a reason to inspect the plant and its condition, not an automatic reason for a broad insecticide application. Another Neophyllaphis species occurs on the same ornamentals.
identification: Adults are tiny, roughly a millimeter or a little more long, with a flattened oval body. Wingless individuals often carry a light waxy dusting, and both winged and wingless females can occur. Colonies gather on young leaves, shoots and fruit stalks. The similar Neophyllaphis varicolor can have yellow, orange, red or purple young and darker reddish adults; color alone can therefore mislead. Photograph several individuals at different stages, their arrangement on the shoot and the host plant. A specialist may need microscopic characters to resolve the species.
actions: Inspect fresh growth and note whether leaves are becoming distorted or whether a colony is declining naturally. Preserve lady beetles and other predators already present. Before sharing cuttings or moving nursery shrubs, check the youngest shoots and keep infested material separate. If growth is suffering, ask extension for a plant-specific approach and identification. Avoid repeated treatments aimed only at old leaf distortion: damaged leaves do not necessarily indicate that living aphids remain. Record new colonies and their host accurately when requesting help.
researchNotes:

proposedDescription: Poet's narcissus is a perennial bulb grown for fragrant white flowers with a small, brightly edged center. It can persist around old gardens and has naturalized along roadsides, in fields and in waste places in parts of North America. A long-lived clump is not necessarily evidence of rapid spread. Like other daffodils, it should be kept separate from edible bulbs and plants gathered for food.
identification: Flat, straplike leaves rise from the bulb, followed by a mostly leafless flowering stalk that usually carries one flower. Broad white floral segments surround a shallow yellow cup with a red, crinkled rim. That small cup distinguishes it from trumpet daffodils. Garden selections and hybrids can blur the pattern; the hybrid with Narcissus tazetta often carries two flowers and a darker yellow cup without the same typical red edging. Photograph the flower face, side profile, stalk and leaves together. Leaves or an unearthed bulb alone are a poor basis for naming a daffodil.
actions: Never taste bulbs to identify them, and keep them out of kitchen storage where they could be mistaken for onions. Wear gloves when handling bulbs or cutting plants if sap irritates your skin. If an unwanted clump needs removal, lift the bulbs and attached offsets rather than repeatedly cutting the flowers. Keep discarded bulbs out of natural areas. For plants persisting at an old homesite, first establish ownership and local significance before digging. Seek prompt poison advice after suspected ingestion.

proposedDescription: Poison hemlock is a highly poisonous biennial that often grows along roads, ditches, streams and disturbed field edges. In its first season it forms a leafy rosette; later it sends up a tall, branching flowering stem. All parts are unsafe to eat, and contamination of hay or other feed creates a risk for livestock. Its resemblance to edible members of the carrot family makes casual foraging particularly dangerous.
identification: Look for finely divided, fernlike leaves and smooth, hollow stems marked with irregular purple blotches. Small white flowers form many umbrella-shaped clusters. Wild carrot usually has hairy stems, while poison hemlock is smooth, but no single feature should be used to declare an unfamiliar plant edible. Young rosettes lack the tall flowering form and can be especially misleading. Water-hemlocks and other hazardous relatives also need careful distinction. Photograph leaves, stem markings and flower clusters without crushing or tasting the plant, and keep children and animals away.
actions: Arrange removal while plants are small, using local weed guidance and protective gloves, long sleeves and eye protection. Avoid creating airborne debris with powered cutting equipment, and never burn the plants. Contain removed material according to local disposal advice; do not feed it to animals or leave it mixed with forage. Large roadside or streamside stands are better handled through the responsible land manager. Recheck treated ground for seedlings. Suspected ingestion requires immediate emergency or poison-control advice, without waiting for symptoms.
researchNotes: Two independent extension sources support hazardous-plant precautions and identification. No pesticide recipe or sensory identification test.

proposedDescription: Polka-dot plant is a small tropical perennial grown for leaves splashed with pink, red or white. It is often kept indoors or used as seasonal bedding, but warm conditions can allow it to persist beyond a garden. Florida's current IFAS assessment predicts high invasion risk and does not recommend it there. That assessment is a regional planting recommendation, not proof that every houseplant is causing ecological damage.
identification: The leaves are oval and paired along the stems, with irregular spots or broad patches of contrasting color. Young stems, leaf stalks and leaves can be conspicuously hairy. Small lavender or bluish flowers appear near the stem tips and leaf axils, though the foliage usually draws more attention. Cultivars vary greatly, and shade or plant condition can affect how much green shows. Other spotted houseplants may have thicker leaves, different leaf arrangement or different flowers. Include the stem joints and an open flower in photographs rather than relying entirely on the color pattern.
actions: Keep outdoor plants contained and check adjacent shaded ground for seedlings or rooted escapes. Collect cuttings and spent plants instead of dumping them in woodland or along waterways. In Florida, choose an alternative consistent with current IFAS recommendations when replacing a planting. For an apparent wild patch, photograph its extent and relationship to nearby gardens and seek a local identification before broad removal. Indoor owners can reduce escape risk by disposing of soil and trimmings responsibly and avoiding distribution of plants that are spreading outside cultivation.

proposedDescription: This pollen beetle is associated with flowering plants and is especially relevant to canola and other brassica crops. Adults seek pollen, while the crop's growth stage influences the significance of their feeding. Beetles visiting open flowers are not equivalent to beetles damaging unopened buds. Older literature may place the species in Meligethes, and it should not be confused with every small dark beetle found inside a blossom.
identification: Adults are tiny, about two to two and a half millimeters long, with an elongated oval body. The wing covers can appear metallic green, blue or bronzy, while the legs and mouthparts are yellowish orange. The antennae end in a distinct club. Brassicogethes aeneus is a close lookalike with similar biology, and confident separation may require a specialist. Photograph several beetles, a close view of the antennae and legs, and the buds or flowers where they were found. Record whether buds have feeding holes or have failed to develop.
actions: Inspect the crop before deciding whether the beetles require intervention, noting crop stage and actual bud injury. Ask local extension to confirm the species and interpret any regional sampling thresholds. Do not import a treatment threshold from another country without checking its relevance to the crop and production system. Protect pollinators visiting open flowers and avoid blanket insecticide use based on beetle presence alone. Retain field and date information with a specimen so an unusual occurrence can be evaluated accurately.

proposedDescription: Polyalthia suberosa is an Asian shrub or small tree in the custard-apple family. Its name refers to the corky bark that develops on older growth. Botanical accounts describe it from forest and thicket habitats, including dry forests and streamside sites. A Bishop Museum report documented a naturalized Oahu tree collected in 2008. That limited record does not establish widespread invasion. Do not borrow the identity or behavior of the much taller ornamental formerly called Polyalthia longifolia.
identification: Older stems have conspicuous corky ridges, while young twigs can carry rusty or tawny hairs. The leaves are simple, relatively small and oblong to narrowly oval, with short stalks and sometimes an uneven base. Small greenish yellow flowers occur singly or in pairs away from, or opposite, the leaf axils. The fruit consists of several small rounded units that become dark purple or blackish. Related custard-apple relatives share parts of this pattern. Photographs of bark, leaf attachment, flowers and attached fruit are more useful than an isolated leaf.
actions: For a cultivated specimen, retain the nursery label and document whether seedlings are appearing independently nearby. Ask a botanical garden or herbarium to verify an unexpected wild occurrence before deciding on control. Keep pruned fruiting branches and collected seeds from being dumped in natural areas. Do not eat unidentified fruit or try medicinal uses based on a shared common name. If removal is being considered, first determine whether the observation is a planted tree, a volunteer beside it or a reproducing population farther away.

proposedDescription: Branchiomma coheni is a marine feather-duster worm that lives in a tube and extends a crown of fine feeding branches into the water. It is native to the Pacific coast of Mexico and Central America. Researchers found it at a Tampa Bay marina in both 2012 and 2014, supporting establishment there. The available synthesis reports no demonstrated impacts for this species, so its introduction should not be presented as proof of ecological damage.
identification: The visible crown resembles a small feather duster, but many native and introduced tube worms share that appearance. In Branchiomma, details of the crown's side projections, eyes and body bristles are important for identification. Similar species include B. bairdi, which is native to Florida and the Caribbean, and other regional sabellids. A photograph of a colorful crown alone is therefore not enough. Photograph the worm in place with its tube and substrate, and leave destructive examination or collection to an appropriately equipped specialist.
actions: Check submerged boating and marina equipment before moving it between waterbodies, and follow local fouling-cleaning procedures that capture removed material. Do not transfer attractive tube worms to another dock or release aquarium specimens. For an unusual population, record the marina, depth, date and substrate and share clear photographs with a marine invasive-species program. Avoid scraping an entire mixed fouling community merely because one worm resembles this species. Confirmed identification is especially important where native Branchiomma occur alongside introduced forms.

proposedDescription: The polyphagous shot hole borer is a tiny ambrosia beetle that excavates galleries in wood and cultivates fungi for food. The beetle and its associated fungi can damage trees, including ornamentals and native hardwoods in California. Its name once covered several nearly identical species, so older reports need care: Florida's tea shot hole borer is now treated as Euwallacea perbrevis, a different species.
identification: Look for small round entry holes with staining, sap, gum or pale sugary deposits around them, depending on the host tree. Branch dieback can follow, but the response varies among tree species. Adult females are small, dark and cylindrical; casual photographs do not reliably separate them from related shot hole borers. A tree with holes is not automatically a reproductive host, since beetles may attack without establishing a successful colony. Photograph the whole tree, affected branches and entry holes with a scale, and record the tree's identity.
actions: Keep suspect logs, firewood and prunings at the site until a qualified arborist or plant-health adviser explains local disposal options. Do not assume that ordinary chipping eliminates every beetle; research found greatly reduced emergence but not complete elimination in all material. Have the tree's condition assessed before deciding between selective pruning and removal. Preserve useful shade and habitat where treatment is justified and feasible. Report unusual attacks promptly, and use professional guidance for any preventive treatment rather than drilling or injecting the tree yourself.

proposedDescription: Pond lovegrass is a fine-flowered grass in a group whose species can be difficult to distinguish without mature heads. Botanical treatments describe it as an annual or sometimes a short-lived perennial, reflecting variation across its broad range. It is native to tropical and subtropical parts of the Old World and occurs in disturbed or wet settings elsewhere. Its common name should not be read as a requirement that it grow submerged.
identification: Plants form tufts of narrow leaves and produce a branched flowering head with many very small spikelets. The head may be narrow and crowded or more open, so overall shape varies. At the junction of blade and sheath is a short membrane with a fringed edge, a useful character to photograph. Individual spikelets contain several tiny florets and break apart as they mature. Many lovegrasses look similar from a distance. A regional key may require measurements of the spikelets, floral coverings and leaf collar that a general landscape photograph cannot show.
actions: Record the soil moisture, habitat and whether the plants are flowering before requesting identification. Obtain close photographs of the leaf collar and several mature spikelets, while keeping collected heads in a closed packet. Avoid assigning a species name solely from an app's suggestion for a delicate grass. In a maintained bed, confirmed unwanted plants can be removed before seed dispersal. For a shoreline or natural-area population, seek local botanical advice before disturbing sediment or surrounding vegetation, especially where several native lovegrasses may occur together.

proposedDescription: Pond water-starwort is a small aquatic plant that can form mats of stems and floating leaf rosettes in quiet water. It reproduces by seed and vegetative growth, and plant material can be carried with wet equipment. Introduced populations occur in parts of the United States, but several native water-starworts look very similar. Correct identification is especially important before disturbing a pond or clearing a shoreline.
identification: Leaves occur in opposite pairs. Those near the water surface are usually oval or spoon shaped and cluster into rosettes, while submerged leaves are narrower. Tiny flowers sit at the leaf bases and are easy to overlook. Mature fruits are the decisive feature: they divide into four parts, each with a thin winged margin. A hand lens or stronger magnification is normally needed to examine them. Leaf shape changes with growing conditions, so a floating rosette alone is not a reliable species identification. Photograph fruiting stems in addition to the surface mat.
actions: Clean plants and mud from boats, waders and sampling gear before leaving the water, and follow local drying or decontamination guidance. Do not empty pond plants or aquarium water into another waterbody. Send photographs and the location of a suspected new patch to the local aquatic-plant program. Wait for a confirmed identification and any necessary permissions before removal; careless raking can redistribute fragments and disturb native plants. Management should reflect the size of the patch, water use and surrounding habitat.

proposedDescription: Welsh poppy is a tap-rooted perennial with yellow or orange flowers, often grown in cool, partly shaded gardens. It is native to western Europe and was long known as Meconopsis cambrica. The name Papaver cambricum is accepted by Kew. Its familiar garden presence should be distinguished from a documented naturalized population, and a plant appearing outside a border is not automatically a serious invasive threat.
identification: Light green leaves are divided into irregular lobes. Slender stems carry bowl-shaped flowers with four broad, delicate petals, followed by upright seed capsules. Flower color ranges from lemon yellow to orange, including cultivated forms. Other yellow poppies and celandine relatives can resemble it, especially when only one flower is shown. Include the entire leaf, branching pattern, flower center and a mature capsule in photographs. The perennial root system and the combination of foliage and fruit are more useful than color alone when separating garden escapes from similar wild plants.
actions: If you want to limit volunteers in a garden, remove spent flowers before capsules release seed and pull unwanted seedlings while small. Keep seed-bearing stems out of garden waste dumped beyond the property. Do not taste the plant or use sap as an identification test. For a patch in woodland or beside a stream, record whether it lies near an old planting and ask a regional botanist to confirm its identity. Leave unfamiliar native lookalikes in place until that comparison is complete.

proposedDescription: Port Jackson fig, or rusty fig, is an Australian evergreen tree planted for shade and sometimes grown as bonsai. proposedDescription: Phytophthora lateralis is a water mold that causes serious root disease in Port-Orford-cedar, also called Lawson cypress. It has damaged native cedar populations in southwestern Oregon and northwestern California. The pathogen can travel in contaminated soil and water, making muddy equipment and drainage routes important pathways. It is funguslike but is not a true fungus, and a declining cedar can have several other causes.
identification: An affected tree may lose its normal green color, then turn rusty red or bronze over much of the crown. Root and collar tissues are damaged, and disease can progress rapidly in small trees. Some infections involve branches or stems rather than beginning visibly at the roots. Drought, other root pathogens and unrelated conifer problems can produce similar browning. Confirm the host tree as well as the disease: names such as cedar and cypress cover several distinct plants. Laboratory assessment of properly collected material is needed for a secure diagnosis.
actions: Respect seasonal road closures and cleaning requirements in cedar habitat. Remove mud from footwear, vehicles and tools before moving from an affected area to a clean one, using the land manager's procedures. Avoid carrying soil, rooted plants or suspect debris between sites, and do not use potentially contaminated water for cleaning equipment elsewhere. Report unusual cedar decline to a forest-health office. Tree removal and access restrictions should be planned professionally, with attention to drainage and remaining healthy trees. No simple garden treatment restores an infected forest site.
researchNotes: Independent US Forest Service and UK Forest Research accounts support soil/water biosecurity. Outdated statement of no resistance from 1990 silvics not repeated; no bleach recipe.
