proposedDescription: Portia tree is a tropical coastal tree with glossy, heart-shaped leaves and hibiscuslike flowers. It has a long history of cultivation and a broad tropical distribution. In central and southern Florida, introduced populations are a concern in coastal habitats, including mangrove edges and sheltered beaches. Current IFAS guidance treats it as invasive in those regions, while its northern Florida assessment differs.
identification: Leaves are alternate, simple and smooth edged, with several strong veins radiating from the base. The showy flowers are yellow with a dark red center and often darken toward maroon as they age. Rounded, relatively firm fruit follows. Sea hibiscus is an important lookalike, and flower color alone does not settle the identification. Photograph both leaf surfaces, the base of an open flower, attached fruit and the whole tree. Young seedlings may show only the heart-shaped leaves, so retain some uncertainty until more characters are available.
actions: Where local guidance discourages portia tree, choose a suitable alternative for new coastal planting. Watch beneath and beyond established trees for seedlings, and remove confirmed small volunteers where permitted before they develop a substantial root system. Keep fruiting branches and seedlings out of dumped garden waste. Mature trees near shorelines require a site-specific plan that protects native vegetation and complies with access rules. Ask a local botanist to distinguish similar coastal trees before removal. After work, check the site repeatedly for surviving seedlings or regrowth.

proposedDescription: Pot marigold is a familiar garden annual with yellow or orange daisy-shaped flower heads. Despite the common name, it belongs to Calendula rather than Tagetes, the genus containing many other garden marigolds. It can reseed in cultivated ground, sometimes reappearing where a previous planting has disappeared. Volunteers in a flower bed are usually a garden-management question, not evidence of a landscape-scale invasion.
identification: Leaves are simple, oblong to spoon shaped and slightly hairy, arranged along branching stems. Flower heads contain a central disk surrounded by broad rays, although double cultivars can obscure the center. The mature fruits are especially useful: they are curved, irregular and often rough, with different shapes within one head. Tagetes generally has divided foliage and differently shaped fruits. Photograph the leaves and mature head as well as the bright flowers. Seedlings without flowers can be harder to recognize among other soft-leaved annuals.
actions: If self-sowing is unwanted, remove spent heads before the fruits mature and pull surplus seedlings while their roots are small. Keep desired plants spaced so their growth can be inspected and maintained. For a patch beyond cultivation, record the setting and nearby garden source before deciding whether removal is necessary. Do not assume that a plant called marigold is edible, and avoid using an uncertain identification for food or home remedies. Garden-grown plants can also have pesticide histories that are not evident from appearance. Dispose of seed-bearing trimmings responsibly rather than dumping them in natural vegetation.

proposedDescription: This potato flea beetle is a small leaf beetle associated with wild and cultivated members of the nightshade family. European sources describe adults feeding on foliage and larvae feeding on roots. The common name is shared or confused with other potato-associated flea beetles, especially Epitrix species. A report of potato flea beetle damage should therefore include the scientific identification before a species-specific management plan is chosen.
identification: Adults are roughly two to three millimeters long and mostly yellowish, with a darker head and a darkened line where the wing covers meet. The enlarged hind thighs can also be dark. Like other flea beetles, they can jump abruptly when disturbed. Several pale Psylliodes resemble one another, while many Epitrix are darker, so color is only a starting clue. Photograph the back, legs and antennae with a size reference. Small holes in leaves do not identify the beetle, and root-feeding larvae are difficult to distinguish without specialist work.
actions: Check which insects are actually present on damaged potato or nightshade foliage, and record the crop stage and extent of injury. Keep a securely contained specimen for extension or an insect collection if identification is uncertain. Do not move rooted plants or attached soil from a questionable infestation into a clean planting. Avoid transferring management advice for tuber-damaging Epitrix directly to this species. A local crop adviser can determine whether feeding warrants intervention and select measures appropriate to the identified insect and crop.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. The independent field account and original key support recognition and referral; potato-tuber injury from Epitrix is excluded. Microscopic confirmation is appropriate and is not itself a reason to hold a correctly scoped profile. Source lineage and access details are recorded in batch-63-notes.md.

proposedDescription: Potato tuber moth is most damaging during its caterpillar stage, when it tunnels through potato foliage, stems or tubers. Exposed tubers and cracks in the soil give females access to places where eggs can be laid. The insect can also develop on other nightshade crops, including tomato. Risk varies with region, weather and crop handling, and damage may continue in poorly protected storage.
identification: Adults are slender gray moths with darker markings and fringed wings. Caterpillars are pale, sometimes pinkish or greenish, with a brown head and a dark plate immediately behind it. In potatoes, look for silk and droppings near an eye and dirty tunnels just below the skin or deeper in the tuber. Wireworm tunnels can look different, but damage alone still needs careful assessment. Leaf mines and small moths have many lookalikes. Photograph the larva, entry point and cut tunnel, and retain the crop's location and harvest date.
actions: Keep growing tubers well covered with soil and reduce cracks through appropriate irrigation and cultivation. Harvest promptly when ready, and remove cull piles and volunteer potatoes that can support breeding. Do not leave harvested tubers exposed in the field longer than necessary. Inspect stored potatoes, separate damaged material and maintain clean, protected storage. Commercial growers can use properly selected pheromone traps with local extension guidance. A trap catch helps monitor activity; it is not a universal treatment threshold for every region or production system.
researchNotes: Independent UC and Idaho accounts support diagnosis and crop precautions; no universal trap threshold, pesticide recipe or cure asserted.

proposedDescription: Poverty brome, also called barren or sterile brome, is an introduced annual grass of fields and disturbed ground. The word sterile is misleading in everyday use: the plant produces seed and can reproduce readily. It is also treated as Anisantha sterilis in some botanical works. A mature flowering head is much more informative than the soft green leaves when separating it from other annual bromes.
identification: The flowering head is open and loose, with long slender branches that often droop. Each branch commonly carries only one or a few wedge-shaped spikelets. Long straight awns project from the floral coverings, giving a mature head a bristly appearance. Leaves and sheaths are often softly hairy, although hairiness varies. Ripgut brome generally has larger spikelets and longer awns, while downy brome usually has smaller spikelets and more on the lower branches. Measure an intact spikelet with its awns and photograph the whole head, leaf sheath and collar.
actions: Remove confirmed unwanted plants before the heads mature and shed seed. In a small bed, pulling or hoeing young annuals is easier than handling dry, awned heads later. Collect mature heads carefully and clean clothing and equipment before entering clean ground. In pasture or a natural grassland, verify the species and retain desirable cover rather than clearing every brome-shaped grass. Ask local extension for a plan where the infestation is large or mixed with crops. Revisit disturbed patches after seasonal germination to catch new plants early.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Independent floras support annual-weed recognition; advice is limited to seed containment and local assessment. proposedDescription: Praxelis is a fast-growing herb with clusters of lilac or blue-purple flower heads. Native to South America, it has become a weed in Florida, including ornamental production areas. It can flower while still relatively young and produce many small seeds that travel on wind, clothing, animals and equipment. Its resemblance to familiar blue-flowered plants has contributed to overlooked introductions.
identification: Leaves occur in opposite pairs and are often diamond shaped or triangular, with conspicuous teeth and hairs. The stems are hairy and can be brittle. Beneath the tiny florets, the flower-head base forms a pronounced cone, an important distinction from the flatter or slightly domed heads of ageratum. Mature seeds carry numerous fine bristles. Native blue mistflower and other related plants can look similar, so flower color alone is unreliable. Photograph the leaf outline, stem hairs and a close view of the head's structure before assigning a name.
actions: Inspect nursery containers and recently disturbed ground regularly, removing confirmed seedlings before they flower. Bag flowering or seeding plants so handling does not scatter their small fruits. Clean soil and seed from tools, footwear and mowing equipment before moving to another site. Keep new nursery stock under observation and address volunteer plants around production areas. In a mixed natural patch, get a botanical confirmation before removal to protect native lookalikes. Follow-up matters because seedlings can appear after the first clearing; one pass is unlikely to resolve a persistent seed source.
researchNotes: UF nursery-management work and Australian government account provide independent practical evidence. Old proposed US federal listing not treated as current law.

proposedDescription: Prickly comfrey is a coarse perennial with bristly foliage and hanging clusters of tubular flowers. It has been grown as an ornamental and is one parent of Russian comfrey, the hybrid Symphytum x uplandicum. That relationship makes names on old garden plants particularly unreliable. Comfreys contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, so a plant's history of medicinal or forage use should not be treated as assurance that it is safe to consume.
identification: Look for large, alternate, oval to elliptical leaves covered in stiff prickly hairs. The stems are not prominently winged by leaf tissue running down their length, a useful comparison with common comfrey. Flowers arise in curled clusters and change from pinkish tones toward blue or purple. The hybrid can show intermediate characters, and color alone does not distinguish it reliably. Photograph leaf attachment, stem surfaces and several flowers at different stages. A botanist may need mature fruit or closer examination to separate a cultivated hybrid from prickly comfrey.
actions: Wear gloves when handling the rough foliage, and keep it out of feed and material intended for food preparation. For an unwanted patch, confirm the species and mark its extent before attempting removal. Avoid distributing rooted divisions under an uncertain comfrey name. Ask local extension for a removal approach suited to the established root system rather than assuming that cutting flower stalks will eliminate a perennial. Record any regrowth and prevent seed-bearing garden waste from being dumped along streams or in unmanaged ground.

proposedDescription: Prickly lettuce is an upright annual weed that often begins as a low rosette before sending up a branching flowering stem. It grows in disturbed soil and can be troublesome in grain crops, particularly where established plants survive harvest and produce more seed. Despite its relationship to cultivated lettuce, an unidentified roadside plant should not be treated as food or used to make herbal preparations.
identification: The most useful clue is a row of stiff prickles along the midrib on the underside of the leaf. Leaf edges are also prickly, and many leaves are deeply lobed with bases that clasp the stem. Some leaves are less divided, so the underside matters more than the outline alone. Small yellow flower heads occur in an open branching cluster, followed by seeds with pale parachutelike hairs. Sowthistles can have similar leaves and milky sap but lack the characteristic lower-midrib prickles. Photograph a leaf underside and its attachment to the stem.
actions: Pull or hoe small plants before they bolt and set seed, removing the crown and as much taproot as practical. Wear gloves around mature prickles. Recheck cut plants because mowing during flowering can leave stems that branch and flower again. Keep field margins and disturbed beds from becoming recurring seed sources, while maintaining desirable vegetation. In crops, obtain advice that fits the rotation and growth stage rather than relying on repeated late mowing. Collect seeding material carefully so its windborne fruits are not shaken into adjacent beds.
researchNotes: Independent Missouri identification and Cornell management synthesis; Cornell full text read. No foraging or pharmacological claims.

proposedDescription: Prickly moses is an Australian wattle with densely arranged, sharply pointed foliage. It is usually a shrub or small tree, and it has naturalized outside its native range, including New Zealand. Its compact prickly form can resemble several other spiny shrubs. An overseas weed designation is useful context, but it does not establish the status or management priority of an unidentified American planting.
identification: The apparent leaves are phyllodes, flattened or needlelike modified leaf stalks. They are short, rigid and pointed, often arranged in whorls or tight clusters around ribbed young twigs. Pale yellow flowers commonly occur in short spikes that extend beyond the foliage, followed by narrow pods. Consider flower shape alongside the arrangement and width of the phyllodes, rather than identifying a plant from one prickly twig. The species is variable, and different forms have broader or narrower phyllodes. Photograph the arrangement around a twig, an intact flower spike and mature pods; avoid grasping a branch barehanded.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and protect your eyes when working close to the sharp foliage. Inspect the ground around planted shrubs for seedlings before distributing seed or rooted plants. If volunteers are appearing beyond the maintained area, document them and ask a regional botanist to confirm the identification. Keep pods and prunings from being dumped in natural vegetation. A large or persistent patch needs locally appropriate removal and follow-up advice, rather than treatment copied directly from a foreign legal program. Retain nearby native shrubs until their identity is clear.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Independent botanical descriptions support identification; unverified US impact does not require treating every planting as invasive. proposedDescription: This tumbleweed is better known in recent research as Salsola ryanii. It arose through hybridization between Salsola tragus and Salsola australis and carries additional sets of chromosomes. Researchers have documented its expansion in California. It is therefore a distinct biological entity, not simply another spelling of ordinary Russian thistle. The shared common name makes casual records difficult to interpret without specialist identification.
identification: Plants have the branching, rounded form associated with Russian thistles, becoming stiff and prickly as they mature. Dried plants can detach and roll, spreading seed. However, overall size, roundness and the presence of spines do not reliably distinguish this hybrid species from its relatives. Research surveys used genetic markers to establish identity. A useful field record includes the whole mature plant, close views of flowers or fruiting structures, the location and the surrounding population. Young soft seedlings provide fewer dependable species-level clues than mature material.
actions: For a suspected occurrence, ask a weed specialist whether a specimen or genetic confirmation is needed before assigning the name. Manage immediate access and seed-spread problems while keeping the identity provisional. Remove unwanted young tumbleweeds before they harden and release seed where local guidance permits, and contain mature material during transport. Wear protective clothing around dry plants. Do not deliberately move this hybrid or its parents for comparison or experiments. Large accumulations near roads or buildings should be referred to the responsible land manager for safe handling.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Taxonomy and original genetics support a profile that requires specialist confirmation and avoids species-specific control claims. proposedDescription: Russian thistle is a branching annual associated with dry, disturbed ground across much of the western United States. Young plants are soft, but mature plants become rigid and prickly; dry plants can break loose and tumble with the wind. Several related species share this habit, so not every tumbleweed is Salsola tragus. Roadsides, bare lots and poorly covered field margins can provide recurring places for establishment.
identification: Seedlings have narrow, fleshy leaves and can resemble tiny pine seedlings. As stems branch, the plant develops a rounded outline and shorter, stiff, spine-tipped leaves. The flowers are small and inconspicuous, usually nestled among the leaf bases; mature floral structures are important for separating close relatives. Salsola paulsenii, S. australis and hybrid taxa can overlap in general appearance. Photograph both young foliage and mature fruiting branches, along with the complete plant. A detached dry tumbleweed is often less useful for precise identification than a rooted plant in season.
actions: Pull or hoe young unwanted plants before they become spiny and begin setting seed. Wear gloves and protective clothing when handling older growth, and keep mature material contained so seeds are not scattered down the road. Improve desirable groundcover where feasible, since repeatedly bare soil invites new plants. Do not assume that cutting a large green plant once will prevent all later growth or seed production. For extensive infestations or hazardous windblown accumulations, coordinate with the land manager and local extension. Keep questionable material out of livestock feed.
researchNotes: UC explicitly treats Russian-thistle complex; Nevada guidance includes tragus/paulsenii and is scoped as group-level prevention. No broad old synonym or winter-annual claim adopted.

proposedDescription: Prickly sedge is a tufted sedge with compact clusters of small flowers and fruits near the stem tip. It belongs to a group of Carex species that can look almost identical in a casual photograph. The common name is also used inconsistently among related sedges. Mature fruiting material and the leaf collar are much more useful than a broad view of a grassy clump.
identification: Look for narrow leaves, a dense tufted base and several crowded spikes along a short flowering axis. The membrane where a leaf blade meets its sheath is unusually long and pointed compared with the rounded, shorter ligules of several close relatives. Basal sheaths may be purple tinged. The small sacs enclosing the fruits taper into beaks and have a thickened, corky base, although that feature can be difficult to see. Carex muricata and C. divulsa are important comparisons. Photograph the ligule, stem base and mature fruiting sacs under magnification when possible.
actions: Leave an uncertain sedge in place while obtaining a regional botanical identification, especially in a wet meadow or other habitat supporting native Carex. Record whether the plant is in maintained turf, disturbed ground or relatively intact vegetation. If collecting is permitted and requested by a herbarium, include mature fruiting material and the basal parts, keeping seeds contained. Do not clear a whole sedge patch based on a shared common name. Any management decision should reflect the confirmed species and local habitat rather than the prickly appearance of its fruit cluster.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Independent sedge treatments support careful diagnosis; current local status is a field question rather than a universal removal instruction. proposedDescription: Downy thorn-apple is a bushy plant with large white trumpet flowers and spiny seed capsules. Many references spell its name Datura innoxia, the spelling accepted by Kew. Its native range includes Texas and Mexico, so it should not be described as foreign everywhere in the United States. All parts are hazardous if eaten, and the attractive flowers do not make it a safe plant for home remedies.
identification: The broad leaves and branching stems are covered with soft, often glandular hairs, giving the plant a gray-green appearance. Flowers open as long upright trumpets, while the rounded mature capsules hang down and bear numerous slender prickles. Datura wrightii and other thorn-apples can look similar, so hair type, floral structure and fruit need comparison. The common name moonflower also applies to unrelated vines. Photograph the whole plant, leaf surface, flower side and attached capsule without opening pods or touching your face after handling it.
actions: Keep children, pets and livestock away from the plant and its seeds. Never taste it or prepare tea from any part. Wear gloves when removing an unwanted plant, avoid contact with eyes, and contain capsules so seeds are not scattered. For a natural-area occurrence within its native region, consult local guidance before removal rather than treating all thorn-apples as invaders. After suspected ingestion, seek immediate emergency or poison-control advice; do not wait for symptoms or attempt a home antidote. Wash hands and tools after handling.
researchNotes: Kew confirms conserved innoxia spelling and Texas-Mexico native range; CDC documents serious poisoning and common-name confusion. Catalog ID preserved; toxicity does not imply introduced status.

proposedDescription: Pride-of-Barbados is a tropical flowering shrub or small tree, also called dwarf poinciana or red bird of paradise. It is widely cultivated for orange, red and yellow flowers and finely divided foliage. Florida's current IFAS assessment does not consider it a problem species in the state, so its presence in a garden is not an automatic reason for removal. Local escape behavior still deserves observation.
identification: Leaves divide twice into many small oval leaflets, giving the plant a light, fernlike appearance. Flowers occur in upright terminal clusters, with broad bright petals and very long projecting stamens. Flat pods develop afterward, turning brown and splitting when mature. Other ornamentals called bird of paradise may be unrelated, and the larger royal poinciana differs in overall tree form and fruit. Photograph a whole leaf, the flower cluster, stamens and pods. Some selections have mostly yellow flowers, so the familiar red-orange color is not essential.
actions: Keep seed pods away from children and pets, since the seeds are poisonous if eaten. Wear gloves when pruning around any prickly stems, and remove unwanted seedlings before they become woody. Inspect beyond the intended planting rather than assuming a vigorous shrub is spreading. Avoid dumping pods or rooted material in natural areas. If a substantial plant conflicts with a path or structure, plan pruning or replacement around its mature size and local growing conditions. Confirm the identity before removing another plant sold under the same broad common name.
researchNotes: NC State morphology/toxicity and UF2026 nonproblem assessment support proportionate profile. Uncertain ultimate native origin not asserted.

proposedDescription: Princess-of-the-night is a climbing or trailing cactus grown for very large pale flowers. Its long stems can scramble over supports and produce aerial roots. Botanical accounts record escapes in Florida, and IFAS currently places the species in its Caution category. That calls for attention to local spread and planting choices rather than assuming every cultivated night-blooming cactus is the same species.
identification: The stems are ribbed rather than flattened into broad leaflike segments. Small clusters of short spines occur along the ribs, and aerial roots may attach the plant to a support. Large flowers have white inner segments, narrower darker outer segments and a long tube bearing hairs and scales. Several Selenicereus species and garden hybrids look similar, particularly without flowers. Other plants called queen or princess of the night may belong to different genera. Photograph stem ribs, spine clusters, aerial roots, the entire flower and its tube from the side.
actions: Keep cultivated stems on a manageable support and check surrounding vegetation for rooted pieces or growth beyond the intended planting. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling tangled stems. Collect cuttings and broken sections instead of leaving them on damp soil or dumping them in woodland. For a suspected escape, document the attachment and extent and seek a cactus specialist's identification before removing a large tangle from a host tree. Follow local planting guidance, and avoid distributing material from a population that is spreading beyond cultivation.

proposedDescription: Princess tree is a fast-growing deciduous tree introduced from China for ornament and timber. Its winged seeds can reach disturbed ground, rocky slopes, forest openings and even cracks around buildings. Large leaves make young plants conspicuous, while mature trees are most noticeable when pale purple flowers open before the new foliage. In regions where it escapes, early recognition prevents a small seedling from becoming a difficult tree-removal job.
identification: Leaves are opposite, broadly heart shaped and velvety, especially beneath. Vigorous young shoots can carry exceptionally large leaves. Upright clusters of trumpet-shaped lavender flowers are followed by rounded woody capsules that persist after splitting. Brown, felted flower buds and old capsules can be visible together on bare winter twigs. Catalpas have similar large leaves but produce long, slender pods rather than rounded capsules. Young velvetleaf can also resemble a seedling princess tree. Photograph leaf arrangement, texture and fruit or buds whenever available.
actions: Pull small seedlings and dig manageable saplings with their roots when soil conditions permit. A cut stump or surviving root can produce vigorous sprouts, so schedule repeated follow-up rather than treating felling as the end of the job. Have large trees assessed and removed by a qualified professional where replacement is appropriate. Avoid planting the species where local guidance discourages it, and choose a tree suited to the site. Check gutters, pavement cracks and nearby disturbed ground for new seedlings after seed dispersal.
researchNotes: Maryland full account read; NC State independent profile supports traits and introduced concern. No timber-growth claims generalized to commercial performance.

proposedDescription: Privet aphid is a tiny sap-feeding insect associated with privet shrubs and hedges. Its feeding can roll leaves into narrow tubes and leave yellow spotting, sometimes making new growth look untidy. Specialist accounts record it as introduced in North America. The damage is usually limited enough that an otherwise healthy hedge does not need treatment simply because a few curled leaves are present.
identification: Look inside a freshly curled privet leaf for small, shiny yellow to greenish-yellow aphids, about a millimeter or a little more long. The paired tubes near the rear of the body have dark outer portions, a feature best seen with magnification. Leaf curling alone is not a species identification, since other insects and growing conditions can distort foliage. Photograph the host shrub, affected shoots and the insects themselves. A specialist may need a specimen to distinguish closely related aphids. Empty old curls can remain after the colony has disappeared.
actions: Inspect new growth during the growing season and judge the amount of live infestation rather than the number of damaged old leaves. Tolerate small colonies where the shrub continues to grow normally. On an accessible shoot, a small colony can be removed by hand while avoiding beneficial insects. Allow naturally occurring aphid predators to work and avoid broad treatment based only on curled leaves. If damage keeps expanding or the plant is declining, ask extension to confirm both the insect and the cause before choosing a response.
researchNotes: RHS provides species-specific low-impact management; Blackman/Eastop supplies independent morphology and North American introduction. UK month-specific life cycle not transferred to all US climates.

proposedDescription: Goatsrue is a perennial legume that can form persistent patches in moist pasture, ditches and other disturbed ground. It was once promoted as forage, but it is toxic to livestock and should never be introduced for grazing. Its clusters of pale pea-shaped flowers can resemble several harmless or native legumes, making careful identification essential before a pasture or wetland is treated.
identification: Plants produce multiple upright stems from a substantial root crown. The alternate leaves are divided into numerous paired leaflets with a terminal leaflet, rather than ending in the grasping tendrils typical of many vetches. Flowers are white to lavender or bluish and occur in elongated clusters; narrow pods follow. The native plant also called goat's-rue, Tephrosia virginiana, is a different species. Photograph the leaf tip, leaflet arrangement, flower cluster and pods, and obtain expert confirmation rather than relying on the shared common name or flower color.
actions: Keep livestock away from a suspected patch and do not include cut plants in hay or feed. Contact your local weed program or extension service for identification and a site-specific plan. Small plants may be removed with their crowns and roots, but established patches need follow-up over multiple seasons. Cutting alone can leave the perennial root system alive and should not be represented as a complete solution. Prevent seed production and avoid moving contaminated soil or equipment into clean areas. For suspected livestock exposure, seek veterinary advice promptly.

proposedDescription: Proso millet is both a cultivated grain and a source of weedy populations. The wild forms can be troublesome in corn and other summer crops, especially when seed travels with harvesting or tillage equipment. A volunteer from birdseed or a planted grain crop does not automatically behave like the most persistent wild biotypes. Management should reflect what the population is doing in that particular field.
identification: This upright annual grass has broad leaves, a hairy sheath and a fringe of hairs at the collar where blade and sheath meet. It lacks the small clasping appendages called auricles. The flowering head is a branched panicle with relatively large, smooth spikelets, often partly enclosed at its base by the upper leaf sheath. Seeds can be pale, reddish-brown or dark. Witchgrass has smaller spikelets, while mature fall panicum is generally much less hairy. Photograph the collar, sheath, complete seed head and a few attached spikelets rather than using seed color alone.
actions: Pull isolated outbreaks before seed matures, and remove flowering material from the field. Young plants can recover from substantial damage, so check after cultivation instead of assuming broken shoots are dead. Clean machinery before moving from infested ground, and harvest affected fields last where practical. In recurrent crop infestations, work with an adviser on rotation and timely cultivation that interrupt seed return. Dense, competitive crops or a suitable perennial forage phase can help, but the choice must fit the farm. Avoid spreading contaminated grain or birdseed waste along field edges.
researchNotes: Cornell management synthesis plus Missouri independent identification. Crop/wild-biotype distinction retained; variable leaf hair and seed colors described without unsupported absolute.

proposedDescription: Lindernia procumbens is a small wet-ground plant with delicate pale flowers. True L. procumbens is an Old World species that resembles the American Lindernia dubia. Similar names and small flowers can complicate older records, and a historical occurrence should not be treated as proof of a current established population. A record carrying the name therefore needs more scrutiny than a simple map dot.
identification: Look for opposite, stalkless leaves with several veins arising near the base and margins that are smooth or only weakly scalloped. Small white to pale pink, two-lipped flowers are borne singly on slender stalks in the leaf axils. The most useful distinction from L. dubia is inside the flower: true L. procumbens has four fertile stamens, whereas L. dubia has two fertile stamens plus modified sterile structures. This requires magnification and an open flower. Overall size, a creeping habit or a damp site will not resolve the identity.
actions: Photograph the leaves, flower stalk and open flower without disturbing the surrounding wetland. Ask a herbarium or regional botanist to examine a suspected occurrence, and provide the original label if the name came from an older survey. Do not remove a patch solely because a historical record calls it introduced. Avoid moving mud or rooted plants to another waterbody while identification is pending. Any response should be based on a confirmed population and local habitat assessment, with care to protect native lookalikes and other small shoreline plants.

proposedDescription: Prostrate knotweed is the low, wiry plant often found in hard-used lawn edges, paths and cracks where soil has become compacted. It usually grows as an annual and can survive routine mowing by staying close to the ground. Its name refers to the joints along its slender stems. It is very different from the tall, cane-forming Japanese knotweed, so their control approaches should not be confused.
identification: Young seedlings can look grasslike before branching into a flat mat. Small, alternate, blue-green leaves attach along tough stems, with a thin papery sheath surrounding each joint. Tiny whitish to pinkish flowers sit in the leaf axils rather than in showy spikes. Prostrate spurge has a similar spreading habit but opposite leaves and milky sap; purslane is noticeably fleshier. Several closely related knotweeds are treated differently among floras, so a precise botanical record may require mature flowers and fruit. Photograph a stem joint and leaf arrangement as well as the whole mat.
actions: Pull young plants before seed matures, taking out the central root where practical. Repeated low mowing is unlikely to solve the problem. Reduce the conditions that favor its return: redirect concentrated foot traffic, relieve lawn compaction when appropriate and maintain turf suited to the site. Mulch exposed planting beds and watch for early spring seedlings. Avoid unnecessary disturbance in a natural area simply because the plant occurs there. For a recurring crop or turf problem, identify the knotweed carefully and choose management suited to that setting.
researchNotes: Penn State and Utah species-specific guidance; NC State compaction response corroborates. UC arenastrum account not silently equated with aviculare. Complex taxonomy acknowledged without forcing new catalog ID.

proposedDescription: Tumble pigweed is a bushy summer annual whose dried stems can break free and roll, scattering seed. It occurs in disturbed ground and cultivated settings, but its native range includes parts of the southern United States and northeastern Mexico. Being a crop weed and being nonnative are separate questions. Its relatively small leaves and pale branching stems give it a different appearance from tall pigweeds with prominent seed spikes.
identification: Look for smooth, pale green to whitish stems that branch heavily from low on the plant. Leaves are alternate, often spoon shaped, with wavy margins and short stalks. Small green flowers are crowded into prickly clusters where each leaf stalk joins the stem. Unlike Palmer amaranth or redroot pigweed, it does not form a large terminal flower spike. Prostrate pigweed stays more matlike and commonly has darker leaves with pale margins. Seedlings are harder to separate, so photograph mature branching, a leaf and several flower clusters before making a firm identification.
actions: Remove unwanted young plants from beds or crop rows before they form mature seed. Wear gloves around the sharp flower bracts, and contain dry plants rather than dragging them across clean ground. Check equipment and moved soil for seed-bearing debris. Keep desirable groundcover where possible, and revisit disturbed areas for later seedlings during the warm season. In a native habitat, assess the actual problem before deciding removal is necessary. A persistent agricultural infestation warrants species confirmation and a crop-specific plan, especially when it occurs alongside other pigweeds.
researchNotes: Cornell and Missouri independent diagnostic accounts; Kew supports southern US native nuance. Early hand removal is proportionate annual seed-prevention advice, not a claimed eradication trial.

proposedDescription: Proteus scale, also called orchid parlatoria scale or variable chaff scale, is a small armored scale insect found on many kinds of ornamental plants. It has been recorded as a pest of orchids in Florida and can travel with infested nursery material. Its broad host range means an orchid association is a clue, not a reliable identification. The insect can be overlooked because its protective cover resembles a tiny patch of plant debris.
identification: Adult females sit beneath flat, oval, partly translucent covers about one to two millimeters long. Covers are tan to pale yellow-brown, with darker shed skins near one end. Male covers are narrower and elongated. Examine leaf surfaces, stems and sheltered plant crevices with magnification. Other Parlatoria species can look almost identical externally, and authoritative identification usually requires a prepared adult female examined under a microscope. Photograph the affected plant and a close view of intact covers, then ask a diagnostic service how to submit material.
actions: Separate a newly acquired plant with suspicious scales from other plants and avoid sharing cuttings until its condition is resolved. Inspect nearby plants, since the tiny mobile crawler stage can spread before settling under a cover. Do not assume every old cover contains a living insect or that wiping visible scales once will clear an infestation. For a nursery, greenhouse or valuable orchid collection, obtain identification and locally appropriate management advice. Keep discarded infested leaves contained and check new growth during follow-up rather than judging success from appearance alone.

proposedDescription: Puncturevine is a low-growing summer annual best known for the hard, sharp burs called goatheads. Those fruits can injure paws and bare feet and puncture bicycle tires. The plant favors warm, disturbed ground and can keep producing new seedlings through summer. Livestock may also be poisoned by eating the foliage, so grazing is not a suitable way to clear a patch.
identification: Stems radiate outward along the ground from a central root. The opposite leaves are divided into pairs of small leaflets, and the stems and foliage are hairy. Small yellow flowers have five petals. The developing fruit separates into hard sections bearing stout spines, a much stronger identification clue than the yellow flowers alone. Related native plants in the caltrop family can resemble it in leaf and flower. Photograph intact fruit, leaf arrangement and the whole plant before removing an uncertain patch; avoid handling burs with bare hands.
actions: Pull or hoe plants before flowering and fruit formation, and collect any burs already present. Check shoes, bicycle tires, carts and mower wheels before leaving the area. Wear sturdy gloves and footwear, and keep pets away while removing spiny material. Mowing usually misses the low stems, so it is not an effective stand-alone method. Revisit the site throughout the warm season and in later years as buried seeds germinate. Reduce bare ground with suitable desirable vegetation or mulch where appropriate. Established biological control programs can help in some regions, but obtain local advice rather than moving insects yourself.
researchNotes: UC management and Montana independent extension diagnosis/prevention support profile. No pesticide recipe or self-directed biological-control release. Native lookalikes retained without unsupported genus-level blanket.

proposedDescription: Melaleuca, or broad-leaved paperbark, is an evergreen tree native to Australasia that became a major invader of southern Florida wetlands. Dense stands replace native plant communities and change the structure of places that formerly supported open marsh or diverse woodland. Florida management has combined repeated removal with carefully evaluated biological control. Trees left as seed sources can undermine that continuing work.
identification: The trunk has thick, pale, papery bark that peels in many soft layers. Narrow leathery leaves alternate along the twigs and have several conspicuous lengthwise veins. Creamy white flowers form bottlebrush-like spikes, followed by small woody capsules crowded around the stems. Capsules can remain attached after flowering. Other cultivated paperbarks and bottlebrushes can share some of these features, so use bark, leaves and fruit together. Photograph a leafy twig with its capsules and the trunk rather than relying on bark color alone.
actions: In Florida, arrange removal of a confirmed tree with local extension or a qualified land-management professional. Small seedlings can be pulled with their roots where this will not damage sensitive vegetation. Larger trees require a planned treatment and repeated checks for sprouts and seedlings. Disturbance can release seed, so avoid casual cutting and hauling of capsule-bearing branches. Follow local disposal directions and clean equipment before leaving an infested site. Do not plant or distribute the tree. Biological control insects belong within approved programs; do not collect and move unfamiliar insects between properties on your own.
researchNotes: UF applied management and independent NSW flora morphology; FWC disturbance-induced seed release corroborates. No historic acreage presented as current; no pesticide recipe or unapproved organism movement.

proposedDescription: Livid amaranth, also called purple pigweed, is a summer annual found in disturbed ground, crop fields and nursery settings. It can spread from bed edges into containers, making early inspection useful where plants are being moved or sold. Its low, branching growth often looks different from the tall pigweeds familiar in farm fields. The name Amaranthus lividus appears in older references to this plant.
identification: A deep notch at the leaf tip is a helpful clue, sometimes with a tiny stiff point in the notch. Leaves are alternate, often widest toward the tip, with smooth margins and stalks no longer than the blade. Stems are smooth and may be green or reddish. Green flowers occur both in the leaf axils and toward the ends of branches. Tumble pigweed has pale bushy stems and flowers confined to axillary clusters; other pigweeds can be difficult to separate when young. Photograph several mature leaves, stem surfaces and both terminal and axillary flower clusters.
actions: Pull unwanted young plants before they contribute seed, especially along nursery bed margins and inside containers. Check pots and growing media before moving them into clean areas. Keep seed-bearing debris contained, and revisit the site for later summer seedlings. Do not identify a pigweed solely by its red coloration or assume all species respond to the same control program. In a recurring crop infestation, ask an adviser to confirm the species and review the management history. Avoid relying on an unfamiliar wild plant as food simply because some cultivated amaranths are edible.
researchNotes: Independent Cornell detailed identification and NC State nursery context. No blanket origin assertion because modern taxonomic treatments vary; no medicinal claims or herbicide-resistance generalization.

proposedDescription: Purple Asian clam is a freshwater clam name applied to some introduced Corbicula populations. Recent studies disagree over whether Corbicula largillierti is a distinct species or belongs within Corbicula fluminea. North American specimens reported under the name therefore need careful review. A purple shell interior does not settle their identity. Keep the original identification, collection location and supporting specimen together rather than treating every Asian clam as this species.
identification: Published descriptions from Argentina mention olive-brown outer shells, violet inner surfaces and relatively low concentric ribs. These features can help document a candidate, but shell shape and color vary, and similar Corbicula forms occur together. Photograph the outside and inside of an already empty shell with a ruler, including the hinge if visible. Do not open a living clam just to check its color. A specialist may need several specimens and both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA evidence to distinguish an introduced lineage from another form. Shell color or a single genetic marker may not reliably establish the species.
actions: Clean mud, plants and small animals from boats, waders and fishing equipment before leaving a waterbody. Drain retained water and follow the local clean-drain-dry procedure before using that equipment elsewhere. Do not release aquarium clams, bait or transport water into a stream or lake. Report an unfamiliar concentration to the relevant aquatic invasive-species program with photographs and the precise location. Ask before collecting or shipping specimens, particularly where native mussels occur. There is no practical reason to disturb an entire riverbed to identify a few shells, and unconfirmed identification should not trigger a chemical treatment.

proposedDescription: Purple deadnettle is a small introduced annual often seen in lawns, garden beds and disturbed ground during cool weather. It commonly starts growing in autumn and flowers early the following season, although timing varies with climate. The reddish upper leaves can make a patch stand out before the small flowers are noticed. It provides nectar for insects, and whether a patch needs attention depends on the site rather than its presence alone.
identification: Look for square stems and opposite, softly hairy leaves with rounded teeth and prominent veins. Upper leaves are crowded, triangular to heart-shaped and often tinted purple, but they still have short stalks. The small pink-purple flowers have a hooded upper lip. Henbit is a frequent lookalike: its upper leaves are rounder and clasp the stem without stalks. Ground ivy spreads along creeping perennial stems instead of behaving as a small upright annual. Photograph the upper leaf attachments and the lower growth together to make that comparison easier.
actions: If the plant is unwanted, remove small patches before they mature seed and revisit the area for later seedlings. In a lawn, address thin turf and bare soil rather than treating each spring flush as an isolated event. In beds, maintain appropriate plant cover or mulch while keeping it away from plant crowns. A few flowering plants in an informal garden do not automatically need spraying. If a larger infestation affects a crop or restoration planting, ask for guidance suited to that land use and the plant's current growth stage.
researchNotes: Purdue supports leaf-stalk and henbit distinctions; Penn State independently covers annual versus perennial lookalikes and management choices. NCSU adds introduced origin and floral characters. No nationwide flowering months, food-use advice or generalized ecological-harm claim.

proposedDescription: Purple false brome, also called annual false brome, is a small annual grass from the Mediterranean region and nearby parts of Eurasia. It grows in dry, open or disturbed places and can become locally abundant in California. Dense growth leaves persistent dry material that can interfere with native seedlings and add to fine fuels. It is different from the perennial false brome that is the focus of some woodland weed-control programs.
identification: Look for short, rough leaf blades and conspicuously hairy joints along stems that may bend at the lower nodes. The flowering structure is compact, with only a few flattened, many-flowered spikelets rather than a broad, airy spray. Individual flower bracts have long projecting awns. A blue-green cast and stiff hairs can help draw attention to it, but neither is diagnostic alone. Photograph the stem joints, leaf collar and complete seed head beside a ruler. A regional grass key is useful because several annual bromes occupy the same habitat.
actions: Mark a suspected patch while seed heads are still recognizable, noting whether it is scattered through other vegetation or forming a dense stand. Avoid carrying mature seed in mowing equipment, footwear or cut material. Before clearing a restoration site, ask the land manager to confirm the species and choose a timing that limits seed production without unnecessarily exposing soil. Return after the next germination period to check the result. Do not assume that recommendations for perennial Brachypodium sylvaticum apply to this annual, and keep species identity attached to any treatment record.

proposedDescription: Purple foxglove is a familiar garden plant that can establish beyond cultivation, especially in moist disturbed ground, roadsides and forest openings. It usually begins as a leafy rosette before producing a tall flowering stalk. In some coastal regions, dense patches replace other vegetation. All parts are poisonous if eaten, so identifying a plant correctly matters even where it is an intentional garden planting rather than an unwanted escape.
identification: Look for a low rosette of large, soft, hairy leaves with toothed margins, followed by a tall stalk bearing hanging tubular bells. Flowers often line one side of the stalk and commonly have darker spots inside; cultivated colors include shades beyond purple. The rosette alone is less distinctive, so include a whole-plant photograph and both leaf surfaces. Do not taste a leaf or confuse it with an edible herb because of its broad shape. A flowering stem, its leaf arrangement and the inside of a bell provide much better evidence.
actions: Keep children, pets and livestock away from removed plants and cut flowers. Where removal is needed, wear gloves and take out the whole plant before seed is shed, with the landowner's permission. Contain flowering or seed-bearing material rather than scattering it through garden waste. Small patches can be hand removed, but repeat inspections are essential because seed can persist in the soil for years. Avoid leaving a large cleared area bare. For a substantial escape into natural habitat, coordinate a longer-term plan with the land manager instead of relying on one afternoon of pulling.

proposedDescription: Purple granadilla, or passionfruit, is a vigorous climbing vine grown for its fruit. In warm regions it can escape cultivation, and Hawaiian guidance describes naturalized vines that overgrow shrubs and trees. Birds and other animals carry the seeds after feeding on fruit. Its usefulness as a crop does not prevent escape, but risk assessments and behavior can differ among locations and cultivated forms.
identification: Mature leaves are typically glossy and deeply divided into three lobes. Tendrils attach the vine to nearby supports, and the showy flowers have a ring of fine filaments around the center. Ripe fruit color varies among cultivated forms, so a yellow fruit does not automatically rule it out. Other passionflowers can have similar flowers or lobed leaves. Photograph a mature leaf, tendril, flower and fruit together, and retain the nursery name if known. Young leaves and nonflowering shoots may not show the full set of useful features.
actions: Inspect the edges of a planting for seedlings and vines climbing vegetation that was not intended as a support. Pick up fallen fruit and keep seed-bearing waste out of natural areas. If an escaped vine is covering a tree, do not pull the entire tangled canopy down and damage the host. Ask the land manager how to separate and address the vine at its base, then check for regrowth and seedlings. Before adding another passionfruit planting near sensitive habitat, consult the current local assessment for the particular form and site rather than assuming all fruit crops are low risk.

proposedDescription: Purple loosestrife is a perennial wetland plant that can form dense stands along marshes, shorelines, ditches and streambanks. Established plants produce many flowering stems and large amounts of tiny seed, allowing disturbed wet ground to fill quickly. Dense stands can crowd out native wetland vegetation. A report is especially useful when plants are still scattered, before a small occurrence becomes difficult to manage.
identification: Look for upright, often branching stems with opposite or whorled, narrow leaves that attach without obvious stalks. The stems are usually angular. Tall spikes carry many pink-purple flowers, typically with six petals, opening at several levels at once. Flower color alone is not enough: native blazing stars and vervains can also have purple spikes. Photograph the leaf arrangement, a close flower and the base of the plant. Include the wetland setting, but stay on firm ground rather than wading into an unsafe shoreline to obtain a picture.
actions: Send the location and photographs to your local invasive-plant or wetland program. Do not plant it beside a pond or move flowering stems between sites. Where a very small patch can be removed without damaging the wetland, the whole root system needs attention and all reproductive material should be contained. Mowing alone can encourage regrowth or move fragments and seed. Larger stands need a coordinated plan; approved biological-control programs may be an option through the responsible agency. Do not release insects or use a terrestrial herbicide in water on your own.
researchNotes: UMN supports leaf arrangement and six-petaled flowers; Kentucky guidance independently covers removal limitations and fragment spread. USGS summarizes approved biological control. Neither local legal categories nor exact treatment thresholds are generalized nationally.

proposedDescription: Purple moorgrass is a perennial grass native to parts of Europe, western Asia and nearby regions. It is planted ornamentally and has been recorded outside cultivation in parts of North America, including New England. Its airy flowering stems can be attractive in a garden, but an observation should distinguish a maintained planting from self-sown plants beyond it. An introduced occurrence alone does not establish that the grass is causing local ecological damage.
identification: Look for a clump of narrow leaves with upright stems carrying a branched flower head. The small spikelets contain several flowers and lack the long projecting awns seen on many other grasses. Purple tones can occur in the flower head and anthers, although color changes with stage and growing conditions. Photograph the whole clump, the branching pattern of the flower head and a close view of several spikelets. An ornamental cultivar may differ in height or color, so a nursery label helps but should not replace botanical identification.
actions: Record seedlings beyond the planted clump separately from the original garden plant. Note the habitat, approximate patch size and whether flowering plants are scattered or increasing. Avoid distributing seed-bearing divisions or dumping garden waste near meadows and wetlands. If a land manager considers an escaped patch unwanted, arrange removal with follow-up checks for seedlings and surviving growth rather than assuming one cut will finish the job. Seek local botanical advice before disturbing a grassland that may contain similar native species. Management should reflect the site's conservation goals, not just the common name on a plant list.

proposedDescription: Purple nutsedge is a persistent perennial sedge of gardens, crop fields and other disturbed ground in warm regions. Much of the plant is underground: rhizomes connect chains of tubers that can produce new shoots after the visible leaves are removed. This is why a patch may return after ordinary weeding. It can become troublesome in cultivated soil, but recognizing its growth system is more useful than treating it as an unusually fast-growing lawn grass.
identification: The upright stems are triangular in cross-section, with narrow leaves arising near the base. Flowering plants have clusters of reddish to purplish-brown spikelets above several leaf-like bracts. Yellow nutsedge usually has paler, golden-brown flower clusters and tubers formed singly at rhizome ends, while purple nutsedge produces tubers in chains. If you are already digging an unwanted patch, photograph the attached underground parts before they break apart. Do not spread soil simply to inspect it. A leaf-only photograph may not distinguish the two nutsedges reliably.
actions: Address small patches early and keep checking for replacement shoots. When digging, account for the tubers and connecting rhizomes instead of removing only the green top. Avoid moving infested soil or nursery stock to clean beds. Check for leaking irrigation or persistently wet soil, while remembering that established nutsedge can survive less favorable conditions too. Repeated attention is normally needed; a single mowing or shallow hoeing does not remove the stored underground growth. For larger infestations, choose a locally appropriate integrated plan that protects nearby plants and matches the confirmed nutsedge species.
researchNotes: UC IPM supplies nutsedge biology and integrated management; Penn State independently distinguishes purple from yellow nutsedge. CDFA repeats UC morphology and is not counted separately. No taste test, chemical dosage or assurance of one-pass removal.

proposedDescription: Purple pampas grass, also called jubatagrass, forms large tussocks on coastal bluffs, dunes and disturbed ground. Introduced as an ornamental and for erosion control, it can spread far beyond a planting through windblown seed. Seeds can develop without fertilization, so one isolated plant can still produce an expanding population. Dense stands can displace lower vegetation and make access or restoration work difficult.
identification: Look for a broad, spreading clump of long leaves and tall stems carrying dense feathery plumes. Young plumes are often violet to pinkish, becoming pale or brown as they age. Flowering stems commonly rise well above the leafy clump. It resembles Cortaderia selloana, the plant most often called pampas grass; plume color alone cannot separate every plant. Photograph the whole tussock, the height of the stems relative to the leaves and the leaf bases. Avoid dragging bare hands along the sharp leaf edges to inspect them.
actions: Report new escapes near natural areas, particularly isolated seed-producing plants that can be addressed before a larger stand develops. Wear suitable protective clothing when working near the foliage. Small seedlings are easier to remove than established tussocks, whose crowns and roots require much more effort. Contain plumes before moving cut material, and keep contaminated equipment from spreading seed. Arrange specialist help for large plants or steep sites. Follow-up matters after removal because seedlings may emerge on disturbed soil; restore appropriate cover rather than leaving a bare patch. Do not use fire as a home control method.

proposedDescription: Purple scale is an armored scale insect most familiar on citrus. It feeds on leaves, twigs and fruit, often in cooler, shaded parts of the canopy. Heavy patches can cause leaf loss or twig dieback, while natural enemies keep many populations below damaging levels. The brownish-purple structures visible on a plant are protective covers; the insect itself sits underneath. Finding a few old covers is not the same as finding an active outbreak.
identification: Female covers are elongated and curved like tiny mussel shells, usually dark brown with a possible purple tinge and old cast skins at the narrow end. Male covers are narrower and shorter. Check shaded inner branches and leaf midribs, and photograph a cluster with a size reference. Glover scale and other armored scales can resemble it. A plant diagnostic service may need adult females mounted for microscopic examination to confirm the species. Include the host identity and whether the covers contain live insects rather than relying on color alone.
actions: Inspect new citrus and other host plants before moving them into an established planting. If scale is present, document its extent and any associated leaf or twig damage. Avoid broad spraying of an otherwise healthy tree, because parasitoids can provide useful control. A local citrus adviser can determine whether treatment is needed and how to time it to the vulnerable crawler stage. Address conditions that interfere with natural enemies, such as heavy dust or tending ants where relevant. Keep infested nursery material in place while its identity and management are being assessed.
researchNotes: Naturalis diagnostic synthesis supports cover shape and microscopic confirmation; UC citrus guidance supplies observed canopy preference, damage and parasitoid-based management. UC general table says biologically controlled; the text avoids interpreting that as never damaging everywhere.

proposedDescription: Purple toadflax is a European perennial cultivated for its slender flowering stems. On Hawaii Island, BIISC reports that a garden escape entered dry native forest near Oceanview and that the known population was eradicated. Slender stems and many small flowers give it a light, airy appearance, but established plants have a persistent rootstock. It should not be confused with yellow toadflax or Dalmatian toadflax simply because the common names overlap; evidence and management for those species are not interchangeable.
identification: Look for narrow, blue-green leaves on upright stems that branch toward the top. Long flower clusters carry small purple or pink flowers with two lips and a curved spur extending behind the flower. Individual blooms are much smaller than garden snapdragons. Round capsules follow the flowers. Photograph a stem with its leaves, a flower from the side so the spur is visible, and mature capsules if present. Flower color varies, so the combination of narrow leaves, flowering arrangement and spur is more useful than a purple bloom alone.
actions: Record whether plants are maintained in a bed, persisting after cultivation or appearing independently outside the planting. Avoid distributing seed-bearing cuttings into roadsides or natural areas. If local managers want a small escape removed, address the rootstock and revisit the ground for regrowth and seedlings. Take care not to remove similar native plants based only on a common name. For larger populations, ask a regional weed specialist to confirm the species and whether control is a local priority. Do not borrow a treatment plan for another toadflax without checking that it applies.

proposedDescription: Purpleanther field pepperweed is a small mustard whose identification depends more on its fruits than its common name. The intended name here is Lepidium heterophyllum Benth., also recorded as Lepidium smithii. A different name with the same spelling has been applied to another pepperweed, so checking the author and underlying specimen is important when comparing databases. A matching search result is not always a matching species.
identification: Look for small white, four-petaled flowers followed by flattened, broadly oval fruits on an elongating stem. Upper leaves attach without stalks and have arrow-like or ear-like bases. The fruits have a broad wing near the tip and a shallow notch, with the slender style extending clearly beyond that notch. Hairy fruiting stalks are another useful detail. Photograph mature fruits from the face and side with a scale reference, along with upper and lower leaves. Several pepperweeds look similar before fruiting, so a leafy rosette alone may remain uncertain.
actions: Keep the location and photographs with any identification request, especially if the plant was found in a seed mix, nursery stock or transported soil. Do not taste it to confirm the pepperweed name. Avoid moving mature seed-bearing plants into other sites. If it is unwanted and a local specialist confirms the identity, address a small patch before further seed dispersal and return to look for seedlings. Local occurrence and land-use goals should guide the response.

proposedDescription: Purpleglume flatsedge is a tufted sedge recorded from wet ground, streambanks and disturbed roadsides. Its native range extends through parts of Africa, Asia and Australia, with introduced records in several southeastern states and Hawaii. Older references may call it Pycreus sanguinolentus. Those distribution records help place an observation in context, but do not by themselves show that a particular patch is damaging a wetland.
identification: Look for smooth, three-sided stems and narrow leaves near the base. The flower head may be compact or have a few short branches, with one or more long leaf-like bracts extending beyond it. Flattened spikelets contain dark reddish-brown to nearly black scales with paler margins. Mature fruits are tiny and flattened rather than prominently three-angled. Many sedges share the overall form, so photographs should include a complete head, individual spikelets and the leaf bases. Color alone is not enough, and a botanist may need mature fruit for confirmation.
actions: Record the moisture conditions, extent of the patch and whether recent soil or equipment movement could explain its arrival. Clean adhering mud from tools and footwear before visiting another wet site. Avoid digging up a shoreline just to obtain an identification; photographs or a carefully requested specimen may be sufficient. If a land manager considers removal necessary, plan it around the wetland's other vegetation and check for renewed growth after disturbance. Do not apply a nutsedge treatment solely because both plants belong to Cyperus. The response should follow the confirmed species and local habitat needs.

proposedDescription: Purpletop vervain is a South American garden plant with tall, open stems and clusters of small purple flowers. It can self-sow beyond a planting, but the name has often been confused with Verbena incompta, a similar plant with less conspicuous flowers. Older records may therefore need rechecking. A flower photograph is particularly valuable because the long flower tube is one of the best clues to the narrower species concept.
identification: Look for sharply toothed leaves and small flower clusters held high on angular stems. In Verbena bonariensis, the colored flower tube projects noticeably beyond the green or purplish calyx surrounding its base. Under magnification, gland-tipped hairs can help with identification. Verbena incompta has much shorter flower tubes that barely exceed the calyx. Plant height and the outline of a whole flower cluster are less dependable distinctions. Photograph several fresh flowers from the side, leaves and stem hairs rather than only taking a distant picture of the purple canopy.
actions: Watch for seedlings outside the intended bed and document escapes separately from planted specimens. Where spread is unwanted, remove seedlings before they become seed-bearing and contain mature flower heads during cleanup. Do not assume that a seed packet or a familiar nursery name settles the identification. If plants are spreading into nearby natural vegetation, ask a regional botanist or land manager which species is present before choosing a response. Retain the photographs and any cultivar label so future records can be compared. Local management should account for the plant's identity and setting rather than treating all ornamental vervains alike.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. Current comparative work supports distinguishing the garden species from incompta; ambiguous historical records remain qualified. The same Gardner paper is counted once, not as multiple website lineages. No US harm is borrowed from incompta. Source lineage and access details are recorded in batch-63-notes.md. proposedDescription: Verbena incompta shares the common name purpletop vervain with a more familiar garden species, Verbena bonariensis. The two were long confused, so older reports can describe a broader group than the name now implies. This South American plant occurs in roadsides, fields and other disturbed places. North Carolina botanists map specimens reidentified specifically as V. incompta, while acknowledging that older bonariensis records still need sorting. Its precise local identity matters before transferring impact claims or control advice from another vervain.
identification: The stems are upright, prominently four-angled and often conspicuously hairy. Toothed leaves attach without stalks and partly clasp the stem. The small blue-purple flowers barely project beyond the calyx at their base, unlike the noticeably longer tubes of Verbena bonariensis. A hand lens and close side-view photographs are useful. Leaves may be broader than those of the garden lookalike, but leaf width alone is unreliable. Include young and mature flower clusters, stem hairs and leaf attachments in a report, since a distant purple flower head cannot resolve the distinction.
actions: Keep a record of where the plant appeared and whether it is associated with a planting, imported soil or roadside disturbance. Avoid moving seed-bearing material to another property. Ask a herbarium or regional weed specialist to check the identification before treating an unfamiliar population. If removal is advised, contain reproductive material and revisit the disturbed ground for new plants. Preserve any specimen number or identification comments with the observation so it does not become another ambiguous bonariensis record. A treatment should be selected for the confirmed local population, not simply for any plant sold as purpletop.
researchNotes: Fresh exact-taxon review, 2026-10-31. A US flora explicitly based on reannotated vouchers supplies the missing local taxon applicability. proposedDescription: Pygmy peaclam is a very small freshwater bivalve native to Europe and parts of western Asia and recorded in the Great Lakes region. Older sources place it in Pisidium. Historical accounts suggest ship transport as a likely introduction pathway, but its ecological effects are not well established. A French reservoir study documented recovery after temporary drying, so drawdown should not be assumed to eliminate it. Its minute size and resemblance to other pea clams make ordinary shoreline photographs unreliable for identification.
identification: Reported adults are only about two to three millimeters long. The shell is rounded to somewhat triangular or trapezoidal, with visible growth ridges and low beaks that barely rise above the upper margin. Distinguishing it from other pea clams depends heavily on the tiny hinge teeth inside the valves. Those structures require magnification and specialist experience. If you find empty shells during legitimate sampling, photograph them with a millimeter scale and retain the collection details. Do not assume that every small pale clam in sediment is this introduced species.
actions: Follow clean-drain-dry guidance for boats, waders and sampling equipment, paying attention to mud and retained water that can carry organisms too small to notice. Do not move sediment or living clams between lakes for comparison. For a suspected new occurrence, contact the relevant aquatic survey or invasive-species program and ask how it wants a specimen documented. Avoid disturbing native mussel habitat or collecting without permission. There is no supported household treatment for an unidentified peaclam population; accurate identification and a traceable location are more useful than attempting broad removal.

proposedDescription: Pyriform scale is a sap-feeding soft scale found on avocado and other ornamental hosts. Unlike armored scales, its visible surface is the insect's own body rather than a separate removable shield. Feeding can leave sticky honeydew that supports black sooty mold. In California, it is more often encountered on landscape avocados than in commercial groves, and natural enemies commonly keep soft scales from becoming serious pests.
identification: Look on leaves for flattened, brownish scales shaped roughly like a rounded triangle or pear. A fringe of white wax may project from beneath a mature female. Young insects are smaller and paler; mature bodies can darken, so color varies with age. Photograph the underside of affected leaves, the outline of individual scales and any white wax. Other soft scales can occupy the same plant, and an official diagnosis may require a mounted adult female examined under a microscope. Sticky residue or sooty mold alone does not identify which insect is present.
actions: Inspect affected plants and new nursery arrivals before moving them. Check whether scales are alive and increasing, and note any leaf loss or reduced growth. Keep natural enemies in mind before spraying: indiscriminate insecticides can remove the predators and parasitoids already helping. Reducing dust and managing ants that protect honeydew producers can be useful in suitable settings. Ask an extension adviser whether a treatment is warranted and, if so, how to target the susceptible stage. Clean foliage is not a reason to move potentially infested plants until the insects themselves have been checked.
researchNotes:
UC avocado guidance supports landscape occurrence, body outline and biological control; Australian national protocol independently provides diagnostic standards. Broad soft-scale recommendations are identified as such and are not inflated into pyriform-specific damage rates.

proposedDescription: Quackgrass is a perennial grass that spreads through underground stems called rhizomes as well as seed. A patch can return after its visible leaves are removed because living pieces remain below the surface. It occurs in lawns, planting beds and open ground, where its spreading growth can compete with desired plants. The underground network is the main reason a quick mowing or shallow cultivation rarely resolves an established patch.
identification: Look for relatively broad grass blades and small clasping projections, called auricles, where the blade meets the stem. New leaves are rolled in the shoot. A carefully lifted edge of an unwanted patch may reveal pale, pointed rhizomes running between shoots. Clasping auricles also occur in some ryegrasses, so combine that feature with the rhizomes rather than using it alone. Photograph the leaf collar closely and, where appropriate, an intact connection between shoots. An isolated blade without its collar or underground structures is much harder to identify.
actions: In a small bed, work patiently to remove rhizomes rather than snapping off just the leaves, and check repeatedly for fresh shoots. Avoid rotary tillage as a quick cure because cut rhizomes can continue growing and be spread through the bed. Clean soil and fragments from equipment before moving elsewhere. Maintain competitive planting cover and prevent seed production while addressing the established patch. If removal would damage valuable plants or the infestation is extensive, ask about a site-appropriate systemic treatment. Any product must be labeled for the location and used with care around desirable grasses and other vegetation.
researchNotes: Cornell independently corroborates rolled bud and clasping auricles; Utah extension supports rhizomes and warns against cultivation fragmentation. Advice targets both shoots and rhizomes and avoids promising single-pass eradication.

claims: Rolled leaves and clasping auricles.

proposedDescription: Quagga mussels are small freshwater mussels that attach to surfaces and can also colonize soft lake bottoms. Dense populations filter food from the water and foul water-intake systems, boats and equipment. Their microscopic young can travel in retained water even when no adult mussels are visible. Some references use Dreissena rostriformis bugensis for the same mussel, so both names can appear in monitoring records.
identification: Quagga shells are variable in color, from pale cream to dark brown, and may have stripes. Compared with zebra mussels, their underside is usually more rounded and the two valves are less symmetrical. A shell may roll rather than rest flat on its underside, but this is a clue rather than a definitive test for every size or form. Photograph multiple views with a scale and record what the mussels were attached to. Young mussels can be difficult to separate from related species without expert examination.
actions:
Clean plants, mud and attached animals from boats, trailers, waders and other gear before leaving the site. Drain retained water as required by local rules, and dry equipment before entering another water body. Arrange an approved inspection or decontamination when required; a quick surface rinse may miss organisms inside a boat's systems. Report suspected new mussel colonies with a precise location and photographs, and ask before transporting specimens. Do not release captured mussels or use saltwater launching as an assumed cure. Prevention needs to include small craft and fishing gear, not only large boats.

Protect hands and feet from sharp shells when cleaning encrusted equipment or walking on affected shores.
