proposedDescription: Red pine scale is a tiny insect associated with serious decline of red pine in parts of the northeastern United States. Matsucoccus resinosae appears in older accounts; modern references generally place it under Matsucoccus matsumurae, also called Japanese pine bast scale. Its feeding can contribute to pockets of tree mortality. In Maine, red pine is the affected native tree, while other native pine species growing alongside it may remain healthy. That host pattern is useful, but it does not replace a diagnosis.
identification: Needles may change from olive green to reddish, beginning on individual branches before the whole crown declines. Look for small white cottony tufts on twigs and beneath loose bark flakes. These include male cocoons and female egg sacs. Adult females are mobile, brick-red and wingless; other stages can resemble tiny waxy pods. Several insects and environmental stresses cause pine decline. Photograph the tree, affected branches and scale material, and identify the pine itself before submitting a sample.
actions: Report suspected new occurrences to the state forest-health service and follow its sampling instructions. Avoid moving infested nursery stock or untreated branches to other sites. Maintain appropriate tree care, but do not add fertilizer simply to stimulate a declining pine; Maine guidance warns that it can worsen infestation. An arborist or forest-health specialist can advise whether treatment is realistic for an ornamental tree and how to handle hazardous trees. Check nearby red pines and record changes over time rather than relying on one inspection.
researchNotes: ScaleNet records resinosae as a junior synonym of matsumurae, and Maine independently documents red-pine symptoms and care. Regional origin remains disputed (ITIS reports native US status); the profile makes no origin assertion and uses the older name transparently. proposedDescription: Red sand-spurry is a small Eurasian herb that has been present in North America since at least the nineteenth century. Spergularia rubra often grows on disturbed ground, paths and open fields. Unlike several sand-spurries associated with salty shores, it also occurs well away from saline places. In New England it is introduced throughout the region. Its presence in a pavement crack or disturbed lawn does not by itself indicate a threat to surrounding natural vegetation. A careful identification is useful before deciding whether any action is needed.
identification: Plants spread low across the ground or rise on slender branches. Narrow, threadlike leaves occur in opposite pairs and are not strongly fleshy. Small papery stipules sit at their bases. The tiny flowers have five pink petals, generally shorter than the pointed green sepals around them. Mature capsules split to release numerous small seeds. Specialists can distinguish sand-spurries using seed surfaces, seed wings, stipules and flower measurements. Those details help separate this species from coastal relatives and from superficially similar little chickweeds.
actions: Photograph a flowering plant with a size reference and include the leaf bases and mature capsules if present. Record whether the ground is salted, coastal or inland, since that context helps identification. In a garden, decide whether the small patch is actually interfering with the intended planting before removing it. Avoid moving seed-bearing soil or sweepings into natural areas. For a plant found in a sensitive coastal habitat, ask a botanist to confirm it before disturbing the vegetation; native sand-spurries can grow in similar-looking patches.
researchNotes: Go Botany independently supplies North American introduction context; the Australian revision-derived key confirms diagnostic structures. Lack of ecological damage or a control trial does not prevent a restrained identification and seed-containment profile. proposedDescription: Purple starthistle is a Mediterranean-region weed with conspicuously armed flower heads. Centaurea calcitrapa grows in disturbed ground, roadsides and grazing land, where its spiny heads can interfere with access and pasture use. Plants may flower in their first year or spend longer as a rosette before producing a branched flowering stem. It spreads by seed, including seed carried with contaminated produce, soil and equipment. Local abundance and management priorities vary, so a newly found patch deserves confirmation and attention before it seeds.
identification: The plant is bushy, with deeply divided basal leaves and pink to purple flower heads. Long, stiff, straw-colored spines project from the bracts surrounding each head. Upper stems lack the conspicuous wings found on some other starthistles. The leaves themselves are not armed like a typical thistle leaf. Iberian starthistle is especially similar; its seeds carry a tuft of bristles, while purple starthistle seeds lack that plume. A photograph of the whole plant, a side view of the head and mature seed is more informative than a purple flower alone.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and protect exposed skin around the spiny heads. Small patches can be removed repeatedly before seed matures, with follow-up for missed plants. Nevada guidance notes that mowing during the bud-to-flower period can reduce seed production, but timing and repeat visits matter. Bag mature seed heads before handling the rest of a plant. Clean equipment used in an infestation and ask local weed staff about larger patches. Revisit the site in subsequent seasons because one cutting does not account for seed already in the soil.
researchNotes: Two independent agency lineages. Legal categories and pesticide recipes omitted. Iberian seed pappus distinction explicitly supported by Nevada; action timing based on Nevada, seed longevity not generalized beyond cited evidence.

proposedDescription: Red valerian is a Mediterranean ornamental that readily seeds beyond gardens in some regions. Centranthus ruber also appears under the newer name Valeriana rubra. Its rounded flower clusters brighten walls, rocky slopes and disturbed coastal ground, especially in climates with relatively cool summers. In parts of the western United States and Hawaii it occurs outside cultivation. The feathery fruits can be carried by wind, so a tidy-looking parent plant may have offspring well beyond its bed. Local setting matters when deciding whether to retain a planting.
identification: This perennial has smooth stems and opposite, somewhat fleshy blue-green leaves. Lower leaves have stalks, while upper leaves sit directly on or clasp the stem. Many tiny tubular flowers form a large, rounded cluster. Individual flowers have five fused lobes and a small spur. Flowers are often rose-pink to crimson, but white forms occur, so color is not a reliable dividing line. After flowering, fine feathery hairs become conspicuous around the fruits. It should not be identified solely by the common name valerian.
actions: Remove spent flower heads before the feathery fruits disperse, and check nearby gravel, wall bases and open ground for seedlings. Small unwanted plants can be dug out where access is safe and disturbance is limited. Avoid pulling plants from unstable masonry or steep slopes without appropriate help. Where red valerian is spreading into nearby habitat, replace it with a locally suitable plant that will stay within the garden. Follow up after removal, since seedlings may appear beyond the original clump and later flowering stems can still set seed.
researchNotes: Accepted-name change noted without changing catalog ID. Cal-IPC card supports digging and dispersal; NCSU independently supports deadheading, US naturalization and morphology. Old Cal-IPC1999 low-threat wording not used as current risk classification.

Spurred flowers, feathery fruits, wind spread and digging small plants.

proposedDescription: Hybrid imported fire ants arise from interbreeding between red imported fire ants and black imported fire ants. Solenopsis invicta x richteri occurs in parts of the southeastern United States where the parental populations have met. These ants can build substantial soil mounds and defend colonies with painful stings. A hybrid colony is not a harmless intermediate between the two parents. However, a red-brown ant or a large mound cannot establish hybrid identity, and ordinary management decisions usually begin with confirming that imported fire ants are present.
identification: Workers vary in size within a colony and range from reddish to brownish. Under magnification they have a two-part waist and ten-segmented antennae ending in a two-segmented club. Their shape combines characters of the parental species, making visual separation difficult even for experienced observers. Specialist laboratories can use chemical profiles of the body surface to help distinguish hybrids. The pale objects carried by workers are developing ants, not seeds. Photograph a mound from a distance and obtain sampling instructions rather than disturbing it to provoke a response.
actions: Keep people and pets away from an active mound, particularly during gardening or play. Contact extension for identification and a management plan matched to the site, whether lawn, pasture or nursery. Treatments must reach the colony, so scattering workers or flattening a mound is not a dependable solution. Check plants, soil and equipment before moving them from an infested area. Follow local movement requirements and product labels, and reassess activity after recommended treatment instead of assuming that a collapsed mound means the colony is gone.
researchNotes: Hybrid retained as hybrid concept, not separate species. Museum diagnostic lineage and multi-institution imported-fire-ant extension management lineage are independent. No hybrid identity inferred from color or medical treatment advice.

proposedDescription: Red-masked parakeet is a green, long-tailed parrot native to Ecuador and Peru. Aratinga erythrogenys is an older scientific name; current references generally use Psittacara erythrogenys. Birds from the pet trade have formed free-living populations outside their native range, including California and Hawaii. Their loud calls and social flocks make them conspicuous in urban landscapes. An introduced flock can be worth documenting without assuming that every individual is a recent escape or that every population has the same ecological effects.
identification: Adults have a broad red facial mask, bare pale skin around the eye and a long pointed tail. Red also occurs at the bend of the wing and on the underwing, best seen in flight. Juveniles may show little or no red on the head. Mitred parakeets are similar, but usually have less extensive red below and behind the eye. Photograph the face and wing pattern when possible. A distant green silhouette or a single loud call is rarely enough to separate these parrots confidently.
actions: Watch from a distance and record flock size, location and evidence of nesting without approaching a nest cavity. Submit clear observations to a local bird-monitoring program so changing populations can be tracked. Keep pet parrots securely housed and arrange a responsible new home if one can no longer be kept; release adds animals to existing flocks or starts new ones. If a bird appears injured or unusually tame, contact a qualified rescue or wildlife service rather than attempting to catch a healthy flying flock.
researchNotes: Cornell recognition and independent Puerto Rican introduced-bird research distinguish the pet-trade introduction from a claim of universal harm. Psittacara is the modern combination; response is observation and avoiding release, not capture or a control prescription. proposedDescription: Red-rim melania, often sold as Malaysian trumpet snail, is a warm-water snail associated with the aquarium trade. Its name appears as both Melanoides tuberculata and Melanoides tuberculatus in references. Native populations occur across parts of Africa and Asia; introduced populations occupy springs, streams and other suitable waters in the United States. The snails graze on fine organic material and algae and may become very abundant. A quiet aquarium population can be a source of introductions if snails, plants or bottom material are released outdoors.
identification: The shell is long and narrowly conical, with numerous whorls and often rusty markings on a pale brown background. A small operculum closes the opening when the animal withdraws. Shell color and sculpture vary, and the tip may be worn. Young snails can be overlooked among gravel. Females brood developing young internally, and many populations reproduce without males, so the absence of visible egg masses does not mean reproduction has stopped. Photograph the shell opening and side profile with a scale for identification.
actions: Keep aquarium animals, plants and gravel out of natural waters, storm drains and outdoor ponds connected to waterways. Inspect plants and equipment when moving material between tanks, since small snails are easily missed. Seek a responsible aquarium rehoming or disposal option if a population becomes unwanted. For a suspected new wild occurrence, send photographs and location details to the relevant aquatic-invasive-species program. Avoid introducing predators or applying pond chemicals on your own; those actions can harm other aquatic life without reliably removing snails hidden in sediment.
researchNotes: USGS and FWGNA use overlapping historical literature; independent FWGNA field observations and life-history synthesis explicitly retained, not USFWS derivative as additional lineage. No human parasite risk or unsupported eradication method.

proposedDescription: Red-whiskered bulbul is a fruit-eating songbird native to southern Asia and introduced to places including Florida, California and Hawaii. Pycnonotus jocosus often uses gardens, orchards and other open wooded settings. In Hawaii it can damage cultivated fruit and spread seeds of invasive plants, including miconia and ivy gourd. Its significance depends strongly on location: preventing movement to another island is a different task from observing an established population on Oahu. A clear sighting record can therefore be valuable even when the bird looks familiar.
identification: Adults have a prominent black crest, a white throat and pale underparts, brownish upperparts, and red patches behind the eye and beneath the tail. The dark band across the breast varies in completeness. Young birds lack the obvious red cheek patch and have a shorter crest. The red under-tail patch alone is not sufficient because other bulbuls can also have red there. Look for the combination of crest, white throat and facial pattern, and photograph the head from the side when possible.
actions: Do not release captive bulbuls or move wild birds between islands or communities. In Hawaii, report sightings outside their established Oahu range through the state pest-reporting service or the local invasive-species committee. Record the date, exact location, number of birds and photographs, while avoiding disturbance to nests. For repeated fruit damage, consult local agricultural or wildlife staff about appropriate exclusion and management. Avoid improvised traps or poisons, which can affect other birds, and seek advice before attempting to capture or relocate any bulbul.
researchNotes: Cornell independent morphology and Hawaii agency impact/reporting. Current state profile consulted; no broad legal import/export summary transferred from potentially changing jurisdictional rules.

proposedDescription: Redbanded thrips is a small leaf-feeding insect found in tropical and subtropical regions, including Florida and Hawaii. Selenothrips rubrocinctus attacks a range of plants, with mango, avocado and ornamental trees among its hosts. Feeding can leave leaves silvery, bronze or brown, and severe infestations may cause considerable foliage damage. The common name refers most clearly to the immature stages. Seeing damaged leaves without the insects is not enough to distinguish it from other thrips or from unrelated causes of leaf discoloration.
identification: Adults are slender, dark brown to black and only about a millimeter long, with narrow fringed wings. Immatures are pale yellow with conspicuous red abdominal bands. Look beneath leaves for both stages, along with dark fecal spots. Damage may occur on leaves and sometimes fruit, where scarring can develop. A hand lens helps reveal moving insects and the red markings of young stages. Include the host name and photographs of both healthy and damaged foliage when requesting identification; tiny adult thrips usually require expert examination.
actions: Inspect leaf undersides, especially where fresh damage is developing, and check nearby host plants rather than judging the entire planting from one damaged leaf. In orchards, edge trees can be useful monitoring points. Preserve predators such as lacewings and predatory thrips by avoiding unnecessary broad insecticide use. If an infestation is increasing, ask extension for a host-specific management recommendation and whether localized treatment is justified. Recheck for live insects after treatment and distinguish old scars from new damage before deciding that another intervention is needed.
researchNotes: UF biology and Northern Territory mango field observations/management are independent. Northern Territory calendar and pesticide advice not transferred to US; monitoring/natural-enemy principles retained.

proposedDescription: Redbay ambrosia beetle is a tiny Asian beetle associated with laurel wilt, a serious disease of trees in the laurel family. Xyleborus glabratus carries the fungus into wood as it bores galleries where the beetles cultivate fungi for food. Redbay and sassafras are important affected native trees in the southeastern United States. The beetle and disease are connected but are not the same organism, and other ambrosia beetles may also occur in dying trees. Moving infested wood can carry the problem beyond its natural rate of spread.
identification: Adult females are shiny dark brown to black and roughly two to two-and-a-half millimeters long. Their wing covers end in a distinctive pointed slope with tiny teeth, features that require magnification. Affected trees can wilt quickly, retain reddish or brown leaves, and develop dark staining in the sapwood. Fine boring-dust tubes or piles suggest ambrosia beetle activity but do not identify this species by themselves. Photographs of the tree, leaves and bark signs help a forest-health specialist decide what samples are needed.
actions: Do not transport firewood, logs or suspect nursery plants from affected sites to other areas. Report unexpected wilting or clustered deaths of redbay or sassafras to extension or a state forest-health service. Follow their instructions before cutting diagnostic wood or moving material. If a tree is hazardous, coordinate safe removal with an arborist and ask how debris should be handled locally. Avoid assuming that spraying visible holes will cure an infected tree; diagnosis and a site-specific plan are essential before spending time or money on treatment.
researchNotes: UF modern beetle taxonomy and Georgia original field spread observations independent. Older Georgia assertion of sole vector not repeated; fungus name avoided pending changing generic treatment. Frass explicitly nondiagnostic.

proposedDescription: Redbelly tilapia is an African and Middle Eastern cichlid introduced to waters outside its native range for several purposes, including aquatic-plant control. Coptodon zillii appears in older literature as Tilapia zillii. In suitable warm waters it can consume substantial vegetation and change habitat used by other fishes. United States reports require care because some historical identifications may represent similar tilapias or hybrids. A fish with a reddish belly is therefore a useful lead, not a complete identification. Local fisheries staff can help establish what is actually present.
identification: The body is deep and laterally flattened, with a long dorsal fin. Breeding coloration can include a strongly red lower body, but appearance changes with age and condition. Like other cichlids, it has a divided lateral line and one nostril opening on each side of the head. Redbreast tilapia is particularly similar and has been confused with this species. Spotted tilapia typically shows a different pattern of strong square side blotches and bars. Photograph both sides, fins and the head without relying solely on bright breeding colors.
actions: Never release aquarium fish or stock a pond with tilapia without checking local fisheries requirements. Do not move a catch alive to another water body. If an unfamiliar tilapia is found outside a known population, record the location and contact the state fisheries agency for identification and handling instructions. Keep photographs and any requested specimen information linked to that exact site. Aquatic-weed control should be planned with qualified local advice rather than by introducing fish that may reproduce, spread or alter habitat beyond the intended pond.
researchNotes: The new Freyhof and colleagues West Asian revision independently supplies exact diagnostic characters. USGS supports introduced US occurrence; uncertainty about particular local impacts is handled by identifying and reporting fish without inventing an eradication protocol. proposedDescription: Red escallonia is an evergreen South American shrub often planted as a hedge. Escallonia rubra is native to Chile and neighboring Argentina and includes several variable forms. Some garden plants have escaped cultivation in temperate regions, but a maintained hedge and an independently reproducing wild population are different situations. In Hawaii, naturalization records include the large-flowered variety macrantha. The broader species name can appear on garden labels without indicating which variety or cultivated form is present, so labels are a starting point rather than a complete identification.
identification: Look for glossy, toothed leaves, resin glands on the paler undersides and clusters of pink to deep red flowers at branch tips. The petals stand close together at their bases to form a short tube, then spread outward. Young stems may be hairy and sticky, and older bark can peel. Leaf shape and hairiness vary considerably within the species. Photographs should include flowers, both leaf surfaces and young twigs. Many cultivated escallonias are hybrids, and a red-flowered hedge should not automatically be assigned to this species.
actions: Inspect ground beyond a planting for separate young shrubs, especially where garden waste has been discarded. Keep prunings and seed-bearing material within managed waste arrangements rather than leaving them on coastal banks or woodland edges. If plants appear to be escaping, record the distance from the parent hedge and whether they are rooted independently. A local herbarium can help distinguish the species, its varieties and garden hybrids. Ask local land managers about the significance of an escape before undertaking substantial removal on a slope or in established vegetation.
researchNotes: New Zealand original flora confirms the variable shrub morphology; Bishop independently confines Hawaiian naturalization to variety macrantha and distinguishes Oahu cultivation. The species profile clearly retains variety and hybrid limitations rather than borrowing a blanket impact claim. proposedDescription: Large-flowered red escallonia is a Chilean shrub grown for glossy foliage and red to pink flowers. Escallonia rubra var. macrantha is recognized as a variety in botanical accounts, although some references describe it within a broader Escallonia rubra. Bishop Museum records distinguish naturalization on Hawaii Island from cultivation on Oahu, and New Zealand records also document naturalization. These distinctions matter: a planted hedge and a wild population are different situations. Keep the variety name attached to a verified observation, rather than assuming every red-flowered escallonia belongs here.
identification: The shrub bears shiny, toothed leaves that are paler underneath, with conspicuous veins and small gland dots. Young twigs and flower structures can be glandular or sticky. Red or pink flowers occur in terminal clusters, followed by small dry capsules. The name macrantha refers to large flowers, but size alone is not a dependable field diagnosis among variable escallonias and their cultivated hybrids. Photograph a flowering branch, leaf undersides and any nursery label. A botanist may need more complete material to distinguish the variety confidently.
actions: Watch for independently rooted shrubs outside a planted hedge and note whether seedlings recur after routine garden maintenance. Keep discarded branches and fruiting material out of gullies, forest edges and unmanaged banks. For a suspected escape in Oregon or Hawaii, provide the location, photographs and nearby planting history to a local botanical or invasive-species program. Retain the variety name when it is known, because a report simply labeled escallonia loses useful information. Seek local advice before removing a large hedge or disturbing vegetation that may be stabilizing a bank.

Recognition can explicitly defer definitive variety identification without inventing a flower-size cutoff. proposedDescription: Strobilanthes reptans is a low, spreading tropical herb also known by the older name Hemigraphis reptans. It is native to Malesia and parts of the western Pacific and has been introduced elsewhere, including Hawaii and parts of the southeastern United States. In Hawaii it is a naturalized lawn weed and also occurs in disturbed moist vegetation. Its creeping habit allows a small patch to extend through rooted stems. That growth form makes it easy to overlook as ordinary groundcover until it reaches places where it is unwanted.
identification: Stems lie along the ground and often root at their nodes, although plants can also form clumps. Leaves are elongated oval to narrowly egg-shaped, with rounded teeth and a somewhat bristly surface. Small white flowers sit among conspicuous leaflike bracts. The dry fruits are narrow capsules. Leaf color alone does not reliably separate it from related ornamental plants; some specimens have purple lower surfaces. Include the shape and hairiness of leaves, rooting nodes, bracts and flowers in photographs, especially when comparing it with red ivy, Strobilanthes alternata.
actions: Inspect the edges of a patch and check whether creeping stems have rooted beyond the original planting or lawn area. Avoid scattering living fragments with dumped clippings or soil moved to another site. If you need to remove plants from a garden, gather the rooted sections carefully and monitor the same area for surviving growth rather than judging success from removed foliage alone. In a natural area, confirm the identity with a local botanist before disturbing surrounding plants. Record flowering and fruiting material because those features make identification more reliable.
researchNotes: Fresh independent NParks landscape guidance recommends manual removal by roots, complementing Hawaiian flora documentation of node-rooting stems. This supports modest garden removal and follow-up, not a demonstrated US landscape eradication protocol.

proposedDescription: Thickhead is an African annual herb that has become a widespread weed in tropical regions. Crassocephalum crepidioides grows on disturbed slopes, roadsides and other open sites, including locations in Hawaii. Its reddish flower tips and later fluffy seed heads can be conspicuous above surrounding vegetation. The plant belongs to the daisy family, but its heads lack the broad outer petals of a typical garden daisy. A small newly disturbed patch can look different over a short period as green plants flower and then release their light fruits.
identification: The upright stems carry alternate, soft leaves with irregular teeth; lower leaves may also have lobes near the base. Several narrow cylindrical heads are grouped near the stem tips. Their tiny florets are reddish brown to orange, surrounded by a row of similarly sized green bracts and a few smaller bracts below. Mature fruits carry fine white hairs. Other small-headed daisies, including Emilia and Erechtites, can look similar at a distance. Photograph leaf bases, a side view of a flower head and the mature fluffy fruiting head.
actions: In gardens and nursery beds, identify the plant while it is small and remove unwanted seedlings before flower heads develop. UF guidance for ornamental production emphasizes early hand weeding and preventing seed production. Contain mature heads before carrying plants away, and inspect newly purchased plants for seedlings before distributing them through a nursery. Keep soil and plant waste out of nearby natural areas. At a restoration site, record the extent and ask the land manager how thickhead fits their weed priorities; check disturbed ground again for new seedlings.
researchNotes: New full UF nursery account directly addresses the missing US management: handweed small plants, prevent flowering and inspect incoming liners. Independent Bishop vouchers support Hawaiian occurrence. Nursery competition is not generalized into all-habitat harm. proposedDescription: Redlegged ham beetle is a small metallic beetle associated with dried animal products and other stored foods rich in protein or fat. Necrobia rufipes occurs widely around the world and can infest cured meats, dried fish, pet food, copra and related products. It also scavenges and preys on other insects, so finding adults does not necessarily identify the original source of an infestation. In a storehouse or pantry, the useful question is which product or hidden residue is supporting its life cycle.
identification: Adults are shiny blue-green with orange-red legs and reddish antennae ending in a dark club. They are only a few millimeters long and can fly. The thorax is narrower than the wing covers, and the body bears noticeable bristles under magnification. Redshouldered ham beetles differ in having red on the thorax and bases of the wing covers, while the blue bone beetle has dark legs. Larvae look quite different from the metallic adults and may feed within food or occupy nearby protected spaces.
actions: Isolate suspect packages and inspect nearby dried foods, pet food and accumulated residues. Clean shelves, cracks and crevices thoroughly, since beetles and pupal chambers can remain away from the obvious food source. Keep sound products in well-sealed containers and check incoming stock. Save a specimen or clear photograph for extension or a pest professional so similar beetles are not confused. For commercial food handling, follow the facility's food-safety and pest-management procedures. Do not spray food or use improvised fumigation; removing the source and hidden residues is central to lasting control.
researchNotes: UF extension management and Leavengood original Florida taxonomic key are distinct research lineages despite shared host institution. No ruficollis red-head claim copied from extension's questionable comparison; key used for thorax/elytral distinction.

claims: Food associations, adults, larvae, sanitation and hidden pupation sites.

proposedDescription: Garden evening-primrose is a tall, yellow-flowered plant widely grown and escaped from cultivation. Oenothera glazioviana probably arose in Europe from hybridization between North American evening-primroses, rather than representing a straightforward wild European species. It occurs in gardens, roadsides and disturbed fields in the United States, including New England. Its large flowers open toward evening, while the plant may spend an earlier season as a basal rosette. A flowering roadside plant can therefore look very different from the low rosette that preceded it.
identification: Look for four large yellow petals, reddish or red-striped sepals, and a long floral tube. The stigma extends above the anthers. Leaves are elongated and may appear crinkled, while stems bear a mixture of short hairs and longer hairs, often arising from reddish swollen bases. Upright capsules remain after the flowers fade. Native and introduced evening-primroses overlap in appearance, so flower size, bud tips, stem hairs and mature fruit are more useful together than yellow petals alone.
actions: Keep photographs of both the rosette and flowering stage when tracking an uncertain plant. If a garden specimen is producing unwanted offspring, remove developing seed capsules before they open and check nearby bare ground in later seasons. Do not assume all tall yellow evening-primroses nearby are the same taxon. In a meadow or restoration area, confirm identity before removing plants, particularly where native evening-primroses occur. A herbarium or extension botanist can use flowering and fruiting material to help resolve a difficult identification.
researchNotes:
FNA details and Kew taxonomy independently support a cultivated hybrid-origin entity and introduced populations. No exact parentage is asserted because treatments differ; species-specific harm/control is not needed for careful identification and preventing unwanted garden seed. proposedDescription: Redshouldered ham beetle is a small scavenging and predatory beetle associated with dry animal material. Necrobia ruficollis occurs on dried fish and other preserved animal products as well as animal remains. It feeds both on decaying material and on other insects found there. A beetle encountered outdoors on carrion has a different significance from repeated discoveries in a food-storage room. Finding the material supporting the beetles is more useful than treating every metallic beetle as a pantry pest.
identification: Adults are mostly metallic blue, with reddish-brown legs, the thorax behind the head and the basal portion of the wing covers. They are typically around six millimeters long. The antennae and abdomen are dark. Redlegged ham beetle has reddish legs but lacks the broad red thorax and wing-base pattern, while blue bone beetle is more uniformly metallic with dark legs. Clear dorsal and side photographs help show these distinctions. Larvae are less easily recognized, so an adult specimen is particularly useful for confirmation.
actions: If beetles are found around stored products, isolate suspect material and seek identification before choosing treatment. Check dried animal products and nearby residues, keeping a record of where adults and larvae occur. Clean accessible storage surfaces and contain infested material so insects are not carried to another room or building. For food businesses, museums or collections, involve the appropriate pest-management or conservation professional. An outdoor observation can simply be documented without removing the surrounding habitat; the species also participates in decomposition and predation rather than only damaging stored goods.
researchNotes: An independent Brazilian university account and Chinese original development paper corroborate the red pronotum/elytral-base pattern and carrion association. Practical storage inspection is a bounded precaution; no borrowed rufipes control efficacy or larval diagnosis is added. proposedDescription: Redstem filaree is a low-growing introduced herb common in open, disturbed places across much of the United States. Erodium cicutarium often grows as a winter annual in California, producing a leafy rosette before flowering and setting its distinctive long-beaked fruits. It occurs in pastures, roadsides, gardens and crop fields, and its importance varies with the site. In some natural communities it competes with native annual plants. In a working landscape, the response should account for both the existing vegetation and how readily seed can arrive again.
identification: The finely divided, hairy leaves give the rosette a feathery appearance. Small pink to purplish flowers have five petals. Fruits form a long pointed beak, which separates into seed-bearing units with twisting awns as they dry. Related filarees are easy to confuse: redstem filaree has more deeply divided leaves than broadleaf filaree. Stem redness alone is unreliable. Photograph a complete leaf and a mature fruit along with the flowers; seedlings also have characteristic lobed seed leaves that differ from their later foliage.
actions: Work before mature fruits disperse where removal is warranted, and avoid carrying awned seeds on tools, footwear or animals into uninfested areas. Small targeted removals may be practical in a garden or carefully managed restoration plot, but hand removal across extensive infestations is labor-intensive. Ask local weed or restoration staff how to protect native annuals while reducing filaree. Recheck after the next germination period and maintain appropriate ground cover. Do not assume a grass-selective treatment will control this broadleaf plant.
researchNotes: UC IPM morphology, USFS ecology and independent Steers restoration trial support scoped guidance. UC Irvine broad statement that hand-weeding is impractical not treated as biological impossibility; trial documents targeted hand removal.

proposedDescription: Redtop is a perennial grass introduced for pasture, erosion control and turf. Agrostis gigantea can persist along wet field edges, ditches and disturbed shores, where underground stems help it form a dense cover. Its reddish flowering heads give the species its common name, although color varies with conditions. A useful erosion-control planting can become unwanted where it spreads into a native wet meadow. Management therefore depends on the purpose of the site and the plants that would replace it, rather than on the grass's name alone.
identification: Flowering stems carry an open, branching panicle of many tiny spikelets, each containing one floret. Leaves are flat and relatively narrow, with a membranous ligule where blade and sheath meet. Underground rhizomes are important identification clues. Other bentgrasses can look very similar, especially before flowering; a reddish panicle is not sufficient to separate them. A grass specialist may need the ligule, a complete flowering head and the base of the plant. Photograph those structures before mowing or collecting a sample.
actions: Check seed mixtures before using them near wetlands or native-plant restoration sites, since redtop may be deliberately included for rapid cover. If it is spreading beyond a managed area, map the patch and consult the land manager before disturbing a bank or wet soil. Its rhizomes mean that cutting a few stems does not remove the whole plant. USDA guidance notes that repeated close mowing can reduce persistence, but that approach is not appropriate for every wetland or mixed meadow. Plan replacement vegetation and follow-up alongside any removal.
researchNotes: USDA NRCS management and regional flora independent. Mowing effect scoped to NRCS agronomic observation, not presented as universal wetland eradication; no herbicide method invented.

claims: Rhizomes, reddish panicles, erosion/pasture use and response to frequent close mowing.

proposedDescription: Reed manna grass is a tall Eurasian wetland grass that can form dense stands along ditches, ponds and slow-moving water. Glyceria maxima spreads through rhizomes and can crowd out other wetland vegetation. Introduced populations occur in parts of the northern United States, including Wisconsin and New England. The ornamental variegated form belongs to the same species and should not be assumed incapable of spreading. Early recognition is valuable because a small rooted patch is a more manageable problem than a continuous stand along a watercourse.
identification: Stems are upright and can grow well above a person's waist. Broad, flat leaves have a prominent midrib and rough edges. The flowering head is a large branching panicle with many several-flowered spikelets and no conspicuous long awns. A membranous ligule sits where each leaf blade joins its sheath. Native American manna grass can look similar, so compare mature spikelets and the roughness and posture of panicle branches rather than relying on height. Photograph a whole flowering stem and close views of these structures.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the state invasive-plant program and avoid transporting rooted pieces, muddy equipment or ornamental divisions. Wetland work may require authorization, so obtain site-specific advice before digging, covering or treating plants near water. Small patches can sometimes be smothered, while established stands usually need repeated management over several growing seasons. Do not use grazing as an improvised control method. Clean equipment after working in the patch, monitor downstream or adjacent areas, and plan recovery of appropriate native vegetation as the infestation declines.
researchNotes: Wisconsin control assessment and Flora Novae Angliae independent. No chemical recipes or livestock-toxicity details; grazing discouraged per Wisconsin. Similarity to native G. grandis retained, not identified by height alone.

claims: Wetland impacts, rhizomes, native lookalike and management.
Small-clone tarping, repeated treatment, grazing caution and wetland permissions.
Eurasian origin, New England records and spikelet/leaf morphology.

proposedDescription: Regal lily is a Chinese bulbous perennial grown for large, fragrant trumpet-shaped flowers. Lilium regale comes from rocky slopes and river valleys in Sichuan and has long been cultivated well beyond that native range. A flowering clump in an old garden may persist after the surrounding planting has disappeared. Persistence at a former homesite should be distinguished from seedlings spreading into nearby vegetation. The common names royal lily and trumpet lily are shared loosely in horticulture, so the scientific identity is worth checking before interpreting an apparent escape.
identification: The upright stem carries many narrow leaves distributed along its length. Large white flowers open into long funnels with yellow toward the throat; cultivated descriptions may also show pink or purple coloring on the outer surfaces. The six tepals surround conspicuous stamens and a long central style. Related trumpet lilies and garden hybrids can be similar, so leaf width, flower orientation and the exterior of the trumpet are useful photographs. A basal clump of leaves without flowers is much harder to identify confidently.
actions: Retain labels for planted bulbs and photograph flowers before cutting stems or moving a clump. If lilies appear outside a known planting, record their distance from it and whether small independent plants recur over several years. Avoid dumping unwanted bulbs, seed capsules or garden soil into natural areas. In an established bed, remove unwanted seed capsules before they mature if you want to limit self-sowing. Ask a local botanist to confirm an unfamiliar wild lily before digging, since native lilies and cultivated hybrids can occur nearby.
researchNotes:
Independent Flora of China and NC State horticultural account support the exact lily and recognition. No US naturalized population or invasive impact is asserted; cultivation and apparent escape observations can be separated without transferring traits from other trumpet lilies.

proposedDescription: Rotylenchulus parvus is a microscopic plant-parasitic nematode associated with roots and their surrounding soil. It was first described from sugarcane soil in Mauritius and has been reported from several crops, including cotton, corn and sweet potato. In the United States, records include southern states and California's Imperial Valley. It belongs to the reniform nematode group, but should not be assumed to have the same crop effects or management responses as the better-known Rotylenchulus reniformis. The exact species and crop matter when interpreting a laboratory result.
identification: Infective young adult females are slender and wormlike. After entering a root with the front of the body, a female remains partly outside and swells as she feeds. Other stages occur in soil close to roots. These organisms are too small for reliable identification with ordinary garden photographs. Poor growth, root injury or uneven crop performance can have many causes, and visible symptoms cannot name the nematode. A laboratory uses extracted specimens, microscopic characters and molecular evidence. Research has found cryptic diversity within material called R. parvus, so a familiar name does not guarantee identical biology in every population.
actions: If a crop is declining, contact an extension or diagnostic laboratory before collecting samples. Follow its instructions for taking representative roots and soil, labeling the host and location, and keeping material in suitable condition. Avoid moving soil from a suspect field on equipment or planting stock. Ask the adviser to interpret nematode numbers alongside crop symptoms and other possible stresses. Do not choose a rotation, resistant variety or nematicide on the basis of a recommendation written for R. reniformis; species-specific host information is essential.
researchNotes: Independent Tanzanian morphology and DNA work corroborates a parvus-like sugarcane population but reveals cryptic divergence from South African material. This strengthens the need for laboratory interpretation; it does not identify a US lineage or justify reniformis management transfer. proposedDescription: Rescuegrass is a South American grass grown as forage and also encountered as a weed in disturbed ground and crops. Bromus catharticus can behave as an annual, biennial or short-lived perennial depending on climate and growing conditions. Its presence in a pasture may reflect deliberate planting, while seedlings in a vegetable field or restoration area may be unwanted. The same species therefore needs different decisions in different settings. Its broad, flattened seed heads are useful for recognizing it among the many brome grasses found in open landscapes.
identification: Flowering stems carry a loose, branching head with large, flattened spikelets. Each spikelet contains several overlapping florets, giving it a broad, layered appearance. The florets have sharply keeled backs and usually very short awns or nearly none. This contrasts with the long, conspicuous awns of ripgut and some other bromes. Leaves are flat, and the sheaths can be hairy. Photograph a complete head, individual spikelets and the leaf-sheath junction; a green tuft without flowers is difficult to identify accurately.
actions: Check whether a patch is part of an intended forage planting before treating it as a weed. Where plants are unwanted, prevent mature seed heads from being carried in cut vegetation or on equipment to another site. In a crop field, request advice matched to the crop and growth stage rather than borrowing a treatment from a different brome species. Record whether plants return from established bases or as new seedlings after cutting. That distinction helps an adviser plan follow-up and decide whether reducing seed production alone will be sufficient.
researchNotes: NZ flora supplies diagnostic spikelets and UC independently lists rescuegrass among cucurbit weeds. The crop list establishes context, not measured impact or an efficacy trial. Advice is limited to confirming the grass and preventing unwanted seed movement. proposedDescription: Reticulated barnacle is a warm-water barnacle native to the Indo-Pacific and spread widely by shipping. Amphibalanus reticulatus attaches to hard surfaces such as hulls, pilings, rocks and shellfish. It has been recorded in the Gulf of Mexico and Hawaii, where its abundance and shore position vary among sites. The adults remain fixed in place, but boats can carry whole fouling communities between harbors. Its main practical significance is therefore connected to movement and maintenance of vessels and equipment as well as to local coastal observations.
identification: The shell is generally conical or somewhat cylindrical, with a toothed opening at the top. Pale shell plates bear dark longitudinal stripes crossed by finer transverse markings, producing the netlike pattern behind the common name. Closely related barnacles can look very similar, and worn or crowded shells may obscure the pattern. Specialists examine the movable plates closing the opening and other internal shell features. Photographs of an intact shell from above and the side help, but a colorful striped barnacle is not automatically this species.
actions: Inspect hulls, submerged equipment and niche areas during routine maintenance, especially before moving between ports. Arrange cleaning through facilities that can contain and dispose of removed fouling material appropriately. Avoid scraping suspect growth into a new harbor or transferring encrusted gear to another coastal site. Report unusual fouling with photographs, the vessel or equipment history and the precise location to the relevant marine biosecurity program. Do not chip barnacles from living shellfish or sensitive habitat merely to obtain a specimen; ask whether photographs or a professionally collected sample are needed.
researchNotes: NEMESIS taxonomy/US occurrence and original Brazilian tugboat field study support different claims; transport claim not double-counted as independent corroboration. Field identification explicitly uncertain; cleaning guidance is conservative prevention inference from documented hull transport.

proposedDescription: Persian clover is a cool-season annual legume used as a cover crop and forage. Trifolium resupinatum is native from the Mediterranean region into western Asia and has been introduced widely, including much of the United States. It can provide useful cover and flowers for insects in managed systems, but plants that set seed may become weeds in a following crop. A patch may therefore be intentional, a volunteer from an earlier planting, or an escape. Its agricultural use should not be confused with a claim that it belongs in every natural area.
identification: Plants have three leaflets, often broadest toward the tip, and small rounded heads of pink to purplish flowers on stalks. Individual flowers are turned into an unusual orientation reflected by the name resupinatum. The calyx enlarges around the developing fruit, producing a swollen, papery-looking structure. Several other clovers have pink flowers or inflated fruiting heads, so inspect mature heads as well as leaves. A photograph taken only during early vegetative growth usually cannot establish the species with confidence.
actions: If growing Persian clover as a cover crop, plan termination before unwanted seed production and select a method appropriate to the field and following crop. California cover-crop guidance includes mowing and other agricultural termination options, but timing and conditions determine success. Watch field margins and subsequent crops for volunteers, and avoid moving mature seed-bearing material into nearby restoration sites. If a clover appears where it was not planted, document flowering and fruiting heads before deciding on removal. Consult local crop advisers when it interferes with production rather than assuming all clovers respond identically.
researchNotes:
Kew native range, Flora Pakistan diagnosis and California cover-crop guidance independent. No blanket invasive-harm claim or invented grazing/livestock advice. Inflated calyx not treated as unique to this species.

proposedDescription: Rabbit hemorrhagic disease is caused by closely related lagoviruses, including RHDV2, which affects domestic rabbits and wild rabbits and hares. RHDV2 has spread through many parts of the United States since its detection in wild populations in 2020. It is not known to infect people, but people can carry contaminated material between rabbit populations on footwear, clothing or equipment. The disease name covers more than one viral type, so a laboratory result should specify which virus was identified rather than treating every historical outbreak as RHDV2.
identification: The virus cannot be identified by sight. Sudden death may be the first sign, sometimes with a blood-stained nose. Sick rabbits can also become lethargic, stop eating or show breathing or coordination problems. These signs are not unique to rabbit hemorrhagic disease, and absence of visible bleeding does not rule it out. Several dead wild rabbits in one area warrant prompt reporting. Photograph animals only from a distance and record the location; diagnostic testing should be arranged by animal-health or wildlife professionals.
actions: If a domestic rabbit becomes ill or dies suddenly, contact a veterinarian promptly and keep other rabbits separate while following professional instructions. Do not move rabbits, cages or bedding to another property. Ask the veterinarian about vaccination and appropriate cleaning and disinfection for your circumstances. Do not release domestic rabbits or bring wild rabbits into a household group. Leave wild carcasses undisturbed and report unusual mortality to wildlife officials. Obtain disposal instructions before handling a dead rabbit, since moving contaminated material can spread the virus.

proposedDescription: Rhesus macaque is an Asian monkey with an introduced free-ranging population around Silver Springs in Florida. Macaca mulatta lives in social groups and uses both trees and the ground. Its adaptability and history of being fed by people can bring monkeys close to visitors, boats and developed areas. A macaque that approaches confidently is still a wild animal. Feeding changes that relationship and can encourage aggressive behavior, so keeping distance is the most useful way to protect both people and the monkeys.
identification: Adults have grizzled brown to gray-brown fur, a paler underside and a largely bare pinkish to red face. The tail is clearly present but shorter than the head-and-body length, unlike the very long tail of some other introduced monkeys. Males are generally larger than females. Young animals may cling to an adult or travel close to the group. Photograph from a distance and include the face, body and tail if reporting an unfamiliar monkey. Location and group size also help wildlife staff distinguish an established group from an escaped animal.
actions: Never offer food, leave food accessible or approach a macaque for a close photograph. Secure food and trash, keep pets away and give a group room to pass. If monkeys repeatedly approach a recreation area or residence, contact park staff or the appropriate wildlife agency rather than trying to catch or relocate them. Do not attempt to retrieve an item by cornering an animal. After a bite, scratch, or contact of macaque fluid with broken skin, eyes, nose or mouth, begin first aid immediately and seek medical care, explaining that a macaque was involved. CDC advises washing exposed skin with soap for 15 minutes or rinsing exposed eyes and other mucous membranes with water or sterile saline for 15 minutes.
researchNotes:
UF Florida field-management research and independent ADW natural-history reference. Medical action limited to prompt care after bite/scratch as supported by UF; no unverified transmission rates or panic claims.

proposedDescription: Rhodes grass is an African perennial grass widely planted for grazing and hay in warm regions, including parts of the United States. Chloris gayana can form leafy tufts and spreading runners, with substantial variation among cultivars. It tolerates conditions that make it useful in agriculture, but it can also spread beyond a planted area and crowd other vegetation. A productive pasture and an unwanted patch at the edge of native habitat call for different decisions. Its history as a forage crop does not remove the need to watch where it grows.
identification: The flowering head has several slender, fingerlike branches arranged near the top of the stem, sometimes in more than one tier. Small spikelets line those branches, which darken as they mature. Leaves are long and narrow, and running stems can root to form additional shoots. Awn length and overall coarseness vary among cultivated types, so one cultivar should not define the whole species. Other Chloris grasses also have fingerlike heads. Photograph the head, individual spikelets and basal runners for a dependable identification.
actions: Inspect boundaries of forage plantings and avoid carrying mature seed heads or rooted runners into nearby natural vegetation. Clean mowing and earthmoving equipment before it leaves an infested area. Where a small unwanted patch is confirmed, seek local advice on removing the rooted plant and checking for regrowth; larger stands need a plan that also restores suitable cover. Repeated mowing can limit standing growth but should not be assumed to eliminate all rooted plants. Match pasture management to the cultivar and location, and avoid copying overseas chemical recommendations.
researchNotes: SANBI original flora, Hawaii forage guidance and Queensland management independent; Hawaii/Tropical Forages shared agronomic sources not counted twice. US impact not generalized from Queensland. No cultivar nematode resistance transferred to whole species.

proposedDescription: Rhododendron whitefly is a small sap-feeding insect found on rhododendrons in North America and Europe. Massilieurodes chittendeni is still called Dialeurodes chittendeni in many gardening references. Its geographic origin remains uncertain, with sources differing over an Asian or North American origin. The practical concern in a garden is the condition of the host plant and the extent of feeding, rather than assuming that every occurrence represents a newly introduced pest. Smooth-leaved rhododendrons and their hybrids can be especially attractive hosts.
identification: Adults are tiny pale, winged insects that rest beneath leaves and may fly briefly when a shrub is disturbed. The oval, flattened immature stages remain attached to leaf undersides after settling. Feeding may produce yellowing, curling and mottling. Sugary honeydew can support black sooty mold, but mold alone does not identify the whitefly because other sap feeders produce it too. Examine the leaf undersides for several life stages and photograph the host. A diagnostic sample should contain the attached immature insects as well as any adults.
actions: Inspect new rhododendrons before adding them to an established collection, and monitor susceptible plants for overwintering immature stages. Keep a suspect potted plant apart while obtaining identification. If the shrub is otherwise healthy, assess whether damage is increasing before choosing treatment. Ask extension for advice appropriate to the plant, season and local whitefly species, since a product aimed at flying adults may miss attached stages beneath leaves. Avoid moving infested nursery plants between properties, and recheck fresh growth and live insects rather than judging success from old sooty deposits alone.
researchNotes: UMass provides exact rhododendron-whitefly recognition under Dialeurodes; the independently authored Norwegian assessment documents its own introduction context and low assessed ecological impact. Origin disagreement is left explicit instead of asserting a foreign origin throughout North America. proposedDescription: Chrysomyxa rhododendri is a rust fungus associated with rhododendrons and spruce, especially Norway spruce in European mountain forests. It can cause conspicuous needle discoloration and premature needle loss. Similar rusts occur on North American rhododendrons and spruces, but they are not automatically this species. Older names in the Chrysomyxa ledi complex have been applied differently, and modern North American guidance distinguishes other fungi, including C. reticulata and C. piperiana. A rusty leaf therefore needs a careful diagnosis before it is interpreted as an introduced European rust.
identification: On affected rhododendrons, rust infections produce yellow to orange spore pustules, often on leaf undersides. In the spruce phase, infected current-year needles develop yellowed areas and fungal fruiting structures, and needles may be shed prematurely. These are useful signs of a rust disease, not reliable species-level characters. Different hosts, spore stages and seasons can change the appearance. Photograph both sides of leaves or needles, identify the host plant as closely as possible, and note which year's foliage is affected.
actions: Contact a plant-diagnostic service before treating a suspected new occurrence or moving affected nursery stock. Keep samples linked to the exact host and location, and follow the laboratory's instructions for packaging fresh material. Avoid using a management program for a different rhododendron rust without confirmation. Removing nearby spruce or rhododendrons on the basis of orange spots alone can destroy healthy plants without addressing the actual problem. For a cultivated collection, monitor new foliage and document whether symptoms recur while awaiting a species-specific diagnosis.
researchNotes: The 2025 European microscopy study independently documents spruce infection, while NRCan distinguishes North American reticulata from the European entity. The profile can explain host alternation and specialist diagnosis without converting North American lookalikes into confirmed introduced rhododendri. proposedDescription: Ribbed paspalum is a perennial South American grass that has been introduced to several warm regions, including parts of the United States. Paspalum malacophyllum is recorded as naturalized on Maui, while some Hawaiian specimens from other islands represent cultivation. That distinction matters when interpreting a map or an old collection label. The plant can form substantial clumps in disturbed vegetation, but a record from an agricultural trial does not show that it escaped or caused ecological damage at that site.
identification: Flowering stems carry many short, one-sided branches arranged along a central axis, rather than just the two or three branches seen in some familiar paspalums. Small spikelets occur in pairs along these branches. The leaves are comparatively broad for a grass, and their surfaces may be hairy or nearly smooth. Short, scaly rhizomes occur at the base. Because several Paspalum species share this general form, identification needs a mature flowering head, close views of spikelets and the leaf-sheath junction. Photograph the whole clump as well as those details.
actions: If you encounter an unfamiliar large paspalum outside cultivation, record its location, extent and proximity to planted grass. Keep seed-bearing cuttings and soil from the patch from being moved into another field or natural area. Ask a local grass specialist or herbarium to confirm the name before choosing treatment, especially where native paspalums occur. In Hawaii, include the island and whether the plants are growing independently of a garden or trial plot. Revisit a suspected escape to see whether the patch persists and new plants appear nearby.
researchNotes: GrassBase gives exact broad blades, many racemes and paired spikelets; independent Bishop vouchers establish island-specific occurrence. Limited Hawaiian naturalization is not generalized into nationwide impact, and no untested control efficacy is asserted.

proposedDescription: Asian rice is a major food crop, and Oryza sativa includes both cultivated varieties and troublesome weedy forms. Weedy rice grows among planted rice, competes with the crop and can shed seed before harvest. The name red rice refers to reddish bran in some forms, but not every weedy type has the same hull or grain color. The species as a whole should not be treated as an invasive weed: the practical problem is an unwanted, reproducing rice population in a particular field or agricultural setting.
identification: Weedy plants can differ from the planted variety in height, flowering time, seed color or the presence of awns, but those characters vary among populations. Easy shattering of mature seed is an especially important clue. Plants may be difficult to distinguish from the crop before flowering, and a single off-type plant is not enough to explain the origin of an infestation. Record the planted variety, the location of suspect patches and photographs through flowering and maturity. An experienced rice adviser can help separate volunteers, mixed seed and established weedy rice.
actions: Use certified planting seed and clean equipment to reduce movement between fields. In California, extension recommends removing identifiable weedy plants before their seed disperses. Handle mature heads carefully so removal does not scatter the seed back into the field. Consult a local rice adviser about follow-up, crop rotation and any herbicide-resistant production system; options differ by region and variety. Continue monitoring over later seasons because dormant seed can survive in the soil. Avoid assuming that a herbicide safe for cultivated rice will selectively remove weedy plants of the same species.
researchNotes: Kew distinguishes the cultivated species and UC documents weedy rice within that species. Crop and unwanted weedy populations are expressly separated; seed hygiene is supported without labeling every planted rice field invasive. proposedDescription: Smilo grass is a perennial bunchgrass from the Mediterranean region and nearby areas, introduced to California and other parts of the United States. Piptatherum miliaceum also appears as Stipa miliacea in California references and as Oloptum miliaceum in Kew's current treatment. It grows along roadsides, ditches and disturbed ground and can spread into riparian areas and canyons. Its tall, loose flowering heads may resemble an ornamental grass, so plants at the edge of a garden can go unnoticed until several clumps have developed.
identification: The plant forms a persistent tuft of upright stems with relatively stiff, narrow leaves. A large, airy, branching panicle carries numerous small spikelets, each with a single fertile floret. It differs from many bromes whose larger spikelets contain several florets and often long conspicuous awns. The leaf-sheath junction has a membranous ligule. Take photographs of the whole flowering head, individual spikelets and the base of the clump. The several scientific names are synonyms used in different treatments, not evidence that separate weeds are present.
actions: Locate small patches before they produce mature seed and seek local advice on removing the complete rooted clump with minimal disturbance. Avoid tilling through established plants, since fragmented roots and disturbed soil can complicate control. Keep seed-bearing material and contaminated soil from being moved along roads or waterways. After removal, restore appropriate vegetation and check for seedlings or surviving growth. Published control information is limited, so do not assume that grazing or burning will eliminate the grass. Larger infestations need a site-specific plan that protects nearby native plants and erosion-sensitive ground.

proposedDescription: Tetraneura fusiformis is a name used in a taxonomically difficult group of aphids associated with elm galls and grass roots. Recent research treats it tentatively as a synonym of Tetraneura akinire, while older literature often linked it with T. nigriabdominalis. Those changing names can make historical host and distribution records hard to compare. The group includes aphids living out of sight on roots as well as gall-forming stages on particular elms. A record called rice root aphid should not automatically be assigned to this exact name.
identification: Root-feeding members of the revised group are small, pale greenish or brownish-white aphids. In the documented Japanese life cycle, gall-forming stages occur on Ulmus davidiana var. japonica, with stalked, spindle-shaped galls on the upper leaf surface. Other Tetraneura species make similar pouches, and gall shape alone is insufficient. Specialists examine tiny structures such as the claws of first-stage root nymphs and may use genetic evidence. Photograph the host, gall or root colony, but expect a specimen to be necessary for a confident determination.
actions: For a suspected crop problem, consult an extension diagnostic service and provide both affected roots and the host identity using its collection instructions. Do not select a treatment from an old aphid name without checking which species that source meant. Avoid moving infested rooted plants or attached soil to another site while identification is pending. An isolated elm gall does not justify removing the tree. Record whether root colonies, galls or winged aphids were actually observed so a specialist can connect the evidence to the appropriate life stage.
researchNotes:
Research gap retained: The 2022 revision only tentatively assigns fusiformis to akinire type B. A later Australian field paper explicitly retains the nomenclatural confusion and cites that tentative conclusion. The latter is new field context, not a type-based resolution of the catalog organism. The additional source check leaves the specific identity or evidence question unresolved. Which of the 2022 revision's cryptic types is represented by the legacy fusiformis record and its underlying specimens? Next action: Obtain the specimen or voucher basis for the catalog record and compare it with the 2022 revision and any subsequent type-based synonym reconciliation; a catalog synonym alone is insufficient. Fresh access is recorded per source; inherited evidence access describes the earlier review and is not a claim that every full text was reread. Practical documentation and containment guidance is bounded editorial synthesis, not a demonstrated eradication result. Remaining scientific questions: Can type-associated material and the catalog records be connected to the revised akinire concept?

proposedDescription: Rice paper plant is a large-leaved East Asian shrub grown for a bold tropical appearance. Tetrapanax papyrifer is associated with Taiwan and has long been cultivated in China. The name refers to paperlike sheets made from its stem pith; it is not the rice crop. In gardens, its most important spreading behavior is the production of new shoots from underground growth. A single ornamental stem can therefore become a wider colony even where cold weather kills the aboveground foliage back.
identification: Large, deeply lobed leaves sit on long stalks and are often concentrated toward the ends of upright stems. The leaf undersides and young parts can carry dense pale brown to rusty hairs. Branched clusters of small cream to yellow-white flowers appear above the foliage, followed by small dark fruits. Fatsia and other large-leaved ornamentals can look similar from a distance. Photograph the leaf underside, attachment of the stalk and flowering structure rather than relying only on leaf size. Numerous nearby shoots may be connected underground.
actions: Choose a planting position where expanding shoots can be monitored and removed without damaging neighboring plants or structures. If it spreads beyond the intended bed, follow the underground connection where practical and remove unwanted rooted growth; cutting off the visible shoot alone may leave the source in place. Check again during the growing season. Keep discarded roots and divisions out of unmanaged land, and do not share plants without explaining their spreading habit. If a colony occurs away from gardens, ask a local botanist to confirm it and assess its significance before larger removal work.

proposedDescription: Rice flatsedge is a warm-season annual sedge associated with moist disturbed ground and crop fields. Cyperus iria is native to Old World tropical and subtropical regions and is established in parts of the United States. It can grow quickly and produce abundant seed, sometimes allowing more than one generation in a favorable season. In rice and other crops, small plants may be overlooked until their branched flower heads rise above the leaves. It is a seed-producing annual, so management differs from that of perennial nutsedges with persistent underground tubers.
identification: Stems are triangular in cross-section, and the narrow leaves are folded into a shallow V. Several long leaflike bracts extend beyond a branching flower head. The flattened spikelets become yellowish to golden brown and contain rows of small scales. Roots are fibrous. Other small flatsedges can look similar, including species with compact heads or different scale patterns, so a photograph of the complete head and close views of spikelets are useful. Do not identify it only from a triangular stem; many sedges share that feature.
actions: Remove small unwanted plants before flowering and seed production where hand weeding is practical, and check again for later seedlings. Keep seed-bearing soil and vegetation from being moved between beds or fields. In crops, coordinate timing with a local adviser because water management and control options depend on the crop and production system. Avoid assuming a treatment for yellow or purple nutsedge fits this annual species. For a wetland occurrence, confirm the identification before disturbing native sedges and follow local guidance on work near water.

proposedDescription: Ripgut brome is an introduced cool-season annual grass common in many western United States landscapes. Bromus diandrus grows in disturbed ground, fields and grasslands, where it can compete with other vegetation and contribute dry fuel after it matures. Its sharp, long-awned florets can injure grazing animals. The green young grass and the dry seed-bearing plant present very different management problems, making timing important. A patch is easiest to address before the stiff fruits are dispersed through surrounding vegetation or carried away on equipment and animals.
identification: The leaves and sheaths are generally softly hairy. Mature plants produce an open, loose, often nodding flower head with large several-flowered spikelets. Each floret ends in a long, straight, rough awn. Red brome has a more compact head, while rescuegrass has much shorter awns. The closely related rigid brome can be especially difficult to separate and may have been included under broader names in older accounts. Photograph the head before it breaks apart, along with a complete spikelet and the leaf sheath.
actions: Plan control while plants are young and before mature seed spreads. Small patches may be hand-pulled or cut where that can be done without excessive disturbance, with follow-up for missed plants. Keep dry seed heads away from pets and livestock, and clean attached seeds from clothing and equipment before entering another site. Extensive grassland infestations need a restoration or grazing plan developed with local specialists. A single late mowing may scatter mature seed, so check seed development first and provide suitable replacement cover after reducing the grass.

UC WRIC grouped brome report used only for clearly applicable diandrus traits; no red-brome desert-specific effects transferred. Independent Flora China differential and Oregon extension hand-removal guidance.

proposedDescription: Rigid brome is a long-awned annual grass from the Mediterranean region and neighboring areas. Bromus diandrus var. rigidus is a historical name; Kew treats it as a synonym of the separate species Bromus rigidus. Other treatments have combined the two more broadly. This naming difference matters because records labeled ripgut brome may include more than one botanical concept. When comparing a local plant with a distribution record or control study, retain the scientific name used by that source rather than assuming all records describe an identical grass.
identification: Plants have hairy leaves and sheaths and a relatively stiff, contracted flowering head. Short branches bear upright, several-flowered spikelets with long, rough awns. Rigid brome has an elliptical attachment scar at the base of the floret. A specialist can compare this with the related ripgut brome, B. diandrus. These are small details requiring magnification and mature material. Head posture alone can change as a plant ages, so photograph complete spikelets as well as the overall flowering head.
actions: Ask a grass specialist to confirm an uncertain identification before applying advice intended for a different brome. Keep mature awned heads from being transported in cut vegetation, soil or equipment to another site. Where a small patch is unwanted, discuss early removal with local weed staff before seed is shed, particularly in a restoration area with native annual grasses. Record the identification used and revisit the patch in later seasons. Do not assume a treatment trial on broadly defined B. diandrus proves the same result for a separately identified B. rigidus population.
researchNotes: Kew treats the legacy variety as Bromus rigidus. The independent SANBI key describes its long awns and elliptic callus scar, while discussing intermediates. This is an explicit name crosswalk and qualified expert identification, not an unresolved species substitution. proposedDescription: River red gum is a large Australian eucalyptus naturally associated with waterways and alluvial soils. Eucalyptus camaldulensis has been planted widely for shade, shelter and timber. In southern California it can establish outside plantings and crowd native vegetation in some locations. Its behavior should be assessed locally: a managed urban tree and a reproducing stand along a stream present different concerns. Several subspecies and cultivated forms exist, so one photograph or a familiar bark color may not represent the full range of the species.
identification: The trunk usually has smooth, patchy white, gray or reddish-brown bark that sheds in flakes or short ribbons. Adult leaves are narrow and lance-shaped, while juvenile leaves are broader. Flower buds occur in groups, commonly seven to eleven, followed by woody capsules with valves projecting above the rim. Bud-cap shape varies among subspecies; a pronounced beak is not universal. For identification, photograph mature buds, capsules, adult and juvenile leaves where available, and the trunk. Other smooth-barked gums can look similar from a distance.
actions: Look beyond a planted tree for independently rooted seedlings, particularly along drainage lines or disturbed ground. If regeneration is spreading into natural vegetation, document its extent and consult local land managers about priorities and suitable replacement cover. Have large-tree work assessed by a qualified arborist, especially near buildings, roads or waterways. Avoid moving seed-bearing debris into uninfested areas and monitor the site after any professionally planned removal. Do not assume that concerns reported for blue gum or another eucalyptus establish the same treatment or impact for river red gum.
researchNotes: Independent NSW morphology and Cal-IPC assessment support river red gum recognition and localized California concern. The absence of a species-specific removal trial does not prevent advice to verify trees and obtain site-specific professional guidance.
