proposedDescription: Rush skeletonweed is a perennial or sometimes biennial weed with a deep root system and a highly branched, nearly leafless flowering form. Introduced from southern Europe, it occurs in western American roadsides, rangelands, fields, and other disturbed open ground. Its early rosette can blend in with other yellow-flowered members of the sunflower family. Later, the wiry flowering stems make the name skeletonweed more understandable. Both seed production and regrowth from roots complicate management, so a patch deserves attention before machinery or soil disturbance carries it farther.
identification: Young plants have a rosette of sharply toothed leaves. As flowering stems develop, those basal leaves often wither, leaving small narrow leaves on the branches. Coarse reddish hairs point downward near the base of the stem, a useful close-up feature. Small yellow flower heads are scattered along the branched stems, and mature seeds carry white bristles. Several other plants have dandelionlike rosettes or yellow flower heads; combine the basal hairs, sparse stem leaves, and overall branching pattern before making an identification.
actions: Mark and report a new patch to the local weed program before disturbing its roots. Avoid tilling an infestation, because root fragments can produce new plants. Cutting before seed development may reduce seed output but does not remove the established root system. Clean equipment after work in affected ground and keep seed-bearing stems contained. Established patches generally require an integrated plan and repeated inspections over time. Ask the weed manager which approaches fit the site and protect neighboring desirable vegetation.
researchNotes: Pacific Northwest university management handbook independently supports root regrowth and repeated follow-up alongside UC botanical/control guidance. Chemical recipes and quantitative yield-loss claims omitted.

proposedDescription: Russian olive is a thorny shrub or small tree introduced as an ornamental, windbreak, and bank-stabilization plant. It has escaped along streams, floodplains, and roadsides in parts of the western United States. Birds carry its fruits, helping seedlings appear beyond the original planting. In affected riparian areas, management often focuses on restoring a more diverse native plant community. Its value as cover or food for some wildlife does not remove the need to assess that local habitat change, and removal planning should consider what will replace the trees.
identification: Leaves alternate along the stems and are narrow, with a silvery or sometimes rusty appearance from tiny surface scales. Branches commonly carry stout thorns. Small fragrant flowers are yellow inside, and the mature olive-shaped fruits are pale cream to brown with a scaly coating. Native silver buffaloberry, Shepherdia argentea, can look similarly gray from a distance, but it has opposite leaves and red fruit. Photograph leaf arrangement, both leaf surfaces, fruit, and thorns before identifying a young tree or planning removal.
actions: Consult the local weed manager for a riparian infestation, particularly near water or unstable banks. Small seedlings or saplings can sometimes be removed with their roots, while cutting a larger tree alone can leave it able to resprout. Plan follow-up for stump growth and new seedlings. Wear protective clothing around the thorns and keep fruiting debris from being spread. For large trees, use trained help and include replacement vegetation and bank protection in the work plan.
researchNotes: USGS restoration synthesis adds an independent management lineage to Colorado botanical and control guidance. It explicitly notes fewer Russian-olive-specific field studies; prose does not transfer saltcedar-specific efficacy findings.

proposedDescription: Russian wheat aphid is a small cereal-feeding insect that can injure wheat and barley as it feeds. Unlike several other common grain aphids, it can produce visible damage at relatively low abundance, so species identification matters when scouting. Its American importance varies by region and year. California guidance describes substantial declines from earlier outbreaks, while Oklahoma accounts emphasize the Panhandle. Neither history means that every field requires treatment. Crop stage, actual infestation, and local advice should guide decisions.
identification: Wingless adults are pale green, slender, and spindle-shaped, with short antennae and no conspicuous long cornicles. A small projection above the tail gives the rear end a distinctive double-tailed appearance under magnification. Feeding can cause leaves to roll tightly and develop pale, yellowish, or purplish streaks. Gently unroll suspect leaves to look for insects concealed inside; the rolled leaf protects them and is more useful evidence than a general patch of yellow crop. Young or winged forms may be harder to recognize, so keep several clear photographs or obtain a diagnostic sample.
actions: Scout the newest growth and record the proportion of tillers with confirmed aphids and characteristic injury. Do not assume every streaked or rolled leaf contains this species. Use regional crop thresholds and consult a farm adviser before selecting a response. Preserve natural enemies where possible and avoid transferring a recommendation for another grain aphid without checking it. After any management action, revisit affected areas to assess living aphids and new growth rather than expecting damaged leaves to recover their original appearance.
researchNotes: UC and Oklahoma State independent cereal IPM support diagnostics, injury and monitoring. No broad virus-vector claim or fixed economic threshold transferred across regions.

claims: Spindle-shaped pale aphid and double-tail diagnostic; California history.
Rolled streaked leaves; unroll to confirm; wheat/barley damage and regional scouting.

proposedDescription: Russian wildrye is a long-lived, cool-season bunchgrass introduced for pasture and conservation plantings in the northern and intermountain West. USDA materials describe its use in Montana and Wyoming, especially where drought tolerance and a long grazing season are useful. Established plants have extensive roots and can compete strongly with other vegetation. That characteristic can be desirable in a managed pasture and undesirable where native plant diversity is the objective. Its presence should be interpreted in the context of planting history rather than treated automatically as an invasive outbreak.
identification: Most foliage is concentrated at the base in a dense tuft of long, narrow leaves. Leaf color ranges from green to blue-green. Flowering stems rise above the leaves and appear relatively bare, ending in short, dense, upright spikes. Small clusters of spikelets occur along the spike axis, and mature seed can shatter readily. The growth form is a bunch rather than a spreading rhizomatous sod. Compare mature spikes and basal foliage with other introduced forage grasses; a blue-green clump alone is not enough to distinguish it from wheatgrasses or other wildryes.
actions: Check pasture or restoration records before removing an unfamiliar clump. Where the grass is intentionally managed, use local forage guidance for grazing and stand condition. Where it is spreading into a native-plant area, map the boundary and seek advice from the land manager about a site-specific response. Prevent unwanted seed movement with equipment and keep seed-bearing material contained. Avoid reseeding a conservation site with this grass without considering the desired plant community and its strong competitive behavior once established.
researchNotes: NRCS provides exact forage and conservation-use context; independent GrassBase morphology corroborates the tufted grass and spikelets. Strong competition in planted stands is not inflated into a nationwide invasive designation or untested removal advice. proposedDescription: Puccinia modiolae is a rust fungus associated with Carolina bristlemallow and other members of the mallow family. A North American study documented it along the Gulf Coast, including Louisiana and Texas, and considered an introduction from South America likely. The same study added hollyhock and common mallow to its reported host range. Those records should not be confused with the much more familiar hollyhock rust, Puccinia malvacearum. Several rust species can occur on related hosts, and the host name alone does not determine which fungus is present.
identification: A rust diagnosis begins with affected leaves and the fungal structures on them, but identifying this species requires specialist examination. Researchers used specimen comparisons and DNA sequences to separate it from other mallow rusts. Photograph both sides of affected leaves, the whole plant, and flowers or fruits that help establish the host's identity. Preserve the connection between each leaf sample and its host rather than combining material from several mallow species. A general image of rusty spots is useful for reporting symptoms but cannot confirm Puccinia modiolae.
actions: If an unusual rust appears on bristlemallow or a garden mallow, contact a plant diagnostic laboratory before moving cuttings or seedlings from the affected group. Follow its instructions for collecting and packing leaves. Keep suspect plant material separate from healthy propagation stock, and retain the date and location of the observation. Do not apply a control program for another rust solely on visual resemblance. For an isolated wild plant, documentation and expert identification may be more appropriate than removing surrounding vegetation.
researchNotes: Independent Berndt and colleagues European collections corroborate exact-species rust identity and expand host evidence, rather than merely reviewing the North American report. The profile retains laboratory confirmation and does not borrow a treatment from malvacearum.

proposedDescription: Uromyces transversalis is one of the fungi that cause gladiolus rust. Current USDA guidance identifies it as established in the United States and distinguishes it from other gladiolus rust fungi that remain a plant-health concern. This distinction matters because older information may describe responses that no longer apply to this species. Rust spores can travel on wind and with flowers, stems, and contaminated plant material. A grower who sees suspicious leaf lesions should seek a diagnosis before deciding how to handle a planting or shipment.
identification: Early symptoms include small yellow spots on either leaf surface. These develop into yellow-orange, powdery pustules that may merge into larger damaged areas. For U. transversalis, the pustules characteristically form short rows across the leaf, perpendicular to its lengthwise veins. That pattern is helpful, but several fungi can cause rust on gladiolus, and other leaf problems can also produce discoloration. Photograph both leaf surfaces and the orientation of the pustules relative to the veins. Keep the host identity and source of the plants with any diagnostic sample.
actions: Buy planting material from reputable growers and inspect plants before adding them to an established collection. Report suspected gladiolus rust to the state plant-health or plant-regulatory office, which can determine the fungus and the appropriate response. Pause movement of suspect cut flowers and planting material while awaiting advice. Avoid destroying an entire planting or applying a treatment solely from an old quarantine notice; current species confirmation should guide the decision.
researchNotes: Current APHIS July 2025 status and response guidance paired with independent UC crop pathology. Older eradication framing avoided. Diagnosis precedes response because other gladiolus rust fungi differ in status.

claims: U. transversalis established; other rusts require distinction; report and confirm before control.
Orange powdery pustules in series perpendicular to leaf venation.
U. transversalis yellow-orange pustules, windborne spores, clean stock and regular monitoring.

proposedDescription: Pelargonium rust is a leaf disease of zonal pelargoniums, the familiar bedding plants often called geraniums. It is caused by Puccinia pelargonii-zonalis. The host distinction matters: this account concerns zonal pelargoniums rather than every plant sold as a geranium. In greenhouse collections, infected plants can introduce the fungus before obvious symptoms appear. Repeated infections can yellow leaves and cause them to fall, weakening the plant. Humid conditions and prolonged leaf wetness favor the disease, so prevention includes how plants are arranged and watered as well as inspection of new stock.
identification: Small pale or yellow spots appear on the upper leaf surface. On the underside, corresponding blisters develop into powdery brown spore pustules, often arranged in rings. In severe cases, pustules may also appear above. Check both sides of several leaves, including recently affected ones, and photograph the paired upper and lower symptoms. Other spots, edema, and insect damage can discolor pelargonium leaves without producing these rusty spore masses. A diagnostic service can confirm an uncertain case, particularly where different pelargonium types are grown together.
actions: Inspect incoming plants and keep new additions separate for at least two weeks when an established collection is at risk. Improve greenhouse ventilation and avoid prolonged wet foliage. Separate affected plants and seek advice before taking cuttings or distributing them. Heavily infected, weakened plants may be best discarded with their diseased material contained. Continue inspecting nearby plants because symptoms can lag behind infection. For commercial production, use a current local disease-management program suited to the confirmed host and pathogen.
researchNotes: RHS disease guidance and Cornell greenhouse pathology independently support specific host, ringed pustules, symptom delay and moisture management. No claims borrowed from unrelated geranium diseases in the Cornell page.

proposedDescription: Rust pine borer is a longhorn beetle associated with conifer wood. Its range and taxonomic history require care: North American taxonomic records include native populations and subspecies, while introduced populations have also been reported in South America. It should therefore not be presented as a uniformly foreign pest throughout the United States. European accounts describe larvae developing in dead conifer wood and adults visiting fallen logs and stumps. Finding a beetle near a woodpile is not, by itself, evidence that it killed a living tree.
identification: Adults are elongated and brown to reddish brown. European descriptions give a body length of about one to three centimeters. Related Arhopalus species can be very similar; specialists examine the pronotum and feet as well as overall proportions. Photograph the beetle from above and from the side, keeping the antennae and legs visible if possible. Record the kind of wood, whether it was recently transported, and whether the beetle emerged from it. A larval tunnel or emergence hole alone is unlikely to establish the species.
actions: For a beetle found in locally sourced dead wood, obtain an identification before treating trees or removing habitat. If it emerges from imported wood packaging or a newly delivered wood product, keep the material contained and contact a plant-health inspector. Avoid moving firewood between regions, since it can carry many wood-boring insects. Retain photographs and purchase information when relevant. Do not assume that an overseas control recommendation applies to a native North American population.
researchNotes:
ITIS North American taxonomic scope, the fully recovered archived Csóka–Kovács Hungarian account, and the Cerambyx European subspecies treatment support a regional account. SENASA supports adult appearance; the 2019 original pheromone study independently reports South American introductions. Native US populations are not represented as foreign; overseas invasion history and conifer dead-wood association are kept geographically qualified. proposedDescription: Rusty banded aphid, also called hawthorn-parsley aphid, is among the aphids encountered on celery. Related accounts include other carrot-family plants such as parsley, fennel, and carrot. In celery production, dense aphid colonies can interfere with growth and contaminate harvested stalks with insects, cast skins, and honeydew. Several species may be present, so a management decision should begin with the crop and the actual infestation rather than the common name. The species belongs to a difficult group whose members can be hard to separate even with close examination.
identification: Wingless adults in this group are small, yellowish gray and wax-dusted, often with a reddish-brown area near the bases of their dark cornicles. Antennae are relatively short. INRAE cautions that visible morphological characters do not reliably separate D. apiifolia from D. crataegi and D. foeniculus. Record the host and where the colony occurs, and obtain a specialist determination when the exact species matters. On celery, inspect leaflet undersides and stalks rather than only the exposed top leaves. Close photographs should accompany host and field information.
actions: Scout several parts of a celery field because infestations can be patchy, paying attention as stalks form and rows close. Check field edges after neighboring aphid-favored crops are harvested. Preserve parasitoids and predators by avoiding unnecessary insecticide use, and remove crop residues promptly after harvest. Consult a local crop adviser if colonies are increasing or contaminating produce. Do not assume that every virus associated with celery aphids is transmitted by this particular species without a diagnosis.
researchNotes: INRAE explicitly states that ordinary morphology cannot separate three close species; independent UC celery guidance names rusty banded aphid and supports crop scouting. The draft preserves that identification limit and does not claim visual species certainty or species-specific virus diagnosis. proposedDescription: Rye brome, also called true cheat, is a winter annual grass that can be troublesome in wheat. In Oklahoma it grows on a seasonal schedule similar to winter wheat, making it difficult to separate from the crop through routine management alone. Competition, harvest interference, and contaminated grain can all matter to producers. The common name cheat should not be confused with cheatgrass, which usually means downy brome, Bromus tectorum. Several annual bromes occur together, and a mature flowering specimen is often the best starting point for identification.
identification: Plants produce branched flower heads with several-flowered spikelets. Mature florets generally have short awns, unlike the much longer awns typical of downy brome. As rye brome matures, the edges of individual florets roll inward, leaving noticeable spaces between them in a spikelet. Fully ripe material is important for seeing that feature. Hairiness is variable and should not be used as the sole distinction. Photograph the whole head and a close side view of a ripe spikelet; a young grassy seedling may require an attached seed and specialist examination.
actions: Prevent seed production in field margins, fence rows, and fallow ground before it can replenish an infestation. Clean cultivation and harvesting equipment before entering clean fields, including combines used by contractors. Avoid moving contaminated hay or seed into unaffected plantings. For an established wheat-field problem, consult a local agronomist about an integrated crop plan and current treatment options. Confirm which brome is present first, and track surviving plants and seed production after management rather than relying only on an early visual reduction.
researchNotes: Oklahoma State crop management and independent Rothamsted/AHDB diagnostic guide support ready draft. Conflicting hairiness descriptions in regional sources avoided; mature floret separation used instead.

proposedDescription: Rye sedge is a Eurasian sedge documented as naturalized in southeastern New York. A 2012 study reported seven North American populations at that time, mainly in highly disturbed urban habitats, including salt-influenced ground. That historical count is not a current distribution estimate. In its native range the species also occupies damp or wet, often saline soils. The researchers did not consider it demonstrably invasive in North America then, but recommended monitoring because of its potential seed production. A new observation is useful evidence, particularly when accompanied by mature fruit.
identification: The flowering stem has male spikes toward the top and female spikes below. A key feature is the sharply two-angled shape of the perigynia, the small sacs surrounding the fruits. The lower spikes have distinct stalks, another important part of the diagnostic combination. These structures distinguish it more reliably than a general picture of narrow leaves. Many native sedges occur in wet places, so obtain close views of mature spikes and individual fruit sacs, along with the full plant. A hand lens or herbarium examination may be necessary.
actions: Photograph a suspected population and record the exact location, habitat, and approximate number of plants. Contact a regional herbarium or botanist before removing a sedge that might be native. If confirmed, repeat observations can show whether the patch is stable or expanding. Avoid carrying fruiting material or wet soil to another site. Any management in a wetland or along a sensitive shore should be planned with the landowner or conservation manager rather than based solely on the plant's introduced origin.
researchNotes: Werier and Naczi original New York findings provide diagnostic fruit characters; independent Verloove Belgian field observations confirm introduced disturbed-ground occurrence. Historical population counts are dated, and neither study justifies blanket invasive harm. proposedDescription: Ryegrass bunt is a fungal disease caused by Tilletia walkeri. It affects ryegrass seed and became particularly important in American diagnostic work because its spores resemble those of the Karnal bunt fungus, Tilletia indica. Surveys in southeastern wheat fields found T. walkeri on annual ryegrass growing among the crop; the study did not find bunted wheat seed or T. indica. That distinction matters when interpreting a contaminated grain sample. A spore detected among wheat grains does not necessarily mean that the wheat itself is infected.
identification: Infected ryegrass seeds may be partly or more extensively replaced by dark fungal spores. The fungus is not reliably identified from a discolored seed alone. Researchers examined spore size, color, surface ridges, and a surrounding sheath, while molecular methods help distinguish T. walkeri from T. indica. Keep ryegrass seed heads associated with the plant from which they were collected. If a grain lot contains weed seeds, record that mixture rather than discarding the unfamiliar seeds before the laboratory sees the sample. Those details can change the interpretation of the result.
actions: For suspect seed or a laboratory finding, contact a seed-testing or plant-health laboratory before moving or marketing the lot. Keep the original sample and its collection information intact. Follow the laboratory's sampling instructions rather than attempting to diagnose a regulatory disease with a hand lens. In seed or grain production, prevent weed-seed contamination and clean handling equipment between lots. A confirmed T. walkeri finding should be interpreted separately from Karnal bunt, with any response based on the actual fungus and host.
researchNotes: Independent Tan and colleagues developed a five-plex diagnostic assay that distinguishes walkeri from indica and other bunts. This complements the separate southeastern US field survey and supports sample-preserving laboratory advice without mistaking contaminated wheat for an infected wheat host. proposedDescription: Ryegrass mealybug is a small plant-feeding insect recorded on grasses and several other plant groups. Older American literature may call it Phenacoccus graminosus, a name now treated as a synonym of Phenacoccus graminicola. California records are well established in the taxonomic literature. Its origin should be handled carefully, and an old collection record does not by itself establish whether a population is native. Reports of pasture damage elsewhere should not be transferred automatically to an American lawn or field. Finding a mealybug and explaining a patch of declining grass are separate steps.
identification: Mealybugs are soft-bodied scale insects typically covered with a pale waxy coating, but that appearance identifies a group rather than this species. Reliable identification of P. graminicola uses microscopic characters of adult females and specialist keys. Its host list includes ryegrasses and other grasses, so host identity provides supporting evidence. Adults may also move onto nearby woody plants to lay eggs, which can make the collection site misleading. Photograph the insect in place, record the plant and exact part occupied, and preserve a sample according to an entomologist's instructions.
actions: Before treating a declining lawn or pasture, have the insects identified and investigate other causes such as water stress or root problems. Keep samples from different host plants separate. If insects occur on nursery material or harvested fruit, retain source and lot information and consult the relevant inspector or crop adviser. Avoid applying a control program for another pasture mealybug simply because the insects look white and waxy. Monitor the affected area so management reflects confirmed damage and population change.

proposedDescription: Sacred bamboo, or nandina, is an Asian shrub widely planted for its foliage and persistent red fruit. Despite the common name, it is a member of the barberry family rather than a true bamboo. In parts of the Southeast it has escaped into woods and floodplains, where spreading plants can form dense patches. Seeds carried by wildlife and growth from underground stems both contribute. Cultivars differ in fruit production, so a compact garden selection may behave differently from a heavily fruiting shrub; current local recommendations remain important when choosing replacements.
identification: Several upright, cane-like stems support large leaves divided two or three times into many pointed leaflets. The whole leaf is much larger than an individual leaflet, a helpful distinction when examining the plant. Foliage can turn reddish or purple in cool weather. Branched clusters of small pale flowers appear above the leaves, followed by rounded berries that become bright red and may persist through winter. True bamboos have grasslike leaves and very different stems and flowers. Photograph the complete divided leaf, stem arrangement, and flower or fruit cluster together.
actions:
Remove flower or fruit clusters from retained fruiting plants to reduce seed spread. For unwanted small plants, remove the roots carefully and revisit for shoots arising from fragments or underground stems. Keep berries and dug material contained rather than dumping them into woods. Consider a locally suitable native shrub for replacement, especially near natural habitat. Established thickets may need an extension-guided treatment plan and repeated follow-up. Do not assume that cutting the visible stems once eliminates the plant.

Keep berries and trimmings away from children and pets; the plant can be harmful if eaten.

Independent UF management and Clemson horticultural guidance support recognition, regional escape, fruit reduction and underground spread. No unneeded wildlife toxicity claim; cultivar recommendations kept local/current rather than blanket safe.

proposedDescription: Sacred lotus brings enormous round leaves and pink or white flowers to shallow, quiet water. This Asian ornamental can escape water gardens and establish colonies in ponds, marshes, and lake margins in the United States. Underground rhizomes allow a planting to expand well beyond its original pot or shoreline position. Dense growth can crowd the water surface, but a patch of lotus should not automatically be treated as this introduced species: American lotus is native to parts of the country.
identification: Look for nearly circular leaves with the stalk attached near the center of the underside. Leaves may float or stand above the water. Unlike many water lilies, the blade has no deep notch reaching the stalk. Large flowers rise above the foliage and develop into a distinctive flat-topped, cone-shaped receptacle containing individual seed chambers. Pink flowers strongly suggest sacred lotus; American lotus normally has pale yellow flowers. White-flowered selections and plants without flowers deserve closer examination before removal.
actions: Photograph the flower, leaf attachment, seed head, and whole colony, and ask an aquatic plant specialist to confirm identification. Avoid planting sacred lotus where rhizomes or seeds can reach natural water. Contain discarded plants and potting material rather than dumping them beside a pond. Small confirmed escapes may be removable with their rhizomes, but shoreline disturbance and larger colonies need a coordinated plan with the waterbody owner and local aquatic management staff.
researchNotes: UF aquatic botany and Wisconsin agency account provide separate identification and escape-management lineages. Native American lotus comparison is central; no blanket removal recommendation.

proposedDescription: Sainfoin is a perennial forage legume introduced from Eurasia and deliberately grown for hay and pasture in parts of the western United States. Its pink flower spikes make a field look quite different from alfalfa. Wyoming and Montana extension specialists describe it as an agricultural crop with useful forage qualities, not simply an unwanted plant wherever it occurs. An isolated roadside plant and a managed forage stand therefore call for different decisions.
identification: The stems rise from a persistent crown and can reach about three feet. Each leaf is divided into numerous small leaflets arranged along a central stalk, unlike the three leaflets typical of alfalfa. Upright clusters carry pea-shaped flowers, usually pink, though flower color varies. The stems are comparatively coarse and hollow. Flowering begins low on the cluster and progresses upward. Record the leaf arrangement and flowers together: pink bloom alone will not distinguish sainfoin from the many other legumes found beside fields.
actions: Before removing a patch, establish whether it belongs to a planted pasture or hay crop. Ask the grower about its purpose and boundaries. Where volunteer plants are unwanted in a garden or restoration area, remove young plants with their crowns before seed production and revisit the site for seedlings. Keep seed and hay handling areas tidy to limit movement beyond the intended field. For a forage stand, use local extension advice about grazing, weed competition, and soil suitability rather than treating the entire planting as an invasive infestation.
researchNotes: Agricultural context supported independently by Wyoming and Montana extension plus Alberta agriculture. No evidence used to infer nationwide invasiveness or ecological harm from introduction.

proposedDescription: Purple salsify is a biennial herb historically cultivated for its root and now found outside gardens. A first-year plant can disappear into surrounding grass because its leaves are long and narrow. In its flowering year, the purple heads and large fluffy seed balls are much easier to notice. Several introduced salsifies occur in the United States, so the familiar common name does not identify a single species.
identification: Look for smooth, upright stems, narrow leaves with sheathing bases, and solitary flower heads. The stalk swells immediately below the head. Long pointed green bracts extend beyond the mauve or purple florets, producing a star-like outline around an open flower. Mature heads release beaked fruits with feathery parachutes. Yellow-flowered western salsify, Tragopogon dubius, also has a swollen stalk below the head, so that character alone is insufficient. Photograph an open flower as well as the leaves and the base of its head; closed heads are less helpful.
actions: In a vegetable garden, decide whether a plant is an intended crop before disturbing it. For unwanted plants, remove the taproot while the soil is workable and before mature seed disperses. Collect developing seed heads carefully rather than carrying uncovered stems through the garden. Check the same sunny, disturbed margins the following season for narrow-leaved rosettes. Avoid using a roadside plant as food on the strength of its common name or resemblance to a cultivated crop. Where identification remains uncertain, take photographs to extension or a local herbarium before widespread removal.
researchNotes: NZ flora provides species morphology; WSU distinguishes purple from yellow salsify. WSU direct open returned403, so evidence is indexed_excerpt. Actions are proportionate seed containment and garden removal, not a nationwide invasive designation.

proposedDescription: Saltcedar is a woody shrub or small tree associated with river corridors, reservoirs, and other moist places in the arid West. Its fine foliage and pink flower sprays can be attractive, but established stands complicate riparian restoration. Many North American plants called Tamarix ramosissima are hybrids with Tamarix chinensis. Research on that mixed population is often more relevant to a western saltcedar stand than a precise species label based only on appearance.
identification: The foliage consists of tiny, overlapping, scale-like leaves on slender branchlets. Numerous small pink flowers are carried in narrow clusters. A whole plant may have several trunks and an airy crown, or become part of a dense stand. Saltcedars differ from native willows in their minute scale leaves, but separating individual Tamarix species is more demanding. Flower structure and flowering shoots can help a specialist; photographs of the overall tree alone usually cannot resolve hybrid ancestry. Preserve the distinction between a confirmed saltcedar and an unverified species determination.
actions: Report new plants near waterways to the land manager and document the location and extent before work begins. Do not clear an established stand without a plan for nesting wildlife, bank stability, replacement vegetation, and follow-up. Cutting alone may leave living root systems that resprout. Small seedlings are easier to address than mature trees, provided removal is permitted and roots can be removed without damaging the bank. Biological control insects should be handled through authorized programs, with attention to local habitat needs. Follow-up surveys are essential wherever seedlings or regrowth appear.
researchNotes: Gaskin and Schaal directly establish hybrid prevalence; USFS management synthesis draws on separate field-control and restoration studies. The profile explicitly addresses saltcedar stands under a historical species label and does not promise visual identification of pure ramosissima or transfer hybrid ancestry to a particular specimen. proposedDescription: Halogeton is a small annual weed of dry, salty, disturbed ground in the Great Basin and other parts of the western United States. Introduced from Eurasia, it can occupy road edges, livestock trails, and degraded rangeland where perennial vegetation is sparse. Its most immediate practical concern is livestock poisoning: the foliage contains soluble oxalates, and sheep and cattle can be seriously affected. Risk varies with the animals, plant condition, and available forage.
identification: Plants branch from the base and often have reddish or purplish stems. The short, fleshy leaves are roughly cylindrical, like tiny sausages, and end in a fine hair-like point. Young plants can resemble Russian thistle. Look closely for cottony hairs where the leaves meet the stems; these help recognize halogeton seedlings. Later, inconspicuous flowers and winged fruiting structures cluster along the stems. Photograph both a whole plant and a close view of leaves and their junctions, since a distant picture of reddish desert vegetation is not enough.
actions: Keep livestock away from a suspicious dense patch until it is identified, especially when animals are hungry after transport or other forage is limited. Contact a veterinarian promptly if exposure is suspected; do not wait for a plant identification to become certain. Prevent soil disturbance and overgrazing that leave bare ground. Small infestations should be addressed before seed production, with local range or weed specialists helping plan follow-up and suitable revegetation. Clean equipment before leaving infested ground, and monitor treated areas because some seeds persist for years.
researchNotes: USDA NRCS guide read in full; Cornell independently supports livestock toxicity and oxalates. Avoided toxic-dose figures and treatment recipes. Rangeland actions emphasize prevention and revegetation rather than disturbance alone.

proposedDescription: Salvation jane, also called Paterson's curse, is a Mediterranean annual or biennial that has become a pasture and roadside weed in several regions, including parts of the western United States. The purple flowers can make a stand look like a desirable wildflower planting. However, its seeds move with hay, soil, vehicles, and agricultural materials, and the plant contains alkaloids that can harm livestock. Horses are particularly important to protect from contaminated forage.
identification: Young plants form a low rosette with broad, hairy leaves. Flowering stems have conspicuous bristles, while their leaves are narrower than those at the base. Purple, trumpet-shaped flowers are a useful clue, but common viper's bugloss, Echium vulgare, is similar. Examine a fully open flower: Paterson's curse normally has two stamens projecting beyond the petals, compared with four in common viper's bugloss. Take a close photograph rather than relying only on the color of a distant patch. Rough nutlets develop after flowering.
actions: Avoid sowing this plant as a bee or ornamental mixture near grazing land. Keep suspect forage away from horses and other livestock and ask a veterinarian about possible exposure. Use clean seed and hay, and remove soil and plant material from machinery before it enters another field. Maintain healthy pasture cover rather than leaving bare patches after control. For a small suspected occurrence, photograph flowers and rosettes and contact local extension or weed staff before it sets seed. Plan repeated checks because seed can remain in the soil long after adult plants disappear.

proposedDescription: Slender joyweed is a small tropical American herb in the amaranth family. The name Alternanthera ficoidea has also been used broadly in horticulture for colorful bedding plants. That history matters when matching a garden plant to a botanical name: foliage sold under one label may belong to a different, closely related joyweed. A Florida assessment under this name applies to the plant concept assessed there, not automatically to every joyweed sold under a similar label.
identification: Botanical descriptions emphasize a low, decumbent herb with narrow elliptic to spoon-shaped leaves and small rounded or short cylindrical flower heads. The flowers are much less conspicuous than the foliage. Photograph leaf shape, leaf arrangement, branching, and several flower heads together. Bright red, cream, or green coloring is useful for describing a cultivar but does not settle species identification. Other Alternanthera species can look similar, and the name sanguinaria should not be confused with the unrelated woodland bloodroot genus Sanguinaria.
actions: Keep intentional bedding plants within the maintained garden and collect trimmings instead of dumping them in natural areas. If seedlings or rooted shoots are appearing beyond the planting, photograph them and ask a local botanist or extension office to compare them with the parent plant. Unwanted small plants can be removed carefully before they spread further, while preserving neighboring vegetation. Avoid treating an entire patch solely because a nursery label says joyweed. A confirmed identity and evidence of actual spread are better guides to the scale of action.

proposedDescription: Santa Maria is an evergreen tropical American tree with dense foliage and small white flowers. Its native range includes Mexico, Central and South America, and parts of the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico. Trees cultivated in Florida under this name require particular care in identification because some records and landscape references concern the Antillean taxon, treated as Calophyllum brasiliense var. antillanum or Calophyllum antillanum. A name used in a nursery is not always a precise statement of botanical identity.
identification: Look for simple, leathery leaves growing opposite one another. The blades are elliptic to oblong, with smooth margins and many closely spaced, nearly parallel side veins. Small white flowers and rounded fruits provide useful additional characters. Take photographs of both leaf surfaces, the way leaves join the twig, flowers, and mature fruit. These features help distinguish a Calophyllum from unrelated glossy-leaved tropical trees, but they do not by themselves resolve every species or variety. A specialist may need a flowering or fruiting specimen.
actions: For an established landscape tree, watch for seedlings beyond the maintained planting and remove unwanted young plants before they become difficult to manage. Keep fruit and nursery waste out of nearby natural areas. If a tree appears to be spreading into habitat, seek identification before arranging removal, particularly in Caribbean places where related populations may be native. Large-tree work should involve a qualified arborist and the landowner. Match any regional planting advice to the confirmed taxon and location rather than applying a Florida assessment throughout the species' tropical American range.

proposedDescription: Santa Maria feverfew, often called ragweed parthenium, is a branching annual of disturbed ground, fields, and nursery areas. It belongs to the tropical and subtropical American flora, and the limits of its native range in the southern United States have been interpreted differently. Elsewhere it is a serious agricultural invader. Its practical significance at a particular site comes from crop competition, seed movement, and the potential for allergic skin or respiratory reactions, rather than from a single nationwide label.
identification: Young plants may form a rosette of deeply divided leaves. Flowering stems become upright and branched, with conspicuous ribs. Numerous tiny white flower heads are held near the ends of the branches. The divided foliage can suggest common ragweed, especially before flowering, but the small white heads are an important distinction. Photograph the lower leaves, stem ribs, and mature flower clusters together. Other white-flowered weeds can occur in the same disturbed places, so flower color alone is not sufficient.
actions: Avoid handling suspected plants with bare hands or creating dust around a mature patch. People who react to the plant should leave removal to others and seek medical advice for significant symptoms. In production areas, prevent contaminated soil, seed, and equipment from moving between clean and infested sites. Ask extension staff to confirm plants while they are young and easier to manage. Control should prevent seed production and be followed by checks for new seedlings. Maintain competitive ground cover where appropriate, and choose methods suited to the crop and site rather than repeatedly disturbing bare soil.
researchNotes: UF nursery biology and independent NSW field guidance support recognition, seed hygiene and careful handling. Native-range boundaries are geographically qualified; overseas severity is not converted to a blanket introduced designation across the southern US. proposedDescription: The Australian sap beetle, Brachypeplus basalis, is an introduced beetle found in stored honey bee hive equipment in Oregon and in pollen stores in California. Those associations matter to beekeepers, but they do not make it the small hive beetle, Aethina tumida, which has a different pest history. Oregon's first report concerned stored equipment rather than active colonies. Its presence alone therefore does not explain a struggling colony or prove that it damaged the comb.
identification: A small beetle found in a hive is a starting point for identification, not a diagnosis. Oregon State's hive-beetle guide illustrates Brachypeplus basalis alongside the small hive beetle and other lookalikes. Clear views from above, the side, and below are much more useful than a distant photograph on a frame. Include a size scale and retain an intact adult if a specialist requests one. Larvae or fragments may be harder to assign, and the presence of damaged comb does not prove which organism caused it.
actions: Record the hive, date, number of beetles, and where they were found, including stored pollen or debris. Ask an extension apiculture specialist or state apiary inspector to confirm the beetle before choosing a response. Keep suspect hive materials contained during examination and avoid moving them to other colonies unnecessarily. Continue normal colony inspections and sanitation, but do not apply a small hive beetle treatment solely on the basis of a superficial resemblance. Photograph any associated damage separately so the investigator can evaluate the beetle and colony condition together.

proposedDescription: Sapodilla is an evergreen fruit tree native to tropical America and widely cultivated in warm regions. In southern Florida, escaped trees can establish in hammocks, where dense seedlings and mature crowns interfere with native vegetation. The same tree may therefore be a valued orchard crop in one setting and an unwanted escape in another. Fallen fruit and wildlife movement are important links between a planted tree and seedlings appearing beyond the garden.
identification: Look for leathery, glossy, elliptic leaves crowded toward branch tips. The leaves are arranged alternately or spirally rather than in opposite pairs. Small pale, bell-like flowers arise near the leaf bases. Mature fruits are brown, round to oval, and have a rough outer surface and dark, hard seeds. Young growth may be brownish and hairy. Florida also has native wild dilly, Manilkara bahamensis, so an unidentified glossy-leaved tree should not be removed on foliage alone. Flowers, fruit, and the arrangement of leaves provide a much better identification record.
actions: In Florida areas where sapodilla escapes, avoid adding new trees beside natural habitat and inspect beneath existing trees and along nearby hammock edges for seedlings. Remove confirmed young escapes while their roots are still manageable, taking care around native seedlings. Collect unwanted fallen fruit and dispose of seeds with contained household or municipal waste rather than in natural areas. Large escaped trees require a site-specific removal plan to protect surrounding vegetation. If the tree's identity is uncertain, ask extension staff or a botanist to compare it with native relatives before work begins.

proposedDescription: Sarawak bean is a creeping or climbing tropical legume used as ground cover and green manure in plantations. It has also become naturalized in Hawaii, where botanical records document occurrences beyond its original plantings. A dense ground-cover planting can be useful in a managed agricultural setting while still needing containment at its edges. Its ability to produce pods close to the ground makes a quick inspection of the visible flowers an incomplete check for seed.
identification: Look for a trailing legume with compound leaves and small yellow pea-shaped flowers. Tropical forage descriptions treat this species alongside Vigna parkeri, a similar creeping bean, so observations should be matched carefully to the correct species. Some Sarawak bean pods develop within the leaf litter rather than standing conspicuously above the foliage. Photograph an entire runner, leaves, flowers, and both exposed and litter-level pods. Do not rely on the name creeping vigna, which is used for more than one plant. A botanist may need mature fruit to confirm the identification.
actions: Keep an intended cover crop within its planned area and inspect the margins, drainage routes, and nearby vegetation for new runners or seedlings. Before moving soil or plant waste, check for pods hidden in the litter. Contain unwanted material rather than using it as mulch elsewhere. Small escapes can be addressed while the patch is still accessible, with follow-up to find plants missed beneath neighboring cover. In Hawaii, report an unfamiliar spreading patch to local extension or invasive-species staff with photographs and a precise location so its identity and extent can be checked.

proposedDescription: SARS-CoV-2 is the virus that causes COVID-19. It belongs to a broader coronavirus species now called Betacoronavirus pandemicum; the older species name severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus should not be read as a synonym for SARS-CoV-2 alone. This distinction separates the virus responsible for COVID-19 from related viruses discussed in taxonomy and wildlife research. For someone concerned about a possible infection, the useful next step is appropriate testing and health advice rather than trying to identify a virus from symptoms.
identification: COVID-19 can resemble other respiratory illnesses. A cough, fever, fatigue, or sore throat cannot reliably establish which virus is involved, and some infections have few noticeable symptoms. Laboratory molecular tests and authorized antigen tests address different diagnostic needs. A negative antigen result does not always exclude infection, particularly early in illness. Follow the instructions for the specific test, including any recommendation to repeat testing, and discuss persistent symptoms or uncertainty with a healthcare professional.
actions: If you are sick, reduce close contact with others and follow current public-health guidance for respiratory illness. Cleaner indoor air and a well-fitting mask can help reduce exposure, especially around people at higher risk of severe illness. Seek healthcare promptly if you may benefit from treatment, because treatment decisions can be time-sensitive. Testing can help guide those decisions and precautions around other people. For severe or rapidly worsening illness, seek urgent medical care. Keep advice specific to COVID-19 when discussing SARS-CoV-2 rather than applying it indiscriminately to every related coronavirus.

proposedDescription: The sawtoothed grain beetle is a small stored-food insect found in grain, cereal products, and other dry goods. Adults and larvae can develop in stored material, so seeing a few beetles on a pantry shelf may point to an infested package nearby. In bulk grain, heavy infestations can contribute to heating and deterioration. The closely related merchant grain beetle often occurs in similar settings, and the two are easily confused.
identification: Adults are slender, flattened, brown beetles about three millimeters long. The sides of the segment immediately behind the head have a saw-like series of projections. Pale, flattened larvae may be mixed with food particles. Both grain beetle species have toothed sides, so this familiar feature identifies the pair more easily than the exact species. Under magnification, the region behind each eye is proportionally longer in sawtoothed grain beetles than in merchant grain beetles. A close, sharply focused adult photograph or preserved specimen is more useful than a picture of damaged food.
actions: Inspect nearby packages, including rarely used cereal ingredients and pet food, rather than treating only the shelf where adults appeared. Discard infested products in sealed waste, vacuum cracks and spilled material, and clean the storage area before restocking. Store replacement dry goods in tight containers that can be inspected easily. Avoid applying pesticides directly to food or food-contact surfaces. In a grain facility, have the insect confirmed and follow an established stored-grain monitoring and sanitation program. Continue checking after cleanup because another overlooked package can sustain the problem.
researchNotes:

proposedDescription: Soybean dwarf virus infects legumes and has been documented in U.S. forage plants as well as in research involving soybean. Its name can suggest that every infected plant will be conspicuously dwarfed, but symptoms and host relationships differ among virus strains. Studies in Illinois found the virus in several clovers, emphasizing that its ecology extends beyond a soybean field. It is distinct from soybean mosaic virus and from viruses sometimes described with similar stunt or dwarf names.
identification: Affected plants may show stunting, yellowing between veins, or discoloration of older leaves. Those changes are not a reliable field diagnosis: nutrient problems, herbicide injury, and other infections can look similar. A plant diagnostic laboratory can test appropriate samples. Aphid transmission is important, but the relevant aphid and efficiency depend on the virus isolate. Illinois experiments demonstrated transmission by Nearctaphis bakeri, while other work found that soybean aphids can transmit certain isolates inefficiently. An aphid on a yellow soybean plant therefore does not establish the virus or its source.
actions: Record the crop variety, plant age, distribution of symptoms, nearby forage legumes, and recent field treatments. Contact extension or a plant clinic before collecting samples so the submitted leaves are suitable for testing. Scout aphids using the local crop program, but do not assume that spraying them will cure an infected plant or reliably prevent this particular virus. Avoid removing surrounding clover habitat solely from a visual suspicion. Once a diagnosis is confirmed, discuss field-specific crop and vector decisions with the advisor and retain the result for future planting and monitoring plans.
researchNotes: Japanese DPV authors provide an independent biological lineage from Illinois field sampling. The later US transmission experiment qualifies the earlier soybean-aphid negative result. Advice is diagnostic and crop-specific, with no claim that spraying cures infection or that every isolate shares one vector.

proposedDescription: Duplachionaspis divergens is an armored scale associated with grasses, including ornamental grasses and sugarcane. It has been documented in Florida and other Gulf Coast states. A colony can be easy to overlook because the insects resemble small pale marks attached to a blade. Confirming the insect matters before linking it to thinning or yellowing grass, since turf and ornamental grasses can decline for many unrelated reasons.
identification: Female covers are white, elongated, and roughly oyster-shell shaped, reaching about three millimeters. Male covers are smaller and more uniformly narrow. Colonies occur along grass leaves. These features separate the insect from some rounder grass-infesting scales, but several white armored scales look similar. Photograph both sides of an affected blade and include an undamaged blade for comparison. The grass species, exact position of the colony, and a close view of several covers help a diagnostic service choose the right identification key.
actions: Inspect newly purchased ornamental grasses and sod before placing them beside established plants. Keep a suspect potted grass separate while an extension office or insect diagnostician checks it. In an existing planting, compare the location of live colonies with the damaged foliage and record whether the problem is increasing. Avoid treating every pale spot as an active insect: old covers can remain after the insect has died. If management is warranted, ask for guidance suited to the host and local growing conditions, including the timing of vulnerable young stages. Keep removed infested foliage contained and revisit nearby grasses after the initial response.
researchNotes: Cenicana describes independent Colombian sugarcane observations, distinct from the Florida Evans/Hodges detections and UF guidance. The account supports grass association and cautions that visible infestation need not mean measured yield loss; no overseas efficacy is imported.

proposedDescription: The scale historically called Eriococcus insignis is now treated in ScaleNet as Anophococcus insignis, with Acanthococcus insignis appearing in other references. It is a felt scale associated with grasses and a range of other plants. A New York population was originally described under the name Eriococcus saratogensis and later placed in synonymy. These name changes can make old records look like several different insects when they concern the same taxonomic concept.
identification: Adult females are elongate and dark red, with a tough yellowish to white felted egg sac. These features can help locate a colony, but other felt scales can look similar. Published hosts include bentgrasses, orchardgrass, and other grasses; host identity cannot settle the species. Reliable identification uses microscopic characters of a prepared female. Photograph the host, the occupied plant part, and several individuals before sampling. Keep roots or basal material associated with the correct plant when a diagnostician requests them, and avoid interpreting weak grass as proof of this scale.
actions: For an unfamiliar colony on a potted grass, keep the plant separate from other stock until identification is complete. In a lawn, meadow, or natural area, record the extent and condition of the host before deciding whether intervention is needed. Do not remove a whole grass community or apply a broad treatment solely because a scale insect is present. Ask extension staff or an insect collection how to preserve a small sample. Repeat photographs of the same plants can show whether the colony is increasing and whether damage actually coincides with it, helping distinguish an identification record from a management problem.

proposedDescription: Pittosporum eriococcin is a small felt scale described from California as Eriococcus pittospori and now generally placed in Acanthococcus. The original collection came from Pittosporum tenuifolium in San Francisco. A later illustrated collection was taken from Coprosma repens in the same city in 1973. These records help explain why a scale on pittosporum or Coprosma is worth documenting, but the host alone cannot identify it. Its original home remains uncertain.
identification: Adult females are reddish brown, with tan egg sacs that may look yellowish. Gill's California account places them mainly on bark and occasionally on leaves. Photograph several insects, their position on the plant, and the leaves and twigs needed to identify the host. Mealybugs and other felt scales can leave similar waxy material. A specialist examines features such as the body bristles and two bristles on each hind tibia under a microscope; the color of an egg sac is not a reliable identification on its own.
actions: Examine new pittosporum and Coprosma plants before introducing them to a hedge or collection. Keep a suspect container plant apart from other nursery stock while an extension office or county agricultural staff identifies the scale. Record whether new growth is affected and whether the colony is spreading, rather than assuming a few insects require treatment. If pruning is appropriate after diagnosis, contain the cut material and avoid distributing it as propagation stock. Ask for host-specific management advice before spraying a dense hedge, where unnecessary treatment can affect beneficial insects and still miss insects hidden within the foliage.

proposedDescription: Coniferous fiorinia scale is an armored scale found on several kinds of conifers. U.S. records include the mid-Atlantic region and California, where infestations have occurred on residential trees and nursery plants. Feeding can produce yellow stippling, needle loss, and reduced growth, although the severity varies. Its history includes confusion with other Fiorinia species, so reports based only on a host list or a common name need care.
identification: Inspect needles closely for attached scale covers, especially where yellow stippling is developing. Fir, cedar, pine, and hemlock are among the recorded host genera. Several armored scales can occupy conifers, and old covers can persist after an insect dies. Expert identification usually requires an adult female prepared on a microscope slide. Fiorinia externa, the elongate hemlock scale, is a particularly important comparison because historical host records have sometimes mixed the two. Photographs should show the whole affected branch, individual needles, and a close view of the covers.
actions: Check conifer nursery stock before planting and retain purchase information if a suspicious infestation appears. Ask extension or state plant-health staff how to submit needles with intact scales. Avoid moving infested nursery plants while identification is pending. On an established tree, determine whether scales are alive and whether needle loss is progressing before choosing treatment. A qualified arborist can help distinguish scale injury from drought, root problems, and other pests. Any management plan should protect neighboring conifers and include follow-up inspections, since a single visible cleanup does not establish that the infestation has ended.
researchNotes: CDFA original California detections and damage assessment plus independent taxonomic/host review support careful diagnostic actions. Modern critical review distinguishes F. externa host errors. No broadleaf host transfer or nationwide establishment assertion.

proposedDescription: Hypogeococcus pungens is a name that has been applied to several closely related South American mealybugs. Recent research distinguishes the narrow species associated with the amaranth family from a separate, still-unnamed cactus-feeding species with several lineages. A cactus-feeding member of this complex has harmed native cacti in Puerto Rico. That makes the identity especially important: a mealybug used against invasive cacti elsewhere should not automatically be treated as the same organism as the Puerto Rican pest.
identification: A wax-covered mealybug on a cactus is not enough for a species-level identification. Record the cactus species, the location of colonies, and any distorted or damaged growth. Photograph individual insects as clearly as possible without moving pieces of the plant to another site. Genetic and host-association studies have separated several lineages hidden under the traditional name. Similar appearance therefore does not establish that two populations have the same host range, geographic origin, or suitability for biological control.
actions: If an unfamiliar mealybug colony appears on native cacti in Puerto Rico or another sensitive cactus habitat, contact the relevant plant-health or conservation staff promptly. Keep infested cuttings and nursery plants from being moved or shared. Ask the receiving laboratory how to package a specimen so insects cannot escape. Avoid releasing predators, parasitoids, or additional mealybugs independently: biological control depends on matching the correct pest lineage and evaluating host safety. For a garden cactus, isolate the plant where feasible and obtain a diagnosis before selecting a treatment or discarding material near other cacti.

proposedDescription: Maskell scale is a tiny armored scale recorded from many woody plants in warm regions. Original specimen studies include insects collected on oleander in Bermuda and Jamaica, alongside a separate Queensland account. Its native origin remains uncertain. A broad host list does not mean every plant or U.S. location experiences serious damage. When inspecting a suspect plant, look for living insects and a matching pattern of injury rather than assuming every dark scale cover represents an active problem.
identification: Female covers are nearly circular, strongly domed, and almost black, with dark shed skins near the center. Male covers are smaller and more elongated. Beneath its cover, the female is pale. These features can help locate a suspect colony, but dark circular armored scales occur in several genera. The clavate scale and some Hemiberlesia can be confused with it. Species confirmation requires microscopic examination of an adult female, rather than simply matching the color of a scale cover.
actions: Inspect new woody nursery plants carefully before placing them among established plants. If you find unfamiliar dark scales, photograph the host, an affected branch or leaf, and several close views with a size reference. Keep a suspect container plant separate and ask a plant diagnostic service how to submit intact specimens. Record whether colonies are alive and expanding before arranging treatment. Avoid scraping every cover away before a sample has been examined, since useful diagnostic material may be lost. For a confirmed infestation, seek advice matched to the host and local conditions and check nearby plants after the initial response.

proposedDescription: Tea parlatoria scale is an armored scale found on tea and other woody plants. Dutch plant inspectors have identified it on imported boxwood, maples and other ornamentals from East Asia, illustrating how it can travel with nursery stock. An interception does not establish that the insect became established outdoors. Older U.S. reports also need care because related Parlatoria species have sometimes been confused. Its common name should not be used to identify every scale found on tea.
identification: The living female is a very small insect beneath a protective cover. A host name or a patch of attached scales cannot reliably distinguish tea parlatoria scale from its relatives. Parlatoria pergandii is a particularly close comparison, with separation depending on microscopic body structures such as a pocket near a breathing opening and the arrangement of pores. Photograph the plant and the occupied surfaces before sampling. Include several intact adult females if the receiving diagnostician requests them; immature insects alone may be less useful.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants apart from other stock and avoid sharing cuttings while identification is pending. Record the plant's source, date of purchase, and whether nearby plants have similar colonies. Check whether insects are alive and whether affected foliage is declining, because persistent covers can outlast the insects beneath them. Ask extension or plant-health staff for a species determination before selecting a control program. If a confirmed infestation requires pruning, contain the material rather than placing it beside other susceptible plants. Continue checking the original plant and its neighbors to judge the response instead of treating an old cover as evidence of continuing infestation.

proposedDescription: The scaly tunicate is a solitary sea squirt native to Australia and introduced to parts of the U.S. West Coast. It attaches to hard surfaces in harbors and coastal waters, including structures and vessel hulls. Many individuals can gather closely together even though each remains a separate animal. Dense fouling has affected shellfish culture in some invaded regions, making equipment and vessel movement important opportunities to prevent further spread.
identification: An individual resembles a small leathery pouch with two short siphons. The outer surface is wrinkled and often brown or reddish, sometimes hidden beneath algae or other encrusting organisms. When disturbed, the siphons contract and may become difficult to see. Similar sea squirts can be hard to separate in the field. Microcosmus exasperatus is a notable lookalike; examination of internal structures, including tiny siphonal spines, may be needed. Photograph the animal undisturbed, its attachment surface, and the surrounding aggregation rather than relying on a scraped fragment.
actions: Inspect boats, aquaculture equipment, ropes, and other submerged gear before moving between waterbodies. Arrange cleaning through facilities that capture removed fouling and wash water instead of releasing living material back into the harbor. Do not transfer shellfish or attached gear from a suspicious fouling site without checking applicable local guidance. Report a suspected new occurrence to a marine invasive-species program with the marina name, depth, substrate, and photographs. Leave sampling of unfamiliar sea squirts to an authorized collector when possible, because confirmation may require an intact specimen.

proposedDescription: This scarab relative is better known as Hybosorus illigeri. In 2021, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature conserved that name over older names including Hybosorus roei. The insect has been collected in Florida pasture surveys, but being caught near cattle dung does not establish that it feeds on dung or harms livestock. Research on the group includes predatory behavior by this species, so it should not automatically be treated like a root-feeding lawn grub.
identification: A small scarab-like beetle needs closer examination than a general body-shape match. Useful photographs show the head, antennae, legs, and both upper and lower body surfaces with a scale. Specialists compare these structures with other hybosorid and scarab beetles. Preserve the context of a sighting: a beetle attracted to a light, found in a trap, or seen on an animal provides different evidence. A grub found in nearby soil should not be assigned to this species simply because an adult was seen in the same yard.
actions: For an isolated sighting, photograph the beetle and leave surrounding habitat undisturbed. If many appear indoors, reduce entry through damaged screens and inspect the immediate entry point rather than treating the lawn. Where there is suspected plant or livestock injury, document the injury separately and ask an entomologist to determine whether the beetle is involved. Retain an intact specimen only as directed by the receiving service. Avoid broad insecticide use based on the word scarab or on an outdated name, since those shortcuts can lead to treating an unrelated insect or a harmless visitor.

proposedDescription: Scarlet firethorn is a thorny ornamental shrub native to Europe and temperate Asia. White spring flowers and clusters of red fruits make it a familiar hedge plant. Birds can carry the seeds away from gardens, and escapes occur in suitable habitats, including parts of California. Regional assessments differ in how they describe its risk: a prediction of invasion potential is not the same as proof of widespread damage at every planted site.
identification: Look for stiff woody branches with sharp thorns, small simple leaves, and dense clusters of small white flowers followed by rounded red fruits. Leaves may remain through winter in mild climates. Other Pyracantha species and horticultural hybrids can be similar, and cotoneasters can also carry red fruits. The presence of thorns is useful when comparing these shrubs, but leaf and fruit details still matter. Photograph a leafy twig, a thorn, flowers or fruit, and the whole plant before identifying an escape solely from its berries.
actions: Inspect areas beneath bird perches, fences, and nearby woodland edges for seedlings from an existing hedge. Wear sturdy gloves when working around the thorns. Remove confirmed young escapes while roots are manageable and contain fruiting branches so seeds are not scattered during transport. Before removing a large hedge, check for active nests and plan work around wildlife and access needs. If replacement is appropriate, choose a locally suitable shrub with lower escape potential. Revisit the site after removal to catch seedlings, and use regional advice rather than assuming all firethorn cultivars behave identically.

proposedDescription: The scarlet malachite beetle is a small flower-associated beetle introduced to North America from the western Palearctic region. Historical records place it in parts of the northern United States and southern Canada. It is also a conservation concern in Britain, illustrating why a species' significance depends on location. Finding an introduced beetle on a flower does not by itself show that the plant is being damaged or that control is needed.
identification: Adults have a metallic greenish or bronze background with conspicuous red markings on the wing covers. Other red-and-dark beetles can look similar, including other malachite beetles. Photograph the entire upper surface, the head, antennae, and the pattern along the wing covers with a size reference. A red beetle on a lily should not automatically be called scarlet malachite beetle, nor should this species be treated as a lily beetle without examination. The plant being visited and the date help an insect specialist interpret the sighting.
actions: For a beetle visiting flowers, observation and a clear photograph are usually the appropriate first steps. Note whether it is feeding on pollen, other insects, or plant tissue rather than inferring its behavior from where it landed. If actual damage is occurring, photograph the damaged tissue and look for the organism doing the feeding. Ask a local entomologist or extension service to confirm the beetle before any treatment. Avoid moving live beetles between gardens or releasing collected individuals elsewhere. In a native-range conservation setting, follow local habitat guidance rather than applying a North American introduction label.

proposedDescription: Scarlet mealybug, also called citrophilus mealybug, is a sap-feeding insect associated with citrus and other plants. It has a long history in California citrus, where natural enemies can keep populations low. A white waxy colony therefore deserves inspection rather than an automatic spray. Mealybugs can hide among closely touching fruit and protected plant surfaces, and their honeydew can support dark sooty mold.
identification: Adult females are oval and covered with white mealy wax. Bare or thinner areas of wax form dark lengthwise lines across the back. Short wax filaments fringe the body, with the rear pair longer than those along the sides. The insect can release red fluid when disturbed, but crushing it is unnecessary and destroys a useful specimen. Longtailed mealybugs and citrus mealybugs differ in filament patterns, while definitive identification may require microscopy. Photograph intact females and the colony's position on leaves, stems, or fruit.
actions: Inspect new plants and fruit clusters, and keep an infested container plant separate until the insect is identified. In citrus, conserve existing predators and parasitoids and address ants and excessive dust with advice suited to the orchard or garden. These steps can be more useful than repeated broad insecticide treatments that disrupt natural enemies. Record whether live colonies and fresh honeydew are increasing before deciding on further action. If a treatment is warranted, use a locally appropriate program for the confirmed species and host. Recheck sheltered fruit clusters afterward, since exposed insects may not represent the whole infestation.

proposedDescription: Scarlet tasselflower is a flowering herb with bright orange to red heads, often encountered as an ornamental. It belongs to a group of similar Emilia species whose names can be confused in gardens and weed records. In particular, Florida tasselflower, Emilia fosbergii, and lilac tasselflower, Emilia sonchifolia, are not interchangeable with this species. A red tassel-like flower is a useful clue, but it is not a complete identification. The cited Florida extension comparison reports that this exact species had not been documented there.
identification: Look at the leaves as carefully as the flowers. University of Florida comparisons describe Emilia coccinea as having bright orange-red heads and leaves that are not divided into the feather-like form seen in its close lookalikes. Photograph several lower and upper leaves, their attachment to the stem, and a fully open head. An image cropped tightly around one flower can conceal the most useful differences. Plants sold under a common name may also differ from spontaneous weeds appearing nearby, so compare both before assuming they are the same species.
actions: Keep an intentional ornamental planting within the garden and remove unwanted volunteers before mature seed is carried elsewhere. Collect spent heads and garden waste rather than dumping them at a natural-area edge. If an unfamiliar tasselflower appears in nursery stock or a restoration planting, ask a botanist or extension office to identify it from flowers and leaves together. Small unwanted herbs can be removed carefully without disturbing surrounding desirable plants. Continue checking the immediate planting area for new volunteers. Avoid applying the growth rates, seed counts, or regional weed status of another Emilia species to a plant identified only from flower color.
