proposedDescription: Scentless false mayweed, also called scentless chamomile, is a daisy-like weed of disturbed land and agricultural fields. Its finely divided foliage can make a young patch look delicate, but established plants compete with crops and can interfere with harvesting. Plants may behave as annuals, biennials, or short-lived perennials depending on conditions. Reproduction by seed makes preventing mature heads especially important.
identification: The leaves are green, hairless, and repeatedly divided into narrow segments. Flower heads have white outer rays surrounding a yellow center. Unlike strongly scented chamomiles and stinking mayweed, crushed foliage lacks a strong characteristic odor, though smell alone is not a dependable test. Similar white daisies can be distinguished by combining leaf shape with flower structure. In scentless mayweed the central receptacle is solid, whereas scented mayweed has a hollow receptacle. Photograph a whole plant, leaves, and a mature flower head before deciding what to remove.
actions: Remove small confirmed patches before seed matures, taking care to collect developing heads rather than scattering them. In a field, ask an agronomic advisor to match management to the crop and the stages of both crop and weed. Avoid allowing a few plants at field margins or equipment parking areas to replenish the seed supply. Clean soil and plant debris from machinery before moving to another field. Revisit treated patches because seedlings can emerge at more than one time of year. Where local rules apply, check the county weed program for the appropriate response rather than assuming every county requires the same control.
researchNotes: Ontario crop identification and King County field-management accounts independent; HRAC diagnostic comparison adds solid/hollow receptacle. No local legal status generalized nationally. Control focuses on seed and repeat emergence.

proposedDescription: Gremmeniella abietina is the fungus associated with Scleroderris canker, a disease of conifers that can kill shoots and damage nursery or plantation trees. Different strains have different histories and effects in North America. Red and Scots pine plantations are among the settings described in U.S. forest-health literature. A browning pine is not automatically infected, but a cluster of affected shoots deserves investigation before nursery plants or branches are moved elsewhere.
identification: Symptoms often become apparent in spring after infection occurred earlier. Needles on affected shoots may turn orange or brown and detach unusually easily. Shoot tips can die back, and a greenish stain may occur beneath infected bark. Small dark fungal structures may develop on stems or around needle bases. These signs overlap with other shoot diseases and environmental injury, so confirmation belongs with a plant pathology laboratory. Photographs should include the whole tree, the pattern of dead branches, and close views of needles and affected shoots.
actions: Contact a forest-health specialist, extension office, or nursery inspector when several conifers show similar unexplained shoot death. Ask how to collect an appropriate sample before cutting or shipping material. Keep suspect nursery lots separate and retain records of their origin and movements. Do not move affected branches, seedlings, or planting stock to another site while the cause is unresolved. Pruning, sanitation, and planting decisions should follow a confirmed diagnosis and local recommendations for the strain and host involved. Monitor neighboring trees through the next growth period rather than assuming removal of visible dead tips has eliminated the problem.
researchNotes: CFIA symptom description and USFS original forest-disease leaflet provide independent regional evidence. Older leaflet range statements not presented as current limits; strain-specific impacts retained. No fungicide recipe or diagnosis from color alone.

proposedDescription: Scotch broom is a European shrub that has escaped cultivation and spread through sunny disturbed ground, roadsides, pastures, and open woodland in parts of North America. Its bright yellow flowering display can conceal a persistent management problem: established shrubs are difficult to remove, and seeds can remain available for later germination. A newly found plant at the edge of an infestation is usually easier to address than an old, densely branched stand.
identification: Look for green, strongly angled stems that remain conspicuous even when leaves are sparse. Lower leaves usually have three leaflets, while upper leaves can be simple. The yellow flowers have the familiar pea-family shape, sometimes with reddish markings. Mature plants are woody shrubs rather than soft annual herbs. Other brooms and yellow-flowered shrubs can resemble it, so photograph the stem angles, lower and upper leaves, and flowers together. The combination is more useful than a distant image of yellow bloom.
actions: Confirm small new occurrences promptly and prevent plants from reaching seed production. Young plants are easier to remove with their roots, especially when the soil is workable. Minimize unnecessary soil disturbance, which can create new germination sites, and revisit cleared ground repeatedly. For mature shrubs, ask the local weed program about a method appropriate to stem size, season, and habitat; cutting and pulling do not have identical results in every situation. Keep seed-bearing branches contained during transport, clean equipment, and reestablish suitable vegetation where removal leaves large bare patches. Do not rely on a single visit as lasting control.
researchNotes: Montana extension identification/management and independent BC invasive council account support diagnostics and repeated control. Exact seed-longevity and regional legal claims omitted; native-range statement scoped to Europe.

proposedDescription: Scotch thistle is a large Eurasian thistle that can make pastures, roadsides, and access routes difficult to use. Its pale, woolly foliage and heavily armed stems distinguish a mature stand from many ordinary roadside weeds. Plants commonly begin as broad rosettes before producing tall flowering stems. Removing a young rosette is much less demanding than working through a mature spiny plant, and preventing seed production is central to long-term control.
identification: The leaves are broad, gray-green to whitish, and covered with dense hairs. Their margins are lobed or toothed and tipped with sharp spines. Wide, spiny wings run down the flowering stems, giving them a distinctive finned appearance. Purple to lavender flower heads develop at branch ends. Native thistles also have spines and purple flowers, so neither feature alone justifies removal. Compare the woolly leaf surfaces, broad stem wings, and overall growth form, and obtain help if the plant has not yet produced a stem.
actions: Wear protective gloves and clothing when working near confirmed plants. Dig or sever young rosettes below the crown before flowering, making sure leafy regrowth is not left behind. Collect mature or developing seed heads carefully and keep them out of loose compost or roadside brush piles. A single mowing may delay seed production without eliminating the plant, so inspect for regrowth. For a large pasture infestation, coordinate with a local weed specialist and restore competitive cover after control. Return in later seasons because the seed supply can outlast the visible plants.

proposedDescription: Scots pine is a Eurasian conifer widely planted in North America for landscapes, windbreaks, and Christmas trees. It has naturalized in parts of the United States, particularly in northern regions. Its role depends on the site: a maintained specimen tree is different from seedlings spreading into an open habitat that managers are trying to conserve. Naturalization alone does not establish the same ecological impact everywhere.
identification: The upper trunk and branches often have orange to cinnamon-colored, peeling bark, a particularly useful clue on mature trees. Needles are short, stiff, somewhat twisted, and blue-green, usually held in bundles of two. Cones are relatively small and may point back toward the supporting branch. Young trees are more regular in outline; older crowns can become open and irregular. Several native pines also have paired needles, so check bark, cones, and needle form together rather than relying on bundle count alone.
actions: If the tree is an intentional landscape planting, monitor its health and look for volunteer seedlings beyond the maintained area. Where seedlings are establishing in a meadow, dune, or other managed open habitat, confirm their identity with the land manager before removing them. Small unwanted seedlings are easier to handle than established saplings, and follow-up prevents a few survivors from becoming seed trees. Large-tree removal should be planned with a qualified arborist. Browning shoots may indicate disease or stress rather than a reason to label the tree invasive; seek a separate diagnosis before moving suspect branches or nursery plants.

proposedDescription: Scots pine blister rust is a fungal disease associated especially with hard pines in Europe and Asia. The name Cronartium pini now includes forms formerly separated as Cronartium flaccidum and Peridermium pini. One form alternates between pine and other plants, while another spreads directly between pines. This is different from assuming that all pine blister rusts have the same hosts or life cycle. A 2024 California assessment reports no North American disease records; older uncertain reports do not establish a current US occurrence.
identification: A suspect pine may develop diseased bark, resinous areas, and conspicuous rust spore structures, but those signs require expert interpretation. Other rusts, cankers, and insects can produce superficially similar damage. The pine species, the part of the tree affected, and the timing of visible spore production are useful diagnostic details. Do not identify this fungus simply because the host is a Scots pine. Laboratory work may be needed to establish the pathogen and distinguish its life-cycle form; nearby herbaceous plants alone cannot provide that answer.
actions: Photograph an unusual rust or canker without cutting and distributing infected material. Contact state plant-health or forest-health staff, particularly if the tree or nursery stock was recently imported. Keep purchase and shipment records available, and ask the receiving laboratory for sampling instructions before sending branches. Avoid moving suspect plants or propagation material to another site. Do not clear nearby wildflowers in an attempt to remove alternate hosts, because the diagnosis and life cycle may be different from what is assumed. A confirmed finding calls for an official, site-specific response rather than ordinary garden treatment.
researchNotes: Fresh review: The modern disease concept is clear. Current CDFA absence wording and older uncertain North American history are dated separately; no present US outbreak is asserted and diagnosis remains a laboratory task. proposedDescription: Scrambling nightshade, also called wetland nightshade or aquatic soda apple, is a sprawling prickly shrub that has invaded Florida wetlands. Long stems clamber through surrounding vegetation and can form difficult, tangled thickets. It occurs around cypress swamps, stream margins, and other wet habitats, although it is not a plant of permanently submerged conditions. Pieces of stem can establish new growth, so careless cutting and disposal can spread the problem.
identification: Leaves are alternate and longer than wide, with deeply wavy margins. Prickles occur on stems and leaf veins, and the plant has star-shaped hairs. Small white flowers have yellow anthers held together at the center. Clusters of pea-sized berries ripen from green through orange to bright red. Other prickly Solanum species occur in Florida, including tropical soda apple and red soda apple. Compare growth habit, habitat, leaf shape, and mature fruit rather than identifying it from a single berry. Do not taste the fruit.
actions: Report an unfamiliar prickly thicket in a wetland to the land manager or local invasive-plant staff. Wear protective clothing and avoid dragging cut stems through clean vegetation or water. Small confirmed plants may be addressable with their root systems, but a large tangled stand needs a plan that protects wetland plants and limits fragment movement. Keep all fruiting and stem material contained for suitable disposal. Clean equipment after working in the patch and check for rooted fragments and seedlings afterward. Any treatment near water should be selected by someone familiar with the habitat and applicable aquatic-use requirements.
researchNotes: UF identification compared with USDA federal weed diagnostic account. Stem regeneration and wetland context confirmed independently; no pesticide recipe or unsupported continuous-flood tolerance. Public reporting does not assert county presence.

proposedDescription: Sea hibiscus is a tropical coastal shrub or small tree also widely known as Hibiscus tiliaceus. Its broad leaves and large yellow flowers make it easy to notice along wet coastal margins. Regional origin needs care: Florida treatments distinguish the introduced variety tiliaceum from a related variety, pernambucense, native to Puerto Rico and parts of tropical America. Advice for an escaped Florida planting should not automatically be applied to every sea hibiscus population.
identification: Look for broad, heart-shaped leaves and large yellow hibiscus-like flowers; the Florida variety has a dark purple center. The leaves are arranged alternately, and their undersides can be softly hairy. Plants may become multi-stemmed and form dense growth near wetlands. Other tropical members of the hibiscus family can share heart-shaped leaves and yellow flowers, so document flowers, leaf undersides, and fruit where present. A photograph of leaf shape alone cannot reliably resolve a variety or distinguish every related coastal tree.
actions: Before removing a coastal thicket, confirm both its identity and regional status with a botanist or land manager. In a Florida landscape where the introduced variety is spreading, check the edges of the planting and nearby wet ground for new growth. Keep prunings and nursery waste out of natural areas, and prevent an intentional planting from expanding into adjoining habitat. Larger removal work should account for shoreline stability and the plants growing beneath or beside it. Where sea hibiscus is part of native or culturally important vegetation, decisions should follow local conservation guidance rather than a broad common-name label.

proposedDescription: Didemnum vexillum is a colonial sea squirt that can spread across rocks, shellfish, dock structures, and other submerged surfaces. Colonies consist of many tiny animals embedded in a shared covering. It has established on both U.S. coasts and can alter bottom habitats or foul aquaculture equipment. Genetic evidence points toward a northwestern Pacific origin, but the exact limits of its native range remain less certain than its introduced occurrence in North America.
identification: Colonies often look like cream, tan, or pale yellow sheets with irregular folds or hanging lobes. On suspended structures, extensions may resemble dripping wax. Tiny openings and darker channels can be visible across the surface. These features are useful for recognizing a suspect colonial tunicate, but native and other introduced sea squirts can look similar. Species confirmation requires a specialist examining colony structures, and sometimes genetic evidence. Photograph the colony in place, its attachment surface, and nearby growth before anyone scrapes it away.
actions: Inspect vessel hulls, ropes, cages, and other submerged equipment before moving them between sites. Use cleaning arrangements that capture fouling material and wash water, rather than releasing scraps into the water. Keep suspect aquaculture gear or shellfish at the site while consulting the relevant marine program. Report a possible new colony with clear photographs, a precise location, depth, and the type of surface occupied. Avoid collecting and transporting living fragments without instructions. For an established infestation, coordinate cleaning and follow-up with the facility or waterbody manager so isolated efforts do not simply move material to another location.

proposedDescription: Seashore vervain is an upright tropical American herb that has naturalized widely, including across the main Hawaiian Islands. Despite its common name, it is not restricted to a narrow strip beside the sea. In Hawaii it occurs in moist or wet pastures, disturbed forest, and other altered sites, where it can displace forage and native vegetation. The base may become somewhat woody as the plant persists.
identification: Leaves occur in opposite pairs, with successive pairs set at right angles. They are narrow, rough-textured, and coarsely toothed along the edges. Small blue, lavender, or purple flowers open along slender spikes at the ends of the branches. The plant can become tall and much branched, but individual flowers remain tiny. Other vervains have similar spikes, so photograph the entire branching pattern, several leaves, and the flower-bearing portion together. The common name vervain is too broad to confirm this species on its own.
actions: In Hawaii pastures or restoration areas, identify scattered plants before a larger patch develops. Remove small unwanted plants with their bases where that can be done without exposing large areas of soil, and keep developing seed spikes contained. Recheck moist disturbed edges and places where maintenance equipment enters the site. Maintaining suitable forage or native cover can reduce the bare ground available to new weeds. For extensive growth, ask local extension or conservation staff to choose a method appropriate to the surrounding vegetation. Do not assume livestock will suppress it adequately; Hawaii management guidance specifically notes that goats do not browse it.

proposedDescription: Seaside barley is a small annual grass associated with saline ground. It is native to the Mediterranean region and has been introduced elsewhere. The common names sea barley, barley grass, and Mediterranean barley have been used inconsistently for several Hordeum species, so an awned grass at the coast should not be assigned this name automatically. Its occurrence can also reflect the soil conditions of a site rather than establish that it is causing ecological damage.
identification: Plants form tufts with narrow blades and short, dense, bristly flower spikes. In the Flora of New South Wales treatment, the leaf collar has a short membranous ligule and lacks the clasping auricles found in some other grasses. Mature spikes break into units, each containing a group of three spikelets. The shape of the small glumes surrounding those spikelets is important for separating closely related barleys. Photograph the collar and whole spike, and retain mature material only if a botanist requests it. A seedling photograph alone is unlikely to be decisive.
actions: For an unfamiliar patch in a salt marsh or coastal grassland, seek identification before disturbing it, because native grasses and other barleys may be mixed together. In a maintained garden or path where a confirmed plant is unwanted, remove it before the spike breaks apart and contain the seed-bearing material. Clean footwear and equipment after working through mature awned grasses. Larger agricultural patches need advice matched to the crop and soil conditions. Avoid applying control recommendations for a different barley grass solely because the common names sound alike.

proposedDescription: Seaside petunia is a small, low-growing plant with miniature pink to purple trumpet flowers. It also appears in older references as Petunia parviflora. Its North American status deserves regional care: California botanical resources treat it as native, while Kew's global checklist places California and other U.S. areas in its introduced range. That disagreement makes automatic removal from natural habitat inappropriate without local botanical advice.
identification: The stems lie along or close to the ground and bear glandular hairs. Leaves are small, narrow to spoon-shaped, and attached without a distinct stalk. Each flower has a short funnel-shaped tube and a shallowly lobed opening. The capsule remains smaller than the surrounding calyx lobes. The modest flowers and creeping habit distinguish it from many large-flowered garden petunias, but small-flowered relatives can still be confusing. Photograph a flower from the side, the leaf attachment, and a developing capsule, using a ruler or another scale reference.
actions: If the plant occurs in a natural wash, shoreline, or other open habitat, record it and ask a local herbarium or botanist about its identity and regional status before removal. Avoid treating a native-status dispute as evidence of harm. In a container or cultivated bed where volunteers are unwanted, remove individual plants before mature capsules release seeds and keep garden waste contained. Check nursery labels carefully when choosing ornamental Calibrachoa, since a horticultural name or hybrid does not necessarily refer to this wild species. Preserve surrounding vegetation while addressing any confirmed garden escape.

proposedDescription: Carex diluta is a Eurasian sedge documented as introduced in Montana, including moist alkaline meadow habitat. It is not simply another name for every pale sedge in a wet pasture. Sedges are a diverse and important part of many native wetland communities, and this species can be difficult to recognize without mature fruit. A new observation is most useful when it includes a precise location and enough detail for a botanist to verify it.
identification: Plants form tufts with short rhizomes, upright stems, and mostly basal, narrow leaves that can look yellowish. The flower stalk carries several separated spikes: an upper male spike and lower female spikes. The leaf-like bract beneath the lowest spike can extend beyond the entire cluster. Mature fruits are enclosed in small, yellowish-green sacs called perigynia, with visible veins and a short beak. Those tiny structures, together with the subtending scales, are more diagnostic than the plant's overall grass-like appearance. Photograph a fruiting stalk and close views without dismantling the whole patch.
actions: Leave an uncertain sedge patch intact while obtaining identification, particularly in a wet meadow where trampling or digging can damage native plants. Mark the location and estimate the patch size so it can be found again when fruit is mature. A herbarium or state botanical program can advise whether a small voucher is needed and how to collect it legally. Avoid moving soil or divisions from an unidentified patch into a restoration planting. If the sedge is confirmed and removal is warranted locally, plan the work with the land manager and monitor the disturbed ground afterward.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Montana provides substantive local morphology and occurrence, while the independent world sedge checklist supports identity. Unmeasured ecological harm does not prevent a carefully scoped identification and reporting profile. proposedDescription: Senegal date palm is an African palm commonly planted for its arching fronds and clusters of leaning trunks. In southern Florida it has escaped cultivation and is assessed as invasive, while its role in its African native range is very different. A mature clump can occupy much more space than a young nursery plant suggests. New shoots and seedlings around an established planting deserve attention before they develop into difficult-to-access growth.
identification: Look for feather-shaped fronds held above slender trunks, often with several stems of different heights in one clump. Older fronds may hang beneath the green crown. Separate male and female plants produce flower clusters, and females can carry small oval fruits that turn orange-brown. Other date palms can look similar, especially as young plants or cultivated forms. Photograph the full clump, the base of the trunks, frond attachment, and fruit rather than relying on a single detached leaf. A palm specialist can help resolve uncertain landscape specimens.
actions: Where Senegal date palm is escaping in Florida, avoid planting it beside conservation land and inspect existing clumps for growth beyond the maintained area. Remove confirmed young volunteers while they can be handled without damaging adjacent native plants. Mature palm work is better left to experienced crews, particularly where crowded trunks and old fronds limit access. Keep fruit and removed plant material out of natural areas. Before clearing a large clump, confirm the identity and arrange a plan for safe removal, disposal, and follow-up. Choose replacement palms according to local habitat and regional escape risk.

proposedDescription: Sepi, Neurolaena lobata, is a tropical American shrub or subshrub also known by several regional names, including salve bush. Its native range includes Puerto Rico and much of the Caribbean and tropical mainland Americas. It has been introduced to Hawaii and other Pacific islands. That geography matters: a plant can belong to the local flora in one U.S. jurisdiction and be introduced in another, without those facts alone establishing the same management need.
identification: Look for a branching leafy plant with alternate leaves and clusters of small flower heads. Botanical descriptions record variation in leaf shape and margins, so the word lobata should not lead you to reject a plant merely because some leaves lack obvious lobes. Fine hairs, including glandular hairs, may be visible on young growth and leaf undersides. Photograph leaves from different parts of the stem, their arrangement, and mature flower heads. Several tropical daisy-family shrubs can resemble it, and common names such as salve bush are not unique.
actions: In native Caribbean habitat, obtain a botanical identification before removing an unfamiliar shrub. In a Pacific garden where it was deliberately planted, watch for seedlings or new plants beyond the maintained area and contain garden waste. If it appears to be spreading into nearby habitat, provide local conservation or extension staff with photographs, location, and planting history. Address small confirmed volunteers before they become woody, while preserving neighboring vegetation. Do not taste the leaves or use a common medicinal name as evidence that a plant is safe to consume. Identification and regional context should guide the response.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent range and Bahamian botany support the plant. Geographic native/introduced limits and lack of measured Pacific harm stay explicit; no medicinal or congener claims are needed. proposedDescription: Coffee senna, also called Senna occidentalis or formerly Cassia occidentalis, is an American plant now widespread in warm regions. It occurs around disturbed ground and agricultural areas. Its seeds can contaminate feed, and veterinary studies have documented serious poisoning in cattle and poultry. The common name coffee senna is not an invitation to use the seeds as a drink or home remedy.
identification: The plant is an upright herb or small shrub with compound leaves divided into several opposite pairs of leaflets. A conspicuous raised gland sits near the base of the leaf stalk. Yellow flowers develop in clusters, followed by long, narrow pods. Leaflet number, shape, and the position of the gland are useful when comparing it with other sennas, including sicklepod and Senna tora. Photograph a complete leaf attached to the stem, a close view of the gland, flowers, and mature pods. A yellow flower alone cannot distinguish the species.
actions: Keep suspect plants and seed-contaminated material out of livestock feed. If animals may have eaten contaminated feed or plants, contact a veterinarian promptly and retain a safely contained feed sample for investigation. Do not wait for visible illness before seeking advice about a credible exposure. Remove confirmed unwanted plants from feed-production margins before pods mature, and check equipment and stored material for contamination. In a garden, collect pods rather than scattering them during cleanup. Regional botanical advice can clarify whether a wild population is native or introduced locally; practical action should focus on the actual exposure or crop problem.
researchNotes: Botanical morphology supported by Flora Malesiana and tropical floras; original cattle/poultry toxicology independent. NCSU edible claims and weak older toxicity language rejected. Native American origin not converted into blanket U.S. nonnative status; no toxic doses.

proposedDescription: Serbian bellflower is a low, spreading perennial grown in rock gardens, borders, and along walls. It comes from the Balkan region and can expand through runners and trailing growth. A planting that starts as a small cushion may gradually occupy neighboring pockets of soil. Horticultural descriptions sometimes call that behavior invasive, but garden spread and demonstrated damage in U.S. natural habitat are different questions.
identification: Look for a mound of small, rounded leaves with slender stems spreading outward. The pale violet-blue flowers open widely into a star-like shape rather than remaining a narrow bell. Flowering stems can extend beyond the leafy mound and spill over a wall or container edge. Other low-growing bellflowers are similar, especially before bloom. Photograph an open flower from above and the side, the leaf shape, and the way stems arise from the patch. Keep cultivar labels if available, because flower color and habit can vary in cultivated plants.
actions: In a maintained garden, check the edges of the planting and lift or trim unwanted spread before it becomes woven through neighboring plants. Remove pieces carefully so the desired plants' roots are not torn out with them. Contain discarded divisions and rooted stems instead of dumping them at woodland or stream edges. If a bellflower is found well away from cultivation, record the location and seek identification before assuming it is this species. Revisit the edge after cleanup to find surviving growth. A manageable garden plant does not require broad treatment solely because it spreads, but repeated escapes merit local botanical advice.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Two independent garden institutions support recognition and spreading garden habit. The profile addresses containment of an unwanted planting, without converting horticultural spread into proven US natural-area harm. proposedDescription: Sericea lespedeza is an Asian perennial legume once widely planted for forage, erosion control, and wildlife cover. In parts of the central and eastern United States, it has spread into grasslands and other open habitats, where dense growth competes with native vegetation. Its deep root system and persistent seed supply make an established stand difficult to eliminate. Young plants and scattered outliers are valuable priorities before a larger patch forms.
identification: Stems are upright, leafy, and increasingly tough or woody near the base. Each leaf has three narrow leaflets with flattened hairs that can give them a grayish or silky appearance. The leaflets are wider toward the outer end and taper toward the base. Small cream-colored flowers with purple or pink markings occur in the upper leaf axils. Native bush clovers and low annual lespedezas can be confused with it, especially in mowed turf. Compare the erect perennial habit, leaflet shape, hairs, and flowers rather than using three leaflets as the sole clue.
actions: Avoid introducing seed into conservation grasslands, and inspect roadsides or equipment routes that border an uninfested site. Remove small confirmed plants with their roots where practical before seed production. For established stands, work with a local grassland or weed specialist on a multi-season plan suited to the surrounding native plants. Mowing, grazing, fire, and herbicides have different consequences depending on timing and habitat; none should be chosen from the common name alone. Clean machinery before leaving a seeding patch and monitor treated ground for both regrowth and seedlings.

proposedDescription: Serrated tussock is a South American perennial grass that has caused major pasture and native-vegetation problems in countries where it is established. Its dense tufts and abundant wind-moved seed make prevention important. U.S. records need particularly careful interpretation: some widely repeated records trace to contaminated seed shipments rather than confirmed growing populations. A suspected plant should therefore be documented and checked, not treated as proof that a state is already broadly infested.
identification: Plants form tight tussocks of very fine, stiff, rolled leaves. At the junction of blade and sheath, a small whitish, papery ligule is a useful feature. The open flowering panicle can have a purple tint and carries small awned fruits. Several native bunchgrasses and other Nassella species look similar when not flowering. Photograph the whole clump, leaf collar, flowering head, and mature fruit if present. Avoid pulling mature heads apart in the field, where loose seed could be scattered before the identification is resolved.
actions: For a suspected U.S. occurrence, contact state agriculture or a local weed specialist promptly and provide precise location information. Keep people and equipment from brushing through mature seed heads, and do not collect or mail living material without instructions. Retain the source information for any suspect seed mixture or ornamental grass purchase. Small confirmed incursions are best handled through a coordinated response that includes disposal and repeat inspections. Avoid assuming that a treatment described for a widespread Australian infestation is the right response to a possible first local detection.

proposedDescription: Sessile joyweed is a creeping herb of wet disturbed places, ditches, pond margins, and cultivated ground. It can also grow in less saturated soil, so its presence is not limited to standing water. Florida plant-health guidance describes introduced populations in the southeastern United States and notes that stems root at their joints. Both seeds and rooted pieces can contribute to movement, including through garden or aquarium material.
identification: The leaves are simple and opposite, with smooth margins and variable narrow to oval shapes. Stems often lie along the ground and produce upright branches from rooted nodes. Small white, papery flower heads sit directly in the leaf axils without a conspicuous stalk. That feature helps distinguish it from alligatorweed, whose flower heads are stalked. Other native and introduced joyweeds also occur in Florida, so use flowers, leaves, and fruit together. Mature fruit can project beyond the surrounding flower parts, a useful close-up feature for a botanist.
actions: Do not discard aquarium plants, cuttings, or garden waste into drains, ponds, or natural areas. If a suspected patch is found, photograph the flower attachment and rooted stems and ask local extension or plant-health staff to confirm it. Keep fragments contained during any approved removal; leaving pieces on damp soil can undermine the work. Inspect nearby drainage routes and the original planting or aquarium source for additional plants. For a larger wetland infestation, coordinate with the land manager before disturbing soil or vegetation. Follow local disposal instructions and revisit the site for new seedlings or rooted fragments.
researchNotes: FDACS directly read for Florida morphology/pathways; independent Australian flora confirms sessile heads and growth. No edible/medicinal advice; native origin cautiously not asserted. Current regulation not needed in public wording.

proposedDescription: The sevenspotted lady beetle is a European aphid predator that became established in North America after repeated introductions and an apparently accidental establishment in New Jersey. It can help suppress aphids in crops and gardens. At the same time, research and long-term observations have raised concerns about changes in native lady-beetle communities where introduced species become abundant. These two roles are compatible: a useful predator can still alter the community around it.
identification: Adults are rounded and domed, usually red or orange with seven black spots across the wing covers, including a shared spot near the front. Pale marks occur near the sides of the head. Spot number and pattern should be checked together with body shape because other lady beetles can be variable. Larvae look very different: they are elongated, dark, and active, with three pairs of prominent legs rather than a smooth adult shell. Photograph larvae as well as adults; unfamiliar larvae among aphids may be predators rather than plant pests.
actions: Leave naturally occurring lady beetles and their larvae undisturbed while assessing an aphid problem. Look for active feeding and changes in aphid numbers before deciding whether treatment is needed. Avoid broad insecticide applications that would remove many predators at once. Do not buy, move, or release sevenspotted lady beetles into new areas on your own. If you are recording lady-beetle diversity, take clear photographs of spot patterns and note the habitat and date. Supporting a varied garden and observing the whole predator community is more informative than trying to eliminate one introduced beetle wherever it appears.
researchNotes: Cornell biological-control account read directly; independent longitudinal community study supports ecological concern. No assertion that every native decline is caused solely by this species; no release recommendation. Historical commercial availability not repeated as current.

proposedDescription: Sewer vine is a twining Asian vine that has escaped into Florida vegetation. It can climb over shrubs and other plants, while stems touching the ground root at nodes and create new points of growth. It is closely related to skunkvine, Paederia foetida, and has often been confused with that species. Both the living vine and discarded stem pieces deserve attention when a patch is being managed.
identification: Leaves are opposite, with smooth margins and relatively long stalks. Small tubular flowers are pinkish to pale lilac with a darker throat. The foliage has a strong unpleasant odor when damaged, but smell does not separate sewer vine reliably from skunkvine. Mature fruit is more useful: sewer vine has flattened, papery, yellowish to orange fruit and winged seed structures, while skunkvine has more rounded fruit. Photograph flowers and fruit along with the leaves. A leafy vine without fruit may need specialist examination before a precise name is assigned.
actions: Avoid planting or sharing the vine, and inspect nursery material and moved soil for rooted fragments. For a small confirmed patch, trace stems to their rooted points before cutting so hidden connections are not overlooked. Cut climbing stems carefully and leave high portions to die in place when pulling would damage the supporting plants. Remove accessible root systems where practical, contain all fragments and fruit, and follow local disposal guidance. Larger infestations require a coordinated plan with repeated checks for resprouting and seedlings. Clean tools and equipment before leaving the site so node-bearing pieces are not carried into another planting.

UF Florida management account and independent Flora of China morphological treatment support identification and context. Florida flora key corroborates flattened fruit vs globose P. foetida. Historical introduction timing uncertain and omitted; no pesticide recipe.

proposedDescription: Shady woodsorrel is a small creeping perennial with yellow flowers and three-part leaves. Despite the common name, it also grows in lawns, gardens and disturbed open places. It is native to Australia and New Zealand, where it can be an ordinary part of the local flora. A plant reported elsewhere needs careful identification because several yellow-flowered woodsorrels have very similar foliage, and their native ranges and underground structures differ.
identification: Look for slender branching stems that spread along the ground, sometimes rooting where they touch it. Each leaf has three small, heart-shaped leaflets. The yellow flowers are followed by short, relatively broad capsules with a tapered tip. Fine hairs on stems and fruits, the small appendages at the leaf-stalk base, and ridges on mature seeds help separate it from related species. Unlike some garden oxalis, it does not produce bulbils. Photograph a flowering stem, a mature capsule and the leaf-stalk base; a leaf-only image rarely settles the identification.
actions: For a new patch, record its size and whether it arrived with nursery plants, lawn material or disturbed soil. Keep soil from the patch separate while seeking an identification. If removal is appropriate in a small bed, lift the creeping stems and rooted portions carefully, then check for remaining growth. Do not assume that advice for a bulb-forming oxalis applies here. In natural vegetation, have a botanist confirm the species before disturbing neighboring plants or making a broader control decision.

proposedDescription: Shaggy soldier, also called hairy galinsoga, is a short-lived annual weed of vegetable plots, nursery containers and other disturbed ground. Its small daisy-like flowers are easy to overlook, but a plant can begin replenishing the seed supply while it is still modest in size. Repeated attention to young plants is more useful than waiting for a large patch to develop. It is closely related to smallflower galinsoga, which often grows in similar places.
identification: Leaves occur in opposite pairs and have toothed edges. The upper stems and flower stalks carry conspicuous spreading hairs, including glandular hairs. Each tiny head has a yellow center and a few short white rays. Shaggy soldier generally has longer white rays than smallflower galinsoga, but hairiness and ray length should be checked together. Young Virginia copperleaf can look similar; its later leaves are alternate rather than opposite. Photograph the leaf arrangement, hairy upper stem and an open flower with a size reference.
actions: Remove seedlings before they flower and return regularly during the growing season. In vegetable beds, avoid leaving gaps where another flush can establish. Use clean mulch and inspect incoming nursery pots, including the soil surface and drainage area. Cultivation works best on very young plants; take care around crop roots and irrigation lines. Farms with persistent infestations can consider rotation into a competitive sod crop where that fits the operation. Choose any chemical treatment for the actual crop or ornamental planting rather than treating all garden beds alike.
researchNotes: Cornell weed synthesis supplies life cycle and cultural management; UF ornamental account and NC flora corroborate diagnostic traits. No edible or medicinal advice carried over.

proposedDescription: Shakeshake, or fuzzy rattlepod, is an upright herb or small subshrub with yellow flowers and conspicuously hairy seedpods. Botanical accounts record it as naturalized on many Hawaiian islands. Its wider native range includes tropical regions on more than one continent, so the meaning of an occurrence depends on the location. It is one of several plants called rattlebox, a shared name that is not enough to identify the species or choose a pasture-management response.
identification: Each leaf is divided into three broad leaflets, usually with spreading hairs on both surfaces. Young stems are also hairy. Yellow pea-shaped flowers occur in elongated clusters and may develop reddish or brown markings as they age. The inflated pods become tan to dark brown and remain covered with spreading hairs. This combination differs from simple-leaved rattleboxes such as showy rattlebox. Photograph a complete three-part leaf, the flower cluster and a mature pod from the side. Avoid opening pods over clean ground simply to hear the seeds rattle.
actions: Document whether plants are scattered through a pasture, concentrated in disturbed soil or growing beyond a cultivated area. Keep unidentified rattlepod material out of hay and feed until an agricultural adviser confirms what it is. For a small unwanted patch, contain mature pods and avoid carrying loose seed with clippings or soil. Review the site's grazing and vegetation cover with local extension before broader treatment. A historical report from another island is useful context, but your observation should include its own date, location and photographs.

The prior lack of US control trials is handled by conditional seed containment, without transferring another rattlebox toxicity claim. proposedDescription: Shamel ash is a large tree planted for shade, timber and landscape use. Native to Mexico and Central America, it has spread beyond plantings in places including Hawaii, where the university's weed-risk guidance advises against introducing it into new areas. Winged seeds allow new trees to appear away from the original planting. An isolated seedling is much easier to address than a mature tree beside a building or among native vegetation.
identification: The leaves are opposite and divided into several toothed leaflets, usually five to nine, with a single leaflet at the tip. Mature bark is gray or brown and becomes furrowed. Flowers are inconspicuous; female trees produce clusters of narrow, papery winged fruits. The tree may retain its foliage in warm climates. Several ashes have similar compound leaves, so include the twig arrangement, buds, leaflet margins and fruits in photographs. A single detached leaflet does not show the full leaf arrangement and can be misleading.
actions: Look around planted trees and nearby disturbed ground for seedlings, recording whether they recur over several seasons. Pull manageable seedlings where removal is appropriate, taking care not to damage surrounding roots or expose unnecessary soil. Have large trees assessed by a qualified arborist or land manager before removal. If cut trees or treated sites produce new growth, arrange follow-up rather than assuming the work is finished. Keep seed-bearing debris away from natural areas, and use local planting guidance when selecting a replacement shade tree.

proposedDescription: Sensitive plant is a low, prickly herb whose finely divided leaves fold when disturbed. That familiar movement makes it popular as a novelty plant, but it can also establish in lawns, roadsides and pastures in warm regions. Hawaiian accounts describe extensive naturalization, and Florida's current assessment predicts a high invasion risk. The moving leaves are a useful clue, not proof of identity: other sensitive plants can respond in a similar way.
identification: Slender stems trail or spread and often carry prickles. Each leaf has one or two pairs of secondary branches, with many small leaflets arranged along them. Rounded pink to lavender flower heads arise on stalks. The short, flattened pods occur in clusters and have bristly edges; mature pods break into seed-bearing sections. Photograph the stem prickles, the complete divided leaf and the pods. Do not identify a plant by repeatedly touching it alone, and avoid confusing it with native sensitive plants that share the same general leaf movement.
actions: Wear gloves when working around a patch and keep seed-bearing material from catching on clothing or equipment. Avoid planting it where local guidance discourages its use, especially next to natural vegetation. For an unwanted patch, confirm the species and plan removal before mature pods disperse. Check the area afterward for new plants. Pasture infestations deserve advice from local extension because prickly growth can interfere with use of the site. Do not introduce grazing animals specifically to control it or transfer old overseas treatment instructions to a different setting.

proposedDescription: Shasta daisy is a garden hybrid grown for large white flower heads with yellow centers. It is related to oxeye daisy, but the two names should not be treated as interchangeable. Different cultivars vary in size and form, and a planted clump is different from a population reproducing beyond a garden. Botanical records describe occasional garden escapes, while local guidance often makes a clearer distinction between this hybrid and the more widely invasive oxeye daisy.
identification: Plants have upright leafy stems and comparatively large daisy heads. The leaves are usually lance-shaped to elliptical with toothed edges; they are not as deeply cut as typical oxeye-daisy leaves. Cultivars may have extra rows of white rays or other altered flower forms. Native fleabanes tend to have many much narrower rays. Include the lower leaves, upper stem leaves, whole clump and flower heads in photographs. A nursery label is helpful, but an unlabeled escape may need specialist examination, especially where related daisies grow together.
actions: Check outside the planted bed for seedlings and record whether they persist without care. If the plant is unwanted, remove flower heads before seed develops and deal with the clump without dumping living plant material into natural vegetation. Confirm an escaped daisy before applying an oxeye-daisy control plan. Do not assume that every modern cultivar is sterile or that every white garden daisy has the same behavior. When replacing a planting near a restoration area, choose a locally suitable plant whose identity and spreading habit are clear.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Hybrid identity and recognition are supported independently. proposedDescription: The sheep blow fly is a metallic fly whose larvae can cause flystrike, a serious skin infestation of sheep. It is especially important in Australian and South African livestock systems; the mix of flies involved in North American cases differs. A green fly near an animal does not establish which species is present. The immediate priority when maggots are found on a living animal is veterinary care, followed by identification and prevention.
identification: Adults have a coppery to green metallic appearance and reddish eyes. Pale, legless larvae may be found in affected wool or tissue, but neither color nor a casual photograph reliably separates this species from other blow flies. Lucilia sericata is particularly similar, and research has documented identification difficulties and hybridization. Specialists use several microscopic characters and sometimes molecular testing. On sheep, irritation, discolored or damp wool and skin damage are reasons to inspect closely, even when the animal still appears to be keeping up with the flock.
actions: Contact a veterinarian promptly for suspected flystrike; do not delay care while trying to identify an adult fly. Increase checks during warm, wet conditions and pay attention to wounds or soiled fleece. Work with your veterinarian on shearing, cleanliness and an appropriate prevention plan for the flock. Keep treatment records and follow product restrictions for the animal and country involved. If samples would help identify the fly, ask how to collect and preserve them safely. Never apply household insecticide or an improvised treatment to damaged skin.
researchNotes: Morphology/hybrid study and NSW veterinary guidance support identification limits and welfare response; Merck distinguishes regional fly assemblages. Cornell synonym claim equating sericata/cuprina rejected. No Australian prevalence or drug protocol applied to US flocks.

proposedDescription: Shell ginger is a large, clump-forming ornamental grown for arching foliage and hanging flower clusters. It spreads locally through underground rhizomes and is also propagated by dividing them. Its appearance outside a bed deserves attention, but it should not automatically be treated like every invasive ginger. Florida's assessment currently lists this species as not a documented problem across its zones. Conditions and management priorities can differ elsewhere.
identification: Long, broad leaves are arranged alternately along leafy shoots; some garden varieties have yellow striping. The stems visible above ground are formed largely by tightly overlapping leaf bases, while the true spreading stems are underground. Flower clusters hang from the shoot tips. The pale, pink-tipped flowers open to reveal a yellow lip marked with orange or red. Photograph the entire clump, leaf arrangement and flowers when present. Foliage alone can be confused with other ornamental gingers, especially if the plant has recently been cut back.
actions: Inspect the edges of a cultivated clump for shoots appearing beyond the intended planting. Keep discarded divisions and soil containing rhizomes out of ravines, waterways and natural vegetation. If removing an unwanted clump, account for the underground rhizomes and monitor for surviving shoots rather than relying only on cutting leaves. For an apparent wild population, record whether plants are connected to a nearby garden and ask for local identification and status guidance. Do not copy a control prescription for kahili ginger or another ginger species without confirming that it fits this plant.
researchNotes: NParks supports rhizomes, flowers and foliage; UF assessment independently documents current Florida conclusion. No claim of harm extrapolated from clump growth or other ginger species.

claims: Rhizomes, alternate leaves, hanging flowers and division.
Not a documented problem species in Florida zones.

proposedDescription: Shepherd's purse is a small annual mustard common in disturbed soil, garden beds and agricultural ground. Many plants begin as a low rosette in cool weather, survive winter and send up flowering stems the following season. The distinctive seedpods explain the common name: they resemble tiny flattened purses or hearts. A few scattered plants are usually a straightforward garden-management issue, while repeated seed production can keep a patch returning.
identification: The basal leaves form a rosette and become variably lobed as they develop. Slender stems carry smaller leaves and tiny white flowers. Below the newest flowers, flat triangular to heart-shaped pods stand out on narrow stalks, with the narrow end toward the stalk. Young rosettes can resemble dandelions and other mustards, so look for flowers and pods before deciding. A hand lens may reveal branching hairs on the leaves. Photograph the full rosette and a fruiting stem rather than relying on the shape of one damaged leaf.
actions: Check beds in autumn and again in early spring so rosettes can be addressed before seed matures. In a small planting, loosen the soil around the taproot and lift the plant carefully; pulling only the slender flowering stem may leave the root behind. Keep mature pods from spilling into clean soil. Maintain appropriate cover or mulch where repeated disturbance leaves an opening for new seedlings. In nursery or crop settings, choose management around the cultivated plants and the local growing season. Revisit the area after the next flush of germination.
researchNotes: Penn State supplies seasonal rosette and taproot management context; Ontario and Texas botany independently support fruits, hairs and leaves. No medicinal/edibility claims or product rates included.

claims: Cool-season annual rosette, taproot and nursery context.
Seed propagation, rosette and stellate hairs.

proposedDescription: This small shield-backed bug was documented as established around Homestead in southern Florida after collections in 2001. The original report linked adults and young bugs to false mallow, Malvastrum corchorifolium, where they fed on the fruits. It was already known from the Caribbean. That history helps explain an identification, but a past collection does not show that the insect is currently present at every nearby site or that it damages unrelated garden plants.
identification: Adults are roughly eight to ten millimeters long, with a pale yellow to reddish-brown back covered in darker punctures. A pale line runs along the middle of the back, and the antennae have contrasting pale and dark sections. The head is relatively narrow and strongly convex. Similar Diolcus species occur in Florida, and an expert may need to examine the antennae, head and underside. Take sharp photographs from above and from the side, include a scale, and record the plant on which the insect was actually observed feeding.
actions: If you find an unfamiliar cluster, note whether both adults and immature bugs are present and photograph the host plant's leaves, flowers or fruits. Send the observations to extension or a regional entomology collection for confirmation. Avoid spraying nearby plants solely because a shield-backed bug is present. If damage is occurring, document the affected tissue separately so a reviewer can assess the relationship. Keep any requested specimen contained and labeled; do not move live insects or their host material to another site for comparison.

proposedDescription: The shiny spider beetle is a tiny scavenger associated with dry stored materials. Its rounded body and long legs can make it look more like a spider than a beetle. Museum pest specialists recognize it as a potential collection pest, but finding one does not show that a whole collection or pantry is infested. The useful next step is to identify the insect and locate the material it came from.
identification: Adults are roughly 3-4 millimeters long, with a smooth, glossy, reddish-brown to dark abdomen and a contrasting yellowish head, thorax and legs. The long antennae are hairy rather than ending in an obvious club. Look for six legs and antennae, which separate a beetle from a spider. Other Mezium species can be very similar, particularly the American spider beetle. Save a close photograph with a scale and, if practical, an intact specimen in a closed container for an entomologist.
actions: Inspect the nearby dry goods or stored collection rather than spraying the room after a single sighting. Keep suspect packages separate from clean material and look for additional beetles, larvae or damage. Spider beetles as a group can persist in overlooked residues, dead insects and old animal nests, so a recurring problem may have a source outside the first package you find. For museum objects, ask a conservator about treatment before freezing, heating or applying anything to the object. Record where and when each insect was found to help narrow the search.

proposedDescription: Lyrodus takanoshimensis is a shipworm: a marine clam with a long, soft body that lives inside wood. The small shells at its front end help it excavate a tunnel, while the rest of the animal remains sheltered within the timber. Despite its name and wormlike appearance, it is a bivalve. A damaged piling or piece of driftwood cannot be assigned to this species simply because shipworm tunnels are present. A 2026 study sequenced an identified Japanese specimen; that finding does not confirm a US population.
identification: A complete specimen and specialist examination are usually needed. Shipworms have paired siphons at the exposed end of the burrow and small structures called pallets that help close its opening. Those features are useful to a marine taxonomist, whereas the hole visible on a timber surface is not enough. Photograph the wood, its setting and any naturally exposed animal without cutting into a working dock or other structure. Include whether the wood was fixed in place, floating or recently transported.
actions: Do not move suspect wet timber or driftwood to another marina while seeking advice. Tell the harbor operator or marine invasive-species program where it was found and whether there is structural damage. Leave inspection of load-bearing wood to a qualified professional. Keep dated photographs and details of any recent timber movement, which can help an investigator distinguish a local occurrence from transported material. Ask how to submit a specimen before removing or shipping wood. An intact animal is more useful for identification than loose fragments, and collection should not compromise a dock or damage neighboring marine life.

proposedDescription: Shoebutton ardisia is an evergreen shrub or small tree introduced to Florida as an ornamental. Birds eat its dark fruits and can carry the seeds into nearby vegetation. In invaded Florida habitats, dense growth can crowd the understory and shade other plants. Its behavior there differs from its role in its native Asian range, where it is part of coastal vegetation. Location matters when deciding what an observation means.
identification: Look for alternate, leathery, oval leaves with smooth edges and reddish new growth. Small pink to mauve flowers grow in clusters from the leaf angles along the branches. The rounded fruits change from reddish purple to black. Florida's native marbleberry, Ardisia escallonioides, is an important lookalike: its flowers are white and grouped at the branch tips rather than in the same pink-flowered side clusters. Photograph the flower placement, leaf margins and fruits together before removing an unfamiliar ardisia.
actions: Avoid planting or sharing shoebutton ardisia in Florida, where UF's current assessment lists it as prohibited. If it is already present, check shaded ground around fruiting plants for seedlings and document how far they extend beyond the planting. Small confirmed seedlings can be removed carefully before they fruit; contain berries so cleanup does not scatter seeds. Larger shrubs and infestations in wetlands need a site-specific plan from the land manager or extension service. Revisit the area for new seedlings rather than judging success by the disappearance of the original shrub alone.
researchNotes: UF plant directory/assessment provides Florida impact, native lookalike and regional restriction; NParks independently documents morphology and native-range ecology. Florida prohibition is regional, not a national claim.

proposedDescription: Shortfruit storksbill is a small annual of disturbed ground, native to parts of the Mediterranean region and Canary Islands. Botanical records list it as introduced in several US states, including California and Oregon. It belongs to a group of similar storksbills whose long fruit beaks are often more useful for identification than their flowers. The common name can be misleading: the complete fruit, including its beak, is not especially short.
identification: Plants grow low or ascend to about 30 centimeters. Lower stems have stiff whitish hairs, while upper parts can carry glandular hairs. The basal leaves are deeply divided, with toothed smaller divisions. Flowers occur in small clusters, commonly one to four, and the mature beaked fruit can measure roughly 6-9.5 centimeters overall. Fine details on the individual seed-bearing segments help distinguish related species. Photograph a whole basal leaf, stem hairs and a mature fruit beside a ruler; keep the fruit attached when possible.
actions: For an unfamiliar patch, record whether it occupies a lawn edge, cultivated soil, roadside or natural grassland. Ask a local herbarium or extension botanist to confirm it before assigning a regional impact or treatment priority. If confirmed plants are unwanted in a small managed bed, removing them before mature fruits disperse is a practical first step; avoid carrying seed-bearing debris to another site. Return after the next period of growth to check for seedlings. A state-level botanical listing is useful context, but it does not establish presence in every county.

proposedDescription: Shortpod mustard, also called summer mustard, is a branching yellow-flowered plant of roadsides, grasslands and disturbed shrublands. Unlike some annual mustards, it can survive for more than one season. In California, rapid growth and shading can interfere with native vegetation, including in recently burned areas. Cal-IPC rates its regional impact as moderate. Its persistence means that a patch deserves follow-up even after flowering stems have been cut.
identification: Look for soft-haired, deeply lobed lower leaves and numerous small yellow flowers with four petals. The most helpful feature is the fruit: short, narrow pods, generally less than 1.7 centimeters long, lie close against the flowering stem. Black mustard has a different overall stature and fruit combination, so a yellow flower alone is not enough. Photograph the lower leaves, branching habit and a section of stem bearing mature pods. Young rosettes are easier to confuse with other members of the mustard family.
actions: Start with small outlying plants before they add more seed to clean ground. Where hand removal is appropriate, work when soil conditions allow the rooted plant to be lifted without unnecessary disturbance to neighboring vegetation. Collect seed-bearing stems rather than spreading them with mowing equipment. Recheck treated ground for surviving crowns and new seedlings. For extensive roadside or post-fire infestations, coordinate with the land manager and use a restoration plan that also protects recovering native plants. Grazing or a single mowing should not be assumed to eradicate an established patch.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC assessment/profile and UC management notes support California context and control planning. UC discussion distinguishes evidence from speculative grazing suggestions; no grazing efficacy or treatment rate asserted.

claims: Short appressed pods, perennial persistence, disturbed habitats and California impact.
Species-specific management context and need for follow-up.

proposedDescription: Shortspike canarygrass is a tufted annual grass with a compact, egg-shaped flower head. It is native to a broad region from Macaronesia and the Mediterranean toward Iran. Several canarygrasses occur outside their native ranges, but they differ greatly in growth form and behavior. This species should not inherit the wetland impacts or rhizome-based management advice often associated with perennial reed canarygrass. Its identification begins with the mature flowering head. A 2016 USDA assessment reports California naturalization while questioning a Texas record.
identification: The upright stems can reach roughly 30-90 centimeters. A membranous flap, or ligule, sits where the leaf blade meets the sheath. The dense head is usually about 1.5-4 centimeters long. Identifying it among annual canarygrasses requires a close look at the tiny units within that head: the outer scales have winged keels, and the reduced sterile scales are only about one-tenth to one-fifth as long as the fertile scale. A grass specialist may need a mature sample. Photograph the whole tuft, ligule and head with a scale rather than relying on the oval outline alone.
actions: Note whether the grass grows among crops, in disturbed soil or near a planting or seed source. Avoid moving mature heads or soil from a suspect patch while the identification is checked. In a small managed bed, confirmed unwanted annual plants can be removed before seed matures, followed by checks for another flush. Larger agricultural infestations need advice suited to the crop and local conditions. Report a new wild occurrence with its precise location; a photograph of an unidentified canarygrass does not establish this particular species.

proposedDescription: Graphium euwallaceae is a microscopic fungus associated with the polyphagous shothole borer in California. Researchers recovered it from beetles and their tunnels in several tree species, including avocado and California sycamore. It is one member of a beetle-fungus association, not a diagnosis that can be made from a dark mark on bark. The practical concern for a tree owner is recognizing a possible infestation and arranging an appropriate inspection. An independent German greenhouse study confirmed the fungus with morphology and four genetic markers in 2026.
identification: There is no reliable leaf, bark or garden photograph that identifies this fungus by itself. Tree symptoms can include small borer holes, staining, gummy deposits or dying branches, but other causes can produce similar damage. Record the tree species, the position of affected branches and when the change first appeared. Take both a whole-tree photograph and close views of the damaged area. Identification of the fungus requires laboratory work; naming it from a beetle sighting alone would be too specific.
actions: Contact a local tree-health specialist or extension office with those details. Keep suspect firewood and pruning debris at the affected site until its handling has been discussed. If branches threaten people or structures, arrange a professional safety assessment rather than collecting a sample yourself. Ask the diagnostic service how it wants samples packaged before sending wood. Treatment decisions should address the confirmed tree and beetle problem as a whole. A record of this fungus should include the laboratory result and collection location, not only a photograph of general dieback.

proposedDescription: Paracremonium pembeum is a fungus associated with the polyphagous shothole borer. Researchers first described it from California beetle tunnels and tested it on cut shoots. A separate Israeli avocado experiment found that it did not persist in living wood as the principal Fusarium associate did, although it remained viable in dead wood. identification: The organism cannot be identified from the color of a trunk stain or the shape of a dying leaf. The original species description used microscopic features and genetic comparisons. For a suspected tree problem, photograph the entire crown, affected branches and any small holes or deposits on the bark. Note whether damage is limited to one branch or is progressing through the tree. Keep the observed symptoms separate from the proposed fungal name when submitting a report so the reviewer can consider other explanations.
actions: Arrange an assessment through extension, an arborist or a plant diagnostic laboratory. Ask which branch or tissue is useful for testing and how to contain it. Keep dated photographs so changes can be compared during follow-up. Any pruning, removal or other treatment should follow the confirmed diagnosis; a suspected fungal name alone is not a reason to remove a healthy tree.

proposedDescription: Annual baby's-breath is a small flowering plant grown in gardens and included in some flower-seed mixtures. identification: Plants commonly reach about one to two feet, with slender branching stems and opposite, narrow leaves. If fruit is present, include it without scattering the seeds. The delicate branching habit alone is not enough to separate it from related ornamental species or cultivars.
actions: Check the scientific name on seed packets and record whether an observation is inside a planted bed or beyond it. If an unwanted patch is confirmed, remove annual plants before the capsules release seed and watch the surrounding soil for seedlings. Avoid dumping flower arrangements or garden waste in natural areas. For a suspected new escape, send the location and photographs to a local botanist rather than assuming an invasive designation. proposedDescription: Showy rattlebox is an introduced yellow-flowered plant of open fields, roadsides and disturbed agricultural ground in the southeastern United States. It was historically planted for soil improvement, but escaped plants can compete with pasture vegetation. Its greatest practical concern around livestock is toxicity: plant material can remain dangerous after drying and may enter hay or contaminated feed. A flowering patch near a pasture deserves prompt identification and attention.
identification: Look for upright, ridged stems and alternate leaves that are single blades, rather than divided into three leaflets. The leaves broaden toward their tips and are hairier underneath. Bright yellow pea-shaped flowers grow in long terminal clusters and may have dark reddish lines. Inflated pods, roughly one to two inches long, darken as they mature and can rattle when dry. Photograph an entire leaf, the flower cluster and the pods. Several unrelated plants share the name rattlebox, so the common name alone is not enough.
actions: Keep suspected plants and contaminated clippings out of animal feed. If horses or other livestock may have eaten them, contact a veterinarian promptly and provide photographs or an identified sample; do not wait for obvious illness. Check hay and seed sources as well as the pasture itself. For a confirmed patch, arrange removal before mature pods scatter, and prevent cut material from becoming accessible to animals. Larger infestations need a pasture-management plan suited to the site and grazing schedule. Recheck after treatment for seedlings rather than relying on one cleanup.
researchNotes: UF veterinary publication supports persistent toxicity and cumulative liver injury; NC extension independently supports morphology, disturbed-field occurrence and feed/equipment pathways. No dose, universal legal status or unsupported eradication promise included.

proposedDescription: Shrubby lespedeza is an East Asian shrub introduced for purposes including erosion control and wildlife plantings. It can spread beyond those plantings into open ground and woodland edges, where dense growth interferes with other vegetation and young trees. Its woody structure separates it from the smaller bushclovers that may grow nearby. A planting that once served a practical purpose can therefore need attention when seedlings begin appearing in surrounding habitat.
identification: Look for arching, branching stems growing from a woody base and alternate leaves divided into three broad oval leaflets. The leaflets are paler underneath and end in a small hairlike point. Pinkish-purple and white pea-shaped flowers appear in loose clusters, followed by small flattened pods. Related ornamental lespedezas can resemble it, and hybridization may blur the differences. Photograph a complete leaf, the flower cluster and the base of the shrub. Avoid identifying every three-leafleted plant as this species; native bushclovers share that general feature.
actions: Check beyond an old hedge or wildlife planting for young plants, especially along disturbed edges. Remove small confirmed plants where that can be done without damaging nearby native growth. Established shrubs can regrow after cutting, so plan follow-up before starting a large clearance. Prevent further seed production and revisit cleared areas over several seasons. The Forest Service notes that control studies are limited and a persistent seed supply can complicate recovery. For larger sites, work with the land manager on a plan that restores desirable vegetation as well as reducing the shrub.
researchNotes: NC extension supports identification and invasion context; Forest Service FEIS independently synthesizes seed persistence and limited control studies. Related L. thunbergii traits are not treated as diagnostic for all bicolor plants.

proposedDescription: Whitehead broom, also called shrubby false buttonweed, is a perennial with small white flower clusters along its stems. It has become troublesome in some south Florida pastures and hayfields, even though UF's broader natural-area assessment does not currently classify it as a documented problem species. Those accounts address different settings. A plant can be difficult to manage in a working pasture without having the same effect in every habitat where it grows. Authorities also disagree about whether it is native to Florida, so that regional status needs separate review.
identification: The plant branches repeatedly, and stems can root where their nodes contact the ground. Narrow, smooth leaves occur in opposite pairs or appear clustered around the stem. Tight groups of tiny white flowers sit at the nodes rather than forming large showy blooms at the branch tips. Photograph a flowering stem close enough to show the leaves and flower positions, plus the whole patch. Other buttonweeds are easy to confuse with it, so a clear view of the growth form helps a reviewer.
actions: In a pasture, note the size of the patch and whether it is spreading after mowing. Clean mowing equipment before entering an unaffected field; mowing alone offers only temporary relief and can redistribute seed. Discuss a site-specific plan with an agricultural adviser because regrowth has followed several tested treatments, and forage species affect the available choices. Whitehead broom also supplies nectar for Larra wasps, so blanket eradication is not automatically the right goal. Prioritize the actual pasture problem, prevent spread and revisit treated patches to check the outcome.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent Kew taxonomy complements UF pasture research while exposing a Florida-origin disagreement. proposedDescription: Paniculate fuchsia is a large ornamental shrub or small tree from Mexico and Central America. Instead of the familiar large hanging flowers of many garden fuchsias, it carries sprays of much smaller rosy-purple blooms. Kew lists introductions in places including California and Hawaii. That broad distribution record does not tell us whether a particular plant was cultivated, escaped or forming a persistent wild population, so the setting of an observation matters.
identification: Look for reddish stems, large glossy lance-shaped leaves and branched clusters of small pink to purple flowers. The flowers have backward-bending sepals and are followed by purplish fruit. Plants can grow well above head height in suitable conditions. Related tree fuchsias and garden hybrids can be similar, so include the entire flower cluster and a close view of a single bloom in your photographs. Record the leaf arrangement and any nursery label as well; a distant image of a pink-flowered shrub may not resolve the species.
actions: If you find it beyond a garden, note the distance from the nearest planting and whether there are younger plants of different sizes. Photograph fruiting branches and the surrounding habitat without spreading fruit or cuttings elsewhere. A local herbarium or invasive-plant program can help determine whether the occurrence is new or significant. Where an unwanted garden escape is confirmed, start with small plants and monitor the surrounding area. Do not assume that the management advice or ecological effects reported for a different fuchsia apply to this one.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent horticulture and taxonomic range support recognition and reported introductions.
