proposedDescription: Bush morning-glory is a tropical American perennial grown for its large pink flowers. Unlike many familiar morning-glories, it can form a woody shrub, although branches may sprawl or climb. It has escaped cultivation in Florida, where it is prohibited and can occupy both terrestrial and wet settings. Its attractive flowers should not obscure the importance of checking the plant's local status before moving cuttings or adding it to a garden.
identification: Look for long-stalked alternate leaves, woody hollow stems and clusters of pale pink to purple trumpet-shaped flowers with a darker throat. The leaves vary from oval to lance-shaped and may have a heart-shaped base. Dry capsules contain conspicuously hairy seeds. Growth form and the complete combination of leaves, stems and flowers are more useful than flower color alone. Photograph a branch with its leaf attachments and a close view of the flower. Avoid damaging a wetland bank simply to inspect a stem.
actions: Do not plant or share it in Florida. If it appears beside a ditch, pond or natural area, record its location and whether stems extend beyond an old planting. Keep pruned pieces and seed-bearing material out of waterways and garden-waste dumps; the plant can be propagated from cuttings. Ask the land manager or local extension service about a containment plan before disturbing a large patch. Keep seeds away from livestock and pets. Treatment around water needs to suit that setting, and follow-up is important before assuming the rooted plant has been removed.
researchNotes: NParks supplies morphology and propagation; USF FLIP/FNAI and UF assessment support Florida escape and prohibition. Hairiness varies among accounts, so not made absolute. No unsupported nationwide native/exotic assertion.

proposedDescription: Siamese cassia, or kassod tree, is a yellow-flowered Asian tree planted widely for shade and ornamental use in warm regions. Older records often call it Cassia siamea. It can become a substantial tree with a dense crown, so an occurrence should be described as a planted tree, nearby seedling or wild-growing stand rather than simply marked present. Those distinctions help explain whether the tree is reproducing beyond cultivation at a particular site.
identification: Leaves are arranged alternately and divided into paired, oblong leaflets. Bright yellow flowers occur in clusters, often gathered into larger groups near branch tips. The fruits are long, flattened pods containing numerous seeds. Botanical accounts describe the leaf stalk and central leaf axis as lacking the conspicuous glands found in some other sennas. Photograph a complete leaf, the flower cluster and a mature pod with a size reference. A close-up of one yellow flower is unlikely to separate it from the many related ornamental trees.
actions: If seedlings are appearing outside a planting, record their number, approximate sizes and distance from the parent tree. Check disturbed edges and drainage routes after fruiting. Keep seed-bearing prunings out of unmanaged areas, and seek a local identification before deciding on removal. Small unwanted seedlings are easier to address than established trees; large-tree work should be planned with a qualified arborist and the property owner. Do not transfer treatment advice from another Senna species solely because both have yellow flowers. A dated series of observations will be more useful than an unsupported claim that every planted tree is invasive.
researchNotes: Fresh review: ICRAF supplies independent species morphology beyond the NParks account. Seedling monitoring and appropriate tree work are conditional practical advice, not claims of a tested US invasive-control protocol. proposedDescription: Siberian elm is a fast-growing Asian tree widely planted for its tolerance of difficult conditions. Wind-carried seeds can produce many seedlings along roads, streambanks, grasslands and other open sites. In parts of the United States, these recruits form dense growth that displaces other vegetation. An established shade tree and a spreading population around it present different management decisions, especially where removing a large tree could affect buildings or people.
identification: Look for relatively small, alternate, oval leaves with pointed tips and toothed edges, along with gray-brown furrowed bark. Small greenish flowers appear before the leaves, followed by round papery winged fruits with a notch at the tip. Native elms often have larger leaves and more noticeably uneven leaf bases, but leaf size alone is not reliable. Photograph a twig with several leaves, the bark and any fruits. Chinese elm has a different flowering season and should not be treated as the same tree simply because a nursery label says elm.
actions: Check nearby open ground for seedlings, especially after a seed crop. Small confirmed seedlings can be pulled while the root system is manageable; protect neighboring native seedlings during the work. Plan removal of larger trees with a qualified professional, including how to address regrowth and replace useful shade where appropriate. Wisconsin lists the species as restricted with stated exceptions, but rules differ elsewhere. For a wild population, share the location and photographs with the land manager and revisit cleared ground for new seedlings before considering the work finished.
researchNotes: Wisconsin DNR provides regional ecology/control and OSU independently confirms tree form, alternate small leaves and weak wood. Tooth-count disagreement in Nebraska account avoided; Wisconsin exceptions not generalized nationally.

proposedDescription: Siberian peashrub is a hardy Asian shrub or small tree long used in northern windbreaks, hedges and wildlife plantings. It can escape into woodland edges, forests and other habitats beyond those plantings. Its pods release seeds as they ripen, creating new plants around an established hedge. The concern is not simply that a shrub survives a cold winter, but that it begins replacing the vegetation outside the area where it was planted.
identification: Each alternate leaf is divided into several pairs of oval leaflets, commonly eight to twelve leaflets in total, without a terminal leaflet. Yellow pea-shaped flowers hang on stalks from the leaf angles. The smooth pods become brown and sharply pointed as they mature. Young twigs are yellow-green, and small spines may remain near the leaf bases. Photograph a complete compound leaf and its attachment, a flower and a pod. That combination helps separate peashrub from other yellow-flowered members of the pea family.
actions: Look for seedlings beneath and beyond old windbreaks, especially where a planting meets natural vegetation. Small plants can be dug or pulled with care, while larger stems may resprout after cutting. Avoid relying on one mowing to remove a mature patch. A broader plan should prevent additional seed production and include several seasons of checks for returning growth. Wisconsin restricts the species with named cultivar exceptions; consult the applicable local guidance before buying or moving plants. In established woodland infestations, coordinate removal and recovery of native cover with the land manager.
researchNotes: Forest Service seed manual provides planting history/origin; Wisconsin DNR provides ecology/control. Forest Service Alaska morphology resolves the distinction between stipular spines and a terminal leaflet. No universal cultivar or national legal claim.

proposedDescription: Siberian squill is a small bulb-forming plant whose blue flowers appear early in spring. It has been planted in lawns and woodland gardens, but can spread beyond them through seeds and new bulbs. Minnesota extension asks people to report populations in unmanaged areas so its wild distribution can be understood more clearly. A blue carpet in a garden and a spreading patch among native spring plants are worth recording differently.
identification: Look for a few narrow, grasslike leaves rising from the bulb and slender leafless flower stems, usually only several inches tall. The nodding blue flowers have six petal-like segments, often with a darker stripe down the center; some cultivated forms have other colors. Photograph the entire small plant and a flower from the side and front. The foliage dies back after the spring display, so mark the patch's location while it is visible. Other early flowering bulbs can look similar from a distance.
actions: Avoid moving bulbs or soil from an escaping patch into new beds or natural areas. For a small unwanted group, carefully lift the bulbs and associated offsets, then return in later springs to check for plants that were missed. Larger woodland patches need a plan that also protects native spring flowers. Wear gloves when handling the plant, and keep bulbs and other material away from children and pets because the plant is toxic if eaten. Report wild occurrences with photographs and a note about nearby plantings rather than assuming every record represents an unmanaged population.
researchNotes: UMN supplies spread/reporting context; NC State independently supports bulb habit and toxicity; MISIN supplies detailed flower recognition. Control advice is limited to cautious small-patch bulb removal/follow-up, not eradication efficacy.

claims: Early spring growth, seed/bulb spread and unmanaged-population reporting.

proposedDescription: Foetid senna is a yellow-flowered tropical plant often called sicklepod, a name also used for the closely related Senna obtusifolia. The two have a long history of confusion in botanical and agricultural records. For a US observation, resolving that identity is more useful than applying the familiar sicklepod name immediately. Information about the widespread agricultural weed S. obtusifolia should not automatically be attached to S. tora.
identification: Look for alternate compound leaves with rounded or broadly oval leaflets, small yellow flowers near the leaf angles and long narrow pods. One useful clue is the position of small glands on the central leaf axis: S. tora commonly has glands between the first two leaflet pairs. Flower and seed details are also important, and gland counts can vary in related material. Photograph a whole leaf close enough to show the glands, an open flower and mature pods. A specialist may need seed or floral details to make a confident distinction.
actions: Label an uncertain observation as a possible Senna rather than forcing a species name. Note whether it was planted, arrived with disturbed soil or is growing among crops. Keep seed-bearing material contained while requesting identification, and do not use an online photograph as the sole basis for a pasture or crop treatment. If removal of a small unwanted plant is appropriate, act before pods disperse and check for later seedlings. Avoid using the plant as food, feed or a home remedy on the strength of a common name shared with another species.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent Queensland comparative diagnosis strengthens separation from S. obtusifolia. The draft still requires mature details and does not attach the other species agricultural harm or treatments to this one. proposedDescription: Siebold viburnum is a large Japanese shrub or small tree planted for its white flowers and colorful fruit. Birds can carry seeds beyond gardens, and escaped plants have formed dense understory growth at some eastern US sites. A Pennsylvania preserve documented long-established plants shading native vegetation. That local history shows why seedlings around an old ornamental planting are worth checking, without implying that every cultivated viburnum behaves identically.
identification: Look for opposite, simple leaves with strongly toothed edges and prominent veins. Leaves can have hairs along the veins and stalks, and crushed foliage has a distinctive unpleasant odor. Clusters of small whitish flowers appear near branch tips. The fruits pass through pink or red before becoming dark blue to black. Native viburnums share several of these features, so compare leaves, fruit color at maturity and the entire shrub. Photograph those details rather than identifying it from a cluster of red fruit alone.
actions: Check woodland edges and ground beneath bird perches near a fruiting shrub for young plants. Ask a local botanist to confirm unfamiliar seedlings before removing them. If an escape is confirmed, prioritize small outlying plants and plan any larger removal with follow-up for returning growth and seedlings. Keep fruit-bearing branches from being dumped in natural areas. Do not assume a named cultivar has the same fruit behavior as the species; ornamental accounts describe differences. Share the location, photographs and planting history with the land manager so treatment can be matched to the actual population.
researchNotes: Kmetz's 2014 preserve account supplies independent local impact; Forest Service comparison supports species recognition, and UF cultivar account cautions against treating Seneca fruit behavior as universal. No nationwide invasion status asserted.

proposedDescription: Lima bean is a widely cultivated food crop native to tropical America. Depending on the variety and growing conditions, it can form a compact bush or a climbing plant and may persist for more than one season in warm climates. Its presence in a vegetable plot is not evidence of an invasion. An escaped plant becomes a different kind of observation when it reproduces beyond cultivation, especially where vines extend into nearby unmanaged vegetation.
identification: Leaves have three leaflets, with the terminal leaflet held beyond the side pair. Small pea-shaped flowers can be whitish, pale pink or yellowish, and the flattened pods contain a few broad, kidney-shaped seeds. Seed color and plant size vary considerably among cultivars. Photograph a complete leaf, the flowers, a closed mature pod and the whole growth habit. Do not identify a wild vine as an edible lima bean from its three-part leaves alone; many unrelated or closely related plants share that feature.
actions: When reporting an escape, say whether there is a nearby vegetable garden, discarded crop material or a former planting. Note whether younger plants are appearing without further sowing. Keep unwanted mature pods from being carried into natural areas with compost or garden waste. Small volunteer plants can be removed where they are unwanted, but a cultivated crop does not need removal without evidence that it is spreading or causing a local problem. Do not taste raw beans or unknown wild seeds to identify them. Ask a local botanist about uncertain plants growing well beyond cultivation.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Taxonomy and independent crop horticulture support identity and variable habit. The profile explicitly distinguishes cultivated crops from unwanted escapes; lack of US invasion trials is not a remaining editorial hold. proposedDescription: Silkleaf is a small member of the daisy family found in open disturbed ground. Its native range includes much of tropical America, while botanical accounts distinguish introduced populations in places such as Puerto Rico. That geography is important: a weedy appearance does not make the plant nonnative everywhere. The small pale flower clusters and softly hairy leaves are more useful starting points than assuming a regional status from the common name.
identification: Leaves are opposite, generally oval, and may have toothed edges, with several main veins arising near the base. The plant can branch, straggle or occasionally root where stems meet the ground. Its compact terminal flower cluster is unusual: it is made from many tiny, single-flowered heads grouped together. The flowers are white or faintly bluish rather than surrounded by large daisy petals. Photograph the paired leaves, their undersides and a close view of the flower cluster. A hand lens can help reveal the individual smaller heads.
actions: Record the habitat and whether the plant occurs as a few individuals or a spreading patch. For an unfamiliar US occurrence, ask a regional botanist to confirm both identity and local status before disturbing natural vegetation. Avoid moving mature flower heads or soil from a suspect introduction into another site. Small unwanted plants in cultivated ground can be removed before seed dispersal, with follow-up for new seedlings. Reports should describe the actual location and behavior rather than converting a tropical distribution list into a claim that the species is harmful throughout the United States.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent field botany and range authority support a geographically scoped account. proposedDescription: Silk oak is an Australian tree with fernlike foliage and orange-yellow flowers. Despite its common name, it is not a true oak. It has been widely planted for shade, timber and reforestation, including in Hawaii, where escaped trees have become a concern in natural forests. Florida's horticultural assessment describes a different regional situation. The surrounding habitat and evidence of seedlings matter more than treating every ornamental silk oak as the same management problem.
identification: Look for deeply divided green leaves with silvery-white undersides and flowers arranged along one side of a cluster, giving a brushlike appearance. The dry, leathery fruits turn gray-brown to brown. Mature trees can be tall, with furrowed bark and substantial spreading limbs. Photograph the leaf surfaces, flower arrangement and entire tree. A leaf that looks fernlike does not mean the plant is a fern; the woody trunk, flowers and fruits establish a very different growth form.
actions: In Hawaii, avoid introducing silk oak to new areas and check around existing trees for recruits beyond the planting. Mark small seedlings for confirmation and removal where appropriate. Large-tree work needs an arborist, especially near buildings or paths, because limbs may break and sawdust can cause allergic reactions. Keep seed-bearing debris from being dumped in natural areas. When reporting a stand, distinguish planted rows from younger trees spreading into surrounding vegetation. Ask the land manager about follow-up and restoration so removal does not leave an opening for another unwanted plant.

proposedDescription: Burma reed is a tall, clump-forming Asian grass that has invaded parts of south Florida, including pine rocklands. Large feathery flower heads release wind-carried seeds, while pieces of its underground stems can travel with soil and construction equipment. Cutting away the tall growth does not necessarily remove the plant: living rhizomes can send up new shoots. Its size and persistence make early attention to small outlying clumps especially useful.
identification: Look for dense upright canes, often branching, with long narrow leaves and a large nodding, silky-looking flower head. At the junction of leaf blade and sheath, a ridge carries a line of hairs. Stems contain soft pith rather than being simply hollow. Common reed and native plumegrasses can look similar, so photograph the leaf junction, stem, entire clump and flower head. Fine details of the tiny flower units may be needed to confirm the species. Do not identify it from height alone.
actions: Avoid moving soil or machinery contaminated with rhizome pieces into clean ground. Where treatment is planned, containing seed heads first can reduce later seedlings. A mature clump usually needs a coordinated control plan and repeated checks for regrowth; mowing or fire alone can leave the underground plant alive. Consult the land manager before working in pine rockland or other sensitive habitat. Florida lists Burma reed as a noxious weed, so use local disposal and treatment guidance. Photograph and report a new patch before it expands or becomes mixed with native grasses.
researchNotes: FDACS provides Florida pathways and resprouting; FNAI cites UF management for seedhead containment; Kew GrassBase independently supports morphology. Common-reed lineage/native-status ambiguity is not repeated. No herbicide rates or casual burning.

proposedDescription: Silky bluegrass, also called Queensland bluegrass, is a tufted grass native across parts of the Indo-Pacific and Australia. It includes forms with different life spans, so describing every plant as a long-lived perennial would be misleading. Botanical sources list introductions in several US states. Those records establish a need for careful identification, not proof that this grass has the same impacts as other introduced grasses called bluestem or bluegrass.
identification: Plants have narrow leaf blades and several slender flowering branches clustered near the top of the stem. The heads can look bluish and silky because of long pale hairs. Stem nodes are hairy, and the tiny flower units include bristle-like awns. Subspecies differ in head length, details of the outer flower scales and annual versus perennial habit. Photograph a whole flowering plant, a node, the leaf junction and a close view of the head. A grass specialist may need mature material to separate it from related Dichanthium species.
actions: Record whether it grows in a planted pasture, along a road or within natural grassland. Keep a suspected new introduction from spreading with hay, seed mixes or soil while its identity is checked. For a small unwanted patch, seek advice on removing the plant before seed dispersal without damaging native grasses around it. Larger grassland work should follow a site-specific plan rather than an assumption that mowing will control all forms. Include the scientific name and, if known, the subspecies in reports so observations of different bluegrasses are not combined accidentally.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent taxonomy and botanical treatment resolve the need for a bounded species overview. Life-span variation is retained, while unassigned subspecies and missing US control trials do not justify borrowed grass impacts. proposedDescription: Silver carp is a large East Asian fish introduced to the United States for uses including plankton control. Escaped populations have spread through many river systems. These efficient filter feeders can reduce food available to native plankton-eating fish, and startled adults can leap from the water, creating a hazard for boaters. An observation should identify the actual waterbody; a regional map does not mean every nearby lake contains silver carp.
identification: Look for a deep, silvery body, very small scales, an upturned mouth and eyes set low and forward on the head. Compared with bighead carp, silver carp usually lack dark blotches and have a smaller head. A sharp belly ridge extends farther forward, past the pelvic fins toward the throat. Young fish are harder to distinguish and can be confused with native baitfish such as gizzard shad. Photograph the side, head and underside when that can be done safely, with a scale and the catch location.
actions: Never move live silver carp or empty a bait bucket into another waterbody. Inspect collected bait carefully rather than relying on its small size to rule out carp. If you suspect a new occurrence, contact the state fisheries agency with photographs and location details, and follow its instructions for the catch. Around jumping fish, slow down and keep passengers protected from impacts. Do not attempt to provoke jumps for a photograph. Prevention at ramps and between fishing trips is particularly important because a few transported fish can create a problem far from an established river population.

proposedDescription: Silver-leaved cinquefoil is a Eurasian perennial recorded across much of temperate North America. Its most useful field clue is the pale, densely hairy underside of the leaves, rather than the small yellow flowers shared with many other cinquefoils. It can occur in open and disturbed places, but the importance of a particular patch depends on the habitat and neighboring vegetation. Identification should come before a decision to remove an unfamiliar cinquefoil.
identification: The lower leaves are divided into several leaflets spreading from a common point. Their margins have a few conspicuous tooth-like lobes and tend to roll downward. Dense silvery hairs cover the undersides, while the basal leaves are noticeably larger than leaves higher on the flowering stems. Other cinquefoils may be gray-haired too, so compare the leaf arrangement, depth of the lobes and both leaf surfaces. Photograph an intact lower leaf from above and below, a stem leaf and the flowers. Do not rely on the word silver in a common name.
actions: For a new record, note whether plants occupy a lawn edge, dry field, roadside or natural opening, and estimate the size of the patch. A regional botanist can help distinguish it from native cinquefoils and similar introduced species. If a small confirmed patch is unwanted, remove the rooted plants carefully before seeds are dispersed and revisit the site for returning growth. Keep seed-bearing debris out of clean soil. In species-rich grassland, avoid broad treatment until the plants have been identified and the likely benefit outweighs disturbance to surrounding vegetation.

proposedDescription: European silver fir is a large evergreen conifer native to European mountain regions. It is grown as an ornamental and in collections outside that range. Its pale needle undersides explain the silver-fir name, but several North American trees have similar common names and foliage. A planted specimen should not be mistaken for evidence of a spreading wild population. Reports are most useful when they distinguish a labeled landscape tree from seedlings established beyond a planting.
identification: Needles are flattened, dark green above and marked by two pale bands underneath. They often appear combed into two rows along the twig, with tips that are notched or split into two small points. Cylindrical cones stand upright on branches rather than hanging down. Young bark is relatively smooth with resin blisters; older bark becomes plated. Photograph a twig from above and below, needle tips and the whole tree. Native firs can share several of these traits, so a nursery label or expert examination may be needed for a confident species identification.
actions: If you notice seedlings near a planted fir, document their distance from the parent tree and whether there are several age classes. Ask an arboretum, forester or herbarium to check the identification before treating them as European silver fir. Before removing a mature tree, confirm its identity and whether seedlings are spreading into surrounding habitat. Where confirmed seedlings are unwanted, address them while small and follow the property owner's guidance. Avoid moving soil or seedlings into natural forest, and retain dated photographs if you are monitoring possible spread over time.

proposedDescription: Common silver-hairgrass is a delicate introduced grass with a loose, airy flowering head. It is recorded in disturbed places, grasslands and woodland edges in New England, and is also widespread in California grasslands. Widespread occurrence does not by itself show severe ecological harm. California's 2006 inventory described its apparent impacts as negligible, a useful reminder to describe the plant's actual local abundance rather than assume that every patch is a major threat.
identification: Look for slender stems and an open head whose fine branches hold tiny flower units apart from one another. In the New England key, those little flower stalks are generally as long as or longer than the flower units they carry. The similar early silver-hairgrass, Aira praecox, has a much narrower, denser head with branches pressed close together. Photograph the whole plant and the head against a plain background with a scale. A grass expert may need mature material because the distinguishing features are very small.
actions: Record whether it is scattered among other grasses or forming a dense patch, along with the site's disturbance history. Avoid treating all fine-stemmed grasses as this species. In a small managed bed where removal is warranted, lift confirmed unwanted plants before seed dispersal and check for another generation. In natural grassland, ask the land manager whether intervention is useful and how to protect native annuals. Clean seed-bearing debris from equipment before moving between sites, and keep regional impact uncertainty visible in reports rather than overstating what an observation proves.

proposedDescription: Silver July croton is a small, hairy herb from tropical America. It belongs to the spurge family and is different from the brightly colored ornamental commonly sold as croton. Botanical accounts describe it from disturbed habitats, but its local status needs to be checked against the exact species and place. Several crotons are native in the United States, so confirm an unfamiliar hairy plant before deciding whether it belongs at the site or needs attention.
identification: Look for branching stems covered in dense hairs and oval to oblong leaves with finely toothed margins. Star-shaped hairs are especially dense on the pale undersides. Short crowded flower clusters contain separate male and female flowers; the female flowers have unequal, divided sepals and lack petals. These are small features that may require a hand lens or a botanist's examination. Photograph the leaf surfaces, stem hairs and a flowering or fruiting tip. Record the scientific name carefully because similarly named crotons can represent different plants.
actions: For a suspected occurrence, note whether it grows beside a levee, in moved soil, on a field edge or in relatively undisturbed vegetation. Send detailed photographs to a regional herbarium or extension botanist before assigning an impact or treatment priority. Avoid carrying fruiting material or soil to another site while identification is pending. If a small confirmed plant is unwanted in cultivated ground, remove it before seeds disperse and check for seedlings later. Do not use it as a home remedy or assume that the toxicity and control advice for another spurge applies unchanged.

proposedDescription: Silver wattle is an Australian tree planted for its soft-looking foliage and masses of yellow flowers. It has escaped cultivation in California, where land managers remove it from some natural areas. Long-lived seeds and shoots from damaged roots can make an established stand harder to manage than a single small seedling. A roadside planting and a colony spreading into nearby habitat should therefore be recorded separately.
identification: The blue-gray to silvery leaves are divided twice into many tiny leaflets. Young shoots often have a pale, frosted appearance. Small round yellow flower heads gather into larger branching clusters, followed by flattened pods. Look closely along the central leaf stalk: raised glands occur where pairs of leaflet-bearing branches meet it. Similar wattles differ in these gland positions, foliage color and young-stem texture. Photograph the whole tree, a complete leaf and a close view of those junctions rather than relying on yellow flowers alone.
actions: Avoid planting it beside sensitive habitat where it is escaping locally. Small confirmed seedlings are easier to address before a seed supply develops. For larger trees or colonies, work with the land manager on a plan that accounts for root shoots and later seedlings; simply cutting stems may not finish the job. Keep pods and contaminated soil from being moved to clean ground. Return after treatment to look for regrowth, and record the extent of new plants beyond the original planting. Mature-tree removal should be handled safely by people equipped for the site.

proposedDescription: Wirilda is an Australian shrub or small tree grown beyond its native range as an ornamental. Older references used Acacia retinodes for a broader group that now includes separate species, notably Acacia provincialis and Acacia uncifolia. That change matters when interpreting reports of escape: an old nursery name may not identify the plant under today's narrower definition. California introduction records deserve that extra check before claims about spread or harm are attached to them.
identification: The leaf-like structures are narrow phyllodes, flattened leaf stalks with one main lengthwise vein. A small gland sits along the edge above the base. Rounded pale-yellow to cream flower heads occur in short clusters, followed by long, narrow pods. These features place a plant near the wirilda group but do not reliably separate all its close relatives. Photograph mature phyllodes, the gland, bark, flower clusters and ripe pods. A flowering branch examined by an acacia specialist is more useful than a distant photograph of the tree.
actions: If plants appear outside a garden, document the parent planting and any nearby seedlings, including where they are establishing. Ask a herbarium or extension botanist to review the name before assigning a control priority. Keep ripe pods and soil containing seed out of natural areas, and remove small unwanted volunteers only after confirming that they are not another species. For established trees, seek a site-specific plan and monitor replacement seedlings. Do not borrow the impact claims or treatment history of silver wattle merely because both are Australian acacias.

proposedDescription: Silverleaf cotoneaster is a Chinese ornamental shrub that has escaped into coastal California scrub, grassland and woodland. Birds and other animals carry its abundant fruits away from gardens, allowing seedlings to appear well beyond a hedge. A large shrub can be persistent after cutting, so management needs to include returning shoots and younger plants around it. The name also covers an identification challenge: several cultivated cotoneasters look very similar.
identification: Look for small, oval, leathery leaves that are dull gray-green above and densely white-felted underneath. White flowers open with their petals spread, followed by red fruits. The related Cotoneaster franchetii often has pink-tinged, more upright petals. Neither fruit color nor leaf size alone is enough to separate every species or possible hybrid. Photograph both leaf surfaces, open flowers and fruiting branches. A confident identification may require a specimen with several of those features, especially where different cotoneasters have been planted together.
actions: Check beneath fruiting shrubs and nearby bird perches for seedlings. Pull small confirmed plants when the soil allows roots to come away without excessive disturbance, and contain fruit-bearing debris. Cutting a mature shrub can leave a living root system, so plan follow-up instead of assuming the missing canopy means it is gone. On natural land, coordinate removal and replanting with the site manager. Replacing a fruiting ornamental with a suitable native shrub can reduce the continuing seed supply. Record uncertain plants as cotoneaster pending identification rather than forcing every escape into this species.

proposedDescription: Silver-sheath knotweed is a small annual herb found in disturbed ground, especially in parts of the southwestern United States. It is not the tall, bamboo-like knotweed that forms large streamside thickets. Its slender flowering shoots and tiny flowers can make it easy to overlook among other weeds. A record should describe the plant and setting directly, without borrowing the much greater impacts or specialized treatment advice associated with Japanese knotweed.
identification: Plants branch from near the base and usually grow more upright than common mat-forming knotweed. Narrow bluish-green leaves become much smaller toward the flowering tips, making the upper stems look almost leafless. Thin papery sheaths surround the stem joints and later break into fibers. Tiny flowers have pale green centers with pink or whitish margins, and the small brown fruits are glossy. Photograph lower leaves, a stem joint and a flowering tip together. The shiny fruit and nearly leafless flowering shoots help distinguish it from common knotweed.
actions: Record whether the patch is in a garden, field edge, roadside or other disturbed soil, and note its extent. Small unwanted plants can be removed before seed dispersal, taking care not to scatter mature fruits. Revisit the site because an annual's disappearance at the end of a season does not mean the seed supply has disappeared. Avoid moving infested soil into clean planting areas. Ask a regional botanist to confirm uncertain knotweeds before large-scale treatment; a species-specific impact or control claim should not be inferred merely from the shared common name.

proposedDescription: Himalayan cotoneaster is an introduced ornamental shrub recorded along the Pacific coast from British Columbia into California. It grows in places including thickets, forest openings, shorelines and grasslands. Birds can carry its bright fruits from planted shrubs into surrounding vegetation. Overseas weed assessments describe dense stands that interfere with other plants, but a US report should still document the local stand and habitat rather than assume the same impact everywhere.
identification: This is generally an upright shrub with a fairly narrow crown and stiff branches. Leaves are small, oval and pointed, shiny green above and paler beneath. Young leaves and shoots have hairs that become less conspicuous with age. The small flower clusters develop bright orange to orange-red fruits. Cotoneaster species overlap in appearance, and regional sources describe flower color and leaf persistence differently, so those features should not be used alone. Photograph the branch arrangement, leaf surfaces, flowers and fruits for a botanist to compare.
actions: Look for seedlings beyond a garden boundary, especially beneath perches and along edges where birds travel. Remove small confirmed unwanted plants with their roots where that can be done without harming surrounding vegetation. Keep ripe fruits and garden waste away from natural areas. Larger shrubs need follow-up after removal, and restoring nearby ground cover helps reduce open space for new seedlings. For a new regional record, provide clear photographs and the location to a herbarium or local land manager. Do not label every red-fruited shrub as Himalayan cotoneaster or apply another country's legal rules to your property.

proposedDescription: Exotic bur-reed is an emergent wetland plant that can form dense colonies along shallow water. The name needs particular care: older botanical treatments sometimes included North American broadfruit bur-reed within Sparganium erectum. US identification guidance separates that native relative from the Eurasian plant addressed here. A broad leaf and a round, prickly-looking fruit head are therefore reasons to investigate, not enough evidence to remove a wetland plant.
identification: Plants have long flat leaves, sometimes floating and sometimes upright, with a raised fold along the underside. Branched flowering stems carry separate rounded male and female heads, and mature female heads become clusters of firm fruits. The shape of individual mature fruits, including their shoulder and beak, helps specialists distinguish closely related bur-reeds. Photograph the entire flowering stem, leaf base and mature fruit heads from the bank if possible. Keep the location and any previous scientific name with the observation so an older record can be interpreted correctly.
actions: Report a suspected exotic bur-reed to the state plant-health or aquatic invasive-species program before moving material or attempting control. It appears on the federal noxious weed list, and native lookalikes make confirmation especially important. Clean plant fragments from equipment before leaving the waterbody. Cutting the leaves alone can be followed by regrowth from underground stems, while digging or machinery can disturb wetland habitat. Let the responsible agency choose a permitted treatment plan. Do not mail a specimen, transplant it to a pond or remove a native stand based solely on an identification app.

proposedDescription: Simple-stem cudweed is a small woolly herb whose inconspicuous flower clusters can be mistaken for several other cudweeds. Botanical sources place its native range in tropical America and record it beyond that range, including North America. Accurate naming is important because similar plants have often been grouped under older Gnaphalium names. A weed report from a South American crop field does not establish the same impact in a US natural area.
identification: The plant usually has one upright woolly stem, although some specimens branch near the base. Leaves are greener and less hairy above, with dense pale wool underneath. Lower leaves are broader toward their tips, while upper leaves become narrower. Small flower heads form an interrupted, spike-like series of clusters rather than one continuous dense cylinder. Close examination of the tiny surrounding bracts and fruits may be needed to distinguish it from Gamochaeta americana and other relatives. Photograph the leaf surfaces, whole stem and several mature flower clusters.
actions: For a useful record, note whether it grows in a lawn, cultivated field, river margin or another disturbed place, and whether it is scattered or abundant. Ask a regional herbarium to verify the identification if the plant is new to the area or the common name is uncertain. Small unwanted plants in a garden can be removed before mature heads release seed, with later checks for seedlings. Avoid broad treatment of mixed cudweeds in natural habitat before confirming their identities. Keep the original photographs and identification history so future name changes do not separate the record from its evidence.

proposedDescription: Three-leaf chastetree is an introduced shrub or small tree found in coastal and disturbed habitats in central and southern Florida. It was planted as an ornamental, including forms with variegated foliage. Florida's invasive-plant assessment places it among species increasing in abundance or frequency, rather than treating that category as proof of severe harm at every site. Its scientific name is important because other plants called chastetree or beach vitex have different habits and regional status.
identification: Leaves grow opposite one another and may be simple or divided into three leaflets. Their upper surfaces are greener, with grayish hairs beneath, and young stems are softly hairy. Small purple or violet flowers gather in branching clusters, followed by small rounded fleshy fruits. Some cultivated plants have white-edged leaves. Photograph a shoot showing several complete leaves, their undersides and the flowers or fruits. Do not confuse this usually upright shrub with the creeping, dune-covering habit of beach vitex, Vitex rotundifolia.
actions: Check around older plantings for seedlings or shrubs establishing in neighboring coastal vegetation. Where it is escaping, choose a suitable noninvasive replacement and contain fruit-bearing cuttings during removal. Small confirmed volunteers can be pulled when the roots come free without disturbing sensitive ground. Larger shrubs and plants in protected coastal habitat should be handled with the land manager's guidance and checked afterward for returning growth. Record the exact species, growth habit and habitat when reporting an occurrence. Do not apply beach-vitex regulations or a different chastetree's horticultural recommendation without checking which plant you have.

proposedDescription: Angled luffa is a climbing vegetable crop also called ridged gourd or Chinese okra. Despite that last name, it is a member of the cucumber family, not the okra plant. Its long fruits have strong lengthwise ribs, unlike smooth luffa grown for similar uses. Florida extension describes it as a cultivated warm-season crop. A plant growing on a trellis is not evidence of harmful spread, although self-sown vines outside a planting are worth documenting.
identification: Look for a vigorous vine using branched tendrils to climb, broad lobed leaves and yellow flowers. Developing fruits are elongated and dark green, with prominent angular ridges running from end to end. Mature fruits become fibrous and contain numerous seeds. Fruit ridges are much more useful than the general leaf shape for separating angled luffa from smooth luffa. Photograph the tendrils, a complete leaf, flowers and a fruit still attached to the vine. Do not use an unfamiliar wild gourd as food simply because it resembles a cultivated vegetable.
actions: Where vines are unwanted, prevent ripe fruits and seed from being dumped with garden waste into surrounding vegetation. Remove small volunteers before they climb through shrubs, taking care not to pull down the plants supporting them. Note whether an apparent escape comes from a nearby crop, discarded fruit or repeated self-seeding. If vines persist beyond cultivation, send photographs and location details to a regional botanist. Management should reflect actual escape and impact evidence, not a blanket assumption that every cultivated luffa needs removal. Check the site again in the following growing season for new seedlings.

proposedDescription: Sirex woodwasp is an introduced pine-associated insect established in parts of eastern North America. Females place eggs, a wood-decaying fungus and toxic mucus into trees; together these can weaken or kill the host. Stressed or crowded pines are particularly important to watch. Its severe effects in some overseas plantations should not be treated as a prediction for every US forest, but moving infested wood can carry the insect to a new area.
identification: Adults are large cylindrical woodwasps with a spear-like plate at the end of the abdomen. Females are usually metallic blue-black with orange legs and a long egg-laying structure beneath the tail. Males have orange abdominal segments. Native woodwasps can look similar, so color alone is not a reliable confirmation. On pines, resin beads or dribbles, declining needles and round exit holes may prompt inspection, but none proves Sirex noctilio by itself. Photograph the insect, host tree and visible damage for an entomologist.
actions: Keep firewood near where it was obtained and do not transport suspect logs to another property for diagnosis. Contact the state forestry or plant-health agency about an unfamiliar woodwasp or a possible new infestation; ask how to submit a specimen safely. A forester can assess tree stress, stand crowding and the need for thinning or removal. Do not release biological-control organisms yourself or spray an entire stand on the basis of round holes alone. Preserve the date and location of the find, since a confirmed occurrence outside the known range is especially valuable.
researchNotes: Cornell field/silviculture guidance and USDA APHIS biology support pine/fungus mechanism and diagnosis; Washington agency supplies firewood prevention/reporting. Native lookalikes and overseas-vs-US severity kept explicit; old 2006 range excluded.

proposedDescription: Sisal hemp is the large, architectural agave once planted for the strong fibers in its leaves. In warm places, an old planting can keep expanding long after its original purpose has disappeared. New plants form around the parent and on its towering flower stalk, giving this succulent more than one way to persist. Florida sources describe escaped plants in coastal uplands, scrub and pine rockland. A planted specimen is not, by itself, evidence that surrounding natural habitat is invaded.
identification: Look for a broad rosette of rigid, gray-green, sword-shaped leaves with a dark, pointed spine at each tip. Mature leaf edges usually have few teeth, unlike the regularly toothed edges of some other agaves. The branched flower stalk rises far above the leaves and bears yellow-green flowers followed by small plantlets. A rosette flowers once and then dies, but nearby offspring can continue growing. Photograph the entire rosette, leaf margins and any developing plantlets without reaching between the sharp leaves.
actions: Keep falling plantlets and removed offsets out of natural areas and drainage channels. If an established clump is unwanted, ask a local invasive-plant program or experienced landscaper to plan removal around the sharp leaves and any remaining offspring. Check the site again after the parent is removed. In Florida, current university guidance calls for preventing escape in central and southern regions; management elsewhere should reflect local evidence. Choose a locally appropriate replacement that will remain within the space you can maintain.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent Kew taxonomy and Mexican origin support the substantive Florida species account. The broad UF origin field is not used as a taxonomic authority; regional caution does not become nationwide harm. proposedDescription: Slender false brome is a perennial bunchgrass that can make a woodland floor look freshly green while other grasses have faded. In parts of the Pacific Northwest, that attractive appearance hides a serious management problem: dense patches can replace the varied plants beneath trees and along trails. It also grows in open ground, so shade alone will not keep it contained. Seeds travel with people, animals and equipment, making trail edges and work routes useful places to notice a new patch.
identification: Look for soft, yellow-green to bright-green leaves with fine hairs along their edges. Flowering stems carry noticeably drooping rows of spikelets attached directly, or almost directly, to the main stalk. The leaf sheath is open, another useful feature for a trained observer. Native Columbia brome can look very similar and deserves protection. Its spikelets have more obvious stalks. Take close photographs of the leaf edge, sheath and flowering head rather than relying on the color of a whole patch.
actions: Ask a local weed program to confirm the grass before removing plants from a woodland. Clean seeds and soil from footwear and maintenance equipment before leaving an affected area. Small confirmed patches can be dug or pulled while soil is moist, removing the roots and containing any seed heads. Return to check for survivors and seedlings. A single mowing usually leaves living plants behind; larger infestations need a planned sequence of treatment and recovery planting that also protects the native vegetation.
researchNotes: Independent Oregon university and state agriculture accounts support identity, spread and habitat impacts. Public advice deliberately excludes grazing and universal herbicide timing.

proposedDescription: Slender meadow foxtail is better known to cereal growers as black-grass. It is an annual grass whose narrow flower heads can rise above a crop, especially where many plants have established together. In British arable fields it is an important competitor for light, water and nutrients. Its presence in a species catalog does not mean every meadow or American farm has the same problem. The setting matters: a confirmed weed patch in a crop needs a different response from an unidentified grass beside a path.
identification: Plants have slender stems and flat, elongated leaves without conspicuous hairs. The dense flower head is narrow and tapered at both ends, sometimes becoming dark purple as it matures. Plants can exceed three feet in height under favorable conditions. Other foxtail-like grasses can look convincing at a distance, so a dark cylindrical head is only a starting clue. Photograph the base, the junction between leaf and stem, and several mature heads with a ruler or another scale.
actions: If you suspect black-grass in a crop, mark the patch and contact an agricultural adviser before harvesting or moving equipment through it. Keep a record of the crop, sowing history and previous control attempts. Correct identification is especially useful before choosing a treatment or changing a rotation. Avoid scattering mature seed while collecting a sample; ask the diagnostic service how to package it. In a garden or small disturbed area, confirm the identity and remove unwanted plants before seed sheds, then watch the same ground for new seedlings.
researchNotes: Two independent British horticultural/agronomic sources support identity and annual habit. Crop impacts are explicitly British context; no US occurrence or resistance status is inferred.

claims: Hairless annual, tapered heads and crop competition.

proposedDescription: Slender oat is an annual wild oat with loose, nodding flower heads that move easily in the breeze. Introduced from Eurasia, it grows in fields, roadsides and other open, disturbed places in western North America. California lists it as an invasive plant, although a pasture, a roadside and a native grassland may have different management priorities. The dry heads are distinctive, but several wild oats occur together, and recognizing this particular species requires a closer look than its overall graceful shape.
identification: Look for an open, branching head with dangling spikelets and long, bent bristles called awns. The flower coverings, or lemmas, have reddish hairs on the lower part and end in two narrow, bristle-like tips. Those tips help separate slender oat from common wild oat. Leaves are flat and relatively narrow; plant height varies with conditions. Photograph a mature spikelet from the side and include the tips as well as the long central awn. A grass specialist may need a specimen to confirm it.
actions: Where slender oat is unwanted, work before ripe seed is shed and keep cut heads contained during transport. Clean mowing equipment after working through a seeded patch. For a small garden population, remove plants while you can still distinguish them from nearby grasses. In native grassland, ask the land manager to choose treatment timing that protects desirable species and follows with recovery of plant cover. Revisit the area in the next growing season, since removing this year's stems does not tell you what remains in the soil.
researchNotes: Independent regional flora and California inventory sources support morphology, introduced status and regional concern. No claim that forage use makes every population harmful.

proposedDescription: This worm-snail is a reminder that a snail does not always carry a neatly coiled shell around with it. Thylacodes vandyensis lives attached to a hard surface inside an irregular tube and feeds with mucus nets extended into the surrounding water. It was described from the artificial reef formed by the sunken USNS General Hoyt S. Vandenberg off the Florida Keys. Researchers considered it a likely non-native arrival, but its original home and wider distribution remained uncertain in the material reviewed.
identification: An attached, winding shell tube and a visible snail head are useful starting observations, but they do not establish this species. Tube-building worms and other worm-snails can resemble one another underwater. The original description used shell structure, the living animal and molecular evidence, including comparison with other regional vermetid snails. Color varies within the species, so an orange or dark head alone is not a dependable test. Take clear photographs of occupied tube openings and the surrounding colony without touching or breaking the growth.
actions: If you notice an unfamiliar colony on a wreck, marina structure or vessel, record the exact location, depth, date and surface it occupies. Share photographs with a marine biodiversity program or a local specialist. Leave attached animals in place during a recreational dive; scraping a colony is not an appropriate identification method. Vessel owners should use approved hull-maintenance procedures and contain fouling waste ashore. A report is useful even when identification remains uncertain, provided it is clearly labeled as a possible worm-snail rather than a confirmed record.

proposedDescription: Slimjim flatsedge is a small, fine-leaved sedge that can pass for a delicate lawn grass. It is native to eastern Australia and New Caledonia, and has also been cultivated as a ground cover elsewhere. A Hawaiian botanical account records it as sparingly naturalized after planting. That history calls for checking where a plant is growing, rather than treating every tuft as an invasive threat. The reviewed sources describe its botany more clearly than any harmful effects in the United States.
identification: The plant forms a dense tuft of very narrow, threadlike leaves, usually shorter than its slender flowering stems. At the stem tip, a small group of flattened spikelets spreads from nearly the same point, with several longer, leaflike bracts underneath. Mature fruits are tiny and dark brown to black. Sources describe stem cross sections somewhat differently, so stem shape alone is not a safe shortcut. Photograph the whole tuft, the flower cluster from above and from the side, and the base of the leaves.
actions: Before removing a sedge from a natural area, ask a botanist or local extension service to confirm the species and its local status. Keep nursery labels if the plant was sold as a lawn substitute or ornamental ground cover. If a planting is escaping its intended bed, document the edge and remove unwanted outlying tufts before spreading soil or garden waste. Avoid applying a general nutsedge treatment simply because the plant is a sedge. Management should follow an identified problem and preserve nearby native plants.
researchNotes: Fresh review: A fresh original Hilo voucher adds geographically precise occurrence evidence to independent morphology. proposedDescription: Small carpgrass, also called hairy jointgrass or small carpetgrass, is an annual grass introduced from Asia. It can form conspicuous patches along moist edges and other disturbed ground. The spreading growth and numerous seeds make a modest-looking patch worth noticing before it fills more space. Its broad little leaves give it a different texture from many lawn grasses. In a restoration area, the important question is whether a confirmed population is expanding into the vegetation people are trying to protect.
identification: Look closely at the leaf bases: they clasp the stem, a useful feature when sorting this grass from other small annuals. The leaves have conspicuous hairs along their margins. In late summer, green to purplish flower spikes appear on branching stems above the foliage. A photograph of the whole patch is helpful for context, but close views of a clasping leaf base and the flowering branches are much better for identification. Do not assume that every low, broad-leaved grass is this species.
actions: Check likely patches before flowering, when a small amount of work can prevent a larger seed crop. Confirm the identity first, then hand-pull manageable populations and contain plants that already carry seed. Clean shoes, tools and mower decks before moving to an uninfested area. Larger sites need a management plan suited to the surrounding plants and moisture conditions; mowing or herbicide use should be chosen with the land manager. Return through the growing season and the following year, recording where seedlings recur rather than treating one cleanup as the end.
researchNotes: Independent NC and Illinois university accounts support identity, Asian introduction and practical recognition. No unverified county occurrence or broad wetland-treatment prescription.

claims: Clasping hairy leaves, late-season spikes and removal before flowering.

proposedDescription: Small geranium is one of the little crane's-bills that can appear among short grass, on open ground and around cultivated places. Its flowers are easy to overlook, while its rounded, divided leaves often attract more attention. It belongs to the true geraniums, rather than the large-flowered bedding plants commonly sold under that name. Several closely related species share this modest appearance. The sources reviewed support careful identification, but they do not justify treating every occurrence as a serious ecological invasion.
identification: Look for small, pale pink to purplish flowers with narrow petals and a shallow notch at their tips. The leaves are rounded in outline and divided into lobes, but they are less finely cut than those of some other crane's-bills. Short hairs on the stalks are useful under magnification; the conspicuous long stalk hairs of dove's-foot crane's-bill are absent. Mature fruit details also help separate the two. Photograph flowers, leaf shape and stalk hairs together, since a leaf-only image can leave the identification uncertain.
actions: If it is growing harmlessly in a tolerated corner, identify it before deciding that removal is necessary. In a bed where it is unwanted, lift young plants before the beaked fruits mature and scatter seed. Keep the surrounding ground covered with suitable plants or mulch where appropriate. For a natural-area record, send photographs to a local botanical group and explain whether the patch is spreading or simply present. Avoid a broad lawn treatment based on the common name alone, especially where native geraniums or other small wildflowers are mixed in.

proposedDescription: Pycnoderes vanduzeei is a small plant bug reported from the Caribbean and parts of tropical America, with an established population documented in central and southern Florida. The Florida account identifies dayflower and spiderwort as reported hosts. That is useful information for looking for the insect, but a host record does not tell us how much injury it causes. The common name 'small green plant bug' is too broad to distinguish this species from the many other small bugs a gardener might find.
identification: Carvalho's type redescription describes a tiny black-and-pale bug with silvery surface markings; the male measured about 2.6 millimeters. A dark crosslike marking on the membranous wing is another clue. These details are more useful than the catalog common name, but they are not a complete field key. The revision also uses male genital structures. Photograph the insect from above and from the side, record its host plant, and ask an entomologist to confirm a suspected record.
actions: Leave healthy host plants alone while the identification is being checked. If a plant is declining, photograph the symptoms separately and note whether the insects are repeatedly present on the affected tissue. Share those observations with an extension diagnostic service, which can assess both the bug and other possible causes. Do not move insects or infested nursery material to another garden for comparison. If a specimen is requested, follow the receiving service's instructions. Avoid spraying solely because a small bug appears on a plant or has a non-native catalog entry.

proposedDescription: Small hive beetle is a bee-colony pest whose larvae can turn stored pollen and honey into a fermenting, slimy mess. Adults may be present in a hive without causing obvious trouble, so a single beetle is not the same as a damaging larval infestation. The insect is native to sub-Saharan Africa and is established in much of the United States. Beekeepers are most concerned when beetles reproduce in comb that the bees cannot adequately defend, including stored equipment and honey awaiting extraction.
identification: Adults are small, flattened, dark brown to black beetles, roughly a quarter inch long, with clubbed antennae and wing covers that leave the end of the abdomen exposed. The pale larvae have small spines along their backs and three pairs of legs near the head. Unlike wax moth larvae, they do not produce webbing. Slimy comb and a fermented odor strengthen the suspicion, but photographs or specimens should still be checked when the identification is uncertain.
actions: Inspect colonies and stored comb regularly, and extract harvested honey promptly rather than leaving filled supers unattended. Keep the honey house clean and avoid transferring infested frames into healthy colonies. Match the amount of hive space to the colony's ability to protect it, and ask a beekeeping adviser about suitable beetle traps and follow-up monitoring. If larvae are actively damaging comb, seek help promptly. Use only treatments currently labeled for the intended beekeeping use; improvised insecticide applications can harm bees and contaminate hive products.
researchNotes: Independent Georgia and Utah extension accounts support life history, larval damage and husbandry. No pesticide dose, threshold or unverified current product approval provided.

proposedDescription: Small lucerne weevil is a broad-nosed weevil associated with damage to lucerne, also known as alfalfa, and other pasture plants. Adults feed above ground, while the larvae work around roots below the soil surface. That split life cycle means a few notched leaves may reveal only part of what is happening. Agricultural accounts from Argentina and Western Australia document the insect, but those reports do not establish its presence or importance on an individual American farm.
identification: Adults are grayish brown, with pale scales forming lengthwise bands on the wing covers. They have a short, broad snout and elbowed antennae. The Argentine account gives a body length of roughly five to nine millimeters. Larvae are pale, curved and legless, with brown heads, and live in the soil. Rounded notches along leaf edges can suggest adult weevil feeding, but many other weevils make similar marks. Take photographs of an adult from above and the side, and document root injury separately.
actions: In a thinning pasture or alfalfa stand, ask an agricultural diagnostic service to examine both the insects and the roots before choosing control. Record whether the problem affects seedlings or established plants, and whether patches are expanding. Keep soil and rooted plants from the affected area on site while identification is pending. A management decision should account for the below-ground larvae as well as visible adults. Avoid treating every leaf notch as evidence of this species, and use locally current crop guidance if a damaging population is confirmed.
researchNotes: Independent Argentine plant-health account and Western Australian research abstract support host injury and life-stage distinction. Australian report abstract only was read; no US distribution or treatment efficacy inferred.

proposedDescription: Small red-belted clearwing is also called apple clearwing moth, a name that points to its best-known host. The caterpillars live beneath the bark of fruit trees, so their activity can be much less obvious than leaf feeding. The moth occurs in Europe and has been documented in Canadian orchards. Finding an unfamiliar clearwing near an apple tree deserves a careful look, but several other clearwing moths also visit gardens, and a flying adult alone does not establish an orchard infestation.
identification: Adults have a slender, dark blue-black body, largely transparent wings and a conspicuous orange-red band around the abdomen. Their wingspan is about three-quarters to one inch. Larvae are dirty white with a reddish-brown head and shield behind it. Bark-associated frass can be a useful clue, although it is not unique to this insect. Photograph the moth and any suspicious bark area separately. Avoid cutting into a healthy trunk simply to look for a larva; let an adviser decide how to inspect it.
actions: Report suspicious orchard damage to a crop adviser or extension diagnostic service and include the tree species, planting source and location of the injury. Keep affected fruit trees, rootstocks and apple wood from being moved while the identity is being checked. An orchard professional can decide whether targeted monitoring with a suitable lure is warranted. Treatment timing depends on the insect's life cycle and the local situation, so do not rely on a general moth spray. Preserve nursery and planting records to help trace a confirmed introduction.

proposedDescription: Small spruce bud scale is a sap-feeding insect that can hide in plain sight on spruce branches. Mature females resemble small brown buds at the base of new growth, so a tree may carry them for some time before anyone recognizes the problem. Feeding produces sticky honeydew that can support black sooty mold. Heavy populations may stunt shoots or damage lower branches, but scattered scales do not automatically mean the tree needs an insecticide treatment. Authorities disagree about whether it is native to North America, so its regional origin should not be assumed from a sighting.
identification: Look around the bases of young shoots for rounded, reddish-brown bodies, often clustered together. Mature females are only about three millimeters across. Check lower branches as well as the outer canopy, and photograph the suspected scales beside real buds. Honeydew, ants or dark surface mold can draw attention to an infestation, but they do not identify the species. Other Physokermes scales have similar appearances, so a specialist should confirm the name when an exact species record or a management decision depends on it.
actions: Ask an arborist or extension service to check whether the scales are alive, how widely they occur and whether feeding is affecting growth. Record the spruce species and take photographs over time. Keep the tree appropriately watered during dry periods without creating persistently wet soil. If treatment is needed, timing should follow local monitoring of the vulnerable crawler stage. Avoid routine broad-spectrum spraying, which can interfere with natural enemies. New nursery trees should be inspected before they are planted beside an existing spruce collection.

proposedDescription: Small tumbleweed mustard is an upright mustard also known as false London-rocket or tall hedge mustard. It is associated with open, disturbed places such as roadsides, rubble and gaps in paving. The name can make it sound interchangeable with other tumble mustards, but it is a separate species and should be identified on its own features. The botanical sources reviewed describe its form and habitat; they do not establish a particular ecological impact at a site in the United States.
identification: Look for a branching herb with yellow, four-petaled flowers and long, slender seedpods. The lower stem is often noticeably rough with spreading or downward-pointing hairs. Leaves are also usually hairy, and the smooth pods can be slightly curved. Many mustards have yellow flowers and narrow pods, so include the lower stem, basal leaves and mature fruits in photographs. A flowering tip alone may be insufficient. A regional flora or botanist can help distinguish this species from the other Sisymbrium plants growing nearby.
actions: In a garden, path or managed work area, remove confirmed unwanted plants before the pods mature and release seed. Keep seed-bearing material contained instead of dragging it across clean ground. Record the size of the patch and check disturbed soil again in the next growing season. In a natural area, first establish both the identification and the management reason for removal. Avoid collecting it as food on the basis of a mustard-like appearance. If it appears in newly delivered soil or planting material, retain the supplier information for follow-up.

Conditional seed prevention in managed ground does not imply a measured US ecosystem impact or nationwide removal need. proposedDescription: Small-leaf climbing fern, often called Old World climbing fern, grows in a way that surprises people expecting a fern to stay near the ground. Its long, twining fronds climb over shrubs and into trees, forming blankets of growth. In Florida natural areas, those blankets can smother vegetation and carry fire upward into tree canopies. It spreads by tiny windborne spores as well as continued growth from its underground stems, making isolated new patches especially valuable to report.
identification: Look for a slender, dark, wiry climbing frond with short side branches carrying paired leaflets. Ordinary leaflets are generally oblong and unlobed; fertile leaflets have a fringed edge where rolled tissue protects the spore-producing structures. Japanese climbing fern has more divided, lobed leaflets and can be confused with it. Photograph both ordinary and fertile leaflets if present, along with the climbing stem. The distinctive feature is the fern frond itself doing the climbing, rather than a separate woody vine carrying fern-like leaves.
actions: Record a suspected patch and notify the property manager or local invasive-plant program. Avoid carrying cut fronds, soil or contaminated equipment into clean habitat. Check clothing and footwear after working near the fern. Small accessible populations may be manageable, but growth high in trees and infestations near water need experienced crews and a site-specific plan. Cutting alone does not remove the underground source of new fronds. Arrange follow-up checks after treatment, and do not try to burn a patch yourself: the climbing growth can carry flames into the canopy.
researchNotes: UF and USDA identification tool provide independent authored accounts; management wording avoids numerical herbicide recipes and self-directed burning. No local occurrence inferred.

proposedDescription: Small-leaf spiderwort is a trailing South American perennial that can turn damp, shaded ground into a thick green carpet. Soft stems root wherever their nodes meet the soil, so a broken piece can become a new patch. Garden escapes and dumped clippings are therefore important to prevent. Florida's university assessment identifies invasive behavior in the northern and central parts of the state. The effect of a particular planting still depends on its setting, and a contained houseplant is different from an expanding woodland mat.
identification: Look for smooth, somewhat fleshy, oval leaves with pointed tips on soft, creeping stems. The leaves are glossy green, and small white flowers have three petals. Stem joints are particularly useful to photograph because they show how the plant spreads and roots. Several related ornamentals are sold under overlapping names, including variegated forms, so a nursery label or leaf color alone may not settle the identity. Include flowers, both leaf surfaces and an intact section of stem in your photographs.
actions: Keep cuttings, repotting waste and removed mats out of streams, woods and ordinary garden dumping areas. In a small confirmed patch, collect the rooted stems carefully and check the ground for fragments afterward. Revisit the site, since overlooked pieces can regrow. Larger mats beneath native vegetation need a plan that limits soil disturbance and allows desirable plants to recover. Clean tools and footwear before leaving. Ask the local weed program about appropriate disposal and treatment near water, and choose a less spreading ground cover for future planting.
researchNotes:
Independent New Zealand Weedbusters and UF assessment lineages. No seedlessness claim extended beyond New Zealand; cultivar taxonomy left for confirmation.

proposedDescription: Smallflower buttercup is a short annual buttercup with flowers so modest that its leaves and developing fruits may be easier to notice. It is native to the Mediterranean region and has become naturalized elsewhere, including documented sites in Kansas. That record confirms that the species can occur outside cultivation, but it does not show that every population is spreading aggressively or causing ecological harm. Careful identification is particularly useful because several small buttercups share rounded leaves and tiny yellow flowers.
identification: The softly hairy stems may spread outward or stand partly upright. Basal leaves are rounded to kidney-shaped, often with three main lobes and toothed margins. Flowers are only a few millimeters across, with small yellow petals and sepals that bend back. The mature fruits are especially informative: each small, flattened fruit has a beak and a surface covered with little bumps bearing hooked bristles. Photograph a mature fruit cluster with magnification if possible, as well as the leaves and flowers.
actions: If the plant is unwanted in a garden or managed lawn edge, remove it before the fruit clusters mature and keep the surrounding ground covered where practical. Wear ordinary gardening gloves and avoid handling an unidentified buttercup as an edible herb. For a natural-area sighting, record the patch and ask a local botanist to confirm it before any larger removal effort. Note whether it is recurring or expanding, and whether the ground was recently disturbed. A new observation can improve knowledge without needing an immediate claim that the plant is invasive.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent mature-fruit diagnosis and original Kansas vouchers support identity and bounded occurrence. Unmeasured harm stays explicit; no toxicity severity or treatment efficacy is invented. proposedDescription: Smallflower tamarisk is a deciduous shrub or small tree with fine, feathery-looking branches and clouds of pale pink flowers. It has been planted as an ornamental and is included in California's invasive-plant inventory. Tamarisks are often discussed together, but their identities and effects should not be treated as interchangeable. A species-level photograph or a general saltcedar story cannot tell you exactly how this tree is behaving along a particular stream. Local vegetation, water conditions and planting history all matter.
identification: Look for tiny, pointed, scale-like leaves along slender branches. In late spring, small pink flowers can densely cover older stems. Smallflower tamarisk typically has four petals per flower, an important clue when separating it from several other tamarisks. The flowers are tiny, so close, sharply focused images are more useful than a distant pink canopy. Photograph flowering branches and leaves together. A botanist may need flower structures under magnification; the overall wispy shape is not enough for a confident species determination.
actions: If a tamarisk is spreading beyond a planting or appearing along a waterway, document seedlings and established plants separately and notify the land manager. Avoid moving soil or cut branches from the site until a removal plan is agreed. Large-scale clearing beside water should account for bank stability, wildlife use and what vegetation will replace the trees. Ask for a species-confirmed, locally appropriate management plan with follow-up monitoring. Do not assume that one round of cutting will complete the work or that every tree labeled saltcedar is this species.
researchNotes: Independent RHS morphology and Cal-IPC species assessment; USFS explicitly distinguishes species-level versus pooled tamarisk claims. No blanket water-use or salinity claim transferred from congeners.
