proposedDescription: Smallflower touch-me-not, also called small balsam or small-flowered jewelweed, is an annual plant with little pale yellow flowers. It is native to parts of Asia and has spread widely in Europe, often in shaded habitats. Washington also treats it as a weed of concern. The familiar touch-me-not appearance can be misleading where native jewelweeds grow, so a suspected patch deserves a careful identification before plants are pulled. Small flowers and finely toothed leaves are more useful clues than the common name.
identification: The stems are fleshy and upright, with swollen joints. Alternate leaves are oval to broadly lance-shaped and have sharply toothed edges. Flowers are pale yellow, sometimes reddish-spotted in the throat, with a short, relatively straight spur extending behind them. Native jewelweeds can have larger flowers and a differently shaped spur, but color alone does not reliably separate all the possibilities. Photograph a flower from the side so the spur is visible, then include a whole leaf and the leaf arrangement along the stem.
actions: Record the location of a suspected population and ask a local weed program or botanist to confirm it. In Washington, follow the county weed program's current instructions for this species. Avoid disturbing mature seed capsules or carrying seed-bearing plants along trails. If removal is advised, work before seed matures and check the site through the season for later plants. Preserve surrounding native jewelweed and other moist-woodland vegetation. Clean footwear after working in a patch, and keep any removed material contained until appropriate disposal is arranged.
researchNotes: King County regional account and Flora of China description through WFO are independent. Washington guidance scoped geographically; native jewelweed protection explicit.

proposedDescription: This smokebush is a sprawling shrub from Madagascar, also known as orange buddleia or Madagascar butterfly bush. Its long branches can scramble through surrounding vegetation, and Hawaiian guidance documents it invading mesic to humid forests. It is a different plant from the familiar purple-flowered butterfly bush, and it is also unrelated to the ornamental Cotinus commonly called smokebush. Those shared names make the scientific name especially helpful when checking a nursery plant or reporting an escape.
identification: Look for opposite leaves with a dense, pale woolly covering underneath, along with hairy young stems. The flowers are small, tubular and orange to dark yellow, gathered in elongated clusters at the branch tips. Fruits are fleshy little berries that become bluish purple, unlike the dry capsules of common butterfly bush. Photograph both sides of a leaf, a flower cluster and any ripe fruit. A large tangle may conceal the original stem, so include a wider view showing how it climbs or sprawls.
actions: Keep garden plants from growing into adjacent woodland, and watch beyond the original planting for new individuals. Do not dump prunings or fruiting branches in natural areas. If a confirmed plant is escaping, consult the local invasive-plant program about removing the root system and managing any resprouting. Large tangled shrubs may need staged work to protect the plants they cover. Recheck the site after removal and replace lost cover with suitable local vegetation. When buying a plant sold as smokebush, verify which species the seller means before deciding it fits the site.
researchNotes: Independent Hawaii university and Queensland-derived weed accounts. The Hawaii page includes B. davidii in brackets; mainland seaboard claims for that species were deliberately excluded.

claims: Woolly leaves, orange flowers, fleshy fruit and Hawaiian forest invasion.

proposedDescription: Smokybrown cockroach is a large, glossy cockroach often associated with outdoor shelter around buildings. It can live in leaf litter, tree cavities, wood piles and gutters, then turn up in garages, attics or other protected spaces. Adults are capable fliers and are attracted to lights at night. Seeing one indoors is unpleasant, but it does not by itself reveal where the population is living. Finding the shelter and entry route is usually more informative than repeatedly treating the room where one appeared.
identification: Adults are uniformly dark brown to mahogany, with a shiny surface and long wings. They can reach about an inch and a half in length. The shield behind the head lacks the contrasting pale pattern seen on some other large cockroaches. Young stages can look quite different, and older nymphs may be confused with Oriental cockroaches. Photograph the insect from above with a size reference, or retain it securely for identification. The casual name 'palmetto bug' does not distinguish this species.
actions: Use monitoring traps to learn where cockroaches are appearing, and check nearby doors, screens, vents and utility openings. Remove damp debris and unnecessary clutter close to the building, and keep gutters clear where access is safe. Repair persistent moisture problems. If sightings continue, ask a pest professional to identify the species and inspect likely outdoor and structural harborages. Choose a targeted plan suited to the source of activity. Avoid scattering insecticides around the home without a diagnosis, and follow the label for any product used.
researchNotes: Catalog common-name typo should be corrected by MAIN separately; ID retained. BugGuide now uses Validiblatta fuliginosa, while extension retains Periplaneta; nomenclature update flagged without silently changing source ID.

claims: Outdoor/structural habitats, dark glossy adult and light attraction.
Species-aware household pest management.

proposedDescription: Smooth brome is a cool-season perennial grass widely planted for hay, pasture and erosion control. Its usefulness in those settings explains why it is so familiar across much of North America. The same ability to form a dense sod can be a problem where it spreads into native grassland. It grows from underground stems as well as seed, so an established patch is more than the visible flowering stems. Management should start with the purpose of the land and the identity of the grass.
identification: Look for broad, flat leaf blades, often with a wrinkled mark shaped like an M across the middle. Flowering stems carry an open, branching head in late spring or early summer. The plant commonly grows roughly one to three feet tall and develops a closely connected stand through underground rhizomes. The leaf mark is helpful but should be checked alongside the flower head and plant base. Related bromes, including native forms treated differently by some floras, make a mature specimen valuable for confirmation.
actions: In a working pasture, ask a forage adviser whether the stand meets the farm's goals before treating it as a weed. In prairie restoration, map the edge and watch for expansion into native plants. Avoid sowing smooth brome into a restoration area that is intended to support native grassland. Established patches require a plan that accounts for rhizomes and protects desirable vegetation during treatment. Clean seed from equipment, retain good replacement cover and check the site over subsequent seasons. One mowing or one visible dieback does not demonstrate lasting control.
researchNotes: Missouri forage account and USFS ecological synthesis support distinct agricultural/native-grassland contexts. Historical FEIS includes infrataxa; no Pumpelly's brome traits or blanket nativity claim applied to all forms.

claims: Forage use, M-shaped leaf mark, panicle and rhizomes.

proposedDescription: Smooth cat's ear is a small yellow-flowered herb that can look like a delicate dandelion from a few steps away. It usually grows as an annual, with a low leaf rosette and slender flowering stems. Introduced from Europe, it is recorded in the Washington flora and has naturalized elsewhere. Its presence is not enough to establish a serious ecological problem. The most useful first step is to separate it from rough cat's ear and other yellow-flowered members of the daisy family.
identification: The leaves stay mostly at ground level and may be toothed or lobed, with little hair or only scattered short hairs. Thin stems carry small yellow flower heads and only tiny bracts rather than ordinary stem leaves. The fruit is particularly useful: outer fruits lack a long beak, while inner fruits have one. Rough cat's ear can overlap in size and hairiness, so the name 'smooth' is not an absolute rule. Photograph the rosette, a complete flowering stem and a mature seed head with close detail.
actions: If the plant is unwanted in a bed or lawn edge, lift the small rosette and root before seed heads mature. Check nearby bare patches and decide whether suitable ground cover would reduce repeated establishment. In natural habitat, confirm the species and the reason for intervention before removing a group of lookalike wildflowers. Avoid assigning livestock effects reported for another cat's-ear species to this one. A botanical record with clear photographs and a date is useful even where the plant's local impact has not been assessed.

proposedDescription: Smooth crabgrass is a warm-season annual familiar in lawns, garden edges and other disturbed ground. It grows low and branches near the base, often filling gaps where the intended vegetation is thin. Much of the next season's population comes from seed, which makes preventing seed production and improving cover useful parts of management. It is a turf weed, but its appearance does not mean the surrounding landscape has an ecological emergency. A response can be matched to the size and purpose of the space.
identification: Look for flat leaves and leaf sheaths that are mostly hairless, sometimes with a few hairs near the collar where blade and sheath meet. The flower head has several narrow, fingerlike branches spreading near the top of the stem. Older plants may become reddish at the base. Large crabgrass usually has much hairier leaves and sheaths, although small details still deserve a close look. Photograph the collar and sheath as well as the seed head; a distant picture of a low grass patch can be ambiguous.
actions: Remove small unwanted plants before seed ripens, especially along the edge of a newly repaired lawn or bed. Review mowing height, irrigation and bare spots so the desired vegetation can compete more effectively. If crabgrass is recurring widely, ask local extension staff about a seasonal plan that fits the turf species and any reseeding you intend to do. Herbicide timing and reseeding restrictions vary by product. Clean seed-bearing clippings from equipment, and judge progress over the following growing season rather than expecting an immediate end to all seedlings.
researchNotes: Independent Missouri and Cornell descriptions support field distinctions. Sources differ about occasional rooting at nodes, so public copy does not make that an absolute diagnostic.

claims: Hairless sheaths, collar hairs, annual habit and fingerlike head.

proposedDescription: Smooth hawksbeard is a short-lived, yellow-flowered plant that often appears in lawns, roadsides and other open, disturbed places. It begins with a rosette and later sends up branching stems carrying many small flower heads. European in origin, it has naturalized in other regions. Several hawksbeards and cat's-ears share this general look, so identifying it is more useful than treating every small yellow daisy as the same weed. The reviewed floras describe its biology without establishing a universal need for removal.
identification: Basal leaves are narrow to spoon-shaped, with edges ranging from toothed to deeply lobed. Smaller upper leaves clasp the stem with pointed bases. The many yellow heads sit on slender branches; their outer petal surfaces may carry a reddish stripe. Mature fruits are small and lack an elongated beak, with white hairs above them. Despite the common name, some parts can be hairy. Photograph the lower leaves, the way upper leaves meet the stem, and both flowering and mature fruiting heads.
actions: In a garden where it is unwanted, remove the rosette or young flowering plant before seed dispersal. Recheck the space later in the season, especially if fresh soil has been exposed. Where small flowering plants are tolerated, first establish whether this species is actually causing a problem. For a meadow or restoration site, have the identity checked against native and other introduced lookalikes before broader treatment. Record how abundant it is and whether it is increasing. Avoid routine spraying based only on a yellow flower head or an app's tentative name.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Two independent floristic treatments support the species-specific recognition details. Local abundance and management need remain observations to establish, rather than assertions about all yellow-flowered weeds. proposedDescription: Smooth joyweed is a low, mat-forming plant with small pale flower clusters tucked close to its leaves. Its native range includes tropical and subtropical America, which makes location essential to understanding an observation in the United States. Kew lists Puerto Rico within its native range and several continental US states as introductions. The name also belongs to a genus containing very different species, so the severe aquatic impacts associated with alligatorweed should not be attached to smooth joyweed without evidence.
identification: Look for spreading branches that can root where they touch the ground. Leaves are oval to broader toward the tip, and young parts may carry pale hairs despite the word 'smooth' in the common name. Small white flower heads sit directly in the leaf axils rather than on long, obvious stalks. Closely related joyweeds require examination of the tiny floral parts for reliable identification. Photograph the leaves, rooting joints and a flower cluster with a scale, and keep the habitat context in the record.
actions: Ask a local botanist or extension service to confirm both the species and its regional status before removing it from a natural area. If an identified patch is unwanted in a cultivated bed, lift rooted sections carefully and keep fragments out of drains or nearby vegetation. Recheck for overlooked pieces. Do not apply an alligatorweed management plan simply because both plants are Alternanthera. A useful report states where the plant grows, how much ground it covers and whether it appears to be expanding, while leaving unsupported impact claims out.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Fresh Kew geography resolves the vague US-applicability concern by separating continental introductions from native tropical territory. Independent voucher-based BSI morphology supports identification; no alligatorweed impact is transferred. proposedDescription: Smooth rattlebox is an upright member of the pea family with leaves divided into three leaflets and clusters of flowers followed by conspicuous pods. It is recorded from disturbed ground, fallow fields and roadsides in the southeastern United States. Some regional accounts identify those plants more narrowly as the variety obovata. That distinction matters when a catalog contains both the species and a variety: they are overlapping taxonomic records, not automatically two separate invaders at the same location.
identification: Look for an erect herb with three leaflets on each leaf stalk and many flowers arranged along an elongated cluster. The pods extend well beyond the small flower calyx. Leaflet shape varies within the broader species treatment; the southeastern obovata form has broad, rounded-to-obovate leaflets and noticeably curved pods. Other rattleboxes may have a single leaf blade or differently shaped leaflets. Photograph leaves, flowers and mature pods together. A leafy plant alone may not support a confident species or variety identification.
actions: If rattlebox appears in a field or planting, confirm the species before deciding on control, and preserve the variety name when a specialist can determine it. Remove unwanted plants before pods mature and keep collected pods contained. Do not introduce an unidentified rattlebox into forage, feed or a cover-crop mixture on the assumption that every pea-family plant is suitable. Ask an agricultural adviser about plants found in grazing or hay areas. In a natural setting, document the extent and nearby vegetation before undertaking a broader removal effort. When counting a patch, avoid duplicating plants already reported under variety obovata.
researchNotes: Fresh review: The species and obovata records intentionally represent broad and narrow identifications, with no incorrect voucher demonstrated. Explain that the same plant can satisfy both concepts, retain the variety where confirmed, and do not count overlapping observations twice. proposedDescription: This smooth rattlebox record refers specifically to Crotalaria pallida variety obovata, rather than to the species in its broadest sense. It is an erect, short-lived plant found in disturbed ground, and North Carolina's flora assigns its smooth rattlebox populations to this variety. Florida's assessment currently advises preventing escape while reassessment continues. The variety and the broader species can describe the same individual plant, so observations should retain the most precise identification actually supported by the specimen.
identification: Leaves have three leaflets, each generally broadest toward the tip, with a relatively smooth upper surface and sparse, pressed-down hairs beneath. Elongated flower clusters bear yellow flowers marked with reddish-brown veins. Pods are several centimeters long. These characters help recognize the form, but other rattleboxes still require comparison, especially when flowers or fruits are missing. Photograph the underside of a leaflet, a flower from the side and a mature pod. Do not assign the variety merely because a plant resembles a photograph of the species.
actions: Keep the variety name on a confirmed record and ask a botanist to check plants that lack diagnostic material. If unwanted plants are producing pods near a field or natural area, contain the pods and remove the plants before seed is scattered. Check disturbed ground nearby for further seedlings. Avoid moving rooted plants or giving away seed while their local suitability is unresolved. For hay or grazing sites, consult an agricultural adviser rather than assuming the plant is acceptable forage. Follow local recommendations when choosing a replacement cover. Do not count the same plants again as a separate species-level population.

proposedDescription: Smutgrass is a tough, perennial bunchgrass often noticed as wiry clumps standing above a pasture or lawn. Florida pasture guidance treats it as an important weed, while botanical sources disagree about the northern limits of its native range. That uncertainty does not prevent managing a damaging pasture population, but it does make a blanket 'foreign invader' label unhelpful. Small smutgrass also needs to be separated from giant smutgrass, a related species with a different scientific name.
identification: Look for a compact clump with tough fibrous roots and narrow, upright flowering stems. The seed head is long and very slender, with short branches held so close that it may look like a single spike from a distance. Some plants have blackened upper leaves or heads associated with a fungus, but not every plant will show that feature. Photograph the entire clump and a close view of the flowering head. A mature specimen is useful for distinguishing Sporobolus indicus from other dropseeds.
actions: In a pasture, map the affected clumps and ask a forage adviser to confirm the species and evaluate the desired grass cover. Prevent seed-bearing material from traveling on equipment, and avoid moving contaminated soil or hay between clean and affected areas. A control plan should include recovery of the pasture after unwanted clumps are treated. In a natural area, resolve local status before broad removal. Monitor the same places over time; a short-term reduction in tall seed heads does not show whether the perennial plants or new seedlings remain.
researchNotes: Fresh review: The southeastern native-range boundary remains disputed, but the exact small-smutgrass account and Florida pasture concern are independently supported. proposedDescription: Snail flower is a twining member of the pea family whose flower shape is more distinctive than its common name. Older references may call it Vigna speciosa or Phaseolus speciosus; these names refer to the same taxonomic lineage now placed in Sigmoidotropis. It is a plant of tropical America, with botanical records describing it as a climbing herb. The reviewed sources establish its identity but do not demonstrate a particular invasive impact in the United States. Other vines sold as snail vine or corkscrew vine may be different species.
identification: Look for leaves divided into three leaflets on a twining stem. The flower has the familiar pea-family arrangement, but the keel is strongly curved into an S-like form rather than simply pointing forward. Florida's botanical key uses the large corolla and sharply bent keel to distinguish it from a related Sigmoidotropis. Slender pods follow the flowers. Photograph the flower from several angles, along with a complete leaf and any pod. A common-name label or a spiral-looking flower alone is not enough.
actions: Keep the original nursery label and any older scientific name when asking a botanist to identify a planting. If a vine has moved beyond its support or appears outside cultivation, document the rooted base and surrounding habitat before cutting it back. Keep removed stems and pods out of natural areas and waterways. Do not assume that management advice for another snail vine applies to this species. Where local escape risk is uncertain, avoid sharing seed or cuttings until the identity and regional suitability have been checked.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Brazilian voucher morphology and updated independent Florida key support exact identification. The ordinary older Vigna/Phaseolus synonyms do not create an entity conflict; US harm remains unasserted. proposedDescription: Sneezewort, listed here under the common name sneezeweed, is a perennial Achillea with loose clusters of white flower heads. It is also grown as a garden flower, so a plant beside an old house may have a planting history worth investigating. This is not one of the Helenium species that also carry the name sneezeweed. Shared common names are especially unhelpful when people are looking up a plant's effects or deciding whether it belongs in a meadow.
identification: Look for upright stems with narrow, lance-shaped leaves that have finely toothed edges. The leaves are simple rather than divided into the feathery segments familiar from common yarrow. Several white flower heads gather near the top of the stem in a loose cluster. Cultivated selections can have fuller-looking heads, so flower shape alone may vary. Photograph a whole stem, the leaf margin and the flower heads, and retain any nursery label. Comparing the leaves is often the quickest way to avoid a mistaken yarrow identification.
actions: Check whether the plant was deliberately planted and whether it is moving beyond that area before deciding on management. If it is unwanted in a bed, remove the established clump carefully and monitor for returning shoots. Keep divisions and garden waste out of nearby natural habitat. For a wild occurrence, ask a local botanist to confirm the identity and regional status. Do not transfer livestock warnings or home-remedy instructions from another plant called sneezeweed. The scientific name is the useful anchor for any further advice.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent horticultural and botanical accounts support species recognition. The shared sneezeweed common name is explicitly separated from Helenium, and no livestock or medicinal inference is transferred. proposedDescription: Snow in summer is the silvery, low-growing perennial often planted over the edge of a wall or along a rock garden. Its pale foliage and white flowers can make a bright patch even in a small space. It spreads by runners and has escaped cultivation in some places, including documented records at Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore. That does not make every maintained planting equally troublesome; climate and nearby habitat influence how readily it expands beyond a garden.
identification: Look for a dense covering of soft white hairs on the narrow leaves and stems, giving the whole plant a gray or silver cast. Flowering stems rise above the low mat and carry white flowers; the petals extend well beyond the surrounding sepals. Small cylindrical capsules follow. Other mouse-ear chickweeds can look similar, especially when not in flower. Photograph the foliage close enough to show the felted hairs and include flowers or mature capsules. A specialist may need those details to separate garden escapes from related plants.
actions: Watch the outer edge of a planting and remove runners that reach unwanted ground before they form a larger mat. Keep divisions and rooted trimmings out of natural areas. If plants are appearing away from the garden, document the distance and habitat and ask a local plant program whether removal is appropriate. Dig small unwanted patches carefully and check afterward for remaining rooted pieces. In a restoration setting, choose a replacement ground cover suited to the local plant community rather than leaving a broad area of bare soil.
researchNotes: Independent NZ flora, Missouri horticultural account and NPS historical occurrence provide morphology, runner spread and a bounded escape example. NPS record is historical evidence, not a current survey claim.

proposedDescription: Snowbush is a tropical shrub grown mainly for its patterned foliage. Kew now treats Breynia disticha as a synonym of Phyllanthus nivosus. Green, white and sometimes pink-toned leaves can make it look as though the branch tips have been lightly dusted with snow. Despite names such as Hawaiian snowbush, its native range is in the southwestern Pacific, including New Caledonia and Vanuatu. It is widely used ornamentally, and the reviewed sources describe cultivation more clearly than ecological harm. A garden shrub should not be called an invader simply because it appears in this catalog.
identification: Look for thin, often reddish branches with small, simple leaves arranged alternately. The leaves are oval to broader toward the tip, with smooth edges; cultivated forms commonly show irregular pale markings. Flowers are tiny, greenish and without showy petals, so they are easily missed beneath the foliage. Small rounded red fruits may follow. Several unrelated plants share names such as snow-on-the-mountain. Photograph the woody branching pattern, leaf arrangement and any flowers or fruit, and keep the nursery label when available.
actions: Monitor the edge of a planting for unwanted shoots and note whether new plants are appearing beyond the maintained bed. Keep prunings and rooted pieces out of natural areas. If the shrub is outgrowing its space, ask a local horticultural adviser about removal or a more suitable replacement. For a suspected wild escape, record whether it is close to a hedge, old garden or dumped material. Confirm its regional status before broader control. A precise observation is more useful than assuming that variegated foliage signals either harmlessness or invasive behavior.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent current nomenclature now links Breynia disticha to Phyllanthus nivosus. proposedDescription: Snowpeaks raspberry is also known as Mysore or hill raspberry. It is a prickly, sprawling bramble introduced to Hawaii for ornamental and food use, where it can form dense thickets that exclude other plants and make forest access difficult. Birds and mammals can carry the seeds after eating the fruit, while vegetative growth expands established patches. Similar problems are documented in the Galapagos. Those regional impacts are more informative than assuming all raspberries, or every occurrence of this one, behave alike.
identification: Look for long, arching canes armed with hooked prickles and compound leaves divided into several toothed leaflets. The leaf undersides are conspicuously pale and hairy. Ripe fruit is dark purple to black. Hawaiian sources describe more than one form, and flower or cane color varies between accounts, so neither should be treated as a single decisive test. Photograph the cane, both leaf surfaces and fruit without pushing into the thicket. Native Hawaiian raspberries and other introduced brambles should be checked before control.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the local invasive-species program, especially near forest or a site being restored. Avoid moving fruiting branches, soil or rooted canes to another place. For small confirmed plants, removal should include the rooted base and a plan to check for regrowth and seedlings. Large thorny thickets need experienced crews and follow-up work rather than a single cutting. Wear protective clothing if working near the canes, keep access routes clear, and restore suitable vegetation where removal leaves exposed ground.
researchNotes: Hawaii state guidance and independent Galapagos observations support regional impacts; Hawaii university morphology adds identification. Flower-color conflicts avoided; no unsupported mainland distribution.

proposedDescription: Soft brome, also called soft chess, is an annual grass introduced from Europe and widespread in many western North American grasslands and disturbed places. Its compact, softly hairy flower heads are a familiar part of spring vegetation. The name covers several subspecies, and different references draw those boundaries differently. A record identified only as Bromus hordeaceus should remain at that level. It should not be silently reassigned to a subspecies simply because that form is common nearby.
identification: Look for softly hairy leaves and stems, with a narrow, crowded cluster of plump spikelets near the top. Each spikelet contains several florets, and their coverings usually carry relatively short awns. The leaf sheath is closed, unlike that of false brome. Size and head shape vary, and mature spikelets are much more informative than a newly sprouted tuft. Photograph the leaf sheath, a complete head and a close view of several mature spikelets. Keep the original identification level on the observation.
actions: In a garden or small managed patch, remove unwanted plants before the heads shed seed. Clean seeds from footwear and mowing equipment before entering a clean site. In a grassland, discuss the aim and timing of control with the land manager so native annuals and perennial grasses are protected. Track whether treatment reduces the next season's seedlings rather than simply removing this year's dry stems. If a subspecies determination is needed for research, arrange a botanical review of mature material instead of guessing from a general field photograph.
researchNotes: Independent Burke morphology and USFS ecology; broader species treatment retained. No species-wide impact automatically assigned to catalog subspecies.

proposedDescription: This record is for the divaricatus subspecies of soft brome, a narrower identification than the general Bromus hordeaceus entry. Botanical references have used several names for plants in this group, so the original identification and the reference used to make it are worth preserving. A subspecies name helps describe variation within soft brome; it does not by itself establish a distinct local impact or a different control program. The evidence reviewed here is strongest for taxonomy and recognition.
identification: British botanical guidance distinguishes divaricatus by a relatively stiff, upright flowering head with many spikelets on short branches and stalks. Its awns curve outward as the fruits mature, whereas the typical hordeaceus form generally has straighter awns. These are mature-plant characters and should be considered together, not as a single-photo shortcut. A grass specialist may also need measurements of the spikelets and their floral coverings. Photograph several mature heads from the same population and include a scale rather than relying on plant height.
actions: Keep a tentative observation at the broader soft-brome level until the subspecies has been checked. If collecting is allowed and a herbarium requests material, ask how to retain mature spikelets without scattering seed. For an unwanted garden patch, prevent seed production and contain cut heads while the identification is reviewed. In natural habitat, base any larger intervention on the site's management goals and confirmed local evidence. Do not count the same plants twice under the species and subspecies entries when describing the size of a population.

proposedDescription: This is the typical subspecies of soft brome, a name used when a plant has been identified more precisely than Bromus hordeaceus alone. It belongs to a variable grass group whose subspecies can overlap in outward appearance. Current Kew taxonomy recognizes this subspecies, and regional keys distinguish its mature flowering heads. That taxonomic detail is useful for a botanical record, but it should not turn a general soft-brome observation into a confirmed subspecies record without the necessary mature material.
identification: Compared with the divaricatus form, botanical guidance describes a flowering head that may droop to one side and have branches of varying lengths. The awns are generally straight and upright at maturity. Spikelet characters are more dependable than the overall height of the plant, which can vary substantially with growing conditions. Take close photographs of mature spikelets and the complete head, and include a ruler. A small plant is not automatically a different subspecies, nor does a crowded head alone settle the identification.
actions: Retain the name used by the identifying botanist and note which regional key was followed. If the plants are unwanted in a small managed area, prevent seed shedding and clean equipment before moving elsewhere. Larger grassland work should protect native plants and include a plan for follow-up and replacement cover. Where only the species is confirmed, report soft brome without adding a subspecies guess. Keep counts at one taxonomic level when mapping the patch so the same individuals are not duplicated in species and subspecies totals.

proposedDescription: Pulvinaria citricola is a soft scale insect whose scientific name has changed as researchers clarified its anatomy. Older references may place it in Takahashia or Saissetia. Those names are useful when tracing a specimen or publication, but they do not make it the same insect as the citrus pest commonly called citricola scale, Coccus pseudomagnoliarum. The material reviewed for this profile is primarily taxonomic, so it supports a careful identification route more strongly than a claim about local damage. This profile follows the 1909 name; a Japanese palace survey separately recorded it on satsuma in 2010.
identification: Egg-laying females produce a developed cottony egg sac, but that feature is shared by several related scales. The research description separates this species using microscopic structures, including the shape and setae of the anal plates and the arrangement of ducts on the underside. Those are specialist characters, not features a gardener can reliably assess from a distant photograph. Photograph the scale and egg sac on the host plant, and include the host's identity, the date and a close view with a size reference.
actions: Keep a newly acquired plant with unidentified scales separate from other plants while advice is sought. Ask an extension diagnostic service or scale-insect specialist whether a specimen is needed, and follow its collection instructions. Note any decline or sticky deposits without assuming that this species caused them. Avoid choosing a citrus treatment simply because the word citricola appears in the name. A useful response begins with confirming the insect and assessing the plant's condition; the reviewed evidence does not support a species-specific household spray recommendation.
researchNotes: Fresh review: The palace survey supplies distinct 2010 material independent of the redescription specimen set. Follow the 1909 name, distinguish the 1914 homonym now called P. nipponica, and do not infer US occurrence or injury. proposedDescription: Urbicola soft scale is a plant-feeding insect with a broad host range, including many unrelated shrubs and trees. It has been documented on tropical islands and in other warm regions, and researchers consider outbreaks potentially damaging. Its cottony egg sacs can be more conspicuous than the females themselves. A white patch on a leaf is still only a clue: several scales and mealybugs look similar, and an exact species name matters before an observation is used to explain a plant's decline.
identification: Young females are yellowish or light green and become browner as they mature. A white, fluffy, somewhat ribbed egg sac extends beneath and behind the oval body, often reaching several times its length. Scales may occur on leaves, stems or roots. Confirmation requires microscopic characters that separate it from similar Pulvinaria species, including cottony camellia scale. Photograph the female and egg sac together, record the host plant and include a size reference. Do not identify it solely from the amount of white wax.
actions: Inspect new nursery plants before placing them among established plantings, and keep a suspicious plant separate while a diagnosis is arranged. For an outdoor tree, document which branches are affected and whether the problem is increasing. Ask a plant-health specialist to assess the living scales, host condition and available natural enemies before choosing treatment. Avoid moving infested cuttings or leaves to another site. If specimens are requested, package them as directed. A targeted response should follow confirmation rather than treating every cottony insect on the property.

proposedDescription: Softseed wild petunia is more often sold as Mexican petunia or Britton's wild petunia. It is a flowering perennial that has been widely planted because it tolerates many garden conditions. In Florida it can spread into natural areas and form dense stands. Seed-producing plants disperse through capsules, while creeping lateral roots allow established clumps to expand. Even a sterile cultivar can spread vegetatively, so a seedless label does not remove the need to watch the edge of a planting.
identification: Look for upright green or purplish stems with opposite, long, narrow leaves. The trumpet-shaped flowers are usually purple, although cultivated forms can be pink or white. Narrow capsules follow fertile flowers. Native Ruellia species and garden selections should be checked carefully before removal, particularly when a plant is not flowering. Photograph the full plant, leaf arrangement and flowers, and keep the cultivar label if one was supplied. A common name such as wild petunia is not precise enough to settle the identity.
actions: If a planting is spreading toward a ditch, wetland or wooded area, contain it early and consult local guidance. Remove unwanted plants with attention to the below-ground growth, since cutting off the tops can leave living roots. Revisit treated ground for new shoots and seedlings. Keep root pieces and seed-bearing waste out of natural areas. Where the plant is invasive, choose a locally suitable replacement. Ask a nursery to identify a cultivar by name rather than accepting an unverified promise that all Mexican petunias are harmless or seedless.

proposedDescription: Soldier's orchid is a small, ground-growing orchid that can turn up where a much showier flower would seem out of place: a lawn, a shrub border, or even a crack in pavement. Native to Asia, it has naturalized in parts of the southeastern United States and Hawaii. Its ability to occupy disturbed ground makes it worth documenting, but finding one plant does not establish that it is damaging the surrounding habitat. An orchid identification matters before deciding whether to remove it.
identification: Look for a short upright plant with narrow leaves arranged around the stem and a crowded spike of tiny flowers. The flowers are white with a yellow lower lip. Plants growing in shade can look dark green, while those in bright sun may be reddish or bronze; color alone is therefore a poor test. Photograph the whole plant, the arrangement of its leaves, and several flowers from the front and side. Flowering plants provide much better evidence than leaves alone.
actions: Leave unfamiliar orchids in place while seeking an identification from a local botanist or extension service. Include the date and whether the plant appeared in maintained turf, a nursery pot, or nearby natural vegetation. If it is confirmed and unwanted in a managed bed, remove it carefully before capsules mature and keep the material contained. Avoid moving soil from the patch into other beds. Return during the next flowering season to check whether it was an isolated arrival or part of a continuing population.
researchNotes: NAOCC supplies direct U.S. naturalization and morphology; Kew independently supports accepted identity and Asian native range. Specific ecological damage or a national eradication requirement was not established. Draft limits impact language accordingly.

proposedDescription: Burnet saxifrage is a perennial member of the carrot family, despite a name that suggests a saxifrage. It grows in grassy and disturbed places, where its pale flower clusters can blend into the summer vegetation. University of Minnesota Extension identifies it as an invader of disturbed grasslands and woodlands and notes that abundant seed helps it colonize open ground. That regional concern is useful context, rather than a reason to assume that every white-flowered plant nearby belongs to this species.
identification: The lower leaves are divided into broad, toothed leaflets. Leaves higher on the stem become smaller and more finely divided, with bases that sheath the stem. The small white, sometimes pinkish flowers form umbrella-like clusters. Plants may approach two or three feet tall. Take photographs of both the basal leaves and the upper stem; a flower-head picture alone leaves out important clues. Wild carrot and several other members of the family can look similar from a distance.
actions: Do not taste a plant to settle its identity. Have a knowledgeable local botanist or extension office check the leaf and flower photographs before handling a patch. In Minnesota, follow the state's reporting guidance for confirmed plants. Elsewhere, ask the land manager whether the species is a local concern. On property you manage, keep confirmed plants from setting seed and arrange follow-up removal of surviving roots or new seedlings. Clean loose seed and soil from equipment before moving to another grassy area.
researchNotes: Minnesota Extension gives explicit species-level invasion and reporting context; Kew independently supports taxonomy, perennial habit, Eurasian native range and morphology. Reporting recommendation remains Minnesota-specific. No wild-carrot control recipe or toxicity claim transferred.

proposedDescription: This wild sorghum is closely related to the sorghum grown for grain and forage. Some floras recognize Sorghum arundinaceum as a species; others place it within Sorghum bicolor as subsp. verticilliflorum. This account concerns the wild form, rather than every cultivated sorghum plant. Different names on two lists may describe the same plant and should not be counted as two separate findings. An observation should also explain whether the grass was deliberately planted or appeared on its own.
identification: Floral descriptions show a tall, leafy grass that is annual or short-lived and lacks spreading underground rhizomes. Its branched flower head can be broad and open or narrower. The small flowering units occur in pairs, with a fertile, stalkless spikelet beside a stalked one. These details are difficult to see in a distant photograph. Record the entire flower head, the leaf base, stem nodes and, with permission, the base of the plant. Do not identify it simply as any tall grass with a sorghum-like seed head.
actions: Keep suspected seed heads out of seed mixtures, animal bedding and garden waste that will be spread elsewhere. Ask an agricultural extension office or herbarium to determine which name and taxonomic treatment fit the specimen. Explain whether it grew from deliberately sown material or appeared independently. If an unwanted plant is confirmed on managed ground, prevent seed maturation and check the site again after removal. Avoid applying johnsongrass advice automatically; that species has a different underground growth habit.

proposedDescription: Sorghum is an important cultivated grass, grown for grain, fodder and other uses. An intentionally planted crop is different from an unwanted volunteer outside the field. The broader species also includes wild forms, some listed separately under names such as Sorghum arundinaceum. This account covers that broader crop-and-wild context without treating the names as additional occurrences. A garden or roadside observation should explain whether the plant was sown, persisted from an earlier crop, or appeared without planting.
identification: Look for an upright, cane-like grass with broad, flat leaves and a branched flower or grain head at the top. Heads vary greatly, from fairly open to compact, and mature grains may differ in color among cultivars. Many cultivated forms are annual and lack rhizomes. Neither height nor grain color is a dependable species test. Photograph the head, leaves, stem nodes and plant base, and keep any seed-packet or crop-variety information associated with the observation.
actions: Do not remove a farmer's crop or a deliberate garden planting because it appears in an introduced-species list. For unwanted volunteers, ask the grower or land manager how they fit the crop rotation and weed-management plan. Prevent seed-bearing material from being carried into clean seed lots or neighboring beds. If identification is uncertain, seek agricultural advice before choosing control measures or using unfamiliar plants as feed. Revisit disturbed ground after removal and record whether further plants emerge from the same site.
researchNotes: Profile evidence reassessed: The independent OGTR crop biology account distinguishes cultivated sorghum, wild forms and crop-wild derivatives. The profile can explicitly cover the broader species while distinguishing cultivated plants from escapes; the adjacent wild-form entry is a narrower concept rather than proof of an additional occurrence. The broader crop-and-wild scope is explicitly supported, rather than pretending the adjacent wild-form entry is unrelated or an extra occurrence. Next action: Owner review of the bounded description can proceed. Preserve cultivated-versus-volunteer context and audit overlapping wild-form records separately. Fresh access is recorded per source; inherited evidence access describes the earlier review and is not a claim that every full text was reread. Practical documentation and containment guidance is bounded editorial synthesis, not a demonstrated eradication result. proposedDescription: Sorghum midge is a tiny fly whose larvae feed where a sorghum grain should develop. A flowering field can look promising while damage is beginning inside its flowers; later, affected heads contain empty or poorly developed grains. The vulnerable period is flowering, so the timing of an observation matters more than simply seeing small flies near a crop. Midge pressure can build through successive plantings, and susceptible late crops may face greater risk. This is a crop-monitoring problem that calls for timely, local advice.
identification: Adults are delicate orange to reddish flies, roughly two millimeters long, with clear wings and long antennae. Look closely at flowering sorghum heads, especially during the morning, without assuming every small flying insect is a midge. Empty-looking florets and small pupal cases projecting from the flower coverings can support a diagnosis. Photograph the insects and the whole head, and record whether fresh flowers are present. Beneficial tiny wasps can also be active around heads and should not be counted as midges.
actions: Begin scouting as heads flower and follow the sampling method recommended by your local crop adviser. Record the variety, planting date, flowering stage and number of suspected midges, rather than acting on a single photograph. Ask about resistant varieties and coordinated planting schedules when planning the next crop. Manage nearby volunteer sorghum and relevant grassy hosts within the farm's weed plan. If treatment is being considered, use current local thresholds and product guidance; larvae sheltered inside florets make poorly timed spraying ineffective.
researchNotes: Independent Queensland and UGA extension sources establish morphology, flowering-stage injury and monitoring. Older UGA source is not used for current pesticide thresholds or product choices. Queensland lists several related hosts; draft avoids UGA's narrower assertion that only two hosts exist.

proposedDescription: Sour cherry is a familiar fruit tree with a second life beyond orchards and gardens. It can produce seedlings outside the planting area and send up suckers that develop into a thicket. That tendency deserves attention near a meadow, woodland edge or other place where a planted tree is meant to stay contained. It does not make every orchard tree an ecological problem. The useful distinction is between a maintained planting and new stems spreading into ground where they were not intended.
identification: Look for a small deciduous tree with alternate, oval to elliptical leaves and finely toothed edges. Clusters of white, five-petaled flowers appear in spring, followed by rounded red fruit in summer. Gray-brown bark can show conspicuous horizontal markings. Sweet cherry and other cherries require careful comparison, especially when fruit is absent. Photograph the leaf surfaces, leaf stalk, flowers or fruit and the relationship between young stems and the older tree. Do not use tasting as an identification method.
actions: Check around the parent tree and along nearby edges for seedlings or connected suckers. On property you manage, remove unwanted young growth and revisit the area, since cutting one stem may not resolve the whole patch. Keep fruit and pruning waste out of natural areas. For a retained fruit tree, use a routine containment plan rather than removing it solely because it is introduced. If a tree outside cultivation appears to be spreading, ask a local botanist or extension service to confirm its identity and advise on appropriate follow-up.
researchNotes: NC Extension supports reseeding, suckering and recognition. Independent NPS records document historic noncultivated occurrence; they do not prove present abundance or current impact. Draft makes no claim that all sour cherry plantings are invasive, and avoids edible-part advice and poisoning detail.

proposedDescription: South African lovegrass is a dense perennial bunchgrass from southern Africa. Its tough clumps can be easy to overlook among other pasture or roadside grasses, especially before flowering. Botanical accounts describe it as a poor grazing grass and document introductions outside its native range. The Flora of North America records it from waste areas beside livestock lots in South Carolina. Those records are useful leads, but they do not establish that the species is widespread or causing the same problems throughout the United States.
identification: Look for tight clumps with narrow, often folded leaves and strongly flattened leaf sheaths near the base. The flowering stems can reach roughly a meter, carrying an elongated, branched head of small, many-flowered spikelets. This species lacks the spreading rhizomes that characterize some other persistent grasses. A reliable identification needs mature spikelets and close examination of the sheath and tiny structures where the blade meets the stem. Photograph those features, along with the full clump and its growing setting.
actions: Avoid moving seed-bearing clumps or loose material from an uncertain patch into clean pasture. Record whether the plants are beside feed storage, livestock yards, disturbed soil or an established grassland. Ask a regional grass specialist or herbarium to examine a permitted specimen before choosing a control plan. If confirmed plants are unwanted on managed land, prevent further seed production and arrange follow-up checks. Keep the patch mapped so that a later visit can distinguish regrowth from new seedlings or a genuinely expanding population.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent PROTA and FNA treatments support recognition and a precise historical South Carolina context. Current distribution is left unverified; germplasm and foreign pasture problems are not converted into US invasion claims. proposedDescription: The South American rice miner is a small fly whose young feed inside developing rice leaves. Damage may be much easier to notice than the insect itself: leaves emerge with pale scars and may tear, leaving the plants looking ragged. Extension reports documented injury in Louisiana and Texas rice during the early 2000s. Those reports establish a real crop association, while the importance of the insect in any present-day field still needs local assessment. Other rice insects can leave superficially similar marks.
identification: Adults are small gray flies. The larvae are pale, legless and concealed within damaged leaf tissue; brown pupae may also be found there. Broad, elongated white mines or lesions tend to run along the leaf veins. When damaged leaves unfold, their tips may break or remain attached by a narrow strip. Photograph a whole affected plant and close views of several leaves. Preserve the connection between the symptoms and any larva found, because a fly photographed elsewhere in the field is weaker evidence.
actions: Ask your rice extension specialist to check suspicious injury, especially when young plants or a late planting are affected. Record the planting date, crop stage, approximate area involved and whether symptoms are increasing. Follow the diagnostic service's instructions for submitting leaf samples; do not move living insects or damaged plants between fields. Keep scouting records alongside other crop observations so that an adviser can separate this miner from other causes of leaf injury. Base any intervention on current regional guidance rather than an old pesticide recommendation.
researchNotes: Independent Texas A&M production guidance and LSU publication establish rice injury and U.S. records. Both are historical sources; draft does not imply an active outbreak or current treatment recommendation. Hydrellia griseola biology and management from California search results were explicitly excluded.

proposedDescription: South American waterweed is a submerged perennial native to southern South America and introduced in parts of Europe. Its slender leafy stems can resemble other waterweeds closely enough that distribution records have been confused. A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service review specifically questioned a reported Washington occurrence because it lacked corroboration and could represent another Elodea. A name in a database is therefore not enough to announce that this species is established in a U.S. waterbody.
identification: Look for long, thin underwater stems bearing narrow, usually flat green leaves. That general appearance is a starting point, not a reliable species identification. Elodea nuttallii has been mistaken for this species, and the common name South American waterweed is also used for Egeria densa. Take clear photographs of an intact stem section, several leaf arrangements and any flowers visible without disturbing the bed. Include a scale and the waterbody location. An aquatic botanist may need a properly collected specimen to decide the identity.
actions: Never empty aquarium plants or pond-cleaning waste into streams, lakes or drains. Before leaving the water, inspect boats and equipment for attached vegetation and follow local cleaning requirements. If you find an unfamiliar submerged patch, report it to the waterbody manager or aquatic invasive-species program and request identification guidance. Avoid pulling apart a large bed on your own; loose material can complicate containment. Arrange any sampling or removal with the responsible manager, and keep observations separate from an unconfirmed species name.
researchNotes: Fresh review: Independent habit description and FWS record audit support a useful cautious profile. Uncorroborated US establishment is stated explicitly; specialist reporting and aquatic hygiene do not require claiming a confirmed invasion. proposedDescription: Bipolaris maydis is the fungus responsible for southern corn leaf blight. It survives in infected crop material, and spores can move with wind and splashing rain when conditions favor infection. Warm, damp weather helps the disease develop. Its history includes the severe 1970 epidemic associated with a particularly susceptible type of corn, but that history should not be used to predict the outcome of every modern field infection. Hybrid resistance, crop conditions and the particular fungal race all affect the practical risk.
identification: Look for tan to light-brown spots that often begin on lower corn leaves. Lesions may lengthen between the veins and develop darker margins; heavily affected leaves can become extensively blighted. Some forms of the disease also affect other plant parts. Leaf spots alone cannot identify the fungus or its race. Photograph both early and advanced symptoms, including where they occur in the canopy, and compare several plants. Other corn diseases can produce brown lesions that need a diagnostic laboratory to separate.
actions: Record the hybrid, growth stage, recent weather and how widely symptoms occur, then contact your extension plant-disease service for sampling instructions. Choose resistant varieties when planning future plantings and discuss crop rotation and residue management suited to the site. Avoid assuming that every spotted leaf needs a fungicide: the value and timing of treatment depend on diagnosis and field conditions. Follow current local guidance if a product is recommended, and continue checking the crop so that management decisions reflect the developing problem.
researchNotes: Cornell, Clemson and Arkansas independently support pathogen identity, symptoms, disease cycle and management context. Race-T epidemic is explicitly historical; no claim of a new introduced outbreak or universal susceptibility. No blanket tillage recommendation or pesticide product/dose included.

proposedDescription: The southern cowpea weevil is a small seed beetle that can turn an apparently sound bag of dried cowpeas into a source of emerging adults. Its young develop inside individual seeds, so the damage often remains hidden until neat round exit holes appear. Infestations can begin on legumes in the field and continue in warm storage. The important setting is therefore a seed lot or pantry, rather than a tree or wooden building. Finding adults near a cupboard should prompt a careful check of stored beans, peas, lentils, and other dried legumes.
identification: Adults are compact, dull-colored beetles with a body that narrows toward the head. Cowpea weevils have dark markings toward the tips of the wing covers and additional dark spots above them. Eggs are attached to seeds or pods, while the pale larvae and pupae remain inside the seed. Several other bean beetles produce similar holes. Photograph both an adult and the damaged seed, preferably with a scale, rather than identifying the species from the hole alone.
actions: Inspect nearby legume packages, contain infested material, and dispose of the affected food or seed lot so emerging beetles cannot reach other supplies. Clean spills and storage corners, rotate older stock first, and move sound supplies into pest-proof containers. Check planting seed before it enters the garden. A persistent infestation deserves identification by an extension office; spraying pantry shelves or stored food is not a substitute for finding the infested package.
researchNotes: Independent UC and Utah extension guidance supports stored-legume biology and sanitation. No building-damage or broad ecological invasion claim.

proposedDescription: The southern green stink bug feeds by piercing plant tissue, with developing fruit, pods, and seeds particularly vulnerable. In vegetable gardens and farms, feeding can leave hard discolored spots or misshapen produce. It uses many host plants, and adults can shelter through colder weather before returning to growing crops. The species is established in warm parts of the United States, but a green shield-shaped insect is not automatically this pest. Some similar bugs have different feeding habits, and the crop's condition matters more than the presence of a single wandering adult.
identification: Adults are dull green and shield-shaped, with a broad triangular plate on the back. Three pale spots near the front of that plate are a useful close-up feature. Young nymphs look very different: dark, brightly spotted stages gradually give way to greener older nymphs. Eggs form orderly clusters on leaves. The similar green stink bug has a pointed underside spine, whereas the southern green stink bug's is rounded. Good top and underside photographs help an expert separate them.
actions: Inspect leaf undersides and developing produce for egg clusters, nymphs, and fresh feeding injury. Record which crop and growth stage are affected before seeking advice. Protect naturally occurring predators and parasitoids by avoiding an automatic broad treatment after one sighting. For recurring crop damage, use local extension scouting guidance and crop-specific thresholds; management should follow confirmed identity and the amount of injury rather than color alone.
researchNotes: UGA independent crop guidance plus UF identification guide. No crop-specific numerical threshold generalized across hosts.

proposedDescription: The southern house mosquito is a brown mosquito whose larvae develop in standing water, often where organic material has accumulated. Around homes, overlooked containers, catch basins, and poorly sealed septic systems can provide breeding sites. Females feed at night on birds and mammals; males feed on plant sugars. This species can transmit West Nile and St. Louis encephalitis viruses, although seeing a mosquito does not establish that it carries either virus. Local mosquito surveillance is the useful guide to current activity and response.
identification: Adults have a fairly plain brown to bronze appearance and narrow pale bands across the abdomen. Those bands curve rather than forming the bold striped pattern familiar on some Aedes mosquitoes. Eggs are laid together as floating rafts, and the immature stages live in water. Closely related northern house mosquitoes and hybrids are difficult to separate without specialist examination. A photograph may establish a mosquito group, but precise species identification often needs a properly collected specimen.
actions: Empty unnecessary water-holding containers, keep drainage routes clear, and refresh birdbath water regularly. Check window screens and arrange repair of a damaged septic lid rather than opening or treating the tank yourself. Use protective clothing and a labeled repellent when outdoors at night. Report persistent breeding in public drains or other inaccessible water to the local mosquito-control service, which can assess the site and choose an appropriate response.
researchNotes: Full UF and Jacksonville municipal pages read. Public-health claim limited to vector capability, not infection likelihood or diagnosis; no fish introduction advice.

proposedDescription: Southern rockbell is a slender bellflower that can be easy to miss until its small blue flowers rise above nearby grass. Botanical accounts describe it as a perennial, with much of its foliage concentrated close to the ground. It occurs in open or disturbed settings, and Hawaiian collections document naturalized plants. A plant growing beside a trail is not, by itself, evidence of serious ecological damage. This entry is best used to recognize and document the species while local status and management needs are checked.
identification: Look for narrow leaves low on nearly bare, wiry stems. The lower leaves can be broader and spoon-shaped, while leaves higher up become much smaller. Flowers are blue to lavender, sometimes white, and have five spreading lobes around a bell or funnel-shaped center. They may appear singly at the ends of long slender stalks. Capture the base of the plant as well as the flower: a close flower picture alone can be confused with other small blue wildflowers.
actions: Before removing a patch, photograph an entire flowering plant, the lower leaves, and any developing capsules. Note whether it is in a planted bed, lawn edge, sandy roadside, or less disturbed vegetation. Send uncertain records to a local herbarium or extension botanist. If it is an unwanted plant on managed ground, keep seed-bearing cuttings and soil from being spread elsewhere, and revisit the spot to see whether additional plants emerge.
researchNotes: Fresh NCSU and Bishop records support a perennial naturalized bellflower with concrete leaf and flower characters. The original missing US impact/control trial is unnecessary for identification and cautious seed containment; neither widespread harm nor treatment efficacy is asserted. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. General documentation and containment actions are editorial precautions, not tested control-efficacy claims.

proposedDescription: Southern root-knot nematode is a microscopic plant parasite that feeds inside roots. It belongs to a group capable of damaging many vegetables, field crops, and ornamentals. Infested plants may grow unevenly, yellow, or wilt despite adequate soil moisture because their damaged roots cannot supply the shoots normally. These aboveground signs resemble several other problems, including nutrient shortages and root disease. The useful first step is to examine roots and obtain a diagnosis, rather than assume that every weak patch needs more fertilizer or water.
identification: Root-knot nematodes cause swellings that are part of the root itself. On legumes, do not confuse these galls with the separate nitrogen-fixing nodules that can often be rubbed from the root. Gall size varies with the host, and some infected plants show little obvious swelling. Seeing galls can suggest the root-knot group, but it cannot identify Meloidogyne incognita specifically. A diagnostic laboratory may need both roots and surrounding soil to distinguish the species and assess the problem.
actions: Ask an extension or nematode laboratory how and when to collect samples before digging extensively. Avoid transferring soil, rooted plants, or runoff from an affected bed to clean ground, and remove adhering soil from tools. Select resistant varieties or rotation crops only after the nematode has been identified, because resistance to one species does not protect against every root-knot nematode. Keep weed hosts managed and plan the next planting around the diagnosis.
researchNotes: UC group-level identification and sanitation explicitly bounded; Maryland species-specific host/endoparasite evidence. No species diagnosis from symptoms, no universal rotation recommendation.

proposedDescription: Southern sailfin catfish, also called Parana sailfin catfish, is a South American armored catfish sold in the aquarium trade under names such as snow-king plecostomus. Its natural range includes the Paraguay and middle Parana river systems. Eschmeyer's current fish catalog treats Pterygoplichthys anisitsi as a synonym of P. ambrosettii; older references retain anisitsi. USGS records nonnative collections in Florida and Texas, but a collection record does not establish that a population still survives at that place. Aquarium names can also cover more than one species. A large armored fish seen in a local waterway therefore needs a careful identification before a species-level report is accepted.
identification: The body is covered in bony plates, and the mouth forms a suction disc underneath the head. These features distinguish armored suckermouth catfish from native North American catfishes, which lack the plates and have a more forward-facing mouth. Pterygoplichthys usually has more dorsal-fin rays than the similar aquarium genus Hypostomus. Separating individual sailfin species requires a specialist key, so a spotted body or tall dorsal fin should not be treated as decisive by itself. A published species key describes a complex pale-and-dark belly pattern with the pale areas wider than the dark areas.
actions: Never release an unwanted aquarium catfish into a pond, canal, or river. Ask an aquarium retailer or suitable rescue about rehoming before the fish outgrows its tank. For an outdoor sighting, record the location, date, estimated size, and clear side photographs if these can be obtained safely. Send the record to the state fisheries agency or USGS nonindigenous aquatic species program, and avoid moving a captured fish to another waterbody.
researchNotes: The independently authored 2006 diagnostic revision supplies the missing exact-taxon key beyond the 2001 Texas occurrence paper. The profile stays with documented morphology and aquarium-release prevention. Current Eschmeyer Catalog of Fishes treats Pterygoplichthys anisitsi as a synonym of P. ambrosettii, while NAS and the 2006 key retain anisitsi. This ordinary name crosswalk does not authorize a catalog remap or establish identity from an aquarium label. proposedDescription: Southern threecornerjack is a sprawling annual with hard, three-spined fruits that can catch on footwear, tires, and animals. It is also called doublegee or spiny emex; some current authorities use the name Rumex hypogaeus. Native to southern Africa, it is a troublesome crop and pasture weed in parts of Australia. Those regional accounts explain its spread and recognition, but they do not establish its current status in a particular American county. The woody fruits are the feature most likely to bring an overlooked plant to someone's attention.
identification: Young plants form a rosette of broad, dull green leaves. Several fleshy, ribbed stems then spread from the crown, often showing purple at their bases or joints. Flowers are small and green. The mature fruit is brown and woody, with three strong spreading spines. Compared with lesser jack, Emex spinosa or Rumex spinosus, this species generally sprawls more and has larger fruits with longer spines. Photograph mature fruit with a ruler as well as the whole plant.
actions: Keep children, pets, and livestock away from a heavily fruiting patch while its identity is checked. Remove attached burrs from footwear and equipment before leaving, containing them for disposal instead of dropping them elsewhere. On your own managed ground, small confirmed plants are easier to address before the fruits harden. Obtain local weed-management advice for pasture or crop infestations, and avoid transporting contaminated hay, soil, or loose plant debris.
researchNotes: Flora of North America independently corroborates the fruit and habit described by NSW, which explicitly links Emex australis to Rumex hypogaeus. Regional Australian harms stay geographically bounded. Burr hygiene and confirmation do not require a US herbicide trial. proposedDescription: Soybean aphid is a sap-feeding insect whose numbers can change quickly during the growing season. It spends winter as eggs on buckthorn, then moves to soybean, where many generations can develop without mating. Feeding colonies can weaken plants and leave sticky honeydew that supports sooty mold. Outbreaks vary considerably among fields and years, so finding a few aphids does not mean a damaging infestation is inevitable. Regular field scouting gives a much better basis for action than the first insect seen on a leaf.
identification: These tiny yellow-green insects have pear-shaped bodies and a pair of black cornicles, often described as tailpipes, near the rear. Both winged and wingless adults may be present. Nymphs resemble smaller wingless adults, and pale shed skins can accumulate near a colony. Early colonies often occupy tender growth, but later infestations can spread through the canopy. Small leafhopper nymphs and other green insects lack the aphid's paired cornicles; a close photograph or hand lens helps reveal that distinction.
actions: Scout plants at several locations across the field and record crop stage, aphid abundance, and whether numbers are increasing. Keep checking resistant varieties too, because resistance does not guarantee an aphid-free crop. Use the current extension threshold and sampling method for your region before treating. Avoid preventive spraying simply because aphids are present; predators, weather, and other natural controls may keep a small colony below damaging levels.

claims: Buckthorn life cycle, body shape, cornicles and sap feeding.

proposedDescription: This entry concerns Phakopsora meibomiae, one of two fungi called soybean rust. It is generally the milder pathogen and must not be confused with Phakopsora pachyrhizi, the more damaging Asian soybean rust fungus. Both infect living plant tissue, and their similar appearance makes the common disease name insufficient for identification. Sources describe P. meibomiae from the Americas, including Puerto Rico. That history should not be converted into a claim that it occurs in every soybean-growing region or causes the losses associated with its better-known relative.
identification: Rust symptoms can include small discolored lesions and tiny spore-producing pustules, especially on the undersides of leaves. Examine the lower canopy when investigating suspicious spotting, but remember that several soybean diseases can look similar from above. Even a convincing rust lesion does not separate the two Phakopsora species. Laboratory testing is needed to make that distinction. Photographs of both leaf surfaces, the whole plant, and the affected field pattern are useful supporting evidence for a diagnostician.
actions: Contact a plant diagnostic clinic or extension crop specialist before assigning the species name or choosing a fungicide program. Ask how to package and submit leaves so the sample arrives in usable condition, and include the crop stage and recent observations. Follow current regional rust monitoring when making crop decisions. Do not apply yield-loss figures or treatment schedules for Asian soybean rust automatically to this separate fungus.
researchNotes: Independent PCR development and Puerto Rico monitoring support species separation and the bounded American context. No Asian-rust yield loss, fungicide schedule, or dated continental absence is imported. Diagnostic referral is a complete appropriate action. proposedDescription: Spadeleaf, often called gotu kola, is a creeping perennial in the carrot family. Its stems can root as they extend, creating low patches of rounded leaves. The name needs particular care in North America: some references place American Centella erecta within Centella asiatica, while other treatments distinguish the plants. Kew gives C. asiatica an Old World and western Pacific native range. This disagreement means that a familiar lawn or wet-ground plant should not be declared introduced or invasive from the catalog name alone.
identification: Look for long-stalked, round to kidney-shaped leaves with a deep notch at the base and a scalloped or coarsely toothed margin. Several main veins radiate from the leaf base. The flowers are tiny and occur in small clusters near the nodes, rather than forming a conspicuous flower head above the foliage. Creeping stems, flowers, and mature fruits are useful evidence alongside the leaves. Similar pennyworts and American Centella require a regional botanical key for a dependable identification.
actions: Photograph the leaf stalk attachment, a section of creeping stem, and any flowers or fruits before disturbing a patch. Ask a local botanist which Centella treatment applies to the record and location. Keep cultivated plants and trimmings within the garden rather than discarding them beside wetlands. If the plant is unwanted, decide on management only after confirming its identity and local status; medicinal or culinary common names are not identification evidence.
researchNotes:
Research gap retained: A 2017 Australian original study independently separates asiatica, erecta and cordifolia using morphology and molecular data. Flora Mesoamericana also names native American erecta material and identifies old asiatica applications as misapplied. This adds a practical diagnostic lead but does not settle whether the catalog's American records denote the native or introduced entity. The additional source check leaves the specific identity or evidence question unresolved. Does the catalog intend cultivated Old World C. asiatica or American plants treated as C. erecta? Next action: Have the catalog owner reconcile its intended Centella entity against a current regional flora and original record determinations before invasive status is attached. Fresh access is recorded per source; inherited evidence access describes the earlier review and is not a claim that every full text was reread. Practical documentation and containment guidance is bounded editorial synthesis, not a demonstrated eradication result. Further evidence review, 2026-10-31. Kew accepts American erecta separately, whereas ITIS retains a broader asiatica treatment; the Kew entry also records a recent alternative treatment. The disagreement cannot be settled by assuming every US lawn plant is introduced.
Remaining scientific questions: Which regional taxonomic concept and verified specimen underlie each US record?
