proposedDescription: Spanish arborvine is a vigorous climbing plant also known as wood rose. Older references use Merremia tuberosa, while recent Florida assessments call it Distimake tuberosus. Its yellow flowers and decorative dried fruits helped carry it into gardens and floral arrangements. In Hawaii, officials describe an aggressive vine that can cover and smother other vegetation. Florida's assessment also identifies a high invasion risk. Those concerns are tied to warm regions where it can persist; they should not be treated as evidence that every planted vine has escaped.
identification: Leaves are alternate and deeply divided into several fingerlike lobes radiating from one point. The large yellow flowers are funnel-shaped, fitting its place in the morning-glory family. After flowering, enlarged sepals become brown and woody around the capsule, producing the distinctive rose-shaped structure. Mature capsules contain dark seeds. Photograph both leaf shape and the fruit structure, because yellow flowers alone occur on other climbing plants and a florist's dried wood rose may still contain seeds.
actions: Avoid moving seed-bearing wood roses between gardens or using locally collected fruits in arrangements that might be discarded outdoors. In affected warm regions, choose another ornamental and ask the local invasive-plant program about removing established vines. Photograph and map a new escape before work begins. Keep cut material and capsules contained, and arrange follow-up inspection; a large vine woven through trees needs a removal plan that protects the supporting vegetation.
researchNotes: Hawaii agency impact observations plus independent UF risk assessment and NYBG morphology; FNAI not counted as an independent UF lineage.

proposedDescription: Spanish broom is a woody shrub with upright green shoots and bright yellow flowers. Introduced as an ornamental, it can form dense stands on disturbed ground and compete with other vegetation. Its long-lived seed bank makes an established patch a continuing management task, even after the mature shrubs are gone. It is one of several plants called broom, and their appearances and local requirements differ. A careful identification is particularly useful where Spanish broom is uncommon but other broom species are widespread.
identification: The shoots are rounded in cross-section and relatively smooth or finely ribbed. Leaves are simple, sparse, and shed early, leaving the green stems conspicuous. Fragrant yellow flowers grow in loose groups toward branch tips, followed by flattened pods. Scotch broom generally has strongly ridged, angular stems and often three-part leaves; French broom usually carries more persistent three-part foliage. Take close photographs of a young stem, leaves if present, flowers, and pods instead of relying only on the shrub's overall silhouette.
actions: Check with the local weed program before working on a new population, especially near roads or natural areas. Small seedlings can be addressed before they develop a woody root system, but larger shrubs need a site-specific plan. Avoid moving mature pods with brush or machinery. After removal, revisit the area for new seedlings and regrowth, keeping the soil disturbance as limited as practical so the work does not simply create another germination bed.
researchNotes: UC management and Washington board independent regional policy support; no pesticide recipe or legal status generalized nationally.

proposedDescription: Spanish cherry is a tropical evergreen tree also called tanjong or bullet wood. Despite its English name, it belongs to the sapodilla family rather than the cherry genus Prunus. It is planted for a rounded crown, dense foliage, and strongly fragrant small flowers. Singapore's botanical records describe it as a familiar roadside tree, while regional Asian floras document native populations. These uses and records explain why it may appear in collections or warm-climate gardens; they do not establish an invasive impact in the United States.
identification: Leaves are simple, thick, and oblong, arranged spirally along the twigs. The small cream-white flowers sit in leaf axils and have many narrow points, giving them a star-like appearance. Fallen flowers can remain recognizable as little rings. Fruits are roughly olive-sized, oval and pointed, turning orange-red as they ripen. Photograph a leafy twig with flowers or mature fruit whenever possible. A common name containing cherry, medlar, or bullet wood is not enough to separate it from unrelated ornamental trees.
actions: For a tree outside a labeled collection, record whether it appears deliberately planted and whether seedlings occur away from the parent. Send photographs of foliage, flowers, fruit, and the whole crown to a local arboretum or extension office for confirmation. Keep unwanted fruits and seedlings out of dumped garden waste. Before removing an established landscape tree, establish its identity and local status and use a qualified arborist for work involving large limbs.
researchNotes: Karnataka specimen-linked flora supplies substantive botanical corroboration beyond the former Malaysian name record. A cultivated ornamental recognition profile can be ready without unproven US harm; tree-removal priority remains local. proposedDescription: Spanish heath is a tall evergreen shrub that escaped ornamental planting in parts of the Pacific coast. Its fine foliage and masses of pale flowers can make it resemble a large garden heather, but it can develop dense stands in suitable moist, acidic settings. Oregon and California agencies document concern along roadsides, rights of way, and other open habitats. The plant produces many tiny seeds, so preventing new colonies is an important part of management. Regional reports should not be read as a nationwide distribution map.
identification: Look for woody upright stems clothed in very small, needlelike leaves. The leaves occur in whorls, usually three or four around the stem, rather than as broad flat blades. Small white to pink bell-shaped flowers mass along the branches; on the Oregon coast flowering can begin in winter and continue into spring. Other heaths are sold in gardens, so size and flower color are not decisive alone. Close pictures of the leaf arrangement and individual flowers are more helpful than a distant flowering shrub.
actions: Report a suspected new escape to the relevant county or state weed program, including photographs and a precise location. Avoid collecting flowering branches from wild patches or transporting soil and debris from beneath them. Clean footwear and equipment after entering an infested area. Choose a locally suitable alternative for new planting. For established shrubs, arrange a control and follow-up plan with the weed program, since removing the visible plants does not account for all seed already present.
researchNotes: Oregon species profile and California rating provide regional evidence. Specific counts and older local distribution totals omitted.

proposedDescription: Spanish lime, also called genip, quenepa, or mamoncillo, is a tropical fruit tree in the soapberry family. It is related to lychee and longan rather than citrus. Native to northern South America, it has a long history of cultivation around the Caribbean and in southern Florida. A Virgin Islands flora also records naturalized plants. This combination of cultivation and escape makes site context important: an orchard tree, an old homestead planting, and a self-sown tree in surrounding vegetation should not be recorded as the same kind of occurrence.
identification: Leaves are compound, usually with two opposite pairs of smooth-edged leaflets. The central leaf stalk may be flattened or winged. Small fragrant flowers occur in clusters near branch tips, and the fruits form loose bunches. Ripe fruits retain a green, thin leathery shell surrounding flesh and a large seed. Photograph a complete compound leaf, its stalk, and a fruit cluster. An isolated leaflet can misleadingly resemble a simple leaf, while the name Spanish lime can invite confusion with citrus.
actions: When documenting a tree, note nearby houses, planting rows, labels, and any smaller trees growing beyond the maintained area. Preserve those details with photographs for a local botanist or extension fruit specialist. Collect unwanted fallen fruit in managed spaces and avoid dumping seeds in natural areas. Ask about local escape behavior before new planting. A naturalized record warrants attention to spread, but it does not by itself demonstrate ecological harm or justify removing a mature tree.
researchNotes: Independent St John flora and Florida crop guidance distinguish naturalized trees from deliberate plantings. The prior missing impact/control evidence does not block a profile that recommends documenting seedlings and avoiding seed dumping without declaring ecological damage. proposedDescription: Sparrow false pimpernel is a small creeping herb associated with moist ground, stream margins, and other wet places. Asian botanical accounts describe slender stems that branch near the base and can root at lower nodes. Its flowers are modest enough that a patch may first be noticed as low green growth between taller plants. The species occurs naturally across parts of Asia and Australia. Its presence in a global plant catalog does not establish a harmful invasion or a current local record in the United States.
identification: The leaves grow in opposite pairs and are longer than wide, varying from oblong to lance-shaped. Small white to pale purple tubular flowers have a distinctly lipped shape, with a three-lobed lower lip. Mature fruits are narrow capsules containing many seeds. Related false pimpernels and other tiny wet-ground herbs can look alike when not flowering. Photograph a whole stem, a close flower from the front and side, and a mature capsule; those details are more useful than a photograph of an undifferentiated mat.
actions: Record the habitat and whether the plants are rooted in open mud, a container, a garden bed, or a natural wet area. Ask a regional herbarium to check an unfamiliar record before assigning a species name. Avoid transferring wet soil or seed-bearing plants between ponds and gardens. If a confirmed patch is unwanted on managed ground, contain removed material and check the same damp spots again, while leaving surrounding wetland vegetation undisturbed until identification is secure.
researchNotes: Both botanical accounts were refreshed and agree on rooting stems, opposite leaves, wet habitat and pale lipped flowers. No US establishment or harm is inferred; documentation and avoiding movement of wet soil are bounded precautions. proposedDescription: Sweet potato chlorotic stunt virus, abbreviated SPCSV, infects sweetpotato and can travel in planting material as well as through whitefly feeding. An infected vine may show only mild symptoms, yet the virus can contribute to much more serious disease when another sweetpotato virus is present. The combination with sweet potato feathery mottle virus is known as sweetpotato virus disease. This distinction matters: a mild-looking source plant is not necessarily suitable for producing clean slips, and the severity of a mixed infection should not be attributed to SPCSV alone.
identification: Possible signs include leaf yellowing or reddening and reduced growth, but some infected plants show little obvious change. Mixed infections may produce distorted leaves and severe stunting. These symptoms overlap nutrient stress and other diseases, so photographs cannot identify SPCSV. A diagnostic service may use laboratory tests, sometimes supported by grafting to an indicator plant. Record the variety, source of the slips, age of the planting, and whether neighboring plants show the same pattern.
actions: Use virus-tested planting material from a reliable clean-stock program when available. Do not take new cuttings from a suspect planting or pass its storage roots to another grower for propagation. Contact an extension specialist about sampling, keeping suspect stock separate, and handling old vines or volunteer plants. Whitefly management should be part of local crop guidance; killing visible insects does not remove virus already inside an infected plant.
researchNotes: A later original coinfection experiment adds a substantive dataset rather than another mirror of the training manual. proposedDescription: Spear saltbush, also known as spreading atriplex or spearscale orache, is an annual of fields and disturbed ground. Despite its name, it is not a woody saltbush shrub. Regional botanical treatments record it as introduced in New England, where it can occur in human-disturbed habitats. Its relationship to similar oraches makes identification more demanding than the common name suggests. In particular, not every spear-shaped leaf beside a road belongs to this species, and occurrence alone is not a measure of ecological impact.
identification: Young foliage can carry a light mealy coating. Mature leaves are often narrow or triangular with a pair of basal lobes, but their shape changes along the stem. The small green flowers lack showy petals. Developing fruits are enclosed between paired bract-like structures whose shape and surface are important in identification. Keep photographs of the lower leaves as well as mature fruits, because the lower leaves may be lost by fruiting time. A regional key can separate it from prostrate and coastal oraches.
actions: For an unfamiliar patch, photograph the whole branching plant, several leaf levels, and ripe fruiting structures with a scale. Note whether it grows in a cultivated field, road verge, or saltmarsh, since habitat helps interpret the identification. Where confirmed plants are unwanted garden weeds, prevent seed production and avoid moving seed-laden soil. Obtain local advice for a large agricultural patch rather than assuming that a treatment recommended for another goosefoot-family weed will fit.

proposedDescription: Spearmint is a familiar aromatic garden herb that spreads by underground stems and can root where stems touch moist soil. A small planting can therefore become a broad patch without relying entirely on seed. Botanical records document naturalized plants in damp places such as ditches and water margins. The same growth that makes it useful in a kitchen garden can make it difficult to keep within a border. A cultivated clump and an escaped population should still be distinguished when reporting its occurrence.
identification: Look for upright, square stems with leaves in opposite pairs. The leaves have toothed edges and usually very short stalks or almost none. Small pale pink, lilac, or white flowers form narrow spikes at the stem tips. Leaf hairiness varies, and spearmint belongs to a genus with hybrids and overlapping characters. Its familiar scent is a helpful clue, but it should be checked against the leaf stalks and flowering spikes rather than used as the sole test.
actions: Grow spearmint where its runners can be contained and checked, such as a suitable container. Inspect drainage openings and nearby ground for escaping stems. Keep rooted trimmings and dug rhizomes out of waterways and dumped garden waste. If a patch is unwanted, remove the spreading underground growth carefully and revisit for missed pieces. Seek a botanical check before treating an unfamiliar wild mint, especially near wetlands where other mint-family plants may be present.

proposedDescription: The spectacled caiman is a crocodilian native to Central and South America and established in parts of southeastern Florida. It is associated especially with freshwater canals and lakes. Florida managers work to detect and remove nonnative caimans while protecting native alligators and American crocodiles, which can be confused with them. A sighting therefore calls for a clear location and professional identification. It does not call for approaching the animal, and a small individual should not be assumed to be harmless.
identification: Caimans can resemble pale-colored American crocodiles, but their snouts are shorter and more rounded. American alligators generally have a broader, rounder snout and darker overall appearance. Size is not a dependable separator because young native crocodilians are also small. A distant photograph showing the head and body together can help a wildlife specialist; there is no need to obtain an underside or close mouth view. Keep the original image and note the animal's approximate length without moving nearer.
actions: Stay well back, keep pets and children away from the water's edge, and never feed or attempt to capture the animal. Report a suspected caiman to the state wildlife agency with the date, precise location, and photographs taken from safety. Leave any removal to authorized specialists. Aquarium or captive animals must never be released, and an owner who can no longer keep one should contact the appropriate wildlife authority about lawful placement.

proposedDescription: Sphaeropsis blight is a pine disease often described in extension literature as Diplodia tip or shoot blight. The fungus has appeared under several names, including Sphaeropsis sapinea and Diplodia pinea. It can persist in apparently healthy tissue as well as dead material, with damage becoming more conspicuous after drought, hail, or other stress. Austrian, Scots, and red pines are among familiar susceptible hosts. A brown branch tip is a reason to investigate, but not proof of this fungus: insects, weather injury, and other diseases can produce similar dieback.
identification: Affected new shoots often carry unusually short, straw-colored or brown needles, sometimes held together by resin. Tiny black fungal structures may appear at needle bases and on cones. Branch cankers can also ooze resin, with foliage beyond them dying back. Photograph the whole tree, the pattern of affected shoots, and a close view of short needles and cones. A diagnostic clinic may need samples because the fungal structures and overlapping pine symptoms are difficult to interpret from a distant photograph.
actions: Reduce avoidable tree stress, including drought stress, and avoid wetting foliage unnecessarily. Ask an arborist or extension clinic to confirm the cause before pruning or choosing a treatment. If infected shoots are pruned, work in dry conditions and clean tools as recommended. Removing visible tips alone may not stop infection because the fungus can remain in cones and other tissues. Any protective fungicide program depends on spring growth timing and local guidance.
researchNotes: Independent Michigan State and Minnesota extension evidence supports symptoms and management. Replaced unstable AWS mirror with current Minnesota publisher page; dry-period pruning verified in its full text. Both Minnesota pages share one source lineage; MSU PDF remains independent. proposedDescription: Spiderwisp is an annual herb with conspicuous projecting flower parts that give its flower clusters a loose, whiskery appearance. Botanical references also call it Cleome gynandra, and Kew currently treats Gynandropsis gynandra as a synonym of that name. It occurs widely in tropical regions and has a history of cultivation as well as spontaneous growth. Name changes can scatter records between databases, so an older label is useful evidence rather than something to discard. These botanical records do not establish a damaging invasive population at a particular American site.
identification: Leaves are divided into three or five leaflets that meet at the end of a shared stalk. Flowers are white to purplish, with long stamens projecting beyond the petals. Long narrow capsules develop on stalklike supports beneath the fading flowers. Stems and leaves may have glandular hairs. Other spiderflowers share some of these features, so count the leaflets and photograph the entire flower cluster, including developing capsules. A flowering or fruiting stem is much more informative than a single detached leaflet.
actions: For an unexpected population, note whether it is inside a vegetable garden, near discarded garden material, or reproducing farther away. Retain photographs and the planting history for a regional herbarium or extension botanist. Avoid sharing seed under an uncertain name or dumping ripe capsules outdoors. If unwanted on managed ground, contain seed-bearing plants before removal and revisit the area for seedlings, without assuming that cultivation elsewhere proves local ecological harm.
researchNotes: Fresh flora accounts under Cleome gynandra support the older catalog combination and its diagnostic flower structure. The ordinary genus synonym is explained without changing the catalog ID. Crop context and seed containment do not claim a US invasion or dietary safety. proposedDescription: The spike-topped applesnail is a South American freshwater snail familiar in the aquarium trade. It was formerly treated as Pomacea bridgesii diffusa, and aquarium labels may still confuse it with Pomacea bridgesii or simply call it a mystery snail. USGS records nonnative collections in the United States, but individual records vary in age and do not demonstrate that every reported population remains established. The distinctions among apple snails matter because their feeding behavior and impacts differ. Claims about a destructive apple-snail species should not be transferred to this one by common name. A New Zealand study independently identified a wild specimen and aquarium specimens using DNA; its single river find did not prove establishment.
identification: The shell is rounded with a relatively pronounced pointed spire and several whorls. Color ranges from yellowish to dark olive-brown, sometimes with striping, so aquarium color forms are not a dependable species test. Egg clusters are described as tan to salmon-colored and are deposited above the water. Photograph the shell from the side and opening, plus any egg mass without disturbing it. A specialist should confirm the identification where native and introduced apple snails occur together.
actions: Keep aquarium snails, eggs, plants, and water from entering outdoor waterways. Arrange rehoming for unwanted animals instead of releasing them into a garden pond that may overflow. For a wild sighting, record the waterbody, precise location, date, and photographs and contact a state aquatic-species program. Avoid destroying unfamiliar snails or egg masses on appearance alone; confirmation protects native species and prevents a report from being assigned to the wrong apple snail.
researchNotes: An original New Zealand specimen and COI sequencing study adds independent evidence for P. diffusa beyond the Rawlings-Hayes taxonomy. Use of reference DNA does not make newly collected and sequenced specimens the same dataset. The study supports aquarium-release context, not borrowed bridgesii feeding claims or demonstrated local impact. proposedDescription: Spiked bur grass is a small annual grass whose flowering head carries tiny hooked structures. These can attach to fur or clothing, helping move the plant's reproductive parts beyond the original patch. Regional African flora records describe it on sandy ground and in open sunny settings, with stems sometimes spreading near the base before turning upward. Its short stature can make it easy to overlook among taller grasses. A specimen-based record is useful for identification, but it is not evidence that the species causes a particular level of harm in an American landscape.
identification: Look for short, relatively broad grass blades with noticeable hairs along their edges. The flowering head is a narrow, dense cylinder rather than a loose branching spray. Its small spikelets carry hooked prickles, giving the head a burrlike texture. Related Tragus grasses need close examination of the spikelets and their arrangement. Photograph the whole plant, leaf margins, and a mature head with a scale; a picture of burrs stuck to clothing rarely shows enough detail for a confident species name.
actions: Inspect footwear, socks, animal coats, and equipment after walking through a fruiting patch, and contain attached material instead of brushing it off at the next site. Record the habitat and whether the patch is expanding along a path or disturbed verge. Ask a herbarium or grass specialist to verify an unfamiliar record. On managed ground, address confirmed unwanted plants before mature heads detach, while avoiding unnecessary disturbance to surrounding grass cover.
researchNotes: The independent New England key breaks the prior dependence on a single African flora network. Species-level glume characters and introduced ballast context support recognition without a US impact or eradication claim. proposedDescription: Spiked speedwell is an herbaceous perennial widely grown for upright spikes of small flowers. It is quite different in appearance from the low, creeping speedwells that can appear as lawn weeds. Garden selections vary in flower color and height, and many plants offered under the broader name Veronica are cultivars or hybrids. A flowerbed label is therefore useful context, but it does not prove that a nearby self-sown plant belongs to the same species. The sources reviewed here support recognition and cultivation, rather than a general claim of invasive harm.
identification: Flower spikes rise above the foliage and narrow toward their tips. The individual flowers are small and star-like, commonly blue in the species, while named garden forms may differ. Leaves are simple, usually opposite, and have toothed or shallowly scalloped edges; some surfaces are hairy. Photograph the full flowering stem and the lower foliage, not just the tip of a colorful spike. Other upright speedwells can look similar, so a regional key or horticultural record may be needed.
actions: Keep the nursery label or cultivar name when documenting a planted specimen. If plants appear beyond the bed, photograph those separately and note their distance from the planting and whether they are producing seed. Remove unwanted flower stems before seed dispersal where containment is the goal, and keep garden waste out of natural areas. Ask a local botanist about uncertain escapes before removing wild plants merely because they resemble an ornamental speedwell.
researchNotes: An independently authored Australian horticultural flora now corroborates opposite hairy leaves, dense terminal racemes and perennial habit beyond NCSU. The detailed Victoria treatment adds botanical evidence; the superseded BSBI account is supplementary stable habitat information only, never current conservation status. No invasive harm is asserted. proposedDescription: The name spiketop apple snail is often used loosely in the aquarium trade. This entry is specifically for Pomacea bridgesii, a name that has frequently been applied to the separate species Pomacea diffusa. A US Fish and Wildlife screening document highlights that confusion and cautions that trade identifications can be unreliable. The practical consequence is simple: a purchased mystery snail is not a verified record of this species. Occurrence reports and impact descriptions need their scientific identity checked before they are combined.
identification: Apple snails have rounded coiled shells and a large opening that can be closed by a hard operculum, or trapdoor. A pointed spire may suggest the group sold under spiketop names, but shell color and a retailer's label cannot establish Pomacea bridgesii. Related species overlap in appearance, and published reports may use older names. Photograph several views of the shell, retain the purchase information if available, and have a mollusk specialist interpret the evidence rather than forcing an identification from one feature.
actions: Keep any unidentified aquarium apple snail securely contained and prevent eggs or live animals from leaving with discarded plants. Never release an unwanted snail into a stream, ditch, or outdoor pond. For a suspected wild population, record the exact location and send photographs to the state aquatic-species program, explaining that the species is uncertain. Let specialists advise on collection or removal; protecting native snails and preserving a reliable record are more useful than acting on a trade name.
researchNotes:
Research gap retained: The refreshed 2025 USFWS synthesis and 2023 South American review explicitly say introduced bridgesii reports probably involve diffusa. The latter follows the Hayes/Cowie evidence lineage rather than independently determining the catalog snails. The 2006 original chapter supplies shell comparisons but does not resolve those introduced records. The additional source check leaves the specific identity or evidence question unresolved. Which voucher-confirmed P. bridgesii records correspond to this catalog entry rather than P. diffusa? Next action: Obtain a specialist determination and current exact-species revision for the catalog records before replacing the hold with a P. diffusa-derived profile. Fresh access is recorded per source; inherited evidence access describes the earlier review and is not a claim that every full text was reread. Practical documentation and containment guidance is bounded editorial synthesis, not a demonstrated eradication result.

Further evidence review, 2026-10-31. The new apple-snail egg study uses the term bridgesii clade, but its tested members are diffusa and scalaris, not true bridgesii. It cannot fill the exact-species evidence gap. USFWS also explicitly warns about the trade-name confusion.
Remaining scientific questions: Which US material has an exact bridgesii determination independent of diffusa trade labels?

Next step: Find a specialist determination tied to a voucher; do not treat a clade name or aquarium label as species-level evidence.

proposedDescription: Spinach is the familiar cool-season leafy crop, Spinacia oleracea. It is grown for foliage and responds to increasing heat and day length by sending up flowering stems, a process gardeners call bolting. That change can make an abandoned crop look quite unlike the low leafy plant sold in markets. Cultivation is the central context for this entry: finding spinach in a garden or agricultural record does not establish an invasive problem. Volunteer seedlings and plants persisting outside a crop should be documented separately from deliberate plantings.
identification: Leaf shape and texture vary among cultivars, from relatively smooth blades to heavily crinkled, or savoyed, foliage. Plants begin with a low leafy form and later elongate into stems carrying inconspicuous flowers. A seed packet or planting record is often more reliable than trying to identify a detached leaf. Several unrelated vegetables are also called spinach, so keep the scientific name with the record. Photograph the entire plant and any flowering stem if a volunteer's identity is uncertain.
actions: In a vegetable bed, harvest and manage the crop according to local cool-season guidance. Remove unwanted bolting plants before seed matures if volunteers are a concern, and keep the planting history with observations submitted to a botanist. Do not report an intentionally grown row as an escaped population. If spinach-like plants occur away from cultivation, seek identification before using them as food or planning weed control; appearance and a familiar crop name are not sufficient.
researchNotes: Independent crop descriptions support recognizable spinach and bolting without implying invasive behavior. The earlier absence of impact evidence is handled by explicitly distinguishing cultivated rows and volunteers; the misleading Delaware New Zealand spinach comparison is excluded. proposedDescription: Spined scale insect is an armored scale found on a broad range of plants. A New Zealand study documented it on kiwifruit and noted other hosts including avocado, citrus, and several fruit crops. That study did not describe it as a major pest of all those hosts, although its presence could matter for movement of produce. This distinction is important: a host record identifies a plant the insect can use, not a guarantee of serious damage. Local identification and plant condition should guide any response.
identification: Like other armored scales, the settled insect sits beneath a protective covering and can resemble a small patch or bump on a leaf, twig, or fruit. That general appearance is not enough to recognize this species. Researchers specifically report that reliable separation from similar armored scales requires adult females mounted on slides and examined microscopically. Photograph the affected plant parts and the pattern of infestation, but retain suitable material only as instructed by a diagnostic service so important identification features are preserved.
actions: Keep a suspect nursery plant separate from other stock and avoid sharing cuttings until the scale is identified. Record the host plant and where it came from, especially if the finding involves recently purchased material. Ask an extension entomologist or plant-health service how to submit a sample. Do not choose a pesticide solely from the name spined scale: treatment timing, live-insect confirmation, host sensitivity, and the identity of similar scales all matter.
researchNotes: Fresh taxonomic history corroborates the exact species independently of the New Zealand field study. The catalog draws on original Comstock and Takagi material predating the New Zealand survey. Identification referral and stock separation are sufficient without a US treatment trial. proposedDescription: Spiny amaranth is an annual pigweed that can grow in fields, gardens, pastures, and disturbed ground. Its sharp stem spines make it particularly unpleasant to encounter while weeding or moving through a mature patch. Like other annual pigweeds, it reproduces by seed, so plants left to mature can add to future weed problems. It also resembles several other amaranths that require different management decisions. Confirming the species is useful before treating a crop infestation or interpreting a report of a resistant pigweed.
identification: The clearest field clue is a pair of stiff spines at the base of a leaf stalk. Stems are otherwise hairless. Leaves are oval to diamond-shaped with smooth margins, and some show a pale V-shaped marking. Greenish flower clusters occur along upper stems and at leaf axils. Palmer amaranth and waterhemp can also have smooth stems, but they lack these paired axillary spines. Photograph the stem nodes closely rather than relying on leaf shape, which overlaps among species.
actions: Wear gloves and use tools that keep hands away from the spines when removing confirmed plants on managed ground. Work before mature seed develops, and contain any seed-bearing tops. Check nearby disturbed areas for younger plants and avoid carrying contaminated soil or equipment into clean fields. For agricultural infestations, ask extension staff to identify the amaranth and select a current integrated plan; a treatment that worked on another pigweed may not work here.
researchNotes: Cornell morphology and Maryland comparative extension support; rice research institute supports annual seed reproduction and hand weeding. No herbicide recipe or universal resistance claim.

proposedDescription: Spiny cocklebur is a branching annual with two different kinds of prickly structures: sharp spines on the stems and hooked burrs enclosing the seeds. It grows in disturbed places including fields, farmyards, floodplains, and water margins. Burrs can tangle in animal coats or wool and move with people and equipment. Washington's weed program also warns that seeds and very young seedlings can poison livestock. The practical concern is to prevent exposure and spread, while confirming the plant rather than relying on the word cocklebur alone.
identification: Look for yellowish spines divided into three points at the leaf axils. Leaves are dark green above and pale or downy beneath; many have a long central lobe and two much smaller side lobes. The flowers are small and greenish, followed by oval burrs covered with hooks. Common cocklebur lacks the distinctive three-part stem spines. Photograph a stem node, both leaf surfaces, and a burr with a scale, keeping hands clear of the sharp parts.
actions: Keep livestock away from suspected seedlings or seed-contaminated material until an agricultural adviser confirms the plant and assesses the pasture. Clean burrs from clothing, coats, and equipment before moving elsewhere. On managed land, remove or cut confirmed plants before burr formation and inspect again for later seedlings. Contain mature burrs during disposal. For a large field or waterside patch, obtain a local management plan that accounts for access, seed persistence, and nearby desirable plants.
researchNotes: Independent California agricultural and NSW botanical accounts corroborate the distinctive spines and seedling hazard. No poisoning dose or treatment is prescribed. Burr containment and acting before seed formation are proportionate precautions. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. proposedDescription: Spiny plumeless thistle is a biennial that begins as a low rosette and later sends up a tall, branching flowering stem. It favors disturbed ground, pastures, fields, and road margins. Dense infestations can replace desirable forage and make grazing difficult. The plant is introduced from Europe and temperate Asia, but the response to a sighting should reflect local conditions and rules. Native thistles also provide wildlife habitat, so identifying the plant before removing a whole patch is especially important.
identification: Both leaves and stems are conspicuously spiny. Leaf tissue extends down the stem as narrow prickly wings, and those wings continue close to the flower heads. The heads are relatively small and pink-purple, appearing singly or in small clusters. Leaves are deeply lobed, often wavy, and hairy beneath. Musk thistle usually has larger, often nodding heads and a less continuously winged stalk immediately below them. Photograph the rosette, upper stem, and underside of a flower head to support identification.
actions: Ask a local weed coordinator to check an unfamiliar thistle, particularly where native species grow nearby. On managed ground, small confirmed rosettes can be dug before flowering, using gloves and a tool to avoid the spines. Contain seed-bearing heads instead of leaving them in loose brush. Maintain healthy pasture cover and inspect disturbed gaps after removal. Larger infestations need repeated follow-up and a site-specific plan rather than a single mowing pass.
researchNotes: Minnesota and Washington independent regional guidance supports morphology, pasture impacts and removal. No national legal obligation implied.

claims: Biennial habit, spiny wings to heads and forage impacts.

proposedDescription: Spiny sowthistle is an annual weed that can move quickly from a low leaf rosette to a flowering stem. It is common in disturbed ground, gardens, roadsides, and agricultural settings. Yellow flower heads eventually become small white seed heads, allowing the fruits to travel on air currents. Its prickly leaves account for the thistle name, but it belongs to a different group from the purple-flowered true thistles. The useful management window is before seed release, especially where several generations or repeated flushes can appear in mild weather.
identification: Leaves are often dark green and glossy, with stiff prickles along wavy edges. Rounded lobes at their bases clasp the stem. Flowers look like small yellow dandelion heads and occur in clusters above a leafy stem, rather than on single leafless dandelion stalks. Cut stems may show milky sap, a feature shared with several lookalikes. Common sowthistle generally has softer leaves and differently shaped clasping lobes. Photograph the leaf base and flower cluster, since a seed head alone is not distinctive.
actions: Remove confirmed unwanted plants from beds while they are young and before the fluffy seed heads open. Use gloves for the prickly foliage and contain plants that already carry mature seed. Check recently disturbed soil and the margins of containers for new rosettes. For a crop field, seek local advice that fits the crop and growth stage. Do not confuse this annual's management with that of a perennial sowthistle spreading from underground roots.
researchNotes: NCSU species-specific recognition and seed prevention plus independent Ontario crop account. UC genus page not used for contradictory species/subspecies invasion wording.

claims: Rounded clasping lobes, prickly foliage, yellow heads and seed prevention.

proposedDescription: Spiny threecornerjack is a prickly-fruited herb also known as lesser jack and, in newer botanical treatments, Rumex spinosus. It originates from the Mediterranean region and is recorded as an introduced plant in several parts of Australia. Its hard fruits can be troublesome in pasture and cultivation. It should be kept separate from southern threecornerjack, Emex australis, which is now often called Rumex hypogaeus. Similar common names can hide meaningful differences in fruit size, growth habit, and the interpretation of older records.
identification: The plant has broad oval to triangular leaves on relatively long stalks and stems that may spread or ascend. Small female flowers develop a hardened fruiting envelope with three sharp outward-pointing spines. Compared with southern threecornerjack, the fruits are smaller and their spines shorter; close measurements are much more useful than a general photograph of the patch. Take pictures of the whole plant and a mature fruit from several angles. Leaves alone can be mistaken for other members of the dock family.
actions: Prevent mature prickly fruits from traveling on footwear, animals, or equipment. If a suspected patch is found near grazing animals, keep access limited while an agricultural adviser checks the identification and site. Record the location and contain any sample as directed by a botanist. For unwanted plants on managed ground, act before mature fruits accumulate and avoid moving contaminated soil. Local guidance is needed before applying overseas pasture-control recommendations to a United States site.
researchNotes:

proposedDescription: This waterflea is a tiny freshwater crustacean, not a biting flea. Daphnia lumholtzi has become established in many United States waters after originating in warmer regions of Africa, Asia, and Australia. Its conspicuous spines can make it harder for some young fish to eat, potentially changing food-web relationships. Studies do not all find the same degree of impact, so local effects should not be overstated. The common name spiny waterflea is also used for other crustaceans, making the scientific name essential when comparing reports.
identification: Under magnification, look for a large pointed helmet on the head and a long tail spine, often about as long as the body. The body itself is only a few millimeters long, and additional small spines occur along the shell margin. These features distinguish it from many familiar native Daphnia, but specialist examination is needed to separate a plankton sample reliably. A stringy accumulation on fishing line is not enough to identify this species and may involve a different waterflea.
actions: Follow local clean, drain, and dry guidance for boats, live wells, nets, and other equipment before moving between waters. Do not transfer bait water or untreated lake water to another waterbody. If a plankton sample appears unusual, record where and when it was collected and ask the state aquatic-species program how to submit it. Keep samples contained, and avoid releasing aquarium or classroom cultures into outdoor water, even when the organisms seem harmless or nearly invisible.
researchNotes: Two distinct original experimental datasets replace reliance on overlapping government reviews. Laboratory and mesocosm predator effects support a cautious food-web description, not a universal local impact claim. proposedDescription: Spinyfruit buttercup is an annual buttercup whose most useful identifying feature appears after the yellow flowers fade. Its fruits have conspicuous projections, unlike the smoother fruits of many similar buttercups. Floristic accounts record it in damp disturbed places, cropland, and sometimes water margins, including naturalized occurrences outside its original range. The flowers can blend into a mixed patch of small yellow weeds. A record should therefore include mature fruits whenever possible, and should not be assigned from flower color alone.
identification: The lower leaves are rounded in outline and usually divided into three broad lobes, with additional teeth or smaller divisions. Stems are branched and largely hairless. Individual flowers have five yellow petals. After flowering, the head holds flattened fruits with prickly surfaces and a noticeable beak. Other buttercups can have lobed leaves and similar flowers, so the mature fruit shape is especially valuable. Photograph both a whole fruiting head and individual attached fruits at close range with a scale.
actions: Ask a regional botanist to check an unfamiliar buttercup before removing plants in a wet meadow or streamside area. Note whether the patch occupies disturbed soil, a cropped field, or intact vegetation. On managed ground where it is confirmed unwanted, prevent mature fruits from being carried with soil or garden debris. Use gloves when handling unfamiliar buttercups and avoid using them as food. A broad damp-area treatment is unnecessary until the identity and extent of the patch are understood.
researchNotes: Independent regional field accounts substantiate the distinctive fruit and disturbed wet habitat in the United States. No nationwide ecological harm is claimed. Confirmation and avoiding movement of fruiting debris are complete bounded actions. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. proposedDescription: Spiral ginger is a tropical perennial grown for its leafy stems and bright flower heads. Costus pulverulentus belongs to the spiral-ginger family and develops from rhizomes. Botanical garden sources place its native range in Mexico, Central America, and South America. The name spiral ginger is shared with other Costus species, so a nursery name alone is not enough for an exact record. In Singapore the species is described as cultivated, a useful reminder that a plant collection entry is not the same as evidence of naturalization.
identification: Leaves wrap around the stem in a spiral arrangement, creating a different pattern from the two-ranked leaves of many familiar gingers. Their bases form closed sheaths, with a small ligule at the junction. Red to orange-red tubular flowers emerge from dense terminal heads with bracts. Horticultural selections may have different foliage colors, so leaf color should not be used as the main distinction. Photograph the flower head from the side, a leaf base, and the entire leafy stem.
actions: For a garden specimen, retain the label and cultivar information and check whether any shoots occur beyond the planted clump. Keep rhizome pieces and unwanted divisions out of dumped garden waste or drainage channels. If plants appear in surrounding natural vegetation, document them separately and seek identification from a tropical-plant specialist. No broad removal recommendation follows from the species name alone; local establishment, site sensitivity, and confirmed identity should determine whether containment or further action is needed.
researchNotes: Fresh botanical and horticultural descriptions agree on spiral leaves, rhizomes and red-orange flowers. A garden plant profile may proceed without treating cultivated occurrence as escape or inventing local ecological damage. proposedDescription: Spiritweed is better known in many gardens as culantro or sawtooth coriander. It is a tropical American herb in the carrot family, grown in other warm regions and capable of seeding itself. Its long, sharply toothed leaves look quite unlike the finely divided foliage of common coriander. That distinction is useful when interpreting planting records, because several unrelated herbs share coriander-based common names. Cultivation and self-seeding explain how it can appear around gardens, but they do not establish a damaging invasive population at every location.
identification: Most leaves form a low rosette. They are elongated, broader toward the outer end, and edged with obvious stiff teeth. When the plant flowers, branching stalks carry small compact flower heads surrounded by pointed, spiny bracts. These structures give a flowering plant a much more prickly appearance than a young leafy rosette. Photograph the rosette and a whole flower head with its surrounding bracts. Aroma can support an identification, but it should not replace visible characters or a reliable botanical name.
actions: Keep the planting label when recording a culinary garden specimen, and note any seedlings outside the maintained bed. If containment is needed, remove unwanted flower stalks before seed matures and contain seed-bearing debris. Wear gloves around the spiny flowering structures. Ask a local herbarium to confirm plants found away from cultivation, especially where native Eryngium species occur. Avoid assuming that every plant called coriander is this species or is suitable for the same culinary use.
researchNotes: Independent American and Indian floristic descriptions corroborate culantro leaf and flower characters. Cultivation and unfamiliar volunteer records remain distinct; aromatic leaves alone are not an eating recommendation. proposedDescription: Spleen amaranth is an annual herb native to Mexico and tropical America. It has been grown and moved beyond that range, and regional floras also record it as a weed of disturbed places. The name is less familiar than the plant's resemblance to other pigweeds, which can make reports uncertain. It is particularly similar in overall form to spiny amaranth, but lacks that species' paired stem spines. Its occurrence in a cultivated or disturbed setting should not automatically be treated as evidence of harmful invasion.
identification: Plants are upright, with green to reddish stems and stalked leaves that are usually oval to diamond-shaped. Small greenish flowers form clusters in leaf axils and longer, sometimes branched spikes near the tops. The absence of paired axillary spines helps separate it from Amaranthus spinosus, but does not distinguish it from every other smooth-stemmed amaranth. Fine flower and fruit characters are needed for a confident identification. Photograph mature flower clusters, stem nodes, and leaves at several levels.
actions: Seek an extension or herbarium identification before selecting crop weed management or reporting a new population. Include the location, planting history, and whether plants are producing seed. For confirmed unwanted plants in a garden, remove them before mature seed is shed and keep seed-bearing material contained. Check disturbed soil for subsequent seedlings. Do not apply resistance reports or control expectations from Palmer amaranth, waterhemp, or another pigweed to this species without evidence.

proposedDescription: Splitlip hempnettle is an annual mint-family plant recorded in fields, meadows, and disturbed ground in northern North America. It is closely related to common or brittle-stemmed hempnettle, Galeopsis tetrahit, and older records sometimes combine them. The common name refers to the shape of the flower's lower lip rather than to a nettle sting. Because the two species are so similar without flowers, a summer photograph can be much more informative than a spring seedling or an autumn stem.
identification: Leaves are opposite and toothed, and the stems have stiff hairs with conspicuously swollen nodes. Small lipped flowers occur around the upper leaf axils. In splitlip hempnettle, the middle section of the lower flower lip has a distinct notch, and its sides turn downward. Flowers are often pinkish, but color is variable and should not be the deciding feature. Common hempnettle generally has an unnotched, flatter lower lip. Take a sharply focused front view of a fresh flower and a side view of a stem node.
actions: For an uncertain record, return while the plant is flowering rather than assigning the species from leaves alone. Note whether the site is a crop margin, disturbed clearing, or meadow, and send the images to a local botanist. If confirmed plants are unwanted on managed ground, prevent seed-bearing stems from moving with soil or cut vegetation. Local crop advice is preferable to treating every hempnettle as the same weed.
researchNotes: Independent floristic keys substantiate the flower distinction that makes this hemp-nettle recognizable. No local treatment trial is needed for a profile focused on confirmation and preventing seed movement. proposedDescription: Spongy moth is a forest insect whose caterpillars can strip leaves from trees during outbreaks. Oaks and many other woody plants can be affected, and repeated defoliation adds stress to trees already coping with drought or other injury. The established European form in much of the eastern United States has one generation each year. Egg masses survive the winter on bark and many outdoor objects, creating a route for people to move the insect. Older sources use the former common name gypsy moth.
identification: Older caterpillars are hairy and show five pairs of blue spots followed by six pairs of red spots along the back. Egg masses are tan and feltlike, often placed in sheltered places on trees, firewood, trailers, or furniture. Males are brownish with feathery antennae; females of the established European form are pale with dark zigzag markings and do not fly. Other members of the broader species complex can differ, so unusual moths or new-area sightings deserve official identification.
actions: Inspect outdoor equipment and stored items before moving them, and follow the destination's current plant-health requirements. Photograph suspected egg masses and report unfamiliar occurrences to the state agriculture or forestry agency. Protect stressed yard trees with appropriate care and seek local advice before treatment. Mechanical egg-mass removal can help around individual trees when done correctly, but a few scraped masses are not a forest-wide solution. Avoid improvised sprays and unattended sticky bands that can catch other wildlife.
researchNotes: UMN identification and Penn State outbreak-management guidance independent. Female flight statement restricted to established European form; no species-wide flight claim.

proposedDescription: Spotfin spiny eel is an elongated freshwater fish also sold as a peacock eel. It comes from Southeast Asian river systems, including the Mekong and Chao Phraya basins. Despite its eel-like shape, its small dorsal spines and extended snout distinguish it from familiar true eels. USGS lists nonnative collections in Florida, but a collection is not proof of a widespread or self-sustaining population. Aquarium trade names are also variable, so reports should retain photographs and the scientific name used by the identifier. Thai researchers have also studied captive spawning and nursery rearing of this species.
identification: The body is long, with a narrow, protruding snout and a flattened tail region. A row of small spines precedes the soft dorsal fin, which carries several dark rounded eye-like spots. Pectoral fins are present, while pelvic fins are absent. The combination of extended snout and dorsal markings is useful, but similar Asian spiny eels need comparison with a key. Photograph the fish from the side with its fins visible if that can be done without unnecessary handling.
actions: Do not release an aquarium spiny eel into a pond, canal, or stream. Arrange an appropriate rehoming option before disposal becomes urgent, and keep aquarium water and live contents out of waterways. For a wild observation, record the location, date, approximate size, and photographs and contact the state fisheries agency. If a fish has already been caught, ask the agency what to do rather than transporting it alive to another waterbody or assigning an identification from a shop name.
researchNotes: An independent Thai captive-breeding experiment corroborates the exact species beyond the shared NAS risk-review lineage. The experiment supports captive reproduction context only; its hormone regimen and local production results are not public management recommendations. proposedDescription: Spotted alfalfa aphid is a small sap-feeding insect that can damage susceptible alfalfa, especially young plants. Feeding introduces substances that stunt growth, and honeydew can leave foliage sticky and support dark fungal growth. Resistant cultivars and natural enemies have made a substantial difference in management, but resistance is not a reason to stop scouting. This profile concerns the alfalfa-feeding form commonly treated as Therioaphis trifolii maculata; EPPO and some crop guides use Therioaphis maculata. The broader T. trifolii name also covers other host-associated forms.
identification: The aphids are pale yellow to grayish, with rows of dark spots across the back. Each spot bears a short spine, best seen with a hand lens. Winged adults have smoky areas along the wing veins. They are smaller and paler than some other common alfalfa aphids; green pea aphids and dark cowpea aphids have different markings. Photograph a colony and a close individual, and note whether it is on new growth or older leaves.
actions: Sample across the field and record plant height, growth stage, aphid numbers, and natural enemies. Use local thresholds rather than transferring a number from a mature stand to seedlings. Check resistant varieties regularly and discuss variety choice with an adviser when planning a new planting. Preserve beneficial insects where possible, including through suitable harvest practices. If treatment is warranted, use current crop-specific guidance and label requirements that account for the next harvest or grazing date.
researchNotes: Kansas and UC crop guidance concerns the alfalfa-feeding form. Blackman/Eastop and EPPO explicitly bridge concurrent T. trifolii maculata and T. maculata treatments; no alfalfa impact is generalized to every host-associated T. trifolii form. Peer-review scope correction incorporated; no universal treatment threshold.

claims: Therioaphis name usage, spots, wing markings and seedling susceptibility.
Feeding damage, resistant varieties, natural enemies and scouting.

proposedDescription: Spotted henbit is more often called spotted deadnettle, a low perennial groundcover grown for patterned leaves and small flowers. Its trailing stems can root where they contact the soil, allowing a planting to widen beyond its original edge. It favors shaded garden settings and can persist around old plantings. Regional advice varies: Maryland extension has recorded some spread into natural areas and advises caution, while other horticultural sources emphasize garden use. That difference calls for local judgment rather than a blanket claim that every patch is invasive.
identification: Leaves grow in opposite pairs and are oval with rounded teeth. Many garden forms have a silvery blotch or broad pale center, although markings vary among cultivars. Small two-lipped flowers are commonly pink or purple, with white-flowered selections also available. The creeping perennial habit distinguishes it from the familiar annual henbit weeds, but a leafy fragment can still be misleading. Photograph a flowering shoot, its leaf pairs, and the rooted trailing stems, keeping any cultivar label with the record.
actions: Watch the edge of an existing planting and remove rooted stems that cross into adjoining natural vegetation. Keep divisions and trimmings out of dumped garden waste, where they may be overlooked. Ask a local extension office about regional escape behavior before expanding a planting near woodland. If plants occur away from gardens, document that population separately. Confirm identity before removal, because common names such as henbit and deadnettle cover several different species.
researchNotes: Fresh horticultural description and independent regional advice support creeping growth and garden containment. Maryland precaution is not converted into proof of widespread harm or measured seed dispersal. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. General documentation and containment actions are editorial precautions, not tested control-efficacy claims.

proposedDescription: Spotted knapweed is a taprooted perennial or biennial that can spread from roads, gravel areas, and field margins into grasslands and other open habitats. Dense patches compete with desirable plants and reduce the value of pasture. The name refers to dark markings on the bracts beneath each flower head, not spots on the petals. North American sources have used several scientific names for this plant, including Centaurea maculosa and C. biebersteinii. Records under those names need interpretation rather than automatic counting as different species.
identification: Plants begin with a rosette of gray-green, deeply divided leaves. Upright branching stems later carry small pink to purple flower heads. Beneath each head, overlapping bracts have dark triangular tips with a fine comb-like fringe, creating the characteristic spotted appearance. Upper leaves are smaller and less divided. Unlike a true thistle, the plant lacks conspicuous sharp leaf spines. Photograph the bracts close up, as several knapweeds have similar flowers and cannot be separated by color alone.
actions: Report unfamiliar patches to a local weed program and protect nearby uninfested ground from seed movement. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling plants. Small confirmed patches may be removed before seed matures, with flowering or seed-bearing heads contained for disposal. Clean equipment used in the patch and inspect the area repeatedly afterward. Established infestations need a plan that combines suppression, follow-up, and recovery of desirable vegetation rather than leaving bare ground for another flush.
researchNotes: UMN and Washington regional programs provide independent guidance. Broad C. stoebe entry does not independently prove subspecies identity or duplicate counts.

claims: Habitat spread, rosette, dark bracts and handling precautions.

proposedDescription: Spotted knapweed is a persistent plant of open disturbed ground and grasslands in North American management accounts. The name Centaurea stoebe subsp. micranthos is still used in older guides; Kew and the updated California assessment place it under C. stoebe subsp. australis. These accounts describe the same subspecies under different names. A record identified only as Centaurea stoebe still needs its original determination checked before it is assigned to this subspecies.
identification: Look for a gray-green basal rosette, later branching stems, and small pink-purple flower heads. The overlapping bracts below each head bear dark fringed tips, giving the spotted appearance. Leaves near the base are more deeply divided than those higher on the stem. These traits support recognition of spotted knapweed, but they do not by themselves resolve every subspecies or taxonomic treatment. Preserve close bract photographs, flowering material, and the name used by the original botanist or source.
actions: For a suspected patch, seek confirmation from the local weed program and explain which scientific name appears in the record. Prevent seed movement on equipment, hay, or soil while identification is being reviewed. Use gloves when handling plants and contain mature heads. A confirmed infestation should follow the local spotted-knapweed management plan, including repeated checks and vegetation recovery. Keep records under the parent species and subspecies linked so the same patch is not mistaken for two separate occurrences.
researchNotes: Kew and the updated Cal-IPC assessment explicitly connect micranthos with australis, resolving the ordinary name change. No species-level observation is silently promoted to a subspecies determination; detailed fruiting and flowering material remains necessary. proposedDescription: Spotted lanternfly is a sap-feeding planthopper introduced from Asia. It can gather in large numbers on woody plants, producing sticky honeydew that supports sooty mold and creates a nuisance beneath infested trees. Grapevines are a particularly important crop concern. Research-based guidance distinguishes that damage from the more limited effects often seen on established landscape trees. The insect is also an efficient hitchhiker: eggs laid on outdoor objects can move long distances with vehicles, equipment, and household goods.
identification: Adults hold spotted grayish forewings over the body; opening the wings reveals striking red, black, and white hindwings. Early nymphs are black with white spots, while the final nymphal stage adds red. Fresh egg masses have a gray coating that later resembles a cracked mud smear on a hard surface. Photograph the insect or egg mass and include the surface it was found on. Tan fuzzy spongy-moth egg masses and other insects can be mistaken for lanternfly evidence.
actions: Inspect vehicles, trailers, firewood, garden furniture, and other outdoor items before moving them from an affected area. Follow current state reporting and movement guidance, since the relevant boundaries change. Report a suspected new occurrence with a photograph and precise location. For an established infestation, use extension management advice suited to the plant and life stage. Avoid indiscriminate spraying or exposed sticky traps that can harm other animals; preserving plant health and preventing transport remain useful first steps.
researchNotes: APHIS pathway/identification and Penn State research management independent. No volatile state count or generalized tree-killing claim included.

proposedDescription: The spotted leopard slug is a large land slug with a pale gray-brown body patterned in darker spots and bands. It occurs in human-modified settings and has been introduced beyond its original range, including California. The striking pattern makes it memorable, but a slug's presence does not establish that it caused nearby plant damage. Species differ in their habits, and native slugs can share the same garden or woodland edge. Identification and a direct look at feeding are more useful than treating every slug as the same pest.
identification: The mantle, the saddlelike area behind the head, usually has spots or broken markings rather than continuous dark stripes. Farther back, the tail often carries longer dark bands that may break into spots. The body can become quite large when fully extended, but contracted animals look much shorter. Similar cellar slugs tend toward greener or yellower coloring and different tail patterns. Photograph an active animal from above and the side, including the mantle, tail, and head, without stretching or injuring it.
actions: Look after dark or during damp weather to see which animals are actually feeding on vulnerable plants. Keep newly purchased pots and their undersides free of unwanted hitchhikers before moving them between gardens. Do not relocate slugs to parks or natural areas. If protection is needed, ask local extension staff for a targeted approach that fits the plants and avoids harming other wildlife. Broad treatment based only on a spotted slug photograph can miss the real cause of damage.
researchNotes: Two independently authored mollusk accounts corroborate the mantle, tail and sole characters. General moisture and shelter management is bounded garden advice; no ecological impact or species-specific bait trial is claimed. proposedDescription: Spotted snapweed is the garden plant usually called garden balsam or rose balsam. It is an annual grown for colorful flowers that sit close to the stem, followed by capsules that scatter seed when ripe. It can naturalize in disturbed places, but it must not be confused with Himalayan balsam, Impatiens glandulifera, a different species with a different invasion history. Florida's assessment currently does not consider garden balsam a problem species there. That regional conclusion is useful context, not a guarantee about every climate or site.
identification: Plants have succulent upright stems with narrow, pointed leaves arranged alternately. The leaf margins are clearly toothed. Flowers are clustered in the leaf axils and may be pink, red, purple, or other cultivated colors; a curved spur projects behind the flower. The green capsules are fuzzy and split readily as they mature. Photograph the leaf arrangement, flower position, and capsule surface. Those features help distinguish garden balsam from other touch-me-nots better than flower color or the shared habit of explosive seed release.
actions: In a garden, remove unwanted seed capsules before they ripen if seedlings are spreading beyond the bed. Keep seed-bearing debris out of natural areas and note any plants growing well away from the original planting. For an unexpected wild patch, ask a local botanist to confirm the species before applying guidance written for Himalayan balsam. Record cultivated plants and self-sown escapes separately, and base management on the confirmed plant and local conditions.
researchNotes: NParks morphology plus current UF status assessment support a cautious, non-alarmist profile. Florida conclusion explicitly regional; no medical or edible-use advice.

claims: Alternate narrow leaves, axillary spurred flowers and fuzzy splitting capsules.
Current Florida not-a-problem assessment and common-name mapping.

proposedDescription: Spotted tilapia is an African cichlid established in Florida and associated with introductions through the ornamental-fish trade. Newer references often call it Pelmatolapia mariae, while older records and this catalog use Tilapia mariae. It inhabits a range of freshwater settings, including canals, ditches, rivers, and lakes. Reports from outside Florida vary in certainty, and some historical records have been questioned because of misidentification. A fish sold as tilapia or observed in a warm spring should therefore not be assigned to this species without supporting evidence.
identification: Adults have a fairly deep, flattened oval body with several dark blotches along the side. Juveniles look different, often yellow-green with stronger dark vertical bars. A diagonal dark stripe through the eye and a dark mark near the front of the dorsal fin can be particularly noticeable in young fish. Photograph the complete side of the fish and its fins, and record approximate size. Comparing an adult photograph with a barred juvenile alone can create a false impression of two species.
actions: Never release aquarium fish or move a captured tilapia to another waterbody. Keep pond or tank contents from escaping during overflow or disposal, and arrange suitable rehoming for unwanted fish. Report unusual outdoor sightings to the state fisheries agency with photographs and a precise location. Ask that agency about handling a captured fish and current local rules. Preserve both scientific names in the report so older records can be checked without inventing additional populations.
researchNotes: Museum specimen-based identification independently supports the USGS introduced-population account. The displayed museum vouchers are a distinct morphological basis from the historical field records summarized by NAS; overlapping general literature is not counted twice. proposedDescription: Spotted-wing drosophila is a small vinegar fly that can infest ripening soft fruit while it still looks suitable for harvest. Females use a serrated egg-laying structure to cut into thin fruit skins, allowing larvae to develop inside berries and other susceptible fruit. That ability distinguishes it from many familiar fruit flies associated mainly with damaged or overripe produce. Damage may become apparent only after picking, when apparently sound fruit softens. Frequent harvest and prompt handling are therefore important alongside monitoring in the planting.
identification: Adults are tiny, with the general appearance of other vinegar flies. Males usually have a dark spot near the leading edge of each wing and dark combs on the forelegs. Females lack those wing spots; their serrated egg-laying structure requires magnification to inspect. Small pale larvae in fruit cannot be identified confidently to this species by eye. Retain adult specimens from monitoring and seek expert confirmation, especially when a first infestation is suspected.
actions: Monitor susceptible fruit from coloring through harvest using local extension guidance, and do not rely on trap numbers alone to judge fruit quality. Harvest frequently, remove infested and overripe fruit from the planting, and cool sound harvested fruit promptly to slow insect development. Keep the canopy reasonably open and correct irrigation leaks where practical. For persistent crop losses, use an integrated plan tailored to the crop and harvest schedule, including exclusion or labeled treatments only when locally appropriate.
researchNotes: AHDB diagnostic guidance independent of UMN crop-management research. No food safety assurance or pesticide recipe; larval identification limitation explicit.

proposedDescription: Spottedheart is a tropical climbing plant in the morning-glory family, with broad, heart-shaped leaves and large funnel-shaped flowers. It can grow as a substantial woody creeper in coastal thickets and forest margins. The name is a useful reminder to examine the tiny dark glands beneath its leaves. Floras document this plant across tropical regions, but those records do not establish that a particular American planting is invasive or that a nearby wild vine belongs to this species.
identification: Look at the underside of a mature leaf with a hand lens: dark gland dots are an important clue. Leaves are broadly oval to almost round, with a heart-shaped base and a pointed tip. The flowers have the familiar morning-glory funnel, while the rounded fruit remains enclosed by enlarged, leathery sepals. Similar coastal vines have been called Ipomoea campanulata, and historical name confusion makes a flower photograph alone unreliable. Include leaf undersides, sepals, and mature fruit in an identification record.
actions: Photograph the entire vine and its supporting vegetation before cutting anything. A local herbarium or extension botanist can help resolve the name and determine whether the plant is an ornamental escape, an established regional occurrence, or a different vine. Keep garden trimmings and fruit out of natural areas. If removal is advised, plan how to detach the vine without pulling down the vegetation beneath it. For a large vine on a tree, seek advice before cutting; removal can damage the support plant and leave seeds or cut material to manage.
researchNotes: Independent Caribbean and Taiwanese floras agree on the gland-dotted leaves and persistent enlarged sepals. The identification profile can proceed without claiming local ecosystem damage or a tested removal method. proposedDescription: Sprawling signalgrass is a low, branching grass whose stems can lie along the ground and root at their lower joints. Botanical accounts place its native range from the Arabian Peninsula through parts of Asia to the Pacific and record introductions elsewhere in the tropics. It is associated with roadsides and disturbed ground. Finding it in a weedy patch is useful information, but neither a tropical distribution map nor a species-list entry demonstrates serious ecological damage at a particular United States site.
identification: The leaves are short and lance-shaped, often noticeably broader than those of fine lawn grasses. At the junction between blade and sheath, look for a fringe of hairs rather than a long membrane. The seed head carries several short branches along a central stalk; paired, crowded spikelets line these branches. Rooting lower stems can make one plant look like a loose mat. Signalgrasses and crabgrasses overlap in general appearance, so preserve photographs of a mature seed head, the leaf junction, and the rooting nodes.
actions: Record whether the patch is spreading beyond disturbed soil and whether it is displacing planted or native vegetation. Ask a grass specialist to confirm a flowering specimen before choosing treatment. For a small unwanted patch, careful removal before seed shed and containment of rooted stems are sensible precautions, with follow-up for new plants. Avoid moving soil or mower debris from the patch into clean areas. For larger patches, ask local extension staff to fit a plan to the site, its surrounding vegetation, and the amount of seed already present.
researchNotes: An independently authored FNA treatment breaks the earlier dependence on a single African flora lineage. The catalog name is retained; regional range statements differ, so habitat and diagnostic spikelets carry the profile rather than an overprecise global origin claim. proposedDescription: Spreading hedgeparsley is an upright herb in the carrot family that can turn a walk through grass or woodland edges into a session of picking burrs from clothing. Its small fruits carry gripping bristles, allowing animals and people to move seed beyond the original patch. It is an introduced weed in parts of the United States, with invasive-management guidance in California and Wisconsin. Its delicate white flowers can blend into other roadside plants, making fruiting material especially useful for confirmation.
identification: Look for divided, parsley-like leaves, slender branching stems, and small white flowers arranged in compound umbrella-shaped clusters. The developing fruits are oblong and become bristly little burrs. Photograph the bristles closely and include the structures beneath a flower cluster; these help distinguish Torilis species. Japanese hedgeparsley and other members of the carrot family can look similar at a distance. Do not identify a plant from white umbels alone or assume a parsley-like leaf means it is suitable to eat.
actions: Pull small, confirmed patches before flowering while the soil is moist enough to release the roots. Bag plants that already carry developing burrs so seeds do not catch on clothing during removal. Mowing around flowering can reduce seed production, but regrowth may require another visit. Clean footwear, pet fur, and tools before leaving a seeding patch. Work with the land manager on larger sites, and check again in following seasons for seedlings rather than assuming one round of pulling has finished the job.
researchNotes: UC weed report and NC State provide independent management and recognition lineages; regional impacts not generalized nationally.
