proposedDescription: The common pleco label does not reliably identify Hypostomus plecostomus. A modern study clarified this South American fish's identity in the Guianas, and a later Canje River survey recorded it in its native region. Many introduced American Hypostomus populations remain less securely identified. An aquarium label or an old occurrence name therefore needs checking before it becomes a species-level record. Findings about a different armored catfish, including its environmental effects, should not automatically be assigned to this one.
identification: An armored body and a mouth adapted to attach to surfaces are useful starting points for recognizing this broader group. They are not enough to distinguish H. plecostomus from other Hypostomus or from the sailfin catfishes called Pterygoplichthys. Photograph the whole fish from the side, its fins when naturally visible, and any clear patterning without chasing or injuring it. Include an estimate of size and the waterbody location. Reliable species assignment may require a fish specialist and comparison with museum material or current diagnostic literature.
actions: Never release an aquarium fish into a pond, ditch, spring, or river. If a pet has outgrown its tank, arrange a responsible return or rehoming option through an aquarium retailer or experienced keeper. For a fish seen outdoors, send photographs and location details to the state fisheries agency or its nonnative-species reporting program. Avoid moving a live specimen to another waterbody. Let agency staff decide whether collection or removal is appropriate; the unresolved identity of a pleco is a reason to improve the record before making species-specific management claims.

Together with the 2012 type-based Guianan revision, this gives new native-range evidence for the narrow species. It does not identify introduced American plecos, and those mapped records still require separate voucher review. New native-range survey evidence and a type-based revision support the true-species account; introduced U.S. voucher identities remain unclaimed. proposedDescription: Suckling clover, also called small hop clover, is a little annual legume with yellow flowers. It often fits between grasses in lawns and other open ground, and Mississippi State describes it as a volunteer component of pasture. Its low stature makes it easy to overlook until small yellow heads appear across a patch. This is a European plant naturalized elsewhere, but that history does not mean every occurrence warrants control. In a lawn, pasture, or conservation area, the useful question is what it is doing at that particular site.
identification: Look for sprawling green or reddish stems, leaves made of three small leaflets, and modest clusters of yellow flowers. The leaflet margins have small teeth. Several yellow-flowered legumes look similar, especially larger hop clover and black medick. Mature fruit can help: black medick develops dark, coiled pods, while the clover does not. Black medick also has a tiny pointed projection at the leaflet tip. Take close photographs of flower heads, leaves, and fruit together; a yellow dot in a lawn is not enough for a reliable identification.
actions: If the plant is simply part of a low-input lawn or pasture, decide whether intervention is needed before treating it. Where a small patch conflicts with a planting or restoration goal, pull plants before seed matures and maintain the desired ground cover afterward. Revisit the area in the next growing season because removing visible plants does not remove seed already present. For pasture changes, seek local forage advice rather than applying a lawn treatment. Confirm the plant first, and avoid broad applications that would also remove wanted clovers and other broadleaf plants.
researchNotes: Three independent botanical/agricultural sources support annual habit, introduced status, forage context and black-medick comparison. Does not claim demonstrated ecosystem invasion. Actions are proportionate site-specific horticultural judgment rather than a species-specific herbicide recommendation.

proposedDescription: Sudangrass is an annual forage grass associated with the Sorghum x drummondii complex. Farmers grow it and related hybrids for livestock feed, so an occurrence may be an intentional crop rather than an invading weed. The name also needs care: commercial sorghum-sudangrass hybrids are not all the same material as traditional sudangrass. Its most immediate management concern in a forage setting can be feed safety. Young or stressed sorghum-family plants may present prussic-acid hazards, and drought can also create nitrate concerns; a green-looking stand does not demonstrate that it is safe to graze.
identification: Typical sudangrass has erect, relatively slender stems, long narrow leaf blades, and an open, branching seed head. The botanical account describes plants reaching several feet tall and paired spikelets along the fine branches. Other sorghums, including forage hybrids and johnsongrass, can look similar from a distance. Photograph the base, leaf attachment, and mature seed head, and keep the seed label if the stand was planted. A farm adviser can use planting history and detailed plant features to distinguish a crop from an unwanted volunteer or another sorghum.
actions: Before grazing or feeding a stressed stand, consult a local forage adviser about appropriate testing and management. Tell them about frost, drought, recent cutting, regrowth, and fertilizer use. Do not rely on a single waiting period or plant height as proof of safety, and do not assume that cutting or drying solves every forage hazard. Where volunteers are unwanted, remove them before seed develops and monitor field margins. Keep crop-management decisions separate from claims about ecological invasion, which require evidence from the location concerned.
researchNotes: PROSEA reconciles the catalog hybrid name and older synonyms, morphology and crop context; South Dakota State supplies current independent sorghum-family safety guidance explicitly including sudangrass. No universal grazing interval, treatment rate or unsupported invasive-impact claim.

proposedDescription: Sudden oak death is a disease caused by the water mold Phytophthora ramorum. It has killed large numbers of susceptible trees in parts of coastal California and southern Oregon, but the same pathogen can cause a different-looking leaf or twig disease on other hosts. A shrub with infected leaves and an oak with a trunk canker do not play identical roles in the disease cycle. This host variation is why moving apparently ordinary nursery plants or contaminated material can matter even when no dying oak is nearby.
identification: On susceptible oak and tanoak hosts, dark bleeding patches or cankers on the trunk may accompany decline. Other hosts can develop leaf lesions or dying shoots. These signs overlap with injuries and other diseases, and neither a photograph nor a general Phytophthora screening test confirms P. ramorum. A trained sampler and a diagnostic laboratory may be needed. Record the host, location, symptoms, and whether nearby plants are affected. Photograph the trunk and foliage without cutting into bark or removing branches to investigate on your own.
actions: Contact the state plant-health agency, extension service, or an established local sudden-oak-death program before collecting or moving suspect material. Keep plants, soil, cuttings, and woody debris from the affected area in place until you receive instructions. Avoid carrying soil on footwear or tools between sites, and follow the receiving program's cleaning and sampling advice. In nurseries, reducing standing water and unnecessary overhead irrigation can help limit conditions favorable to spread. There is no simple cure for an infected tree; treatment or removal decisions require the host, diagnosis, site, and applicable movement rules.
researchNotes: Independent APHIS, UC IPM and APS disease lesson support pathogen, host-dependent symptoms, diagnostic confirmation and prevention. Avoids diagnosing from bleeding alone, guarantees of cure, unauthorized sampling and fixed quarantine geography.

proposedDescription: Sugar cane root scale is a small armored scale insect that can live in sheltered parts of its host, including beneath leaf sheaths and near the base of stems. Despite the common name, it is not confined to exposed roots, and published host records extend beyond sugarcane. California's pest assessment describes it as a sugarcane pest in the Caribbean and Florida but notes that it is usually a minor pest. Finding a few scales therefore calls for identification and inspection, rather than an assumption that severe crop loss is inevitable.
identification: Female scale covers are thin, roughly circular, and fairly flat, with a pale to darker brown or purplish-brown appearance. The cast skin is near the center. Male covers are smaller and more elongated. Those features help locate a possible infestation under sheaths, but other armored scales can look much the same. The insect beneath its cover and microscopic characters are important for reliable identification. Photograph the host and the position of the scales, and ask a diagnostic service how to submit a small sample without spreading infested material.
actions: Inspect planting material before it is taken to another field or property, paying particular attention to protected stem bases and leaf sheaths. Keep suspect material separate while identification is pending. Healthy planting cane and natural enemies are useful parts of sugarcane pest management, but the appropriate response depends on infestation level and the host involved. Ask a local crop adviser about monitoring and whether treatment is justified. Do not copy a quarantine rating or pesticide instruction from another jurisdiction, and avoid moving infested cane or ornamental plants while their status is being checked.

USDA ARS independently supports healthy seedcane and natural-enemy context for the named sugarcane scales; kept group-level. CDFA document is a 2021 proposal, so no present legal rating asserted.

proposedDescription: Sugarcane borer is a moth whose caterpillars feed on grasses and tunnel inside stalks. In sugarcane, this can reduce stalk weight and sugar yield, and injury near a young shoot's growing point can kill the shoot. The importance of the insect differs among production regions: Louisiana guidance treats it as a major crop pest, while Florida reports substantial historical suppression associated with natural enemies. That difference matters when deciding whether a sighting calls for routine monitoring or an urgent crop-management response.
identification: The caterpillar is pale cream to yellowish with a brown head and rows of dark spots along the body. Adults are straw-colored moths, but a moth's color alone is not enough to separate related borers. Look for larvae feeding beneath leaf sheaths before they enter stalks, as well as entry holes, internal tunnels, weakened stems, or dead central shoots. Several other borers can produce similar injury. Photograph an exposed larva and its feeding site, record the crop and growth stage, and have uncertain specimens checked by extension staff.
actions: Use local crop scouting guidance, with attention to larvae still feeding outside the stalk. Once larvae are deep inside, a treatment aimed at exposed insects is less likely to reach them. Keep records of infestation levels and the variety grown, since crop susceptibility and tolerance vary. Protect established natural enemies and discuss treatment thresholds with a regional crop adviser rather than spraying after seeing a single moth. Select healthy planting cane and avoid transferring suspect stalks to new plantings. Recheck affected areas to determine whether fresh injury continues after any management decision.
researchNotes:
UF supports morphology, feeding injury and Florida natural-enemy context. Independent LSU supports scouting before boring and variety-dependent decisions; Texas A&M corroborates lookalikes. No numerical threshold generalized beyond Louisiana or pesticide recipe included.

proposedDescription: Sugarcane delphacid is a small sap-feeding planthopper associated with sugarcane. Perkinsiella saccharicida has become established outside its original range, including Hawaii and Florida. It can transmit Fiji disease, but finding the insect does not establish that the disease is present. Florida extension guidance reports little economic damage from the insect there and specifically distinguishes that situation from disease outbreaks elsewhere. The useful question is whether a correctly identified population is damaging the crop or carrying a pathogen, rather than whether any hopper is present.
identification: Check sugarcane leaves and sheaths for the insects and for egg clusters inserted into plant tissue, particularly near the midrib. Exposed egg ends may have a small white waxy covering. Several other hoppers live on cane, so color, jumping behavior or a distant photograph will not reliably identify this species. Photograph the insect from above and from the side, include a size reference, and record the host. An entomologist may need magnified structural characters to confirm the identification.
actions: Keep unfamiliar insects and affected planting material at the site while seeking advice from extension or plant-health staff. Record how many plants are affected and whether fresh feeding damage is increasing. Do not assume Fiji disease from the presence of a known vector, or apply a broad insecticide simply because hoppers occur. A crop specialist can distinguish direct insect injury from disease and decide whether monitoring or treatment is warranted. Avoid moving infested cane between growing areas.
researchNotes: UF Florida crop observations and Delaware taxonomic treatment support distinct claims. NSW cites Bartlett/Delaware and is not counted separately. Disease-vector presence is explicitly separated from pathogen presence.

proposedDescription: Sugarcane leafminer is a tiny moth whose caterpillars feed inside cane leaves. The name Dicranoctetes saccharella appears in older accounts; modern treatments place it in Elachista. A Louisiana survey following its discovery there in 2006 found mines on a minority of sampled stalks, mainly on older foliage, with substantial parasitism. That study did not consider it an economic threat under the conditions observed. A leafmine is therefore worth documenting, but it is not by itself evidence that a crop needs treatment.
identification: Look for a narrow mine that widens into a blotch within the leaf. The damaged area lies between the leaf surfaces rather than being an open hole chewed through the blade. Photograph the whole leaf and a close view of the mine, including any larva or emergence opening. The moth itself is minute, and similar grass-mining moths can be difficult to separate. Confirmation may require rearing an adult or examination by a specialist; do not rely on the mine shape alone.
actions: Record the crop variety, date, affected leaf position and approximate frequency of mines. Keep a suspect leaf in place until a diagnostic service explains how it should be sampled. Avoid moving live larvae or infested plants between fields. Ask a crop adviser whether damage is continuing on new growth and whether natural enemies are already limiting it. The historical Louisiana findings support careful assessment, not an automatic spray recommendation or a promise that the insect is harmless everywhere.
researchNotes: An Ecuadorian field guide adds substantive moth and mine recognition beyond the original Louisiana survey. The older Dicranoctetes and Elachista combinations are retained as a name crosswalk, not separate species; no broad yield-loss or spray conclusion follows. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. proposedDescription: Sugar gum is a South Australian eucalyptus planted for shelter, shade and timber. It can also establish beyond plantings, including in parts of coastal California. That distinction matters: a mature planted tree and a group of self-sown seedlings tell different stories about spread. California resources identify sugar gum as a plant to watch, making nearby self-sown seedlings especially useful observations to record and follow. Its local effects should be assessed directly rather than borrowed from blue gum or another eucalyptus species.
identification: Look for smooth, patchy bark in pale gray, cream, yellow or brown tones. Adult leaves are narrow and glossy, with a noticeably darker upper surface and paler underside. Young leaves are broader and often rounded. A useful feature is the placement of flower clusters on leafless portions of branchlets within the crown. The white flowers leave small barrel-shaped or urn-shaped woody capsules with their valves tucked inside. Include bark, leaves, buds and capsules in photographs because foliage alone can be misleading.
actions: Check around established trees for seedlings in places that were not planted, especially along disturbed edges. Record their distance from the likely parent and whether they are surviving among native vegetation. Consult the land manager before removing trees or disturbing habitat. Small seedlings are easier to assess and address than established trees, but mature-tree work needs a qualified arborist. When considering replacement planting, use locally appropriate species and ask about sugar gum spread at comparable nearby sites.
researchNotes: Australian diagnostic treatment and independent California records support recognition and bounded introduced context. Fire risk, toxicity and treatment performance are not inferred from the genus or other eucalypts. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. General documentation and containment actions are editorial precautions, not tested control-efficacy claims.

proposedDescription: Sulfur cinquefoil is a long-lived Eurasian perennial that can form dense patches in open grasslands, pastures and disturbed ground. It grows from a substantial root crown and produces many seeds, allowing a small infestation to persist after the first visible plants are removed. Its pale yellow flowers are attractive, but it can displace other vegetation and reduce the usefulness of pasture. Native cinquefoils grow in many of the same settings, so careful identification comes before any removal.
identification: Look for upright, leafy stems and leaves divided like a hand into usually five to seven narrow, toothed leaflets. Flowers have five pale yellow, notched petals around a deeper yellow center. Long stiff hairs stand out from the stems and leaf stalks rather than lying flat. Compared with some native relatives, both leaf surfaces are similarly green and the plant carries many leaves along the stem. These are useful clues together; leaflet number alone is not enough to distinguish every native cinquefoil.
actions: Photograph the flowers, leaf undersides and stem hairs before planning control. For a small confirmed patch, ask the local weed program about digging the root crown and preventing mature seed from scattering. Simply cutting the flowers does not remove the established root system. Clean soil and seeds from equipment before leaving the site, and revisit treated ground for seedlings. Larger infestations need a coordinated plan that also restores desirable vegetation. Follow local requirements and current site-specific guidance if chemical control is considered.
researchNotes: USFS synthesis and Missouri weed identification support complementary identification/control. NPS repeats USFS and is not counted independently. No blanket legal requirement or fixed herbicide recipe.

proposedDescription: Sulphur cosmos is a warm-season annual grown for its yellow and orange flower heads. Native to Mexico and nearby parts of Central America, it has escaped cultivation in several regions of the United States. It readily reseeds, which can be useful in a garden but deserves attention when seedlings appear beyond the intended bed. An escaped plant is not automatically evidence of severe ecological harm. The location, persistence and extent of spread help distinguish a few garden volunteers from a population needing closer review.
identification: Look for opposite leaves deeply divided into narrow but visible segments, branching stems and daisy-like flower heads held above the foliage. The central disk is surrounded by yellow, orange or reddish-orange rays. Common garden cosmos has much finer, threadlike leaf divisions and usually different flower colors, although cultivated varieties complicate quick comparisons. Photograph the leaves as well as the flowers and dry fruits. A flower-only picture may not show the features needed to separate similar ornamentals.
actions: Keep intentional plantings distinct from observations of self-sown plants. If it is spreading where unwanted, remove flower heads before mature seed is released and lift young volunteers while the roots are manageable. Avoid tipping garden waste into roadside vegetation or natural areas. Check the same ground in the next growing season for new seedlings. For plants established away from gardens, share photographs and the setting with a local botanical or extension service before assuming they need extensive control.
researchNotes: Independent horticultural accounts corroborate foliage, flowers and annual growth. Reseeding in gardens supports modest seed containment, not a nationwide ecological harm claim. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. General documentation and containment actions are editorial precautions, not tested control-efficacy claims.

proposedDescription: Avocado sunblotch is caused by a viroid, a small infectious RNA rather than an insect or a conventional virus. It can reduce fruit quality and tree performance, yet some infected trees show no obvious symptoms. Those quiet infections matter when buds, grafts or nursery plants are shared. A tree that looks healthy is not necessarily suitable propagation stock. The disease is associated with avocado, and its presence should be established through plant-health testing rather than inferred from a discolored fruit alone.
identification: Look for narrow pale, yellow or pink streaks along green twigs and sunken streaks or blotches on fruit. Affected fruit may be small or misshapen, and older bark can develop a rectangular cracking pattern. Sunburn can resemble some fruit symptoms, while symptom expression varies with cultivar and growing conditions. Photograph fruit, young branches and the whole tree together. A laboratory result is needed to distinguish infection from lookalike damage and to detect trees that carry the viroid without visible signs.
actions: Do not take grafting wood, seeds for nursery production or cuttings from a suspect tree. Contact a plant diagnostic service or avocado extension adviser and follow its sampling instructions. Use tested nursery material for new plantings, and ask about appropriate tool sanitation before pruning other trees. Keep records of where planting material came from and which trees were propagated from it. Finding symptoms does not justify insecticide treatment: the practical concern is infected plant material and mechanical transfer, not a visible insect vector.
researchNotes: Independent UC IPM and Plant Health Australia guidance support symptoms, symptomless infection and propagation safeguards. Australian reporting pathways are not prescribed to US users.

proposedDescription: Mexican sunflower is a warm-season ornamental grown for its bright orange flowers. Tithonia rotundifolia is often visited by butterflies and other flower-feeding insects, but a useful garden plant can still produce seedlings beyond its intended bed. Its name is easily confused with Tithonia diversifolia, a different Mexican sunflower with a different invasion history. A Florida flora explicitly separates the annual species from its perennial relative. This profile should not turn reports about its larger relative into a claim that this species causes the same problems throughout the United States.
identification: Look for upright, slightly ridged hairy stems and large, rough leaves arranged alternately. Leaves may be oval, triangular or three-lobed, with toothed edges and hairy undersides. Flower heads commonly have orange-red outer rays around an orange-yellow center and can reach about three inches across. Photograph both the leaf outline and the flower head; a close-up of orange petals alone is not enough to separate all similar ornamentals. Include the whole plant and note whether it was deliberately planted.
actions: If plants appear outside cultivation, record the distance from the nearest garden and whether seedlings return in later years. Remove unwanted young plants on your own property before they set seed, and contain mature seed heads rather than scattering them in yard waste. There is no reason to treat every planted Mexican sunflower as an established invasion. Ask a local herbarium or extension office to confirm the species when a wild population is spreading, especially where the name is being used interchangeably with Tithonia diversifolia.
researchNotes: The new Florida flora supplies independent species separation from perennial Mexican sunflower. The common-name trap is addressed without importing T. diversifolia impacts; ordinary garden seed management remains appropriate. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. General documentation and containment actions are editorial precautions, not tested control-efficacy claims. proposedDescription: Sunn hemp is a fast-growing annual legume used as a cover crop and green manure. Despite its common name, it is not cannabis. Fields of Crotalaria juncea are often intentional agricultural plantings, so a photograph of a crop is not evidence of an invasive population. Seed production and persistence depend on the cultivar, climate and planting date. Its use as forage also needs care: guidance for a selected cultivar should not be applied to every sunn hemp seed lot or to other Crotalaria species.
identification: Plants have upright, branching stems, narrow simple leaves and clusters of bright yellow pea-shaped flowers toward the top. The short pods are inflated and become brown as they mature. Look closely at the leaves: each has a single narrow blade, unlike species with three separate leaflets. Photograph the flowers, pods, leaf attachment and whole plant. Other rattleboxes can look similar and may present different livestock risks, so a common name or a field of yellow flowers is not a reliable identification.
actions: For an unexpected roadside or field-edge population, note whether sunn hemp was recently planted nearby and whether plants are producing mature pods. Ask extension staff to confirm the species before making forage or control decisions. Keep unidentified rattlebox seeds out of animal feed, and do not assume that a cultivar described as suitable for grazing makes every plant safe. Manage an intentional cover crop according to its cultivar and local planting plan. Remove unwanted volunteers before seed develops when that can be done without disturbing protected habitat.
researchNotes: Two regional extension crop accounts support the bounded annual cover-crop context. Neither genus-wide toxicity nor absence of all risk is inferred; feeding choices are referred to local livestock advisers and cultivar identity. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. proposedDescription: Surinam cherry is an evergreen shrub or small tree introduced as a hedge and fruit plant. In central and southern Florida it can escape into natural areas, where dense growth competes with native vegetation and limits regeneration. Birds and mammals carry its seeds away from cultivated plants. Regional context matters: Florida guidance identifies the strongest concern in the south and uses caution categories farther north. A clipped garden hedge and a spreading population in a hammock should be recorded separately, even when both belong to the same species.
identification: The most distinctive feature is the deeply ribbed fruit, shaped rather like a small flattened pumpkin. Fruits can ripen red, maroon or nearly black. Leaves occur in opposite pairs, have smooth edges and are oval to lance-shaped; new growth is often bronze or reddish. White flowers carry many conspicuous stamens. Photograph a leafy branch and mature fruit together, because other Eugenia species are also sold as hedges. Avoid using taste as an identification test, and do not assume that any red-fruited shrub is Surinam cherry.
actions: Where the plant is invasive, choose a suitable native replacement rather than planting more. Pull small seedlings where permitted, keeping soil disturbance modest, and check nearby shaded areas for additional seedlings. Larger shrubs can resprout after cutting, so repeated clipping alone may not resolve an infestation. A land manager or extension adviser can help plan removal and follow-up for established plants. Keep fruits and seed-bearing debris contained, and record regrowth after treatment so that apparently cleared areas are checked again.
researchNotes: UF provides Florida impact and control context; NParks independently supports morphology and fruit variation. No nationwide legal status or herbicide rate asserted.

claims: Florida thickets, dispersal, resprouting and seedling removal.
Opposite leaves, many stamens and ribbed fruit colors.

proposedDescription: Water spinach is a trailing wetland vine also cultivated as a vegetable under names such as kangkong and ong choy. When it escapes into suitable waterways, it can crowd other plants and spread beyond the place where it was grown. Cultivation and possession rules vary by jurisdiction; Texas, for example, includes it among regulated aquatic species. An edible use does not make releasing it into a pond or ditch appropriate. A record should distinguish a managed crop from plants growing freely along a waterway.
identification: Look for a soft vine at the water edge, with alternate leaves that are often arrow-shaped but can vary considerably. Stems root at their joints, and flowers resemble morning glories: broad funnels in white, pale pink or lilac. Floating stems can hold leaves above the water. Photograph several leaves, the stem joints and any flower, along with the surrounding habitat. Other wetland vines and morning glories can resemble it, so an arrow-shaped leaf by itself is not enough to confirm the identification.
actions: Do not release live plants, roots or cut stems into drains, ponds or natural wetlands. If you find an apparent escape, record its location and extent and contact the state aquatic-plant program before attempting removal. Avoid chopping or dragging plants through water, where rooted pieces may be displaced. Check current cultivation and movement requirements with the relevant agency rather than assuming that supermarket availability authorizes outdoor planting. Keep any removed material contained and follow local disposal instructions; do not move a live sample to another waterbody for comparison.
researchNotes: FWC/UF-derived identification counted together; USDA summary references Lee/Austin for impact; Texas regulator independently supports current restrictions. No nationwide permit claim.

proposedDescription: Swamp mahogany is an Australian eucalyptus planted for timber, shelter and shade in warm regions. In Hawaii, forestry accounts describe regeneration through both seedlings and shoots from cut stumps after disturbance. Florida assessments identify a high predicted invasion risk, which is a risk evaluation rather than proof that every listed county has an established wild population. A useful observation records whether a tree was planted, whether younger trees are appearing beyond it, and whether those recruits persist in surrounding vegetation.
identification: Look for thick, fibrous rough bark and broad adult leaves that are darker above than below. Side veins meet the central vein at a wide angle. Large buds and cylindrical woody fruits are particularly useful: the fruit valves can remain joined across the opening. Photograph bark, both leaf surfaces, buds and mature capsules together. Many eucalyptus species share rough bark or glossy leaves, so those features alone are insufficient. Juvenile foliage differs from adult foliage and should be labeled as such in a report.
actions: Check around established plantings for seedlings, especially after logging, soil disturbance or canopy opening. Photograph and map new growth before removing it where permitted. Small seedlings are more manageable than mature trees, but cutting established trees may produce coppice shoots that need follow-up. Use a qualified arborist for work involving large stems or nearby structures. Avoid relocating seedlings into natural areas, and ask the local land manager which eucalyptus species are priorities before treating an entire stand based on its common name.
researchNotes: EUCLID morphology, USFS Hawaii silvics and UF predictive assessment serve different roles. Predicted risk is explicitly separated from county establishment and from blue gum impacts.

claims: Bark, discolorous leaves and joined fruit valves.

proposedDescription: Sweet alyssum is a low flowering plant widely used along garden edges and in containers. It comes from the Mediterranean region and can reseed outside cultivation. A California field flora documents it in waste places and along roadsides, but those records do not establish severe ecological effects at every site. Some plants are short-lived escapes close to a planting; others may continue producing seedlings. Recording that distinction helps separate an ornamental occurrence from a population that is maintaining itself without gardening.
identification: Look for spreading or mounded growth with narrow, alternate leaves and clusters of tiny flowers. Each flower has four separate petals, commonly white but also pink or purple in cultivated forms. Mature plants develop small, short seedpods rather than the long narrow pods seen in many other mustards. Photograph the foliage, flowers and fruit together, including a size reference. Similar Alyssum species may require examination of plant hairs and fruit stalks, so a white-flowered mat should not be identified from color alone.
actions: For plants beyond a garden, note the surrounding habitat and whether new seedlings appear after the original plants die. Remove unwanted volunteers before seed matures on property you manage, taking care not to disturb neighboring native plants. Keep seed-bearing garden waste away from dunes, roadsides and other natural areas. A local flora or herbarium can help confirm an unusual population. The available sources support monitoring and preventing unwanted reseeding; they do not justify a blanket recommendation to eradicate every cultivated alyssum planting.
researchNotes: An authored California field flora adds independent fruit and leaf detail plus naturalized context. Local escape and garden reseeding are distinguished from demonstrated ecosystem damage. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. proposedDescription: Sweet autumn clematis is a woody climbing vine introduced as an ornamental. It can escape into forest margins, stream edges and disturbed ground, covering nearby vegetation with dense growth. Its abundant white flowers are followed by wind-carried fruits, helping new plants appear away from a garden. Native clematis vines can flower at a similar time and look remarkably alike from a distance. Correct identification is especially important before removing a vine from a streamside or woodland edge.
identification: Examine mature leaves rather than relying only on the flowers. Sweet autumn clematis usually has opposite, compound leaves with three to five glossy leaflets and mostly smooth edges. Native virgin's bower commonly has clearly toothed leaflet edges. Young growth can be less straightforward, so include several mature leaves, white flowers and the feathery fruit heads in photographs. The vine climbs using its leaf stalks. A dense white-flowered cover over shrubs is a clue, not a complete identification by itself.
actions: Avoid planting the species where it escapes, and use a locally appropriate native vine instead. Pull small seedlings where permitted, or remove established plants with a plan for the roots and subsequent regrowth. Cutting the visible stems alone can leave a living root system. Contain fruiting material and keep cuttings out of unmanaged yard-waste piles. Revisit the site for seedlings and returning shoots, and ask for an identification check before treating a vine that might be native virgin's bower.
researchNotes: UF control, Smithsonian Chesapeake history and Michigan morphology independently support claims. Michigan juvenile-tooth caveat preserved; Clemson control referral not counted as independent control evidence.

claims: Habitat, root regrowth and removal safeguards.

proposedDescription: Sweet basil is a familiar culinary herb with many cultivars selected for leaf color, scent and size. It is grown widely in gardens and commercially, and occasional plants escape near cultivation. In New England, botanical accounts describe these escapes as likely short-lived. That is different from evidence of persistent ecological damage. A basil plant beside a garden should be recorded as cultivated or escaped as appropriate, rather than automatically labeled an established invasive population.
identification: Look for opposite leaves on branching, square stems and small, lipped flowers arranged in groups along an upright flowering axis. Leaves are often oval and green, but cultivars can be purple, variegated, small or strongly textured. Scent varies too, so a familiar basil smell does not identify every cultivar or separate all related species. Photograph the whole plant, a leaf pair and flowers. Do not taste an unknown herb to identify it, especially when its growing conditions or treatment history are unknown.
actions: If basil appears beyond cultivation, record its distance from planted beds and check whether it survives or produces new plants in later seasons. Pull unwanted volunteers before seed disperses where you have permission. Keep garden waste within managed disposal routes rather than dumping it in nearby habitat. A suspected persistent wild population deserves a botanical identification, particularly in a warm climate where its behavior may differ from New England. The current evidence supports documenting escapes, not treating ordinary kitchen-garden basil as a nationwide ecological threat.
researchNotes: Independent New England flora distinguishes short-lived escapes from deliberate basil cultivation. No invasive harm evidence is needed to document a volunteer or prevent unwanted seed; uncertain garden hybrids are not assigned from scent alone. proposedDescription: Bay laurel is a Mediterranean evergreen grown for its aromatic leaves and as a hedge or container plant. Records outside its native range include California, but a record of a nonnative tree does not by itself show that it is spreading or damaging habitat. Planted specimens can remain for many years. For this species, the most useful field detail is whether young plants are appearing independently beyond a maintained garden, rather than simply whether a mature tree is present.
identification: Leaves are alternate, leathery and narrowly oval, often with wavy edges. The upper surface is glossy dark green. Small yellow-green flowers occur in clusters, and female plants can develop shiny black, oval fruits. Photograph leaf arrangement, the edge of the blade and any fruit. Several unrelated plants are called laurel or bay, including California bay and cherry laurels, so the common name is not a dependable identification. Do not taste a leaf to decide whether a plant is the culinary bay species.
actions: Document seedlings as well as the adult tree, noting whether they occur in irrigated beds, dumped garden material or surrounding natural vegetation. Ask a local herbarium or extension office to confirm an apparent escape before planning removal. Unwanted small plants can be removed from managed ground before they mature, while larger trees require a site-specific assessment. Avoid distributing seedlings into natural areas. For a mature landscape tree, discuss any proposed work with the owner and an arborist, using the observed seedlings and surrounding vegetation to explain the concern.
researchNotes: California occurrence data independently supplement the detailed Oregon horticultural description. No cooking instruction is offered for an unverified laurel; planted trees are separated from seedlings beyond cultivation. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. General documentation and containment actions are editorial precautions, not tested control-efficacy claims.

proposedDescription: Winter honeysuckle is a Chinese shrub grown for fragrant flowers that open when few other garden shrubs are blooming. It has escaped into woodlands and disturbed places in parts of the southern and eastern United States. Dense growth can limit light and space for native plants and tree seedlings. Its seasonal behavior differs from some other invasive honeysuckles, so advice or photographs labeled only bush honeysuckle should be checked against the species rather than copied without qualification.
identification: Look for a tangled, rounded shrub with arching branches and opposite, simple leaves. Small creamy-white tubular flowers have a strong lemon-like scent and can appear in winter or early spring, depending on climate. Orange-red to dark red berries develop later, often partly hidden by foliage. Leaves are broadly oval and relatively dull rather than strongly glossy. Photograph flowers, a leafy branch and the whole shrub. Native honeysuckles deserve protection, and flowering season plus leaf and fruit features is more useful than a red berry alone.
actions: Where winter honeysuckle is spreading, avoid planting additional shrubs and consider a native replacement suited to the site. Document seedlings beyond the garden before removing them where permitted. Young plants are easier to address than an established thicket; larger shrubs need a removal plan and repeated checks for returning growth. Keep fruiting branches contained rather than placing them in woodland brush piles. If identification is uncertain, ask extension staff to review photographs before treating a shrub, and record follow-up observations after any removal.
researchNotes: NC State species-specific impact and Oregon State morphology used. Generic hollow-pith diagnostic and other honeysuckle treatment calendars intentionally omitted.

claims: Thickets, seasonal flowers, opposite leaves and fruit.

proposedDescription: Sweet cherry is a Eurasian fruit tree that is widely cultivated and occasionally escapes into surrounding landscapes. An orchard tree, an old homestead planting and a self-sown tree in woodland represent different kinds of records. This distinction matters when deciding whether a population is spreading. The available botanical accounts support naturalization in parts of the United States, but they do not establish the same ecological impact everywhere. Native cherries and other planted cherry species should not be grouped under this name without identification.
identification: Look for alternate, oval to oblong leaves with finely toothed edges and conspicuous reddish glands near the top of the leaf stalk. White flowers appear in clusters, followed by fleshy fruits containing a single stone. Fruit color varies among cultivated forms, from yellow or red to very dark. Bark can be reddish brown and peel with age. Photograph the leaf stalk glands, flower arrangement, fruit and bark together; fruit color alone is not enough to distinguish sweet cherry from other Prunus species.
actions: For a tree away from cultivation, record nearby orchards or abandoned gardens and look for smaller trees that may be seedlings. Ask a local botanist or extension office to confirm the identification before removing a tree from natural habitat. Remove unwanted young plants where authorized, and use an arborist for mature trees when removal is appropriate. Do not use unknown leaves, stems or pits as food or animal feed. A useful report explains how the tree is growing and reproducing, not simply that cherries are present.
researchNotes: An Alaska field guide independently corroborates glands, flowers and localized escape records. The profile does not turn all cultivated cherry trees into control targets; local seedlings and site effects guide the response. Next step: Editorial review of this bounded identification and prevention profile; no release is authorized. General documentation and containment actions are editorial precautions, not tested control-efficacy claims. proposedDescription: Common fennel is a tall perennial herb that can form dense stands in disturbed grassland, coastal scrub and other open habitats. Once established, its root crown can survive cutting, while abundant seed helps maintain the population. California management accounts describe effects on native plant recovery. The culinary name can be confusing: some regulatory treatments exclude bulbing Florence fennel, so a vegetable bed and a wild stand should not automatically receive the same interpretation. Local guidance should determine whether a particular planting or population is a management priority.
identification: Look for finely divided, threadlike foliage and broad umbrella-shaped clusters of small yellow flowers. Plants are often much taller than nearby herbs, with several stems arising from a substantial base. The leaves and stems have an anise-like scent, but scent should not replace a careful identification. Photograph the whole plant, leaf divisions and flower clusters. Do not taste an unknown carrot-family plant: other members of the family can be dangerous, and a casual resemblance to a kitchen herb is not a safety check.
actions: Address small patches before mature seed spreads. Where removal is permitted, work carefully around the root crown and minimize soil disturbance. Mowing alone usually leaves the plant able to regrow, and cutting seed-bearing stems can distribute seed. Contain those stems and clean tools before moving to another site. Plan follow-up visits for seedlings and returning shoots, and restore appropriate vegetation rather than leaving bare ground. Large stands need a sustained land-management plan; a single cutting is not evidence that the population has been eliminated.
researchNotes: Cal-IPC report read in full; King County independently confirms regional classification and Florence-fennel exclusion. Historical chemical rates omitted; Cal-IPC-derived public words kept below 200.

claims: Morphology, root-crown survival, seed and restoration guidance.
Local classification, native grassland effects and cultivar exception.

proposedDescription: Sweet orange scab is a citrus disease caused by the fungus Elsinoe australis. It produces corky blemishes on fruit and can reduce marketability, while severe early infection can distort fruit or contribute to premature drop. The fungus moves with infected plant material and locally with water splash. It is different from the more widespread citrus scab caused by Elsinoe fawcettii. Similar names and overlapping symptoms make laboratory confirmation important, especially when a finding could affect plant-movement requirements.
identification: Look for raised, scabby areas on young citrus fruit that change from pale pink or light brown to darker, cracked or warty patches. The pattern may reflect splashing water, but weather injury, citrus canker and other fungal diseases can look similar. Photograph several fruit at different stages and the host tree as a whole. Note the citrus variety if known and when symptoms first appeared. A photograph can document the problem, but it cannot reliably identify which Elsinoe species caused it.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants, grafting material and fruit at the site while contacting state plant-health staff or a citrus diagnostic service. Follow their sampling instructions rather than mailing material without notice. Check current movement rules before transferring citrus out of an affected area. Disease management may reduce future infection, but it does not erase existing fruit scars or replace official identification. Record irrigation practices and recent plant purchases to help investigators understand possible spread, and avoid treating an unfamiliar scab as harmless cosmetic damage without checking it.
researchNotes: APHIS and EPPO support distinct regulatory and biological claims. Leaf-symptom differences and conflicting cure/control phrasing avoided; management is not represented as a cure. No quarantine map inferred from state presence.

claims: Fruit symptoms, reporting and movement safeguards.
Distinct scab species, water spread and need for diagnostics.

proposedDescription: Annual wormwood, also called sweet Annie, is an aromatic Eurasian herb introduced across much of North America. It occurs in gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Unlike perennial wormwoods that return from established underground structures, this species completes its life cycle in one growing season and persists through seed. Some regional accounts describe escaped plants as short-lived at a particular site. A record therefore needs context about repeated recruitment and habitat, rather than assuming a lasting invasion from one tall plant.
identification: The green leaves are finely divided two or three times into narrow lobes and are usually nearly hairless. Upper branches carry many tiny, nodding flower heads without conspicuous ray petals. The foliage has a sweet or fruity scent. Biennial wormwood can look similar, but tends to have a tighter, more upright flowering arrangement and much less scent. Photograph the whole flowering branch, a lower leaf and an upper leaf. Those details are more useful than a close view of green foliage alone.
actions: On managed ground, remove unwanted plants before the small seeds mature and scatter. Record whether the same patch produces new plants the following season, especially where garden waste or disturbed soil may be involved. Confirm the identity before removing native Artemisia species nearby. Avoid distributing seed-bearing stems or treating the plant as a home remedy on the basis of its traditional uses. The available evidence supports identification and prevention of unwanted reseeding, while site-specific ecological harm and management priority still need to be established.
researchNotes: Independent New England and Illinois accounts support annual wormwood recognition and seed persistence; absent local impact trials do not prevent a bounded botanical profile. Hilty supplies field observations distinct from Flora Novae Angliae. The text describes unwanted reseeding without claiming nationwide ecological damage or medicinal efficacy. Retain local recruitment observations when assigning a site management priority.

claims: Annual habit, nodding heads and biennial wormwood comparison.
Hairless divided leaves, seed reproduction and ephemeral escapes.

proposedDescription: Sweet vernalgrass is a small, early-flowering grass introduced from Eurasia. It grows in hayfields, pastures, roadsides and some natural grasslands, where its early growth can make it conspicuous before other grasses flower. Its sweet smell is familiar in drying hay, but that smell does not make a plant native sweetgrass. Whether a patch warrants removal depends on the habitat and the plants it is replacing. A pasture occurrence and a spreading population in a native meadow deserve different management decisions.
identification: Look for upright tufts with narrow, often hairy leaves and compact, spike-like flower heads that turn yellowish brown. At the junction of leaf and stem, a membranous ligule is present and clasping ear-like auricles are absent. Mature spikelets help separate this perennial from the related annual Anthoxanthum ovatum. Native sweetgrass, Anthoxanthum nitens, generally has a more open flower cluster and long spreading rhizomes. Photograph the whole clump, leaf collar and flower head rather than relying on scent or a single grass blade.
actions: In a confirmed small infestation, digging out the complete plant and below-ground growth can be useful where disturbance will not damage sensitive habitat. Mowing before seeds mature may reduce seed production, but grazing alone is not a dependable removal method. Keep seed-bearing material from entering clean meadow areas on equipment or in hay. Ask a local grass specialist to verify uncertain plants before work begins, especially near native sweetgrass. Revisit the site during the next early flowering season and record surviving clumps.
researchNotes: Independent flora, weed identification and western management sources. No forage toxicity or local harm inference from scent. Native sweetgrass comparison protects lookalikes.

claims: Early flowering, ligule, hairs, roots and pasture habitat.
Digging, mowing and grazing limitations.
Annual and native sweetgrass distinctions.

proposedDescription: Sweet violet is a low-growing garden perennial introduced from Europe and nearby regions. It can persist around old plantings and spread into lawns, disturbed ground and woodland edges. A violet patch is not automatically an invasive population: many North American violets are native, and cultivated flowers may remain close to their original planting. Regional floras document sweet violet outside gardens, but the evidence reviewed here does not establish the same ecological effects across all locations. Confirming the species comes before deciding what to remove.
identification: The plant forms a low mat of heart-shaped leaves and usually fragrant violet or white flowers. Leafy runners, called stolons, are especially useful to photograph. A close examination of the hairy ovary or developing capsule can help distinguish it from common blue violet, Viola sororia, which lacks those leafy stolons and has a smooth ovary. Color and fragrance alone are not enough, particularly in garden selections. Include the leaf bases, runners and developing fruits in a report, and avoid pulling apart a patch just to obtain a picture.
actions: If sweet violet is spreading where it is unwanted, first establish which plants belong to it and which are native violets. Remove confirmed small plants and their runners only where you have permission, then watch for new growth around the edge of the patch. Keep garden divisions and soil containing runners out of nearby natural areas. For an observation record, note whether plants are maintained, abandoned or growing beyond a garden. A local flora or botanist can resolve an identification before more extensive work is considered.
researchNotes: Sweet violet is adequately distinguished by leafy stolons and hairy fruits; regional impact and historical Vermont misidentifications can remain explicit limitations. Go Botany identification and the independent New Zealand flora substantiate the plant concept. No Vermont occurrence is asserted and no native violet is targeted from flower color alone. Use flowering and fruiting material to check uncertain violet patches before removal. Rhizomatous perennial with basal heart-shaped leaves and hairy capsules; exotic in New Zealand.

proposedDescription: Sweet William catchfly is a European garden flower that has escaped cultivation in parts of North America. It is also treated under the scientific name Atocion armeria, so records using either name need to be matched carefully. It usually grows as an annual or biennial in disturbed ground, roadsides and former gardens. Botanical records establish that escapes occur; they do not by themselves show serious ecological harm at every site. This plant should not be confused with native catchflies or with the separate garden species called sweet William.
identification: Look for upright, relatively smooth stems carrying opposite, gray-green leaves and clusters of small pink flowers. The upper leaves clasp the stem. Sticky bands below some upper joints are a helpful feature, although they are not always obvious in a distant photograph. Each flower has five shallowly notched petals above a long, narrow calyx tube. Photograph a flower cluster, a stem joint and the leaf attachment. These details distinguish a useful botanical record from a general picture of a pink garden flower.
actions: Record whether the plants were deliberately sown, are persisting in an old bed or are appearing in surrounding unmanaged ground. If confirmed plants are unwanted, remove small patches before seed capsules open and avoid scattering their seed with garden debris. Check the same disturbed ground in later seasons for seedlings. Do not remove a native Silene on the strength of the common name catchfly. Where the identity or ecological significance is uncertain, submit photographs to a local botanical resource before planning wider removal.
researchNotes: Atocion armeria and Silene armeria refer to the same garden catchfly in the reviewed floras, with enough agreement for recognition and seed-containment advice. Spencer 1997 and Flora Novae Angliae are separate botanical treatments. Variable annual or biennial terminology is retained rather than converted into a false fixed life span. Confirm local escape status separately from intentional sowing and avoid assigning impacts from other catchflies. Inherited URLs retained for provenance, not refreshed as evidence in this revision (some redundant or unavailable): https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?basic=silene&isprofile=0&taxonid=279050.

claims: Synonym and introduced disturbed-ground records.
Sticky stems, clasping leaves and pink flower structure.

proposedDescription: Sweetbriar rose is a thorny shrub introduced from Europe and widely associated with old plantings, roadsides and open ground. It can spread by seed and vegetative growth, forming difficult thickets in suitable settings. Its importance varies by region, and a watch-list entry should not be mistaken for a statewide removal requirement. Native roses support wildlife and can look similar from a distance. A reliable identification is therefore an important part of deciding whether a rose patch is an unwanted introduction or a plant worth protecting.
identification: Look for arching woody canes with stout, curved prickles of different sizes. Leaves are divided into usually five to seven leaflets with toothed margins. Small glands, especially on the leaflet undersides, give the foliage a characteristic apple-like scent when handled gently. The flowers typically have five pink petals, followed by orange-red to red hips. Photograph the whole shrub, prickles, leaflet undersides and flowers or hips. Do not rely on a pink flower alone, and use gloves when working around the canes.
actions: Where sweetbriar is confirmed and spreading, avoid adding new plants and plan removal while the patch is still small. Contain fruiting material so hips are not moved to a new site. Larger thickets need a coordinated approach because remaining growth can return after cutting; ask local land managers about methods appropriate for the surrounding vegetation. Check for seedlings and renewed shoots after work. A report should describe the extent of the patch and nearby native plants, not simply label every rose in the area as invasive.
researchNotes: NRCS, Washington weed board and Oregon State support identification and regional concern. Conflicting sepal persistence omitted. Watch-list status not portrayed as mandatory control.

Monitor status and identification.
Naturalization, foliage and hips.

proposedDescription: Sweet pea is a Mediterranean ornamental grown for fragrant flowers, often on fences or garden supports. It is generally an annual, unlike some perennial plants that share the name pea. Finding it beside a garden does not establish an invasive population, and the sources reviewed here do not support a uniform claim of ecological harm. Cultivated plants, discarded garden material and plants reproducing away from cultivation should be recorded separately. This flowering ornamental is also different from the peas grown for food.
identification: The climbing forms use tendrils to hold onto supports and have winged stems with paired leaflets. Showy, fragrant flowers appear in many cultivated colors, so color alone is not a dependable identification feature. Photograph a complete leaf with its tendril, the stem wings and a flower from the side. Native Lathyrus species and perennial ornamental peas can resemble it. A botanical identification should consider the whole plant and its life cycle rather than assigning a name from a seed packet found nearby.
actions: Do not eat ornamental sweet pea seeds or offer them as food; poison-plant references distinguish this species from edible garden peas. If unwanted plants are confirmed, remove them before pods open and keep seed-bearing trimmings out of natural areas. For plants beyond cultivation, note the location of nearby gardens and whether new seedlings appear in later seasons. Ask a local botanist to check uncertain peas before removal, especially in native vegetation. No broad treatment recommendation is warranted without evidence that this particular population needs control.
researchNotes: Sweet pea identity and its separation from edible peas are supported; lack of a local invasion trial is a scope limit rather than an identity gap. NC State supplies ornamental morphology and UC authors provide independent poison-plant guidance. The profile does not prescribe treatment or assert a self-sustaining invasive population. Document recurrent seedlings away from cultivation before elevating local management concern.

Ornamental sweet pea safety distinction.

proposedDescription: Sweetpotato is a familiar food crop and an ornamental vine in the morning glory family. Plants selected for colorful leaves and plants selected for useful storage roots belong to the same species, but they do not necessarily perform well for both purposes. Trailing stems can cover a surprising amount of ground during warm weather. Its appearance in a planted bed is evidence of cultivation, not proof of ecological invasion; a useful observation records whether the vine was planted or appeared independently outside a garden.
identification: Look for trailing stems with alternate, heart-shaped or deeply lobed leaves. Cultivars range from green to lime, purple, or variegated foliage, so color alone is unreliable. Occasional flowers are funnel-shaped, often lavender or pink with a darker center. The swollen underground parts are roots and lack the surface eyes found on ordinary potatoes. Other morning glories can have similar leaves and flowers, making the planting history and several views of the whole plant helpful.
actions: Keep cultivated vines within their intended bed or container and collect trimmings rather than discarding them on a natural-area edge. Photograph unexpected plants where they grow, including the stem, leaves, and any flowers. Note nearby ornamental plantings or vegetable beds before calling a patch an escape. If vigorous regrowth repeatedly appears beyond cultivation, ask local Extension staff to verify it and advise on removal. Use known planting material for gardening; an identification photo is not a food-safety assessment.
researchNotes: NC State and UF horticultural accounts independently support habit and recognition. No broad invasive-impact conclusion is inferred from cultivation or catalog inclusion.

claims: Ornamental versus root cultivars; trailing habit; cultivar leaf variation
Root lacks potato eyes; leaf form and venation; lavender funnel flowers

proposedDescription: Cereus repandus is a large, branching cactus often called apple cactus. The catalog name sweetpotato cactus should not be read as a connection to the sweetpotato vine. Mature plants can become tree-sized, with upright fleshy columns and conspicuous flowers that open at night. Kew accepts the species and places its native range in the southern Caribbean and northern South America. Horticultural sources use older names and sometimes conflicting origin accounts, so a cultivated cactus label deserves checking before it becomes a wild-species record.
identification: Look for blue-green to grayish columns divided into prominent longitudinal ribs, with clusters of spines along their outer edges. University of Arizona's cultivated plants have large white flowers, reddish outer tips, and smooth pink to red fruits. Rib number varies and is not a reliable shortcut to species identification. Photograph a complete branch, its ribs and spine clusters, and any flowers or fruit. The name Cereus peruvianus appears in older horticultural treatments and in Kew's synonym list.
actions: Treat a planted specimen as a garden tree unless there is evidence of separate establishment beyond the planting. Keep fallen pieces and pruning material contained rather than leaving them on open ground. Large, spiny branches are awkward to handle; arrange suitable professional help for substantial pruning or removal. For an unexpected roadside or natural-area cactus, submit clear photographs and the location to a botanical specialist. Do not collect fruit or remove a plant solely because a nursery label matches this catalog entry.
researchNotes: Kew supports the accepted Cereus repandus concept and Caribbean-to-northern-South-American range, while Arizona documents cultivated morphology. Origin differences are attributed rather than merged; nursery use of Cereus peruvianus is not accepted as proof of a wild voucher identification. No US ecological damage is claimed. Have unexpected wild cactus records checked using flowers, fruits and complete branches.

sources.title: University of Arizona Campus Arboretum: Cereus repandus

claims: Accepted name; southern Caribbean to Colombia/Venezuela range; C. peruvianus synonym
Branching ribbed cactus; spine clusters; night flowers and smooth fruit

proposedDescription: Sweetpotato whitefly is the name commonly used for Bemisia tabaci, a group of extremely similar whiteflies associated with many crops and ornamentals. The name covers a cryptic species complex rather than one easily recognized biological unit. Feeding can discolor or distort leaves, and some members transmit damaging plant viruses. Sticky honeydew and the dark mold growing on it are often the first noticeable signs. The host plant and local growing conditions matter when judging risk; a cloud of white insects alone does not establish which member is present.
identification: Adults are tiny, with pale yellow bodies and white wings held at a slight angle over the back. Look underneath leaves for the flattened immature stages, which remain attached while feeding. Late immature Bemisia generally lack the obvious waxy fringe or long filaments of several other whiteflies. These clues help separate groups, but ordinary photographs cannot resolve the cryptic species. A diagnostic laboratory may need molecular evidence; older B- or Q-biotype names should not be treated as photo-identifiable forms.
actions: Inspect new plants, especially leaf undersides, before placing them beside established crops. Monitor affected plants and keep a record of host, location, and symptoms. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding indiscriminate insecticide use, and reduce dusty conditions that disrupt them. Small infestations may be managed with removal of heavily affected leaves or other locally recommended measures. If crop injury or suspected virus symptoms are spreading, ask Extension staff for diagnosis and a current host-specific plan before choosing a product.
researchNotes: UC IPM supports signs, morphology and conservative management; independent 2024 ARS-associated study supports cryptic species limits. No biotype-level identification or universal virus claim.

sources.title: USDA ARS: Bemisia species delimitation study

claims: Sap feeding, honeydew, leaf underside stages, group characters, natural enemy protection
Cryptic species complex; molecular and reproductive evidence required for boundaries

proposedDescription: Sweet William is a familiar cottage-garden flower, usually grown as a biennial or a short-lived perennial. Compact clusters of pink, red, purple, or white blooms can persist as conspicuous traces of old planting. Many cultivars have been selected, including small plants and double flowers, so a garden escape may look different from a field-guide illustration. The evidence reviewed here establishes its horticultural identity but does not establish harmful invasion throughout the United States. A record should distinguish a maintained border, an abandoned planting, and self-sown plants.
identification: Plants typically reach about one to two feet tall, with opposite, narrow leaves and dense rounded flower clusters. Individual flowers commonly have five petals with toothed or fringed edges, although double cultivars obscure that arrangement. Leaves are smooth and may be green or somewhat gray-green. Dry capsules release numerous small, dark seeds. Compare the whole plant with other cultivated pinks rather than relying only on flower color; photographs of leaf arrangement, the flower cluster, and its green base are especially useful.
actions: If you want to limit volunteers, collect spent flowering stems before capsules open and check nearby disturbed soil for seedlings. Keep garden waste out of woodland and meadow margins. Photograph an unexpected patch before disturbing it, and record whether an old house site or garden lies nearby. Ask a local herbarium or Extension office to confirm uncertain plants, particularly when a management decision depends on identity. A planted Sweet William does not warrant removal simply because it appears in a nonnative-species catalog.
researchNotes: Go Botany adds independent evidence that Dianthus barbatus escapes cultivation in North America, supplementing NC State horticultural morphology. This replaces the weak garden-use-only second source. The new evidence establishes escape context, not a new impact or control experiment. Retain the distinction between maintained plants, abandoned plantings and spontaneous recruits. Inherited URLs retained for provenance, not refreshed as evidence in this revision (some redundant or unavailable): https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/Portals/0/Kemper%20Gardens/Fact%20Sheets/Bird%20Gardening%202023_pdf.pdf?ver=er-QPfMhbn2rlu_xxCRb1w%3D%3D.

claims: Biennial or short-lived perennial; cultivars; opposite narrow leaves; fringed flowers and capsules
Eurasian garden plant widely escaped in North America; dwarf and double-flowered cultivars.

proposedDescription: The eel swimbladder nematode is an internal parasite of freshwater eels. It is native to eastern Asia and has been introduced into other regions, including North America. Eels acquire infection by eating infected small crustaceans or other hosts in the food web; the worms eventually occupy the swimbladder. This organ helps regulate buoyancy, so infection can be important even when the eel looks ordinary from the outside. Evidence of infection is not, by itself, proof that the parasite caused a local eel-population decline.
identification: An observer cannot reliably identify this parasite from the eel's skin, body color, or swimming behavior. Adult worms live inside the swimbladder, and laboratory examination is needed to distinguish them from other parasites and assess associated damage. Older publications use Anguillicola crassus for the same organism. If an eel is examined through an authorized fisheries survey, retain the host identity, collection location, and sampling details with the parasite record; a worm photograph without that context is much less useful.
actions: Do not move live eels, bait organisms, or water between waterways. Anglers should follow current local bait and fish-movement rules rather than trying to inspect or treat wild eels themselves. Report an unusual finding from a legally caught or professionally examined eel to the state fisheries agency, with photographs and collection information. Ask the agency how it wants a specimen handled before transporting it. Fish-health professionals should direct testing or treatment in aquaculture, where preventing movement of infected stock is especially important.
researchNotes: Original South Carolina recruitment research and the separate upper Potomac study provide independent American-eel infection evidence beyond the shared agency summaries. The 2013 South Carolina samples and Zimmerman and Welsh 2012 Potomac samples are different field studies. Neither demonstrates that the parasite caused a regional eel-population decline; laboratory diagnosis remains appropriate. Use fisheries-directed specimen examination and avoid transporting live eels or suspect water. Inherited URLs retained for provenance, not refreshed as evidence in this revision (some redundant or unavailable): https://invasions.si.edu/nemesis/chesreport/species_summary/anguillicoloides%20crassus ; https://nas.er.usgs.gov/queries/FactSheet.aspx?speciesID=3830.

proposedDescription: Swollen fingergrass is a warm-climate grass with a distinctive crown of fingerlike flowering branches. It commonly occupies disturbed, open ground, including roadsides and sandy places. Published accounts disagree about its original range: Singapore's botanical account places its origin in tropical America, while Kew treats the tropical and subtropical Old World as native. That disagreement should not be hidden behind a single global label. For a US observation, check the identification and the regional flora before deciding whether the population is an unwanted introduction.
identification: Plants are usually upright annuals, sometimes with lower stems leaning over and rooting at their joints. Narrow leaves sit in two ranks along the stem. A flowering head commonly has seven to seventeen branches radiating near the tip, with purplish spikelets that give it a soft, brushy appearance. Tiny hairs and the structure of the individual spikelets matter in separating it from other Chloris grasses. A distant picture of a windmill-shaped seed head is useful for finding the group but usually insufficient for a confident species name.
actions: Photograph a whole flowering plant, its stem base, and a close view of the flowering branches. Include a scale and record the habitat rather than collecting loose seed heads. Ask a local grass specialist or Extension office to compare it with other windmill grasses before undertaking control. Where removal is appropriate and authorized, work before seed matures and keep seed-bearing material contained. Brush accumulated seeds and soil from equipment before leaving a patch, especially when moving from disturbed ground into a conservation area.
researchNotes: Flora of North America independently supports Chloris barbata morphology; its origin differs between Kew and Singapore accounts and is now explicitly scoped. The disagreement concerns geographic origin, not a demonstrated mismatch of specimens. The profile avoids a single global origin claim and does not transfer Singapore naturalization status to US sites. Use a regional flora and mature spikelets to determine the status of a particular windmill-grass population.

proposedDescription: This large, soft-textured fern is sometimes listed simply as swordfern, a name also used for quite different ferns. Macrothelypteris torresiana forms a tuft of broad, finely divided fronds and readily colonizes disturbed sites where conditions suit it. In 2026, the University of Florida assessment places it in the high invasion risk category throughout Florida using a predictive screening tool. That is a regional risk conclusion, not a claim that every fern with this common name is invasive or that measured damage has been documented at every site.
identification: Look for broadly triangular to oval fronds divided repeatedly into smaller segments, rather than the simple ladderlike outline associated with many familiar swordferns. Fronds can be pale green to blue-green and feel soft; the stalk base is enlarged and scaly. Fine hairs and the small spore-bearing structures on the underside help specialists distinguish it from related ferns. Photograph both surfaces of a mature frond and the base of the plant. Its old names include Thelypteris torresiana and Dryopteris uliginosa.
actions: Check nursery labels and spontaneous ferns in pots before moving plants between gardens. In Florida, choose a locally suitable alternative rather than planting this high-risk species. Have unfamiliar ferns identified before digging, since native species can share the same general appearance. If removal is warranted, contain mature fronds and follow local disposal advice rather than spreading them with garden waste. Revisit disturbed soil and nearby pots for new plants, and record whether the fern returns after the original clump is removed.
researchNotes: Independent UF predictive risk assessment and NZPCN authored botanical account. Florida risk is not represented as measured nationwide impact; NZPCN's broad Hawaii-range wording is not adopted.
