proposedDescription: Threecorner leek is a bulb-forming perennial that can create dense seasonal patches after escaping gardens. Its narrow leaves and nodding white flowers are attractive, but established colonies can be difficult to separate from the many small bulbs beneath them. Australian weed guidance documents dense stands that displace native ground vegetation, especially in moist shady sites. Its significance in the United States depends on local conditions and records; an overseas designation does not establish a nationwide rule for every garden.
identification: The flowering stalk is distinctly three-sided in cross-section, the feature behind the common name. White, bell-shaped flowers hang in a cluster and have green markings running along the floral segments. Leaves are narrow and arise from the base. Other onions, onion-scented plants, and white-flowered bulbs can be confused with it before flowering. Do not taste a plant to establish its identity. Photograph the stalk, entire flower cluster, and leaf arrangement, and ask a botanist to check an uncertain patch.
actions: Where the plant is unwanted, work before seed matures and remove bulbs as completely as practical. Collect loose bulbs and soil carefully rather than spreading them along a path or into a compost area beside natural vegetation. Recheck the site in the next growing season, because missed bulbs can produce fresh shoots. Avoid moving contaminated soil to another bed. For a dense colony beside a stream or in woodland, seek local weed-management advice before digging extensively or choosing any treatment near water.
researchNotes: VicFlora and the Australian weed account support Allium triquetrum recognition and bulb-focused follow-up; absence of a US trial need not hold the profile. The botanical description and weed guidance have distinct purposes and underlying treatments. Overseas impact remains attributed and no overseas legal rule or chemical rate is imported. Contain bulbs and seed-bearing material and consult local staff before digging dense streamside patches.

proposedDescription: Threeflower ticktrefoil is a low, wiry legume whose stems spread over the ground and can root at their lower joints. It often blends into short vegetation until its small pea-like flowers or jointed fruits become visible. Modern treatments also use the name Grona triflora. Floras document it across tropical regions and in disturbed habitats, but that broad distribution does not mean every occurrence is harmful or that a United States lawn patch deserves an invasive-species label.
identification: Each leaf has three small leaflets, often with a slight notch at the tip, and the lower surfaces can be hairy. Flowers occur in small clusters close to the leaf axils rather than on a long, showy flowering spike. The fruit is divided into separate joints. Desmodium adscendens and D. barbatum can resemble it in general habit, while ordinary clovers also have three leaflets. Flower arrangement, stipules, and the shape of fruit joints help separate these plants; photograph those details together.
actions: Check the identification before removing a mixed patch of low legumes. Record whether the plant stays in a maintained lawn or is expanding into a nearby natural area. Where a small garden colony is unwanted, lift rooted stem sections carefully and collect the fruits before moving clippings or soil. Revisit the edges for surviving rooted nodes. Regional status and tested control remain incomplete in this review, so pasture or conservation-site decisions should be made with local botanical and land-management advice.
researchNotes: The authored East African and Indian floras support Desmodium triflorum morphology under its modern Grona triflora combination. Gillett, Polhill and Verdcourt 1971 describe creeping rooted stems, small notched leaflets and jointed fruits independently of the Indian regional flora. The Kew page supplies this substantive hosted treatment, not only name corroboration. Use flowers and mature jointed fruits to distinguish similar low legumes and check local native status before removal. proposedDescription: Threelobe false mallow is an upright, branching member of the mallow family with small yellow flowers. It can grow as an annual or persist longer, and botanical accounts document it in disturbed tropical and subtropical habitats. Its leaves are not always conspicuously three-lobed despite the common name. A roadside plant with a yellow mallow flower may belong to several different species, and neither a weedy appearance nor a foreign-sounding scientific name establishes that it is locally invasive.
identification: Look for toothed leaves that range from broadly oval to narrower shapes, sometimes with shallow lobes. Hair type varies across the plant and among its subspecies; magnification helps reveal simple and star-shaped hairs. Small yellow flowers arise near leaf axils, with three narrow bracts outside the main calyx. Mature fruits break into separate segments, whose structure is useful for identification. Sida species and other false mallows are important lookalikes. Include a ripe fruit and the bracts beneath a flower rather than relying on a single petal photograph.
actions: Have an uncertain plant checked before removing native mallows from a natural area. In a cultivated bed, remove a confirmed unwanted plant before its fruits mature and collect loose fruiting material. Note whether new plants appear repeatedly from disturbed soil or spread beyond the original patch. Avoid carrying fruit-bearing stems on mowing equipment into clean ground. The reviewed sources establish botanical identity and regional records, but United States site-specific impact and an evaluated control program remain unresolved and should guide any larger response.
researchNotes: The Saudi specimen paper and IISc regional flora independently support Malvastrum coromandelianum, while subspecies variation requires restraint in the hair description. The Saudi study concerns a named subspecies and includes a key; its exact subspecies characters are not generalized into a US invasion claim. Broad recognition and fruit documentation remain useful. Check flower bracts and mature fruit segments with a local mallow specialist before removing natural-area plants.

proposedDescription: Threespike goosegrass is a small perennial grass from South America that can establish in lawns, gravelly ground, and other disturbed places. Its short stature makes it easy to overlook until the compact finger-like seed heads appear. The name suggests three branches, but plants can have two to four. Agricultural accounts from Argentina describe crop competition, while New Zealand records concern scattered naturalized populations. Those different contexts should not be collapsed into a single claim of severe impact everywhere.
identification: The plant forms low tufts, with folded leaves and blunt, boat-shaped tips. A few short, stout flowering spikes cluster at the stem tip, each carrying densely arranged spikelets on one side. The common annual goosegrass, Eleusine indica, is usually larger and often has more and longer spikes. Check the perennial base and complete seed head together, because spike number alone varies. Close views of the leaf tip, blade-sheath junction, and spikelet arrangement are particularly helpful for a grass specialist.
actions: In a lawn, identify the grass before treating it as annual goosegrass, since a surviving perennial base changes the follow-up needed. Small unwanted tufts can be lifted before seed matures, taking care to remove the crown. Repair bare areas with suitable cover and avoid transferring seed-bearing soil or clippings. In crops, use local agronomic advice rather than importing a treatment from another country. Regional United States impact and tested control are still gaps in this account, especially for natural-area settings.
researchNotes: Argentina's plant-health account and New Zealand's flora-derived description independently establish Eleusine tristachya's perennial habit and compact seed heads. Crop competition is attributed to Argentina, not assumed for US lawns or natural areas. The distinction from annual E. indica supports crown removal and appropriate follow-up. Confirm the perennial base and seed-head structure, then seek local agronomic advice for crop infestations.

proposedDescription: Chilli thrips is a tiny introduced insect that damages tender plant growth rather than merely gathering harmlessly inside flowers. It has become a concern on ornamental plants and crops in parts of the southern United States and California. Feeding can discolor and distort young leaves and shoots, reducing a plant's ability to grow normally. Blueberry guidance from Georgia describes its importance to southeastern fruit production. The effect depends on the host and infestation, so a curled leaf alone is not a diagnosis.
identification: Adults are very small and pale, with darker fringed wings and faint abdominal markings. Look at newly expanding leaves, buds, and shoot tips for insects and feeding scars. Broad mites, aphids, herbicide injury, and several other thrips can produce similar symptoms. California guidance specifically warns that field appearance cannot reliably identify chilli thrips to species. A diagnostic laboratory should examine collected insects when the identification matters, especially on nursery plants or in a new production area.
actions: Inspect new plants and isolate suspicious stock before placing it beside susceptible plants. Monitor new growth frequently, using a consistent sample of shoots so changes are visible over time. Contain heavily infested prunings and remove nearby discarded plant material that could shelter pests. Ask extension staff about conserving predators and choosing a crop-appropriate integrated program. Repeated use of one pesticide is not a durable plan. Document the plant host and damage when reporting a suspected new occurrence to a local plant clinic.
researchNotes: Georgia blueberry observations and UC landscape diagnostic guidance provide independent regional evidence. Generic thrips color is not treated as a species diagnosis; lookalike damage is explicitly discussed.

claims: Southeastern blueberry impact and adult appearance
California occurrence, symptom lookalikes and need for specialist identification

proposedDescription: Melon thrips is a warm-climate crop pest that can also persist in protected growing spaces. It spread from Southeast Asia to many tropical and subtropical regions, with United States records including Hawaii and Florida. Vegetables such as eggplant and cucurbits can suffer feeding damage, but host suitability is not identical across all vegetables. In particular, tomato should not be assumed to support the same populations simply because several other thrips attack it. Greenhouse conditions can make a local risk different from the outdoor climate.
identification: Adults are tiny, slender, yellowish insects with narrow fringed wings; young stages lack developed wings. Feeding may leave pale or bronzed surfaces, but damage and body color overlap with other thrips. Examine the affected host and the distribution of insects across leaves and flowers rather than naming the pest from a sticky-trap silhouette. A specialist can inspect microscopic characters. Preserve the crop identity and growing conditions with the sample, because those details help interpret an otherwise ambiguous finding.
actions: Inspect incoming transplants and keep suspect lots separate while seeking identification. Scout regularly instead of waiting for widespread damage, and remove crop residues promptly after harvest. Predators can suppress populations, and research in Guadeloupe found that excessive insecticide use could worsen problems by disrupting that regulation. Work with an adviser on a crop-specific program that includes sanitation and natural enemies. Do not move infested plants or make treatment choices based solely on the general word thrips on a product label.
researchNotes: UF species account and original INRA work in Guadeloupe are independent evidence lineages. Regional crop limits and disruption of natural control are retained without generalizing every thrips host.

proposedDescription: Thrips parvispinus, often called short-spined or pepper thrips, is an emerging pest of ornamental plants and crops. It was confirmed in Florida in 2020, and later reports document spread associated with plant commerce. Texas extension describes specimens from hibiscus and pepper that were confirmed by a specialist in 2025. Such records deserve attention, but an interception at a retailer and an established outdoor population are different findings. The plant's source and location matter when interpreting a report.
identification: Females are dark brown, with the head and thorax often paler than the abdomen; males are smaller and lighter. Both can hide in protected plant parts, and feeding may scar or deform new growth. Several other dark thrips can look similar without magnification. Photograph the affected plant and its fresh damage, then arrange for microscopic identification of actual insects. A leaf photograph alone cannot separate this species from mites, other thrips, or some growth disorders.
actions: Hold suspect nursery stock apart and avoid selling, gifting, or moving it until local plant-health staff advise what to do. Keep purchase and shipment information available so a confirmed finding can be traced. Inspect nearby plants, especially fresh growth, and use a consistent monitoring routine after any intervention. Commercial growers should work with extension and regulatory staff on sanitation, biological control, and resistance management. Home gardeners should seek confirmation early rather than repeatedly applying broad insecticides to every damaged plant in the garden.
researchNotes:
UF's species synthesis and Texas A&M's independently documented, specialist-confirmed Texas specimens support the account. Current state-specific regulatory details are deliberately not converted into nationwide instructions.

proposedDescription: Thymeleaf dragonhead is a small herb in the mint family, with modest bluish flowers rather than the large blooms of ornamental dragonheads. Botanical records show it outside its native region, including an unusual historical Massachusetts occurrence. A recent Polish study documented a railway population persisting for more than a decade. That is useful evidence of establishment at that site, but it does not demonstrate aggressive spread or ecological damage across the United States. Sparse records call for careful observation rather than an inflated threat label.
identification: Look for opposite, toothed leaves and small blue to purple flowers with a two-lipped outline. The floral tube sits within a toothed calyx, and the plant is upright rather than a creeping mat of true thyme. Other small mint-family herbs can look similar, so flower size, calyx structure, and the leaves directly below the flowers deserve close photographs. Record the entire plant and its habitat as well as the flowers. A regional herbarium can compare it with native dragonheads and related mints.
actions: If you find an unfamiliar population, record how many plants occur, whether they are flowering or fruiting, and whether imported soil or transport corridors are nearby. Have the identification checked before removing a rare native lookalike. In a garden, a confirmed unwanted plant can be removed before its fruits mature. Avoid redistributing seed-bearing material. United States impact and control evidence are insufficient here, so conservation-site work should follow a local botanical assessment rather than a generic invasive-mint response.
researchNotes: Independent New England flora and original Polish field observations support Dracocephalum thymiflorum; unknown US damage is a geographic limitation, not a missing identity. The Polish survey documents persistence at its own railway site. It is not evidence of US expansion or a tested control method. Confirm flowering plants and record repeated recruitment at the actual US site before escalating management.

proposedDescription: Thymeleaf sandwort is a small annual that can disappear into gravel, short turf, or other open ground until its tiny white flowers catch the light. Its branching stems and pointed little leaves give it a wiry appearance. Floras document it as naturalized in several regions, but a modest patch in disturbed ground should not automatically be treated as a major ecosystem invader. Correct identification is especially useful because several native and introduced plants share its small white flowers.
identification: Leaves are small, opposite, and pointed, with fine rough hairs. Each flower has five white petals that are shorter than the surrounding pointed sepals. The mature capsule is swollen near the base, rather like a tiny flask, and opens with six short teeth. Chickweeds can resemble it but commonly have deeply divided petals, while the closely related slender sandwort requires careful fruit and seed comparison. Take close photographs of the sepals and a ripe capsule; flowering stems alone may not resolve the distinction.
actions: In a garden bed or gravel path, small unwanted plants can be pulled before capsules shed seed. Keep disturbance shallow so management does not continually create new bare ground. In a lawn, assess whether thin turf or repeated soil exposure is encouraging annual weeds and address that underlying condition. Avoid broad treatment of a mixed spring flora without confirming the species. Local ecological impact and a species-specific United States control program remain unresolved in this account, so larger interventions need a site-based reason.
researchNotes: The closely related leptoclados concept can be addressed by checking mature capsules rather than withholding the Arenaria serpyllifolia profile. New Zealand and NSW offer independent floras, although their species boundaries differ. The draft already asks for capsule-based confirmation and does not assign local ecological damage. Use the local flora's narrow or broad treatment consistently when verifying a sandwort specimen.

proposedDescription: Thymeleaf speedwell is a low perennial with small pale flowers, often growing in damp lawns, short grass, and open wet places. Its lower stems can lie along the ground and root at the joints, while flowering tips rise above the leaves. The name covers plants whose regional and subspecific treatment varies, including forms associated with mountain habitats. A species-level listing should not erase that variation or automatically classify every local population as an introduced weed.
identification: Leaves are opposite, rounded to oval, and nearly smooth, with shallow teeth that can be hard to see. Small pale blue or whitish flowers occur along an upright terminal cluster, often showing darker lines on the petals. The fruit is flattened and notched at the top. Threadstalk speedwell has more conspicuous individual flowers on long fine stalks, while purslane speedwell is annual and has almost unstalked flowers. Close views of flowers, fruit margins, and the rooted stem base help resolve the identification.
actions: In a lawn, consider whether the plant is causing a practical problem before removing it. Where a patch is unwanted, carefully lift rooted stems and improve thin turf using practices suited to the local grass and drainage. In wetlands or mountain vegetation, seek botanical confirmation before disturbance, because local status may differ from that of garden weeds. Record the habitat and flowering date with a sighting. This review leaves regional native status and species-specific ecological impact open rather than prescribing broad removal.
researchNotes: The humifusa boundary and uncertain regional origin are openly documented in the current Washington flora, allowing a cautious Veronica serpyllifolia profile. The FNA-derived Washington account describes intergrading characters; the independent New Zealand flora supports morphology. The draft avoids a blanket invasive or removal designation. Determine the regional taxon and native-status treatment before managing an unfamiliar patch.

proposedDescription: Tickclover is a legume with trailing to upright stems and jointed fruits that readily catch on clothing or animal fur. It is native to tropical and subtropical America, while the Hawaiian flora documents naturalized populations on several islands. That distinction matters: a plant can be a familiar native in one region and an introduced pasture or roadside plant in another. Its ability to hitchhike makes cleaning clothing useful, but sticky fruits alone do not demonstrate serious ecological harm.
identification: Leaves have three leaflets, usually elongated or oval, with a larger terminal leaflet. Some show a pale mark along the middle, but the mark is not universal. Pink to purple pea-like flowers occur in elongated clusters. Mature fruits divide into several flattened, roughly semicircular joints covered in tiny hooked hairs. Other ticktrefoils share three-part leaves and clinging fruits, so a single leaflet is a weak identification. Include the flower cluster, lower leaf surface, and a complete mature fruit in photographs.
actions: Brush attached fruit segments from clothing, pet fur, and equipment before leaving an infested site, disposing of them where they will not start another patch. In a garden where the plant is unwanted, remove it before fruit matures and revisit for regrowth or seedlings. In pasture or natural vegetation, confirm regional status before choosing control. Do not assume a tropical American native is an invader everywhere. Local impact and management evidence remain incomplete in this account, especially outside the Hawaiian introduction context.
researchNotes: PROSEA adds a substantive independent Desmodium incanum account while Smithsonian records corroborate Hawaiian naturalization. The live Smithsonian species page and Puerto Rico page were unavailable. Its indexed Hawaiian family checklist and the independently authored PROSEA account support a profile with region-specific origin and no US impact claim. Match the jointed pods and leaves to a local flora before interpreting a new population as introduced. claims: Desmodium incanum recorded as naturalized on several Hawaiian islands.
Independent tropical forage account with morphology, habitat and seed dispersal.

proposedDescription: Tidalmarsh flatsedge is a perennial sedge associated with wet ground. Botanical treatments describe underground runners ending in tubers, which allow it to persist beyond a single season. Its broad Eurasian range and scattered records elsewhere need to be interpreted locally; the common name does not mean that every plant occurs in a tidal marsh. A tuft in an irrigated field, a shoreline stand, and a conservation-sensitive wetland population present different questions about identification and management.
identification: Plants have firm, three-angled stems, long narrow leaves, and a branched cluster of flattened brownish spikelets. Several leaf-like bracts extend beyond the flowering cluster. The underground tubers are useful clues, but digging them from a wetland just to make an identification may be inappropriate. Other flatsedges and nutsedges share much of this appearance. Mature spikelets and fruits, including the number of style branches and fruit shape, are important specialist characters. Photograph the full flowering head and a close view of individual spikelets.
actions: Have a flowering plant identified before treating a wet area for nutsedge. Record water conditions and whether the patch is spreading through soil moved during ditching or cultivation. Where removal is justified, plan for the underground propagules rather than repeatedly clipping the leaves alone. Keep excavated wet soil and plant fragments from being transferred to clean sites. Any work in a marsh or drainage channel should follow local habitat and water-management guidance. United States ecological impact and a tested species-specific response remain unresolved here.
researchNotes:
Flora of North America directly establishes Cyperus serotinus in northeastern US tidal marshes, resolving the prior US-applicability gap. FNA is independent of the Chinese flora displayed by Shanghai. Tuber and stolon biology supports careful soil handling; overseas rice-control results are not presented as local treatment trials. Preserve fertile material and inspect connected underground parts when confirming a new marsh occurrence. proposedDescription: Tiger grass is a tall, clump-forming grass with broad leaves that can make it look like a bamboo screen. It is native to tropical and subtropical Asia and is also known under the older name Thysanolaena maxima. The University of Florida's predictive assessment rates it as high invasion risk. That is a forecast based on its traits and behavior, not proof that every Florida county has an established damaging population. Its ornamental appeal should be weighed against that regional assessment.
identification: Arching, reed-like stems arise from short underground rhizomes and can reach several meters tall. The broad, smooth, leathery leaf blades alternate along the stems. A small membranous collar occurs where each blade meets its sheath, and the mature flowering branches form a large airy head. It lacks the familiar woody branching structure of many true bamboos. Photograph both the base and a flowering stem, since broad leaves alone can be confused with other large ornamental grasses.
actions: In Florida, choose a locally recommended alternative when a tall screen is needed. For an existing planting, watch the surrounding ground and nearby disturbed areas for young plants, and prevent seed-bearing cuttings from being dumped beyond the garden. A clump that has outgrown its site may require staged removal of the persistent base and follow-up on new shoots. Ask local extension staff about suitable methods before working near drains or natural vegetation. Retain a record of escapes separately from the original cultivated clump.
researchNotes: UF's predictive assessment is explicitly distinguished from observed invasion. Singapore NParks and Kew provide botanical evidence independent of the Florida risk conclusion.

proposedDescription: Timothy grass is a familiar cool-season hay and pasture grass introduced from Eurasia. It greens up early and produces dense, cylindrical flowering heads that stand above broad blades. It also escapes cultivation and persists in old fields and other disturbed places. Those escapes can matter in a restoration area, but a managed hayfield is not automatically an invasive-species problem. Decisions should reflect the purpose of the site and whether the grass is displacing vegetation that managers are trying to conserve.
identification: Look closely at the tight cylindrical head: each small spikelet has two short bristles, giving it a tiny horned appearance. Plants form tufts and often have a swollen stem base rather than a spreading rhizome network. The leaf junction has a pale membranous ligule and no clasping auricles. Meadow foxtail can look similar from a distance, but the placement and form of its awns differ. Native alpine timothy has a shorter, more compact head and should not be removed on a casual comparison.
actions: Keep useful forage management separate from natural-area restoration. Where timothy is unwanted, identify the stand before seed matures and work with the land manager on preventing further seed input while establishing suitable replacement vegetation. Small isolated tufts may be dug out if soil disturbance is acceptable. Avoid introducing hay or seed mixtures containing timothy into projects intended to restore native grassland. Revisit treated areas for seedlings and surviving crowns rather than assuming one cut has removed a perennial.
researchNotes: Illinois and Utah extension accounts provide independent agronomic and morphological descriptions; Alaska's guide supports native lookalike caution. Managed forage is not described as universally invasive.

proposedDescription: Tiny vetch is a slender annual legume that scrambles through surrounding vegetation using tendrils. Its small pale flowers are easy to miss, and the most revealing feature may be the short hairy pod that follows. It occurs as a weed of cultivation in botanical accounts from several regions. That status should not be confused with proof of serious ecological damage everywhere it grows. The common name hairy vetch is also used for other species, making the scientific name particularly useful.
identification: Each leaf carries several pairs of narrow leaflets and ends in a tendril that may branch. Flowers are small, dull white to pale blue, and grouped on a stalk. Mature pods are short, hairy, and usually contain two seeds, becoming dark as they ripen. Larger purple-flowered vetches are a common source of confusion, while other small-flowered species need closer comparison. Photograph a complete leaf, the flower cluster, and an intact ripe pod; counting leaflets alone is not enough.
actions: Where tiny vetch is unwanted in a garden or young planting, remove it before pods mature, gently freeing the tendrils so neighboring plants are not uprooted. Check whether the vine is actually smothering seedlings or simply occupying an open gap before intervening. Avoid transporting mature pods with cut vegetation or contaminated seed. Crop fields require local advice that considers the crop and season. United States site-specific impact and tested control are not established by the floras reviewed here, so broad natural-area removal needs further justification.
researchNotes: Independent New Zealand and Indian botanical accounts adequately support hairy tare recognition and seed containment. A missing US control experiment does not invalidate a carefully limited annual-weed profile. The advice targets confirmed unwanted plants before pod maturation rather than extrapolating treatment efficacy. Document local density and crop context before deciding whether broader intervention is warranted.

proposedDescription: The titan acorn barnacle is a large marine barnacle native to the eastern Pacific from Mexico toward Peru. Introduced populations have been documented on the United States Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts. Adults attach firmly to hard surfaces, including boats, buoys, and other structures, making hull fouling a plausible transport pathway. Larvae can also move through water. Its presence deserves documentation, but local abundance and ecological effects vary; a few large barnacles are not evidence of a shoreline-wide impact.
identification: Adults can reach several centimeters in height and width and often have a conspicuous pinkish-red shell. The shell opening and the plates closing it are important identification features. The related California barnacle, Megabalanus californicus, differs in shell pattern, ribbing, and the relative size of the opening. Age and crowding can alter shape, so color alone is insufficient. Photograph the entire attached animal from the side and above, with a scale, and let a marine specialist examine uncertain specimens.
actions: Inspect hulls, trailers, and equipment before moving them between coastal waters. Use an appropriate haul-out or cleaning facility that captures removed organisms rather than scraping living fouling directly into a new harbor. Do not move a colonized buoy or shell as a souvenir. Report unfamiliar large barnacles to the local marine invasive-species program with the exact location and substrate. Broad chemical treatment of docks or natural shores is not justified by a photograph; management should focus on confirmed identification and transport prevention.
researchNotes: Smithsonian's invasion synthesis supplies regional history. A separate 2014 taxonomic specimen study supports shell variation; derivative NEMESIS regional pages are not counted as independent sources.

proposedDescription: Titan applesnail is the name historically applied to a large introduced freshwater snail in southeastern Florida. USGS retains a Pomacea haustrum profile, but Smithsonian's taxonomic discussion explains that the name and the identity of the green-egg-laying Florida snail require further research. This is a real evidence conflict, not a reason to silently substitute another applesnail. The catalog record should remain under review until its intended species concept is reconciled with current specialist taxonomy.
identification: Historical accounts describe a very large rounded shell, potentially around nine to twelve centimeters high, and distinctive green egg masses laid above water. Shell shape overlaps strongly with other large Pomacea, including the spotted applesnail, and Florida also has a native applesnail. Egg color and shape can help guide an expert, but neither a large shell nor an unfamiliar clutch settles the name. Photograph the shell from several angles and the egg mass in place, including a size reference and the waterline.
actions: Do not release aquarium snails or move aquatic plants carrying eggs into another water body. Report a suspected unusual applesnail to a local aquatic-species specialist and keep the exact location and photographs. Avoid destroying every snail or egg mass on the assumption that all are nonnative. If removal is recommended, obtain local instructions that protect native species and address the confirmed population. Claims about crop destruction or control methods from other Pomacea species should not be assigned to this unresolved taxon.

proposedDescription: The tokay gecko is a large, vocal lizard from Southeast Asia whose repeated call helped give it its name. Introductions associated with the pet trade have produced established populations in parts of Florida and Hawaii. It is mainly active at night and can use trees, rocky shelter, and buildings. Finding one near a porch light documents an animal using that site; it does not by itself measure its effect on native wildlife or prove that a breeding population occurs throughout the neighborhood.
identification: A typical tokay has a large head, broad gripping toe pads, and gray to bluish-gray skin marked with orange or reddish spots. Adults are much larger and more robust than the small pale house geckos commonly seen on walls. The loud repeated call can support an identification when heard with a visual sighting, but recordings alone may be misleading. Photograph the animal from a safe distance, including its head, body pattern, and toes; do not grab it to obtain a closer view.
actions: Never release a pet tokay outdoors. If an unwanted captive animal needs a new home, arrange a responsible surrender through a qualified organization. For a free-ranging sighting outside an established area, record the location and contact a local wildlife or invasive-species program. Keep pets away and avoid glue traps or indiscriminate poisons that also harm native animals. Any capture or removal should follow local guidance and be handled by someone prepared to work safely with a large gecko.
researchNotes: CNAH's cited regional history and a separate UF educational account support introduction context and morphology. Ecological harm is not inferred from predatory diet or isolated sightings.

proposedDescription: Tomato pinworm is a small moth whose caterpillars damage tomato leaves and fruit. Young larvae begin within leaves, then may fold leaves with silk or enter fruit, where their feeding is harder to reach. It is a recognized production pest in southern California and other warm growing areas. A pinhole in a tomato is not a diagnosis on its own, however, and seasonal crop damage should be assessed separately from claims about an insect's native or introduced status.
identification: Adults are small grayish moths flecked with darker markings. Young caterpillars are pale and relatively smooth, while older larvae may show reddish or purplish bands. Look for blotchy mines and folded leaves as well as fruit injury. Ordinary leafminer tunnels are typically narrow and winding, and leafminers do not fold the leaves. Tomato fruitworms are different caterpillars with more obvious early bristles and bumps. Photograph the larva, its shelter, and damaged fruit before submitting material for confirmation.
actions: Inspect transplants and scout leaves before damage becomes concentrated inside fruit. Remove infested crop residues after harvest and manage volunteer tomatoes or other confirmed host weeds that bridge cropping cycles. In a home garden, promptly containing badly infested leaves and fruit can reduce the amount of occupied material left behind. Commercial growers should use local guidance on monitoring and integrated control, including host-free periods where appropriate. Avoid moving infested transplants between gardens or assuming a spray will reach larvae already protected inside fruit.
researchNotes:
UC IPM's crop and home accounts are one lineage, while Texas A&M provides a separate field account. Leafminer and fruitworm distinctions are evidence-backed; no blanket introduced status is assigned.

proposedDescription: Tomato thrips is a brown thrips associated with tomato and other nightshade-family crops in tropical regions. An original 2017 study reported it from Asystasia gangetica flowers in Miami-Dade County, Florida. That occurrence does not establish damage in Florida vegetable fields. The common name is not unique, and the similar Ceratothripoides claratris has a separate research history. Reports about virus transmission or severe losses in that relative must not be reassigned to C. brunneus without species-specific evidence.
identification: Adults are brown, with paler feet, tibial tips, and parts of the antennae. Both sexes have developed wings. Reliable identification depends on microscopic features, including the eight-segmented antennae and the placement of particular head and body hairs. These characters are beyond a typical garden photograph. C. claratris and other members of the genus are important comparisons. Send actual insects to a diagnostic service and record the host plant, affected tissue, and whether the insects came from imported or locally grown material.
actions: Keep suspect transplants separate and avoid distributing them while identification is pending. Inspect adjacent plants and retain shipment or purchase details so a confirmed detection can be traced. Crop damage should be assessed alongside other possible causes before treatment is chosen. Ask local extension or plant-health staff for a response appropriate to the location; an overseas quarantine instruction is not automatically a United States rule. The Florida flower record supports presence, while local crop impacts and a tested management response still need species-specific evidence.

The paper anticipates possible crop detections but does not demonstrate Florida crop losses or virus transmission. proposedDescription: Toothed dock is an annual or sometimes biennial dock that often occurs in moist disturbed ground. Its native range stretches across a broad part of the Old World, and botanical records also place it outside that range. The name refers to teeth on the structures surrounding the fruit, not simply to a jagged leaf edge. Like other docks, it can be difficult to name when young. A rosette in a wet field needs more evidence before it is classified as this species.
identification: The lower leaves are longer than wide and may have a squared or slightly heart-shaped base. Upper leaves become smaller and narrower. Flowering stems carry clusters of small flowers that mature into fruits enclosed by enlarged inner flower segments, often called valves. These valves have conspicuous narrow teeth and may carry raised grain-like swellings. Several other docks have toothed valves too, so their shape, tooth length, and swellings need comparison. Photograph mature fruits with a scale and retain views of the lower leaves.
actions: In a cultivated bed, remove a confirmed unwanted plant before the fruit clusters mature, collecting seed-bearing material rather than scattering it. Note whether repeated seedlings follow irrigation, soil movement, or disturbance. Do not assume treatment for a deep-rooted perennial dock fits this shorter-lived species. A regional herbarium or crop adviser can confirm identity and local relevance. This review does not establish a species-specific United States impact or control program, so extensive work in wet natural habitat should wait for a site-based assessment.
researchNotes: The refreshed Iraq and East African flora excerpts and Indian habitat record support a bounded Rumex dentatus profile. The floras allow variation in life span, fruit teeth and tubercles. The draft avoids an inflexible subspecies diagnosis and does not promise a US control outcome. Use mature fruiting valves, not leaf shape alone, to verify an unwanted dock population.

proposedDescription: Torpedograss is a persistent perennial whose most important growth happens out of sight. Long, pointed underground stems spread through soil and can produce new shoots from fragments. In Florida it is an invasive wetland and shoreline plant, and Hawaii also documents it in disturbed and natural settings. Dense colonies can replace other vegetation. Although it produces flowering heads, vegetative growth is central to its persistence, so simply stopping seed production does not solve an established infestation.
identification: Look for upright green to blue-green grass shoots and an open, branched seed head. At the leaf junction is a very short membrane fringed with hairs. The namesake clue is a stout, sharply pointed, pale rhizome with scale-like leaves. Several grasses share narrow blades and creeping growth, so an aboveground photograph may be insufficient. Where digging is appropriate, photograph a small exposed rhizome in place; do not scatter fragments while trying to identify the plant.
actions: Avoid moving soil, sod, or ditch-cleaning debris from an infested area into clean ground. Small patches require careful removal of underground stems and repeated follow-up; incomplete digging can leave many growing points. Mowing may keep shoots short without eliminating the colony. For shorelines, canals, and wetlands, consult a qualified local manager about site-appropriate treatment and protection of desirable aquatic plants. Work from isolated patches toward larger stands, monitor regrowth, and restore suitable vegetation rather than leaving newly disturbed soil open.
researchNotes: Florida's current assessment and Hawaii's species-specific weed account are treated as separate regional evidence. Seed uncertainty is retained; rhizome fragmentation and aquatic-site management drive practical advice.

proposedDescription: Phyllostachys edulis is usually called moso bamboo, a large running bamboo cultivated for useful stems and shoots. Tortoise-shell bamboo more specifically refers to the tortoise-shell form often sold as Heterocycla, whose lower stem sections are irregularly shortened and swollen. The species and that form should not be treated as identical descriptions. Florida's predictive assessment rates the species as high invasion risk, while horticultural guidance warns that it spreads. Those conclusions concern planting risk, not proof that every cultivated grove has escaped.
identification: Moso develops tall, stout woody culms, with younger surfaces often powdery and finely hairy. The protective sheaths on emerging shoots have dense brown hairs and spots. Specialist bamboo identification uses these sheaths, branching, and leaf characters together. Ordinary moso culms need not show the distorted pattern associated with tortoise-shell bamboo. Photograph a young shoot with its sheaths, mature culms, branch attachments, and leaves. Height alone cannot distinguish it from other large running bamboos or native cane.
actions: Before planting, consider the Florida risk assessment and obtain locally appropriate alternatives for screening. Existing groves need regular inspection beyond their intended boundary, because underground growth can produce shoots away from the visible clump. If removal is necessary, plan repeated work on new shoots and the rhizome system rather than a single cutting of the tall culms. Do not dump rhizome-bearing soil or divisions into natural areas. A species-level identification does not establish that a plant is the tortoise-shell form.

proposedDescription: Trailing indigo is a creeping legume historically used as a tropical cover crop. Stems can root at the nodes and form a dense layer over the soil. It has often been confused with Indigofera spicata. A Taiwan field study distinguishes the two, while a U.S. germplasm review found that many southeastern accessions labeled hendecaphylla were actually spicata. That history makes old livestock-toxicity reports difficult to assign. Neither a cover-crop label nor an uncertain name is assurance that a plant is safe to graze.
identification: Leaves are divided into numerous small leaflets, commonly nine to eleven in the reviewed treatment. Pink to brick-red pea flowers form elongated clusters, followed by slender downward-pointing pods. The similar I. spicata typically has fewer, broader leaflets, but dependable separation also uses small flower structures. A sprawling plant with pink flowers cannot be identified securely from growth habit alone. Photograph complete leaves, flowers from the side, mature pods, and the rooting stems, and ask a legume specialist to examine uncertain material.
actions: Keep an unidentified creeping indigo out of hay and grazing areas until it has been assessed. If livestock may have eaten it and seem unwell, contact a veterinarian promptly rather than relying on a plant photograph. For an unwanted patch, prevent movement of rooted stems and seed-bearing soil and plan follow-up after removal. Do not apply toxicity figures or control claims from I. spicata automatically. A regional record needs a verified specimen before its identity can be matched confidently to older accounts of harm.

proposedDescription: Trailing shrubverbena, usually called trailing lantana, is a low woody plant with spreading stems and clusters of small lavender flowers. It comes from South America and is widely grown in containers and as ground cover. In warm conditions it can naturalize beyond gardens, and Florida's predictive assessment rates it as high invasion risk. Its popularity with flower visitors does not resolve that planting concern. Risk also varies with climate and cultivar, so a cold-season bedding plant and a persistent escaped mat need different assessments.
identification: Leaves are opposite, oval, toothed, and rough above, with softer hairs beneath. Slender stems trail along the ground and may root where they touch soil. The flower heads contain many small tubes, usually purple to pinkish with pale centers and yellow throats. Other lantanas and cultivated hybrids can resemble it; a yellow-flowered nursery selection may be a hybrid rather than this species. Photograph leaves, stems, flowers, and fruit together and retain the cultivar label when available.
actions: In Florida, choose a locally recommended alternative instead of planting a species assessed as high risk. Inspect established plants for seedlings and rooted stems beyond the bed, and contain fruiting prunings. Wear gloves when handling the plant and keep it out of grazing material or edible-plant harvests. If removing a mat, check for rooted nodes left behind and revisit after new growth resumes. Do not assume a cultivar is sterile without reliable documentation for that exact selection.

proposedDescription: This trapjaw ant is known from tropical American regions and Florida, where it can occur around homes and in coastal habitats. Published work has debated whether Florida populations are native or introduced, with range expansion and disturbed-site associations supporting introduction as a possibility. That uncertainty deserves to remain visible. A large ant with snapping jaws is not automatically this species, and Florida also supports native trapjaw ants, including species associated with sensitive natural habitats.
identification: The elongated jaws, narrow waist, and spine-topped waist node identify the general trapjaw form, but species separation needs much closer inspection. In O. ruginodis, the rear face of the waist node has conspicuous transverse wrinkles, and specialists compare head sculpture, body size, and other structures. Color varies and is not sufficient. O. brunneus and O. haematodus are important comparisons. Photograph the ant from the side and above without handling it, and seek identification from an entomologist familiar with regional ants.
actions: Avoid moving colonies, occupied soil, or potted plants between properties. If ants are entering a building, document their route and obtain an identification before selecting a pest-management response. Outdoor ants in a natural area should not be treated simply because their jaws look alarming. Keep children and pets from disturbing a nest and leave any necessary collection to someone equipped to do it safely. Species-specific ecological effects, origin in Florida, and an appropriate local control recommendation remain unresolved in this review.
researchNotes: Original Nearctic revision and Longino's separate Costa Rican collections support Odontomachus ruginodis identification while leaving Florida origin uncertain. Uncertain exotic status is retained as an explicit regional limitation rather than used to withhold natural history. The profile does not direct eradication of a potentially native ant. Ask for specialist determination and local status interpretation before considering nest removal. proposedDescription: Tree mallow is a large, soft-wooded mallow with rounded lobed leaves and pink to purple flowers. Older sources often call it Lavatera arborea. It is associated with coastal habitats in parts of its native range and has naturalized elsewhere, including California and the Southern Hemisphere. Australian botanical guidance documents competition and hybridization concerns involving a native mallow. Those specific impacts should remain tied to that region rather than becoming a claim that every coastal tree mallow threatens the same species.
identification: Plants can grow into a substantial shrub, with pale woody stems and soft hairs on younger parts. Leaves have several broad shallow lobes. The flowers have darker veins near the throat, and three broad outer bracts sit beneath the main calyx. The ripe fruit is a flattened ring of separate segments rather than a fleshy berry. Other tall mallows can resemble it, so photograph the outer bracts, leaf shape, and mature fruit. The old Lavatera name may still appear on nursery or herbarium labels.
actions: Check local status before planting near dunes, seabird habitat, or coastal reserves. Where removal is appropriate, tackle small plants before fruit matures and contain seed-bearing branches. Large stems may require careful cutting and follow-up on the base, especially on unstable coastal soil. Avoid clearing vegetation from nesting areas without land-manager guidance. This review leaves United States site-specific impact and control unresolved, so a botanical confirmation and a local habitat assessment should precede extensive removal.
researchNotes: Independent South African and Victorian floras establish tree mallow morphology; Calflora independently documents California nonnative occurrence. Regional effects remain attributed and Lavatera arborea is treated as an ordinary synonym. Missing local trials do not prevent identification and proportionate seed containment for unwanted plants. Check local recruitment and site goals before treating established tree mallows.

proposedDescription: Tree marigold is a tall, soft-wooded shrub with large yellow flower heads, also known as Mexican sunflower. It is native to Mexico and Central America and has been planted widely in warm regions. The Hawaiian flora records naturalized populations on several islands, while Florida's predictive assessment rates it as high invasion risk. A large flowering hedge can therefore deserve attention beyond its garden value. The risk assessment and documented naturalization are different kinds of evidence and should not be confused with a measured impact at every site.
identification: Look for a substantial branching plant with broad leaves divided into three to five lobes. The conspicuous heads have yellow outer rays surrounding many small disk flowers. Stems are soft-wooded, and mature fruits are flattened, dry, and associated with small persistent awns or scales. Other sunflowers, including the commonly grown annual Tithonia rotundifolia, can cause confusion. Record the overall woody habit, leaf shape, flower head, and fruit rather than identifying it from yellow rays alone.
actions: In Florida, select a locally recommended alternative for new planting. Where an existing shrub is spreading, prevent mature heads and cut branches from being dumped into natural areas. Young escapes are easier to address before they become large and produce more reproductive material. Plan follow-up after cutting because removing the visible canopy is not a complete monitoring program. On slopes or stream edges, coordinate removal and replacement vegetation with the land manager to avoid leaving exposed soil.
researchNotes: Florida predictive risk and Smithsonian's Hawaiian flora are independent assessment and regional botanical lineages. Naturalization is not inflated into quantified local impact, and the annual ornamental lookalike is distinguished.

proposedDescription: Tree tobacco is a branching shrub or small tree with blue-green leaves and long yellow flowers. Native to South America, it has naturalized in warm regions, including disturbed streambanks and roadsides in the southwestern United States. It can grow quickly after favorable rain and produces many tiny seeds, allowing new plants to appear on open ground. Unlike cultivated tea or an ordinary edible herb, this tobacco is poisonous and should not be used for food, smoking, or home remedies.
identification: The smooth, often waxy-looking leaves give the plant a gray or bluish cast. Flowers are narrow yellow tubes borne near branch tips, and the plant develops a woody framework rather than remaining a small leafy rosette. Other tobaccos and yellow-flowered shrubs can resemble parts of this description, so use the leaves, woody habit, flowers, and fruit together. Never taste a leaf to confirm the name. Photograph the whole plant and the point where a leaf joins the stem.
actions: Keep livestock and children away from an unwanted plant and ensure cut material does not enter feed or garden harvests. Small seedlings are easier to remove before they become woody and set seed; use gloves and avoid scattering mature capsules. Established plants and streamside stands need a local removal plan with follow-up for new seedlings. Do not dump cut branches into a wash where water can move the debris. If ingestion is suspected, seek prompt professional poison or veterinary advice rather than waiting for a botanical identification.
researchNotes: NC State provides toxicity and horticultural morphology, while UC Irvine documents southwestern disturbed-site ecology and seed production. Conflicting pollinator and leaf-arrangement snippets were excluded from the draft.

proposedDescription: Tree-of-heaven is a fast-growing deciduous tree that can turn a vacant lot, forest opening, or roadside into a thicket. Introduced from China, it spreads through winged seeds and shoots from an extensive root system. This combination makes established trees difficult to remove: a trunk that disappears may be followed by many new stems. In the eastern United States it competes with native vegetation and crops, while urban trees can also become persistent problems around buildings and neglected ground.
identification: Follow one whole leaf from the twig to its tip. It is a long compound leaf made of many pointed leaflets, rather than a branch of separate leaves. Most leaflet edges are smooth, with a few gland-bearing teeth near the base. Native sumacs usually have toothed leaflets and clusters of red, fuzzy fruits; tree-of-heaven produces loose bunches of twisted, papery wings. Walnuts can look similar, but their twigs have chambered pith rather than the spongy center of tree-of-heaven. Photograph the leaflet bases, twig, and fruits together.
actions:
Confirm the tree before cutting, especially where native sumacs and walnuts grow nearby. Small seedlings can be removed with their roots, but established root sprouts require a different plan. Cutting an older tree alone commonly triggers vigorous regrowth. Ask an extension forester or qualified arborist to plan treatment and safe removal, taking nearby structures and desirable trees into account. Mark the treated area and revisit it for root shoots and seedlings over subsequent seasons. Avoid distributing seed-bearing branches in mulch or yard waste.

Wear gloves when handling seedlings or cut material.
researchNotes:
Independent Virginia Tech and UConn extension accounts support recognition, root sprouting and repeat management. Chemical choice and timing intentionally deferred to site-specific professional advice.

proposedDescription: The triangle barnacle is a small crustacean that spends its adult life fixed to a hard surface. Its larvae develop in the water before reaching a stage that attaches and changes into a juvenile. Its Pacific and Indian Ocean range includes places where it is native, while Atlantic populations are introduced. Along the southeastern United States it occurs on submerged rocks, shells, dock structures, and vessel hulls in salty coastal water. Smithsonian's account reports fouling but no demonstrated species-specific economic or ecological impact, so fouling alone does not show that it is harming the surrounding habitat.
identification: Look for a low cone with six shell plates, pale vertical ribs, and pinkish or purplish coloration. The opening at the top is roughly triangular. The strongest diagnostic clue is much smaller: the closing plate called the scutum has rows of little pits. Other striped acorn barnacles can resemble it from above, and weathering or attached growth can hide the useful features. A close photograph with a scale helps, but a specialist may need to examine the shell plates to distinguish it reliably from related barnacles.
actions: Record the harbor, substrate, approximate depth, and whether the barnacles are on a boat or a natural surface. For an unexpected record, send photographs to a local marine extension or invasive-species program before collecting material. Boat owners can reduce transport by inspecting submerged fittings and arranging hull cleaning where removed growth and wash water are contained. Do not scrape fouling into another marina or move encrusted equipment between water bodies. Leave barnacles on natural shores undisturbed unless a responsible management program requests removal.
researchNotes: SERC invasion history, Texas A&M field recognition, and original Hong Kong larval experiment support separate claim sets. SERC also cites that experiment, which is not recounted as independent corroboration of larval biology.

proposedDescription: Tropical almond is the broad-canopied coastal tree whose horizontal branches often form conspicuous tiers. It is native in parts of the tropical Indo-Pacific and widely planted for shade elsewhere. Its buoyant fruits can travel in coastal water, giving a planted tree a route beyond the garden. In Florida it is a nonnative tree with an invasive-plant listing; that regional concern does not change its native role on shores such as Singapore's. A beachside seedling deserves a location-specific identification and assessment.
identification: Large leathery leaves crowd near the branch tips and broaden toward their rounded ends, giving them a paddle-like outline. Older leaves can turn red or yellow before falling, an unusually autumn-like display in a tropical landscape. The fruits are flattened and almond-shaped, changing from green toward reddish or purplish tones as they mature. Combine these features with the layered branching pattern. The common name does not make this the commercial almond tree, and leaf color alone is too variable to identify a seedling.
actions: Where tropical almond escapes into coastal habitat, check beneath parent trees and along adjacent shorelines for young plants. Record seedlings separately from intentionally planted shade trees so the observation describes actual spread. Remove small unwanted seedlings only with the landowner's permission and arrange professional help for large trees. Keep collected fruit and rooted garden waste out of dunes, mangrove edges, and drainage channels. For a replacement shade tree, use a locally appropriate species and check coastal planting guidance rather than assuming every tropical shoreline needs the same treatment.
researchNotes: Florida IFAS listing supplies regional concern; Singapore NParks supplies independent native ecology, fruit dispersal and recognition. No statewide legal-control requirement inferred.

proposedDescription: Tropical creeping cudweed has a misleading common name: botanical descriptions characterize Euchiton sphaericus as an upright or ascending annual without creeping runners. It is a small member of the daisy family, often noticed as a leafy stem topped by a compact ball of tiny flower heads. Australian and New Zealand floras recognize it, and New Zealand treats it as indigenous. Those accounts provide a sound identification starting point but do not establish harmful invasion at a particular United States site.
identification: Examine both sides of a leaf. The upper surface is green and may become nearly hairless, while the underside carries a pale woolly covering. Leaves narrow toward the base and can be spoon-shaped to slender and tapering. Several long, leaflike bracts extend beyond the rounded terminal flower cluster. Basal leaves may have withered by flowering time. Other cudweeds share the woolly appearance, so include the whole plant, the terminal cluster, and the stem base; a genuine network of runners would be a reason to reconsider this identification.
actions: Photograph a flowering plant before routine mowing or garden cleanup removes the useful features. A herbarium or extension botanist can compare it with regional cudweeds and check whether the name is appropriate for the location. If it is simply an unwanted garden annual, removing it before mature seed is a reasonable containment precaution. Avoid moving seed-bearing soil from the patch into another bed. Broad habitat clearing is not justified by the common name or this catalog entry; local impact and control evidence remain a research gap.
researchNotes: Two independent floras explicitly describe Euchiton sphaericus as an annual without stolons, resolving the misleading implication of the common name. The scientific species concept is consistent. The profile already explains that creeping in the common name is not evidence of runner formation, and it makes no US impact claim. Confirm terminal flower heads and the annual root system rather than identifying this plant from its common name.

proposedDescription: Tropical dropseed is a slender annual grass with a seed head so fine that it can resemble a little cloud above the leaves. Kew places its native range in southern Mexico and tropical America and records introductions in Florida, Hawaii, and other warm regions. A Bishop Museum account discusses it as an easily overlooked garden weed in Hawaii, possibly moved with potted plants. That account considers major environmental damage unlikely, which is a useful distinction from the more troublesome grasses that share its genus.
identification: The open seed head is narrow in overall outline but loosely branched, with threadlike branches and extremely small spikelets. Leaves are narrow, and the leaf junction has a fringe of hairs. Unlike many weedy dropseeds, the head is not a dense spike. It can resemble Sporobolus pyramidatus, but its branches are not arranged in the same whorled pattern. Another lookalike, Eragrostis amabilis, has several florets in each spikelet; tropical dropseed has one. A hand lens and a mature flowering specimen are more informative than a distant lawn photograph.
actions: Inspect nursery pots, garden edges, and disturbed soil for plants that are setting seed. For a small unwanted patch, remove the annuals before the delicate heads shed their seed and keep the material contained during transport. Clean soil from tools before using them in another bed. Record whether plants persist after the initial disturbance or occur beyond cultivated ground. A local botanist should verify uncertain grass records; neither a new occurrence nor an introduced-range listing alone establishes that an aggressive eradication program is warranted.

The Bishop paper repeats FNA morphology, which is not counted again; its garden and potted-plant observations are the independent evidence. The larger inherited mirror was not downloaded. Record repeated seedlings and clean soil from equipment before movement; treat the proposed nursery pathway as a hypothesis. proposedDescription: Tropical fanpetals is a bristly herb or small subshrub that may stand upright or lean through surrounding vegetation. Small pale yellow flowers gather in compact clusters where leaves meet the stems. Flora of North America records it from disturbed sites in Florida, including a Broward County discovery in 2008. It also occurs widely in tropical regions. These records establish identity and occurrence, but they do not demonstrate the same ecological impact as better-studied invasive shrubs.
identification: Look for pointed, heart-based leaves with toothed margins and long, stiff hairs along the stems and flower cups. The flower buds have conspicuously drawn-out tips, and the flowers sit close together rather than on long, widely separated stalks. Mature fruits separate into five small units. Several Sida species have yellow flowers, so flower color is a poor shortcut. Include the leaf base, hairy calyx, clustered flowers, and a mature fruit in photographs. The leaning habit and long-pointed buds are particularly helpful clues in the North American flora.
actions: Note whether the plant is confined to a recently disturbed verge or is expanding into adjacent vegetation. Ask a local herbarium to confirm a flowering and fruiting example before reporting it under this name. Wear gloves when handling the bristly stems. In a small garden patch, removing unwanted plants before fruits mature can limit seed movement; keep fruiting material out of soil or yard waste destined for natural areas. A larger control recommendation should wait for local evidence of establishment and impact, which was not resolved by this research.

FNA and the independent African flora treatments support Sida urens recognition while differing origin accounts remain geographically bounded. The 2008 Florida record in FNA is occurrence evidence, not proof of ecological damage. The draft uses bristly growth and mature fruits for confirmation and avoids transferring impacts from other Sida species. Preserve flowers and mature fruit units when checking a new local Sida record. proposedDescription: Tropical girdlepod is a branching annual whose small white flowers gather into tight clusters along a leafy stem. It belongs to the coffee family, although it looks more like a modest field weed than a woody coffee plant. Botanical treatments describe plants that can become somewhat woody near the base. The species is recorded in tropical floras, but the sources reviewed here do not establish its local United States impact or support treating every occurrence as an invasive infestation.
identification: Opposite leaves are narrow to oval and sit close to the stem. At their bases, a small sheath with bristlelike tips joins the leaf pair, a useful detail to photograph with a hand lens. Hairy, rounded flower clusters occur at the stem tips and leaf joints. The fruit offers a stronger distinction from similar buttonweeds in Spermacoce: a Mitracarpus capsule opens around its middle like a tiny lid. The seed has a characteristic cross-shaped pattern. Those details are too small for an ordinary landscape photograph and often require specialist examination.
actions: Start with photographs of the branching pattern, opposite leaves, and both flowering and fruiting clusters. Ask a botanist to resolve the species if buttonweeds grow nearby or the record would be new locally. Small unwanted garden plants can be removed before capsules release seed, with flowering material kept contained. Avoid spreading soil from the patch on equipment or transplanted plants. For a roadside, pasture, or natural area, document abundance and surrounding vegetation before choosing treatment; species-specific local management evidence remains incomplete.
researchNotes: Independent Singapore and Costa Rican flora treatments supply readable Mitracarpus hirtus morphology beyond the previously difficult source endpoints. The Singapore flora includes original specimen-based illustrations; the Costa Rican treatment independently describes the unusual capsule. Neither supplies a US management trial, which is not claimed. Use opened mature capsules and seeds for confirmation before removing similar small white-flowered herbs. proposedDescription: Aedeomyia squamipennis is a tropical mosquito with unusually patterned wings, documented in southern Florida through surveillance and specimen examination. A Palm Beach County study confirmed specimens collected in 2021-2022 using both morphology and DNA, following earlier records near Homestead. Its immature stages are associated with freshwater vegetation, especially floating plants such as water lettuce. An adult collected in a mangrove area does not establish that the mosquito breeds in salty water; researchers explicitly noted that distinction in the Florida Keys.
identification: Adults have broad white, yellow, and brown wing scales that create a striking mottled pattern. Short, thick antenna segments and tufts of scales near the ends of the middle and hind femora are additional clues. These are small structures best checked under magnification by mosquito-control staff. The familiar description 'tropical mosquito' is not an identification, and a blurred picture of a biting insect cannot separate this species reliably from other mosquitoes. Preserve the location and date even when a usable specimen is unavailable.
actions: Send an unusual patterned-mosquito observation to the local mosquito-control program, including a sharp photograph if one can be taken without attracting insects to bite. Report nearby floating vegetation and persistent water rather than assuming ordinary household containers are the only source. Do not move aquatic plants between ponds or release them into canals. Routine mosquito precautions and maintenance of screens remain sensible, but a sighting is not evidence of a local disease outbreak. Wetland vegetation removal or larval treatment should be planned by the responsible water or mosquito-management agency.
researchNotes: Independent Palm Beach and Florida Keys surveillance papers used, with the latter's morphology credited to the earlier diagnostic literature. No human disease-vector claim or brackish breeding claim inferred.

proposedDescription: Culex panocossa is a mosquito first documented as established in southern Florida in 2016. The original report found large adult collections and larvae near Homestead, with larvae associated with water lettuce. Later blood-meal research found that Florida mosquitoes fed on birds, mammals, and reptiles. Those findings make the species relevant to surveillance because it can encounter several kinds of vertebrate hosts. They show potential connections in virus transmission, not proof that a photographed mosquito is infected or that a local outbreak is occurring.
identification: Species-level identification belongs with a mosquito laboratory. This mosquito is part of the Melanoconion group, where similar-looking species cannot be reliably separated by overall brown color or the fact that they were found near a canal. Useful records include the collection site, date, whether adults or larvae were seen, and the vegetation in the water. A clear specimen allows specialists to examine diagnostic structures. Water lettuce is a habitat clue from the Florida study, but its presence alone does not identify the mosquitoes living around it.
actions: Contact the local mosquito-control district when an unusual concentration occurs near vegetated freshwater. Staff can sample the habitat, identify the mosquitoes, and decide whether surveillance or treatment is justified. Keep ornamental floating plants out of canals and natural wetlands, and coordinate any removal with the water manager so fragments are contained. At home, maintain screens and remove avoidable standing water as routine mosquito prevention. Do not attempt to catch adults by exposing skin, and do not interpret a single adult observation as evidence of disease transmission.
researchNotes: Two original UF studies address different questions: 2017 establishment and 2024 blood meals. Vector potential is explicitly separated from demonstrated Florida transmission; diagnostic morphology not invented.

proposedDescription: Tropical signalgrass is a low, mat-forming grass that can spread along the ground on creeping stems. Australian botanical descriptions allow either annual or perennial growth, and Florida's assessment recognizes it as an introduced grass of tropical Asian origin. That assessment does not currently regard it as a problem species in Florida natural areas. A patch in turf or a garden may still be unwanted, but a maintenance problem should not be presented as evidence of widespread ecological invasion.
identification: Look for short flowering stems above the mat and a small seed head with two or three branches. Spikelets sit in orderly rows along one side of those branches. The leaves are narrow to lance-shaped, and the ligule at the leaf junction is a fringe of hairs. Creeping stems and the small head distinguish the general growth form, but several signalgrasses and crabgrasses look alike. Names including Brachiaria distachya and Urochloa subquadripara appear in older or regional treatments, so a specimen should be checked against the taxonomic concept used locally.
actions: For an unwanted lawn patch, first determine which grass is present and whether the problem is spreading stems, seed production, or both. Small plants can be lifted carefully, with creeping stems gathered rather than scattered by raking. Keep rooted fragments and soil out of clean garden beds. In a natural area, record the patch's extent and ask a botanist or land manager whether any intervention is needed. Local turf recommendations should guide larger treatments; this profile does not support labeling all Florida occurrences as damaging invasions.
researchNotes: AusGrass supports the narrow Urochloa distachya morphology, while the Florida assessment's broader synonym usage is explicitly kept separate. A broad-versus-narrow taxonomic overlap does not itself prove a mismatched specimen. The draft attributes the assessment and asks users to verify the local concept before applying it. Match flowering spikelets to the local flora and do not transfer a subquadripara record automatically.

proposedDescription: Tropical soda apple is a prickly perennial shrub that can turn a southeastern pasture into a dense, difficult-to-use stand. Its round fruits begin green and white, then ripen yellow, and animals can move the many seeds they contain. The species is native to South America and has become a serious pasture weed in the United States. Winter dieback does not necessarily end an infestation: established plants can return from surviving roots when conditions improve.
identification: Look for large, hairy leaves with deep, irregular lobes, straight pale prickles on stems and leaves, and small white flowers with five spreading or reflexed lobes. Young fruits resemble miniature mottled watermelons, but ripe fruits are bright yellow. Other prickly nightshades can share the leaf shape or flower color, so photograph both young and mature fruits together with the leaf surfaces. The combination is much more useful than a thorny stem alone. Do not taste the fruit as an identification test.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to local extension or the state agriculture department, especially on land where livestock or hay move between farms. Keep fruiting plants and contaminated soil off equipment headed to clean fields. Mowing can delay seed production, but it does not kill established plants and can spread material once fruits are present. Work with a pasture specialist on a complete control plan and follow-up for regrowth. Use gloves and protective clothing around the prickles, and keep removed fruit contained rather than leaving it where animals can carry it.
researchNotes: Alabama extension and NC State supply independent regional management and morphology accounts. Federal listing noted in sources but profile avoids making a new legal determination or prescribing chemical rates.
