proposedDescription: Verdolaga-francesa is a soft, succulent herb also grown as waterleaf or Surinam spinach. Pink flowers rise above fleshy green leaves, followed by capsules containing many small seeds. Its presence in a vegetable bed is not evidence of an invasion. Kew places its native range in tropical and subtropical America, including Florida, while introductions are recorded elsewhere. Published accounts disagree about its origin and whether to describe its life cycle as annual or perennial, so those details deserve regional interpretation.
identification: Look for broad, spoon-shaped leaves that narrow toward the base and have smooth margins. The flowering stalk is triangular in cross-section, a useful detail when comparing plants sold under the older name Talinum triangulare. Flowers occur in a branching cluster and the capsules contain shiny black seeds. Photograph the stalk, a whole leaf, flowers, and mature capsules together. A fleshy leaf alone is insufficient to separate this plant from purslane or another Talinum, and common vegetable names are especially easy to confuse.
actions: Keep a cultivated plant labeled and check seedlings beyond the bed before deciding they need removal. In a natural area, ask a local botanist whether this is a native occurrence or an introduction; do not clear a population simply because it appears in an invasive-species catalog. Where volunteers are unwanted, remove them before capsules open and keep seed-bearing garden waste contained. Do not use a common name to judge an unfamiliar succulent safe to eat. Observe local spread and ask which regional flora applies; conflicting origin accounts do not establish harm at your site.
researchNotes: Finding: The two botanical accounts agree on the succulent plant and triangular flower stalks, while disagreeing about broad origin and longevity. Rationale: Kew flora and NParks are independent accounts; regional origin disagreement is disclosed rather than converted into a nationwide alien-status claim. proposedDescription: Vermiculated sailfin catfish is an armored, bottom-feeding fish associated with aquarium introductions and established populations in Florida. Its downward-facing mouth scrapes food from submerged surfaces. Laboratory work on this exact species shows unusually mobile jaws that help it work across uneven surfaces. Florida research also documents repeated spawning within the breeding season. Although abundant populations can raise ecological concerns, USGS describes important uncertainties about the magnitude of species-specific impacts; observations of other armored catfish should not automatically be assigned to this one.
identification: The broad, flattened head, plated body, suckermouth, and conspicuous sail-like dorsal fin identify the general kind of fish. On this species, dark markings on the belly merge into winding, connected patterns. The similar Pterygoplichthys pardalis usually has more separate spots, but intermediate patterns and confused historical names make expert review important. A side photograph alone can miss the most useful character. Record the fish in place, and obtain belly and fin photographs only when it is already being handled safely by trained personnel.
actions: Never release an aquarium catfish or move a wild fish to another pond. Ask a retailer or aquarium rescue about responsible rehoming before an animal outgrows its tank. Report an unfamiliar armored catfish to the state fisheries agency with the date, location, and photographs. Leave bank excavation and removal programs to the waterbody manager; disturbing a burrow is not a reliable way to identify its occupant. If a fish is caught during authorized work, follow the local instructions for documentation and disposition.
researchNotes: USGS population and reproductive synthesis, an independent jaw-mechanics study, and an original Indian identification report support the draft. Genus-level bank erosion claims were not promoted to species-specific certainty.

proposedDescription: Verticillium wilt is a disease name, not a dependable identification of a single fungus. The catalog name Verticillium albo-atrum has historically covered organisms that later research separated into different species, including V. alfalfae and V. nonalfalfae. That matters because host range, movement pathways, and management advice attached to an old name may describe a different organism. Older alfalfa or hop wilt reports need their original identifications checked before they can describe the narrowly defined fungus.
identification: Wilting, yellowing, poor growth, and discolored vascular tissue can prompt a plant-disease investigation, but none identifies this fungus by itself. Drought, damaged roots, and other wilt pathogens can produce overlapping symptoms. A diagnostic laboratory needs the host identity, affected plant parts, and growing history, and may require culture and molecular tests. When reading a laboratory report, note whether the identification is to Verticillium, to the older broad albo-atrum concept, or to a currently recognized species. Preserve the exact wording rather than simplifying it.
actions: Contact a plant diagnostic clinic before removing an entire planting or choosing a replacement crop. Ask how to collect a sample from the active edge of the problem, and keep it separate from healthy propagation material. Until the diagnosis is clear, avoid sharing suspect rooted plants or moving their soil to clean growing areas. Record which hosts are affected and how the symptoms progress. Crop rotation and resistant-variety recommendations should follow the confirmed pathogen and crop, not a general web description of Verticillium wilt.

Which host records have a post-split molecular determination? proposedDescription: Northern giant hornet is a large Asian social wasp whose brief establishment in Washington prompted intensive detection and nest removal. Washington and USDA declared it eradicated from the United States in December 2024 after three years without confirmed detections. That dated result should accompany older invasion accounts. It is not a reason to identify every large wasp as this species. Colonies can attack honey bee colonies, but the practical public response is careful reporting of credible observations, not indiscriminate trapping. Colonies grow through summer, and newly mated queens overwinter before founding nests the next spring.
identification: A broad orange head, robust body, and alternating dark and orange-yellow abdominal bands are useful starting points. The unusually wide head is more informative than size alone. European hornets and native cicada killers are frequent sources of mistaken reports, and photographs should show the head and body pattern without approaching a nest. A distant blur or a statement that a wasp looked enormous is not a confirmed identification. Nest entrance shape alone also cannot establish the species.
actions: If you see a convincing candidate, step back and take photographs from a safe position. Record the location and date, then send the observation to your state agriculture department or its invasive-insect reporting program. Do not follow a hornet into vegetation, attempt to collect it, or open a suspected nest. Avoid homemade broad-spectrum trapping that can kill unrelated insects. Beekeepers should document unusual attacks and request agency guidance. The eradication announcement describes the known US incursion; a new report still requires a fresh expert assessment.
researchNotes: The 2024 WSDA-USDA declaration supplies the dated eradication result. UF entomology supplies independent natural-history and identification discussion; no claim of a current US established population is made.

proposedDescription: Viburnum leaf beetle can turn a leafy shrub into a network of bare veins. Both its larvae and adults feed on viburnums, giving the plant more than one period of damage in a season. Repeated heavy defoliation can seriously weaken susceptible shrubs. The insect is introduced in North America and has spread through parts of the Northeast and Great Lakes region. Its presence is a reason to identify the shrub and inspect it closely, rather than assuming all viburnum species respond equally.
identification: In spring, examine the undersides of damaged leaves for small, pale larvae marked with dark spots. Adults are small brown beetles and appear later in the season. The most helpful winter clue is a line of covered egg-laying pits along young twigs. These capped cavities distinguish the beetle problem from many ordinary chewing injuries. Photograph the insects and twig scars together; holes alone could have several causes. Keep a record of the viburnum species or cultivar, because susceptibility varies substantially.
actions: During dormancy, inspect young shoots and prune out confirmed egg-bearing twigs before spring hatch. Contain and dispose of the cut material so eggs do not remain beside the shrub. Recheck leaves as they expand, when a small larval population is easier to address. An extension office can recommend a response suited to the shrub, season, and nearby pollinators. For replacement plantings, choose regionally appropriate viburnums with better resistance. Avoid stripping out healthy native shrubs merely because the beetle has been reported elsewhere in the county.
researchNotes: Wisconsin extension supplies regional surveillance and damage context; Cornell documents its own New York invasion observations. UF management guidance is retained as extension synthesis, not a separate original detection.

proposedDescription: Heartleaf philodendron, also called vilevine, is the familiar tropical climber with cascading, heart-shaped leaves. It can trail from a pot or climb with roots produced along its stems, and gardeners commonly propagate it from cuttings. Native to tropical America, it is mainly an indoor plant where winters are cold. Florida assessment results for the typical variety describe low invasion risk and no documented problem at the time of assessment. That finding does not make discarded cuttings an appropriate addition to a woodland.
identification: Look beyond the heart shape. The leaf stalks are not grooved, and new leaves emerge with conspicuous separate protective stipules that later dry and fall away. These details help separate heartleaf philodendron from golden pothos, Epipremnum aureum, which is often confused with it. Leaves alternate along slender stems and usually have a pointed tip. Flowers are uncommon in indoor cultivation. Photograph the newest growth, a leaf stalk, and the stem roots when asking for an identification, especially for variegated cultivars.
actions: Keep garden and houseplant trimmings in a contained waste stream instead of dropping them over a fence or beside a drainage ditch. For an outdoor escape, document whether stems have rooted independently and seek a local identification before removal. A contained indoor plant does not warrant eradication simply because its name appears here. Maintain drainage and avoid persistently saturated potting mix. Keep the plant away from children and pets that chew foliage, since its calcium oxalate crystals can irritate the mouth and other exposed tissues.
researchNotes: NCSU provides species identification and cultivation information; the UF assessment is explicitly for var. hederaceum. No species-wide invasive designation or claim of proven ecological harm is inferred from outdoor occurrence.

proposedDescription: Vine mealybug is a small sap-feeding insect that can remain hidden beneath grapevine bark long before it is obvious on fruit. In California it is an important vineyard pest, with several generations possible during a year. Its waxy colonies and honeydew can contaminate bunches, and managing an infestation requires attention to the vine and to material moving through the vineyard. Oregon treats confirmed infestations as a plant-health concern with restrictions on movement from affected properties. Rules and priorities should always be checked for the actual growing region.
identification: Adult females are oval, segmented, and covered in white powdery wax, with pinkish tissue sometimes visible beneath it. The short wax filaments and absence of long tail filaments help distinguish them from several Pseudococcus mealybugs on grapes. A darker central stripe may be visible. Look beneath loose bark, around the graft union, and in protected places rather than checking only exposed leaves. Citrus mealybug can look similar, so a farm advisor or diagnostic laboratory should confirm an important vineyard finding.
actions: Mark suspicious vines and contact the local extension viticulture specialist or agricultural commissioner. Avoid moving cuttings, fruit containers, or equipment from the affected block until you have guidance about cleaning and any local restrictions. Inspect planting stock before it enters the vineyard. A monitoring plan can combine close vine inspection with appropriate traps, but a trap catch and a visible colony answer different questions. Management should account for the hidden life stages, beneficial insects, and season; a quick spray of the visible fruit is not a complete plan.

proposedDescription: Violet crabgrass is a small annual grass of disturbed ground, gardens, and other open sites. Its stems may root at lower joints, allowing a plant to occupy more ground than its modest height suggests. The Flora of North America account describes an introduced species established mainly in the southeastern United States. Other floras record it as a weed in their regions, but those observations do not demonstrate severe habitat damage at every American occurrence. Its small seed structures are more useful than its common name for recognizing it.
identification: Look for several slender seed-bearing branches arranged like fingers near the end of a stalk. The crowded spikelets are usually in groups of three and only about 1.2 to 1.8 millimeters long. Mature fertile bracts become dark brown to nearly black. Smooth crabgrass, Digitaria ischaemum, is particularly similar, so branch arrangement alone is insufficient. A hand lens helps, but reliable separation may require stronger magnification to examine the hairs and veins on the spikelets. Include mature seedheads rather than sending only a lawn photograph.
actions: In a garden, remove confirmed unwanted plants while the seedheads are still immature, taking rooted lower joints with them. Keep nursery pots and soil-moving tools free of seed-bearing clumps. If the grass occurs among native vegetation, identify it before disturbing the patch, and record how much ground it occupies rather than assuming it dominates. Revisit the same spot after the next germination period. Broad herbicide treatment is a poor first response to an uncertain identification among closely similar grasses.
researchNotes: Independent North American and New South Wales floras agree on minute ternate spikelets and disturbed-site occurrence. The draft distinguishes established introduction from an unsupported nationwide impact claim.

proposedDescription: Helicobasidium longisporum belongs to a group associated with violet root rot, but that disease name cannot identify a fungus. A 2026 study connected lineage III with cranberry fairy ring in New Jersey and Massachusetts. A separate 1972 Queensland report found the named fungus on Verbena stems and roots without associated root decay. These records concern different hosts and methods; they do not establish that every purple root crust is the same lineage or has the same effect.
identification: In the cranberry study, diseased vines carried characteristic infection cushions and occurred in affected patches. These signs should prompt laboratory investigation, not a field-level species diagnosis. Root discoloration, declining vigor, and a ring-shaped pattern can have other causes. The fungus also has differently named life stages: the study linked the root-associated form with a rust-parasitic Tuberculina stage on nearby plants. A photograph of a purple crust, or the presence of rust alone, cannot resolve this complex life cycle.
actions: Cranberry growers should map changing patch boundaries and contact a crop specialist or plant diagnostic laboratory before altering drainage, applying treatments, or removing surrounding vegetation. Ask what roots, vines, and soil the laboratory needs and how to package them. Avoid transferring suspect planting material or soil to an unaffected bed while diagnosis is pending. Keep laboratory names and sequence-based identifications with the field record. The cranberry findings concern one genetic lineage. Let the laboratory diagnosis and crop specialist guide the response for that particular bed.

Rationale: Separate specimens and study designs establish independence without proving identical lineages. proposedDescription: Violet tanbark beetle is a longhorn beetle associated with dead conifer wood, especially material that still carries bark. Larvae feed beneath the bark and later enter the wood to pupate, so an adult emerging from stored timber does not by itself mean a living tree is under attack. Forest research describes it as Holarctic. Its status should therefore be assessed regionally rather than treating all North American records as evidence of an alien forest invader. Wood movement and the condition of the material are the practical concerns.
identification: Adults have a broad, somewhat flattened longhorn-beetle shape and a conspicuous blue-violet metallic appearance. Forest accounts give a body length of roughly 8 to 18 millimeters. Inspect the context as well as the beetle: bark-covered conifer logs and broad galleries beneath the bark are relevant clues. Other longhorn beetles can emerge from firewood, and old damage alone is not diagnostic. Photograph the adult from above with a size reference, along with the bark and exit area, without breaking apart structural timber.
actions: If adults appear indoors, first check recently brought-in firewood or bark-bearing wood products. Keep suspect material from being moved to another property while an extension entomologist or wood-pest professional identifies the insect. Use locally sourced firewood and avoid storing unnecessary bark-covered wood inside. Where a building member may be affected, request a professional assessment of both the insect and the wood rather than assuming a photograph establishes structural damage. Historical recommendations involving tar or burning are not adopted here; present-day advice should fit the material and local requirements.
researchNotes:
Finding: Separate authored European beetle treatments support dead conifer wood use and diagnostic appearance; regional origin must remain geographically qualified. Rationale: Csoka-Kovacs and Slama-based treatment include separate authored biology and reared material, not merely taxonomic name lists. Next step: Review the dead-wood and reporting scope without labeling every North American occurrence alien. proposedDescription: Violetflower petunia is a South American wild petunia with purple to violet funnel-shaped flowers. It is related to familiar bedding petunias, but a garden plant carrying a petunia label is not automatically this species. Kew recognizes Petunia integrifolia and places its native range from southern Brazil to northeastern Argentina. Botanical research has examined a complex of closely related plants under this name, making exact identification particularly important when interpreting an old garden escape or herbarium record.
identification: The plant is a branching herb with sticky glandular hairs, angular stems, and simple leaves that vary from oval to narrower shapes. The flowers stand on slender stalks and open into a broad purple funnel. Photograph the calyx behind the flower, the leaf arrangement, and stem hairs as well as the colorful face. Cultivated petunia hybrids can overlap in flower color and habit. A purple bloom does not separate this species from those hybrids or settle the boundaries of the integrifolia complex.
actions: For an unexpected roadside or garden-edge plant, record the nearby planting history and seek a herbarium identification before assigning the species name. Keep spent plants and seed-bearing capsules out of natural areas. If seedlings are unwanted in a cultivated bed, remove them before more seed is shed and check whether they return. There is no basis in the sources reviewed here for a nationwide invasive designation or a large-scale control campaign. Local persistence and ecological effects need evidence tied to an accurately identified population.
researchNotes: Finding: The named species can be described narrowly while garden hybrids and P. inflata are excluded from its range and impact narrative. Rationale: The original 113-population morphology study is independent of the Flora Zambesiaca account; hybrid variation does not make every named profile unresolvable. Next step: Review the narrow botanical account and keep uncertain garden specimens provisional.

proposedDescription: Viper grass is an annual whose seedhead branches point upward when young, then bend back and separate from the central axis at maturity. It occurs in open and disturbed ground across parts of Africa and Asia and has been introduced elsewhere. Flora of North America cites historical reports from Maryland ore piles and North Carolina. Those transport-associated records do not establish a currently spreading or damaging population; a new American observation should be checked and dated in its own right.
identification: Look for a leafy, often spreading plant with a narrow, branching seedhead. Lower stems can lie against the soil and root at their joints. The stiff, short branches carry wedge-shaped spikelets; their long outer bracts extend well beyond the smaller flowers inside and end in diverging pointed tips. The backward-bending mature branches are a useful clue, but many grasses have superficially similar comb-like heads. Collect photographs at both young and mature stages and ask a grass specialist to check the spikelets.
actions: Where it is confirmed as an unwanted annual in cultivation, prevent mature seedheads from being moved with soil, nursery pots, or cut vegetation. Small plants can be removed before seed matures, followed by checks for new seedlings. In a natural area, photograph and map the patch before intervention, particularly if this would be an unusual regional record. A local herbarium or extension service can establish whether a report belongs to this species and whether management is warranted. Do not infer a grazing recommendation from reports that livestock sometimes eat it overseas.
researchNotes: Finding: Flora of North America records historical Maryland ore-pile and North Carolina reports, giving bounded US occurrence context without proving present establishment. Rationale: Barkworth FNA is independent of the Chinese diagnostic flora. Historical transport-associated reports are not an impact measurement. Next step: Review the dated report scope and require a fresh voucher before describing a current local population. proposedDescription: Snake plant, also called viper's bowstring hemp, is now often named Dracaena trifasciata. Its upright, banded leaves make it familiar as a durable houseplant, but outdoors in a warm climate it is a spreading perennial rather than an inert decoration. Underground stems produce additional shoots, and discarded divisions can become new patches. UF/IFAS rates it as a high invasion risk in Florida. That regional assessment should guide outdoor decisions there without implying that a contained pot in a cold-climate home is an established invasion.
identification: Look for stiff, flat, sword-shaped leaves rising together from the base, with irregular bands in contrasting greens. Some cultivars have yellow edges or form short rosettes, so height and color vary. The plant lacks the woody trunk seen in many other dracaenas. Cylindrical-leaved snake plants are different taxa. Include a photograph of the whole clump and its basal growth when seeking identification. Nursery labels may still use Sansevieria trifasciata, which refers to the same species under the older classification.
actions: Keep divisions, leaves intended for propagation, and potting waste away from vacant lots and natural areas. In Florida, choose an appropriate alternative for outdoor planting and consult extension about removing an established escape. Digging a small patch requires attention to the underground connecting stems; simply cutting off the leaves leaves those structures behind. Recheck the site for new shoots. Indoors, maintain a contained plant with suitable drainage, and do not treat the change in scientific name as evidence that your plant has become a different species.
researchNotes: NCSU and NSW confirm the Dracaena synonym treatment; Florida provides a separate risk assessment. Management language is bounded to rhizome containment and regional review, with no unsupported nationwide legal claim.

proposedDescription: Wakasagi is a small Japanese smelt introduced to California waters. Its importance to monitoring comes partly from its resemblance to the native Delta smelt: confusing the two can distort records for a fish already of major conservation concern. USGS lists wakasagi as a nonindigenous fish, while recent field programs have paired visual identifications with laboratory and genetic checks. A credible identification is therefore more valuable than a confident guess based on a silvery fish in a net. Research in Japan has found both lake-resident and migratory forms spawning in the same lake.
identification: Wakasagi is a slender smelt, but general shape, small size, and silvery appearance are not sufficient to distinguish it from related species. The US Fish and Wildlife Service describes a two-stage process in which field identifications are checked by experienced laboratory staff, with a subset independently verified genetically. Early life stages are especially difficult. A photograph can document an observation but may not show the anatomical features needed to resolve it. Record the waterbody, collection circumstances, and life stage without claiming certainty that the image cannot support.
actions: Do not move small fish between lakes or use an unidentified smelt as live bait elsewhere. If you encounter a possible wakasagi during authorized fishing or monitoring, follow the waterbody's instructions and ask the fisheries agency how to document it. Avoid collecting additional fish solely for a casual identification where protected native species may be present. Clean and drain equipment before leaving the water. For historical records, preserve the original name and note whether the identification was visual, independently checked, or genetically confirmed.
researchNotes: USGS provides introduction context; the 2023 USFWS/UC Davis poster reports original identification validation. Exact external separation is intentionally not oversimplified, and no unsupported population impact estimate is included.

proposedDescription: Walking catfish became established in Florida after aquarium-related introductions in the 1960s. These air-breathing fish can wriggle over wet ground, helping explain sightings on roads or between shrinking pools. There is an important naming problem, however: the Florida Museum notes that the introduced population traditionally called Clarias batrachus may not be that species in the strict sense. Research restricted the true species to Java while recognizing a wider complex. Florida observations describe the introduced walking-catfish population; an exact-species attribution requires a current determination.
identification: The Florida fish has a long body, a flattened catfish head with barbels, and dorsal and anal fins extending along much of its length. Wild individuals are commonly gray-brown with pale flecks, although unusually pale forms occur. These characters distinguish the walking-catfish type from many local fishes but do not resolve the species complex. A fish moving on land is not automatically identified by that behavior. Record head, side, and fin photographs from a safe position and note the exact locality.
actions: Never release aquarium fish, and do not carry a stranded catfish to a different pond or canal. Report an unfamiliar walking catfish to the state fisheries agency, especially beyond its known regional occurrence. Stay out of traffic when documenting roadside fish and avoid bare-handed handling of the fin spines. Fisheries staff should determine whether a specimen is needed and how it should be managed. Historic impact descriptions and distribution records need review against the taxonomic uncertainty before they are presented as exact-species evidence.

Which current name should the historical Florida records carry? Next action: Locate a post-revision voucher or genetic reassessment of Florida fish and ask the catalog curator which species concept is intended. proposedDescription: Wall bedstraw is a delicate annual that can disappear into dry grass and roadside vegetation until its small branches are examined closely. European botanical accounts describe it in dry grasslands and disturbed ground, including vineyards and orchards. It grows from a slender root and completes its life cycle through seed. Those agricultural associations do not make it a damaging invader everywhere. For an American observation, local occurrence and impact should be established separately from the fact that the species is weedy in parts of its range.
identification: The narrow leaves form rings, or whorls, around a slender, four-angled stem. Upper whorls commonly contain about six leaves, and fine prickles can make the stem and leaf edges feel rough. Flowers are extremely small and greenish to reddish, held in a narrow branching arrangement. The dry fruit separates into two parts. Other small bedstraws can look very similar, particularly as seedlings; the tiny flower, fruit surface, and branching pattern matter more than the whorled leaves alone. Use a close photograph with a scale.
actions: If this plant is competing with crops or appearing in a newly disturbed bed, confirm the identification before deciding how much to remove. Small unwanted annuals can be pulled before mature fruit develops, with follow-up checks where seed has already fallen. Avoid carrying seed-bearing plants with soil or harvest waste. In a meadow or natural area, leave uncertain bedstraws in place while a botanist checks them, since native relatives may be present. Document abundance and neighboring vegetation so a local reviewer can judge whether intervention is justified.
researchNotes: Finding: Authored French weed flora supplies detailed recognition, and North American taxonomic evidence corroborates introduced status without a measured harm claim. Rationale: INRA morphology and the independent Trieste regional flora supply substantive recognition and ecology; ITIS is supporting taxonomic context, not the second biological source. Next step: Review recognition and modest seed containment; avoid treating an introduced record as proof of displacement. proposedDescription: Wall hawkweed is a perennial with a leafy basal rosette and a loose cluster of yellow flowerheads. It can occur on roadsides, woodland edges, and rocky ground, including introduced populations outside its European range. Its name covers a notoriously difficult group: regional floras recognize substantial variation, and the British Columbia flora explicitly warns about the taxonomic complexity. A broad yellow-flowered hawkweed patch therefore deserves closer examination before its name, origin, or management priority is assigned.
identification: Look for broad, stalked basal leaves, often with coarse teeth near the base, and relatively few leaves on the flowering stem. The flowerheads contain strap-shaped yellow florets rather than a contrasting central disk. Dark gland-tipped hairs on the flowerhead bracts are important, as are the types of hairs on the leaves and stalks. Similar hawkweeds cannot reliably be separated by flower color. Photograph the rosette, the whole stem, leaf bases, and the underside of a flowerhead; a specialist may need a properly collected specimen.
actions: Before treating a patch, have a local botanist distinguish it from native hawkweeds and other introduced members of the complex. Record whether the patch is expanding and whether its identity was checked beyond a photo application. If removal is advised, take out the perennial crown and prevent mature seedheads from being scattered. Revisit the site for regrowth and seedlings. Avoid broad spraying through mixed woodland vegetation. For historic records labeled H. murorum, retain the original name and flag the possibility that a regional taxonomic treatment used a broader concept.
researchNotes: Finding: Independent NSW and British Columbia floras support the regional broad H. murorum concept and disclose its apomictic complexity. Rationale: The profile can use that stated regional concept without inventing a microspecies assignment or measured local harm. Next step: Review the broad-concept caveat and require specialist determination for a new regional record.

proposedDescription: Wall-lettuce is a slender plant whose airy spray of tiny yellow flowerheads can look much less substantial than its broad lower leaves. It is also encountered under the name Lactuca muralis. Regional North American assessments recognize it as a nonnative plant, with concern varying by place; Massachusetts classifies it as likely invasive. A regional assessment should not be expanded into a national claim that every occurrence causes the same level of harm.
identification: Each small head usually has five narrow, yellow, strap-shaped florets. Lower leaves are deeply lobed and clasp the stem, while the upper leaves become fewer and smaller as the branches spread. The smooth or slightly bluish stem releases milky sap if damaged, and mature fruits carry a pale tuft of hairs. Count florets in several heads and photograph the lower leaves. Many wild lettuces and nipplewort can resemble it from a distance, so a yellow flower cluster without leaf detail is not enough.
actions: For a small confirmed escape, remove plants before the tufted fruits are ready to disperse and collect seed-bearing tops carefully. Minimize soil disturbance among desirable woodland plants, then revisit the site for seedlings. Tell a land manager about a new patch in a conservation area, including its size and distance from a trail or disturbed edge. Do not confuse this wild plant with a food-crop recommendation. Where identity or local impact is uncertain, an herbarium determination and a few repeat observations are more useful than an immediate large-area treatment.
researchNotes: Alaska identification guidance and the Massachusetts regional assessment form two evidence lineages. No single national invasion designation is inferred, and practical actions are limited to confirmed unwanted plants.

proposedDescription: This wallaby grass forms a narrow-leaved tussock rather than a creeping lawn. New Zealand flora describes a native grass forming green clumps with flowering stems rising well above the leaves. A 2025 Bishop Museum specimen review confirmed it on Molokai and Maui while correcting some older records to another wallaby grass. The common name wallaby grass applies to many related species, however, and Hawaiian specialists emphasize that distinguishing them requires magnified examination. An occurrence under the common name alone is not dependable evidence for Rytidosperma biannulare.
identification: Leaves are narrow and often rolled, with a short fringe of hairs where the blade meets the sheath. The flowering stems can reach about 85 centimeters, carrying a relatively compact cluster of spikelets. Young leaves may be more hairy than mature ones, so a single leaf can mislead. The decisive differences from other Rytidosperma lie in the small flowering structures, especially the lemmas. Photograph the entire tussock and retain close views of a mature head; ordinary distant grass photographs cannot resolve those details.
actions: Ask a grass specialist or herbarium to verify a suspected population, particularly when it would add a new locality or support a claim of invasion. Keep any submitted material tied to its date, location, and habitat. Do not buy or spread seed identified only as wallaby grass for restoration outside its native region. If a confirmed planting is producing unwanted seedlings, contain mature heads and monitor nearby ground. Evidence for US ecological harm and locally validated control is still insufficient here, so removal priority should be decided by the local land manager.
researchNotes: Finding: The 2025 Bishop Museum specimen review confirms biannulare on Molokai and Maui while correcting some historical identifications to gracile. Rationale: The Hawaiian re-examination is original specimen work independent of the NZ flora; shared key citations do not erase its separate specimens. Next step: Review confirmed-island context while retaining the warning that old unreviewed Hawaiian records may be misidentified. proposedDescription: Wami tilapia is an East African fish introduced to waters outside its native range through human activity. USGS describes historical stocking in southern California for aquatic vegetation and insect management, but also says that ecosystem impacts of this species there have not been adequately studied. It feeds on material such as algae and detritus and can occur in fresh or brackish water. The name has a complicated history involving hornorum and Mozambique tilapia, so records of unspecified tilapia cannot simply be assigned to this species.
identification: It is an oblong, deep-bodied fish with a continuous dorsal fin and a rounded snout. Smithsonian descriptions note dark markings on the side and gill cover, while mature males can become very dark with orange fin margins. Color changes with age and condition. Closely related tilapias and hybrids can look similar, and reliable identification may require fin-ray, scale, and gill-raker counts. Photograph the side, head, and fins if a fish is already being handled during authorized work; do not treat color as a complete field key.
actions: Do not release pond or aquarium tilapia, and do not transfer fish between drainage systems. If an unfamiliar tilapia is found, send the state fisheries agency the location, photographs, and any known stocking history. Keep the record separate from reports of other tilapia until an expert verifies it. Managers considering vegetation control should use locally approved methods rather than repeating historical stocking practices. The uncertainty about ecological impacts is a reason to prevent new introductions and gather better evidence, not a declaration that introductions are harmless.
researchNotes: USGS documents historical introductions and explicitly unknown impacts; Smithsonian provides separate morphological detail. Hornorum history and hybrid identification are retained as cautions without changing the assigned species ID.

proposedDescription: Wand mullein is a tall, usually biennial herb that begins with a low rosette and later sends up a slender flowering stem. Its yellow flowers are more widely spaced than the dense, woolly flower spike many people associate with common mullein. It occurs outside its native range as a naturalized plant of disturbed places. Because it resembles moth mullein, records can be overlooked or assigned to the wrong species. A careful look at the short flower stalks and small bracts is especially useful.
identification: Upper stems and flower parts carry gland-tipped hairs, giving them a different texture from the thick felt of common mullein. Flowers sit on very short stalks, commonly no more than a few millimeters long, with small additional bracts near the base. Some nodes carry more than one flower. Moth mullein, Verbascum blattaria, generally has longer flower stalks and lacks those bracteoles. Photograph the side of the flowering stem and the developing capsules as well as the bloom. Distinguishing the two becomes harder when the relevant structures are cropped out.
actions: Where a verified plant is unwanted, remove the rosette or flowering plant before seed capsules mature, taking the root crown rather than only snapping off the stem. Bag mature seed-bearing tops and avoid shaking them along a path. Keep disturbed soil covered with appropriate vegetation and revisit the site for new rosettes. In a natural area, confirm identity and local priority before treating a larger patch. The sources support recognition and naturalization, but do not justify assuming that every roadside individual poses a major ecological threat.
researchNotes: Burke Herbarium/FNA morphology and the independent Belgian botanical treatment agree on short pedicels and bracteoles. A Florida indexed key appeared to reverse the names and was not used as supporting evidence.

proposedDescription: Ward's weed is a small annual mustard that can be easy to overlook among other spring-flowering weeds. Its divided leaves and pale yellow flowers are followed by unusually shaped pods. It is a weed of dry regions in Australia and has attracted weed-management attention in the southwestern United States. San Diego County includes it in its invasive weed watch material, while Arizona lists it among noxious weeds. Those regional concerns should be kept tied to the place, rather than treated as a uniform national status.
identification: The plant branches near the base and carries bristly hairs on its stems and deeply divided leaves. Flowers have four pale yellow petals with purple veins. The fruit is the strongest clue: a small rounded seed-bearing portion ends in a flattened, spoon-like extension. Other small mustards, including peppercresses, can have similar divided foliage, but their pods differ. Photograph several mature fruits from the side with a scale, plus the flowers and a whole lower leaf. Seedlings without fruit can be much less distinctive.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the local weed program before mature pods scatter, especially in a region where early detection is a priority. If removal is recommended, work from the edge of the patch and keep seed-bearing material contained. Clean soil and plant debris from boots and tools before visiting another site. Avoid moving infested soil or garden waste into open land. Follow up after seasonal rains, since removing visible annual plants does not show that every seed has been eliminated. Confirm current local requirements with the responsible agency.

proposedDescription: Warehouse beetle is a stored-product pest that may turn up in a pantry as readily as in a commercial storage building. Its larvae can feed in a wide range of dried foods and other plant or animal materials. Shed larval skins, crawling larvae, and small adult beetles may be the first clues. The problem is usually a hidden food source, not evidence that the building itself is being eaten. Careful inspection and removal of the infested material are more useful than treating every visible adult separately.
identification: Adults are small, roughly one-eighth of an inch long, with a mottled covering of pale, orange, and dark hairs or scales. Larvae are hairy and become golden brown, with conspicuous tufts toward the rear. They resemble other dermestid beetles, including the much more consequential khapra beetle, so an important commercial finding needs expert confirmation. Photograph both larvae and adults and keep a sample securely contained if the diagnostic service requests one. A loose hairy skin alone should not be used to name the species.
actions: Inspect dry pet food, grain products, spices, seeds, and forgotten packages, including unopened-looking containers with damaged seams. Seal and discard infested products, then vacuum spilled food and debris from cracks and shelf edges. Store replacement food in pest-resistant containers and rotate stock so old packages do not remain indefinitely. Avoid consuming food contaminated with hairy larvae or cast skins. In a warehouse or imported shipment, contact the responsible pest professional or plant-health authority before redistributing goods. Monitoring traps can help locate activity but do not replace source removal.
researchNotes: Utah State extension provides species-specific household IPM; Argentina's plant-health system independently describes larvae and hidden stored-product infestations. Similarity to khapra beetle is an identification caution, not a diagnosis.

proposedDescription: Marsh dewflower, also called Asian spiderwort or wartremoving herb, is an annual wetland plant that can form a tangled mat over shallow water and saturated ground. It is introduced from Asia and has spread through parts of the southeastern United States, with records in the Pacific Northwest as well. Its stems root at the joints, and both seeds and detached plant pieces contribute to spread. This combination makes it a poor choice for an informal pond planting and makes careless pulling capable of leaving substantial material behind.
identification: Look for narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately along succulent, creeping or partly upright stems. Small flowers have three petals and may look pink, pale purple, or nearly white. The leaf bases sheath the stem. Other dayflowers and spiderworts share the three-petaled appearance, so include the whole stem, leaf arrangement, and where the plant is rooted in identification photographs. A floating piece may still carry useful nodes and leaves. Do not infer medicinal value from the common name wartremoving herb.
actions: Report a new wetland patch to the landowner or local invasive-plant program before attempting a large removal. For small authorized work, collect loose fragments as carefully as the rooted stems and keep the material from washing downstream. Inspect boots, nets, and equipment before leaving. Follow-up visits are essential because missed fragments and buried seed can produce new plants. Avoid applying ordinary garden herbicides in water; any treatment needs to fit the site and its aquatic requirements. Native wetland plants interwoven with the mat should be protected during management.
researchNotes: NCSU supplies exact-species morphology and spread; Virginia DCR supplies an independent regional management account. The FWS high-risk assessment was consulted but is not counted as a wholly independent underlying biology lineage.

proposedDescription: Water chestnut is a rooted annual aquatic plant that spreads its floating leaves into rosettes at the surface. In parts of the northeastern United States, dense beds interfere with boating and other water uses and crowd the water surface. Its hard, sharply pointed fruits can remain an unwelcome presence on shorelines after the leafy plants are gone. This is the plant called Trapa natans, not the familiar edible water chestnut sold as a vegetable. The shared common name is a frequent source of confusion.
identification: Floating leaves are roughly diamond-shaped, with toothed edges and swollen leaf stalks that help hold the rosette at the surface. Small flowers have four white petals. The hard fruit has sharp projections and is more informative than a distant view of a green mat. Underwater structures look quite different from the floating leaves. Other Trapa taxa also occur in North America, so include fruit photographs when reporting a find. Avoid handling the pointed nuts with bare feet or casually reaching into a pile of them.
actions: Report a new bed to the waterbody manager or state aquatic-invasive-species program. Organized hand removal can help with small infestations when done before mature fruits drop, but permission, access, and follow-up matter. Remove the entire plant where feasible and contain fragments and fruits for disposal away from water. Clean boats and trailers after visiting an infested site. A single successful pulling day does not establish eradication, because subsequent plants can arise from remaining seed. Keep monitoring the same shorelines and access points in later growing seasons.
researchNotes: USGS supplies botanical and distribution context; Michigan provides an independent state identification/reporting account, and NY DEC documents local hand-control experience. No claim of a uniform national legal status is made.

proposedDescription: This water flea is a minute freshwater crustacean also listed as Eubosmina coregoni or Bosmina (Eubosmina) coregoni. It is an introduced zooplankton species in parts of North America, but it is not the large, conspicuously spined water flea that anglers sometimes find on fishing line. A 2025 sediment study in British Columbia found remains decades older than the first modern regional observation. That result illustrates why a first detection date is not necessarily the date an organism actually arrived.
identification: Individuals are generally less than a millimeter long. Identification relies on microscopic details of the head, antennules, shell-like carapace, and postabdominal claw. The rear spine called a mucro is absent or extremely small in the USGS account. Females vary in shape, and related Bosmina can be difficult to separate. A photograph of cloudy water or a mass of tiny swimming animals cannot establish this species. A trained zooplankton specialist should examine a properly documented sample before a new locality is accepted.
actions: For ordinary lake visits, the useful response is prevention: drain retained water from boats and equipment and clean and dry gear before moving to another waterbody. Do not transfer untreated lake water with live bait or aquarium material. Report unusual findings to the local aquatic monitoring program and let staff specify sampling and preservation methods. Avoid trying to remove an entire plankton community. When reviewing records, distinguish a microscope-confirmed modern sample from sediment evidence, and keep uncertainty about the introduction pathway separate from uncertainty about identification.
researchNotes: USGS morphology and the independent 2025 Kootenay sediment study provide distinct evidence lineages. Alternative genus combinations are retained; no predatory-spiny-waterflea traits or large economic impacts are borrowed.

proposedDescription: Water foxtail, also called kneed foxtail, is a low grass of wet ground whose stems often bend sharply near the base and root where they touch the soil. Compact cylindrical flowerheads rise above those spreading stems. Its geographic origin is not consistently described across botanical references: Kew treats North American occurrences as introductions, while some older regional floras describe a broader native range. That disagreement matters when an invasive-species catalog is used to make removal decisions. A local determination needs more than the common name foxtail.
identification: Look for a short, soft-looking cylindrical head and a stem base that runs outward before turning upward. The membrane at the junction of blade and sheath is conspicuous, and the tiny flowers carry fine awns extending beyond their outer bracts. Other wetland foxtails can resemble it closely. Examine mature flower structures with a lens and photograph the bent stem base, leaf junction, and head together. Bristly seedheads of unrelated grasses commonly called foxtails should not be treated as the same plant.
actions: Before removing a wetland patch, ask a local herbarium to confirm both the identification and its regional status. Record whether it is in a pasture, drainage ditch, or relatively undisturbed wetland, since that context changes the management question. Where confirmed plants are unwanted in a managed area, prevent seed-bearing clumps from moving with soil or mowing equipment and recheck rooted stem fragments. Avoid draining or broadly treating a wet area solely to eliminate an uncertain grass. Keep the regional origin disagreement visible, and assess the actual patch before assuming ecological harm.
researchNotes: Finding: The grass is identifiable, but authorities disagree about western North American nativity; the disagreement can remain regional and explicit. Rationale: NZ morphology, Kew taxonomy and GRIN/FNA origin statements support a bounded account without selecting one nationwide origin by assumption. Next step: Review regional origin wording and retain local identification before intervention. proposedDescription: Water hyacinth is a floating plant whose attractive violet flowers can conceal how quickly a pond surface is being occupied. Often now named Pontederia crassipes, it produces daughter plants along connecting stems and can gather into thick wind-driven mats. Warm conditions favor sustained growth, while cold limits its persistence. In invaded waterways, the practical problems include blocked access and crowded water surfaces. A garden-pond plant can become a source for new infestations when flooding or discarded material carries it into connected water.
identification: The rounded, glossy leaves rise from a floating cluster, often on swollen, spongy stalks. A curtain of fine, dark roots hangs below. Flower spikes bear conspicuous pale purple to violet blooms. Frogbit and American spongeplant can resemble young floating plants, so inspect the roots, leaf stalks, and flowers together. The inflated stalks may be less obvious in crowded growth. Take a close photograph of a single plant as well as the whole mat, without carrying live material to another waterbody for identification.
actions: Do not plant or release it where floodwater can reach natural waterways. Report a new patch early and coordinate removal with the pond owner or aquatic plant manager. Small accessible groups may be lifted out, with plants and connecting pieces contained on land away from drainage routes. Large mats require a planned response that accounts for access, disposal, and water quality. Do not treat the entire pond casually with a garden product. Inspect boats and trailers carefully, and revisit the shoreline after removal for overlooked daughter plants.
researchNotes: NCSU supports the Pontederia name and clonal spread; Kentucky fishery guidance provides separate field recognition and pond management. A Kentucky statement denying biological controls was not generalized beyond its local guidance.

proposedDescription: Water mannagrass is a grass of shallow, still, or slow-moving water, with stems that may float or spread along a muddy margin. Its loose, narrow flowerhead carries long spikelets rather than the dense cylindrical head of water foxtail. Regional floras describe it as naturalized in places outside its native range. The name has also been used within a broader group of similar mannagrasses, which makes old distribution and impact statements easy to misread. It should not inherit the reputation of the much larger invasive Glyceria maxima.
identification: Look for flat or folded leaves, a conspicuous membranous ligule, and a loose flowerhead that often leans to one side. The elongated spikelets contain several florets. In the New Zealand flora, the flowering bracts called lemmas are about 6 to 7.5 millimeters long, an important distinction from several close relatives. Their tips are not deeply toothed like those of Glyceria declinata. A grass specialist may need mature spikelets; a floating leaf alone cannot reliably distinguish the species or exclude a hybrid.
actions: Leave an uncertain wetland grass in place while obtaining an identification, especially among native shoreline vegetation. Photograph the habitat, leaf junction, and mature heads, and ask whether the regional flora uses a narrow or broad species concept. If confirmed plants require management in a ditch or other maintained area, avoid moving contaminated mud and rooted pieces downstream. Plan any removal with the waterway manager. Local origin, ecological effects, and treatment evidence remain incomplete here, so a blanket eradication response would be premature.
researchNotes: Finding: NZ and Spanish botanical treatments independently corroborate the narrow floating sweet-grass diagnosis; local damage and efficacy remain unmeasured. Rationale: Different regional floras support lemma and wet-habitat traits. Broad range uncertainty does not prevent a carefully identified profile. Next step: Review the narrow morphology and local-priority advice, keeping efficacy claims out.

proposedDescription: Water spangles, or common salvinia, is a small floating fern that can join into a continuous cover over quiet water. It has no showy flowers: what looks like a root beneath each leafy section is actually a finely divided submerged leaf. The species is problematic in parts of the southern United States, including Mississippi. It is smaller than giant salvinia, but small size is not a dependable measure of either identity or management importance. A fragment carried with pond plants or equipment deserves attention.
identification: Pairs of oval floating leaves sit at the surface, with the divided third leaf hanging below. A lens reveals water-repellent hairs on the upper surface. In common salvinia, each hair branches and its tips remain separate; in giant salvinia, the branches join at their ends into an eggbeater-like structure. This is a much better distinction than leaf size alone. Photograph the hair structure, the paired floating leaves, and the submerged portion. Duckweeds have a simpler appearance and do not have this arrangement of fern leaves.
actions: Inspect ornamental pond plants and equipment before placing them in clean water, and never empty aquarium or pond contents into a ditch or stream. Report a new mat to the waterbody manager. Small patches may be collected with appropriate fine-mesh equipment, but tiny missed pieces make follow-up important. Keep removed plants contained well away from the water's edge. Larger infestations need an aquatic management plan; do not assume a method used for giant salvinia will work identically here. Clean boats, trailers, nets, and footwear before moving to another site.
researchNotes: USGS and Alabama supply species-specific hair and leaf characters; Mississippi extension independently identifies regional management concern. Shared salvinia accounts are used only where they explicitly distinguish S. minima.

proposedDescription: Water yam, also called winged yam or ube, is both a cultivated food plant and a troublesome escaped vine in parts of Florida. Those roles should not be confused. In Florida natural areas, vigorous vines can climb over shrubs and trees, spreading large leaves across the supporting vegetation. Underground tubers allow regrowth, and aerial tubers called bulbils can start new plants. The familiar crop name does not make an unidentified wild tuber safe to eat, and cultivated food value does not erase the effects of escaped populations.
identification: Inspect the stem for four narrow wings or ridges and the upper leaves for an opposite arrangement. The leaves are broad, often heart-shaped, with prominent veins. Lower leaves may alternate, so one section of vine can mislead. Air potato, Dioscorea bulbifera, is a close lookalike, but winged stems are a particularly useful clue for D. alata. Photograph stem cross-section, leaf arrangement, and bulbils together. Do not use a guessed direction of twining as the only deciding character.
actions: In an invaded Florida site, collect fallen bulbils before they establish and prevent them from leaving with garden waste. Cut climbing vines near the ground without pulling heavy growth down from the canopy. Small underground tubers may be dug where this will not damage nearby roots or soil; large plants need a planned response and repeated checks for regrowth. Ask local extension about appropriate treatment. The beetle used against air potato does not control winged yam, so moving those insects is not a solution for this species.
researchNotes:
Flora of China independently verifies winged stems and variable leaf arrangement. UF provides Florida impact and management, including the explicit lack of control by the air-potato beetle; FNAI derivatives are not double-counted.

proposedDescription: Watercress is a familiar vegetable that also grows outside cultivation in springs, ditches, and shallow flowing water. It is a perennial aquatic or semi-aquatic herb, often spreading across mud or along the water surface. The species is introduced in many North American settings, but a patch should be evaluated in its own watershed rather than labeled harmful simply because the plant is edible and nonnative. Thick growth can raise a local management question, while correct identification remains the first step.
identification: Look for hollow, smooth stems, leaves divided into rounded leaflets, and small white flowers with four petals. The terminal leaflet is often larger than the side leaflets. Mature slender seedpods are especially helpful because related watercresses, including Nasturtium microphyllum and hybrids, may be difficult to separate without fruit. The garden flower commonly called nasturtium belongs to Tropaeolum and is a different plant. Photograph stems, a complete leaf, flowers, and pods together; a handful of rounded leaflets is not a secure identification.
actions: Do not transplant wild watercress or empty cultivation water into a natural stream. For an unwanted patch, coordinate with the landowner or waterway manager and collect loose stems so they are not carried downstream during removal. Avoid disturbing an entire spring margin merely to clear a small uncertain plant. Recheck the site after flow conditions change. Treat a wild identification separately from a food-safety decision: an edible species name does not establish the cleanliness of the water or authorize harvesting from a particular place.
researchNotes: USGS provides nonindigenous aquatic context and NSW flora provides independent exact-species morphology. Similar watercress taxa and hybrids require fruit-based review; no claim that all naturalized patches are invasive is made.

proposedDescription: Phaedon laevigatus is a small European leaf beetle sometimes listed under the common name watercress leaf beetle. That label is a poor guide to its biology. Authored European keys associate the species with hemp-nettles, Galeopsis, and a Latvian specimen review independently confirms the beetle while correcting an earlier misidentification. The watercress-feeding Phaedon cochleariae is a different species. Neither a common-name list nor holes in a watercress leaf demonstrate that P. laevigatus caused the damage or is a harmful local invader.
identification: The adult is tiny, about 2.5-3 mm long, with a nearly rounded, strongly convex body and a dark bronze or copper sheen. Fine rows on the wing covers are much more delicate than those of several similar Phaedon. These are useful clues, but color alone is unreliable and the detailed key characters require magnification. Photograph the beetle from above and the side with a scale, and record its host. Note whether it was actually feeding rather than merely resting on a plant.
actions: Ask an entomologist to confirm a suspected record, especially before attributing crop damage to it. Keep any requested specimen contained and attach the date, location, host identity and close photographs of the injury. Do not move beetles between gardens for comparison. If a cultivated watercress bed is affected, obtain crop- and water-site-specific advice before treatment; a recommendation for a different leaf beetle may be unsuitable. For a wild observation, report the association without assuming harm. Local seasonal development and effective management have not been established by the European records used here.
researchNotes: Finding: An authored beetle key and an independent Latvian specimen study establish P. laevigatus morphology and Galeopsis associations, replacing the prior name-list-only evidence. Rationale: The key separates laevigatus from watercress-associated cochleariae; the 2009 study examined two 1991 specimens and corrected a misidentification. Neither proves US crop damage. Next step: Review the rewritten exact-species recognition and avoid treating the watercress common name as a verified crop association. proposedDescription: Watermelon is a warm-season annual crop, not a plant that should automatically be presented as an invasive threat. Its long vines spread over the ground and produce familiar large fruits after successful flowering and pollination. Cultivars differ greatly in fruit size, rind pattern, flesh color, and seed production. A volunteer beside a compost pile may simply reflect discarded seed. A persistent population outside cultivation would need its own evidence before being described as a local ecological problem.
identification: Look for a trailing, tendrilled vine with deeply divided leaves and small yellow flowers. Male and female flowers occur on the same plant; a developing fruit sits beneath a female flower. The mature fruit is a thick-rinded melon, but young vines can be confused with other cucurbits. Leaf shape, flowers, tendrils, and fruit should be considered together. Older botanical accounts used the name more broadly for several crop forms, so do not assume every wild Citrullus record represents a modern sweet dessert watermelon.
actions: In the vegetable garden, give vines adequate space, drainage, and warm growing conditions, and protect pollinator access during flowering. Poor fruit set may reflect weather or pollination rather than an invasive pest. Remove unwanted volunteer plants before they fruit if they interfere with the garden plan, and keep discarded fruit from repeatedly seeding nearby unmanaged ground. If a vine is growing far from cultivation, document it and ask a local botanist for confirmation. Never use an uncertain wild melon identification as permission to taste the fruit.
researchNotes: NCSU provides crop growth and care; University of Michigan supplies independent vine and flower morphology. Original pollination research supports the importance of flower visits; the species is explicitly not labeled inherently invasive.

proposedDescription: Waterpoppy is an aquatic ornamental with rounded floating leaves and yellow flowers that can brighten a pond while its creeping stems spread below. It grows in still or slowly moving water and can establish from stem fragments. Outside its native American range, it has become a management concern in places such as New Zealand, where dense mats are targeted for control. US sources document escapes in several warm regions, but those records should not be treated as proof of the same impact in every waterbody.
identification: Each flower has three broad yellow petals around a darker center. The floating leaves are shallowly heart-shaped, and the midrib on the underside is conspicuously inflated. Count petals carefully: yellow floatinghearts have five, often fringed petals, while yellow waterlilies have a different, many-parted flower. Swamp lily can share a three-petaled form but has white flowers and lacks the inflated underside midrib. Photographs of both leaf surfaces and a complete flower are much more useful than a distant yellow bloom.
actions: Keep ornamental ponds separated from drainage routes that can carry plants into streams. Do not discard waterpoppy fragments, mud, or aquarium contents into natural water. Report a new escape to the aquatic plant manager and ask how to contain it before removal. Pulling through a large tangle can create pieces that drift away, so plan fragment collection and disposal as part of the work. Revisit nearby margins for new growth. Use locally applicable guidance rather than importing New Zealand legal restrictions into a US recommendation.
researchNotes: New Zealand flora provides detailed independent recognition and fragment spread; the 2025 FWS assessment supplies US occurrence context while clearly citing its underlying sources. Geographic impact and legal scope remain separated.

proposedDescription: Wavyleaf basketgrass is a low, spreading grass that can turn a shaded woodland floor into a continuous green carpet. In the mid-Atlantic region it is an introduced invader, with Maryland records dating to 1997. Its stems root at their joints, and later in the season its seeds acquire sticky bristles that attach to clothing, pets, and equipment. That makes an ordinary walk through a patch a potential transport event. The rippled leaves are attractive, but the spread can interfere with native woodland vegetation.
identification: The leaves have obvious crosswise ripples, like shallow pleats, and the stems and leaf sheaths are noticeably hairy. Long trailing stems lie along the ground and root at nodes. Seedheads carry paired spikelets with long awns that become sticky. Japanese stiltgrass and small carpetgrass can cause confusion, so inspect the leaf surface, stem hairs, and rooting habit together. A photo of the wavy blade plus the lower stem is especially helpful before the seedheads appear. Avoid brushing against mature seedheads just to obtain a closer picture.
actions: Stay out of seeding patches and keep dogs on trails near affected woods. Check clothing, footwear, fur, and equipment before leaving the site. Small patches can often be hand-pulled when soil is moist, with careful removal of rooted stem sections and protection of native plants mixed among them. Prioritize trail edges and other places where people can carry seeds away. Bag seed-bearing material instead of composting it. Tell the land manager about a new patch and return for follow-up, since one removal visit rarely captures every stem and seedling.
researchNotes: Maryland DNR field identification and management observations are supported by independent botanical morphology from Kew/GrassBase. Maryland Extension is used for practical pulling guidance but shared DNR observations are not counted twice.

proposedDescription: Wavyleaf sea lavender, commonly sold as statice, is a short-lived perennial often grown as an annual for cut and dried flowers. The lasting color comes largely from papery calyces that remain after the small corollas fade. It is native to the Mediterranean region and nearby areas and has escaped cultivation in parts of the western United States. A garden escape is not automatically a severe invader, and the name sea lavender should not be confused with either true lavender or native coastal Limonium species.
identification: Look for a low group of hairy, deeply lobed leaves and upright, branched flowering stems with conspicuous wings. Small flowers sit in crowded clusters, surrounded by persistent colored calyces. Cultivars may be purple, pink, yellow, or other colors, so flower color alone is unreliable. The divided leaves and winged stems are particularly useful when distinguishing it from other sea lavenders. Photograph the basal leaves and a section of stem as well as the flower spray. A dried florist's stem may lack the most useful vegetative characters.
actions: For a garden planting, provide well-drained soil and avoid persistent overwatering that encourages root and crown problems. Check adjoining paths and unmanaged ground for unwanted seedlings, especially where plants have repeatedly matured seed. Keep discarded seed-bearing arrangements and garden waste out of natural coastal areas. If you find it away from cultivation, record the nearest possible garden source and request a botanical identification before removal. Evidence reviewed here supports horticultural use and occasional escape, not a blanket claim that this species threatens every American salt marsh.
researchNotes: NCSU supplies exact-species cultivation and morphology; the UCLA Santa Monica flora records local escapes independently. Native coastal relatives are not labeled invasive, and no generalized impact claim is imported from other Limonium.

proposedDescription: Pulvinaria delottoi is an iceplant scale, despite the broader catalog label wax scale. It feeds on certain succulents and was studied in California alongside a different iceplant scale, Pulvinariella mesembryanthemi. The two should not be treated as interchangeable. Original California work found P. delottoi concentrated on mature, lower portions of plants and described one annual generation there. A later British report documented it on an imported Cheiridopsis plant. These records make nursery and collection hygiene relevant, but leave questions about geographic origin and current local importance.
identification: Young adult females can be bright green, later becoming reddish brown and wrinkled as they mature. Females produce an irregular white egg sac beneath the body. Similar iceplant scales can look alike in life, and a white cottony patch on a succulent is not a secure species diagnosis. Photograph the insect, egg sac, and host plant, including the older lower stems. A scale specialist may need slide-mounted adults and a taxonomic key. Keep the host label with the sample rather than reporting simply that it was on an aloe.
actions: Separate an affected potted succulent from other plants and inspect nearby pots before sharing cuttings. Ask a diagnostic service to identify the scale before choosing treatment or discarding a valuable collection. Check older growth as well as tender tips, since the two iceplant scales can occupy different parts of a plant. Avoid moving infested nursery material outdoors or between properties. Historical biological-control success is not permission to release insects yourself. Ask the adviser to consider the host and setting; the historical California result does not promise the same outcome in another collection.
researchNotes: Finding: California field work and a separate British interception report support exact-species biology; broad origin metadata disagreement is not an identity failure. Rationale: The 1982 California biological-control observations and 2011 imported-plant specimens are distinct original studies. California outcomes are not promised elsewhere. Next step: Review the geographically attributed observations and keep any modern treatment decision local. proposedDescription: Webbing clothes moth is a small indoor pest whose larvae damage animal-based materials such as wool, fur, and feathers. The adult moths are a clue to the infestation rather than the stage chewing holes in a sweater. Quiet, undisturbed storage gives the larvae places to feed, especially where garments or furnishings retain food residues and body oils. This is a household-material problem, not a reason to treat every small moth seen near a light as an invasive species requiring outdoor control.
identification: Adults are pale tan or golden, with narrow, unmarked wings and a tuft of reddish hairs on the head. Larvae are pale caterpillars with darker heads. Their silk forms feeding tubes attached to the material. This differs from the portable case carried by a casemaking clothes moth larva. Pantry moths and carpet beetles can also appear indoors but point to different sources. Inspect beneath rugs, along upholstery edges, and inside stored woolens, and photograph the larva, silk, and damaged material together.
actions: Find and isolate the affected items before treating the room. Clean garments by a method suitable for the fabric, such as professional dry cleaning when appropriate, then store clean items in sealed containers. Vacuum lint, hair, and debris from storage areas and beneath furniture, and inspect nearby articles that have not been used recently. A trap can help monitor adult activity but does not remove larvae inside textiles. For valuable textiles or extensive damage, consult a conservator or pest professional rather than experimenting with heat, chemicals, or mothballs.
researchNotes: Minnesota extension supplies adult identification; Maryland independently distinguishes attached webbing from portable cases and supports cleaning and sealed storage. Outdated fumigant advice was not reproduced.

proposedDescription: Weeping bottlebrush is an Australian shrub or small tree with hanging branchlets and red brush-like flower clusters. Some botanical treatments call it Melaleuca viminalis, while others retain Callistemon. It is widely cultivated, but local behavior matters: UF/IFAS currently rates it as a high invasion risk in Florida. Its ornamental value therefore should not be used as evidence that it is suitable beside every wetland or natural area. Conversely, that Florida assessment is not a claim that all planted specimens everywhere are causing measurable harm.
identification: Look for narrow leaves along flexible, drooping branches and cylindrical red flower clusters made conspicuous by their many long stamens. Woody capsules follow the flowers and release seed annually, unlike bottlebrushes that retain seed for many years. Other bottlebrush species and cultivars share red flowers, so the weeping habit alone is not conclusive. Include leaves, branch arrangement, flowers, and old capsules in photographs. Retain nursery labels where available, and recognize that Callistemon viminalis and Melaleuca viminalis may refer to the same plant under different generic treatments.
actions: Before adding one to a warm-climate landscape, consult the current regional assessment and choose an appropriate alternative where invasion risk is high. Watch existing trees for seedlings beyond the maintained planting, especially near drainage routes. Remove confirmed unwanted seedlings while small and keep capsule-bearing prunings out of natural areas. An established tree should be assessed for both ecological concern and safe removal access. Do not assume the control history of the invasive paperbark Melaleuca quinquenervia applies to this species simply because one classification places both in Melaleuca.
researchNotes: The Australian Native Plants Society provides independent native-region description; UF supplies a current Florida risk assessment dated through 2026. Genus-name disagreement is explained without importing paperbark impacts.
