proposedDescription: Weeping fig is a familiar indoor tree that becomes a much larger evergreen outdoors in frost-free climates. Its flexible branches carry glossy leaves, and older landscape trees can develop substantial surface roots. That can make it a poor fit beside pavement, pipes, or small structures even where ecological invasion is not documented. UF/IFAS currently does not consider it a problem species in Florida, and its plant account says ecological impacts have not been documented there. Structural root damage and invasive ecological behavior are separate questions.
identification: The leaves are alternate, oval to elliptic, glossy, and drawn out into long pointed tips. Slender branchlets hang down, giving the crown a soft, weeping outline. Small figs may occur in pairs and change color as they mature; the flowers are enclosed inside them rather than displayed as showy blossoms. Other ornamental figs can have similar leaves, and pruning can obscure the usual crown shape. Photograph a leafy twig, leaf attachment, and any figs, and keep the cultivar label if the plant was purchased.
actions: Indoors, provide bright indirect light and drainage, and avoid abrupt changes in growing conditions that can trigger leaf drop. Outdoors, consider the eventual tree and root size before planting. Ask an arborist to assess existing root conflicts instead of cutting major roots or attempting to remove a large tree yourself. Record any seedlings growing beyond a cultivated site and verify them before assuming the parent has naturalized. A well-kept houseplant does not need invasive-plant treatment, and an isolated fig sighting should not be turned into a claim of widespread habitat damage.

proposedDescription: Weeping lovegrass is a warm-season perennial bunchgrass with long, fine leaves that arch toward the ground. It has been planted in the United States for erosion control and forage, while in Australia it is a serious introduced pasture and roadside weed. Dense tussocks can become difficult to manage where grazing pressure or disturbance opens space for establishment. These different histories matter: a useful planting in one setting does not establish suitability in another, and an Australian weed designation does not automatically describe every American field.
identification: Look for a tight basal tussock, very narrow leaves, and an open, branching seedhead held above the foliage. Leaf blades may be flat or rolled, and their long tips droop conspicuously. At the junction of blade and sheath, the ligule is a short fringe of hairs. Other lovegrasses and fine-leaved native bunchgrasses can look similar when sterile. Photograph the base, ligule, and mature seedhead rather than relying on the weeping shape alone. A local grass key or extension identification is useful before disturbing a mixed grassland.
actions: Prevent seed-bearing hay, soil, and equipment from carrying plants into an uninfested site. Where this species is an unwanted invader, map the scattered plants beyond the main patch and prioritize them before they produce seed. Small tussocks may be removed when doing so will not destabilize the ground, followed by revegetation with suitable local cover. In pasture, seek advice on grazing and recovery of desirable grasses rather than repeatedly creating bare ground. Large stands need a staged management plan and follow-up; mowing alone should not be assumed to eliminate perennial crowns.
researchNotes: USDA NRCS documents US planting history and growth form; NSW provides independent invaded-pasture identification and management context. Benefits and harm are geographically qualified rather than generalized globally.

proposedDescription: Weeping willow is a fast-growing deciduous tree native to China, widely planted for its long curtains of hanging branches. It favors moist settings and can naturalize along waterways beyond its native range. Detached branches can root, so maintenance debris can matter as much as seed in some populations. Its beauty beside water should be weighed against root space, branch failure, and local riverbank-management needs. Many trees sold or recorded as weeping willow are hybrids, making the scientific name worth checking before assigning a regional impact.
identification: Typical Salix babylonica has slender green to brown-green hanging twigs and long, narrow leaves with finely toothed edges and extended tips. Leaves are greener above and paler beneath. Small flowers appear in catkins rather than showy blossoms. Hybrid weeping willows can closely resemble it, and leaf shape alone is not always decisive. Record the young twigs, both leaf surfaces, and catkins if available. Native American willows can also occupy wet banks; a willow on a stream is not automatically this introduced ornamental.
actions: Avoid leaving live willow cuttings or pruned branches where they can lodge in wet soil or wash downstream. Seek a local identification before removing trees from a riparian site, and coordinate any work with the land manager so bank stability and native vegetation are protected. A large planted tree near a building or path merits professional assessment when roots or weak branches create conflicts. For replacement planting, select a locally appropriate tree with enough space to mature. Do not assume Australian restrictions or hybrid behavior apply unchanged to a US specimen.
researchNotes: NCSU supports horticultural traits and native origin; NSW botanical treatment independently documents vegetative spread and diagnostic features. Hybrid identity is cautioned without assigning seed sterility or Australian legal status globally.

proposedDescription: This hybrid weeping willow has a complicated naming history. Traditional horticultural accounts describe Salix x sepulcralis as a cross involving white willow and weeping willow, and the name includes familiar planted weeping forms. Regional floras have applied related names differently, including Salix x pendulina. Washington herbarium records recognize S. x sepulcralis as introduced in wet and disturbed places, but the identity of a particular tree cannot be settled by the common name alone. A clear regional taxonomic treatment is needed before older records can be combined into a range or impact account.
identification: Expect a deciduous tree with hanging branches, narrow toothed leaves, and catkins. Some traditional treatments distinguish this hybrid group by hairier young leaves and particular ovary characters compared with other weeping hybrids. Those are specialist distinctions, not a promise that every golden-twigged willow is the same hybrid. Photograph new growth, mature leaf undersides, twigs, and flowers at the appropriate season. Keep a record of any cultivar label and the botanical source used. A bare winter silhouette cannot establish the parentage.
actions: For a planted tree, assess space, drainage, and structural condition before deciding whether any action is needed. If it has established along a stream, ask a regional herbarium or willow specialist to confirm the name and advise the land manager. Keep live pruning waste out of wet banks and waterways while identification is pending. Do not clear nearby native willows on the basis of similar hanging branches. Management guidance should follow the locally identified hybrid and site conditions, with bank protection and safe handling of large limbs included in the plan.

proposedDescription: Calomycterus setarius, often called the imported longhorned weevil, is a small plant-feeding beetle introduced to North America from Japan. Adults may gather on vegetation or wander into houses during summer. Their presence indoors is unsettling but should first be treated as an entry problem, not evidence that stored food or the building structure is being consumed. Outdoors, adults feed on foliage and larvae feed on roots. The importance of that feeding depends on the crop, the number of insects, and the actual damage observed.
identification: Adults have a dark body covered with gray-brown scales and hairs, often giving a mottled appearance where scales are missing. They are only a few millimeters long, with a short snout and elbowed antennae. Other broad-nosed weevils can resemble them, particularly in a dim indoor photograph. Take a close image from above and from the side, including the antennae and legs, and add a size reference. On plants, record fresh notches or feeding damage separately from the insect so an identification can be tied to an observed problem.
actions: Vacuum up indoor strays and examine door thresholds, window screens, and other entry points before reaching for a spray. Keep collected insects contained while obtaining an identification. In a garden or nursery, inspect the plants where adults gather and ask extension staff whether the observed feeding justifies action. Do not assume every root problem nearby has the same cause. Avoid moving infested potted plants or soil to another property until assessed. A confirmed damaging population calls for crop-specific management, while occasional adults may require only monitoring and exclusion.
researchNotes: UMass provides species-specific introduction, host, and recent diagnostic context; Minnesota independently addresses home-invading adults and recognition. No stored-product or structural-infestation claim is made.

proposedDescription: Exomias pellucidus is a European broad-nosed weevil that has become established outside its native range, including North America. Older literature often calls it Barypeithes pellucidus, and common names include hairy spider weevil and juniper root weevil. The spider name describes an impression, not a relationship to spiders. Published accounts describe root-feeding larvae and adults active around the ground and low vegetation. Nursery and horticultural records make it worth identifying, but effects attributed to a whole community of introduced root weevils should not automatically be assigned to this species alone.
identification: Adults are about 2.9-4 mm long, shiny chestnut to darker brown, with paler legs and conspicuous long hairs on the wing covers. The eyes are small and sit high on the head. A similar introduced species, Exomias trichopterus, makes close examination important: E. pellucidus has denser hairs near the rear and an additional row of long hairs beside the rear wing-cover seam. Photograph the snout, legs and hair pattern with a scale. These clues guide a specialist; they are not a guarantee that a phone photograph will settle the name.
actions: In a nursery, isolate suspect stock and avoid moving its potting soil until an entomologist has identified the weevil. Inspect both foliage and roots when a plant is failing, rather than assuming the visible adult explains all symptoms. A confirmed finding can guide the choice of a crop-appropriate response and help locate the source of movement. Do not transfer insects between gardens for comparison or attempt an unverified biological-control release. Ask the adviser to connect any treatment decision to identified insects and observed injury; the sources do not establish a universal local damage threshold.
researchNotes: Finding: The original New Zealand arrival study supplies a practical combination of adult characters, while the North American manual adds the crucial E. trichopterus comparison. Rationale: NZ collected specimens and North American diagnostic and historical records are separate evidence; the manual repeats NZ arrival and that repeated claim is not double-counted. Next step: Review the strengthened diagnosis and retain specialist confirmation and the absence of a locally measured treatment threshold.

proposedDescription: Pachyrhinus elegans is a North American broad-nosed weevil, not a species that should be labeled an alien invader simply because it appears in a pest list. A 2021 revision recognizes it as one of three North American Pachyrhinus species and brings several older names into its synonymy. Canadian collection records document it across a broad region, with pine associations noted in the literature. Those facts support a native-fauna and plant-health account, but they do not establish an invasive range or a need for routine control.
identification: The scales on the wing covers form a relatively even pattern rather than the mottled patches of the other Nearctic Pachyrhinus. They can look iridescent green, but copper and other color variation make color alone unreliable. A specialist uses magnification and the revised key to check the scale characters. Photograph the beetle from above and the side with a scale and record the host tree. Older labels such as P. lateralis and P. miscix should stay attached to their original records when the updated identification is added.
actions: For an insect found on a pine, photograph any fresh feeding separately from old needle damage and send both records to an extension or forest-health specialist. Keep a requested specimen contained and label the tree accurately. Avoid removing a healthy tree or spraying an entire stand merely because a weevil is present. Other insects, disease, drought, and physical injury can produce similar-looking decline. The recent taxonomic revision can help a specialist interpret older names. A native weevil on a pine needs a plant-health assessment, not an automatic invasive-species response.
researchNotes: Finding: The modern revision and Canadian specimen study support a North American native-fauna account, rather than an unsupported alien-invader warning. Rationale: The 2021 taxonomic work and 2007 original New Brunswick collections are independent; lacking an introduced range is a scope correction, not a missing fact to invent. Next step: Review the native-fauna framing and require diagnosed injury before recommending control.

proposedDescription: Phyllobius oblongus is an introduced leaf-feeding weevil found in parts of North America, including northern hardwood forests. Adults use a range of deciduous trees, while the immature stages live below ground and feed on roots. Experiments with insects from Wisconsin and Michigan showed that adult feeding and egg production varied with the tree species offered. That is useful evidence of host relationships, but it is not a prediction that every occupied tree will decline or that all related weevils cause equivalent damage.
identification: Adults typically combine a dark head and thorax with brown wing covers and fine pale hairs, rather than the bright blanket of green scales seen on some other leaf weevils. Their body is elongate, with a short snout and elbowed antennae. Color can vary with lighting and wear, so compare structural features using a regional key. Photographs should include the full beetle, antennae, and legs. Note the tree species and fresh feeding marks; finding the insect on a leaf does not prove that it caused every hole nearby.
actions: Inspect young growth and record whether feeding is increasing before deciding on treatment. In an orchard or nursery, ask an extension entomologist to confirm the species and assess the crop stage and damage. Do not transplant laboratory host preferences into a blanket spray recommendation for woodland trees. When moving nursery stock, check foliage and root-associated material for unwanted insects and follow local plant-health advice. In a natural woodland, submit a well-documented observation and protect surrounding native insects while the importance of the population is assessed.
researchNotes: The Canadian taxonomic treatment supplies exact-species appearance, while Pinski and colleagues provide original feeding and reproduction experiments. The laboratory design is explicitly distinguished from field damage or an intervention threshold.

proposedDescription: Polydrusus formosus is a bright green introduced leaf weevil recorded in North America. Older North American studies often used the name Polydrusus sericeus for this insect. Adults occur on deciduous vegetation, and recent research has documented it in Minnesota hazel plantings. Its presence warrants accurate identification and observation of feeding, but a green weevil on a hazel leaf is not, by itself, evidence of economically important crop loss. Several native and introduced relatives can occupy similar settings. In Great Lakes populations, larvae feed on roots and overwinter in soil before adult emergence in late spring.
identification: The green appearance comes from scales covering a darker body; worn patches can therefore look black. Identification keys describe brownish-yellow legs and antennae and a small tooth on the femur. Similar Polydrusus species differ in leg teeth, scale coverage, and antenna proportions, while Phyllobius has a different arrangement of the antennal grooves. These details may need magnification. Take clear upper and side views, avoid rubbing the scales off, and record the size and host plant. Do not identify the species from green color alone.
actions: In a hazel planting, inspect multiple plants and record adult numbers alongside fresh feeding and plant condition. A regional extension specialist can use those observations to decide whether additional sampling or management is justified. Avoid transferring insects or infested nursery material to another site. Protect beneficial insects while identification is pending, and do not apply a general leaf-weevil treatment simply because the species is introduced. For a woodland record, supply photographs, date, and tree identity. Keep older sericeus records linked to their original publications so taxonomic changes remain visible during review.
researchNotes: The 2024 original Minnesota study provides exact-species hazel observations; Hoebeke taxonomy uses older independent identification work. The review is used for naming and key characters, not counted as independent replication of Minnesota ecology.

proposedDescription: Rhinocyllus conicus is a thistle flowerhead weevil deliberately introduced to control certain nonnative thistles. Its history is also a warning about unintended effects: original prairie research documented populations developing in native Platte and wavyleaf thistles. Larvae feed inside flowerheads, reducing the resources available for seed production. The insect should therefore not be presented as a universally helpful thistle control. A native thistle can be an important plant in its own right, and its association with this weevil deserves careful attention.
identification: Adults are small, short-snouted weevils with dark bodies and mottled pale hairs. They may be found on developing thistle flowerheads. Eggs are placed near the head bracts and covered with material, while larvae develop within the head. Other thistle weevils, including Larinus species, can be confused with it, so pair close photographs of the beetle with a reliable identification of the thistle. A damaged head alone is not enough: native insects also feed in thistle flowerheads, and opening heads destroys part of the evidence.
actions: Do not collect and redistribute this weevil as a do-it-yourself biological control. Current agency guidance restricts its interstate movement because of risks to native thistles. If you suspect it on a native or conservation-interest thistle, leave the plant in place and contact the land manager or extension entomologist with photographs and location details. Ask before taking flowerheads for a sample. For an unwanted nonnative thistle patch, use a locally approved management plan that distinguishes the plant species and protects native relatives, rather than introducing an insect with a documented broader host range.
researchNotes: USFS supports life cycle and recognition; Louda original prairie work independently documents non-target use. North Dakota agency guidance verifies current interstate movement restrictions. Mirrors of Louda papers are treated as the same lineage.

proposedDescription: The nut leaf weevil is a small European beetle established in parts of northeastern and northwestern North America. Adults feed on foliage of several woody plants, including hazel and oak, rather than belonging to just one host. European forestry studies have examined damage in plantations, but that does not establish a comparable problem at a particular American site. A weevil on a tree is a reason to look more closely, not a reason to treat the whole tree.
identification: Look for a squat, oval beetle about 4 mm long, with conspicuous projecting eyes and a short, broad snout. Brownish and pale scales cover much of the body. A useful feature is the exposed, shiny black strip near the front of the seam between the wing covers. Take a sharp photograph from above and another showing the head; a distant picture of a brown beetle or a chewed leaf is not enough for confirmation.
actions: Record the plant it was actually feeding on, the date, and whether damage is scattered or increasing. Photograph fresh injury as well as the insect. If repeated feeding threatens nursery plants, ask an extension entomologist to confirm the species and assess the need for treatment. Leave ordinary woodland observations undisturbed while identification is checked. Do not introduce fungi or other biological-control agents based on overseas experiments; experimental results are not local treatment instructions.
researchNotes: Hoebeke and colleagues provide North American identification and establishment context; Danish government research documents a separate European plantation setting. Keep geographic impact distinctions explicit and do not turn experimental fungal control into public instructions.

proposedDescription: This tiny ambrosia beetle has been reported from tropical southern Florida and other parts of the Americas. Older accounts use the name Xylosandrus zimmermanni, while a later North American revision places that name under Xylosandrus curtulus. The published synonym explains the older label; records should retain the name originally used alongside the later treatment. Florida accounts describe breeding in unhealthy, broken or recently cut branches, which is quite different from assuming that the beetle caused a healthy tree to decline.
identification: Females described under the older name are only about 1.3-1.5 mm long. Specialists examine the rear slope of the wing covers and the direction of a small tuft of hairs on the pronotum, the plate behind the head. Those details usually require a microscope. Entry holes, sawdust and wilting twigs can help document the setting, but cannot separate this beetle from other ambrosia beetles by themselves.
actions: Photograph the branch, its condition and any holes before disturbing it. Note whether the wood was already cut or damaged and ask an extension diagnostic service how to provide a contained sample. Keep potentially infested branches on site until you have disposal guidance rather than moving them as firewood. Avoid spraying a healthy tree solely because a beetle emerged from dead wood. A confirmed identification and the condition of the host should guide any response.
researchNotes: Finding: The published revision explicitly places zimmermanni under curtulus, and the original Florida survey reports small dead-material breeding without living-host attack. Rationale: This is a traceable published synonym, not an unresolved biological entity; retain the catalog ID and state the current combination in prose. Next step: Review the synonym-qualified profile without changing identifiers or transferring damage from other Xylosandrus. proposedDescription: Weld, also called dyer's mignonette, is a Eurasian plant found outside cultivation in parts of North America. Its narrow flower spikes can rise above disturbed ground, roadsides and fields. The common name reflects its history as a dye plant, rather than a particular ecological impact. A garden specimen and a reproducing roadside population should be recorded differently; the sources reviewed here do not justify describing every occurrence as a damaging invasion.
identification: Look for an upright plant with narrow, simple leaves and a long, slender spike of small pale-yellow flowers. The leaves are not divided into separate leaflets. Mature capsules are small, roughly rounded and open at the top. Close photographs of flowers, their short stalks and the capsules help separate weld from fragrant mignonette, Reseda odorata, which has larger capsules and differently divided petals. Record the whole plant as well as these small details.
actions: If it appears outside a planting, note the size of the patch and whether young plants occur nearby. Photograph fruits before any permitted removal, and keep seed-bearing material contained so it is not carried into new ground. On a managed property, ask the land manager whether the plant is a local priority before clearing it. Follow up where mature plants were removed. Identification and local spread matter more than the presence of an unfamiliar flower alone.
researchNotes: Finding: Victorian and New England botanical accounts support weld recognition and introduced occurrence without a demonstrated local impact threshold. Rationale: Entwisle and the New England flora are separate regional botanical treatments. The profile can recommend modest seed containment without promising eradication. Next step: Review the regional identification and garden actions with ecological harm left unclaimed.

proposedDescription: Sporobolus pyramidalis is a tall, tough, clump-forming grass treated as one of the giant rat-tail grasses in Australia. Botanical sources place its origin in Africa and nearby regions. The label West Indian dropseed can refer to a different Sporobolus, so use the scientific name when checking records. Australian accounts describe pasture degradation by the giant rat-tail group, which includes this species. Those overseas observations justify checking an escape, but do not establish the same impact or legal status in the United States.
identification: Established plants form substantial tussocks with narrow, wiry leaves. The flower head can look narrow when young and open into an elongated, branching pyramid as it matures. Several introduced Sporobolus grasses and native dropseeds look similar. A seed-head photograph alone is not a dependable species diagnosis: include the whole tussock, leaf bases and a close view of the small structures where each leaf meets the stem. A grass specialist may need mature material.
actions: Have an unfamiliar pasture infestation identified before mowing it or moving hay. Mark patches and keep soil, seed-bearing equipment and cut material from spreading into clean areas. Where the grass is confirmed, a pasture adviser can help combine seed prevention with recovery of competing vegetation and follow-up monitoring. Avoid copying overseas herbicide recommendations; products and permitted uses differ. For a small reported population, the most useful first steps are good photographs, a precise location and a record of its extent.
researchNotes: Finding: The scientific name supports giant rat-tail grass in the African-Australian treatment; West Indian dropseed can denote a different Sporobolus and must not drive Florida claim transfer. Rationale: AusGrass morphology and Queensland management observations are distinct sources; US trials under jacquemontii or older varietal labels are excluded. Next step: Review the exact-name profile and common-name caveat; verify a US specimen before attaching local impact or control results.

proposedDescription: West Indian rattlebox is an upright tropical African legume that has been grown and has escaped cultivation elsewhere. Older references may call it Crotalaria zanzibarica. It can grow into a tall, branching plant with long sprays of yellow flowers and inflated seed pods. The reviewed botanical accounts describe roadsides, clearings and other open ground, but they do not establish how much ecological harm a particular United States population causes.
identification: Each leaf has three leaflets, usually elongated or broadly lance-shaped. The stems are ribbed, and hairs are more noticeable beneath the leaves. Flowers are yellow with reddish or purplish markings and occur in long upright clusters. The cylindrical, inflated pods contain many small seeds; mature pods are especially useful for confirming the species. Photograph a complete leaf, the side of a flower, and mature pods. Other rattleboxes share yellow flowers, so color alone is not a reliable identification.
actions: For a plant growing beyond a garden, record whether it is an isolated individual or part of a patch with seedlings. Keep pods from being scattered while documenting or removing a confirmed plant with the landowner's permission. Do not use an unidentified rattlebox as food or livestock feed. A local botanist or extension office can check the name and help decide whether the population needs management. Revisit disturbed ground nearby rather than assuming that removal of the largest plant finishes the work.

proposedDescription: West Indian sage is a small, spreading herb of the mint family. Caribbean botanical accounts include Florida within its native range, along with the Caribbean and parts of tropical mainland America. That matters: its appearance in a national introduced-species catalog should not turn every Florida observation into an invasive-plant warning. The plant can occur in open, moist places, where its low branches and small flowers may be easy to overlook among taller vegetation.
identification: Look for a loosely branching plant with flowering stems rising from a sprawling base. Leaves are paired along the stem, roughly diamond-shaped to oval, with a narrowed base and noticeably toothed edges. The flowers and their surrounding cups are small. Other small salvias occur in the same region; leaf shape, hairiness and flower details are more useful than a general resemblance to garden sage. Photograph the leaf pairs and flowering branch rather than relying on scent or taste.
actions: Leave a suspected native plant in place while its identity and regional status are checked. A helpful report shows the whole patch, leaf edges and flowers, with the date and location. Explain whether it is growing spontaneously or was planted. If it is appearing somewhere outside its documented range, ask a regional herbarium or extension botanist to review it before choosing a response. Protect nearby native herbs and keep an uncertain observation at the level that the botanist can actually confirm.
researchNotes: Finding: Authored Caribbean botanical accounts support the species and its Florida-Caribbean native context, so nationwide alien framing is unnecessary. Rationale: The St John flora and Leon Levy Preserve botanical account are separate regional works; local harm is not inferred from garden weed behavior. Next step: Review the native-range qualification and seek local priority advice before removing natural-area plants. proposedDescription: West Indian woodnettle is an annual nettle that can arrive in growing areas with plants or potting materials. Hawaii's agriculture department documented it in Oahu nurseries in 2012 and highlighted its spread and irritating hairs. Its history elsewhere is less straightforward: Flora of North America describes the Florida population as possibly introduced. Keep that uncertainty separate from the well-documented nursery concern in Hawaii rather than giving the entire country one origin label.
identification: The leaves are broad, toothed and arranged alternately, one at a time along the stem. Small greenish flowers grow in branching clusters. Stinging hairs occur alongside softer hairs, and the leaf stalks may be reddish. Plants can approach a meter in height. Do not run a finger along a stem to check for hairs. Native woodnettles and other nettles can look similar; photographs of leaf arrangement, flower clusters and the whole plant are safer identification tools.
actions: Inspect new nursery plants and the surface of their potting mix before setting them among other plants. If a small infestation is confirmed for removal, protect your hands and exposed skin; Hawaii's advisory recommends gloves and containing mature seed-bearing plants. Keep contaminated potting material from being shared or dumped outdoors. Ask the nursery or local plant-health service about larger infestations and appropriate disposal. Recheck the growing area for seedlings, and document the source of recently received stock if that might help trace an introduction.
researchNotes: Finding: Hawaii nursery detection and FNA morphology support a precise stinging-nettle account while Florida origin remains explicitly uncertain. Rationale: HDOA original detection is independent of Boufford FNA. The latter says possibly introduced in Florida, which is not converted to certain alien status. Next step: Review the handling precautions and regional uncertainty without adding unmeasured ecological losses. proposedDescription: Western flower thrips is a tiny insect native to southwestern North America that has spread widely with horticultural trade. It feeds on many ornamental plants and crops, often hidden inside buds and flowers. Feeding can scar leaves and petals, and the insect can carry plant viruses such as tomato spotted wilt virus. Native origin in one region does not make it harmless in a greenhouse, but neither does every thrips observation establish this species or a virus infection.
identification: Adults are slender and less than 2 mm long, with narrow, fringed wings visible under magnification. Color varies from pale yellow to brown, so color is not a dependable species test. Silvery scars, distorted flowers and small dark specks may suggest thrips feeding. Several other thrips make similar damage. Species confirmation usually requires a specialist to examine fine body hairs and antennae; sticky-card counts are useful for tracking activity but are not an identification on their own.
actions: Inspect incoming plants and cuttings, especially flowers and tender new growth. Keep suspect stock apart while a diagnostic service checks it. In a greenhouse, track insects with regular inspections and sticky cards, remove plant debris in closed containers, and investigate virus-like symptoms promptly. Ask a crop adviser for an integrated plan if damage persists. Repeatedly using the same insecticide can select resistant thrips, and spraying without identifying the insect may harm natural enemies while leaving the actual problem unresolved.
researchNotes: NC State supplies regional origin and crop distinctions; UF supplies diagnostic limits; UConn supplies greenhouse sanitation and monitoring. Keep greenhouse advice scoped and virus infection distinct from thrips presence. Each source supports a separate portion of the draft.

proposedDescription: Tilletia caries, also called Tilletia tritici, is one of the fungi that cause common bunt of wheat. The disease replaces developing grain with spore-filled structures and can contaminate seed lots during harvest. Another fungus, Tilletia laevis, causes similar symptoms. This profile is about common bunt, not every disease described as wheat smut; separating those diseases matters because their biology, diagnosis and management are not interchangeable.
identification: Infected plants can be difficult to recognize until their heads develop. Affected heads may stay green longer, with the outer structures spread around rounded, spore-filled kernels called bunt balls. When these break, they release dark powder and can give grain a strong, unpleasant odor. Do not deliberately crush or smell suspect kernels to identify them. A plant-disease laboratory can distinguish the causal fungi and rule out other grain problems using appropriate examination.
actions: Keep a suspect grain or seed lot separate and contact an extension crop specialist or diagnostic laboratory before planting or moving it. Ask how to collect a contained sample without spreading spores. Clean affected harvesting and handling equipment according to agricultural guidance, and avoid unnecessary dust exposure. Prevention generally depends on clean tested seed, suitable resistant varieties where available, and locally recommended seed treatment when needed. These are decisions for the next planting; applying a treatment to visibly affected mature heads will not restore the missing grain.
researchNotes: Agriculture Victoria explicitly connects T. caries with T. tritici and distinguishes common bunt from other smuts. Nebraska provides independent symptom and prevention guidance. Do not conflate laboratory species confirmation with field recognition or offer pesticide rates.

proposedDescription: Myxobolus cerebralis is the microscopic parasite responsible for whirling disease in trout and salmon. Its life cycle involves both a fish and a bottom-dwelling aquatic worm. Infection damages developing cartilage, making young fish especially vulnerable. Some waters contain the parasite without obvious disease or a measured decline in fish numbers, so detecting the organism and documenting its effects are different findings. Mud, water and infected fish can carry it between places.
identification: Affected fish may swim in tight circles or show a dark tail, a twisted spine or an abnormal head shape. Those signs are reasons to report a concern, not a reliable diagnosis by themselves. The parasite cannot be identified from an ordinary photograph, and fish that look healthy may still carry it. Record the fish species if known, how many fish are affected, and the exact water body. A short video of unusual swimming can be especially useful to fish-health staff.
actions: Report unusual fish behavior or deformities to the state fish and wildlife agency without moving fish to another water body. Remove mud and plants from boots, waders and equipment, drain retained water, and dry gear thoroughly before the next trip. Follow local decontamination guidance where provided. Do not discard fish parts into the water or transfer live bait between sites. These precautions focus on preventing spread; a home treatment poured into a stream cannot safely solve an established infection.
researchNotes: USGS supplies disease mechanism, Wisconsin separates parasite presence from population impact and gives prevention guidance, and North Carolina supplies field signs. No old state-count claim, unsupported eradication promise, or hazardous hatchery chemical recipe reused.

proposedDescription: White bladderflower, often called moth vine, is a climbing plant with pale flowers and conspicuous inflated fruits. It can scramble over shrubs and small trees, covering the foliage that needs light. Overseas weed accounts document this smothering behavior in natural areas and orchards. A planted vine is not the same as an established wild population, but seedlings beyond a garden or vines spreading through surrounding vegetation are worth recording and checking.
identification: Look for opposite leaves that are triangular to broadly oval, greener above and paler beneath. White or pale-pink flowers occur in small clusters. The large, green, somewhat pear-shaped pods eventually open and release seeds with silky hairs. Damaged stems release milky sap, but do not break a stem just to test this: the sap can irritate skin and eyes. Photograph leaves, flowers and intact pods to help distinguish it from other milkweedy vines.
actions: Keep pods contained before they open, and avoid carrying cut vines or fruit into uninfested areas. Wear protective gloves and clothing if handling a confirmed plant. Small plants can be removed with their roots where permitted; established vines need a plan for both the climbing growth and the root system. Do not pull heavy vines out of a living tree if that could tear its branches. Ask a local weed adviser about larger infestations and return to check for seedlings and regrowth.
researchNotes: Finding: Cal-IPC supplies California occurrence and a Watch assessment, while the NSW flora and weed account provide recognition and overseas management context. Rationale: The California assessment is independent of the NSW flora; NSW WeedWise cites that flora and is not counted as a second botanical lineage. Next step: Review California context as a regional assessment and keep Australian control methods geographically labeled.

proposedDescription: White bryony is a perennial climbing vine from Europe that can spread across fences, shrubs and small trees. A large underground root helps established plants return after their tops are cut. In parts of the inland Northwest it is a serious weed because dense growth shades the vegetation beneath it. Its berries and other plant parts should not be eaten. The word white refers to the plant's name, not the color of its ripe berries.
identification: Look for curling tendrils, alternate leaves with three to five broad lobes, and small greenish-white flowers where leaves meet the stem. Ripe berries are dark, commonly black. The foliage can resemble native wild cucumber, so include fruit and tendril photographs rather than identifying it from a lobed leaf alone. White bryony has a substantial fleshy root, but you do not need to excavate one just to make an initial report.
actions: Keep children and animals away from the berries and avoid bare-handed handling. Report suspected vines to the land manager or local weed program, especially where they are climbing native shrubs. With permission and an appropriate removal plan, young plants are easier to address before they build a large root or produce fruit. Cutting the vine alone is not a lasting solution because the root can resprout. Contain berries, protect surrounding vegetation during removal, and revisit the site for new shoots and seedlings.
researchNotes: Washington's weed account and the NRCS Inland Northwest guide give compatible identification and lookalike information. National Park Service guidance supports root-regrowth and handling cautions; no jurisdiction-wide legal requirement or precise herbicide recipe is asserted.

proposedDescription: White clover is a low, creeping perennial familiar in lawns, pastures and other open places. It is non-native in North America and has long been deliberately planted. Its flowers provide food for some pollinators, while its spreading stems can compete with lawn grasses or other vegetation. Whether it needs management depends on the setting and the vegetation you are trying to support; a few lawn flowers do not call for the same response as spread into a sensitive planting.
identification: Each true leaf usually has three rounded to egg-shaped leaflets, often with a pale V-shaped mark. The white flower heads, sometimes flushed pink, are made of many small pea-like flowers. Stems creep along the ground and can root where their joints touch soil. Yellow-flowered lookalikes are not white clover, and strawberry clover can resemble it closely. Take photographs of a flower head and a complete leaf rather than assuming that every three-leaflet plant is this species.
actions: First decide whether the patch conflicts with your goals. Tolerating some clover in an existing lawn may be more practical than trying to eradicate it. If you need to limit its spread, address the conditions weakening the desired vegetation and remove small patches with their creeping stems. Avoid unnecessary soil disturbance that creates new openings. In habitat plantings, favor locally appropriate native groundcovers. If chemical control is being considered, use local extension guidance and protect flowering plants and visiting insects from exposure.
researchNotes: Maryland Extension provides current lawn context and management nuance; UC IPM independently supplies growth and lookalike descriptions. Benefits and competition are presented together without equating all lawn occurrences with ecosystem damage.

proposedDescription: White deadnettle is a Eurasian perennial with nettle-like leaves and conspicuous white flowers. It has become established outside its native range, including parts of North America. Underground creeping stems allow it to form patches in disturbed ground and grassy or wooded edges. Its local effects deserve observation rather than an assumption that every patch causes the same ecological harm. An Alaska assessment cites a 2009 Glacier Bay Lodge observation of a persistent patch that was not spreading; that is a useful local limit, not a prediction for every site.
identification: Look for hairy stems, paired toothed leaves and clusters of white, hooded flowers around the stem. Lower leaves have longer stalks and a heart-shaped base. The flowers are much larger and more conspicuous than the tiny greenish flowers of a stinging nettle. Field mint and hempnettles can also resemble it before flowering. Use photographs of the flowers and leaf arrangement; touching an unidentified nettle-like plant is not a sensible way to test its name.
actions: Document where the patch ends and whether it is extending into nearby native vegetation. If removal is appropriate on your property, work carefully enough to lift the creeping underground stems, not just the flowering shoots. Keep removed material from being dumped at a woodland edge and revisit the site for regrowth. Ask a regional botanist to confirm plants without flowers before disturbing a large area. A manageable garden escape and an established natural-area population may need different priorities and follow-up.
researchNotes: Finding: The Alaska assessment records a persistent Glacier Bay Lodge patch reported not to be spreading, adding local context without proving ecological displacement. Rationale: The Alaska field observation is distinct from the NZ flora. Modeled or inferred rhizome risk is distinguished from the observed patch. Next step: Review the dated Alaska observation and retain modest garden containment rather than an eradication promise. proposedDescription: White Egyptian lotus is an African waterlily, despite the common name lotus. It grows from a tuberous base in sheltered water and is cultivated as an ornamental. Flora of North America reports introductions in Florida and Louisiana. More recent Florida botanical discussion notes difficulty separating it from the similar Nymphaea pubescens, so older records need their treatment and identification retained. Neither a historical report nor white flowers on a pond proves that the narrowly named species is spreading or causing harm there.
identification: Mature leaves are broadly rounded, with a deep notch and distinct teeth along the margin. Their undersides have prominent branching veins. The large white or cream flowers are held above the water and often open from evening into the following morning, although flowering behavior varies. Photograph the leaf edge, the notch, both leaf surfaces where safely visible, and an open flower. American white waterlily has a different leaf margin, while true lotuses belong to the separate genus Nelumbo.
actions: Keep ornamental waterlilies in contained water gardens rather than releasing plants, tubers or pond waste into natural waterways. For an unfamiliar wild patch, report its location, approximate extent and photographs to the water body's manager. Do not wade into unsafe water or uproot native lilies to obtain a sample. Identification should come before any removal plan, and aquatic treatments require advice suited to the actual water body. Record whether the plants are intentionally planted or spreading beyond a maintained pond.
researchNotes:
Finding: FNA documents introduced Florida and Louisiana reports under lotus; the identity and current behavior of an individual pond still need checking, particularly against pubescens. Rationale: African flora and Wiersema FNA are distinct botanical treatments. A 2026 Florida flora warns that narrow separation from pubescens can be difficult, so historical reports are attributed. Next step: Review the historical FNA context without presenting every white pond lily or old lotus record as a confirmed narrow-species invasion. proposedDescription: The white garden snail is a Mediterranean land snail that has established populations in southern California. It feeds on a range of plants and can travel unnoticed on nursery stock, equipment and freight. One unusual habit makes it particularly important to check above ground: during dry weather, groups can rest on stems, fences and other upright surfaces instead of hiding only beneath debris. An apparently inactive cluster may still contain living snails.
identification: The shell is usually ivory-colored, sometimes with brown bands, dots or broken lines; other individuals have little pattern. Adults are rounded, roughly half an inch across in many cases, with a relatively low spire. Color alone is unreliable because it varies within the species. Photograph the top, side and opening of the shell with a size reference. Other pale land snails can look similar, so a plant-health specialist should confirm a suspected new occurrence.
actions: Inspect pots, packing corners, fence posts and equipment before moving them out of an affected area. Do not relocate snails outdoors or send live specimens through the mail without instructions. Share photographs and the source of recently received plants with your county agricultural office. For an established garden problem, use a locally appropriate combination of monitoring, habitat management and targeted control. Avoid indiscriminate baiting or releasing predatory snails, which can harm native mollusks and create another problem. Check treated areas again because inactive snails may be missed.
researchNotes: UF's morphology and dormancy account is paired with UC's California field/landscape review. Older sources claim establishment only in San Diego; omitted that potentially stale exclusivity. No quarantine claims without current jurisdiction-specific confirmation.

proposedDescription: White garland-lily, or butterfly ginger, is a tall ornamental ginger with fragrant white flowers. Its thick underground stems let clumps expand and return after the leafy shoots die back. Hawaii's weed-management guide describes creeping growth that can overwhelm low vegetation in wet forests and pastures. Florida's assessment, however, does not currently classify it as a problem species. Those different regional findings belong in the description rather than a single nationwide label.
identification: Look for upright leafy stems with long, broad, bright-green leaves arranged in two ranks. Large white flowers with a butterfly-like outline appear at the tops of the shoots. White garland-lily differs from yellow ginger and kahili ginger, which have yellow flowers; kahili ginger also has conspicuous orange floral parts in an upright flower cluster. Photograph an entire flowering stem, its leaf arrangement and the edge of the clump. Do not assume every tall ginger has the same impact or treatment needs.
actions: Keep garden divisions and discarded underground stems out of streams, forest edges and unmanaged ground. Where it is spreading into natural vegetation, show the land manager photographs of both the clump and surrounding plants. Small patches may be manageable by removing the underground growth, but leftover pieces can require follow-up. Large established patches need a site-specific plan, especially near water. Avoid borrowing herbicide instructions for other Hedychium species; the Hawaii guide discusses several gingers whose treatment responses differ.
researchNotes: Independent Hawaii management, LSU identification and Florida assessment support explicit regional nuance. No imported kahili/yellow ginger chemical results. This is review-ready with clear geography, not a claim of invasive behavior everywhere.

proposedDescription: White leadtree is a fast-growing shrub or small tree introduced to many warm regions for fodder, shade and other uses. Outside managed plantings it can produce dense thickets and many seeds. Florida accounts describe displacement of native vegetation along disturbed edges, coastal areas and gaps in tree cover. Its useful history does not prevent it from spreading; the important question is whether seedlings and thickets are extending into surrounding habitat.
identification: The leaves are divided twice, with rows of small leaflets along several side branches, giving them a feathery appearance. Round, pale flower heads occur near branch tips. The flattened pods hang in clusters and turn brown as they mature, holding glossy brown seeds. Several native and introduced legumes have similar foliage and puffball flowers. Include photographs of a whole leaf, flowers and pods so a botanist can distinguish white leadtree from other local species.
actions: Avoid planting it where local invasive-plant guidance recommends alternatives. On your own property, remove confirmed seedlings while their roots are still small and keep pods from being carried into new areas. Established trees can regrow after cutting, so plan follow-up rather than treating one cut as completion. Have an arborist handle plants near buildings or wires, and ask a weed adviser about larger infestations. Restore suitable native vegetation where practical and watch the cleared ground for seedlings after rain and disturbance.
researchNotes: UF's Florida account provides U.S. impact and seedling management; Queensland independently describes pods, seed movement and root regrowth. Avoid transferring Australian legal requirements or claiming all fodder cultivars behave identically.

proposedDescription: White mango scale is a small armored scale insect found especially on mango leaves, twigs and fruit. Infestations can blemish fruit and damage foliage, while infested plants and fruit can carry the insect to new areas. A white coating on a mango is not automatically this species: several scales may occur on the same tree. Identifying the insect matters before deciding whether the finding is a routine orchard problem or a new plant-health concern.
identification: Female covers are roughly circular and whitish to translucent, with a darker spot formed by older shed skins. Male covers are smaller, narrow and white, often gathered in conspicuous clusters. Yellowed areas on leaves or pinkish blemishes on fruit can accompany feeding. These are screening clues only. Specialists usually identify slide-mounted adult females by microscopic structures. Photograph colonies close up and show the affected fruit, leaf or twig as well as the whole tree.
actions: Keep newly acquired mango plants apart while checking their leaves and stems. If you find suspicious scales, contact an extension diagnostic service or plant-health office and provide the plant's source and movement history. Avoid giving away infested cuttings or moving affected nursery stock before advice. In an established orchard, management should be timed to the insect's vulnerable stages and protect beneficial insects. Do not assume that washing fruit or treating one visible colony eliminates scales hidden elsewhere on the tree.
researchNotes: Finding: Exact-species diagnostic morphology and independent Costa Rican mango field observations support a bounded scale-insect profile without a US efficacy claim. Rationale: Naturalis traces diagnostic work to Cunningham and other earlier studies; the 2023 Costa Rican observations are separate sampled data. EFSA is synthesis, not an extra experiment. Next step: Review inspection and crop-adviser actions; retain geographic labels on mango damage and natural-enemy observations. proposedDescription: White moneywort, also called alyce clover, is a low legume with small pea-like flowers and jointed pods. Its native range spans Africa and parts of Asia and Australia, and it occurs outside that range. The Florida assessment currently treats it as not a problem species, which is important context for a catalog entry. Being non-native or growing in a lawn does not, by itself, show that it is damaging nearby natural habitat.
identification: Unlike a typical three-leaflet clover, each leaf has a single leaflet. Leaf shape varies from oval to elongated, and the plant may spread close to the ground or stand more upright. Small flowers can show pink, purple or orange tones. The narrow pods are divided into a short row of segments rather than forming a broad, flat bean pod. Photograph the leaf attachment and mature fruit; these details help separate it from other small legumes with similar flowers.
actions: If you notice it beyond a maintained planting, record its location, patch size and whether it is increasing over time. A regional botanist can confirm the identification from flowering and fruiting material. Where it interferes with a garden or restoration planting, address small patches before mature pods are moved with soil or mowing equipment. There is no reason to clear an entire area solely because this species appears in the catalog. Let the condition of the surrounding vegetation and local assessment guide the response.
researchNotes: Finding: The current UF assessment considers A. vaginalis not a problem species in Florida; botanical recognition is independently supported by Kew flora. Rationale: Taxonomic morphology and the Florida status assessment are separate substantive lines; absence of a harm trial is consistent with a restrained profile. proposedDescription: White mulberry is a cultivated Asian tree that has escaped into fields, woodland edges and other open habitats in North America. Birds eat its fruit and can carry the seeds away from planted trees. In addition to competing with surrounding vegetation, it can hybridize with native red mulberry. Protecting the native tree makes careful identification especially important; an unfamiliar mulberry should not be removed simply because its fruit is dark or its leaves are lobed.
identification: Leaves are alternate, toothed and often glossy. Their outlines can vary considerably on the same tree, from unlobed to deeply divided. The fruits resemble elongated blackberries and may ripen white, pink or dark purple, so the name is not a dependable color guide. Photograph several mature leaves from both surfaces, the twig and any fruit. Red mulberry and hybrids can be difficult to distinguish, and a regional botanist may need more than one leaf to assess them.
actions: Look for seedlings beneath fences, perches and nearby trees, especially around fruiting plantings. Remove confirmed young white mulberries with their roots where you have permission and can avoid disturbing desired plants. Established trees require a safe removal and regrowth plan; use an arborist near structures or utilities. Before replacing a tree, choose a locally appropriate native species from a source that can verify its identity. Continue checking the site for seedlings rather than assuming that removing the parent tree prevents all future arrivals.

Wisconsin's page contains questionable flower/native-lookalike wording and an unrelated Artemisia citation, so those parts were not reused. Fine red/white/hybrid discrimination remains expert-led.

proposedDescription: White mustard is an annual crop and occasional escape, also known as yellow mustard. It is grown for seed and as a cover or green-manure crop. A field planted intentionally with mustard should not be treated as an invasive outbreak. The useful observation is whether plants are reproducing outside cultivation or persisting as unwanted volunteers, and what effect that has on the neighboring crop or habitat.
identification: The flowers are yellow, despite the name white mustard. Leaves are stalked and divided into irregular lobes, often with noticeable bristles. Mature pods provide a stronger clue than flower color: they are relatively short and stout, usually bristly, and end in a long, flattened beak. Other yellow-flowered mustards, especially wild mustard, can look similar before fruit develops. Photograph lower and upper leaves together with several mature pods and a size reference for a more useful identification.
actions: If mustard appears unexpectedly, check whether it came from a recent cover crop, seed mixture or disturbed agricultural soil. Record that context rather than assuming a new wild introduction. Prevent unwanted plants from producing mature seed when removal is appropriate, and clean equipment before moving it from a seeding patch. Farmers should coordinate control with the crop rotation and any cover-crop plan. In natural areas, confirm the species and local priority before broad treatment; the sources here do not establish identical ecological harm across all places where it grows.
researchNotes: Finding: CFIA crop biology and WSU regional green-manure observations support an agricultural account, not a universal harmful-mustard claim. Rationale: CFIA biology synthesis and WSU seed/cultivation observations are separate; WSU results apply to tested crop varieties and planting timing. Next step: Review the crop-versus-volunteer distinction and avoid generalizing seed dormancy findings to every mustard population. proposedDescription: Pseudogymnoascus destructans is the cold-loving fungus that causes white-nose syndrome in hibernating bats. It grows on skin, including the muzzle, ears and wings, and can disrupt hibernation so bats use up energy needed to survive winter. The fungus can persist in places where bats hibernate. Finding the fungus in an environment is not identical to confirming disease in a bat, a distinction that matters when interpreting surveillance reports.
identification: Possible warning signs include white growth on a bat's face or wings, unusual winter daytime flight, damaged wings, or several sick or dead bats near a roost. None of these signs confirms the disease by itself, and infected bats may lack obvious white growth. Wildlife specialists use laboratory examination to establish the diagnosis. Observe from a distance; approaching a hibernating bat for a better picture can disturb it and create unnecessary risk.
actions: Report unusual, sick or dead bats to your state wildlife agency with the location, date and photographs taken without handling them. Do not touch, capture or move bats. Respect cave closures and follow the current decontamination instructions for shoes and gear before visiting another cave or roost. Never apply disinfectants to bats or inside a cave yourself. If there has been direct contact with a bat, contact a health professional or local health department promptly; that exposure question is separate from white-nose syndrome.
researchNotes: USGS pathology guidance distinguishes signs from diagnosis; the 2025 Oregon agency detection report supplies independent surveillance context and public action. Excludes stale state counts, DIY bat sampling and chemical formulas. Health contact advice follows agency guidance.

proposedDescription: White peach scale is an armored scale insect that feeds on bark, especially on trunks and larger branches. It affects peach and other woody plants, including mulberry, and heavy infestations can weaken or kill branches. The conspicuous white covering is made by many small insects, not a fungus. Its close relative, white prunicola scale, can occur on similar hosts and is more likely in some northern settings, so the two should not be merged without identification.
identification: Female covers are rounded and whitish or grayish, often with a yellowish spot from earlier shed skins. Male covers are narrow, ridged and bright white; dense groups can make bark look snow-covered. The tiny mobile young are called crawlers. A photograph can show the infestation, but separating white peach scale from white prunicola scale usually requires a specialist to examine prepared specimens. Include the host plant's name and the location, not just a close-up of white spots.
actions: Inspect trunks and substantial branches when assessing a tree that is losing vigor. Ask an extension service to confirm the scale and check whether insects beneath the covers are still alive before planning treatment. On a small ornamental plant, gentle brushing may reduce accessible colonies, but avoid damaging the bark. Larger infestations need monitoring and carefully timed management, often focused on crawlers. Preserve natural enemies where possible and do not use an ornamental-plant treatment on edible fruit unless its label permits that use.
researchNotes: NC State supplies scale-cover biology; Virginia Tech supplies microscopic separation and overlapping geography; UMass supplies bark management limitations. The draft avoids fixed nationwide generation timing and preserves edible versus ornamental treatment distinction.

proposedDescription: White peppermint is a fine-leaved eucalyptus native to Tasmania, where it belongs to dry forests and woodlands. It is also grown as an ornamental tree elsewhere. A cultivated tree, a naturalized seedling and an invasive stand are different situations; the sources reviewed here do not establish broad United States ecological impacts for this particular eucalyptus. Claims about blue gum or other large eucalypts should not be transferred to it simply because they share a genus.
identification: The adult leaves are exceptionally narrow and almost linear, giving the crown a light, fine texture. Much of the trunk has smooth, pale gray to whitish bark, sometimes with rougher bark near the base. Flowers are pale and the fruits are small woody capsules. Several peppermint eucalypts and their hybrids can resemble one another. Photograph mature leaves with a ruler, the trunk from base to branches, and attached buds or capsules rather than identifying it by smell alone.
actions: For a tree beyond a known planting, record whether seedlings of different sizes are appearing nearby. Ask a herbarium or qualified arborist to confirm the species before choosing management. Do not remove a mature tree on the assumption that all eucalyptus species have the same behavior. If seedlings are spreading into a managed habitat, discuss their extent and removal priority with the land manager. Any work near overhead lines or buildings should be handled professionally; documenting the tree does not require climbing it or cutting branches.
researchNotes: Finding: EUCLID and the NZ flora independently identify white peppermint and document cultivation-associated escape; US impact claims are unnecessary. Rationale: Australian diagnostic work and NZ plantation-edge observations are separate regional data, not generic eucalyptus fire or water-use claims. Next step: Review leaf, bark and capsule recognition and site-specific advice without transferring harms from other eucalypts. proposedDescription: White poplar is a Eurasian tree planted for shade and its pale foliage. In parts of North America it spreads beyond old plantings through root suckers, forming colonies along roads, fields and woodland edges. Several stems in a patch may therefore be connected underground rather than representing separate seedlings. That growth pattern explains why cutting down one trunk can leave the colony in place or encourage additional shoots.
identification: The leaves are green above and densely white-haired beneath, often with several rounded lobes. Young branches and buds may also have pale hairs, and younger bark is comparatively smooth and light colored. Leaves vary across shoots, so include both mature branches and vigorous suckers in photographs. Native aspens and cottonwoods lack the same combination of white hair and leaf shape, but hybrids complicate identification. Ask for confirmation when the foliage is intermediate rather than deciding from trunk color alone.
actions: Map the outermost suckers as well as the main trees before planning removal. Small confirmed shoots may be manageable, but repeated cutting alone can stimulate more growth and requires follow-up. Work with a land manager or arborist on established colonies, particularly near wetlands, buildings or utilities. Avoid moving root-bearing soil to another site. After treatment, revisit the entire colony for new shoots and restore suitable plant cover so the cleared space does not become an opening for another unwanted species.
researchNotes: Forest Service synthesis supports clonal spread, hybrid caution and cutting response; North Carolina flora independently supports regional recognition and habitat. No claim of abundant pure-species seed production is made. Management is colony-level, not a one-cut cure.

proposedDescription: White prunicola scale is an introduced armored scale often found on cherry laurel and related ornamental plants. Its waxy cover protects the insect while it feeds on stems. Dense populations can contribute to poor growth and branch dieback, although a few old covers do not necessarily mean a plant has an active, damaging infestation. Checking the insects underneath is more useful than treating every white mark on the bark.
identification: Female covers are small, rounded and white with a yellowish center. Male covers are narrower and elongated, sometimes making crowded branches look dusted with white material. Newly hatched crawlers are much smaller and briefly mobile before settling. White peach scale can look almost identical and was historically confused with this species. Record the host plant and photograph the whole affected branch, then ask an extension specialist whether a sample is needed for microscopic identification.
actions: Start by checking the plant's overall condition and whether live scales are present. Prune badly affected branches only where this will leave a healthy plant, and dispose of infested material without spreading it to other plantings. Monitor for crawlers before choosing a treatment; the protective covers make poorly timed spraying less effective. An extension service can help match monitoring to local conditions and the host plant. Avoid broad spraying simply to remove the appearance of old covers, and preserve beneficial insects that help suppress the population.
researchNotes: Maryland Extension provides current host, cover and management information. Virginia Tech supports microscopic distinction from P. pentagona; its shared use in the preceding profile is limited to the taxonomic distinction rather than copying general scale biology twice.

proposedDescription: Onion white rot is caused by Stromatinia cepivora, also widely described as Sclerotium cepivorum. It attacks garlic, onions and other alliums, rotting roots and bulbs. The fungus leaves tiny resting bodies in soil that can survive for many years without a crop. Moving contaminated planting stock, soil or equipment can establish a problem in a previously clean bed, which makes prevention more useful than relying on a short crop rotation.
identification: Affected plants may yellow, wilt and lose older leaves. Around the bulb base, look for fluffy white growth that later contains very small black, seedlike bodies. Roots can decay so badly that the plant becomes loose in the soil. These signs deserve examination, but other diseases can also produce white fungal growth; southern blight usually develops larger tan to reddish-brown resting bodies. Send photographs and request diagnostic instructions before mailing bulbs or soil.
actions: Keep suspect garlic cloves, onion sets and transplants out of clean growing areas. Mark affected beds, avoid moving their soil, and clean soil from tools and footwear before working elsewhere. Do not put diseased bulbs or contaminated debris into ordinary garden compost. Ask an extension plant clinic to confirm the disease and plan future use of the site. A brief break from onions and garlic does not eliminate the resting bodies, and home remedies should not be treated as a dependable cure for an infested bed.
researchNotes: UC IPM white rot and southern blight guidance supports prevention and differential diagnosis; RHS independently supports allium host scope and long persistence. Avoids UK-only pesticide availability claims, unverified garlic-juice cures and numeric treatment recipes.

proposedDescription: Amylostereum areolatum is a wood-decay fungus closely associated with woodwasps. Female Sirex noctilio can introduce it into pine wood while laying eggs, and the fungus helps support the developing larvae. Tree injury involves the insect, its secretions and the fungus together; white rot alone is not evidence of this particular association. Research has also found distinct fungal strains with native North American woodwasps, so it is inaccurate to label every occurrence a newly introduced Sirex infestation.
identification: In a suspect pine, resin drips, declining needles, round emergence holes and tunnels may prompt a woodwasp investigation. None identifies the fungus on its own. Many organisms decay conifer wood, and native woodwasps can leave similar holes. Reliable fungal identification needs specialist laboratory work, while identifying the insect may require an entomologist. Photographs of the tree, bark damage and any adult insect are useful starting evidence without cutting open the trunk.
actions: Report an unusual cluster of declining pines or a suspected nonnative woodwasp to a state forestry or plant-health service. Leave logs and firewood near their origin while the situation is assessed, rather than moving potentially infested wood to another property. Do not remove every decaying conifer or native woodwasp as a precaution. A forester can evaluate tree condition, identify the organisms involved and decide whether stand management or removal is warranted. Laboratory results should retain the host and locality details needed to interpret them.
researchNotes: Finding: Separate 2009 US isolation and genotype studies support the fungal-woodwasp association while showing that North American origin cannot be reduced to one introduction. Rationale: Wilson and colleagues isolated fungi from pine wood; Nielsen and colleagues compared strains carried by different wasps. These are distinct original data sets. Next step: Review the strain-qualified origin and diagnostic laboratory advice; keep woodwasp-complex harm separate from fungus-only causation. proposedDescription: White sweetclover is a tall, branching legume introduced from Eurasia and now widespread in open, disturbed habitats. It can produce dense growth along roads, riverbanks and grasslands. Its ability to fix nitrogen and produce persistent seed helps it occupy places where maintaining native plant communities is a priority. It is also a cultivated forage and bee plant, so management depends on the setting rather than its presence alone.
identification: Leaves have three narrow, toothed leaflets. Numerous small white pea-shaped flowers form long, narrow clusters, unlike the rounded flower heads of white clover. Plants are usually biennial, with much taller flowering growth in their second season. Yellow sweetclover is very similar when not flowering; fresh flower color is more useful than dried blooms, which can both look cream colored. Photograph the whole plant and a flowering cluster as well as the leaves.
actions: In a restoration area, identify young plants before they set seed and plan follow-up over several seasons. Cutting flowering stems before seed matures can reduce replenishment, but timing and repeated checks matter. Avoid carrying mature seed on mowing equipment or moving seed-bearing cuttings into clean habitat. Hand removal may suit a small patch where it will not damage neighboring native plants. For larger infestations, a land manager should coordinate control with the desired vegetation and site conditions; a single mowing should not be presented as permanent removal.
researchNotes: Maine control guidance and Missouri field observations supply independent context; USFS synthesis supports seed persistence and variation in life cycle. Retains Melilotus albus catalog identity despite databases that lump sweetclovers; no unsourced nationwide harm or fixed control success promised.

proposedDescription: White upright mignonette is a Mediterranean-region herb that has been grown ornamentally and recorded outside cultivation in North America. It can behave as an annual or persist longer from a woody base. Its presence in a plant catalog documents an introduced plant, not proof that it is displacing native vegetation everywhere it occurs. Local spread and impacts need to be assessed separately from identification.
identification: Look for upright, ribbed stems and leaves deeply divided into numerous narrow lobes. The flowering stems carry many small white flowers with divided petals, giving the clusters a finely textured appearance. The fruits are elongated capsules rather than the long, narrow pods typical of many mustards. Yellow-flowered mignonettes are different species, and a distant picture of a pale flower spike is not enough to separate them. Photograph leaves, close flower details and mature capsules with a size reference.
actions: If you find it outside a garden, record whether it is a single escape or a patch containing flowering plants and younger individuals. Share those photographs with a regional herbarium or botanical group, especially where records are scarce. If removal is appropriate on land you manage, avoid scattering mature capsules and check the site again after disturbed soil produces new seedlings. Do not infer a need for landscape-wide spraying from the common name alone. The reviewed references support recognition and introduced records but do not establish a species-specific United States control program.
researchNotes: Finding: NZ flora supports white mignonette morphology and California records corroborate a nonnative occurrence context without demonstrating harmful spread. Rationale: An authored flora and separate California occurrence assessment support a bounded profile; collection presence is not an impact experiment. Next step: Review recognition and seed containment, retaining the distinction between occurrence and measured harm.
